Introduction

Opera Historica, Part II — the Chronicon Hirsaugiense and Chronicon Sponheimense — is the second half of Trithemius's collected historical works: his two great monastic chronicles. The Chronicon Hirsaugiense narrates the foundation and progress of the monastery of Hirsau, in the diocese of Speyer, down to 1520; the Chronicon Sponheimense does the same for his own former house of Sponheim, in the diocese of Mainz. Together they are the fullest record of the Benedictine reform world he inhabited — though, like his Frankish history, they must be read with caution for the fabricated sources woven into the genuine documentary labour.

This is the 1601 Frankfurt edition (Marne; dilibri witness), the standard early-modern collected edition, companion to Part I (prdl-70289). The Latin was re-OCR'd from the page scans and translated by GPT-5.5. This is among the roughest-OCR work in the corpus — its 184 newly-translated tail chunks are the ones graded by GLM-5.2 rather than Claude (see the Methodology honesty note) — and the translation sits in the top tier (S).

Opera Historica, Part II — Chronicon Hirsaugiense & Sponheimense

Johannes Trithemius of Spanheim, first abbot of Spanheim, then of St. James the Greater at Würzburg, a man most learned in his age: two distinguished chronicles of the second part.

I. Of the monastery of Hirsau, in the diocese of Speyer: comprising its foundation and progress from the year of Christ 830 down to the year 1370.

II. Of the monastery of Spanheim, in the diocese of Mainz: comprising its foundation and progress from the year of Christ 1143 down to the year 1526; or rather the memorable events carried out in the whole Church and Empire during those eight centuries.

Of these, the former is issued more correctly and fully through collation with the archetype written in the author’s own hand; the latter, now for the first time rescued from darkness, is brought to light in the best faith because of its outstanding usefulness.

There are added his familiar letters, written after his departure from the monastery of Spanheim to princes and distinguished men, full of the histories of that age.

From the library of the distinguished Marquard Freher, Palatine councillor.

With a very full index.

Frankfurt, from the Wechelian press, at Claudius Marnius and the heirs of Johann Aubrius. 1601.

To the most reverend and most illustrious prince, Lord Johann Adam, Archbishop of Mainz, Archchancellor of the Holy Roman Empire throughout Germany, and Prince Elector, etc., my most gracious lord.

From the time when, as a boy, I began to perceive the wondrous delight of history, and, as my years increased, learned also to appreciate its usefulness, I long ago resolved that nothing more right could be done in letters, and nothing for which this age ought more to be congratulated, than that learned men should labor, as if in rivalry, to bring forth from every side all writings that serve to illuminate the earlier age, and not only those monuments of the highest antiquity but also those of the middle period, and should eagerly contribute them to the public. Since in this kind of work the republic of letters has also thus far willingly credited some things to our little efforts, I desire, meanwhile, that this not regrettable work of Trithemius’s Annals should stand in no last place: a work which, known until now only by its title, and alike desired and lamented by the learned, has at last by me, by good fortu[unclear] recovered, I at once judged it worthy of publication and of continual use by posterity. He, a prelate by no means among the lowest in your diocese, but more by the merit of his learning having acquired a most celebrated name (a rare thing in that age, when knowledge even a little above the common level could give rise to slander about magic), among other memorable affairs carried on throughout the Church and Empire, recorded especially the affairs of Mainz with a diligent pen and preserved them for posterity. When, according to custom, I was looking about for a suitable patron for him, I could not reckon whose name it might more justly be inscribed to, and indeed ought to be inscribed to, than yours, Most Reverend Prince-Elector. I also easily commended this plan to your chancellor, a truly noble man, Philipp Wolf von Rosebach (a man whom I count it part of my good fortune to be connected with by some affinity of family, but still more by the union of minds and studies). And this not so much because that author of ours, as I have just said, committed to writing with particular care the affairs of your Church above all others, so that I would venture to say that an almost continuous Chronicle of Mainz is contained in these commentaries, as because he accurately noted the principal moments and changes of the whole German Empire; in which you, by your great merit, hold that dignity joined to so ample and ancient a prelacy, which the Greek author Nicetas Choniates, speaking of some one of your predecessors, calls [unclear Greek], logothete.

For to your care and ordering belong the dispatch, recording, and publication of affairs to be carried on throughout wide-stretching Germany by the Caesars; to yours the preservation of justice and of the imperial tribunal; to yours the ordering of diets and solemn assemblies. To you, therefore, belong archives, record offices, and chartularies. In these, I do not know whether it is of less public concern that monuments of this kind and commentaries on deeds done in every age be preserved than any other class of acts and registers; without them we would surely be involved in great ignorance of very many matters of the highest importance. Certainly we have this Trithemius, just as he had diligently gathered, turned over, and excerpted the writers and all the remains of preceding ages, so too as a most ample witness of the deeds of his own age, on which he chiefly expatiates. But I have always judged, and I do not yet repent of the opinion, that History, which is called the Witness of Times, cannot better give credibility to its words than if it gives the reason for its knowledge from its own proper perception, as the sons of advocates say. For this reason learned men certainly judge that those old writings, of whatever kind, should be religiously preserved, rather than that new ones should continually be hammered out and compiled according to one's own inclination. Would that Trithemius himself, and after him Nauclerus, Aventinus, and others, had done this: indeed, how much more gladly would we have read the authors whom they follow than those men themselves.

But since those authors either lie hidden somewhere, captive or buried, or have even very plainly perished, meanwhile we must be content with this Cato, as Augustus used to say. In the meantime, if I should present this Trithemius just as he came into my hands, with the best faith, sincere and unblemished, I thought that I would have discharged the duty of a faithful editor as properly as the editor is by no means obliged to guarantee the good faith and truth of the writers themselves. For those men are not to be tolerated who wish to be clever in other people's writings, especially writings of antiquity; still less those who wish to be bold; least of all those who permit themselves to alter anything in the authors of history according to their own judgment or feeling. But if it is counted a fault in a historian to have inserted judgment among the things narrated, what of his editor? And let them indeed have written as each one pleased, as it seemed, as it was discovered; since we wish it to be free for us to believe as we please, and to judge about what has been believed. Let it suffice for us to have used such conscientiousness in editing that we did not allow ourselves to change a single little word, but rather checked it carefully against the author's archetypes, manuscripts of venerable antiquity and remarkable elegance, and, as far as possible, left it to its own integrity. Whatever this work is, it has been completed at that very point of time and [unclear] you to come forth into the light, when you, most illustrious prelate, with your most highly praised predecessor departing from life, were taking up the helm of that most ample [unclear] succession; and of that fortune most friendly you recently had the most serene prince Frederick, the Palatine Elector, your colleague, my lord, as one congratulating you; and this very thing, besides the earlier reasons, seemed to supply a further new occasion, and even to give me courage, to congratulate you with humble devotion on that same honor owed to your virtue and merit, and to pray from my heart that God Most High may will it to be firm and lasting for you, and salutary for your Church and province. That you may deign, in your extraordinary clemency, to regard this zeal of mine favorably, most clement lord, I humbly and earnestly ask and beseech with all the submission of spirit that I can. Farewell. From Myrtiletum, May 31, in the year of Christ 1601.

Most devoted to Your Most Reverend Highness,

Marquard Freher.

To the Most Reverend and Most Illustrious Prince Johann Adam, of the Most Noble Family of the Bickens, Archbishop-Designate of Mainz, Elector of the Empire.

Up to this point, having duly been called to great affairs, endowed with the keen valor of Pallas, offspring of the Bicken stock; and, the difficulty and mass of business overcome, raised to an illustrious summit, you touch the stars with your lofty head, O long-lived Adam, appointed to the office of supreme prelate after the faithful [unclear] of the lords of Dalberg fell through great age. All congratulate you on this honor, at the same time on this burden, on this tiara.

For how great is the care of the weary empire, and of the realm already threatening collapse and drawing with it whatever props are applied to walls that are to be well sustained, you know most clearly; and you know the manner in which the commonwealth ought justly to be ruled and administered. With this better Minerva as pilot, when the ship is shaken by the motions of the wave-tossed sea and its oarsman is weary, you as helmsman will steer it and will set the swimming keel in a fixed station amid the slippery whirlwind.

You have Philip Rosebach, a relief to your weary right hand, ready to bring you aid, a pillar of equity, a safeguard of Justice. But you yourself, divine prince, with how many and how great arts are you more elegantly cultivated, and with gifts of talent! Abundant plenty [unclear], and much knowledge of languages adorns the man; elegant historians, critics, and philosophers delight you as you read. Indeed you also examine poetry inwardly, acting, as we know, as a competent censor. Therefore a marvelous love burns freely in you toward the learned company: among whom Themis loves to set, under the auspices of sacred law, the distinguished Freher, now bringing forth many serene monuments of historians into the breezes, some shaken free from ancient decay, some lying almost buried, and some by private labor published for public reading.

You, highest prelate, patron of men of Mercury, will rightly think him both to be cherished and to be embraced before the rest with a singular affection of mind and with triple Grace. His candor deserves this, and his learning, virtue, keenness, and the watchful lamps of his works: through them monarchs, and the famous deeds of Caesars and kings, and the lineages of princes, gain an immortal name, never to perish in any other age.

Paulus Melissus, a Franconian, Count Palatine and golden knight, citizen of Rome.

Chron[unclear] An Excellent Chronicle of the Monastery of Hirsau, of the Order of St. Benedict, published by Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim.

The ancients applied incredible diligence to the writing of histories, believing that the commonwealth could be adorned by them no less than defended by arms. For history is, as it were, a preserver of memory, an example of virtue, the companion of prudence; and by itself alone it renders immortal, with a certain everlasting renown, the fame of good men who strove to surpass others in wisdom, holiness, and courage.

Who would make known today to those who do not know it the origin of the world, the reckoning of the years, and the things done in the meantime? Who would persuade unbelievers of the incarnation, the birth from the Virgin, the teaching, miracles, passion, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ, our Savior and the Son of the eternal Father? Or who would disclose to the ignorant, in writing, the sufferings of the martyrs, the lives of the saints, the destruction of the Trojans, the wide empire of the Romans throughout the world, the various deeds of kings and princes, and the other matters of antiquity worthy of remembrance that have become known to us; or even, if the possibility were granted to narrators, who would believe them, if no writers of histories had existed before us? History alone, therefore, is that by which it comes about that we, who are separated from the ancients by the interval of a very long time, seem to have been present at their deeds and to have lived in the same times. Indeed, history bestows immortality among mortals upon human beings; it adorns and preserves the commonwealth; by seasoned prudence it keeps it free from many dangers; it instructs faith, raises up hope, sets before us the reward of eternity, and adds strength to laws; since it has shown that everything which sense either desires or fears is nothing other than a dream, it cares for the immortality of the soul and renders men eager for the contemplation of divine things.

The difficulty of writing human history.

How great a benefit comes to us from the reading of histories no one who has even moderate understanding can be ignorant. Knowledge of the deeds of the ancients, if they were good, teaches and instructs us toward the imitation of virtues and toward the wisdom and courage of heroes. But if they were evil or wrongly done, then by warning us not to become imitators of the depraved it makes us cautious and prudent. For history, the living model of the dead and the inextinguishable light of mortals, sets before us the merits, virtues, and praises of good men in such a way that, stirred by their glory, fame, and immortality, [unclear] to be what they themselves were, so that we too may leave to posterity an example of virtue and holiness such as we received from those who preceded us in time and in virtue.

But when it shows readers the impious deeds, disgraces, and deserved punishments of the wicked, should we suppose that these things were written as though proposed to us for imitation? Rather, we should believe that we are being warned, lest, by committing similar acts, we incur like punishments to those that they paid. Add that prudence can be grasped by us only through experience of many things; and to this, since art is long and life is short, no easier access lies open to anyone than to the man who, from love of truth, runs through whatever histories of past time he has found with diligent inquiry of mind.

Since this is so, I should believe, most excellent Blasius, distinguished Abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, that you were moved not by a zeal for vanity but rather by the divine Spirit: you who do not cease to urge me, by so many importunate prayers, indeed by so many magnificent benefactions, that I should be willing to write, for the knowledge of posterity, the history of that same monastery over which, by God’s favor, you preside, from the notes and records offered to me by you and from the various chronicles of our men, of which there is a great abundance among us.

There are two precepts of history: tru—

For among the many precepts given to those who wish to write history, two especially must be observed. The first is that in the narrative the truth should everywhere remain inviolate; the oth— Of the Monastery of Hirsau

... secondly, that the very integrity of the narrative, most aptly adorned with proper and fitting words, may by its antiquity attract those who behold it. In the first matter, indeed, I do not deny that I both can and wish to give sufficient satisfaction, since the monastic profession itself, indeed the Christian faith, does not permit me to be a liar, as Sacred Scripture attests when it says, “The mouth that lies slays the soul.” And since I am a lover of truth, no necessity compels me to lie. In the second matter, however, I do not promise that I shall be obedient, unless perhaps a tepid will may suffice, which, moved by brotherly reasoning, neither sufficiently wills nor, if it desires, can do much. For I wished to accommodate myself to those lovers of simplicity for whom I am about to write the history, for their benefit; and, because of my rusticity, as all will judge, I easily could.

There are three kinds of histories. One is called general, embracing the solemn deeds of the kings and princes of the whole world or of many provinces. In this kind of writing there were Titus Livius, Orosius, Eusebius the bishop, Cornelius Tacitus, Cassiodorus, Freculphus the bishop, Vincent of Beauvais, Marianus Scotus, monk of Fulda, Martinus the preacher, Antoninus the archbishop, Hernandus the monk, Rupert the monk, Hugh of Fleury the monk, John de Columna, Jacobus Philippus of Bergamo, Marcus Antonius Sabellicus the Venetian, Sebald Schedel of Nuremberg, and many others.

The second kind is special, which describes the deeds of one kingdom or a few kingdoms, provinces, or a people. In this kind Josephus, Hegesippus the Jew, Bede in the deeds of the English, Gregory of Tours the bishop, Windichinus the monk of Corvey, Saxo, Regino abbot of Prum, Otto bishop of Freising, the aforesaid Marcus Antonius Sabellicus in the history of the Venetians, and many others, whose number is uncertain, made use of it.

The third kind of histories is called topical or local, which narrates the history of one city, family, or place. In this kind there were Bede the monk, Sigebert the monk of Gembloux, Strabus of Fulda, and very many others who wrote the histories of their own monasteries. In this very kind of writing also, out of love for the brothers of Hirsau, I have resolved, driven by their exceeding charity, to weave a history. And although I cannot apply to it the polish of eloquence, I nevertheless promise that I shall observe truth before all, so far as it pertains to my conscience.

The materials have been taken from those whose names are these. From the annalistic records and the letters of privilege of the aforesaid monastery of Hirsau I received the names and successions of the abbots, together with their deeds. I have also obtained many things from various authors, histories, legends of saints, and letters. The authors are Windichinus the monk in the history of the Saxons, another who completed that same history, Regino abbot of Prum in the history of the people of Metz, Berno abbot of Reichenau in the history of the Alemanni, Theoderic the monk in the history of the people of Trier, Golscherus the monk in the deeds of the same, Marianus Scotus, monk of Fulda, in an all-embracing German history, Otto bishop of Freising in his history, Andreas monk of St. Emmeram of Regensburg in the deeds of the dukes of Bavaria, Henry of Erfurt in the history of memorable things, Godfrey of Viterbo in his chronicle Pantheon, Gottfried the monk of St. Pantaleon in the history of the people of Cologne, John of Hildesheim, Carme-[unclear], Hugh the monk of Fleury, John the monk of Kastl in the book on the illustrious men of our order, Everwinus the monk of Segenburg in his chronicle, Bernard the monk of Corvey in his history of the Saxons, and Bertrand the monk in the history of the people of Hersfeld. And from many other various histories of the Bavarians, Swabians, Mainz people, Speyer people, and from the deeds of the counts palatine of the Rhine, described by a certain monk of the monastery of Lorsch, I have inserted here and there, scattered throughout, not without great labor, those things that seemed to me to pertain to the plan of the history.

Finally, many things by digression [unclear], cannot lie hidden in the narrow confines of one monastery, but by the zeal of men, not to say curiosity, had at last been drawn out and had come into the hands of very many to be examined. Therefore, so that it may nowhere proceed empty and may become burdensome to no one, I wished, with a certain moderation, to adorn it with the more memorable clauses of events carried out in Germany. Insofar as the variety of things...

The Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

The foundation of the monastery of Hirsau, made by Count Erlafrid and Notting, his son, bishop of Vercelli, in the year of the Lord's incarnation 830.

[unclear]

With God's help intending to write the history of the distinguished monastery of Hirsau, I have thought it worthwhile to begin from its first foundation, and to show what cause moved the founders themselves to undertake this matter. At the time when Louis the First governed the empire of the Romans, Erlafrid, count of Calw, was a rich and powerful man with the emperor. He had a son named Notting, a man learned in every doctrine of the Scriptures, who, because of his knowledge of letters and the honorableness of his life, had obtained the bishopric of the church of Vercelli under the Emperor Charlemagne, father of Louis. After he had ruled his church well for some time according to the canonical ordinances, there came upon him a sweet desire to see his homeland; and, lest he should seem to have returned to it empty-handed, he began to consider what special gift he might bring with him by which he could make it more illustrious.

Indeed, not long before, at very great cost he had obtained the relics of the most holy bishop of the [Rediciani?], Aurelius Armenius, more precious than jasper and gold; and, carrying them to his own church of Vercelli, he placed them in a very beautiful mausoleum which he had prepared. And so, when he had resolved, on going to see his homeland and his dear parents, to bring this treasure to the Germans, wavering in mind between hope and fear lest this removal should perhaps displease Saint Aurelius, or, if it were learned by the people of the church of Vercelli, he should be forced to draw back from his purpose, he committed the whole matter to be settled by divine counsel. Therefore, turning his whole mind to God, and lying sleepless prostrate on the ground beside the tomb of Saint [unclear] the most gentle Aurelius, he addressed Aurelius himself, the divine friend of Christ, with burning desire and tears, saying: Holy father Aurelius, my glory, and after God the protection of my soul, to you I lay open the desire of your servant, which, being joined to God, you undoubtedly cannot fail to know. I beg you, by the divine love which has made you venerable to me, celebrated in the Church, and one with God, holy and immortal, do not permit me to waver longer in this uncertainty, but hear me, your servant prostrate before you, and teach me, that I may know what I ought to do according to God's will and yours.

When he had persevered for a long time in prayer, in tears and lying on the ground, wearied by prayer and the prolonging of his vigils, he fell asleep for a little while. To him as he slept, divine Aurelius, clothed in pontifical vestments and more splendid than the sun, soon stood by; and, addressing Notting by name, said: Peace be with you, brother Notting. Rise; do not weep. I have come for this purpose, that I may go with you into Germany, to bring more peoples there to Christ when dead than if, still living among the nations and preaching, I were shining with miracles. When you come there, you shall establish a monastery of servants of God in the place where you shall suddenly behold a blind man meeting us restored to sight. Having said these things, he vanished.

But the venerable bishop Notting, rising from sleep, joyfully opened the sarcophagus in secret at once in that very night, and secretly carried the relics themselves of the most sacred bishop Aurelius home. The mausoleum, most carefully closed again, deceived the people of Vercelli for a long time, since they thought they had a guest whom they did not have. But Bishop Notting, when all things had been prepared which seemed to pertain to the plan of the journey, took as companions of so great a pilgrimage certain of the more faithful among his household; and, placing on a pack-animal the little bundle containing the sacred relics of Aurelius, accompanied by the best guide for the journey, he entered upon the road he had set before him.

And when, having happily entered Germany, he came after some days into his own homeland, he was received with great joy by his people; and what a treasure he was bringing into the region he showed to his father and to all the other inhabitants of the land, while absent by letters, and while present by words and by the display of the deed. But since there was not at hand a place consecrated by the gift of blessing and worthy of so great a guest, and since they were unwilling to keep such venerable relics beyond three days [unclear], rising early in the morning Bishop Notting with his household, and Erlafrid his father with his other son, Ermefrid, the pontiff's brother, together with very many of the more noble [unclear].

Notting sets out for Germany. and commoners, whom the count, in honor of such great guests, had caused to be present; and, after the necessary things had been arranged in reverence for the saint, they began to carry the holy body, circling along the slope of the mountain, to the aforesaid chapel of Saint Nazarius. When they came to the place where today the monastery of Saint Aurelius has been built, behold, a certain blind man, coming among the crowd to meet the holy relics, began to cry out in a loud voice, saying, “Give me sight, most holy worshipper of God, Aurelius, by your prayers, just as you promised.” To him the bishop said, “Where did Saint Aurelius promise that he would give you sight?” He said, “Lord, this night, as I was sleeping, in the anguish of my mind, a certain [unclear] in the midst of [unclear] said: ‘[unclear] of Christ, you will be given sight.’ And I said, ‘Lord, who are you?’ ‘I am,’ he said, ‘Aurelius the bishop, a new guest in Germany, whom the son of your lord Count Erlafrid brought here some time ago.’”

When these things had been said, he cried out again: “Saint Aurelius, help me, that I may see you.” And immediately his eyes were opened, and he saw perfectly. All who were present, seeing so unusual a miracle, magnified God, saying, “Praise be to you, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God.” And each said to the one standing at his side: “Oh, how great is this saint, who can even give sight to the blind.” Bishop Nottingus said to Erlafrid the father: “Father, Saint Aurelius has chosen this place for his dwelling”; and, climbing the mountain at a quickened pace, the pontiff, after offering the sacrifice of our redemption, placed the relics that had been made in the prepared place.

Then, after a few days, Bishop Nottingus explained to the patrician Erlafrid and to his brother Ermesrid the vow which he had long before conceived in his mind, at Saint Aurelius’s urging in dreams, admonishing, asking, and beseeching them that, for love of almighty God, in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of Saint Aurelius the bishop, [they should build?] a monastery [unclear]. The thirtieth year [unclear], the seventh of Louis the first emperor, the two hundred and thirty-first from the passing of our most holy father, which with swift completion he happily finished in seven years. Indeed that land produces an abundant supply of both stone and timber, so that there is no need for these to be brought from elsewhere, as [unclear]. Meanwhile [unclear] provision would be made more freely for God. He also sent gold crosses and silver chalices for the service of divine worship, and books too, and various ornaments for the adornment of the house of the Lord, all of which he knew to be necessary for this.

But Erlafrid kept saying that the undertaking was impossible [unclear]; if he himself, overtaken by death, should depart, the unfinished work would either be completed more slowly or be abandoned altogether. For although Ermesrid, the son, was a collaborator with his father in this holy work, nevertheless, because of his youthful age, the zeal of divine love did not seem to burn in him as much as so great an undertaking required.

Therefore, in the seventh year after the monastery of Hirsau had begun to be built, it was completed; this was from the birth of the Lord 837, in the fifteenth indiction, through the untiring diligence of Count Erlafrid, who spared no expense in order to complete what he had conceived in his mind. The church was quite beautiful, built in the manner of the ancients without the support of columns, spacious, covered above with a wooden ceiling, and adorned within with four altars. Moreover the arrangement of the cloister, in imitation of the ancients, had been spacious indeed, but of a simpler construction, likewise covered above with a wooden ceiling, such as [unclear] not so much for the dwellings arranged around the circuit of the cloister as for the custom of that time.

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

[unclear] contained, were quite handsome and well ordered; although, if our monks today were shut up in similar little cells, they would cry out that they had been handed over to chains and darkness. We shall give the reason for this. The monks of old once had cells, churches, and other dwellings that were humble and dark, but their hearts were very bright in the love of almighty God and in the knowledge of the divine Scriptures. Our men, however, now build churches, cells, houses, and all dwellings exceedingly bright, but their hearts are dark, full of vices and idleness, since they neither love God as they ought nor apply their minds to readings of the Scriptures. Thus too, when the chalices once were of copper, the priests were of gold; today, however, the chalices are of gold, and the priests of copper. This monastery, built by Erlafrid, had been in the place where, as we have said, the blind man was enlightened, and where he himself, because of his hunts, had a house in the forest. Yet after almost two hundred thirty-four years, as we shall say below in its proper place, it was demolished by Count Adelbert and reformed into the shape in which it is seen today. For today no trace at all of the earlier monastery remains, although the site of both is one and the same.

When and whence the first monks were brought to Hirsau, and who was appointed their first abbot.

After the most noble Count Erlafrid, having completed so notable a work, had brought his purpose to effect, not without very great expenses, he was impatient of delay, since he said that he desired nothing more than to live to see that day on which he might behold choirs of monks in his little estate praising God together. He began anxiously to consider whence he might obtain for the new monastery gloriously founded by him monks of the old way of life, religiously instructed according to the rule of the most holy father Benedict, who would both themselves be most holy in their conduct and fit for that same purpose, [unclear].

At that time, it was said that the religion of monks flourished very greatly at Fulda above many others, and that they were learned. Hence many of them were raised in various churches to the summit of the pontificate. Therefore Erlafrid sent messengers to Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, [unclear]. The praise and memory of the monks of Fulda was in the mouths of all, and was held in great esteem among emperors, kings, and princes, not only because of the holiness of their life, but also because of their incomparable knowledge of the Scriptures. [He asked] Rabanus [Maurus], abbot of Fulda, for the monks and an abbot to be brought into his monastery which he had built; and he promised that he would do everything that, in their judgment, should seem fitting for the usefulness of monastic institution.

In the year 838, in the first indiction, Abbot Lindbert came to Hirsau with fifteen monks, sent by Rabanus, abbot of Fulda. In the year 839, [unclear] religious men, and for the most part most learned in the sacred Scriptures. Therefore Rabanus, having heard [unclear], sent [unclear]. The most devout Count Erlafrid, receiving with great rejoicing the abbot himself and the monks appointed for him, joyfully brought them into the new monastery, and thereafter discussed [matters] by their counsel. At that time they were still keeping the body of Saint Aurelius in the chapel of blessed Nazarius the martyr, since the church of the monastery had not yet been consecrated. Therefore after a few months, so that everything might obtain the desired effect, Count Erlafrid [went] to the imperial court at Frankfurt with many other princes [unclear].

6. Of the Monastery of Hirsau

Assembly of the princes of the Franks and dukes of Germany.

summoned, and, when the affairs of the empire for which the convocation of princes had been proclaimed had been settled, he asked, invited, and obtained Otgar, archbishop of the church of Mainz, who was then present with many other bishops, to consecrate the new monastery. In what manner this consecration was carried out must next be told.

When, by whom, and in whose presence the dedication and consecration of the first monastery of Hirsau was made.

Since at that time a grave dispute over the empire was being waged between Emperor Louis and his sons, it happened that the convocation of princes to which we have said Erlafrid was called was transferred from Frankfurt to the city of the Nemetes, which in common speech we call Speyer. Since this is not far from Hirsau, it gave the most Christian count occasion for the dedication of the newly founded monastery to be performed with greater solemnity. For many bishops, abbots, and princes had assembled, summoned to the imperial synod, and, at the invitation of Count Erlafrid, a good number of them took part in the office of dedication. Therefore in the year of the Lord 838, in the first indiction, in the month of September, Otgar, most reverend bishop of the church of Mainz, at the request of Count Erlafrid and his son Ermefrid, consecrated the monastery of Hirsau in honor of Peter, prince of the Apostles, and of Saint Aurelius, bishop, in the presence of many princes, bishops, and abbots who at that time were following the emperor’s court. Present there were Hildebold, archbishop of Cologne; Willeric, bishop of Bremen in Saxony; Ebo, bishop of Hildesheim; Thiagrius, bishop of Halberstadt; Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda; Bruno, abbot of Hersfeld; [unclear] of Lindbert, the first abbot of this Hirsau; Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis, [unclear] archchaplain of the palace; Duke Henry; Duke Bernard; Ludolph, his son; Count Erlafrid, founder of the monastery; Ermefrid, his son; Count Ortrung; Count Adelhard; and many others, whose names, together with the foregoing, were not entered in the book of the deeds of Bishop Otgar, or perhaps were omitted through the carelessness of scribes. When the consecration of the church had been solemnly performed, as was the custom, Archbishop Otgar, together with the other bishops, abbots, and princes, [unclear] the body of the most holy prelate Aurelius, brought with great devotion from the chapel of Saint Nazarius, honorably [unclear] at the high altar; through his merit many miracles were performed. But when, after fifty years, under Emperor Arnulf, the Northmen were devastating Worms, Abbot Hardrad, fearing that such holy relics might by some fraud or violence come into the hands of foreigners, and with the counsel of the brothers added to this, made an underground vault in the church, in which he placed the body of the precious confessor of Christ Aurelius in a stone sarcophagus, with an inscription of his name and dignity, and again covered that chamber with earth in such a way that thereafter no one could suspect that anything was hidden there. Thus so great a treasure of relics remained hidden beneath the earth for almost one hundred and seventy years.

Lindbert becomes abbot in Hirsau.

The body of Saint Aurelius is [unclear] into the monastery.

Thus so great a [unclear] of relics of the time of the precious confessor of Christ Aurelius, placed in a stone sarcophagus, with an inscription of his name and dignities, and the chamber itself was again covered with earth in such a way that thereafter no one could suspect that anything else was hidden there. Hence, however, so great a treasure of relics was thus hidden beneath the earth for almost one hundred and seventy years.

The earlier donation of the monastery made by the count.

[unclear] received [unclear] of all. Then Count Erlafrid, approaching the altar with his son, before the [unclear] who were present, handed over to almighty God and to his saints, Peter the Apostle and Aurelius the bishop, the monastery itself which he had built, with little villages, woods, and pastures.

Names of the villages which he gave.

The church also in Deckenpfronn, with everything that he had there. In Gültstein he gave twelve hides. In Münchingen twelve hides and the church. In Döffingen a good estate. And these are the names of the vil[unclear] inserted in the document, which he handed over at that same hour to Saint Aurelius: Lutzelhart, Altburg, Luzenhart, Ebersbuel, Kallenbach, Kugelbach, Nagalthart, Ottenbrunnen, Hugsteten, Gumprecht, Wilar, half the villa of Altriburan, and many other good estates, which were written down in the book of donations.

When this donation had been solemnly made, the aforesaid Archbishop Otgar, in the place of the Apostolic Lord Pope Gregory IV and of the most pious Emperor Louis I, fortified it with the ban of perpetual stability, and delivered the monastery itself, with all donations already made and those duly to be made in future, into the hands of the aforesaid abbot Lintbert and of his successors, to be canonically appointed according to the rule of our most holy father Benedict, to be possessed forever. This was on the condition that the monastic life, according to the standard of the aforesaid father, should remain vigorous in it all its days; and that, whenever the monks should happen to be bereft of a spiritual pastor, they should have free power, without contradiction from anyone, to choose another suitable man, either from among themselves or from another monastery of the same order, in place of the deceased father.

The aforesaid archbishop appointed Count Erlafrid himself advocate of the monastery of Hirsau, under this condition: that when the father died, the son should not succeed in the advocacy unless he had been taken up into it by the abbot and the monks who should be there at the time, by their free and spontaneous will. For the most devout count feared lest the monastery, after his death, should suffer some injury or violence through his son or grandsons, as we see happening today among many, if the advocacy were to pass to descendants by hereditary right. Therefore he decreed that it should depend on the abbot's will whom he wished to have as a suitable advocate for his monastery. And this liberty, confirmed in the course of time by many privileges, both apostolic and imperial, has remained inviolate in the monastery of Hirsau down to the present day.

In the same year, too, this privileged endowment and delivery, made by Count Erlafrid, was confirmed by Emperor Louis the Pious. For when all things had been completed that pertained to the solemn office of dedication, [unclear].

Imperial confirmation.

The liberty of this monastery, concerning its advocate.

Nottingus, bishop of Vercelli, who was the first author of the foundation of the monastery of Hirsau, had sent many things for the adornment of the house of the Lord: gold and silver crosses, chalices, books, and various ornaments of the divine ministry. Whether he was present at this dedication we do not know for certain. But now [unclear] to the emperor Louis in the city of Speyer, where he was at that time, as we have said, holding court with his sons, together with the venerable archbishop and certain others; and when the document of donation had been read before him, he obtained from him perpetual confirmation of all things.

Life of Saint Aurelius, bishop.

Therefore blessed Aurelius, born in Armenia of Christian and most noble parents, as soon as his age permitted, was given over to letters. Instructed by divine prudence, and in a short time making no small progress in every learning of the Scriptures, he turned everything that he could either learn or know to the exercise of divine love. [unclear] as the plan of this work requires, we have gone through the old history of his way of life that was offered to us, so that we omit very much of the words, but either nothing or little of the thoughts.

As his years increased, [born] of Christian and most noble parents, as soon as his age permitted, he was given over to letters. Instructed by divine prudence, [unclear] not in mediocrity an example of Christian [unclear], adorned with all virtues, he shone with outstanding holiness and was made, to the admiration of all, the standard and example of Christian conduct: as one who, though young in age, appeared by his character and wisdom older than many old men. Hence, through all the grades of the ecclesiastical order, he deserved to ascend, though reluctant, to the summit of the episcopate in the city of Rediciana, with the greatest applause of the people no less than of the clergy; and, established in this honor, he shone more brightly with greater virtues than before.

The form of the Lord's flock.

He presented himself as irreproachable [unclear], and stirred the people to the observance of God's commandments no less by example than by speech. He was a father of the poor, furthermore a consoler of widows; whatever he could have, he ministered it all to the uses of the needy.

Aurelius was a true bishop in deed and speech.

He was of so holy and irreproachable a way of life that there was no one at that time in Armenia who did not fear Aurelius the bishop, servant of God, with proclamation of praise. He was accustomed to visit all the villages of the diocese of Rediciana, admonishing and preaching in his own most holy person, ministering the word of salvation to all. He instructed the ignorant, strengthened the faint-hearted, raised up the downcast, and exhorted the good and humble, in order that they might advance to better things.

S. of the Monastery of Hirsau

Dionysius, bishop of Milan, is sent into exile into Armenia.

... he pricked the idle [unclear], and recalled the proud and restless to penitence. Meanwhile, while he was intent upon these holy works, it happened that blessed Dionysius, archbishop of the church of Milan, because he refused to subscribe to the blasphemies of the Arians, was relegated by command of the emperors to exile in Armenia, namely to that city of Rediciana, over which Saint Aurelius was set as bishop. This relegation of the most holy man Dionysius was made by the impious bishops of the Arian faction under Constantine and Constans, emperors, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 361, Liberius presiding as pope over the Roman church; and he himself also was sent into exile in the same year.

But Saint Aurelius received blessed Dionysius, when he came into his city Rediciana, as a true disciple of Christ, with great joy, and after [unclear]. The greatest charity between them. When he heard [unclear], “Brother, restrain your tears; the earth is the Lord’s and the fullness thereof, and the whole world is a homeland for a Christian.” Bishop Dionysius was received by blessed Aurelius with the greatest reverence, and provided for by him with no less kindness of hospitality and generosity; and in that same city he remained, relegated in exile, until his death. Therefore, when the habit of mutual association had been established, a great friendship and familiarity arose between them, which then began in time and now remains and is perfected in eternity.

So great, indeed, was the holiness of them both that their fame ran through all Armenia and drew all people into admiration. The sick flowed together to them and were cured of long-standing illnesses; those also possessed by demons were freed by the prayers of these men. For almighty God deigned to work such miracles through these servants of his that, as a merciful father, he converted all Armenia to his worship by their virtue and teaching. Finally Saint Aurelius, by his teaching and preaching, most diligently warned each of the faithful to flee the pestilence of the Arian heresy and to remain with the church of the saints in the faith of the Holy Trinity.

Although blessed Saint Dionysius was held under guard, as exiles were customarily kept at that time, nevertheless access to him was open to Saint Aurelius whenever he wished; and they were joined to one another by such great affection that they agreed both to live together while alive and to be buried together when dead. But after some years, when blessed Dionysius saw that death was near him, he addressed blessed Aurelius in these words, saying: “I know, dearest brother, that the end of my living in this world is at hand, and the time of my dissolution is now near. I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. In the present age there remains one thing that I ask of you: when I have died, as soon as you can, carry my body back to my Milanese church, so that the church which could not have me alive may at least deserve to have me dead. Let not the inconvenience of a long journey frighten you; the Lord will be with you, and your reward will be very great.” Saint Aurelius, bound to him by great affection and love, consented and promised that he would do what was asked.

And so the holy confessor of Christ, indeed also martyr, Dionysius, having completed the order of his life, died on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the year of the Lord 379. There are those who write that he was relegated to Cappadocia, died there, and that his relics were sent back to Milan to Saint Ambrose through Saint Basil the bishop. But this difference of opinions can easily be reconciled among those who know the histories. After a long space of journeying, Saint Aurelius [unclear]. The body of Dionysius is brought into Milan.

With what great exultation of all the corpse was received, no one could easily say, since all regarded it as worthy of reverence, as though sent back from heaven. Aurelius sets out for Italy. Aurelius dies. But Saint Aurelius, to be brief, after the duty of piety had been performed, when he was thinking of returning to his own church, at the urging of Ambrose, whom he considered it unlawful to contradict, remained [unclear]. “When the Lord calls you to the joys of eternal happiness, you will die, and beside the little chapel of my poor body [unclear] desired [unclear].”

Dionysius appears to Aurelius. Ambrose. Concerning Ambrose and the prayer made at the burial of Aurelius. Ambrose.

And when he entrusted to the Lord that his pilgrimage should be directed [unclear] daily, after the revolution of the year in which he had come to Milan, Saint Dionysius appeared to him, saying, “He has heard [unclear].” And, making his testament, he bade farewell to his homeland, and took care to teach and inflame [unclear]. And when in his daily prayers [unclear], commended into the hands of the holy Ambrose, bishop of Milan, he yielded up his spirit to the Lord on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, that is, on the same day on which Saint Dionysius also had departed in Armenia three years before, in the year of the Lord 383, Gratian ruling with his brother Valentinian. He was buried in his own sarcophagus at the side of Saint Dionysius in the Milanese church. The most blessed bishop Ambrose followed his funeral rites with many tears, and delivered to the people that notable sermon which begins: [unclear].
