... we have lost a brother and most beloved pastor; rather, we have sent ahead an advocate. In this he raises to heaven, with great powers of eloquence, the praises and encomia of that holy bishop Aurelius. He remained buried at Milan for 437 years. Thus the body of Saint Aurelius, buried there and shining with many miracles, remained from the time of the empire of Gratian until the reign of Charles the Great, for almost 437 years, until Nottingus, bishop of Vercelli, having obtained it with great entreaties from the archbishop of Milan, transferred it to his church in the fifth year of the first Emperor Louis. Not long afterward, under the same Louis, he carried it away into Germany, his homeland, and, as we have said before, placed it in the monastery of Hirsau, where to the present day almighty God works many virtues and great wonders through his merits.

10. On Lintbert, the first abbot of this monastery, who presided for sixteen years, and on his manner of life and the deeds of that time.

838.

In the year of the Lord 838, therefore, under the most pious Emperor Louis, Lintbert, a monk of Fulda, was appointed first abbot of this monastery by the election of the brethren who had come with him from the bosom of the monastery of Fulda. He was given the pastoral staff by Otgar, most reverend archbishop of the church of Mainz, and presided over the government of this monastery for sixteen years. He was born in Swabia of parents not of the lowest rank, according to worldly dignity, the brother of Buno, abbot of Hersfeld, who himself also had been for many years a monk of Saint Boniface under Abbot Baugolf. Moreover Lintbert, devoted to God from infancy, became a monk in the monastery of Fulda in the eighteenth year of his age, under the aforementioned Abbot Baugolf, who had succeeded Saint Sturm; and as his age increased, both under Baugolf himself and under his successors Eigil and Rabanus, he made great progress in holy conduct and in learned knowledge. Thus he put on the monk in the year of the Lord 796, in the fourth indiction. But he was sent to Hirsau and received the abbacy, as we have said before, in 838, in the [unclear] year of his age and the forty-second of his conversion, and ruled for sixteen years.

He was a very reverend man, known and familiar to kings and princes. From the time when he entered the monastery he not only lived irreproachably, but, what is judged to belong to greater virtue, shone with such holiness that in his way of life he furnished to all an example of true perfection. Some compositions of his teacher Rabanus on sacred letters are extant addressed to him, which seem to have been requested by the talent of a studious man. I have read under the name of Abbot Lintbert a most beautiful little work on the Song of Songs of Solomon, in which he described the desire and condition of the faithful soul thirsting for its God so beautifully, elegantly, and fittingly that, in my judgment, no one whom I have read has ever treated this subject more clearly. But that the author of this work is the same as our abbot Lintbert of Hirsau I do not hold as sufficiently proved. Yet one might persuade someone willing to believe it, because whoever he finally was, he wrote under Emperor Lothar, the son of Louis, as is clear from the preface of the work itself.

Since, however, this Lintbert our abbot was for a long time the hearer and fellow student of Rabanus of Fulda, a man most learned in all respects, it must be believed that he could only have turned out most learned. For Rabanus himself, while still a monk, had held the public monastic school in the monastery of Fulda, which he continued also as abbot; in it he instructed the monks in every way, not only in sacred Scripture but also in secular letters. Nor did he train only the monks of the monastery of Fulda, but also many pupils in every kind of learning who had been sent to him from various other places. Of these, very many afterward in the course of time were promoted to great dignities. He had had as teacher, from among the disciples of Bede the English monk, the most reverend man Albinus, monk and abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours, formerly teacher of the great Emperor Charles; from him he himself had drawn in Gaul what he later taught others in Germany.

But Lintbert, first the fellow student and afterward the hearer of Rabanus, did not neglect as abbot what he had learned as a monk from a good teacher. He was indeed a most zealous cultivator of regular discipline, who not only [unclear], but, going before them as a good pastor, was open to view by the example of good work. His meditation, day and night, was always continued in the law of the Lord; praying without ceasing to the Lord, he remained to the end a true disciple of Christ. As the fame of his holiness and learning spread through every region round about, many noble men entrusted their sons to be instructed by his teaching. Very many also of those who seemed distinguished among men in the world, The Monastery of Hirsau.

Corvey is founded in Saxony.

[unclear] submitted themselves to that discipline for love of the heavenly kingdom; hence the number of brothers, soon increased, began to grow greatly, and their temporal substance was enlarged by the offerings of many. In these same times the monastery of Corvey in Saxony, under the rule of our holy father Benedict, took the beginning of its new foundation; it began to be founded in the year of the Lord 822, in the fifteenth indiction, and, having been completed almost at the same time as this monastery of the holy bishop Aurelius, began to be inhabited. At almost the same time the monastery of the martyrs Saints Marcellinus and Peter, in the place called Seligenstadt in the diocese of Mainz, under the rule of our holy father Benedict, was first founded by Emperor Louis, with the cooperation of the venerable man Einhard, formerly chancellor, but then a monk and the first abbot of that same monastery; [unclear], in which the bodies of the aforesaid two martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, brought from Rome in the month of November in the year of the Lord 838 through the emperor’s agency, were honorably laid to rest.

840. Distinguished men of our order. Foundation of the monastery of Seligenstadt.

In the times of Lintbert, first abbot of Saint Aurelius of Hirsau, around the year of the Lord 840, under the most pious Emperor Louis and his sons, many very celebrated men flourished in our Benedictine order, distinguished for holiness and learning in the Scriptures; like stars of heaven, they wonderfully illuminated the whole Church by their morals and doctrine. Rabanus Maurus, abbot of Fulda, of whom we spoke above, was held in esteem by everyone in these times because of the integrity of his life and the inestimable discipline of his knowledge. What and how much he wrote, both in our book On Ecclesiastical Writers and in the second On Illustrious Men [unclear].

842.

Finally, in the year of the Lord 842, which was the fourth year of Abbot Lintbert, stirred up by the deceits of certain men, he left the monastery of Fulda and, fleeing to Louis, son of the elder Emperor Louis, remained almost as an exile until the death of Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, who had expelled him for what cause I do not know. But after five years, when [Otgar?] had died, he was appointed in his place in the year of the Lord 847, in the tenth indiction, by the vote of all, and sat for nine years.

Haymo [unclear], third bishop of Halberstadt, who in the year of the Lord 840, in the third indiction, was ordained bishop and presided for thirteen years, was outstanding in all holiness and doctrine. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which we have made mention in our aforesaid books. Einhard also, from imperial chancellor a monk, and from monk the first abbot in Seligenstadt, a learned and most religious man, among other monuments of his learning wrote the deeds of Charles the Great, emperor, in one volume; also a history of his own time, and certain other things, by which he showed himself skilled not only in the Latin language but also in Greek. Frechulf, a monk of Fulda, who wrote a very notable chronicle from the origin of the world down to the incarnation of the Lord, which he entitled On the Seven Ages of the World, was bishop of Lisieux in these times.

There also flourished around these times Hetti, from abbot of [Mediolanum?] archbishop of Trier, who founded, at the admonition of Saint Maternus in dreams, a monastery of regular canons at Koblenz, where the Moselle flows into the Rhine; into it he transferred and placed the body of Saint Castor from Karden. But [unclear] of Saint Castor [unclear] the eighth, in which Hirsau was founded, he died, and he was buried at Saint Matthias outside Trier.

Hilduin also, abbot of Saint-Denis of Paris, a man most learned in every respect, wrote the life and passion of Saint Dionysius for Emperor Louis the First. In the year of the Lord 827 he transferred the bones of the holy martyr Sebastian from Rome into Gaul; after many years, his head was placed by its founder in a monastery of our order in the diocese of Trier, which is called Viridisaugia.

At the same time Theodulf, from abbot of the monastery of Fleury bishop of Orléans, was in great esteem among the Gauls, venerable to all the people no less for the holiness of his life than for his learning in the Scriptures. Placed in custody by Emperor Louis, I know not on account of what suspicion of conspiracy with the sons who were then very much at variance with their father, he composed the hymn which we are accustomed to sing on Palm Sunday, at the station. When on that day, as the emperor was passing near the prison in solemn procession, he had sounded it forth in sweet melody with tuneful voice, that man, delighted Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

... he, moved both by the man's constancy and by the sweetness of the harmony, soon ordered him to be released by the voice of a herald. The hymn itself, composed in suitable verse, begins: "Glory, praise, and honor be to you," etc.

Strabus also, a monk of Fulda, the pupil and scribe of Rabanus, flourished in the same times. He wrote many various works, as we have declared in other published books on writers. He began the Chronicle of the monastery of Fulda, which, continued by others who succeeded him, gave us no small help in the publication of this work. But Angelomus, a monk of the monastery of Luxeuil, appeared in this period most learned in expounding the divine Scriptures. Of him we have made mention elsewhere.

Ansegisus, formerly abbot of the monastery of Bobbio, archbishop of Sens, a man learned in the Scriptures and very highly celebrated in the councils of kings, wrote several works, of which an account is given elsewhere. John, abbot of Vercelli, a Scot by nation, very learned in Greek and Latin, flourished in these times. At the command of Charles, son of the first Emperor Louis, he was the first of all to translate the books of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite into Latin, and adorned them with commentaries not to be despised. He also composed a book of great subtlety On the Division of Nature, together with several other works which we have not seen. Alderic, abbot of the monastery of Ferrieres, of our order, after Jeremiah but immediately before Ansegisus archbishop of Sens, was made in these times. The bodies also of the saints Severus, bishop of Ravenna, Vincentia his wife, and Innocentia his daughter, were translated with the greatest honor to Mainz by Archbishop Otgar.

Ansegisus, formerly abbot, bishop of Sens. John, abbot of Vercelli. Alderic, formerly abbot, bishop. Saint Severinus is translated. The king of the Danes is baptized. Monks of Corvey preach. Amalarius, formerly monk, archbishop of Trier.

Heriolus, king of the Danes, with his wife and sons, is baptized at Mainz in the time of this first Abbot Linthert. A great part of the Danes are converted to the faith of Christ through the monks of the monastery of Corvey, who, out of love for heavenly happiness, had entered Dacia to preach the holy Gospel to the nations. Amalarius Fortunatus, a monk of Luxeuil, afterwards archbishop of Trier, and then cardinal of the holy Roman Church, wrote in these days to Emperor Louis books on the divine offices.

In the twenty-third year of Emperor Louis, under Linthert, the first abbot of this monastery, the Northmen first landed on the borders of Holland and Gaul; afterwards, for many years, wandering here and there with a strong army, they perpetrated boundless evils.

In the year of the Lord 838, which was the first year of Abbot Linthert, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, Saint Frederick, the eighth bishop of the church of Utrecht, in the treasury of the same church, after the solemnities of Mass, while he was devoutly intent upon prayer, was cruelly slain by two attendants hired for pay by the empress Judith, and became a martyr of the highest truth. For the bishop had said to the emperor: "It is not lawful for you to have Judith, daughter of the duke of Bavaria, near to you in blood, as your wife: either cast her away, or I shall excommunicate you by the authority of the Almighty." Exasperated by these words, the impious Judith not long afterwards killed the herald of truth. When Gregory IV, the pope, heard of this monstrous crime, he placed Emperor Louis in the monastery of Soissons to perform penance. And Jesse, bishop of Amiens, placed a veil on the empress Judith, a second Herodias, and made her a nun.

By this empress Louis had a son, Charles, surnamed the Bald, who afterwards, in the year of the Lord 876, was made emperor. He appointed him duke of Bavaria, Swabia, and Burgundy, while his other sons by his former wife bore this with considerable displeasure.

Finally, in the year of the Lord 840, when Emperor Louis, after completing his penance, was pursuing his future [unclear] son Lothair, who had rebelled against his father, and came to the monastery of Hersfeld, he fell gravely ill; reduced to a cart and then by boat, he immediately died at the imperial palace of Ingelheim, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the twenty-sixth year since he had received the empire. His corpse was honorably buried at Metz, in the church of Saint Arnulf, by Drogo his brother, bishop of Metz. This Drogo was a son of the great Emperor Charles, brother of Louis the First, a learned man and a lover of religion; from a monk he was made bishop of the aforesaid church of Metz, for whose adornment he did much.

When the most pious Emperor Louis had died, his son Lothair succeeded him and ruled as emperor for sixteen years. He had three brothers by his father: Pippin, whom he made duke of Aquitaine; Charles the Bald, to whom in the paternal division the western part fell, from the British Ocean as far as the river Meuse; and Louis, who obtained the eastern kingdom, that is, all Germany as far as the streams of the Rhine, together with certain other adjacent cities and districts across the Rhine, perhaps because of the abundance of wine. Lothair himself, the eldest by birth, received in his portion the name of emperor together with the whole kingdom which to the present day we call from his name Lotharingia, although now it is a duchy, the whole province, and also all the kingdoms of Italy together with the city of Rome itself. He had as wife Egilla, daughter of the king of England, who bore him two sons, Lothair and Louis, later emperor.

Strabus, monk of Fulda. Angelomus, monk. Ansegisus, formerly abbot, bishop of Sens. John, abbot of Vercelli. Alderic, formerly abbot, bishop. Saint Severinus is translated. First incursion of the Northmen. Saint Frederick, bishop of Utrecht, is martyred. Great wickedness of the empress Judith. The emperor is deposed together with his wife. Charles the Bald, son of Louis. Emperor Louis dies. Drogo, brother of the emperor, formerly monk, bishop. Louis has sons. A division is made among the brothers. Lothair, emperor. Monastery of Hirsau

Alfrid flourished in these times, formerly a monk of the monastery of Corvey, the fourth bishop of Hildesheim, a man truly beloved of God and most holy in his whole life. He governed the Church committed to him vigorously for 28 years, and built the greater church of the aforesaid city, in which he was also buried. He was elected bishop in the ninth year of Abbot Lintbert, which was the year of the Lord’s incarnation 847, in the tenth indiction.

848.

Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, at the command of Emperor Lothar, convened a synod of bishops and abbots at Mainz in the year of the Lord 848, in the eleventh indiction. In it he condemned a certain heretic, a priest named Gottschalk, and established many things for the adornment and utility of the Church. Among others there were present the most celebrated men, the bishops: Hetti, archbishop of Trier; Hildebold, archbishop of Cologne; Alfrid, bishop of Hildesheim; Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt; Luderic, bishop of Bremen; Lintbert, this first abbot of Saint Aurelius of Hirsau; Waldo, abbot of Fulda; Einhard, abbot of Seligenstadt; Brunwart, abbot of Hersfeld; Bertolph, abbot of Mettlach; Adventitius, abbot of Metz, afterward bishop there; Radulf, abbot of Saint-Médard of Soissons, afterward archbishop of Bourges; and many other bishops, abbots, and monks, among whom several were most renowned for life and learning.

In these days a certain woman, pretending that an angel of God had appeared to her and had announced that the last day of judgment was soon at hand, deceived many, both of the clergy and of the people, throughout the diocese of Mainz. At length, when she had been seized by Archbishop Rabanus, she confessed that she had been led into this, for the sake of gain, by the counsel of a certain priest [unclear].

849.

In the eleventh year of Abbot Lintbert, the body of the holy empress Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, was transferred from Rome to Gaul by the monk Theogisus, and was placed in the territory of Reims; her head is shown today in the church of Trier.

For in the thirteenth year, a very severe famine so devastated Germany that a father [unclear] his son [unclear]. In these days of the most excellent Abbot Lintbert, his mercy toward the poor greatly increased both his own name and the profit of the monastery of Hirsau. For the more he distributed to the use of the poor, the greater things he received. Rabanus the archbishop also displayed great generosity to the poor while [unclear] endured.

Around these times Adolphus, the most Christian king of England, going to Rome under Pope Leo IV, out of very great devotion to the Roman Church made his province tributary, instituting that from each house each year a silver coin should be paid to Saint Peter.

851.

In the thirteenth year of Abbot Lintbert, Lupus Servatus the priest, a most learned man, to whom Rabanus, while still abbot, once wrote eight books on the Epistle of Paul to the Romans, departed to the Lord. Two years earlier, being present at the synod of Mainz, he had plainly overcome and confuted before all who were there, in a very powerful disputation, that priest Gottschalk, who held erroneous opinions on free will, predestination, and the blood of Christ, and was troubling many. He also, for a clearer declaration of the truth, among other things that he wrote, composed a very fine treatise on these matters as well.

853.

In the fifteenth year of Abbot Lintbert, which is the year of the Lord 853, Saint Haymo died, the third bishop of Halberstadt, formerly a monk of Hersfeld, a man beloved of God in every respect, who by word, writing, and example recalled many to the paths of righteousness; he was buried in the greater church of Halberstadt. Saint Hildegrin succeeded him in the episcopate for almost 34 years.

Saint Ansgar flourished in these times, formerly a monk of the monastery of Corvey, the first archbishop of Bremen, before whom there were three bishops, namely Wilhard, Willeric, and Luderic, under the archbishop of Cologne. But Emperor Lothar, after [unclear].

Leo IV, pope, formerly a monk.

At this time there also flourished Pope Leo IV, formerly a monk of the monastery of Saint Martin in the city, then of our order, first cardinal priest of the title of the Four Holy Crowned Saints [the text breaks off].

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

13

[unclear] ordained by Pope Sergius; and, succeeding him after his death in the supreme pontificate, he presided for eight years and three months. He was a learned man, of most holy life, who after his death was entered in the catalogue of the saints; his feast is observed on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August.

853.

Lintbert, the first abbot, a very venerable man, after many labors borne in holy religion for the love of God, and worn out with age, sighing for Christ with his whole heart, died on the third day before the Ides of June, under Emperor Lothar, in the year of the Lord 854, in the second indiction, in the seventy-sixth year of his age, and before the sixteenth year of his administration of the abbacy had yet been completed. He had laudably and usefully presided over this monastery, and through his most holy conduct acquired many goods for it by the donation of the faithful. Gerungus, a monk, succeeded him in the abbacy of this monastery for thirty-two years; concerning him we shall see below.

The Northmen harass Gaul.

In this very year in which the most reverend abbot Lintbert died, the Northmen cruelly devastated Brittany, Gaul, and Francia; they overthrew the city of Nantes, and killed the bishop, who on Holy Saturday was intent upon the consecration of baptism, together with all the clergy.

A woman obtained the papacy.

They also [unclear] the churches of Saint Martin of Tours.

With [the account of] Lintbert completed, let us turn the pen to his successor.

Concerning the venerable Gerungus, the second abbot, who presided for thirty-two years, and what things were done in his times.

Therefore, after the most reverend abbot Lintbert had died and been buried, not without great sadness on the part of the brothers, since they were held by the greatest love for him, they immediately proceeded to an election [unclear].

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

Gandersheim is founded in Saxony.

[a convent?] in Saxony, called Gandersheim, in which he placed nuns living according to the Rule of our holy father Benedict. After him came his son Duke Liudolf, who completed the work begun by his father. The first abbess of the same monastery was Hadmodis, the elder daughter of that same Duke Liudolf; she presided over the virgins of Christ for twenty-two years, in great holiness of life and conduct. When she died, her sister, named Gerburga, succeeded in the abbacy for 14 years, herself also a most holy virgin, who shone forth in life and after death with many bright virtues. When she too was at last taken from their midst, a third daughter of Duke Liudolf was elected abbess, named Christina; by living religiously in the holy resolve of virginity she did not depart from the holiness of the sisters who had preceded her. The same Duke Liudolf also built another monastery of virgins in Saxony, called Brunshausen, and obtained confirmation of both from Pope Nicholas, together with many relics of saints. In these times there flourished from the monastic order many most excellent bishops, distinguished for holiness and knowledge of letters, and also abbots and monks very celebrated both for life and for learning in the Scriptures, who published many and varied volumes in literary study for the edification of posterity.

Abbo, from being abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus, became bishop of Auxerre; his brother Helibald had been bishop there before him. Both were energetic and most holy men, and nobly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular knowledge. Christianus, also called Druthmar, a monk of Corbie and a venerable priest, composed in these times many volumes in exposition of the divine Scriptures. Of him we have made fuller mention in other books on ecclesiastical writers. Egil, abbot of the monastery of Prum in the parish of Trier, was appointed in the first year of Gerung: a noble and very learned man, a friend of kings and princes, who acquired a very great name of praise in regular observance.

855.

In the second year of Abbot Gerung, which was the year of the Lord 855, the Emperor Lothar, worn out with age, summoned the leading men of the realm and divided the empire among his sons: to Louis he entrusted Italy, and appointed him emperor; to Lothar he granted the kingdom which, from his name, we have said was called Lotharingia; and to Charles, who was the younger by birth, he gave the kingdom of Provence. When these matters had been duly arranged, bidding farewell to his people he left the world and entered the monastery of Prum under the aforesaid Abbot Egil, and was made a monk. Having lived laudably in holy religion according to the Rule of our most holy father Benedict until the end, he at last died most happily on 29 September, and was buried there. Therefore, after Lothar became a monk, his son Louis reigned as emperor for twenty-one years.

856.

In the third year of Abbot Gerung, which was the year of the Lord 856, King Lothar, brother of the Emperor Louis, took as wife Theutberga, daughter of his uncle Charles the Bald, later emperor. But not long afterward he repudiated her and brought in Waldrada, his former concubine, sister of Gunther, archbishop of Cologne, from which union [unclear]. In the same year Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, died, and in the monastery of Saint [unclear]; for in a time of famine, which in the thirteenth year of Abbot Lintbert had oppressed all Germany, he relieved the need of the maimed. For at that time he was staying in a certain estate in his parish, where, receiving those coming from various places, he daily sustained with food more than three hundred, from among those who were constantly fed in his presence. One day, among the other beggars, there came a certain woman, almost consumed by starvation, with a very small boy; before [unclear] she breathed her last. The child, drawing out the breast of his dead mother as she lay there, as though she still lived, and trying to suck, compelled all who looked on to groan and weep. There followed him [unclear].

The invasion of the Northmen. The districts are destroyed by the Northmen.

Note his mercy in misfortunes.

Around these times the Northmen, together with the Danes, landing with fleets in Holland in a great multitude, utterly destroyed the very famous village called Dorestad, in which there are remembered to have been fifty-five parish churches, after all its inhabitants had been killed. Then, taking the city of Utrecht, they destroyed it, cruelly killing utterly all the people together with the whole clergy. Hunger, bishop of Utrecht at that time, escaping in flight with a few canons, came to Lothar, formerly emperor, in the monastery of Prum.

859. Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

859.

In the sixth year of Gerung, abbot of Hirsau, Huchertus, formerly a duke, a monk, and abbot of the monastery of Saint Richarius, brother of Queen Thiedberga, flourished: a wise and energetic man, to whom Lotharius entrusted the duchy between Mount Jura and Mount Veneris to govern. But when Lotharius later cast off Queen Thiedberga, Huchertus’s sister, after taking the concubine Wuldrada in addition, he found the abbot his enemy; through his action he was at last compelled to receive his sister back.

860.

In the seventh year of Abbot Gerung, which was the year of the Lord 860, and the fourth of Emperor Louis, in the city of Mainz the devil was plainly exercising his wickedness and hatred toward man. He hurled stones from the windows of houses at people, struck the walls strongly by night and by day as if with certain hammers, knocked at the doors of many people, and from there, speaking openly, everywhere disclosed thefts and sowed great discord among men. Then he stirred up the minds of all against one man, as if for that man’s sin the others were suffering such things; he set fire to that man’s crops, heaped together into one place. Wherever that man entered, at once the house was set on fire by that demon, so that now no place remained for him to stay except in the fields. Because of this, while priests were conducting litanies and sprinkling blessed water, the enemy of human nature for some time ceased from throwing stones. When they withdrew, the devil, shouting horribly, said that while the blessed water was being sprinkled he had hidden under the cope of one priest, whose name he stated, as if with a familiar friend; he accused him publicly of having lain with the steward’s daughter. And so it persisted continuously for three years, until in that place it consumed many buildings by fire. It was heard shouting, howling, speaking, knocking, striking the walls, and throwing stones at people, but absolutely nothing was seen. Yet elsewhere we read that these things happened not in the city of Mainz, but in a certain village of its diocese.

In this same seventh year of Gerung, in the eighth indiction, Probus, priest and monk of Saint Alban’s, died at Mainz, a holy and most learned man, whose conduct and zeal wonderfully adorned that same church of Mainz.

In this same year Saint Meginradus, formerly a monk of the monastery of Reichenau and a hermit in the Black Forest, was martyred by night in his cell by two robbers, who thought that they would find a large sum of money with him, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February. His body, brought back to the monastery of Reichenau and buried, shone for a long time with countless miracles. Moreover, the thieves, betrayed by two ravens which Saint Meginradus had reared, and with these repeatedly pursuing them, were broken on the wheel according to the laws of the country. In these days Egilo flourished, formerly a monk of Sens, afterwards archbishop after Wanlo, a man conspicuous for every goodness, a worthy shepherd of Christ’s sheep.

In the same year Ego, abbot of Prum, voluntarily resigned his abbey, and Ansbald succeeded him. [unclear]

At that time a great famine and mortality raged through the kingdom of the Franks; it converted very many to the love of the heavenly fatherland.

In the same times Mico, monk of Saint Richarius, flourished, a very studious and learned man, who wrote many varied works, excellently composed both in meter and in prose. Among these we have read a book of various epigrams, also excerpts from the poets, a book of riddles, and certain other things. Notgerus, formerly a monk of Saint Gall and bishop of Liege, is held to have been famous in these times among ecclesiastical writers; he first devised the use of sequences, which Pope Nicholas I consented should be sung in the church on this side of the Alps. The disciple of this Notgerus was Salomon, formerly a monk and afterwards bishop of Constance, who himself left to posterity some monuments of a distinguished talent. Wandelbertus also, monk of the monastery of Prum under the venerable abbot Ansbald, flourished at this same time; among other little works of his talent, he comprised in two books the life and miracles of Saint Goar, priest and hermit, resting beside the Rhine in the parish of Trier.

861.

In the eighth year of Abbot Gerung, Waldo, abbot of Fulda, was deposed by Emperor Louis, and Thuode succeeded him.

863.

In his tenth year, which was the year of the Lord 863, Charles of Mainz died, and Lintbertus succeeded him. To this Lintbertus, Otfridus, monk of Weissenburg, wrote, [unclear]

The devil terribly harasses Mainz for three years.

Wickedness of this demon.

Saint Probus, monk and priest, dies.

Meginradus the monk is martyred.

Ego, formerly a monk, archbishop.

Ansbald, famous abbot.

Mico, monk of Saint Richarius.

Notgerus, formerly a monk, bishop.

Wandelbertus, monk of Prum.

Salomon, formerly a monk, bishop.

The abbot of Fulda is deposed.

Otfridus, monk of Weissenburg.

Huchertus, abbot, formerly a duke. 16

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

[unclear], a pupil of Rabanus, [wrote?] four books of the Gospels in verse in our Teutonic language, formed according to certain rules, so that very few are found today who understand his writings. He also wrote many other things, of which we made mention in the smaller catalogue of the Germans.

Werenbertus also, a monk of St. Gall, a man most learned in every kind of knowledge, both secular and divine, is held to have been distinguished among writers in these times; he composed many monuments of his talent for posterity to read.

Ruthardus too, a monk, one of the first of this monastery of Hirsau sent from Fulda, formerly a hearer and disciple of the monks Rabanus and Strabus, a man most learned in every respect, excelling in meter and prose, was among the writers of this age of a most celebrated name. As Meginfridus, monk of Fulda, writes in the Chronicle, he was a man conspicuous in every kind of knowledge and holiness, and of such learning and uprightness that, when Emperor Louis, after the death of Bishop Haymo, wished to ordain him bishop in his place for the church of Halberstadt, he refused to consent, uttering a memorable saying: “Give the bishopric to another who is fit for it; I have held the quiet of the regular life and the study of the Scriptures incomparably preferable to all the riches and honors of the world.” Among the other little works of his talent he wrote the passion of St. Boniface the archbishop, most beautifully in heroic verse, in two books. He was the first, among all whom I have read, who ventured to gloss with a commentary the Rule of our most holy father Benedict. The prologue of that exposition begins thus, after the opening of the Rule itself: “the third, logic, that is, moral; for physics, [unclear], that is, natural; the second, ethics, that is, rational; for physics is derived from what is physis, nature,” etc. He wrote, in addition, several little works on music, geometry, arithmetic, and the other arts of humanity. For he himself was the first, in the monastery of St. Aurelius, as Meginfridus is witness, to begin to have the monks read the divine Scriptures and secular letters, according to the custom of Fulda. He was indeed so learned in every kind of knowledge that not only monks from other monasteries, but also secular persons, flocked eagerly to hear him.

865.

He died full of days and holiness in the twelfth year of Abbot Gerung, which was the year of the Lord 865, in the fourteenth indiction, and was buried in the church of St. Aurelius on the eighth day before the Kalends of November.

Ruthardus, the aforesaid head of the school of the monks.

“O you who duly go along this road, traveler, I ask you, halt your step a little, and read this inscription: remember in supplication the very [unclear] of the buried man; pious [unclear] of Ruthardus, say: ‘Have mercy, O God.’”

[unclear] the aforesaid of Weissenburg, our Ruthardus here of St. Aurelius, wrote many letters; he sharpened his talent by publishing various things; appointed publicly, after Notger, to the school of the monks, he left after him several disciples most learned in every wisdom. Saint Pope Nicholas I [unclear] King Lothar, brother of the emperor, on account of Queen Theutberga, [unclear] brought the case to the hearing of the apostolic see. For the same cause Gunther of Cologne and Theutgaud of Trier, archbishops, were deposed by the same pope, and, all the way to the lay estate, received the worthy reward of their wickedness. For, by false charges artfully fabricated, they presumed to condemn an innocent queen.

866.

These things were done in the thirteenth year of Abbot Gerung, which was the year of the Lord 866. But [unclear] of Emperor Louis II, through fear of the Northmen, from Glanfeuil to the monastery of Fossés in Burgundy [unclear]. When he attempted to return to the worship of paganism, his father, resuming his belt and royal attire, pursued him with [unclear], seized him, and, his eyes having been put out, thrust him into prison. And placing his younger son in the kingdom, he returned to the monastery and remained in the monastic profession until death.

859.

In the sixteenth year of Abbot Gerung, the body of St. Maurus, disciple of the holy father Benedict our abbot, because of fear of the Northmen, was transferred from Glanfeuil to the monastery of Fossés in Burgundy. In these times Hincmarus, archbishop, flourished among the Gauls in great esteem Chronicle of Jo. Trithemius.

bishop of Rheims; from being a monk of Saint-Denis of Paris, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, who wrote many distinguished volumes, of which we have made mention elsewhere.

871. In the eighteenth year of Abbot Gerung, after the deposition of Archbishop Thietgaud, Bertholf, abbot of [Mediolanum?] of our order, became archbishop of Trier, a man keen in intellect, who did not allow the privileges of his church to be violated even in the least; in his time the people of Trier, from fear of the Northmen, hid all the ornaments, holy things, and relics in underground chambers.

882. In the nineteenth year of Abbot Gerung, Saint Edmund, king of the English, martyred by the Northmen, was renowned for countless miracles.

883. In his twenty-first year, which was the year of the Lord 874, in the Italian region, in the city of Brescia, blood rained from heaven for three days, and the Northmen did many evils to the Christians.

In these times Walo flourished, after Christianus, a monk and himself [from a monk?], bishop of Auxerre; brother of Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens, of whom we spoke at length above, in the first year of Abbot Lintbert. This Walo was a man distinguished in learning and conduct. His greatest zeal was to embrace teachers and professors of letters charitably, to use their counsels, to enjoy their conversations, and rather often to refresh them at his own table. In all his conduct he always wished to have certain men of the clergy with him, lest even a slight occasion be given to laymen for [unclear], so that no trace of habitation remained at all.

About these times flourished Eric, a monk of Auxerre, [chaplain?] of Bishop Walo, [unclear] in prose, concerning which we have made mention in the Catalogue of Writers.

876. In the twenty-third year of Abbot Gerung, in the month of June, a sudden and excessive inundation of waters occurred, so that a certain village in Saxony, far removed from torrents and rivers, was in a moment, with men and beasts, with trees and buildings, with church and altar, wholly swallowed up, so that no trace of habitation remained at all.

About these times [unclear]; whence he was accustomed to say, “Let laymen not know what clerics do, and let equals be joined with equals.”

887. In the twenty-fourth year of Abbot Gerung, but the 877th year of the Lord, in the tenth indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, Emperor Louis II died at Frankfurt, and in the monastery of [Lorsch?], then of our order, [unclear] chaplain, a man most learned from every side, who composed many and various little works in meter and prose, concerning which we have made mention in the Catalogue of Writers [unclear], concerning which we have made mention in the Catalogue of Writers.

878. In the twenty-sixth year of Abbot Gerung, which was the 876th year of the Lord, there was a certain Jew named Sedechias, formerly, as report has it, a natural philosopher and physician [unclear]. [Hucbaldus?] wrote to Hatto On Music, a by no means contemptible little work, and certain other things. And Bertram too, a monk, most learned in all literature, wrote to King Charles On Predestination; likewise On the Body and Blood of the Lord, with many other works which have not come to the knowledge of our reading. [unclear] feet, which, placed before them in a basin, with blood flowing, he displayed for all to see; and these he immediately restored to the places from which they seemed to have been cut off, without harm to the man. Passing through the air, he was seen and heard by all; he was thought to perform in the clouds, in the air, hunts, races, and other things which we are accustomed to carry out on the earth. He performed so many and varied tricks that all marveled beyond what can be believed.

King Edmund is martyred. [unclear]. Walo, from monk to bishop. Eric the monk. Emperor Louis dies. Hunibald the monk. Milomarzachus. [Hucbaldus?] the monk. Bertram the monk. A Jewish magician did wondrous things. Bertholf, from abbot to bishop. One village was wholly swallowed up.

Of the Monastery of Hirsau.

882. In the thirtieth year of Abbot Gerung, the Northmen, with an inestimable multitude, burned and destroyed Cologne, Traiectum, Tongres, Bonn, with all the villages and castles adjoining them. They also laid waste with sword and fire the palace of Aachen, the monasteries of our order, Stavelot, [Mundarium?], Prum, Saint-Walaric, and Saint-Riquier, sparing no sex, no age, but killing all whom they could find. After this they set Trier on fire, killed the citizens, and carried off the booty. Advancing to the city of Metz, they joined battle with the citizens and emerged victorious; in that battle Walo, bishop of Metz, fell with many others. But Bertolph, archbishop of Trier, slipped away in flight and escaped; nevertheless he died in the following year.

In the same year the emperor Charles the Bald, setting out from Italy into Gaul, died after being given poison. Pope John VIII anointed Louis, his son, as emperor. The Romans, moved by this, ordered the pope to be held under guard as a captive; they chose Charles, surnamed the Fat, as emperor. Together both held the name of emperor for two years, until Louis, son of Charles the Bald, died after taking poison. And this Charles the Fat alone ruled as emperor for twelve years.

885.

In the year of the Lord 885, in the third indiction, Gerung, the second abbot of Hirsau, died in the thirty-second year of his rule and the seventy-first of his age, on the first day of the month of August. He was buried in the church of Saint Aurelius, beside Lintbert, his predecessor. He was a man in all things devoted to God, no less circumspect in temporal matters than capable in arranging spiritual ones. Reginbodo succeeded him; in his time the Northmen overthrew Worms, as we shall say.

Concerning Reginbodo, the third abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, who presided for six years; concerning the deeds of that time in Germany.

When Gerung, the venerable second abbot of this monastery, had died and been buried, the brothers, whose number was already great, came together in the place appointed for this and elected as abbot an elderly monk named Reginbodo, a quiet, pious, merciful man, who presided over the monastery for six years. He was, as Meginfrid bears witness in the Chronicle, a Bavarian by nation, born of a notable family. When in his youth he had been handed over by his parents to teachers to learn letters, in time he became learned in all knowledge, both human and divine. Then he was made a canon in the church of Constance; there, abounding in many riches, he began also to flow away in spirit. At last, having returned to himself, he began to groan over the vanity of the present life and to consider how brief a man's sojourn in this world is. Finally, after many turnings of fluctuating thoughts, he came to Hirsau, despising all the things which men are accustomed to love in the world, and for the love of God became a monk under the venerable abbot Gerung. Thereafter, turning all his zeal toward piety, always, so far as human weakness permitted, he was intent either on prayer or on reading sacred scripture. [unclear] After Gerung's death he was elected abbot by the unanimous consent of all. In the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 885, in the third indiction, he presided, as we have said, for six years. For, weighed down by old age and unable to endure external occupations, since he had already long since experienced the sweetness of the contemplative life and could not bear to be torn away from it, at last in the sixth year in which [unclear]. A monk and priest, most learned in divine as well as secular letters, he was [unclear]; indeed, by exercising his talent after the example of the ancients he wrote many things, although none of them has come to our knowledge. After the election of Reginbodo as abbot, Concerning the tyrant who disturbed the brothers... A certain tyrant named Edvid began greatly to disturb the monastery and the brothers of Saint Aurelius, saying that there was owed to him a by no means small sum of money, which to Abbot Gerung Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius, 19 had lent. Since he was threatening many injuries, the brothers, who knew the man’s falsehood, began to implore divine aid, and entrusted to Saint Aurelius the defense of the cause of his monastery against the tyrant’s wickedness. And behold, one night, when the day of the plea had been fixed for the morrow by both parties, the holy bishop Aurelius appeared to the tyrant in dreams, saying: “Impious tyrant, what have you to do with me and my brothers, whom you are planning unjustly to despoil of their goods? It will not go unpunished for you.” When these words had been said, the holy man, raising the pastoral staff which he carried in his hand, struck the tyrant in his sleep, saying, “Receive in me the first-fruits of your deserts; you will shortly receive heavier things, unless you quickly take care to make satisfaction to me and to my brothers.” But the tyrant Edwinus, awakened both by fear and by the blow, filled the whole house with so great a cry that all were turned to amazement. On the next day, lying in bed, he called to himself the brothers of Saint Aurelius and, in the presence of his wife and sons, sought pardon for his injuries. He asked them to pray to the Lord for him, promising that he would do great good to the monastery if, through their intercession, he recovered. Not many days later he recovered, and, with many gifts offered, he strove to render Saint Aurelius, the bishop of Christ, favorable to himself.

886.

In the first year of Reginbodo, Bertolphus, archbishop of Trier, a monk of our order, died, as we have already said above; Ratbodo, abbot of the abbey of Mettlach, a learned man and most prudent in affairs, succeeded him in the archbishopric. He acquired many gifts and possessions from the emperors for his church of Trier. He presided in the archbishopric for almost 36 years and did many good things.

887.

In the second year of Abbot Reginbodo, Ansbaldus, the most reverend abbot of Prum, died on the fourth day before the Ides of July, a man of the highest sanctity and religion, who happily passed to the heavenly fatherland. Farabertus, a venerable father, succeeded him in the abbacy on the eighth day before the Ides of August.

In these times Reinibodus, formerly a monk of the monastery of Corvey in Saxony, flourished as archbishop of Bremen, a man most learned in divine Scriptures and secular letters, who for many years presided gloriously by teaching publicly in the school of the monks in the aforesaid monastery. He ruled the church of Bremen for 9 years, and at his death was entered into the catalogue of the saints; his feast is observed on the day before the Nones of February. He was buried in the church of Bremen, shining with many miracles.

Almannus also flourished around these times, a monk of Alt[u]itar[um?], a man most learned on every side, who left many splendid monuments of his talent; of these we have made mention elsewhere.

Adrevaldus, formerly a monk, [unclear] bishop. The archbishop of Bremen, a man learned in knowledge of all things, who himself also displayed the liveliness of his talent by a manifold publication of books, is held famous among the monks in these same times. Remigius also, a monk of Auxerre, later presided over a certain church, as they say, as bishop, a man in divine writings [unclear] left behind. After him Harderadus, a monk, a Frank by nation, received the office of teaching, [unclear] was enrolled; a man excellently learned in the knowledge of secular letters, he illuminated these times by teaching and writing, and in the knowledge of secular [letters] [unclear]; of whose little works we have made mention in the second book of the illustrious men of our order.

889.

In the fourth year of Reginbodo, which was the year of the Lord 889, in the seventh indiction, Richbodo, a monk of this monastery, died. He had presided over the public school at Saint Aurelius after the master Ruthardus for almost 24 years, and left several disciples well instructed in every branch of knowledge. After him Harderadius, a monk, [unclear].

Arnulphus, son of Carloman, ruled in his place for 12 years. But Charles, dying not long afterward, was buried in the monastery of Reichenau on the day before the Ides of June.

In the same year also Lintbertus, archbishop of Mainz, died; Saint Sunderoldus, a monk of Fulda, succeeded him, a man conspicuous for every sanctity and religion, whom the Northmen killed a little later. In these times, after Emperor Charles had died, the Italians divided the kingdom: one part of them chose as king Berengarius, son of Eberhardus, who held the duchy of Friuli; the other chose Guido, son of Lambertus, duke of Spoleto. When battle had been joined between them, Guido came out victorious and expelled Berengarius from the kingdom. Salomon, from being a monk of holy ConThe Monastery of Hirsau

Salomon.

Salomon, bishop of the church of Constance, died in this year. He was succeeded by Salomon of the same name, abbot of Saint Gall, a man distinguished not only by nobility but also by prudence and wisdom, who is known to have been the third bishop of that name of the aforesaid city.

In the same year Arnolphus, bishop of Würzburg in Saxony, was killed quite cruelly during the solemnities of the Mass, after he had presided over the aforesaid church for 37 years and 7 months. Arnaldus or Arnulphus, emperor of the Romans after Charles the Fat, had as wife Lucarda, daughter of Welpho, duke of Bavaria, who bore him two sons and one daughter. The first-born of these, Ludovicus, was afterward emperor. The second-born, named Conradus, was duke of Lotharingia; his son, of the same name, was also afterward made emperor. Moreover the daughter, named Lucarda, who was given in marriage to Otto, duke of the Saxons, bore Henry, afterward the first emperor. But the aforesaid Conradus, duke of Lotharingia, son of Arnulphus, [unclear] count of Bamberg, whom Henry, nephew of the emperor, when made emperor, through the deceit of Hatto, archbishop of Mainz, seized and beheaded, as we shall say below in its proper place.

890.

In the year of the Lord 890, however, Abbot Reginbodo, weighed down by old age, when he felt that through the occupations of household business he was being drawn back from contemplation of inward sweetness, and rejoiced that he could return to the state of his former quiet, voluntarily resigned his abbacy on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, when the sixth year of his promotion had not yet been completed. He returned to the state of private life; and all the brothers, not recognizing in him such penitence and austerity of life, greatly wondered at the fervor of the old man. Indeed, the rigor of monastic life, which he had once undertaken, he did not abandon up to death. He was constant in prayer and compunction of mind, and afflicted himself so greatly with vigils and fasts for love of the heavenly homeland that all his elders pitied the aged man. When he was once asked by the brothers why he afflicted himself so greatly, since he had committed no serious sin in religion, he replied: “Even if, with the grace of God protecting me, from the day on which I became a monk I do not remember having committed any serious sin, as you say, nevertheless in the meantime I have negligently omitted many exercises of good work; and especially from that time when I began to be abbot, [unclear]. Therefore, brothers, it is fitting for us, as long as we live, to do penance, and not to cease from good works up to death.” And that venerable old man Reginbodo persevered firm and constant in his holy way of life up to death.

Concerning Haderadus, the Fourth Venerable Abbot of This Monastery of Hirsau, Who Presided Energetically for Twenty-Eight Years.

After the resignation of Reginbodo, a most holy man, the brothers came together as one and unanimously elected as abbot Haderadus, a venerable monk, who had been in charge of the school of the brothers. He was young in years, namely about thirty years old, but in conduct and prudence older than many old men. He was elected in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 890, in the eighth indiction, on the very same day, namely the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, on which his predecessor resigned, and he presided over the monastery for twenty-eight years. He was a Frank by nation, born of honorable parents, and had entered the monastic order as a young adolescent under Abbot Gerungus; and he had lived so piously and religiously, ready for every obedience, that he was called by all another Placidus, and not undeservedly. For he was of so gentle a mind that no one ever remembered him disturbed by anger. He was truly so studious in the Scriptures that, after the death of his venerable master Richbodo, he was substituted in his place and energetically governed the public school of the monks in this monastery of Saint Aurelius, which at that time was held a great honor. For a monk most learned not only in the divine Scriptures but also in secular letters was required for this office. In those times in the monasteries of our order--there were no others in Europe, Germany, and Gaul--there was this very celebrated custom: that schools of monks were maintained in almost every monastery. Over these were placed not secular men, but monks most renowned in morals and learning, who were regarded as learned not only in the divine Scriptures but also most deeply instructed in Mathematics, Astronomy, [unclear] sciences. Of these many were learned not only in the Roman language, but Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

... but also very expert in Hebrew, Greek, and Arabic, as is easily discerned from their works; although, through the fault of the scribes, who gradually began to degenerate from the teachers' original training, few corrected copies are found in our times.

How great was the ancients' diligence in letters.

Whenever an abbot did not have in his own monastery a monk suited to undertake this office, it was no cause for shame to seek a suitable one from some other monastery. For they considered it the greatest disgrace to neglect the teachable minds of monks; and, so that they might instruct them well in morals and letters, they spared neither labor nor expense. Thus that most learned monk Sigebert of Gembloux was for a long time instructor of the monks in the monastery of St. Vincent at Metz, although he belonged to another monastery. So too Strabo, a monk of Fulda, in Hersfeld; Notger of St. Gall in Stavelot; Albinus, an English monk, in Fulda; Milo of Saint-Amand in Corbie; and many others in other monasteries held the office of teaching for a time where they had not begun their monastic conversion.

This most holy custom first began in England, where that venerable monk and priest Bede, made instructor of monks, left after him many very learned disciples.

How useful the study of letters is for monks.

How greatly this instruction of monks benefited our order no one is ignorant who has studied the histories of the ancients with some care. For many monks, because of their incomparable knowledge of letters, were raised to the honor of the episcopate, and they wonderfully adorned our order by life and learning. For even if the study of letters conferred nothing on the order except a useful occupation for monks, it would nevertheless deserve to be promoted by us with the greatest respect; for unless the mind of a cloistered person is occupied by some agreeable exercise, it slips into many and varied miseries. Understanding this well, the holy fathers wished the reading of the Scriptures to be altogether familiar to monks.

Linthelmus becomes master of the school.

He embraced this holy [unclear], so that within a short time he became most learned in all literature, both secular and divine. After he had been raised to the abbacy, he placed over the monastic school Linthelmus, once his fellow student, a monk most learned in every branch of knowledge, by nation [unclear]; and it happened that many also became bishops.

The emperor against the Northmen.

Around this period in Abbot Haderad's abbacy, the emperor Arnulf, overcoming the army of the Northmen in battle, almost destroyed it; nevertheless, after recovering their strength, they afterwards perpetrated many evils in the empire.

891.

For in the following year, which was the year of the Lord's incarnation 891, the city of Worms [unclear].

Archbishop Sunderold is martyred.

The body of St. Aurelius is hidden beneath the earth.

In the church of St. Aurelius he made a subterranean [chamber], in which he hid the body of that saint, together with a tablet containing an inscription of his name and dignity, so carefully that it could not have been found by any human being. It remained there, altogether unknown, down to the time of Count Adelbert.

For not long afterwards, when the Northmen had been driven from the empire, the Hungarians began to devastate Bavaria, Swabia, and Saxony; and since battle after battle against them followed throughout every province of Germany, the body of the most holy prelate necessarily remained concealed in safety.

Hatto, abbot of Augia, becomes archbishop of Mainz.

The same man was obscure in lineage, distinguished by no nobility, but keen in intellect; regarding him it is difficult to judge whether he was better in counsel or worse. He presided over the church of Mainz for twenty-one years.

892.

In the third year of Abbot Haderad, which was the year of the Lord 892, the Hungarians invaded Carinthia, and, when battle was joined on Holy Saturday, they were defeated and slain.

The Northmen invade Prüm again.

In the same year the Northmen again invaded the monastery of Prüm. The abbot, slipping away in flight with the brothers, barely escaped. After entering the monastery they killed some of the monks, and, slaughtering a great many of the household, led the rest away captive.

The Monastery of Hirsau

In the same year Farabert, abbot of Prum, with the consent of the king of the Franks, voluntarily resigned his abbacy; Regino, a monk of the same monastery, succeeded him, a man most celebrated for his life and learning, who, among other little works of his talent, wrote a Chronicle of past time, addressed to Adelbero, archbishop of Trier, beginning from the origin of the world down to his own times, a work indeed most celebrated and most worthy to be read by learned men.

Around these times there flourished at Mainz, in the monastery of Saint Alban, Rupert, a monk most learned in every respect, skilled in Greek and Latin, who, publicly presiding over the school of monks in the same place, left to posterity many monuments of his talent. His Homilies and Sermons, not without elegance, are extant; he also described in verse the life and passion of Saint Alban. He composed some works on musical proportion. Sebulco also, abbot of Saint-Denis, a noble and powerful man, is held in esteem among the Gauls; even kings feared him because of his admirable wisdom and prudence.

When he was pressing the assault upon a certain castle situated in Aquitaine with too much ardor, he was struck by the blow of a stone and died in the following year. Around these times Liutprandus, deacon of Ticinum, flourished, a man skilled in Greek and Latin and not at all poorly learned in secular letters; among other little works of his talent he published a history of the deeds of the Berengars, which he called by the Greek word Antapodosis, that is, “retribution.” For in writing he repaid Berengar, the tyrant raging in Italy against the empire, because, driven out by him, he had been compelled to go into exile. He began this history of his at Frankfurt, not far from Mainz, and completed it in Greece.

In these times also there flourished in Burgundy Berno, formerly a count, founder and first abbot of the monastery of Gigny, a man venerable for holiness and religion, who also, by the gift and at the expense of his grandmother the countess, built the monastery of Cluny, over which he set as first abbot Saint Odo, once a musician of Tours, a learned and most holy man, who wrote several distinguished little works of his talent, of which I have already made mention in the second book on the illustrious men of our order. Paschasius Ratbertus also, abbot of Corbie, is held to have been famous in these days; he wrote to Abbot Placidus a little book, not to be despised, on the sacrament of the altar; also the life of Saint Adalhard; and also a very beautiful work on the Lamentations of the prophet Jeremiah. Since he was not ignorant of the Greek language [unclear] of Bremen flourished in these times and governed his church energetically for twenty years, a learned and most holy man, whose feast is celebrated on the Ides of May.

In these times, under Abbot Haderad and the scholasticus Luthelm, many studious and most learned monks flourished in this monastery. Of these, one named Sigismund, elected bishop of Halberstadt, presided energetically by word and example over the people entrusted to him for almost thirty years, and lies buried in the same church. Cuntzigo also, a very venerable monk, in the reign of Arnulf was made abbot of the monastery of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch, in the diocese of Worms; yet, scarcely surviving one year, he died and was buried in the same monastery.

There was also among them another monk named Herdericus, a man most learned in all literature, both secular and divine, who wrote many and various works, especially on music, and very beautiful chants in honor of the blessed Mary and of various saints. He also wrote many poems of different kinds; of these I have seen nothing except these two little verses, which Meginfrid attributed to him in the Chronicle, to be said over the blessing of food and drink:

May the right hand of Christ bless the gifts set before us; May the kindly right hand of God bless our drink.

896

In the sixth year of Abbot Haderad, which was the year of the Lord 896, in the fourteenth indiction, a great synod was celebrated at Tribur, at which there were twenty-six bishops with many abbots from Saxony, Bavaria, Swabia, Gaul, Lotharingia, and other provinces. Among the bishops, however, these were the more famous: Hatto, archbishop of Mainz, of our order, formerly abbot of Reichenau; Ratbod, archbishop of Trier, of our order, formerly abbot of [Mediolanum?]; Hermann, archbishop of Cologne; Adalgar, archbishop of Bremen, of our order, formerly a monk of Corbie; Sigismund, bishop of Halberstadt, of our o Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius, 23

[unclear] and most holy: Sigehard, bishop of Hildesheim; Ludhelm, bishop of Toul, of our order, formerly a monk of Saint Maximin at Trier; Rudolph, bishop [unclear]; Salomon, bishop of Constance, of our order, formerly abbot of Saint Gall.

Moreover, among the abbots these were the chief men: Heriger, abbot of Fulda; Harderad, abbot of Hersfeld; Haderad, abbot of Saint Aurelius at Hirsau; Burchard of Saints Marcellinus and Peter at Seligenstadt; Adelbert, abbot of Corvey; Wilhard, abbot of Saint Alban at Mainz; Bertulf, abbot of Saint Ferrucius at Bleidenstadt. In this holy synod the bishops sitting with the abbots of the monasteries enacted many things for ecclesiastical advantage, and especially against certain laymen who were striving to depress and diminish episcopal authority. On these matters, therefore, and on many others, they established decrees, which they strengthened by common subscription, as is the custom.

Haderad was present.

Alfred, king of the English, was held famous in these times; in the thirteenth year [unclear]. Alfred, king of the English.

In the ninth year of Abbot Haderad, Regino, abbot of Prum, as he writes in his chronicle, was deposed. He did not, however, set forth the causes of his deposition, but says thus: In the year of the Lord 899, Richar was appointed abbot of the monastery of Prum; but how it was done toward me I have therefore deferred noting in this place, lest perhaps, provoked by injuries, I should [unclear]. Dividing day and night into three parts, he spent the first eight hours in reading, writing, meditating, and praying, another eight in arranging the affairs of the kingdom, and the remaining eight in care of his body, by a most prudent distribution.

Regino the abbot is deposed.

In the tenth year of Abbot Haderad, which was the nine-hundredth year of the Lord's Nativity, the Hungarians, having heard of the death of Emperor Arnulf, gathered a very great army and invaded the borders of Bavaria; they tore down castles, consumed churches with fire, and killed peoples without distinction of sex, age, or order. And, in order to strike greater fear into all, [unclear]. The empire was thrown into confusion, while the Romans and all the peoples of Italy grieved that it had been transferred into Germany. For this reason German emperors were not thereafter invested by the supreme pontiff until the first Otto. Hence in Italy [unclear] of Berengar usurped the empire.

From these words we can conjecture that he was deposed from the abbacy amid injuries, although the cause [unclear].

In the same year Emperor Arnulf died on the third day before the Kalends of December, and was buried [unclear]. Emperor Arnulf died. His son Louis succeeded. A war with the Hungarians takes place on the [Lyrum?].

In the fourteenth year of Abbot Haderad, Falco, archbishop of Reims, [unclear].

Ambrose. [unclear], a man very learned both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters, wrote a distinguished volume on the Song of Songs, and also on the Psalter and on the Apocalypse of blessed John [unclear]. Nearly a thousand of them are said to have been killed. But the Hungarians, after laying ambushes, at last emerged victorious, and then overran the kingdoms of the Bavarians, Swabians, and Franks, and burned everything while devastating it.

In the fourteenth year of Abbot Harderad, he was most cruelly killed by a certain [unclear] of Baldwin, count of Flanders, on account of the abbey of Saint [unclear], since the count judged that it should by no means be granted to him. The archbishop of Reims [unclear]. The bishop of Wurzburg is expelled.

In the same year, Adelbert, count of Bamberg [Babenberg?], drove Rudolph, bishop of Wurzburg, from his church and devastated the whole diocese.

[unclear] of the emperor, who was the brother of this emperor Louis, as already above [unclear]. Of the emperor, because he was the brother of this emperor Louis, as already above [unclear].
