The Monastery of Hirsau

as we have said, the same Count Adelbert killed [him] in a certain battle in Hasilia, near Fritzlar, on the third day before the Kalends of March. For that same count was an adversary of Emperor Louis, because his father, Duke Conrad, had previously killed his brother.

In the same year, the fifteenth of Abbot Haderad, in the month of July, King Louis held a general assembly of the princes at Tribur, a royal estate not far from Mainz and situated above the Rhine, which, now deserted, keeps no trace of its former honor except the ruined walls of a castle. It is a place between Oppenheim and Mainz, on the right hand for those descending the Rhine, where once this imperial estate had been situated with a castle and a most beautiful monastery; now it has only a few small houses of peasants. Then Louis, moving his army through Franconia, surrounded with a siege and took a certain castle of Count Adelbert, called Tharissa, which is now a monastery of our order in the diocese of Würzburg. Count Adelbert, however, was not in it; but while he was in the castle of Bamberg with his very strong army, [unclear], by the treachery and deception of Hatto, archbishop of Mainz, [unclear], he was beheaded on the fifth day before the Ides of December. Moreover that castle Tharis was changed into a monastery of our order, in which the same Count Adelbert is said to be buried. It is four of our German miles distant from Bamberg by the descent of the Main.

905.

In the same year, the fifteenth of Abbot Haderad, which was the year of the Lord 905, after the death of Pope Benedict IV, Leo, a monk of our order from Brandalo, elected supreme pontiff, the fifth of that name, sat forty days, [unclear] a certain priest named Christopher, a deceitful man, who, led by lust for rule, cast the pope into chains, where not long afterwards he died of grief of mind. And, invading the pontificate, which as he had acquired it wickedly, so after seven months he shamefully lost, and thrust by Sergius into a monastery, unwillingly he was made a monk.

Leo the monk becomes pope.

Sigbertus.

In the nineteenth year of Abbot Haderad, Wymo, a monk of Corvey in Saxony, of our order, a learned and holy man, was elected archbishop of Bremen and presided for eighteen years. Afterwards, for the love of God, he entered Gothia, preached the word of God to those peoples, and after some years died and was buried there, shining with many miracles.

In these same times there flourished in the same monastery of Corvey a very learned man, Sigbertus, a monk, disciple of the aforesaid Wymo, most holy bishop, and companion of his pilgrimage. After Wymo had died among the Goths, Sigbertus returned to the monastery and described his life in a twofold style, that is, in verse and in prose. He also wrote certain other things, of which we have already made mention in the second book of the illustrious men of our order.

910.

In the twentieth year of Abbot Haderad, which was the year 910 of the Lord’s nativity, the East Franks and Saxons waged many wars with the Hungarians, but made little progress.

Incursion of the wanderers.

Adelbero.

In the same year Adelbero, a monk of this monastery of Saint Aurelius of Hirsau, a disciple of Luithelm, was made scholasticus in the monastery of Saint Alban near Mainz, where at that time a great multitude of monks flourished. Because he instructed them so gloriously in every knowledge of the scriptures, both secular and divine, he acquired among all the people round about a great fame for his learning. After a few years Archbishop Hertiger made him abbot of Saint Ferrucius. For he was a man worthy of honor, not only because of the teaching of incomparable knowledge, in which he was distinguished before many others, but also because of his prudence and the complete holiness of his life.

912.

In the twentieth year of Abbot Haderad, Emperor Louis died without children. He had indeed had as wife Lutgard, daughter of Ludolf, duke of the Saxons, sister of Duke Otto, but he received no children from her. In his place Conrad I was elected by the princes, son of Conrad, duke of Lotharingia, and brother of the aforesaid Emperor Louis, whom Count Adelbert of Bamberg, as was said above, killed in battle. This Conrad was the last emperor from the stock of Charlemagne, and he ruled for seven years. Against him many princes rose up, namely Arnulf, duke of Bavaria, whom he compelled to flee to the Hungarians with his wife and children; Burchard, duke of Swabia; Eberhard, count of the Franks; Giselbert, duke of Lotharingia; and Henry, most powerful duke of Saxony and Thuringia, son of Otto Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

25

... emperor after Otto. Yet Conrad quickly drew all these men over to his side, as much by wisdom as by courage.

DCCCCXIII

In the twenty-fourth year of Haderad our abbot, and in the nine hundred and fourteenth year of our Lord Jesus Christ, the second of Conrad’s empire, the Hungarians again devastate all Germany with sword and fire, coming as far as Fulda, Alsace, and Basel.

In these times Betto, a monk of our order, provost of Saint Columba, became bishop of Auxerre, a learned and religious man, who from his boyhood had been excellently instructed in monastic disciplines.

In the twenty-second year of Abbot Haderad the archbishop of Mainz died; Heriger succeeded him.

Betto.

Hatto dies.

[DCCCCXVII?]

In the twenty-seventh year of Abbot Haderad, Saint Ratbod, bishop of Utrecht, passed to the Lord on the third day before the Kalends of December. He was a learned and most holy man, full of the spirit of prophecy, and also wrote many small works in praise of the saints. He rests at Deventer, exalted by miracles.

The monastery of Gembloux is founded.

Ratbod the bishop dies.

Around these times Wipertus flourished, a noble man, rich and powerful in the world, who founded a monastery of our order in the diocese of Liege, named Gembloux. When he had completed its construction, and monks and an abbot had been introduced, he himself laid aside secular dress and, becoming a monk in the same monastery, shone forth as renowned in life and conduct.

In these days also Wiberadis, a consecrated woman, flourished at the monastery of Saint Gall. Enclosed for the love of God, and devoting herself day and night to prayers, fasts, and holy meditations, she deserved to be enlightened by the spirit of prophecy. She foretold to Saint Udalric, then living among the monks at the head of Saint Gall, that he would become bishop in the church of Augsburg; afterward the outcome of the matter proved this true.

[DCCCCXVIII?]

In the year of the Lord 918, in the sixth indiction, Harderadius, the fourth abbot of this monastery, died on the fourth day before the Ides of August, in the twenty-eighth year of his rule. Rudolphus, a monk, succeeded him in the abbacy. He presided over the monastery and the brothers for seven years, as we shall say: a man advanced in age, not very useful for governance.

Concerning Rudolphus, fifth abbot of this monastery, who presided for seven years, with certain deeds of that time in Germany.

After the death of the venerable Abbot Haderad, as we have said, in August, and after he had been honorably buried according to custom, Rudolphus, a certain monk advanced in age, was substituted in his place. He presided over the perfection [unclear] of the brothers for seven years; under his rule regular discipline did not greatly prosper. For he was a pious man, excessively liberal, and I will not say prodigal, who took pleasure in drinking-cups and banquets. Hence he neglected temporal affairs and by no means preserved spiritual ones. Therefore, when after years the brothers wished to depose him, they could not, because of the support of friends, many of whom among secular persons he was said to have gained for himself by gifts and presents.

In the same year in which the venerable Abbot Haderad died, Conrad, the first emperor, died on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, and was buried in the monastery of Fulda beside the altar of the Holy Cross. Before he died, lying on his bed, when he was asked by the princes whom he advised them to elect as his successor, he replied: “I know no one better than Henry, duke of the Saxons, who is an excellent man, prudent and renowned, through whom the empire can easily be restored to its former condition. Elect him with confidence, because he is powerful to defend you and to recover what has been lost.”

Henry, first emperor, dies.

[DCCCCXIX?]

And so Henry, duke of the Saxons, elected to the empire on Conrad’s advice, ruled for eighteen years. He began in the first year of Abbot Rudolphus, namely in the year of the Lord’s nativity 919: a peaceful man, a cultivator of justice, magnificent, and a most vigorous extirpator of the wicked.

In the third year of Abbot Rudolphus, when the brothers themselves wished to depose him from his office because of his disorderly way of life, they could not, because of the force and threats of his friends, whom partly by blood and partly by gift he had made and had as defenders for himself. Therefore, compelled, they bore it patiently, until the Lord God should arrange to dispose the matter otherwise.

28

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

In the same year Adelbero, a monk of this community, who some years before had been appointed scholasticus of the monks at St. Alban's in Mainz, by election of the brethren and promotion by the archbishop of Mainz, became abbot of the monastery of St. Ferrutius, which by another name is called Blidenstadt. In this same year Luithelm, monk and scholasticus at St. Aurelius, died, a man most renowned for life and learning, leaving after him many most learned disciples, many of whom became abbots in different monasteries, and some even bishops.

At about these times a monastery of our order in Saxony, called Ringelheim, was founded by Theodoric, count of that place. This count's daughter Mechthild was taken as wife by Emperor Henry I; she bore him three sons and four daughters: Bruno, who was afterwards archbishop of Cologne; Otto, the first emperor; and Henry, duke of Bavaria. Mechthild, the first daughter, was abbess of our order at Quedlinburg. Gerberga, the second daughter, first married Lothar, king of the Franks; after his death she married again, to Giselbert, duke of Lorraine. The third daughter, named Rixa, married Rudolf, duke of Bavaria. The fourth, named Hadwig, married Hugh, count of Paris, who afterwards became king of the Franks.

922.

In the fourth year of Abbot Rudolf, King Henry expelled from his borders the Hungarians who were ranging through Saxony to exact tribute, their armies having been cut down. In these times, after Luithelm, Dierhard, a monk, presided over the public school of the monks in this monastery, a man most learned in all literature, both divine and secular. He is said to have written some little works, but they have not come to our knowledge.

In these days there also flourished Gilderic, formerly abbot of the monastery of Saint-Germain of our order, bishop of the church of Auxerre, a man very venerable in morals and learning, who by his labors [unclear] many good things for the church entrusted to him. Rutger also, archbishop of the church of Trier after Rabbod, is held to have been distinguished in these times; among the other monuments of his talent he composed a book of decretals, which, producing it publicly in a synod before his suffragans at Trier, he approved.

Around these times Emperor Henry founded [the church of] Meissen, and placed an episcopal see in it. He honored its bishop with great privileges, and gave him many lands, villages, estates, and castles, so that through him he might more easily be able to resist the Hungarians when they raided the land. Meanwhile also, when he had made [peace?] with the Hungarians for nine years, he saw to it that many cities in Saxony were made very strong with walls and ditches, so that if the enemies broke in again, the Christians might defend themselves by the protection of walls.

924.

In the sixth year of Abbot Rudolf, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 924, a certain monk of this community, named Adelhard, died. Once under Abbot Haderad he had been fully instructed in divine and secular writings; but by some occasion or other he fell into such an affliction of the head that after two years he became blind. When the light of sight had been lost, however, the pain of the head also ceased, and apart from blindness the man became very healthy. Thereafter, since, now made blind, he had lost in great part the sweetness of the present life, he made a virtue out of necessity, devoted himself wholly to divine exercises, and strove with all the virtue he could to show himself a faithful worshiper of God. From then on no one ever saw him intent on worldly business, frivolous in conduct, or idle in speech; he was always intent either on prayer or meditation, though more often on contemplation. He is said to have been of such compunction and devotion that whenever anything about the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ was said or read before him, at once dissolved in tears he would cry out with a groan, so that he also stirred others who were present to weeping.

His way of life was so pure and pleasing to God that he deserved to receive the spirit of prophecy. For he often foretold many future things, which the outcome proved true. Indeed, three years before he was to die, he foretold so clearly the [unclear] of the monastery, which followed almost eighty years later, as if he saw it present before his eyes. At his passing, as the monk Meginfrid writes, the sweetest voices of angels singing were heard in the air; lamps were seen at night over his tomb, and certain other signs of sanctity. He died in the aforesaid year, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, in the twenty-third year from when he had lost his sight, but the seventy-eighth of his age, in the first indiction.

925.

In the following year, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 925, Abbot Rudolf also died in the month [unclear].

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

in the month of March; Meginfrid did not record the day, in the seventh year of his rule. The aforesaid monk Adelhard was said to have secretly foretold this to certain of the monks. Abbot Rudolph dies; under him discipline grew slack.

For, as we said before, he was a frivolous man, wholly given to feasts and drinking-bouts, caring little or nothing for regular observance. Hence the monks, especially the younger ones, not yet grounded in the fear of God, having once grown accustomed to these laxities, could never afterwards be recalled to the inner conversion of the spirit.

On Diethmar, sixth abbot of this monastery, who presided for twenty-seven years, and on the various events of that time in Germany.

After the death of Abbot Rudolph, great difficulty arose among the brothers in choosing a successor. Dissension occurs in the election. For some of the elders, who had the discipline of the regular life at heart, desired to have such a shepherd as would wish and be able, by word and example, to revive that former fervor of monastic religion, now almost extinct in this monastery. On the other hand, the greater, though not healthier, part of the brothers, who by the [bad?] example of Abbot Rudolph [unclear].

At last, after many discussions, with the venerable Hildebert, abbot of the monastery of Fulda, interposing his counsel, they unanimously chose Diethmar, a monk of Saint Gall, already known to them before, since, when Linthelm once held the school of Saint Aurelius, he had lived among them for two years. By the counsel of Hildebert, abbot of Fulda. Diethmar becomes abbot.

Choosing him, therefore, as abbot on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, they received him, brought with honor from the monastery of Saint Gall, in the same year in which Rudolph had entered the way of all flesh, namely in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 923, in the thirteenth indiction, in the sixth year of Henry, king of the Romans. He presided for twenty-seven years. Life of Abbot Diethmar.

He was born in Swabia, begotten of his father Arnold and his mother Helwiug, who, indeed, in respect of worldly rank, were marked by no prerogative of nobility, but who made humble lineage bright by the love of Christ. For they offered this son of theirs, while still a little child, in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Gall, to serve almighty God, trusting that by his merit they too could be reconciled to God.

But the boy, once devoted to God by his parents, like another Samuel began to act more zealously in all things that pertained to conduct, and to preserve most diligently what was said by the elders. He was docile in mind and, while still a little boy, flourished with such liveliness of memory that it was regarded as a marvel [unclear].

At that time there was a monk named Hartmond, who after Notger presided for many years over the school of the monks at Saint Gall; we have already made mention of him earlier. [Adelhard?] the scholastic. His talent is commended. Since he had a singular gift for teaching, he took Diethmar, together with others, to be instructed, and in a short time made him more learned than those of his own age.

He was indeed [unclear] in talents; when he had come to [unclear], he became learned in all philosophy, both secular and ecclesiastical, no less distinguished for the integrity of monastic conduct than for learning in letters. In his twenty-eighth year he received the grade of the priesthood. And after seven years, when he was thirty-five years old, [unclear]. Age of Abbot Diethmar.

Not many years later, when Hartmond had died, he succeeded him in the direction of the literary [school]. He was sparing in food, still more sparing in drink; and by most prudent governance he recalled regular discipline in this monastery, almost collapsed, to its former state. The character of his conduct. In every business to be done he conducted himself prudently; almighty God [bestowed?] on him the grace of his blessing in many ways. He was not only learned, but also in the Roman language as [unclear].

He bore the weaknesses of his brothers so prudently and patiently that no one was ever seen so insolent that, through his most prudent long-suffering, he did not make progress toward better things.

927.

In his third year, Heriger, archbishop of Mainz, died on the Kalends of December. In the archbishopric there succeeded him that most reverend Hildebert, abbot of Fulda, a Fran[unclear] by birth. Hildebert, abbot of Fulda, becomes archbishop. 28

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

[unclear], archbishop of Mainz, a man of wondrous holiness and, besides the natural wisdom of his mind, also sufficiently distinguished in knowledge of letters; among the other gifts of graces he is also said to have had the spirit of prophecy. This is Hildebert, a bishop beloved of God, by whose counsel, as we said above, Diethmar was taken from Saint Gall two years earlier as abbot of this monastic dwelling. He presided over the church of Mainz for fourteen years. This venerable prelate anointed Otto the emperor first as king.

928.

In the fourth year of Abbot Diethmar, Emperor Henry, fighting against the Hungarians, Danes, and Bohemians, came away victorious, killing almost twenty thousand of them and leading away nine hundred.

In these days Diethard, abbot of the monastery of Hersfeld, was made bishop of Hildesheim in Saxony, ninth in order; he presided over the aforesaid church for twenty-two years, and in his place Burchard was made abbot.

Around these times Ratherius flourished, from a monk of the monastery of Bobbio bishop of Verona: a man of great simplicity, yet renowned for learning both in secular literature and in ecclesiastical literature. Driven from the bishopric of Pavia into exile by Hugh, king of Italy, which [unclear] he composed in a lowly style. He also wrote many other things useful to readers, of which we have made mention elsewhere. He labored much by writing and preaching against the heresy of the Anthropomorphites, which in his time had begun to sprout again in Italy, saying: that God consists of a body and human limbs.

At the same time Hildewin flourished, from abbot of Bobbio bishop of Verona immediately before Ratherius, and afterward appointed archbishop of Milan by Hugh, king of Italy.

929.

In the fifth year of Abbot Diethmar, Emperor Henry, by entreaties, threats, and immense gifts, extorted from him the lance of wondrous workmanship, sanctified by the nails of Jesus Christ crucified, which is said to have belonged to the first and great emperor Constantine and which Count Samson had given to Rudolph, king of Burgundy. He left it to posterity as an emblem and protection of the empire. In our own times the Nurembergers profess that they possess this, together with the other insignia of Charlemagne, and we have seen it.

In these times also Emperor Henry built that famous convent of nuns under the rule of Saint Benedict in Saxony, which is called Quedlinburg, in honor of blessed Servatius, once bishop of Tongeren, and appointed as first abbess his daughter Mechthild, a virgin renowned for many virtues, namely the sister of Otto the first emperor and of Bruno, archbishop of Cologne.

933.

In the eighth year of Abbot Diethmar, in the city of Genoa a spring of blood flowed forth very abundantly, perhaps portending the imminent ruin of that city, which followed in the same year. For that city, when African unbelievers sailed to it with a large fleet, was captured in the same year, and all the citizens were either slaughtered or led away captive.

In the same year Burchard, abbot of Hersfeld, was made bishop after Diedo in the church of Wurzburg; in the abbacy Megingus succeeded him, a vigorous man and distinguished for honorable morals.

875.

In the tenth year of Abbot Diethmar, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 935, a great synod of bishops and abbots was celebrated at the city of Erfurt in Thuringia.

Many marvels preceded the death of Emperor Henry in this year. The sun, in clear weather, belched forth flames in many places, [unclear] where Henry was afterwards buried. The left hand of a certain man, cut off with iron, was restored whole to him after a year while he slept; and, as a sign of the miracle, there remained at the place of joining a fine line of blood-red color.

In the following year King Henry, after subduing the nations all around, when he had determined to set out for Rome, was seized by illness and abandoned the journey. When he saw that he was about to die, he summoned the princes and all the people, designated his eldest son Otto as emperor, distributed estates with treasures to his other sons, and died on the fourth day before the Nones of July, at about the sixtieth year of his age and the eighteenth of his reign. He was buried at Quedlinburg in the monastery of nuns which he himself had begun and his wife completed. His son Otto the First succeeded him and ruled for thirty-eight years, Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

... lived; in his first year the Hungarians, devastating Francia, Germany, and Gaul as far as the Ocean, and entering Italy by a circuit, finally returned to their own lands with immense booty.

936.

Thus in the second year of Abbot Diethmar, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 936, in the tenth indiction, Otto I was anointed king by the hands of Hildebert, archbishop of Mainz.

For when two bishops, namely those of Trier and Cologne, were contending with one another as to which of them ought by right to perform this office of consecration, by the judgment of the nobles it was assigned to Hildebert, bishop of Mainz.

He went up to the altar, took from it the imperial sword with its belt, turned to the king, who was bending his knees before him, and said: “Receive this sword, by which [unclear] all enemies of Christ, barbarians and bad Christians, handed over to you by divine authority, with all power of the whole empire of the Franks, for the most firm peace of all Christians. Amen.” Then, taking the bracelets and cloak, he clothed him, saying: “By these horns hanging down to the shoulders, be reminded with what zeal for the faith you ought to burn, and that you should persevere constant in defending peace to the end.” Next, taking the sceptre and staff, he said: “By these signs be warned that with fatherly correction you should rebuke those subject to you, and that first to God’s ministers, then also to widows, orphans, and wards, you should always show yourself protector and defender, and mercifully extend to them the hand of mercy.” After this, when the oil of consecration had been poured upon his head, he said: “The Lord has anointed you king over his people, so that the oil of mercy may never fail from your head, whereby here and in the future you may obtain mercy from him, your Creator. Amen.” Last, he placed the royal crown upon his head, saying: “He has crowned you with a crown of justice, by which you are to be reminded that you ought to administer justice to your subjects, so that, fortified by this royal ornament, you may appear revered by your own people and terrible to your enemies, and after the end of this life may be crowned with an everlasting reward with the angels. Amen.” When the bishop’s blessing had been completed, they placed the king on the royal throne with all joy.

937.

In the twelfth year of Abbot Diethmar, the monasteries of St. Gall in Swabia, of Boniface at Fulda, and of the Scots were consumed by fire.

In the same year Duke Eberhard captured Henry, the emperor’s brother, whom his father, after expelling Arnolf, had appointed duke of Bavaria; but when the Bavarians were soon defeated by Otto, his brother was released from prison.

In these times, after St. Odo, Adamarus, abbot of Cluny, flourished, a man distinguished enough for holiness of life and learning in the Scriptures, who at last, deprived of the light of his eyes, [unclear] succeeded, who built the monastery of St. Peter the Apostle outside the walls of Mainz to the north.

940.

In the fifteenth year of Abbot Diethmar, [unclear], formerly abbot of our order, as we said above, archbishop of Mainz, died; Frederick succeeded him. The monastery of our order was founded in the city of Hildesheim, later transferred outside the city onto a mountain, which we call Berg. This foundation Otto I, emperor, began and completed; the first abbot of the monastery was Anno of St. Maximin of Trier, a man very learned in both divine and secular writings, and venerable no less for integrity of morals than for knowledge.

943.

In the eighteenth year of Abbot Diethmar, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 943, Diethard, monk and scholasticus of this place, died; he had presided over the public school of the monks for twenty-two years after Luthelm the monk. He was a man most learned in every knowledge of the Scriptures, and no less notable for [unclear] than for doctrine. He died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, in the first indiction. In the office of teaching there succeeded him Meginrad, a very venerable monk, who in his youth had been a hearer of Luithelm, who was abbot of the monastery of St. Gall, a man very learned in every knowledge; after his death, under the aforesaid monk Diethard, he made great progress in every knowledge, both divine and secular, and left behind him many very learned hearers.

In the same times there flourished in the monastery of St. Gall a man very learned in every knowledge...

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

...of the liberal arts, the monk Helpericus, once a fellow pupil of Diethmar, who, after the death of the monk Adelhart, the scholasticus and his teacher, obtained the office of teaching in the same monastery, and left after him many distinguished disciples trained in every branch of learning. How many small works he wrote we have sufficiently set forth elsewhere, where we treated of writers.

Concerning the wife and sons of Emperor Otto the First

In this same year died Edith, daughter of the king of England, the first wife of Emperor Otto, a holy woman and very devoted to Christ, buried in the aforesaid monastery of Magdeburg. She bore Otto two sons, Liudolf, duke of Saxony, and William, who after Frederick was archbishop of Mainz. After this he took as wife Adelaide, daughter of the duke of Burgundy and a widow, by whom he likewise had two sons, Otto [unclear] Quedlinburg.

In the same year also died Matilda, mother of Otto the First and empress, and she was buried in the aforesaid convent of nuns beside her husband Henry.

In these days Wenceslaus, prince of Bohemia, a holy and most Christian man, was martyred by his brother, while ambition for rule was raging. In vengeance for him Emperor Otto declared war on Boleslaus the fratricide, and there was a long contest between them for fourteen years.

Around these times Arigandus, abbot of the monastery of St Peter in Francia, was held famous for religion and sanctity in the city of Sens; he took care to reform the monastic life in that place splendidly, no less by example than by word. In these days also, after William, Germandus, a monk of St Germanus of Auxerre of our order, became archbishop of Sens, a learned and religious man; after he had governed the church of Sens energetically for some years, he passed to the Lord and was buried in his own monastery of St Germanus, from which he had been taken. After him Hildemannus, a monk of St Denis of Paris of our order, a very learned man, was made archbishop of Sens. In the twenty-first year of Abbot Diethmar, a great famine prevailed in Gaul. The Hungarians fought with the Bavarians and the emperor, and were defeated. In the twenty-third year Emperor Otto conquered the Danes and [unclear] their king Gotfrid. Moreover he established the archbishopric of Magdeburg, and built that city.

951

In the twenty-sixth year of Abbot Diethmar, which was the year 951 of the Lord’s Nativity, Emperor Otto celebrated his wedding with Matilda, his second wife, in the city of Pavia, with the greatest pomp and solemnity; in the previous year he had freed her from the chains of Berengar, after defeating him.

In the following year, which was the last of Abbot Diethmar, the aforesaid tyrant Berengar entered, conquered, and overcame the same man, and drove him from Italy. Finding nowhere that the sole of his foot might rest, he at last at Augsburg submitted himself with his wife in surrender to the emperor; and, sent to the castle of Bamberg and committed to custody, not long afterwards he [unclear]. In this year great earthquakes occurred in various places in Germany and Gaul.

952

In the same year of the Lord’s Nativity 952, in the tenth indiction, on the fourth day before the Nones of May, in the twenty-seventh year of his rule and the seventy-first of his age, [he died and was] buried in the church of St Aurelius: a man in every respect worthy of God, who splendidly reformed, by word and example, the regular observance in this monastery when it had almost collapsed. Nor did he show himself zealous only in the observances of regular discipline, but he also exercised great diligence in preserving and enlarging the possessions of the monastery. For he greatly ennobled this place with books and relics of the saints, and adorned it with many ornaments. A great multitude of monks flourished in this monastery under his rule; some of them were very distinguished for holiness of life, while more were held in very celebrated repute because of their knowledge and learning in the Scriptures. There also remained much zeal among our monks from various [places]. Monks, if any seemed suitable for being instructed for various monastic [unclear], were sent out in order to obtain fuller education. For in all the monasteries of our order, especially in Germany and Gaul, there were scholastici from among the monks, who [taught] the younger also [unclear]

A great multitude of the monastery.

The very great zeal of the monks. A monk had scholastici.

The very great zeal of the monks. A monk had [unclear].

The very great zeal of the monks. A monk [unclear] [Blank page in the source scan.]

...men outstanding in talent, they would instruct in the first rudiments of literary learning, and afterwards send on to higher studies those who had been found capable. But only in the more famous monasteries, which had both a more abundant supply of temporal goods and a larger number of monks, the most learned monks of all were appointed to the office of teaching others; and they were educated not only in sacred but also in secular letters. To them monks were sent from monasteries of lower rank to be instructed in the higher disciplines. Whoever among them had acquired in the order the reputation of greater learning also had more pupils sent to him for the instruction of monks.

Among the monasteries having this custom of studies, the principal at this time were the monastery of Fulda, of Saint Gall, of Reichenau, of Hersfeld, our Hirsau, of Saint Alban at Mainz, of Corvey, of Prum, of Mediolacense, of Saint-Denis at Paris, of Saint Alban at Mainz, of Reims, of Auxerre, of Tours, of Stavelot, and of Wissembourg; of Saint Maximin at Trier, of Reims, of Auxerre, of Tours, of Stavelot, from whose community in each [unclear], in all of which there were many very studious monks, from whom the more excellent was appointed scholasticus. The abbots, moreover, who desired to have monks learned in every branch of knowledge, used to send some of their own to different monasteries to be instructed. Would that such study were maintained today in our monasteries: how many good things would be done, how many countless evils would be prevented. But not all know [unclear].

But let us return to the order of the history. Diethmar, of blessed memory, the abbot of whom we are speaking, knowing the usefulness of knowledge of the Scriptures, resolved with the greatest effort to educate his monks in every doctrine of letters; for this reason he appointed as master to them a very learned [unclear] and was buried. Two once made our order glorious, by merits of life [unclear], as was said above, he set over them as scholasticus; to whose instruction [unclear]. Few notice this in these times; as their knowledge is, so is their manner of life [unclear]. Diethmar, of whom we are speaking, knowing the usefulness of knowledge of the Scriptures, resolved with the greatest effort to educate his monks in every doctrine of letters; for this reason he appointed as master to them a very learned [unclear] and was buried. Two once made our order glorious, by merits of life. He who was able to say the above was filled with admiration. How great Windichinus was in knowledge of the Scriptures, we shall say later.

Concerning Siger, the seventh abbot of this monastery, who presided for almost 30 years, his character, and certain deeds of that time.

When Diethmar, the most reverend abbot of this monastery, had died, as we said before, Siger, a monk, who had held the office of dean, was immediately elected in his place: a man reverend in conduct and life, excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters. He presided over this monastery for almost 30 years in all holiness of religion. He was elected abbot on the same day on which his predecessor had died, namely the fourth nones of March, in the year of the Lord's nativity 912, which was the sixteenth year of the emperor Otto I. This Siger, born at Mainz, when he was twenty-four years old and was powerful in the world with many riches and honors, spurned and despised them all for the love of God and became a monk under Abbot Diethmar, his predecessor. He advanced so far in the holy life of religion, in wisdom, and in knowledge of the Scriptures, that when Diethmar had entered the way of all flesh, he himself, by the unanimous consent of all, was appointed shepherd of the sheep of Christ.

What kind of man he showed himself to his subjects, how zealous for regular discipline, how kind to the good, how severe to the negligent, no one could write better than one who deserved to see him and live with him in the monastery. In all things, indeed, he was solicitous always to present himself to his subjects as a living example of good works and virtues, lest either, preaching good things, he should neglect himself in deed, if he lived otherwise, or, withholding the teaching of the word, he should seem a useless pastor to his subjects and a mute dog unable to bark. Hence whatever he did not teach by example, no one else was able to perform.

853. In the first year of Abbot Siger, Emperor Otto I surrounded the city of Mainz with a siege. In the second year, which was the year of the Lord 954, Wifrid, archbishop of Cologne, died in the twenty-ninth year of his pontificate. Then the bereft clergy and people, by unanimous deliberation, agreed upon the man of God Bruno, brother of the emperor Otto I; and, after the leading men of that church had been sent, they obtained him as bishop. The monuments of his watchful [unclear], with buildings and the adornment of churches, are seen in many forms at Cologne down to the present day.

Bruno, brother of the emperor, becomes archbishop of Cologne.

Life and doctrine illumine our order [unclear].

The study of Abbot Diethmar.

Siger is elected abbot [unclear].

What the life of this Siger was like. [Blank page in the source scan.]

The Monastery of Hirsau

In the same year Frederick, archbishop of Mainz, died. He was succeeded by William, son of Otto the First, the emperor, who writes thus about him in the Chronicle: “In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 954, in the twelfth indiction, lord Frederick of blessed memory, archbishop of the holy church of Mainz, died on the eighth day before the Kalends of November.

“In the same year I, William, unworthy of so great a succession, was elected in his place, with the consent of the clergy and people of that holy see, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, at the place called Arnsteden, and was ordained at Mainz on the ninth day before the Kalends of January.” These are William’s words.

At these times there flourished in Saxony Widukind, monk of St. Vitus at Corvey, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most highly educated in secular writings. As we said above, he wrote to Mechthild, daughter of Otto the First, the emperor, namely the abbess at Quedlinburg, a history of the deeds of Henry the First, of Otto the First, and of the origin of the Saxons, arranged in three little books. He also wrote the Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit and the Passion of Saint Thecla the Virgin in a double style, that is, in prose and in verse, and also many other works, of which elsewhere we have already made mention. For many years he publicly presided over the school of monks in the aforesaid monastery of Corvey, and left after him several most learned disciples, many of whom were taken up into various bishoprics and abbacies. In that little book which he wrote on the studies of the ancients, he admits that, stirred by the reputation of Meginrad the scholastic and of the monks of St. Aurelius, he came to Hirsau and had conversation with them for many days, and that he saw there such study and fervor among the monks for the knowledge of the Scriptures, and found men so learned, that he could not marvel enough; and he extols that same Meginrad the scholastic with particular praises, saying that he was another Jerome and inferior to none of the ancients in learning.

Around these times there flourished Gregory, a priest, son of the king of England, a pilgrim for Christ, and Everard, a monk, both solitaries in the Black Forest beside the cell of St. Meginrad, the martyr of Reichenau. The first of these, Gregory, though he was the son of a king, despising his father, kingdom, fatherland, and all the pomp of the world for love of the heavenly kingdom, and fleeing secretly, remained unknown to men in great holiness in the Lord in the aforesaid place until his death.

The other, Everard, although he was dean of the church of Strasbourg, by divine inspiration despised the world and, when an angel of God revealed the aforesaid place, lived there a most holy life with St. Gregory the pilgrim until death. This most holy Everard was very familiar with and beloved by blessed Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, by whom he was often accustomed to be visited. He was of such merit before God that, living and dead, he shone forth with many miracles, and he foretold his own death to the aforesaid holy bishop Ulrich long beforehand. From these two most holy hermits, that same place in which the monastery of our order now stands, built not much later, has from then until the present day been called “At the Hermits”; to it a great concourse has been accustomed to be made for many years past, although the monks dwelling there in these times are of a most dissolute life.

In these days Saint Ulrich, bishop of Augsburg, also flourished, a man renowned before God, who shone forth, illustrious with many miracles in life and after death. While he was still a young man he was brought up in the monastery of St. Gall and instructed in the necessary Scriptures. At length he was made bishop of Augsburg, and founded a monastery of our order in the same city, in honor of St. Afra the martyr, in which he himself at last became a monk.

He died, moreover, and was buried there, in the year of the Lord 973, which was the twenty-first year of Abbot Siger, in the first indiction, on the fourth day before the Nones of July, in the eighty-third year of his age and the fiftieth of his having assumed the episcopate, under Otto the Second, emperor.

Saint Maiolus also, the fourth abbot of the Cluniac monastery of our order, is held to have been renowned in these same times for learning and holiness. In the sixth year of his conversion, when St. Ademar yielded because of weakness of body and failing of the eyes, he was appointed shepherd of the Lord’s flock and shone forth, illustrious with many virtues. His feast day is kept on the fifth day before the Ides of May.

In the year of Abbot Siger, Otto the Great, emperor, overthrew the Hungarians with great slaughter, with great danger to himself and his men, in the place called Lechfeld, not far from Augsburg; in that battle Duke Conrad fell, with many others. Henry also, duke of Bavaria, the emperor’s brother, died in the same year.

In the following year Hademar, abbot of Fulda, died, who [unclear] his monastery, long before, a fire [unclear].

The Hungarians [unclear].

957.

A fire [unclear].

[Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Johann Trithemius 31: he constructed [unclear] with magnificent workmanship; Hatto, the son of his sister, succeeded him, and afterward became archbishop of Mainz.

In the same year Rupert, archbishop of Trier, died. Henry succeeded him; he built the regular workshops and cloister of Saint Peter around the church, and ordered the rule of the canons to be observed there. This is the greater church of Trier, in which at this time, as also in the other ancient churches, the canons lived in common according to the rule prescribed for them, having one table, one purse, and one common dormitory, just as today we live among ourselves according to the norm set before us.

DCCCCLVIII.

In the sixth year of Abbot Siger, which was the year of the Lord 958 and of the reign of Otto the great emperor, crosses appeared on people’s garments, terrifying many and bringing them back to salutary repentance. The garments of some also appeared as if marked by leprosy and infected with spots.

Around these times also a monastery of our order was founded in Saxony, called Hildesleuen, and many convents of nuns under the rule of our holy father Benedict were built in various regions, especially in Saxony. In this year also Willa, formerly the wife of King Berengar, after he had died under the emperor’s custody at Bamberg, despised the world, entered a monastery, and lived religiously under the habit of holy religion, in the eighth year of Abbot Siger. Envoys of the Turks came to King Otto, asking of him some learned man who might instruct them in the way of truth; for them, at their request, he sent Adalbert, formerly a monk of the monastery of Corvey, a bishop, a learned and holy man, who scarcely escaped from their hands.

DCCCCLXII.

In the tenth year of Abbot Siger, Emperor Otto, invited by the Romans against the insolence of Pope John [XII?], went to Rome; and when the pope, receiving him gladly, was honorably placing him under the Augustan chair, and by a solemn blessing [unclear] him emperor [unclear], with the pontiff promising amendment concerning the accusations brought against him, with glory [unclear]. Willa, formerly the wife of King Berengar, after he had died under the emperor’s custody at Bamberg, despised the world and entered a monastery; [unclear] who might instruct them in the way of truth, for whom, at their request, [he sent?] Adalbert, formerly a monk of the monastery of Corvey, a bishop, a learned and holy man. Likewise [unclear] the father Benedict. It is called Hildesleuen; in various regions, chiefly in Saxony, it was built.

DCCCCCLXII.

Likewise [unclear] the father Benedict. It is called Hildeleuen; Hildesleuen, so called, was founded in various regions of Saxony.

The pope was deposed for crimes of every kind.

A synod is held at Rome in the emperor’s presence.

Pope John is deposed.

The heads of the charges for which John was deposed were these: he celebrated Mass and did not communicate. Likewise [unclear] the father Benedict. Leo, protoscriniarius of the Roman see, a venerable and approved man, was elected pope by the unanimous consent of all, and was led to the Lateran palace, while the Romans praised what had been done [unclear]. When he was despising [unclear], indeed threatening that he would excommunicate the synod, by decree of the emperor and of all the fathers present in the synod he was deposed on the tenth day before the Kalends of December. 34

The Number of Those Who Were in This Synod

Forty-eight in number; all of them, together with the leading Romans and the whole people, with one voice deposing John from the papacy as a monster and slave of the devil, by unanimous vote elected Leo, the eighth of that name, as supreme pontiff, swearing that they would never depart from him, nor thereafter elect a pope without the consent of the emperor and his son.

When these things had been done, the holy emperor, not wishing to burden the Romans with too great an army, and at the same time believing that they would remain steadfast in the promised loyalty, granted many leave to depart. When the deposed John learned this, knowing the instability and greed of the Romans, he secretly sent messengers to them, promising that he would give them all the treasures of the Church if they would butcher the emperor together with the holy pope Leo. The Romans, at once trusting in the small number of the imperial army and encouraged by the promise of money, when the trumpet sounded, hastened and strove against the emperor in order to kill him.

The holy emperor met them on the bridge of the Tiber, which the Romans had blocked with carts. His very brave soldiers, accustomed to war, boldly leapt upon them and, like hawks, terrified the multitude of birds, with no one resisting. Neither hiding-places, nor baskets, nor hollow logs, nor crypts, nor receptacles of filth could protect those who fled. And so the Romans were killed without number, without mercy, without distinction of persons. Not even one of them all would have remained alive, had not the most pious emperor, moved by mercy toward those to whom no mercy was owed, [unclear] his soldiers while they were still killing them. After hostages had been received, the venerable pope Leo, having fallen at the emperor’s feet, begged that the hostages be restored to the Romans and that he be entrusted to their loyalty. Moved by his request, the holy emperor restored the hostages, and, knowing what was to come, entrusted the pope himself to the loyalty of the Romans like a lamb to wolves. When these things had been done, he withdrew from the city.

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

DCCCCLXV.

In the thirteenth year of Abbot Sigert, which was A.D. 965, the aforesaid Bruno, archbishop of Cologne of holy memory, died, and was buried in the monastery of St. Pantaleon, which he had begun the preceding year and, when at the point of death, ordered to be completed. He was buried in the twelfth year of his pontificate. He did many wondrous things in his time, and governed the duchy entrusted to him by the emperor his brother for the peace of the faithful so prudently that he did not on that account neglect the office of bishop, as many do. Wolmar succeeded him in the archbishopric for four years.

Bruno the archbishop dies.

DCCCCLXVII.

In the fifteenth year of Abbot Siger, Otto the Second, at Rome, at the request of Pope John and in the presence of his father, was consecrated emperor. In the following year William, son of the emperor and archbishop of Mainz, died; in his place Hatto, abbot of Fulda, the second of this name, was ordained archbishop. He is said, in a time of famine, to have burned a great multitude of poor beggars together in one barn, as though they themselves were bringing famine upon his region by their begging and idleness, wishing in this to take counsel both for their want and for the common advantage. Hence they say that, before the third year of his archbishopric had yet been completed, the vengeance of divine correction proceeded against him and punished him harshly enough with a wondrous kind of torment, unheard of before by many. For so great a swarm of mice, bursting forth upon him from every side, is said to have rushed upon him in a mass that, wherever he turned, he was oppressed by the deaths of beasts of this kind. If he was in a high place, or in any more elevated place, the mice climbed up the walls; but if he was shut in, they entered through the cracks and, overwhelming him with an infinite multitude, bit him, tore him, and utterly strove to devour him. So great was their importunity that the more forcefully they were driven back, the more violently they attacked; and when he saw that he was nowhere safe on land, the now pitiable pontiff surrounded himself with the protection of waters, and, carried by boat, ascended a tower near the town of Bingen, in the middle of the Rhine, formerly constructed for the defense of the country, hoping that the mice would by no means come to that place through the rushing of the wavy river. But there is no place where divine power is prevented from exercising its vengeance: swimming through the waters in infinite multitude, the mice again climbed the tower by the walls, entered, harassed the pontiff, gnawed him, assailed him, and at last, when he had been overwhelmed by their excessive multitude, miserably killed him. To this tale we neither give authority nor withdraw it, since we read it as described by the ancients down to the present day, and we know that it is told by the inhabitants of the land to their descendants as something received by hearsay from their forefathers. The tower, however, standing in the middle of the river Rhine, retaining its name from the event, is called the Mouse Tower, in which the pontiff Hatto is said to have been consumed by those little beasts.

Otto, son of the emperor, is crowned emperor at Rome.

Hatto, from abbot, becomes archbishop of Mainz.

Hatto burned the poor in a barn.

The unheard-of vengeance for Hatto’s crimes.

The bishop is surrounded by mice in every place.

The bishop is consumed by mice near Bingen in the Rhine.

The Mouse Tower is still so called.

In this same year Meginrad, a monk and most learned scholasticus of this monastery, died in a good old age, a man in whom the discipline of Hirsau had been established with complete perfection in every kind of learning.

Meginrad, monk and scholasticus, died.

DCCCCLXVIII.

He died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, A.D. 968, in the eleventh indiction. Reinhard, a monk, succeeded him in the governance of the monastic school, a man indeed sufficiently learned, but he did not attain the measure of his teacher; nor was he moved by so great a zeal for teaching the monks what he knew that he might be hoped to leave learned disciples after him. Nevertheless, from the instruction of Meginrad the scholasticus there were very many learned monks in the present monastery, of whom one, named Eginard, was made bishop in a certain church of Saxony. Werner was appointed abbot at St. Alban’s in Mainz, and Bernolph at the monastery of St. Michael.

Eginard.

Werner and Bernolph, abbots.

DCCCCLXX.

In the eighteenth year of Abbot Sigert, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 970, Theodoric, bishop of Metz, cousin of Emperor Otto, founded a monastery of our order on an island near the city of the bishopric of Metz, in honor of the holy martyr and Levite Vincent, and richly endowed it with many estates and ornaments.

The monastery of St. Vincent at Metz is built.

At this time the Bulgarians were ruled by two sons of Simeon the monk, Peter and Baianus. Baianus was most learned in the magical art, and through it did many wondrous things. As often and whenever he wished, he changed himself into a wolf, or into the form of any other beast, or so that he was seen by no one at all; and he both could do and did other wondrous things, by which he was accustomed to bring men into great amazement.

Baianus is renowned as most learned in the magical art.

In these times Richard, formerly a monk of St. Germanus of Auxerre and bishop, flourished: a man of excessive simplicity and of less practical capacity than these times seemed to demand, yet very venerable for the merit of his virtue and his zeal for religion.

Richard.

Richard. Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

... a little book On the Calamity and Desolation of the Fatherland, another little book, and certain other things, as Meginfrid reports.

In this year Theodoric, archbishop of Trier, died. Under him the canons of the major church there, having cast aside the regular life which up to this time their predecessors had maintained in the same church, ceased to be regulars and became secular in name and in manner of life. By their evil example the canons also of St. Paulinus at Trier, of St. Castor in Koblenz, those of Mainz and Speyer, and those of very many other churches, at different times indeed but with one spirit of impiety, cast aside the community of the regular life.

In this same year Rupert, archbishop of Mainz, successor of Hatto II, also died. Willigis, a good man and an outstanding worshipper of God, succeeded him. He built the churches of St. Martin the bishop, which is called the major church, and of St. Stephen the protomartyr, in which he was also buried. He also enlarged the monastery of St. Victor outside Mainz, and did many good things for many churches and monasteries.

In these times Robert, king of France, flourished, a just, learned, pious, and religious man, a lover and defender of monks, clerics, and all learned men. Among other little works of his talent he composed that sequence on the Holy Spirit which we sing in our order at Mass on the second and third day of Pentecost, which begins: “Come, Holy Spirit, and send from heaven the ray of your light.” He also published the responsory “Judea and Jerusalem,” and that one concerning St. Peter the apostle, “Cornelius the centurion,” along with many others. He was of such great religion that, enrolled in the catalogue of the saints, he shone with many miracles.

At the same time Æthelwold, a monk of Glastonbury, disciple of St. Dunstan, first abbot of Abingdon and then bishop of Winchester, flourished in England, a learned man and distinguished both in life and in learning. The teacher of this Æthelwold was, as we have said, St. Dunstan, a monk of our order, then abbot of Glastonbury, afterwards bishop of Winchester before him, and finally archbishop of Canterbury, a man of most holy life and distinguished by the radiance of miracles. His feast day is observed on the fourteenth day before the Kalends [of June?], on which he also died, in the thirty-third year of his pontificate, the seventieth of his age, and the year 988 of the Lord’s nativity.

980.

In the twenty-eighth year of Abbot Sigerus, which was the year 980 of the Lord’s nativity, Adalbert died, formerly a monk of the monastery of St. Maximin at Trier of our order, the first archbishop of Magdeburg in Saxony, from the pain of the stone, in the thirteenth year and eighth month of his episcopate, and in the [unclear] indiction, a devout and very learned man.

After his death, Otheric, a monk of Corvey, was elected, a holy man and most learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters. For some time after Windichinus he had charge of the monastic school in the aforesaid monastery. He consented unwillingly to the election made of him, and prayed the Lord not to permit him to become bishop; and this he obtained. For on the journey to the Roman curia for confirmation, he died, not without a reputation for sanctity.

In the thirtieth year of Abbot Sigerus, Emperor Otto II waged a dangerous war in Calabria. In it Henry, bishop of Augsburg, was killed with many other bishops, Duke Otto with many nobles, and Werner, abbot of Fulda, with many others; and the emperor barely escaped by swimming.

In these times Adalbert, formerly a monk of the monastery of Fulda and bishop of Prague in Bohemia, flourished, a learned and holy man and an outstanding propagator of the Catholic faith. After he had undergone many labors for Christ, he was crowned with martyrdom by the Prussians for the Christian faith and enrolled in the catalogue of the saints. His feast day is observed on the ninth day before the Kalends of May. Oswald also, formerly a monk of Fleury, a monastery of our order, archbishop of York, a [learned?] man [unclear].

982.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 982, on the Kalends of September, Sigerus, abbot of this monastery, in the thirtieth year of the rule he had undertaken, [died]. He was buried before the altar of the holy father Aurelius, a devout and religious man; down to St. William no one like him succeeded in the abbacy of Hirsau. Lupoldus is recorded [unclear].

The canons of Trier become seculars from regulars.

Willigis.

Robert, king of France, learned and holy, flourished.

Adalbert.

St. Dunstan.

Otheric, from a monk, archbishop.

Dukes and abbots are slain.

Oswald.

Sigerus, abbot of this monastery, dies in September. 36

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

Abbo, most learned abbot of Fleury and martyr. Aymonius.

There also flourished in these times that most learned abbot of Fleury, named Abbo, a man very renowned for his life and zeal for regular discipline; among other little works of his talent he wrote a booklet, not to be rejected, on the calculation of Victorius. At last, preaching the word of God to the peoples in Gascony, he was reddened with martyrdom and ascended to heaven. Aymonius too, a monk of Fleury under the aforesaid Abbo, at the same times adorned this age by learning and conduct. By command of the same abbot, his Abbo, he wrote a quite handsome work on the growth and beginnings of the Gauls; also a booklet on the miracles of our most holy father Benedict, and certain other things, of which we have made mention elsewhere.

Herigerus.

Herigerus too, abbot of [Bobiensis?], whom Berno, abbot of Reichenau, mentions in his book on the Advent of the Lord, flourished in the same times. He wrote many things, an account of which we have recorded in the second book of the illustrious men of our order. He was indeed a man most learned in every respect, and very famous both by reason of his way of life and of his doctrine.

About these times Saint Wolfgang also flourished. Saint Wolfgang.

About these times Saint Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg in Bavaria, flourished, a man of great holiness and performer of many [unclear]. He was [unclear] to have been a monk of Trier of our order. This man [unclear] Saint Ulrich of Augsburg [unclear] little works, a fuller memorial of which we have made in the aforesaid booklet of illustrious men.

972. Roswitha, nun, most learned.

There also flourished at this time Roswitha of the monastery of Gandersheim, of our order, in Saxony, a consecrated virgin, very devoted to and learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters either, practiced in verse and prose. She wrote many works not unpleasing; [unclear] a little work to ecclesiastical burial.

In the twentieth year of Abbot Siger, which was the year of the Lord 972, Volimarus, archbishop of Cologne, died. He was succeeded by Gero, son of Count Christian and of Wiburga, sister of the count of Magdeburg. This Archbishop Gero, with his brother Count Diethmar, founded a monastery of our order in Saxony which is called the monks’ new castle, which we commonly call Munchennuenburg by its customary name.

About these times Hermann, duke of Saxony, built the monastery of Luneburg in Saxony in honor of Saint Michael the Archangel. In it he placed monks of our order, and set over them as first abbot a monk taken from the monastery of Saint Pantaleon in Cologne, named Luderic, a man venerable in character and learning.

973. The first Emperor Otto died. Otto the second.

In the twenty-second year of Siger, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 974, in the second indiction, Otto the first emperor died, in the thirty-eighth year of his reign and the thirteenth of his empire. His body, with great funeral rites of those mourning, was buried in the church of Magdeburg, which he himself had built. When the first emperor Otto had died, as we said before, his son Otto, the second of this name, succeeded him and ruled as emperor for almost ten years after his father. While his father was still living he had married Theophanu, daughter of John, emperor of the Greeks; by her he begot a son Otto, who after his father ruled as the third emperor. He also begot three daughters: Sophia, who was abbess of our order in Gandersheim; Adelaide, who was also abbess of our order in Quedlinburg; and Jutta, whom Ulrich, duke of Bohemia, took as wife, violently carrying her off from a certain convent of nuns in Regensburg.

In these times too Gero, archbishop of Cologne, founded a distinguished monastery of our order in his diocese, which is named Gladbach, only one mile distant from the town of Neuss, and he enriched it with many estates and ornaments. The first abbot of the same monastery was Sanderadus, a man of most holy life and of regular discipline; after death he was inserted into the catalogue of the saints, and his feast day is kept on the ninth day before the Kalends of September.

About these times also the monastery of Saint Martin in Cologne, of our order, was founded. Its first abbot was Mymborinus, a Scot by nation, a man much venerable for religion and holiness. Hence Scots inhabited that monastery for many years, on account of their incomparable holiness of life, until at last, growing lukewarm from their former fervor and relaxed into every dissolution, they were expelled from that one, as also from certain other monasteries of Germany.

977. Werenbold, monk of Hirsau.

In the twenty-third year of Abbot Siger, Werenbold, a monk of this monastery, died on the fourth day before the Ides of November. Since he was a studious and learned man, he wrote a beautiful little book on the praise of the martyrs;

The monastery of Gladbach is founded at this time. Saint Sanderadus, abbot in Gladbach. The monastery of Saint Martin in Cologne is founded. The monastery of Gladbach is founded at this time. Sanderadus, abbot in Gladbach. The monastery of Saint Martin in Cologne founded. The monastery of Gladbach I found, and I make Sanderadus abbot. 38

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

Concerning Lupold, the eighth abbot of this monastery, who presided for only 4 years; concerning his character and the deeds of his time.

After the most reverend Abbot Siger had been buried, as we have set forth above, the brethren came together as one, to provide themselves with a shepherd according to the rule of our most holy father Benedict. After the casting of votes, as is customary, they unanimously elected as abbot one Lupold, a monk from among themselves, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord 982, in the tenth indiction, in the eighth year of Emperor Otto II: a very old and venerable man, who presided over this monastery for only 4 years and 3 months. This Lupold was Bavarian by race, Regensburg by nation, born of parents of middling rank but nevertheless honorable. He entered the monastic order under Diethmat, abbot of this monastery, while still young, in which he lived more than 40 years most religiously and without complaint, walking before his own face in peace and tranquility of spirit, troublesome to no one, burdensome to no one. For he was a man of very great simplicity, and perhaps quieter than the morals of his subjects and these times required; he was an example of monastic life, not a preacher, since his own holy life commended him, and no impiety of others stirred him.

In these times, after Gero, archbishop of Cologne, Warinus was bishop of the church for 9 years. He renewed the monastery of St. Martin in Cologne, of our order, concerning which we spoke above, magnificently endowed it, and handed it over to the Scots to possess forever, under the rule of our most holy father Benedict.

Around these times Erhard, monk of Luneberg in Saxony, flourished, very devoted to the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters. He left many little works of his talent for posterity to read; for among them he wrote, from choice reading, commentaries on Genesis, on Exodus, on Leviticus, and on most other books of the Bible.

Alger also, a monk of Corbie in Saxony, and for many years a scholastic, before his conversion of seculars and after his conversion of monks, a man most learned both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters, flourished in the same times. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote on the Sacrament of the altar and on free will, little works not to be despised. Arnulph also, or in our German manner Arnold, a monk of this [unclear] although the remaining little works of his talent are [unclear], nevertheless we do not doubt that he wrote more and other things. For the talent of so great a man could not have been summoned to writing by the publication of one little work only, or have ceased.

In these days there also flourished holy monks of our order, namely Benedict, Nathanael, John, Isaac, and Christian, disciples of blessed Adelbert, bishop and martyr of Prague, concerning whom it was said above. After they had, with the Lord’s help, accomplished by their preaching the conversion of many people in Hungary, Prussia, and Poland, at last in Poland they were crowned with martyrdom for the name of Christ, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May.

At about these times there also flourished Libatius, monk of the monastery of St. Alban the martyr near Mainz, a man most holy in character and way of life. Pope Benedict VII ordained him and sent him into Russia to preach the Gospel to the nations, where by word and example he acquired for Christ an innumerable people.

Orthwin also, the tenth bishop of Hildesheim, from a monk of the monastery of Magdeburg of our order in Saxony, learned and fervent with zeal for religion, is held to have been distinguished in these times; and he presided over the church of Hildesheim for almost 29 years.

Odo also, abbot of Corbie, made bishop of Beauvais in France, was distinguished around these times. Both for his learning in the Scriptures and for the integrity of his way of life, he was held in great reverence among all, and more than once fulfilled apostolic and royal embassies in his greatest affairs.

In these days there also flourished Bruno, from a monk of the monastery of Corbie in Saxony made bishop of Verden, brother of Duke Hermann, a man worthy of a prelate, since he is said to have been nobly instructed both in monastic institutes and in ecclesiastical disciplines.

Gebhard also, bishop of Augsburg, formerly abbot of the monastery of our order called Ellwangen, situated in the same diocese, flourished in these times; by his character and learning he adorned both horns of the altar.

983.

In the first year of Abbot Ludolph, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 983, in the eleventh indiction, Egbert, archbishop of Trier, instituted a bannitum fast in the third week after the feast Chronicle of Trithemius.

to celebrate the feast of Easter, because of the excessive drought, which grievously afflicted the whole region.

982.

In the following year, which was the second of Abbot Lupold, Otto died at Rome on the sixth day before the Ides of December, and was honorably buried in the church of St. Peter, prince of the apostles. His son, Otto of the same name, succeeded him and reigned for almost eighteen years. He had as wife Maria, daughter of the king of Aragon, who was barren, whence he received no offspring.

985.

In the third year of Abbot Lupold, Warinus, archbishop of Cologne, died; Everger succeeded him. In these times Lubentius, archbishop of Bremen in Saxony, formerly a monk of Hersfeld, flourished, a man zealous in the holy Scriptures, who vigorously governed the people committed to him for twenty-five years.

Osdacus also, formerly a monk of the monastery of Reichenau, afterward made bishop of Hildesheim after Othwin, is held to have been distinguished about these times, and he vigorously ruled the church divinely committed to him by word and example for twenty-nine years.

In these times also there flourished in England Osbern, a monk of the monastery of [unclear] of our order, a man very renowned both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters; indeed there exists a notable work in which, beginning from the origin of that city, he describes the deeds of the bishops of [unclear], inserting the life or passions of several saints.

He also composed, on music, various chants with sweet melody, and also another monk of our order, of the monastery of [unclear].

In these same times also at Mainz, in the monastery of St. Alban the Martyr of our order, Theoderic the monk flourished, very learned in divine Scriptures and in secular letters. He wrote the successions and deeds of the bishops of Mainz. He also commented on the Song of Songs; likewise he composed very fine commentaries on the Gospel of John. But he left to posterity many other splendid monuments of his talent, the titles of which do not now occur to memory.

In the same year also Willigis, archbishop of Mainz, anointed [unclear] the third as king, and after three years he was consecrated emperor at Rome by Pope Gregory V. Overcoming Lothar, king of the Franks, who was attacking Lotharingia, near Verdun, he put him to flight, and compelled him to restore all the abbeys. About these times there also flourished Bruno, a monk of the monastery of St. Vitus of Gladbach, of our order, in the diocese of Cologne, a very studious man and excellently learned both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters. He is said indeed to have written many works, but few of them have come to our knowledge; of these we have made mention elsewhere.

In these times also there flourished in this monastery of Hirsau a noble man, studious and excellently learned in every variety of writings, a priest and monk named Adelbert. On account of the merit and eminence of his life, his learning, and the philosophy of his reputation, he was taken up as abbot of the monastery of Klingenmünster. Would that he had been placed over this monastery; perhaps the condition of the monastery of Hirsau would never have fallen into such desolation and ruin, of whose misery we shall speak after a little. He governed the aforesaid monastery [unclear], taking care to show [unclear] in all things. In all Germany his name was famous, and princes and bishops of churches depended much upon his counsel.

Concerning Hartfrid, the ninth abbot of this monastery, who presided for only two years, and concerning certain deeds of that time.

In the year of the Lord 986, in the fourteenth indiction, Lupold the abbot, after completing the fourth year and three months of the rule he had undertaken, died on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, and was buried in the church of the monastery of St. Aurelius. He was, as regards his own person, an excellent man, to whom nothing was sweeter than monastic quiet, silence, and contemplation. Yet he was somewhat more indulgent concerning the sins of others and readier for mercy.

Therefore, after Abbot Lupold had died and had been given ecclesiastical burial according to the custom of Christians, the monks of this monastery, deprived of a shepherd, after long discussions held among themselves, at last chose for themselves as abbot Hartfrid, a monk, young indeed in years, 40

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

but such in prudence and morals that no small hope of an excellent shepherd was held concerning him. He was therefore elected in the year of the Lord’s nativity 986, on the same day on which Lupold died, the eighth day before the Kalends of December, and he presided scarcely two years. He was a Swabian by nation, about thirty-six years of age, very finely adorned with monastic morals, by no means poorly learned in all erudition of the Scriptures, handsome in face, and proportionately raised up in manly stature, keen in intellect and eloquent in speech, and such a man as seemed easily able to persuade his hearers of whatever he wished. And indeed, unless untimely death had snatched him from the midst before his time, with the Lord’s help he could have preserved this place from the extreme dangers and evils in which not many years later it was entangled; this one could very readily foretell from the beginning of his rule. For as soon as he was raised up and became abbot, he took care with all his strength that all the monks in the monastery should live according to the purity of the Rule of our most holy father Benedict; and if he found anyone behaving otherwise, he did not tolerate him, but, after he had been admonished once and again and had not amended, he was accustomed to punish him rather severely before everyone according to the norm of the order. And lest anyone could accuse him as he corrected others, he strove to show himself in all things irreproachable, a follower of good works and a living example of virtues to his subjects.

987.

In his first year, Emperor Otto III entered Bohemia with a strong army and compelled its duke, together with the whole people, to surrender. In these times Adelbertus was renowned.

[unclear] of Worms, a very learned man, afterward bishop, learned in the divine Scriptures and very erudite in secular letters, while he was still a monk in the aforesaid monastery of Bobbio, held the public school of the monks and left behind him many very learned pupils. He also transmitted to posterity many lucubrations of his talent.

Engelbertus also flourished in these times, a monk of St. Eucharius at Trier, which today is called by the name of St. Matthias the Apostle, a Mosellan by homeland, a man trained in every respect, very learned in meter and prose. Among the other little works of his distinguished talent he wrote, in verse, the life and passions of the twelve Apostles; he composed certain treatises on music and on the composition of the monochord, and many other things that have not come into our hands. Later he was elected abbot of a monastery whose name I have not been able to find; after some years he rested in the Lord on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, as is clear in his epitaph set below:

In this tomb reclines the abbot ever memorable, Engelbertus, rejoicing, dwells in the stars as a spirit; He died in the month of March, on the twice-sixth Kalends. He built the church which holds his tomb.

In the second year of Abbot Hardfrid, a very great pestilence, famine, and mortality grew exceedingly strong throughout all Germany, and there was such dryness that almost every kind of grain sown in the earth perished because of excessive drought, since it did not have the moisture by which it could have grown. Meanwhile [unclear] attacked [unclear] faithfully, and, as it appears to us, was the occasion of its entire destruction, which followed a little later. For in a short time, namely four months, sixty monks of this monastery were consumed by so lamentable a calamity; all of them died in this mortality of pestilence. Finally, when so many brothers had died and the end of the danger was thought to be at hand, the shepherd followed the sheep.

988.

For in the same year, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 988, Hardfrid, the ninth abbot of this monastery, died on the third day before the Nones of December, in the thirty-eighth year of his age and the second year after he had assumed rule. After his death there immediately arose, alas, the inextinguishable seedbed of the imminent destruction of this monastery. After the deaths, twelve monks remained surviving in it, in whom rested the chief authority for appointing an abbot in place of the deceased. Would that they had consulted their own affairs more prudently, and had not, through contentions and schisms, handed over a place consecrated to God into the hands of outsiders. The highest virtue of monks is humility, and their greatest vice is pride; for while one strives to surpass another through the lust of ruling, a monastery of the servants of God is changed into a pit of demons. Such an evil befell this monastery in these times after the death of the aforesaid man, since the dissension of the brothers who disagreed in the election utterly destroyed it, so to speak. Whence came this evil to this so celebrated place, Lord God, in which so many most holy men, burning before [unclear] for your name, pleased you? Behold, the better men and those who had zeal for regular discipline have been removed from the midst; and Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

..., and useless, proud, haughty, and carnal monks remained, to destroy by their [unclear] a most celebrated place consecrated to your name. Why, Lord God, who judge justly, did you will this to happen in this way? Surely you did not will the impious to prevail and consume the just? Far be it. We see your judgments, Lord; we do not know their causes, nor does it belong to us to examine the causes of your judgments, which we may without sin not know. Rather, to your most holy name we give such thanks as we can, you who allowed that monastery to fall for causes [unclear], so that it might rise again at once into a better state and condition. For if we wish to compare the monastery of Hirsau which we see today, with its persons, goods, substance, and buildings, with the old one whose miserable collapse we lament, we shall find no comparison of the past with the present. For present-day Hirsau surpasses and exceeds that old monastery with all its conditions as much as it seems later in time. But, pursuing the history in due order, let us faithfully and briefly set forth the deed as it has been transmitted to us by the testimony of old writings.
