For even if it may contribute little to the edification of readers, nevertheless knowledge of it will be a not useless warning to all who pass their life in cloistered conversation under a similar lot, by which they may learn that in elections of abbots they should seek not themselves, not their own advantage, but the honor of God alone.

Concerning Conrad, the tenth abbot of this monastery, who presided for about twelve years, and concerning the very bad dissension which occurred in the election.

When, indeed, the venerable abbot Hardfrid had died, with sixty monks, as we have said, twelve survivors remained from the convent. After almost three months they came together bodily in one place to elect an abbot; yet in mind, as will soon appear, they were far separated from one another. For by choosing two men in dissension, Conrad, who received the gift of confirmation from the bishop, and the fugitive Eberhard, who despoiled the monastery, they, alas, furnished the seedbed and material for the destruction of this place to the impious. One party indeed adhered to Conrad as legitimately and canonically elected; the other proclaimed that Eberhard was the true and legitimate pastor according to the first sanctions. Nevertheless Conrad prevailed by right and, as elected by the sounder part of the brethren, received ordination from the pontiff. Meanwhile Conrad was concerned about the gift of blessing; Eberhard, after carrying off all the treasures, chalices, ornaments, and whatever he could steal, hastened with two monks of his party to the count, who was otherwise already gravely hostile to the monastery, to seek aid. The count received him not only willingly but even very gratefully, rejoicing, as afterwards clearly appeared, that an opportunity had been given him by which at last he might satisfy the mind that had long gaped after the monastery’s goods. Immediately the robber savagely invaded the possessions of the monastery, long before offered by Christ’s faithful to God and Saint Aurelius; he tore them away and granted them for distribution as pay to his soldiers, as if in repayment for service rendered. He invaded villages, courts, fields, houses, and whatever he had learned belonged to the monastery’s right; and, under the pretext of the just defense of Eberhard, the abbot, as he himself said, he gradually confiscated the monastery’s property for his own uses. Whom could the monks invoke as protector, having no defender in all these matters, when all either feared the count’s power or were led by greed for the monastery’s spoils? Moreover Eberhard, given over to a reprobate mind and alienated in mind, incited the soldiers to plunder, saying that he was abbot and that it was lawful for him to permit the goods of his monastery to whomever he wished. Meanwhile Abbot Conrad and the monks consenting to his party were oppressed by insults and injuries; they hastened to the bishop, asking aid against the attacks of tyrants. But it is agreed that nothing was done at that time for the restoration of what had been taken away; rather, the violence grew greater day by day, since the count now publicly declared that it was lawful for him to reclaim what had been offered by his ancestors. Every occasion seemed blessed to him by which he might satisfy the avarice into which he had gravely fallen from the spoils of the monks. And so Conrad, now a poor and miserable abbot, with a few monks, and not all of them faithful, remained in the monastery, struck by the greatest fear and dread, scarcely having the means to feed and clothe himself and his own.

989.

He was elected in the year of the Lord’s nativity 989, in the second indiction, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, and he presided over the monastery in many tribulations and miseries for almost twelve years. He was by nation a Frank, born of humble stock, and for that reason less fit to resist such great evils and so many tyrants. He was a good and simple man, born more for handling the mysteries of religion than for governing a monastery prudently and usefully amid such great disturbances. Moreover that most wicked apostate Eberhard, when he was threatening that he would soon invade the monastery with a strong hand and cast Abbot Conrad into prison, was overtaken by death.

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius, 43

The bones of Charles the Great, once emperor, until then unknown to many, were sought and found at Aachen by Otto III, emperor.

In the same year Evergerus, archbishop of Cologne, died; Saint Heribert happily succeeded him in the archbishopric. He built, opposite the city of Cologne beside the river Rhine, where a castle had been destroyed, a monastery of our order in honor of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, which we call Deutz; in it he established an abbot and monks according to the rule of Saint Benedict, and enriched it with many estates and ornaments.

In the same year the emperor, with many cardinals, bishops, abbots, and princes, [unclear] was about to visit Poland with a strong army, among other affairs of the kingdom, the tomb of Saint Adalbert, bishop of Prague, lately martyred for the faith of Christ, as we said above. At that time it shone forth in Poland with innumerable and astounding miracles. He obtained one arm of the same martyr from Boleslaus, duke of Poland, and, receiving it with great devotion, placed it at Rome in the church of Saint Bartholomew. The same emperor also, in honor of the most holy martyr Adalbert, with the consent of the supreme pontiff Sylvester II, appointed his brother Gaudentius, a monk of our order, as first archbishop of the church of Prague, where his brother had been bishop. Since he was a learned and most holy man, by his preaching he converted many peoples round about to the faith of Christ.

In these times Ansfridus flourished, formerly a count, then a monk of our order, and from monk the eighteenth bishop of Utrecht. Others say that from bishop he was made a monk in the monastery of Saint Mary of our order, which he himself built. And this agrees more with the truth and with the chronicle of the people of Utrecht, which says that in the year of the Lord 1005, as a son chastened by God, he lost the light of his eyes and received the habit of sacred religion in the aforesaid monastery, now called Saint Paul’s, of which he was the founder, and persevered in holy purpose with much devotion and sanctity. He presided over the church of Utrecht for [unclear] years, and in his time did many good things for monasteries and churches.

After him Adelboldus, a monk, as some report, of Bobbio, of our order, ruled the church for eighteen years, a most learned and prudent man, who for some time was chancellor and counsellor of Emperor Henry II, of whom we shall speak in his own time. Exercising the dexterity of his talent, he wrote many distinguished little works. For he arranged the deeds of his lord Emperor Henry II in one volume; he was the first and only one after Charles the Great among the emperors to deserve to be enrolled in the catalogue of the saints. He also wrote various little works, both in verse and in prose, on the praises of the Holy Cross, of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, and of various other saints. He also waged many wars for ecclesiastical liberty against Theodoric, count of Holland.

Around these times a certain monk, returning from Jerusalem, was lodged for some time with a certain hermit in Sicily near Mount Etna, which was vomiting flames. When he had heard from him that in that same mountain, Vulcan, the souls of the dead were being tormented by flames, and that many of them were freed every day through the prayers of the faithful, and especially of the Cluniacs, he made it known to the abbot; by whose ordinance the commemoration of faithful souls was established in the aforesaid monastery on the day after the feast of All Saints, and [unclear], about which we have made mention elsewhere.

Remigius, abbot of Mettlach of our order in the diocese of Trier, also flourished in these same times, a man most zealous in the divine scriptures and eminently learned in secular letters. He maintained a public school of monks in his monastery, in which he instructed not only his own subjects but also monks sent to him from various other monasteries.

Theodorus, monk of Saint Matthias the Apostle, also flourished in these times: Theodorus, a monk of Saint Matthias of Trier, a contemporary and fellow-pupil of the above-mentioned monk Theodoric, a man distinguished in morals and learning. He presided gloriously for many years over the public school in the same monastery, and by writing various works took care to make his talent known to posterity. Of these there survives a collection of readings on the Apocalypse of John, not to be rejected. He composed various works on music and astronomy. After many labors in holy religion he happily departed to the Lord to receive his reward; his disciples placed this epitaph for him: Of the Monastery of Hirsau died. But the monks who had gone out from the monastery with him, once they had become fugitives, remained so, and did not return again to the monastery. And indeed Everard received this end, worthy of his malice, he who was the author and occasion of the destruction of this monastery. When he was dead, Conrad the abbot and the monks who had remained were able to live in the monastery with greater peace and security, since he who had been the chief of all the evil had been removed from their midst. But of the things which had been carried off from his monastery, whether by the apostate or by the count and the other ministers of those men, absolutely nothing was restored; rather, as far as could be done, more things were continually alienated and came into the hands of laymen. In this misery and affliction Conrad the abbot, with his brothers, now reduced to a small number, grew old as long as he lived; after his death, twelve years later, as we shall say, the monks were expelled and laymen were introduced by the count.

In the same year in which Conrad was elected abbot, they say that grains of wheat and little fish rained from heaven in Gaul; yet these were of no use for human consumption, because within they were quite plainly too corrupt and foul. In that year also St. Dunstan, archbishop, whom we mentioned far above, migrated to the Lord on the 14th kalends of June.

In this same year, when Pope John XVI died, Bruno, a German by nation, a kinsman of the emperor Otto, became pope, and was called Gregory V. He crowned Otto to the Roman Empire. In the second year of Conrad the abbot, Theophanu, mother of the emperor, died, and was buried in the basilica of St. Pantaleon at Cologne, in the southern apse, which while she lived she honored with the highest reverence and munificently endowed with her own goods. She also, among other things, brought from Italy to the aforesaid monastery of St. Pantaleon the body of St. Alban the martyr, who had once suffered for Christ in Britain.

DCCCCXCIIII.

In the fourth year of Conrad the abbot, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 994, the monastery of St. Michael the Archangel at Hildesheim, of our order, began to be founded by St. Bernward, bishop of the same city, who was also buried in the same monastery and shone forth with countless miracles.

DCCCCXCV.

In the following year St. Adalbert, formerly a monk of our order and bishop of Prague, about whom we spoke above, who converted the Hungarians to the faith, completed his martyrdom among the pagans in Prussia, pierced through seven times and at last beheaded, on the 9th kalends of May. Pope Gregory V, having gathered a synod, decreed, with the Romans and all the clergy consenting, that the Roman Empire ought to remain among the Germans for all future times, so that the princes of Germany appointed by Otto III should have the right and power of electing the emperor. This constitution has now been observed down to our time, through five hundred and six years, with inviolable stability.

In these times flourished Gerbert, a monk of our order from the monastery of Fleury, a man in mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, arithmetic, and almost all the other [unclear]; Emperor Otto too is said to have been by no means among the last. Because of his incomparable knowledge, he was first appointed archbishop of Reims in Gaul by Hugh, king of France, and then driven out; by Emperor Otto he was appointed archbishop of Ravenna; and finally he became supreme pontiff in the city of Rome and was called Sylvester II. He wrote a fine work on the sphere. Also on the construction of the astrolabe and the quadrant. In arithmetic too he made fine compositions. Many greatly commend the dialogue which he had with Leo the abbot, the apostolic nuncio. We have seen several letters which he wrote to the more inquisitive of his disciples. This is Pope Sylvester, who is accused by very many of having entered into a pact and treaty with demons; on this matter we neither wish nor ought to give judgment. He sat in the supreme pontificate for four years.

In these times also, after the death of St. Maiolus, abbot of Cluny, of our order, St. Odilo, a man of outstanding holiness, was made abbot at Cluny. He presided over the same monastery with the greatest fervor of religion for nearly fifty-six years. Since he was a learned man, he is said to have written some little works, and especially sermons to the brothers, in which he showed the dexterity of his talent.

In the third year of Conrad, which was the thousandth year of the Lord’s nativity, the bones of Emperor Charles M[unclear].

Great earthquakes occurred in Europe.

Maiolus and Odilo, abbots of Cluny.

Writings of Gerbert himself, a most learned man.

Constitution concerning the empire of the Germans.

The monastery of St. Michael in Hildesheim was founded.

The empress Theophanu dies.

Nothing is restored of the things carried off.

Wheat and a little fish rained from heaven in Gaul. The Monastery of Hirsau

Here rest the limbs of Theodore the monk, who is buried here: vigorous in piety, renowned for simplicity, a priest by office, fulfilling it in due order; [unclear] in the praises of the highest Lord; prudent and learned, second to none in piety. All that he learned, he soon handed on to others, so that the just and pious Lord might increase a hundredfold the talent entrusted to him, by well praising it. He passed away on the Nones of December, with a happy end. You who read this inscription, pray to God for him.

1001.

In the twelfth year of Conrad, Emperor Otto, setting in motion his third expedition into Italy with a vast army, laid waste to the Romans, defeated them, and overcame them. Moreover he caused Crescentius, who had seized the principate of Rome and had committed many evils against the Church of God and the vicars of Christ, to be beheaded. And when, while staying at Rome for some time, he began to deal rather leniently with the Romans, and they began to hold him in contempt, they formed a conspiracy, killed several of his soldiers, and besieged him stoutly in the palace. By the efforts of Henry duke of Bavaria and Hugh the margrave, after a feigned agreement, he was scarcely extricated, and departed from Rome, accompanied by the pope. And because the wife of Crescentius, a most beautiful woman, who had long consented to the emperor in acts of Venus, saw, and grieved, that the emperor had gone away leaving her behind in hope of reigning, she arranged for a poisoned drink for him; after drinking it, he died in Italy on his way back.

The pontiffs, however, and the princes who were with him, skillfully arranged the corpse, clothed in purple, upon a horse as if he were alive, lest perhaps a tumult should arise in Italy if the emperor’s death had become known; and, removing the entrails, they left them at Augsburg, but buried the body in the basilica at Aachen.

Henry, sprung from the dukes of Bavaria, but in office count of Bamberg, succeeded him by election of the princes, and at Mainz received the diadem of the kingdom from Archbishop Willigis. This is Henry, the second emperor of this name, who deserved to be written in the catalogue of the saints; of him we shall speak later in his own place, whom we have noted here in anticipation.

1002.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 1002, in the fifteenth indiction, Conrad, the tenth abbot of this monastery, died on the Ides of February; when he had been buried with the lamentations of the brothers in the church of Saint Aurelius, the abbacy of Hirsau was vacant for sixty-three years, as we shall say in order in what follows.

Concerning the abbacy of this monastery being vacant for sixty-three years, and certain deeds in the meantime of the monastery, the order, and Germany

When Conrad, the venerable, not to say pitiable, tenth abbot of this monastery, had entered the way of all flesh, a few monks in number remained surviving in this place; and, since even now they had not entirely returned to the way of truth, they brought upon the rest a tribulation greater than they had experienced up to that point. For when they were consulting among themselves about the election of a new pastor, the count violently and with armed hand thrust himself into their affairs, promised that he would give them an abbot, and utterly forbade them to proceed to an election.

In order that, under the appearance of piety, he might gradually make the monastery empty, and might hand over to his own greed all that remained, he set over them as steward one of his own household. He knew [unclear] would come, and would govern everything according to the Rule; then he promised, in humble words and deceitfully, that he would never [unclear] the gifts which he had taken away. In truth, however, he was seeking this, which happened not long afterward: that, when the monks were either dead or expelled, he himself might be called to his own right over all.

For after almost three years, when a certain dissension arose between the brothers and the steward, the monks, except for two who had long adhered to Eberhard and had always defended the count’s party, were expelled from the monastery.

They were four or five in number, who, as they departed, were persuaded among themselves by a prudent indeed, but useless, [unclear]

Monks Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

By common counsel, before they were separated from one another, they chose an abbot; yet he could by no means come into possession of the monastery. They choose the [Albasian?], but he does not reach the monastery. For, dispersed over all the land, they everywhere disclosed to all the injuries they were suffering; but there was no one who either wished, or even could, bring aid against such a tyrant.

Meanwhile, while they were wandering from monastery to monastery, and each settled where he could maintain himself, after some years, when those two monks also who had been permitted to remain in the monastery had died or been expelled, I do not know for certain, secular clerics were ordered to inhabit the monastery. Secular clerics inhabit the monastery.

And so from that time until Count Adelbert, of whom we shall speak in his own place, the monastery of St. Aurelius stood empty, and became a dwelling of clerics and a brothel of whores. Meanwhile, if anything remained that the count and the other thieves had not carried off, the clerics, consuming it little by little upon their concubines and whores, reduced it to nothing, so that they could not even spare the books, of which a huge quantity had been collected there through the diligence of the ancient monks, whom we have shown above to have been most learned. The notable library of this monastery.

For since at that time, when the craft of printing books was not yet in use, volumes were sold at a higher price, those unlearned scoundrels in a few years [unclear] that most precious treasure of the library. From the fact that from the first foundation, for almost 180 years, many most learned men flourished in that same monastery, succeeding one another in order, as is very clear from what has been said above, we can most especially infer how precious, and heaped up with many volumes, that library was. [unclear] succeeding one another, not only Hirsau in that time [unclear], which they adorned by their learning, left after them a very great and precious treasure of books in the library of this monastery. But when all these had been sold and scattered by the clerics, [unclear], shamefully consuming them upon their concubines and whores, within a few years they brought the monastery, by neglecting the repair of walls and roofs, into utter ruin. The clerics consumed [unclear].

It therefore remains fixed with me, firmly concluded beyond all doubt, that [unclear] without books, or for the adornment of the library, which every learned man especially loves, added nothing by writing in his own time. Rain fell upon the most holy altars of the church; cattle were received as stables within the walls of the cloister; everything seemed to be hastening utterly toward desolation. The count not only did not prevent these things, but even rejoiced greatly that they were happening, since he saw that by them the name and place of the monastery would soon be reduced to nothing, according to his desire. The monastery is laid waste.

But we, intending to carry the sequence of years from here down to the restoration of the monastery of Hirsau, since we do not have [unclear] Cunigund, with whom, because of love of chastity, [unclear] was assumed to the empire by election, as we have said, had as wife the daughter of Sigifrid, count palatine of the Rhine, named [unclear], in those things which we have undertaken to touch upon, either concerning our order or concerning deeds in Germany, [unclear], as we hasten toward the future shepherd of the place. For it would be tedious to write for a long time without a guide; let us therefore assign, very briefly, the events that present themselves in the years while the monastery was vacant, even by leaps, as is usual, so that the promised integrity may not be wanting to the history itself.

St. Henry the Emperor observes chastity with Cunigund.

Accordingly, in the first year while the monastery was vacant, Henry, count of Bamberg, as we said above, was assumed to the empire by election. He had as wife Cunigund, daughter of Sigifrid, count palatine of the Rhine; with her, because of love of chastity, [unclear].

The bishopric of Bamberg is founded.

[He founded] [unclear] with the counts palatine of the Rhine, to which he appointed Eberhard as first bishop, and [unclear].

The monastery on Mount [Ma-] of monks is founded.

[unclear]

The monastery of Schuttern is restored.

[He founded it] by repairing it when it was ruinous from extreme age; he repaired it by founding it. It is called from a little river [unclear]. For the sustenance of the monks he provided quite abundantly for necessary things. The monks who dwell in this monastery report concerning it that in 603, when Theodoric, king of the Franks, was waging war with Theodebert and Lothar, inflamed with love of the heavenly fatherland, [unclear] visited the thresholds of the Apostles; then, departing through Alsace, [unclear].

[unclear] the patrician, inflamed, visited the thresholds of the Apostolic court, and thence through Alsace to the departure of his [unclear]. And this is the history of the Monastery of St. Gall. Because lord Henry, who was king of the Germans, and his successor Sigifrid, who was emperor, and his successor Cunigund, who was queen, and his successor Giselbert, who was abbot palatine, and his successor Arnulf, who was archbishop of the diocese of [Terginensis?], and his successor Eberhard, who was bishop of the diocese of [Augiensis?], and his successor Conrad, who was [unclear] the monastery of St. Gall, which was in the region of [Arduingensis?], and his successor William, who was master of soldiers, and his successor Otto, who was king of the Franks, and the successor of that Otto, who was Pope Gregory III, and his successor Paschal, who was pope, and his successor Boniface, who was apostle, and his successor Clement, who was pontiff, and his successor Paul, who was patriarch of Constantinople, and his successor Simon, who was patriarch of Antioch, and his successor Theophanus, who was patriarch of Alexandria, and his successor Michael, who was patriarch [unclear], and his successor Innocent, who was patriarch of Antioch. And this is the history of the Monastery of St. Claren Of the Monastery of Hirsau ...to have first built that monastery by the counsel and aid of a certain Saint Pirminius, one of the disciples of the blessed abbot Maurus, at that time a bishop; to have introduced monks of the rule of Saint Benedict; and also to have provided the necessary revenues.

The Hungarians are converted to the faith through Gisela [unclear] of the Hungarians, with their king Stephen. For that holy woman herself, by her insistence, brought the king to desire that he and his whole people be baptized; in baptism he was called Stephen, and thereafter he adorned his life with such great holiness that after death he was enrolled among the number of the saints.

M X.

In the sixth year while the abbacy was vacant, Bruno, from a monk of our order made archbishop [unclear], after being afflicted with many tortures and having his hands and feet cut off, at last completed his martyrdom by beheading.

About these times flourished Burchard, formerly a monk of the monastery of Gembloux, or, as others prefer, of Bobbio, bishop of Worms, a man most zealous in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, once a hearer and disciple of Albert, monk of Bobbio and afterwards abbot of Gembloux, as we have said above. Among other little works of his talent, he laboriously and quite usefully brought together from various sources into one that great volume of Decrees, divided into twenty books, which the ancients, from the author’s name, called the Burchard.

There also flourished in these times Meginfrid, monk of Fulda, a chronographer, who, like a rose among thorns, shone out clear as a studious and learned man among the idle, carnal, and ignorant monks of his monastery. He, among other little works of his talent, [unclear] of the holy abbot of Gembloux, a certain hearer and disciple, as we have said above. [Unclear] inserted those succeeding one another in time, and briefly noted the deeds of each; he also made mention, in like manner, of those monasteries to which he knew either monks or abbots had been sent from Fulda, and by interweaving their successions of abbots and more memorable deeds, described them concisely. From the labors of this man, I confess that I have necessarily inserted much in this work of ours concerning the history of Hirsau.

About these times there occurred a wondrous deed of the emperor Henry. A certain young man, by the maleficium of two old women, was changed into the form of an ass, so that to all who saw him he appeared an ass. This seems impossible to many, who do not understand that by divine permission the evil spirit can deceive the eyes of men with astonishing illusions. In these times also Balderic, bishop of Liege, the immediate successor of Notker, founded the monastery of Saint James on the island of Liege, in which he placed monks of our order.

M XI.

In the ninth year while the abbacy was vacant, the greater church of Bamberg was consecrated, with the emperor and forty-six bishops standing by. And in the same year Willigis, archbishop of Mainz, died.

About these times, when Ezzelinus, count palatine of the Rhine, brother of Saint Cunigund the empress, opposed the king, and for ten continuous years, [unclear] and, with his magnanimity confirmed to his opinion, by oaths and public pledge from all the Lotharingians, all royal honor [unclear]: the king, judging it more prudent to placate an excellent man with benefactions than to trouble him with any annoyances, sought his friendship. Having obtained it, he granted to him, to be possessed by his children as a perpetual inheritance, the island which is in the Rhine of Saint Suitbert, with all its appurtenances, Duisburg also and Saalfeld, no small supports of the kingdom.

This count had taken a wife named Mechtild, daughter of the empress Theophanu and sister of Otto III, from whom there were born to him three sons and seven daughters: Hermann, afterwards archbishop of Cologne before Pilgrim, surnamed Noble; Everard, after Poppo archbishop of Trier, namely from being provost of Worms; and Ludolph, successor of his father’s duchy. Mieszko, duke of Poland, took Richiza, the first daughter, as wife. Adelheid in Nivelles, Theophanu in Essen, Helwig in Neuss, Mathildis in Dietkirchen, and Willichalda in the monastery of Saint Mary at Cologne on the Capitol, and Sophia likewise in the monastery of Saint Mary at Mainz and Gandersheim, were all at that time placed in positions of rule as abbesses of nuns of our order.

This count Ezzelinus, a rich and vigorous man, built a monastery of our order not far from Cologne in honor of Saint Nicholas, formerly archbishop of Myra, which is called Brauweiler; he adorned it with many estates and ornaments, and in it he was buried. In these also times...

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius 47

In these times Reinhardus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter the Apostle at Senones, flourished: a learned and most religious man, who gloriously restored the buildings of his monastery, ruined by excessive age, and, instructing the monks in the regular path, brought them back to the former fervor of their way of life. He also maintained a public school of monks, and fully instructed his monks in all letters and sciences, both secular and divine.

Reinhardus of Senones, most learned. 1012.

In the year of the Lord 1012, which was the tenth year while the abbacy was vacant, when Rupertus, priest of the church of Saint Magnus the Martyr in Saxony, had begun the first Mass on the night of the Nativity of the Lord, a certain layman Otbertus, leading a dance in the cemetery with fifteen other men and three women, and making a din with secular songs, caused no small distraction to the celebrant. When the priest ordered them through the sacristan to be silent and to desist from such frivolities on so holy a night, and they did not obey his command, he was moved, and standing at the most holy altar said: “May almighty God make it so that you must remain dancing thus for a whole year.” Wonderful to say, the effect at once followed the voice of the one uttering the curse: thus, for the space of a whole year, they danced without interruption day and night; they did not eat, nor [unclear].

People dance for an entire year. The curse of the priest Rupertus.

They seemed to be sunk up to the soles of their feet, trampled beneath them. The son of that priest too, when he tried with violence to pull his sister out from the middle of the dancers by seizing her arm, tore her arm from her body; but she, as if she had suffered nothing, neither felt pain nor uttered a sound, nor did a single drop of blood fall, but continued the dance with the rest.

At last, when the year had passed, Saint Heribertus, archbishop of Cologne, came to the cemetery, absolved the dancers from the curse, and, bringing them into the church, reconciled them to the Lord. Of these the women soon died, and some of the men shortly afterward; they are even said to have been illustrious for miracles after death, since they had undergone a sufficiently hard penance. But the rest, to whom it was permitted to live longer, showed by the trembling of their limbs what they had suffered.

Saint Heribertus absolves the cursed persons from the bonds.

When around these times the monks of the monastery of Fulda had become a mockery to all the people because of their most deformed way of life, and, though often warned by the holy emperor, scorned to amend their wicked habits, since he knew that they had become insolent through an excessive abundance of riches, he ordered many goods and possessions to be taken from them and distributed them to other monasteries.

A cloud [unclear] submerged many thousands of people.

In the twelfth year while the abbacy of Hirsau was vacant, a great cloud suddenly fell in Flanders, and [unclear].

Saint Heribertus dies. Piligrinus.

[Unclear] and in the monastery of Deutz, which he himself had founded, he is buried. Piligrinus succeeded him for almost fifteen years.

In the same year Erekenbaldus, archbishop of Mainz, died; Aribo succeeded him, a learned and very venerable man, who among the other little works of his talent published a not contemptible little work on the fifteen Gradual Psalms.

In these times many very excellent men flourished in our order, distinguished for learning and holiness.

Berno, abbot of Reichenau, a monastery of the diocese of Constance, a man [unclear] in divine scriptures [unclear].

Guido Aretinus, monk and distinguished musician.

Guido Aretinus also, a monk of the monastery of the Cross of Saint Leufridus, a studious and learned man, and notably skilled in secular letters, a philosopher, rhetorician, and musician [unclear].

Ewerbertanus, most learned in theology among the Treverians.

Euerbinus also, abbot of the monastery of Dolciensis, which lies in the diocese [unclear] in the borders of Lorraine, [unclear] German miles distant, flourished in the same times: a man very learned both in divine scriptures and in secular letters, who wrote the life of Saint Simon, monk of Trier, about whom we shall speak later under Poppo of the same city.

Simon, monk of Trier, about whom we shall speak later under Poppo of the same city [unclear].

Berno, abbot of Reichenau. Erckenbaldus. Aribo, archbishop of Mainz. Erkenbaldus. Aribus, archbishop of Mainz. Guido Aretinus, monk and distinguished musician. Ewerbertanus, most learned in theology among the [unclear].

Euerbinus, abbot of the monastery of Dolcienensis, who works under this name in the diocese of Saint Leofridus, and did many other things in the arts of letters; and on account of this excellence and remembrance he exchanged his diocese with the archbishop of Mainz, because it was there, and he had great honor and fame. And afterward he was a master and priest in the church of Trier, and carried his letters and his studies through the regions of the whole world, namely in Germany, Norway, Denmark, Scania, Pomerania, Livonia, Poland, Hungary, Bohemia, Dalmatia, Illyricum, Gaul, Burgundy, France, Spain, Portugal, Italy, the kingdoms of the Gauls, Turkey, Armenia, Persia, India, and it is still scarcely ended. And then he came into Italy and lived at Bologna, and at Florence, and at Vercelli, and at Monreale, and at Saint Peter, and at Saint Anthony, and at Saint Marcellus, and at Saint George, and at Saints Peter and Marcellus, and at Saint Paul, and at Holy Cross, and at Holy Cross, and at Saint Nicholas, and at Holy Cross, and at Saints Cosmas and Damian, and at Saint Benedict, and at Saint John the Baptist, and 48

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

archbishop. He also wrote the deeds of the same Poppo; also certain compositions on fasting, almsgiving, and penance. He held a public school in theology for monks, and wrote many other things unknown to us.

At this time there also flourished in England St. Elphegus, formerly abbot of the monastery of our order called Bath, first bishop of Winchester and afterward archbishop of Canterbury, a learned and most holy man, who, after many labors undertaken for the love of Christ, was crowned with martyrdom. His feast is observed on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May.

In these days there also flourished in the city of Trier St. Simeon, monk of Mount Sinai, a Greek by nation. Poppo, archbishop of Trier, returning from overseas regions, brought him with him and, for the love of Christ, enclosed him in the aforesaid city, in a certain tower, to lead the life of a hermit. For he was a man of many virtues, and one who endured much from demons and wicked men. After his death he was immediately enrolled in the catalogue of the saints, and began to shine with countless miracles. Everwin, abbot of Dolcia, of whom we have already spoken, described his life in a brilliant style. I have in my possession three leaves of the Greek Psalter of this most holy man Simeon; because of his merit I value them as highly as if I possessed a precious treasure of gold and silver. His feast is kept on the Kalends of June.

Around these times there also flourished St. Gerard, formerly a monk of our order, bishop of Morisena in Hungary. After he had preached the word of God to the nations for a long time, he was afflicted with very severe torments by the impious and pagans, and suffered martyrdom for our faith.

Saint William also, abbot of Dijon, of our order, flourished in this same age: a learned man and of most holy life, burning with the greatest zeal for regular discipline. In life and after death he was renowned for many miracles in the diocese of Liege and throughout all Gaul, distinguished also for the performance of many miracles; in his time he magnificently restored monastic discipline, which had almost collapsed. His feast is kept on the eighth day before the Kalends of February.

Richard also, abbot of Verdun, [unclear] of Stavelot. In these same times there also flourished Meginfrid, formerly a monk of a monastery of our order, renowned in these times, whose most holy life was marked by many virtues; by his learning and his religion he brought many back to the path of a more corrected life.

Around these times there also flourished Brando, formerly abbot and then bishop of the aforesaid church for twenty-seven years. Around these times there also flourished St. Burchard, near Wurzburg, sixth archbishop of the church of Magdeburg, appointed by St. Henry, a learned and very religious man, who presided over the aforesaid church for sixteen years. He built a monastery of our order near the city of Hildesheim in honor of St. Bartholomew the Apostle, which in our times is called St. Gotthard after his name, since he was buried in it.

In these days Poppo, son of Liudolf, duke of Austria, archbishop of Trier, of whom we spoke before, who brought St. Simeon the monk with him from the monastery of Blessed Mary in Bethlehem to Trier, is held to have been very renowned. He is said to have converted the Danes to the faith of Christ, as is contained in the deeds of the Treveri, and he obtained from Pope Benedict the canonization of the same St. Simeon on account of the very great performance of miracles. He gloriously presided over the church committed to him by God for forty-one years. He died in the year of the Lord 1057, in the tenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July.

In the year of the Lord 1023, in the sixth indiction, while the abbey of Hirsau was vacant, in the twenty-first year, Aribo Munginus, archbishop [unclear], held a synod of bishops and abbots in the monastery of Saints Marcellinus and Peter in Seligenstadt, for the peace of the clergy and the advantage of the Church, where many things were established with the highest prudence. In this holy synod, as we read from its deeds, there were present Burchard, bishop of Worms, concerning whom it is written; Werner, bishop of Strasbourg; Bruno, bishop of Augsburg, who was the brother of St. Henry the emperor; Everhard, bishop of Bamberg; Meginhard, bishop

A council is held in the monastery of the Holy Savior in the Salzburg city. Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

[unclear] bishop of Wurzburg, and also Richard, abbot of Fulda, Arnold, abbot of Hersfeld, Reginbold, abbot of Saint Nazarius of Lorsch, Hericho, abbot of Saint Maximin at Trier, Eberwin, abbot of [Doley?], Henry, abbot of Saint Burchard at Wurzburg, Sizicho, abbot of Schluchtern, Gerbert, abbot of Saint Alban, Adelbert, abbot of Klingenmunster, and Rudolph, abbot of Blidenstadt, men of our order, distinguished in conduct and learning.

MXXIII.

In the year when the abbacy had been vacant for 22 years, in the 6th indiction, Emperor Henry II died on the 13th day before the Kalends of July, and was buried in the greater church of Bamberg, which he himself had founded. When Henry had died, the prince-electors chose Conrad, the second of this name, to the empire: a Frank by birth, a good and vigorous man. He had taken as wife Gisela, widow of Bruno, duke of the Saxons; by her he begot a son Henry, who ruled after him, and a daughter Cunigunde, who lies buried in the monastery of Limburg. This Emperor Conrad II built the aforesaid monastery of Limburg, of our order, in the diocese of Speyer, which he adorned with many estates, ornaments, privileges, and liberties. They write that previously a castle had been built in the same place, and that through him it was changed into a monastery of monks.

MXXXI.

In the year of the Lord 1031, which was the 29th year with the monastery vacant, A [Athon?], archbishop of Mainz, died; Saint Bardo, abbot of Hersfeld, of our order, succeeded him and presided over the church of Mainz for 20 years. He was a learned man and of most holy conduct, and after his death was enrolled in the catalogue of the saints. He died in the year of the Lord 1051, in the 4th indiction, on the 2nd day before the Ides of June. Around these times Thietagus, from being a monk of the monastery of Corvey in Saxony, of our order, became archbishop of Prague after Gaudentius. He was a man outstandingly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, and venerable no less for the merit of his life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures.

MXXXV.

In the year of the Lord 1035, which was the 33rd year with the monastery of Hirsau vacant, Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne, died. Hermann succeeded him, son of Ezelin, count palatine of the Rhine, concerning whom we spoke above.

In the same year Rudolph, abbot of Hersfeld, of our order, was made bishop of Paderborn, a learned man and venerable for integrity of character.

But in the 35th year with the monastery vacant, Saint Cunegund, formerly empress, died. After the death of Emperor Saint Henry, for love of almighty God she had despised the world, and in the monastery of Kaufungen, taking up the habit of holy life, she remained until death as a nun with the holy virgins of Christ, and herself a virgin. In the same year Saint Bardo, archbishop of Mainz, dedicated the church of Saint Martin at Mainz, with Emperor Conrad and many bishops and abbots present, on the 4th day before the Nones of November.

MXXXVII.

Saint Stephen also, king of Hungary, died in this same year. Henry his son succeeded him, a holy man and beloved of God; he too, together with his father, was enrolled in the catalogue of the saints.

In the same year too Saint Simeon, monk and recluse, died at Trier on the Kalends of June. We have already made mention of him above. He soon shone with such great miracles that, at the request of Archbishop Poppo, he was canonized by Pope Benedict IX immediately after death. His life, as we said before, Eberwin, abbot of [Doley?], described in elegant speech.

MXXXIX.

In the year 1039, which was the 37th year with the monastery vacant, in the 7th indiction, on the day before the Nones of June, Emperor Conrad II died and was buried in the church of Speyer, which he had built and endowed with many benefactions. By the election of the princes his son Henry, the third of this name, succeeded him, and ruled as emperor for 17 years after his father. He had as wife Gunhild, daughter of the king of the Danes; when she died without children, he took as his second wife Agnes, daughter of William, count of Poitou. By her he had Henry, the fourth emperor of this name, who reigned after him, and two daughters: Gisela, a nun, and Adelaide, who was abbess of our order in Quedlinburg.

MXLII.

In the same year Eberhard, first bishop of Bamberg, died; Suidger succeeded him, who afterward became pope. Reginbold, bishop of Speyer, also died; Sibicho succeeded him.

In the 40th year with the monastery vacant, Helias, abbot of the monasteries of Saint Martin and Saint Panta50

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

of [Saint Pantaleon?], of our order, in Cologne, a Scot by nation, died, a learned and holy man, who had led a strict life with his monks.

Guimundus.

In these times Guimundus, archbishop of Aversa, formerly a monk of our order, flourished: a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, who left many distinguished monuments of his lively talent. Among these, that famous work is commonly known which he published, divided into three books in dialogue form with Roger the monk, on the body and blood of the Lord, against the new errors of Berengar, deacon of the church of Angers. The same Roger, monk of the monastery of the Cross of Saint Leufridus of our order, a studious and learned man, afterward a monk of Saint Pantaleon in Cologne, wrote, among other things, the deeds of Bruno, archbishop of Cologne and founder of the same monastery, and certain other little works not contemptible for reading. In the same times there also flourished Theodoric, monk of Hirsfeld, who wrote to Richard, abbot of Fulda, on the life and praises of our most holy father Benedict, certain little works, and certain others, whose titles we have arranged in the second book of Illustrious Men.

Roger the monk of [unclear]. Theodoric the monk.

1043.

In the following year, which was that of the Lord’s Nativity 1043, in the second indiction, Amichadus, a monk of Fulda and a Scot by nation, died. For many years he had been enclosed in the same monastery for the love of Christ, a man of most holy life; over his tomb lights were seen at night.

There also flourished about these times Clarus, monk of the monastery of Saints Marcellinus and Peter in Seligenstadt, in the diocese of Mainz, of our order, a learned man of most religious conduct. In that same place, enclosed for the love of God, devoting himself day and night to prayer and contemplation, he is said to have attained the spirit of prophecy. His feast day is kept on the Kalends of January.

Engelwot archbishop. Engelwot archbishop. Angelpertus in Neuburg is founded. Of the monastery of Seligenstadt. Saint Clarus, monk of Seligenstadt. Engelwot archbishop.

In the year of the Lord 1044, which was the forty-second while the monastery of Hirsau was vacant, in the twelfth indiction, Anshelmus, abbot of the monastery of Lorsch, of our order, founded a provostry in honor of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle near Heidelberg, in the diocese of Worms. In it he placed a provost and monks; afterward, in the year of the Lord 1195, Conrad, count palatine of the Rhine, with the consent of Sigehard, abbot of Lorsch, changed it into a monastery of nuns of the same order of ours, and appointed Cunegund as its first abbess.

1046.

In the year of the Lord 1046, which was the forty-fourth while the monastery was vacant, Saint Guido, abbot of Bobbio in Italy, of our order, born in the suburb of Ravenna in the villa of Casa Marensis, a man of most holy life, who raised a certain monk named Martin from the dead and performed many other miracles, died on the day before the Kalends of April, in the forty-eighth year of his rule. His feast is celebrated on the Kalends of May, for on that day his holy body was translated from Italy by Henry IV to the city of Speyer and honorably deposited in the church consecrated in his name.

In these times there also flourished Bruno, formerly a monk of the monastery of Monichenneburg of our order in Saxony, bishop of Verden, brother of Count Frederick, a wise and learned man, who energetically governed the church entrusted to him by word and example.

In the forty-fourth year while the monastery was vacant, Emperor Henry entered Italy and deposed the three men contending for the papacy, namely Benedict IX, Sylvester III, and Gregory VI; appointing Suitger, bishop of Bamberg, as the true vicar of Christ, he called him Clement II. From him he received the crown of the Empire on the day of the Lord’s Nativity. But Pope Clement died in the ninth month of his pontificate and was buried in the choir of the greater church of Bamberg.

1047.

In the following year Poppo, archbishop of Trier, died. He was succeeded by Eberhard, son of Ezelin, count palatine of the Rhine, about whom we made mention above, [unclear] the church.

Bishop Poppo dies. Eberhard.

In these times Heribert, bishop of Auxerre, flourished, a learned and very famous man. After some years, during which he energetically presided over the church of Auxerre, he abandoned the world and became a monk of our order in the monastery of Saint Saviour in the district of Sens.

Also at this time there flourished there, in the monastery of Saint Gall of our order in Swabia, Hermann, who was called Contractus, a monk most learned in every respect, in Greek, Latin, AraChronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

51

skilled in [unclear], a philosopher, rhetorician, astronomer, poet, musician, and mathematician, the most celebrated of all men of his time; he published many distinguished volumes, of which we have made mention elsewhere. He also composed that antiphon concerning the blessed Virgin Mary, Salve regina misericordiae. He is said to have published another as well, Alma redemptoris, concerning the same most holy Mother of God.

1048.

In the year of the Lord 1048, in the forty-sixth year of the vacancy of the monastery of Hirsau, Bruno, bishop of Toul, by the appointment of the emperor and the election of the cardinals, became pope of the city of Rome, called Leo IX, and he sat for almost six years. He was the son of the count of Egisheim and a monk of our order, a learned and most holy man. When he was going to Rome to take up the papacy, he heard voices of angels singing in the air: “The Lord says, I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction.” He placed Christ, in the form of a leper, upon his bed. He also wrote against the heresies of the Greeks to Constantine, emperor of Constantinople, and chants concerning various saints. At the urging of this pope Leo, the monastery of Hirsau began to be restored, as we shall say later.

In these days there also flourished Humbert, from a monk of our order, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, a most learned man, whom Pope Leo had brought with him to Rome, and whose counsel he used in the conduct of all affairs, especially those of the order. We have treated more fully of this man’s little works in the second book of the illustrious men of our order.

Lambert, a monk of our order from the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liege, once a pupil of Adelman the grammarian, bishop of Brescia, a man certainly splendidly learned in every science, also at this time wonderfully adorned our order by his learning. He wrote the life of Saint Heribert, bishop of Cologne, and many other works, of which we have spoken elsewhere.

1050.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 1050, in the third indiction, the holy Pope Leo IX, having left Rome with many cardinals in order to settle affairs and the state of the churches and to restore peace to the Gauls, came into Germany. At that time Count Adelbert of Calw was advocate of the monastery of Hirsau, but a patron of its desolation. He not only scorned to restore the things impiously taken from Saint Aurelius by his forefathers, but, thinking that he possessed everything by just title, [unclear] nothing less than the restoration of the monastery, the forty-eighth [unclear], which was advocate of the monastery’s desolation, but above the thousandth year of the Lord, as we have said, the fiftieth; because the same most holy Pope Leo, joined by blood to the aforesaid count, having gone out from Rome and crossed Italy, directed his journey through the borders of the Swabians [unclear], as was his custom, sowing the word, and eagerly strove to raise the minds of his hosts to love of the heavenly homeland.

One day the pontiff, for the recreation of his spirit, having embraced the count with his right hand, went out from the castle, not far, to the summit of a neighboring mountain, and while speaking said to him: “How suitable a place this would seem to me, O son, surrounded everywhere by mountains,” which place, he said, “O son, would seem to me suitable, surrounded everywhere by mountains.”

Hastening to meet him on the way, he prevailed upon him with most humble prayers that he should not disdain to enter the lodging of his humble nephew. The pope, moved both by the devotion of the one inviting him and by the tie of blood, assented to the petitioner and entered the count’s castle. Received very courteously, [unclear] of saving doctrine [unclear] he should direct himself to Mainz. When the aforesaid Count Adelbert learned this, namely that his uncle, the pontiff of the holy Roman and universal Church, was to pass through his lands, he hastened to meet him and prevailed upon him with most humble prayers that he should [unclear] into the lodging of his nephew [unclear].

“[Unclear] in my [unclear], in honor of a certain Saint Aurelius, whose body is also said to have been buried there, long ago constructed as a dwelling for monks, with the remaining necessary buildings. Since abundance makes it useful for a dwelling of monks and solitude makes it quiet, in which [unclear] of servants ought to be established, who, paying continual praises to our Creator, would pray for the salvation of many.” To him the count said: “There is, most blessed father, nearby a church built by my ancestors in honor of a certain Saint Aurelius, whose body is also said to have been buried in it, long ago for the dwelling of monks, with [unclear]. After monks had served religiously there for not a few years to almighty God, and finally, miserably growing sluggish from regular discipline, since they would yield to no admonitions of their superiors, they were cast out from there by my progenitors as a scandal to the people.”

When the most holy pontiff heard these things, he went personally to the place and turned over the books that remained, wishing to know the truth of the history. There was there, among the other clerics, a [unclear] named Berthold, who had once seen monks serving God in the place. He disclosed the whole matter to the pontiff just as it had happened, and how the grandfather of Count Adelbert had stripped the monastery of all its goods and, after expelling the monks, had put a few clerics in the place.

When these things were known, the holy prelate groaned, but prudently concealing the grief of his heart, he asked the same cleric where the body of Saint Aurelius was kept. When he said that he had heard from his elders that the sacred relics of Saint Aurelius, at the time when the Northmen devastated [unclear]

Pope Leo IX of our order, a most holy man.

Humbert, from a monk, cardinal.

Lambert, monk at Liege.

Pope Leo comes into Germany.

Pope Leo addresses the count.

The count’s words to Saint Pope Leo.

The holy pope personally approaches the place of Saint Aurelius. [Blank page in the source scan.]

52

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

[unclear] Gaul, had been hidden under the earth by a certain abbot of this place, and had remained unknown to all until this day. The holy pope, having summoned workmen, began to dig the earth in various parts of the church and to search diligently for the hidden treasure; but after the craftsmen had labored long with fruitless effort and had found absolutely nothing, all who were present began to despair of finding the saint’s body.

Then, while the holy pontiff was prostrate in prayer, and while he himself urged the craftsmen not to despair, one of them, more skilled than the others in his craft, who had recently come with his sons from the dominion of the Venetians, and who bestowed much good upon this place by his labors, searched each place industriously. At length, from the reverberation of the hammers, he perceived that the earth beneath was hollow. On his advice the craftsmen began to dig in that place, and at last, not without great difficulty, when the soil had been removed, they found a subterranean chamber, formed quite beautifully, in which a sarcophagus appeared, very ornately arranged on the outside.

When the most holy pope saw it, filled with great joy, he ordered that all [unclear]. When the prayer had been completed, Saint Leo came nearer and ordered the tomb to be opened. When it had been opened, the most sacred bones of the most sweet confessor of Christ, wrapped in silken cloths and beautifully arranged in due order in the form of a body, [were found], and at his head a lead tablet containing these words: “The body of Saint Aurelius, bishop, deposited in the time of King Arnulf, under Abbot Herderad, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September.” When the holy pope had read this inscription before all, he groaned and said: “Woe to those who have despoiled this place, sanctified by the presence and merits of so great a prelate.” The sarcophagus was closed, lest the relics of the saint be taken away in any manner, and he returned with his people to the count’s castle.

On the next day, when the holy Pope Leo saw that the time was suitable for fulfilling his intention, he summoned the often-mentioned count Adalbert and Wiltrud, his wife, a most devout woman, in the presence of the holy cardinals, all the rest being excluded, and said to his nephew: “Yesterday, dear nephew, we saw the sacred relics of this confessor of Christ despoiled of due honor, and that place itself, for love of the heavenly fatherland, duly dedicated of old by your ancestors to almighty God and to sacred monastic religion, and for many years inhabited by the servants of Saint Peter, which your forefathers and grandfather, led by the worst and cruel avarice, caused to be despoiled of the abbot’s possessions and goods. This is more wicked than every crime: after the monks had been expelled, the workshop of holy virtues was turned into a den of all vices by most dissolute secular clerics.

“You also, adhering to the depraved footsteps of your ancestors, as we have learned by proved testimony, not only possess without fear of God those things which they, polluted by sacrilege, most unjustly took from the monastery of the servants of God, but you also, utterly forgetful of salvation and penitence, have seized everything which they, by sparing it, had left untouched. By provoking God and Saint Aurelius, indeed all the citizens of the heavenly fatherland, you have made them your adversaries. Nor should it be regarded as a small sin when it is committed against the saints of God, since even among men themselves the unjust usurpation of property belonging to another’s right is judged a very grave crime. Behold, you, together with your ancestors, have violated the covenant and corrupted [unclear], with [unclear] added, the holy testament: the things which they had offered to almighty God with simple and holy devotion for the remedy of souls.

“You, inflamed by impious cruelty and cruel avarice, did not fear to despoil God and his saints. Having been made an enemy and adversary not only of God and his saints, but of yourself and your own race, [unclear] the cruel bishop, declining as an enemy, will destroy your very offspring from your seed, the generation failing, so long as it is polluted by a sacrilegious inheritance, even unknowingly, or, failing within a few generations, [unclear]. But what hope of obtaining eternal happiness will there be for you, O my son, when through such a manifest crime of sacrilege you have made almighty God, with all his saints, hostile to you by your injuries, and your enemy and adversary? It is dangerous for you, and utterly damnable, believe us, to have God opposed to you; for although he may seem to be patient and to endure injuries done to him in this present time, yet, since he is an avenger and a just judge, he will without doubt avenge this patience after death with eternal punishments.

“But we, to whom the care of your salvation and that of your people belongs, not only by reason of the height of pastoral office, whereby, though unworthy, we are bound by office to the salvation of all, but also by kinship of blood, by the authority of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, whose place we hold on earth, warn and require you; and under threat of eternal damnation, and by the strict judgment of God, we adjure you; and, under anathema, strictly commanding, we order you: that, the clerics being expelled from the aforesaid place, from which by apostolic authority [unclear] every benefice of residence in this same [place], you establish there, according to the rule of the divine father Benedict, monks of this our order, as they are remembered to have been there from the beginning; and that you restore to them, without delay, each and all the things taken away by your ancestors, by you, or by any others whatsoever. If anything further is required to accomplish these things, [provide] what is necessary from your own substance faithfully and without any contradiction [unclear] eternal 54

Of the Hirsau Monastery

1056.

In the year of the Lord 1056, in the fifty-fourth year of the monastery's vacancy, Pope Victor II, having departed from Italy, came into Germany, and was honorably received by the emperor at Goslar, around the feast of the Nativity of Blessed Mary, in the presence of many pontiffs, abbots, princes, and nobles.

In the same year Arnold, bishop of Speyer, died; Conrad succeeded him.

In the same year also Emperor Henry III, when he perceived that death was at hand for him, established Henry as king in the presence of the Roman pontiff, by the election of the princes; and, having arranged affairs as best he could, he died on the third day before the Nones of October. He was buried in the church of Speyer, Pope Victor II standing by with many other cardinals, patriarchs, bishops, and princes. He was succeeded by his son Henry, the fourth of this name, a boy of five years, and he reigned for fifty years. His mother, the empress Agnes, prudently governed the empire for some time. At length Saint Anno, archbishop of Cologne, by the counsel of the princes, took the boy king away from his mother, and governed the empire with others appointed for the purpose, until lawful age made the boy fit to rule by himself.

1058.

In the fifty-sixth year of the monastery's vacancy, in the second indiction, Pope Victor died. Frederick, abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino, son of Duke Gothelon and brother of Duke Godfrey, of whom we have already spoken above, succeeded him in the pontificate, being called Stephen IX by name; he presided for ten months. In this same year also the city of Paderborn, together with two monasteries, was miserably burned by fire on the Friday before Palm Sunday.

At that time there was in the monastery of the same city, which today is called Abdinghof, a certain monk of our order named Paternus, a Scot by nation, who for many years [unclear], always devoutly intent upon contemplation. Foreknowing this very fire by the prophetic inspiration of the Holy Spirit, he foretold long before it happened that it would occur, if men neglected to appease God by saving penitence. But when the monastery already stood amid the flames, and the brothers, after breaking the locks, tried to draw him out of his enclosure, he would not consent, saying that he had long since committed himself to the divine will, [unclear] of his enclosure. The approaching flame compelled the brothers, anxious for their own lives, to flee as quickly as possible. But it consumed Paternus together with his cell.

In these times Lambert, monk of the monastery of Hersfeld of our order, flourished, a [religious?] and learned man. Among the other little works of his talent, he composed a chronicle of his monastery, brief indeed, but not useless. He also wrote, concerning the affairs of emperors, pontiffs, and princes carried out in Germany, a fine and not unpleasant work, which, beginning from the times of Charlemagne, who was the first of the Teutons to rule as emperor, he continued down to the year of the Lord 1077, filled with the remembrance of many events. Since he was contemporary with Emperor Henry IV, he described that emperor's deeds very fully in the same volume. From this very volume we have been helped not a little.

In the same times also flourished Anselm, a monk of Reims, a man learned in every branch of letters, who wrote the itinerary of the holy Pope Leo IX, of whom we have spoken before, from Rome into Germany and Gaul. In it he recounts his deeds in synods held in various places: namely, with how much justice and authority he examined ecclesiastical cases, [unclear] monastery.

Peter Damian also, formerly a monk of our order, bishop of Ostia and cardinal of the holy Roman Church, is held to have been famous in these times: certainly a man most learned among the learned men of his time, venerable no less for holiness than for erudition. He produced many distinguished volumes of his talent, whose titles we have fully arranged elsewhere. Out of love for holy religion he left his episcopate and returned to the monastery.

Around these years also flourished Lambert of Liege, a monk of the monastery of Saint Matthias at Trier, a most learned man, learned in every respect, practiced in verse and prose, who of many, you should lawfully expend for love of eternal life. These things, to be carried out by you as quickly as possible, together with your wife, beloved to us, and to be completed, we earnestly enjoin upon you by the authority of almighty God, for the remission of your sins. But if, which may it not be, you neglect this and are found a despiser of our commands, know that you have incurred the indignation of almighty God and of Saints Peter and Paul the apostles and of all Christ’s elect, and that, bound by the bond of anathema by apostolic authority, you will be subject to the judgment of the divine examination, to be punished with the most grievous torments of Gehenna without end among the impious. Compuncted by this speech of the pontiff, the count fell at his knees, and, publicly confessing with tears that he had sinned gravely, promised that he would do, to the best of his strength, everything that he was ordered. Asking pardon for his offenses and absolution, he heard from the pontiff: “If you carry out those things which, at our command, you promise that you will do, we shall grant you not only pardon for your offenses with absolution, but we also promise you again the manifold rewards of eternal blessedness laid up for you in heaven.”

When these things had duly been done, the most blessed Pope Leo, continuing the journey he had begun to Mainz, at last arrived there with his people, where, in the presence of the emperor, he celebrated a synod with forty-two bishops and many abbots and clerics, and enacted many things for ecclesiastical utility. In this synod Sibicho, bishop of Speyer, cleared himself by holy communion of the crimes of which he was accused. From there the most holy pope, after the synod had been completed, went down to Aachen; there he waited for the emperor, who was conducting an expedition against Baldwin, count of Flanders, until he should return. This most holy Pope Leo IX did many good things in Germany, and, after churches, chapels, and other ecclesiastical matters had been moderately arranged, returned to Rome.

In the same year the emperor celebrated Pentecost at Paderborn, where Saint Bardo, archbishop of Mainz, after delivering a sermon at Mass, foretold that his death was at hand, but [unclear]. He at last arrived with his people, where, in the presence of the emperor, he celebrated a synod with forty-two bishops and many clerics, and enacted many things for ecclesiastical utility. In this synod Sibicho, bishop of Speyer, cleared himself by holy communion of the crimes of which he was accused. The [unclear] pope, after the synod had been completed, went down to Aachen; there he waited for the emperor, who was conducting an expedition against Baldwin, count of Flanders, until he should return. This most holy Pope Leo IX did many good things in Germany, churches, chapels, and other ecclesiastical matters having been moderately arranged, and returned to Rome.

In the same year the emperor celebrated Pentecost at Paderborn, where Saint Bardo, archbishop of Mainz, after delivering a sermon at Mass, foretold that his death was at hand, but [unclear]. He came at last with his people, where, in the presence of the emperor, he celebrated a synod with forty-two bishops and many clerics, and enacted many things for ecclesiastical utility. In this synod Sibicho, bishop of Speyer, cleared himself by holy communion of the crimes of which he was accused. The [unclear] pope, after the synod had been completed, went down to Aachen; there he waited for the emperor, who was conducting an expedition against Baldwin, count of Flanders, until he should return. This most holy Pope Leo IX did many good things in Germany, churches, chapels, and other ecclesiastical matters having been moderately arranged, and returned to Rome.

In the following year, namely the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1051, which was the forty-ninth of the monastery’s vacancy, the emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Worms, where the most holy Pope Leo, bidding him farewell, [unclear]. He celebrated with abbots and clerics, and enacted many things for ecclesiastical utility. In this synod Sibicho, bishop of Speyer, cleared himself by holy communion of the crimes of which he was accused. From there the most holy pope, after the synod had been completed, going down to Aachen, waited there for the emperor, who was conducting an expedition against Baldwin, count of Flanders, until he should return. This most holy Pope Leo IX did many good things in Germany, and, after churches, chapels, etc., and ecclesiastical matters had been moderately arranged, returned to Rome.

In the same year the emperor celebrated Pentecost at Paderborn, where Saint Bardo, archbishop of Mainz, after delivering a sermon at Mass, foretold that his death was at hand, but [unclear]. He arrived at last with his people, where, in the presence of the emperor, with forty-two bishops and many clerics, [unclear]. He was accused of these things, cleared himself by holy communion. The [unclear] pope, after the synod had been completed, went down to Aachen; there he waited for the emperor, who was conducting an expedition against Baldwin, count of Flanders, until he should return. This most holy Pope Leo IX did many good things in Germany, and, after churches, chapels, and other ecclesiastical matters had been moderately arranged, returned to Rome.

In the following year, namely the year of the Lord’s Nativity one thousand and fifty-four, a man much venerable in holiness and authority, who after death shone with miracles. Hirsau venerates this holy pontiff of the highest and most universal Church among its two principal patrons, at whose admonition and by whose agency it exists today as more notable among many abbeys, and [unclear] Pope [unclear] of Saint James the Greater the Apostle, which he enriched with many estates, gifts, and ornaments, and in which he is also buried.

In the same year the emperor celebrated Pentecost at Paderborn, where Saint Bardo, archbishop of Mainz, after delivering a sermon at Mass, foretold that his death was at hand, but [unclear]. He at last [unclear] arrived, where, in the presence of the emperor, with forty-two bishops and many clerics, [unclear]; he was accused of these things, cleared himself by holy communion. This most holy Pope Leo IX did many good things in Germany, churches, chapels, and other ecclesiastical [unclear].

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

...wrote down the legends and histories of many saints, both in prose and in various kinds of verse. Of these we have made mention in the second book of the illustrious men of our order. Theodoricus too, a monk of the monastery of St Alban the martyr outside Mainz, is held to have been renowned among writers in these times; since he was a learned man, he wrote much both in metre and in prose, the titles of which we have recorded more fully elsewhere.

In these times there also flourished Lanfranc, formerly abbot of the monastery of Caen of our order, archbishop of Canterbury in England. Since he was, by the testimony of all learned men, the most learned man of his time in every secular and divine science, and had gloriously directed public schools among the French and the Italians for not a few years, at length, moved by the divine Spirit, he despised all earthly things and, receiving the habit of holy conversion in the monastery of Bec, humbled himself with such humility that he was thought by all to know nothing. For the man who had been great in the world wished, for Christ, to be seen as small in the monastery and to lie hidden in the abjection of humility. Hence, when one day he was reading according to the monastic rule while the brethren were seated at table, and in the course of reading pronounced something as he ought, the prior, who was not very learned, interrupted the reader's voice and, not knowing who he was, ordered him to read otherwise than he ought. But the servant of Christ Lanfranc, correcting what he had pronounced rightly, said [unclear]. The divine [unclear] could not conceal his learning [unclear]; obeying the command of his abbot, he held a public school for monks in the monastery, and left after him many very learned disciples. Then, after some years, he was made abbot of the monastery of Caen [unclear].

In the same year, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, died Meginher, abbot of the monastery of Hersfeld, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, in the German regions [unclear], great in the virtues of Christ, and in this age a singular example of monastic living. He was buried on the seventh day before the Ides of December in the monastery of St James, which he himself had built. He had for not a few years a lawsuit with Burchard, bishop of Halberstadt, concerning the tithes in Saxony. Against his dishonesty, when neither secular nor ecclesiastical laws had any effect, and when the wise abbot, having brought his complaint before the law, had told a story to deaf tribunals, at last he appealed to the tribunal of Jesus Christ the judge. When he died shortly afterward, the bishop, by divine vengeance, followed him with his bowels burst, in a pitiable death; yet before he died, wailing and crying out, he said that he had been summoned to God's judgment by the abbot of Hersfeld, and ordered the tithes to be restored to them. He also sought [unclear] from the monks through a messenger.

In these days there was also renowned Ruthard, monk of the same monastery, who succeeded the aforesaid Meginher in the abbacy of Hersfeld, a studious and learned man, since for a long time he had publicly presided over the monastic school at Corvey and left learned disciples after him. He had once been ordained abbot in that same monastery of Corvey, but, falsely accused, as is believed, of certain crimes, after losing the abbacy he had spent some years as a private person in various monasteries; at length, on account of his learning, he was made abbot at Hersfeld. He wrote a very fine little book On the Tranquillity of Life, in which he consoles himself by many forms of reasoning, saying that a mortal man ought not to be disturbed on account of whatever [unclear], and certain other works, the titles of which for mortals in other places I have already set down.

Of the Monastery of Hirsau: concerning the second restoration of the monastery of St Aurelius, made by Adelbert, count of Calw, begun in the year of the Lord 1059.

In the one thousand and fifty-ninth year of the Lord’s nativity, which was the fifty-seventh year of the monastery’s vacancy, and the two hundred and nineteenth year from the first foundation of this place, which had been made by Count Erlafrid and his son Notting, bishop of Vercelli, Count Adelbert, being a strong young man, rich and wholly immersed in worldly cares, seemed gradually to forget the words and threats of his most holy uncle, Pope Leo IX, and his own promise and oath, and he kept putting off from day to day the restoration of the monastery of St Aurelius of Hirsau, which he had sworn, by promise, to hasten under obligation of anathema. Wilterud, his devout wife, a handmaid of Christ, fearing and at the same time dreading that too long a delay might utterly void her husband’s holy [vow?], or that, if death should befall him, thereafter none of the things that the holy pontiff had commanded would be brought to the desired effect, began to press her husband urgently with frequent admonitions, praying and beseeching him that, mindful of the words and threats of the most holy pontiff and uncle Leo, and of how harsh a sentence of excommunication and eternal damnation he had thundered against him if he neglected it, [unclear]; that he should finally spare the whole offspring of his lineage, which in future time would succeed its parent, if he had resolved to be wholly more cruel to himself; and that he should take care to commit to execution as quickly as possible the things that the most holy man had commanded. Otherwise, she said, she greatly feared that the justice of almighty God, once provoked, would at last punish with a most grievous and eternal penalty the disobedience presumed against the commands of so great a pontiff.

When his wife was frequently impressing these and like matters upon the count her husband, and daily recalling to mind the terror-filled words of the supreme pontiff, and when she saw that, though he said he would shortly do everything according to the command of the holy lord and would restore the monastery of St Aurelius, [unclear] was being put off from day to day, and that always graver obstacles were being added to grave ones, she resolved to overcome by importunity him whom she considered she could not overcome by gentleness and mildness. Therefore from then on the devout woman ceased neither by day nor by night to admonish, beg, and with a certain seasonable force drive her husband to begin as quickly as possible the work promised, lest he provoke against himself the wrath of almighty God. Accordingly, overcome by her excessive importunity, he resolved to redeem his fault. Craftsmen were sent for the work; seeing that the church of blessed Aurelius, built with wooden boarding according to the custom of the ancients, and half-ruined through the negligence of the clerics and the evil of the times, could not stand together with the other dwellings of the cloister, they gave the advice that, after the old structure, too simple as it was, had been taken down, he should begin a new monastery of stone, whose firmness would both remind posterity of the deed and, being most stable, would not allow the expenses to go to waste. For, as we said much earlier in the first foundation, the church first founded by Count Erlafrid was indeed sufficiently spacious, but, in the manner of the ancients, too simple and less firm, and it seemed unable to stand long without danger. Therefore Count Adelbert, having received the advice both of architects and other craftsmen and of prudent men experienced in the dimensions of monasteries, had the first [site?] for the new church cleared, to be restored according to the form handed over to him by experts.
