Meanwhile he had squared stones from a nearby mountain, timber, and the other things necessary for so great a work brought in at great expense, and whatever was required for the new building very abundantly prepared.

1060.

Then, in the following year, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1060, in the thirteenth indiction, while [the monastery] was vacant, the foundations of this church of St Aurelius, which we now see, were made, and within a few years the restoration of the monastery was completed, as we [said?] in its place. In the same year, in the territory of Paris, they report that blood rained from heaven on the feast of all Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

...of all the saints over the people at the time of the divine sacrifice of the Mass. Conrad, bishop of Speyer, also died in this year; Einhard succeeded him in the episcopate.

Around these times Count Eberhard and Countess Ida built in Swabia a monastery of our order, called Schaffhausen, which they endowed with great estates and goods. Their son was Udo, archbishop of Trier after Eberhard, of whom we have spoken above.

In these times Marianus flourished, a Scot by nation, first a monk of St Pantaleon at Cologne, then of Fulda, and finally a recluse at Mainz for the love of Christ, a man devoted to God and studious in the divine Scriptures. He wrote a concise chronicle from the beginning of the world down to the year 1084, neatly divided by notation of the years; its reading could be useful enough and pleasing to students for knowledge of chronology.

1064.

In the year of the Lord 1064, which was the 52nd with the monastery vacant, in the twelfth indiction, Saint Cunno, whom the emperor had sent to the church of Trier to receive the insignia of the then-vacant archbishopric, was martyred by Count Theodoric, because he had been appointed by the king without the election of the people; and on the third day, after being hurled down from a mountain, he passed to the Lord. Buried in the monastery of Tholey of our order, he soon began to become renowned through many signs. Afterwards the count, intending to do penance for the crime he had committed, went to Jerusalem and there ended his life. All the others who had consented to the crime were soon consumed and perished by an evil death. Udo, son of Count Eberhard, of whom we have already spoken before, succeeded him. In the same year also Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, Gunther, bishop of Bamberg, Otto, bishop of Regensburg, William, bishop of Utrecht, together with many others, more than seven thousand in number, set out for Jerusalem for the sake of prayer and devotion, and scarcely two thousand returned.

In this year also, when Arnulph, bishop of Worms, a man of episcopal modesty and holiness, died, Adelbero, a monk of St Gall of our order, brother of Duke Rudolf, succeeded him, altogether lame in one foot, a man in every respect worthy of spectacle. For he was of great strength, excessive voracity, and such corpulence that it struck those who saw him with horror rather than admiration.

In these times Williram flourished, from schoolmaster of Bamberg a monk of Fulda [unclear] he flourished in Saxony, a man very learned in both divine and secular writings, practiced in verse and prose, who for many years illuminated the public school of the monks in the same monastery by teaching and writing various things; not least learned also in secular letters, he had taught philosophy gloriously for many years in the Parisian school. Among the other little works of his talent he wrote three little books on the Song of Songs, divided between verse and prose. He also wrote several other things not yet seen by us.

Bernard too, a monk of Corvey of our order, in the same times [unclear] in Saxony, by teaching and writing, illuminated various things. He described in verse, not inelegantly, the life and passion of St Cyriacus the martyr, together with many other things which have not yet reached us.

Theoderic too, abbot of St Trudo of our order, most learned, fully instructed both in secular letters and in the divine Scriptures, wrote in elegant verse the life of Trudo, and also of Saint Bavo, Saint Reinold, and very many others.

In these times Saint Arnulph also flourished, a monk of the monastery of Blessed Medard at Soissons. Saint Arnulph.

Saint Maurilius also, from being a monk of the monastery of Fécamp of our order, archbishop of Rouen after the deposition of Malger, is held to have been renowned in these times, a man adorned with the beauty of many virtues, an outstanding cultivator of charity and abstinence; concerning his holy manner of life exalted proclamations of praise are reported.

In these times Saint Anno, archbishop of Cologne, built a monastery of our orThe Monastery of Hirsau

of our order in Westphalia, which in the language of that people is called Grafschaft, in which he placed an abbot and monks who were to live according to the Rule, and provided them with all necessities. The holy archbishop Anno also founded a third monastery of our order on the borders of the Slavs, which is called Salvedia, in which he likewise placed monks of the Rule of our most holy father Benedict with an abbot, and enriched them with many estates and gifts.

In these times a certain monk of our order came from Ireland, who was called John, into the territory of Mecklenburg in Saxony, preaching the word of God to the inhabitants. On account of his zeal for the faith and his tireless constancy in evangelizing, the Roman pontiff set him as bishop over those peoples; and at last, crowned with martyrdom for faith and justice, he passed to the Lord.

Hermann also, from being a monk of the monastery of Saint Felicitas in Schwarzach, not far from Würzburg, of our order, in these days after the death of Gunther, bishop of Bamberg, succeeded in his place. There are those who write that this Hermann had been vicedominus of Mainz, and that by the entreaties and money of friends he bought the bishopric; but afterward, led by repentance, he entered a monastery.

When and whence the first monks came to Hirsau in this second foundation or restoration. Of Count Adelbert at Constance.

Meanwhile, while the work begun in the foundation of the new church of Saint Aurelius the Pontiff was being continued by Count Adelbert, every delay seemed too long to the holy woman, since she both knew that her husband’s mind was slack and inconstant, and knew that, not yet sufficiently grounded in the fear of God, he could easily be turned back from his holy purpose. Therefore, by what seemed a shrewd counsel, she decided that the completion of the monastery was not to be awaited, lest perhaps death or some impediments should intervene, if it carried off either her or the count before the work was finished. The devoted wife therefore moved her husband, and at last persuaded him to introduce monks without waiting for the date of completion, which still seemed far distant; with their counsel he would finish what was not yet completed in the construction of the monastic dwellings and cells. The count therefore gave consent to the woman who urged him, and took counsel as to whence monks might be brought who would live blamelessly according to the monastic Rule. At that time there was a monastery of solitaries, which from ancient times, as we said far above, was called Ad eremitas, in the Black Forest, praised above the other monasteries of Swabia for the good reputation and rule of life of the monks dwelling there. Led by the glory of its good fragrance of fame, the count and countess resolved to seek monks from it, if they could obtain them. Therefore, after an embassy had been sent to the abbot of that monastery, Count Adelbert asked that monks outstanding in life and conduct be sent to him, to possess under the Rule of the holy father Benedict the monastery founded by him. Accordingly brothers were sent from the aforesaid monastery with Frederick, a venerable man, whom they appointed abbot over themselves.

1065.

And they came to Hirsau in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1065, in the third indiction, on the day before the Nones of December, in the sixty-third year from the desolation of the first monastery, and in the 227th year from its first foundation. When the devoted handmaid of Christ, Countess Wiltrud, saw them, she received them with incredible joy; and after arranging everything that seemed necessary for the sustenance of the servants of God, she, together with the consenting count, handed over the monastery to them in perpetual possession. But when Abbot Frederick and the brothers said that this conveyance was by no means sufficient unless, before the bishop, in the face of holy mother Church, with suitable witnesses called for this purpose [unclear] concerning the possessions which both he himself and his forebears had long ago violently seized from the monastery: although he restored some for the use of the brothers, he kept back more, and perhaps would not even have restored those, had he not been overcome by the excessive insistence of his religious wife. But after the death of Abbot Frederick, when the most reverend Abbot William was placed over the government of the monastery [unclear], by his dove-like purity and simplicity [unclear] the count’s [unclear] and the pure liberty of this monastery, both from the supreme pontiff and from the emperor, with suitable Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

...obtained with the consent of Count Adelbert, as we shall say more fully in its proper place.

But after the brothers had been admitted into possession of the monastery, although it had not yet been completed, they began to labor most diligently so that the church might be finished as quickly as possible, hoping that they would then without doubt obtain the necessary provision of temporal things also, according to the promise of our Savior in the Gospel and of the blessed father of monks in the Rule, since before all else, in the rendering of service to almighty God, they had put forward the duty of obedience owed to him.

The brothers were twelve in number. When the holy woman Countess Wiltrudis saw their fervor and devotion, she strove with all the strength she could before her husband, lest anything should happen to be lacking for the completion of so holy a work. Hence she showed her munificence toward the brothers and her piety toward God by many benefactions; and whatever she understood to be necessary for the support of the servants of the Lord, she generously furnished, now openly, now even secretly. And although the brothers, together with the craftsmen whom the count had hired at his own expense, pressed on strongly and diligently with the work begun, nevertheless they could not bring it so quickly to the desired completion. For over nearly ten years the church was completed, together with certain other dwellings necessary for the manner of life of the monks. Indeed, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1060, as we have said before, the new church, the old one having been taken down in the preceding year, was begun with stone foundations laid; and at last in the year 1070 it was completed, and, as we shall say later, in the seventy-first year it was consecrated by Henry, bishop of Speyer. Thus for ten years labor was spent on the construction of the monastery.

But Abbot Frederick, although he applied an unwearied hand to the work, was not able to see the completion of the church, together with the other dwellings of the monastery, because after three years, having been ensnared by the false accusations of certain men, as we shall say, he was deposed from the office of his dignity, and not long afterward he died. The dedication, transfer, and liberty of this foundation and monastery, although in this place, according to the order of the narrative, we ought to set them forth before we take up writing the deeds of Abbot Frederick, nevertheless, because they occurred after his death under Abbot William, we have judged that they too should be referred to his times.

Concerning Frederick, the eleventh abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, who presided for three years, and concerning his character and the deeds of his time.

Thus, when the brother monks came from the monastery of the hermits to Hirsau at the request of Count Adelbert, as we have already said, twelve in number, Frederick was placed over them as the first abbot of this restoration; he was the eleventh abbot from the original foundation of the monastery of Hirsau. He was elected in the year of the Lord 1065, in the third indiction, in the sixty-third year after the abbacy had become vacant, was ordained by Einhard, bishop of Speyer, and presided for three years. Concerning his life and manner of conduct, so far as pertains to the purpose of this work, a few things must first be set down by us.

Therefore Abbot Frederick, of whom we are speaking, was born of freeborn parents, from the people of the Swabians, of an ancient family, not among the lowest according to the nobility of this world. In his youth he was set by them to learn letters, and, as far as his age allowed him, he made sufficient progress in learning over time. But afterward, when he began to have some wisdom and understanding, he turned himself to God, not without fervor of mind, admirable indeed in a boy; and in the monastery of the hermits, namely at the cell of Saint Meinrad, with the support of his parents he sought and obtained a dwelling among the monks. From then on he spent all his time, for not a few years, in monastic exercises and regular discipline, quite quietly, troublesome to no one and burdensome to no one, but walking in simplicity before your face; he thought little about the affairs of this world. For, devoted from youth to the reading of the divine Scriptures and to inward compunction, and well instructed by the solicitude and foresight of his teachers, he learned, as though led in by a certain habit, to have absolutely no dealings with the world. Indeed, at that time the monks in the often-mentioned monastery were leading before God and men an excellent regular life and purity, without complaint; they instructed boys and young men whom [unclear]

But after many years, when Count Adelbert of Calw, as we have said, humbly sought monks and an abbot from the community of the Solitarians, no one then seemed better than Frederick.

The number of brothers in the monastery of their prince.

In ten years the church of Saint Aurelius was completed.

Praise of the Solitarian monks. The Monastery of Hirsau for he seemed able, not only by words but also by examples, to inflame the hearts of his subjects more powerfully than all others to contempt of the world and love of heavenly things. For in the disposition of his body, no less than of his mind, he was venerable with a certain majesty of dignity: of middling stature, so that he was considered neither very short nor excessively tall; full and rounded in the face, strong and robust, and yet not notably fat; with black hair sprinkled here and there with gray, and not stripped by any baldness. When he had taken up the name and dignity of pastoral care, he omitted either nothing or very little of his former holy discipline, but, devoting himself day and night to prayers, readings of the Scriptures, holy meditations, and contemplation of inward things, he did not readily admit the distractions of secular business. He also did not love wandering excursions away from the monastery; afflicting his body continually with vigils and fasts for the love of God, he strove to offer himself to the Lord as a living and spotless victim. Toward the poor he was very merciful, and, as far as he could, for the love of God [unclear]; for if he found a poor man even somewhat hungry, immediately and without delay, as far as he could, he relieved that man’s need both in clothing and in food. For, according to his name, he was in all things peaceable, gentle, sweet, and quiet, full of the charity of God and brotherly love, serious in [unclear], sweet in speech, and adorned with a beautiful gravity of conduct. Indeed he had learned so to humble himself before God that even in his outward manner of life a certain brightness of spiritual grace shone forth, openly showing to all the inward humility of his heart. For among the other scribes, an office which among the old monks was very commonly in use, he was not ashamed to take his place with the brethren, where, in turns, when free from prayer, he might usefully occupy himself. In his dress he differed in nothing from the monks subject to him, who at that time, content in accordance with the rule with every usefulness and utmost plainness, wore cowls underneath and cloaks above. Thus, carefully preserving his life in this humility and innocence, Abbot Frederick nevertheless could not escape the rashness of the wicked, which from the beginning of the world has always been hostile to good men; but he lay exposed even to the outrages of evil men to such a degree that at last, as we shall say later, he was most unjustly deposed from the office of his dignity.

  1. In the first year of Abbot Frederick, Sigfrid, archbishop of Mainz, returned from the lands across the sea; and of the seven thousand whom he had led away with him, he brought back scarcely two thousand. In the same year the kingdom of England was miserably afflicted by William, bastard of the Normans, who killed its king Harold and reigned in his place. He soon sent almost all the bishops of that same kingdom into exile; the nobles and princes were killed; men of middling rank he handed over into servitude to his soldiers; he joined the wives of the natives in marriage to his newcomers; and in the city of York he cruelly killed more than one hundred thousand priests. Also at the Easter feasts in this same year a comet appeared in the sky for about fourteen nights.

  2. In the second year of Abbot Frederick, which was the year 1067 of the Lord’s Nativity, in the fifth indiction, Einhard, bishop of Speyer, died; Henry, a canon of Goslar, succeeded him, a man of such dignity [unclear], mature in age, and advanced to this not so much by election of clergy or people as by the favor of the king, to whom in his boyhood he had been very intimately attached.

At this time Marbod, from a monk bishop of Rennes, flourished, a man [unclear] in the divine writings [unclear]. He left monuments of his talent to posterity, and among other things wrote a distinguished work on the Song of Songs, also the Passion of the holy Theban martyrs and the Life of several [unclear]. For utility and advantage in external matters he seemed to be able or willing to provide absolutely nothing. A man worthy of every honor the monks, utterly [unclear], not only do not revere, but even despise while persecuting him; and him whom, with the highest honor, from the ends of the earth, if opportunity required it, they ought to have called to themselves, they do not shamefully fear to repel from themselves and to cast away. The leaders of the faction, monks utterly ungrateful to God and men, approach Count Frederick: they denounce their abbot Adelbert as idle and slothful, insufficiently [unclear], and falsely invent, in one phrase after another, how useless he is to the monastery. And indeed they easily turn the count’s mind against the holy and innocent man, since he, accustomed to worldly affairs, was thinking of nothing less than the inward quiet of the religious life. The count had also long been not a little hostile to the abbot, because, with the monks themselves also advising it, he had tried rather more freely than was in his mind to require that the transfer of the monastery be strengthened by pontifical authority. Hence he gladly admitted the brothers’ accusations against Abbot Frederick, and would soon have deprived him of the abbatial honor, had he not been for some time prevented by the counsel of his most devout wife. But the cause of accusation brought to him did not seem sufficient, for which an abbot should be deposed: not because he had regard in this to the principle of justice, but lest he be accused among men of fickleness, if, on so slight a complaint of the monks, he had removed from the prelacy a man otherwise of good fame and reputation among all.

Meanwhile, while these things were being done, Abbot Frederick, a lover of holy simplicity, intent as was his custom on heavenly disciplines, wholly ignorant of the machinations being prepared for his destruction, did not turn aside the deceits and frauds of [unclear]. But when the wicked accusers perceived that by this way they could not succeed in utterly casting down the man of the saints, they found a manner of [unclear] of fornication. For, having taken counsel among themselves at the devil’s suggestion, they found a crime. The diseased sheep lay fornication upon their shepherd, so that by injury they might overcome him whom they could not conquer. When this report was brought to the count, he did not examine the case according to the rule of equity, did not have witnesses produced free from suspicion of wickedness, but [unclear] the violence of the man set over them, and therefore admitted as witnesses against the innocent man those whom he had as accusers in a matter not pertaining to him. Therefore the presumptuous judge deposed the holy and innocent man, whom, though accused, he had removed: not confessed, not [unclear] by lawful testimony. And although the principle of an action of this sort does not pertain to a layman, nevertheless ambition presumed [unclear].

The Monastery of Hirsau

he began to grow weak and rested in peace with a holy end. When he had died, an iron chain was found against his bare flesh, which he is believed to have worn in secret for many years, not without pain, as the scars impressed upon his flesh could show. He was buried in the same place, not without a reputation for holiness; over his tomb at night lights were seen to shine forth, as many testified, signs shown by God. And this indeed was the end of Abbot Frederick, whose soul we trust has been brought into the joys of heaven, since, while set in the flesh, it always loved Christ with all its inmost being, and for love of him patiently endured many things.

On William, the twelfth abbot of this monastery, who presided for twenty-two years; on the deeds done by him, and on his most holy way of life.

After the deposition of the most devout man, Abbot Frederick, no small dispute arose among the brothers as to who should suitably be put in his place: one who by word and example would show himself a useful shepherd to the sheep, and who would not neglect the provision of temporal things, without whose support religion cannot subsist. For they feared the violence of the count; since with his help Frederick had been deposed from his dignity, they not unwisely feared his anger if they presumed the same against a successor.

At that time there was in the monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg a certain monk named William, a very learned and religious man. Some of the brothers had known him before, and the rest had often heard his reputation for good conduct widely celebrated.

Therefore, after long deliberations held among themselves, at last, inspired by a wise counsel from God, with concordant unanimity they resolved that they would elect no one other than the aforesaid monk William, whom they knew, as one very well imbued with the Scriptures and adorned with holy morals, would be a pastor not without usefulness. So they sent two from among themselves, with an embassy from Count Adalbert, to the monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, to ask in the name of all that William be given to them as abbot. The messengers came to Regensburg and set forth their embassy to the abbot and community, as they had been ordered. They sought William as the shepherd of their souls and, after showing their necessities, obtained him. This William, when [unclear] was received with the joy of the brothers, soon [unclear] into abbot, by the consent of all who [unclear], did not raise himself up in pride, but by fasts and prayers entrusted the matter wholly to the Lord. Compelled by the command of his superior, however, after a few days he set out on the journey with the brothers who had been sent, and, with the Lord accompanying him, came to the monastery of Hirsau.

He was received with great joy by the brothers; soon, by the consent of all who [unclear], [unclear] began [unclear] the count, so that he might restore an innocent man to his former dignity. When he saw him obstinate in his rashness, he considered returning to his own monastery whence he had come. When this became known to the brothers, they threw themselves at his feet and very humbly begged him not to abandon them, so desolate; [unclear] they wrap him about, and at last with difficulty obtain that he remain. He refused either to be ordained by the bishop, or to stand or sit in the place of the abbot, as long as he knew that Frederick, his predecessor, was still surviving in this life. When he, not many months later, departed to the Lord, William at last consented to his own ordination. But he would not consent before the monastery was handed over in every way to freedom. For the advocate-counts had entirely reduced the monastery into their own jurisdiction, and did not wish to permit any freedom to the place offered, in accordance with the terms of the first foundation, in the fullest manner.

Count Adalbert, therefore, seeing the constancy of Abbot William, namely that he would by no means involve himself in the governance of the monastery unless the count himself withdrew his hands from it and granted the place perpetual freedom, pretended that he would obey in all things, whatever he foresaw to be necessary for the business of this matter. And so, at his insistence, Count Adalbert, with secular cunning, composed false [charters?], which he obtained to be secured with the royal seal. But after five years, understanding the deceit, William overcame it through the mercy of God, as we shall say in order in its proper place. Therefore, since William was holy and innocent, truthful and faithful, measuring all by his own virtues, and believing that the monastery had now been freed from servitude, he consented to be ordained as abbot.

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

1069.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1069, in the seventh indiction, on the holy day of the Ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was the fourth day before the Nones of June, the monastery not yet being completed, William was appointed abbot; and in the presence of many nobles, both clerics and laymen, he was ordained according to custom by Henry, bishop of Speyer, and placed in the seat of the abbacy, not without a flood of tears.

He presided in great religion and holiness for twenty-two years; during these he wonderfully enlarged the state and condition of this monastery, both in persons and in temporal goods. He was born in Bavaria, begotten of honorable parents, by whom, in his boyhood, he was offered to almighty God by his most pious parents in the aforesaid monastery of the holy martyr Emmeram at Regensburg. There, both in conduct according to the purity of the Rule and in literary learning, he advanced so much with time and diligence that, I will not say in the monastery, but not even in another, did he have an equal in his age.

His intellect was most subtle, and learned in every science, both human and divine, as his distinguished volumes show, which he published both as a monk and afterward as abbot. If anyone carefully turns them over with understanding, he will know with what keenness of intellect he was endowed. For from his boyhood, as we have said, being established in the monastery, all that time which could remain over from the regular and other monastic labors he devoted either to prayer or to the study of good letters. No one ever saw him idle, in the monastery or outside it: he was always occupied with some spiritual, or certainly literary, intention.

In those arts which are called liberal he was most learned, so that he far surpassed even his own teachers. For he was a most acute philosopher, and so subtle in disputations that he was completely overcome by no one. In music he shone with singular learning, since in praises of the saints [unclear]. He was so illustriously learned in mathematics and astronomy, in arithmetic and in the calculatorial art, that he was considered by all the most learned in these things, as it were [unclear].

What he published, however, we shall indicate in passing. For he wrote on music, on the composition of the monochord, on the astrolabe and its composition, on the correction of the Psalter, and on the method of ecclesiastical computation. He himself also was most devoted in the sacred Scriptures, in the reading of which, as long as he lived, he was accustomed to have sweet companionship.

He was in every respect a man worthy of honor; even the disposition of his body [unclear] from those who looked upon him. Indeed, he was tall in stature, bald on the front part of the body [i.e. head], [unclear] somewhat drawn out, and the fingers of his hands slender with beautiful length; in the rest [unclear] he had rare [unclear], a face of blue color mixed with whiteness, beautiful [unclear]. His speech to men was such as, with a certain natural adornment of words, has been accustomed to make any excellent orator [unclear]. Hence he was very powerful in exhorting, so that, outstanding most modestly through sweetness of voice and a certain authority of speech, he seemed to have the minds of his hearers in his power, since whatever he wished to say he could persuade his hearers with admirable ease and beauty.

In correcting delinquents, even if he seemed somewhat severe, nevertheless he acted with wonderful prudence and discretion, and with such sagacity [unclear] that they could have worked the salvation of [unclear]. For the love of Christ he afflicted his body with almost continual fasts and vigils, and he [unclear] himself with such tears of holy compunction into a sacrifice of praise that you would have believed he would soon lose the light of his eyes. He was pleasant in brotherly conversation, not dissolute; and there was in him, together with pastoral gravity, a sweet affability, by which he easily drew all into favor toward himself.

He was of such humility that he did not disdain not only to be taught by inferiors in those things which he perhaps seemed not to know, but also many times to be corrected. He cherished his brothers and sons in Christ with a wonderful affection of love, and he strove to care for the causes and necessities of each one no less than his own soul. No one ever came to him, however sad or tempted, for the sake of consolation, who did not depart magnificently consoled by the sweetness of his words.

He was of the greatest mercy toward the poor, and all the sick, needy, and weak whom he found he cherished with fatherly affection, to such an extent that many times he stripped himself of his own garments, with which he might cover the nakedness of some poor man. For he distributed many things to the poor and to guests with a generous hand, and

Hirsau Monastery

Nevertheless, in all things he did not neglect the care of the brothers. In that conflict which, between the supreme pontiff Gregory VII and King Henry IV, was turning to the peril of many souls, he could by no means be induced to consent, even in the least, to those who were attacking the vicar of Christ. Nor did he wish only to defend and observe the side of the Apostolic See, but he also brought back to obedience to it, publicly and privately, by word and example, all whom he could, without regard for the indignation of the malicious.

He was a great lover of great charity, so that he rejected no one who wished to serve God. He did not consider poverty or the ignorance of persons, but admitted all who came to the service of the Creator, noble and ignoble, rich and poor, learned and unlearned, without distinction of family or nation. In food and clothing he was neither fastidious nor excessive; he loved moderation in all things. At table he never agreed to use special foods or drinks, but as soon as anything of that kind had been set before him, he ordered it to be distributed to the weaker brothers. He taught from the Rule that every mark of singularity in outward conduct was to be avoided by a monk; yet in inward conduct he was, laudably, very singular. For in contrition of heart, in devotion of mind, and in the fervor of divine love he was very singular, so much so that in the daily sacrifice of tears and prayers he offered himself wholly [unclear] to the Lord. His purity of life was so holy, so innocent, and so religious that, since it was confirmed by magnificent signs and miracles, it cannot be doubted that it was most pleasing to the almighty Lord.

Finally, when the fame of his religious way of life, which could not long remain hidden, spread far and wide through Germany and Gaul, many nobles and rich men of this world, and men of great dignity and learning, began eagerly to flock to him and humbly to bind themselves to divine service under his instruction. Of these, several who had been prosperous in the world brought much of their paternal inheritance with them to the monastery for the support of the brothers and the acquisition of necessary revenues.

Throughout all the days of his life he had great trust in the mercy of almighty God, and showed himself such in holiness of morals toward the Lord that in no necessity was he ever abandoned by him. For on a certain day, when the brothers to whom he had entrusted the care of temporal affairs, constrained by the greatest and unavoidable necessity, were urgently demanding from the pious shepherd, who had not a single penny, five pounds of silver to be applied to the common utility of the domestic estate, he began to console them with very sweet words, saying that one must in no way despair of the mercy of God. But they, oppressed by excessive necessity, paid no heed to words of consolation. And so the most reverend abbot, rising from the midst of the brothers in order to beseech the Lord for the pressing necessity of his own, went out; and immediately some unknown man met him, placed the aforesaid weight of silver in his hands, and at once departed.

Many miracles were performed through the man of God William; since they are very fully described in the history of his life, it would be superfluous for us to write them again. Having met on the bridge near the monastery of St. Aurelius a lame man supporting himself on two staffs, he restored him to his former health by invoking the name of Christ. In a grove, when he was about to do some work [unclear], he fed many men from a few loaves, raising himself up with great faith in Christ. Taking pity on Gebhard, a monk, who after the man of God had been carried to heaven after death succeeded him in the abbacy of the monastery, and who was contracted in his whole body, he obtained by prayers sent up to the Lord the health of his right arm, so that he could help himself with it in eating.

At a certain time a fish set before him from theft, though he had been instructed by no indication of human revelation, but inwardly taught by a prophetic spirit, he rejected; and, when the crime was disclosed, he reproved them sufficiently severely. Also a vessel which, through the negligence of the servants, [unclear] was suddenly found again full of wine, and he ordered it to be distributed to the poor. Then, secure in the examples of the supreme shepherd Jesus Christ concerning the mercy of God, he ordered a brother who had labored all day with the brothers in fishing, trusting in the Savior's kindness, to go out again and let down his net for a catch; and at the first draw the brother caught eight pikes of great size. Immediately the holy father invited the poor to a feast, so that he might eat with them the gift divinely offered.

When in a time of famine he was refreshing the poor with a generous hand, and the storehouses, exhausted of grain, now appeared altogether empty, Christ's servant William did not on that account lessen the works of piety; and behold, the grain chest, which in the evening had been carefully inspected, [unclear]. Why do I dwell upon miracles, when the greatest of all miracles is his restoration of the monastic order and of regular discipline, of which I have not yet made mention? For he is the man who strove to reform our order, miserably collapsed in almost all the provinces of the German kingdom, and in many monasteries he also wonderfully reformed it. For whatever monks he could, by word [unclear].

The Monastery of Hirsau

[to have] renewed, which formerly we knew to be renowned only in the primitive life of the monks. Oh, how beautiful it would have been in that time to be present at the life of so many servants of God, who, of one mind in spirit and concordant in will, walked in the house of God with agreement; although their bodily dwelling was in the present age, yet their mind and desire were occupied in heaven.

For the fuller instruction of morals and minds this holy father issued decrees conformable to the holy Rule. After brothers had been sent to Cluny to learn and bring back their customs, he compiled these in one volume with varied and beautiful distinction. The book of these customs is found today in many monasteries, a witness of the ancient religion and sanctity of the monks of Hirsau, although through the publication of the new Bursfeld constructions it seems now almost abolished from use.

It is pleasing to touch briefly on the institution of the lay brothers, wisely made by Saint William the abbot, so that posterity may know with what solicitude, diligence, and zeal the brothers of this monastery sought their salvation under a most pious shepherd. All were to come to the church for the night vigils with the greatest haste and reverence, to say their prayers most devoutly, and all things with [unclear]. And lest they be burdened beyond their strength by the excessive length of the vigils, matins were sung briefly for them; when these were finished, those who wished were permitted to return to bed, or, if they preferred, to remain in the church until the night offices were completed by the monks in choir.

In the morning every day all heard the high Mass. When it was finished they assembled at the chapter of faults, where, accusing themselves for the negligences they had committed, they received fitting penance from the master. Then, if anyone wished, he confessed his faults to the priest, so that he might complete the day with more fervent cheerfulness in the love of God. After this each went to the work assigned to him, and all labored with incredible fervor of charity, just as if each man were bound by his own labors to provide what was necessary for all.

For each had duties assigned to him within or outside the monastery, which they administered so faithfully, diligently, and honorably as if they had been divinely commanded. Among them there was the greatest devotion of mind toward God, and they were joined together among themselves in such charity and brotherly love in unity of spirit that no disturbance and no displeasure ever weakened their peace and tranquillity. They all lived in common, guarding the renunciation of all property so strictly and inviolably that they seemed to wish or feel nothing at all of the world.

They were most prompt, cheerful, and always willing in obedience to their seniors, ready for whatever those men wished to command, not only in light matters [unclear], but also in those which seemed impossible. Among them there were not only no quarrels or disputes, but not even an idle word or one provoking laughter could be heard from any of them. Every day all the lay brothers came to the church together with all the monks, and each, communicating, received the body of our Lord Jesus Christ with the greatest reverence and devotion [unclear].

At compline, [unclear], and, applying themselves to compunction, they lay down in their beds to sleep, so that at the appointed hours [unclear]. They fulfilled the cloistral life according to the custom of the church [unclear] so studiously, so devoutly, and so fervently did they order their life that, though later in time, yet in morals, observance, and regular discipline they were held before God and men to be wholly equal to the most ancient monks in the Egyptian desert. But now at last let us return to the narration of the history, because there is no need to insert in order into this work of ours the life and morals of the most holy man, which are contained written in a special volume.

Therefore, when Frederick, the former pastor, had been removed by the count because of the importunity of the brothers, and William, the most reverend abbot, had at length, after many impediments, been ordained, neither had the foundation of the monastery been completed, nor had the necessary donation been lawfully confirmed by the count himself according to the custom of the time.

Concerning the consecration of the new basilica of Saint Aurelius, and the endowment, manumission, and liberty of the monastery which William procured.

Since, therefore, the church of the monastery had not yet been completed when William came to Hirsau, as we said above, nor had the endowment by Count Adelbert [unclear].

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

...by word and example most strict in the observance of regular discipline, kindled by the ardor of the Holy Spirit, he recalled; with the greatest zeal he desired in a wondrous way to bring back to the monks of his own time that former fervor of spirit with which our holy fathers Benedict, Maurus, Placidus, Columbanus, Aegidius, Gregory, Boniface, Lullus, and almost innumerable others once burned toward God. Indeed, he erected seven monasteries of our order in different provinces, partly by himself in his own person, and partly through his monks and disciples, and built them from their foundations for the honor of God.

Of these the first was the cell of St. Gregory, which is called Richenbach, concerning whose foundation we shall speak more fully below. The second is the monastery of St. Gregory the martyr in the Black Forest, in the diocese of Constance, in which he placed monks from his own Hirsau community, men approved and most renowned in every religious observance. Over them he appointed as abbot Henry, his disciple, a monk of this monastery, a man of tested religious life, who by word and example encouraged his subjects to contempt of present things and love of things to come. The third, indeed, he founded in Bavaria in honor of St. Martin the bishop, where likewise from his own community he set monks and an abbot; and they, without doubt, having been trained in regular observances under a most holy father, could not easily have failed to be most religious, especially since the father, full of God, was accustomed with most prudent consideration to send to new plantations not any of the weaker monks, but the better ones whom he had.

The fourth he founded in Thuringia, in the territory of Erfurt, a monastery in honor of the holy apostles of Christ Paul [unclear], in which likewise he placed brothers from his own Hirsau community; and he entrusted that monastery and the brothers to Gilbert, formerly a monk of Hirsau and at that time abbot in Reinhardsbrunn, to be governed and managed until he had provided them with an abbot. But since the brothers who today inhabit that monastery of Erfurt say that Dagobert, king of the Franks, was their founder, perhaps someone will be able to accuse us of falsehood because we dare to call William, abbot of Hirsau, its founder. Therefore we bring forward as a witness of the truth the history of his life, in which the things we have said about this matter are plainly contained. Nor do we fear dispute, since if Dagobert was the first founder, William was not the first, but, after the ruin of the earlier monastery, the second founder.

The fifth monastery of our order he founded in [unclear] of the most glorious mother of God, the Virgin Mary, at the Double Water, building it anew; in it he placed monks and a rector from his own community, men venerable in their manner of life. The sixth he established as a monastery of the servants of God in a certain village called Wielheim; yet afterwards it was transferred to Mount St. Peter, to which likewise he gave monks and a shepherd. The seventh monastery of our order he founded in the province of the Charentini, which is called Lavense; to it he sent brothers from his own community, men of approved conduct, and he appointed over them as abbot Wetzilo, a venerable monk.

Moreover, many monasteries of our order in the provinces of Germany, almost collapsed through excessive age, he restored to their former state; some begun by others, but not completed, he carried on and brought to completion. Furthermore, after the holy father William had provided monks, abbots, and stipends, with the mercy of the Almighty cooperating with him through the offerings of the faithful, he wondrously increased the number of the brothers and provided all necessities. For he had one hundred and fifty monks under his discipline, praising the Lord daily, for whom he provided, frugally and according to the rule of our most holy father Benedict, what was necessary for body and spirit. In addition to this number of monks he had several other bearded brothers, whom in the customary term we call conversi; they, applying themselves to the labors of their hands, managed the care of temporal things according to the commands of the seniors and provided bodily necessities for the monks, who were always devoted to contemplation and prayer. They report, finally, that this most reverend father William first either instituted, or rather restored after it had been abolished, the use of conversi of this sort in the monasteries of Germany...

After the act had been done for Adalbert and confirmed by the necessary fortification, the holy father, together with his brothers, whose number was then still small, began earnestly to take action with the greatest care, diligence, and zeal, by admonishing, promoting, and cooperating, so that the work begun might be completed as quickly as possible. And when they applied themselves most diligently to the work begun, Count Adalbert and his most devout wife providing the expenses, and no less also the faithful round about, noble and low-born, contributing by the largess of their alms, the whole building was completed in a short time.

1071

For in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1071, in the ninth indiction, the structure of the church, begun almost ten years before, was completed with God’s help, together with the remaining dwellings of the monks begun at the same time. Therefore in that same year, which was the second year of Abbot William, on the day before the Nones of September, the same church was dedicated by Henry, bishop of Speyer, the ordinary in whose parish the monastery was built, at the request of Count Adalbert and his most devout wife Wiltrudis, and of Abbot William.

When these things had been done, since William, a lover of truth, believed that the monastery had been handed over to complete freedom according to the count’s promise, and suspected no fraud, he rejoiced in the Lord and carried out his purpose according to the rule of our most holy father Benedict. But after a few years had passed, the most devout handmaid of Christ, Countess Wiltrudis, hearing from her husband how deceitfully and fraudulently he had circumvented the holy man in the imperial letters granted for the freedom of the monastery, took care to reveal this very secretly to Abbot William, to see whether he could in some way restrain the deceiver’s frauds, admonishing him to obtain new letters concerning the freedom of the monastery after the earlier ones had been cancelled, and saying that she would diligently see to it that, with her husband’s consent, none of the sons should set himself against it. With how great sadness and bitterness the holy man groaned over the fraud committed not against himself only, but against God, [unclear].

And what he had despaired of being able to obtain from the fraudulent man, he knew he would easily receive through the mercy of God. And [unclear] the Almighty, who does not despise the prayers and tears of his poor, [unclear] the calamities which he suffered, they confirmed to the man, as it were with one mouth, unless he restored the monastery of Hirsau, which he had unjustly occupied, to complete freedom.

But he delayed nothing and promised that he would do everything; and, having called to himself the most reverend Abbot William, after the letters had been annulled and utterly cancelled, he offered into his hands the complete freedom of the monastery and of all things belonging to the right of the monastery. And by a firm declaration before his wife, his sons, and many others, he renounced forever, for himself and for his sons and heirs, every right or property by reason of advocacy or of any other jurisdiction or lordship. Therefore after a few days Abbot William, giving due thanks to God, [unclear]. Then he instructed the abbot to draw up, either by himself or through any others, letters concerning this perpetual freedom of the monastery, in whatever form and tenor seemed to him more expedient, saying that whenever he wished he would go with him without delay to the royal presence, and would faithfully and without deceit do everything that pertained to the confirmation of this matter. [unclear] the form of the letters, with the counsel of prudent men, for perpetual freedom; and, going with Adalbert, he personally approached the king and offered into the hands of King Henry IV himself the testamentary page which he had drawn up, to be strengthened by the protection of the royal seal.

And because the sum of the entire freedom, endowment, or, to speak properly, restoration of the monastery of Hirsau made by the often-mentioned count is known to be contained more fully in those same letters, it will not be useless if we faithfully insert into this work of ours the form of that royal instrument word for word.

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

Page: Charters of Liberty

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by the favor of divine clemency king: let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present namely and future, know that in our kingdom there is situated a certain regular monastery, in the province which is called Teutonic Francia, in the bishopric of Speyer, in the district called Wernigau, in the county of Ingersheim, in the forest which is called the Black Forest beside the river which is called the Nagold, which is named Hirsau or the cell of St. Aurelius, where also that same saint rests in body. In the time of King Louis the Pious it was honorably built in honor of St. Peter and of Aurelius the bishop, and dedicated to God by Erlafrid, a certain noble and religious senator, and by Notting, his son, the most reverend bishop of Vercelli, and by other kinsmen of Count Adalbert of the castle of Calw; but [unclear] by their descendants it was dispersed.

Now however that same Count Adalbert, touched by the prompting of God, and also repeatedly urged by his wife Wiltrud, has now restored that monastery, and has restored the monastic life which for some time had failed there; and the estates which in ancient times had been handed over thither by his kinsmen, but had been partly seized by their descendants and partly possessed even by himself as if by hereditary right, he has restored. Moreover, from his own property he has handed over to the aforesaid place so many and so great expenses, that the service of God, now carried out there by fifteen brothers under the Rule of St. Benedict, may by the grace of God be maintained and established there; his sons, the aforesaid Bruno, Adalbert, and Gosfrid, and his daughters Vita and Irmingard, agreeing with him in this and in all things consonant with this ordinance.

And first, namely, the place itself, Hirsau, with all the lawful endowments and appurtenances now at present conferred there, and whatever things in their entirety, he has restored, delegated, and handed over upon the altar of St. Aurelius to the Lord God, to Saint Mary, to Saint Peter the Apostle, to St. Aurelius the bishop, and to St. Benedict, into their power and ownership. And all things of the aforesaid monastery to the abbot named William, and to his successors, for free disposition [unclear], so that, as by his kinsmen, the service of God may thereafter be able to be [unclear] there, prudently to profit and [unclear] the same cell with all its appurtenances now conferred and duly to be conferred, from this [unclear] domination, ordering, and power.

Thus they [unclear] it with the right and privilege of complete liberty, and for the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom in Christ, in every way for hope of sins [unclear], with his wife, sons, and daughters aforesaid, he faithfully renounced [unclear]. But this whole thing the truly happy merchant prudently effected: first for the pledge and reward of eternal life, for the remission of sins, for the health of bodies, and the everlasting [unclear] of souls, and also of all kinsmen, descendants, blood-relations, friends, and all who belong to the care of holiness. Also for the memory of kings, bishops, and lords, for the diligence of the aforesaid monastery and of those still to be gathered in Christ, so that they may be able more safely and freely to serve the Lord God in the service of holy profession, he endowed them with this kind of gift of liberty.

And whenever they shall be bereft of their spiritual father, they shall have free power among themselves, according to the Rule of St. Benedict, or from anywhere where there is need, not only of choosing an abbot for themselves but also of constituting him. Whomever the brothers shall have regularly chosen, thereafter, as is customary, the prior of that place shall take the staff of government from the altar of St. Aurelius, in order to set him in the choir as monk, and without any contradiction whatsoever shall hand it into the hand of him whom the whole body of brothers [unclear], private greed having been removed, [unclear]. He, then, having been canonically ordained abbot, without domination or impediment by any person, shall fulfill the ministry he has received [unclear] among his own, and shall serve God alone freely according to his order, if he shall be bound in all things.

The count also grants that the advocacy of the beloved cell should be made [unclear] from among his descendants, if, however, with the counsel of the brothers of that place, he finds such a one among them who, just as the count himself now, is solicitous and zealous not for earthly advantage but for eternal reward, good and conChronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

The aforesaid count also decreed that if anyone of his posterity, or a man of whatever persons, rashly and unjustly takes away from the aforesaid cell one vineyard, one mansus, one mill, or even one serf or anything of that sort, compelled by the royal power of us and of our successors, he shall pay three talents of gold to the king’s treasury, first restoring to the church the revenues which he had [unclear]. But if any one of them, which God forbid, violently alienates [unclear] or anything in the village from it, or proves to be a manifest invader of its goods, or if he shall most presumptuously attempt to break this testament or any court pertaining to them, he shall likewise pay one hundred pounds of gold to the royal chamber; and according to the laws he shall likewise make composition for what had been taken away, so that his intention may become altogether void. He also grants to the ministers of the household of the sanctuary the law and service which the others freely have in our kingdom, so that thereafter they may serve their [unclear] in all things as before.

... so that, insofar as they may, they may both receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict judge, the rewards of eternal recompense.

Pope Gregory VII delivered this privilege of the liberty that had been instituted to Abbot Wilhelm; a copy of it, written out again by his own hand, he deposited in the chest of St. Peter, as testimony to all the aforesaid things and as a perpetual memorial of the liberty.

Finally, out of the exceeding affection of charity with which the apostolic man embraced the abbot, and as a sign of love, he bestowed upon him some relics of saints, which he carried with reverence to the monastery. While the blessed father was staying for some time in the same city of Rome, he fell into a very grave illness from swelling of the belly, which grew so severe that even the most experienced physicians despaired of him.

At length he ordered himself to be carried to the church of Blessed Mary ever Virgin; and, placing his wounded belly at the altar, he implored the aid of that same advocate of the poor with most earnest supplication. And suddenly, amid the words of prayer, he began to recover, and, restored in a short time to his former health, and the business for which he had come to the curia having been completed, he happily returned to Hirsau, with the Lord accompanying him. His brothers received him with great joy and gave thanks to almighty God through him, both for the safety of their father and for the privileges obtained from the Apostolic See.

When these things had thus been accomplished, the most reverend Abbot Wilhelm, since he believed that adequate provision had been made for that monastery, its brothers, and the possessions acquired and legitimately to be acquired in future, by a sufficient privilege of liberty and immunity, from then on devoted all his zeal to winning the souls of many for Christ. And indeed in a short time the possessions of the monastery, by God’s bounty, were notably enlarged under him through the offerings of the faithful, so that from these he could maintain a plentiful number of monks without much burden.

He therefore gathered together all who wished to serve God in truth, noble and low-born, rich and poor, learned and unlearned, without regard to persons; and although the monastery had been endowed by Count Adelbert at the beginning for fifteen monks, he himself [unclear] one hundred fifty [unclear] under Wilhelm. Number of monks under him was 124.

Hence, since the site of the monastery of St. Aurelius seemed too narrow for receiving so great a multitude, he built a new monastery across the bridge with stone flooring, of which we shall speak later. But now, after we have recorded the consecration, endowment, liberty, and the other privileges of the monastery obtained through Abbot Wilhelm, together with the foundation by Count Adelbert, let us resume the order of the history, long interrupted; and, beginning from the first year of Wilhelm, let us touch more briefly upon the sequence of times and the more noteworthy things done in Germany, especially concerning the order, in such a way, namely, that while attending to matters outside, we nevertheless do not neglect the abbot’s deeds and the growth of the monastery under him.

Therefore, in the first year of Wilhelm, Peter Damian, cardinal bishop of the holy Roman church from our order, of whom we made mention much earlier above, was sent by Pope Alexander II as legate to King Henry in Germany, and at [Francen-] [unclear] expounded with great [unclear] and wisdom.

In the same year Megimward, abbot of Hildesheim, took up the abbey of Augia, an entrance to it having been opened by a great largesse of money. For in these times in which Henry IV was reigning, bishoprics, abbeys, provostships, and the other ecclesiastical dignities were not conferred upon the worthy by election; and the simoniacal heresy stained almost the whole Teutonic kingdom with its depravity. From this many evils arose in Germany, because the king, on account of this and many other matters, was excommunicated by Christ’s vicar, was rebellious and contumacious toward the supreme pontiff, and persecuted all who obeyed him even unto death.

In the following year, which was the year 1070 of the Lord’s Nativity, Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, Hildolf, archbishop of Cologne, and Hermann, bishop of Bamberg, summoned by Pope Alexander, came to Rome. There the bishop of Bamberg was accused of having invaded the episcopate through the simoniacal heresy, with money having been given; yet he pleased the Roman pontiff so much with gifts that he returned from him to his homeland not only unpunished, but even rewarded with the pallium, as though an archbishop. Adelbero also, bishop of Worms, made from a monk of St. Gall, as we said above, died in this same year, suffocated, as they report, by his own fatness; Adelbert succeeded him.

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

When, therefore, the most reverend abbot Wilhelm had obtained a charter of this tenor, concerning the restoration, donation, liberty, and immunity of his monastery of Hirsau, fortified by the hand and seal of the royal majesty, he gave thanks to God, who does not forsake those who hope in his mercy; and, so that the donation, strengthened by the king, might also be confirmed by the supreme pontiff and secured with greater stability, on the advice of his friends he resolved to go personally to Rome, to obtain from that vicar of Christ also, according to the canonical sanctions, a perpetual privilege of liberty.

Abbot Wilhelm resolves to go to Rome.

Count Adelbert [unclear] provides for the holy abbot.

Pope Gregory VII.

This purpose of the holy man Count Adelbert, now wholly turned to God, advanced not only by counsel but also by help, providing everything that seemed necessary for the accomplishment of so great a matter and for the expenses of the roads. After some days, therefore, the holy father undertook the proposed journey, and, with the Lord protecting him, arrived safe and unharmed at the apostolic see.

At that time the most reverend pope Gregory VII, formerly called Hildebrand, presided over the holy Roman universal Church. He had been taken up as pope from being abbot of the monastery of St Paul outside the city walls, of our order: the most vigorous cultivator and defender of justice and ecclesiastical liberty. When Abbot Wilhelm came to him, he was received by him honorably and lovingly; and, when the causes of his coming had been learned, he most willingly granted all that he had requested for the liberty of the monastery.

Pope Gregory VII.

First, he received the place itself, Hirsau, with all things acquired and lawfully to be acquired in the future, persons, bondsmen, present and future possessions, under the protection of the holy Roman Church. Then he confirmed by apostolic authority the royal privilege, a copy of which we have set forth above. Third, he gave such a privilege concerning all these things.

Privilege of Pope Gregory VII

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Wilhelm, abbot of the monastery of Saint Aurelius, which is called Hirsau, in the bishopric of Speyer, and to his successors forever. Since the holy apostolic faith ought, from the general providence of pastoral rule, to provide and take counsel for the welfare and security of all the sons of the Church, then indeed it is necessary more eagerly and more earnestly to receive the vows of pious intention and religious devotion and to bind them to salutary affection, so that it may gladly meet the petitions of good endeavors, and may establish, to be held firmly by the solidity of its authority, those things that have been instituted for the praise and glory of the divine name. Therefore we too, rejoicing together at the praiseworthy desire of our beloved son Adelbert of Calw, have decreed to assent to his prayers humbly directed to the holy apostolic see, and have effectively granted what was religiously requested. For he, kindled by love of eternal recompense, has restored and finely repaired on his estate called Hirsau a monastery built of old by his forefathers, recently lost, and has more amply enlarged the [unclear] of the brothers serving God there by adding and handing over many possessions and revenues. And, lest in the future the audacity of perverse men should presume to diminish or violate this establishment of his liberality, they request that it be fortified by the privilege of apostolic authority and strengthened by the guardianship of the holy Roman Church, with an annual pension of a gold bezant being given, considering this indeed: that while honor, fear, and obedience are shown by the faithful of holy mother Church to the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, what has been made solid and strengthened by their decree and in their name may not be shaken by the unlawful presumption of any [unclear].

Wherefore we generally embrace under the guardianship and protection of the holy apostolic see that same aforesaid monastery, with all things justly belonging to it at this time and legally conferred, and thereafter to be conferred by authentic conveyance of whatever persons; and, under the [unclear] of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, we confirm by the testimony of the present writing that they are to be possessed freely and absolutely, and ordered regularly and usefully, by you, son Wilhelm, and your successors, with the disquiet of all those causing trouble removed and forbidden.

We also establish that the forms of constitution, immunity, and liberty which the aforesaid illustrious count Adelbert inserted in his written deed of conveyance and caused to be impressed with the royal seal, are to be diligently observed for the caution of posterity and for [unclear] the attacks of those causing trouble: only those, that is, which do not obstruct the canonical sanctions, so that no one may be neglectful in permitted matters, nor may anything be inflicted concerning forbidden ones. Therefore we decree that the things contained in this page of our [unclear] command and decree are to be observed forever both by you and by all who shall succeed in the rank and place in which you are. But if anyone of the order of priests, clerics, judges, and secular persons, recognizing this page of our constitution, shall attempt to come against it, let him lack the dignity of his power and honor, and let him know that he is guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity committed. And unless he restores those things that have been wrongly taken away by him, or with fitting penance laments the things unlawfully done, let him be subject to the vengeance of the most sacred [unclear]. But to all who preserve what is just for the same place, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which72. Of the Monastery of Hirsau

1071.

In the second year of Abbot William, King Henry took the duchy of Bavaria away from Otto, which his mother the empress had previously given him; in his place he appointed Welf, a vigorous and warlike man, a Swabian by nation. Thereupon Duke Otto, fleeing to the Saxons, was made commander of the war against the king. In the following year many princes conspired against King Henry and the Saxons, and with a most bitter spirit toward him they waged many battles against him.

At this time Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, went to Galicia, to St. James, for the sake of prayer; and on his return, turning aside to Cluny, he resolved to remain there, in contempt of the world. On the Sunday which preceded the feast of St. Michael the Archangel, he again publicly professed regular obedience before all, into the hand of the abbot. But when hirelings tried to purchase the bishopric of Mainz from the king for money, he was compelled by the obedience which he had promised the abbot under the Rule of St. Benedict to return to his see; and on the eighth day before the Ides of December he returned to Mainz, and governed his see for another twelve years. Thus Archbishop Siegfried founded in Thuringia a monastery of our order, which is called Hasungen, in which he too was buried.

The first abbot of that same church was Giselbert, a monk of this monastery of Hirsau, whom Abbot William, at the urging of Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, sent to that place with the whole necessary convent. This Giselbert was a venerable abbot, a man learned in good letters and conspicuous for integrity of morals, a very great lover of regular discipline, who in a short time gathered many monks into the aforesaid monastery to serve the Lord.

But since they were in no way willing afterward to consent to King Henry, excommunicated by the supreme pontiff Gregory VII, they were all expelled from the monastery together with the abbot. More than seventy in number, they came to Hirsau and were honorably received by the holy Abbot William; he kept them with him for some time, and afterward assigned to them the cell of St. Gregory for a dwelling, as will be said more fully in its proper place. The same archbishop also established the cloister of Blessed Mary ever Virgin ad Gradus, in the city of Mainz, which he endowed with many estates and ornaments.

1072.

In the fourth year of Abbot William, which was the year 1073 of the Lord’s Nativity, when Pope [unclear] had died, [unclear] archdeacon [unclear], and he presided for twelve years; he was called Gregory, the seventh of that name, a man certainly of much learning and great piety, prudence, justice, constancy, and religion, who both did many good things for the defense of ecclesiastical liberty and endured adversities.

He had first been a monk of Cluny and was ordained by Pope Leo IX as archdeacon of the holy Roman church at the monastery of St. Paul. In this year, after Alexander, he was created supreme pontiff by the consent of all. Holding a synod at Rome, he decreed, under the great penalty of excommunication, that all priests and deacons should as quickly as possible cast off from themselves concubines and all women, except those whom the rule and the holy synod admitted, and should live chastely according to the canons. Finally he forbade laymen to presume to hear the masses of priests who had concubines. In the same synod he also excommunicated all who sold or bought bishoprics, abbeys, provostships, deaneries, canonries, prebends, priesthoods, diaconates, subdiaconates, tithes, and the other ecclesiastical offices.

After the crimes and evils perpetrated, when [the king], often summoned to Rome by messengers and letters for synodal answers, scorned to come, he excommunicated him; whence evils were multiplied in the kingdom and the Church.

Very clear and celebrated in these times throughout Germany and Gaul was the memory of St. Sebald in Nuremberg and of St. Heimerad in Hasungen; and they were visited daily by a great concourse of peoples because of the healings which were very often divinely granted there to the sick. The latter of these, namely Heimerad, was a priest of most holy life, who died in the year of the Lord 109[unclear], in the indiction [unclear], on the twenty-fourth day before the Kalends of July. Over his tomb Archbishop Siegfried built a monastery of our order, as we have said; its patron is St. Heimerad, who shone there with many miracles.

1075.

In the sixth year of Abbot William, King Henry attacked the Saxons in war, and after many had been killed on both sides he at last obtained the victory.

In the same year Henry, bishop of Speyer, died; Hutzmann succeeded him.

1081.

Duke Otto of Bavaria is deposed. Archbishop Siegfried becomes a monk of Cluny. The monastery of Hasungen is built. Giselbert, abbot from our nation, is sent to Hasungen. Hildebrand from abbot becomes Pope Gregory. Concubinary clerics are excommunicated. Simoniacs also are excommunicated. The pope excommunicates the king. St. Heimerad, etc. The king wars against the Saxons. St. Sebald in Nuremberg, famous for miracles. [Blank page in the source scan.]

The Monastery of Hirsau

[unclear]. The primate of England, sanctified by God, a man most worthy of every praise, sanctified this place by his presence, and showed himself so accessible to the brothers in humility and charity that you would have thought him not an archbishop, but any one of the least monks.

He sat among the brothers as though one of them, speaking about Holy Scripture, the formation of regular conduct, the love of God, and the salvation of souls; to everything asked, especially questions proposed from Scripture, he gave with the greatest goodwill a fitting answer to each and all. With great longing he commended himself to the brothers’ prayers; and, seeing their tranquillity, peace, and concord, he lamented his own cares and hardships, calling himself wretched because he was forced, a little or much, to interrupt inward purity. But [he called] those blessed and thrice happy to whom, in the silence of monastic solitude, [unclear] the sweetness of contemplation, because of the cares of the world, or to stain otherwise [unclear].
