And I, Anselm, consulting with the same men, hearing their words and knowing their opinions, composed this concerning the same matters, and wrote and published the same.

From all Anselm’s letters which he wrote to Abbot William, [unclear] to set before us, so that no one of later generations may be ignorant how highly a man of such holiness and eminence valued the merits of the brothers of this Hirsau community. For after some years, when the count of Calw, excommunicated by the supreme pontiff along with many others because of his adherence to King Henry, intruded himself into the divine offices, and greatly disturbed the brothers of this monastery because [unclear] with the supreme pontiff [unclear], Abbot William made the case known to blessed Anselm by letter, together with certain other questions, and asked his counsel on these matters. Saint Anselm wrote back to him from England in this manner:

To the lord and reverend father William, abbot of the brothers of Hirsau, Anselm, unworthy minister of the church of Canterbury: in this present life lasting prosperity, in the life to come eternal happiness. From the time when your [unclear] deigned to grant me knowledge of itself, I conceived so great an affection that your memory is always sweet to me; I have learned that this has not happened undeservedly, since your life is worthy to exist in love and reverence, and your fatherhood is not without a feeling of sweetness toward my littleness. For often brothers coming from you have not only edified me by report of your holiness, but have honored me by the greeting of your condescension. In this matter, although whatever is in my whole self can scarcely answer to such merits, it is nevertheless mine to show what love and reverence I can. But committing these things to be preserved and increased by God in us, I shall answer, not presumptuously but rather obediently, to those matters on which your prudence has deigned to consult my insignificance: perhaps not what suffices for the subject, but what seems right to me.

Your count, who, though excommunicated, thrust himself in while you were celebrating the divine office, seems to me to need humble admonition, lest by despising the sentence [unclear] a man can [unclear]. Therefore it is better for him to abstain from these things through salutary humility, from which, unless by humility, [unclear] profit, while things always presumed in disorder do harm; nor ought he, with no advantage to himself and with the gravest harm to you, to force you, when you do not wish to offend him, to provoke God and apostolic authority grievously. To pacify them you cannot have him as adviser; and the Apostolic lord will receive his reasons more readily and kindly if he knows that his sentence has been reverenced.

God is to be feared more than man. Therefore I judge that either action should be taken toward him according to the apostolic sentence already issued, or the Apostolic lord himself, or someone acting in his stead, should be consulted about this very matter. Concerning priests who, by open commerce of lust, show themselves reprobate and rejected by God, what apostolic providence has established with ecclesiastical and just rigor must be held altogether.

For it is in no way fitting that reverent attendance be given there where men, persisting in open shameless lust, serve the sacred altars while despising the prohibition of God and the saints; indeed, they do not serve them, but, so far as in them lies, shamefully defile them. This is not so that anyone should think the things they handle contemptible, but rather the very persons who handle them, so that those who do not reverence the presence of God and the angels may, when repelled by the [unclear] of men, cease to pollute sacred things. Nor is it in any way fitting that those should be companions of those who partake from the altar who Of the Monastery of Hirsau

By these letters and counsels of blessed Anselm, the holy abbot William, strengthened in the Lord and wholly kindled with divine love, and no less stirred by zeal for souls, throughout all that time during which the wretched schism against the Church of God endured, while the impious King Henry raged against the vicar of Christ, encouraged with salutary counsel, with all his strength, all whom he could to preserve and protect the unity of the Church. And because with a pure and simple eye he pressed on in so holy and so necessary a matter, whatever he did was pleasing to the minds of all religious; whatever he said soothed the hearts of all good men with the inward affection of love. Together with dove-like simplicity, serpentine prudence always flourished in him; and because in all things he sought not his own glory but God’s, God gave him his grace, so that he acted prosperously in all matters, such that he seemed to surpass all the prudent men of this world in prudence, and was honored without envy by those who professed divine wisdom.

In these times there also flourished in England Gilbert, abbot of our monastery which is called Westminster, a disciple of blessed Anselm, a man excellently learned both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters. Among the other monuments of his talent he wrote, against the Jews, a fine disputation in no inelegant style.

In these times too there flourished Diemo, an abbot of our order in the city of Salzburg, who, because of the excommunication of King Henry IV, was expelled from his monastery, since, siding with the holy Roman Church, he refused to communicate with the excommunicated. Therefore, drawn by the fame of Saint Abbot William to the institution of the monasteries, he came to Hirsau; and, living humbly among the brothers, when he had seen the laudable ordering of their life, he resolved to remain with them in the Lord forever. And so, made a monk anew, he lived religiously under William, giving thanks to God that he had deserved to be enrolled in so holy a congregation. Then, after some years, he was raised to be archbishop of the church of Salzburg, and, compelled by obedience, was unwillingly forced to withdraw from the monastery. He presided over the aforesaid church vigorously in word and example, offering many inducements to virtues. At length, inflamed by divine love, he resolved to go with many others to the Holy Land and to visit the Lord’s sepulchre; and on the way, captured by pagans, he was crowned with martyrdom along with most of the other companions of his pilgrimage. His deeds are extant.

Around these times Rupert, formerly abbot of Reichenau, was deposed by Pope Gregory VII, the mandate being carried out by Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and every exercise of ecclesiastical order was forbidden him except psalmody, because, though summoned to Rome a third time to clear himself of the charges brought against him, he refused to go. Later, despising the prohibition of the supreme pontiff, he received from King Henry the monastery at Gengenbach, where, while according to his custom he devoted himself too immoderately to temporal gains, he was killed with another monk of the aforesaid monastery, of by no means hopeless character, against whom, after advancing upon the possessions of the monastery and his own right, he himself wished to defend himself by warding off force. In these times Pope Gregory VII, for ecclesiastical causes, sent as legate into Germany and Gaul a venerable man, outstanding in learning in the Scriptures and in [unclear], [unclear] to this our monastery of Hirsau, subject to the archbishop. From this the most reverend abbot William, with the permission of [unclear], most holy abbot of Cluny, arranged in two books, in a fair order, the statutes and customs transmitted to him, with certain things reasonably to be changed according to consideration of place, region, and climate, and handed them down to his brothers and successors to be observed for the preservation of monastic life.

1079.

In the tenth year of Abbot William, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1079, Hidolph, archbishop of Cologne, died, and Sigeuinus succeeded him. In this same year King Henry fought fiercely against the Saxons, of whom many perished.

1080.

But in the [unclear] year of Abbot William, at Brixen, a city of the Noricans, another synod of thirty bishops and many abbots and clerics was held by command of King Henry against Pope Gregory VII.

In the same Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

...who through uncleanness make themselves excluded from service at the altar. Concerning those fallen persons who have sacred orders, however, it must not by any means be asserted that, as they ought to be considered with voluntary humility, they can no longer in any way make use of those same orders, if, appeasing God by the sacrifice of a troubled spirit and of a contrite and humbled heart, they have earnestly striven to advance in virtue. For neither before God is anyone's office rejected because of a fault which he himself forgives, nor among men is the dignity of sacred order discolored because of a person whose sin they themselves do not know; for by these two causes a fall of the flesh bars access or return to sacred orders.

But since it is almost always hidden whose iniquities have been remitted, whose sins covered, and whose by no means, it is always safer for one conscious to himself of a crime, and [unclear], to abstain through praiseworthy humility than to presume through culpable security. For the former can always be done without God's disapproval; the latter ought not be done unless God approves it. But anyone who grants assent to this opinion, by which after a fall return to the office of sacred order is allowed, unless he is supported by some reason or by the authority of the Scriptures, wishes to attribute agreement to the legal epistle of blessed Pope Callistus directed to all the bishops established throughout Gaul, and to blessed Gregory to Secundinus [unclear]; for there they establish this opinion with such firm and almost identical reasons and authorities that it in no way needs the proof of others. But since the same blessed Gregory forbids this very thing in certain other epistles of his, lest he be contrary to himself, he is understood to have forbidden it in open cases, but to have allowed it in hidden cases after fitting penance. For a crime which is neither imputed by God nor thought to exist by men does not reject nor disfigure, as we have already said; nevertheless, in such a matter it is safer for anyone before God to fear more than to [unclear].

That he must necessarily be prohibited who of his own accord reveals a hidden crime by humble confession I by no means think, lest the saving power of confession be obstructed for many; for who would be able to choose it at all, if by this occasion he should be led from a hidden [unclear] into the certainty or suspicion of some crime? For it is established that they should confess their sin, but no one is compelled by custom, without his own consent, to cease from the office of his order. Rather, he seems guilty of a great crime who [unclear], because by thus compelling [unclear] he drives and compels many, still not confessed, to fear and flee confession.

For it is plain enough how much less evil it is for any sinner, after an offering [unclear] and with hope [unclear], to approach the altar with a humble mind, than with hatred of confession, despair of pardon, a hardened heart, desire, or even as if [unclear], to thrust himself in. Therefore he to whom permission is granted is by no means [unclear]; he commands a lesser fault, in which he has involved another not by consenting but by prudently guarding against a greater one. But he would seem to be a participant in, and author of, the greater crime, if by helping he drives many, even if unwillingly, yet inordinately by fearing more what is lesser than what is greatest. But it is manifest that those who, by humble contrition, trample upon proud shame, denouncing themselves and consenting of their own accord to the judgment of cessation, minister much more safely when permitted, or even ordered, than those who, with human shame, refuse justly to judge themselves between God and themselves. Although this is thus allowed, it is very dangerous to forbid the unwilling, as has been said above, rather than the willing. And since it is necessary for both, either to abstain for a time [unclear], because those who do not gladly cease from that to which they have not well advanced are then to be relaxed; but those who abstain of their own accord are even to be recalled to that which they do not presume. For in the former, if they are recalled, presumption is cloaked under the covering of obedience; but in the latter humility is aided by the strength of obedience. This renewal is not to be undertaken indifferently, but is to be carried out with great confession of the prelate receiving it and with discretion.

For it often happens that someone does not shrink from the office assigned to him through horror at the crime committed, nor overcome human shame by a life of humility, but through the darkness of folly, the very hard obstinacy of shamelessness, [unclear], or through negligence does not desire his office. But a man of this sort is never either to be recalled to sacred office or [unclear], unless the prelate is moved not so much by [unclear] as by the humility of supplication, by the intercession of a contrite change of life; then indeed, if the prelate, comforting him not so much concerning any merits as concerning the great mercy and multitude of the compassions of God, sends him back to his office or invites him, he seems to have acted not so much rashly as prudently.

For in matters of this kind pusillanimity must often be anticipated, suspicion of contempt excluded, benevolence shown, compassion displayed. In this way those who are such persons, the more kindly they are advanced to perfection, the more effectively they are bound more strictly in a good purpose. I could have inserted more than has first been written here, but because the brevity proper to a letter, which protests that it has already extended itself too much, does not allow it, I have simply set forth, at your fatherhood's command, what I thought about the matters asked. May almighty God so direct us in these and in all things that must be done by us in the uprightness of truth that for them he may repay himself as the reward. If I were present before you and your holy congregation, of which, by the merits of many, I daily hear greater things in concord, from which much good is reported and eagerly sought, I would prostrate my whole body with a suppliant mind, so that you might grant me again and more fully in fraternal charity to be a perpetual participant in the good things which God works in your holy monastery. But since, being very far away, I cannot do this, I presume, from [unclear], to ask of your holiness that you ask this very thing for me, not with body humbled but with kindly [unclear]; not concerning merits, but to ask of your holiness that you ask this same thing for me and grant it to me with that [unclear], and that you ask it for me from the same your sons and grant it with that. Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

In the same year war was again waged between Rudolf and King Henry, and Rudolf himself fell with many others. He was carried by his men to Merseburg, where he died and was buried. It is said that, when he was at the point of death and looked at his severed right hand, he said with a heavy sigh to the bishops who happened to be present: “Behold, this is the hand with which I confirmed by oath my fidelity to my lord Henry; alas, at your urging I did not keep it, and behold, wretched as I am, I am compelled to forsake life together with the kingdom. See, you who made me ascend the throne against my lord, whether you have led me by the right path as I followed your counsels.” Having said this, he expired. In his place the Saxons and the princes of Alemannia elected a certain Hermann, a very powerful nobleman from Germany; but before long he began to be regarded with contempt as a stranger, and therefore after a few years, laying aside the title of king, he betook himself to Henry’s favor.

1081.

In the twelfth year of Abbot William, and in the 1081st year of the Lord’s nativity, King Henry sought Italy with an army; and coming to Rome on the vigil of Pentecost, with Pope Gregory and the Romans resisting him, he set up fortifications before the castle of Saint Peter. There also, though harassed for two years by the frequent attacks of the townsmen, with a small force he performed many deeds bravely. He therefore besieged the city continuously for two years, and at last took it in the year of the Lord 1083, in the sixth indiction, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, which was the Friday of Pentecost week. Pope Gregory, however, fleeing secretly, withdrew to Salerno, and remained there until the day of his death. In his place, at the request of the Romans, King Henry appointed Wighert, bishop of Ravenna, as pope; he was called Clement, the third of this name. King Henry took Rome by besieging it. This [installation?] of Wighert the antipope was made while the siege of the city was continuing. In a synod of thirty bishops, as we have said, at Brixen, they falsely accused [unclear] of having invaded the apostolic see by the art of magic, necromancy, and the aid of demons, and with many other falsehoods they deposed him in his absence. When Pope Gregory heard this, after an assembly of bishops and abbots had been gathered, he excommunicated the invader of the apostolic see together with all who had been in the synod of Brixen, and also King Henry with all his supporters, and cursed them with great severity.

Mainz is consumed by fire together with the church.

In the same year also of Abbot William, namely the twelfth, the city of Mainz was for the greater part consumed by fire, together with the principal church and three monasteries. Henry, the fifth king of this name, was born. The monastery at Bamberg too was burned on the vigil of holy Easter.

One hundred fifty monks and forty lay brothers of this monastery.

1082.

In the year of the Lord 1082, when the number of monks of this community under the most reverend Abbot William, the Lord bestowing his blessing, had greatly increased, so that because of their multitude the narrowness of the place at Saint Aurelius could scarcely contain them; for there were more than one hundred fifty monks, besides the lay brothers, of whom there were no fewer than forty; the holy man began to take counsel with those same brothers of his about enlarging the aforesaid monastery somewhat. But since this could not suitably be done, because of the narrow and less convenient situation of the place and the arrangement of the buildings, after taking counsel he [decided?] on a new monastery across the river in a somewhat higher place and for that reason also healthier, [unclear]. The [cloister?] of the monastery begins to be founded at Hirsau. The monastery at Bamberg too was burned on the vigil of holy Easter. When he had begun to prepare the necessities for this work, [unclear] of timber [unclear].

The marchioness gives expenses to the abbot.

At that time a certain powerful and wealthy margrave named Hermann, drawn by the divine spirit and despising the world with all its possessions and pomp for the love of God, fled secretly, with no one except his wife knowing, and went unknown to the monastery of Cluny; and, having received from Saint Hugh the abbot the habit of holy conversion, for love of the supreme Shepherd he became shepherd of the livestock of that same monastery. After the departure of the aforesaid husband, the wife of this most excellent man, wishing God to be heir of her goods, [gave?] costs and expenses to the holy Abbot William for building the new monastery that had been begun, [unclear] so that he would leave it unfinished with hands withdrawn. Yet from what she had previously contributed, so much of the expenses remained that nearly all the rest that was left was completed. But the most reverend Abbot William began to build the larger monastery in the thirteenth year of his rule, which was the 1082nd year of the Lord’s nativity, in the fifth indiction, and in nine years the whole [unclear].

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

...completed the building, so that in the tenth year the church was consecrated. It is to be believed that he had no other craftsmen for this building than his own monks, since they were nearly two hundred in number; among them were stonecutters, carpenters, blacksmiths, and architects undoubtedly most experienced in every art and science of architecture. Thus they completed the whole work without the help of secular craftsmen, with excellent timberwork, as the church is seen today. For the other buildings of the monastery, apart from the church, were almost all changed in the course of time by various abbots.

1083.

In the following year, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1083, Abbot Wilhelm founded the cell of Saint Gregory in Reichenbach. We have thought it better to insert the sequence of this foundation in his own words rather than in those of another.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Wilhelm, by no merits of my own but by the mercy of God alone abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, desire it to be known to all, both future and present, that a certain free elder named Bern gave his little estate, situated in the Black Forest, in the place which is called Reichenbach from the stream that there flows into the Murg, to Saint Aurelius of Hirsau, in the presence of suitable witnesses, as an eternal inheritance, requesting this in return: that I should arrange for a monastery to be built there. Therefore, having received the common and concordant counsel of our elders, [unclear] we sent three of our brother monks and five lay brothers to that little estate, bristling with very dense woodland, so that, the forest having been cleared and the place made ready, they might build a monastery for blessed Gregory.

And so, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1082, indiction 5, around the Ides of May, when those brothers came to the aforesaid place, for not a few days they made use of bare fir-wood as a hut. One of them was called Ernest, an upright and courtly man, who had already some time before given himself and all his possessions to our obedience; him, together with all his goods, we assigned to the same place as a helper. This Ernest therefore became provider for the place and the brothers, and as it were a second father: for the clearing of the forest, the preparation of the site, the building of the monastery, and the construction of workshops, he himself especially gave the expenses and suitably procured resources from every side. I therefore judged it fitting that his memory and that of his parents, as also mine and my people’s, should be celebrated there, and I gladly confirmed it. Indeed, the foundation of the church was laid in the fourteenth year of the aforesaid Abbot Wilhelm, when [unclear] was completed.

In the aforesaid monastery of Reichenbach there is a priory of our order, which from the time of its foundation down to the present day has been immediately subject to the abbot of this monastery in full right and lordship. To him belongs the right of instituting and removing the prior of that place as often as there is need, and of consecrating monks there, and of doing the other things which are recognized today as held by custom and privilege. He also has similar jurisdiction over the priory in Schönrain, situated in the borders of Franconia, which is simply and immediately subject to the abbot of Hirsau in all things; he has the right of instituting and removing the prior and of arranging each matter that is known to pertain to the authority of priories of this kind. The provostry also in Rode, in the diocese of Augsburg, belongs immediately to the right of the monastery of Hirsau; its provost is subject in full right to the abbot of Hirsau. But the holy Abbot Wilhelm at that time still possessed under his jurisdiction several more priories of our order, which in the course of time, having been changed into abbeys, were alienated from the jurisdiction of the monastery of Hirsau. At this time the monastic order flourished in this monastery, highly distinguished not only by the number of monks but also by the rank of persons and the quality of their merits.

For, as we said in the preceding sections, when the fame of the most holy man Abbot Wilhelm had been spread far and wide through the world, many men began to flock to him, noble and wealthy in the world, who, despising all the things and pomps of the world, undertook to bear the sweet yoke of the Lord under his obedience. And although it is not within our power to preserve the memory of all of them, nevertheless, lest we seem to have recited a tale to those ignorant of the glory of the old monks of Hirsau, let us set forth at least the names of a few out of many, joining to them the dignities over which they presided.

Gebhard, son of the duke of Alemania and brother of Duke Berthold, a man distinguished not only by nobility of blood but also by wisdom, eloquence, and learning in the Scriptures, despised the world and, for love of God, became a monk in this our monastery under the holy father Wilhelm. He was afterward ordained bishop of Constance, and together with his brother Duke Berthold did many good things for this monastery of Hirsau. Another Gebhard of the same name, a noble and learned man, became a monk in this our monastery under the same father Wilhelm; he succeeded Wilhelm himself in the abbacy, and at length was appointed bishop of the church of Speyer...

80

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

But to the monastery of Lauense, which Father S. built in the province of the Carinthians, as was said above, he appointed as abbot Wetzillo, a vigorous man, revered for religious severity, and sufficiently imbued both with monastic institutions and with knowledge of the Scriptures.

Segewinus, a monk of the monastery of Hirsau, sent into Carinthia with the aforesaid abbot Wetzillo without the permission of Abbot Gebhard and of the brethren of Hirsau, received the abbacy of Rosati near Aquileia. When he learned that this displeased his brethren, he returned, contrite, to the monastery of Hirsau, and in the meantime resigned that abbacy of his. Abbot Gebhard, to test his penitence and contrition, made him sit in the last place of the congregation. When he saw that he bore this humbly, with the counsel of the brethren he restored him to his proper place. But another certain man of ours, named Gaudentius, who had gone with him, having likewise obtained an abbacy without the consent of the brethren of Hirsau, did not return to the monastery for penance, and therefore is not counted among the abbots sent from Hirsau. They also rejected Manegold, a monk of the convent of Hirsau, who without the consent of the abbot and brethren had obtained the abbacy of Campidonum in the diocese of Constance from King Henry V through the intervention of friends, by the unanimous counsel of his brethren and abbots.

To the monastery which is called Beinwil, a certain monk of the monastery of Hirsau was given as abbot, named Esso, a man mature in morals and life and a fervent zealot of regular discipline, under Abbot Gebhard, who succeeded St. William.

But to the monastery in Odenheim of the diocese of Speyer, the abbot who had been sent gave Everard, a very notable monk of the convent of Hirsau; concerning its foundation we shall make mention hereafter in its own time. Gerung also, a monk of Hirsau and prior of St. Aurelius across the bridge, certainly a very religious man, was made abbot of the monastery of Paulinzelle in Saxony, in the diocese of Mainz, under Abbot Bruno; concerning his praiseworthy way of life, when we have come to the year of the Lord 1107 and the times of that Bruno, we shall speak more fully. To the same place, Paulinzelle, after Gerung, Ulrich was taken up as abbot, a monk of this monastery of Hirsau, a man revered in morals and life, and no less worthy and fit for pastoral care by his learning in the Scriptures than by his conduct.

To the monastery also in Godifangia of the diocese of Speyer, the venerable monk of this house named Wolpeto was sent as abbot, a man of great virtues and very well experienced in spiritual as well as temporal matters. To the same monastery also, at another later time, Burchard, a monk of the monastery of Hirsau, was appointed abbot, a distinguished lover of regular discipline.

But to the monastery of Mons Monachorum near Bamberg in East Francia, Wölfran, a monk, was transferred at the insistence of the brethren serving God there, and was solemnly ordained abbot. Evernold, a monk of this monastery of Hirsau, was appointed abbot at the monastery of Briuernugense, a man most holy in knowledge and conduct; he is said to have shone with many miracles in life and after death, and his life and conduct, together with his miracles, written in two little books, are preserved more fully in the aforesaid monastery.

Drutwin, a monk of this monastery of Hirsau, was sent with twelve monks to a newly built monastery of the diocese of Mainz in Hesse, and was ordained abbot in the year of the Lord 1119, under Abbot Bruno. The name of the monastery is called Breitenau; concerning it we shall speak more fully afterward in its own place and time. Egbert, a monk of this monastery, was sent to Passau about the same time and appointed abbot, a man not at all poorly learned, of venerable reputation among us both for morals and for learning in the Scriptures. To the same place also afterward the venerable [unclear] of this [unclear] was appointed abbot, who was a distinguished cultivator of regular discipline. Reginbold, a monk of the monastery, was sent to a certain monastery which is called Navy, and at the insistence of many was ordained abbot. Adelbert also, a monk of this monastery, after the death of that Reginbold, was sent as abbot to the same place, a man worthy of so great an honor, since he was venerable no less in life than in knowledge.

Another Adelbert also, a monk of this monastery, a man distinguished in morals and knowledge, was sent to the monastery in Echlingen of the diocese of Augsburg at the insistence of the monks of that same place, and was solemnly ordained abbot. Since he was a very religious man Chronicle of Jo. Trithemius.

was appointed, as we shall say below in its proper place. Dietgerus also became a monk of our monastery under the holy father Wilhelm, a man distinguished in character and learning; on account of the merit of his life and his learned knowledge, he was ordained bishop in the church of Metz. Many monks from our monastery, both under the holy father Wilhelm and under his various successors, were at different times given as abbots to other monasteries. Of these, some in the course of time became bishops in various places. We have the names of all of them, although we do not know the dates of some; therefore, lest any be overlooked in the reckoning of the years, we have resolved briefly to arrange in this place a universal catalogue of all who have been reported to us.

Sigefrid, a monk of our house under the holy father Wilhelm, was ordained by the same Wilhelm as abbot in the monastery of Schaffhausen, of our order, in the diocese of Constance. That monastery, almost collapsed through age, the holy father restored with fine panel-work and gave to the aforesaid abbot and monks. Heinrich too, a monk, an energetic man and a most upright zealot for regular discipline, was appointed by the holy father Wilhelm as first abbot of St. George the Martyr in the Black Forest, which he himself had built from the foundations, as we said far above. To the monastery of Petershausen, in the same diocese of Constance, he gave as abbot Dietheric, a venerable man, distinguished in character and knowledge, a monk of this house, who was a fervent cultivator and restorer of regular discipline and led many by word and example to contempt of the world.

To the monastery in Hasungen, in the diocese of Mainz, situated in the regions of Thuringia, about which we spoke above, he sent as first abbot one of his monks, with a whole community, named Giselbert. After he was later expelled by King Heinrich IV because of the excommunication of the supreme pontiff, and returned to Hirsau with seventy monks, he appointed him abbot of the monastery in Reinhardsbrunn, on the borders of Thuringia, in the same diocese of Mainz; he also undertook the governance of the monastery of Erfurt.

To the monastery in Zwiefalten, in the diocese of Constance, he also gave as abbot Notger, a monk, a man very well imbued with monastic disciplines, suitable in every respect, who could instruct the monks by words and examples according to the norm of regular life.

To the monastery in Camburg, in the diocese of Würzburg, which has now been transferred from the order, he gave as abbot Gunther, a monk, a man venerable for prudence and religion, who before his conversion had gained a great reputation for experience in courtly affairs.

To the cell of St. Peter, which had been transferred from Weilheim above, he appointed as abbot Adelbero, a man not moderately distinguished in monastic disciplines and experience; taught under his mastership the whole foundation of the institution of regular life, he converted many to piety by his example.

To the monastery in Altdorf, in the diocese of Strasbourg, he gave as abbot, by name Welchio, a venerable monk, very well instructed in monastic life. Trained by the best teacher in all disciplined conduct, he strove to show himself a not useless shepherd to the sheep of Christ.

To the monastery called Buren, in the diocese of Augsburg, he sent as abbot Azelmus, a venerable monk, who, born of illustrious family, [unclear]. Otto, a monk of our house, was appointed abbot after Azelmus. Whether this was done under Wilhelm or under his successor Gebhard, we do not know sufficiently. The same Otto afterwards also undertook the governance of the monastery of Rheinau, in the diocese of Constance.

To the monastery of St. John of Magdeburg in Saxony, whose foundation we described far above, he sent as abbot the monk Hildebold, a very venerable man, about whom many proclamations of praise are reported. To the same house later Brother Hugo, a monk of our Hirsau community, was sent and ordained abbot, a man of great prudence, honesty, and religion.

To the monastery situated in the diocese of Constance, which is called Isny, the holy father ordained as abbot a monk of his community, of much religion and devotion, named Erckenbald, very well instructed in monastic institutions. To the same place Bruno, a monk of the Hirsau house, was afterwards ordained abbot, a man venerable and very distinguished in piety and religion, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures.

Dietgerus, bishop of Metz.

Hildebold, abbot at Magdeburg; Hugo.

Erckenbald, abbot at Isny.

Bruno, abbot of Hirsau. Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

Religious and prudent, he enlarged the monastery entrusted to him, adorning it in no small measure in both estates.

Adelhelmus also, a monk of this Hirsau monastery, a learned and religious man, of whom someone sang thus:

This man by his conduct drew the loves of all, And did not change his pious ways because of honors.

He was first appointed abbot of the monastery called Ammineberg; and then, after some years, having been transferred to the monastery of Mediolac in the diocese of Trier, he undertook, by public consent and at the request of all the monks dwelling there, the abbacy of that place to be governed, which he administered energetically and laudably all the way to the end of his life.

To the monastery of St. Peter in Erfurt, in the diocese of Mainz, after the death of Abbot Rupert, there was sent from this Hirsau monastery, in the year of the Lord 1128, under Abbot Volmar, a venerable monk named Vernerus, who, having been appointed abbot there, acquired many goods for that monastery by his own industry. With marvelous ingenuity and no small expense he began an aqueduct into the monastery and brought it to a sufficiently useful completion.

After the death also of Drutnuinus, first abbot in Breitenau, of whom we spoke above, Henricus, a monk of this Hirsau monastery, was appointed abbot of the place in the year of the Lord 1132, in the tenth indiction, under Abbot Volmar; of him more broadly must be said at the proper time.

Diethericus, however, a monk of this Hirsau monastery, under the same Abbot Volmar, was sent to the monastery of St. Felicitas near the city of Würzburg, which is called Schwarzach, at the insistence of its monks and the prayers of the bishop of Würzburg, and was ordained abbot.

Conradus, a monk of Hirsau, a very venerable man, was first made prior in the monastery of Schōrein, and then, ordained abbot of the monastery of Amorbach in the diocese of Würzburg, he notably enlarged it with buildings and revenues, and in his time magnificently renewed there the fervor of regular discipline, already almost collapsed.

Another Conradus of the same name, also a monk of this Hirsau monastery, was given as abbot to the monastery of Schwarzach beside the Rhine in the diocese of Strasbourg, at the petitions and insistence of the brothers and of the bishop of that place. He was a very religious man, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures.

Burchardus also, a monk noble by birth, but nobler in virtue of conduct and in learning of the Scriptures, was given as abbot far away to the monastery called Vinea, commonly Weingarten, in the diocese of Constance, in the time of Abbot Manegold.

Dithmarus, a man of reverend memory, after the death of Burchardus was sent to the same place from this Hirsau monastery and ordained abbot; by life and conduct he took care to show himself, in word and example, a worthy shepherd for the sheep of Christ.

Rupertus also, a venerable monk of this Hirsau monastery, was given as abbot to the monastery of Gottesaue in the diocese of Speyer under Abbot Manegold; because of the wickedness of his subjects, he at last resigned the abbacy and returned to Hirsau, and after the death of Manegold was elected abbot of this place in the year of the Lord 1165, in the tenth indiction. Of him we shall make suitably fuller mention at the proper time.

To the monastery of Tharis, which is situated in the parish of Würzburg, about five miles distant from Bamberg downstream along the Main, Rudigerus, a monk distinguished in conduct and learning, was given as abbot from this Hirsau monastery under the venerable Abbot Manegold.

To the monastery called Besselbornen, in the diocese of Augsburg, Lupoldus, a monk from this Hirsau monastery, was sent as abbot: a man not ignoble according to fleshly kinship, but by virtue of mind and knowledge of the Scriptures far nobler than many of the most noble.

Diepoldus, a monk of this monastery, a very studious man and an exceptional lover of books, was sent to the monastery in Schaffhausen, in the diocese of Constance, and solemnly ordained abbot.

To the monastery of Zwiefalten in the diocese of Constance, another Godfridus, also a monk of this Hirsau monastery, a man worthy of honor, was ordained abbot; he always most diligently strove to feed the flock entrusted to him by word and example.

Furthermore, to the monastery of Lorsch in the diocese [unclear], which the Premonstratensians inhabit today, Sigehardus, a monk from this Hirsau monastery, outstanding in life and conduct, was given as abbot; he magnificently restored that place in both estates.

Sigehardus, abbot in Lorsch. 82

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

To the monastery also of Saint Ferrucius in Blidenstad, in the diocese of Mainz, which about three years before this had been transferred by the order, Henry, a monk of this monastery, was sent and was ordained legitimate abbot.

Rudolph also, a monk of Hirsau, having been ordained abbot for the monastery of Gotifau in the diocese of Speyer, by his prudence and by the zealous care of his observance brought back the depraved morals of the monks to the standard of regular observance. Megingus, a monk of this monastery, on account of his diligence and praiseworthy way of life was first appointed prior in Richenbach, and afterwards, ordained abbot of the monastery of Weingarten in the diocese of Constance, presided not idly over the flock entrusted to him.

But to the monastery of Gotifau in the diocese of Speyer, after the death of Abbot Rudolph, at the petitions of the brothers of that place, Conrad, a monk of this monastery of Hirsau, was sent and legitimately ordained abbot.

Another Conrad also, of the same name, a monk of this monastery, was ordained abbot of the monastery of Alpersbach in the diocese of Constance: a man very diligent and experienced in conducting worldly affairs, and not ignorant of divine institutions, who vigorously presided over that monastery and took care to show himself in all things a useful pastor, both by word and by example.

To the monastery in Hornbach in the diocese of Metz, to me the death of Abbot Rudolph, Conrad of the same name, the abbacy of Alperbach. 10

to me, at the petitions of the brothers of the same place, Conrad, a monk there of the monastery of Hirsau, was legitimately ordained as abbot.

Another Conrad also, of the same name, a monk of this monastery, was ordained abbot of the monastery of Alpersbach in the diocese of Constance: a man very diligent and experienced in conducting worldly affairs, and not ignorant of divine institutions, who vigorously presided over that monastery and took care to show himself in all things a useful pastor in all respects, both by word and by example.

To the monastery in Suerzach beside the Rhine, in the diocese of Strasbourg, Hildebert, a monk of this monastery, was given as abbot; adorned in no low degree with morals and learning, he was held worthy of such an honor.

But Marquard, a monk of this monastery, himself also a man of many virtues and a zealous lover of the divine scriptures, was sent to the monastery in Deckingen in the diocese of Augsburg at the request of the monks staying there, and was duly ordained abbot for it.

To the monastery also in Alpersbach, to me, in place of an abbot of venerable memory, [unclear] of this monastery of Hirsau, named Berthold, who for some time was prior of the cell of Saint Gregory in Richenbach, a man worthy of every honor.

But to the monastery in Otrenburen in the diocese of Augsburg, William was directed as abbot: first a monk of this monastery of Hirsau, and then provost in Roth, of the same diocese of Augsburg, from there called to the abbacy by the bishops and monks of the aforesaid monastery.

To the monastery in Schuttera in the diocese of Strasbourg, of whose foundation we made mention much earlier above, John, surnamed Wedel, a monk of this monastery, was given as abbot. He first existed for some years as claustral prior in this place; then he was made prior in Richenbach; and finally, under Abbot Blasius, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1492, indiction 10, when John Phul, abbot in Schuttera, had died, who first took up our reformation commonly called Bursfeld, he was ordained abbot in his place: a man mild in disposition, yet not lax; sufficiently diligent in handling temporal cares; irreproachable before all who knew him in zeal for regular discipline and in making his life honorable. Since he is still considered to be present in life, we are admonished by religious propriety to refrain from his praises. But now, with the names of those who, from this monastery, from the time of Abbot William down to the present year of the Lord’s nativity 1501, in which we have written these things, Maximilian ruling the Romans, were appointed abbots for various monasteries, having been duly marked in order as far as they have come to our knowledge, although through the negligence of the ancients the names of many have been omitted, we must at last return to the order of the history undertaken.

1083.

Therefore in the fifteenth year of Abbot William, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1084, King Henry, the fourth of this name, with Bertha his wife, on the holy day of Easter at Rome received the imperial blessing from the antipope Clement. Afterwards, departing from there and crossing Italy, he besieged and took Augsburg, the city of the Raetians, which had been invaded by the Alemanni.

1085.

In the following year, which was the sixteenth of Abbot William, a great synod of bishops and abbots was celebrated at Mainz, in the monastery of the holy martyr Alban, by order of King Henry against Saint Pope Gregory VII. He himself was personally present at it with the envoys of the antipope Clement, and all [unclear], who, although he was weak in body, nevertheless, with his mind lifted upward to God, always remained sound and firm in the contemplation of divine things. His manner of life was an example to all; in his character the highest religion, true wisdom, and perfect charity shone forth. By the appointment of Abbot William, Diethericus, a monk, a man worthy of every honor, succeeded this holy man in the priorship of this monastery. He was afterward made abbot of the monastery of Petershausen in Constance, as we have said above, where by word and example he called back the flocks entrusted to him by God to the paths of righteousness. After him the holy father William appointed as prior Otto, a monk, a venerable old man, mature in character and conduct and worthy of reverence by all, who was prior for a few months indeed, but cellarer of the monastery for many years. For in arranging temporal affairs and domestic matters he was vigorous with the greatest foresight; hence it came about that, while he wisely disposed all outward things, the holy father was more freely intent on leisure within. And although, by reason of care for the household, he was compelled with Martha to be anxious about many things, nevertheless he did not neglect Mary’s spiritual leisure, but always cared for temporal things in such a way that he did not omit the holy exercises of spiritual life. After him the holy father appointed as prior Gebhard, a man of noble birth and, in all matters to be done, admirable for exceptional prudence; he also succeeded to the abbacy of this monastery, as we shall say later, and of his character and life we shall speak in its proper place.

1089.

In the twentieth year of Abbot William, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1089, Sigewinus, archbishop of Cologne, died; Hermann the third, surnamed the Rich, succeeded him in order.

After the death of Dietmar, bishop of Worms, which occurred in the year of the Lord 1085, in the [unclear] indiction, Eppo was ordained bishop and flourished in these times; many wonderful things are told about him, and he presided in his episcopate for not a few years. The emperor celebrated his marriage at Cologne, taking as wife a certain widow of Margrave Udo, named Praxedis, daughter of the king of the Rus’, by whom he received a son named Henry, who after his father ruled, Conrad having been repudiated, and a daughter named Agnes. Then, departing to Aachen, he caused his elder son Conrad to be anointed king; nevertheless he later repudiated him after Henry the fifth had been born.

In this year there was a very great pestilence in the western part of Lotharingia, where many, as a fire arose within and consumed their inward parts, rotted away, their limbs eaten off and blackening like coals, and either died miserably or, their hands or feet having rotted, were left maimed for a still more miserable life. Many others, distorted by contraction of the sinews, were tormented by a miserable kind of torture. There were great earthquakes in different places of Europe.

1090.

In the twenty-first year of Abbot William, which was the year of the Lord 1090, the emperor entered Italy again and remained there for almost seven years. He surrounded Florence with a siege and committed many crimes.

1091.

In the twenty-second year of Abbot William, not yet completed, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1091, the greater monastery of Hirsau, which that holy father himself had begun eight years before, was, as it is seen today, completed from the beginning of its foundation in the new [unclear] year. The [unclear] of the apostles of Christ Peter and Paul having been completed, and this dedication having been made, the holy father burned with a wondrous desire to be able to have some relics of the holy prince of the apostles, in whose honor he had built so costly a church. Therefore, having consulted the counsel of the elders, he sent to Cluny his prior Gebhard, a learned and very prudent man, to Hugh, the venerable and most holy abbot, asking that he would deign to send him some relics of Saint Peter the apostle. But the holy father Hugh, abbot of Cluny,

Diethericus, prior of this place.

Otto, prior and cellarer of this place.

Hermann.

The emperor entered Italy again.

A dreadful plague was among the people.

The emperor [unclear] entered [unclear].

Completion of the new monastery.

Note [unclear] for father William [unclear].

Gebhard, prior of Cluny, minister [unclear]. and he forcibly compelled all who were against Gregory to swear obedience to that same Clement. This synod was presided over by Wezilo, archbishop of Mainz, successor of Bishop Siegfried, about whom we remember having already said more above; he pronounced Pope Gregory deposed. This Wezilo was a learned man, both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, sweet in speech and most eloquent, and in his time he was held to be so great a preacher of the word of God that he had no equal. William, the most holy abbot, summoned to this synod by royal letters, scorned to come, [unclear] by a subtle contrivance, preferring boldly to subject himself to dangers to his property and body in defense of the vicar of Christ rather than to be stained by agreement with the wicked.

In the same year Pope Gregory VII died at Salerno. He was first succeeded by canonical election by Desiderius, abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino, of our order, who was called Victor III.

1086.

In the seventeenth year of Abbot William, which was the year 1086 from the Lord’s Nativity, King Henry, angry at Saxony and the country on every side, laid it waste with a great army by plunder and fire. Hermann, however, whom the Saxons, by order of Pope Gregory, had set up as king against Henry, gathered as large an army as possible and met him near Würzburg in the place called Bleichfeld; there, when battle was joined, an innumerable multitude on both sides [unclear]. Hermann obtained the victory and took the city of Würzburg; yet King Henry soon recovered it by the strong hand of his men.

In this same year the Carthusian order began to be founded in the diocese of Grenoble, which happened as follows. Saint Hugh, then bishop of Grenoble, saw in a dream that in the solitude of Chartreuse a dwelling was to be built for God by his favor, and also seven stars providing him guidance for the journey. And behold, drawn by the odor of his holiness, seven men came to him; all of them, kindled by one desire, were seeking a place suited to the eremitic life, but had not yet found it. The first of these was Bruno, born at Cologne, master in theology at Paris, a man most famous for religion and learning; the other four were men of letters and two were laymen. Saint Hugh received them graciously and made them attain their wish. For by his counsel, aid, and companionship, they entered the solitude of Chartreuse and built the dwellings necessary for their purpose. Around the same time flourished Stephen the Levite, a man most renowned for miracles, abstinence, and holiness; born in Auvergne, he migrated to the territory of Limoges and practiced the eremitic life for almost fifty years with the few who had gathered to him. From him the order of Grandmont began.

In this same year Marianus Scotus, monk of Fulda, a distinguished chronographer, about whom we made mention far above, died at Mainz, enclosed for the love of Christ, and was buried with due honor in the greater church of Saint Martin.

1087.

In the eighteenth year of Abbot William, which was the one thousand eighty-seventh year of the Lord, Pope Victor died after drinking poison in the sacred chalice; many report that this was done by the plots of King Henry and Wibert the antipope.

After him Otto, bishop of Ostia, was elected as true vicar of Christ, and was called Urban II; he sat twelve years and four months. He was first a cleric of the church of Reims, afterward became a monk of Cluny of our order, then prior of the same monastery, from prior bishop of Ostia, and finally from bishop was made pope.

Hermann, having laid aside the false name of king, returned to his own possessions by permission of the emperor; after a few days he was killed and died in the siege of a certain town.

The empress Bertha died and was buried at Mainz, but afterward she was transferred by the emperor to Speyer.

1088.

In the following year, which was the nineteenth of Abbot William and the year of the Lord 1088, Wezilo, archbishop of Mainz, died; Ruthard succeeded him. In this same year the city of Augsburg was taken by the treachery of the Swabians on the Lord’s Supper day, and on the second weekday after the feast of Easter it was destroyed by the same men.

At these times Adelbert the monk was illustrious in this monastery of Hirsau; under the father Saint William he carried out the office of prior energetically for not a few years. For he was a man adorned with every beauty of virtues, in holiness of conduct by no means degenerate from a good master [unclear].

[Cluniacensis?], having received the letters of his very dear Wilhelm and learned of his desire, sent with letters, by the hands of that same prior Gebhard, most precious and true relics from the hair of St. Peter the Apostle. But before Gebhard returned to Hirsau, the servant of Christ Wilhelm passed to the Lord, as we shall say in its proper place. For after the dedication of the new monastery he survived only nine weeks; and therefore, because of the shortness of the time, the congregation did not leave the monastery of St. Aurelius while the holy abbot was alive.

Therefore, as the feast of the most blessed apostles of Christ Peter and Paul was approaching, an illness seized the most reverend abbot Wilhelm. Although he was weak in body, he nevertheless attended the night watches and the divine offices with most devout presence. On the feast day of those Apostles he celebrated Mass privately at the principal altar of the new monastery, and this was his last; he was supported by the hands of the brothers on both sides, since he was wholly unable to stand by himself. Thus with the greatest devotion of mind toward God, as if about to depart to him whom he had faithfully served in this life and about to receive the reward of his work, he began the Mass with as loud a voice as he could, saying in the words of the most blessed Apostle Paul: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to keep my deposit until that day, the just judge.” On the fourth day before his death he had himself carried into the chapter, and, all having been summoned, with Mass [unclear] before him, he received the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ from the hand of the priest with great devotion. [Unclear] they might make progress, first admonishing them to maintain continual love of God, zeal for monastic religion, the observance of mutual charity, and hospitality to be carefully kept. And, like another Moses in Deuteronomy, he repeated everything whatsoever he had taught them from the beginning. Then, on the third day, he again had himself carried into the oratory of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin, which he himself had built on the southern side, and, Mass having been celebrated before him, he received the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ from the hand of the priest with great devotion. Then, joined with the sacred oil, he was carried back to his cell, where, saying farewell to the brothers, on the following day he happily rested in the Lord, on the fourth day before the Nones of July, in the year of the Lord’s nativity [unclear], in the twenty-second year of his rule, and in the sixty-fifth year of his age.

Two bishops, five abbots, and many clerics with the people came to his funeral rites; for five continuous days they celebrated his obsequies. When these had been completed, they buried his holy body with honor and reverence in the middle of the new church which he had built, and they adorned his tomb with suitable construction.

After the holy abbot Wilhelm had died, and while prior Gebhard was absent, great sorrow overtook the brothers, because to remain long without a shepherd seemed full of danger to them; and they did not dare to establish [unclear]. But while they were awaiting the arrival of their prior, behold, after a few days the man they desired arrived, bringing with him the precious relics of the prince of the Apostles, namely true hairs from his head, which St. Hugh, abbot of Cluny, sent as a great gift to the most reverend father Wilhelm as a sign of mutual love. But Gebhard, using prudent counsel, did not immediately bring the relics of the blessed Apostle into the monastery, but entrusted them to a certain faithful priest living nearby, until at an opportune time, with fitting honor, [they might be brought] to the monastery. But very many other monasteries also, under the title of mutual confederation, were received by the holy abbot Wilhelm into the same confraternity of the monks of Hirsau; excessive antiquity of time has not allowed their names to come down to our memory. Canons also of secular churches, and likewise of cathedrals, established in various provinces, and many noble princes and powerful bishops in the world, having heard of the most holy way of life of Abbot Wilhelm and of the monks of Hirsau, commending themselves most devoutly to their prayers, prayed the more urgently to be received into their confraternity. For such great good things were spoken everywhere, in Wilhelm's time, by all who loved God, about that most holy congregation, that all who had been admitted into their confraternity believed themselves blessed. Nor among many at that time was this famous remembrance of the monasteries, amassed [unclear], idle; for the souls of the dead [unclear] many noble [unclear] and powerful bishops in the world, having heard of the most holy way of life of Abbot Wilhelm and of the monks of Hirsau, commending themselves most devoutly to their prayers, prayed the more urgently to be received into their [unclear]. For these agreements stipulated that whenever anyone deceased from a monastery received under the aforesaid confraternity had been announced in the monastery of Hirsau, the appointed prayers, vigils, masses, disciplines, and alms should immediately be made for him.

Therefore, when the most holy abbot Wilhelm had happily died, the abbacy was vacant for twenty-seven days because of the absence of Gebhard, the future abbot, then indeed prior, whom, as we have said, had been sent to Cluny for the relics of St. Peter the Apostle.

Concerning Gebhard, thirteenth abbot of this monastery, who presided for fourteen years and three months; concerning the deeds of his time.

After the most reverend and most holy abbot had happily entered the way of all flesh, and after the abbacy of this monastery had been vacant for 27 days, the brothers came together as one for the election of a new shepherd, on the day which is called the feast of Peter in Chains, when, as we have said before, the hairs of the same Apostle, in the presence of many abbots, monks, and faithful, had been brought into the monastery [unclear].

The abbacy was vacant for 27 days.

they unanimously elected this Gebhard, their prior, as abbot: a man sufficiently fit for the governance of souls, a Swabian by nation, singularly imbued with learning and eloquence. He was elected, as is reported, on the first day of the month of August, in the year of the Lord 1091, indiction 14, under Emperor Henry IV and Pope Urban II, and presided over the monastery for 14 years and 3 months. When these had elapsed, he was elected bishop of the church of Speyer, as we shall say in its proper place.

He was, as we have said, of Swabian origin, born of noble stock, in bodily stature neither too short nor ungainly through excessive height, but proportioned with due moderation; adorned with black hair around his head, stout in body, and disposed with handsome balance. When he was still a boy, he was handed over by his parents to teachers to learn letters; in these, over time, he made such progress that he scarcely had an equal in all literature, both secular and divine. For he was a man most learned in every respect and endowed with singular eloquence, both in the Roman and in the Teutonic language.

At length, when the years of boyhood had been passed in the study of letters, he was made a canon in the church of Strasbourg. There, when he daily increased in wealth and honors, he thought of nothing less than conversion. For contrition is rarely accustomed to be present among the rich, especially clerics, because the more they devote themselves to worldly cares, the less they are solicitous for their own salvation. So also this Gebhard the canon, of whom we are speaking, when he was vainly raised up above himself by nobility of birth and abundance of riches, not only showed no good to the poor of Christ, and especially to monks, but even, despising and contemning them, was accustomed to inflict many wrongs upon them.

For the wine which, from the donation of the faithful, accrued in Alsace to the brethren of the monastery of Hirsau, he seized by violence and, against the will of all, turned to his own uses. He was able to do this the more easily because he knew that the holy man William, who agreed with the Roman Church, could hope for no aid of defense from King Henry, to whom he was subject. Yet, admonished by good men concerning this rash deed, he came to Hirsau to reach an agreement with Abbot William, swollen, proud, and exalted, showing in dress and gestures nothing less than love of religion. But almighty God, in whose power are the hearts of all men, who made Saul, the persecutor of the Christian faith, into Paul, its defender, suddenly changed the mind of this man also to another purpose.

For with keen consideration he began to observe the manners and way of life of the brethren, and he heard the holy father discoursing on contempt of the world. Captivated by his speech, with the Holy Spirit acting within, he suddenly changed his purpose; and, bidding farewell to the pomps and cares of the world, he became in this monastery, under the monastic habit, a servant of God.

After he had for some time lived laudably among the brethren, sound and unharmed, in order that his patience might be proved before all, [unclear]. For apart from his tongue, up to that time he could move none of his members. But one day the man of the Lord William entered the cell of the sick man and exhorted Gebhard, as he lay there, to seek from the Lord with devout prayers at least the use of his right hand. He refused, [saying that] with [unclear] purged away he could reach God. But the kindly father, moved by mercy, took his right hand, blessed it, prayed, and kissed him; and suddenly, with all looking on, restored him to his former health.

After a few days, however, the wife of this Gebhard’s brother, a noble lady, came with a large household for the grace of visitation. He was carried to her in a carrying-chair; and when, in conversation, he brought forward the miraculous healing of his arm, she took that healed right hand and, in womanly fashion, kissed it as though it were something sanctified. Then, with all looking on, what had happened suddenly occurred: soon at the touch of the woman his arm was miraculously returned to its former rigidity. Then the holy abbot William said: “This is the punishment for your rashness, brother, because you offered to be kissed by a woman, out of the touch of empty glory, the hand consecrated to God and healed by his own compassion.” Admonished by what had happened, although the devoted [woman] [unclear], he concealed what had occurred, greeted his brother’s wife, and had himself carried back to his cell.

His arm [unclear]. The [unclear] of Saint Abbot William. Gebhard limped on one foot.

[He was] a man as distinguished by nobility of birth as he was lofty in sharpness of intellect and notable for the prerogative of constancy of mind, wisdom, knowledge, and singular eloquence, and also of great repute in the world: ...of reputation he was scourged by the Lord's pious chastisement, lest perhaps, when all things were succeeding prosperously, his mind should slip into the sickness of pride.

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

Restored to health, since he lived religiously in all things, he was appointed prior of this monastery, on the counsel of the brothers, by the holy father William. In that office he showed great diligence, and always zealously went before the brothers in all humility, patience, charity, and regular observance.

Afterwards, when the holy father William was much occupied in the construction of the new monastery of Hirsau, and saw that the completion of the labor he had undertaken was drawing near, and wished to appoint Saint Peter, prince of the Apostles, as patron of his church, he desired with great longing to have some relics from his most sacred body, which he might place in the new church founded by him. Therefore he sent his venerable prior Gebhard, with letters and commendatory epistles, to Rome to the supreme pontiff Urban II, who had once been a monk at Cluny, asking that something of the relics of the most blessed prince of the Apostles be sent to him.

When Prior Gebhard came to the pope, he was indeed kindly received by him, but he could not obtain the relics requested. Gebhard heard from the supreme pontiff himself that true relics of the hairs of Saint Peter were kept in the monastery of Cluny; and the pope advised that Abbot William, as a friend of Saint Hugh, should ask for something from them, which was later done. But the pope, lest he send the envoy back empty, destined relics of certain others for the blessed Abbot William by the hands of the same Gebhard, as a gift of charity.

When Prior Gebhard returned to Hirsau, he reported the words of the supreme pontiff to the holy father, and with joy presented to the abbot the particles of relics delivered to him by the same. When the holy Abbot William heard that something of the hairs of the blessed prince of the Apostles Peter was held at Cluny by Abbot Hugh, who was most loving toward him, he rejoiced greatly, trusting that absolutely nothing could be denied him by one whom he had found, through many benefits, to be charitable toward him. Therefore, after a few months, again to [unclear].

Monastery of Hirsau 90

... his little works, the Life and Miracles of the aforesaid blessed abbot Wilhelm; yet another brother afterwards, wishing to enlarge it, made it shorter. He also wrote some sermons and homilies, which for the most part are mistakenly ascribed to another man of the same name, Haymo, formerly a monk and then bishop of Halberstadt, an equally learned man, of whom we made mention much earlier. And so the homilies of both Haymos are found mixed together, so that only a very keen reader can distinguish the sayings of one from those of the other from the very phrasing, and even then with difficulty.

When Gebhard had been ordained abbot, the congregation first [unclear] to the monastery. [unclear] he constructed the cloister. All the buildings necessary for the dwelling of the brothers, which the holy father Wilhelm, overtaken by death, either had not begun or, having begun, had not finished, he completed, with a certain Wigand, a citizen of Mainz, abundantly supplying him with the expenses. He was very capable in managing household affairs, and in all things more shrewd than one would have believed, since, for the sake of advantage, he often feigned one thing while keeping another stored in his mind. He had extremely acute hearing, so that he could very easily perceive by ear things that were said in a place apart.

He was very renowned for his wisdom and eloquence throughout all Germany, not only among religious and spiritual persons, but also among secular men, nobles, and princes; for whoever had once heard him either giving counsel or speaking formally was immediately led into admiration and proclaimed Hirsau blessed, which had deserved to have such a shepherd. He was frequently summoned to the public councils of princes, in all of which he always appeared admirable, since both the honeyed force of his eloquence, by which he surpassed all, displayed in him a wonderful wisdom, and his incredible wisdom made that admirable eloquence fruitful. Under his rule the temporal affairs of the monastery were enlarged in a wonderful fashion: estates were increased, possessions extended, and annual rents and revenues grew in number and value. For many noble and very wealthy men handed over both themselves and their property, for love of the kingdom, to the brothers of the monastery of Hirsau, under the governance of Abbot Gebhard.

In the same year in which this Gebhard was elected abbot, namely three and seventy days before the death of the holy father Wilhelm, in the year of Christian salvation 1091, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, died that venerable and most holy abbot of the monastery of Brauweiler, named Wolfhelm, a man excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, whose most holy way of life profited many unto salvation. There was a great intimacy between those two most reverend men, Wilhelm of Hirsau and Wolfhelm of Brauweiler, matched by equal holiness, which remained inviolate until the death of both.

The same blessed Abbot Wolfhelm wrote little works not unworthy of reading, but few of them have come to my notice. I have read under his name a small book On the Sacrament of the Altar, full of learning, which he wrote against the errors of Master Berengar of Tours. He also composed poems on Saint Benedict and on various other saints and subjects, together with many sermons. This man was first abbot of Saint Pantaleon in Cologne; afterwards he became abbot in Gladbach, in the diocese of Cologne. From there he was transferred to Brauweiler in the same diocese, and was established there as the third abbot in order.

His life, full of virtues and signs, Conrad, a monk and his disciple, described in a truthful narrative addressed to Everard, abbot of Brauweiler, and Hermann, abbot of Saint Pantaleon. This Conrad, since he was by no means poorly learned in sacred and secular letters, and was excellently imbued in every branch of knowledge by a good and most learned teacher, also composed certain other little works, by which he transmitted the acuteness of his intellect to the knowledge of posterity.

There also flourished in the same times in this monastery of Hirsau, under Abbot Gebhard and certain of his successors, a very learned monk named Conrad, who by his admirable knowledge and learning obtained immortal fame. For he was not only studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, but also most learned in secular letters: the most celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, musician, and poet of all of his time in Germany. He composed many excellent volumes of his intellect, to be read by posterity, in a most ornate style; in them, out of humility, he hid his own name under the name Peregrinus.

Among these there excels that very famous work which, on holy virginity, under the names of Peregrinus the priest and Theodora the nun, dividing it in the manner of a dialogue into eight books, he called The Mirror of Virgins: a work indeed so useful and necessary for the virgins of Christ that it cannot be adequately praised by a mortal man. Likewise on the Gospels, which through the cycle of the year 92 Of the Monastery of Hirsau … the bishop of Mainz, Wezilo by name, a very learned man, at first in agreement with him but afterward opposed to him, he afflicted with many injuries.

He also drove his successor, Ruthard, a venerable man, from the see of Mainz, and compelled him to live in exile for nine years in the greatest misery in Thuringia. The abbot [Giselbert?], a son of this community, together with sixty monks, he expelled from the monastery of Hasungen because of the obedience which they were showing to the supreme pontiff, and he miserably dispersed the possessions of that monastery.

He also furiously drove many pontiffs from their churches, expelled abbots and their monks from monasteries, and utterly destroyed many monasteries together with churches. By many visions of saints his attempts were always hindered, as a certain holy abbess in the regions of Bavaria, instructed by a vision, used to relate. Moreover, as long as Emperor Henry IV lived and ruled, the brothers were distressed among themselves by frequent threats and terrors concerning the destruction of this monastery, threatened by him. Yet, trusting in the help of the Most High, for whose love they had the earthly king as an enemy, they strove without ceasing to defend their cause not with arms but with prayers.

M X C I I.

In the second year of Abbot Gebhard, Conrad, son of Emperor Henry, born of his first wife Bertha, began to rebel against his father and, persuaded by letters of the Roman pontiff, to draw the empire to himself. But it will be worthwhile to have set out from the beginning the cause of this rebellion. King Henry, the father of Conrad, had taken Praxedis as his wife at Cologne seven years earlier; he began to hate her with excessive hatred, so that the hatred was greater than the love with which he had previously loved her. Therefore, inflamed with excessive hatred against her, he placed her in custody; he allowed many of his agents to do violence to her, while he himself looked on. Indeed he came to such madness that he even invited his own son Conrad to have intercourse with her. When Conrad refused to defile his father’s bed, the king, exhorting him to the illicit embraces of his stepmother, said among other things:

“Why do you timidly delay to lie with the woman assigned to you, who is not your stepmother? For you are not my son, as you suppose, but the son of a certain foreign prince of Swabia, whose likeness you plainly bear imprinted.” Beyond measure indignant at these words, the son nevertheless prudently concealed his anger. After a few days, with certain men who agreed with him, he went to the supreme pontiff Urban II; by him he was honorably received, and he was solemnly [unclear] as king; in Italy and Lombardy he reigned against his father.

He was, moreover, an excellent man, conspicuous for every goodness and uprightness, humble, modest, full of charity, and of the highest reverence and piety toward the clergy and monks. But, surviving only a few years after his coronation, he was carried off by an untimely death. The queen, however, after many injuries and unheard-of evils innocently inflicted upon her, by God’s mercy escaped from custody and, fleeing, came to Matilda, the most powerful queen of the Lombards.

Matilda received her with honor and brought her to Urban, the supreme pontiff. Therefore the empress, prostrate at the feet of the bishop, miserable, with abundant tears and deep [unclear], made known the whole misery of the calamity she had endured. The pope, having compassion on the queen, after words of necessary consolation, gathered a synod in the city of Rome. In it, publicly declaring King Henry a heretic, a simoniac, the chief of the Nicolaitan heresy, and disobedient and rebellious toward holy mother Church, he excommunicated him again for the unheard-of crimes committed against his own wife, and [declared] him a schismatic, enemy of God [unclear]. A dragon was seen in the sky; a great pestilence and mortality of men and beasts followed.

The deeds of this pilgrimage have been very fully described by many; to insert it into this chronicle would be too lengthy and tedious.

But this Peregrinus of ours, following Ciceronian eloquence, in the manner of the ancients, without superfluous citations, continues a clear, sound, whole discourse.

Now this Godfrey was count in Bouillon and duke in Lotharingia, a brave and vigorous man, who, about to undertake this arduous pilgrimage for love of the heavenly kingdom, sold his county of Bouillon, with all its revenues and appurtenances, to the bishop of Liege for thirteen hundred marks of purest silver, which he gladly spent on that same expedition.

Hence down to the present day the bishop, in honor of Godfrey, afterward made king of the Jerusalemites, has been accustomed to write [unclear]. But before this pilgrimage began, namely in the year [unclear] of Abbot Gebhard, many signs and prodigies were seen in the air.

For around the Nones of October a comet appeared, standing toward the southern quarter, extending its mild brightness obliquely like a sword. Another star also was seen in the east on the sixth Kalends of March; it changed its place over a long interval with frequent leaps.

Many writers of that time testify that they saw blood-red clouds rising both from the west and from the east, meeting one another on their way in the middle of the sky; and, at about midnight, fiery [unclear] often rising from the north; and also torches flying through the air.

Not many years before these events, a certain priest of venerable life, named Suiggerus, in [unclear] Cologne, at about the ninth hour of a certain day, saw two horsemen charging together in the air and fighting with one another for a long time; one of them, who seemed to hold in his hand a cross of no small size with which he struck the other, finally came forth the victor.

A certain priest also, named Gerlacus, while walking in a wood at midday with two companions, saw a sword of wondrous length carried by a whirlwind to an unknown [unclear] place; and until the height lifted it from sight, he distinguished both the crash with his ears and the metal with his eyes.

Some reported that at night they had seen a city hanging in the air, [unclear]. A city flying in the air. A sword flying in the air. Horsemen [unclear] in the air. A two-year-old boy, born [unclear], speaks.
