Provoked by these words, not only peasants and persons of no rank, but also kings, dukes, princes, bishops, abbots, monks, priests, laymen, nobles, the wealthy, the poor, men, women, virgins, and nuns, a nearly innumerable multitude, after selling in part their possessions, or even [unclear], with the cloisters wholly neglected, as if driven by some divine frenzy, all resolved with one mind and on one road to go to Jerusalem, to rescue the holy sepulcher of the Lord, together with the whole surrounding region, from the hands of the infidels and restore it to the Christian world. I marvel at that wondrous spirit which impelled so many thousands of people to so extraordinary an undertaking, especially all the women. The women, virgins, and nuns without number who went out on this expedition were dressed in male clothing and walked armed among the men.

Gathering together as one, they took up the proposed journey; and when they had come as far as Pannonia, a great part of them was killed, and not undeservedly. There Godfrey himself was elected king by the people of God; after he died some years later and was buried beside the Sepulchre of the Lord, his brother Baldwin succeeded to the kingdom and greatly enlarged the borders of the Christians round about.

In the same year of the Lord, namely 1066, the abbatial monastery of our order, Reinhausen, in Saxony, in the diocese of Mainz, not far from Gottingen, was founded and suitably endowed for the support of monks.

The first abbot of this monastery, called Reinhard, was a learned and very holy man, who was renowned for many miracles in life and after death; through his merit, down to the present day, Almighty God is said to cure in that same place the disease which they call epilepsy, for those who devoutly invoke him.

This same most holy abbot Reinhard wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he showed the excellence of his talent to those present. Of these the chief are said to be commentaries on the prophet Ezekiel, on the prophet Isaiah, on the Psalms, on the epistles of Paul the Apostle, also a metrical work on Job, and certain other things which do not now come to my memory.

At this time the venerable abbot Gebhard, having compassion on the labors of the brothers in drawing water from the river, after taking counsel with highly experienced architects, caused an aqueduct to be built at no small expense through hidden underground channels, and brought an abundance of water into all the workshops of the monastery.

1097.

In the sixth year of Abbot Gebhard, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1097, the emperor Henry IV, on the holy day of the Epiphany of the Lord, made his younger son Henry king at Aachen, after rejecting Conrad, his elder son, whom he had previously caused to be crowned. And unless this Conrad himself, overtaken by an untimely death, had died before his father, Henry V could not have attained the empire.

1098.

In the following year Ruthard, archbishop of Mainz, who refused to favor the excommunicated king Henry, lost his favor, and, withdrawing into Thuringia, remained there for some years as though placed in exile. Around this time the Cistercian order began, and its first monastery at Citeaux was founded in this very year; in the course of time it grew greatly, and was wonderfully increased both in number and in wealth. Many writings are found here and there concerning its beginning and progress.

Also around this time, not far from Worms, for many days and nights a very great multitude of armed horsemen and foot-soldiers appeared, as if about to proceed to a meeting for an agreed conference or to war; and now running this way, as if in companies, about the ninth hour of the night they returned to the neighboring mountain from which they were accustomed to come forth.

At length, on a certain night, a monk of the monastery of Limburg, which lay not far from the mountain from which they were accustomed to come out, took certain others with him and went to the place of the mountain; and, fortifying himself with the sign of the holy cross, he stoutly adjured those coming out of the mountain, by the power of the holy and undivided Trinity, to say who they were. One of the company answered him: We are not a phantom nor a living troop of soldiers, but the souls of men once in this world serving a prince of earthly men, slain not many years ago in this place. The arms, dress, and horses, which while we lived were instruments of sin for us, are even now after death certain signs of torment upon us. Everything that you now discern around us is wholly fiery for us, although you see our fire very little. And when the monk asked whether they could be helped by human beings, the spirit replied: We can be helped by fasts and prayers, and especially by the offering of the body and blood of Christ, and we ask for it. When this had been said, all that multitude of spirits cried out as if with one voice three times: Pray for us, pray for us. Soon all dissolved into fire [unclear] emitted a noise.

Also in these times the monastery of Bursfelde in Saxony, in the diocese of Mainz, was founded and built in honor of Saints Thomas the Apostle and Nicholas the Bishop. In the eighth year of Abbot Gebhard, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1099, there was great mortality in Germany.

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

In the same year Conrad, bishop of Utrecht, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, after the celebration of masses, while lying prostrate in prayer in his house, was cruelly killed by a certain Frisian.

The occasion of his killing was this. When the same bishop had decided to build a monastery of canons in a certain marshy part of the city, and because of the muddy site had been unable to lay a foundation, there was present among others a certain Frisian, a very skilled mason, named Ploberus, who promised, under pledge of his head, that by a certain secret art he could build the church in that same place according to the bishop’s will.

But when he demanded an immoderate sum of money for this, the bishop, concealing his intention, won over the son of that Ploberus with generous gifts; and, learning from him the secret of this art, he soon completed the church already begun without any further mastership. For this reason the same Frisian conceived great resentment against the bishop, because he seemed to have been defrauded by him of his profit, and thereafter thought of killing him, which he carried out most cruelly. Therefore, after Bishop Conrad had been killed and buried, Burchard, a pious and devout man, succeeded in the bishopric of Utrecht.

In the same year also Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, died; Frederick succeeded him. This Archbishop Frederick newly built a monastery of nuns on the island of the Rhine which is called Roland, not far from the town of Bonn, and placed in it nuns of our order. He also built at his own expense the neighboring castle Rolandseck, and another, called Wolkenberg, situated very high not far from Bonn, together with the city of Andernach and the provostry of St. Apollinaris of our order beside Remagen, immediately subject to the abbot of Siegburg. Conrad, bishop of Eichstatt, also died in this same year; in his place another Conrad of the same name was ordained.

Pope Urban II also, once a monk of our order, died in this same year. This Pope Urban II, in the seventh year of his pontificate, at the request of the venerable Abbot Gebhard, confirmed and strengthened with fuller grace the privilege of Pope Gregory VII graciously granted to the blessed William, abbot of his monastery of Hirsau. The tenor of this bull follows, and is as follows:

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son [Gebhard?], abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, and to his successors to be regularly substituted forever. Since we stand indebted by the authority and benevolence of the Apostolic See to all households of the Church and to its sons, nevertheless it is fitting that we attend with more ready zeal of charity to those places and persons which adhere more especially and familiarly to the Roman Church, and which stand forth by a fuller grace of religion. Therefore we, following the form of our predecessor of blessed memory Gregory, grant to you and to your legitimate successors the same things which he granted and confirmed to his predecessor William in the same monastery, at the prayers of Count Adalbert.

He, kindled by love of eternal reward, recently restored and beautifully repaired on his estate, which is called Hirsau, a monastery built long ago by his ancestors and lately lost, and enlarged it with many possessions and revenues for the uses of the brothers serving God there. He asked that this institution of his liberty be strengthened by the protection of the minister of the holy Church in a privilege, lest hereafter the audacity of perverse men presume to diminish or violate [unclear]. For this reason, specially embracing the aforesaid monastery under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See, by the page of the present privilege we decree that whatever that same monastery today justly possesses, or in the future, by grant of pontiffs, by the liberty of princes, or by offerings of the faithful, it shall be able justly and canonically to acquire, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors.

Among these we have thought that the following should be designated by name: the cells of St. Gregory, which is called Reichenbach; of St. Martin, which is called Vischbachona; and the estate which is called Gilstein, which was given for the cell of St. Peter, which is called Wilhelm. We decree that neither you, dearest son Gebhard, nor any of your [unclear], may rashly or violently presume to destroy the aforesaid cells, or to diminish those things which have already been granted to them or shall be granted.

Furthermore we decree that it be lawful for no man at all [unclear] the same [monastery?]; [the monks?] shall choose according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. Consecrations of altars or of basilicas, and also ordinations of clerics, holy oil, and the other things pertaining to the episcopal office, you shall receive from the bishop in whose diocese you are, provided however that he is catholic, [and] communion with the Apostolic [See?] [unclear].

[unclear] they are to be preserved entire and unmixed for the uses of those for whose support and governance they have been granted, and are to be wholly profitable.

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

Otherwise, however, it shall be lawful for you to approach whatever Catholic bishop you wish, and to receive from him the sacraments of consecrations, who, supported by apostolic authority, may grant what is requested. Moreover, we appoint as advocate and protector for you Godfrid, son of the aforesaid Count Adelbert, provided this shall be granted him by God: that he show due honor to the church and to the servants of God, and be a more zealously useful defender of the aforesaid monastery. But if not, let it be in your power to choose a suitable protector for your church, who without the profit of secular [exaction?] might exercise [unclear], who, supported by apostolic authority, may grant what is requested. Moreover, as advocate [unclear] of his church, let him show due honor to the servants of God, and be a more zealously useful defender of the aforesaid monastery. But if not, let it be in your power to choose a suitable protector for your church, who without the profit of secular exaction may render that service of divine servitude vigorously and reverently. Therefore you, sons most dear in Christ, ought to judge more carefully and devoutly according to the institutions of regular discipline, so that, inasmuch as you are free from secular tumults, you may strive the more zealously to please God with all the powers of mind and soul. Especially be zealous to observe the venerable decrees of the Roman Church, by whose protection, by the Lord’s aid, you are fortified from every yoke of [the living?].

As a sign of this liberty granted by the Roman Church, you shall pay each year one gold bezant to the Lateran palace. But if in future any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, count or viscount, judge, or any person, great or small, knowingly attempts rashly to go against this page of our privilege, and makes void anything of those things which have been granted or established, having been warned a second and a third time, if he does not amend it with fitting satisfaction, let him know that he is bound by eternal anathema and separated from the body of Christ, the Church, by the authority of apostolic [unclear]. But for those who preserve these things, may peace from the mercy of God be preserved in the present and future ages. Amen. Given at Piacenza, by the hand of John, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church, on the Ides of March, in the second indiction, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1095, and in the pontificate of lord Pope Urban.

These things were done under the venerable Abbot Gebhard, in the fourth year of his abbacy; he could easily obtain from the supreme pontiff what he wished, since he had previously been known to him and singularly loved by him. Nor indeed could it have escaped the pope how well the brethren of the place thought with the Roman Church, opposing the excommunicated king, and how most steadfastly they had always stood for Roman liberty.

Moreover, when Abbot Gebhard was still claustral prior, having been sent to the pope by Saint Wilhelm, as we said above, he had obtained acquaintance with him through familiarity.

That venerable Pope Urban also gave another privilege to the monastery of Hirsau, of greater exemption, liberty, and quiet; since it is quite notable, we have thought it should be inserted in this work word for word.

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of the Teutonic region. Since we are about to grant this charter and this privilege in the name of Christ, it is not beside the point if we first make known what is the cause, or what the necessity, of this privilege. Monasteries and dwellings of the servants of Christ, which are built with pious will and excellent zeal, if they were loved no less by posterity than by their founders and ancestors, their condition would not be so weak. Likewise, if all those who are called bishops cared worthily for their office and strove to benefit as much as to preside, this too would contribute not a little to the fitness of monasteries. But now, as we have rather often experienced, what the ancestors build, if their descendants do not destroy it, they omit more from human shame than for God. Yet from the very alms of their parents they exact so much secular service that there is no worthy solicitude for that service which is owed to God.

This too has been seen to happen more than once: that one who seemed to be a prelate of Christ, solely through this occasion, namely that an abbot had to be blessed by him, would [unclear] the congregation of brothers and the election of the abbot [unclear], and would ordain no one other than the one whom he himself chiefly wished, the will of the brothers being wholly set aside. Once he had been ordained, moreover, he thereafter commanded him as if he were his tributary, and as if he had been appointed solely for this, to serve in a secular manner. For that most malignant pest, namely the simoniacal heresy, with its author the devil, goes about the earth and walks through it, so that there is no church which can be secure from its violent invasion. On account of these several things, since the Lord’s dispensation has so ordained concerning our mediocrity that we ought to be servants of the servants of God, it is not fitting for us to omit or neglect whatever aid or support the mercy of Christ may give against hostile incursions, so that we may be able to confer it upon these same our lords.

There is a certain monastery in the district of Speyer and in the forest which is called the Black Forest; the name of that monastery in the Teutonic tongue is Hirsau. When it had come by hereditary right into the power and possession of the most noble Count Adelbert and of his wife Wiltrud, it did not seem sufficiently to avail toward the salvation of their souls if they retained it in their own hand, as it had been left to them by their parents. Therefore the first little fruit of the labor of their good will was that, in place of the canons formerly living there, the ordered life of monks was introduced. This having been done, they also wished that the heir of the same monastery should be more religious than Saint Peter and the Roman Church. It was assigned to Saint Peter and confirmed as his own, by the offering of their devotion...

... in the book. And so that each year you pay one gold piece to the Apostolic See as census, and that it be subject to no other mortal in any earthly matter. And now what remains to be added and completed by us? Chiefly concerning the appointment of an abbot, and concerning the advocate or defender of the place.

Therefore, whenever it shall happen that an abbot is to be ordained, we do not wish, indeed we wholly forbid, any person to be present at his election except the monks, only those who have professed obedience to the title of the monastery. Let the man whom they have chosen receive the pastoral staff from one of the senior brethren, so that no ecclesiastical or secular authority be sought for this. After he has received investiture of the office, let him be sent on behalf of the congregation to whichever of the bishops seems most suitable, who for charity’s sake will come, as is customary, to bless him as abbot. Concerning the other brethren to be ordained to any order of this kind, as to the priesthood or the diaconate, let what is more opportune be done: either let them be ordained in the monastery itself, or let them be directed to an absent bishop making ordinations elsewhere. For this reason we most earnestly beseech all our fellow-bishops, especially all those in Germany together, that they not disdain to favor and consent to this our decree.

And if it was not unworthy in the very text of his ordination to profess obedience to the Apostolic See of the Roman Church, whoever shall have dared to cavil at or contradict our command, as though it were known to be unlawful for anyone to profess obedience, we admonish and ask them, or, if they prefer this, by the authority of the Apostolic See we command them, that in whatever we have ordained concerning this, so far as lies in them, they not in any way show themselves disobedient. If any of them has been asked to come for the blessing of the abbot, let him not fail to come, if he can, unless prevented beforehand by ill health or by some other necessity of this sort. Likewise, if he has been asked for the conferring of other ecclesiastical orders, in this also let him not fail to comply with the wish of the brethren, if [unclear]. We beseech all, that they may deserve to be true sons of the promise.

[unclear] in [unclear]. No law [unclear].

... to reach the land of promise truly: they have also now decreed, according to the ancient discipline of the fathers, to serve as soldiers for Christ [unclear], so as to have no fellow-soldier [unclear] than once those very men [unclear]. He indeed, who is the Word, spoke with the fathers from the twentieth year upward. If there are any younger, these, no doubt, [unclear]. That renowned father, Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Cy[prus?]

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

...with the permission and blessing of their venerable pastor, withdrawing to the hermitage of a neighboring solitude, and imitating the purpose of the ancient anchorites, they despised all the comforts of this world for love of the heavenly kingdom. This institution of arduous life was not permitted to be undertaken indiscriminately by just anyone, but only by those whom the holiness of their past life, under the testimony of all the brethren, together with more advanced age and experience in fighting against the devil, had commended. We read that some of these men, even after death, were not without miracles, to which even an angelic vision gave authority. Indeed, so holy in these times was the life of the monks of Hirsau that they admitted none into their fellowship except holy men; or certainly, having received them, they tested them more harshly and sanctified them according to the Rule. No one among them, unless he was good and sought God in truth, could remain, since he necessarily would have had to endure as many very severe censors of his wickedness as he found monks in the monastery. For this was the greatest desire of them all: to seek God in truth, and, despising transitory things, to love him above all things. Therefore, since all were of one and the same purpose, they could by no means endure among themselves a man of another will. But now at last let us fittingly call back the pen to the history that has been interrupted for a little while.

Therefore, when Pope Urban had died, as we said before, in the eighth year of Gebhard, and in the one thousand ninety-ninth year of the Lord, Reiner, an abbot of our order, first succeeded in the pontificate by election. He was called Paschal II, an Italian by birth, a devout and steadfast man, who by wisdom and diligence steadfastly freed the Roman Church from the tyranny of the wicked. He sat eighteen years, five months, seven days. He was descended from the Roman nobility, of holy conduct and good testimony; from being abbot and cardinal of Saint Clement, both by the designation of Pope Urban when already at the point of death, and by revelations of the saints, he was elected by the unanimous consent of all.

1101.

In the ninth year of Abbot Gebhard, which was the one thousand one hundredth year of the Lord's Nativity, Wibert of Ravenna, invader of the Apostolic See, died: a man indeed distinguished in talent, eloquence, nobility, and dignity of person, but then of no good use either to Rome or Ravenna. He, who mounted above one man still living, although he was compelled, as they say, himself outlived three men succeeding one another in turn, being an exile from both sees, namely the Roman and that of Ravenna.

Some of his supporters testified among the people that divine lights had shone at his tomb. Therefore the supreme pontiff Paschal, already named, inflamed with zeal for God, ordered that he be dug up and cast into the Tiber; and this was done.

In the same year Godfrey, king of Jerusalem, died; his brother Baldwin was compelled by the election of the people to succeed him in the kingdom.

Otto, bishop of Strasbourg, also died.

1102.

In the following year Hartwig, archbishop of Magdeburg, who by another name was called Udo, died by sudden death. Concerning him that terrible sentence of the strict judge Jesus Christ is circulated, who in the aforesaid church of Magdeburg, called in Greek Parthenopolis, that is, [unclear].

[unclear] but in the order of bishops of the same diocese he was the eighth; he governed with energy, by word and example, the church committed to him by God. His most holy life, written in a clear discourse, is extant; his feast is observed on the day before the Kalends of October. He was buried before the high altar of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Michael, in which he had been a monk.

In the same year Conrad the king, son of Emperor Henry, of whom we made mention above, died in Italy and was buried at Florence.

Rupert, bishop of Bamberg, also died. In his place was appointed Otto, from the monastery of the community of Monk's Mount outside the walls of the same city, a man of our order and of most holy conduct, who was famous for many signs and miracles in life and after death. Because he was the son of a most powerful count, he founded a certain monastery of our order in the diocese of Würzburg, which is called [Vraugia?], in honor of Saint Lawrence the martyr, and magnificently endowed it with estates and possessions for the support of the monks. The first abbot of this monastery of [Vraugia?], appointed by Saint Otto, was Eckhard, a venerable monk.

The monastery of [Vraucia?] is built.

Eckhard, first abbot in [Vraue?], a very learned man.

Of the Monastery of Hirsau. The Monastery of Hirsau

... may be able to have support in the future. And because the archbishop is especially likely to send to the Apostolic See for the pallium, if he asks the abbot to be his legate for such a matter, and gives him everything necessary for the journey, we approve that he should not refuse to go. For it serves the matter if by this office he should be bound more familiarly to his friendship; which, without injustice from us, a son and member of the household may obtain more than one who has not been so privileged.

Likewise, whenever the bishop of Speyer is to be ordained, it is expedient that, if he has not neglected to be present there also, before he is ordained he should remind the archbishop what he should do, and seek assent for this decree of ours. Or if he wishes anything else, let him see what the archbishops do for those commended to them; and if need be, let the matter come even to our notice or that of our successor. But if God has given to that bishop this spirit, that he should not unwillingly favor the humble servants of Christ, then, lest we seem to have passed him over here without honor, we command that in your convent of brothers, on any private day, Psalm ninety-nine be said for him throughout his life. After his life, however, for him and for his predecessors from this day henceforth, all those who have not opposed the present precept, let a private Mass of the dead be held every Monday. He can know that this is more expedient for the profit of his soul than if he were able to rule in the monastery by his own vow.

As advocate, however, we appoint the Roman emperor, who is also our advocate. Yet because of his many cares and the arrangements of the realm, the abbot and the brothers may choose from the family of Calw, if a suitable man is found, who is willing to defend the often-mentioned place not for the sake of gain or because of his own necessity, but for the remedy of his soul and of his parents. But if not, being free from every side, they may choose another, who, when summoned into the presence of the abbot and the brothers, shall also swear with his household under oath that he will not act against the privileges of the Church. Thus brought into the presence of the lord emperor, he shall confirm it in like manner. Not only over the greater cell may the abbot appoint subordinate advocateship, but also throughout each of his estates and cells, where no right is withdrawn from him by those priors established there in providing benefices or even in investing churches. But if the advocate so appointed should have acted contrary to the privileges, let the abbot have full power to reject him as excommunicated by our ban and to provide for that same monastery another useful to himself, from wherever he pleases, even with the help of the emperor if there is need.

[Note: This privilege the venerable abbot Gebhard, induced by the counsel of the brothers, favorably obtained from the supreme pontiff Urban II himself, going to him in his own person; and with Ruthard, archbishop of Mainz, consenting in his own person as far as pertained to him, he brought it into use and practice.]

Furthermore, this statute, of which mention is made in the bull, namely that no one should be received as a member of the monastery before completing his twentieth year, the holy father William had begun with the counsel of the brothers, knowing indeed that the observance of regular discipline is tolerable not for boys, but for strong men. For just as today we see in all places where boys are admitted to religion, little or no observance of monastic integrity flourishes. Therefore the most excellent men, brothers of this monastery, fearing that in the course of time this holy institution might perish by some occasion, with prudent counsel offered it to be confirmed by the approval of the Apostolic See.

[Note: For in those times, in this monastery under Gebhard, the venerable abbot, there were men great both in number and in wisdom, who illuminated our order like the brightest stars of heaven; many of them, before entering religion, had been of great name and honor in the world. At that time the greatest charity flourished among them, and such observance of regular discipline [unclear] prelates of churches of great name, who nevertheless, after they had been converted to the order, cast themselves down with such humility among the poor for the love of Christ, as if during all the days of their life they had been ignorant peasants, servants, or wretched beggars in the world.]

Many among them were most learned in all knowledge of the Scriptures; many also [unclear]. Several adopted the solitary life.

Of these, some, after they had absorbed the discipline of the order to the very nail, as the common saying goes, in order to preserve tranquility of mind in the highest contemplation of divine things, with [monk] of the often-mentioned monastery of Mons Monachorum, a man most learned both in divine Scripture and in secular letters, an eminent rhetorician and poet, and no less renowned for his way of life than for his knowledge. Among the other little works of his talent, in imitation of Boethius and of his predecessor Martianus Capella, for the consolation of monks, he wrote a very beautiful volume in a double style, divided into five little books, which he entitled The Lantern of Monks. He also compiled a brief history of the deeds of his own time, which we once saw in the aforesaid monastery. He was buried in the middle of the church of the same monastery, not without a reputation for sanctity.

In the same year died Egilbert, the seventy-ninth archbishop of Trier, a magnificent restorer of his church and most generous toward the poor. He was succeeded in the archbishopric by Bruno, born in Franconia, which in ancient times was called Eastern Francia, son of Count Arnold and of Countess Adelheid; and he was consecrated at Mainz on the Ides of January. This Archbishop Bruno restored from the foundations, with marvelous stone paneling, the monastery of Saint Eucharius near Trier, of our order, which is now called Saint Matthias, and which through excessive age had almost collapsed. In that restoration the body of Saint Matthias the Apostle was found, and from that time the name of the same Apostle has remained with that same monastery down to the present day. For before that it had been called after Saint Eucharius. The same archbishop also newly built another monastery of the order, in the diocese of Speyer, in the district called Kraichgau, in the county of Bredheim, near the village of Odenheim, in the place Wigoldesberg, which in common speech is called Odenheim, in the twenty-first year of his pontificate. This is contained more fully in the letter of foundation of the same monastery, given by Emperor Henry, the fourth of this name, in the year of the Lord 1122, indiction 15, on the third day before the Nones of March, at Nuhusen. Pope Paschal II confirmed this foundation under a privilege of an annual payment of one gold bezant. But he built this monastery [unclear] of monasteries is counted, [unclear] is condemned forever with its authors and followers by a sacred anathema.

In these times Abbot Gebhard began gradually to act somewhat more laxly, especially in providing the alms appointed for the poor. 1102.

For it had been established by the holy father William, with the common counsel of the brothers, that some of the lay brothers coming for conversion, in the [unclear] of the poor under secular clothing, should receive the cellar and clothing [unclear]. Abbot Gebhard changed this statute, ordering that the servants of the poor should receive the necessities of their life from nowhere other than from that alms itself. From this occasion, when the provision for the poor had been diminished, a lamentable thing occurred: the customary mercy was withdrawn from pilgrims and the needy, to such a degree that, shut out from lodging through the freezing nights of winter, they would very often cry out wretchedly in the street from hunger and cold, and would repeatedly disturb the brothers lying in the dormitory. When, about these matters and similar ones, though often admonished by the elders, he made no correction at all, a certain elder monk of holy conduct saw himself, on a certain night of the Lord’s Ascension, in a vision, present among the glories of the saints; there, among the others, he recognized the holy abbot William, once very familiar to him, shining in countenance and habit, standing between two most splendid bishops, one of whom was Saint Conrad, bishop of Constance, and the other Saint Ulrich of Augsburg.

And after many words had been exchanged between them, Saint William said these things to the monk seeing the vision: “On behalf of the supreme majesty of God I command you to tell the abbot, the prior, and the other brothers of Hirsau that, according as they received from us, they should serve the needy and guests with every affection of charity, and should correct their manners and their life according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. Before all else, casting away anger, hatred, indignation, and detraction, by which they continually offend God, together with all malice, let them preserve sincere and continual love for one another; and unless they observe this, let them know that they will undoubtedly experience divine vengeance.”

When these things had been said, Abbot William, leaving behind the man with whom he had been speaking, went with the others to certain higher secrets of heaven. But that elder to whom these things had been revealed, when [unclear]

Saint William [unclear] of Abbot Gebhard.

A synod celebrated at Rome, in the year. Saint Matthias is restored. The monastery of Odenheim is built. The negligence of Abbot Gebhard. Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

...he dared, he made all things known to the abbot through another elder. The abbot ordered that the former ordinance of Abbot Wilhelm concerning alms for the poor should indeed be observed.

The other matters with which he had disturbed the monastery he left uncorrected. Therefore, according to the aforesaid warning of the holy father Wilhelm, scarcely anything thereafter prospered for him. For after a few years, removed from the governance of the monastery and invested with the episcopal mitre at Speyer, he stirred up the hatred of everyone against himself by his foolish conduct, and not long afterwards, consumed by a miserable illness, he died, as we shall say later.

In these times a certain young nobleman seized the possessions of the monastery in the village of Almendingen, which had once been conveyed to this monastery by lawful donation by a certain Winther, a convert, under Abbot Wilhelm, invading them after the death of both as though he were the nearer heir. When one day, under pretext of that inheritance, he was carrying away from there two cartloads of wine and certain other things with reckless audacity, suddenly the foot of one of the oxen that were drawing the booty was broken. The plunderer himself also suddenly fell from the horse on which he was sitting, lost his speech, and for three whole [days?] fell into madness. Then, lifted up by the hands of others, when after some days he returned to his senses and feared the scourge of God, he had himself carried to the monastery of Hirsau; and there, changing his secular habit together with his mind, he faithfully bound himself to God. After a few years he faithfully fell asleep in holy rest.

In the same year Henry, count of Northeim, founder of the monastery of Bursfelde of our order, of whom mention was made above, died and was buried in the same monastery. In the same year Burchard, monk of Hirsau, was made abbot at Erfurt on the sixth ides of February; immediately in that same year he began to found the new church of the holy apostles Peter and Paul on the same mountain.

1103.

In the twelfth year of Abbot Gebhard, which was the year 1103 of the Lord’s nativity, Henry IV, emperor, celebrated the Lord’s Nativity at Mainz. Entrusting the whole of his affairs to his son Henry, he promised that he would go to Jerusalem, but he did not do so. But the younger Henry was consecrated emperor at Rome by Pope Paschal.

In the thirteenth year of Abbot Gebhard, which was the year 1104 of the Lord’s nativity, Emperor Henry celebrated the Lord’s Nativity at Regensburg.

1104.

In this same year, in the bishopric of Speyer, blood was seen to have flowed from loaves of bread, and it was also found prodigiously in a dish of lentils. It was conjectured, according to the likeness of ancient Roman history, that this portended civil, indeed intestine, war.

This year, around the summer solstice, the weather having changed into a storm, it is said that in the district of Würzburg ice of such great size fell among the hailstones that, when divided into four parts, it seemed impossible for as many men to carry them.

1105.

In the fourteenth year of Gebhard, and the year 1105 of the Lord’s nativity, Henry, son of Emperor Henry IV, seized the kingdom and began to reign while his father was still living. The elder Henry wished to invade Saxony with a hostile force, because all the Saxons, as true Catholics, were well disposed toward the pontiffs of the Roman Church; but he could not, because his son detested him, as did all the faithful, since they declared that he had been excommunicated by three prelates of the Apostolic See, namely Gregory VII, Urban II, and likewise Paschal II. In that expedition in which he was attempting to enter Saxony, his son fled one night from his father’s army with a few men. When his father learned this, he was saddened and abandoned the expedition. The son, going to Swabia, was absolved from the sentence of excommunication by Gebhard, bishop of Constance, legate of the Apostolic See.

Then, aided by the counsel and help of Margrave Diepold, of Count Berengar, of Otto [unclear], of Franconia, and of the other neighboring men, of the most powerful duke and of all the princes, bishops, and abbots of Saxony, Swabia, Bavaria, and [unclear], he began to order the kingdom most prudently, and he pleased all the peoples in a wondrous way.

First, in the ninth year after Ruthard, archbishop of Mainz, had been driven by his father into Thuringia, he restored him to his own see. He also restored many other bishops of churches who had been driven out by his father on account of obedience to the Apostolic See, and deposed those who had been introduced by his father’s violence. He also announced a general council of bishops and abbots at the royal estate of Nordhausen, on the fourth kalends of June, where the discipline of ecclesiastical institution, now excessively corrupted, was to be treated. In this council, after the decrees of the fathers had first been read concerning the pressing judgments, whatever matters could be corrected praiseworthily were corrected for the present; certain matters that seemed more serious were referred to apostolic obedience.

Monastery of Hirsau

At length, when the synod had been completed, Henry V, intending to celebrate Pentecost, went to Merseburg, and there had Henry, long ago designated archbishop of Magdeburg but impiously rejected by the emperor’s adherents, consecrated. Then he shut Mainz up under siege, while his father was inside; and afterwards, coming to Wuerzburg, he expelled a certain Erlung, whom the emperor had designated after the death of Bishop Emehard, and through Ruthard, archbishop of Mainz, enthroned Rupert, provost of the same church, who had been elected both earlier and then by the clergy and people.

After this, entering Bavaria, he besieged the castle of Nuremberg, held by those favoring the emperor’s party against the Church, and after almost three months successfully took it. Departing from there, he disbanded the army and betook himself to Regensburg, where he held an assembly of the princes.

Summoned to this royal conference, Gebhard, abbot of Hirsau, attended; by his wisdom and eloquence he drew all alike into admiration and love of him. It happened, however, that John, bishop of Speyer, died in those same days. When Henry the younger king learned this, by the counsel of Ruthard archbishop of Mainz, Henry of Magdeburg, Rupert of Wuerzburg, Udo of Hildesheim, Frederick of Halberstadt, Gebhard of Constance, Eppo of Worms, and other bishops and princes then present, he designated the venerable Gebhard, abbot of this monastery, who was present, as bishop for the widowed church of Speyer, also conferring on him the abbey of [Lorsch?], of our order, situated in the diocese of Worms.

Then, driven away from his father through the treachery of the people of Regensburg, the king came to Speyer. Having obtained it together with his father’s treasures deposited there, he had this Gebhard consecrated bishop with great solemnity by the often-mentioned archbishop of Mainz, Ruthard, and enthroned him on All Saints’ Day, that is, on the first day of November, in the year of the Lord 1105, indiction 13, while Paschal II was ruling the Roman Church, in the sixth year of his pontificate, in the forty-eighth year of Emperor Henry IV, in the fourteenth year, four months, and one week of this Gebhard’s abbacy at Hirsau; after the election made at Regensburg concerning his person, [unclear].

Before his episcopate, however, as long as he was abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, he was always of great name and most celebrated fame among all Roman pontiffs, cardinals, bishops, abbots, kings, dukes, counts, princes, nobles, and peasants; and among all men the abbot of Hirsau was held, proclaimed, and praised as a good, religious, learned, wise, and most eloquent man, with great glory of honor. For wherever his name was brought into conversation, admiration of his virtues, wisdom, prudence, and integrity of life always stirred the hearers to love and praise of so great a man.

But after he left the monastery of Hirsau, which at that time seemed not much inferior to the church of Speyer in riches, revenues, fame, and honor, and assumed the episcopate, he immediately lost the renown of his name and the excellence of his reputation together with the abbacy. All men, noble and low-born, friends and enemies, household members and strangers, began to contemn, despise, and mock him as proud, vain-glorious, greedy, and foolish, since he had left so distinguished a monastery and a place glorious with most celebrated fame, obedient sons devoted in all things, and holy men, for the sake of an episcopate. For he was held in greater reverence and veneration as abbot than as bishop. For although as abbot he was noble by birth, composed in morals, circumspect in speech, gentle, wise, and eloquent, nevertheless, as soon as he assumed the episcopate, by some manner of divine permission, I know not how, he so completely lost all these things together that in morals he was rustic, in speech unskilled, and in conduct began to be burdensome to everyone.

It is to be feared, however, that all these things, together with not a few other adversities, befell him by divine ordinance for this reason: that he neglected to amend what had been commanded to him by the holy father William through the vision of the elder, of which we have spoken, just as he had threatened. Those who revered the abbot mocked the bishop. Moreover, on a certain day, while he was present, seeing and hearing through the windows, citizens with women and boys, in a certain place where he was staying, led dances and sang songs mockingly composed about him, to his insult. But this did not turn out well for them. For knights who were his friends, when they had heard these insults against their bishop, came running and suddenly scattered those [beaten?] people.

As soon as it had become known to the brothers in the monastery that their spiritual father, otherwise Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

103

when, indeed, though sufficiently beloved, he had been elected bishop by all, a certain contention began to arise among them. For to some it seemed that it could contribute greatly to the utility and peace of the monastery if they were to have the same man as abbot whom they also had as bishop, who would not only bring upon them none of the troubles of the preceding bishops, but would also by his authority resist those who wished to bring them on. But the others, with sounder consideration, maintained the contrary, saying that to have the bishop as abbot was not a remedy of defense, but rather the beginning of the destruction of the monastery and of its goods and possession, especially because the bishop, surrounded by a multitude of soldiers, coming often by necessity to the monastery for the sake of visitation, or certainly sometimes having quarters in the estates and possessions of that same monastery, would in a short time utterly consume whatever he found laid up by the great care and labor of the brothers. This too, they said, was no small thing to fear: that he might by his power take away the estates of the monastery and confer them as benefices on his friends and stipendiaries, just as they saw had happened to very many monasteries in the region, now almost desolated.

Meanwhile Gebhard secretly caused the minds of the brothers to be solicited and entreated through the advocate Gotfrid and others whom he judged suitable for this purpose, indeed even to be adjured, that they should be mindful of the benefits they had received from him; in view of these he earnestly begged that they should not consent to another abbot being ordained in his place, but should suffer him to be over them at once as bishop and abbot, promising that he would do many good things for the monastery and for each of them. These and similar things he caused to be communicated, not to all indeed, but only to those whom he hoped would agree with him, by letters, by messengers, and through intermediaries. But because at that time there were many very prudent men among the monks of this monastery, who, when they detected Gebhard's hidden schemes, took counsel together, and, so that they might forestall his cunning by cunning, hastened the election of an abbot according to the tenor of the apostolic grant.

Concerning Bruno, fourteenth abbot of this monastery, who presided for fourteen years, three months, twenty-two days, and concerning his deeds.

[unclear]

Therefore, after Abbot Gebhard had been taken up to the pontificate of the church of Speyer, as we have said, and was laboring greatly so that he might retain the abbacy of this monastery together with the episcopate, the elders of the convent, wise and most devout men who knew his cunning, lest they be forestalled by him through any scheme, appointed among themselves the day of election according to the privilege granted them by Pope Urban II, namely the last day of the month of November, which was the day of Saint Andrew the Apostle. And so the brothers came together as one, and, after scrutiny had been made among them according to custom, from the votes of the individuals the greater part of them elected Bruno, a monk and venerable old man, as abbot on that same day. There were, however, some among them directing their votes to others, to whom the election of Bruno seemed not to be pleasing because, being rather weighed down by old age, he was less suited to enduring such great labors; nevertheless, without obstinacy and following the majority, being fewer in number, they consented to him without delay. Therefore by the unanimous consent of all, Bruno the elder was elected abbot of this monastery on the day before the Kalends of December, that is, on the day of Saint Andrew the Apostle.

In the year of the Lord 1105, in the thirteenth indiction, he was ordained by Richard, bishop of Ostia and legate of the apostolic see, here in the monastery, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, that is, on the day of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, in the presence of very many abbots, monks, and other faithful people. He presided for fourteen years, three months, and twenty-two days. This Bruno was a Swabian by nation, born of noble and most powerful lineage; after the first rudiments of letters, when he had reached manly age, he was made a canon and matricularius of the greater church of Speyer. There, when he saw many going through the precipices of vices into perdition, to whom riches, honors, and the delights of the flesh had offered the occasion, after some years had been spent in that state, and at last, by the mercy of God, having obtained compunction, despising the world with all its vanities, he betook himself to the monastery of Hirsau, and under the most holy Abbot William, converted to God with his whole mind, he assumed the habit together with the monastic purpose. Having lived in it most religiously for several years, at last he was ordained abbot. As far as the composition of his body was concerned, he was great in stature and fittingly proportioned in manly form, somewhat bald, and his head sprinkled with a certain venerable whiteness. And although he appeared fittingly large in body, yet he was not strong and laborious, but through a certain weakness was exceedingly frail and altogether unable to endure labors. Therefore whatever matters in the monastery seemed to need ordering or arranging, he did not do through his own industry, but through that of his subjects [unclear].

[Marginal notes:] An alteration arose among the brothers on account of the bishop [unclear]. By the counsel of the sounder party, that of the abbot and of those choosing others. The bishops is solicited [unclear] for abbot [unclear]. Gebhard's attempts [unclear] concerning the abbacy having been made void, he functioned. The day of election of the abbots is appointed. Bruno the monk is elected abbot. Abbot Bruno is elected. Bruno's life and homeland. He becomes a canon of Speyer. He becomes a monk of Hirsau. Of the Monastery of Hirsau

...were being disturbed. But he himself, a quiet man, faint-hearted, mild, and gentle, not sufficient to bear the burdens of secular business, withdrew to inward things and devoted his attention to prayer, reading, meditation, and the contemplation of spiritual exercises. He was elected, indeed, because of fear of Gebhard, the aforementioned bishop of Speyer, who was trying to retain that abbey for himself: so that, if he attempted to begin any injury or violence against the monastery and its monks, he would be restrained by the authority of Bruno, the full brother of that abbot, who was the most powerful among all the Swabians. He also had very many other men, distinguished by riches, power, and nobility, joined to him by blood and friendship, who by their power would easily have hindered all the bishop’s attempts. But when the bishop saw that the brethren had ordained another abbot for themselves, he indeed took it badly; nevertheless he attempted no evil against them. For he was so involved and occupied in the cares and business of the church of Speyer that he was allowed little time to think about others’ affairs. Therefore Bruno, confirmed in the abbacy, entrusted the ordering of secular business to suitable brethren; and he himself, attending with the others to inward matters, showed his life to his subjects as an example of good works. Although he was noble and weak by nature, nevertheless he was never costly or singular even in his food.

1106. While the first year of his rule was still running, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1106, Henry the younger king, son of Emperor Henry IV, announced a meeting of princes at Mainz at Christmas; and there was so great a gathering of bishops, abbots, and princes as had not been seen for many cycles of years. There the legates of the apostolic see arrived, the bishops of Albano and Constance, testifying that the sentence of anathema had been thundered against Henry the elder, the emperor, by so many supreme pontiffs and other bishops, and proclaiming that he had been and was cut off from the communion of all the faithful for many years [unclear]. He resigned the scepter, orb, and crown before the princes and legates, and promised thereafter to take counsel for his soul. In this order Henry, the seventh of this name, after his father and then by all the princes of Germany, was now elected king a second time; and, confirmed as Catholic by the apostolic legates through the laying-on of hands, after receiving the oaths according to the custom of the time both from the bishops and from the laity, he began to reign, in the year, as has been said, of the Lord’s Nativity 1106. And from then he ruled for 20 years.

In the same year Henry the elder, Emperor Henry IV, father of Henry V, died at Liège, in the fiftieth year of his reign and the twenty-third of his empire; and he was first buried in a certain deserted church, until, through the intervention of his son, after absolution by the pontiff of the apostolic see, he was carried to Speyer and entombed. But, to comprise in a brief summary the evil history of that man, let us insert what the ancients wrote about him. That this Henry was a man [unclear], and by just judgment cast out from the Church, was truly evident to all in his time. For he sold all spiritual things; he was disobedient to the apostolic see; and, after the vicar of Christ, Pope Gregory VII, had been put to flight, he set up the idol Wibert of Ravenna in that very see. Against his lawful wife, a most honorable matron, he committed unheard-of crimes; and, renewing the Nicolaitan heresy, he prostituted her against her will to be violated by many by force. For these and many other crimes, excommunicated by many Roman and other pontiffs, he [unclear] the curse of the apostolic see, spurned it, and held it in contempt. From this there followed a very great persecution in the Church of God, through envy and discord, while one persecuted another even to death; and there was such a pernicious schism in the Church of God, with some adhering to the pope, others to the emperor, that apostolic censure was held for nothing, and no one cared about the sentence of excommunication itself. And although in all these things the emperor was most obstinate, so that he would not by any reasoning recognize the authority of the apostolic see, [unclear] when at some time he was sitting for the necessities of nature, certain men wishing to pierce him through were captured as assassins. Many princes also, who committed many evils against him and inflicted great contempt upon him, as soon as they had prostrated themselves before him and sought pardon, he mercifully forgave everything. Toward the poor he was very merciful and bestowed much alms upon them, and he had more compassion than can be said for all the afflicted. But obstinacy obscured all these good things, on account of...

Apostolic censure held in contempt.

The mercy of Emperor Henry.

Distress of mind.

Of the Hirsau Monastery

Around the feast of the Nativity of Saint Mary, very early in the morning, while he was sleeping in the palace at Goslar, suddenly a thunderclap came and shook the wall that was at the head of his bed; then, by the force of the lightning, it knocked several nails from the king’s shield, and scorched at the point the sword that the king had placed at his side. Terrified beyond measure by this, the king leapt outside.

1108.

In the second year of Abbot Bruno, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1108, a monastery of our order was newly founded in the diocese of Augsburg, called Lorch; and for the support of the monks it was magnificently endowed by Frederick, duke of the Swabians, father of Frederick the first emperor.

In the same second year of Abbot Bruno, and the year of the Lord 1108, when Gebhard, bishop of Speyer, formerly abbot of this monastery, was afflicted by continual pains of illnesses, so that he seemed wholly useless for managing the affairs of his church, having taken counsel with familiar friends, he resolved to abandon the bishopric entirely, together with its cares, and to return to the monastery of Hirsau, from which he had been absent, so that, since he had not wished to remain alive with those whose abbot he had been, at least when dead he might be able to remain with them forever. And when, after everything necessary for the journey had already been arranged, he began to make his way, seated in a vehicle, from the mountain of St. Michael called Ebernberg, where he was staying, a rumor spread among the people of Speyer that their bishop had hastened to go into flight and desert them. Therefore, gathering in a great crowd, before the bishop had completed half the journey, they seized him, begging that he not remove himself entirely from them; he began to resist vigorously, and said that he did not wish to burden them with his long illness. And when, after many words exchanged between them, they would in no way permit him to depart, one man rose from the midst before them all and said: “Men of Speyer, it seems to me neither just nor honorable to send away from us our bishop, whom we have lawfully received, because of illness, and to burden the monks of the monastery of Hirsau with his sickness, contrary to the order of brotherly charity. Let us rather, from a few suitable men, provide him the necessities of his life as long as he lives.” This man’s counsel pleased them all; and after assurance had been given to the bishop by oath that, when it should please God, they would bring him dead to Hirsau, since they had prevented him while alive, he too gave his consent to their will. Therefore a dwelling suited to his illness and sufficiently pleasant was chosen among the marshes of the Rhine, which to the present day is called Bruchsal. There, after suitable and faithful attendants had been assigned, they caused the bishop to remain, and through the same attendants they provided him everything that was necessary. Thereafter, remaining in that same place for only three months, as his illness became much more severe, he died on the Kalends of March, in the year of the Lord 1108, in the first indiction. His body was brought back by the people of Speyer to this monastery of Hirsau, in accordance with the promise they had made to him while he lived, and was buried with great honor in the greater monastery before the principal altar of Saints Peter and Paul. And this was the end of Bishop Gebhard, who after Saint William the abbot had presided over this monastery for fourteen years and three months, and then, having been ordained prelate of the church of Speyer, presided for only one year and four months. Bruno, also called Einhard, succeeded him.

In this same year Ruthard, archbishop of Mainz, grieving deeply over the desolation of the monastery of Saint Disibod the bishop, in the county of Spanheim, which before the present time had been miserably despoiled and destroyed by its [unclear] for many years, expelled the clerics, unjust possessors of the holy [unclear], and, transferring the monastery, which had collapsed from excessive age, onto the mountain, founded it anew. At that time Burchard, abbot of Saint [unclear], was held in esteem among the people of Mainz. To him the aforesaid Archbishop Ruthard committed the monastery of Saint Disibod with all its appurtenances, and appointed him its first abbot as well as abbot of Saint James. This Burchard, by order and at the expense of the aforesaid archbishop, on the day before the Kalends of July in this year, placed the first foundation stone on the aforesaid mountain for the new monastery; and, having received monks from the mountain of Saint James, he established a community according to the rule of our most holy father Benedict. This same Archbishop Ruthard also built one provostry of our order in the Rheingau, not far from Vinicella, on a mountain that is commonly called Bischoffsbergk, and willed it to be subject to the greater monastery of Mainz. To this provostry Rudolph, count of Rheingau, and Dancmodis his wife, with the consent of their son Louis, handed over estates and not inconsiderable revenues for the remedy of their souls. Their aforesaid son Louis also, despising the things of the world, for love of the kingdom of heaven, in the same place Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

...because of which he was excommunicated by Pope Gregory VII and was deposed from the empire by a synodal decree of the bishops, although he did not care. He himself, moreover, is the first among all the emperors to have been deposed by a pope. The scholastics dispute, and the case is still undecided, whether a pope can depose an emperor; since that question does not pertain to us, let us leave it undiscussed. In this same year also Magnus, duke of Saxony, died, and the duchy, together with the march, was entrusted to Count Lothar of Supplinburg, who afterward became emperor.

In the year of the Lord 1107, which was still the first year of Abbot Bruno, the venerable and holy woman Paulina died, on the day before the Ides of March. For many years she had led a life almost eremitical, enclosed for the love of Christ near the borders of the Thuringians, in the diocese of Mainz, where both in life and after death she shone with countless miracles. Present with this matron in her illness were Werner, her son, a monk of this monastery; Gerung, first abbot of the cell of St. Paulina, once also a monk of this monastery; and many other brothers. After celebrating the solemnities of masses in the place where she was ill, they commended her passing to the Lord. When at last she had happily died, they carried back her holy body, enclosed in a little vessel, to the cell previously founded by her; and, after celebrating her obsequies with due honor, they reverently buried her before the altar of the Holy Cross. And because mention has occurred of Abbot Gerung, who was a monk of our monastery of Hirsau, it seems fitting that we should recount his merits somewhat more fully.

Gerung was by nation a Swabian, born from the family of the Buchaugienses, who, after he had for some time learned manners and letters in the city of Augsburg, proved to be a young man of good disposition and became a monk under Abbot William in the monastery of Hirsau. He was so zealous in learning and keeping monastic discipline that [unclear]. Thereafter he fulfilled the office of cantor for some time with sufficient distinction; in this office both his art commended his voice, and his voice his art, with singular harmony. He was also a most tenacious emulator of regular discipline, and for that reason was twice sent by the holy father William to Cluny to learn the order of monastic life. For he was of mature gravity, and in the censorship of monastic rigor very severe, especially toward those who, having often been proclaimed for some transgression, had neglected to amend. Yet he did not lack the virtue of discretion, since, in caring for the diseases of souls, he mingled the austerity of strictness with a certain gentleness. Weighing each matter prudently, he was by no means lax toward offenders. In bodily stature he was handsome, well proportioned, so that he was neither excessively short nor monstrously tall. In conduct he knew how to present himself as an example to all, so that he knew how to adapt himself without fault to individual assemblies, both secular and religious. Because [unclear]. He copied out [unclear] with his own hand. For he was an excellent scribe. When the new monastery had been completed by St. William, and after his death the congregation had passed from St. Aurelius to that larger monastery under Abbot Gebhard, Gerung was appointed by him prior of the brothers who had remained at St. Aurelius. At last, by the election and counsel of his brothers, he was ordained first abbot of the aforesaid monastery, which is called the Cell of Paulina down to the present day, and he was sent with ten other monks of this monastery of ours for the establishment of the order according to the desire of St. Paulina. For St. Paulina herself, in that place of her paternal inheritance where she took up the service of Christ and continued for many years in most holy life until death, founded at her own expense a monastery of our order, in the times of Emperor Henry IV, which she handed over to the monks of Hirsau, and [unclear]. Whoever desires to know the merits of this man more fully should read the Life and Deeds of the often-mentioned St. Paulina. Gerung was, as we have said, a man of holy life, and since he was well disposed toward the Roman Church and Christ’s vicar, he suffered many persecutions and wrongs from the servants and friends of Henry [unclear].

In the aforesaid year a great controversy arose between King Henry and the apostolic lord Paschal concerning the investiture of prelates, which was the seedbed of many evils in the Church. Hence the pope in the council of Troyes confirmed by his ban that no one should receive investiture or ecclesiastical dignity from a lay hand, until this question between him and the king should have been settled by synodal discussion.

The first emperor deposed by a pope. Lothar, duke. St. Paulina dies. She is buried in the monastery which she herself founded. The life of Gerung. He was cantor. Twice sent to Cluny. Bodily stature. [Unclear]. He was a scribe and lover of books. He became prior at St. Aurelius. Gerung becomes abbot. Foundation of the monastery Cell of Paulina. A dispute arises between pope and king. The Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

He was made a monk there, and, living most religiously according to the rule of our holy father Benedict, he persevered in holy conduct until the end of this present life. Within the precinct of the same monastery, namely beside the church, the aforementioned bishop built a little convent for nuns, in which he placed virgins serving Christ most devoutly in holy virginity. These, established together with the monks under the care of one provost, always remained enclosed, despising the world with all its pomps in contemplation of heavenly things. In this same convent the aforesaid count and countess of Rineck, Richolf and Danckmodis, also offered their daughter Werdrudis to almighty God, to serve forever, together with a portion of their inheritance. At length the successor of this Archbishop Ruthard raised the said provostship into an abbey, as we shall say in its place, in the year of the Lord 1130, in the thirteenth indiction.

The nuns were with the monks.

Werdrudis, a nun.

1109.

In the third year of Abbot Bruno, which was the year 1109 from the Lord’s nativity, in the second indiction, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, Saint Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, died, the greatest supporter and lover of the brethren of Hirsau; of him we made mention much earlier in connection with Blessed William.

Saint Anselm died.

In the same year Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, also died, on the third day before the Kalends of May; he too was a father and a most wholehearted lover of the men of Hirsau, whose life was distinguished by many virtues and signs.

Saint Hugh died.

Adalbert becomes bishop of Mainz.

In the same year also Ruthard, archbishop of Mainz, died; Adalbert, the king’s chancellor, succeeded him in order.

1111.

In the fourth year of Abbot Bruno, a great synod of bishops and abbots was held at Rome, with the lord pope presiding, where many useful measures were enacted. King Henry, at Liège, married Matilda, daughter of Henry king of the English, who had been betrothed to him; by her he had no children.

The king came to Rome.

In the following year, coming to Rome, he was indeed received honorably by the Apostolic lord; but when they had sat down and discussion was held concerning ecclesiastical and royal affairs, suddenly a tumult was stirred up by the faction of the Romans. The king was so hard pressed by their wickedness that he was now almost taking to flight, had not Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, come to his aid with a strong force and compelled the Romans, overcome with great slaughter, to flee. Having therefore gained the victory, he led the pope away. Yet afterward, having returned to concord, they again returned to Rome; and, after peace had been made with the Romans, the pope consecrated the king as emperor. During communion the king [unclear].

The emperor is blessed.

In the following year [Pope?] Dominic called a great synod, and, in a synod of one hundred twenty-five bishops held at Rome, excommunicated all who sided with the emperor against him; and evils in the Church were renewed. When Emperor Henry entered Italy, he had in his army thirty thousand armed men, besides servants and many others following the army without order.

The army.

1112.

In the sixth year of Abbot Bruno, which was the year 1112 from the Lord’s nativity, a dispute was forced between the princes of Saxony and the emperor, in which Duke Wibert and Count Palatine Siegfried lost the emperor’s favor. And Wibert [unclear].

Conspiracy of the Saxons against the emperor.

In this year a comet appeared. In the same conspiracy with the Saxons against the emperor were these princes: Lothar, duke of Saxony; Rudolf, margrave; Wibert, duke; the aforesaid Siegfried, count palatine, whom we have mentioned; and Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz, who for this reason was captured by the emperor and in this same year was consigned to custody for nearly three years.

Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz, is captured.

In the same year a conspiracy for liberty was made in Cologne.

1113.

In the seventh year of Abbot Bruno, in the year 1113 from the Lord’s nativity, Gertrude the marchioness, widow of Count Henry of Northeim, surnamed the Fat, obtained the sacred relics of Saint Auctor from Bruno, archbishop of Trier; and, transferring them with great honor into Saxony, she deposited them outside the walls of Brunswick in the place where today the monastery of Saint Giles the confessor is situated within the city walls. For when the aforesaid marchioness [unclear], after receiving the counsel of prudent men of our order, in the same place [unclear] magnificent [unclear].

Saint Auctor is transferred from Trier into Saxony.

The monastery of Saint Giles in Brunswick is founded.

In the same year a conspiracy for liberty was made in Cologne. In this year a comet appeared. In the same conspiracy with the Saxons against the emperor were the [unclear] princes: Lothar, duke of Saxony; Rudolf, margrave; Wibert, duke; the aforesaid Siegfried, count palatine, whom we have mentioned; Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz, who for this reason was captured by the emperor and in this same year was consigned to custody for nearly three years. In the same year a conspiracy for liberty was founded in Cologne. In this year a comet appeared. In the same conspiracy with the Saxons against the emperor were the [unclear] princes: Lothar, duke of Saxony; Rudolf, margrave; Wibert, duke; the aforesaid Siegfried, count palatine, whom we have mentioned; Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz, who for this reason was captured by the emperor and in this same year was consigned to custody for nearly three years. In the same year a conspiracy for liberty was founded in Cologne.

In the same year a conspiracy for liberty was made in Cologne.

In this year a comet appeared. In the same conspiracy with the Saxons against the emperor were the [unclear] princes: Lothar, duke of Saxony; Rudolf, margrave; Wibert, duke; the aforesaid Siegfried, count palatine, whom we have mentioned; Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz, who for this reason was captured by the emperor and in this same year was consigned to custody for nearly three years.
