The Monastery of Hirsau

constructed, in which he placed the body of the same saint. This monastery, at the instance of Lothar, duke of Saxony, later emperor, who had as wife the daughter of the aforesaid marchioness, was consecrated in the year of the Lord 1115, after the glorious victory won against the emperor, by Theodoric, legate of the apostolic see, and Reinhard, bishop of Halberstadt, in honor of St. Giles the Confessor, and was magnificently endowed by him.

In this same year, the seventh of Bruno, Burchard, abbot of St. James at Mainz, died, in the sixth year after he had undertaken the governance of the abbey of Mount St. Disibod the Confessor by command of Ruthard, archbishop of Mainz, on the third day before the Nones of March. Adelhunus succeeded him in the monastery of St. Disibod, a man vigorous in every work and distinguished for uprightness of conduct; he presided for fifteen years.

In this same year St. Bernard, about twenty-two years old, entered Citeaux with more than thirty companions under Abbot Stephen, who had succeeded Alberic.

The whole Church of the faithful solemnly celebrates the praises of this most holy man Bernard. His life, miracles, and most celebrated deeds are contained in five little books, written in sufficiently lucid style by William, abbot of St. Thierry. Later, being ordained the first abbot of Clairvaux, he illumined the whole world by sanctity and learning. Besides the 140 monasteries of his order built by him, indeed at others’ expense but for the greater part through his own labor, direction, and care, he also by his preaching converted innumerable souls to Christ. Moreover he wrote many outstanding little works of his most excellent talent, the titles of which we have for the most part noted in the book On Ecclesiastical Writers.

1114.

In the eighth year of Abbot Bruno, which was the year 1114 from the Lord’s nativity, Emperor Henry moved a great army against the people of Cologne. Around these times the monastery of Laach of our order, in the territory of the diocese of Trier, was founded in honor of Blessed Mary ever Virgin and Mother of God, and of St. Nicholas the bishop, not far from Andernach. For Henry, count palatine of the Rhine and lord of Laach, with the consent of his wife Adelheid, began the foundation of that monastery in the aforesaid place of his paternal inheritance in the year of the Lord 1093, in the first indiction. Prevented by death, he entrusted its completion to his stepson Siphid, heir of the same palatine county and of all his goods. When he had neglected this for some time, as being a young man, at last, led by repentance, he completed it, namely in the year of the Lord 1112, in the fifth indiction, and magnificently endowed it with estates and revenues for the support of the abbot and monks.

1115.

In the ninth year of Abbot Bruno, the emperor, to the injury of Lothar, duke of the Saxons, occupied Brunswick and laid waste Halberstadt. Against him the same duke, with the Saxons, joined to himself Frederick the archbishop and the people of Cologne, also Frederick, count of Westphalia, with his brother Henry, and Hermann of Calvelage, and Henry, duke of Limburg, and with Reinhard, bishop of Halberstadt, hastened to battle in the place called Wulpheholtz, on the day after the virgin Scholastica. On that day battle was joined twice; the emperor with his men turned his back, and the Saxons triumphed gloriously. In that battle, on the emperor’s side, the count of Mansfeld fell with a very great multitude of men, and the emperor himself barely escaped. Departing from there to Mainz, he celebrated Easter there, and, compelled by the princes, restored to the citizens Adelbert, archbishop of that place, who had already been held captive for three years.

1116.

In the tenth year of Abbot Bruno, the one thousand one hundred sixteenth from the Lord’s nativity, on the Nativity of the Lord, many bishops, abbots, and princes assembled at Cologne, by the counsel and authority of Theodoric, cardinal and legate of the apostolic see, whose reputation was now celebrated throughout the kingdom, to deliberate on the affairs of the Church. But the same cardinal died on the journey, and his body was brought to Cologne to be buried.

In this year there was great irregularity of the air.

1117.

In the eleventh year of Abbot Bruno, which was the one thousand one hundred seventeenth from the Lord’s nativity, the monastery in Breitenau of our order, in the diocese of Mainz, in Hesse, began to be founded by Count Werner, a most excellent man. After he completed it, he magnificently endowed it in the third year thereafter; and he obtained an abbot and brethren, as we shall say, from this monastery of Hirsau.

In the same year, on the octave of St. John the Evangelist, there was an earthquake twice between day and night,

Foundation of the monastery of Breitenau.

Bishop Adelbert is freed from captivity.

Assembly of princes at Cologne. Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

during the night, throughout almost the whole world, it was so dreadful and terrible that many buildings collapsed and countless people perished, especially in Italy, where it was so dangerous and horrible that various cities, castles, and villages, together with the people dwelling there, suddenly perished in a chasm of the earth. For mountains were split apart; rivers, swallowed by the earth, were completely dried up, so that those who wished could have crossed on dry feet. The Po also, one of the four greater rivers of Europe, lifting itself high from its place, stood raised from the earth like an arch, so that between the earth and the water a path lay open for those passing through. After the water had hung in the air in this way for some time, at last it fell back upon itself from on high with such a crash that the sound of it was heard for many miles. When these dreadful signs had been reported throughout all Europe, everyone believed nothing other than that the last day was at hand. But by fasts and three days of prayers, performed throughout all Italy by all the people, they sought to mitigate the sentence of the Lord.

Meanwhile, while these proclaimed fasts were being carried out with great fear, at Cremona a little infant lying in a cradle, wrapped in swaddling-clothes, opened his mouth, contrary to nature, in his first act of speech: to his elder brother, who was tearfully asking for bread, and to his mother, who was preparing food for him, he said to both: “Cease, mortals, to prepare foods, O you who are soon to perish: behold, the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, before the tribunal of Christ, with most urgent prayers, is beseeching concerning the judgment of the dread sentence which the most just Judge himself had intended against the world because of the sins of men.” And although these signs terrified all who saw and heard them, nevertheless they corrected few. For in the same year many evils were committed by men, especially in Gaul and Germany: unjust conspiracies, burnings, murders, burnings of churches, seizures of the goods of those serving God in them. Citizens rise up against citizens, despoil one another, plunder goods, destroy and cut down cities, castles, villages, and houses; they tear apart and kill men not in human fashion but like cattle. There was an eclipse of the moon in the same year, namely on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July; on the fourth day before the Ides of December.

A wondrous sign also, mixed with various colors, appeared in the sky on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January.

1117.

In the twelfth year of Abbot Bruno, which was the 1118th year of the Lord’s Nativity, Buggo, the most reverend bishop of the church of Worms, who had succeeded Eppo, consecrated that church of his at Worms, renewed with handsome stone paneling, on the Ides of June, many bishops being present there: Bruno of Trier, Eberhard of Eichstätt, Albuin of Merseburg, Hartwig of Meissen. In the same year, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, Pope Paschal II died, who had formerly been of our order. John succeeded him, a monk of the Cassinese monastery of our order, cardinal deacon and archchancellor, a man most renowned for learning in letters and integrity of conduct; he was called Pope Gelasius II and presided over the Church for only one year. He had first been a monk of the monastery of Cassino under Subabbot Oderisius; then, because of his admirable knowledge and the probity of his life, he received from Urban II the office of secretary in the Roman Church. Afterwards, made cardinal deacon and chancellor by Paschal, he was at last, as we have said, ordained pope. Cuno, legate of the apostolic see and bishop of Palestrina, sent as legate from Paschal to the kingdom of the Teutons, and confirmed by Gelasius through the bishop of [unclear], came to Cologne and celebrated there a glorious synod of bishops and abbots. Under the just and venerable Abbot Bruno, the substance of the monastery grew quite considerably, both through the offerings of the faithful and through prudent governance. For many noble men, rich and powerful in the world, for the remedy of their souls, [unclear] many estates [unclear], for love of the kingdom of heaven, scorning the things of the world, to the habit of holy religion [unclear] goods to this monastery [unclear]. [Hemma?], with her sons Henry and Hugo, for herself and for her husband Count Hugo, gave to the monastery, in Eichweiler, for Saint Peter and Paul, patrons of Hirsau, under her sons Henry and Hugo, for herself and for her husband, and also sums of money, a gift of no small valuation, all of whose value or price rose to almost 200 marks of silver. Luitgardis also, sister of this Bruno, gave over to this monastery no small amount in gold and silver for the remedy of her soul. But Count Berthold of Eberstein, together with his wife Adelheid, with the consent of his sons Berthold, Eberhard, and Hugo, gave the fourth part of the village of Eltingen, with all its right, to this monastery, in the presence of Count Gottfried of Calw and Count Eberhard of [unclear].

The terror at the dry places overturned men.

Mountains were split apart.

Wondrous raising of waters.

An infant, going against nature, speaks.

Words of the infant.

Men, not amended by terrors, heap up sins upon sins.

A sign appeared in the sky.

Pope Paschal II was of our order.

Pope Gelasius II was of our order.

A synod is celebrated at Cologne.

The substance of the monastery under Abbot Bruno [unclear]. Hemma, countess. Geba, countess.

Luitgardis. Count Berthold of Eberstein. [Blank page in the source scan.]

The Hirsau Monastery

Diemar the knight becomes a monk and gives all his possessions.

... of Helfenstein, of Count Hugo of Tubingen and Ulrich of Lustenau, Reginbodo of Tallacker, Mascelinus of Rupburg, and very many others under the same venerable abbot Bruno. Diemar also, a knight, noble, rich, powerful, and very famous among the princes of Eastern Francia, having his more usual residence in the diocese of Wurzburg, in the county of Mergentheim, at Rutingen beside the river Tauber, drawn by divine inspiration, gave by solemn donation to this our monastery of Hirsau all that belonged to him by right, both in that same place Rutingen and in other places, for the remedy of his own soul and of the souls of his parents. And at last, offering himself to God and to his holy apostles Peter and Paul as a perpetual servant, under Abbot Gebhard he received the monastic habit in the present monastery, and persevered in holy conduct until death. This solemn donation of Diemar the knight was made in the time of Abbot Gebhard, in the year of the Lord 1103, in the second indiction, under Emperor Henry IV, on the day of St. Prisca, virgin and martyr, in the presence of Count Ebo of Mergentheim and many other witnesses.

Another knight also, of no obscure family, from the village of Merlenheim, named Conrad, was made [unclear] in this monastery of Hirsau under the venerable Abbot Bruno; before he had [unclear] the holy monastery, he handed over to this monastery, by solemn donation made upon the altar of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, all the goods that he possessed by hereditary right, in the presence of Abbot Bruno himself and the whole congregation, with many others. The confirmation of this donation was made in the presence of Bruno, bishop of Speyer, Egbert, count of Speyer, Stephen, brother of this Conrad, and many others.

In the year of the Lord 1109, while Emperor Henry V was reigning, Hermann, count of Leiningen, and Diemar, count of Brachfeld, for themselves and for all their kin, handed over to God and blessed Peter, as the perpetual right of the monastery of Hirsau, one hundred hides in Roth and in the little surrounding villages in the bishopric of Augsburg, on this condition, namely, that by the provision of the abbot of the same monastery the service of God according to the Rule of St. Benedict should be established there. And this was done. For in the same place a monastery was built by the work and expenses of the abbot of Hirsau, with the help of the faithful round about, in which brothers sent from this monastery established the regular life, having over them a provost with [unclear], going out and coming in, [unclear] to the abbots.

In the time of the same Abbot Bruno there was a certain citizen of Speyer named Bebo, a very rich man and a very great lover of the brothers of Hirsau, who for the remedy of his own soul and of the souls of his parents did many good things for this monastery. For at various times, either for relieving the needs of the brothers or for acquiring estates, both in his lifetime and at his final departure, he bestowed on this monastery more, in the value of pure silver, than 450 marks, as can be found more clearly in the book of donations. William also of Hissigheim [unclear] bestowed on the monastery, in the presence of Bruno and the whole congregation. This donation he afterwards confirmed anew for perpetual stability at Ingersheim, in a public court of laymen, in the presence of the same Abbot Bruno, Count Adelbert, and many others. Count Frederick also, brother of St. Otto, bishop of Bamberg, bestowed certain estates on this monastery of Hirsau in perpetuity by solemn donation in the time of Abbot Bruno. Abbot Bruno himself also, in the time of his rule, acquired many goods, estates, rents, and revenues for the advantage of this monastery through the hands of his brothers, to whom after him the chief management of affairs had been entrusted. Many counts also, nobles, citizens, and villagers, in his time bestowed many goods on this monastery; their names are written in the book of donations of the monastery [unclear], handing themselves over to the Hirsau monastery for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, and taking up the habit of holy conversion, and becoming monks, they remained until death in regular observance.

In the thirteenth year of Abbot Bruno, which was the year 1119 from the Lord’s nativity, in the twelfth indiction, Drutwin, a monk of this monastery of Hirsau, was ordained the first abbot at Breitenau, in the diocese of Mainz in Hesse, concerning whose foundation it was said above. Sent by Abbot Bruno at the request of Count Werner the founder, he came with twelve monks to the aforesaid monastery of Breitenau on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, and presided for fourteen years: a man venerable in character and learning, and an outstanding founder, propagator, and preserver of regular discipline.

112 Of the Monastery of Hirsau

[unclear], a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and very learned in secular letters, whose learning and wisdom were of great repute and fame throughout all Gaul and Germany. He wrote many volumes, by which he made himself useful to those then present and to those who would live long afterward. Among these I have found an outstanding volume of histories of past time; also one book On the Illustrious Men of Our Order. He described the life of Saint Theodoric, bishop of Metz, in heroic verse; also the life of King Sigebert. He composed the life and passion of Saint Lucy the virgin in elegiac verse. He wove together a history of the translation of her body to the city of Metz. He also wrote, in heroic verse, the passion of the Theban martyrs; also the life of Saint Guibert the monk, founder of Gembloux. [He wrote] a chronicle [unclear] against those who slandered the masses of priests who had concubines. At the request of the same persons he replied to the people of Trier concerning the fasts of the Four Times. Likewise he published a little book on famous writers, brief indeed, but not useless. On Ecclesiastes, too, he composed a threefold exposition in heroic verse. He also wrote many letters to various persons; sermons, homilies, antiphons, responsories, concerning various saints. This Sigebert, summoned from his own monastery to the monastery of Saint Vincent at Metz, of our order, on account of his learning, presided there publicly for some time over the school of the monks. Afterwards, recalled to his own monastery, he spent all the time of his life in the study of letters, learning, writing, and teaching.

Rudolph also, of our order, abbot of the monastery of Saint Trudo in the diocese of Liege, a man excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, practiced in verse and prose, in these times, among other monuments of his talent, wrote an outstanding volume against the simoniacs, which he divided into seven books. He also compiled a short chronicle of the deeds of past time. But he is said to have written many other things, which we have not yet seen.

1121.

In the fifteenth current year of Bruno, which was the one thousand one hundred twenty-first year of the Lord’s Nativity, Count Werner, the first founder and endower of the monastery at Breitenau, died, a man wholly devoted to God. Frederick, bishop of Liege, also died; in his place Adelbero, brother of Duke Godfrey, was appointed.

In the same year also Godebald, bishop of Utrecht, founded a monastery of our order not far from the city of Utrecht itself, in a marshy solitude, in honor of Saint Lawrence the martyr; it is called Oesborch down to the present day. In it he established an abbot and monks, for whom he provided the necessary things abundantly. It is reported that there was a very large congregation of monks in that place, who lived in such strictness of monastic conduct that the place itself, long afterward, was called by the inhabitants of the land “the prison of religion.” For those who could not be corrected in other monasteries were sent there to do penance. He also joined to the previously established monastery of men a monastery of nuns, or women religious, in which he placed many virgins serving Christ, and for them also he provided necessities.

In the same aforesaid year of the Lord’s Nativity, the one thousand one hundred twenty-first, in the fourteenth indiction, Bruno, the venerable abbot of this monastery, after many labors undergone in holy religion, and weighed down by age, began to be ill; desiring Christ with his whole longing, he at last happily passed from this misery.

In that year, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, after the fourteenth year of his rule had been completed, with three months and twenty-two days, he was buried in the church of Saints Peter and Paul, before the altar of Saint Lawrence the martyr; a man certainly worthy of remembrance, [unclear] for the people: a rule of right conduct, who from that day on which he once took up the habit of holy conversion in the present monastery, always advancing toward what lay ahead, did not look back. In prayer he was constant; in the offering of the body and blood of the Lord, daily. For from that time, out of love for God, he despised [unclear], began to be a monk, so wholly betook himself to inward things, so despised the cares and all the business of the world, and so cast himself down, for the sake of our Lord Jesus Christ, in such great humility and simplicity, that to those who did not know him he seemed the simplest of all. Thereafter no one ever saw him idle; but always occupied in the mental exercise of the spirit, either he burned with tears in prayer, or was intent on the reading of the divine Scriptures, or in meditation.

His Praises.

A lover of humility and simplicity.

Never seen idle. Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

iii

In the same year Pope Gelasius died at Cluny and was buried there; [Guido], archbishop of Vienne, succeeded him, was called Calixtus II, and sat for six years. Holding a synod in the city of Rheims at the feast of St. Luke the Evangelist, he, with the bishops and abbots, excommunicated the emperor. Adelgot, archbishop of Magdeburg, died; Rutger succeeded him. The excommunicated emperor, in the archbishop’s absence, was honorably received by the people of Cologne. Therefore the divine offices were interdicted to them by that bishop. An assembly of the emperor and princes was held at Mainz on the feast of Sts. Peter and Paul. In the same year Otbert, bishop of Liège, died; Frederick succeeded him for one year and some months.

10

In the fourteenth year of Abbot Bruno, which was the year 1120 of the Lord’s nativity, the Premonstratensian order began in the diocese of Laon, under Bishop Bartholomew, when Louis was king of the Franks, under Father Rupert, a man of venerable sanctity, establishing him with the Rule of St. Augustine and with thirteen companions around the feast of Easter; Pope Calixtus confirmed him. This order, growing wonderfully afterward in a short time, was enlarged.

In the same year Emperor Henry entered Italy and restored peace with the Roman pontiff Calixtus; he was absolved from the sentence of excommunication. But the letters concerning the concord made between the Church and the Empire, both the pope’s and the emperor’s, [unclear] with fifteen companions establishing [unclear] around the feast of Easter; Pope Calixtus confirmed him. The offices were interdicted by that bishop. An assembly of the emperor and princes was held at Mainz on the feast of Sts. Peter and Paul. In the same year Osbert, bishop of Liège, died; Frederick succeeded him for one year and some months.

1120

In the year of Abbot Bruno [unclear], which was the year 120 of the Lord’s nativity, the Premonstratensian order began in the diocese of Laon, under Bishop Bartholomew, when Louis was king of the Franks, under Father Rupert, a man of venerable sanctity, establishing him with the Rule of Saint Augustine and with thirteen companions around the feast of Easter; Pope Calixtus confirmed him. It pleased us to insert these matters, whatever they are, into the work for the knowledge of posterity. Thus therefore the pope wrote to the emperor: In the fourteenth year of Abbot Bruno, which was the year 1120 of the Lord’s Nativity, the Premonstratensian order began in the diocese of Laon, under Bishop Bartholomew, when Louis was king of the Franks, under Father Rupert, a man of venerable sanctity, establishing him with the Rule of Saint Augustine and with thirteen companions around the feast of Easter; Pope Calixtus confirmed him. It pleased us to insert these matters into the work for the knowledge of posterity. Thus therefore [unclear] between the pope and the emperor:

I, Calixtus, bishop, servant of the servants of God, grant to you, beloved son Henry, by the grace of God august emperor of the Romans, that elections of bishops and abbots of the Teutonic kingdom, which pertain to [unclear], be held in your presence, without simony and without any violence. If any discord should arise between the parties, then by the counsel or judgment of the metropolitan and provincials you are to give assent or aid to the sounder party. The elected man, however, shall receive the regalia from you by the sceptre, and shall do what he rightly owes you from these. But from the other parts of the empire, once consecrated, he shall receive the regalia from you by the sceptre within six months, and what is rightly owed to you from these [unclear], excepting all things which are known to pertain to the Roman Church. Concerning matters about which you make complaint to me and seek aid, I shall give you aid according to the duty of my office. I give true peace to you and to all who are or were on your side in the time of this discord.

When the emperor had received these letters from the pope, he gave him letters of the same tenor:

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Henry, by the grace of God august emperor of the Romans, for the love of God and of the holy Roman Church and of lord Pope Calixtus, and for the remedy of my souls, remit to God and to God’s holy apostles Peter and Paul and to the holy catholic churches all investiture by ring and staff, and I concede that in all churches which are in my kingdom or empire canonical election and free consecration ought to take place. The possessions and regalia of Blessed Peter which from the beginning of this discord down to the present day, whether in the time of my father or also in my own, have been taken away, and which I have, I restore to that Roman Church. Those of the churches and princes and others, clerics as well as laymen, which have been lost in this war, [I shall restore] by the counsel of the princes and of others, clerics as well as laymen. And by the counsel or justice of the princes, what I have I shall restore; what I do not have I shall faithfully help to be restored. And I give true peace to lord Pope Calixtus and to the holy Roman Church and to all who are or were on his side. And in matters in which the holy Roman Church seeks aid from me, I shall faithfully help; and concerning matters about which it makes complaint to me, I shall do the justice owed to it.

All these things were done with the consent and counsel of the princes, whose names are written below: Adelbert, archbishop of Mainz; Frederick, archbishop of Cologne; H., bishop of Regensburg; Otto, bishop of Bamberg; Ulrich, bishop of Constance; H., abbot of Fulda; Duke Henry; Duke Frederick; Margrave Diebold; Godfrey, archbishop of [unclear]; H., bishop of Augsburg; Godehard, bishop of Utrecht; Count Ulrich; Margrave Engelbert; Count Berengar; Theodoric Frederick, count palatine; Otto, count palatine; Margrave Engelbert; Count Berengar; Theodoric Frederick, count palatine; Otto, count palatine; Engelbert, margrave-count; Berengar, margrave-counts; and many others.

This concord, however, was made in Germany after the emperor’s return from Italy and after the decrees against Burdinus the antipope. For Pope Calixtus, having returned to Rome from Apulia after the departure of Emperor Henry, sent three cardinals to him in Germany as legates to confirm peace between him and the Church. When, by God’s ordinance, they came to him and restored peace, as we have said before, in a public assembly of the princes at Mainz, this Pope Calixtus, among the other little works of his talent, wrote a booklet, not of contemptible reading, on the miracles of Saint James the Apostle, which he had read here and there or had heard from trustworthy persons, when he was still [Blank page in the source scan.]

[unclear], or by contemplation, he was lifted upward to God. And because by his works he fulfilled the counsel of a wise man, namely the blessed bishop Prosper, who says, “Wisdom fills a tranquil mind, free from cares, and will be the guest of a peaceful breast,” therefore the spirit of saving wisdom rested upon him; and, as it wondrously illumined his mind, he appeared more learned even among the most learned, especially in those matters that pertained to the way of salvation, the discernment of virtues, and the instruction of monastic life. He was so apt, so elegant, and so persuasive in this place that not only his brothers and subjects, but also outsiders, both religious and secular, whoever heard him, were greatly astonished at his speech. Hence, through his most gentle admonitions, many noble and wealthy men, knights, canons, and men greatly honored in the world, were brought to contempt of the world.

When the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him to utter the word of exhortation, and he opened his mouth to his hearers, he seemed to speak not human but divine words.

He was therefore buried before the altar of blessed Lawrence, as we have said, and lay under the earth for three hundred thirty-nine years; and at last, when exhumed, he gave sight to a blind man.

Exhumed in the year 1460. For in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1460, in the eighth indiction, on the third day before the Kalends of September, when, after the death of Abbot Wolfram, called Meiser, a burial-place was being prepared in that place where the body of Lord Bruno, the aforementioned abbot, lay buried, with an inscription of his name [unclear].

The Monastery of Hirsau

Volmar the abbot presided for 35 years and 10 months. The Life of Volmar.

By providence and ordinance he vigorously presided over this monastery for thirty-five years and ten months. He was born in Swabia of rather free/noble stock; from his earliest age he devoted himself to the study of letters, and became sufficiently learned both in secular letters and in divine Scripture. For, having obtained by nature a good and teachable intelligence, he seemed fit for learning anything at all. Then, having become a monk, he walked blamelessly in the sight of his brothers, a devoted lover and cultivator of the rule of our most holy father Benedict and of the traditions of the fathers.

He was of tall stature; and, so far as concerns the proportion and outward disposition of the body, the outward bearing of his body too seemed to display a certain majesty of soul lying hidden within. Being mature in all his words and deeds, he bore before him a certain severity of spirit, so that he appeared worthy of reverence and fear not only to religious men, but also to secular persons of every sort. He detested all frivolity and looseness, of mind as well as of body; he was always firm, stable, and consistent in his manner of life, and at no time was he ever seen to change toward laxity. For in his morals he was always accustomed to be so composed, so mature, so religious, that in his presence even dissolute and otherwise most frivolous men, as though violently restrained within by some divine power, displayed nothing but propriety and maturity. At times he was cheerful, but never unrestrained; and he was accustomed to moderate even his cheerfulness with his usual gravity, so that, when he laughed with holy Job, no one would believe it laughter.

He was also endowed with great wisdom, and not only in those matters which pertained to the order of the monastic state, but also in all worldly business he was so circumspect and intelligent, and most skilled in both Latin and the native tongue, and so distinguished by such eloquence in each, that in his time he had no equal among the Swabians. Whatever he wished to say, he said so aptly, so ornately, and so elegantly that, persuading men to everything, he seemed to have the minds of his hearers in his power. Endowed with wisdom.

Now as soon as he was ordained abbot, he took care with all zeal to show himself a useful shepherd to the brothers; and not only by words in exhorting, which he could do excellently, but also by going before them in morals, which few do, he diligently led the sheep committed to him to the pastures of life. He was a most bitter enemy of vices, and immediately corrected offending subjects, without respect of persons, according to the tenor of the holy rule. Hence at all times he was solicitous with the utmost zeal for monastic discipline, both with respect to himself and to his subjects; he continually went before them by good example, and with pastoral authority he ceaselessly urged them to follow.

But the brothers, seeing in Abbot Volmar such love of regular discipline, zeal, diligence, and irreproachable conduct, cherished him with great love, showing themselves his helpers in all things with the greatest cheerfulness. Therefore, when by the grace of God he was notably increased, almighty God blessed them, and through the offerings of the faithful their temporal substance was increased in many ways. For many princes, nobles, and rich men in the time of this Abbot Volmar bestowed many gifts on this monastery on account of the holy manner of life of the brothers.

Of these, to recount a few: [Udafo-Hildebrandus?], count palatine, bestowed on Saint Peter and Paul in the monastery of Hirsau estates of no small utility; yet Godfrey himself violently drew these to himself and received their produce as long as he lived. When he was now about to die, in the presence of many he resigned them into the hands of Wolfram of Weinsberg, to be restored to the monastery of Hirsau. Then, after a short time had passed, Welf, son-in-law of that Count Godfrey, not only restored what had been taken away, but also added much greater things from his own possessions; all these are contained by name and expressly in the book of donations.

Hildebrand of Burbiltingen also bestowed certain estates on this monastery for the remedy of his soul, placing no small hope in the prayers of the brothers. [unclear], many estates and goods on this monastery in the time of Abbot Volmar, and humbly commended himself to the prayers of the brothers. But Henry, dean of the church of Worms, a rich and devout man, pursuing the brothers of Hirsau with great love, bestowed many goods on this monastery, both in ornaments and in money, and commended himself to the prayers of the brothers. Many others also, under Volmar, bestowed many things for the honor of God on the holy apostles Peter and Paul and on the brothers of Hirsau; to recount the names of each one would be too wearisome and wholly contrary to the laws of history. Nor did only people nearby and dwelling within the borders of Swabia bestow their benefactions on the men of Hirsau, but also from places very far removed from Hirsau, neglecting monasteries near to themselves— Of the Hirsau Monastery

of [Martin?] the bishop, through the ministry of Adelbert, archbishop of Mainz, and with a solemn gift and endowment having been made, in the presence of that archbishop himself, and also of Buggo, archbishop of Worms, Volbert, abbot of Saint Alban, Werenbold, abbot of Saint James, Adelhun, abbot of Saint Disibod, and very many other prelates, counts, and nobles, monks of the order of Saint Benedict were enthroned there, twelve in number, taken from the monastery of Saint James at Mainz and Saint Alban. The first abbot, named Bernhelm, came from the aforesaid monastery of Saint Alban at Mainz and presided over the monastery for twenty-seven years, a man distinguished for learning in letters and for the merit of his life. These things were done in the year written above, under Henry, king, but the fourth emperor, while Pope Calixtus II presided, on the seventh ides of June. On the same day Abbot Bernhelm was appointed to this abbacy of mine at Spanheim, etc. Thereafter, on the calends of July, which was the Nativity of Blessed John the Baptist, he received the office of consecration from the same archbishop at Mainz in the monastery of Saint Alban, in the presence of four abbots, namely of Saint Alban, Saint James, Saint Disibod, and Blidenstadt, and of many prelates and nobles.

In the same year Bruno, archbishop of Trier, founder of the monastery of Odenheim, died and was buried in the greater church of Trier. Gotfrid, dean of the same church, succeeded him. Hail of great mass fell in this same year on the [unclear] calends of August. An eclipse of the sun occurred on the third ides of August. There was a great famine and a very harsh winter. In these times also a monastery of our order in Saxony, in the diocese of Halberstadt, named Ballenstetten, was founded, namely after the death of Count Otto of that place; and monks with an abbot were enthroned there, provided with sufficient endowment.

Around these times Rupert of the monastery of Deutz of our order flourished, opposite [unclear]. Bruno, archbishop of Trier: death. Foundation of the monastery of Ballenstadt. Miracle. He wrote many volumes. A useful hand flourished. Rupert, abbot of Limburg. The manner of observance of individuals at Limburg. Inscriptions of the writer. They abstained from meats, fish, eggs, dairy foods, and wine. Abbot Rupert is summoned by the bishop. Accusation of the bishop against the abbot.

The names and titles of those matters which have come to our knowledge we long ago set down in the book On Ecclesiastical Writers. In life, moreover, he was renowned for many miracles, concerning which we have written elsewhere. Rupert also, abbot of a monastery of our order in the diocese of Speyer, of whom we spoke above, a man devoted both to divine scriptures and to secular letters, became sufficiently learned. At length returning to his own homeland, that is, the city of Worms, he exchanged secular philosophy for divine; and, becoming a monk in the aforesaid monastery of Limburg and then abbot, in these times he imposed upon himself and his monks, contrary to the custom hitherto usually observed in that monastery, such distinction, fasting, and abstinence of conversion that some of the monks, though fewer in number, fled from the monastery and, going to Arnold, bishop of Speyer, who had succeeded Bruno, stirred up a grave persecution against him. For as abbot he introduced such a manner of living that they not only abstained altogether from meats, according to the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, but also from fish, eggs, and dairy foods, and generally from all things which had ever lived or could have lived, content with vegetables alone, peas and beans, after the example of the ancient holy fathers, both in the desert and in monasteries, [unclear]. Outside illness they did not drink wine, as we read of Saint Martin and his monks.

Arnold, bishop of Speyer, having assembled [unclear] of secular men, summoned this Abbot Rupert into his presence. When he appeared in the city of Speyer, together with the more important monks from the convent, before Bishop Arnold and many other prelates and clerics, men of different orders, the bishop, with all listening, said to the abbot: “By whose authority, or fortified by whose permission, are you abbot, that without our consent in our parish, over which, by God as author, we preside, [you avoid?] the cenobitic life instituted by the holy fathers with discreet moderation, and now from the very [unclear] of bodies Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

115

their neighbors, gave gifts, presents, and estates in various places to this monastery, both under Abbot Wolmar and under various others, inflamed with wonderful devotion. For a certain woman in the city of Cologne, moved by the reputation for holiness of the monks of Hirsau, named Liberadis, gave to the men of Hirsau, before the citizens and the council, the house she owned in Cologne, of great price and value, to be possessed forever for the remedy of her soul. Volmar himself also, the abbot, since he was a prudent man, most experienced both in secular affairs and in spiritual actions, by acquiring many estates, goods, revenues, and rents through his own industry, won them for the use of the brethren. Hence the resources of the monastery under his rule, by the Lord's bounty, were sufficiently enlarged, and the brethren serving Christ deservedly increased in number.

For he used great industry, and looked after everything so diligently that, if you had seen his zeal for spiritual exercises, you would have believed that he had had no care at all for temporal affairs. Again, if you had considered the labor and care that he expended in procuring and arranging temporal matters for the peace of the brethren, you would altogether have thought it impossible that he could have had any solicitude for spiritual exercises. For thus, as the proverb says of Aod, he was ambidextrous, so that he could reasonably attend to one without detriment to the other.

1122.

When his first year was completed, which was the one thousand one hundred twenty-second year of the Lord's Nativity, Pope Calixtus II sent Lambert, bishop of Ostia, as legate into Germany. He absolved all from the general excommunication.

Cuno, bishop of Strasbourg, was deposed in the same year; another, by the name of Bruno, succeeded him. Gebhard was appointed bishop of Wurzburg.

In the same year Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, with the people of Cologne bringing aid, besieged, captured, and destroyed the emperor's castle, named Carpena.

In these times flourished Hugh, formerly abbot of Saint Germanus of our order, bishop of Auxerre, nephew of Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, a man distinguished in learning and character and to be celebrated among posterity in eternal memory. He greatly loved the Cistercian order, then very new, did many good things for it according to his ability in his diocese, and supplied its necessities.

1123.

In the second year of Abbot Volmar, which was the 1123rd year of the Lord's Nativity, the foundation of the monastery of our order at Odenheim in the diocese of Speyer, by Bruno, archbishop of Trier, and his brother Poppo, count of Bretheim, as we said above, was completed. There, after a solemn endowment and confirmation had been made by Emperor Henry V, monks were introduced, twelve in number, sent from this monastery of Hirsau at the request of the aforesaid archbishop and count. Eberhard, a monk of this Hirsau community, a man renowned in life and conduct, who was sufficiently experienced and useful both in spiritual and in temporal matters, was placed over them as first abbot. Almost three years ago this monastery, after the monks with their abbot apostatized from the order, was deformed into a secular church; how this happened we shall tell in its own time.

In this same year Bruno, bishop of Speyer, died and was buried in the monastery of Limburg before the steps of the presbytery. Concerning him Rupert, abbot of Limburg, relates wonderful visions, saying that he [unclear] incurred a grave sentence before the inner judge because he permitted him to be buried in the church, and that he scarcely escaped the danger of death through the intercessions of the saints.

In the same year, when the servant of God Norbert came to Cologne to seek relics of the saints, after he had proclaimed a fast to his followers and they were devoting themselves to prayer, one of the number of the eleven thousand virgins appeared and disclosed her name and the place where she lay. On the next day she was solemnly raised and, together with other relics of saints, was transferred by him to the monastery of Premontre. On the following day, spending the night at Saint Gereon's in Cologne, when morning came, in the middle of the church, where no sign of burial appeared, he ordered digging to be done. He found the body of that same Saint Gereon whole except for part of the head; it was raised from the earth with great joy of the people, and a part of it was given to the man of God.

1124.

In the [third?] year of Abbot Volmar, which was the 1124th year of the Lord's Nativity, in the second indiction, Meginhard with his wife Mechtilde, and Rudolph with his wife Richarde, counts of Spanheim, consecrated their church as a monastery in honor of Saint Mar-

At Cologne a house is given to Hirsau.

Abbot Volmar purchased many things.

He was industrious in both states.

An apostolic legate is sent into Germany.

Hugh, from abbot, bishop of Auxerre.

Completion of the monastery of Odenheim.

An abbot with brethren is sent from Hirsau.

Foundation of the monastery at Spanheim. Chronicle of Jo. Trithemius.

...observed laudably down to us by their successors without any legitimate reproach from anyone, you dare, by a certain new superstition, to change it, forbidding men the use of those things which none of the saints is ever read to have forbidden. For you ought not to think yourself greater than your holy lawgiver Benedict, who in the Rule which you too have professed, though he forbade monks the eating of meat, did not forbid fish, eggs, dairy foods, or wine. By what rashness, then, do you presume to forbid monks those things which the holy man lawfully permitted?

To this the man of God Rupert replied humbly and fearlessly: "By the authority and leave of almighty God and of the whole heavenly court, I have forbidden gluttony and delicacies, as seemed right to me, to my abbots, who of their own accord follow my purpose for the love of God, knowing that abstinence is pleasing to God and especially adorns the monastic institute. And you, lord bishop, who think that I have presumed this by some new superstition, what great injury you do to me and to our holy fathers of God, who once in the desert and likewise in monasteries, for love of the heavenly kingdom, mortified themselves with greater abstinence than we do, abstaining even from the vegetables which we permit, content with bread and water and a little salt, all who are even moderately wise now understand. If you are a bishop, if a good shepherd of souls, if a lover of God, you ought by all means not to forbid the voluntary frugality of your subjects, undertaken for the love of God, but rather to pursue it with fitting favor, and to encourage the sheep committed to you not toward easier things but rather toward difficult ones. Why do you blame us for that in which you, as shepherd, ought at all times to have gone before us as sheep? Abstinence, voluntarily undertaken by us at divine command for our sins, you [unclear], although it appears in many places in the sacred Scriptures commended as good. But if it is bad, why then is it commended in Daniel with his companions, who, scorning the royal foods, were fed on vegetables out of love for their paternal tradition? If, I say, that manner of abstaining is bad and blameworthy, why does holy mother the Catholic Church also commend it so greatly in the holy fathers Anthony, Paul, Macarius, Arsenius, Moses, Bambo, Onuphrius, and many others? Or do you entirely reject the life of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, and of the holy monks in the monastery with him, who in their own time observed this manner of life and abstinence, which you reproach in us sinners, much more strictly than we do, or do you wish to forbid it? For if you should persist in wholly forbidding us our way of living, [unclear] to God rather [unclear] through many [unclear] wonderful proclamations of this abstinence were held.

When the little book had been read publicly before all, the wise men who loved God found [unclear], as those who had always known Rupert to be a religious man and one who feared God.

Again the bishop said to the abbot: "We knowingly intend to ordain nothing against the divine will; but we cannot, nor ought we, quickly give credence to your unproved revelations, since Scripture says, 'He who believes quickly is light of heart.' And the holy apostle Paul says, 'Test the spirits, whether they are from God.' What sign, therefore, do you give, so that we ought to believe that these revelations of yours are not feigned, not false, but sent from God?"

When the abbot replied: "I am not a prophet, so that in your sight I might raise the dead or cause fire to come down from heaven. But in this matter I have been sent by God and his saints to announce to you [unclear] of the command of the highest majesty [unclear]. But if you do not believe, the Lord who sent me [unclear]. You have done well [unclear], and you have freed your soul. This will be a sign for you: [unclear] he will judge you; he will cut off your root from the land of the living, and you will live only a short time. Nevertheless I am prepared to undergo whatever judgment you decree, so that you may take proof of the things I have said."

Therefore, after taking counsel with the men present, the bishop imposed on the abbot, under the precept of the Lord's body and blood, a test of his revelations. And so, when the celebration of Mass had been performed by the bishop in the sight of all, the body of our Lord...

The Monastery of Hirsau 118

The oath which the abbot made.

Offering [the body?] of Christ into the abbot’s hand, before he received it, he ordered him to swear thus: “I, Rupert, by the grace of God abbot of the church of Limpurg, say, affirm, and swear before almighty God, all his saints, and you, lord bishop Arnold, upon my soul and upon this true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was born of the Virgin Mary, suffered and was sacrificed on the altar of the cross for us, that these revelations which I have written, in part and in whole, are not invented, not false, not phantasmal, not diabolical, not devised by man, not deceitful, nor coming by human contrivance, but revealed to me from God, true, sober, angelic, divine. So may God, and this body of our Lord Jesus Christ which I hold in my hands, help me, save me, and receive me now in the final hour of my death and on the last day of judgment. And if it shall be otherwise than I have said and sworn, may this venerable body of our Lord Jesus Christ not pass through my throat, but stick in my jaws, choke me, suffocate me, and kill me immediately in an instant. Let there be no place for me in heaven with the elect of God, but let my portion be with Dathan and Abiron in hell, with Judas the betrayer, with Herod and Pilate, who crucified the Lord, with the devil and his angels, in the center of Gehenna, immediately [unclear] my Jesus Christ.”

Attestation added by the bishop.

And the bishop added: “If those things which have been read before us have not truly been revealed to you by God, but have come either through you or through another by human means, invented, false, diabolical, deceitful, or phantasmal, may this body of our Lord Jesus Christ not come to you for salvation nor pass through your throat. But may it bring judgment upon you, at once kill you, and may you, by the authority of almighty God and ours, be handed over to Satan for the destruction of body and soul forever, as a proof of the truth, so that all may learn, warned by your destruction, not to mock or deceive the holy church of God.”

The abbot communes undaunted.

And when he had received the sacrament of the life-giving body of the Lord without difficulty, with great devotion he made clear to those standing by the trustworthiness of his revelations. Having therefore been dismissed, by the counsel of those standing by he returned with his brothers to his own place, and together with them continued the abstinence he had begun. But Bishop Arnold not only did not believe the revelations of Abbot Rupert, but also considered taking vengeance on him. Hence, after a few months had passed, he came to Limpurg with men like himself, who mocked the abbot’s words as dreams, wishing altogether to forbid any trust being placed in them. Therefore, exasperating the holy man with great arrogance, and receiving from him a repeated proof by oath, though unwillingly, he scorned belief.

Then Abbot Rupert, standing in the presence of all, said to the bishop as if with a certain authority: “Behold, God sends his commands to you; you do not believe. I underwent a dreadful proof; you despise it. And now, since we cannot by any reasoning [unclear] you to this desire, that you place faith in our words, it will be necessary that we leave you to divine judgment. And let this be a sign to you: if you, Arnold, survive this year, God has not spoken in me, but all the things I have said have been invented, and you will condemn me as a deceiver according to your will. But if God has spoken in me, you, bishop, will without doubt die this year, to receive from our Lord Jesus Christ, who sent me, the reward of your unbelief.”

When he heard these things the bishop was afraid, and perhaps would have corrected his error, had he not been deceived in his infancy [unclear] by the counsel of his men, who said: “Far be it from you, lord, that you put faith in this foolish madman and his ravings. It is not fitting that your authority be deceived by the dreams of monks, so that you come into scandal and reproach before all the people, and it be said of our lord that, infatuated by little women, at the voice of one mad torrent he was changed from his purpose.”

In the same year the bishop dies.

Strengthened, indeed deceived, by this wicked counsel of his men, the bishop returned to his own affairs and died. After his death, when Rupert steadfastly persisted in his purpose, he was again accused through envy before Arnold’s successor Sigefrid, and for nearly six years was troubled by his rivals with many injuries and persecutions.

At length, by the authority of that bishop of Speyer, he was expelled from the monastery of Limpurg and sent into Hesse, banished to Breitenau, a monastery of our order. Henry, formerly a monk of Hirsau, a learned and holy man, then presided over it as abbot after Drutwin, as we shall say, so that, corrected by his instruction, Rupert might return from his purpose to the common order and practice of living. But since he persevered in his observance, abstaining from everything by which he lived or could have lived, and Henry the abbot could not recall him to the common ways, he wrote letters to the bishop concerning each matter done with him, asking him to recall Rupert to his own monastery of Limpurg, lest he infect the brothers at Breitenau with his singularity.

At length, returning to his monastery of Limpurg, and persevering in his resolve of abstinence together with his brothers, most devout men, until death, he endured many persecutions from his rivals, and not long afterward rested in holy peace. He wrote several little works not to be despised for our reading, of which these have come to our reading:

In Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

He composed a beautiful work on the Song of Songs, divided into four little books, in which he explained all the words quite appropriately as praises of the most blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary. On Contempt of the World, two little books. On Saint John the Baptist, one. Also one book of his various revelations, and certain homilies or sermons. The rest of what he wrote has not come to my knowledge.

In the same prescribed year of the Lord, namely 1124, Pope Calixtus II died. Lambert, bishop of Ostia, succeeded him, and, called Honorius II, presided for 5 years and 2 months.

He summoned Pontius, abbot of Cluny of our order, to Rome and ordained him cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, a man learned in every respect and no less [unclear]. The monastery of [Schonau?], at a distance from Bingen on the other side of the Rhine, was founded by a certain noble and wealthy man named Hildelin, who, when the monastery had been completed, became a monk and its first abbot. He also built the adjoining stone monastery of nuns of our order, in which thereafter a great religious community of Christ's virgins flourished.

1125.

In the fifth year of Abbot Volmar, King Henry, the fifth but the fourth emperor of that name, died at Utrecht in the week of Pentecost, and, having been brought to Speyer, was buried. He left no children. Then at Mainz, on the third day before the Kalends of September, by the election of the princes, Lothar II, duke of Saxony, was established as king, and at Aachen, on the Ides of September, was crowned, as is customary, by the hands of Frederick, archbishop of Cologne. In the same year, when King Lothar wished to introduce Otto, whom he had appointed duke, to the Bohemians, in the following winter Ulrich, who had occupied those lands, was striving to claim the duchy for himself. But while the soldiers were trying to make a way for themselves through the forest with iron, the enemies suddenly came upon them and killed Otto himself together with many other brave men. Margrave Adalbert was captured. Frederick, duke of Alsace, contriving certain new things against the king, was condemned by the judgment of the princes.

In this same year Arnold, bishop of Speyer, died according to the word of Rupert, abbot of Limburg, of whom we have spoken, namely a few months after he had threatened him with death. Siegfried, succeeding him, presided for 21 years. Hartwig, bishop of Regensburg, also died; in this very year Cuno, abbot of our order from the monastery of Siegburg in the diocese of Cologne, was substituted for him, and presided for 6 years. Henry, duke of Bavaria, also died.

In these times there was a certain heretic named Tanchelm, living in the lower regions, who also denied that the sacrament of the Lord's body and blood was of benefit for salvation to those receiving it. And going about in costly attire and gilded garments, with his hair twisted in a triple cord, he enticed his followers, who followed him armed to the number of about 3,000, by persuasive words and the provisions of banquets, and through them, by committing murders against those resisting him, he gained support. The people of Antwerp and almost all those round about believed him and revered him as a saint and as one sent by God, to such an extent that they even carried off as the greatest relics the water with which he had washed his body, and drank it.

Yet he was of such great incontinence and impurity that he corrupted daughters in the presence of their mothers and betrothed women while their husbands looked on, and asserted that this work was spiritual. At length, after he had disseminated many errors among the people and many murders had been committed against the clergy and the faithful of the Church, while he was sailing in a boat he was struck in the brain by a certain priest inflamed with zeal for the faith, and died. But not even after his death could the error which he had sown be so easily rooted out. For this reason, by the clergy of that place, a church with some revenues was given through the hand of the bishop to Norbert, founder of the Premonstratensian order, for the building of a monastery. Indeed, while he was preaching, men and women, moved to compunction, [unclear] the Lord's body which [unclear].

The Monastery of Hirsau

...which they had stored away in little chests and holes for more than ten years out of contempt and unbelief, they brought to him in repentance; they were restored to the right catholic faith.

1127.

In the sixth year of Abbot Volmar, which was the year 1127 from the Nativity of Christ, King Lothar celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Cologne.

In the same year King Lothar, with the duke of Bohemia, besieged Nuremberg for two months and withdrew without result. William, prince of Burgundy, was killed by his own men. Charles also, count of Flanders, a lover, cultivator, and defender of justice above all the princes of his time, while set in prayer before the altar, was killed by his own men, who hated justice.

G., archbishop, dies. When Nuremberg was besieged.

In the same year Gotfrid, archbishop of Trier, weighed down by old age, resigned the episcopate, which he had ruled for two years and ten months; surviving one year, five months, and sixteen days, he rested in the Lord. Meginher succeeded him; going to Rome, he was consecrated by Pope Honorius II and given the pallium. Returning then to Germany, by command of the pope he excommunicated Conrad, duke of Swabia, afterwards emperor, [unclear], who was then troubling Lothar's empire; this did not turn out well for him.

Conrad is excommunicated.

For when afterward he too strongly reproved the incontinence of his clerics, and on that account became hated by all wicked men, he resolved to go to Rome so that he might be helped by the pope. But at Parma, betrayed by his own clerics, he was captured by Duke Conrad, whom he had excommunicated, imprisoned, and deprived of the light of his eyes; at last, tortured by excessive misery, [unclear] in Germany. By command of the pope he excommunicated Conrad, duke of Swabia, afterwards emperor, [unclear], and Lothar, who was then troubling his empire; this did not turn out well for him.

In the same year several bishops died: Theodoric, bishop of Münster; Ulrich, bishop of Constance; Eberhard, archbishop of Strasbourg; Rutger, archbishop of Magdeburg; the bishop of Paderborn; and the bishop of Liege. Godebold, bishop of Utrecht, founder of the monastery of Saint Lawrence of our order in Oesbrog, of whom we spoke above, weighed down by old age, resigned his episcopate in this year, entered the aforesaid monastery, took up the habit of holy religion, and as a monk happily rested in the Lord on the day before the Ides of November. After his resignation Andrew succeeded in the pontificate of the church of Utrecht.

A bishop becomes a monk of our order.

Norbert, the first founder of the Premonstratensian order, a man of wondrous holiness and an outstanding preacher, was ordained bishop for the church of Magdeburg. For it happened by a remarkable chance that he was made bishop: when the aforesaid archbishop Rutger had died, and Arnold, who had invaded the episcopate, had been killed by the citizens, the clerics sent messengers to the emperor and asked that a bishop be given to them. By chance this Norbert was present, a man most renowned throughout the whole world for knowledge and holiness; with the counsel of the princes, the emperor appointed him archbishop. These things were done in the year of the Lord 1128, in the city of Speyer. Moreover, Alexander was ordained bishop for the church of Liege.

1128.

For the church of Paderborn, however, a certain man named Bernard was appointed, in the seventh year of Abbot Volmar, which was the year 1128 of the Lord's Nativity. Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter in Erfurt, formerly a monk of Hirsau, died; Werner, also a monk of this monastery of Hirsau, succeeded him in the aforesaid abbacy by the unanimous election of the brothers and with the permission and blessing of Abbot Volmar, a man of much prudence and [unclear]; he introduced [unclear] into that monastery, to the wonder of all.

Werner becomes abbot in Erfurt.

In the same year, when King Lothar was celebrating Christmas at Wurzburg, he learned by flying rumor that Conrad, brother of Frederick, duke of Alsace, had usurped the royal name for himself. For this reason the bishop of Mainz, with the others present, excommunicated the same Conrad; afterward Pope Honorius confirmed that excommunication through Meginher, archbishop of Trier, as we have said. King Lothar therefore came with his princes and besieged Speyer, where Conrad himself, after expelling Bishop Sigfrid, had placed his garrison; but, after receiving hostages, he departed.

Duke Conrad usurps the royal name for himself. Speyer is besieged.

In these times, under Pope Honorius II, there came to Rome a certain priest, Arnolph, a man of great of great devotion and an outstanding preacher. While proclaiming the word of God he rebuked the wantonness, lust, greed, and excessive pomp of the clergy, and set before all for imitation the poverty of Christ and his apostles and their most blameless life. He was indeed praised by the Roman nobility as an ancient disciple of Christ, but he was held in excessive hatred by the cardinals and clergy, by whom he was seized at night and secretly killed.

Arnulphus, preacher of truth, is killed at Rome by the clergy.

This martyrdom of his had previously been divinely revealed to him while he was still in the hermitage, when he was sent by an angel to preach at Rome. Hence he said publicly: “I know that you seek my life; I know that shortly you will kill me in secret. But why? I tell you the truth: I rebuke the pomp, pride, greed, luxury, and excessive zeal which you wretched men devote to acquiring riches; for this reason I do not please you. I call heaven and earth as witness that I have announced to you those things which the Lord commanded me; but you despise me and your creator, who redeemed you through his only-begotten Son. Nor is it any wonder if I, a sinful man announcing the truth to you, am delivered to death by you, since even if Saint Peter were to rise again today and rebuke your vices, which have been multiplied beyond measure, you would by no means spare him.”

How freely he rebukes the vices of the clergy. Nor would they spare Saint Peter.

When he had cried out with this loud voice, he added: “For my part, I do not fear to undergo death for the truth; but to you I proclaim in the word of the Lord that almighty God will not spare your impurities. For you, full of every filthiness, go before the people entrusted to you down to hell. God is the avenger.” And when the hatred of the clergy began to rage against him because of the truth, he was seized by their treacheries and drowned.

1129. In the eighth year of Abbot Volmar, which was the year 1129 of the Lord’s nativity, in the western regions, by a miracle against men wearing long hair by evil custom, the hair around the heads of twenty men suddenly began to burn, having been miraculously set on fire in many cases.

Speyer is captured.

The boy king [unclear]. [unclear] perished through the gate/harbor [unclear].

[Henry?], bishop of Verdun, was also deposed by Matthew, bishop of Albano, legate of the Apostolic See. But Bruno, bishop of Strasbourg, after being expelled for four years, [unclear].

The abbey of St. John in Rheingau will be erected.

In this year the boy Philip, son of Louis, king of the Franks, was anointed king at Reims. [unclear] he obtains the favor of the queen and of the bishops of the king. Frederick also, archbishop [unclear], having been convicted, confessed that he had received thirty solidi for the consecration of a certain church. Perhaps meeting him, he threw him headlong from his horse; [unclear] following, in this year he was reconciled. The bishop of Cologne, who for three years had carried on enmities against the king, was reconciled.

[Henry?], bishop of Verdun, was also [unclear] by Matthew, bishop of Albano, of the Apostolic See [unclear], to be anointed king. [Henry?] also, bishop of Verdun, by Matthew of Albano, priest, son of King Louis of the Franks, because for the consecration of certain churches [unclear] to reconcile. “For my part, I do not fear to undergo death for the truth [unclear] by night [unclear] the king to be anointed, expelled from the kingdom; he was expelled.” [Henry?] also, [unclear] of Verdun, priest, son of King Louis of the Franks, because for the consecration of a certain church [unclear] to reconcile. “For my part, I do not fear to undergo death for truth [unclear] by night [unclear] the king to be anointed, expelled from the kingdom; he was expelled.”

122

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

was celebrated under King Lothar; Matthew of Albano, legate of the Apostolic See, presided over it. Many bishops were present there: St Otto, bishop of Bamberg; Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz; Buggo of Worms; Sigfrid of Speyer; Embricho of Würzburg; the bishops of Augsburg, Eichstätt, Hildesheim, and many others. To this council also Wolmar, abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, summoned by the archbishop of Mainz, came together with many other abbots.

In the same year died Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, founder of the monastery of nuns of our order on the island of Roland, a man magnificent in every respect; by his generosity and authority that most reverend abbot of Deutz, the great Rupert, composed almost innumerable works. He died in his castle, which he himself had newly built on the highest summit of a mountain, and for that reason called Wolenberg, and was buried in the monastery of Siegburg of our order, in the chapter-place. In the archbishopric he was succeeded by Bruno, dean of St Gereon, provost, son of Count Adolf of Althene, ordained by the judgment of Emperor Lothar, the princes, and three cardinals or legates of the Apostolic See then present at Cologne, against the will of many.

1131.

In the same year also, the tenth of Abbot Wolmar, namely the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1131, King Lothar set an expedition in motion against the Danes and Slavs, and subdued them. Eckebert, bishop of Münster, formerly dean of the greater church of Cologne, died at Cologne at the time when the aforesaid election of Archbishop Bruno was being held, and, carried back to his own see, was buried. Werner succeeded him.

About these times, a little before these years, namely in the year of the Lord 1100 or thereabouts, that noble abbey of our order, Reichenbach in Bavaria, was founded by the count of Vohburg, who enriched it with many estates, revenues, and ornaments, and raised it up splendidly.

In the year of the Lord 1106 also, a certain rich and powerful count of Montbéliard began to found an abbey of our order in honor of St Walpurga the virgin, situated in the diocese of Strasbourg, not far from Haguenau; he endowed it with many goods for the support of the monks serving God.

The same count of Montbéliard also, in the same wood near the village called Bibelis, at a cannon-shot from the aforesaid monastery of St Walpurga, founded another monastery of nuns of our order. In it he appointed as first abbess his daughter, named Gunthera, a holy virgin. Renowned for miracles, she was at last buried in the middle of its dark church. In these times also Count Otto of Scheyern in Bavaria, of the stock of Emperor Charles the Great, from whom all the dukes of Bavaria who now exist have descended, converted his castle Scheyern, almost collapsed from excessive age, into a monastery and abbey of our order in honor of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin. Cooperating in this were Count Conrad, Count Otto of [Tochauie?], the other Otto, count palatine in Wittelsbach, and Count Otto, with seven other counts, all of whom bore the names and arms of the aforesaid castle of Scheyern, although at that time [unclear] lived there.

All these, with Agnes, wife of the aforesaid count, with the greatest devotion offered forever to the Blessed Virgin every right which they had in that castle, building a distinguished monastery in which they appointed burial for themselves and their posterity. But there was one among them, Count Arnold of Scheyern, [unclear] to offer to the Lord God; and when he perceived that one man could hinder many, he threw his glove into the air and before everyone offered his share to the devil, saying: “You lords of the devil, take my share among yourselves!” And immediately invisible demons visibly carried off the glove, which never afterwards appeared anywhere.

1132.

In the twelfth year also of Abbot Wolmar, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1132, died the venerable [Drutwin?] of Hirsau, of whom we made mention above under lord Abbot Bruno, in the year of the Lord 1119. He presided for thirteen years, a man magnificent in every respect. In the governance of the abbacy of the aforesaid monastery of Breitenau, Henry succeeded this Drutwin: a monk of this monastery of Hirsau, in all his time most learned in divine Scriptures, who wrote many and varied works, both in verse and in prose.

Of these, when we once stayed for two days in the aforesaid monastery of Breitenau, we received Many bishops were present: Saint Otto, bishop of Bamberg; Adelbert, archbishop of Mainz; Buggo of Worms; Sifridius of Speyer; Embricho of Wurzburg; the bishops of Augsburg, Eichstatt, and Hildesheim; and many others. To this council also Wolmarinus, abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, was summoned by the archbishop of Mainz,

In the same year died Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, founder of the monastery of nuns of our order on Rolandswerth, a man magnificent in all things; through his munificence and authority that most reverend abbot of Deutz, the great Rupert, composed almost countless works. He died in his own castle, which he himself had newly built on the highest summit of a mountain, and therefore called Wolenberg. He was buried in the monastery of Siegburg of our order, in the chapter-place. In the archbishopric Bruno succeeded him, dean of Saint Gereon, provost, son of Count Adolf of Althene, ordained by the judgment of Emperor Lothar, of the princes, and of three cardinals, or legates of the Apostolic See, then present at Cologne, against the will of many.

The king is admonished concerning the Slavs.

Bruno succeeded in the bishopric.

Hirsaugiensis [unclear], many being present: Saint Otto, bishop of Bamberg; the bishops of Augsburg and Eichstatt; Sistridius of Speyer; Embricho of Wurzburg Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

[unclear] the following: a dialogue in the persons of the rich feaster and of poor Lazarus resting in Abraham’s bosom. On contempt of the world, which begins thus: “A man, lover of an unstable kingdom.” Likewise a little book of several prayers vowed to God, which likewise begins thus: “O wretched one, my soul.” Likewise a little book on the conflict of the virtues and vices, which begins: “With various vices [unclear] to learn of the virtues [unclear].” Likewise a little book on the twelve abuses, beginning thus: “It is agreed that the abuses of the world are said to be twice six.” Likewise a little work on the fall of the first man and on weariness of the present exile, which begins thus: “The serpent [unclear] Adam to sin.” Likewise a little work on the City whose name is “The Lord is there,” which begins thus: “Since [unclear] I should like to write the gift.” Likewise a little book on the habit of a virgin and on blessedness, beginning thus: “A virgin exceedingly dear,” etc. Likewise a little book on the resurrection of the saints, which begins thus: “Christ, the salvation [of] all things.” Likewise a little work on thinking upon mortality, which begins thus: “Why does the human race.” Likewise a little book on our Lord Jesus Christ, beginning thus: “I, poorer than all, [unclear] the city.” Likewise a little work on the mystical body of Christ, which begins thus: “A true son of the Church, who has received the catholic [faith].” Likewise a little book on the Catholic faith, which begins thus: “A son of the Church [unclear],” which he entitled “Little Flowers,” beginning thus: “In my manner, in the field of Scripture.” Likewise a work of many hymns in various kinds of verse, which begins thus: “Praise of wheat from the dead grain.” Likewise a volume of letters to various persons, which begins thus: “To the venerable bishop of Chartres,” that is, “on passibility.” He also wrote various sermons and diverse little works, whose order and titles I have not retained in mind. He was indeed a learned man and very studious, and no less by sanctity and the merit of his life than by erudition in the Scriptures was of most celebrated fame and reputation throughout all Germany; in life and after death he shone with many signs and miracles.

His deeds are found described quite clearly. Abbot Henry [unclear] shone with miracles. Rupert, abbot of Limburg. To this Henry, as to a holy, learned, and proven man, Rupert, abbot of Limburg, of whom we have spoken above, was banished to Breitenau by order of the bishop of Speyer, on account of his abstinence of unwonted novelty, so that, brought back by him to the common mode of living, he might depart from his singularity. Concerning him the same Saint Henry the abbot makes mention more fully in a certain letter to the bishop of the church of Speyer. Finally, because of the fame of his most excellent sanctity, many men noble, powerful, and honored in the world, for the love of God, became monks in Breitenau under Saint Abbot Henry. Among these the foremost was Adelbert, count of Schoenberg, who, having despised the things and pomps of the world, although he was powerful and very rich, became a poor monk for Christ; and he lived with such purity that, not without miracles, he showed to all the monks in that place the traces of great sanctity. In this same year of Abbot Volmar II, a very violent force of winds overthrew countless buildings.

In the same year Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, the first founder of the Carthusian order, a man singular among the bishops of his time in life and conduct, died. Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, dies. [unclear] the provost succeeded him, who raised from the earth with great honor the body of Saint Gotthard the bishop, which had lain buried for almost a hundred years. Berthold also, bishop of Hildesheim, died, and Bernard of the same church [unclear] of Cologne, of our order, of whom they spoke above, succeeded him. The spirit Hudelin, appearing in Saxony, performed many miracles.

In these times a certain malicious spirit, in the diocese of Hildesheim, appeared visibly for a long time to many people in rustic garb, his head covered with a cap; whence the country people commonly called him “the capped one,” that is, “ein Hedeckm” in the Saxon tongue. This spirit Hukin did many marvelous things and took pleasure in being with human beings, speaking, asking, and answering everyone familiarly, appearing sometimes visibly, sometimes invisibly. He harmed no one unless he had first been harmed, but mindful of injuries or mockeries, he hindered in turn those who inflicted insult upon him.

The county is occupied by him. When Burcard, count of Luca, had been killed by Count Hermann of Winsenburg, and the county of Winsenberg itself seemed exposed to plunder, the spirit [unclear] came to Bernard, bishop of Hildesheim, sleeping in his bed, and woke him, saying: “Arise, O bald man; summon the army, because the county of Winsburg, empty and desolate on account of the homicide, will easily submit to his command.” Rising, he summoned his soldiers, invaded the county, and obtained it; with the emperor’s consent he joined it forever to the church of Hildesheim. The bishop [unclear] on the walls.

The same spirit also, without being asked, often used to warn the same bishop of many dangers. Appearing rather frequently in the court of the same prelate, he was generally accustomed to serve the cooks quite diligently, and often to mingle conversations with them in the kitchen.
