124. Of the Monastery of Hirsau

Injuries, etc.

Hence, when by now through habit he had become familiar and was feared by no one, a certain little boy serving in the kitchen began to despise him, mock him, and assail him with insults, and as often as he could he poured the filth of the kitchen upon him. When he had often asked the master of the kitchen to restrain the boy from his insults, and had at last threatened that he would [avenge?] the insults, he was laughed at by him, who said: “You are a spirit, and do you fear a boy?” To him the demon replied: “Because you scorn to correct your boy at my request, in a few days I shall show you how much I fear him.”

Having said this, the spirit departed in anger. Not long afterward, when one day after vespers the boy, alone in the kitchen, was sleeping from weariness, the spirit came, suffocated him, cut him into pieces, put him in a pot, and began to cook him at the fire. When the master of the kitchen perceived this, he began to curse the spirit. The latter, provoked, on the next day, when a roast had been set on spits at the fire for the bishop and the courtiers, pressed [unclear] and sprinkled it over with horrible toads, with the blood of the same and venom. And again, having been assailed with insults, he hurled him from on high by an illusory bridge into a pit; and, while keeping watch most diligently above the walls of the city’s castle, he compelled all the guards to keep watch.

A certain man, about to set out on a long journey, since he had an unchaste wife, said to the spirit Hutgin, as if in jest: “Good companion, I entrust my wife to you until I return; see that you guard her.” And when, in the man’s absence, the woman would set out her portion with adulterers and would try many lovers in succession, this spirit always placed himself invisibly in the midst, and, throwing the men from the bed to the ground, permitted none to come even to touching the woman herself, to say nothing of unlawful intercourse. Thus the woman, almost every single night and almost at every hour through the whole time, brought in ever new lovers; yet as soon as each tried to touch her, the spirit threw him far off onto the ground. At last, when the husband was returning and was still far from home, the spirit entrusted with the charge met him gladly, saying: “Your arrival is very welcome to me, for by it I am freed from the very restless labor which you imposed on me.” To whom the husband said: “Who, then, are you?” “I am,” he said, “Hudgin, to whom, when you were lately going away, you entrusted her to be protected; behold, I have guarded her for you, though with the greatest and continual labor, safe from adultery. But I beg you not to wish henceforth to hand her over to me to guard. For I would rather guard the pigs of all Saxony than your one wife herself; by so many tricks she tried to get around me, by so many ways and so many methods to misuse her own body.”

This spirit also performed innumerable other miracles, both serious and ridiculous, all of which cannot easily be written down; nor, if they were written, [unclear]. They say that by means of a ring made from laurel leaves, with certain other things added, he made [unclear] very learned for some time. At last, eliminated by the aforesaid bishop Bernard through ecclesiastical censures, he was compelled to withdraw from the province.

1133.

In the twelfth year of Abbot Volmar, which was the year 1133 of the Lord’s Nativity, King Lothar set out for Rome with a very great army of princes, bishops, abbots, nobles, and knights, to restore Innocent to the apostolic see. Passing therefore through Italy, he took very many fortifications that resisted him; and at last, on the second day before the Kalends of May, he entered Rome with the highest favor. Since Anacletus, who was Peter Leonis, was now dead, he restored Innocent to the apostolic see. By him Lothar himself was consecrated emperor on the third day before the Nones of June, at the Lateran in the church of Saint John; after some wars and victories he returned to Germany, bringing with him as captive a certain prince of Italy.

In the same year, on the fourth day before the Nones of August, on the twenty-seventh day of the moon, at the sixth hour of the day, an eclipse of the sun occurred, to such an extent that stars appeared in the sky. Great irregularity of the air and an inundation of rains followed through the whole harvest-time. The cousin also of Emperor Lothar, having crossed [the river?] with Goitido his brother, Hermann of Cuch was killed.

1133.

In the thirteenth year of Abbot Volmar, Emperor Lothar celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Cologne. There a rash tumult of the townsmen arose before him, and, before it had yet been quieted, he departed thence. But he celebrated Easter at Halberstadt with a great attendance of princes. There Magnus, king of the Danes, placed himself in the power of the emperor, gave hostages, and swore an oath that he and his successors would not obtain the kingdom except by permission of the emperor and of his successors. After this, allowed to return in peace to Dacia, on the day of holy Pentecost he was killed by his rivals, together with five bishops, sixty priests, and his father Nicholas. Meanwhile Emperor Lothar, celebrating the feast of Pentecost at Merseburg, performed with great solemnity and pomp the wedding of his daughter Gertrude, giving her as wife to Henry, duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Proud, a very strong and daring man. He added to him also the duchy of Saxony, from whom all the dukes of Brunswick and Lüneburg who exist today have descended by succession, as in the histo126 Monastery of Hirsau

In these times also the convent of nuns of our order at Lobenfeld, in the same diocese of Worms, in the district called Kreichau, about two miles from Heidelberg, was founded through the work and at the expense of the aforesaid bishop Buggo, and was sufficiently endowed for the support of the virgins of Christ. Around these times too the count of Leiningen, named [Emicho?], founded a monastery of brethren, canons under the rule of Saint Augustine, in the thickets, commonly called Heyna or Hegina, in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and enriched it with many goods and revenues. Its church the often-mentioned bishop Buggo, in whose diocese the monastery was built, consecrated in the year of the Lord 1122, and appointed Hartung as first provost; he first instituted there the life of regular canons.

In the fifteenth year of his rule, Abbot Volmar, provoked by the insolence of certain secular ministeriales of his, went to the emperor Lothar while he was celebrating the Nativity of the Lord at Speyer, and called upon him as helper and defender of his monastery of Hirsau and of the brethren and the dependents of the same. He at once ordered the disturbers of holy religion to be brought before him; such great fear seized them that, while Volmar lived, no one presumed to trouble the men of Hirsau.

1136.

In this same year, which was the 1136th from the Lord’s Nativity, on the second day before the Kalends of January, there died, of holy memory, Jutta, a most devout virgin of Christ, sister of Count Meginhard of Spanheim, founder of St. Disibod, who, enclosed with certain other noble holy virgins, led an eremitic life. She was enclosed in the year of the Lord 1112, in the fifth indiction; three others were with her, namely the holy virgin Hildegard, who later, as we shall say, founded a monastery of nuns on Mount Rupert, in that place where the Nahe flows into the Rhine very near the city of Bingen; Jutta, the daughter of her brother; and another virgin of the same name. The number of virgins under her instruction increased. As long as she lived, St. Hildegard did not withdraw from her side. This holy woman, among other miracles of her holiness, changed water into wine and crossed the waters of the river Glan with dry feet.

She was buried in the aforesaid monastery of St. Disibod, which at that time was of our order, in which she herself, holy woman, had taken the habit of conversion. Her life, conduct, deeds, and miracles are found written down.

In the same year, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November, there was a very great wind, which overturned many towers and buildings. The sea also, having gone beyond its bounds, suddenly and unexpectedly submerged a great part of Flanders together with its inhabitants.

In the same year, around the feast of the Assumption of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, the emperor Lothar launched an expedition into Italy against Roger, prince of Apulia, at the urging of Pope Innocent II.

1137.

In the sixteenth year of Abbot Volmar, which was the 1137th from the Lord’s Nativity, the emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord and Easter in Italy, but Pentecost at Bari with a general assembly of the Italian princes. There Bruno II, archbishop of Cologne, died and was honorably buried in the church of Saint Nicholas. Hugo, dean of St. Peter’s at Cologne, succeeded him by [unclear] command of the emperor, and Pope Innocent ordained him there; yet in the same year he died in exile in Italy, before the city had learned of his ordination. Roger, prince of Apulia, on account of whose insolence the emperor, invited by the pope, had entered Italy, had placed [unclear], who by land and sea were oppressing the region with unheard-of calamities. In similar fashion he had acted through almost all Italy. After celebrating Pentecost, the emperor surrounded the castle of Bari with his army; taking it at last with great labor, he burned it and leveled it to the ground. The robbers seized around the burned tower were all hanged, more than five hundred in number.

Roger, prince of Apulia, enemy of the Roman Church.

Robbers are hanged.

The church of Mainz is burned.

Adalbert died.

Speyer is burned.

At that time Mainz was burned, together with the principal church.

In the same year Adalbert the elder, archbishop of Mainz, died on the ninth day before the Kalends of June. In the following year Adalbert the younger succeeded him, as we shall say. The greater church of Speyer also, with no small part of the city, and the town of Goslar, were consumed by fire on the same day on which Mainz was burned.

Meanwhile The Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

...as we have shown in the history of the dukes of Bavaria. This duke of Bavaria and Saxony begot, by the aforesaid wife, the daughter of Emperor Lothar II, Henry surnamed the Lion, duke of Brunswick and Saxony, a warlike and remarkable man, about whom the ancients sang marvelous things in German songs, and whom princes have been accustomed to depict in their halls down to the present day.

The story of his pilgrimage tells how, namely, sewn into a horse-hide and carried away from a ship by a griffin, he escaped the peril of the sea; how he fought with griffins, killed a dragon, crossed the sea with a lion, and at last, when his wife Matilda, daughter of the king of England, was preparing to take another husband, he was suddenly brought back unharmed by a demon, together with the lion, the companion of his journey and [unclear] danger, from very remote places to his castle. There are many similar things, which one should believe were written more from the invention of poets, under a certain mystical meaning, than that they actually happened. For the ancient Germans, after the custom of the Greeks, with whom it is known they had much intercourse, were accustomed to cast the brave deeds of heroes into songs fit for teaching, and, by concealing the deeds of mortals under the symbols of figures and riddles, to compare them with the immortals.

1134.

In the same year also, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1134, Saint Norbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, first founder of the Premonstratensian order, an outstanding propagator of holy religion, died on the eighth day before the Ides, and passed to the Lord in the eighth year of his episcopate. Conrad, son of a certain count, succeeded him.

In the same year Emperor Lothar besieged Speyer and, when it had at last been worn down by long famine, took it; and he received Conrad, duke of Swabia, rival of the kingdom and empire, into surrender and favor.

1135.

In the fourteenth year of Abbot Volmar, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1135, the emperor celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Aachen. In this same year the body of Saint Matthias the Apostle was found at Trier, in the monastery of Saint Eucharius of our order; from him the name of the monastery was thereafter changed, and it is called Saint Matthias down to the present day. Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, and Frederick, duke of Alsace, who were not well disposed toward the emperor, were judged worthy to be reconciled through the intervention of the princes.

At the feast of Pentecost, by order of the emperor, a great assembly of princes was held in the city of Magdeburg, at which the king of Denmark and many other princes were personally present; all of them swore a very firm peace for ten years, and the rest of the multitude was compelled to do the same.

In the same year Emperor Lothar expelled the nuns from the monastery of Lutera in the diocese of Halberstadt, and, after restoring the place for the better, introduced monks of our order from the monastery of Bergen near Magdeburg, appointing as their first abbot Everhard, a venerable monk of the aforesaid monastery. Moreover, the church itself [unclear] in honor of the holy apostles [unclear] was called by the common people. But after it had been changed and newly restored by King Lothar, it was called royal Lutera, that is, Königslutter, down to the present day.

In these times also, namely in the year of the Lord 1135, Buggo of the church of Worms established the monastery of Frankenthal. In it he placed a multitude of virgins serving Christ in chastity, after providing the necessary things. But after almost three hundred and twenty-six years, the most reverend bishop founded the monastery of Frankenthal, not far from Worms, in the time of Reinhard, bishop of Worms, when, with his consent, the regular brothers from Windesheim in the lower parts had undertaken to reform that monastery of Frankenthal, and they extinguished the abbatial title with which it had previously always been distinguished; and he placed in the monasteries canons living in common under the rule of Saint Augustine, for whom the church abundantly provided the necessities of the body.

He also established a monastery of nuns of the same religion next to the aforesaid [unclear] monastery, [unclear] the aforesaid seminary, after the nuns had been expelled, he joined it to the monastery of the brothers. CHRONICLE OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS. 127. [The OCR of this page is badly interleaved (two columns merged), with phrases repeated; the recoverable narrative follows.]

Meanwhile, matters in Italy having been prosperously accomplished, the emperor Lothair, when he had now begun to return home, on the very journey, situated not far from Nuremberg, in a certain castle of Welf, duke of Bavaria, by age as much as by infirmity, closed his last day, the 2nd [day before] the Nones of December—an outstanding man, and worthily to be called father of [his] country; whose body, brought back into Saxony, was honorably laid to rest in his monastery of Königslutter, which he had built, as we said.

In the same year died the bishop of Auxerre, [risen] from [being] abbot of the monastery of St Germain of our order, a man of great sanctity and religion. When he labored with [his] last sickness, and felt the final day to be at hand, around the ninth hour of the day he admonished the brothers standing around with these words: "Dearest brothers, let us pay to the Lord the hours of the day which remain, which we owe; for, the hours finished, I shall sleep and rest in the Lord." They therefore sang praises to the Lord, and, compline said, as he had foretold, the holy man rested in peace, and is buried in the church of St Germain, where he had earlier been abbot.

After Hugh, archbishop of Cologne, whom we said died in Italy, Arnold, provost of St Andrew in Cologne, son of the count of Wied, is raised to the archbishopric—who at length, by Pope Eugenius III in the council of Rheims, was suspended from the pontifical office, as we shall say in [its] place.

The emperor Lothair being dead (as has been said), Adelbero, bishop of Trier, fearing lest Henry, duke of Bavaria surnamed the Proud, son-in-law of the emperor—of whom we made mention above, to whom the regalia had long since been committed by Lothair himself—should prevail in the assembly of the princes (he who already so far reckoned himself secure of attaining [the kingdom] that he did not deign to make words about the kingdom to any of the princes): [Adelbero] acted with great industry, and, together with duke Conrad himself and the bishop of Worms, [arranged] that they should meet in conference at Coblenz in mid-Lent, the see of Mainz being vacant; where Arnold, the aforesaid archbishop of Cologne, met Adelbero, and, treating counsels together among themselves, they swore that they would elect Conrad king.

[1138.] In the year of abbot Volmar 17, which was of the Lord's nativity 1138, Conrad III of that name, duke of Alemannia or Swabia, brother of Frederick duke of Alsace, elected king of the Romans, reigned 14 years. But against this Conrad the princes of Bavaria and Saxony elected Henry the Proud, duke, son-in-law of the emperor Lothair, as king; and evils were multiplied in the land: for Conrad cunningly acquired the regalia which were with him, deposited by Lothair, and wished to deprive him [Henry] of the duchy of Saxony, [it] being given to the same Adelbert, margrave of Soltwedel. Hence slaughters, plunderings, and burnings through all Saxony.

In the same year king Conrad celebrated the Lord's Easter at Cologne. Thence going up, in the third week after Easter, he was received at Mainz with great favor of clergy and people. There Adalbert the younger, nephew through a brother of the deceased elder [Adalbert], by the common consent of all, by command of the king, was designated archbishop. Now the elder Adalbert, Saint Bernard of Clairvaux cooperating, while he yet lived, founded a monastery of the Cistercian order at Eberbach, almost two miles from Mainz, in the Rheingau, in which also he was buried.

In the same year king Conrad held a court of the princes at Bamberg for the feast of Pentecost, where the princes of almost the whole kingdom had assembled, except Henry, duke of Bavaria. There Adalbert of Mainz, elected, on the Saturday of the Ember days, was consecrated by Saint Otto, pontiff of the church of Bamberg. …This monastery [of St Disibod], collapsed by age, was newly built by Willigis, archbishop of Mainz, about the year of the Lord 976, and afterward (as we said) by Adalbert the archbishop, and Ruthard… The Monastery of Hirsau his predecessor, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 113[unclear], translated to the mountain newly founded a second time; and when this was at last completed, the tomb of the holy prelate Disibod, which Archbishop Willigis had closed, was opened, and the relics were translated into the new monastery and laid away behind the greater altar in a new sarcophagus. At this translation there were present Cuno, abbot of that place, with his whole congregation, since they are not far distant from one another; Gerard, abbot of St. Maximin at Trier; and very many of the clergy and nobles of the land of the county.

  1. In the eighteenth year of Abbot Volmar, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity [1139?], King Conrad celebrated the Lord’s Nativity at Goslar. Then, around the feast of James the Apostle, he moved an expedition into Saxony against Duke Henry. But when Henry met him manfully with a great army near the little town called Creutzberg, the king was compelled to return with the business unfinished. Those who took Duke Henry’s side were the counts palatine of the Rhine, the dukes of Bavaria, and Conrad, archbishop of Magdeburg. Days for bringing about concord between the king and Duke Henry were appointed by the princes at Quedlinburg; when Duke Henry had come there with his men, he ended his life by poison, as is reported: a powerful and warlike man, and the boldest of all in his time. He was buried in the monastery of our order at Konigslutter beside Lothar, his father-in-law, the emperor. His duchy Adelbert the margrave, mentioned above, obtained from King Conrad. Against him almost all the princes of Saxony conspired.

At about these times, when Embricho, bishop of the church of Wurzburg, was going to Mainz to carry out certain business, on the journey he had meeting him a certain monk, named Christian, a Scot by birth, who, bending his knees to the ground, begged that bishop that, for love of St. Kilian the martyr, who had been a Scot, he should grant to monks from Scotland, journeying abroad for Christ, a place or hospice in his city. Embricho provided letters strengthened with his seal, which we have seen and read whole and sound. For among the other miracles that he performed in this life, since he abstained entirely from wine for the love of God, and one day, sitting at table in the midst of magnates, could not have water, after making the sign of the holy cross over a vessel of wine set before everyone on the table, he changed the wine into water. All who were present marveled, since they had tasted wine that was excellent and suddenly saw it changed into water. Present at table in their own persons for this miracle were Piligrin, abbot of St. Burkhard, then of our order; Gebhard, provost of the New Monastery; Burekerus, Hentricus, Mukolinus, and Iringus of Zabelstein, with many others, both clerics and laymen. To transmit to posterity the perpetual memory of this most famous sign, the aforesaid Bishop Embricho, by the common counsel and assent of the whole clergy, gave and assigned forever, in the greater church of Wurzburg, a full and perpetual canonical prebend to the Scottish monks of the said monastery and their successors; thereafter they possessed and received it down to the present day.

In the nineteenth year of Abbot Volmar, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1140, there died Diemo, monk of this monastery of Hirsau and formerly prior, a most devout man who was believed to be filled with the spirit of prophecy. For he is said to have foretold many things, the truth of which certain [unclear] proved. That holy Henry, abbot of Breitenau, formerly a monk of this monastery, of whom we spoke above, was present at his burial; he had come, not by chance, but rather, as we believe, called by divine ordinance, for the spiritual consolation of the brothers.

In the same year the king celebrated the feast of the Purification at Worms, and Easter at Wurzburg. St. Otto, bishop of Bamberg, of our order, died in this same year and was enrolled in the catalogue of the saints. Gebhard too, bishop of Strasbourg, died. Adelbert auChronicle of Johannes Trithemius

[unclear], the younger, archbishop of Mainz, went to Rome, having been summoned by Pope Innocent, and was honorably received by him.

Discord between the pope and the king.

Since in these times King Conrad was attempting to invade the kingdom of Sicily against the will of Pope Innocent, the pontiff, by entreaties and money, dealt with the dukes of Bavaria, Henry and his brother Welf, that they should block his access into Italy. They undertook this the more willingly because they had previously regarded the king as hostile and hateful. And so, when King Conrad wished to prepare an expedition into Italy, while Duke Henry was still living, Duke Welf stoutly resisted.

War between the king and the dukes of Bavaria.

Thus a very severe battle took place between that Duke Welf of Bavaria on the side of Pope Innocent and Frederick, duke of the Swabians, on the king’s side, in the diocese of Augsburg, near Neresheim, a monastery of our order; and when many had been slain on both sides, Duke Frederick at last won the victory, and Welf fled with his men into a stronghold. Finally, after the death of Duke Henry, Duke Welf, mindful of the loss he had suffered, gathered a great army and renewed the war against Duke Frederick near the village called Ellenhofen, not far from Weinsberg. In this battle Duke Welf himself fell, and the greater part of his army was laid low.

Weinsberg is taken.

Thereupon, in this same year, King Conrad besieged Welf’s town, which is called Weinsberg; and, receiving it in surrender, he granted this liberty to the matrons and women: that whatever they could carry away on their shoulders should be permitted to them by royal munificence. They, neglecting their household goods, took up on their shoulders their husbands and men, as many as they could, and carried them out beyond the gates while all looked on and marveled at their resourcefulness. When the duke advised that such things not be allowed to happen, the king said that it was not fitting for the word of a ruler to be changed.

Note the change of [unclear] made [unclear].

The duchy of Bavaria is transferred to the Austrians.

Moreover, the king conferred the duchy of Bavaria on Leopold, margrave of Austria; yet afterwards Emperor Frederick I restored it to the legitimate heirs.

John de Temporibus died.

In this same year died John, called de Temporibus, who had lived three hundred and sixty-one years from the time of Charles the Great, whose shield-bearer he had been; he was a man of a very temperate constitution.

Hugh of Saint Victor of Paris died.

In the same year died Hugh, canon at Saint Victor of Paris, a man second to none in his time in religion and in knowledge of letters, and in knowledge of the seven liberal arts. He wrote many excellent little works of his talent for the benefit of readers; of these we have made fuller mention in the book On Ecclesiastical Writers.

A pseudo-emperor deceived many.

In these times a certain pseudo-emperor arose in Germany. Living for some years in enclosure at Solothurn and then coming forth from there, he pretended that he was Emperor Henry. And when he was causing scandal to many, [unclear], when he was cited to it, he appealed to the apostolic see; and thus escaping, [unclear], by seducing, he had attracted people to himself to such an extent that serious battles and killings took place on his behalf, some receiving him as the deceased Emperor Henry, others openly crying out that he was a deceiver. Finally, when his falsehood had been made clear, he was shorn as a monk at Cluny.

Synod against Peter Abelard.

In the same year of the Lord, [unclear] 19, in the city of Sens in Gaul, a synod of bishops and abbots was held in the presence of Louis, king of the Franks, against Master Peter Abelard, who was scandalizing the Church by a certain profane novelty of words and meanings. When he was cited to it, he appealed to the apostolic see; and thus escaping, [unclear], by seducing, he had attracted people to himself to such an extent that serious battles and killings took place on his behalf, some receiving him as the deceased Emperor Henry, others openly crying out that he was a deceiver. Finally, when his falsehood had been made clear, he was shorn as a monk at Cluny.

The same Peter founded a convent of nuns. His wife was the first abbess.

The philosopher, who from his own marriage built a convent of nuns in the territory of Troyes, in a certain meadow where he had been accustomed to lecture; gathering there many nuns by episcopal authority, he named the convent after Saint Paraclete, and in [unclear].

Epitaph of this Peter Abelard.

Our Aristotle, among logicians, whoever they were, known to the world of studies as either equal or better; first in talent, varied, subtle, and keen, surpassing all by the force of reason and the art of speaking: Abelard was such. But then he conquered all the more, when, professing the Cluniac monk and way of life, he passed over to the true philosophy of Christ. In this, completing well the final things of a long life, [unclear] to be numbered among the good philosophers. Hope The Monastery of Hirsau. The eleventh [unclear] gave hope, with May renewing the Kalends.

1141.

In the twentieth year of Abbot Volmar, which was the year 1141 of the Lord's Nativity, King Conrad held his court at Regensburg on the feast of Pentecost, where some princes of Saxony were present. Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz, conspired with the Saxons against the king, but not long afterward, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, he died. Marolph succeeded him in the archbishopric of the church of Mainz; he had previously been provost of the church of Aschaffenburg in the same diocese, and he did not complete two years in the pontificate.

In the same year Lady Richiza, empress, wife of Emperor Lothar, died and was buried beside her husband in the monastery of Lutter. Conrad, archbishop of Magdeburg, also died; Frederick, custos of the cathedral church, succeeded him by election of the brethren. Henry, margrave of Brandenburg, likewise died without children and left the march free in the hands of the king and the empire; King Conrad, by counsel of the princes, granted it as an imperial fief to Adelbert, count of Salzwedel. The same king also gave to his brother, Count Henry, as wife the daughter of Emperor Lothar, left as widow of Henry, duke of Bavaria, and created him duke of Austria.

1142.

In the [twenty-first?] year of Abbot Volmar, in the year [1142?] of the Lord's Nativity, the king celebrated Pentecost at Frankfurt, where almost all the princes, bishops, and abbots of the whole kingdom assembled; and there the marriage rites were celebrated for fourteen days. The king joined Gertrude, daughter of Emperor Lothar and widow of Henry, duke of Bavaria, in marriage as wife to his brother Henry, the first duke of Austria. There Henry, surnamed the Lion, son of Henry, duke of Bavaria, and of Gertrude, the aforesaid daughter of Emperor Lothar, received the duchy from the hand of King Conrad.

In the same year Marolph, archbishop of Mainz, died. Henry, provost of the cathedral church, succeeded him; in the presence of two cardinals, legates of the Holy Roman Church, at Frankfurt he received investiture of the regalia from King Conrad himself.

In the same year Henry of holy memory, abbot in Breitenau, of whom we spoke above, obtained from Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, four bodies from the company of the eleven thousand virgins; these, on the sixth day before the Nones of July, with the greatest honor, to the monastery [unclear].

Henry, archbishop of Mainz.

The winter was very severe.

In the following year Adelbero, archbishop of Trier, expelled the monks from the monastery of Saint Maximin at Trier because of their disorderly life, and, restoring others in their place, set over that monastery an abbot named Siger.

In this year the winter was hard and very severe. Gertrude also, daughter of Emperor Lothar, whom we have said was married to Henry, duke of Austria, after the death of her former husband, reached her last day because of the difficulty of childbirth; and, with the inhabitants of Saxony [unclear] mourning, she was buried in the monastery of Lutter with her father and mother and her former husband, Duke Henry. Pope Celestine II died; Lucius II succeeded him.

1143.

In the [twenty-third?] year of Abbot Volmar, and in the one thousand one hundred forty-fourth year of the Lord, blessed Felix, pope and martyr, appeared to Saint Henry, most reverend abbot of the monastery of Breitenau, [formerly?] a monk of this monastery of Hirsau, as was said above, revealing to him his head, which had lain hidden for many years in the apse of that church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September. The holy man raised the head of the holy martyr from the earth with the greatest reverence, and sent one small part to the brethren of Hirsau as a very great gift of charity.

1144.

In the [twenty-fourth?] year of Abbot Volmar, Pope Lucius died; Eugenius, abbot of Saint Anastasius, of the Cistercian order and formerly a monk of Saint Bernard, succeeded him.

1145.

In the [twenty-fifth?] year of Abbot Volmar, which was the year 1145 of the Lord's Nativity, a great earthquake occurred fifteen times; a comet appeared, and in the following year a great pestilence followed.

Earthquake.

A comet appeared.

In the same year, on the Nones of December, Buggo, bishop of Worms, died, a man of many virtues, and through the hands of Gunther, bishop of Speyer, in the monastery of Schönau, which he himself had built and consecrated in honor of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, but

Buggo. CHRONICLE OF JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS. 131.

…was buried. He presided over the church of Worms strenuously for 36 years; to whom in the episcopate succeeded Conrad, the first of this name, who sustained many persecutions from many. For in his time Conrad, count Palatine of the Rhine, brother of the first emperor Frederick, violently plundered the possessions of the churches; whom, since no one could resist (because the days were evil), the ministers of the Lord were compelled either to redeem the things taken away with money, or patiently to tolerate the injuries with loss. There is extant a letter of this bishop Conrad to the holy virgin of Christ Hildegard, abbess on the Mount of St Rupert near Bingen, in which he mentions the calamities which he suffers, and humbly asks her counsel and the support of [her] prayers. To whom the holy virgin writes back words of holy admonition, divinely inspired, and makes [him], as he had asked, a participant in her prayers.

[1147.] In the year of abbot Volmar 26, which was of the Lord's nativity 1147, an eclipse of the sun occurred, the 7th [day before] the Kalends of November, around almost the fourth hour of the day. In that year a famine followed. After the famine, too, pestilence and a great mortality followed, incredible to all posterity.

In the same year too Embricho, bishop of Würzburg (of whom we spoke above), returning from Greece, dies at Aquileia, and is buried there; for whom Siegfried is constituted bishop. Eggebert, bishop of Bamberg, also dies, in whose place Everhard is ordained. Conrad the king entered Hungary with a strong hand.

In the same year the greatest army of the Christians—from all Germany, Gaul, Italy, Spain, England, Hungary, indeed from all Europe—after the paschal feast, was moved to recover the holy land, the cross being preached by Bernard, by command of Pope Eugenius, against the infidels; whose journeyings and deeds, since they have been copiously described by many, we have resolved to pass over in silence.

In the same year St Malachy, archbishop [of Armagh], coming from Ireland to Clairvaux to visit holy Bernard, migrated to the Lord, the 3rd [day before] the Nones of November, a man of apostolic life, the very form of all perfection and the example of virtue; who, among the other marks of his virtues, raised a dead man, reformed the faith in Ireland, [and] wonderfully spread holy religion. So holy a man, Bernard the abbot, described [his life]. About these same times the same St Bernard the abbot, to preach the cross of the Lord against the infidels, by command of Pope Eugenius, was traveling through Germany, and shone forth everywhere with many signs and miracles. For in the territory of Constance, in one day he enlightened eleven blind men, healed ten maimed, and to eighteen lame, the powers of walking restored, fully reformed [them]. When he was in that very city of Constance, the fame of [his] virtues spreading everywhere, the abbot of the monastery of Reichenau sent to him a blind man, whom by his alms[deeds]…

The Monastery of Hirsau

preaching with confidence, he showed himself to be a true servant of God. From there, carried by ship, he reached the town of Bingen, where in the monastery of St. Rupert, duke, on the other side of the River Nahe, the virgin beloved of God, St. Hildegard, as mistress, presided over devout virgins serving the almighty Lord under the rule of our holy father Benedict. To her he had previously sent by letters words of holy admonition, together with certain small gifts, which are preserved in that same place as relics.

When Bernard, the man of God, came to the holy bride of Christ, after a mutual greeting in Christ he ordered the books which that virgin had written by divine inspiration to be brought to him. After he had examined them carefully and admired them beyond measure, he is said to have told those standing around: “These writings are not human inventions, but divinely inspired through the Spirit; nor can any mortal man understand them unless he has first been truly reformed inwardly in his soul according to the likeness of God.” To this the chaplain of the holy virgin, a monk of most devout conduct, replied: “Reverend father, what you have said is indeed true. But many people, not only unlettered laymen but also religious and learned men, torment the spirit of Christ’s handmaid with daily slanders, when they assert that these things are not divinely inspired, but are either women’s dreams and ravings of a ruined brain, or deceitfully sent in by demons.”

To him the man of God said: “We do not wonder, dearest brother, if those sleeping in sins regard divine revelations as dreams, knowing as true what the holy Apostle said: ‘The animal man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God; for it is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand, because it is examined spiritually.’ For to all those who, as though sleeping, [lie?] in the sins of lust, greed, and pride, divine admonitions seem to be dreams deceitfully sent in. But those who say that these things are sent in by demons have not known the hidden and mystical signs of divine inspirations; and they should be judged like those who said that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ cast out demons by the power of Beelzebub.”

He also said to holy Hildegard: “And you, dearest daughter, do not fear the reproaches of men, since you have God as your defender; for they will perish like straw, but the truth of the Lord remains forever. We too, for love of you, will take pains that these writings of yours, once read and confirmed by the lord Apostolic, may safely be brought into the light.”

The holy virgin Hildegard offered to the man of God, at his request, a particle of the relics of St. Rupert, duke and confessor. In return for these he too afterward [unclear] certain things [unclear] of the count of Sponheim, under whose temporal authority the aforesaid monastery was built, and in which he also had a daughter, a nun named Hiltrud, a virgin of most holy conduct, who with blessed Hildegard had been [instructed?] in the love of God under the teaching of blessed [Jutta?]. Present there with that count were Cuno, abbot of St. Disibod, and Bernhelm, first abbot in Sponheim, with many other clerics, monks, and laymen. There at that time Bernhelm, abbot of Sponheim, obtained the body of St. Rupert.

At Boppard [unclear] a paralytic. At Trier [unclear]. At Cologne he also cured twenty-two. At Aachen miracles [unclear]. Meginhard, duke and count in Sponheim, was present.

Meginhard, duke and count in Sponheim, under whose temporal authority the aforesaid monastery had been built, obtained the body of that duke, whole with skin and flesh, from blessed Hildegard and her whole congregation of holy virgins; and with great reverence and honor, as he continued the descent of the Rhine to his monastery, he cured at Boppard, in the midst of the people, a paralytic, [one with a disabled hand?], and a deaf woman in the same city, with all the people looking on. Finally, after staying for three days in the city of Cologne, he cured twelve lame persons, two maimed persons, five blind persons, and ten deaf persons, restored speech to three mute persons, and performed countless other signs. At Aachen, when he was celebrating Mass, he restored walking to a lame man and sight to four blind persons before a multitude of peoples. In the cities also of Liège and of the Nervii, which is now called Cambrai, he restored speech to many, hearing to the deaf, sight to the blind, walking to the lame, and health to those sick with any disease.

1149. In the aforesaid year of Abbot Volmar, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1149, in the twelfth indiction, Crafto, count of Sponheim, son of Meginhard the elder and brother of the younger, betrothed as his wife Clementia, daughter of Adolf, count of Homberg, a beautiful and modest virgin most devoted to Christ. Since she had resolved to devote the flower of her virginity to Christ, she sought and obtained the consent of her mortal bridegroom. Therefore that venerable virgin Clementia became a nun of our order in the monastery of St. Irmina in Oeren at Trier, and served almighty God in great holiness for many years. Moreover that same Crafto, bridegroom of the holy virgin, [Blank page in the source scan.]

[unclear] in my aforesaid monastery of Spanheim, under Abbot Bernhelm, he became a monk; in it he conducted himself so religiously and so prudently that, when Bernhelm died, he was ordained abbot in place of the dead man, as we shall say in what follows.

1150.

In the twenty-ninth year of Abbot Volmar, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1150, fire and water brought about countless disasters and losses throughout various parts of the world. That whole year, full of miseries, was a portent of the one following. The winter was very severe and excessively long. Fiery battle-lines were seen in the sky. The whole city of Utrecht, with its churches, was consumed by fire; there a certain wooden cross, falling from on high, while the roof of the church with its beams fell down upon it, remained unharmed [unclear]. Even after it had lain for a very long time in the fire, it was afterwards found uncorrupted, except only that the iron nails of the crossbeam, by which the image of the Lord was held, had melted. This cross, in memory of the miracle that occurred, is honorably preserved in the church of St. Boniface.

In these times Pope Eugenius III came to Trier with eighteen cardinals and many bishops and abbots, invited by Adelbero, archbishop of that city, who for three months provided the pope and all the others who were present, at his own expense, most abundantly with food and drink. There Pope Eugenius dedicated the newly repaired church of the monastery of St. Matthew the Apostle on the day before the Kalends of February. He also held a synod there of bishops, cardinals, and abbots; there Henry, archbishop of Mainz, and St. Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, reported to the supreme pontiff the marvels that God was working in his handmaid Hildegard, abbess of Mount St. Rupert the Confessor.

When he had heard these things, the pope was astonished, and, wishing to investigate the matter more diligently, sent Adelbert, bishop of Verdun, with other trustworthy men to St. Hildegard, so that with humility and gentleness, without noise or curiosity, they might inquire of her what the matter was. When they had come to the monastery in which the holy virgin was living, and, according to the apostolic commission, were humbly inquiring the truth from her, she simply [unclear]. After these things had been examined for the pope, he ordered the volumes of the holy virgin that had been sent to him to be read publicly before the cardinals, archbishops, abbots, and all the clergy; and he himself, performing the office of reader, read no small part, through which the minds of all were turned to amazement, and their voices to praise [unclear]. He gloriously granted her [the authority?] of writing whatever she had learned through the Holy Spirit, and encouraged her to write down without fear the things revealed to her. The tenor of his letter was:

“Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter in the Lord, Hildegard, prioress on Mount St. Rupert, greeting and apostolic blessing. We marvel, O daughter, and we marvel beyond what can be believed, that God in our times is now showing new miracles, since he has so filled you with his spirit that you are said to see, understand, and utter many secrets. This we have learned from certain truthful persons [unclear] having [the keys?] of knowledge, so that we might close and open; and do we neglect, through folly, to do this prudently? We rejoice in the grace of God, and we rejoice also in your love; and we admonish you of this, that you know that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. Therefore preserve and guard through humility the grace that is in you, so that the things which you perceive in the spirit should be brought forth you may prudently bring forth, whereby you will hear that saying from the Lord: ‘Open your mouth, and I will fill it.’ What you have signified to us concerning that place which you foresaw there in the spirit, let this be done with our permission and blessing and that of your bishop, namely, that you live there regularly with your sisters according to the Rule of St. Benedict, within the enclosure of that same place.”

The birth of Blessed Hildegard.

To these things the virgin of Christ, divinely inspired, sent letters of reply back to the supreme pontiff, in which she admonished him concerning the secrets that he had in his heart, and indicated the divine will and good pleasure concerning these matters. This most blessed virgin Hildegard was born from the county of Spanheim, in the village called Bickelnheim, begotten of her father Hildebert and her mother Mechthild, in the times of Emperor Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1098, in the sixth indiction. Her father Hildebert, a noble man, served as a knight in the court of Count Meginhard of Spanheim, a most noble and at that time very powerful man; he was rich and honored in the world. But Hildegard, in the eighth year of her age, was handed over by her parents to be instructed in monastic disciplines by the lady virgin Jutta on Mount Disibod, enclosed there for love of Christ, the sister of the aforesaid Count Meginhard, of whom mention was made above; and by her she was laudably educated in the fear of the Lord, Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

and many others. Also through the provosts of the regulars in Flamheim, of the regulars in Heyna, of the regulars in Vestera, of the Premonstratensians in Herde, of the nuns of our order in Himelauue, of the nuns of the Cistercian order in the Valley of God, of Cappenberg, of Saint Victor at Mainz, of Saint Castor in Koblenz, of Saint Andrew in Cologne, of Erfurt, of the major church of Mainz, of Saint Simeon at Trier, in Ruestede, of Frankfurt, of the major churches of Trier, Cologne, Bonn, and many others.

Also through the abbesses of Saint Elisabeth of Schonau of our order, writing in the same spirit; of Gandersheim; in Wechterswinckel of Altzen of our order; in Altwyich in the diocese of Utrecht; in Krunchen of Saint Mary at Regensburg; in Keysungen of Saint Cyriacus at Erfurt; in Lubbelsberg; in Widergoldesdorff; in Sebach of our order; in Gronechtal; of Saint Theodore at Bamberg of our order; in the Old Monastery at Mainz; of Olfaten; in the Upper Monastery at Regensburg; in Nussia of our order; of the Holy Virgins in Cologne; in Didenkirchen; in Andernach; of Saint Glodesindis at Metz; in Erdendal; and through many others. But also through priests, philosophers, and masters, both from remote and from nearer places, not a few letters were sent, to which responsive letters of hers, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and full of mysteries and secrets, are joined.

For she was accustomed to aid all who sought from her the consolation of the Holy Spirit, or asked for a word of holy admonition, by writings and prayers; and she never despised anyone, however weak, lowly, or poor. She was renowned for many miracles both in life and after death, and by her prayers in the name of Christ she cured the sick, burdened in whatever way, who flocked to her. Her life, conduct, and wondrous deeds [unclear] by Theodoric [unclear] of Spanheim, brother of the blessed Hiltrudis, a nun, and formerly husband of the most devout virgin Clementia, daughter of the count of Homberg, a nun in the monastery of Saint Irmina, which is called the Granary, of whom we made mention above. He was a man very devoted in the fear of the Lord, and no less distinguished by humility than by blood. By his earnest prayers he obtained the head of Saint Irmina, a venerable virgin, [unclear] and first abbess of the aforesaid monastery of nuns, daughter of Dagobert, king of the Franks, whom Saint Willibrord the bishop [unclear] as a bride to Christ; this head is held to the present day in that same monastery of mine at Spanheim.

In this same year there was a severe famine, and a great mortality of men followed. Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, died; Arnold the second, provost of the major church and chancellor of the king, succeeded him in the pontificate. In this same year there also died Conrad, landgrave of Thuringia, and Frederick, archbishop of Magdeburg; Wichmann, son of the count of Tegenburg in Bavaria, succeeded him, governed for forty-two years quite usefully, and was buried in the monastery of Husburg of our order.

1152.

In the thirty-first year of Abbot Volmar, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1152, Conrad the third, king of the Romans, lying ill in the city of Bamberg and sensing that the day of his death was near, handed the royal insignia to Duke Frederick, his brother’s son, commended to him his own son Frederick, still a little child, and asked him to speak to the princes about acquiring the kingdom for him. Having arranged his affairs, he died on the second day before the Kalends of March, in the fourteenth year of his reign; he was buried in the same city and did not receive the imperial benediction from the pope. After his death, a celebrated assembly of princes and bishops was held at Frankfurt. There, with the highest favor of all, the aforesaid Frederick, duke of Swabia, was elected king of the Romans, a vigorous man and one of many works, as we shall partly say in what follows. He reigned as emperor for thirty-seven years.

In the same year Adelbero, archbishop of Trier, died, a high-minded man and [unclear].

The Monastery of Hirsau

... learned to love nothing except heavenly things. In the same place she served almighty God for many years in humble chastity, until at last, after the death of the venerable Jutta, when the number of virgins had increased, instructed by divine revelation, she moved to the mountain of Saint Rupert near the town of Bingen, where the Nahe flows into the Rhine, with eighteen nuns subject to her. There, with the help of Count Meginhard of Sponheim and other faithful of Christ, she built a monastery for sacred virgins, in the very place where Saint Rupert the duke, together with his mother, a holy woman named Bertha, had had a castle and dwelling in the times of Emperor Louis I.

Under her direction, among the other sacred women, was Hiltrud, a most devout virgin, the very beautiful daughter of the aforesaid Count Meginhard, concerning whom mention was made above. For love of the heavenly kingdom she rejected broad dominion on earth and received the habit of holy life under the discipline of Jutta, her father's sister, on the mountain of the holy bishop Disibod. Out of regard for this virgin her father, Count Meginhard, bestowed many goods on that monastery, and the right of the place, which belonged partly to the church of Mainz, partly to [unclear] of Disibod, [unclear]. Out of regard for this virgin her father, Count Meginhard, [unclear] many goods to that monastery, and handed it over to Saint Hildegard, giving and granting her every kind of freedom to choose whatever protector she wished; and he released that place forever from his own lordship, power, and advocacy.

Furthermore, Saint Hildegard, virgin of Christ, visited from childhood by divine revelations, although, apart from the Psalter and simple psalmody, she had learned from no human being either the art or the practice of the Latin language, nevertheless, wondrously illumined by the grace of the Holy Spirit, wrote many things and dictated many things, distinguished partly in Latin, partly in German speech, which she learned not by human perception or understanding, but rather by divine inspiration; and therefore her writings can be understood only by spiritual persons.

She wrote a large book of much subtlety, which she entitled Scivias, which begins: "And it came to pass in a new year." Likewise, three books On Divine Works. Three books On the Merits of Life. On the Causes and Remedies of All Diseases of the Human Body, an outstanding work, which she entitled Medicine when she had composed it, and it begins: "God, before the creation of the world, was and is without beginning." Likewise [unclear], which deservedly turns readers to astonishment. This little work begins thus: "Charity, which with abstinence from sins instructs faith." Instructed from heaven by vision, she also wrote the life of Saint Disibod the bishop, a brief indeed but useful little work, beginning thus: "And I, [a poor little one in female form?]." Likewise, to the thirty very subtle questions of Wibert the monk, put before her by letter, taught by the Holy Spirit, she replied so profoundly, properly, and catholically that [unclear]. She wrote [unclear] full of [unclear]; indeed, she was also present in person in this monastery, concerning which we shall make mention when, in weaving the history, we shall have come to the times of Abbot Manegold.

Finally, in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Rupert there survive to the present day copies of letters and epistles sent to Saint Hildegard herself by Conrad II and Frederick I, Roman emperors; by Eugenius III, Anastasius IV, Adrian IV, and Alexander III, Roman pontiffs; by the archbishops of Mainz, Henry, Arnold, and Christian; by the [Trier?], Cologne, Bremen, Salzburg, Jerusalem, and Magdeburg archbishops, and several others; also by bishops and abbots [unclear]. Of Monks' Mountain, Bamberg, Speyer, Constance, Verdun, Liège, Utrecht, Prague, and many others from Germany, Gaul, and Italy; by holy abbots, first of all Bernard of Clairvaux, Adam of York, by the [Eberbach?] abbot, by that of Saint Anastasius from Rome, by that of Kaisheim, by Manegold of Hirsau, by that of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, by that of [Monichen Nuenburg?], by that of Saint Mary ad Martyres at Trier, by that of Saint Matthias at Trier, by that of Saint Disibod, by those of Kempten, Ellwangen, Maulbronn, Monks' Mountain, Bamberg, Zwiefalten, Sponheim, Salem, Besonis villa of Saint Martin, Cologne, Brauweiler, [Wetel?], Heilsbronn, Bellevaux, [Cariloc?], [Clarefontes?], Charity, Bethany, Sprengersbach, Rodenkirchen, El...
