of regular censure.

When Lothar the emperor had received the royal insignia at Aachen on the holy day of Easter, this man publicly excommunicated his brother Simon and, under the Gospel, with such [unclear], in the presence of the emperor himself, compelled him to leave the church. But from the monastery of St. Matthias and the other monasteries of monks he violently seized many things and converted them to his own uses. Hillinus, dean of the greater church, succeeded him in the archbishopric and presided for eighteen years. Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, having set out for Rome, was ordained by Pope Eugenius; by him he was sent back to his see with the pallium and honor.

1153.

In the thirty-second year of Abbot Volmar, which was the year 1153 of the Lord’s nativity, Henry, archbishop of Mainz, by order of Pope Eugenius, on the holy day of Pentecost, was deposed by two cardinals, Gregory and Bernard; and he died in the same year, on the Kalends of September. St. Hildegard foretold to him this shortness of life two years before; in a certain letter to him she says thus: “Hear, you who neglect me amid many inquiries. Heaven is opened for the vengeance of the Lord, and now the boundaries have been released to enemies. But you, rise, because your days are short; and remember that Nebuchadnezzar fell, and that his crown perished. And many others fell who rashly exalted themselves into heaven. Ah, you ashes, why are you not ashamed to scatter yourself on high, when you ought to be in corruption?”

Therefore, when Henry had been deposed from the archbishopric, Arnold, the king’s chancellor and provost of Aachen, succeeded; he was afterward slain in the monastery of St. James outside the walls of Mainz, as we shall say in its place. To him St. Hildegard writes thus, among other things: “O father, living in human fashion, these words he gave me for you. Why are you not strong in my fear? And why do you have zeal, displaying as it were [unclear], so that by separating you cast down what is contrary to you? But this I do not will. Wipe away, from the eye of your heart, an unquiet mind; and cut off injustice from your people, because the time of wars now stands in the morals of men, so that they are neither in discipline nor in the severity of the fear of the Lord. You shall endure; do not be afraid, because the Son of God suffered the same things. Therefore rise to God, because the time is at hand [unclear] will come.”

In the same year also, when Henry, bishop of Minden, could not clear himself concerning a certain cleric who had been [unclear] in the city by his men, with his own consent, as was said, being wearied by many adversities, he renounced the bishopric before the aforesaid cardinals. Werner, provost of the same church, succeeded him.

Pope Eugenius III also died. Conrad, abbot of the monastery of St. Rufus in the diocese of Velletri, of our order and a cardinal, succeeded him and was named Anastasius IV; he sat one year, four months, and twenty-four days. This Pope Anastasius sent, in the first year of his pontificate, letters to St. Hildegard the virgin, full of paternal affection and showing devotion, in which he wonderfully extols her writings and humbly commends himself to the prayers of her and of the whole congregation, beseeching from her with great prayers a divine response. The holy virgin, taught divinely through revelation, wrote back to him all the things that were necessary for him for the amendment of life, even the most hidden things.

In the same year at Cologne, a certain man born of a Jewish father, but a convert, after he had received by mouth the sacrament of the body of Christ at the solemnity of Easter, and had gone out of the church and thought of carrying it home, intending I know not what to do with it, was struck with divine terror and shuddered; and, not knowing where to turn, he made a pit in the cemetery and buried in it the most holy body of the Lord. But a priest came upon him, and, learning the matter, opened the pit; finding the form of a little child, and reverently lifting him in his hands, he wished to carry him to the church. But, wondrous to say, when light was sent from heaven, the little boy slipped from the hands of the one holding him and, ascending in that light, penetrated the heavens.

1154.

In the thirty-third year of Abbot Volmar, which was the year 1154 of the Lord’s nativity, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March, Mechtild, a nun and virgin, died in my monastery of Spanheim, enclosed for the love of Christ for twenty-nine years, the sister of Bernhelm, the first abbot of the same monastery. She was first enclosed at St. Alban’s in Mainz for seven years; then, when Bernhelm her brother had been ordained abbot of Spanheim, for greater quiet and solitude, to the city Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

...to the same monastery, with the consent of the archbishop of Mainz and the abbot of St Alban, she transferred herself, and served almighty God most devoutly in fasts and prayers, day and night, until the end of her life. She was buried in the middle of the choir beside the tomb of her brother, Abbot Bernhelm, not without a reputation for holiness. For the harmony of angels was heard at her passing, and various visions were shown; and St Hildegard, while she was still living in the flesh, bore witness to her holiness.

Around the feast of St Michael King Frederick set out for Italy with a great army. The expedition of the king into Italy. Meanwhile Pope Anastasius died. Nicholas the Englishman, first a monk of St Rufus, then abbot, afterward cardinal bishop of Albano of our order, succeeded him, called Adrian IV, and sat for 4 years and 10 months. King Frederick, after his army had crossed into Italy, at the first assault subdued Piacenza, a city of Emilia; he also devastated certain castles by fire because of the insolence of the Milanese and Cremonese. Then he burned Spoleto, the very wealthy city of Umbria, entirely with fire. And so, passing with his army toward the sea [unclear], he came to Rome, where he was honorably received by the Roman pontiff and the whole senate, was consecrated emperor, and, after the solemn ordination, when a sedition had been stirred up by certain common people at noon, he was unexpectedly attacked in battle. But the emperor and his men, suddenly armed, drove the enemy across the Tiber with drawn swords, and raged against them with such slaughter that the very bed of the river was entirely changed by the blood of the slain. Having carried out this bloody victory on 18 June with a small band of his men, he did not delay on the following day but began his return, and led his army back unharmed into his homeland.

In these times the bishopric of Lübeck was transferred from Oldenburg, and Gerold was ordained the first bishop there.

1155.

In the 34th year of Abbot Volmar, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1155, there was a serious war between Arnold, archbishop of Mainz, and Hermann, count palatine of the Rhine. War between the archbishop of Mainz and the count palatine. But Frederick the Emperor, returning from Italy, so subdued the disturbers of the kingdom and of peace that in a short time a very firm peace was restored by the terror of his arrival. For the emperor himself had established Arnold as archbishop, against the wishes of many powerful men round about, since they knew him to be a just and severe man, in no way consenting to their wicked designs. Therefore, while the emperor was in Italy, Hermann, count [unclear], Emicho, count of Leiningen, Godfrey, count of Sponheim, Henry, count of Katzenelnbogen, Conrad, count of Kirchberg, and Hericus, count of Didesheim, with certain others, took up arms against the pontiff. Counts on the side of Hermann. The emperor, therefore, returning from Italy, celebrated the Lord’s Nativity at Worms, and, by the counsel of the princes, imposed satisfaction as penance on the aforesaid counts together with the aforesaid Archbishop Arnold, because they had violated the peace that had been commanded. For the aforesaid counts Emicho, Godfrey, Henry, and others, on the side of the aforesaid Count Hermann, carried dogs at the emperor’s command; and so Lord Arnold the archbishop absolved them from excommunication. But on the side of the bishop himself, Count Louis of Lohun, Count William of Glitzberg, and others began to carry dogs, but out of reverence for the archbishop they were ordered by the emperor to desist. The carrying of dogs as satisfaction.

In the same year Bernard, bishop of Hildesheim in Saxony, because he had been blind for ten years and was useless for ruling, resigned the bishopric; and in his place Bruno, dean of the same church, was ordained, a holy man and most devoted to blessed Mary ever virgin. He was the first to celebrate the octaves of her Nativity, and solemnly instituted their celebration in his diocese. And the most holy Virgin herself once visibly appeared to him at matins while he was celebrating those same octaves, and, giving thanks to him for so great a service, [unclear] great consolation and hope of future recompense. The emperor, dismissing his wife, marries [unclear]. [unclear]

In the course of the 35th year of Abbot Volmar, Arnold, archbishop of Mainz, provoked by the injuries of certain men, came into the presence of Pope Adrian; honorably received by him, he obtained from him the apostolic legation, and then, returning to Mainz, was received with honor.

In this same year the emperor Frederick took as wife Agnes, daughter of the prince of Burgundy, having repudiated his former legitimate wife at Constance; from this a very grave [unclear] in the church.

Hermann, count palatine, died. He was succeeded by the emperor’s brother on his father’s side, named Conrad, a man forgetful of God, who by violence inflicted many injuries on churches and monasteries and their ministers, especially on Conrad, bishop of Worms.

The Monastery of Hirsau

Another Conrad also, a monk of this monastery, at about the same time, with the consent of Abbot Volmar himself, was ordained abbot for the monastery in Schwarzach in the diocese of Strasbourg. Burchard also, a monk of this monastery, was elected abbot at Weingarten, a man shrewd in ability, and in affairs very provident and experienced.

After his death Diethmar, our monk, by the election of the brothers of that place, was made abbot; by his industry he did and acquired many good things for that same monastery.

At the same time when Hartwig, from being provost, became a monk under Abbot Volmar, the cloistral prior was Manegold, a Frank by nation, who was afterwards elected abbot of this monastery, concerning whom we shall speak. He loved Hartwig with great charity, a wise man, magnificent in all his actions. Hence, when promoted to the cellarership of the monastery, he watched with much solicitude over the necessity of the brothers; ministering well in the lower office, he deserved a higher rank.

After him Adelhelm was appointed prior, first at Amöneburg, afterwards abbot at [Mediolacum?] in the diocese of Trier, a man venerable for wisdom and religion. In his place Heymericus was substituted as prior, an old and weak monk; when he died shortly thereafter, Gerlach succeeded him. After him Manegold was again ordained prior, and he remained in that office until the death of Abbot Hartwig.

In this very year of the installation of Abbot Hartwig, which was the year 1157 of the Lord’s Nativity, Adelhelm, as we have said, having been lawfully ordained by Hillin, archbishop of Trier, visited the holy virgin Hildegard at Bingen and returned to Hirsau, where he was received with the greatest joy of the brothers, as a shepherd of most upright charity.

The emperor celebrated Easter at Worms, where almost all the princes of the German kingdom assembled, and swore that in the following year they would go with the king into Lombardy against the rebels of the empire. Afterwards in this same year the emperor, by his great industry, brought it about that abbots, provosts, and indeed many of the better ministerials of the church of Mainz promised into the hands of certain of his friends that, should Archbishop Arnold depart for any reason, they would not elect another without his counsel and assent.

In the same year Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, the second of this name, died, a man acute in ability and most experienced in military affairs, who, having always followed the emperor into Italy, spent much for his empire. He [unclear] of the monasteries of Rindorf near [Bundericus?], the second of that name, in which he was buried; to him Frederick [unclear], was consecrated pope at Rome, and, having received the pallium, [unclear] of Cologne, was consecrated by Pope Adrian at Rome, and, having received the pallium, returned with honor to Cologne. Against him, amid very grave dissension, Gerard, provost of Bonn, was elected; but at Regensburg, by the emperor’s command of the princes, he was compelled to yield to Frederick.

At the same time very grave contentions began to arise from a slight occasion between Pope Adrian and Emperor Frederick. Pope Innocent II had once caused his own image to be painted on a wall at Rome, as though he were sitting on the pontifical seat, with Emperor Lothar before him with folded hands, bent down, receiving the crown of the empire.

When Emperor Frederick saw this while he was at Rome, urged on by his own men, he took it badly. To this affront, if it is right to call it so, there was added another thing very similar, which was a great seedbed of new commotion and dissension.

When the emperor was holding a court with the chief men of the kingdom in the city of Besançon in Burgundy, two cardinals were present, carrying letters of Pope Adrian, in which, among other things, this was contained: “We have conferred on you the benefit of the crown, nor would we be moved by regret if your Excellency had received greater benefits from us.” This word, namely “benefit,” those who were about the emperor interpreted in its customary sense and asserted that it had been put there as an insult to him; they stirred his mind to anger. He cast the cardinals, after they had been subjected to insults, quickly from his sight, saying: “We have the crown from God alone; that is, we attribute the crown of the empire not to the Roman pontiff, but to God alone. We acknowledge the first voice of royal election as belonging to the archbishop of Mainz; we allow the royal consecration to the archbishop of Cologne; we assign the imperial consecration to the Roman pontiff. Therefore let the painting and the writing be removed and corrected; otherwise concord and peace will not be able to exist between kingdom and priesthood.” But the Romans, fearing the indignation and anger of the emperor, [offered] another interpretation Monastery of Hirsau

In the same year, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 1156, the emperor came to Cologne around the feast of All Saints, and was received with sufficient honor both by the citizens and by Archbishop Arnold. There a certain knight named Bernhard, who had been convicted by the duke of the Saxons of having conspired in the murder of Hermann of Winceburg, was beheaded by order of the emperor.

1157.

In the following year, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 1157, in the fifth indiction, Volmar, the fifteenth abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, departed from this world on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, around the first watch of the night, and rested in the Lord: a man worthy of remembrance among all posterity, since by his industry, wisdom, and piety he did many good things for this monastery of his. He increased its revenues, enlarged its income, restored the ruined buildings of the cenobium, constructed anew several houses and dwellings necessary for the convenience of the brethren, increased the number of monks serving God, and showed himself, by word and example, an excellent pastor to all his subjects. He was buried in the greater church, before the altar of Saint Michael.

Concerning Hartwig, Sixteenth Abbot of This Monastery, who presided for only two months, and concerning his life and conduct.

[unclear] — the emperor holds court at Cologne. Abbot Volmar dies.

After the most reverend and God-beloved abbot Volmar had been buried, although the brethren were held by the very great love they had for him, and could not erase from their hearts the memory of so most pious a father, not, I say, quickly, but not ever entirely, whom they had always found to be in all things a useful, pious, and most gentle pastor; nevertheless, lest the malice of the times, which then abounded in the land, should introduce anything sinister by the suggestion of depravity, it seemed to them that they should not delay in the election of a new pastor.

Therefore on the same day on which they had committed Volmar to ecclesiastical burial, they came together [unclear] temporal matters, so that one useful and suitable for the rule of the monastery might be considered. Accordingly, after the grace of the Holy Spirit had been invoked, as is the custom, they unanimously and concordantly elected as abbot a monk named Hartwig, a venerable old man, in the year of the Lord 1157, in the fifth indiction, on the octave of Saint Agnes, virgin and martyr, which is the fifth day before the Kalends of February. When the election, according to custom, had been publicly announced in the person of Hartwig, he fell to the ground before the whole convent and tearfully begged the brethren, with supplication, that he be spared so great a burden. “If I had wished,” he said, “indeed, if I had been fit to rule souls, I would have remained in that state in which I had been before my entrance into religion. But because I know my imperfection, and that it is more expedient for me to be subject than to preside, therefore I gladly gave up my house, provostship, dignities, and the benefices that I had, though all my friends and kinsmen opposed it, so that without care and anxiety for temporal affairs I might be able to render pleasing service to almighty God in the simplicity of my heart.”

And when the brethren strongly pressed him to take up the burden of rule imposed on him by God as upon one fit for it, at last, consenting, he said: “To despise your prayers, most beloved brethren, I judge [unclear]; yet I know myself wholly insufficient for so great a weight of rule. Nevertheless I trust in the mercy of almighty God, for love of whom I once despised all worldly things, that he will not long permit me to live in this misery, if he knows before himself that this care of souls, which inexperienced men demand, will harm my soul.” And so, yielding to the very great insistence of the brethren, he undertook the burden of pastoral care for the love of Christ, and went down with certain monks to Hillin, archbishop of Trier, for the gift of benediction. He refused, however, to be blessed by Günther, bishop of Speyer, for certain reasons; and therefore, according to the tenor of the privilege long since granted by the Apostolic See to the monastery of Hirsau, he went down to Trier. Thus on the Sunday of Quadragesima, which in that year had fallen on the fourth day before the Nones of March, he was blessed in the greater church of Trier by Archbishop Hillin, in the presence of several abbots.

While he was on that journey, he visited the most holy bride of Christ, Hildegard, of whose holiness, miracles, writings, and revelations he had heard many things. When he heard her speaking, he was turned to amazement and shed tears for exceeding joy. Having obtained an opportunity to speak with her privately, he opened to her the whole state and grief of his mind, and simply related in what great anxieties he was because of the care of souls imposed upon him. And he humbly asked that, for the love of Jesus Christ, she would deign to inquire into the divine will concerning his state, and what he ought to do regarding those thoughts in which he was engaged concerning pastoral care.

The Monastery of Hirsau.

Manegold is elected abbot.

... some impediment might intervene through the contrivance of the wicked because of a long vacancy, and might somehow have been able to weaken that most free election of a new pastor. After much deliberation beforehand, the brothers who had votes in the election immediately came together on the same day as one, with the mind and intention of setting a new pastor over themselves. Therefore, after the grace of the Holy Spirit had been invoked, in the year of the Lord 1157, in the fifth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, at about the third hour of the day, while Frederick I was reigning as emperor, in the sixth year of his reign, the conventual monks of this monastery unanimously elected as abbot Manegold, a venerable monk, a Frank by birth, sprung from the kin of Hartwig his predecessor, being almost sixty years of age. After a long and humble refusal, yielding to the prayers of the brothers, he took up the burden of pastoral care, but deferred the office of blessing until the Saturday of the Ember fast after the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, because he resolved to offer himself to be well tested by the brothers.

He is consecrated at Speyer by Bishop Gunther, and presided for eight years.

At length, scarcely induced by the urgent prayers of the brothers, he set out for Speyer to be blessed, with a large and distinguished company; and on the aforesaid Saturday of the autumnal fast, after twenty-five of his monks had been promoted to holy orders by Gunther, bishop of Speyer, he himself on the following Sunday solemnly received from the same pontiff the gift of blessing, six abbots standing by, vested in sacred vestments.

Life of Abbot Manegold.

He presided in the abbacy for eight years, four months, and six days, a man of good and praiseworthy conduct, and he did many good things for this monastery. He was a Frank by birth, as we have said, born of honorable parents; when he was set to learning letters in his youth, he turned out sufficiently learned and educated. He had, so to speak, drunk in the fear of the Lord from infancy; hence he was accustomed to take delight not in games, not in running about, not in the frivolities of boys, but rather to devote himself, so far as his age allowed, to the study of letters and to prayers.

Manegold becomes a monk.

For, having by nature obtained a good intelligence, and having drunk in the taste of eternal wisdom, he learned to love nothing more in this life than the knowledge of the Scriptures. At length, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, he was made a monk under Abbot Volmar, and lived among the brothers so piously, so religiously, and so humbly that he scarcely had an equal in the whole congregation. Walking before God and men in all tranquillity of mind and action, he was burdensome to no one, troublesome to no one, but in all things showed himself a worthy monk according to the Rule of our holy father Benedict.

He becomes succentor.

He was indeed short in bodily stature, but great and distinguished in the virtues of the soul. Finally, after the years of his initial monastic training had been completed, he was appointed succentor by Abbot Volmar; and while placed in that office he caused more than sixty volumes to be copied for the adornment of the library and the use of the brothers, his friends and secular kinsmen providing the expenses for this. After this, when in all things he had shown himself lowly and irreproachable, upon the death of Ditho the prior he was appointed prior in his place, and by word and example he was a rule of holy conduct for the brothers. In admonishing he was gentle, pious, and meek; in correcting, serious, since he knew very well that the governance of souls is the most difficult of all arts, and therefore must be exercised with greater zeal. To the [unclear] and [disobedient?] he showed himself stern and fearsome. Hence it came about that the good and humble embraced him with the greatest love, while the slothful and those who had no care for their own souls feared him as a lord and a singular avenger of their iniquity.

He becomes cellarer.

Then, so that he might be tested in all things, he was appointed chief cellarer by Abbot Volmar, and Adelhelm was substituted in his place; not long afterward Adelhelm was appointed at Mediolacum in the diocese of Trier. When he had been made cellarer, he applied great care and solicitude in administering his office, and yet did not neglect the inward conduct of the spirit. Again, after some years, when Gerlach the prior had died, he became prior a second time, and in his usual manner vigorously carried out zeal for regular discipline. Always first and last in choir, he promoted the worship of the divine service with the greatest diligence. He loved the divine Scriptures wonderfully, and as long as he lived he devoted all his zeal to the copying of authentic books of the saints.

He is elected abbot.

Finally, after the passing of Abbot Hartwig had been happily completed, he was elected the seventeenth abbot of this monastery, as we have said, in the year of the Lord 1157, in the fifth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April; and on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, that is, on the Sunday of the autumnal Ember fast after the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, which was the day of Saint Maurice the martyr, receiving the office of blessing from Gunther, bishop of Speyer, he presided for eight years, four months, and six days. He is consecrated at Speyer. He was a man adorned with holy morals: gentle, calm, humble, peaceable, mild, and affable, and chaste in mind and body to indicate that the pastoral office should be left behind. But the virgin Saint Hildegard, in her manner raising the sight of her mind to the invisible light, gave Hartwig this reply: “The living light says to you: O man, your mind is made subject to me in my will, and I shall not cast you away. For the man who is ready to serve me, for the honor of my name, in feeding my souls, and seeks nothing else, remains in me. But I know who [unclear] in prelacy, and I shall not abandon him. And he who reigns without me, him I do not [unclear]. But you, be ready, because I am soon to come.” Then, having returned to Hirsau, he did not live long, as we shall say.

Hartwig was by birth a Frank; as a young man he was set to the study of letters and became sufficiently learned and educated, not only in divine but also in secular letters. When at length his years increased, he was made a canon of the greater church of Speyer, where he conducted himself so wisely and religiously that by the consent of all he was elected first chamberlain and then provost of the same church. He was a man of good conscience, of gentle heart, and of most honorable conduct; although he abounded in riches and earthly honors, yet with his mind always raised upward to God he devoted himself to good and holy studies. For though he had abundant wealth, he by no means set his heart upon it, but opened his hand to the needy and most readily relieved the necessities of the poor as far as he could. Among other works of piety, while he was still living a secular life, he was bound by great affection to the brothers of this monastery of Hirsau, and bestowed many benefits on them. He often visited them, and whenever anyone from the monastery of Hirsau happened to come to Speyer on any business, it was permitted to find lodging nowhere but in the provost’s house. His house, like a monastery, was furnished with a most honorable household, into which no dishonorable person at all had entrance. By his good and God-fearing morals he was held honorable by all; in his presence no one dared to speak or do base or dishonorable things. Being also inwardly bound in devotion to almighty God, he allowed no idle time to pass in which he did not add some good work to the due measure of his service. He was frequent in prayers and devoted to the reading of the holy Scriptures, as one who had learned by daily meditation the fruit and sweetness of spiritual exercises.

When, however, he saw that many of his fellow canons were going through the steep paths of vices, he applied the medicine of fraternal correction, both by reason of his office and by obedience to the command, and showed, by manifold witness of the Scriptures, how the ministers of the Lord ought to live. But when he perceived that his admonitions profited little among most of them, it wearied him to live in the office of prelacy, in which he saw that he was uselessly set over the rest. Therefore, after mature deliberation had first been held, he resolved for the love of God to abandon all worldly pomp and honor and to bind himself wholly to almighty God by the monastic [unclear]. To undertake this holy and arduous purpose he was especially moved by the sermons and miracles of the holy father performed at Speyer, at which he had been present, and which, as long as he lived, he was accustomed to recount to everyone with the greatest devotion.

Therefore, having sold many of his possessions, and [unclear] the price. He also brought with him to the monastery many things in gold, silver, precious vessels, and various furnishings; all these he resigned into the hands of Abbot Volmar before the whole congregation. Receiving the habit of holy religion from the hands of Abbot Volmar, he thereafter gave himself wholly to God, and was always intent, either in mind or in body, upon his service. To be present at psalmody and at the hours prescribed by the rule, both by night and by day, was always pleasant and most sweet to him; and he groaned that he had lost all the time which he had not devoted to the service of the Creator. He took care to bring his body into servitude to the spirit by abstinence and fastings, and to show himself imitable to all in good works. In all his conduct among the brothers he was peaceful, tranquil, and quiet, and so abounding in charity toward all that he deservedly was called the mother of the congregation. No one ever saw him disturbed; no one heard him murmuring; but walking before his face in true humility, he caused absolutely no one sorrow.

At the same time Siegfried, dean of Pforzheim, who gave many goods to this monastery [unclear] Conrad, as is contained in the Book of Donations, became a monk under Abbot Volmar, a man of singular learning and wisdom, provoked by the instruction and example of Hartwig himself. Likewise very many other notable men, distinguished in wisdom, birth, and wealth, were stirred by the example of the provost of Speyer and were made [monks] in this monastery of Hirsau in the abbacy of Volmar. They [unclear] for the use of the brothers many [unclear]. And he was first appointed prior in Schöntal, then, by Volmar’s consent, abbot in Amorbach: a man well suited to govern both in spiritual and in secular matters. For he was very learned in the holy Scriptures and endowed with singular experience in affairs.

The response of Hildegard. The life of Abbot Hartwig. He is made provost in the church of Speyer. He was merciful to the poor. He loved the monks of Hirsau. In his manner of life he was devout. Armed with zeal for righteousness. He is moved to compunction by St. Bernard. He becomes a monk at Hirsau. In the divine office [unclear] diligent. Never [unclear] disturbed. The dean of Pforzheim, under Volmar, [unclear] Amorbach. Monk. Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

[They] put forward the [interpreta]tion of this name, saying that “benefice” ought to be understood as though “a good deed.”

In these times Saint William flourished, formerly count of Poitou, a most renowned hermit, who wore a mail-shirt against his bare flesh and mortified his body with the greatest abstinence, glorious for many miracles.

When he was obstinately siding with the schismatics against Pope Innocent, Saint Bernard, by means of the most sacred body of the Lord, so firmly terrified him and brought him to such compunction that he not only laid aside all obstinacy, but, what is more, abandoned his county, despised all honors and riches, fled men, and entered the wilderness. In these times too the wondrous vision of the knight Tondalus is said to have taken place in Ireland; since it is everywhere very well known, there is no need for it to be inserted into this work.

In these times there flourished in the Church of God many very learned men, who published various little works for the instruction of the simple.

Gilbert, surnamed Porreta, a Frenchman by nation, formerly a scholastic of Paris and then bishop of Poitiers, a man most learned in every respect, wrote a notable exposition on the Psalms; likewise on the Gospel of John, and also on all the epistles of Paul; on Boethius, On the Holy Trinity; and in philosophy he published many subtle treatises.

Lucas also, abbot of Saint Cornelius, of our order, a very learned man, among other little works of his studies, published in these times a work on the Song of Songs of Solomon, not to be despised in reading. Richard of Saint-Victor, a Parisian canon, a man in these times, by everyone’s judgment, by far the most learned in the sacred scriptures, and distinguished no less by the holiness of his manner of life than by his literary learning, published many excellent volumes, the reading of which is set before both the learned and the [unclear]. He also wrote commentaries on the Psalms and on the Epistle, which are quite useful. We have already long since made mention of his little works in the book On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Around these times too Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, gathered from various sayings of the holy fathers and transmitted to posterity the four books of the Sentences; today they are of such authority in the schools of theologians that they are preferred in daily reading to almost all others. He also wrote commentaries on the Psalms and on the Apostle, which are quite useful, and certain other works which have not come to our knowledge through reading.

In these same times another Peter also was famous, a priest of Troyes, whom people commonly call Comestor. He wrote an outstanding work to William, archbishop of Sens, and certain other little works not to be rejected in reading. Richard, a monk of Cluny, of our order, is held in esteem among the chronographers in these times; among the many things he wrote, he composed a history of the events of past time, quite pleasant and useful.

In these times also, under the first Emperor Frederick, Joachim, abbot of the monastery of Fiore in Calabria, of our order, flourished: a man indeed studious and learned, who, being regarded by many as a prophet, was also accustomed to foretell future things. He wrote on the prophet Jeremiah, on the prophet Daniel, on the Gospel of John, and on the Apocalypse of John; in all these he always attempts to foretell future things. He also wrote several works to Henry VI. Likewise on the Seven Seals in the Apocalypse; on the Psalter of ten strings; likewise the book Concordia. Likewise, concerning twenty-five future Roman pontiffs after his own time, he wrote one prophecy. He also composed many letters to various persons, and various works concerning future times. In this very year of the Lord’s nativity 1357, the sign of the cross appeared plainly in the moon.

In the same year the lord Hartwig, the aforesaid abbot of this monastery, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, around the first watch of the night, released from the flesh, rested in the Lord, on the fifty-sixth [unclear].

[Unclear] gathered into one book of Decrees from the various opinions, decrees, and writings of the holy fathers, and offered it to be confirmed by the supreme pontiff.

[Unclear] in his mercy, according to his desire, removed him from the midst after a short time, lest wickedness should change his understanding; for prelacy is often accustomed to deceive the mind.

Concerning Manegold, the seventeenth abbot of this monastery, who presided for 8 years, 4 months, and 6 days, and concerning his life and manner of conduct.

After he had entered, and after the burial had been entrusted to him, not without many tears of the brothers, Chronicle of Jo. Trithemius 743

chaste, who in his time did not diminish the substance of the monastery, but increased it, as [unclear] in the book Donation. For in his time many people, for the love of God, handed over many goods to this monastery, and he himself also bought several things for a price. Among others, moreover, there was at that time a certain canon named Ruthardus, who had a brother in Hirsau, a monk, [and was] resident in the church of Mainz; for the remedy of his soul he handed over to the monastery of Hirsau an estate at Bingen, which his brother the monk, by order of the abbot, sold for [unclear] marks of silver, and spent the price for the use of the brothers.

After some time, however, Hedericus, nephew through his brother of the aforesaid Ruthardus, himself also a canon of Mainz, conferred twelve talents on this monastery; for these, Hugo his paternal uncle, at the request of Abbot Manegold, bought three yokes of vineyards in Gruningen for the monastery.

Rupertus also of Tubingen [gave] many goods to the monastery of Hirsau in the time of the abbess [unclear], and also to co-purchasers and others of the convent, of accounts and of others for the common matter. But that benefits of this sort are not as if by the authority of the kingdom or empire, but by the authority of the monastery itself; nevertheless they are held in this way, as if they had been by the authority of the Kingdom or Empire, and ought to pertain to it. And therefore it is said that this is the donation of the monastery of Saint George in Tubingen, which Johannes, bishop in Tubingen, had made. And for that reason it is said that this monastery is now in the possession and hand of the church of Saint George in Tubingen, which Johannes, bishop in Tubingen, had held, who founded this monastery. And all men who have been benefited from this donation shall have this monastery, just as also all men who have been benefited from the donation of Johannes, bishop in Tubingen.

In the first year of Abbot Manegold, that is, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1157, there was a great earthquake in Asia in various places, which utterly destroyed Tripoli, Damascus, and a certain other city. Moreover the city of the Catanensians was completely overturned; in it almost up to twenty thousand of a very great multitude of men, women, young people, and children perished, suffocated in a miserable disaster. In these days Sophia of Holland, wife of Theodoric, count of Holland, flourished: a holy woman and most devoted in the love of Christ, continually intent on prayers, fasts, vigils, and almsgiving; she is said to have been illustrious for miracles both in life and after death.

When this holy woman, about to visit the threshold of the holy apostle James in Galicia, had fallen among cruel robbers, who wished not only to despoil her of her jewels but even to deprive her of life, she so constrained and bound them by the power of her prayers that they could in no way move from the place or lay hands upon her. Therefore, astonished, they sought pardon from her; having received it, they suddenly fled away. At last, however, after many works of piety, when she had already set out in terror to visit the holy sepulcher of Christ at Jerusalem, and had most devoutly visited the sacred places, on 26 September she happily rested in the Lord; and she was buried in the hospital of the Teutons in Jerusalem.

In the second year of Abbot Manegold, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1158, Emperor Frederick, with the princes of the German kingdom, around the feast of Pentecost entered Lombardy with a strong hand, and took the city of Brescia with many others. Moving his army from there, with fifty thousand fighting men he besieged Milan, and assaulted it fiercely for many days. And when the Milanese saw themselves surrounded by a tight siege, and could expect no help from anyone, they handed the city over to the emperor. When this had been done, the emperor sent his German soldiers back to their homeland for the most part, and imposed on the defeated Milanese an annual payment of tribute.

In the same year Godfridus, abbot of Saint James of Mainz, and Burchardus, provost of Saint Peter’s, together with almost the whole clergy and the citizens of Mainz, began to hold their archbishop in great hatred, and petitioned the emperor against him. Only the Creopoli, whom they call butchers, defended the archbishop’s side with all their strength; whence both by Emperor Frederick and by the archbishop of Mainz, who succeeded Arnold, they were granted a certain singular liberty and privilege, down to the present day, for such great fidelity.

In the third year of Abbot Manegold, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1159, the emperor [unclear] were assembled.

1158.

1159.

Donation of Ruthardus.

Donation of Hedericus.

Religion of the Hirsau brothers.

Various donations.

Earthquake.

Sophia, most [unclear] countess, a holy woman.

Robbers [unclear] without [unclear].

The emperor moves his army into Lombardy.

Milan is taken by the emperor.
