144 Of the Monastery of Hirsau

having [gathered?] the whole army, he besieged and took by storm Crema, a very strongly fortified city, over seven months, while the Cremonese brought assistance. At last, when they could not withstand the force of the soldiers, they submitted themselves and the city to the emperor’s power, taking away no small hope from the Milanese.

In the same year, after the feast of Saint Remigius, the adversaries of the archbishop of Mainz entered a synod with armed force and wished to kill him. But when the counts, together with their men, resisted bravely, they were compelled to depart shamefully. For this reason Arnold himself, archbishop of Mainz, after the feast of All Saints, went to Lombardy, intending to make complaint about the matter to the emperor; and his adversaries, by no means inactive, followed after him.

In the same year Frederick II, archbishop of Cologne, died in Italy; his body was brought back to his homeland and buried in a certain monastery at Aldenburg. When he had been buried, the people of Cologne sent envoys to the emperor in Italy, asking from him Reinhold the chancellor, whom he had chosen as archbishop. The emperor, glad that he had found an occasion to confer honor upon him, consented with grateful mind and granted Reinhold as archbishop to those who asked. Not long afterward the same Reinhold, having received the emperor’s permission, came to Cologne, took possession of the archbishopric and all that belonged to it, and, after arranging affairs briefly, returned again to the emperor in Lombardy with three hundred chosen soldiers.

In the same year, when Pope Adrian was preparing to excommunicate Emperor Frederick because of the discord concerning the marriage, he was overtaken by death and departed this life in the month of October. After his death a great disturbance followed in the Church of God. For the cardinals, disagreeing among themselves, chose two pontiffs for themselves: Roland the chancellor, whom they call Alexander III, and Octavian, whom they named Victor IV. Alexander, the old vicar of Christ, approved in every respect the sentence of his predecessor Peter [unclear], but Victor favored the emperor very greatly. This Pope Alexander confirmed the Carthusian order and gave them certain privileges, receiving that order itself under the protection and defense of the holy Apostolic See.

1160.

In the aforesaid year of Abbot Manegold, not yet completed, which was begun as the year 1160 of the Lord’s Nativity on the octave of Epiphany, Emperor Frederick ordered a council to be held at Padua, at which he received Victor, who was present, as pope, but condemned Alexander, who was absent. When the council had been completed, Arnold, archbishop of Mainz, having received permission from the emperor, returned to Mainz. At last, when on the day of the Nativity of blessed John the Baptist he had gone out for devotion’s sake to the monastery of Saint James outside the walls of Mainz, Godfrey, abbot of that place, and Burchard, provost of Saint Peter’s, together with the other associates of the conspiracy, sent out assassins whom they had hired from ambushes, and they cruelly killed the archbishop in that same monastery, a great part of the citizens consenting. When the crime had been committed, the perpetrators of the monstrous offense withdrew with haste to the city; and immediately the counts and ministeriales of the murdered archbishop, together with the butchers, violently drove out the monks, plundered that monastery itself, set it on fire, and utterly overthrew all the dwellings of the monks. But Abbot Godfrey, with the rest of the accomplices of his impiety, had betaken himself into the city, where the authors of the crime, together with the clergy, though compelled by violence, set aside the fidelity which they had given into the emperor’s hands three years earlier and elected as archbishop Rudolph, son of Conrad, duke of Zähringen; and when, by the counsel of his men, he intended to appease the emperor with gifts, he stripped the church of its ornament.

At that time there was in the church of Mainz a most precious cross, which Willigis, archbishop of Mainz, in the time of Emperor Otto III, had ordered to be made for the adornment of the house of the Lord. Its crossbeam was of cypress wood, covered above with gold plates and precious stones. The large image, however, made wholly of the purest gold, weighed six hundred pounds of gold, as the verse carved on it showed, in words of this tenor:

This golden cross holds the following pounds of gold.

Marcelphus the archbishop took one foot of this image and sent it to Rome for the pallium. The other, with the legs, Arnold the above-mentioned archbishop took away, and with it rebelled against Hermann, count palatine. All that remained, this Rudolph, with the consent of the people of Mainz, took, intending to appease the emperor with it; in [unclear] the count palatine of the Rhine, the emperor’s brother, rejected and drove out Rudolph, and raised Christian, a certain noble man, to the archbishopric; he at last to the pontificate [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

...did not at that time attain the [unclear], because Conrad, brother of Otto, count palatine of Wittelsbach, was placed over him by the emperor, as we shall say.

In these times the pernicious heresy of the Poor of Lyons, which by another name is called Waldensian, began through a certain wealthy citizen of Lyons, who, after leaving everything behind, professed evangelical poverty; and, after certain books of Sacred Scripture had been translated from Latin into the French tongue, he took upon himself the office of the apostles, and both by himself and through his accomplices in error preached everywhere the Scriptures badly understood. They despised the rulers and prelates of the churches, together with their constitutions, and made nothing of established orders. When they were admonished to come to their senses, they were accustomed to reply that God must be obeyed more than men. At last, stubborn and obstinate in wicked errors, they were driven from the Church, excommunicated, and declared heretics.

About these times, when Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, passed from this life, which happened in the year of the Lord 1153, in the first indiction, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the sixty-fourth year of his age, a dreadful vision was shown to the bishop of Langres. For there appeared to him a certain dead hermit, whom he had once known while living; moved by fear of God, some years earlier, when he was called a wealthy dean, he had despised everything and entered a hermitage for the love of Christ. But among the other places which he sanctified by his presence, he also came to Hirsau, and Abbot Manegold and the community of brothers received [him] with inestimable joy, as an angel of the Lord coming from heaven. But she, after the customary prayer, sitting in the midst of the brothers, opened her mouth in the name of Christ; the word which the Holy Spirit had entrusted to her, so fervently [unclear] others were sent to purgatory; all the rest, by the sentence of the just judge, were condemned and went down to hell, to be tormented forever.

In the third year of Abbot Manegold, which was, as we have said, the year 1160 from the Lord’s nativity, Saint Hildegard, virgin of Christ, abbess of the monastery of the holy confessor Rupert near Bingen, compelled by the Holy Spirit, personally announced the word of God to people in many places. Among the other places which she sanctified by her presence, she also came to Hirsau, and Abbot Manegold and the community of brothers received her with inestimable joy, as an angel of the Lord coming from heaven. But after holy prayer, sitting in the midst of the brothers, she opened her mouth in the name of Christ and delivered to her hearers the word which the Holy Spirit had entrusted to her, so fervently, soberly, and prudently that all were turned to amazement. A wondrous thing happened. While she spoke the word outwardly, the Holy Spirit inwardly worked its effect in the hearts of the hearers; and he poured over all so great a grace of compunction that they were compelled, from deep feeling and because of the sweetness of mind, to shed tears. Among the other discourses of her sweetest sermon, she foretold to the brothers that, unless they cautiously guarded against the snares of the ancient enemy, they would within a very short space of time experience some tribulation. This happened in that same year in the pernicious dissension which, at the devil’s instigation, arose between Abbot Manegold and the community; of this we shall speak in its proper place. All together, in those matters which concerned the community, instructed by the Holy Spirit, she reproved hidden and manifest faults, and showed with most prudent reasoning what things in their assembly or conduct displeased the divine majesty. Proceeding from there, she went to the monastery of Zwiefalten of our order, and there likewise announced both to the nuns and to the monks what the Holy Spirit had commanded her. In many monasteries and places of Swabia, too, she opened the word of the Lord to the people with the attestation of miracles, and by her admonitions turned many away from iniquity.

1161

In the fourth year of Abbot Manegold, which was the year 1161 from the Lord’s nativity, a grave discord arose, according to the prophecy of blessed Hildegard, through the devil’s instigation, between the abbot of Hirsau himself and his brothers; this spread great scandal and evil report among the people in almost every region of the Swabians. For it seemed to Prior Diemo and to the brothers that the abbot, by indulging his familiars too much, yielded to whatever they wished, and that by dissembling he tolerated many dissolutions and insolences of theirs against the peace of the community and monastic propriety. Hence, when he had several times been admonished about this by the seniors, and, using free power too much, seemed to amend none of the things being put forward, the brothers, thinking themselves held in contempt by him, conceived the gravest displeasure against him. This grew so much that it came to the knowledge of all dwelling in that region, not without disgrace, confusion, and detestation [unclear]. And since the dissension among the brothers thus produced many ordinances against the abbot, insults, and murmurings against him, the abbot, provoked against them, not with paternal mildness, as it seemed to them, but with severity, punished harshly whomever he could catch; the less affection of paternal gentleness he showed, the greater [unclear].

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

...provoked their displeasure against himself. But when Abbot Manegold saw that he could by no means bring the brothers back to concord, being a lover of his own salvation he wished to resign the abbacy. But lest he should rashly offend the eyes of the divine majesty, he sought counsel on this matter through a trusted messenger and by letters from the blessed virgin Hildegard, to whom he sent this letter:

To the most holy lady and his venerable mother Hildegard, Manegold, unworthy abbot of Hirsau, [sends] prayer with service. I have indeed heard that among the Cyrenians there is a certain [unclear] vein of waters, and [unclear]; I know you, and have found by experience among the Alemanni, good mother, to be the vein [unclear] of those entering and going out, and the bosom of kinds in things, like the pupil of the eye [unclear]. For you draw, O my lady, and pour forth; you give form and distinguish into species; and in practical matters [unclear] into contemplation [unclear]. Therefore it has been my impulse, and long has been, to love you, to honor you, to admire you, to serve you and yours, and in all things, by word and deed, to be yours and of your women, in prayers insofar as is right for me, and in services. I ask you, my mother and lady, remember me in your most holy prayers; love one who humbly loves you; acknowledge one who reveres you in Christ; and write back to me by letter concerning the questions asked, having been petitioned in God. When the blessed Hildegard, virgin of Christ, had received these letters and heard the words entrusted by the abbot to the messenger, to...

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

... who has sinned, if he does not have the one who anoints him, straightway flees into despair and withers away, because no medicine is administered to him according as he himself can bear it. Now, dear sons, hear the voice of the living light: Take hold of mercy, which has arisen not from us, but which comes from God. And therefore do not withdraw it from those to whom it must be shown. Therefore draw them back to the health of their souls.

After the brothers of Hirsau had received these letters from Saint Hildegard, handmaid of Christ, they rejoiced in a wonderful manner; and, changing their plan, they began to treat among themselves concerning peace and the tranquillity of concord. But Abbot Manegold too, according to the counsel of the lady virgin Hildegard, forestalling them in a spirit of meekness and gentleness, showed himself in all things, in word and deed, a most loving father. The brothers likewise, through the sweetness of his fatherly promise, promised that they would show themselves humble and obedient sons in all things, and would never thereafter provide an occasion for discord. Thus, therefore, by the merits, prayers, and counsels of the blessed Hildegard, virgin of Christ, concord between the abbot and the convent was restored with the Lord's help; and thereafter, while Abbot Manegold himself lived, both sides firmly preserved it inviolable among themselves.

1162.

In the fifth year of Abbot Manegold, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1162, the emperor Frederick, while he was in Lombardy together with the leading men of the church of Mainz, passed over Christian the prior, or rather despised him, and set up as archbishop of the aforesaid church Conrad, brother of Otto, Count Palatine of Wittelsbach; and he presided for two years.

In the same year also, when the Milanese, forgetful of their pledged faith and oath, refused obedience to the emperor, the city of Milan itself was again besieged by Caesar and was shortly captured. The people were expelled, the wall all around was stripped bare, and all the buildings, except the churches of the saints, were destroyed down to the ground, so that, at the emperor's command, a plow was drawn through the middle of the city in the form of a cross. Reinhold, archbishop of Cologne, taking away from Milan, with the emperor's consent, the bodies of the holy Magi who had adored Christ in the cradle, transferred them to Cologne and placed them in the greater church of Saint Peter, where [unclear] they promised to do [unclear]. On Tuesday the men of Brescia swore similar things.

At the same time Louis, king of France, sent envoys to the emperor for arranging peace and unity of the holy Church, and he received them graciously. Therefore, when a general synod had been proclaimed in the town called Leona, on the river Saone, in the bishopric of Besancon, the emperor was present with Pope Victor and many archbishops and abbots on the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist. The king of France, however, had arrived the day before on the other side of the river, but by the counsel of Pope Alexander and those obedient to him, he remained in a nearby castle and did not come to the emperor. Waldemar, king of the Danes, was present at this synod, and there he received the crown of the kingdom of Denmark from the hands of the lord emperor. Therefore the emperor and the aforesaid king of the Danes, with that assembly of bishops, abbots, and princes, just as in the first and second synod, named Victor universal pope, but designated Alexander with his adherents as schismatics.

1163.

In the sixth year of Abbot Manegold, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1163, the emperor celebrated Easter at Worms, and in the octave held a solemn court at Mainz. But almost all the citizens, except for a few of the lower sort, fled from the city so that they would not be found by the emperor, on account of the murder of Archbishop Arnold, committed in the monastery of Saint James, concerning which I have spoken above. [Unclear], having been brought to court, received a capital sentence. Godefrid, abbot of Saint James, was presented to the emperor so that he might clear himself of the charges brought against him, and received a delay. But when he could not clear himself of the killing of that archbishop, by decree of the emperor and the princes he was expelled from the abbacy and was compelled also to abjure his homeland and the province of the church of Mainz. But the monks of the same monastery, all shut up in one house by order of the emperor, who had previously been obedientiaries, seeing that they had been placed in an evil situation, sought flight, some through the windows, others by whatever device they could. The rest, the older men, the weak, and the sick, who were unable to flee, were permitted to depart. And so, when the abbot had been expelled together with all the monks, and the monastery of Saint James had been utterly destroyed, that place remained desolate without inhabitants for fourteen years, and thus...

The brothers began to treat among themselves concerning peace.

Peace between the abbot and the brothers was restored.

Conrad becomes archbishop of Mainz.

The bodies of the three holy Magi are transferred to Cologne.

[Unclear] presents obedience to the emperor.

A synod of two popes is held.

Waldemar, king of the Danes.

The emperor comes to Mainz.

The abbot of Saint James is expelled from his abbacy and homeland. Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

... he knew [them] to be incorrigible, he resigned the abbacy after he had governed it for some years, preferring to remain in humility with his Hirsau brothers as one cast down than to preside fruitlessly in an abbacy over reprobate monks. Having therefore left the abbacy of the aforesaid Gotzaugian monastery, he returned to Hirsau and, received by the brothers with great charity, obtained the place of prior and continued among them a tranquil life, as he had been accustomed before, without reproach.

Afterwards, however, at the monastery of Schonrem, by the counsel and assent of the brothers of this community, he was appointed supreme prior and rector by Abbot Volmar; there he presided for almost ten years with sufficient usefulness, and enlarged that priory no less in spiritual than in temporal matters.

At length, after the death of Abbot Manegold, since no one more useful than he was found among the brothers at Hirsau, by common counsel and the unanimous consent of all he was elected abbot of this monastery in the aforesaid year of Christ’s nativity 1165, in the fourth indiction, on the Nones of August, and he presided, as we have said, for eleven years. In the observance of regular discipline he was quite zealous and fervent; but because the days were evil, and it was necessary to redeem the time, he governed the brothers not as he wished, but as he could. For already then they had begun to grow lukewarm from the fervor of their first institution, nor was it easy to call back all at once those who were slipping away too much. For this reason he received many injuries from weak subjects. Therefore, compelled by necessity, lest from bad they become worse, he kept silent and, with prudent moderation, as far as he was permitted, passed things over for the better course. [The monastic profession?] had grown lukewarm at this time.

As for the state of temporal affairs, he did not diminish the substance of the monastery, but enlarged it; and besides the many donations made by the faithful in his time, which are contained in the Book of Donations, he himself also acquired not a few estates and meadows for the use of the brothers. This Abbot Rupert also built, in the greater monastery of Hirsau, on the northern side, a chapel with beautiful woodwork in honor of St. Nicholas, the great archbishop of Myra, in which he was accustomed rather often to celebrate the solemnities of Mass. The chapel of St. Nicholas is founded.

This chapel, after 278 years, Abbot Wolffram, since it had almost collapsed from excessive age, destroyed with the consent and permission of Reinhard, bishop of Speyer; and transferring that altar itself into the church of the monastery, to the left side of the altar of the Holy Cross, he consecrated it in honor of Saints Peter the Apostle, Nicholas, Ulrich, and Aurelius, bishops, and Gall, abbot, through the ministry of Peter, bishop of Myra, vicar-general in pontificals of the aforesaid prelate Reinhard, as we shall say in its place.

In the course of the first year of Abbot Rupert, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1162, St. Elisabeth, nun, the holy and God-beloved virgin Elisabeth, a nun of our order, mistress of the virgins of Christ at Schönau in the diocese of Trier, sister of Eckbert, abbot there in the monastery of monks, of whom we made mention above, in the thirty-sixth year of her age, the twenty-fourth of her conversion to the order, and the thirteenth of the visitation of heavenly grace, with the Lord calling, [unclear: of Saints Peter the Apostle, Nicholas, Ulrich, and Aurelius, bishops, and Gall, abbot, through the ministry of Peter, bishop of Myra, the aforesaid vicar-general in pontificals of Bishop Reinhard, consecrated it], as we say in its place.

For in the eleventh year of her religious life, which was the twenty-third of her age, [unclear], she was buried in the monastery of men, there in the principal church toward the north [unclear]. Her life, manner of life, miracles, and revelations her brother, the aforesaid Abbot Eckbert, described for the edification of many. This virgin, when she was twelve years old, was given to the monastery of the poor virgins of Christ at Schönau, to the Lord God under the rule of our holy father Benedict and under the direction of Hildelin, first abbot and founder of both [monasteries?]; [unclear] angelic [visitations?], and, divinely illumined, to reveal the secrets of minds. And for as long as she lived thereafter, she was refreshed by divine revelations, and this especially on Sundays and on the feasts of saints; she had been given there, where she lived so holy, so pure and religious a life that she deserved more often to be divinely consoled in this mortality by many wondrous revelations.

For the [manner?] of the visions, or revelations, was this. A certain suffering of the breast came upon her, so that, having suddenly fallen in the church, she would remain as if lifeless, lying quietly or sitting motionless, and no breath could be perceived in her. While this rapture lasted, her spirit was carried away to various places, and in the meantime she was instructed by angelic speech. At length, after a long rapture, having recovered her spirit, she would utter most holy words, sometimes in the Teutonic tongue, which was her native language, and sometimes in Latin, although she had almost no [knowledge] of the Latin language 143

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

the services of divine praise there were interrupted. Finally, to curb its insolence, the wall around the city was, by order of the emperor, entirely destroyed and reduced to dust. And thus Mainz remained without a wall for thirty-seven years.

In this same year certain heretics of the sect of those who are called Cathars, coming from the parts of Flanders to Cologne, began to live secretly in a certain barn near the city. But since they did not enter the church even on the Lord’s day, they were brought in by the people living round about. They were therefore brought to the examination of holy mother Church, and were found to be most obstinate heretics.

In these times flourished Eckbert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Florinus the Confessor in Schönau, of the diocese of Trier, of our order, brother of the blessed Elisabeth, a consecrated virgin, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and of great name and reputation in his time among ecclesiastical teachers. Therefore the clergy and the leading men of the city of Cologne, knowing him to be a man no less venerable for the holiness of his conversion than distinguished for his learning in the Scriptures, summoned him to Cologne by letters and messengers to examine the aforesaid heretics. When Abbot Eckbert came to Cologne, in the aforesaid year 1163 of the Lord’s Nativity, in the eleventh indiction, on the second day of the month of August, he entered upon a public contest of disputation with three heresiarchs who seemed more acute than the rest, namely Arnold, Marsilius, and Theodoric. Although they were very sharp, nevertheless by disputing vigorously he convicted them, so that they were altogether unable to contradict him.

And since by no arguments, no authorities, and no admonitions could they be induced to renounce their error, but persisted most obstinately in their purpose, they were cast out completely by the Church and handed over into the hands of the laity. These led them outside the city and, on the Nones of August, handed them over to the flames: eight men and two women. Among them was one young woman; when, through the pity of the people, she was almost being saved, in case perhaps, terrified by the death of the others, she might acquiesce in sounder counsel, she suddenly slipped from the hands of those holding her, threw herself voluntarily into the flames, and perished.

These heretics were entangled in many errors, Cataphrygians, or Cathars, so called because they said that they themselves were pure and the only Christians, but all other people impure and heretics. Despising the rulers of churches, prelates, priests, and all the clergy, they called them deceivers of souls and snares of the devil. They mocked the sacrament of the Church and denied the most holy body and blood. Lust committed among themselves in whatever manner or with whomever they said was not a sin, alleging: “All things are pure to the pure.” They also professed many other abominable errors, about which we blush to write for the sake of decency.

Against these Cathars, Saint Hildegard, inspired by the Holy Spirit, wrote a letter to the canons of the greater church of Mainz, which begins thus: “In the month of July of the present year, which is the 1163rd of the Lord’s Incarnation,” etc. The origin [unclear] of this heresy had its source from the dregs of Tanchelm, about whom we spoke much earlier, in the fifth year of Abbot Volmar; in the lower regions, and especially in Antwerp, he disseminated most foul errors and revived the heresy of the Adamites.

And although through the brothers of Saint Norbert, the first founder of the Premonstratensian order, that same heresy was then for the greater part extinguished, especially in that region, nevertheless meanwhile it has so often sprouted again in various provinces of the world, and especially in the kingdom of Bohemia, in Alsace, and in Thuringia, that down to the present day it has infected many with the venom of its depravity; nor is it even today believed to be wholly extinct, although it is very hidden and known to very few. For, through fear of fire, the professors of this error have always been accustomed to love hidden lurking-places. Since mention has fallen upon Abbot Eckbert, we must say who and how great he was. He was [unclear] of the aforesaid most devout [unclear], abandoned the world and all things that are in the world for the love of Christ, and under Hildelin, first abbot of the monastery of Schönau, became a monk.

When he died, succeeding in his place, he was appointed abbot by the election of the brothers. He was a man, both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, in his time among [unclear], ready and eloquent before the people, and he left to posterity many little works of his talent, written in a polished style. Of these few have come down to our reading. Against the heretics

Verdastus was.

Little works of Eckbert.

The Cathar heretics.

Eckbert, Abbot of Schönau, of our order.

He overcame the Cathar heretics by disputation.

The Cathars burned at Cologne.

The errors of the Cathars were very wicked among many.

Hildegard writes against the Cathars. The origin of the heresy of the Cathars.

This heresy is not yet extinct.

This Abbot Eckbert, who was Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

Against heretics he wrote one book. This book of his against the Cathars is extant, printed at Cologne in the year [1530?]. Also, On the Beginning of the Gospel of John. Also, on the Gospel, 'The angel was sent': a fine treatise, not to be despised. He also composed several letters to various persons, and many and varied sermons. He also wrote the life, conduct, revelations, and death of his blessed sister Elisabeth, of whom we shall speak later. He also published several poems of different kinds, and prayers suited to devotion, concerning the Lord Jesus, and concerning his most holy mother, the Virgin Mary, and many other diverse saints.

He was abbot of Schonau. At length, when Hildelin, first abbot of the aforesaid monastery of Schonau, had died, on the Nones of December in the year of the Lord 1167, by the unanimous consent of the brothers he was appointed abbot in the same monastery. He presided for eighteen years, and on the fifth day before the Kalends of April he passed from this life, not without a reputation for sanctity.

He was of such great learning that, in a public assembly of learned men at Koblenz, in the first disputation he convicted a certain heretic, [of Gardena?] by origin, who held wrong opinions and taught most wickedly concerning the body and blood of the Lord, and who, because of the subtlety of his mind and the fluency of his tongue, was formidable even to all the most learned; and he called him back from his error to the profession of the truth.

1163.

In the seventh year of Abbot Manegold, and in the year 1164 of the Lord's nativity, the archbishop of Salzburg was cruelly killed by the ministerials of St. Rupert. The Emperor returned again into Italy.

The archbishop of Salzburg is slain. The sea oversteps its bounds. The ocean in the lower regions, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, went beyond its boundary for twelve miles and submerged many thousands of people of both sexes and of different ages, especially around the river Weser.

In the same year, on Good Friday, namely the fourth day before the Ides of April, while Pope Alexander, who was also Roland, was celebrating the divine rites at Sens, horrible darkness came on; and then such a dreadful lightning bolt fell, and after it such a great crash thundered, that the pope, leaving the altar, and the deacon, leaving the reading, and all who were present judged that they must look to their safety by flight.

Dreadful tempest of the air. In that same year Pope Victor died at Lucca and was buried there. Wido, bishop of Crema, was ordained by Henry, bishop of Liege, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, and was called Paschal III.

Pope Victor died; Paschal III succeeds. Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, is expelled; Christian is elected. In the same year Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, of whom we spoke above, bound himself by faith and oath to Pope Alexander and against the will of the Emperor, and withdrew from the Emperor and his antipope. Therefore the Emperor, indignant, expelled him from the archbishopric of Mainz and compelled him to flee to that father Alexander himself. When he had been expelled, Christian was appointed in his place; as we said above, the men of Mainz had elected him before Conrad. There is extant a letter of this Archbishop Christian to Saint Hildegard, in which he asks and obtains. At length, however, after Christian, Conrad again [unclear] to the archbishopric.

On the appointed day for battle, on the second feria of Rogation week in the field of Andernach, after the men of Cologne had been reconnoitered by scouts, Conrad the Palatine did not dare to come, although he had been awaited by them for twelve days.

In the same year, on the Kalends of October, the Emperor returned from Italy and held a famous court at Bamberg in the octave of St. Martin, where he restored peace between Conrad, count Palatine, his brother, and Reinold the elect and the men of Cologne.

In the eighth year of Abbot Manegold, which was the year 1165 of the Lord's nativity, Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury in England, while he was stoutly defending the freedom and rights of his church against the tyranny of the king of the English, was driven by him from his country and at the same time from his archbishopric. Coming into the kingdom of the Franks, he first stayed in the monastery of [Pontigny?]. Afterwards he was maintained at royal expense at Sens, in the monastery of St. Columba.

Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, is exiled. In the same year a son named Henry was born to the Emperor at Nijmegen. In that same year the Emperor held a very celebrated court at Wurzburg on the day of Pentecost, where both the Emperor himself and all the other princes swore that their pope Paschal[...]

[unclear] they would never desert, nor would they ever go over to the party of Alexander. There, then, Rainald, elect of Cologne, was first ordained priest on Ember Saturday, together with many others newly elected. Afterwards, on the sixth day before the Nones of October (October 2), he was elected archbishop of Cologne by Philip, bishop of Osnabruck, Emperor Frederick being present together with his empress.

In the same year also, on the day of Peter in Chains, which is the Kalends of August (August 1), after midday, Manegold, the seventeenth abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, in the sixty-ninth year of his age, and in the eighth of his abbacy, with four months and six days completed, departed from this life to the Lord, and was buried before the altar of St. Michael the Archangel. He was certainly a man worthy of remembrance: although he sometimes endured the murmurings of his brothers, as we have said before, nevertheless the cause of the displeasures arose not from evil, but rather from a good zeal for regular discipline. For he was a most fervent lover of the monastic life; and when he corrected delinquent monks rather harshly according to the monastic rule, he provoked the hatred of the weak against himself. But after he was once admonished by St. Hildegard, he changed severity into the greatest kindness, and supreme peace between him and the brothers prevailed until his death.

Concerning Rupert, the eighteenth abbot of this monastery, who presided for eleven years, and concerning his way of life and certain deeds of that time.

In the year of the Lord's nativity 1163, on the second day after the feast of Peter in Chains, which was the fourth day before the Nones of August (August 2), after Manegold, the venerable abbot, had died and been buried, as we have said, the brothers of this monastery came together as one to provide themselves with a new shepherd. After many necessary discussions among themselves, and after humble invocation of the grace of the Holy Spirit, they elected as abbot the venerable man Rupert, at that time prior in [Schonrain?]. But once elected, only with the greatest difficulty could he at last scarcely be induced by the brothers to consent, since, taught by experience, he had learned that there is more danger than honor in the prelacy of cloistered men. For he had previously been abbot in Gottesaue, as we shall say; and from this he had learned very fully in many matters how much the prelate of monks must necessarily suffer. He therefore refused to accept the abbacy of this great and distinguished monastery, [unclear]. At last, overcome by the prayers of the brothers, after he had long resisted, he gave his consent, and for the love of God humbly accepted the burden of pastoral care to be borne; in it he served the Lord strenuously for eleven years. The office of blessing, which he had once received in the abbey of Gottesaue, sufficed also in this one.

He was born of honorable parents in Eastern Francia, and, having been set to the study of letters in boyhood, advanced diligently, as his years increased, in good morals and in knowledge of the Scriptures; in a short time he surpassed many of his contemporaries in both. Then, as his years increased, touched by divine inspiration, he became a monk in this monastery under Abbot Volmar, where he gave himself wholly to spiritual exercise, so that as a young man he became an example of virtues even to many elders. As far as bodily constitution is concerned, he was [unclear]; he was resonant [of voice?], mature and eloquent in speech. In morals he was composed and gentle, ready and cautious in counsel, and circumspect in all his actions. He was of the mildest and most tranquil conduct among the brothers, and never offended anyone by injury. Finally, he applied himself with such diligence to serving almighty God that he always entered the choir among the first and left among the last; and day and night he devoted himself almost continually to the reading of Scripture, holy meditations, and prayers. At length, when the fame of his virtues spread everywhere, even to outsiders, the brothers of the monastery of Gottesaue, which is four miles distant from Hirsau, moved by his name and reputation, when they were bereft of a shepherd, sought him as abbot over them by unanimous election and obtained him. After a humble excuse, at last, constrained by the command of his abbot, he accepted that burden of pastoral care, and was solemnly ordained according to custom by the bishop of Speyer. Once ordained abbot, he applied all his zeal to [unclear], and made no small progress in the restoration of temporal affairs. But in spiritual matters he could not make progress to the same degree, because the insolence of certain brothers stood in the way not a little. And when, with the insolence of the monks standing in the way, he saw that he was making little progress, leaving to them those Of the Monastery of Hirsau

and that you may know my innocence and that of our abbot, and may be able to make it known to others. I beseech you, moreover, both that you make me a sharer in your prayers, and, as the Spirit of the Lord shall suggest to you, that you write back to me some words of consolation. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.

MCLXVI.

In the year noted above, in which the holy virgin Elisabeth departed from the body, which was the first year of Abbot Rupert, the winter was very harsh, and there followed a great famine with pestilence and many evils.

MCLXVII.

But in the third year of Abbot Rupert, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 1167, Henry, bishop of Wurzburg, died; Herold, succeeding him, presided for 7 years, 5 months, and 10 days. To this Bishop Herold, Emperor Frederick was the first to confirm the duchy of Franconia under a golden bull, with all ducal power and jurisdiction.

MCLXVIII.

In the following year Arnold, archbishop of Mainz, was cruelly killed by his own citizens in the monastery of St. James on the day of St. John the Baptist. The leaders of this conspiracy among the clergy were Godfrey, abbot of St. James, and the provost of the churches of St. Peter, with many others consenting to the same deed against the bishop. When the murder of the venerable prelate had been carried out, the cruel killers elected as archbishop Rudolf, son of Conrad, duke of Zahringen; and so that he might appease the emperor for himself with gifts, he stripped the whole Church of its ornaments. But, being despised by the emperor, he by no means attained to the see of the pontificate. Meanwhile, while Rudolf was going to the emperor, who was staying in Italy, Conrad, count palatine of the Rhine, brother of the emperor himself by one parent, raised a certain Christian to be archbishop. But when both had been rejected, the emperor [unclear] Conrad, brother of Otto, count palatine of Wittelsbach, to be ordained archbishop [unclear], stripped the whole Church [unclear]. We shall say, he expelled him, and ordained the aforesaid Christian in his place. After the murder of Arnold, the venerable bishop, the monastery of St. James was destroyed by his supporters, and the dwellings of the monks were utterly scattered, so that for nearly twelve years no harmony of divine praise was celebrated in that place. The monks were scattered here and there, and the abbot stood [unclear]. But all the citizens who had consented to the murder of the bishop, except the poor and beggars, saved themselves by flight before the emperor's return from Italy.

MCLXX.

But in the fifth year of Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 1170, Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, because he adhered to Alexander, the third pope of the city of Rome, against the sentence of the emperor, was driven from his church. In his place the emperor caused the above-mentioned Christian to be ordained; he presided for 13 years, and after his death Conrad returned to his church. Meanwhile, fleeing, he turned aside to the pope; received by him with honor, he accepted from him the bishopric of Sabina for the sustenance of his life. Therefore, as long as he lived, even after returning to Mainz, he wrote himself in all letters archbishop of Mainz and bishop of Sabina.

MCLXXII.

In the seventh year of Abbot Rupert, Emperor Frederick I subdued Henry, duke of Brunswick, who until then had been rebellious against the empire, both by the forces of the princes and by imperial censure, and compelled him to come to obedience.

In the same year the emperor celebrated Pentecost at Mainz, together with his wife and his son Henry and many princes; and on the same day in the monastery of St. Alban outside the walls he established [unclear] for the benefit of the commonwealth. There [Heminus?], count of Flanders, subjected himself in obedience to the emperor, and promised that same county to the emperor's son, provided he died without children.

In the same year also Louis, the second margrave of Thuringia, died, a man of great deeds and always unconquered in spirit.

MCLXXIII.

In the eighth year of Abbot Rupert, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 1173, the head of the holy virgin Irmina, daughter of Dagobert, once king of the Franks, who had been the first abbess of our order in the granary at Trier, was translated, at the petition of Lord [Craston?], the second abbot, to my monastery of Spanheim, with the consent of Hillin, archbishop.

MCLXXIIII. 152 The Monastery of Hirsau ... might have understanding. For the Spirit who spoke in her formed the words as he wished. Her whole life was, as it were, a certain long martyrdom, since, placed under regular discipline, she bore the Lord’s yoke for a long time under the manifold scourge of sufferings. For the hand of the Lord was always stretched out over her, and the scourge of her pious Creator was never lacking to her, weighing down her soul and crushing her weak body with continual illness. Although she was vexed by continual infirmities, nevertheless, always patient, always cheerful, mortifying herself by [unclear] chastisement, she offered an acceptable sacrifice to the Lord.

Instructed by divine revelations, moreover, she wrote several works for the edification of the faithful, among which we have read the following: The Ways of God, a beautiful and necessary work, in which several sermons are set down concerning the way of contemplatives, of active persons, of martyrs, of married persons, and of the continent; it begins thus: “It happened in the fifth year of my visitation,” etc. Likewise, instructed by angelic revelation, she issued a little work on the history, origin, discovery, and names of the eleven thousand, which begins thus: “To you who bear pious affections toward those things which are holy, I, Elisabeth, little woman of the handmaids of the Lord who are in Schönau, reveal the things which have been revealed to me through the grace of God.” Likewise she composed three books of various revelations, on various matters, causes, and propositions, containing one hundred forty-four chapters, in which she described many beautiful and useful things. The first of these begins thus: “You ask of me, brother; you have come for this, that I may recount to you the mercies of the Lord.” The second thus: “Benign is the mercy of our God.” The third thus: “The angel of the Lord took me up in the spirit to a place of great height.” Likewise, to the question [unclear] Saint Hildegard, mistress of the sisters at Bingen, which, after careful consideration, it has pleased us to insert word for word into this work of ours, as follows:

“To Lady Hildegard, venerable mistress of the brides of Christ who are at Bingen, Elisabeth, humble nun, mistress of the sisters who are at Schönau, offers devout prayers with all affection. May the grace and consolation of the Most High fill you with joy, because you have kindly had compassion for my disturbance, as I understood from the words of my consoler, whom you diligently [unclear] concerning my consolation. For, as you said that it had been revealed to you concerning me, I confess truly that recently I conceived in my soul a certain cloud of disturbance, because of the false words of people saying many things about me which are not true. But I would easily endure the words of the common people, if those who walk in the habit of religion did not grieve my spirit with bitter words. For these men, driven by I know not what goads, mock the grace of God in me; concerning things of which they are ignorant they do not fear to judge rashly. I hear that certain letters written from their own spirit are being circulated under my name, defaming me as having prophesied concerning the day of judgment. This, certainly, I presumed to do, since its coming escapes the knowledge of all mortals. But I shall disclose to you the occasion of this report, so that you may judge [unclear].

Many foolish persons mocked the visions of the holy virgin. [unclear] wished to [unclear] his [unclear] servants. She was struck by an angel. She reveals her visions to her abbot.

“On a certain Sunday, when I was in an ecstasy of mind, an angel stood by me, saying: ‘He has also frequently shown me through his angel what things would come upon his people in these days, unless they did penance for [unclear]; gold in the mud, that is, the word of God which has been sent through your mouth onto the earth because of the misfortunes of prophecy. Why do you hide it? Not that it may be hidden, but that it may be made manifest to the praise and glory of our Lord and the salvation of peoples.’ And when this had been said, he lifted over me a scourge, which with very great anger he inflicted on me five times most bitterly, so that for three days I was weak in my whole body from that blow. After this he placed his finger on my mouth, saying: ‘You will be silent until the ninth hour, when you will reveal the things which the Lord has worked with you.’ I therefore remained mute until the ninth hour. Then I signified to the mistress that she should bring me a certain little book, which I had hidden by my instruction, containing in part those things which the Lord had done with me. When I offered it into the hands of Abbot Hildelin, who had come to visit me, my tongue was loosed in these words: ‘Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory.’ After this, when I had revealed certain other things to him, which I had not wished to commit to writing, namely concerning the great vengeance of the Lord which I had learned from the angel would in a short time come upon the whole world, I asked him very diligently to keep that word hidden with himself. But the lord abbot himself commanded me to devote myself to prayer, and to ask the Lord to grant me understanding whether he wished the things which I had said to be governed by silence or not. And when for some time I had applied myself to prayer over this matter, the angel of the Lord stood by me, saying: ‘Cry out strongly, say “alas” to all nations, because the whole world has been turned into darkness. And you shall say: Come out; he has called you, who formed you from the earth; and say: Do penance,’ The Monastery of Hirsau

Concerning Conrad, the nineteenth abbot of this monastery, who presided for 12 years, and concerning his way of life and certain deeds of his and of that time.

Conrad becomes abbot of Hirsau.

After the resignation of the most reverend father, Lord Abbot Rupert, lest the monastery long feel the inconveniences of its widowhood, the prior and brothers of this community appointed a day for the election of a new shepherd. When it arrived, and all who were required to be present at the election had assembled in the chapter place, the grace of the Holy Spirit having been invoked, as is customary, after mature deliberation they unanimously elected as abbot the venerable man Conrad, a monk of this community, brother of Count Hermann of Kilberg, a holy and excellent man. After humbly excusing himself, he was at last overcome by the prayers of the brothers, gave his consent, and accepted the dignity with its burden. Thus elected by the common assent of the brothers, after a few days he was ordained abbot by the bishop of the church of Bamberg, and he presided vigorously over this monastery for 12 years. He refused, however, to be ordained by the bishop of Speyer, because that bishop adhered to Emperor Frederick, long since excommunicated, against the supreme pontiff.

This Conrad, as we have said, was sprung from the noble stock of the Swabians, the son of the noble count of Kilberg and the brother of Count Hermann. From his earliest age he was set to learning letters, and he made no small progress in every branch of knowledge, both divine and human. At last, when he had grown into a mature man, and was held glorious and distinguished for riches and honors and for the nobility of his lineage, he despised all things as dung for the love of God, betook himself to the present community, and, becoming a monk, lived in all religion and holiness. For the higher and nobler he was by birth, the humbler he showed himself in all things in his way of life. He never saddened anyone, offended no one wrongfully, but lived among the brothers without complaint and went about without offense. He was gentle in disposition and ready for obedience, so that he had no equal in the community. For in humility, obedience, patience, and uprightness of conduct he surpassed all, and by continence both of body and mind he was of singular chastity. He was dark in face, of middling stature, grave in gait, contemptible in habit, but excellent and gracious in virtue of soul.

When he had been ordained abbot, he strove in all things to show himself the form of the flock by word and example, tempering modestly the former measure of his humility, so that to the good and well-disposed he seemed a companion in manner of life, but to the hard and disobedient he was to be revered through the censure of justice. In his whole life he always lived most chastely, giving greater care to the soul than to the body. He was gentle in disposition, subtle and calm, cautious, ready, and circumspect in counsel, succinct, eloquent, and orderly in speech. In arranging temporal affairs he was strong in great sagacity and prudence, and he abundantly supplied to his subjects the necessities both of mind and body, according to the Rule of our most holy father Benedict. At table before the brothers and guests he was sufficiently generous and bountiful, and, receiving in Christ with all charity all who came, he treated them liberally according to the command of the Rule. He was dear to all, and held in the greatest reverence and honor by his subjects.

1177.

In the first year of Abbot Conrad, which was the year 1177 from the Lord’s Nativity, at Bingen, in the monastery of Saint Rupert, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, died Saint Hiltrudis, a virgin nun of our order, daughter of Count Meginhard of Spanheim and sister of Lord Crafto, the second abbot of my monastery of Spanheim. Blessed Hildegard, her mistress, is said to have borne witness to her sanctity both in life and after death.

1178.

In the second year of Abbot Conrad, the monastery of Saint James on Mount Speciosus near Mainz, destroyed nine years earlier on account of the murder of Arnold, archbishop of Mainz, began to be rebuilt by permission of Frederick, the first emperor, and with the aid of Archbishop Christian.

In the same year Reinhard, bishop of Würzburg, died. Godfrey succeeded him and presided for 6 years, eight months, and 24 days. This Bishop Godfrey dedicated the greater church of Würzburg in honor of Saint Kilian the martyr, and governed his church quite usefully and vigorously.

1180.

In the fourth year of Conrad, abbot of this community, which was the year 1180 from the Lord’s Nativity, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, died Saint Hildegard, a nun of our order, foundress and mistress, of the diocese of Mainz, of whom mention has been made above, in the [unclear] year of her age. She was buried in the middle of the choir of her monastery before the high altar; she, by many things both in life and after Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

153

[unclear], for the kingdom is near. Therefore, moved by this sermon, the lord abbot began to spread the word before the officials of the Church and men of religion. Some of them received the word with reverence; others, however, did not, but spoke ill of the angel who was familiar to me, saying that he was a deceiving spirit and transformed into an angel of light. Therefore the lord abbot himself bound me by my obedience, ordering that, when he appeared to me again, I should adjure him by the name of the Lord to tell me whether he was a true angel of God or not. But I, judging this presumptuous, accepted this command with great fear. Therefore one day, when I was in my ecstasy, in the usual manner he presented himself to me and stood in my sight. And trembling I said to him: I adjure you by God the Father and the Son and the Spirit. But tell me rightly whether you are a true angel of God, and whether the visions which I saw in my ecstasy are true, and the things which
