1174.

In the ninth year of Abbot Rupert, Craffto, the second abbot of my aforesaid monastery, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of June; he was the son of Count Meginhard of Spanheim, aged fifty-eight, and was buried in the middle of the choir, in one sarcophagus with his predecessor Bernhelm. Adelger, a monk and custodian of my monastery, succeeded him and presided for six years, [unclear] month, and only three days. Before entering religious life he had for a long time been in charge of the public school at Mainz, and left behind after him many distinguished pupils.

Adelger becomes abbot of Spanheim.

In the same year Herold, bishop of Würzburg, died; Reinhard succeeded him and presided for four years, ten months, and fifteen days.

1175.

In the tenth year of Abbot Rupert, which was the year 1175 of the Lord’s Nativity, there was great disturbance throughout the whole Roman Empire because of the disobedience and rebellion of Frederick, the first emperor, against the apostolic see. Rupert himself, abbot, and the brothers of this monastery, openly taking the side of the holy Roman Church from the first, suffered many troubles and injuries in goods and persons from the emperor’s supporters, until at last they were freed by the counsel of friends.

Great disturbance of the Roman Empire.

Therefore, since throughout all Germany there was an enormous disturbance of the people and of the clergy, because the excommunicated emperor was persecuting the pope with words, writings, and arms, and held in excessive hatred all who agreed with him, and both by himself and through his men inflicted many losses and inconveniences on them and permitted many injuries to be done, good and God-fearing men, seeing that they were placed in an evil situation, desired to save themselves either by flight or by silence.

The emperor persecutes the pope.

But since Rupert, the distinguished abbot of this monastery, was among those prelates who had agreed with the supreme pontiff, and was not the least of them, and daily endured many injuries from his rivals, fearing a general loss to the monastery because of the emperor’s personal hatred, and wishing to give place to anger, he resolved to resign the abbacy for the peace of the brothers and the benefit of the monastery.

Abbot Rupert agrees with the pope.

1176.

Therefore, in the eleventh year of his promotion, which was the year 1176 of the Lord’s Nativity, already greatly weighed down by age and cares, he freely resigned the abbacy into the hands of his brothers, and for the support of his life received from the brothers the provostship at Roth. There he lived for some time amid many labors, and at last rested in the Lord, being buried there, according to his prior arrangement, on the threshold of the church, so that he might be trodden by the feet of the brothers; this was a great sign of his humility. For he was, as we said above, a good and [unclear] man, who was accustomed to live among the brothers in all peace and tranquility.

Rupert resigned the abbacy.

For this reason he had formerly left the abbacy at Götzau, in which he could not live peacefully, and returned to his monastery of Hirsau. The monastery of Götzau is of our order, in the diocese of Speyer, in the county of Vorchheim, in eastern Francia, in the district called Albegau, beside the river called Alba; it was built by Count Berthold of Hennenberg in the year 1010 of the Lord’s Nativity, which was the eighth year during which this abbacy of Hirsau was vacant after the death of Abbot Conrad. In it Rupert presided for almost ten years. When he compelled the monks, who had strayed too far from the right path of monastic life, to observe regular discipline, he provoked the hatred of many against himself. Therefore he gave up both the place and the dignity, preferring to live humbly among his brothers of Hirsau rather than, among wicked and rebellious monks, to suffer harm to his soul under the burden of a pastor.

The monastery of Götzau is founded.

In the same year in which Rupert resigned the abbacy of this monastery of Hirsau, Clementia, a nun of our order in the monastery of Horrea at Trier, daughter of the late count of Homburg, died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. She was of most holy conduct, and by day and night intent upon [unclear] and contemplation, desired nothing more than to please God in all things.

Saint Clementia the virgin dies.

This most holy virgin had formerly been betrothed by her father, Count Adolf, to Lord Craffto, son of Count Meginhard of Spanheim; but since she had a holy purpose of virginity, with the consent of her betrothed she became a nun at Trier in the aforesaid monastery. Her betrothed, however, became a monk in my monastery of Spanheim under Bernhelm, the first abbot, succeeded him in the abbacy, and rested in holy conduct.

Craffto, abbot of Spanheim.

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

after death she was illustrious through miracles. This most holy virgin deserved to be visited by divine revelations from her youth, and by divine command wrote many things for the benefit of posterity.

1181.

In the following year, on the fifth day before the Nones of July, Adelgerus, the third abbot of my monastery of Sponheim, died, a good and very learned man, who greatly increased and maintained the observance of regular discipline; concerning him I have made fuller mention in the chronicle of that same monastery of mine. Baldemarus, the fourth abbot, succeeded him in the abbacy, and presided for 17 years, 2 months, and 17 days, a sufficiently good man and a lover of piety.

In the same year Pope Alexander III died; [unclear] sat for 4 years and 2 months, and was by nation a Tuscan.

Pope Alexander died.

In the same year also Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, defeated Saladin, king of the Egyptians, not far from Ascalon, and put him to flight.

1182.

In the sixth year of Abbot Conrad, Emperor Frederick entered Italy with a great army, and committed many evils against the pope and the Roman Church with sword and fire.

1183.

In the following year, which was the seventh of Abbot Conrad, Christian, archbishop of Mainz, died; and Conrad, whom the emperor had formerly expelled because of his obedience to the Apostolic See, returned to the see of Mainz and presided for 2 years, and retained, together with the archbishopric of Mainz, the title of bishop of Sabina, which the pope had conferred on him when he was expelled from Mainz.

1185.

In the ninth year of Abbot Conrad, which was the year 1185 of the Lord's Nativity, Godfridus, bishop of Wuerzburg, died while on pilgrimage overseas to the sepulchre of our Savior Jesus Christ, and was buried in Antioch. Henry III succeeded him, for 2 years.

In the same year Pope Lucius III died, by nation a Tuscan; Urban III, by nation a Lombard, succeeded him and presided for only 2 years. Emperor Frederick deprived all the cities, except Pistorium, of their agrarian jurisdiction, and accomplished many things in Italy against the rebels of the empire.

1186.

In the tenth year of Abbot Conrad, Godridus, formerly count palatine and a monk of this monastery of Hirsau, died, a man once vigorous and illustrious in the world, but in religion [unclear], devout, who brought with him no small gifts to this monastery, and after many [unclear]. [unclear] III, by nation a Roman, [presided] for three years, five months, and 16 days, who came to agreement with the emperor. [unclear] of his brothers.

1187.

In the eleventh and last year of Abbot Conrad, which was the year 1188 of the Lord's Nativity, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, there died in the monastery of Schoenau, of the Cistercian order, in the diocese of Worms, not far from Heidelberg, a devout virgin of Christ named Hildegundis, who, having disguised her sex and presenting herself as male, had there taken the habit of a novice among the monks; and, changing her name, she called herself Joseph, and remained unknown until death. Caesarius, monk of Heisterbach, wrote her life at sufficient length in the first distinction of his Dialogues.

In the same year Frederick, emperor of the Romans, and Philip, king of the Franks, together with Richard, king of the English, and Clement, the supreme pontiff, [unclear] for the aid and recovery [unclear]. He went on certain causes and business to the cell of St. Gregory in Reichenbach; when he had arrived there, he began to be struck by frequent burning fevers, and, lying in bed, was ill there for some time. As the disease grew day by day, he turned himself wholly to the Lord with most intent mind; and, after first making humble confession and receiving the sacraments of the Church with great devotion, at last on the fifth day of the month of September he rested in the Lord with a blessed end. His body through brought by the brethren to Hirsau, it was buried with reverence and honor in the greater monastery at the entrance of the church before the altar of All Saints, not without the tears of his subjects. In the same year also died Ulrich, the forty-first bishop of Speyer, who had presided for 8 years; Otto, the forty-second bishop, succeeded him for 2 years.

Concerning Henry, the twentieth abbot of this monastery, who presided for 8 years; concerning his character and certain deeds of that time.

After the most reverend abbot Conrad had died and been buried, as we have said, and after the funeral rites had been celebrated in Christian fashion with the customary solemnity, the prior and the brethren, assembling on the day appointed for the election in the chapter place, after the invocation of the Holy Spirit, by unanimous consent elected as the twentieth abbot of this monastery Henry, a conventual monk, who at that time held the office of cantor. But after his election he resisted for a long time, until at last, overcome by the prayers of the brethren, he gave his consent to the election. He presided for eight years.

He was from eastern Francia, born of honorable parents; having been set to letters in his youth, he made no small progress over time by learning, so that, instructed by long practice both in divine and in human philosophy, he became exceptionally learned. Afterwards, touched by divine inspiration, he began to consider in his mind the vanity of this world and the brevity of the present life; and after mature deliberation had first been held, he came to Hirsau and, by putting on the monastic habit, undertook monastic customs. Once made a monk, he lived among the brethren without complaint, always first with the last in the divine service, to which he wholly bound himself. Afterwards, since he seemed zealous in the divine offices and was not ignorant of music, he undertook the office of cantor, which he fulfilled for some years so studiously and eagerly that he yielded to all as an example through admiration. He also used to be intent with the greatest diligence upon the labors of his hands, according to the Rule of our holy father Benedict, planting vineyards, cultivating gardens, and grafting trees of various kinds.

By his own zeal and labor he also greatly adorned the church, [unclear] from day to day he advanced more and more in religion, and was dear and beloved to all the brethren; the fame of his name began also to spread abroad to outsiders, [unclear] with manifold praise. He was elected abbot by the brethren of the same monastery, [unclear] received with much honor and reverence.

Having been ordained abbot at Brauweiler, he took care with all zeal to instruct the monks in the observance of regular discipline and to forbid all the vices of the monks more strictly under a fixed censure. But, affected by weariness because of the poverty of the place and the excessive importunity of the brethren, when he saw that he could make less progress, he repented of having undertaken so arduous a burden of pastoral care. Therefore, after long and mature deliberation, he resolved to lay down the abbacy he had undertaken and to return to Hirsau, whence he had come. And so he then resigned the office of pastoral care and, having returned to the monastery whence he had come, was again appointed cantor, persevering in the same humility after the abbacy in which he had lived before.

After this, when the venerable abbot Conrad had died, as we have said, he was substituted in his place and presided over the monastery of Hirsau for 8 years: a good man, gentle in disposition, who at the beginning of his advancement for some years ordered both his own life and that of his subjects modestly enough and according to the Rule, and took care in all things to show himself a useful pastor in each state. But in the course of time, too much weighed down by the cares and anxieties of secular affairs, he turned his mind away from the rigor of holy observance; and, becoming more lax in the custody of monastic discipline, he relaxed in himself and toward his subjects the fervor of a holy superior. Hence, when 8 years had been completed in the abbacy, he brought back to memory the negligences of his past life and, fearing the punishment of divine vengeance, abdicated the abbatial dignity, as we shall say in its place, and accepted the provostship in Reuth for the support of his life.

As far as the disposition of his body is concerned, he was a man of middling stature, his body somewhat spread out in [unclear]. In his way of life he was very humane and affable to all with a certain sociability; though he was quickly moved to anger, he could be placated by a quick satisfaction. In his time, the holy observance of religion had declined not a little in the present monastery, since he immersed himself wholly in the cares of temporal affairs and did not seem to give as much thought as he ought to the spiritual advancement of his subjects.

1189.

In the first year of abbot Henry, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1189, when Frederick, emperor of the Romans, was in the Holy Land and held Syria, and [unclear] to the Christians against the infidels Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

...he was preparing what seemed necessary, when, while bathing in a certain river, the passages of life being closed, he was suffocated, and miserably entered the way of all flesh. After his death, the princes took his son Henry, the sixth of this name, as king of the Romans; Philip, archbishop of Cologne, crowned him at Aachen according to custom, and he reigned after his father for ten years, having reigned with him, while he was alive, for almost twenty-two years. He took as wife Constance, daughter of William king of Apulia, by the counsel and dispensation of Pope Clement III, because she had been a nun for many years and was the only daughter of the aforesaid king. With her he obtained the kingdom of Apulia and Sicily, the pope lending favor and assistance. And although she was fifty years old, nevertheless she bore him a son named Frederick, later Frederick II, emperor, of whom we shall speak in his own place.

The emperor Frederick dies.

Henry his son becomes emperor.

[Unclear] countess.

Saint Margaret, nun.

Eclipse of the sun.

1190.

In the second year of Abbot Henry, Ida, countess of Spanheim, became a nun of our order in the monastery of Mount St. Rupert near Bingen, in which thereafter, all the days of her life, she lived most religiously, second to none in continual humility and obedience, in prayers and meditations on the divine Scriptures. Her sister was Margaret, a virgin of most holy life, [unclear], who carried out the office of prioress for many years in the same monastery, and, renowned for miracles, at last passed to the Lord. The feast day of her commemoration is observed on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, when she passed from life.

1192.

In the [unclear] year of Henry, Philip, archbishop of Cologne, died in Apulia, having been established with the emperor. Bruno III, provost of the major church, succeeded him and presided for three years, and afterward became a monk. There was an obscuration of the sun, and famine followed in the land, and no small barrenness of fields and vineyards.

In this same year also Philip, king of the Franks, and Richard, the renowned king of the English, with their army joined together in Syria, at first waged war prosperously against Saladin. But soon discord between them having arisen at the devil’s instigation, Philip returned to Gaul. Richard, however, vigorously pursued the war he had begun in this same year; but in the following year he too returned home, not without harm to the Christians, whom he left afterward exposed to many dangers in the Holy Land.

In the same year also Pope Clement III died. Celestine III succeeded him and presided for six years and eight months. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, after celebrating his pontifical coronation at the solemnity of Easter, on the following day he crowned Henry VI, king of Rome, as emperor of the Romans.

In these times the Order of the Teutons began in the Holy Land through certain citizens of Bremen and Lubeck, who, crossing the sea with Count Adolf of Holstein under Emperor Frederick I, took poor, sick pilgrims into their care for the love of God and, as far as they were able, supported them by nourishing them under tents. They built at Acre the first house and church of this undertaking; calling it the house of the Teutonic brothers, they gave the order its name. The work of this order is to serve sick pilgrims. Around the same time also began the Order of the Holy Trinity for the redemption of captives, whose more important monasteries are established in France. The work of this order is cheerfully to expend its substance for the redemption of Christians who are held captive among the unbelievers in the Holy Land, and to aid them by ministering to them with all its strength.

In the fourth year of Henry, abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, a grave dissension arose because of the insolence of his servants, who were disturbing the peace of the brothers with excessive importunity. But when the brothers had often asked the abbot either to cast the wicked and restless servants out of the monastery or at least to correct them, and [unclear], certain of the younger men, offended in spirit, calling upon the aid of outside friends, violently drove some of the abbot’s own household out of the monastery. In that tumult one of the abbot’s servants, named Adelbert, was gravely wounded, and after eight days he died from the same wound. From this arose a great dissension between shepherd and sheep, not without danger to souls, until Otto, bishop of the church of Speyer, interposed his authority with the counsel of friends and restored concord.

Vision of a certain monk.

1193.

In the fifth year of Abbot Henry, which was the year 1193 of the Lord’s nativity, Rupert, the fourth prior of my monastery of Spanheim, beheld a wondrous vision of the joys and punishments of the life to come. When he revealed it in public with too little prudence, he was soon gravely struck by paralysis and suffered punishment for almost the space of a year.

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

In the same year Albert was born, later surnamed the Great, in a village of Swabia whose name is Laugingen. There was also an eclipse of the sun.

1193.

In the following year, which was the sixth of Abbot Henry, Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, resigned his episcopal office into the hands of Emperor Henry VI and became a monk of the Cistercian order in the monastery of Altenberg. His brother, named Adolf of Altena, a canon of the cathedral church, succeeded him in the archbishopric and presided for twelve years.

1195.

In the seventh year of Abbot Henry, the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1195, Henry VI, emperor of the Romans, took Sicily with a mighty hand, and Tancred, the usurper of the kingdom, having been captured and his eyes gouged out,

In the same year Conrad, Count Palatine of the Rhine, who was dwelling at Heidelberg, changed the provostship of the monastery of our order near the town of Heidelberg itself, which is called Neuburg, in the diocese of Worms, into a monastery of nuns of the same order of ours, with the consent of Sighard, abbot of Lorsch, to whom that provostship belonged by full right and without intermediary. There Cunegundis, a very devout and religious virgin, was appointed by him as the first abbess.

1196.

In the following year, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1196, when Henry, abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, called to mind the negligences of his past life and the wrongs he had committed, and fearfully pondered the vengeance of divine retribution, inwardly touched with sorrow of heart, he began to discuss with certain friends the resignation of the abbacy. But although all who knew themselves to be his intimates and friends opposed his will with one steadfast resolve, nevertheless they could not turn him away from his decision so as to prevent him from carrying out in deed the thought he had conceived in his mind. For he was moved to resign the abbacy chiefly by two causes: [first, that] he knew he had committed [unclear] in temporal matters; for these, unless the occasion of affairs were cut away, he could by no means [make satisfaction?] as he desired. The other was that, [unclear] with peace and tranquillity, much exhausted in body, he had greatly declined, and could no longer usefully attend to the affairs of the monastery as he ought.

And so, pierced in heart, grieving and repentant for his past negligences, in order to save his soul, in the eighth year of his rule, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1196, indiction 14, in the month of [June?], he freely and voluntarily resigned his abbacy into the hands of his community before them all. After the resignation had been made, he received from the brothers the provostship in Rothe for the support of his life, where, surviving for almost [eleven?] months in sorrow of spirit and continual tears, at last in the following year, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, he rested in the Lord. His body was buried with reverence beside the body of Rupert, formerly abbot, here in the same monastery, at the very entrance of the church.

[H.] after [a year?] died in Rothe.

On Marquard, twenty-first abbot of this monastery, who governed for 8 years, 6 months, and 21 days, and on the events of his time.

After the resignation, therefore, of Dom Henry, the twentieth abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, which took place in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1196, indiction 14, on the last day of the month of June, that is, on the feast of the Commemoration of Saint Paul the Apostle, on the same day the brothers, invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit and proceeding to the election of a new shepherd, after much deliberation at last unanimously elected as the twenty-first abbot of this monastery Marquard, a conventual monk, a venerable and most prudent man. Confirmed and blessed according to custom, he governed this monastery vigorously for 8 years, 6 months, and 21 days, a man of great deeds and many virtues, who prudently and bravely defended the rights of the monastery against the attacks of tyrants, resisting without fear.

Under Abbot Marquard [unclear].

He was by origin from Swabia, born of most noble parents, drawing his descent from the counts of Montis Solis; in writings both divine and human he became sufficiently learned. From his youth he was instructed in the way of the Lord in fear; when he had reached the years of discretion, despising the world, his parents, brothers, kinsmen, the splendor of a great patrimony, and also the nobility of his lineage for the love of God, he became a monk in the present monastery of Hirsau under Abbot Conrad, his maternal uncle Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

... made profession. When he had learned the monastic discipline according to our most holy father Benedict, he strove to conform his conduct wholly to it, and, living among the brothers without complaint even in the lowest rank, he showed everyone an example of humility. After he had been ordained abbot, he took every care to show himself a shepherd worthy of his sheep, and to teach no less by example than by word.

As for the disposition of his body, he was a robust and strong man, handsomely proportioned in stature, somewhat exceeding middle height, with a sound and not small head, surrounded all about with much hair tending toward black. He had a resonant and trumpet-like voice, by which alone he was accustomed to strike terror into the wicked. In speaking he was sufficiently eloquent, whether the discourse had to be delivered in Latin or in German. He was of a very gentle nature, and was not easily moved to anger; but when he was angry with reason, he did not quickly let the matter pass into oblivion. In all things generous, he was of such benevolence toward his subjects, and of such loyalty, charity, and affection toward his friends, that he had no equal in his time.

Nevertheless he was marked by certain stains of negligence and tepidity in those matters that seemed to pertain to the complete observance of regular discipline, chiefly for this reason: that he had many continual occupations, labors, and cares in household affairs, and that at the beginning of his promotion he necessarily endured dangers, injuries, and innumerable tribulations, both from the advocate of the monastery, Count Adelbert, and from various others whom it was necessary to resist.

For the aforesaid Count Adelbert, advocate of this monastery, forgetful of the duty of his office, undertook, contrary to the liberty and privilege formerly granted by the supreme pontiffs and emperors, to burden, harass, and disturb the household and servants of the monastery. A certain tyrannical advocate. For, at the devil’s instigation, he strove so greatly to violate and infringe the rights and liberties of the monastery, which he ought to have defended, that one day he seized the chamberlain of the monastery before the gate, and, with his hands bound behind his back, [unclear] the innocent [unclear], while the abbot protested.

Compelled by necessity, the abbot first went to Rome in his own person, and afterward, once and again through messengers, laid the violence of the advocate before the examination of the most holy apostolic see; he sought and obtained the counsel and aid of the supreme pontiff against the tyranny of the count. For, when the privilege of liberty had been renewed, and a declaration made concerning the law of the advocate as limited, [unclear].

The conduct and character of his life. The disposition and condition of his body. He was an excellent and humane man. A certain tyrannical advocate. Abbot Marquard went to Rome. Of the Monastery of Hirsau

In the same year also Luthold, bishop of Basel, Baldwin, count of Flanders, Adelbert, count of Spanheim, and many other princes, proceeding through Greece with a great army toward the Holy Land, took Constantinople and made Alexius, son of Isaac, formerly emperor of Constantinople, emperor. When he was soon killed by the Greeks, Baldwin, the aforesaid count of Flanders, received the empire. Through his agency the union of the Eastern and Roman Church was confirmed. He ruled over the Greeks for almost seven years.

In the same year also Conrad, count of Zollern and burgrave of Nuremberg, established in the presence of King Otto, freely and willingly resigned forever to Conrad, bishop of Speyer, and to his successors, the castle of Rietburg, which he had received in fief from the church of Speyer.

1201.

In the sixth year of Abbot Marquard, namely in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1201, King Philip, gathering an army again, crossed the Moselle, besieged Cologne, took the archbishop, and thus compelled the city and the whole province to surrender. Afterwards, coming to Aachen with many princes, he placed himself, together with the queen, on the seat of the kingdom.

In the same year, after King Philip had prosperously returned to the upper parts, King Otto, having gathered an army of his men, ascending again to the upper parts, reached as far as Wissembourg; but, unable to advance farther, he returned to the lower regions of the land.

In the same year also, around the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, Guido, cardinal bishop of Palestrina, came to Cologne and declared King Philip and all those who agreed with him excommunicated, commanding all men by apostolic authority to accept Otto as king and to abandon Philip, under penalty of excommunication. There then for the first time Siegfried, elect of Mainz, was ordained priest and archbishop by the hands of that cardinal; and, having proceeded to Rome with them and with letters of mandate from King Otto, he was confirmed by Pope Innocent III with the pallium, as is customary.

In the same year King Philip held a solemn assembly of princes in Bamberg, where many bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, and nobles gathered. There the bones of the holy emperors Henry and Cunegund were raised up, and they shone forth with many miracles. There was a very great gathering of peoples there, from both distant and neighboring regions. At about these times the order of the Friars Preachers began, through the institution of St. Dominic, a man of outstanding holiness, who was originally from Spain. Pope Innocent confirmed his institution.

1202.

In the sixth year of Abbot Marquard, namely in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1202, King Otto and Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, with other princes, held a conference at Maastricht by the Meuse concerning the commonwealth and various affairs of the kingdom; and among other matters they restored peace between the duke of Brabant and the count of Guelders, who with great opposing armed forces had often already prepared themselves for war, not without very grave injury to the poor.

In the same year Conrad, bishop of Strasbourg, died. Henry of Veringen succeeded him, a good, religious, and devout man, a lover of peace and a most upright defender of the clergy; in the fourth year after his election he was scarcely able to obtain consent from Pope Innocent to receive the office of consecration from the archbishop of Sens, because he was compelled to side with King Philip, which displeased the pope, who always favored Otto for the reasons alleged above.

In the same year also, on the feast of St. Nicholas, bishop of Myra, Conrad, bishop of Würzburg, formerly chancellor of the imperial court, was cruelly killed in the public street of the city of Würzburg by Bodo and Henry, knights of Ravensburg, and by their servants Herald and Conrad. Henry, called Cascus because he took delight in cheese, succeeded him and presided for four years, seven months, and [unclear] days; he was a learned man and very much instructed in all Scripture, who governed his church quite well. Those parricides, however, led by penitence and seeking Rome, after two years received from the supreme pontiff such a penance as he gave in his letters patent, sounding as follows: Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to all the faithful of Christ who shall inspect these letters, greeting and apostolic blessing. What an execrable crime and singular outrage they committed who, with sacrilegious daring, wickedly laid impious hands upon the Christ of the Lord, cruelly killing Conrad of Würzburg, bishop of good memory and chancellor of the imperial court, it is more fitting to weep over than to relate. But since Of the Monastery of Hirsau

... having died at Palermo (as we have said). For Adolf, archbishop of Cologne, and Theodoric, archbishop of Trier, maintaining that the election of the king belonged to their jurisdiction, held counsel at Andernach with Duke Bernard and with other bishops, counts, and many nobles, and proclaimed to all the princes a general court at Cologne for the Sunday Oculi mei, to celebrate the election of a new king. Meanwhile the eastern margraves, Conrad archbishop of Mainz, Bernard duke of Saxony, the archbishop of Magdeburg, and other higher princes, meeting at Erfurt, elected Philip duke of Swabia as king of the Romans, namely the brother of the deceased emperor Henry.

Therefore, on the appointed day, the aforesaid princes, coming to Cologne, waited with great desire for the arrival of Bertold, duke of Zahringen, whom they had promised that they would elect. But when he had received from Philip 1,000 marks of silver together with the duchy of Swabia, and had renounced the election, he disdained to come. When this became known to the aforesaid princes, greatly indignant, they elected Otto, count of Poitou, son of the late Henry duke of Saxony, as king of the Romans against Philip. And evils were multiplied in the land: wars, burnings, destruction of cities, and the slaughter of the poor.

But when Philip heard of Otto's election, he sent ahead to Aachen three hundred armed knights with many other shield-bearers, so that they might keep Otto from entering the city and preserve the city and the seat of the kingdom for him. But Otto, with his supporters, surrounding that city with a siege at harvest time, took it by force and held it; and after sitting for three days in the seat of the kingdom, he departed from there, entrusting it to his faithful men to guard. Meanwhile Philip, having gathered an army, entered Alsace; and because it was near harvest, he destroyed all the grain found in the fields. Thus there were many wars between this Philip and Otto for almost eight years, during which Philip lived in the kingdom, until at last, after his death, peace was in some measure restored, as we shall say in its place.

In the year noted above Celestine III, pope, also died; Innocent III succeeded him, by nation a Campanian, and he presided for 18 years. Because he hated King Philip on account of his father and brother, who had committed many acts against the Roman Church, he held Otto's side, and crowned him emperor, as we shall say later.

In the same year a battle was joined between King Philip and his adversary Otto, not far from Koblenz beside the Moselle, but nothing worthy of memory was done, except the plundering of the poor and the desolation of all the provinces round about.

In the same year Baldemar, the fourth abbot of my monastery of Sponheim, died. Rupert succeeded him as fifth abbot, and presided for 14 years and 2 months. He was a man very learned in both divine and secular letters, and venerable no less for his life than for his knowledge.

Otto, bishop of Speyer, died.

Likewise in the same year, on the Kalends of July, Baldemar, the fourth abbot of my monastery of Sponheim, died. Rupert succeeded him as fifth abbot, and presided for 8 years. In the same year [unclear], who had previously been chancellor of the imperial court, a prudent man and for a long time sufficiently experienced in many varieties of affairs, [died?]. He governed his church well, increasing its revenues and restoring what had been ruined. There are those who write that he had first been bishop of the church of Metz.

Also in the year noted above, the third of Abbot Marquard, and the 150th from the foundation of this house, King Philip besieged Strasbourg, destroyed Rubiacum and many strongholds of the bishop of Strasbourg and of Count Adelbert of Dagsburg, and leveled them to the ground. At last, through the mediation of Lord Berthold duke of Zahringen and other princes, concord was made between them, so that the bishop, abandoning Otto's side, would give Philip, for retaining the governance of the kingdom, aid and support with his son as far as he could. This same thing the count of Dagsburg promised that he would do thereafter.

This year, on the Assumption of blessed Mary ever virgin, King Philip held a great court of his princes at Mainz. Since Conrad, its archbishop, was still in the Holy Land with other princes, the archbishop of Tarentum there, in place of the aforesaid archbishop, anointed Philip as king. In the same assembly King Philip, as [unclear], gave crowns to him and to his wife. At that time the empress Constance died in Sicily, and her son Frederick, after many hardships, at last obtained the kingdom of Apulia and of Sicily.

In the same year, around the beginning of October, King Philip, together with the new king of the Bohemians, crossed the river Moselle with a strong force and a numerous army, invaded the territory of the people of Cologne against Otto, and burned Remagen, Bonn, and many surrounding villages with fire.

In the same Of the Monastery of Hirsau

In the same year also Theoderic, count of Holland, died, and the province, together with the daughter of the deceased, was handed over to the count of Lo. William, Theoderic’s brother, taking this very ill, gathered soldiers, expelled that same count of Lo from Holland, and took his brother’s daughter.

In these times also Pope Innocent III composed five books of Decretals, which he ordered to be read in the schools and observed everywhere in legal proceedings; this was done, and is done down to the present day. Lupold, bishop of Worms, who had sought the archbishopric of Mainz, as we said above, adhered to King Philip against King Otto and Pope Innocent, and committed many evils throughout the whole province. In all the wars he was personally present with Philip his king against Otto; he fought as a knight, plundered the poor, and spared neither monasteries nor churches. And when the soldiers said to him, “Lord, it is not lawful for us to plunder churches and monasteries,” he would answer, “When you take away the bones of the dead, then you are plundering churches and cemeteries.” At last he was excommunicated by Pope Innocent and deposed from his pontificate because of the countless crimes he had committed. Finally, out of hatred for King Otto, he was restored to his office and benefice.

1204.

In the eighth year of Abbot Marquard, which was the year 1204 of the Lord’s Nativity, around the month of [unclear], King Philip, having assembled a very great army, entered Thuringia and burned and devastated a certain city of the landgrave, named Wizen[see?]; also [unclear] the king of Bohemia with a very great [unclear]. The landgrave, seeing the ruin of his land and that he could not resist the king’s anger, came to him as a suppliant through the intervention of certain princes, seeking his favor, and obtained it. After this, through the mediation of the archbishop of Trier and the bishops of Speyer and Constance, he gained over to himself Adolf, archbishop of Cologne, at a council at Andernach: in order to make the duke of Brabant and the remaining nobles of Lotharingia faithful to himself, he gave him nine thousand marks, restored Saalfeld, long before taken away from the church of Cologne, and promised that he would give very many other things. Enticed by these promises, Adolf, archbishop of Cologne, making little of the oath he had formerly sworn to Otto, and not fearing perjury or the pope’s excommunication, came after the feast of St. Martin to that same Philip with the duke of Brabant at Koblenz. Both offered him the oath of fidelity, which afterward did not turn out to his prosperity.

The princes go over to Philip. Philip again gains Thuringia for himself.

1205.

In the ninth year of Abbot Marquard, on the feast of the Epiphany in the year 1205 of the Lord’s Nativity, in the eighth indiction, King Philip held a great assembly of the princes adhering to him at Aachen, where the archbishop of Cologne came to meet him with very great display. There the king, after taking counsel with his men, so that the princes might not lose their free election according to the ordinance of antiquity, laid down the royal name and crown, and asked and obtained that he be re-elected by all in concord. Adolf, archbishop of Cologne, with great solemnity, together with Maria his wife, daughter of the emperor of Constantinople, again anointed and crowned him, while Otto was held by a very grave illness and deprived of the help of almost everyone. In this year the summer was dry, the winter harsh.

In the same year the most reverend Marquard, abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, after he had energetically and usefully governed this cenobium for eight years, six months, and twenty-one days, at last weakened by a subsequent dysentery, rested in the Lord on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the year of the Lord 1205, in the eighth indiction, and was buried, not without the tears of the brothers, before the altar of St. Nicholas. [Unclear], he triumphed over all. In many things he increased the revenues of the monastery; he restored the supply of resources [unclear] with many other structures; he began, in excellent stonework, the wall before the doors of the monastery, which, forestalled by death, he did not complete. For he was a man noble in blood and character, distinguished in intellect and wisdom, known to kings and princes, who in the time of the schism of the empire between Philip and Otto conducted himself so prudently toward all that he won merit before God and praise from men.

Concerning Lutfrid, twenty-second abbot of this monastery, who presided for 2 years and 15 days; concerning various deeds and affairs of that time.

After the most reverend Marquard, abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, had died in the aforesaid year and day, and after his body had been committed with honor and reverence to ecclesiastical Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

At the same time the Lotharingians, whom Otto had summoned to his aid near Andernach, being unable to withstand King Philip and fearing for their own skins, secretly favored his side, perpetrating many unheard-of crimes in that region. It will be enough to have set down one of these, from which the other unspeakable things they committed may be weighed. They stripped a certain nun of all her clothing, smeared her with honey, rolled her in bed-feathers, and, thus made monstrously shaggy, put her on a horse, with her face turned toward the horse’s tail. And when they had led this ridiculous, indeed pitiable, spectacle around for several days, the matter became known to King Philip, who, inflamed with zeal for God, ordered all those guilty of this crime to be handed over to boiling water. The town of Andernach also was burned by the army of the same King Philip. Afterwards he returned to his own territories.

Meanwhile King Otto entered Saxony with his army and began to attack Goslar, together with the other neighboring towns. But when King Philip came upon him, he was compelled to desist from his purpose and withdraw. Henry, Count Palatine of the Rhine, brother of King Otto himself, and the landgrave of Hesse and the duke of Brabant, together with Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, returned from the lands overseas, the affairs of our men there having been left in a bad condition. But the aforesaid archbishop, hearing of the discord between Philip and Otto over the kingdom, resolved to make some stay in Italy until he should deliberate what he ought to do in so grave a matter of disturbance in the commonwealth. At this time grave [unclear].

In the year of the Nativity 1200, Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, returning from Hungary, whither in the preceding year he had gone to restore peace between two brothers contending over the kingdom, after concord had been made in the parts of Austria, in the territory of Passau, released from the flesh, passed over to the Lord for his merits. Wolfher, bishop of Passau, with solemn obsequies brought his body back to Mainz, where it was buried with great honor. Meanwhile a serious tumult arose in Mainz because of the election of a new pontiff. For certain men, by the will and favor of King Philip, elected Lupold, bishop of Worms, as archbishop; [unclear] having been taken, Siegfried drove him thence with an army. But Siegfried, seeing that he and his men were making too little progress, betook himself with his men to King Otto, by whom he was graciously received; he received the regalia from him, and, relying on his authority, with an army [unclear] to the diocese in Philip’s [unclear] came to Bingen, and there what they had intended concerning the election of Siegfried [unclear].

... divine mercy surpasses human impiety, and the miseries of men cannot be compared with the compassions of the Lord; since the Lord does not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he should be converted and live, as one who is patient and very merciful, [unclear] over wickedness. We, who, although unworthy, exercise his office on earth, knowing that there is greater joy among the angels over one sinner doing penance, however much homicides of this kind may have offended, nevertheless could not, nor ought we, close the approach to pardon to the penitent, since we know that the Lord said through the Prophets: “In whatever hour the sinner has been converted and has groaned, I shall no longer remember any of his iniquities.”

Therefore Bodo, Henry, his vassal, knights, with Herold and Conrad, his servants, came into our presence, confessing that they had killed the aforesaid bishop. Since they tearfully repented of their excesses, they humbly asked that penance be enjoined upon them by us for the enormity of so great a crime. Because the door of indulgence must not be closed to the penitent, by the counsel of our brothers we committed them to our beloved son Hugh, cardinal priest of the title of St. Martin, to be heard. After hearing their confession, he made them stand for several days before us, naked in their breeches, with ropes around their necks, in the presence of crowds of people; and by our command he enjoined upon them this penance: that henceforth they should never use arms, except against the Saracens or in defense of [unclear]. They should not wear vair, gray fur, ermine, or colored cloths. They should not go to public spectacles; they should not contract marriages after the death of their wives. As soon as they are able, they should go into the province of Jerusalem, to serve the Lord there for four years against the Saracens. Bodo, however, who was the greater [offender?], should bring with him three men, or at least one, at his own expense. And until those four execrable homicides [unclear], they should make fifty genuflections. They should not presume to receive the body and blood of the Lord except at the very last moment of death. When they are overseas, they should fast on water on Wednesday and Friday and on the vigils of saints. They should keep three Lents in the year, namely before the Resurrection, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord. They should not eat meat except only on those three feasts; and on the day on which the aforesaid bishop was killed, they should not eat meat forever. They should recite the Lord’s Prayer one hundred times between day and night; they should make fifty genuflections. Also in the year noted above, the Tartars, having come out from the mountains of India with their wives and children, plundered the neighboring provinces, to which they had always been accustomed. Then they sought the Parthians; with equal terror they overran Media, Assyria, Persia, Armenia, and the Sarmatians in no long time; at last they fixed their settlements around the Maeotic marshes and did many evils to the neighboring Christians.

M.CC.III.

In the sixth year of Abbot Marquard, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1203, King Philip, having gathered a strong army, entered Thuringia in order to humble Hermann the Landgrave, because he had abandoned him, adhered to Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, against his will, and supported him, and because he had converted to the uses of his enemy, that is, King Otto, the revenues and proceeds of the church of Mainz falling due in Thuringia. The Landgrave, perceiving openly that the duke of Bohemia was surrounding the city with a siege, and that Philip would capture him, consumed everything by fire, and thus betook himself with his men into Erfurt. When the counts in that Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

... from the burial. The prior and convent, lest they wander any longer like sheep without a shepherd, unanimously appointed the third day thereafter, that is, 23 January, for the election of a new abbot. When that day arrived, and those absent who ought to be present at an election of this kind had meanwhile been summoned, all assembled in the chapter-place in the morning; and, after the grace of the Holy Spirit had been invoked in the customary manner, after long and mature discussions held among themselves, they at last elected as the twenty-second abbot of this monastery Lutfrid, a monk of this convent, a gentle and religious man. After he had been confirmed by the Ordinary, the bishop of the church of Speyer, he received the office of benediction from Guido, cardinal of the holy Roman Church, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See throughout Germany. He presided over this monastery for eleven years and five days. For he refused to be blessed by his own bishop of Speyer, who favored King Philip against the mandate of the supreme pontiff; and for that reason, in accordance with the privilege long before granted by Pope Urban under Abbot Gebhard, [unclear].

Lutfrid becomes abbot of this place, 2a.

Abbot Lutfrid is blessed by Guido the cardinal.

[unclear] he was accustomed to be reproached; but, from earliest age devoting himself to peace and silence, even while still a boy he already seemed to live as one who had become a monk. When he had grown older, he resolved to renounce worldly affairs utterly for the love of Christ, and to serve the almighty Lord in tranquillity of mind and body. He therefore came to Hirsau, and under Abbot Conrad became a monk. He lived among the brethren without complaint and, after being tested for a good many years in certain lesser offices, at last, after the death of Marquard, as we have said, he was ordained abbot.

His family and origin.

He was born in East Francia, begotten of free and honorable parents. As a young man he was set to letters and made moderate progress in study. For he did not immerse himself, as many do, in the games of the people and temporal affairs, but rather entrusted himself to necessity. [unclear]

How he became a monk [unclear].

At about the same time at which his election was held at Hirsau, namely in the year of the Lord 1205, Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, and the bishop of Cambrai, appointed commissioners and judges by the Apostolic See, came to Cologne. In the greater church of St. Peter, before the clergy and the whole people, they publicly announced that Adolf, archbishop of Cologne, had been excommunicated by Pope Innocent, and they ordered that, in all the conventual and parish churches of the same city, on each Sunday and feast day, he should be declared excommunicate. They also had this in their mandate: that if, within a month after [unclear], he persisted in defying the censures of the supreme pontiff, the aforesaid commissioners should again come to Cologne. In the greater church, before the clergy and people, in the presence of King Otto, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, by definitive sentence and apostolic authority they deposed the same Adolf from every office and archiepiscopal dignity, and by the same authority ordered the canons to elect another bishop. Obeying the apostolic commands, they elected Bruno of Sayn, provost of Bonn, as archbishop; and countless evils followed.

Adolf is excommunicated.

Adolf, archbishop of Cologne, is deposed.

Bruno becomes archbishop of Cologne.

For Adolf, going to King Philip, on account of whose adherence he had been deposed, while Philip was holding court with the princes at Speyer, explained what he was suffering and sought counsel and help. Therefore, by the common decree of the princes, the king gathered a great army against Bruno and the people of Cologne; and after the Nativity of Blessed Mary ever Virgin he crossed the Moselle. On the feast of St. Michael the Archangel he encircled Cologne with a siege; when this was finally abandoned, he besieged and captured Neuss, which he gave to the deposed Adolf. When these things had been done, by burning, plundering, and miserably afflicting it everywhere, he devastated the whole province and captured many fortifications. He also built in his time a handsome and very strong castle called Landskron, to subdue the people of Cologne.

King Philip [unclear] an army into Cologne.

Landskron Castle.

There was very great calamity in all the land at these times, and especially in the land of Cologne, because of the deposition of Adolf, and in the diocese of Mainz because of Siegfried, who had deposed him; and nowhere was faith secure, but a thousand dangers raged everywhere.

Calamity of the province of the Rhine.

1206.

In the first year of Abbot Lutfrid, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1206, Henry, bishop of Wurzburg, a learned man and master of sacred letters of the University of Paris, died. Otto of Ladenburg succeeded him in the episcopate and presided for sixteen years and five months, a magnanimous prince, feared for wisdom and dignity.

Henry died.

Lutfrid becomes abbot of this place, 2b.

1206. In the first year of Abbot Lutfrid, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity. In the year of Bishop Henry [unclear].

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

In the same year Baldwin, count of Flanders, emperor of Constantinople, died, a most Christian prince, who accomplished many things for the defense of Christians. His brother Henry succeeded him in the empire of the Greeks, and ruled vigorously for eleven years.

In the same year also King Philip again entered the territories of the people of Cologne. Adolf, formerly archbishop, came to meet him, and with counts and a great army he traversed the whole bishopric, subjecting everything to his will. But King Otto and Bruno, who in the same month had been ordained archbishop by Siegfried of Mainz, with two bishops from Britain sent by the king of England and with four hundred horsemen and two thousand foot soldiers, set out from Cologne and resolved to fight with Philip. Therefore, when these two kings joined battle with their armies at Wassenberg, Otto and his men turned their backs, and King Philip obtained the victory. Among many other nobles he also captured Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, whom he took away with him bound in iron manacles, and kept in close custody for more than the space of a year. Meanwhile the people of Cologne, considering that the whole empire was opposed to them and that their efforts were everywhere frustrated, took the counsel and assistance of the duke of Brabant, went to King Philip while he was staying at Boppard, and, asking pardon for their offenses, were received back into his favor at Cologne. They also afterward, when Conrad had been sent [unclear]. King Otto, leaving Cologne, came to Brunswick in Saxony, and there [unclear] came by ship across the sea into England, where he was received with honor by the king of England, namely his uncle, and remained for some time.

In the same year, on the second day before the Kalends of March, at the tenth hour of the day, there was an eclipse of the sun, and many testified that they had seen a human head in the sun.

1207.

In the second year of Abbot Lutfried, which was the year 1207 of the Lord’s Nativity, Conrad, bishop of Speyer, granted in perpetuity to the provost in Denkendorf the church of the Holy Sepulchre at Speyer, in which there were nuns, with all its rights and appurtenances, so that, when the nuns who were then in it had died or had been transferred to other [places?], their necessities of life being preserved, he might establish there a convent of men of his own [profession?], which nevertheless would be subject to the jurisdiction of the bishop of Speyer for the time being.

In the same year, around the feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle, King Philip held a great assembly of princes at Augsburg. There two cardinals appeared, namely Hugh, bishop of Ostia, and Leo, priest of [Holy Cross?], sent by the supreme pontiff Innocent to restore peace in the kingdom. Through the king’s intervention, they released Adolf, formerly archbishop of Cologne, from excommunication, and sent him to the examination of the apostolic see for satisfaction. At their prayers also King Philip [unclear] Bruno the archbishop [unclear]

who, after being admitted, drew his sword and killed the king himself, and immediately fled with his men before the deed became known. The body of the slain king was first [buried?] there in the major church; [afterward?], together with his nephew by his brother, they were transferred to Speyer and buried in the major church with the kings. He was killed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July, and the empire remained vacant until the feast of Saint Martin. Moreover the murderer, Count Otto, became a fugitive and was outlawed from the land, and after a few years was killed by Philip’s marshal.

In the same year, on the feast of Saint Martin the bishop, through the agency of Conrad, bishop of the church of Speyer and chancellor of the slain King Philip, who at that time had the royal insignia in his possession, a very great assembly of princes, nobles, and prelates was held at Frankfurt. There King Otto, formerly Philip’s adversary, was again unanimously elected by all and confirmed in the kingship; he also took the daughter of King Philip as his wife.

In the same year also, after King Philip had been killed, Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, from RoChronicle of Jo. Trithemius

from Rome, where for two years he had held the cardinalatial title of the church of Saint Sabina, at the command of Pope Innocent he returned with honor to the see of Mainz; and, with the blind Lupold, bishop of Worms, a most unjust invader, set aside, by the authority of the lord pope he was received by all at Mainz with glory. For Lupold, protected by the power of King Philip, had occupied the see of Mainz for a full two years after Siphrid had been expelled, despising the pope’s excommunication, because he was a wicked man, as we have said.

At the same time Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, sent by the pope together with the aforesaid Siphrid, archbishop of Mainz, returned to Cologne; and on the feast of the holy martyrs Protus and Hyacinth he was received with the greatest exultation and joy by all the people and clergy of Cologne. At his arrival peace was restored to the lands, the province, purged of robbers, was quiet, and the counts and nobles of the land subjected themselves to him by oath in obedience. Adolf also, formerly archbishop, came to him and promised him obedience according to the apostolic mandate. But this fair weather in the province did not last long. For after everything had gone according to his wish, Archbishop Bruno was seized by illness, and in the same year, on the day after the feast of All Saints, he departed from this life and was buried in the greater church, not without the tears of many, all of whom hoped that, while he lived, they would have peace in the province. After his death Theoderic, provost of the Apostles, with the counsel and aid of King Otto, was unanimously elected archbishop and presided for twenty-six years.

1209.

In the fourth year of Abbot Lutfrid, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1209, Pope Innocent, hearing that the princes of the whole empire had elected Otto as king, and that by their counsel he had taken in marriage the daughter of King Philip, although she was joined to him by blood relationship, for the good of peace and concord, praised the deed, and again sent the cardinals Hugh and Leo into Germany, so that [unclear] was received at [unclear]. At his arrival the counts and nobles of the land subjected themselves to him by oath in obedience. Adolf also, formerly archbishop, came to him and promised him obedience according to the apostolic mandate. But this fair weather in the province did not last long. For after everything had gone according to his wish, Archbishop Bruno [unclear] of many departed from this life and was buried in the greater church, not without the tears of many, all of whom hoped that, while he lived, they would have peace in the province. After his death Theoderic, provost, was unanimously elected and presided for twenty-six years.

In the same year King Otto entered Italy with great splendor, where the princes of all Lombardy came to meet him, received him with glory, subjected cities and castles to his lordship, and handed over into his hands an infinite amount of money from taxes and tributes reserved from the time of Emperor Henry. After this, proceeding to Rome, with the pope and the cardinals coming to meet him, he was received with honor by the senate, and on the following Sunday after the feast of Saint Michael, that is, on the fourth day before the Nones of October, in the greater church of blessed Peter the Apostle, he was crowned emperor by Pope Innocent himself.

Around the same times Saint Francis began the order of the Friars Minor in Italy with much religion and holiness; in it, in the course of time, many holy and most learned men shone forth, who by word and example magnificently illumined the church.

This year the summer was very violent with thunders, lightning-bolts, and rains, and the winter exceedingly hard and most harsh, and it lasted a long time.

1210.

In the fifth year of Abbot Lutfrid, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1210, very grave dissensions arose between the pope and Otto IV, emperor, concerning the March of Apulia, which the emperor asserted belonged to the empire, but the pope to the Roman church, by the testamentary donation of Lady Matilda, daughter of the famous Prince Roger of Sicily and wife of King Conrad, son of Henry IV, emperor. The pope said that this donation, made by a woman without the consent of the princes, was valid for the church; the emperor said it was invalid. At last, when the emperor would not concede that march to the pope, he was excommunicated by him and finally deposed from the empire.

1211.

In the fifth year of Abbot Lutfrid, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1211, Emperor Otto, enjoying prosperous successes, subjected all Apulia and Calabria to himself, received the cities in surrender, entrusted castles to his soldiers to be guarded, attempted to exterminate utterly King Frederick, son of Emperor Henry VI, and scorned to obey the apostolic commands. Wherefore the pope, moved by this, ordered Siphrid, archbishop of Mainz, to announce throughout all Germany that the emperor was excommunicated and deposed from the empire; this he did. When this had been done, Henry, count palatine of the Rhine, the duke of Brabant, and many other princes and nobles favoring Otto began, around the feast of Saint Michael, to devastate the whole bishopric of Mainz with fire and plunder, leaving nothing untouched except fortified cities and the strongest castles, but despoiling villages, churches, and monasteries by laying them waste, the whole land almost in [unclear].

Siphrid, archbishop of Mainz, returns.

Bruno returns to Cologne.

The pope sent legates into Germany.

King Otto enters Italy with [unclear].

King Otto is crowned emperor at Rome.

Beginning of the Order of Minors.

Discord between the pope and the emperor. Cause of the dissension.

The emperor obtains all Apulia.

The emperor is excommunicated. Persecution of the church of Mainz. 172. Of the Monastery of Hirsau

was excommunicated, and afterward, by Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, legate of the Apostolic See, was deposed at Cologne, in the greater church, from every office, benefice, and pontifical function. Having gone to Rome, he long sought the favor of restitution, but could not obtain it.

MCCXV.

In the tenth year of Abbot Lutfrid, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1215, Adolf, count of Berg, besieged and took the castle of Werden, and by mighty force freed Otto, bishop of Münster, who had there been put in chains by the emperor, as we have said, namely on the vigil of St. James the Apostle.

In the same year Pope Innocent held at Rome, in the Lateran church, a synod of 130 bishops for the recovery of Jerusalem; in it he condemned as erroneous certain little books of Joachim, abbot of the Florensian monastery in Calabria. Sending his letters throughout all the borders of Christendom, he ordered all suitable persons to preach the cross. Hence throughout various provinces an innumerable multitude were signed for love of Christ and the liberation of the Holy Land. Among them were Frederick, king of the Romans and of Sicily; Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz; also the bishops of Liège, Bamberg, Poitiers, and Strasbourg; Duke Henry of Brabant; the duke of Moravia; the duke of Limburg; the duke of [Ancei?]; the count palatine of Tübingen; the margrave of Baden; the count of Looz; the count of Jülich; the count of Sayn; the count of Berg; and many others, all of whom took up the cross at Aachen when John, scholasticus of Xanten, preached it.

In the same year Theodoric, archbishop of Trier, came to Cologne; through the agency of Duke Henry of Brabant he brought the citizens back to peace and to submission to King Frederick, according to the apostolic mandate, and absolved them from the excommunication and interdict under which they had lain for a year and five months. On the fourth day of the month of August he solemnly celebrated masses in the greater church of St. Peter before all the people.

On the same day Frederick entered the city and was received with great honor; after receiving the homage of fidelity, he remained for seven days.

In the same year also lord Lutfrid, venerable abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, obtained from Frederick II, illustrious king of the Romans and of Sicily, confirmation of all privileges granted to that monastery by kings and emperors, together with further concessions, as appears in the letters of that confirmation, which were issued at Haguenau in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1215, on the sixth day before the Ides of July, in the third indiction.

In the same year, when Theodoric, formerly archbishop of Cologne, had long labored at Rome before the pope for his own restoration and made no progress, he was compelled to return empty-handed; the pope wrote to the people of Cologne that they should elect another as archbishop. Assembling together, they elected as archbishop Engelbert, provost of the greater church and son of the count of Berg; he presided for almost ten years, a very good man, a lover of the clergy and defender of the poor. Frederick, count of Isenburg, his kinsman, afterward cruelly killed him.

In the same year Walter, bishop-elect of Basel, being accused of having entered office uncanonically, was summoned to Rome by Pope Innocent. Since he could not canonically clear himself of the charges brought against him, he was deposed by the same pope; Henry, succeeding by canonical election, was confirmed.

In these times there were many hidden heretics of both sexes, who sowed various errors in Germany, France, and Italy; many of them, when detected, were burned in the flames. In the city of Strasbourg, indeed, in this year more than 80 in number were seized together at one time, of whom few were found innocent. Brother Conrad of Marburg, the apostolic inquisitor, was accustomed, if they denied the heresy, to test them by the ordeal of glowing iron; those whom the iron burned he handed over as heretics to the secular court to be burned. Hence, with few exceptions, all who had once been accused and brought to his examination were condemned by him to the fire. There were those who believed that many were condemned innocently, because glowing iron found no one free from sins, even if he had never been infected by any stain of heresy.

MCCXVI.

In the eleventh year of Abbot Lutfrid, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1216, Pope Innocent died. Honorius III was appointed; he presided for ten years and two months. He confirmed the orders of Preachers and of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis.

In the same year King Frederick held an assembly of princes around the beginning of the month of May at Nuremberg 170 Of the Monastery of Hirsau

they carry on devastation. But Siegfried the archbishop, suffering all these evils on account of obedience to the apostolic see, safe nowhere in his homeland, fled to Hermann, Landgrave of Thuringia, and remained there for some time.

In the same year, around Lent, Otto the Emperor returned from Italy, excommunicated by the pope and declared so throughout all Germany.

MCCXII.

In the seventh year of Abbot Lutfrid, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1212, Otto the Emperor, around the feast of Pentecost, held an assembly of princes at Nuremberg, setting forth to the princes the cause of the dissension between himself and the pope. After this he launched an expedition into Thuringia against Hermann the Landgrave, who opposed him, where he destroyed two very strong fortifications, Rotenberg and Saltzungen. Advancing from there, he surrounded the town of Wizense with a siege, which he also took, apart from the citadel. There then for the first time began to be used the war engine which is called a Tribock.

In the same year Liège, on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, was captured by Henry, duke of Brabant, after Bishop Huard had been put to flight; and very great booty and inestimable treasures of riches were plundered by the soldiers and [unclear], to the harm of many. In this same year a very great multitude of people of both sexes and every age, from all Germany and Gaul, and also Burgundy, set out on the road toward Italy: old men and young, boys and adolescents, married women and virgins, poor and rich, without order, without a leader, without authority, led by their own presumption, mutually marking themselves with the cross, saying that they wished to cross the sea against the Saracens and recover the Holy Land. But when they came to the sea, some perished from hunger and want, others were seized by pirates and sold, and the rest returned home with great confusion, many carrying back the reward of their own corruption.

In the same year an expedition of those marked with the cross was made by the duke of Austria and certain barons of the land, and other men of diverse condition, from Austria, Saxony, Westphalia, Frisia, and all Germany, in aid of the count of Montfort, to attack the Albigensian heretics, who were also called Ruptarii or Coterelli, from the land of Saint-Gilles, at the pope’s command. When they heard that so great an army was coming against them, some abandoned their cities and castles and fled; others, having returned to the unity of the Catholic faith, promised obedience under oath to the cardinal sent for this by the pope. When these things had been done, the aforesaid duke of Austria, Leopold, with a great army of Christians, proceeded into Spain against the Saracens, sent by ship by Massamutus, king of Maroth. There, when battle had been joined with those same faithful, the Christians gained the victory, an infinite multitude of Saracens being slain and the rest drowned in the sea.

In the same year also Otto the Emperor celebrated his wedding at Nordhausen, taking as wife the daughter of King Philip, previously betrothed to him, as we said; on the fourth day after this she departed from human affairs. Meanwhile Pope Innocent, seeing the stubbornness of Otto, whom he had formerly always favored against Philip and raised on high, since Otto labored neither for absolution nor for any settlement, sent into Sicily and brought out from there the above-mentioned Frederick, a son of the former Emperor Henry, and sent him into Germany with letters and commands, instructing and commanding the princes of the empire that, Otto being excommunicated, deposed, and annulled, they should elect him emperor, receive him, uphold him before the others, and stand by him manfully in all things, and that each in his own place should honorably provide safe-conduct for him as he passed through their lands. And this was done. When Otto learned of Frederick’s arrival, abandoning his attack on the Landgrave, he set out with an army to meet him. When they had come together in the regions of Swabia, Otto with his men was compelled to give way and could not prevail, because many were leaving him on account of his obstinacy. Yet, still having confidence in the duke of Zähringen alone, he went down as far as Breisach, a royal town, wishing to await the outcome of the matter, to see whether in some way he could have the means to resist. While he was staying there in garrison, and his retainers, provoking the townsmen with robberies and injuries, were violently plundering wine, fodder, and whatever pertained to provisions, the citizens gathered as one and drove him with all his men from the town, some being wounded and mutilated in their limbs. Departing from there, he returned into Saxony, certain nobles of that land escorting him.

After this, since Frederick was being received by all as king, while the citizens of the imperial town of Hagenau still persisted in loyalty to Otto, he surrounded the city with a siege and received its surrender. Advancing from there from city to city, he was received by all with honor as king, and in a short time obtained the whole realm of the empire. Also on the feast of Saint Andrew: Of the Monastery of Hirsau

A most vigorous defender of his liberties, nor did he ever permit any violation of them to be endured. He was steadfast in spirit, and could not easily be overcome by those doing him injury, since prudence made him provident in his affairs, and inborn kindness, together with humble patience, made him glorious in suffering.

1217. Lupoldus.

In the first year of Abbot Eberhard, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1217, Lupoldus, bishop of Worms, died. Caesarius, monk of Heisterbach, mentions him in the second distinction of his Dialogues, chapter nine, bearing witness to his wicked manner of life. After his death Henry, provost of Neuhausen, son of the count of Saarbrücken, succeeded; he presided for nearly seventeen years.

In the same year Andrew, king of Hungary, Lupoldus, duke of Austria, with many bishops, counts, nobles, and a numerous multitude of those signed with the cross, crossed the sea for love of Christ in aid of the Holy Land. Likewise William, most powerful count of Holland, George, count of Wied, John, count of Spanheim, with Juvanus, sixth abbot of my monastery, and many other men of Germany signed with the cross, set out to recover the Holy Land. Among them were also the bishop of Bamberg, his brother the duke of Merania, Poppo also, count of Henneberg, Ludovicus, count of Oettingen, and one cardinal, legate of the apostolic see.

1218.

In the second year of Abbot Eberhard, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity [1218], on Palm [Sunday], the duke of Austria, Lupoldus, with the pope’s legate, the Templars, the Hospitallers, and a numerous army, approaching the borders of Egypt, besieged for some time the very wealthy city of Damietta. By storming it on the vigil of Saint Bartholomew they took the very strongly fortified tower beside the shore of the Nile, which is called the Key of the Land; afterwards they also obtained the city, which however they could not hold for long, as is read in their acts.

In the same year Berthold, duke of Zähringen, died, a strong and warlike man, who in his life waged many wars with adversaries.

Also in the same year the sea, passing beyond its bounds in Phrygia and going out far, occupied the land in length round about, destroyed entire villages, and overthrew churches, houses, castles, and innumerable towns; it consumed more than one hundred thousand people. There are those who write that the cause of this flood was a certain irreverence shown to the venerable sacrament of the Lord’s body by a drunken man, who had struck the hosts from the pyx in the priest’s hand to the ground with his fist; hence divine vengeance raged.

1219.

In the third year of Abbot Eberhard, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1219, Jerusalem, queen of cities, which seemed impregnable, was destroyed by Coradinus, son of Saphadinus. Its walls, inside and outside, together with its towers, were reduced to heaps of stones, except for the temple of the Lord, the church of the Holy Sepulchre, and the citadel which they call the Tower of David.

In the same year King Frederick set out for Rome with the greatest display for the imperial blessing; around the feast of Blessed Cecilia he was anointed and crowned emperor by Pope Honorius. Proceeding further into Apulia, with a great army of his men he waged many wars there and subjected all the land, together with Sicily, to his empire. Immediately dissensions followed between him and Pope Honorius, which lasted for many years to the loss of both parties.

Also in the same year the duke of Lorraine, with the consent or connivance of the bishop of Strasbourg, entered Alsace with a strong army, intending to take the vengeance he had planned upon certain men who had injured him.

1220.

In the fourth year of Abbot Eberhard, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1220, Emperor Frederick, being established in Apulia, waged many wars with the neighboring Saracens; after many had been cut down and killed, he compelled the rest to be subject to his lordship. Henry, his son, a boy of about ten years, meanwhile was said to govern the kingdom of Germany in his father’s absence through Otto, bishop of Würzburg, to whose guardianship he had been entrusted, with the cooperation of Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne.

In the same year there was serious discord between Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, and Conrad, Wildgrave count of Dhaun, on account of the advocacy in Heimbach: so much so that the archbishop, after excommunicating him, placed his land under ecclesiastical interdict. At length, when friends intervened, a concord was made in this manner, that the count [unclear] one hundred of silver

Conrad, Wildgrave count.

Frederick the Emperor [unclear] Apulia.

A flood submerged about [unclear] thousand people.

Jerusalem is overthrown by the Saracens.

The duke of Lorraine. Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

of Andrew the Apostle, he held a celebrated court at Mainz, where many princes swore an oath of fidelity to him.

In this same year also Lupold, bishop of Worms, through the intervention of King Frederick and with the pope’s permission, returned to his see and was received into the grace of the apostolic see: out of hatred, as it seemed to most, of Otto, who, after King Philip had died, with the pope’s consent had proscribed him into exile. Meanwhile Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, for as long as he stood in Otto’s favor, also governed the church of Worms, especially with regard to ordinations and sacraments.

The court at Mainz. Lupold. 1213.

In the eighth year of Abbot Lutfrid, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1213, Frederick held a celebrated assembly of princes at Aachen on the feast of Saint James. There, with the consent of all the princes, he was called king and placed on the throne of the realm. There too, together with many others, he was signed with the cross against the Saracens for the recovery of the Lord’s Sepulchre, Master Conrad preaching the cross, then dean, who afterward was made bishop of Hildesheim in Saxony, a holy and most learned man.

King Frederick first took as wife Maria, daughter of the king of Aragon, who in this same year, while bringing aid to the Albigensians [and?] to the count of Toulouse, was killed.
