By her he begot Henry, king of the Romans, who died before his father, and Conrad the king. After his first wife died, he took a second, the daughter of John, king of Jerusalem, who had a son named Jordan. After she too died, he took a third.

Frederick: wives, etc.; children. 1213.

In the year of Lutfrid [unclear], the king of France entered Flanders with an army, to drive out Count Ferrand and subject the land to his own dominion. But [unclear] two daughters, two daughters, Frederick king of Tuscany, Eric king of Lombardy, Agnes wife of the landgrave of Thuringia, and Constance wife of Louis, landgrave of Hesse. By a concubine he begot Manfred, king of Sicily.

In the same year Leuthold, bishop of Basel, died; Walter succeeded him.

In the same year also Philip, king of France, entered Flanders with a very great army, to drive out Count Ferrand and [unclear] the land to his own lordship; when [unclear] had been killed, he could not fulfill his desire, for very many of his men were killed there, and with great loss and disgrace he was compelled to return to France.

Around autumn also Duke Henry of Brabant, fighting with the bishop of Liège, was defeated, with almost all his men either captured or killed. Theoderic, archbishop of Cologne, stubbornly disobeying the apostolic mandates, openly supported the party of Otto against Frederick, and by this brought much calamity upon his diocese. It happened in that year that the bishop of Münster came to Cologne; he was seized by certain supporters of the deposed emperor, sent to Werden, and at his order consigned to chains. On account of this the people of Cologne were excommunicated by Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz and legate of the Roman pontiff, and the celebration of divine offices in Cologne was forbidden.

In the same year also, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, Rupert, the fifth abbot of my monastery of Spanheim, died. Juvanus, succeeding him as sixth in the order of abbots, presided for 39 years and 3 months.

1214.

In the year of Abbot Lutfrid [unclear], but of the Lord’s Nativity 1214, Otto, formerly emperor, devastated the land of the count of Guelders with fire and sword. In the month of July the same Emperor Otto, together with the king of England, his maternal uncle, and also Henry, duke of Brabant, Ferrand, count of Flanders, of whom mention was made before, and many others, marched to war against Philip, king of the French; when battle was joined, he was defeated by him near Tournai. There Count Ferrand, with many nobles both of Flanders and of Lotharingia, was captured; all of them were sent to Paris and consigned to chains.

At the same time Frederick crossed the Moselle with a very powerful army and by fear of him compelled all the nobles of that land to his obedience. Then, crossing the Meuse, he resolved to attack Henry, the aforesaid duke of Brabant, in war. Terrified by his swift arrival, Henry came to him as a suppliant, swore fidelity, gave his son with many other nobles as hostage, and withdrew from Otto, the deposed emperor.

In this same year, on the day before the Nones of March, a comet-star appeared.

In the same year also Brother Conrad of Marburg, of the Order of Preachers, began to preach in Germany by apostolic authority; he continued for nearly [unclear] years and caused many to be burned as heretics, with no one preventing it. At last, as we shall say, he himself was killed. Theoderic, archbishop of Cologne, because of disobedience to the pope’s mandate and his continued adherence to Otto, the former emperor who had been deposed, first [unclear]

Brother Conrad of Marburg. Theoderic, archbishop of Cologne, is deposed. Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

... celebrated at [Nuremberg?], at which Peter of Santa Pudenziana, sent by the pope, was present. There [unclear] Engelbert, elect of Cologne, was confirmed as archbishop by the same cardinal. Likewise in the same year Otto, formerly emperor, abandoned by all, made ill by sorrow of mind, died after many distresses.

In the same year also Abbot Lutfrid, seized by illness and old age, after many labors by which he had governed this monastery quite usefully for 11 years and 5 days, rested in the Lord in April: a man gentle in disposition and of singular meekness, who lived as both monk and abbot in all tranquility and peace among the brothers; he made various buildings, and did not diminish the revenues.

Concerning Everhard, twenty-third abbot of this monastery, who governed for 15 years; concerning the various events of that time in Germany.

When the venerable Abbot Lutfrid had entered the way of all flesh and had been given ecclesiastical burial according to custom, the brothers, deprived of their shepherd, assembled together and began to deliberate on the election of a new abbot. At length, after mature deliberation among themselves had first been held, and after the grace of the Holy Spirit had first been invoked, by unanimous consent they elected as twenty-third abbot of this monastery lord Everhard, a professed monk of this community, a man of complete integrity, distinguished in learning and morals. Canonically elected, confirmed by Conrad, bishop of Speyer, and solemnly ordained according to custom, he governed this monastery vigorously for 13 years and some days.

He was born in Swabia, begotten of free and noble parents; in his boyhood he was set by them to love letters, and, advancing with age in all studies of the liberal arts, he became learned. Then, coming to the religious life, he was made a monk and was ordained among the brothers. Ordained, moreover, in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s nativity 1216, in the fourth indiction, in the month of April, as we have said, he took every care to show himself to all, in morals and life, a useful shepherd, instructing those subject to him in regular observance no less by example than by word, which he both greatly increased and maintained.

For he was so circumspect in ordering external affairs for the benefit of the monastery and the brothers that one would openly attest that he could in no way be wholly free for the spirit of inward life. For he was wholly intent upon the observance of monastic discipline, and so solicitous and circumspect concerning the conduct of the brothers that he was both called and truly was the shepherd of all. He was also diligent and provident in the care of temporal affairs.

Against the provost of Roth.

The abbot, against the rebellious [unclear], wishing to avoid obedience, appealed to the bishop of the aforesaid church of Augsburg, thinking, in the manner of the other abbots of the said church, that he was immediately subject not to the abbot but to the bishop. Abbot Everhard, taking this provost’s rashness ill, opposed him steadfastly, and before the aforesaid bishop and the whole chapter of the church of Augsburg he triumphed gloriously by judgment. For when the rights and privileges of the monastery of Hirsau had been examined, it was there declared by all that the provost in Roth was subject not to the bishop, but without any intermediary to the abbot of this monastery for the time being: namely, in such a way that his institution and deposition, according to the rule of our most holy father Benedict, belonged to the abbot alone, and that no one else whatsoever should in any way interfere in his ordination. For Abbot Everhard was [unclear] of the rights, liberties, privileges, properties, and goods of the monastery...

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

having received [unclear] marks from the chapter of Mainz, he resigned the advocacy, and was absolved from the sentence of excommunication or interdict.

In this same year, on the Nones of August, St. Dominic died, the first founder of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man of incomparable holiness.

1221.

In the fifth year of Abbot Everhard, the year of the Lord's Nativity 1221, the city of Damietta, which the Christians had taken and possessed in the preceding year with the greatest labor and much shedding of blood, was restored by the Christians to the Sultan of Babylon for the liberation of the captives in his kingdom and of Coradinus his brother. There is no doubt that this was done because their sins deserved it. For Saladin, a little before, seeking peace with the Christians, had promised that he would restore the kingdom of Jerusalem, rebuild that city itself, and grant Damietta, with the adjacent region for twenty miles, to be possessed in peace, provided they proceeded no farther into his land; and now the Christians seek his favor.

In the same year, on the day of St. Margaret, virgin and martyr, the city of Worms was burned by an accidental fire, and many houses, especially around the market and the surrounding streets, were consumed, so that almost half the city was destroyed. The church of St. Paul likewise was also burned, and endless losses were inflicted on the citizens.

In this same year the Friars Minor, entering Worms for the first time, built there a monastery of their order from the alms of the faithful.

1222.

In the sixth year of Abbot Everhard, the year of the Lord's Nativity 1222, Conrad, bishop of Speyer, hearing that the nuns at Hausen of our order near Durkheim had departed too far from the path of regular observance, and were living a wicked and excessively shameful life, united their convent, with the consent of Lord Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, to the monastery of Limburg of the same order, and wholly extinguished the title of a convent of nuns, so that when those who were then living had died, none should thereafter be received there, and the abbot of Limburg, through his monks, should have divine services celebrated there for the time being, according to the capacity and revenues of the place.

In the same year, on the seventh Ides of May, which was the Sunday nearest before Ascension Sunday, Henry, son of Emperor Frederick II, at the instance of his father and with the consent of the princes, while still a boy, was consecrated king of the Romans by Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne.

In the same year also, on the third Ides of January, in the morning at the first hour of the day, there was a great earthquake in Cologne and round about, and it overthrew many buildings. In Cyprus too two cities in the same year collapsed from an earthquake, with many people killed. In Italy also and Lombardy there were very great and terrible earthquakes this year, to such an extent that people abandoned the cities and lived in tents. For on the very day of the Nativity of the Lord, and throughout the two following weeks, almost every day twice in Lombardy there was a dreadful earthquake, which in many places overturned buildings and very strong churches, and crushed people together with priests. It also overthrew almost the whole city of Brescia with its people, tore rocks from the mountains, cast down castles, and wretchedly killed many thousands of people in various places. At Rome also earth mixed with blood was seen to fall from the clouds like rain.

In the same year also, Valdemar, king of Denmark, together with his son, was captured by Count Henry of Schwerin, and for two years was held and kept in custody by him in the very strong castle of Dannenberg.

1223.

In the seventh year of Abbot Everhard, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1223, Otto, bishop of Wurzburg, died on the Nones of December. Theoderic succeeded him and presided for one year, two months, and fourteen days.

In the same year Everhard, abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, obtained from Emperor Frederick II confirmation of indulgences and privileges with fuller favor, as is clear in the letters, which were given at Precima in the month of January of the aforesaid year.

In the same year also, after the death of the wife of Emperor Frederick, namely the first, the daughter of the king of Aragon, there was betrothed to him as a second wife the daughter of John, king of Jerusalem, whom not long afterward he took as wife.

In this same year there arose a very great pestilence among cattle, which, lasting almost three years, began from Hungary and infected all Germany and Gaul with its foulness, so that scarcely a green third part of the cattle and draft-animals was spared from so great a pestilence.

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

In the same year Henry, bishop of Strasbourg, also died; Berthold, a prudent man, a vigorous defender and supporter of the Church, succeeded him. In that same year also King Henry, son of Emperor Frederick, held a court of princes at [Nordhausen?], where Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, labored greatly for the liberation of the king of Denmark.

In the same year, as Philip, king of France, was dying, he bequeathed one hundred and fifty thousand marks for the aid of the Holy Land. In this same year also Pope Honorius, sending messengers everywhere, ordered the cross to be preached to the faithful, announcing to all that after two years, on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, they should be ready with Emperor Frederick to cross the sea and again liberate the Holy Land.

In the same year also Pope Honorius III, with the consent of the cardinals, confirmed the Order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis on the third day before the Kalends of December, two years before the death of that same holy confessor of Christ.

1223.

In the eighth year of Abbot Eberhard, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1224, Conrad, bishop of Speyer, died. Berengar of Entringen succeeded him, the forty-fourth bishop of the church of Speyer, namely on the sixth day before the Kalends of April; he presided over it for almost nine years.

In the same year Theoderic, bishop of Würzburg, died. Hermann of Ladenburg succeeded him and presided for almost twenty-six years; he endured many pressures and persecutions from his citizens on account of the excommunicated Emperor Frederick, but always obtained victory.

In the same year also, around the middle of the month of May, King Henry held a court of princes at Frankfurt, where messengers of the emperor were present with his letters, announcing that he would come from Sicily to Germany as quickly as possible, and would hold counsel with the princes concerning the recovery of the Holy Land and the maintaining of possession by force.

In the same year Pope Honorius sent as legate into Germany Conrad, bishop of Porto and cardinal of Santa Rufina. As he was about to go down to Cologne, he made his journey through Swabia, and came with his men to Hirsau, where he was received with honor by Abbot Eberhard and the brothers.

At the same time Henry, with the aforesaid legate of the Apostolic See, Engelbert archbishop of Cologne, and certain princes, set out for Saxony for the liberation of the king of Denmark and the restoration of the land of the empire unjustly possessed by him. There that same king, with his son, was being held captive by Count Henry of Schwerin in the very strong castle of Dannenberg. When the aforesaid counts came to the river Elbe, they sent ahead Hermann, master of the Hospital of the Teutons, who had been sent by the emperor into Germany for the sake of reconciliation and of making an agreement between both parties, namely the king and the count. Through his mediation, the same king was induced to restore all the land taken from the empire, to receive the crown of the kingdom of Denmark from the hand of the emperor, and furthermore to promise to give one hundred thousand marks for his liberation. When the princes who were present with the king accepted this, Albert, count of Orlamünde, [unclear] son of the king, and the barons of Denmark rejected this agreement, annulled what had been promised, and, boarding ships, departed in indignation, taking with them the immense sum of money that they had brought to redeem the king. And the aforesaid princes, the affair unfinished, returned in confusion to their own lands.

1225.

In the ninth year of Abbot Eberhard, the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1225, King Henry, son of Emperor Frederick II, held a court of princes at Frankfurt, in which he dealt with many matters.

In the same year, after the Nativity of the Lord, Count Albert of Schwerin resolved to attack; Henry met him, and when battle had been joined with great fierceness and much bloodshed, they fought from the first hour of the day until evening, with many falling there. There also Count Albert himself, with many nobles of Denmark, was captured by Count Henry and committed to custody in the castle of Dannenberg.

In this same year the winter was very long and very harsh. There was also a great and unheard-of famine, lasting for two years, in every province.

In the same year also, on the Ides of September, Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, the second of that name, died; Siegfried III succeeded him and presided for twenty-four years, a man [unclear].

Henry, bishop of Strasbourg, died.

The cross is again preached everywhere.

The Order of the Friars Minor is confirmed.

Conrad, bishop of Speyer, died.

Theoderic, bishop of Würzburg, died.

Assembly of princes.

Conrad, apostolic legate.

King Henry enters Saxony.

The king of Denmark.

Hermann, master of the Hospital.

Count Albert of Orlamünde.

Great famine.

Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, died. [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

...a man of great virtues and deeds, who was of such steadfastness that, by order of the pope, he publicly declared Emperor Frederick excommunicated and pursued him as such.

In the same year Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, was cruelly killed by Frederick, count of Isenburg, his brother’s son, with thirty-eight wounds. His body, buried in the greater church, soon began to become famous through countless miracles. But when the killer was, not long afterward, broken on the wheel before the walls, the miracles at once ceased. He was succeeded in the archbishopric by Henry of Molenarck, provost of Bonn, who presided for twelve years and destroyed the castle of Isenburg.

Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, is killed.

In the same year also Henry, king of the Romans, son of Emperor Frederick II, took as wife the daughter of Leopold, duke of Austria; the wedding was celebrated at Nuremberg with great solemnity, where a capital sentence was given against the killer of the archbishop of Cologne.

Henry the king takes a wife.

1226.

Now in the tenth year of Abbot Eberhard, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1226, Saint Francis, first founder of the Order of Friars Minor, rested in the Lord on the fourth Nones of October, and two years later was enrolled in the catalogue of the saints by Pope Gregory IX.

St. Francis dies.

In these times Henry, bishop of Worms, raised from the foundations a convent of nuns of the Cistercian order at Kirsgarten, outside the city walls, installed nuns there, and provided them with necessities. But after 217 years Frederick, bishop of Worms, expelled the nuns because of the enormity of their life, and put in their place regular canons of Saint Augustine of the Windesheim observance; they inhabit that place itself, with profit, up to the present day. Between the aforesaid Bishop Henry and the citizens of Worms a serious dissension arose over ecclesiastical liberty. Since they disdained to obey his command, he placed the city under ecclesiastical interdict, and also ordered all the clergy, except the parish priests, to leave the city, strictly forbidding the parish priests to confer the sacraments on the sick unless they promised the pontiff that they would obey him in all things if they recovered. Nor were the bodies of the dead permitted to be buried in holy places. But when these evils had lasted for the space of a year, some of the citizens, affected by weariness of the troubles, began to incline to the bishop’s side. Seeing this, those who were in charge of the consulship, and fearing to experience worse things, accepted peace.

Dissension between the bishop and his people of Worms.

In the same year the Lombards, rebelling against Emperor Frederick at the suggestion of Pope Honorius, formed an association, which for a long time was called that of the Lombards, to no small detriment of the Roman Empire and an impediment to the recovery of the Holy Land.

The association of the Lombards against the empire.

And in the same year Pope Honorius III himself died. Gregory IX succeeded him and presided for fourteen years and three months.

Pope Honorius dies.

1227.

In the eleventh year of Abbot Eberhard, and in the one thousand two hundred twenty-seventh year of the Lord’s nativity, Henry the king, son of the emperor, coming to Aachen around Passion Sunday, held a very celebrated court of the princes and nobles of almost all Germany. Among them the chief were the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne, and Salzburg, with many bishops, the dukes of Bavaria, Carinthia, Brabant, and Lorraine, Henry count palatine of the Rhine, the landgrave of Thuringia, the count of Flanders, who for twelve years had been detained in captivity at Paris by the king of France and had been released the previous year, with many other counts and nobles. In this assembly of princes, the wife of Henry, king of the Romans, daughter of Leopold, duke of Austria, was consecrated as queen by Henry, archbishop of Cologne, and, with great solemnity, placed on the royal seat beside the king.

The queen is crowned at Aachen.

In the same year, on the day of St. Mary Magdalene, the king of Denmark, a violator of the faith and oath that he had pledged in the previous year for his absolution, prepared to avenge himself: after gathering an immense multitude of armed men, he challenged Henry, count of Schwerin, to war. By him, with the aid of the archbishop of Bremen and Albert, duke of Saxony, he was defeated and scarcely escaped by flight, four thousand men on his side having been slain, and many captured from the Danes.

Emperor Frederick is excommunicated by the pope.

Because of this, he was excommunicated by Pope Gregory IX, and the archbishop of Mainz announced him as such. Yet many princes of Germany, counts, dukes, barons, and nobles, notwithstanding the emperor’s contumacy, prepared to cross the sea. Among them were Louis, the fifth landgrave of the Thuringians, the first margrave of Meissen, husband...

The Monastery of Hirsau [unclear]. The temporal substance of the monastery, however, was well preserved under him, because he was sufficiently experienced in the ordering of household affairs and solicitous with singular attention in the care of temporal business.

1232.

In the first year of Abbot Ernest, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1232, the emperor Frederick, staying at Ravenna, prepared war against the Lombards; but he made no progress, since the Lombards blocked the route to the king, Henry his son, and to the German soldiery whom the emperor had summoned to him at Ravenna.

In this same year the Sultan of Babylon sent the emperor a tent constructed with marvelous art, in which images of the sun and moon, moved artificially, completed their course through fixed and proper intervals and indicated the hours of day and night infallibly. The value of this tent was said to have exceeded the price of five thousand florins.

In the same year a great war was made between Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, and Conrad the Landgrave. Taking the town of Fritzlar, he almost utterly destroyed it. In the same place men were captured by the Landgrave himself. At last peace was made between them.

Also in the same year Frederick II, emperor, abolished from the monastery itself the principality of a monastery of our order, not far from Worms, called Lorsch, with every honor, vassals, ministeriales, towns, castles, villages, rights, revenues, and its appurtenances, which the abbot of that place had always been accustomed to hold; and he gave almost all the canonry-rights of the aforesaid town to the archbishop and the church of Mainz forever, whose value exceeds the price of one hundred thousand florins. Pope Gregory IX, at the archbishop’s request, confirmed this donation, commanding him that, after the monks of our order had been expelled from there, he should put Cistercians in their place. When he had done this, our men, grieving that they had been expelled from their monastery so unjustly by the archbishop, returned one night to the monastery, relying on the help of friends; and they attacked the Cistercian monks found there, who feared nothing of the kind, struck them, wounded them, and expelled them from the monastery; and they began to inhabit the place again. But not many days later the archbishop arrived, and with a strong hand expelled them once more from the monastery, and recalled his Cistercians again. And on a certain night, during matins, when the Cistercians believed themselves to be safe, our men again came with their friends to Lorsch, attacked them again, cut them down, struck them, and expelled them once more, declaring that they would kill them all if they presumed to return again to that monastery of Lorsch. Therefore from that day the Cistercians could no longer be induced to return to Lorsch. The monastery was thus vacant for some time, since neither they nor our men [unclear] safely place themselves there. [He] commanded, in the second year of his pontificate, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1246, that he should put monks of whatever order, or certainly secular canons, back into the monastery, lest it remain vacant any longer. Having taken counsel, he [unclear] monks of the Premonstratensian order from the monastery of All Saints in the diocese of Strasbourg for this purpose [unclear] 764, built and magnificently endowed it. In it afterward Saint Ermenold was made the fifth abbot of this monastery, although he resigned the abbacy because of a scruple of conscience; and, translated into Bavaria, he was appointed the first abbot of the monastery of Saint George in Prüfening, where he was renowned for many signs and miracles, as is read in his Life.

This year the summer was dry and very hot; excellent wine grew.

1233.

In the second year of Abbot Ernest, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1233, the emperor Frederick violently took Messina, a city of Sicily rebelling against him, and burned all his rebels in it with fire.

At the same time in Germany many noble and non-noble persons, clerics, monks, nuns in178

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

Louis, husband of St. Elisabeth. Bernstein is taken. Henry, Count Palatine. The Emperor Frederick crosses the sea. The coronation of the kings of Bohemia belongs to the archbishop of Mainz. War between the bishop of Strasbourg and the count of Pfirt. Jerusalem is handed over to the Christians. Dissension between the pope and the emperor. Concord is made between the bishop of Strasbourg and the count of Pfirt. The king of Leon attacks the Saracens. Majorca is taken by the king of Aragon. The archbishop of Cologne. The duke of Limburg. The emperor is absolved. Duke Leopold dies.

St. Elisabeth of Marburg, a most pious prince, who died on the third day before the Ides of September in a certain city of Sicily called Otranto; his bones were brought back to Thuringia and buried in Reinhardsbrunn, a monastery of our order. Louis also of Castel, Louis the elder of Stolberg, and the bishop of Augsburg, who himself also died on the journey, not without suspicion of poisoning.

In this same year also Berthold, bishop of Strasbourg, besieged the castle of Bernstein, stormed it, and after a month obtained it.

In the same year lord Henry, Count Palatine of the Rhine and lord of Brunswick in Saxony, gave his daughter Gertrude as wife to Otto, duke of Bavaria, with whom [unclear].

1228.

In the twelfth year of Abbot Eberhard, and in the year of the Lord's Nativity 1228, the Emperor Frederick, having already for many years been signed with the cross, at last undertook the journey overseas with many other princes; nevertheless Pope Gregory meanwhile caused him, as excommunicate, to be proclaimed throughout all Germany, especially by the Friars Preachers.

In the same year Odakar and Wenceslaus, kings of Bohemia, gave such a privilege to the church of Mainz that the consecration of the kings of Bohemia should belong to the archbishop of Mainz for all future times forever. This was observed for many years, until at last by a certain archbishop of Mainz this right was sold to the church of Prague.

Also in the year noted above a grave dissension arose between Berthold, bishop of Strasbourg, and his kinsmen, the counts of Pfirt; and as it grew stronger day by day, almost the whole province for nearly three years was laid waste and lay open to the fire and plundering of robbers. Therefore, after many injuries had been suffered, the bishop, having gathered an army of his men, together with Albert, count of Habsburg, who himself also had sustained many losses, prepared himself to resist. The counts of Pfirt, then, having as aid Egon, count of Freiburg, and the imperial cities between Blodelsheim and Hirnfeld, met the bishop with a very great army; and when battle was joined, they were defeated by him, many of them being killed, others wounded, others led away into captivity.

1229.

In the thirteenth year of Abbot Eberhard, and in the year of the Lord's Nativity 1229, the holy city of Jerusalem, with certain castles, was recovered by the Emperor Frederick II, under certain conditions, from the sultan of the Egyptians without any engagement or shedding of blood, and was handed over again into the hands of the Christians. The Emperor Frederick himself, moreover, on Laetare Sunday entered Jerusalem crowned; and after making truces with the Saracens for ten years, on the next day he set out for the ships and returned to his own land. But when he entered Sicily, he found that many towns, castles, and fortifications had gone over to the pope's side. Recovering all these by the strong hand of the Germans, he utterly destroyed some of them; and from that time grave enmities arose between him and the pope.

1230.

Now in the fourteenth year of Abbot Eberhard, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1230, concord was made between King Henry, the counts of Pfirt, and Berthold, bishop of Strasbourg, and the land fell silent from the tumult of wars. But it could not be cleansed of thieves and robbers, who by night, breaking the doors of monasteries and churches, since they had been accustomed to live from plunder, secretly carried off whatever they could find.

In the same year in Spain the king of Leon and his son the king of Castile, taking up arms against the Saracens, occupied a great part of the land, powerfully taking the city of Merida with many castles from their hands. The king of Aragon also, in this same year, took by armed force the island of Majorca, which was once a kingdom and had for many years been possessed by the Saracens; he led away its king captive with the whole royal household, entrusted the island to his Christian knights to be guarded, and carried off much spoil.

In the same year also a dissension arose between the archbishop of Cologne and the duke of Limburg over the advocacy of the monastery of Siegburg of our order, which each contended belonged to his own right. From this fires and plundering followed around the territories of both, until at last truces were interposed by King Henry.

In this same year the Emperor Frederick was absolved by Pope Gregory at the entreaty of Leopold, duke of Austria, and restored to the communion of the Church. This duke, after the treaty of peace had been completed, died at San Germano in Campania; his entrails and flesh [unclear] in the chapter house [unclear].

[Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

179

...of the monastery of Cassino of our order were buried, the bones having been carried back into Austria. At this time the impiety of many heretics, who had long lain hidden in Germany, Italy, and especially in Lombardy, was detected, and very many of them were burned with fire. The sect of the Nico-[unclear]. The heresy of the Lombards is detected. Their errors. They despised the Church and prelates; they also ate meat in Lent; and they did many evil things, secretly drawing into their error whomever they could. Their very great multitude. Every year from Germany, Gaul, and Italy they used to send an annual tribute to Milan, where the primacy of diverse heresies and errors was exercised. Certain of them, when captured, publicly confessed that so great was the number of those in error everywhere that, if anyone, setting out from Cologne, wished to go to Milan, every night he would find a host of their sect, in whose house [unclear] mother, wife, daughter; and they had small signs around the doors of the houses, or above the dwellings of their accomplices, [wherever] they could find them.

MCCXXXI.

In the fifteenth year of Abbot Eberhard, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1231. Ludovicus, duke of Bavaria, is killed. Ludovicus, duke of Bavaria, returning from overseas regions, when he had come to Kelheim, was stabbed through with a knife and killed in the sight of his household by a certain messenger of the Old Man of the Mountains, sent for this purpose; Frederick the emperor, as was reported, having procured this crime. For the aforesaid Old Man of the Mountains, prince of the Saracens, allied with the emperor, wishing to avenge the many injuries which the same duke had inflicted on the emperor, sent his servant to kill him. And [unclear] in his place, so that if anyone, setting out from Cologne, wished to go to Milan, [unclear] every night he would find a host of their sect, in whose house [unclear] mother, wife, daughter; and they had small signs around the doors of the houses, or above the dwellings of their accomplices, [wherever] they could find them.

In the same year, on the third day before the Kalends of December, died Saint Elisabeth, daughter of the king of Hungary, wife of Lu-[unclear]. Otto, duke of Bavaria, count palatine of the Rhine. In Hesse she dies. [unclear] of the count palatine of the Rhine dwelling at Heidelberg, and after him his son Otto succeeded to that same palatinate in the duchy of Bavaria; he had as wife Gertrude, daughter of Henry [unclear], and joined the duchy of Bavaria to it down to the present day. From her he begot two sons, Henry and Ludovicus, of whom we shall speak later in their proper place.

In the same year also Antonius of Padua, of the Order of Minors, disciple of Blessed Francis, a learned and most holy man, died.

In the same year also Eberhard, abbot of this monastery, after many labors undertaken for the defense of the rights and liberties of the place, rested in the Lord, a man worthy of eternal memory, who in every respect did good to the monastery during the time of his rule. Saint Elisabeth dies. He adorned the church, [built] many buildings for the brethren [unclear] from the second to the glorious [unclear], on the penultimate day of the month of December, after he had presided for 15 years, 8 months, and 20 days, in the sixty-fifth year of his age; he was buried in the greater monastery with reverence and honor, not without many tears of the sons whom he left behind.

Concerning Ernest, twenty-third abbot of this monastery, who presided for 13 years, one month, and three days, and concerning the various deeds of that time.

After the death of the most reverend and God-beloved abbot Eberhard, the brothers of this monastery, assembling together on the last day of the month of December, which was the second day after the death of their shepherd, began to have discussion among themselves about the necessary substitution of a new abbot. Therefore, after the customary prayers had first been said, at length they unanimously elected Ernest, a good man, born of respectable parents in Swabia, who, ordained abbot by Berengar, bishop of Speyer, presided over this monastery for 13 years, one month, and three days. The life and character of Abbot Ernest. And he was, as we have said, a good man of honorable conduct, yet more inclined to temporal affairs than to the observance of monastic discipline. Hence it came about that the integrity of discipline gradually failed under him, since he cared less for the inner life of the brothers, but rather for external things...

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius, 181

[unclear] enclosed women, townsmen, citizens, and peasants, in various places of Germany, were condemned to punishment by fire under the name of [Luciferians?] by a certain friar of Marburg of the Order of Preachers, who had been appointed general inquisitor of heretics by the apostolic see, with too hasty a sentence, as it then seemed to many. For, as someone writes, on the same day on which a person was accused, whether justly or unjustly, with no refuge of appeal or defense availing him, he was condemned and cast into the cruel flames.

Among the many who were then accused, the count of Sayn was denounced to him, falsely defamed for heresy; for his purgation or defense King Henry held an assembly of many princes at Mainz. For this reason Brother Conrad, the minister and author of this persecution among the Germans, fell into the hatred of many nobles and commoners.

Departing from Mainz with an army, he entered Bavaria, having in his host six thousand fighting men, whom he brought out to battle against the duke of Bavaria in the fields of the river Lech near Augsburg of the Raetians; in a short time he received the duke himself, with all Bavaria, in surrender. Meanwhile, while these things were being done in Bavaria, Theoderic, count of Montbeliard, was killed on the road with arms near the borders of Alsace. His body lies buried at Marburg.

At the same time King Henry, leaving Mainz with the princes, began to depart with a strong hand, after certain men had been captured together with booty; when behold, a clamor arose, and the people of the land pursued those fleeing. The count was again captured with many others and handed over to the custody of the bishop of Strasbourg. The bishop, returning from the Bavarian expedition, received security and permitted him to go free.

In the same year also the bishop of Chur was killed by certain wicked men. In the year noted above Berenger, bishop of Speyer, also died; Conrad of Thann succeeded him, and was the forty-fifth in the order of the bishops of Speyer. He presided for almost four years usefully enough.

In this same year, on the third day before the Kalends of March, a concord was made between the bishop and the citizens of Worms in the town of Frankfurt, through Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, Conrad the aforesaid bishop of Speyer, and the margrave of Baden, by the order and command of King Henry, son of Emperor Frederick.

1234. In the third year of Abbot Ernest, which was the year 1234 of the Lord's nativity, Pope Gregory IX caused the cross to be preached against the Stedingen peoples, situated on the borders of Frisia and Saxony, surrounded by roads, marshes, and rivers. Because of disobedience, their offenses, and the withholding of tithes, they had for many years been excommunicated and placed under interdict by the apostolic see, and had shown themselves despisers of the ecclesiastical keys; fighting often with bishops, counts, and other neighboring nobles, they were frequently victors and rarely defeated. But when an army of crusaders came against them, they were overcome and defeated; more than two thousand of them were slain, and the rest fled to their neighbors. Their confederation against the Church came to an end.

In the same year the city of Worms, set alight by an accidental fire, was burned in great part, not without irrecoverable loss to many citizens. This fire began on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, at night, and lasted two days.

In the same year also, on the day before the Ides of September, Henry of Saarbrucken, bishop of Worms, died and was buried with honor in the middle of the choir of his cathedral church. Landolph succeeded him and presided for three years. He expelled the nuns of our order from the monastery commonly called Nonnenmunster, in the suburb of the city, because of their disorderly life, and introduced others of the Cistercian order there; they inhabit that place down to the present day, as we see.

In this year also King Henry summoned an assembly of princes at Boppard, where, after accepting the counsel of wicked men, he made a conspiracy against his father, Frederick II, to his own destruction and the danger of very many. From that day onward he began to solicit whomever he could, with threats, entreaties, and promises, to leave his father and follow him, and he gained many. But the Worms men and the others who, because of their oath, refused to defect from the father, he troubled for a long time with many injuries. Seeing this, the margrave of Baden, faithful to the emperor, set out for Sicily to the emperor, urging him to return to Germany as quickly as possible; otherwise his native land would be [unclear], and he himself would lose [unclear].

Many heretics are burned in Germany.

Brother Conrad of Marburg.

The count of Sayn is accused.

The army of Brother Conrad [unclear]; expedition of the king into Bavaria.

Theoderic, count of Montbeliard.

Berenger, bishop of Speyer, dies.

The Worms men are reconciled with the bishop.

The cross preached against the Stedingen.

The Stedingen are slaughtered after being defeated.

Henry of Worms dies.

Nonnenmunster of our order is transferred.

King Henry conspired against his father.

The margrave of Baden recalls the emperor. Monastery of Hirsau

whom the duke himself had formerly unjustly oppressed, or had driven from his land, devastated all Austria and subjected it to the emperor, except for a few very strongly fortified castles, into which the duke had withdrawn. But the emperor, after arranging his affairs in Lombardy as best he could and leaving part of his army there, returned to Austria; and, remaining in the city of Vienna through the winter, he began to make arrangements concerning the condition of that duchy newly subjected to him, and to secure it with his own soldiers, having with him the army brought back from Italy.

MCCXXXVII.

In the sixth year of Abbot Ernest, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1237, Emperor Frederick, being established in Austria, caused his son Conrad, still a boy, born of his overseas wife, to be elected king of the Romans. He was elected by the archbishops of Mainz and Trier, and also by the king of Bohemia and the duke of Bavaria, Otto count palatine of the Rhine, with the consent of the other princes who were present. When this had been done, the emperor himself, leaving a garrison of soldiers there at that time, went up to Regensburg and summoned an assembly of princes at Speyer. When they came there at the appointed time, he again caused his son Conrad, the boy, to be designated king. After this, having sent Count Eberhard of Eberstein into Austria with two hundred soldiers to guard the city of Vienna, he himself set out again for Lombardy with the rest of the army; and around the feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle he had a battle with the Milanese, and, after gaining the victory, captured and killed many thousands of them.

In the same year before autumn, a quarter of wine was being sold for sixteen denarii in Alsace; in the preceding year there had been such abundance of it that a quarter of wine was sold for one denarius, as was said above.

In the same year also Pope Gregory IX excommunicated Emperor Frederick, who was laying waste Lombardy, which was in rebellion against him, and caused him to be denounced everywhere by the Friars Minor; and countless evils followed in every land subject to the Roman Empire and to the Church.

In this same year, in the month of April, Emperor Frederick resigned in perpetuity to Archbishop Siegfried and his successors, with all its appurtenances, the fief of the advocacy of the village of Bischoffsheim on the borders of Franconia, which is [unclear] by the church of Mainz in the name of the duchy of Swabia.

In the same year, at the end of Lent, Henry, archbishop of Cologne, died; Conrad of Hochstaden, a warlike man, succeeded him. At that time many troubles of wars arose in the provinces of Mainz, Trier, Cologne, and especially in the land of Liège; because of these there were many incursions of wars, plunderings, and burnings, followed not without the shedding of blood. At the end of this aforesaid year, on the vigil of the Nativity of Christ, Conrad of Tann, bishop of Speyer, died. He gave the church of Deidesheim, with all its revenues, to the canons of the greater church of Speyer for their common use, as a perpetual possession. At his urging also, Cuno, abbot of Wissembourg, with the consent of his convent, handed over the church in the village of Billigheim, not far from Landau, with all its revenues, to the canonical church of Speyer. And the abbot of the monastery of Klingenmünster, then of our order but now of secular clerics, at the persuasion of the said pontiff, gave the right of patronage of the church in Offenbach to the chapter of Speyer. He [held office] almost eight years.

MCCXXXVIII.

In the seventh year of Ernest, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1238, Henry, the last landgrave of Alsace, died without heirs. He had held many fiefs from the Empire, from the church of Strasbourg, and from others; after his death these reverted to their lords. Moreover, the title of the provincial countship has remained with the church of Strasbourg down to the present.

In the same year Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, Conrad, bishop of Speyer, [unclear] Conrad his son into Germany with the aforesaid archbishop of Mainz, [unclear] set out, with whose help he fought many battles there. But after a short time, commending him and the affairs of the kingdom to his loyalty and protection, [unclear].

In the same year Henry, bishop of Basel, died; Lütold of Röttelnheim lawfully succeeded him by election of the canons. In these times the Tartars, an immense multitude also pouring out from their own places, miserably destroyed Hungary, Poland, and Moravia, and all the adjacent lands, devastating them with fire, plunder, and sword. Against their incursions, many princes, signed with the cross, assembled at Merseburg; and in the year 182 — Of the Hirsau Monastery

... the empire, with the princes and his son conspiring against him. But when the emperor heard this news, he sent the margrave ahead into Germany and promised that he himself would come as quickly as possible. But Henry the king, the emperor’s son, took it badly that his father had been informed of the things he had committed and would be returning to Germany by his counsel. Therefore, having gathered an army of his men, he entered his territory and contrived great evils against him. But the margrave, certain of the emperor’s coming, defended himself and his men stoutly and put the king’s army to flight.

In the same year the count of Holland, in a certain tournament at Corbie, in the diocese of Amiens, was miserably suffocated and died, expired.

Likewise in this same year Frederick, count of Pfirriß, being held in captivity, was cruelly killed by his own son, after a long starvation in prison.

1235.

In the year [unclear], with 4 subtracted, which was the Sunday of the Nativity, 1235, Henry the king, son of the emperor, hearing that his father would shortly come into Germany, and fearing him, began to seek the friendships of princes and cities for himself; and beginning from Basel, he received hostages from all the cities with which he was confederated in Alsace, as a precaution, lest they should fall away from him when the emperor came, but should remain firm with him against his father in the conspiracy already begun until the end.

But the emperor, returning from Apulia around the Nativity of John the Baptist, came through Austria into Germany. Soon, after sending his messengers throughout the whole kingdom, he summoned the princes to an assembly to be held at Mainz on the feast of the Assumption of the blessed Mary ever virgin. Meanwhile Henry the king, who because of fear of his father was staying in the very strongly fortified castle of Driuels, at the persuasion of Hermann, master of the hospital of the Teutonic Knights, came to his father at Worms on the Nones of July, where he was with certain princes. He immediately placed him in custody, first at Worms, in a very strong house near the church of Saint Andrew the Apostle; then in Heidelberg castle, under the custody of Otto, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria. Afterwards he was led from Heidelberg to Alzey, and finally, sent to Sicily, he was held in close custody until death for five years: God rendering to him the way according to his merits, since he had made the noble kingdom of Germany common to robbers, had violently oppressed religious and ecclesiastical men with unjust services and exactions, and had exposed the province to such plundering by the impious that there was now no security of peace for travellers.

When the feast of the Assumption of the blessed Mary ever virgin arrived, a very great multitude of princes, bishops, abbots, counts, and nobles from all parts of Germany assembled at Mainz according to the emperor’s edict. There the emperor, crowned on the octave of the feast of the Assumption, proceeded and ordained many things for the peace and advantage of the empire. In this assembly there are those who testified that more than twelve thousand noblemen and soldiers had gathered. In the same assembly of princes the discord which had lasted for almost eight years between the emperor Frederick and Otto, duke of Saxony, was settled by the counsel of friends. For when Henry, count palatine, who was also lord of Brunswick and Lueneburg, had died eight years before and left two daughters, Otto, duke of Bavaria, taking the first daughter, Gertrude, as wife, as was said above, obtained with her the county palatine of the Rhine; but the margrave of Baden took the second as wife, with whom he received the lordship of Brunswick as dowry, which he sold to the aforesaid emperor Frederick for a certain sum of money. And when the emperor had sent his men to Saxony to take possession of the lordship newly purchased, Otto, duke of Saxony and Lueneburg, taking it very ill that the inheritance of his forefathers, which they had possessed by right for a long time, had come into the emperor’s hands, constantly opposed himself. By violent force he compelled the soldiers sent by him to leave Brunswick.

The duke comes into the emperor’s favor.

Albert of Anhalt becomes duke of Saxony.

But Duke Otto, persuaded by the counsel of friends, came into the emperor’s favor in the aforesaid assembly of princes at Mainz, where concord between them was confirmed in this manner, with the consent of the princes: that the same Duke Otto, for himself and his heirs, should hold in perpetuity the duchy of Brunswick and Lueneburg. Further, the emperor transferred the title of the duchy of Saxony to Albert of Anhalt, who was in the county of Lauenburg, creating him duke of Saxony and prince elector. And so that the integrity of the history may more easily become known to the reader, let him who desires to know the truth know that Henry, once duke of Saxony, who on account of his wonderful deeds obtained the name of the Lion, concerning whom there is that famous battle of the lion and the griffin, and the long [unclear] at sea...

Of the Monastery of Hirsau

After his deposition he entered Italy, and afflicted the pope and the peoples subject to him with such great evils that the pontiff grew weary of living, and wished that he had never thought of deposing him. [unclear] lasted almost to this day, for two hundred and sixty years, not without the shedding of much blood. For those who followed the party of the Roman pontiff, to whose supporters the name Guelfs had been given, strove with all zeal and all strength to pursue and utterly destroy the supporters of the emperor, who were called Ghibellines. Nor with less zeal did the Ghibellines pursue the Guelfs. But what was done concerning the Empire after King Henry died, or even after the emperor died, we shall tell in its proper order after six years.

1245.

In the year of the Lord’s nativity 1245, indiction 2, Ernest, the twenty-fourth abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, died on the day of Saint Blaise, bishop, which is the third day of the month of February, in the fourteenth year of his rule, begun but not completed, and at about sixty-three years of age. He was a good, tranquil, peaceable man, who [unclear].

On Volpold, Twenty-First Abbot of the Monastery, Who Presided Twenty Years and as Many Days; on the Various Events of That Time.

When Ernest, the venerable abbot of this monastery, had died, as we have said, and had been buried with the reverence of his sons, as is customary, in the year and on the day prescribed above, the brothers, bereft of a shepherd, came together on the first suitable day following in the chapter place and began to take counsel concerning the election of a new abbot. Therefore, after the customary prayers had first been said, at length, confirmed by Conrad, bishop of Speyer, and, as is customary, ordained with great solemnity in the greater church of the said city of Speyer, he presided over this monastery of Hirsau for twenty years and as many days. He was a man of middling stature, inclining more to corpulence than to slenderness of body. He was a Swabian by nation, born of honorable parents, and, according to the custom of that time, had been adequately instructed in the Scriptures for necessity. Having become a monk, he lived quietly and peacefully among the brothers at all times, walking without reproach. He is not found to have alienated anything. Moreover, the fervor of monastic life at that time had grown not a little lukewarm in this monastery, as in almost all others; he could not easily revive it, nor did he labor greatly on that account.

In the course of his first year, the year prescribed above, which was, as we have said, 1245 from the Lord’s nativity, in the month of November, Conrad of Eberstein, the forty-sixth bishop of Speyer, died. Henry, son of the count of Leiningen, chancellor of the imperial court, succeeded him and presided for twenty-seven years. This Henry, elected but not yet confirmed, besieged and took by armed force the castle called Starkenberg, which pertains to the principality of the monastery of Lorsch, after driving out from it the guardians of the church of Mainz. From this a great dissension arose between him and Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz. At length Pope Innocent, at the instance of the aforesaid archbishop, entrusted the case to certain judges for determination and restored peace.

In the same year, on the vigil of Saint Andrew the Apostle, at night, Otto, the first of the dukes of Bavaria to be count palatine of the Rhine, died. At the beginning of his rule he was a pious, just, and most merciful prince. Afterwards, when he sided with the excommunicated and deposed Emperor Frederick, as we have said, he himself was excommunicated by the pope, and he began to persecute the clergy out of hatred for the pope; this did not turn out well for him. For on the aforesaid vigil of Saint Andrew, when he was cheerful and well with his wife, sons, and household, he was found dead suddenly in that very night, excommunicate. He left two sons, Louis and Henry, who governed his principality for ten years in fraternal community. But after ten years, that is, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1255, they divided the principality between themselves. Henry received Landshut with Lower Bavaria as his legitimate portion. But Louis [unclear].

[unclear] his pilgrimage is depicted as having been fabricated; he begot two sons, namely Otto, the fourth emperor, and William, duke of Saxony and Brunswick, concerning whom there is nothing relevant to the matter at hand. But he begot as his third son Henry, who married Agnes, daughter of Conrad, count palatine of the Rhine. She bore him two daughters: namely Gertrude, whom Otto, duke of Bavaria, as we have said, had as wife, and with whom he also obtained the palatinate of the Rhine; and Adelaide, whom [Ericus?], margrave of Baden, married, and with whom, as has been said, he obtained the duchy of Brunswick, which, as we have already said, he sold to Emperor Frederick.

This Henry, from the dukes of Saxony count palatine of the Rhine, after the death of Agnes, daughter of Conrad the count palatine and mother of his daughters Gertrude and Adelaide, took a second wife, namely Agnes, daughter of the count of Landsberg, but by her he had no children. Therefore, when concord had been made between Emperor Frederick and Otto, duke of Brunswick, mentioned above, in the aforesaid assembly of princes at Mainz, the emperor, after the solemnities of the masses on the octave of the Assumption, invited the princes to a feast. Because of the very great multitude of people, this had been prepared at great expense outside the city in an open place, the emperor himself rejoicing with all the others that he had increased the Roman empire by the creation of a new duke.

Not long afterward the archbishop of Besançon, a wise and glorious man, in the same assembly of princes at Mainz, closed his last day. His body was brought back to the church over which he had presided, and was buried with honor in Christian fashion. After this the emperor invited the third [unclear] on the octave of the Assumption to a feast, which, because of the very great multitude of people, had been prepared at great expense outside the city in an open place, the emperor himself rejoicing with all the others that he had increased the Roman empire by the creation of a new duke.

After the celebration [unclear], he sent her after the wedding to Haguenau, in Alsace, and remained there with her for almost the whole winter together with his princes. On the feast of All Saints the emperor held an assembly of princes at Augsburg, where the king of Bohemia was present, receiving from the emperor ten thousand marks for the part of the duchy of Swabia which had devolved by hereditary right to his wife. From there the emperor returned to Haguenau and wintered there. Among other princes there were the count of Toulouse, who received the March from the emperor as a fief, after giving the oath of fidelity, as is the custom; and the count of Provence, in his fiftieth year, whom the emperor made a knight, although he resisted in part, because the counts in his family did not believe they could live long after they had attained the rank of knighthood. Nor would he even then have consented to knighthood, unless the kings of France and England, each of whom had taken his daughters as wives for their sons, had compelled him to this order of knighthood, judging it unworthy that their father-in-law should not be a knight. There were also envoys of the king of Spain, bringing very beautiful destriers and precious gifts to the emperor with greetings.

1236.

In the fifth year of Abbot Ernest, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1236, on the kalends of May, Saint Elizabeth was raised from her subterranean tomb at Marburg by the archbishops of Mainz and Trier and the bishop of Hildesheim, apostolic commissioners, in the presence of Emperor Frederick and many princes, bishops, abbots, counts, prelates, nobles and commoners, the number of all of whom was estimated at twelve hundred thousand. There, before all the people, countless miracles occurred at the invocation of her holy name. The emperor lifted the first stone from the sarcophagus, and reverently placed upon the sacred head of the saint the golden crown brought forth from his treasures. Her body was placed in a golden tomb, because she had been canonized by Pope Gregory IX. After this the emperor moved his army into Italy against the Lombards, who for many years past had gone out in rebellion against him.

In the same year, before the emperor’s aforesaid expedition into Italy, the Jews dwelling in the town of Fulda secretly killed certain Christian boys in a mill in order to obtain their blood. When this crime was discovered, many of them were burned. The bodies of the boys, however, were presented at Haguenau for the emperor to inspect, and there were buried with honor as if they were martyrs; and a great persecution of the Jews followed.

In the same year there grew a very great abundance of wine, especially in the regions of Alsace, so that one quartal of wine was bought for one denarius. And so the emperor, coming into Italy with a strong army of his men, in the first encounter took Vicenza, and, setting it on fire, destroyed it for the greater part. Mantua also and Padua, after long rebellion and many dangers, came into his surrender. Meanwhile, while these things were being done in Italy, the king of the Bohemians and the duke of Bavaria, with certain bishops, by the emperor’s command entered the land of the duke of Austria with a strong army, on account of the manifold excesses and grave crimes by which that same duke had been defamed. When they had come into Austria, with the nobles of the land joining themselves to them, whom Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

1239.

In the eighth year of Abbot Ernest, which was the year 1239 of the Lord’s Nativity, the greater church of Mainz, newly repaired by Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, was consecrated with great solemnity.

The church of Mainz [unclear].

In the same year there occurred a failure of the sun, which the Greeks call an eclipse, and a great pestilence followed it in very many regions. In these times there was much persecution of the ministers of God’s Church, especially in the kingdom of Germany, on account of the excommunication of Emperor Frederick II, who did not cease persecuting all who agreed with the pope, despoiling churches of their ornaments and revenues, and afflicting prelates, monks, and priests with many injuries.

1240.

In the ninth year of Abbot Ernest, and in the year 1240 of the Lord’s Nativity, Pope Gregory IX died; Celestine IV was elected pope.

Celestine IV, succeeding him, presided for only seventeen days. After his death, because the cardinals did not agree, the Apostolic See was vacant for one year and nine months, not without danger to many souls.

1241.

In the following year, which was the tenth of Abbot Ernest, Pope Innocent IV, elected after Celestine, presided for eleven years and three months.

In the same year, a mountain in Burgundy, splitting away from the mountains and constricting the valleys, wretchedly crushed many thousands of farmers.

1242.

In the eleventh year of Abbot Ernest, and in the year 1242 of the Lord’s Nativity, Theoderic, archbishop of Trier, died in the thirtieth year of his pontificate, in the fifteenth indiction, on the first day before the Kalends of April; he was buried in the greater church of Trier before the altar of St Martin. Arnold succeeded him, provost of the greater church, son of the count of Isenberg, nephew by his sister of the aforesaid Archbishop Theoderic, and he presided for almost sixteen years. Against this Arnold, elected by the greater and sounder part of the chapter, Rudolph, provost of St Paulinus, born of Ponte, elected by a few, set himself, trusting in the aid of the duke of Lorraine and the counts of Luxembourg and of Sayn, and resisted as much as he could the election that had been made of him. At length agreement was made between them. Pope Innocent confirmed Arnold as archbishop and granted to him, for his table, that he might lawfully retain all the ecclesiastical benefices that he had held before.

Worms perished by fire.

In the same year, on the Ides of April at the hour of Vespers, the city of Worms, set on fire by a chance blaze, was half consumed by that fire, and more than three hundred people perished in the same fire.

1243.

In the twelfth year of Abbot Ernest, which was the 1243rd year of the Lord’s Nativity, [unclear] archbishop [unclear], monks of the Premonstratensian order, began to inhabit that famous monastery of Lorsch of our order, as we said above by anticipation.

1244.

In the following year, which was the thirteenth of Abbot Ernest and the 1244th of the Lord’s Nativity, Emperor Frederick II, cited by Pope Innocent to that famous council at Lyons and not appearing, was [unclear] from the imperial majesty. Henry [unclear], provincial count of Hesse, having been elected king against Frederick, defended his party as much as they could. Henry, once elected, had a war with Conrad, the emperor’s son, in the fields near Frankfurt, and, emerging victorious, overcame Conrad.

Therefore, bearing the royal name for five years, he accomplished nothing worthy of memory, but died without ever obtaining the crown of the empire. For as long as Emperor Frederick lived, for almost six years none of the princes could prevail against him; but, not heeding the pope’s sentence, which he called unjust and frivolous, he conducted himself as emperor, and had a great adherence of princes, nobles, and cities until his death.

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

... took as wife Mary, of the duke of Brabant, a very beautiful woman; by her he had no children, but killed her in the third year of Abbot Volpold, because of suspicion of adultery, as we shall say there in its own place and order. But his brother Henry took as wife Elizabeth, daughter of Hungary, niece through her brother of St. Elizabeth of Marburg; by her he begot three sons, Otto, afterwards king of Hungary, Louis, and Stephen, dukes of Bavaria. We shall mention them below in order; they divided Bavaria among themselves.

1246.

In the second current year of Abbot Volpold, which was the year 1246 of the Lord’s Nativity, after Emperor Frederick had been deposed, as we have said, Conrad, the younger son, usurped the empire for himself. Against him Henry Raspe, landgrave of Hesse, son of Saint Elizabeth, elected king by certain princes, went forth to war, defeated him near Frankfurt, and drove him into Italy.

In the same year Ludolph, bishop of Worms, died, and was buried with great pomp and honor before the high altar in the convent of nuns called Nonnenmünster, which he had taken away from our order. After his death the canons of Worms unanimously elected as bishop Cuno, dean of the greater church of Mainz, a good man and worthy of the honor of the episcopate. After he had presided for twenty days, he was taken off by death, perfected in a short time, and fulfilled many times, lest malice should change his understanding. When he had died, Richard, a native of Trier, was elected bishop and presided for nearly fifteen years, a good man and provident governor of his church, who did many good things in his time.

1247.

In the third year of Abbot Volpold, which was the year 1247 of the Lord’s Nativity, Louis, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, had his wife Mary, strongly suspected of the crime of adultery, killed at Werd in Swabia; she died slain with remarkable severity, without children. In satisfaction for so great a crime committed, he afterwards had the monastery of Fürstenfeld built in Bavaria, which he magnificently endowed with many goods and revenues.

In this same year the aforesaid Louis, count palatine and duke, built from the foundations the very strong castle called Friedberg, for the defense of the duchy of Bavaria against the bishop of Augsburg. After this he took a second wife, Anna, daughter of the king of Poland; by her he begot three sons, Louis, duke of Bavaria, Rudolph, count palatine of the Rhine, and the other Louis, afterwards Roman emperor. Of these we shall speak below in order.

1248.

In the fourth year of Abbot Volpold, and the year 1248 of the Lord’s Nativity, Conrad, archbishop of Cologne, a rich and magnanimous man, began to build that great and distinguished greater church of Cologne, laying the first stone on the vigil of the Assumption of Blessed Mary ever Virgin. Although that work takes increase daily by the labors of craftsmen, and has now for two hundred and fifty-four years been [unclear] without interruption [unclear], he himself also being a good man.

In the same year a very great famine oppressed Germany and killed many.

1249.

In the following year, which was the fifth of Abbot Volpold and the year 1249 of the Lord’s Nativity, in the seventh indiction, Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, died on the Ides of March: a man of great works, who magnificently enlarged his church in honor and possessions, and amid so many evils, so many wars, and so many dangers by which the empire was tottering, ruled it most wisely. To him in [unclear] ... as we have said, a few years before, by certain princes, at the command of Pope Innocent, [unclear] came. He died of a flux of the belly and was buried in his town of Eisenach. After Henry’s death, William, count of Holland, son of Count Floris, was elected king of the Romans by certain princes at the village of Wörnich, against Emperor Frederick and his son Conrad, in the presence of Pietro Capocci, cardinal deacon of the Golden Veil and legate of the Apostolic See. When he was elected, he was still a young man of twenty years, and he reigned nearly seven years; although he did not obtain the crown of the empire, nevertheless [unclear].

William becomes king of the Romans. Of the Monastery of Hirsau

[unclear] king by nature. [He] had obedience. But on the last day of the month of October he entered the royal city of Aachen with a great multitude of nobles, and on the following day, that is, on the feast of All Saints, having been presented in the church by two bishops, of Minden and of Munster, to the archbishop of Cologne to be blessed, two other bishops, of Utrecht and of Liege, clothed him with a dalmatic in the manner of a deacon; and the aforesaid archbishop Conrad, with great solemnity, anointed and crowned him king of the Romans.

When the consecration had been completed, the same archbishop placed him on the royal seat, saying: May you sit upon the throne of the glorious seat, and do judgment and justice on earth.

Christian, archbishop of Mainz, anointed his right hand outwardly with sanctified oil, saying: May almighty God deign to consecrate you as king of the Romans, who commanded David to be anointed by the hand of Samuel the prophet over the people of the Hebrews.

Arnold, archbishop of Trier, placed his hands upon his head, saying: May the spirit of wisdom, understanding, knowledge, piety, strength, and counsel descend upon you, and may you be filled with the spirit of fear of the Lord.

Ludwig, count palatine of the Rhine, arch-steward of the kingdom, placed the golden orb in his hands, saying: Receive the spherical orb, that you may subject all the nations of the earth to the Roman empire, and may be able to be called a glorious Augustus.

The margrave of Brandenburg, the king's chamberlain, handed the ring into his hand, saying: Receive the seal of the monarchy, that you may preserve the Roman empire in its vigor and defend it with unconquered virtue from every incursion of the barbarians.

Duke of Saxony.

King of Bohemia.

The duke of Saxony, the king's sword-bearer, gave him the sword, saying: Receive the royal scepter, that you may powerfully afflict rebels with severe reproof, and govern all the well-disposed in tranquil peace.

The king of Bohemia, cupbearer of the empire, with the consent of the archbishop of Cologne, placed the silver crown on the king's head, saying: Receive the splendid diadem, that you may be so radiant on earth with virtuous deeds that you may deserve to have the crown of eternal blessedness in heaven. Amen.

After these things he kept the octave there solemnly. And all the princes and nobles of the lower parts offered him obedience, except for certain castellans still faithful to Frederick.

Among them was the castellan of Kaiserswerth, whom King William, surrounding him with a siege, could not overcome, because he defended himself strongly.

1250.

In the sixth year of Abbot Volpold, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1250, in the eighth indiction, Emperor Frederick II died at Taranto, in the fifty-seventh year of his age, leaving two sons: one, named Conrad, king of Jerusalem, whom he had long before designated king of the Romans, although he had been expelled from Germany; the other, named Manfred, by a concubine, who invaded the kingdom of Apulia after his father's death, though his brother resisted him, but he did not reign long.

In the same year Hermann, bishop of Wurzburg, died. Eringius of Reinstein succeeded him and presided for sixteen years, amid much disturbance and discord which he had with his citizens of Wurzburg.

In this same year the winter was very harsh and exceedingly long-lasting, abounding greatly in snow and ice; when these were at length dissolved into water, a very great flood followed, which overthrew many buildings.

1251.

In the seventh year of Abbot Volpold, and in the one thousand two hundred [unclear] year of the Lord's Nativity, [Conrad], once the son of Emperor Frederick II, took up the kingdom of Apulia; then in the following year he died, destroyed by poison, as is believed, his brother Manfred, as we have said, having contrived it.

In the same year the archbishop of Mainz died; [unclear] succeeded him and presided for nine years, a magnanimous and very prudent man, named Gerard, who, like the others, supported the party of King William.

1252.

In the eighth year of Abbot Volpold, and in the one thousand two hundred fifty-second year of the Lord's Nativity, in the tenth indiction, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, the holy virgin Jutta died, formerly attendant of blessed Elisabeth of Marburg, landgravine of Thuringia and Hesse, concerning whom mention was made above. This holy virgin is said to have been renowned for many signs and miracles both in life and after death; she had been privy to all the virtues and works of her lady while she was still living among men, a zealous co-worker in all things, and to the utmost of her strength she most steadfastly took care to imitate her until death.

In the same year, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, Ibanus of my monastery of Sponheim Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

[unclear], the sixth abbot, whom Johannes de Schonberg, cantor, succeeded; he presided for 12 years, 4 months, and 21 days.

In the ninth year of Abbot Volpold, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1253, there was a great and dreadful wind, which in various places overturned many buildings, tore up several very strong trees from the earth by the roots, and with infinite losses crushed many people.

In the same year Manfred, son of the late Emperor Frederick by a concubine, after Conrad had, as they say, been killed by poison in the preceding year, occupied the kingdom of Sicily, and held it for a few years while he lived.

MCCLIII.

In the following year, which was the tenth of Abbot Volpold, and of the Lord’s Nativity 1254, in the twelfth indiction, Pope Innocent IV died, and the Apostolic See was vacant for two years because of discord among the brethren.

In the same year, in the month of February, the citizens of Worms and Mainz, who for a long time had stood in mutual dissension, established perpetual peace, concord, and confederation among themselves. In these times also Count Emicho of Leiningen, brother of the bishop of Speyer, bearing a hostile spirit against Richard, bishop of Worms, strove with every effort to capture him; but Richard, defended by the aid of his own citizens and admitted into Worms, although before this he had been in discord with the citizens, escaped his threats. In those times there was great tumult in the kingdom, and various dissensions, because not all [unclear] of King William of the Romans.

In the year noted above, when the cities of these parts that sided with King William, such as Mainz, Worms, Frankfurt, Boppard, Wesel, Bingen, Oppenheim, Gelnhausen, Friedberg, Fritzlar, and certain others, while he was in the lower regions, had no defenders against their adversaries, after counsel was held at Mainz on the day of St Margaret, virgin and martyr, they joined themselves together in a very firm mutual confederation, to defend everything against all persons whatsoever, laying aside the tolls which they had for the common peace.

MCCLV.

In the eleventh year of Abbot Volpold, and of the Lord’s Nativity 1255, King William held an assembly of certain princes at Worms, where envoys and legates sent from many cities were present. But on a certain day, when the queen his wife was proceeding from Worms to the castle of Trifels, which now belongs to Duke Alexander, not far from Landau, with an honorable company, she was captured by Hermann, knight of the castle of Rieberg, together with the count of Waldeck and certain others, and was brought to the aforesaid castle of Rieberg. He kept her captive for some time; afterwards, stripped of all her jewels and possessions, he allowed her to go, to no small disgrace of the king and of the whole country.

Afterwards in the same year, since the Apostolic See had been vacant for almost two years, not without danger to many souls, Alexander IV was at last elected pope by the cardinals, a Campanian by nation; he sat for six years and as many months, and canonized St Clare of the Order of Minors.

MCCLVI.

In the twelfth year of Abbot Volpold, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1256, King William resolved to set out for Rome for the imperial crown, when suddenly the most restless people of the Frisians, stirred up by a tumult, began to rebel, and, having entered the borders of Holland, to devastate everything with plundering and fire. But the king, seeing that their ferocity had to be subdued by the sword and no otherwise, gathered a huge army of his men and advanced against them at the end of this year, that is, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January; and, showing them many kinds of hardship, he overcame them with a strong hand, building the castle of Corenburg against their assault. After this, intending to advance farther, when the harshness of winter had drawn ice over the waters and marshes, he went ahead of the army on horseback, alone, to investigate all the hidden places of the enemy, as he thought. But behold, when the ice broke, his horse sank and stuck fast in a marshy ford, unable to go forward anywhere. Seeing this, the Frisians, who were hiding in the reeds, ran together and killed him, not knowing that he was the king, in the seventh year of his reign, the twenty-first of his countship of Holland, and the twenty-seventh of his age, and buried him in a certain house. But afterwards his body was transferred to Middelburg and honorably entombed in a certain monastery. After his death his son Florentius, a boy of six months, received the countship of Holland, and [unclear] it for almost forty years.

1257.

In the thirteenth year of Abbot Volpold, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1257, after the death of William, king of the Romans, the princes came together to appoint a new king, lest, if they neglected the matter too long, they should suffer some impairment of their right. But, being at variance with one another, they elected two men.

For Conrad, archbishop of Cologne, and Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, elected Richard, count of Cornwall, brother of the king of England, as king.
