Arnold, electing the king of Castile as king of the Romans, sent formal envoys to him, asking that he would deign to come as quickly as possible to the regions of the Rhine to take up the government of the kingdom, promising that he would provide counsel and aid to the best of his powers.

But King Alfonso, either despising or not caring for the Roman Empire, sent the envoys back with honor, after bestowing great gifts on them, promising that at a suitable time he would follow with an army of his men. Yet, content with his own kingdom, and because he was a most excellent philosopher and astronomer, he disdained to come to Germany, nor did he involve himself in any way in governing the Roman kingdom, except for the title alone, which, out of regard for those who had elected him, he retained for a time in his letters.

Moreover, the aforesaid Count Richard, summoned from England by Conrad, archbishop of Cologne, came into Germany; elected at Frankfurt, he willingly assumed the empire and was consecrated as king by the same archbishop. Then, by the favor and support of his princes, he was received as true king with great honor by the people of Cologne, Boppard, Wesel, Mainz, Frankfurt, Worms, Speyer, and many other cities, and was led around these parts with great pomp. And when, going up through all the cities of the Rhine, he made his way as far as Basel, and the money spent far too lavishly for acquiring the kingdom was now on the point of running out, all the princes left him and returned to their own places, silently indicating that up to that point they had followed the booty, not the king. He [entrusted?] the administration of the Wetterau to [unclear] of Falkenstein, whose sister he had married because of her extraordinary beauty; to Philip of Hohenfels [he entrusted?] Boppard, Wesel, and the other adjacent cities of the empire. Then, taking his wife with him, he returned to England and did not come to Germany again.

In the year written above, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, Richard, bishop of Worms, died; he had had many disputes with his citizens. He had as his adversary Eberhard of Badenberg, who in the beginning had been elected against him by many; Count Emicho of Leiningen supported him, who [unclear] all the episcopal revenues accruing outside Worms, [unclear].

After Richard had died and been buried, Conrad of Durekem, dean of the greater church of Mainz, was elected bishop of the aforesaid church; he presided for only twenty-two days, died, and was buried in the church of Mainz before the altar of Saint Peter. After him the brothers of the chapter, for the peace and advantage of the church, unanimously elected Eberhard of Badenberg, provost of the church of Saint Cyriacus in Nuhusen; he presided for nearly twenty years, did many good things for the canons of Nuhusen, and had disputes with the people of Worms.

In the fourteenth year of Abbot Volpold, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1258, Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, [unclear] the church of Saint Catherine in Oppenheim, [unclear] in the presence of Ge-

In the same year Richard, count of Cornwall, who had been elected in the preceding year by Conrad, archbishop of Cologne, was crowned at Aachen as king of the Romans, in the presence of Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, and certain other princes. After his coronation, as we have already said, he was led by them through all the cities of the empire along the Rhine, began to conduct the business of the kingdom, received the obedience of the citizens, and held assemblies of the princes, until at last he was deserted by them.

In the year Chronicle of Jo. Trithemius.

1259.

In the fifteenth year of Abbot Volpold, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1259, the monastery of Saint Disibod, of our order, in the county of Sponheim, in the diocese of Mainz, near the town of Sobernheim, was transferred from our order by Gerard, archbishop, and the canons of the church of Mainz, and given to fathers of the Cistercian order. Their first abbot, named Johannes, as though in thanksgiving for the benefit received, with the consent of his brethren, promised back to the canons of the aforesaid church, from the revenues of the same monastery, an annual rent of one hundred malters of wheat, to be rendered every year at Mainz for all time, as appears from the letters drawn up concerning this matter, whose date is the day before the Nones of March, in the aforesaid year, at Mainz, done in the presence of many witnesses.

In the same year Albert, surnamed the Great, of the Order of Preachers, of the convent of Cologne, a Swabian by nation, a man most learned in every respect, by the provision of Alexander IV was made bishop of Regensburg in Bavaria, when he was sixty-six years of age; but not long afterward he resigned.

Also in the same year Arnold of Isenburg, archbishop of Trier, in the town called Montabaur, in the seventeenth year of his pontificate, closed his last day; he lived magnificently in every respect and did many things vigorously in peace and war. He took the very strong castle of Thuron after it had been besieged for two years. He most beautifully fortified anew a great part of the city of Trier with a wall, and likewise enclosed the monasteries of Meinfeld and Koblenz with a wall. When he had died and had been buried with honor in the greater church of Trier before the altar of the Holy Trinity, two men were elected by the chapter in disagreement, namely Arnold of Sleyda and Henry of Bolanden. When they were contending over their elections before him at Rome in consistory, Pope Alexander IV, by the counsel of the brethren, annulled them, and [unclear], provost of the church, and he presided for twenty-four years and six months, a man excellent in ability and prudence, who ordained the bishop; and when he came to Trier with the pallium and apostolic letters, he was received by all the clergy and people of the city as archbishop, and he presided for twenty-seven years, a steadfast and [unclear] man.

Also in the aforesaid year, on the last day of the month of April, the city of Worms, again set alight by accidental fire, burned through the whole night around the hour of Compline, and with the loss of many people was consumed almost by half.

1260.

In the sixteenth year of Abbot Volpold, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1260, in the third indiction, Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, died. Werner of Falkenstein, provost of the greater church, succeeded him and presided for four years, a man excellent in ability and prudence, who governed his church very well and greatly increased its revenues.

In the same year two knights, Jacob of Lapide and Simon of Guntheim, [unclear] enmities [unclear]. For in those times, since there was no king in the lands, [unclear], movements of robbers [unclear], things were done rather at whim.

Also in the aforesaid year, on the last day of the month of April, the city of Worms, again set alight by accidental fire, burned through the whole night around the hour of Compline, and with the loss of many people was consumed almost by half.

1261.

In the seventeenth year of Abbot Volpold, and the year of the Lord's Nativity 1261, in the fourth indiction, Conrad of Hochstaden, archbishop of Cologne, died; he had many disputes with his citizens during his pontificate. He was buried in the greater church of Cologne. Engelbert II of Valkenburg, provost of Saint Gereon, succeeding him by election of the chapter, presided for almost fourteen years; he too had many and continual dissensions with the people of Cologne.

In the same year Pope Alexander IV died. Urban IV, a Frenchman by nation, succeeded him and presided for three years, one month, and four days. He instituted the feast of the Body of our Lord Jesus Christ, to be celebrated every year on the Thursday after the octave of Pentecost throughout the whole Christian world, and granted indulgences in its favor. The kingdom of Sicily also, which Manfred, duke of Swabia, son of the late Emperor Frederick II, had occupied after the death of [Conrad, his brother?], as we have said, Urban conferred on Charles, count of Provence, brother of the king of the Franks, and summoned him from Gaul into Italy through legates; and he occupied Sicily after Manfred had been put to flight, not without the bloodshed of many.

The monastery of St. Disibod is transferred from the order.

Albertus Magnus is ordained bishop.

Arnold, archbishop of Trier, dies. Two [unclear].

Henry [unclear], archbishop of [unclear], dies.

Worms is burned by fire.

Very great floods of water.

Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, dies.

[Unclear].

Pope Alexander dies. Pope Urban.

Conrad, archbishop of Cologne, dies.

Manfred is [driven?] from Sicily. The Monastery of Hirsau

1262.

In the eighteenth year of Abbot Volpold, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1262, Richard the hermit died, formerly a priest and monk of our order in Alsace, in his hermitage near Paffenborn, on the Kalends of November, that is, on the feast of All Saints; he had for many years led a hard life in the strictest penance.

In the same year Werner, archbishop of Mainz, excommunicated Philip of Hoenfels, whom King Richard, after returning to England, had appointed captain in the regions of the Rhine, placing his land under ecclesiastical interdict, because he was oppressing too heavily, with new and unwonted exactions and demands, the courts and goods of the clergy of Mainz situated in his lordship, and, though often admonished, had refused to desist. But afterwards, changing his purpose, he remitted the unjust exactions he had presumed to impose on the clergy; and, agreement having been made between them, he was absolved.

1263.

In the nineteenth year of Abbot Volpold, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1263, the citizens of Cologne, after long disputes, wars, and losses, suddenly shut up in a certain house Engelbert their archbishop, who was in the city and suspected no such thing, together with Theoderic of Valkenburg his brother, and compelled him to conditions of peace, although thereafter no such concord was maintained between the parties.

In the same year there was great discord between the aforesaid archbishop and the count of Juelich, which grew even to arms. And so, when the forces of the parties advanced to battle, the archbishop, relying on the aid of Henry, bishop of Utrecht, and of the Hollanders, defeated the men of Juelich, with many slain.

1264.

In the following year, which was the twentieth of Abbot Volpold and the year of the Lord's Nativity 1264, the hermit brothers of the rule of Saint Augustine, whom the common people call Augustinians, entered Worms and there built a convent and monastery of their order, with Bishop Everhard consenting and the citizens providing aid and support.

In the same year, on the second day before the Kalends of May, John, the seventh abbot of my monastery of Sponheim, died. He was succeeded by Peter, the eighth abbot, who presided for twenty-five years and four months; in the first year of his rule he gave the church in Genzingen, with the right of patronage, tithes, and all its revenues, to the canons of the greater church of Mainz, for perpetual possession for the augmentation of their prebends.

In the same year also Pope Urban IV died, and the Apostolic See was vacant for five months, until the following year, because of the discord of the brethren.

1265.

In the following year, which was the twenty-first, begun, of Abbot Volpold, and the year of the Lord's Nativity 1265, after the Apostolic See had been vacant for five months, Clement IV was elected supreme pontiff, by nation a Narbonese, from the town of Saint-Gilles. He presided for three years, nine months, and twenty-one days, a man of holy conduct and illuminated, as was said, by a prophetic spirit. He enrolled with great honor in the catalogue of the saints Hedwig, formerly duchess of Poland, a widow of wondrous holiness, who had been canonized.

In the same year Abbot Volpold, touched by grave illness, ended his last day on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, having been healthfully fortified by good confession and the ecclesiastical sacraments, after completing the twentieth year of his rule with the same number of days; he was a man of modest conduct and very solicitous about the condition of household affairs, although the monastery in both its conditions declined not a little in his time, and also under certain other abbots, as we shall say in what follows.

Concerning John, the Twenty-Sixth Abbot of This Monastery, who presided for 10 years, 3 months, and 4 days, and concerning the various deeds of that time.

[unclear]

After Abbot Volpold had died and been buried in the year and on the day written above, according to custom [unclear] to lament the misfortunes, they appointed the day for the election of a new shepherd, the penultimate day of the month of February; on that day they assembled, and, after the customary prayers had first been offered and the other things that are accustomed to be done in the act of election, after various discussions had been held among them, at last the greater and sounder part elected John, prior of this monastery, as abbot, the rest being divided among various others. Yet these, yielding to the election of the greater number, all unanimously consented to him.

The elected Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

Elected, moreover, and confirmed by Henry of Liningen, bishop of Speyer, and solemnly ordained according to praiseworthy custom, he presided over this monastery of Hirsau as the twenty-sixth in the order of abbots for 10 years, 3 months, and 4 days. He was Bavarian by nation; having become a monk under Eberhard, the twenty-third abbot of this monastery, and then having been appointed prior under Volpoldus, his predecessor, he continued the weak discipline that he found. At length, when ordained abbot, he cared little for the integrity of regular observance, but rather pursued external things, the pomp of power and the vanity of glory. Among the abbots of his time he was not of the lowest reputation, because of a very celebrated fame acquired by many labors [unclear] and abstinences. For the observance of the order of our most holy father Benedict had, in the time of this abbot, failed to such an extent in almost all the monasteries of the German nation that no trace of the former institution was discerned in their morals. Everything was corrupted, everything collapsed; the monks together with the abbots fell headlong into the abyss of vices. No one cared about this deformation of our order; no one seemed to have grieved over it: not the king, not the pope, not the princes; indeed no prelate at all gave any thought to the reform of the monks. For the transgressions of the monks were so public that they were thought lawful. Hence it came about that the deeds and actions of the abbots of this monastery, from this point down to Abbot Frederick, the thirty-seventh, have been transmitted to our memory in very small number, because of the obscurity of the times and the negligence of ignorant monks.

In the year noted above, in which John was elected abbot, Iringus, bishop of Wurzburg, and the clergy suffered many injuries from the citizens; for these, at length, the citizens themselves were compelled to make satisfaction in two hundred and two thousand marks of silver and to return to obedience to the bishop.

1266.

In the first year of Abbot John, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 1266, the aforesaid Iringus of Reinstein died, the forty-first bishop of Wurzburg, a steadfast, warlike, and magnanimous man. Berthold of Sternberg succeeded him and presided for almost 18 years.

In the same year Charles, appointed king of Sicily by Pope Urban, cruelly killed Manfred, king of Swabia, duke, son of Frederick II the emperor, after he had been defeated not far from Benevento. After his death Conrad, whom the Italians called Conradin, grandson of the former Emperor Frederick through his son Conrad, a very handsome young man and the last duke of Swabia, sought the kingdom of Apulia by right of his paternal inheritance; but, having been unjustly repelled by Pope Clement IV and Charles, count of Provence, of whom we spoke above, he did not attain the kingdom. Indeed, after two years he was miserably killed by that same Charles.

1267.

But in the second year of Abbot John, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 1267, a monastery of the Friars Preachers of St. Dominic was founded in the city of Speyer, from the alms of the citizens and other faithful, with the consent of Henry, bishop of the same [unclear]. [unclear] cruelly killed. In the same year a very great sedition arose between the citizens and the council of the city of Cologne. For when the rulers of that city seemed to burden the citizens with unusual levies and exactions, the citizens, following the counsel of wicked men, rashly opposed the council; and after a very grave sedition had been stirred up, rushing to arms, and attacking one another in a mutual gathering within the city itself, they wounded one another with weapons, with not a few killed on both sides.

1268.

In the third year of Abbot John, in the year of the Lord's nativity 1268, Conrad, grandson of Emperor Frederick through his son Conrad, the last duke of Swabia, having gathered an army of helpers from Germany and from wherever he could, determined to enter Apulia against Charles and to recover his paternal kingdom. Charles defeated him in the borders of the Alban territory, captured him, and cruelly killed the most noble youth. In him the genealogy of the illustrious Swabians came to an end; under it the Roman empire, resting securely for more than one hundred and twenty years, had received its growth.

In the same year, on the day before the Nones of June, Henry, bishop of Utrecht, died in the twenty-fifth year of his pontificate; John of Nassau succeeded him. In these times knights fighting with one another at night in the regions of Holland are said to have appeared in the air with arms. A great calamity of that people followed this prodigy. For the untamed common people rose up against the princes and nobles of the land and, after forming a conspiracy, resolved by unanimous consent to extinguish them all and utterly destroy them, and to claim every kind of liberty for themselves The Monastery of Hirsau [unclear]. Therefore, assembling armed in a very great multitude, they brought forth a huge army; and coming to Utrecht, they were gladly admitted by the citizens as defenders of liberty. They at once expelled all the nobles from the city with disgrace, distributing their goods to the poor and needy. Advancing from there, they seized many towns, castles, and fortifications of the nobles, and utterly destroyed some. Then, when they were vigorously besieging a certain town named Harlem, situated in Guelders, the townsmen, through the effort of a certain knight and with the aid, it seems, of the aforesaid bishop of Utrecht and the count of Guelders, defeated in battle those confederates of the Sotularian faction, many being captured and more being killed. And thus the Sotularian society of peasants, reduced to nothing, vanished.

1269.

In the fourth year of Abbot John, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1269, a great quarrel arose between Berthold, bishop of Würzburg, and the counts of Henneberg, Castell, and Hohenlohe. As it gradually grew exceedingly, they finally came to arms; and when battle was joined near the town of Kitzingen, many on both sides fell wounded.

In the same year certain men proscribed from the city of Cologne fled to Engelbert the archbishop, who was staying at Bonn. They were kindly received by him, because he was not in good accord with the people of Cologne. Having taken counsel, they approached Cologne by night and tried to enter through a hidden underground passage, made by someone for a price, laboring to hand the city over into the hands of that bishop. But when the plan was discovered, they accomplished nothing, although many perished on this evil occasion.

1271.

In the fifth year of Abbot John, in the one thousand two hundred seventieth year of the Lord’s nativity, Pope Clement IV died, and the see was vacant for nearly two years.

In the same year peace and concord were made between Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, and the citizens, through the mediation of Albert the Great, bishop of Regensburg.

In this same year there were many seditions in various cities and several wars among the princes of the land, not only in Germany but in all the neighboring provinces, and many thousands of men fell.

1281.

In the following year, which was the sixth of Abbot John and the year of the Lord’s nativity 1271, in the fourteenth indiction, after the two-year vacancy of the apostolic see, the cardinals elected as Roman pontiff the archdeacon of Liège, named Theobald, who at that time was in Asia with the army of the Christians fighting against the infidels. Summoning him to Viterbo, they made him pope, and he was called Gregory X. He presided for four years, a man worthy of so great an honor, if indeed a mortal man ought to be deemed worthy to hold on earth the place and vicariate of our Lord the Savior, who sits in heaven. He celebrated a general council at Lyon in the second year of his pontificate, at which many cardinals, archbishops, abbots, and other prelates of various ranks appeared. Many things [were done] concerning the election of the supreme pontiff, the expedition against the Saracens, the union of the Greek and Latin Church, and the peace of Christians [unclear] from Poland, [unclear], on the fourth nones of March. And he presided for thirty years, a good and [unclear] man, who ruled the church well.

1282.

In the seventh year of Abbot John, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1272, Henry of Leiningen, the forty-seventh bishop of Speyer, died on the day of Saint Prisca the virgin, that is, on the fifteenth kalends of February. He was buried in the greater church of Speyer, under white marble. Frederick of Westerburg succeeded him and presided for twenty-four years and five months, a man patient of labors and not ignorant of war.

1273.

In the eighth year of Abbot John, and in the one thousand two hundred seventy-third year of the Lord’s nativity, Pope Gregory X, hearing of the disorder of the Roman Empire and the plunderings by the princes, [unclear], so that within a fixed time, according to the power entrusted to them, they should elect a king suitable for the empire; otherwise he himself wished to provide the Roman Empire with a ruler. AssembChronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

Rudolf is elected king of the Romans.

Therefore the princes, assembling in the aforesaid year at Frankfurt, after many and various negotiations, at last unanimously elected as king of the Romans Rudolf, count of Habsburg, who was then absent and besieging Basel with a great army. As soon as he heard that he had been elected king of the Romans, he raised the siege and came with great display to Frankfurt; going down with the princes to Aachen, he received the rite of consecration in the customary manner. There the princes, after swearing peace and obedience into the hands of the new king, received their fiefs from him, promising him firm and faithful assistance, to the best of their powers, against all men.

Rudolf reigned nineteen years.

Thus Rudolf, having received the kingdom, reigned vigorously for eighteen years and ten months. He restored peace in the land, checked robbers, and destroyed many of their strongholds and fortifications; he repaired, as far as he could, the fallen empire, and in a short time recovered by his labor and industry many things that had been alienated from the kingdom. He had as wife Elisabeth, daughter of Burchard, count of Haigerloch, by whom he begot three sons and four daughters.

The sons of King Rudolf.

The first son was Albert, whom he afterwards made duke of Austria; he succeeded Adolf in the kingdom of the Romans, as we shall say in its place. From him our illustrious king Maximilian is descended, together with all the dukes of Austria who have lived in the meantime. The second son, Hartmann, was drowned in the Rhine not far from Basel. The third son was Rudolf, count of Habsburg and duke of Swabia, who married the daughter of Ottokar, king of Bohemia.

The first of the daughters married Wenceslaus, brother of the king of Bohemia. The second, named Mechthild, married Louis, count palatine of the Rhine. The third married Albert, duke of Saxony. The fourth married Charles, king of Apulia. Thus Rudolf, the renowned king, advancing with his army from city [to city?], was everywhere received as the true lord.

Count Albert, father of the king.

The father of King Rudolf was Albert, count of Habsburg, who had once been landgrave of Alsace and captain of the city of Strasbourg, a warlike man, of whom many wars are reported to have been bravely fought. After his death Rudolf, rising in his place, like a lion in the midst of shepherds, so overcame all his adversaries without fear. While still a count, by military force he claimed the county of Kyburg, Baden, and Mersburg from the hand of the count of Savoy, and he obtained Molenberg, Grötzingen, Durlach, and a great part of Swabia.

1274.

In the ninth year of Abbot John, which was the year of the Lord's birth 1274, Eberhard, count of Württemberg, the count of Montfort, the count of Helfenstein, and the count of Dockenberg, with eleven other counts and certain nobles, having formed a conspiracy, strove with all their might either to capture or to kill King Rudolf. Against them he led a great army; he defeated them all and bound them forever to obedience to himself and to the empire, and [unclear] peace in [unclear]. [Asked when he would set out for Rome] with an army for the crown of the Roman Empire, he would answer: “Italy has consumed many kings of the Germans. I shall not go to Rome. I am king, and I trust that I shall do no less for the benefit of the commonwealth than if I had been crowned at Rome.” Reigning, therefore, for almost nineteen years, as we have said, he did not receive the crown of the empire from the supreme pontiff, for the reason he stated.

[Unclear date].

The king's expedition into Bohemia.

In the tenth year of Abbot John, and in the year of the Lord's birth [unclear], around the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Mary ever virgin, King Rudolf set out with a great army into Bohemia against King Ottokar, who was occupying lands of the empire. For when the duke of Austria had died in the preceding year [without?] children, and that duchy itself, together with the counties of Tyrol and Carinthia, was vacant to the Roman Empire, the aforesaid king of the Bohemians invaded and occupied those lands, alleging a certain hereditary right, without the authority of the empire. But Rudolf, raised to be king of the Romans, admonished him by letter to restore to the empire what had been unjustly taken away, or else to expect danger. Scorning his commands, he said to those standing by: “Behold a new thing: the count of Habsburg, who was the captain of our army and the servant of our majesty, has sent commands to us as if he were lord. By our crown, we shall not be his obedient subjects.”

The duchy of Austria is vacant to the empire. Rudolf defeated the king of Bohemia.

Moved by this, King Rudolf led an army into Bohemia, defeated him in war, and compelled him to terms of subjection. Later, as we shall say, when he violated his promises, Rudolf defeated him again in battle in the fourth year of his reign, killed him, and gave the duchy of Austria to his son.

Pope Gregory died. Innocent V sits for six months.

In the same year Pope Gregory X died and was buried at Arezzo; Innocent V succeeded him in the pontificate and presided for only six months, an excellent man, from whom all good things were hoped. He had previously been called Peter of Tarentaise, of the Order of Friars Preachers of St Dominic, a most learned theologian, who wrote most profoundly on the four books of the Sentences and certain other works; and when he became pope he strove with all zeal to restore peace in Italy.

The Monastery of Hirsau

In the year of the Lord's nativity noted above, John, the twenty-sixth abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, afflicted by the severe trouble of fevers, passed from this mortal life to eternal life on 3 June, after ten years, three months, and four days of his rule had been completed. His body was buried in the greater monastery.

Concerning Voland, the twenty-seventh abbot of this monastery, who presided for 6 years, 8 months, and 14 days, and concerning various deeds.

After the death of John, the twenty-sixth abbot of this monastery, which occurred, as we have said, on 3 June in the year of the Lord's nativity 1275, on the same day after his burial the brothers, lacking a shepherd, assembled in the chapter place. After many and various discussions held among themselves, they elected as abbot Voland, a certain monk of the same monastery. He was soon confirmed and ordained by Frederick of Bolanden, bishop of Speyer, and presided over this monastery for 6 years, 8 months, and 14 days: a wholly useless man, a dissipater of the monastery's substance, who pursued pleasures and the comforts of the flesh. He had no care for regular observance, and no thought for the governance of public honesty and advancement. By nation he was an Alsatian, born not far from Strasbourg; from the monastery of Gengenbach, under lord Abbot John, I do not know on what occasion he came to Hirsau, and, received by the brothers into the convent, became one of them. But when Abbot John had died, he was put into his place by cunning and artifice, governed badly, and in a few years disposed of many goods of the monastery by pledging them, sold them, and alienated them.

For in the second year of his rule, as we shall say below, he unjustly alienated a very profitable tithe, without the consent of the diocesan bishop and the brothers.

1276.

In the first year of Abbot Voland, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 1276, when Odacharus, king of Bohemia, did not keep the agreements which in the previous year he had promised to Rudolf, king of the Romans, King Rudolf himself again entered Bohemia with a great army, overcame Odacharus in war, killed him, and subjected the whole kingdom to his power.

Moreover, the duchy of Austria, together with Styria and Carinthia, belonging to the empire, as we have said above, he conferred upon his first-born son named Albert; and with the consent of the princes he placed him, from the number of the counts, into the college of dukes. Thus the duchy of the house of Austria came by imperial munificence to the counts of Habsburg, and remains with them down to the present day. From this Albert all the dukes of Austria have descended in order down to Maximilian, who reigns today, and his son Philip, duke of Brabant, as we shall say in what follows.

In the year noted above Pope Innocent V died, of the order of the Friars Preachers, and was buried at Rome in the Lateran church. He was succeeded in the pontificate by Othobonus, Genoese by birth, cardinal deacon of St. Adrian, nephew of Pope Innocent, called Adrian V; he presided for one month and ten days, and died at Viterbo before the office of consecration, and was buried there in the convent of the Friars Minor. This pontiff [unclear] King Rudolf by letters, and [unclear] his son Conradin [unclear] had conferred upon himself. In Rome he did everything according to his own will, God avenging the wrong done to them. But Rudolf, entangled in the Bohemian war, could not satisfy the pontiff. When Adrian also had died within forty days, Peter, bishop of Tusculum, a Lisbonese by birth, succeeded to the pontificate and was called John XXI. He presided for eight months; when he at last died at Viterbo, a new chamber having fallen upon him, the Apostolic See was vacant for six months. He was most learned in medicine and philosophy, and wrote many things. Among them there is extant a certain little summa, which they call the Treasure of the Poor, a work indeed pleasant, delightful, and not useless in medicine.

1277.

In the second year of Abbot Voland, which was the year of the Lord's nativity 1277, this Abbot Voland, excessively given to banquets and pleasures, spending the substance of the monastery prodigally by distributing it to his friends and kinsmen and other useless persons, began, when money failed, to dispose of and alienate the immovable property of the monastery. And first he sold the tithe, with all its revenues in Elmendingen and the half share in Wyl, to the grave and perpetual loss of this monastery; and he spent that money for the uses of his own people, not for the advantage of posterity, as he ought to have done. Several other [goods?] of the monastery also [unclear] alienated immovable goods during the time of his administration; their names an excessive lapse of time thereafter brought into oblivion. Indeed, this age was full of sloth, and the monks did not take care to bring deeds done to the knowledge of posterity through writings, but, having become ignorant and carnal, they pursued the vain and useless things of the world.

In the same year Henry of Vinstingen, archbishop of Trier, built the castle beside the Moselle that is called Bernkastel; he surrounded the town itself with a wall. Since it is otherwise enclosed by very high mountains on the east, south, and north, and by the river Moselle on the west, it could seem impregnable by the protection of nature.

Also in the same year Hartmann, a youth, the third-born son of Rudolf, king of the Romans, was drowned in the Rhine not far from Basel, and was buried with his mother in the church of Basel itself.

Also in the year noted above, Eberhard, bishop of Worms, who was in Italy, died. His body was brought back to Germany and buried in the monastery of Otterburg, of the Cistercian order. Frederick succeeded him in the episcopate and presided for almost six years.

In the same year, on the day of St. Heribert the bishop, William, count of Jülich, with three sons and noble armed knights, entered Aachen secretly in the evening, about the ninth hour, wishing to take the city and subject it to his own lordship. When this was learned, the citizens ran to arms, attacked him and all his men in the middle of the marketplace, and killed them, so that not one escaped. For the expiation of this deed they were afterward heavily fined. For in the end they were compelled forever to give to the counts of Jülich a third part of the offerings in the church of the blessed Mary ever virgin, whether coming from the devotion of pilgrims or accruing from any source whatever. The counts of Jülich, who are now dukes, also received from that time until the present day the institution of the provost of the church of Aachen. But when William, count of Jülich, had died, Siegfried, archbishop of Cologne, long before an enemy of his, allied with the people of Aachen, entered his land, bereft of its prince, with armed force, destroyed everything with sword and fire, captured towns, occupied fortifications, and reduced the whole county to his power. Against him the duke of Brabant, with the aid of the kinsmen and friends of the slain count, led an army, but accomplished little. At length, when Pope Martin IV interposed his offices, peace was made; the archbishop restored all the lordships, towns, castles, and villages that he had taken away.

Also in the year noted above, after the apostolic see had been vacant for six months, the cardinals at last elected John Gaetano, a Roman by country, of the Orsini family, as supreme pontiff. He was called Nicholas III and presided for three years, eight months, and twenty days.

[unclear] became an enemy of the archbishop.

In these times also, under Frederick, bishop of Worms, the convent of nuns of the Order of Preachers at Hocheim near Worms was founded in honor of the blessed Mary ever virgin by Dirolphus the knight and Agnes his wife, who [unclear].

Spanheim, the castle Bickelnheim, is situated not far from my monastery of Spanheim, [unclear], with many killed on both sides. Among the chief men whom [unclear] on the side of that count [unclear], the count of Velingen, with many other nobles, most distinguished men, all of whom were held in captivity for two years, until between the archbishop and the aforesaid counts [unclear], to serve the Lord there perpetually in holy virginity.

In the fourth year of Abbot Volandus, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1279, a fierce war was waged between Werner, archbishop of Mainz, and John, count of Spanheim, in the field near Sprendlingen, one mile from Kreuznach. In it the count with his men was overcome, with many captured and many more killed on both sides. Among the chief men whom the aforesaid archbishop led away captive were the count of the Rhine, count Emicho of Leiningen, [unclear], the count of Veldenz the younger. They handed over to that same convent all movable and immovable goods [unclear] the daughter [unclear] with all movable and immovable goods. [unclear], to serve there perpetually in holy virginity.

In the same year Henry, count of Veldenz, seneschal of the church of Mainz, [unclear] entered into a treaty [unclear] with lord Werner, archbishop of Mainz, for himself and his heirs. At length, through Rudolf, king of the Romans, peace was made at Mainz in the year of the Lord 1281, in the ninth indiction, on the [unclear] day of December; in it all the captives, after taking an oath of peace, were released.

198 The Monastery of Hirsau and his successors, in which they promised one another faithful assistance against any injurers whatsoever, as is clear in the letters of the same confederation, which were issued in the aforesaid year on the Kalends of September at Mainz.

1280.

In the fifth year of Abbot Volandus, in 1280 of the Lord’s Nativity, Albertus Magnus of the Order of Preachers died, formerly bishop of [unclear] in Bavaria, in the eighty-seventh year of his age. He was buried at Cologne in the middle of the choir of his convent, not without a reputation for sanctity.

In the same year Pope Nicholas III, in the third year of his pontificate, confirmed all the privileges, liberties, and goods of this monastery of Hirsau, at the request of the abbot and convent, giving them a bull under lead at Avignon, as is customary, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December. He also gave the same persons another bull confirming their privileges at Rome at St. Peter’s, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the first year of his pontificate.

1281.

In the sixth year of Abbot Volandus, in 1281 of the Lord’s Nativity, Rudolph, king of the Romans, after matters in Austria and Bohemia had been carried out prosperously, and after he had given his daughter in marriage to Wenceslaus, son of Otakar, king of Bohemia, whom, as we said above, he deprived of life and kingdom, surrounded [unclear] with a siege and took it. He also defeated the count himself, who came against him for battle with a very great army, and compelled him to surrender. Returning from Burgundy, he captured by assault Colmar, Zurich, [Bern?], and Hagenau, cities joined in rebellion; the leaders of the rebels were partly slain and partly outlawed, and the land was silent before him in peace.

In the same year Pope Nicholas III died at Rome, at St. Peter’s, and was buried with honor; and the Apostolic See was vacant for five months because of the discord of the cardinals. When these months had passed, at last they elected Simon, cardinal priest of St. Cecilia, a Gaul by nation, born in the city of Tours, who was crowned on the tenth day before the Kalends of April and called Martin IV. He presided for four years and one month, a man of most holy conduct, who is said to have been renowned for miracles.

1282.

In the following year, which was 1282 of the Lord’s Nativity, since Abbot Volandus, by his bad rule, had inflicted very grave losses on this distinguished monastery, both in spiritual and temporal matters, the brothers, no longer able to bear his insolence and excessive prodigality, using the counsels of friends, finally induced him to resign the abbacy, which he had not been able usefully to govern and rule. Therefore he resigned the abbacy into the hands of the brothers on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the year of the Lord 1282, in the tenth indiction, after he had ruled it badly for six years, eight months, and fourteen days, not without damage to the monastery.

Concerning Lord Crafto, the twenty-eighth abbot of this monastery, who presided for eleven years, and concerning various deeds of that time in Germany.

[unclear]

Crafto became abbot [29?]. He presided for thirty-one years.

In the aforesaid year, King Rudolph violently captured Richenstein and Schonek, very strongly fortified castles of robbers, and utterly destroyed them.

Also in the same year, on the second weekday after the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, the citizens of Mainz, after making an uprising against the Jews, killed many and drove the rest out of the city, stripped of all their goods; and soon afterward a general persecution of the Jews followed throughout all Germany.

Year [unclear].

Nikhestein. Schneck. Persecution of the Jews. Johannes Benedictus. Gottfriedus Hartmanns. Rodericus Munsterm. Stephanus Wernher. Theodoricus Schoenecker. Joachimus Krebs. Matthias Ludwig. Dominicus Freytag. Georgius Steinmetz. Jacobus Dietrich. Stephanus Reichardt. Martinus Pfaffenberger.

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

1283.

When the first year of Abbot Crafto had been completed, in the year of the Lord's Nativity 1283, on the day of St. Potentiana the virgin, the counts of Henneberg led an army against Berthold, bishop of Wurzburg, and burned with fire the very strong town of Schwarzach near the Main. Plundering the monastery of St. Felicity of our order, situated there outside the walls, they carried off everything they had found.

In the same year Pope Martin IV sent into Germany as legate a latere the bishop of Tusculum. Coming to Wurzburg, in the presence of Rudolf, king of the Romans, and of many princes, bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, and nobles, he held a council. There, among other matters, the legate himself in the name of the pope, and the king from the whole people of the empire, began to demand most urgently a contribution of the tenth penny from the clergy, many princes consenting to their view. But Siegfried, archbishop of Cologne, and Henry, archbishop of Trier, strongly opposing the unaccustomed and excessively burdensome exaction, wholly revoked the business.

1284.

In the second year of Abbot Crafto, in the year of the Lord's Nativity 1284, Frederick, bishop of Worms, died. Simon of Schoneck succeeded him and presided for eight years, three months, and fourteen days, a just man and of remarkable integrity, who did many good things.

In the same year, on the second day of the month of April, Werner of Falkenstein, archbishop [unclear], held a council; there, among other matters, the legate himself in the name of the pope, and the king from the whole people of the empire, began to demand most urgently a contribution of the tenth penny from the clergy, many princes consenting to their view. But Siegfried, archbishop of Cologne, and Henry, archbishop of Trier, strongly opposing the unaccustomed and excessively burdensome exaction, wholly revoked the business.

1285.

In the year of Abbot Crafto [unclear], with two having been elected in disagreement, namely Peter, canon of the greater church of Basel [unclear], bishop of Mainz, buried in the greater church; and the see of Mainz was vacant for almost three [unclear]. In the said church at the Steps, together with one tower adjoining the greater church and the new shops, it was burned.

In the same year Berthold, the forty-second bishop of Wurzburg, died and was buried in the greater church. Mangold of Neuenburg succeeded him and presided for twelve years.

1285.

In the third year of Abbot Crafto, in the year of the Lord's Nativity 1285, the church of Blessed Mary ever virgin at Mainz, called "at the Steps," together with one tower adjoining the greater church and with the new [unclear].

In the same year, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, the citizens of Wurzburg expelled from the city all the canons and clergy, stripping them of all their goods.

In this same year Louis, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, son of Otto, died. He was the first of the dukes of Bavaria to obtain the Palatinate, as was said in the preceding sections. Louis was buried in the monastery of Furstenfeld in Bavaria, which he himself had newly built in Bavaria in satisfaction for the wife he had killed. He left two sons: Rudolf, count palatine of the Rhine, who had taken as wife Mechthild, daughter of Adolf, king of the Romans, by whom he begot Rudolf, Rupert, and Adolf, concerning whom we shall speak later [unclear] count of Holland, Zeeland, and Hainaut and lord of Frisia; Otto called "the Roman," because he had been born at Rome; and Louis, the other duke of Bavaria. The mother of the aforesaid dukes was Margaret, sister of the king of France and daughter of William, count of Holland; after her father died without sons, she obtained the paternal county of Holland, Hainaut, and Zeeland, and assigned it to her son William, as we shall say in its proper place.

In the same year also Pope Martin IV died at Perugia and was buried in the greater church. At his tomb many sick persons brought there, blind persons led there, and mute and lame persons recovered their former health. Honorius IV, a Roman by origin, formerly called Jacob, cardinal deacon, succeeded him in the pontificate and presided for one year and eleven days, a good and upright man, a true lover of knowledge and honesty.

1286.

In the fourth year of Abbot Crafto, and in the year of the Lord's Nativity 1286, the aforesaid Pope Honorius, after annulling the election of the canons of Mainz, which they had made two years before Of the Monastery of Hirsau, concerning Peter the Physician and Gerhard of Epstein, he appointed Henry, bishop of Basel, as we said above, of the Order of Minors, as archbishop of the church of Mainz; he presided for one year, eleven months, five days. In the same year Rudolf, king of the Romans, driven by money, committed a shameful deed for a prince: he sent his chancellor into Italy, who, after receiving money, was to make peoples free, especially those who redeemed themselves by payment. The Lucchesi paid twelve thousand gold coins on this account, but the Florentines six thousand. Having immediately been made wholly free, they created the magistracy which they call the priors of the arts, with the addition of the standard-bearer of justice. In this way most of the other cities also, with money intervening, brought themselves into liberty.

MCCLXXXVII.

In the fifth year of Abbot Crato, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1287, the Jews stealthily seized a certain Christian boy, born from the village of Wamraid, named Werner, and brought him with them to the town of Wesel by the Rhine; and, in order to receive his blood, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, piercing him with needles and knives, after a long martyrdom they cruelly killed him. His little body, buried in the town of Bacharach, is shown incorrupt in a certain chapel up to the present day, and is venerated by the inhabitants of the place as a martyr, and is said to have been renowned for many signs.

In the year noted above Pope Honorius IV died, and the Apostolic See was vacant for ten months. He, after changing the striped mantles of the Carmelites into white ones, confirmed the Carmelite order, not sufficiently approved in the council, and the order of the hermits of Saint Augustine, which had been disapproved at Paris. He was buried at Rome in the church of Saint Peter.

MCCLXXXVIII.

In the sixth year of Abbot Crato, and the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1288, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, brother Henry of the Order of Minors, archbishop of Mainz, died and was buried in the major church at Mainz. After him two men were again elected in dissension: Gerard of Epstein, canon of Mainz and archdeacon of Trier, whom we have said was elected before Henry against Peter, and Emeric of Schoneck, scholasticus of Mainz. But while these things were happening at Mainz, the Apostolic See, Pope Honorius having died, as we said, was vacant; for this reason their case could not be concluded either in those regions or at Rome.

Meanwhile Henry, archbishop of Trier, died, and the aforesaid Gerard was postulated as archbishop by one part of the chapter against Bohemund. At length, after Nicholas IV had been created pope, Gerard went to Rome with a double election, and was ordained archbishop of Mainz by the pope himself against Emeric of Mainz and Bohemund of Trier. He presided for sixteen years, a prudent and magnanimous man, who ruled his church well and usefully and did many things vigorously in peace and war. Bohemund, however, having been ordained archbishop of Trier, presided for eleven years; he too did many things uprightly and defended the rights of the church.

In the year noted above the duke of Limburg died without children, and over his duchy a great dissension arose between John, duke of Brabant, and Reinhard, count of Guelders. [unclear] war [unclear] Waring. Henry, count of Westerburg, and also the count of Jülich, Everard count of Mark and his brother, and also the count of Saint-Pol, the count of Loon, the bishop of Liège, [unclear] the Cologne men, and many other very strong nobles. Moreover with Reinald, count of Guelders, were Siegfried, archbishop of Cologne, Henry [unclear]. Men fell on both sides, and at last John, duke of Brabant, obtained the victory. There, among many other nobles, Henry count of Luxembourg and his brother Walram fell. Reinald, count of Guelders, captured by the duke of Brabant, was compelled not only to yield his right to the duchy of Limburg, but also, for his own release, to give many castles, dominions, and a huge sum of money. Siegfried also, archbishop of Cologne, captured by Adolf count of Berg, was kept in custody for seven years, and could not be released before he freed himself from him, at great loss, with money, castles, and many revenues. Many others also were captured, and still more were killed. There are those who write that in that battle a hundred thousand men came together for the conflict of war.

In the same Chronicle of Jo. Trithemius. 201

In the same year, after the apostolic see had been vacant for ten months, the cardinals at last assembled at Perugia and elected as pope Jerome, cardinal priest of St. Sabina, of the Order of Friars Minor. He was called Nicholas IV and presided for 4 years, 1 month, and 8 days, a good man, a lover of religion and peace.

Nicholas IV is elected pope.

1289.

In the 7th year of Abbot Crafto, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1289, King Rudolph again led an army into Burgundy; and first, besieging the city of Payerne, he took it. Afterwards he captured the count of Burgundy, a rebel and perjurer, and put him in chains. He likewise captured the count of Savoy and the count of Montbeliard, and compelled them to swear to his dominion.

The king again into Burgundy.

1290.

In the same year Emicho, count of Lingen, Diether, son of Eberhard, count of Katzenelnbogen, Walter, count of Geroldseck, Gerlach the elder, lord of Limburg, also the count of Welingen and the count of Rieneck, died at one time near the Black Forest [unclear].

Counts [unclear] died.

Henry, duke of Bavaria, dies.

In the 8th year of Abbot Crafto, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1290, Henry, duke of Bavaria, son of Otto I from the dukes of Bavaria, count palatine, brother of Ludwig, of whom mention was made above, died. He had as wife Elisabeth, daughter of King Bela of Hungary; she bore him Otto, king of Hungary, and Ludwig and Stephen, dukes of Bavaria. These two, after their father’s death, held the lordship in Landshut.

Peter, abbot of Sponheim, died.

1291.

In the same year, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, Peter, the eighth abbot of my monastery of Sponheim, died. John II succeeded him and presided for 7 years and 11 months; with every zeal he took care to adorn the church, and in his first year he also had it dedicated anew, together with the altars. In these times, while Siegfried, archbishop of the church of Cologne, was for seven years, as we have said, captive under the custody of the count of Berg, Walram, count of Julich, raging with sword and fire through the lands of the church of Cologne, inflicted many harmful losses on the poor. Among other things he took a very strong castle of the church called Zulpich and utterly destroyed it. Stirred by a similar madness, Eberhard, count of Mark, entered Westphalia with a powerful army of his men, and devastated by burning and plunder the duchy of Angria belonging to the lordship of that archbishop, and subjected to himself many fortifications of the land, castles, and towns.

Assembly of the princes.

King Rudolph dies at Speyer.

1291.

In the 9th year of Abbot Crafto, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1291, Rudolph, king of the Romans, held a solemn assembly of the princes at Frankfurt, where with many entreaties, means, and methods he tried to induce the princes to elect his son Albert, duke [of Austria], as king. Yet he could not obtain this, although after the death of Adolf of Nassau that same son was at last made king, as we shall say in its place. Rudolph therefore went with his friends to Strasbourg for the sake of refreshing his spirit, and fell into an illness that could not be cured. Therefore he had himself quickly brought to Speyer, where his predecessors, kings and emperors, had been buried. When he had arrived there, he soon died in the aforesaid year, on the octave of the Division of the Apostles, and was buried there in the greater church; and the empire was vacant for almost one year, because of the discord of the princes.

Nicholas IV [unclear].

1292.

In the 10th year of Abbot Crafto, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1292, at the beginning of the month of May the princes assembled at Frankfurt, after the empire had been vacant for almost a year, in order to elect a king of the Romans. After many counsels and negotiations had been held among them, they [unclear] Adolf [unclear], who, having received the kingdom, ruled for 6 years. Against him Albert, duke of Austria, son of the late King Rudolph, exerted himself with the aid of certain princes, saying that the empire belonged to him by paternal right, and that no one else should be elected so long as someone fit for the kingdom could be found from the royal lineage. Therefore, on all the days that Adolf lived, Albert regarded him as an enemy, until at last, deserted by the princes, he was killed by him in the field of Worms.

Adolf, count of Nassau, becomes king for 8 years.

Albert, duke of Austria.

In the aforesaid year Gerhard, archbishop of Mainz, summoned a provincial synod to be celebrated with his suffragans and prelates at Aschaffenburg, where they assembled

Synod of Mainz. 202. Of the Monastery of Hirsau

the bishops of Eichstätt, Speyer, Würzburg, Bamberg, Hildesheim, and Worms, with many other abbots, provosts, deans, and priests, who enacted many and various measures useful in ecclesiastical affairs. When the council was dissolved, and each had set out on his own journey, Gerhard, provost of Utrecht, son of Eberhard, count of Katzenelnbogen, seized Frederick, bishop of Speyer, on the road beside a little village situated near Mainz, called Keferbach, and led him away captive, until, through the intervention of a pact of concord, he was released by him.

1293.

In the second year of Crafto, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity [1293], a great part was again consumed by a terrible fire. In the same year also, on the day of Saint Othmar the abbot, Simon, bishop of Worms, died and was buried in the monastery of Schönau. After his death Gerhard, son of the count [Hirluti?], commonly called Raugraf, was elected as his successor; before he could be confirmed, while the Apostolic See was vacant, he was overtaken by an untimely death. After him, in the following year, Eberhard of Strahlenberg was elected; he presided for only ten months, and died.

In the same year also, Adolf, the new king of the Romans, led an army against the margraves of Meissen, and made that very march subject to the Roman Empire and obedient, together with its princes. Between Philip, king of the French, and Edward, king of the English, in this same year there began a war which lasted for some years, with great loss to both, not without the bloodshed of many.

In these times also Eberhard, count of Württemberg, siding with Albert, duke of Austria, persecuted Adolf, king of the Romans, inflicting many losses upon him and receiving many in return. This Count Eberhard, a man impatient of peace, a lover of war, always in commotion, always restless, had disputes with all the kings who in his time governed the Roman Empire; he was hostile to all, rebellious and opposed to all. Allied with Rudolf the First, he rebelled with fourteen counts, as we said above. Later, in persecuting Adolf, he clung most firmly to Duke Albert. Then, after Adolf’s death, he was no less opposed to Albert than he had, with all his strength, persecuted the other kings before him.

In the year noted above Crafto, the twenty-eighth abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, died, having completed the second year of his rule; he was indeed a good man in his time, but by no means to be compared with the ancient fathers in zeal and fervor for monastic integrity, since he found the observance of regular discipline fallen into ruin and left it so.

Concerning Godfrey, Twenty-Ninth Abbot of This Monastery, who presided for seven years; and concerning various deeds of that time in Germany.

When the venerable Abbot Crafto had died and been buried, the brothers of this monastery came together in the chapter-place for the election of a new shepherd; after prayers had first been offered for counsel, they began to hold mature discussion among themselves. At length, after many deliberations, they unanimously elected Godfrey, a venerable old man, who had for a long time held the office of custodian, a Swabian by nation, born of honorable parents according to [unclear], who, confirmed by Frederick, bishop of Speyer, and blessed according to custom, was the twenty-ninth in the order of abbots of this monastery and presided for seven years. He was a man of great stature and elegant appearance, born of a [unclear] family, prompt and capable in carrying out affairs, subtle in intellect, cautious and prudent in counsel, eloquent in speech, outstanding in action, mature in life and conduct. He would gladly have restored the fallen observance of regular discipline to the former state of its integrity; but, with the monks, long since accustomed to laxity, opposing him, and the malice of the times resisting, he could not bring the holy purpose of reform to its due [unclear]. He bore their vexations [unclear]; and since he was a prudent man, he easily surpassed them all in counsel.

1293.

In the course of his first year, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1294, after the Apostolic See had been vacant for two years and almost four months, by divine ordinance at last, as was believed, Celestine V was elected pope: a hermit, professed under the rule of our holy father Benedict, from whom the order of Celestines took its beginning; a man of most holy conduct, called Peter before his pontificate. He presided for only five months and renounced the papacy.

Chronicle of Jo. Trithemius [unclear]. Boniface VIII succeeded him and presided for 8 years, 9 months, and 17 days; because of his scheming Celestine had resigned.

In these times also a great dispute arose between Philip, king of France, and Edward, king of England; on that occasion a fierce war was begun between them. The king of England summoned Adolf of Nassau, king of the Romans, to his aid for one hundred thousand marks of silver, on this condition: that the money be divided among the princes of the empire and that, by common agreement, they assist him against the French. But King Adolf, after receiving the money, held it back for his own uses, despising them. Hence, spurned by them also, and unable to keep his promises to the king of the English, he incurred great disgrace.

1295.

In the following year, which was the 2nd of Abbot Gotfrid, and the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1295, indiction 8, Albert, duke of Austria, son of Rudolf, formerly emperor, aspiring to the Roman kingdom, pursued King Adolf with all his strength, inflicting many losses on him.

The king of England [unclear] despised the princes, held back [unclear]. Hence, spurned by the same men, and unable to keep his promises to the king of the English, he incurred great disgrace.

1296.

In the same year Siegfried, archbishop of Cologne, after seven years of his captivity, was nevertheless freed from the hand of the count of Berg at a great price. Not long afterward, when the same king had resolved to deprive [him] of the duchy, overcome by fear of the princes adhering to him, he was compelled to change his plan.

Albert, duke of Austria, pursues King Adolf.

Siegfried.

The count of Berg is captured by treachery.

In the same year Siegfried, archbishop of Cologne, after seven years of his captivity, was freed [unclear] of the whole kingdom. Not long afterward the same archbishop, using craft and industry, against the oath of alliance, seized the same count, who feared no such thing, and consigned him to harsh imprisonment until death. The count, captured and detained in very great affliction, freely and of his own accord promised that he would restore to the archbishop everything that he had extorted from him, and would add greater things for his liberation; but he was not heard by the pontiff. Rather, he received from him this reproachful reply: “St. Peter has the means by which, from your goods and promises, he may maintain his servants; therefore you shall not be released while I live, but you shall undergo death in prison, and you shall learn how you ought to hold an archbishop captive.” And so the count died in custody.

In the same year also John, duke of Brabant, was killed in a tournament.

1297.

In the 3rd year of Abbot Gotfrid, the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1296, Manegold, bishop of Würzburg, died. Andrew of Gundelfingen succeeded him and presided for 22 years; he too had many disputes with his citizens, from whom he suffered various injuries.

Duke of Brabant.

Andrew becomes bishop of Würzburg.

Count Florentius of Holland is killed.

In the same year Florentius, count of Holland, in the 42nd year of his rule, betrayed by his own men, was cruelly killed at the hands of his adversaries on the third day before the Kalends of July. John, his son, succeeded him; he had taken as wife Elizabeth, daughter of Edward, king of the English, by whom he had no children. He ruled Holland only three years and six months, and waged many wars and battles.

In the same year also Pope Boniface VIII transferred John, bishop of Utrecht, to the church of Toul, and appointed in his place as pontiff Wilhelm, born at Mechelen, auditor of causes in the Roman Curia. He presided for 5 years amid many tribulations, and at length was killed in war.

Frisians killed.

1298.

In the 4th year of Abbot Gotfrid, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1297, John, count of Holland, having gathered a large army of his own men and Zeelanders, entered Frisia, and on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, after battle had been joined with the Frisians near Alkmaar, killed 4,000 of them.

King Adolf of the Romans.

Conspiracy of the princes against Adolf.

In these times also Adolf, king of the Roman Empire, [brought] many calamities and dissensions into the land among those who had peace. For at his command Hermann, count of Geroldseck, and a certain other count, appointed provincial prefects in Alsace, were exceedingly troublesome to Conrad of Lichtenberg, bishop of Strasbourg, and to all the people of Alsace, and inflicted many injuries, insults, and losses. Hence, provoked to impatience, the aforesaid bishop, the citizens of Strasbourg, the counts of Ochsenstein, the landgrave of Alsace, the count of Freiburg, the count of Zweibrücken, and the count of Hohenlohe, with many other princes, counts, nobles, and peoples, conspired unanimously against King Adolf; and, despising his commands and orders, [unclear], until, when many princes had joined in the same opinion, they at last deposed him from the kingdom and deprived him at once of life and honor, as we shall say in its place.

1298.

In the 5th year of Abbot Gotfrid, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1298, Siegfried, archbishop [unclear], died.

Boniface VIII. [Blank page in the source scan.]

204. MONASTERY OF HIRSAU.

…bishop of Cologne, buried in the church of Bonn, whom Wichbold, dean of the greater church, succeeded, and presided nearly 4 years; whom Bohemund, archbishop of Trier, weighed down by age and disease, soon took as his coadjutor.

In the same year, when king Adolf was weakening the empire, nourishing discords and wars, burdening the people with unaccustomed tributes, fostering robbers and oppressors of the poor, and despising the princes: Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, with certain other princes, called Albert, duke of Austria and count of Habsburg, son of Rudolf the former king of the Romans, from Austria to Mainz, promising that he—Adolf being deposed—would be elected king of the Romans. These [things] known, duke Albert came to the Rhine with a very great army of his [men], whom the princes of Alsace and the aforesaid counts, together with Everhard, count of Württemberg, meeting at Strasbourg with a great army, promised aid against Adolf. The Strasbourg-men, too, receiving four thousand warriors as aid, led [them] to Strasbourg. King Adolf, hearing these [things], soon walled Rouffach with a siege, but, the matter unfinished, [his men] lost, he betook himself into the city of Speyer, awaiting the outcome of the new affair. Meanwhile duke Albert, with a great army of dukes, counts, nobles, and soldiers gathered from Austria, Bohemia, Swabia, and Alsace—accompanied by the bishop of Constance, the bishop of Strasbourg, the provincial count of Alsace, and the aforenamed counts—with none resisting, came to Mainz, where he found Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, Wichbold, elect of Cologne, with certain other princes, assembled. There, therefore, on the vigil of the nativity of St John the Baptist, the princes, king Adolf having been deposed from the kingdom by sentence on account of grave excesses, unanimously elected duke Albert himself as king, and promised him fidelity, obedience, and assistance against whatsoever adversaries. These [things] accomplished at Mainz with great solemnity, Albert the new king, with his whole army, crossed to the town of Alzey, set in mid-journey from Worms to Kreuznach, destroying the whole of it except the castle, and there, tents fixed, settled, about to fight against king Adolf. Meanwhile king Adolf, hearing that he was deprived of the kingdom, and Albert elected by the princes, was dismayed in mind, and, gathering a great army of warriors from the cities faithful to him—Speyer, Worms, Oppenheim, Frankfurt—together with his princes (namely Rudolf, count Palatine and duke of Bavaria, his son-in-law; the count of Isenburg also; the count of Sponheim; the Hairy count; and many others), betook himself to Oppenheim, and for ten days awaited the aids of the friends to whom he had written. But, ten days elapsed, before the promised aids of [his] friends came, impatient of delay, inconsiderately and too precipitately, unequal in strength, he advanced to battle, between the village called Göllheim and the nuns' monastery called Rosenthal, not far from the Worms field; where, battle joined, it was sharply fought, and many fell on either side. King Adolf himself, too, fought most bravely with his own hand; to whom, when victory now seemed to be approaching, his [men] began to flee, and he, deserted in the midst of [his] adversaries, was killed in the same place, and his son captured—the count of Isenburg also, the bravest captain on his side. [Margin: The king is buried at Rosenthal. Albert is made king. The offspring of Albert. The king's six sons.] Otto, count of Oxenstein, supreme captain of Albert, fell there too, with sixty companions and the chief nobles of the land. But the body of the slain king Adolf was buried in the aforesaid monastery of Rosenthal, until the times of Henry, king of Luxembourg, by whose command it was brought with honor to Speyer and placed in the tombs of the kings. There are [those] who write that all those who conspired against king Adolf perished by an evil death, divine grace avenging his injury. For Albert himself, the usurper of the kingdom, was killed by his brother's son, as we shall say in [its] place; the count of Holloch and the count of Oxenstein were likewise killed; the archbishop of Mainz, sitting on his chair, was carried off by an unexpected death; the count of Zweibrücken was drowned in the bank called Glan; Conrad, bishop of Strasbourg, before Freiburg, was slain by a sword by a certain peasant; the count of Leiningen became frenzied and was made wretched by various calamities; and almost all the rest passed from this world by a similar destruction. But Albert, escaping the victor with his princes, sets out for the city of Aachen, and there is crowned king of the Romans by Wichbold, archbishop of Cologne, and reigned 10 years. He had as wife Elizabeth, daughter of Meinhard, duke of Carinthia, of whom he begot six sons and five daughters. The first-born was Rudolf, king of Bohemia. The second, Frederick, duke of Austria, who was elected against Louis the Bavarian, the emperor, as we shall say below. The third was Leopold, duke of Carinthia and Styria. The fourth was Henry the duke, who had as wife Elizabeth, daughter of the count of Virn[eburg]… [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

Virnenburg. The fifth was Duke Albert, who founded the monastery in Gimeneo; through him the line of dukes is continued. The last of the sons was Duke Otto, who had as wife Elisabeth, daughter of the duke of Bavaria. Of the daughters, the first, Agnes, married Andrew, king of Hungary, and after him the duke of Vratislavia. The second, Elisabeth, married Frederick, duke of Lorraine, to whom she bore Rudolf, who succeeded his father in the duchy. The third, Anna, married Hermann, margrave of Brandenburg. The fourth was Catharina, who was betrothed to Henry of Luxembourg, king of the Romans; when he died before the wedding, she married Rupert, king of Apulia. Ulrich, count of Oetingen, a vigorous and warlike man, took as wife the fifth and last of his daughters, named Gutta.

In this same year in which Albert was elected king of the Romans, the city of Cologne, which for seven years, the same number of months, and nine days had lain under excommunication and ecclesiastical interdict because of disputes and dissensions held with Archbishop Sifrid, with the consent of Wichbold, his successor, was absolved by Pope Boniface VIII, and divine offices were again permitted to be celebrated in it. In the same year also, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, John II died, the ninth abbot of my monastery of Spanheim; Dietlib, formerly chancellor of John, count of Spanheim, succeeded him and presided for six years and six months. He renewed again the observance of regular discipline, which had utterly collapsed.

In the same year, on the fifth day before the Ides of November, Bohemund, archbishop of Trier, died. He had built anew from the foundations the castle of Neumagen, near Trittenheim, the village of my birth, on the Moselle. He was buried at Hemelrad, a monastery of the Cistercian order.

After him Diether of Nassau, brother of the former king Adolf, not elected nor postulated, but out of hatred for King Albert ordained archbishop by Pope Boniface VIII, was sent to Trier. He presided for almost eight years. He was of the Order of Preachers, and although he was always opposed to Albert, he was nevertheless able to do nothing.

In the same year also, on the vigil of Saint James the Apostle, lord Emicho, bishop of Worms, died, buried in the major church under the monastic habit, as they say. Eberwin of Kronenberg succeeded him and presided for three years and [unclear] months. At the insistence of his citizens he consented that from the community sixteen men should be admitted to the council of the senate, which had not been done before.

In his time the convent of nuns of the Order of Preachers, which is called Liebenau, outside the walls of the city of Worms near Neuhausen, was founded by a certain citizen named Jacob Engelmar, abundantly provided with the necessary goods for the support of the handmaids of Christ, and that foundation itself was confirmed by him.

1299.

In the sixth year of Abbot Gotfrid, which was the one thousand two hundred ninety-ninth year of the Lord’s nativity, Pope Boniface VIII condemned the heresy of those who called themselves Fraticelli, and utterly destroyed it everywhere.

In the same year, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, John, count of Holland, died at Haarlem, without children. After his death John, count of Hainaut, son of Adelaide, sister of the former William, king of the Romans, assumed the duchy by right of kinship and joined all Holland to his dominion. He had taken as wife Philippa, daughter of the count of Luxembourg, by whom he begot John, the first-born; William, successor as count of Holland; John, lord of Beaumont; Henry, canon of the church of Cambrai; Margaret, countess of Artois; Adelaide, countess of Clermont; Mary, countess of Bourbon; and Mechtild, countess of Nyede. Against this John, King Albert held an assembly of princes, asserting that the county of Holland had fallen vacant to the Roman Empire; yet by the counsel of the princes he granted it to him in fief.

1300.

In the seventh year of Abbot Gotfrid, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1300, Pope Boniface VIII first instituted at Rome the jubilee of plenary remission and indulgence of all sins from punishment and guilt, and commanded that it be celebrated again after a hundred years. This was a new thing, previously unheard of: because such indulgences had been announced throughout the whole world in the preceding year, so great a multitude of people set out from all Germany for Rome that it seemed utterly infinite and innumerable. And from that time the use of the jubilee began in the Roman Church; there had previously been no account of it. Among the many princes, bishops, abbots, and other prelates who then sought Rome, Gotfrid too, the twenty-ninth abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, went there with certain brothers for the grace of the jubilee, in hope of eternal reward. So great a multitude of people came to Rome from all sides in that year that it was scarcely possible to walk through the city, broad and vast though it is.

The daughters of King Albert were [unclear].

The people of Cologne are released from the interdict.

Abbot John.

Bohemund, archbishop of Trier, died.

Emicho died.

The monastery of Liebenau is founded.

The heresy of the Fraticelli is condemned. John, count of Holland, died.

The jubilee year is instituted by the pope.

Gotfrid, otherwise Romanus, is recorded.

Gotfrid, otherwise Romanus, is recorded. [Blank page in the source scan.]

206. Of the Monastery of Hirsau

In the same year Albert, king of the Romans, entered the lower parts of Germany with a strong hand, with the mind and intention of making war on John, count of Hainaut, who, as we have said, had occupied Holland. And when he had come to Nijmegen, a town of Guelders, he caused letters such as these to be published throughout the whole region: “Let all men know that Albert, king of the Romans, ever unconquered, has powerfully incorporated into the Roman Empire the vacant principality of Holland, which Emperor Charles, once called the Great, gave as a fief to Count Theoderic.” But when John heard that the king was about to come against him with an army, he gathered a very great multitude of armed men. The king, fearing his boldness and at the same time his strength, entered into peace with him through the mediation of the archbishop of Cologne, and granted him the county of Holland, always to be received as a fief from the Empire.

In the year noted above, while the Jubilee was still continuing at Rome, lord Gotfrid, abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, died in the twenty-ninth year of his rule and the sixty-eighth of his age, a good, mature, prudent man, who governed honorably enough and usefully.

Concerning Henry the Second, Thirtieth Abbot of This Monastery, Who Presided for Seventeen Years; Concerning Various Deeds in His Time

When Abbot Gotfrid had died and been buried, the brethren, bereft of a shepherd, assembled together at the time already appointed by the senior monks through the prior. After many counsels and various deliberations, at last they unanimously elected as the thirtieth abbot of this place Henry, the second of that name. Confirmed and ordained, as is customary, by Frederick of Bolanden, bishop of Speyer, he governed this monastery badly for seventeen years, and at last, by command of Emperor Louis IV, was deposed because of the deformity of his life and the squandering of the substance of the monastery, as we shall say in its proper place. He was by nation a Swabian, born of respectable parents; when he was eighteen years old, under Abbot Voland, he became a monk. He was a man given over to quiet idleness, ready and prompt with words for anything whatever, but slow and inept in work and action. Once ordained abbot, he soon began to conduct himself licentiously in all things, and, given over to idleness and sloth, shamefully neglecting both the household property and regular observance, he reduced it almost to nothing. For the temporal condition of this monastery, which he found in good state, he finally left in bad state when he yielded office. He pledged many of the monastery’s goods, sold many, and secretly alienated many without the consent of his subjects; and the price he partly gave to his blood-relatives and worthless persons, and partly consumed uselessly. In morals he was dissolute, wholly secular, since by day and night he was accustomed to have nothing else among his delights than banquets and pleasures. He neither possessed in himself the observance of regular discipline, nor took care to reform it in his subjects. Finally, he was not free from suspicion of a graver crime, because the curtain of vices is accustomed to draw after it a curtain.

1301

In the first year of Abbot Henry, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1301, a comet appeared in the sky. Many evils followed, seditions and rumors of wars in various regions.
