In the same year, on the fourth day before the Nones of July, William, bishop of Utrecht, was killed in war by his enemies, after he had governed the church of Utrecht for almost five years amid many storms of tribulation and persecution. Guy, canon and treasurer of the church of Liege, succeeded him and presided for sixteen years, a man magnificent in all respects. His natural brothers were Botzard, bishop of Metz; John, bishop of Cambrai; John, count of Holland; and Florentius, prince of Morea.

Also in the same year, on the day of Saint Mary Magdalene, Henry, count of Luxembourg, set up his camp beside the church of the Holy Cross, and laid waste everything round about: hamlets, houses, vineyards, wine-presses, and orchards. He would have advanced further, had not almighty God, through the merits of his saints resting at Trier, sent upon them, on the eleventh night after they had arrived, a spirit of dizziness, so that they struck one another and fled, with no one pursuing.

1302

In the second year of Abbot Henry, but of the Lord’s Nativity [1302], in February, Frederick of Bolanden, bishop of Speyer, died; he was buried in the monastery of Eußerthal of the Cistercian order. Sibodo of Lichtenberg succeeded him and presided for eleven years.

In the same year Gerard, archbishop of Mainz; Diether, archbishop of Trier; Henry, archbishop of Cologne; Rudolf, count palatine of the Rhine,

Frederick, bishop of Speyer, died. Sibodo succeeded in the episcopate. John, count of Hainaut, renowned. Gotfrid, abbot of this place, died. Henry is elected the thirtieth abbot. The origin and life of this abbot. The substance of the monastery is squandered. A comet appeared. William, bishop of Utrecht, is killed. Henry, count of Luxembourg. [Blank page in the source scan.]

of the Rhine, and certain other princes, swore among themselves a great and very firm league and confederation; Albert, king of the Romans, took it very ill, as made to the detriment of his power. Therefore, bringing a great armed army from Austria and Swabia, he first entered the lands of Rudolf, count palatine of the Rhine, and, inflicting much damage on the poor, received him graciously when he came to surrender. Then, moving his army against the archbishop of Mainz, among the other losses that he brought upon him, he also surrounded Bingen, a town on the Rhine, with a siege. But the archbishop, seeing himself unequal in strength, sought and obtained the king’s grace; and coming to Bingen he lifted the siege by entreaties, and accepted the conditions of peace proposed by the king, resigning into the king’s hands the towns of Bingen and Lahnstein, with the castles Klopp, Ehrenfels, Scharfenstein, and certain others. When matters had been pacified with the archbishop of Mainz, King Albert led his army against the archbishops of Cologne and Trier, and subjected both to his rule; he forced them vigorously, not without losses on their part, to seek his grace.

In the same year, when a multitude had been stirred up in France against their rulers, craftsmen and men of the lowest condition revolted from the French; and, having become lords of the province, they overcame in war the great forces of the king of France and slew them most cruelly. But their savagery did not last long before they were all destroyed.

A.D. 1303.

In the third year of Abbot Henry, and of the Lord’s Nativity 1303, in the first indiction, Philip, king of the French, bearing with an unjust mind the arrogance of Pope Boniface VIII, caused him to be seized at Anagni, in his father’s house, while he was sleeping at night and fearing no such thing, and brought under guard to Rome. Worn out by grief of mind, he died thirty-five days later and was buried in the church of St Peter, after having first been taken from the tomb. Benedict XI, by nation a Trevisan, previously called Nicholas, cardinal of Ostia, succeeded him in the pontificate and presided only nine months.

A.D. 1304.

In the fourth year of Abbot Henry, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1304, on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, Gerhard, archbishop of Mainz, born of Eppstein, died. After his death the see of Mainz was vacant for some time. Meanwhile, in the same year, at the beginning of the month of June, Pope Benedict XI died at Perugia, in the church of the Friars Preachers, of whose order he had previously been a professed member. He was buried with great pomp, not without a reputation for sanctity, and the Apostolic See was vacant for two months, until the following year, not without loss to the salvation of many souls.

In the same year, between Guy, count of Flanders, and William, son of John, Eberwin, bishop of Worms, [unclear]; Emerich of Kronenberg succeeded him and presided for ten years, a peaceful and devout man. Also in the aforesaid year, on the third day before the Kalends of May, Eberwin, bishop of Worms, died; Emerich of Kronenberg succeeded him and presided for [unclear]. On the Ides of September the aforesaid John of Holland and Hainaut died [unclear]; and in the same year, on the fifth Ides of July, magnificent disputes arose in Holland, which, growing into very grave wars, miserably consumed many vigorous men on both sides. [unclear] a magnificent man, who had as wife Joan of Valois, sister of the king of France; by her he begot John the count, Margaret empress of England, William, heir received in the county, [unclear], Philippa queen of England, and Elizabeth, who died as a young woman.

A.D. 1305.

In the fifth year of Abbot Henry, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1305, after a long vacancy of the Apostolic See, the cardinals at last assembled at Perugia and unanimously elected Bertrand, bishop of Bordeaux, as pope. He was called Clement V and presided eight years, ten months, and eighteen days. He transferred the curia from Rome into France, not without the greatest inconvenience to Italy, and especially to the city of Rome; and there it remained continuously for seventy-four years.

To this Pope Clement, while he was staying at Poitiers, Henry, count of Luxembourg, sent Master Peter of Aspelt, his most experienced physician, to obtain the archbishopric of Mainz for his brother Baldwin, for at that time, after the death of Archbishop Gerhard, it was vacant, as we have already said. When Peter came into France to the pontiff, he set forth the embassy of his lord, the aforesaid count, and poured out many prayers to obtain the archbishopric of Mainz for the aforesaid brother of his lord. But the pope, after very many reasons had been alleged, would not listen to the petitioner, and refused to give the church of Mainz to Count Baldwin. Meanwhile it happened that the pontiff himself fell gravely ill, who by the art and skill [unclear]

The king’s expedition against the princes. Bingen is surrounded with a siege. League [unclear] in France. Benedict [unclear]. Gerhard, archbishop, dies. Eberwin, bishop of Worms, dies. A savage war in Holland. William, count of Holland. Pope Clement V is elected. Peter, physician of the count of Luxembourg. [Blank page in the source scan.]

208. Of the Monastery of Hirsau

Clement the pope, sick, is cured. Peter the physician becomes archbishop of Mainz.

[unclear] of the same Peter, having been cured, with the consent of the cardinals, he ordained him archbishop of the often-mentioned church of Mainz, and, after giving letters and the necessary provisions, sent him back to Mainz with the pallium. The clergy, together with all the people, obeying the apostolic commands, received him with honor and reverence, and peacefully admitted him into possession of the church of Mainz. For he was a learned and magnificent man, worthy of the pontificate itself, who established many things useful for morals in synods, and presided vigorously for fifteen years. Hearing this, Henry, count of Luxembourg, who had sent him to the pope on behalf of his brother Baldwin, was angry, although afterward he confessed that the whole thing had been done by divine ordinance. For through the agency of the same master, Baldwin was afterward made archbishop of Trier, and Henry himself king of the Romans, as we shall say.

King Albert holds the funeral rites at Speyer.

In the same year, on the day of the commemoration of Saint Paul the Apostle, Albert, king of the Romans, celebrated with great pomp the obsequies of the recently deceased king of Bohemia in the greater church of Speyer, with many princes, bishops, and abbots standing by. Among them Henry, the aforementioned abbot of this house, was present, not of the lowest reputation. There, during the ringing, the great bell fell, and, breaking two vaults, fell to the pavement and was split into two parts.

In these times also a great discord arose between Diether, archbishop of Trier, and the townsmen of Koblenz, the pontiff oppressing the townsmen with exactions, and they refusing obedience. At last the archbishop, unable to endure their insolence any longer, hired fighters with money, besieged Koblenz, took it, and received its surrender, the townsmen being compelled to obedience. He spent much money on the preparation for this victory; to obtain it he pledged almost all the estates of his diocese.

1306.

In the sixth year of Abbot Henry, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1306, on the day of the Purification of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, when the ice and snows had melted, there was a very great inundation of waters around the Rhine and the Main, which brought almost infinite losses upon the people living round about, overthrowing many houses and dwellings, and with incredible fury devastating gardens, vineyards, fields, and meadows. By its excessive force it threw down the bridge over the Main at Frankfurt, partly overturned the walls of Mainz, utterly overthrew two towers in the wall of Cologne, and drowned many people in various places. In these times the Hospitallers of Saint John of Jerusalem, aided by Christian forces, after vigorously besieging the island of Rhodes, together with five others adjacent in the Mediterranean Sea, continuously for four years, finally obtained them; the Turks were killed and expelled, and they have peacefully held it down to the present day, for 196 years.

In this same year the Jews throughout the kingdom of France, after all their goods had been brought into the fisc, were killed; others were driven from the kingdom half-naked.

1307.

In the seventh year of Abbot Henry, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1307, indiction 5, when Diether of Nassau, archbishop of Trier, had alienated very much because of the multitude of expenses for the preparations of war, he was denounced by his clergy and summoned to the examination of the Apostolic See in Gaul. But before the date for appearing arrived, he was seized by illness and departed from this life on the twenty-third day of November. He was buried in the church of the Preachers, of whose order he had previously made profession, in the city of Trier. After his death, lord Peter, archbishop of Mainz, had such influence with Pope Clement V and brought it about that Baldwin, brother of Henry, count of Luxembourg, a young man in the year of his age [unclear], to whom two years before he had denied the church of Mainz because of his minority, as we have said, was raised to the archbishopric of Trier. After being ordained, and received honorably as archbishop by all the clergy and people of Trier, he presided for forty-six years, one month, and eighteen days, a man in every respect vigorous and magnificent, who ruled his church excellently and recovered everything alienated.

1308.

In the eighth year of Abbot Henry, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1308, Albert, king of the Romans, when he had crossed the Rhine by boat with a few men, while the rest of the army waited for the boat on the other side of the bank, as is customary, John, his nephew through his brother, approached with the associates of his conspiracy and killed him when he feared no such thing; slipping away in flight, he escaped. The cause was this: Rudolf, duke of Swabia, brother of King Albert, when about to die, entrusted the aforesaid John, his son, still a boy, together with his whole duchy, to his guardianship. When he had grown up, he asked his uncle for his paternal duchy, asserting that he was now sufficient to govern. But since Albert [text breaks off] Chronicle of Jo. Trithemius.

...we despise. The aforesaid Brother Bernard, however, had many illustrious men as witnesses of his innocence, and likewise letters of John the king, son of the Emperor, and of archbishops and bishops who were present at the Emperor's death and excused him in a clear voice, namely those of Milan, Genoa, Perugia, Lucca, and Strasbourg.

The opinion of [Genosus?] is justly refuted.

Nevertheless Henry, count of Flanders, and the other noble courtiers, on the contrary, steadfastly affirmed that Bernard was guilty of the Emperor's death, and that he had poisoned him in the sacrament of the body of Christ. Hence a great persecution of the Order of Preachers arose, with too little justice, even if that brother had not been innocent of the charge laid against him, since the crime of one man should not have been referred to the whole order. In these times there was a great famine everywhere in the land, and a great pestilence followed, and in both dangers many people perished.

1314.

In the fourteenth year of Abbot Henry, which was the year 1314 of the Lord's nativity, Pope Clement V died, in the ninth year of his pontificate not yet completed; and the see of Peter was vacant for two years, three months, and seventeen days, because of discord among the brethren.

In the same year, on the day before the Ides of January, Sibodo of Lichtenberg, bishop of Speyer, died. Emicho of Liningen succeeded him and presided for fourteen years, not without dissension among his citizens, as is their custom.

In the same year also, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, Emericus, bishop of Worms, died. Henry, son of the Wildgrave of Dune, provost of the house, succeeded him and presided for five years.

In the same year also, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, the princes of the empire assembled at Frankfurt for the election of a new king; and when the votes were divided in different directions, Peter, archbishop of Mainz, Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, Volmar, margrave of Brandenburg, and John, king of Bohemia, elected Louis, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, as king of the Romans. Against him Henry, archbishop of Cologne, [unclear], and it lasted eight years; then at last Louis prevailed and reigned alone, captured Frederick, and forced him to surrender. His own brother Rudolf, count palatine of the Rhine, who obstinately took Frederick's side, he proscribed from his homeland and banished to England until the end of his life; there, living in great poverty, he finally died. Thus he held the Palatine county, with the other things that had belonged to Rudolf, for some time, but all [unclear]. This Louis had as wife Margaret, daughter of William, count of Holland; she bore him six sons: Louis, margrave of Brandenburg; Stephen, duke of Bavaria, dwelling in Landshut; Albert in Straubing; William, duke of Holland, afterwards count; Louis called the Roman, because he had been born at Rome; and Otto, duke, who was called the Brandenburger.

In the year noted above, three moons appeared at once in the sky. A brightness also, which they call a comet, shone in the sky for three months.

1315.

In the fifteenth year of Abbot Henry, which was the year 1315 of the Lord's nativity, there was a very great famine throughout all Germany, in which many thousands of people perished from want; and it lasted for two years. Afterwards an immense pestilence among people followed everywhere.

In the same year a battle took place between Louis, king of the Romans, and Frederick, duke of Austria, his adversary, near the city of Speyer, where Leopold, Frederick's brother, burned several villages round about with fire and inflicted much damage on the poor. Yet Louis came out victorious, and compelled Frederick his adversary, with his men, to flee shamefully. The famine, as we have said, was very great; but through the provision of Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, nothing necessary was lacking to the army.

In the same year also, in the city of Krems in the diocese of Passau, in the duchy of Austria, several most abominable heretics, investigated by the brothers Preachers, were found and burned. The first of the articles of their heresy was this: they said that Masses were vanity, and of no reverence or usefulness. The second article was: they said that Lucifer, with his demons, had been driven from heaven unjustly and was at last to be restored with all his own to blessedness; that Michael and all the angels were to be assigned to eternal torments; and that human beings outside their sect were likewise to be damned. Hence, when they greeted one another, they said: May he who suffered injury greet you, that is, Lucifer.

A most wicked heresy.

The third article, most abominable, was this: for they said...

Chronicle of Johann Trithemius.

keeping him in suspense from day to day with fair words, he pretended not to return what had been entrusted to him; the nephew, using the counsel of wicked men, resolved to kill him. Thus, having found an opportunity, he ran him through with a sword on the bank of the Rhine, as we have said, not far from Schaffhausen, on the day of Saints Philip and James the Apostles, which was the first day of May. His corpse was brought to Speyer the following year and was buried with honor among the kings in the greater church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September.

In the same year, in the month of November, the prince-electors assembled at the village called Rhense, not far from Boppard, near the royal seat; and, through the agency of lord Peter, archbishop of Mainz, they unanimously elected as king of the Romans Henry, count of Luxembourg, brother of Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, a good and vigorous man, worthy of imperial honor. They solemnly made public his election at Frankfurt on 27 November; and thereafter, on the feast of the Epiphany of the Lord in the following year, he was anointed and crowned king of the Romans at Aachen by the hands of Henry, archbishop of Cologne. He reigned four years and nine months. Soon after he had been crowned and came from Aachen to Speyer, he caused the bones of Kings Adolf and Albert to be brought to the greater church of Speyer and buried with honor. He had as wife Margaret, daughter of John, duke of Brabant, by whom he begot John, king of Bohemia, of whom we shall speak later.

John Scotus, the Subtle Doctor, dies.

In the year already noted, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, John, the Subtle Doctor, of the Order of Minors, died at Cologne and was buried there in his convent at the entrance to the sacristy. How much he wrote, and how subtle and profound in receptive theology, all theologians know, and we have noted it in our book on ecclesiastical writers.

In these times also Peter, archbishop of Mainz, newly constructed from the foundations a monastery of monks of the Carthusian order outside the walls of Mainz, and provided for it magnificently.

1309.

In the ninth year of Abbot Henry, the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1309, on the day of Saint Michael the Archangel, Dietlib, the tenth abbot of my monastery of Sponheim, died: a good man and an outstanding lover of regular observance. He presided usefully in both states, for he both took away the private property which his predecessors had allowed the monks, and suitably enlarged the revenues of the monastery. In the abbacy of Sponheim he was succeeded by lord Willich, a conventual monk, son of the count of Westerburg, brother of the countess of Sponheim; and he presided vigorously for 27 years, [unclear] months, and 14 days. Concerning his life, morals, and governance we have arranged a full history according to the sequence of years in the Chronicle of the aforesaid monastery of Sponheim.

In the same year, when the king of Hungary died without children, the nobles of the land and the elders unanimously elected Otto, duke of Bavaria, son of Duke Henry, as king of Hungary, as the nearest heir, because through his mother he was the grandson of King Béla. Summoning him from Bavaria, they received him with great honor. But not long afterward, changing their mind, they drove him out of Hungary. Returning to Bavaria, he died not much later, leaving an only son, Henry, an infant of fourteen days, by his wife, the daughter of the duke of Poland; he was called prince of [Notterberg?].

1310.

In the tenth year of Abbot Henry, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1310, Henry, king of the Romans, held a great assembly of princes at Speyer. There Elisabeth, daughter of a former king of Bohemia, appeared in person and sought from the emperor to be enfeoffed with her father’s kingdom. But King Henry, using the counsel of the princes, with the consent of the nobles of Bohemia gave this same daughter, together with the kingdom of Bohemia, as wife to his son John, count of Luxembourg. The wedding was celebrated there with great solemnity, and he sent him with an army into Bohemia, joining to him Peter, archbishop of Mainz, once his physician. When John came into Bohemia, he was received as king with great honor by all the inhabitants of the kingdom, and was solemnly crowned by the same Peter, archbishop of Mainz, to whom by ancient right that office belonged. More than three hundred thousand people were said to have been present at this coronation. When the coronation had been performed, the king, among other small gifts, gave the archbishop a seat adorned with gold and gems, which, after it had been brought into the church of Mainz, the common people have been accustomed to call the seat of Saint Martin down to this day. Meanwhile, while these things were being done in Bohemia, King Henry, moving his army from the assembly at Speyer, directed his way into Italy to receive the imperial crown, having with him, among many other princes, Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, his brother, Rudolph, count palatine of the Rhine, and Leopold, duke of Austria. On that journey he took many cities, towns, and castles of the rebels in Italy, and fought many battles bravely Chronicle of Johann Trithemius.

1317.

In the seventeenth and last year of Abbot Henry, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1317, Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, with King Louis's consent, redeemed with money the imperial castle of Sterrenberg, which had been pledged, and joined it to his church of Trier. For he was a magnificent man, and always obedient and pleasing to the emperors, which greatly benefited the church of Trier.

In the same year, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, Guido, bishop of Utrecht, died. Frederick of Sierck, provost of the greater church, succeeded him and presided for five years, afflicted by many adversities.

Also in the same year Henry, the thirtieth abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, by order of Louis IV, emperor, was deposed from his abbatial dignity and recalled to private life. For, as we remember saying at the beginning, he was a man given to leisure and idleness, who, indulging too much in banquets and the comforts of the flesh, shamefully neglected the whole state of the monastery in temporal and spiritual matters. He sold off many movable and immovable goods of the monastery, alienated [unclear], and spent all the money badly. Therefore, when he disdained to amend his ways, after often being [unclear] by the more prudent men, the matter was brought by the brothers to the bishop, and through him to the king, and by his mandate he was deposed.

Concerning Sigismund, the thirty-first abbot of this monastery, who presided for twenty-four years, and concerning the various events of that time.

After Abbot Henry had been deposed and recalled, as we have said, to private life, there followed among the brothers a great examination of merits, lest, if they chose someone as pastor with too little deliberation and with hasty counsel, they should be subject to similar, or certainly graver, dangers and evils, and should inconveniently reduce both states of the monastery to extremes. Therefore, after mature deliberation had first been held for the election of a new pastor, at last they proceeded and directed their votes toward two men. One party, stronger in number and in maturity of counsel, strove to set over [unclear] Sigismund, formerly prior. When both elected men had first come to the judgment of the bishop of Speyer, and then to the audience of Louis, king of the Romans, after the process of the election had been heard, Sigismund, by the sentence of the doctors, was confirmed in the abbacy. Having been ordained according to custom, he presided vigorously over this monastery for twenty-four years, and in spiritual matters governed all things well. He was a Swabian by nation, born of noble stock, of seemly stature, neither short nor misshapen by excessive height. In manners he was humane, in disposition gentle and subtle, prompt in counsel and circumspect with singular prudence, eloquent in speech, and venerable through a certain severity. He managed the affairs of the monastery prudently and orderly, and restored to the monastery's possession many things alienated by his predecessor, Abbot Henry.

1318.

In his first year, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1318, Andrew, bishop of Wurzburg, died. Godfrey of Hohenlohe succeeded him and presided for nine years; after many disputes held with his citizens, he finally obtained victory and compelled them to obedience.

In the same year the people of Cologne, at the command of Emperor Louis, called to their aid John, king of Bohemia, who was then at Luxembourg with a great army, William, count of Holland, John his brother, count in Hainaut, Gerhard, count of Julich, Adolf, count of Berg, and John, count of Sayn, with certain others. Proceeding to war against Henry, archbishop of Cologne, who was violating the pacts and treaties of peace and siding with Frederick, duke of Austria, they inflicted much damage on him; and among other things, they besieged the castle called Bruhl for the space of four months. But at last, peace having been interposed and satisfaction made, they withdrew.

1319.

In the second year of Abbot Sigismund, the year of the Lord's Nativity 1319, Henry de Dune, from the count of Wildberg, bishop of Worms, died in the fifth year of his pontificate and was buried in the greater church; and the bishopric was vacant for two months and eight days. Afterward Cuno of Schoneck was elected, a son [unclear] of Worms. Some, however, think that he presided longer, but they have been found by us, after very diligent examination of the sequence of time, to be in error by ten years.

1320.

In the third year of Abbot Sigismund, however, in the year of the Lord's Nativity 1320, on the day before the Nones of June, died master [unclear].

Guido the abbot.

The castle of Sterrenberg is redeemed.

Abbot Henry is deposed.

A division was made in the election.

Sigismund, thirty-first abbot.

The life of Sigismund.

Andrew died.

War against the archbishop of Cologne.

Henry died.

Cuno of Schoneck becomes bishop of Worms.

[unclear].

Guido the abbot.

[Sigismund?] and Sigismund and Hildegard on this account in the church [unclear] granted to Louis the custom of having elections and elected men. he carried on. And first, indeed, at Milan, he was crowned according to custom with the iron crown; and then at Rome, at St. John Lateran, he was exalted with the golden crown and the imperial blessing by three cardinals sent for this purpose by the pope from Gaul, with great pomp and solemnity, on the day of holy Pentecost. After he had been crowned, he made Rudolf, count palatine of the Rhine, and many others knights in the same church. Meanwhile, while the emperor was staying in Italy for almost two years, the third army, which he had left in Germany, advanced bravely in fighting against the counts of Württemberg, rebels against the empire for many years, and obtained seventy-two of their eighty fortifications and castles, and killed many of them in war. But the emperor, waging many wars most bravely in Italy, defeated and overcame with a strong hand the Lombards, the Pavians, the Turinese, the men of Asti, the Veronese, the Piacentines, the Genoese, the Pisans, the Sienese, and also the Romans, and all the rest who resisted him, and powerfully compelled them to come into submission to him. This Emperor Henry was a wise, just, and gracious man, vigorous in arms, a most upright worshipper and defender of the Christian faith, ready in counsel and courage, a lover of the clergy and defender of the poor.

1311.

In the second year of Abbot Henry, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1311, Pope Clement V proclaimed that the Council of Vienne was to be held; it lasted two years. In it the book of the Clementines was published, and many things were decreed for the benefit of the Church. There the order of the Templars, which had stood for almost 184 years, was condemned by Pope Clement himself and destroyed throughout the whole world in a single day, at the urging of Philip, king of the Franks, through whose promotion that pope had been elected. The Templars were very wealthy; in order to acquire their possessions for himself, as many maintained, the king charged them with the false crime of heresy and prepared to extinguish them entirely.

In the same year Guido, bishop of Utrecht, coming to the Council of Vienne, was made a cardinal by Pope Clement V through the mediation of the king of the Franks and certain cardinals who spoke on his behalf; nevertheless, being content with his church of Utrecht, he did not conduct himself as a cardinal.

1312.

In the twelfth year of Abbot Henry, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1312, Otto, king of Hungary and duke of Bavaria, died, leaving one son, fourteen days old, whom, together with the two sons of his brother, Henry, aged six, [unclear] he entrusted to citizens in Landshut and in Straubing to be brought up under guardianship. But after his death, when Louis, duke of Upper Bavaria, together with the nobles of the land, opposed this commission, he carried off the boys.

In the same year Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, received from Henry the emperor himself, his brother, Boppard and Wesel, towns on this side of the Rhine, with certain others, as a pledge for the expenses which he had incurred in Italy and elsewhere on account of the empire, as is clear from letters given in the camp before Florence, in the aforesaid year of the Lord 1312, in the tenth indiction, on the sixth day before the Ides of December. After receiving these, the archbishop, leaving the emperor in Italy, returned to Trier.

In the same year also died John, duke of Brabant. John the third of the same name succeeded him; he had as wife Margaret, daughter of Louis, king of the Franks, by whom he begot three sons, all of whom died before him without children, namely John, Godfrey, and Henry. He also had three daughters, of whom the first, Joanna, first married William, count of Holland. After he was killed by the Frisians, she was betrothed to Wenceslaus, count of Luxembourg, brother of John, king of Bohemia, and of Charles, the fourth emperor. The second was Margaret, who married Louis, count of Flanders. The third was Mary, who married Reynald, duke of Guelders.

1313.

In the thirteenth year of Abbot Henry, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity [1313], Henry, emperor of the Romans, the seventh, in Italy, having raised new armies and being about to advance against Robert, petty king of Apulia, was overcome on the journey at Buonconvento by the disease of dysentery, and died on the day of Saint Bartholomew, not without great loss to the whole Roman Empire; and the empire was vacant for one year. There are those who write that he perished by poison, through the administration of Brother Bernard of the Order of Preachers, his confessor and chaplain, by whom they say he was poisoned in the consecrated host when receiving communion on the day of the Assumption of Blessed Mary ever virgin; and for that reason all the Preachers were marked by the pope with this punishment, that up to this day and thereafter, when communicating persons at the altar, their priests give them communion with the left hand. But since we think this wholly fabricated, we therefore with just reason refuse to give credence to those who say such things.

King Henry is blessed as emperor at Rome.

War of the empire against the Württembergers.

Imperial wars in Italy.

The Council of Vienne is celebrated.

Defense of the order of the Templars.

Otto, king of Hungary, dies.

Boppard is given to the church of Trier.

John, duke of Brabant, dies.

Wenceslaus, count of Luxembourg.

Emperor Henry dies.

The emperor poisoned by a Dominican. Of the Monastery of Hirsau

“If Mary remained a virgin after childbirth, she gave birth not to a man but to an angel; she was not a virgin after childbirth.” Likewise they said that they had twelve apostles, who each year surveyed the whole empire, and that two of them, senior in rank and profession, entered paradise each year and received from Elijah and Enoch the power of binding and loosing, which they communicated to others established in the same sect.

They mocked the sacrament of baptism, saying, “If baptism is a sacrament, then every bath is a sacrament, and consequently every bath-attendant would be God.”

They shamefully corrupted the sacrament of penance, confessing not to priests but to laymen generally, expressing their sins specifically, hoping that from this confession they would receive full remission of all sins, both from penalty and from guilt.

They did not believe in the sacrament of the Lord’s body, calling the consecrated host a fictitious God. They also called the sacrament of lawful marriage “sworn prostitution” in the vernacular.

They mocked the sacrament of extreme unction, and when asked what they thought about it, they answered unanimously: “We believe that vegetables are the better the more they have been seasoned with oil.” They said that the consecrations of churches and cemeteries, and the blessings of palms, salt, water, and the other things that are done in the church, were nothing.

Likewise they said that God neither knew nor punished evils that were done beneath the earth. Hence, gathering in underground caves and caverns, father with daughter, brother with sister, and son with mother indiscriminately practiced the foulness of their flesh.

They said that the Roman Church was not Christ’s but belonged to unbelieving gentiles, and they despised all the statutes of the Church together with its prelates and ministers. They mocked fasting; they ate meat at every season, even on the sixth day of Parasceve. They did not observe feast days, but worked on Easter day. They said that perjury was not a sin.

They denied that the merits and intercessions of any saints could provide assistance to human beings before God. But they also professed many other articles of error, the lengthy insertion of which would, I fear, cause weariness to these readers. There was a great number of them in Austria, Bohemia, and the neighboring lands. For, as a certain one of them burned at Vienna, named Novus Magister, confessed, there were at that time in Austria, Bohemia, and its borderlands more than eighty thousand persons, all sworn and professed into that sect, apart from those who were in other lands.

From this filth Bohemia, then infected, down to the present day abounds in the same errors and foul practices, as we shall say more fully below in the seventeenth year of Abbot Blasius. At that time many in Austria were burned in various places; all of them unanimously remained most obstinately in their errors until death, with great cheerfulness.

Among them was a beautiful girl named Giswa. When she was already about to be burned, she was asked by the judge whether she was still a virgin. She answered before everyone: “Above ground I am still a virgin, but underground by no means.” For the fools believed that virgins could not be deflowered underground, even if they were known by a thousand men, and that such illicit intercourse was not a sin.

In the sixteenth year of Abbot Henry, which was the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1316, Louis, king of the Romans, with all the princes and cities consenting to him, decreed peace throughout the whole kingdom. But Henry, archbishop of Cologne, with those who followed the party of Frederick, did not observe this treaty of peace, and for that reason subjected himself and his diocese to many calamities.

For in the same year King Louis himself, with the assistance of Baldwin of Trier and Peter of Mainz, archbishops, accomplished many things against Frederick’s party. He also encircled with a siege the fortifications of Wiesbaden and Scharfenstein; when he made no progress there because of the strength of the places, he left the matter unfinished and turned to other things.

In the same year, after the apostolic see had been vacant for two years, three months, and seventeen days, the cardinals, at last assembling at Lyon, elected as pope on the fifth day of September James of Cahors, bishop of Porto; called John XXII, he presided over the Roman Church for eighteen years and four months.

In the same year also a battle was fought near Strasbourg between Louis, king of the Romans, and Frederick, duke of Austria, his adversary; in it Frederick’s army was routed and defeated by Louis, and was forced to flee again.

In the year Of the Monastery of Hirsau

Peter the physician, archbishop of Mainz, dies.

Master Peter of [Aspelt?], physician and archbishop of Mainz, a man magnificent in every respect, died; he newly founded the Carthusian house outside the walls of Mainz, and first established the college of canons of the church of St. Catherine at Oppenheim, endowing it quite magnificently. After his death the canons of Mainz petitioned for Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, as their prelate. But Pope John XXII, refusing to give consent to their petition, gave them as archbishop lord Matthias of Buseck, a professed monk of the Order of St. Benedict, an excellent man, worthy of such an honor. He was solemnly introduced at Mainz by lord Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, and by apostolic authority was honorably received by the clergy and people; and he presided for eight years. He immediately allied himself with Baldwin; strengthened by the help of his presence, he enclosed with a siege and took the town called [zu den Giessen?].

In the same year the citizens of Cologne, again proceeding to war on behalf of the Emperor Louis against Henry their archbishop, took his castle of Vrechem and utterly destroyed it.

MCCCXXI.

In the fourth year of Abbot Sigismund, which was the year 1321 of the Lord’s nativity, Frederick, duke of Austria, with his brother Leopold, entered Bavaria with a strong hand and a great army against King Louis, and devastated the whole region with fire and sword, everywhere inflicting many losses on the poor; meanwhile Emperor Louis kept himself in his fortifications, because of the absence of his army, beseeching strong fortune with prayers.

MCCCXXII.

In the following year, which was the fifth of Abbot Sigismund and the year 1322 of the Lord’s nativity, there was apprehended at Cologne a certain Lollard named Walter, the leading master of the school of heretics of that sect of which we made mention above, in the fifteenth year of Abbot Henry II. In the city of Cologne and outside it in many places he had secretly disseminated his errors, especially among little women, and had seduced many. He wrote little books in the German language suited to his errors, in which, by interpreting the words of sacred Scripture badly, he perverted them and applied them to his errors, and distributed them to women to read. When he was seized, however, he vigorously defended his errors; hence, condemned to the fire by sentence, he was burned, leaving behind, as he himself admitted, many hidden professors, cultivators, and disciples of his errors in the city of Cologne and outside it.

In the same year Isabella, wife of Edward king of the English, daughter of the late Philip IV, king of the French, seized Edward himself, her husband, and committed him to custody until death, because of the desolation, as she said, which he had caused in the kingdom with his servants.

MCCCXXIII.

In the sixth year of Abbot Sigismund, and the one thousand three hundred twenty-third year of the Lord’s nativity, Frederick, duke of Austria, again gathered a great army, more than five thousand fighting men from Austria and Hungary, intending to fight against Emperor Louis. Duke Leopold of Austria, his brother, met him with two thousand men, and, after many had been hired on every side, they entered Bavaria again and set about devastating everything. But Emperor Louis, having assembled a very great army of more than thirty thousand fighting men, together with John king of the Bohemians, Baldwin also archbishop of Trier, and Matthias archbishop of Mainz, met Frederick, his adversary, in Bavaria between Ottingen and Molendorf. There, battle having been joined, Duke Frederick was defeated, captured by the king of Bohemia, and presented to Emperor Louis under conditions of life; Louis committed him to custody in a certain very strong castle. Afterwards, while Duke Frederick was thus held in captivity, it happened that a certain magician came to Leopold his brother in Austria, promising that by his art, through the ministry of a spirit, he would bring Duke Frederick back to him from captivity safe and wholly unharmed in one hour, if he wished to promise and give him a fitting reward. He answered: “If you do what you promise,” he said, “I will honor you with a fitting reward.” And so, at an hour suitable to him, the magician entered the circle of conjuration together with the duke and called the spirit accustomed to obey his commands. When it appeared to him in human form, by the power of his conjurations he ordered it to bring Duke Frederick, freed from the emperor’s custody, back to him in Austria as quickly as possible without injury. The spirit answered him and said: “If the captured duke himself is willing to come with me, I will gladly obey your commands.” Having said this, the spirit at once flew off into Bavaria, flew through it after assuming the form of a pilgrim, and entered the prison where Duke Frederick was being held captive. When he had seen him, the spirit sent to him said: “If you wish to be freed from captivity, mount this horse; they will bring you safely and without injury into Austria to your brother Duke Leopold.”

[Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

215

... I will bring [you]. The duke said to him, “Who, then, are you?” To him the spirit replied, “Do not ask who I am, because [unclear] has nothing to do with the matter; but mount this horse, which I offer you, and I will bring you, safe and unharmed, freed from here, back to Austria.” When he heard this, a certain horror seized the duke, otherwise a most daring man; and presently, when he fortified himself with the sign of the holy cross, the spirit disappeared together with the black horse which he had offered. He returned empty-handed to the one who had sent him, and, when reproached by him because he had not brought the captive, he narrated the course of what had happened. At length Duke Frederick, released from custody, confessed that this had happened to him in captivity on the recorded day. After this, Emperor Louis, having received an oath and the necessary guarantees from Duke Frederick that he would no longer involve himself in the kingdom, let him go free. He ruled alone for nearly thirty-three years, a strong man, exceedingly bold.

In the same year also Pope John XXII enrolled Thomas Aquinas, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a most acute theologian, in the catalogue of the saints, forty-eight years after his passing.

1324.

In the seventh year of Abbot Sigismund, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1324, Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, John, king of Bohemia, his nephew through his brother, who was then staying at Luxembourg, and also the duke of Lorraine and the count of Bar, together with certain other counts and nobles, entered into alliance with one another and with a great army besieged the city of Metz. Since they could not take it by storm, they laid waste everything round about by devastation.

In these times Emperor Louis, desiring to enlarge his dominion, violently took away the wife of a certain powerful man, and joined her in marriage, with pomp and solemnity, to his son Otto, margrave of Brandenburg; while her husband, with whom she had lived matrimonially for eleven years, protested and invoked the aid of the supreme pontiff, though in vain. For the emperor said that between him and her there existed an impediment of consanguinity. But another cause moved him The Monastery of Hirsau There at length he redeemed himself with money, after giving letters and sureties that in his own days he would not complete the castle begun in Birckenfeld, over which there had been a dispute.

In the same year also Cuno of Schoneck, bishop of Worms, ordered that the feast of the Body of Christ, according to the institution of Pope Urban, be solemnly celebrated throughout the city of Worms and the whole diocese.

1326.

In the ninth year of Abbot Sigismund, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1326, Louis IV, emperor, raised Reinhard, count of Geldern, to duke; he had kept his father, of the same name, captive in custody for almost eight years until his death. And from then onward the princes of the land of Geldern began to be dukes, retaining the title of the county of Zutphen down to the present day.

And in this same year, on the seventh day before the Ides of October, his father died in captivity. When Frederick, bishop of Utrecht, had died, two men were named amid disagreement: James, dean of the greater church, was elected by the greater part of the chapter; James of [Suden?], bishop, was postulated by the smaller part at the urging of William, count of Holland.

But the former, James the dean, prevailed and was confirmed as bishop of Utrecht. When he died after a short time, the canons of the greater church unanimously elected John of Bruchorst, provost of the church of Saint Saviour in Utrecht, an excellent man, who at once took up the rule and administration of the whole episcopate as the true pontiff canonically elected. Meanwhile John of Diest, provost of Cambrai, came from Avignon, having been appointed and consecrated bishop of the church of Utrecht by Pope John XXII at the urging of the duke of Brabant, Reinhard duke of Geldern, and William count of Holland. Entering Utrecht with armed force and great display, after expelling John of Bruchorst, the elected bishop, he assumed the pontificate, which he governed for almost fourteen years.

In the aforesaid year also a certain Jew, receiving baptism in Hainaut, was lifted from the sacred font by William, count of Holland and Hainaut. Passing and living among Christians, he pretended to be devout, though filled with Jewish malice. For on one occasion, passing alone in the church of a certain monastery, he unworthily beheld a most beautifully painted image of blessed Mary ever virgin.

At once filled with his old hatred and inborn fury, he drew a dagger and, bursting out in words of blasphemy against the holy Mother of God, struck the bright face of the image and foully wounded it. And behold, immediately abundant blood, issuing from the wounded image, began to flow around. Seeing this, the wretch secretly fled from the church. But the blood, preserved by the faithful, was a remedy for many illnesses.

But after the perpetrator of so great a crime had lain hidden for some time and could not be discovered by anyone, the most blessed Mother of God, Mary ever-virgin and ever undefiled, appearing in dreams to a certain blacksmith as if pierced with wounds, showed him the perpetrator of the crime and encouraged him to a duel against the faithless man for the declaration of the truth. The smith came to the judge and accused the Jew of the crime; when sufficient testimonies for proof of the charged crime were not [unclear], or that he would deign to entrust the office of imperial consecration to one of the cardinals, as Pope Clement V had done with Henry VII, saying that it was neither suitable for him nor according to the custom of the Roman Empire to be blessed and crowned anywhere else. But the pope refused both, ordering him to come to him at Avignon.

In the tenth year of Abbot Sigismund, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1327, Louis, king of the Romans, went to Rome with many princes and a great army for the crown of the empire, and by [unclear] although he was often invited by him, he did not believe it safe for him to go. Therefore he asked the pontiff by letters, both his own and those of the Romans and of other princes, that either he himself come to Rome, [unclear] deposed, a heretic, a schismatic, and deprived of every pontifical honor,

1327.

King Louis is professed at Rome. [unclear] had him crowned emperor, in the thirteenth year after his election. When this had been done, by the counsel of his [unclear]. Louis is crowned at Rome. Ludeonius the ruler. By presumption, deposed, a heretic, a schismatic, and deprived of every pontifical honor.

then had it proclaimed; and, appointing Peter of Corbara, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man indeed learned and fit for conducting affairs, as pope, he called him Nicholas V, from whom he received anew the crown of the empire with greater solemnity.

But when Peter was created, not as pontiff but as antipope, he created as cardinals and bishops men very like himself, and in all things conducted himself as a true pope. But after the emperor’s return into Germany, the antipope, left at Pisa, was captured by Boniface, count of Pisa, and brought to Avignon to Pope John, where, cast into prison, he exchanged life for death; although he acknowledged his error, nevertheless he could [not] be freed.

In the same year Gotfrid, bishop of Würzburg, died. He was succeeded by Wolfram of Grumbach, forty-sixth in the order of bishops, and he presided for six years, a man very well suited to rule, who compelled his citizens to every kind of subjection.

In the same year also Matthias, archbishop of Mainz, celebrated a provincial synod of his suffragans, abbots, and prelates, in which he issued many constitutions for the benefit of the Church.

1328.

In the second year of Abbot Sigismund, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1328, in the second indiction, on the Ides of September, Matthias, archbishop of Mainz, of the Order of Saint Benedict, born of Buseck, died, a man upright in [unclear] conduct and worthy of every honor and perpetual memory; and he was buried in the greater church of Mainz. After his death, the clergy again postulated Baldwin, archbishop of Trier; but since he was unwilling to abandon his own church of Trier, which he had already made wealthy, Pope John XXII gave the church of Mainz to Henry of Virneburg without the consent of the canons, and, having ordained him archbishop, sent him to Mainz with apostolic letters and mandates. But the canons, alleging many crimes against him, appealed to the Apostolic See. Therefore, while they litigated for three years before the pope in Avignon, lest the church of Mainz, again deprived of a pastor, incur grave losses, the pope, at their request, entrusted that church of Mainz to the aforesaid Baldwin, archbishop, in the name of administrator until the outcome of the suit.

After he had been appointed administrator, he took into his power the towns, castles, and fortifications of the whole diocese, and he began to build everything anew from the foundations, strongly and with great diligence, against the incursions of the wicked; and he surrounded the village itself on every side with a wall. Meanwhile the people of Mainz, fearing, as they said, a siege by Baldwin, but in fact [unclear] because of ecclesiastical liberty, with the former defending their rights and liberties, while the latter, on the other side, labored to infringe and violate everything.

Therefore, to repress the rashness of the people of Mainz, Baldwin the administrator [unclear].

Baldwin becomes administrator of the church of Mainz.

The castle called Eltville, situated two miles from Mainz down the river Rhine, he defended with wisdom. In these days there was great dissension between the clergy and the citizens of Mainz because of ecclesiastical liberty; and they destroyed in great part the notable buildings and structures of Saint Alban the Martyr, of Saint James the Apostle on the Fair Mountain, and of Saint Victor, belonging to secular canons, together with the castle in Weisenau, monasteries of our order distinguished by buildings and structures, as the traces especially in the monastery of Saint Alban show down to the present day.

Henry, archbishop of Mainz.

The monastery of Saint James, however, because it was very near the city, they utterly overthrew, together with its distinguished church. For this rashness they were afterward summoned to the emperor’s chamber, and by judicial sentence condemned to pay a very great sum of money to those monasteries. The monasteries were rebuilt in the course of time, but they did not attain their former splendor. From that time, however, until the capture of the city, which took place in the third year of Wignand, abbot of this monastery, with the power avenging the wrong done to the saints, fortune was always adverse to the people of Mainz. With God avenging the wrong done to the saints, fortune was always [unclear] to the people of Mainz, until at last, having lost their liberty, they were reduced to perpetual servitude.

After three years, however, judgment was given for Henry of Virneburg, who, confirmed as archbishop, was sent again to Mainz, and to Baldwin [unclear] the administration [unclear]. He was buried in his greater church; his successor was Berthold Burheck of the Order of the Teutonic Brethren, and he presided for one year, being transferred to the bishopric of Strasbourg, as we shall say later in its proper order.

In the same year also Eberhard, count of Württemberg, with the consent of Pope John [unclear].

King Louis made an antipope. The antipope is captured and imprisoned.

Gotfrid died.

Provincial synod [unclear].

[Malvoius?] died.

Contention of the clergy and [unclear] archbishops.

Baldwin becomes administrator of the church of Mainz.

Eltville castle is constructed.

The monastery of Saint Alban, Saint James, and Saint Victor is erected.

Henry, archbishop of Mainz, died.

Emicho died.

Zinichy died. The Monastery of Hirsau

The college was transferred to Stuttgart.

[unclear] 22. [He] transferred the college of canons of Beutelsbach, together with the church in which the burial place of the counts of Wurttemberg was, to Stuttgart; the occasion of this transfer was as follows.

Since in earlier years under Henry VII, who began to reign in the eighth year of Henry the second abbot, as we have said, the nobles and citizens of the empire, by the king's command, had waged war for almost ten years against the aforesaid Count Eberhard, and out of his eighty fortifications had captured almost seventy, and these were destroyed, as we briefly recorded in the tenth year of the aforesaid abbot; among them was the castle of Beutelsbach, where the collegiate church had been situated, in which the counts, as we said, had their burial place. What we are about to relate then happened. The imperial troops, after the fortification was captured, forgetful of God and unmindful of their own salvation, to the insult of the living,

Cruelty against [unclear].

for they opened and broke open the sarcophagi, drew out the bones of the dead counts, and did not fear to scatter them among stones and ashes. Count Eberhard, taking very grievously this injury and insult inflicted on the dead resting in the earth, transferred the church with the burial place from Beutelsbach with apostolic consent. This count died in the same year on the day of St. Boniface, archbishop and martyr, leaving a son who survived him by ten years.

1329.

In the twelfth year of Abbot Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1329, Cuno of Schoneck, bishop of Worms, died. After his death, the canons of the cathedral unanimously took Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, as administrator, against Gerlach Schenk of Erbach, who had ambitiously invaded the bishopric, which he also afterward obtained.

In the same year also Berthold, bishop of Speyer, was transferred by the pope's authority as bishop to the church of Strasbourg; and the aforesaid Archbishop Baldwin was taken up into the administration of the church of Speyer, now ruler of four churches.

1330.

In the thirteenth year of Abbot Sigismund, which was the year 1330 from the Lord's nativity, Walram, from the counts of Veldenz, by the promotion of Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, was made bishop of Speyer, and presided for six years, a good and merciful man.

In the same year, when Archbishop Baldwin resigned the administration of the church of Worms, Gerlach Schenk, about whom we spoke in the preceding year, secured the bishopric and presided for two years, not elected nor postulated, but violently intruded with the help and favor of friends, and, as was said, not confirmed by anyone.

In this same year, after a long contest held in the papal curia, Henry of Virneburg was sent to Mainz by the authority of Pope John XXII, and, having been ordained archbishop, was received by the clergy and people at the apostolic command, in the presence of two legates; and he presided for almost fifteen years, Baldwin resigning the administration by order of the pope and the legates of the apostolic see. This Archbishop Henry completed the castle of Eltville below Mainz beside the Rhine, which had been begun by Baldwin the administrator.

1331.

In the fourteenth year of Abbot Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1331, Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, purchased for a price the chapel of St. Alban, with a very broad garden adjoining it, from the monastery of St. Matthias outside the walls of Trier, and began to build a monastery for Carthusian monks. Completing it in eight years and endowing it magnificently, he consecrated the new foundation. The same archbishop also built anew at this time, at great expense, a stone bridge over the Moselle near Koblenz.

In the same year John, formerly count of Luxembourg, king of Bohemia, entered Italy with a great army and received Brescia, Parma, Reggio, and Modena into his power.

In this same year also a great dissension arose between Henry, duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Upright, on one side, and his brother Otto and the younger Henry, Otto's son, from the dukes of Bavaria and king of Hungary, on the other side, over the duchy of Lower Bavaria. Emperor Louis, on behalf of Otto and the younger Henry, having summoned the Hungarians to his aid, was preparing an army against the elder Henry. When this became known, the king of Bohemia, father-in-law of the elder Henry, with certain other princes joined to him, proclaimed a meeting for the disputants at Rambingen, Scharding, and other surrounding castles, fortifications, and villages. But to Otto his brother, his lot assigned Burghausen, Ottingen, Traunstein, Halle, and the rest as far as the Salzburg Alps-

Contention among the dukes of Bavaria.

Dissension of Lower Ba[varia?].

The Carthusian house of Trier is built.

The bridge at Koblenz.

John, king of Bohemia.

But to Otto, Straubing, Scharding, Traunstein, Halle, and the rest as far as the Salzburg Alps.

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

219

the Salzburgers. Moreover Henry the Younger, in the division, received Dingolfing, Landau, Vilshofen, Deggendorf, Campurg, Kelheim, and other places situated round about.

1332.

In the fifteenth year of Abbot Sigismund, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1332, Henry the Elder, duke of Bavaria, again began to contend for the duchy with his brother Otto and Henry the Younger. When Emperor Louis ordered peace for him, and he did not desist, he gathered an army and in his own person surrounded the town of Straubing with a siege and attacked it vigorously for eight weeks, until at last the aforesaid John, king of Bohemia, arrived and restored peace between them.

Straubing is surrounded with a siege.

In the same year, on the fifteenth day before the kalends of January, Gerlach Schenk, bishop of Worms, died. He was succeeded by Salamannus, born at Mainz, who presided for twenty-three years, confirmed by Pope John XXII but ordained by his successor Benedict XII. When the people of Worms refused to admit him, they were marked by the pope with an ecclesiastical interdict; and many of the canons, especially those of Saint Cyriacus, disobedient to the apostolic commands and rebellious against Salamannus, were excommunicated. At length, after satisfaction had first been made, he reconciled them by apostolic authority.

1334.

In the sixteenth year of Abbot Sigismund, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1333, Wolfram, bishop of Würzburg, died on the day before the kalends of July. Otto Wolfskeel succeeded him and presided for fifteen years, having been promoted and ordained at Liège on the twenty-first day of July by Pope John XXII against Hermann of Lichtenberg, Emperor Louis’s chancellor, out of hatred for the emperor, who wished him to be ordained bishop. For, as we said above in its place, after Emperor Henry VII had died in Italy, Louis, count palatine and duke of Bavaria, brother of Rudolf, count palatine of the Rhine, by the election of the princes and after Frederick, duke of Austria, had been defeated, was raised to be king of the Romans in the year of the Lord 1314. He soon fell into great discord with Pope John XXII on such an occasion, as was reported.

Thus Otto becomes bishop of Würzburg.

Cause of the dissension between pope and emperor.

In the same sixteenth year a certain chancellor, Ulrich by name, a native of Augsburg of the Rhaetians, a rash and proud man, hostile to the clergy and to religion, and a very great hater and adversary of ecclesiastical dignity and liberty, in letters to the pope in the emperor’s name put certain unworthy things in that beginning, and among other things called the pope himself the beast rising from the sea, and wrote many insults against him. Provoked by these, not undeservedly, to indignation, the pontiff excommunicated King Louis. This chancellor, already near death, publicly confessed this wickedness of his before many people. Hence Louis, having set out for Rome in the year of the Lord 1327, wishing to be reconciled to the pope, while he was staying at Avignon, as we said above, in the ninth year of Abbot Sigismund received the office of blessing from a certain simple bishop, and remained in the dispensation of Pope John, appointing another as antipope. To this excommunicated Emperor Louis there came into Bavaria William of Ockham, of the Order of Minors, English by nation, a man indeed learned in philosophy and sacred letters, but exceedingly rash, excommunicated by Pope John XXII, against whom he wrote many things in blasphemy, as we have said more fully in the book On Ecclesiastical Writers.

In the same year Henry the Younger, duke of Bavaria, son of Otto, king of Hungary, died.

In this year a very great abundance of wine grew, so that casks were lacking.

1333.

In the seventeenth year of Abbot Sigismund, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1354, Henry, archbishop of Cologne, died. He was succeeded in the archbishopric by Walram, son of Gerard, count of Jülich, provost of Liège and treasurer of Cologne, who presided for sixteen years, six months, and nineteen days, a man very learned in both laws, energetic and peaceable; he governed the church committed to him quite energetically, peacefully, and profitably in its condition. This Archbishop Walram, among the many buildings which he erected in various places during the time of his pontificate, also built anew the monastery of the Carthusians in Cologne, which he honorably and abundantly endowed for the necessary support of the brothers.

Walram becomes archbishop of Cologne.

The Charterhouse at Cologne is founded.

In the same year, on the day before the nones of December, Pope John XXII died at Avignon in the ninetieth year of his age, leaving an inestimable quantity of gold in his treasuries. He was succeeded in the pontificate by Benedict XII, of Toulouse, of the Cistercian Order, doctor of sacred theology, previously called Jacques Fournier, and he presided for seven years, three months, and eighteen days. He was a man of the most perfect uprightness, who gave a constitution to our order for its reform, which [unclear]

Benedict becomes pope, John having died. 220. The Monastery of Hirsau

they call [it], whose true original under lead is kept at Trier at St. Matthias, and similarly in very many other monasteries.

1335.

In the fifteenth year of Abbot Sigismund, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1335, on the day of the apostles Simon and Jude, a very great and exceedingly tempestuous wind blew in the regions of the Rhine and Swabia; it overturned trees and many buildings in various places.

In the same year Otto, duke of Bavaria, of whom we made mention above, son of Duke Stephen and brother of Henry the Elder, died without children; his duchy devolved by right to his brother.

1336.

In the following year, which was the nineteenth of Abbot Sigismund, Willichin, or Wilhelm, the eleventh abbot of my monastery of Sponheim, died in the twenty-eighth year of his rule, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.

In the same year, on the day of St. Augustine the bishop, Walram, bishop of Speyer, died and was buried there in the church of the Preachers before the high altar. Gerard of Ehrenberg succeeded him, elected on the day of St. Catherine, and presided for twenty-seven years, one month, and six days. But after Willichin, Henry, born at Kreuznach, was appointed twelfth abbot of my monastery of Sponheim; he presided for two years, one month, and six days, not with sufficient usefulness, as the time required.

1337.

In the twentieth year of Abbot Sigismund, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1337, there was everywhere a great mortality of men and livestock, and grain was sold at a high price, so that the poor were oppressed by great want, and many perished from hunger and lack of food.

1338.

In the following year, which was the twenty-first of Abbot Sigismund, Edward the Second [III?], king of England, came to Emperor Louis at Koblenz, seeking aid from him against Philip, king of France. Louis, after receiving money, promised him much support, but could not keep his promises, because he had princes unwilling to obey; and the king of England, frustrated in his hope, lost the money spent without profit.

In the same year Reinald, count of Guelders, who was afterward raised to duke, led out a great army and declared war against the people of Liege and the Brabanters, because in the previous year, while he was with the emperor, they had miserably laid waste his land by fire and plunder. He had with him Adolph, bishop of Liege, whom the citizens had formerly shamefully expelled. In this war more than nine thousand men fell on both sides. The victory went to Count Reinald; from it he became not only rich, but famous in every land and acceptable to all the princes.

1339.

In the twenty-second year of Abbot Sigismund, which was the year of the Lord's Nativity 1339, on the day of St. Kilian the martyr, around midday, there was a great eclipse of the sun for almost two hours.

In the same year, around autumn, the Suitenses [men of Schwyz?], after a dissension had arisen in the city of Berne, cruelly killed several of the citizens.

Also in the same year Emperor Louis held a solemn assembly of the princes at Frankfurt, where, among other things, he raised Reinald, count of Guelders, to duke, adding to his duchy the county of Zutphen, because of his singular prudence and the magnificent deeds done by him. For he had been the eleventh from the beginning in the line of the counts of Guelders, a prudent, bold, warlike, fortunate man, and in every respect magnificent, who vigorously accomplished many things in peace and in war.

At the same time also Wilhelm, count of Julich, was created margrave by Emperor Louis with the consent of the princes: a man worthy of such honor, since he [unclear]. In this year there was a fierce war between Philip, king of France, and Edward, king of England, over the county of Normandy, which each contended belonged to him by right. For the king of England, having hired troops at great pay, entered France with a strong force, laying waste to everything by plunder and fire, although it profited him little, because he did not obtain Normandy.

Also in the same year, on the [unclear] feast of St. Oswald, king and martyr, Emperor Louis, after the death of his brother Rudolf, Count Palatine of the Rhine, whom in England Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

(had driven out), as we said in the fourteenth year of Abbot Henry, summoned his sons Rudolph, Adolf, and Rupert, and divided among them their paternal inheritance, or rather restored what had been taken away, saying: “The father sinned against me, not the sons; therefore it is not just that others should undergo the penalty for the crime.”

Rudolph, Count Palatine of the Rhine. Rudolph, the firstborn of Rudolph, brother of Emperor Louis and Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, a man of no great wisdom, had as wife the sister of the king of Hungary. By her he begot a single daughter, Margaret by name; Charles, king of Bohemia and afterward emperor, took her as wife. By her he received Wenceslaus, after his father king of the Romans; John, king of Bohemia; Sigismund, king of Hungary and afterward Roman emperor; Helen, who married the king of England; and Margaret, wife of the margrave of the Old March.

Adolf, Count Palatine of the Rhine. Adolf, the second-born son of the elder Rudolph Palatine, from whom the succession of the Counts Palatine of the Rhine is continued, took as wife the daughter of the count of Oettingen. She bore him Rupert, or, as very many maintain, Adolf, father of Rupert, afterward king of the Romans, by Beatrice, daughter of the king of Sicily; concerning him we shall speak more fully in his own place, when we come to him.

Rupert, Count Palatine. Rupert, however, the third-born son of the elder Rudolph, Count Palatine of the Rhine, died without children, although he had taken two wives. The first of them was Mechtild, duchess of Brabant; the second Beatrice, daughter of the duke of [Montenfis?].

The University of Heidelberg is founded. This Rupert first founded the universal school of Heidelberg, which Pope Benedict XII confirmed. Likewise afterward Pope Urban VI confirmed it. Its first director and moderator was Marsilius of Inghen, doctor of sacred theology, canon of Paris and treasurer of the church of St. Andrew in Cologne, as I remember that we said some time ago in the book On Ecclesiastical Writers. He also raised up from its foundations, founded, built, and endowed the collegiate church in the New City of the diocese of Speyer, with beautiful stone vaulting; in it he was afterward buried.

1340.

In the twenty-third year of Abbot Sigismund, and the year of the Lord 1340, there was a very great pestilence throughout all Germany, and it struck down many thousands of people. There was also a great famine [unclear], having gloriously triumphed over the captives, bringing no small booty to the English.

In this same year, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, Henry of Kreuznach, the twelfth abbot of my monastery of Sponheim, died. Willichin II of Sponheim succeeded him and presided for only one year, three months, and four days.

In the same year also, on the twelfth day of the month of February, Rupert, Count Palatine of the Rhine, died and was buried in the choir of the church of the New City, which he had raised from its foundations.

1341.

In the twenty-fourth year of Abbot Sigismund, and the year of the Lord 1341, a certain count in Isenburg, at the fair of St. Remigius in Cologne, in a friendly joust, publicly killed against his will Stephen, knight of Oersbeck, who, his neck broken, expired at once, nevertheless remaining seated on his horse as if alive, until he was found and taken down by the hands of servants, in all respects good and magnificent.

In this same year also, John, duke of Brabant, and Engelbert, bishop of Liège, [unclear] Pope XII, whom Clement VI succeeded, presiding for eleven years, a man full of piety and clemency; and [unclear], the rest being turned to flight, until at length they accepted terms of peace.

In the same year, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, Sigismund, the thirty-first abbot of this monastery of Hirsau, died in the twenty-fifth year of his governance, an excellent man and to be honored with every honor; he presided in both states usefully enough and did many good things.

Pestilence occurred.

The king of England moves his army into France a second time.

Willicho, abbot.

A knight is killed in a joust.

Clement VI is elected pope.

Wilhelm, abbot of Sponheim.

Sigismund is moved here as abbot.

Sigismund is moved here as abbot. 222. Of the Monastery of Hirsau, concerning Wighard, the thirty-second abbot of this monastery, who presided for 12 years, and concerning various deeds of that time in Germany.

After the death, therefore, of the most reverend abbot Sigismund, the conventual brothers of this monastery of Hirsau assembled in the chapter-house, in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s nativity 1342, in the tenth Roman indiction, in order to elect a new shepherd of their souls in the place of the deceased. After the necessary deliberation had first been held, at last they unanimously elected Wighard, a monk of their convent, a Swabian by birth, a man proved in temporal affairs not without experience. Having lived in the monastery under the abbots Henry and Sigismund, he seemed, according to the customs of that time, more suitable and better than the others for the necessity of the place, although he was little fitted for the restoration of regular discipline, which at that time had fallen into ruin in almost all the monasteries of our order throughout Germany. Nevertheless he preserved the manner of living in the monastery which he found there, allowing private property to the monks, as his predecessors had done. Confirmed, however, by Gerard, bishop of the church of Speyer, and solemnly ordained abbot, as is the custom, he presided for 8 years and 3 days, as will be clear to one who calculates.

Wighard becomes abbot [unclear]. Life and conduct of abbot Wighard. Confirmation by the bishop of Speyer.

In his first year he obtained from Emperor Louis IV the confirmation of the royal privileges of his monastery.

In this same year of the Lord’s nativity 1342, while abbot Sigismund was still living, on the 23rd day of the month of January, at the first hour of the night, when a dreadful storm of clouds had arisen, thunder was heard, lightning and flashes appeared, with hail and heavy rain, so that a storm seemed to have arisen in the middle of summer.

In the same year, on the vigil of Saint James the Apostle, the river Main, suddenly rising contrary to its nature and custom, poured into the Rhine so great a force of waters as no one living at that time remembered having seen. For it caused much damage to men and overturned whole villages situated around the Rhine.

MCCCXIIII.

While the first year of abbot Wighard was still running, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1343, Reinald, the first duke in Guelders, of whom we have spoken above, died. His son, a boy of ten years, undertook the governance of his duchy, later taking as wife the lady Mary, daughter of John, duke of Brabant; both of them died without children. Some years afterward his brother Edward, led by desire for rule, captured him and kept him in custody for ten years, and [unclear] the duchy of Guelders; concerning his deeds and death, so far as it has become known to us, we shall speak in its proper place.

In the same year, the second of abbot Wighard, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity MCCCXLIII.

In the [unclear] year of abbot Wighard, on the [unclear] day of the month of July, Ulrich, count of Württemberg, son of count Eberhard, of whom we have already spoken above, died, leaving two sons, Ulrich and Eberhard. The first of these died after 26 years without offspring, as we shall say in its proper place. But the second, Eberhard, living for a long time, waged many wars with the cities of the empire and with nobles for almost 46 years; concerning whose deeds and death, so far as [unclear], it has not been customary.

In these times Pope Clement VI, having sent legates into Germany, caused a general passage against the unbelieving Turks to be preached, promising to those contributing in support of the pilgrims from their goods to the chests publicly appointed for this purpose in the churches not only the customary indulgences, but also certain unusual ones: so that he granted to those who had put in their goods, assessed at a fixed amount, the eating of eggs on Fridays and of milk foods, and on all other days outside Lent on which they were permitted; something which until then had not been customary in Germany.

Baldwin of Trier and Walram of Cologne, archbishops, together with certain others, then obtained from the Apostolic See, after a considerable sum of money collected from their people had been spent on the crusade, that all persons established in their dioceses might be allowed in perpetuity, outside Lent, at every time to use milk foods, butter, and eggs; and this is observed so down to the present day. For the people of Trier and Cologne use milk foods and eggs throughout the whole year, with Lent alone excepted, on all vigils of saints and ecclesiastical fasts.

But Henry, archbishop of Mainz, who clung obstinately to the excommunicated Emperor Louis, did not have the favor of the Apostolic See; and therefore he neither wished to contribute anything to the crusade nor cared for the indulgences. Hence it is not lawful, down to the present day, throughout the whole diocese of Mainz, to use eggs at the time of any ecclesiastical fast.

And so Christians, assembled from almost all Europe, were carried in a great fleet against the Turks; and first taking the town of Smyrna, thereafter they fought often, with great slaughter of both peoples.

A very great storm in January.

The use of eggs is granted to the people of Trier and Cologne. A crusade against the Turks is preached. Henry, archbishop of Mainz. Expedition of the Christians into [unclear]. The Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

227

[unclear], increasing exceedingly, and showing a terrible blaze, at length with a great rumbling it passes away through the sky.
