In the same year also Pope Clement VI died; Innocent VI, likewise, a Limousin by birth, succeeded him and presided for nine years and eight months, a good man and a lover of religious, a very great canonist, who afterwards crowned Charles emperor.

Innocent VI becomes pope.

1353.

In the eleventh year of Abbot Wighard, and in the year of the Lord 1353, on the eve of St. Thomas the Apostle, Henry of Virneburg, formerly archbishop of Mainz, long before deposed by Pope Clement VI, as we said above, died. Even after his deposition, as we have often said, he conducted himself as archbishop as long as Emperor Louis IV lived, although Gerlach, promoted and ordained by the pope, had the greater obedience, and very many cities, towns, and castles, in Thuringia Erfurt, and in Hesse almost all, which at first obeyed the apostolic commands. But when Henry died, Gerlach peacefully obtained the church of Mainz, and presided alone for sixteen years.

In the same year, on the day of St. Erasmus, Louis margrave of Brandenburg, Rupert, also called Adolph, the elder count palatine of the Rhine, and John burgrave of Nuremberg, elected for the public advantage, as chosen arbitrators, made a further division of the lands of Upper Bavaria among the dukes, the sons of the late Emperor Louis IV, namely Stephen, William, and Albert, as is clear in the letters. [unclear]

In the year also noted above, celestial flames again appeared, astonishing to behold, drawing after them a long extinguished trail.

A flame in the sky.

1354.

In the twelfth year of Abbot Wighard, and in the year of the Lord 1354, Charles, king of the Romans, in the month of January held a solemn assembly of princes at Mainz; there, among many things which [unclear], he treated of [unclear], which happened in the following year.

In the same year, on the kalends of February, Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, died, a man worthy of perpetual remembrance; he amended and corrected the ordinary of the whole breviary for years, restored it to the form in which it now is, and magnificently enlarged his church with many riches and honors beyond all his predecessors. Boemund of Edendorf succeeded him.

[unclear] For that time was clouded and full of the darkness of ignorance, when regular observance perished, not only in this monastery of Hirsau, but also in all the monasteries of our order, almost throughout all Germany; and the monks, given over to the pleasures of the flesh and utterly casting away the study of letters, which had once made our forefathers glorious, thought of nothing less than writing down the deeds of their prelates. Hence there came about the shameful silence concerning the memorable acts of this distinguished monastery also, because there was no one from the time of Abbot Eberhard down to Frederick, the second of that name, for almost two hundred and seventy years, who clearly described the deeds and successions of the abbots, as others had once done. Therefore through all that time we have necessarily passed briefly.

Concerning Wighard the Second, thirty-third abbot of this monastery, who presided five years, two months, and twenty-one days, and concerning various acts.

When, however, lord Wighard the First, thirty-second abbot of this monastery, had died, and his poor body had been committed to ecclesiastical burial according to the custom of the order, lest the sheep should long be without a shepherd, or incur some danger to their souls, and lest the dead man’s household property, as often happens, should suffer loss, on the day appointed for electing, as the matter required, a new pastor, the brothers came together in one place in the year noted above, namely on the Sunday of the Nativity, 1354, in the seventh Roman indiction, on the morrow of St. Gregory the pope, which was Friday and the thirteenth day of the month of March. After they had held among themselves the necessary discussion concerning the form of election, the greater part of the brothers, with the others assenting, elected lord Wighard, the second of that name, [unclear].

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

The emperor’s crime

In the same year, Emperor Louis expelled John, son of the king of Bohemia, from the duchy of Carinthia, which he had previously given him after receiving money; and he joined his wife, seized without a judgment of the Church, to his own son, to the scandal of many. Hence for this as well as for many other crimes he was again excommunicated by Pope Clement VI, and at last, as we shall say, deposed from the empire.

1345.

In the third year of Abbot Wighard, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1345, William, count of Hainaut, Holland, and Zeeland, and lord of Frisia, around the feast of the Nativity of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, led a great army against the Frisians, having with him the count of Horn and many [unclear].

William, count of Holland, is killed in war.

In the fifth year of Abbot Wighard, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1345, William, count of Hainaut, Holland, and Zeeland, and lord of Frisia, around the feast of the Nativity of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, led a great army against the Frisians, having with him the count of Horn and many other nobles and very brave men. But the Frisians, surrounded by ditches full of water, came out against them in great fury, and, using their customary skill, when they had them enclosed among the marshes, killed some with the sword, while others they miserably drowned by suddenly releasing the waters. Among these Count William too was suffocated and died without children. After his death, his sister Margaret, wife of Emperor Louis IV, as the nearer heir, by decree of the emperor and princes, came down into Holland with her son William in great state; she at once subjected all her brother’s land to her own authority; and with the consent of the inhabitants she handed it over to her son William to govern. When matters had been settled in peace, she returned with her people to Bavaria. Therefore William, having obtained his uncle’s dominion, was accustomed to prefix such a title to his letters: William, by the grace of God count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, count of Hainaut, Holland, and Zeeland, and lord of Frisia, etc. He was, however, a proud, restless, and warlike man, who did not know how to defer to his own mother. From this time the aforesaid counties began to belong to the dukes of Bavaria; by them they were governed in quiet possession for almost eighty years, until the year of the Lord 1425; then they passed to the dukes of Burgundy.

In the aforesaid year Henry, archbishop of Mainz, having been summoned by Pope Clement VI and not appearing at the curia, was excommunicated.

1346.

In the fourth year of Abbot Wighard, but the year of the Lord 1346, Pope Clement VI, in a public consistory and with the consent of the cardinals, by sentence deposed in his absence Henry of Virneburg, archbishop of Mainz, contumacious and rebellious against the apostolic commands, previously, as we have said, summoned and excommunicated; he stripped him of every pontifical honor, and substituted Gerlach of Nassau in his place. Yet Gerlach did not obtain possession of the archbishopric [unclear], dealing with Gerlach not without great harm to the church of Mainz and the subject people.

In the same year a very grave dispute arose between the brothers Edward and Reinard over the duchy of Guelders; it lasted for sixteen years, to their great loss and the devastation of the whole land. For while quarrels and wars were being waged between them, many thousands of men were killed, villages were deserted without inhabitants, castles too were destroyed, and the land of the whole duchy remained untilled, the peasants having either been killed or put to flight. But finally Edward, after Reinard had been thrust into custody, alone obtained the duchy, as we shall say in its place.

In the same year also Pope Clement VI, who said that he had deposed Louis from the empire by sentence, commanded the princes that within a fixed term which he had set for them, unless they wished to lose the right of election, they should elect another emperor in Louis’s place, one who would obey the commands of the Church as a son should; otherwise he would necessarily have care of the empire as supreme head. Accordingly, assembling at Rhens below Boppard near the Rhine on the second day of the month of July, Baldwin archbishop of Trier, Walram archbishop of Cologne, Gerlach, to whom the pope, as we have said, had provided the church of Mainz, John king of Bohemia, and the duke of Saxony, unanimously elected, in his presence, Charles, firstborn son of the aforesaid John, king of Bohemia, as king of the Romans. The archbishop of Cologne anointed him in the town of Bonn with great pomp, as is the custom. For they could not safely go down to Aachen, because the people of Aachen zealously followed Louis’s party. But Adolf, count palatine of the Rhine, Henry archbishop of Mainz, although deposed by the pope, the margrave of Brandenburg, the dukes of Bavaria, and almost all the cities of the empire followed and defended Louis’s party with all their strength until his death.

In the same year King Edward of England entered France again with a great army Hirsau Monastery

[unclear], having with him John, king of Bohemia, father of Emperor Charles IV, and, when battle had been joined, he triumphed gloriously. But the king of Bohemia, wounded by the arrow of a certain Frenchman, fell. This John was the son of Emperor Henry VII and the father of Charles IV, as we said above, formerly count of Luxembourg; when his father was raised to the empire, he received Elizabeth, daughter of Wenceslaus king of Bohemia, together with the kingdom, as his wife, as we set out more clearly in the tenth year of Henry II the abbot; with him the duchy of Luxembourg passed to the Bohemians. He reigned in Bohemia for thirty-six years; when he died in this year, his son Charles succeeded him a little before he was elected to the empire, reigning with his son Wenceslaus for almost thirty-two years. The vines and the clusters hanging on them in this same year, during the octave of the Nativity of Blessed Mary ever Virgin, perished from cold and frost in many places, especially in the regions of Swabia and in many others.

1347.

In the fifth year of Abbot Wighard, which was A.D. 1347, on the day of St. Gereon the martyr, Emperor Louis IV died, and he was buried in the church of Blessed Mary ever Virgin in his city of Munich with pomp and honor. There were those who said that he had died by the poison of a certain duchess of Austria, whom, because of the ugly arrangement of her face, they called Maultasch, that is, “mouth-bag” or “sack”; whether this is true or not, we do not have it sufficiently established.

He left six sons, namely Louis, also called Otto, margrave of Brandenburg, the eldest by birth; Duke Louis, surnamed the Roman because he had been born at Rome; Duke Otto the younger; Duke Stephen; Duke William; and Duke Albert, whom he begot from Margaret, daughter of William, count of Hainaut, Holland, and Zeeland, as was said above in its place. How these six sons, after their father’s death, divided his duchy among themselves, we shall say below in the seventh year of Abbot Wighard. After Emperor Louis died, Henry archbishop of Mainz, although, as we said before, deposed by the pope, Adolf count palatine of the Rhine, Otto also called Louis, margrave of Brandenburg, and the other princes of Bavaria immediately came together; after taking counsel among themselves, they unanimously elected Edward, king of England, to the Roman empire against Charles. They also soon endeavored to summon him by letters and solemn envoys, promising that they would steadfastly provide him counsel and aid until death. Giving thanks to them, he sent back word that he was so occupied in governing the kingdoms of England and France that he could in no way attend to the empire of the Romans.

When these things were known, the aforesaid princes sent envoys with letters to the margrave of Meissen, son-in-law of the deceased Emperor Louis, and called him to the empire. Agreeing to them, he promised that he would come with an army as quickly as possible, although he did not come, having been skillfully forestalled or corrupted by Charles, as we shall say later.

1348.

In the sixth year of Abbot Wighard, A.D. 1348, when Charles learned that the margrave of Meissen had been elected against him as king of the Romans, as we said before, he nevertheless [bought him off?] from it for ten thousand pounds of silver. Hearing this, the aforesaid princes, gathered again at Frankfurt, elected Günther, count of Schwarzburg, a Thuringian, as king of the Romans.

In the same year Otto, bishop of Würzburg, died. Albert of Hohenlohe succeeded him and presided for twenty-four years; in the sixth year of his pontificate he surrounded the citizens of Würzburg, rebellious and disobedient to him, with a firm siege for three weeks and brought them back to obedience.

In the same year also William, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, count of Hainaut and Holland, and lord of Frisia, entered the lands of the church of Utrecht with a very great army of his men; miserably devastating everything with sword and fire, he annihilated the whole province. At length he paid the penalty for his cruelty, being made, by God’s vengeance, [insane?].

In the same year also Conrad de Deck was treacherously killed by a certain knight, [Suikerus?] of Gödelfingen, in his own house, which he had in the Bavarian city of Munich, from long-standing hatred.

1349.

In the seventh year of Abbot Wighard, and A.D. 1349, there was a great pestilence throughout the whole world, beginning from India and breaking everywhere into all the provinces, over the space of three years as far as Germany, England, and all peoples miserably

A very great pestilence in the whole world. The Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius.

225

[unclear] raging, it scarcely allowed half of mankind to remain among the living. A pitiable calamity: for as soon as anyone had been infected with this plague, by his very breath alone he also infected others. At this time the human race, especially in Germany, was afflicted by three plagues: namely pestilence, which laid low almost countless thousands of people throughout nearly the whole world. The cause of this calamity was ascribed to the Jews, because they had infected the springs and the air with poison. Hence there followed a very severe persecution of them by the Christians. For in various regions of the world, when this belief of the Christians had been spread abroad against them, some were miserably suffocated, others thrown down, others drowned, others beheaded, others burned, others pierced through with swords and lances, others killed by various kinds of torments. Some of them, seeing that they had fallen into evil, first killed their children and wives, lest they be handed over into the hands of Christians raging cruelly to be tortured, and then, setting fire to their houses, willingly destroyed themselves by burning. This persecution against the Jews, beginning in the year already noted, lasted two years and consumed many thousands of them in all the provinces. The second plague was a flux of blood, which also carried off a huge multitude of people by an unheard-of kind of torment. The third was the burning of the sacred fire, as that disease is commonly called; it raged with such savagery that whomever it attacked, it at once utterly consumed the flesh down to the bones; nor was it hostile only to the living, but, attacking also the unburied corpses of the dead, it consumed the flesh before they could be buried. These were times full of calamities and overflowing with such great dangers that, except for the universal flood, no one has written of worse.

In the year already noted, Gunther, count of Schwarzburg, elected king by these [unclear], waited for Charles's arrival before the city with tents and camps for [unclear] days and six weeks. Moreover the citizens of Frankfurt were well disposed toward Gunther. Likewise the remaining cities of the empire in Upper Germany, except the people of Strasbourg, who were of Charles's party.

When Charles heard that Gunther had come to Frankfurt, he gathered an army of his men and advanced against him; but seeing that he was stronger than himself, using the skill of Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, he at last drew the duke of Bavaria to his side by many promises. Hence Gunther, seeing that he had been deceived, began to negotiate for concord through the mediation of Otto, margrave of Brandenburg; and having received two thousand two hundred marks of very pure silver, and two cities in Thuringia held for life for his expenses, [unclear].

Likewise the remaining cities of the empire in Upper Germany, except the people of Strasbourg, who were of Charles's party.

[unclear] of the archbishop of Trier, the duke of Bavaria was at last drawn to his side by many promises. Hence Gunther, seeing that he had been deceived, began to negotiate for concord through the mediation of Otto, margrave of Brandenburg; and having received two thousand two hundred marks of very pure silver, and two cities in Thuringia held for life for his expenses, [unclear].

Likewise the remaining cities of the empire in Upper Germany, except the people of Strasbourg, who were of Charles's party.

In the year already noted, Gunther, count of Schwarzburg, elected king by [unclear] ... When Charles heard that Gunther had come to Frankfurt, he gathered an army of his men and advanced against him; but seeing that he was stronger than himself, using the skill of Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, he at last drew the duke of Bavaria to his side by many promises. Hence Gunther, seeing that he had been deceived, began to negotiate for concord through the mediation of Otto, margrave of Brandenburg; and having received two thousand one hundred marks of very pure silver, and two cities in Thuringia held for life for his expenses, [unclear].

Likewise the remaining cities of the empire in Upper Germany, except the people of Strasbourg, who were of Charles's party.

[unclear] of the archbishop of Trier, the duke of Bavaria was at last drawn to his side by many promises. Hence Gunther, seeing that he had been deceived, began to negotiate for concord through the mediation of Otto, margrave of Brandenburg; and having received two thousand one hundred marks of very pure silver, and two cities in Thuringia held for life for his expenses, [unclear].

Likewise the remaining cities of the empire in Upper Germany, except the people of Strasbourg, who were of Charles's party.

In the year already noted, in the seventh year of Abbot Wighard, on the vigil of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Walram, archbishop of Cologne, died; he, because of many [unclear].

[unclear], the mother of Wenceslaus, king of Bohemia and later emperor. The second was from France; after she also died without children, he took as his third wife the daughter of the prince of Swabia, by whom he begot a daughter, whom he gave as wife to the margrave of Brandenburg. The fourth wife was Elisabeth, daughter of the duke of Pomerania and Stettin, by whom he begot Sigismund, king of Hungary and later emperor of the Romans, and Johann, duke.

At the same time a certain new heresy arose, taking its beginning in Hungary, which in a short time was striving to infect all Germany with its poison. Ignorant, rustic, and unlearned people, under the pretext of penance, which they imposed on themselves without the judgment of a priest, men and women mixed together, walking half-naked, carried wooden crosses in their hands.

The heresy of the flagellants arose in Hungary. with head, hood, and cap, but with their private parts covered by a linen covering, they publicly scourged themselves in church and outside, even to the shedding of blood, with whips having three knots and spikes at the tip; singing certain songs mostly either contrary to or suspect in the Christian faith, and more often prostrating themselves on the ground in the form of a cross, they cried out in prayer. But the pontiffs of the churches, considering that this sect was not sincere and would bring no small harm upon the faithful peoples, hastened, by the authority of Pope Clement VI, to remove it from their midst as quickly as possible, leading back the correctable, through public penance and the renunciation of error, to the way of truth; but the obstinate, handed over to secular judgment, they burned with fire. And so at length the new and foolish presumption of the Flagellants ceased.

Also in the aforesaid year there was a division of the duchy of Bavaria among the six sons of Louis, formerly emperor. Louis, who was also [unclear], the first-born, margrave of Brandenburg, Louis the Roman, duke, and the younger Otto, duke, received by lot Upper Bavaria, with all things belonging to it. But Stephen, William, and Albert received into possession Lower Bavaria, Holland, and the lordship of Frisia, although afterward another division was made.

In the same year there was a great earthquake in Germany; it overthrew the city of Villach, and many buildings, both in Italy and in Germany, fell from the violence of this commotion.

1350.

In the eighth year of Abbot Wighard, and in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1350, Pope Clement VI, by a solemn constitution previously issued on the matter, recalled the twentieth year of indulgences, which they called the Jubilee in imitation of the Hebrews, from the hundredth year, as Boniface VIII had instituted it, to the fiftieth, moved by the pious consideration that the very brief span of human life grants to very few the ability to live to the hundredth year. Accordingly the second Jubilee is celebrated this year in the city of Rome, by command of Pope Clement, with many flocking there from every side.

In the same year William, fourteenth in order, abbot of my monastery of Sponheim, freely and voluntarily resigned the abbacy into the hands of his community around the feast of Saint Lawrence the martyr; weighed down by old age and infirmity, he died in the same year, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, and was buried in the chapel of the blessed Mary ever Virgin, which he himself had founded from the foundations in the cloister. After his resignation Philip Meyvvin, the fifteenth abbot, succeeding by election of the brothers, presided for twenty-four years, one month, and twelve days, confirmed by Gerlach, archbishop of Mainz, because Henry, as we have said, had been deposed and excommunicated by the pope and was not regarded as bishop by good and religious men.

1351.

In the ninth year of Abbot Wighard, and in the year of the Lord 1351, Emperor Charles IV, in order to please his princes, by whose help and favor he had come to the empire, established many new tolls around the Rhine and granted them to them, to the very great harm of the commonwealth. But when the merchants, too heavily burdened by this, avoided the traffic of the Rhine and brought their complaint to the cities, all with one accord opposed themselves to the emperor. They could in no way go either up or down from [unclear]. But when the princes saw that through this they were being deprived of the revenues of both the old and the new toll, they entered into concord and peace with the citizens and, content with the old and ancient tolls, renounced the new ones.

In the same year the empress Margaret, formerly wife of Emperor Louis IV, having assembled a great army of Bavarians and others, moved an expedition against her son William, count of Holland, who was oppressing his poor men and subjects very cruelly, after being invoked by the inhabitants as the sole daughter of that land. But when a naval battle was joined on the Meuse, on the fourth day of the month of July, that is, on the feast of the Translation of Saint Martin, the mother was defeated by the son; fleeing with a few, she went down to England.

Also in the same year, in the month of December, a comet appeared beneath the very north; when it had disappeared, violent storms of winds followed, and a heavenly beam, burning at its front part, was seen to glide through the sky.

1352.

In the tenth year of Abbot Wighard, which was the year of the Lord 1352, Reinhard, son of [unclear] of Sponheim, and Ernest of Molenack, canons of the greater church of Cologne, on the Friday before Palm Sunday, in the court of the official of Cologne, were killed very cruelly for a trivial cause, from rashness, by the leading men of the city.

In the same year, after sunset, a heavenly flame between the west and the south very broadly Of the Monastery of Hirsau

his sister’s nephew, certainly a man at that time better than many in knowledge, character, and experience; he, confirmed and ordained by Gerhard of Ehrenberg, bishop of the church of Speyer, with great solemnity presided over this monastery of Hirsau for 5 years, 2 months, and 21 days. He was elected on a Friday and, after the space of a month, confirmed; he received his benediction here in the monastery on the feast of the holy apostles Philip and James. Since either nothing or little concerning his deeds has been committed to writing, we too have been able to insert only a few things in this work of ours and make them known to posterity. We have set down the reason for this openly a little earlier.

In the aforesaid current year of the Lord 1354, which was the first begun year of this Wighard, Salmann, bishop of Worms, died. Theodoric succeeded him, the son of a certain knight, from the family of those who to the present day are called the Bavarians of Boppard, an ancient and formerly privileged family; he presided for nine years and had disputes with the citizens.

In the same year also, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, Pope Innocent VI, before the third year of his pontificate had yet been completed, at the request of Abbot Wighard confirmed all and individual goods and privileges of this monastery, while residing at Rome at St. Peter’s.

1355.

In the second year of Abbot Wighard, which was the year of the Lord 1355, King Charles, having set out for Rome with a great company of princes, nobles, knights, and foot-soldiers, received, together with the queen, the crown of empire with great solemnity and tranquillity. There are those who write that he received the crown of empire from the hand of the cardinal of Ostia, sent for this purpose by Pope Innocent from Avignon.

In the same year, in the month of September, on a certain day around the ninth hour, a great earthquake occurred around Basel and Strasbourg; under its force a great part of the city of Basel was overthrown, and many surrounding buildings and walls and very strong castles in the mountains collapsed, and they wretchedly crushed many people.

Also in the aforesaid year, John, the third of that name, duke of Brabant, when he saw that he was about to die from illness, assumed the monastic habit of the order of St. Benedict; fortified with the saving sacraments, on the sixth day of the month of December he most devoutly rested in the Lord. He was buried in Veleer, a monastery of our order, leaving one only daughter, named Joanna, whom Wenceslaus, count of Luxembourg and brother of Emperor Charles, had taken as wife; with her he contended that the duchy of Brabant had passed into his right. Hence a grave dispute arose between the bishop and Louis, count of Flanders; at length they were reconciled by choosing as arbitrator William, count of Hainaut and Holland, son of the late Emperor Louis.

1356.

In the second year of Abbot Wighard, but the year of the Lord 1356, Emperor Charles, having returned from Italy, held a solemn assembly of princes in the city of Metz, where all the princes and nobles of the whole kingdom, even from France, gathered. Charles himself was known and dear to them, since he had long ago devoted himself to letters at Paris, and at one time, with his father the king of Bohemia, was about to fight in aid of the king of the French. Present at this solemn assembly of princes was a certain archbishop, legate of the Apostolic See, for confirming the peace of the whole kingdom; out of reverence for the supreme pontiff, he alone ate at one table with the emperor, while the other princes, the electors, served according to the nature of each one’s office, once, and afterward sat in their own place according to custom. There William, margrave of Julich, with the consent of the princes, was raised by Charles to be duke, and his margraviate of Julich was changed into a duchy with great pomp. Wenceslaus, too, count of Luxembourg, brother of Emperor Charles and son-in-law of John, the last duke of Brabant, whom we said died in the preceding year, was likewise elevated to be duke. This Duke Wenceslaus, son of John king of Bohemia, grandson of Emperor Henry VII, and brother, as we have said, of Charles IV, a man most noble in birth, learned in the education of letters, vigorous in military affairs, hardly second to anyone in life and character, magnificent in justice, clemency, and piety, was, by I know not what divine judgment, always unfortunate; he frequently had the outcome of all his principal actions contrary to his wishes and liable to losses. He obtained the duchy of Brabant with his wife, which he governed together with Luxembourg for almost 28 years; concerning his death we shall write later under the year of the Lord 1383. In the same assembly of princes held at Metz, the county of the land of Bar was [unclear] into a margraviate Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

229

...was raised to a [duchy?], although among the common people, and among many even today through ignorance, the name of county remains. The same Charles, having summoned an assembly of the princes for the advantage of the commonwealth, caused the so-called Golden Bull, so called because it is strengthened with a golden seal, concerning the election of the Roman emperors, to be written and confirmed with the consent of all the electors and of the realm. When these matters had been duly completed and the assembly dissolved, he passed with his wife from city to city, from monastery to monastery, everywhere most diligently seeking out the relics of saints; and from those he found he carried many into Bohemia, by entreaties which no one could refuse, for the glory and adornment of the churches of his nation.

1357.

In the fourth year of Abbot Wighard, and the year of the Lord 1357, Wilhelm, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, Count of Holland, Hainaut, and Zeeland, and lord of Frisia, son of Louis, formerly the fourth emperor, about whom we have said much above in its proper places, after he had governed those lands for almost twelve years, not without tyranny, having taken poison, by the contrivance of I do not know whom, as was said, became mad. Committed to custody, he remained thus for twenty years until his death; he died mad in prison in the year from the birth of the Lord 1377, as we shall say below. And because he had no sons, Albert his brother, taking up after him the counties and lordships of Holland, Hainaut, and Frisia, governed them vigorously for forty-seven years; and he was twenty-first in the order of succession of the counts of Holland. He had as wife Margaret, daughter of the Duke of Brieg, who bore him two sons: Wilhelm, who succeeded his father in the aforesaid counties, and John, bishop of Liège, of whom mention will be made in their proper places; and one daughter named Catherine. She was first betrothed to Edward, Duke of Guelders, who was the brother of Duke Reinhard the captive. But before the wedding was celebrated, he was killed in a certain war, in the year of the Lord 1371, as we shall say there. When he had died, his betrothed, still a virgin and now a widow, thereafter agreed to be joined in marriage to no one unless he was of the blood of the dukes of Guelders. Therefore at length she married Wilhelm, son of the Duke of Jülich, by Sophia, daughter of the illustrious man Florentius of Mechlin, first wife of Reinhard, first Duke of Guelders, father of Edward her former betrothed, about whom we spoke above.

1358.

In the [fifth?] year of Abbot Wighard, which was the year of the Lord 1358, Albert, Duke of Austria, son of Albert formerly King of the Romans, died, leaving after him Leopold his son, duke, from whom the genealogy of Maximilian our king, who rules today, is continued, as will appear in order in what follows; also Albert, Duke of Austria, who founded the University of Vienna in Austria; also Rudolf, duke, who founded the provostship of St. Stephen the protomartyr in Vienna and joined the county of Tyrol to the duchy of Austria, and who had as wife Catherine, daughter of Emperor Charles IV; Frederick, duke, who died without children. He also left two daughters: Margaret, Margravine of Brandenburg, and Catherine, abbess of St. Clare in Vienna.

In the same year there was a great pestilence from the beginning of August until the Nativity of the Lord throughout almost all Germany; many thousands of people perished from this disease in a very short time.

Also in the year noted above, very serious wars arose between Louis, King of Hungary, and the Venetians over the kingdom of Dalmatia, which the Venetians had possessed for many years while the kings of Hungary protested. And so King Louis, having gathered a great army both of his own men and of Germans, entered Dalmatia in strength. First he obtained the city of Zadar, then the maritime cities, and finally all Dalmatia. Thereafter he also entered the borders of the Venetians, and after some of their fortifications had been captured, he struck great terror into them. Hence, compelled by necessity, they sought peace. The king not only granted it to them, but also restored their fortifications, which he had taken by right of war, except for the kingdom of Dalmatia itself, after receiving an oath from them that they would in no way harm or punish anyone in those lands which he had restored to them because of loyalty previously shown to the king; nevertheless they by no means kept this.

1359.

In the sixth year of Abbot Wighard, and the year of the Lord 1359, Edward, King of England, released John, King of France, and his son Philip, whom he had captured in battle the previous year, under certain conditions. When these were not observed, in the following year, with more than one hundred and fifty ships armed, he led a huge army into Gaul and, besieging Paris, afflicted the whole province with great slaughter, devastating everything with fire and sword.

230 The Monastery of Hirsau

In the same year, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, which was the Wednesday after the feast of St. Urban, pope and martyr, Wighard himself, the second abbot of this name, but the thirty-third in the order of abbots, died, in the sixth current year of his rule.

Concerning Wignand, the Thirty-Fourth Abbot of This Monastery, who presided for 20 years, 10 months, 20 days, and concerning various events.

Abbot Wighard dies.

Wignand becomes abbot.

He presided for nearly twenty years.

The author complains that the monks did not write annals.

An excuse for the vain ignorance of monks.

Without history faith would be [unclear].

Delft, a town of the chief place of Holland.

An assembly of princes at Esslingen.

Esslingen is surrounded with a siege.

A contention between the archbishop of Trier and the count of Sponheim; Enkirch is subjected.

Now, after Wighard, the second of this name, the thirty-third abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, as we have said, had entered upon the way of all flesh and had been buried with due solemnity, as the custom then was, the prior and brothers, bereft of their spiritual shepherd, soon in the same year, on the last day of the month of May, which was the Friday after Urban’s day, came together in the chapter-place for the election of a new father. After the necessary counsels and discussions had meanwhile first been held, they set over them as thirty-fourth abbot of this monastery Wignand, a monk from their own company. Confirmed and ordained according to custom by Gerhard von Ehrenberg, bishop of Speyer, he presided in the abbacy for twenty years, ten months, and twenty days. Of his deeds, because of the sloth and idleness of the monks, we can bring down either nothing or little to the knowledge of posterity, since they were done beyond the memory of those who live today, and were committed to writing by no one, as ought to have been done. For after love and zeal for letters began to fail among monks, together with the discipline of regular observance, it is not surprising if no one either wished or was able to write the chronicle of the monastery for the instruction of posterity. Shameful to say, I am compelled to state what many abbots, who profess the holy observance of regular life with their monks, and who are ignorant of the usefulness of history, object against us. For they say: “What advantage can it bring us to know the antiquity of the foundations of monasteries? What does it contribute to recall to memory either the successions or the deeds of abbots, who sleep in the dust of death and are not soothed by any praises?” O you already buried, idle men though alive, whose memory will perish with a noise: how asinine and crude in wit you are, you openly show, since you despise the good of histories, which you cannot attain. History is written for the living, both present and future, not for the dead; therefore, if you lived in understanding, you would certainly love histories. For if history were taken away, neither would the memory of the most holy Gospel nor the martyrdoms and passions of the saints have come down to our knowledge. Let men alive yet buried in ignorance therefore fare well, and let them live for themselves alone, content with their own idleness, useful to none, and imitable by none in good actions or zeal. But let us pursue our own subject.

Around these times Albert, duke of Bavaria, count of Holland and Zeeland, and lord of Hainaut and Frisia, captured the town of Holland named Delft because of the disobedience and rebellion of its citizens. After taking it he overthrew its walls and gates down to the ground. He also utterly destroyed the castle of Heemskerk.

In the second current year of Abbot Wignand, in the year of the Lord [1360?], the emperor Charles summoned the princes of the empire to the Swabian town of Esslingen for certain affairs of the empire. There, when one day in the refectory of the Friars Minor he was discussing his counsels with them, a disturbance of the citizens arose against the emperor and princes, and a tumult was stirred up. Soon withdrawing from the town, he entrusted it to Eberhard, count of Württemberg, to make compensation for so great an affront inflicted upon him. He, after an army of his own men and of the imperial cities had been gathered together, encircled Esslingen with a siege and began to attack it vigorously. But when the citizens saw that they were placed in an evil situation and could not resist so great a multitude, they accepted peace through the intervention of money, paying to the emperor sixty thousand gold pieces in satisfaction, and thirty thousand to Count Eberhard for the expenses incurred. And thus the disturbance of the tumult, purchased for one hundred thousand, came to rest.

At these times serious disagreements had arisen between Boemund, archbishop of Trier, and the counts of Sponheim and Starkenburg, over certain castles and lordships. But through the intervention of friends, Count Walram of Sponheim soon returned into concord with the archbishop. The count of Starkenburg, however, began to lay waste grievously with sword and fire the fields, villages, and possessions of the church of Trier, and inflicted much damage. But the archbishop, having gathered an army, [attacked?] Enkirch, a village of the count situated on the bank of the Moselle, together with the fortification itself.

To the Reader.

Thus far, not only the earlier Basel edition, produced under the care of Guilhelmus Radens, but also the autograph itself, compared by us with that edition, which is preserved in the most splendid Palatine Library, copied with astonishing elegance by the careful hand of Trithemius. It is uncertain, however, whether the author carried the work further, and perhaps down to his own time, as he did the Spanheim chronicle. This raises a doubt, because in the preface to the Spanheim chronicle, written in the year 1506 in that monastery, he says as follows: “The chronicle of the monastery of Hirsau, begun here indeed, but at length completed at Würzburg, the city of the Franks: a great work, and divided into two volumes.” But in the letter to Rogerius Sicambrus, which is found among his familiar letters printed at Hagenau, p. 320, dated at Würzburg in the year 1507, he writes thus: “At the request of Blasius, abbot of Hirsau, I undertook to write the chronicle of that same monastery and completed the greater part; but after his death I have meanwhile halted its publication, uncertain with what reward his successor will recompense the labor.” Again, in the Breviarium of the Annals of the Franks, published at Paris, fol. III, he says: “We long ago wrote, at the urging of the abbots Blasius and Johannes, two volumes, of no small size, of the chronicles or annals of the distinguished monastery of Hirsau of our order, which is situated in the diocese of Speyer on the border of the Nemetes; in the first of which,” etc. It therefore appears either that the writing was suddenly broken off at this point by him in indignation, after the greater part, as he said, had been completed; or it must be regretted that a further volume of these annals, of equal size besides, is wanting. Yet this loss, if such it is, the following complete Spanheim chronicle, brought down to the author’s own time and now first published by our efforts, will be able in large part to repair.

the fortification which he had made beneath the castle of Starckenburg for exacting a toll from those sailing, though he, as prince of the land, opposed it, he seized and utterly destroyed. Seeing this, the count, fearing worse things, sought the pontiff’s favor through messengers, and received it together with pardon.

In these times also the emperor Charles IV, since he was a learned man, inasmuch as he had devoted himself for a long time to letters in the school of Paris, and loved learned men above others, laudably established the university of Prague for the adornment of the kingdom of Bohemia. It was distinguished by him with many privileges and donations, and in a short time grew beyond all the universities of all Germany in glory and in the number of persons, until at length, after almost fifty years, stained by many heresies, which are known to all, it was reduced to nothing. The bishop of the church of Prague also, for the honor of the kingdom, who until then had been a suffragan under the archbishop of Mainz, he raised by apostolic authority to an archbishop, and adorned him with many privileges, subjecting to him suffragans and bishops after the manner of the others. In Bohemia he founded many new churches, and churches founded both by himself and by his predecessors he magnificently honored with relics, ornaments, paintings, jewels, and various gifts. The hall of the village of Ingelheim, not far from Mainz and the Rhine, which the emperor Charles the Great once had as a castle of residence for his majesty [unclear], in which he was born, and where, according to the belief of the inhabitants, he received from heaven the sword sent by an angel when he was about to fight against the Saracens, which is shown yearly at Nuremberg, he changed into a monastery of canons of the rule of St. Augustine, decreeing that no one should be received into religion there unless he had been born in Bohemia. This has been observed up to now, and even to the present day, for no fewer than one hundred forty-four years. He subjected that monastery, however, to the abbot of the monastery of St. Charles in Prague for the time being, to whom its visitation was to belong. He also obtained from the pope, with great indulgences, graces, and remissions of sins, that the feast [unclear] every year on the Friday after the octave of Easter throughout the whole world of Christ [unclear], after a long contest among the brothers over the duchy of Guelders.

MCCCLXI.

In the third year of Abbot Wignand, which was the year of the Lord’s nativity 1361, on a certain day in the month of February toward evening the sky seemed to burn. That night William, the first duke of Jülich, a warlike and magnanimous man, died.

In the same year Gerhard, count of Mons, and Arnold, count of Blankenheim, laboring under an inveterate hatred against one another, killed each other in the city of Cologne while jousting with sharp lances, each pierced by the other.

In the same year also, after a long contest among the brothers over the duchy of Guelders, after many fires and homicides, at last Edward, coming out victorious, captured his brother Reinald. He kept him committed to custody until the end of his life for ten years, and, having obtained the duchy of Guelders, ruled without anyone’s opposition.

MCCCLXII.

In the fourth year of Abbot Wignand, and the year of the Lord 1362, certain brigands coming out of England were roaming through Spain and France, by plundering, fire, and sword inflicting many losses and injuries on the inhabitants of the land in villages, especially where there was no defense. When they had grown together in number and in boldness, they set over themselves a captain, whom in common speech they called the archpriest. That multitude of robbers, however, was called the Great Company or the English Company, having more than 40,000 men going forth to battle. After roaming through Spain and France, they at last entered the territory of Trier, laying waste everything with fire and rapine. On hearing of their arrival, Boemund the archbishop sent against them Kuno of Falkenstein, his coadjutor, Wenceslaus of Luxembourg, duke of Brabant, Walram, count of Spanheim, also the count of Veldenz, and the count of Starckenburg, with many other counts, nobles, and fighters. As soon as they understood that so many princes had assembled against them, they turned their backs and withdrew from the territory of Trier. Entering Alsace, they inflicted many losses on the villagers around Strasbourg, snatching away whatever they found.

Therefore that cursed company came by night to the walls of Strasbourg, stationed itself around the city, and consumed with fire Köningshonen and all the villages situated nearby. The gates of the city, however, were kept closed, and no one was permitted to go out as long as they remained there. Whomever they found afflicted in the field or in hamlets, they butchered with unheard-of tortures, unless it was permitted to pass safely, without their safe-conduct; and whatever safe-conduct they had given to anyone, they preserved with inviolable firmness. Women, virgins, nuns, and young girls, as many as they found, they violated with an insatiable kind of lust, and many Of the Monastery of Hirsau

They killed [unclear]. They kept young males captive in servitude. But because report of them had preceded their arrival, the peasants had carried whatever was movable into the cities and fortified places. They did indeed surround several towns with a siege, but since they lacked the engines necessary for assault, they were able to capture none at all. Meanwhile the citizens of Strasbourg, together with the Alsatians, sent letters and messengers to Emperor Charles, then at Frankfurt with the princes, to implore aid; the emperor promised them that he would come shortly with an army. But, though often entreated, since he always promised his arrival and always put it off, he gave the Alsatians great [suspicion] concerning himself of a conspiracy secretly entered into with the English Company, because he allowed so noble a province to be laid waste by the basest little robbers. At last, compelled by shame and necessity, he sent an army into Alsace. As it approached, the band of robbers withdrew in flight; and when our men decided to pursue them, they used such speed in fleeing that our men could not cover in four days the journey they made in one day. But after the robbers’ departure, the emperor’s army, ranging through Alsace, did the inhabitants very great damage, trampling down and destroying the grain in the fields, since it was close to harvest-time, so much so that they seemed to have suffered heavier losses from friends than from enemies. Hence a great famine followed, which grievously afflicted all Alsace for six continuous years.

In the aforesaid year Bohemond, archbishop of Trier, burdened by gout and old age, caused Cuno of Falkenstein, canon of the church of Mainz, formerly coadjutor of Archbishop Henry against Gerlach, to be created canon of the church of Trier, and took him on as coadjutor, entrusting to him the handling of the affairs of the whole church and country. He, triumphing everywhere most gloriously against the enemies of the aforesaid church, soon at the beginning of his appointment accomplished wonderful things. Therefore Bohemond, rejoicing, obtained by his prayers from Pope Innocent VI consent to resign the archbishopric of Trier to Cuno. When the pope gladly assented to this, Bohemond abdicated the pontificate and had Cuno as successor, receiving from him for his own support, for as long as he should live, the town and castle of Saarburg with their appurtenances and revenues; he survived five years.

In the year written above Pope Innocent VI died. Urban V succeeded him, abbot of Marseille, of the Order of Saint Benedict; he presided for eight years, a learned man of most holy life, who caused the cross to be preached against the Turks and accomplished many good things. In his time flourished the devoted servant of Christ, Saint Bridget, formerly queen of Sweden, illuminated by many divine revelations; she scorned worldly rule for love of the heavenly, and, going out from her land and kindred, made pilgrimage to the thresholds of the saints, continually devoting herself to fasts, alms, and prayers. She came to Avignon to Pope Urban V, sent by our Lord Jesus Christ for the confirmation of her rule, which she had made.

Also in the aforesaid year William of Gennep, archbishop of Cologne, died, leaving an enormous treasure in gold, silver, wine, and grain. The see was vacant for ten months.

MCCCLXIII

In the fifth year of Abbot Wignand, and the Lord’s year 1363, Gerard, bishop of Speyer, died and was buried in the major church. Lampert of Buren, abbot of the monastery in Gengenbach, of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Strasbourg, immediately succeeded him and presided for eighteen years; when these had elapsed, by the authority of Pope Urban VI, he was transferred to the noble exempt bishopric of Bamberg.

In the same year John of Virneburg, dean of the major church, was elected archbishop of Cologne by the chapter. He went in person to the curia for his confirmation; but Pope Urban not only refused to confirm his election, [unclear].

Adolf was thus archbishop of Cologne [unclear] of Speyer.

[unclear] he raised up the will of the chapter; he presided only ten months, and afterwards resigned. [He held] for a long time episcopal churches of no mean dignity, such as Hildesheim in Saxony, Augsburg in Vindelicia, Culm in Prussia, and Constance in Swabia.

MCCCLXIV

John becomes bishop of Worms.

Of Worms.

Becomes.

Chronicle of Johannes Trithemius

1363.

In the sixth year of Abbot Wignand, which was the year of the Lord 1364, Adolf, archbishop of Cologne, having been accused before the apostolic see of being a squanderer of ecclesiastical property and of possessing nothing worthy of the pontificate, resigned the archbishopric, not by force or fear, but voluntarily.

Adolf, archbishop of Cologne, is deposed. Engelbert becomes archbishop of Cologne.

With the consent of Pope Urban V, provision was newly made, as was then the custom, for Engelbert of the Mark, bishop of Liege, his paternal uncle, to the church of Cologne; he presided for four years, not very usefully. Adolf, after resigning the pontificate, not without loss to the church of Cologne, married a certain girl, the sister of the count of Mark, through love of whom he hoped to obtain the county of Cleves; although he held the bishopric of Munster for five years, and, relying on the presumed confidence of [unclear], he at length obtained with his wife the county he had desired, so that both counties, namely Cleves and Mark, have remained joined even to the present day, although Cleves was afterwards, as we shall say in its place, gloriously raised to a duchy.

1365.

In the seventh year of Abbot Wignand, and the year of the Lord’s nativity 1365, Emperor Charles IV again entered Italy; and, after finding Pope Urban in Rome and holding with him a discussion of certain secrets, he returned safe to Germany with his nobles.

The emperor returns from Italy [unclear]. Severe winter, famine, and pestilence.

There was famine everywhere and a great pestilence in Germany, and many people died, some from cold, others from hunger. John of Rupescissa, led astray by I know not what spirit, unless his own, foretold many things soon to come concerning Antichrist, the general trampling-down of the clergy, and the reduction of the whole world to the faith [unclear].

John of Rupescissa, of the order of Saint Francis, on Antichrist.

He wrote many and various things about these matters to a certain cardinal, which are extant; but whether they have held true as he predicted, let those who have read his books, learned judges of histories, decide.

In these times a great and very firm confederation was made among the imperial and free cities, which even to the most powerful princes seemed formidable at its beginning.

The Worms contention against John [unclear], bishop. Great confederation of cities.

Among the people of Worms there was great disagreement over the establishment of the council and the office of Schultheiss, and over certain other matters belonging to jurisdiction; this was at last brought back to peace by Rupert, count palatine of the Rhine, who was also Adolf, and by the councils of Mainz and Speyer, on the day of the Conversion of Saint Paul in the aforesaid year. We often read that such confederations, which they commonly called leagues, “Bund,” were sworn and confirmed not only among cities but also among princes, and likewise we see it every day; but human instability preserves nothing inviolate for long. Hence the fitting proverb is:

The fickle crowd is always moved along with its prince.

1366.

In the eighth year of Abbot Wignand, but the year of the Lord’s nativity 1356, between the bishop and the citizens [unclear].

Bohemond, archbishop, dies.

Cuno, archbishop of Trier, was buried in the greater church of Trier. After him Cuno himself of Falkenstein, lord of Minzenberg, born of a mother who was the daughter of the count of Saarwerden, while Bohemond was still alive, as we have said, was ordained archbishop and presided very usefully for twenty-one years.

Boppard and Wesel are pledged.

This Archbishop Cuno, for the services rendered in many ways to Emperor Charles IV, obtained Boppard and Wesel, with half of Sterrenberg, which Baldwin, the former archbishop, had obtained in pledge from his brother Emperor Henry on account of the expenses of the empire incurred in Italy, by a more artful pledging, for the sum of [unclear] of eternal goodness, indeed a very great one, so that the amount of the later pledge was greater than that of the earlier. For Cuno was a very prudent man, whom nature had made for the rule even of many churches, nor was there readily found anyone like him.

The quarrel of the counts of Eberstein and [Wertheim?].

[unclear], and the counts of Eberstein, which soon turned into great loss for both parties.

The Monastery of Hirsau

grew up. Therefore, when the man of Württemberg was one day in the natural bath which we commonly call Wildbad, the count of Eberstein came secretly with an army and encircled the place with a siege, hoping that he would capture the count inside. But vain confidence deceived him. For, led by a certain peasant by night through the woods to safer places, he escaped his hands without injury; and very serious wars, burnings, and plunderings followed between them. For almost all the nobles, conspiring with the aforesaid count of Eberstein against the man of Württemberg, except only the citizens in Esslingen, who sided with Count Eberhard, took up arms and stirred up battles.

In the same year also Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, weighed down by very great burdens of debt, and also not moderately disabled by paralysis, feeling that on this account he was less equal to the government of the pontificate, with the consent of his chapter took as coadjutor Cuno, the above-mentioned archbishop of Trier, to whom, with Pope Urban V approving, he committed the whole administration of the church in spiritual and temporal matters. Archbishop Engelbert, however, after this provision had been completed, withdrew to the tranquillity of private life, retaining certain revenues for the use of his life; he did not long survive.

1368.

In the tenth year of Abbot Wignand, and in the year of the Lord one thousand three hundred sixty-eight, Count Eberhard of Württemberg died, leaving two sons, namely Ulrich and Eberhard, who afterwards waged many battles against him [unclear].

In the same year, on the twenty-first day of the month of August, Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, died; after his death the archiepiscopate was vacant for two years. For Cuno, archbishop of Trier, although he was postulated by the chapter, did not wish to be archbishop; but by order of Pope Urban, under the name of administrator, he governed that church together with his own Trier church quite strenuously and usefully. In the aforementioned year, in Lent, a comet appeared from heaven.

In these times also Cuno, the often-mentioned archbishop of Trier, built quite handsomely the castle Engers with its fortification beside the Rhine, between Koblenz and Andernach, and wished it to be called, from his own name, Cunenergers, although few attach his name to it.

1369.

In the eleventh year of Abbot Wignand, and in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1369, around the feast of Easter, Emperor Charles IV, after a very great army of his men had been assembled, entered Lombardy to fight against the Milanese; ranging about here and there until the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel, he could not defeat those who were in fortifications. For he wished to reduce the lordship of Milan to the empire by arms, and to avenge the wrongs of Pope Urban V, which he had once received from the Visconti, when he was still in minor orders: they had forced him to eat the apostolic letters brought against them. But when plague had violently invaded the army, after receiving a great sum of money as a sign of the superiority of the empire, he returned to his own lands, not without great displeasure on the pope’s part.

In this same year the citizens of Cologne, having attempted to infringe the privileges and liberties of the clergy, were subjected to an ecclesiastical interdict for two years; the clergy, leaving the city by order of Cuno, administrator of the church of Cologne, remained outside for eighteen months.

In the same year also Gottfried, count of Arnsberg, with the consent of his wife, handed over his county of Arnsberg, with all its appurtenances, castles, villages, and revenues, to the church of Cologne to be possessed forever, just as it is also possessed today by the archbishop.

1370.

In the twelfth year of Abbot Wignand, and in the year of the Lord one thousand three hundred seventy, a great battle took place on the vigil of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle between Wenceslaus, duke of Brabant and Luxembourg, brother of Emperor Charles, and William, duke of Jülich, near Baesweiler; more than eight thousand men were slain on both sides. The duke of Jülich himself emerged as victor and led away Duke Wenceslaus captive with many other nobles; at length, after eleven months, out of fear of the emperor, he released him freely without exaction. But from the others he extorted an almost boundless amount of money for their liberation.

LECTO- Chronicle of Trithemius

Here happily begins the letter of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to the chronicle of that same monastery of his.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict, to dear posterity: to fear God, and never to depart from the path of the regular life.

Letter to posterity.

I had often resolved with myself to write the origin, foundation, and progress of this our monastery of Sponheim, together with the successions of its abbots; but, always hindered by various occupations of the world, I have not until now been able to satisfy my desire. For it seemed to me that it would be worthwhile if I brought to the knowledge of posterity those things which, over a long time, with great labor, I was able to gather from various monuments of the ancients, lest through oblivion they should wholly perish from the memory of mortals. Many abbots and monks in various monasteries did this before us: for the common advantage of those then present and afterward of those to come, they wrote in order of time the histories of their monasteries and the names and successions of their abbots. Provoked by their example, I have taken care, with studious reflection, to arrange into one orderly book, according to the sequence of the years of the Lord, whatever I could find anywhere concerning this present monastery of Sponheim. Indeed, neither diligence was lacking in my labors, nor did continual solicitude ever abandon our inquiry. For almost fifteen years, at certain intervals, I labored much before I was able to bring the series of the abbots’ successions into one order. For the negligence of those who preceded us in time in this present monastery of Sponheim doubled my labor, since they committed nothing, or little, to writing that would serve my purpose; even that very material which they had received from others as committed to writing seemed almost wholly consumed by decay and age. Yet I did what I could; I have brought together a history, though not altogether such as I wished. For beginning from the first foundation of the present monastery, I arranged the narrative of the histories that occurred according to the years of the Lord’s nativity, and in agreement with these I placed in order the names and successions of the abbots from the first down to me, who am the twenty-fifth. I have [unclear] integrity. Whoever reads these things after my death, say, I pray, with faithful mind: God have mercy on the soul of Trithemius, who compiled these things.

And at the same time I ask the reader not to condemn anything of what we have written before he has diligently examined it, or has found a manifest error. For it is a detestable race of men that gnaws with impious tooth at the slips of men, which they can neither imitate nor improve, and tears apart with presumptuous rashness what they are unable rightly to discern. Rather, if anywhere you find a manifest error, be present as a benevolent corrector, because I gladly admit those who correct with sincere charity. But enough now about these matters. Moreover, there is a reason why I am moved to set down in order all my lucubrations which I have published during the twenty-three years that I have been abbot of this present monastery of Sponheim: that posterity may know that I always wished well, although, hindered by the insolence of Nayaths, I could not at all accomplish the good that I wished.

Reason for undertaking the work.

First I published a large work, On Vices and Virtues, in 2 books. Likewise, On the Temptations of Monks, 1 book. On the Rule of St. Benedict, 1 book. Exhortations to Monks, 2 books. On the Brevity and Misery of the Present Life, 1 book. On the Visitation of Cloistered Persons, 1 book. On the Manner of Celebrating a Provincial Chapter, 1 book. Also the Statutes of the Provincial Chapter, 1 book. Also the Statutes of the Annual Chapter, 1 book. The Chronicle of the Monastery of Hirsau I indeed began here, but at last completed at Würzburg, a city of the Franks: a large work, divided into two volumes. Likewise, the Chronicle of the Dukes of Bavaria, to Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, 1 book. Also the Chronicle of this monastery of Sponheim, to which I have prefixed this Letter, 1 book. On the Ruin of Our Order [unclear], 1 book. On the Praise of Manual Scribes, 1 book. Praises of the Order of Carmelites, 2 books. Praises of St. Anne, 1 book. On the Institution of the Priestly Life, 1 book. On Ecclesiastical Writers, 1 book. On the Illustrious Writers of Germany, 1 book.

Sponheim.

On the Illustrious Men of Our Order, 4 books. On the Ecclesiastical Computus, 1 book. On the Threefold Region of Cloistered Persons, 3 books. On the Spiritual Exercise of Monks, 1 book. A Breviary of the Same, 1 book. Questions on the Gospel of John, 1 book. Questions on the Psalter, 1 book. On Continence and Virginity, 1 book. On Widows, 1 book. On the Crosses Appearing on Men’s Garments, 1 book. Four books of letters to the archbishop of Mainz. Many and various sermons, with certain addresses in chapters, and other things. With these matters set forth, reader, farewell. On the last day of October, in the year 1506.

The Chronicle of This Monastery of Sponheim, from the Beginning of Its Foundation, Briefly Comprising the Successions of All the Abbots, Begins Happily.

[unclear]

In the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1043, the illustrious Count Eberhard founded the church in Sponheim. It was called in ancient times “of the field”; he founded it in the fifth year of Emperor Henry, the third of this name, in the time of Pope Benedict IX, when the holy church of Mainz was governed by Bardo, the venerable bishop, a man in all respects most holy, who also consecrated that same church in honor of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God and Virgin, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord 1056.

Count Eberhard, for the remedy of his soul, conferred on that same church no few goods, from the proceeds of which those who served the altar in that church might live. First, the tithe of the village of Sponheim, with the household and demesne land in fields, vineyards, gardens, meadows, pastures, woods, cultivated land, uncultivated land, and land to be cultivated, roads and trackless ways. Also in Pedersheim, two manses. In Rudesheim near Kreuznach, three manses of demesne land. In the same place, four and a quarter manses, which tenants possessed. In Hagenheim, two manses and two iugera of vineyards. In Basenheim, a manse and six iugera. In Dromersheim, half a manse and four vineyards. In Mannendal, a manse. In Bockenau, two manses. In Auen, four and a quarter manses. In Moncecha, a plot with buildings and twelve iugera of vineyards. In Wernigsbach, two manses. In Escelbrun, eight maldra of wheat and sixteen of rye, from the manse called Eberhard’s.

These and certain other things the aforesaid count conferred on the church founded by him, and he installed in it certain clerics who were to read masses. But he reserved to himself and his heirs the right of instituting clerics to benefices in that church. Saint Bardo, the aforesaid archbishop, also confirmed this solemnly made donation. And so for almost seventy years the church of Sponheim stood before it was raised into a monastery. There were four altars in it, which, according to custom, were conferred on successive priests by the elder count of Sponheim.

How and When the Church of Sponheim Was Raised into a Monastery by Stephen, Count of Sponheim, and His Son Megenhard.

In the year of the Lord 1101, in the ninth indiction, when Emperor Henry IV held the Roman Empire and Ruthard, the venerable archbishop, governed the church of Mainz, Stephen, the illustrious count of Sponheim, forewarned by divine inspiration, took care to raise into a monastery his church on the Montis Campi, founded long before by his ancestors, as we have said. He was a good man and feared God; for God’s honor he bestowed many benefactions on the ministers of the church and on the poor. In the year noted above he began to build places and dwellings for monks, suitable according to the rule of Saint Benedict. But, almost hindered by various occupations intervening, he did not continue the work begun. Therefore, when at last he saw that he was already on the point of dying, he called to him his son Megenhard, heir of his paternal estate, and entrusted to him the task of completing the building begun for the monastery; and so he rested in the Lord on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, in the year of the Lord 1118.

But Megenhard, the renowned count, after his father’s death, vigorously took up the work begun long before and completed it in a few years. In the middle of the church, beneath the tower, he established a choir for the monks, which Chronicle of Trithemius

...he beautifully adorned it with stone paneling, with images of the twelve Apostles and Prophets, as is still seen. To this holy work Mechthildis, his wife, a most devout woman, contributed many benefactions with great eagerness; and she did not cease to press the count himself, her husband, with continual prayers, admonishing and beseeching him that he would deign to bring the work begun to completion as quickly as possible. For that most religious woman feared that delay, which is customarily harmful and dangerous to all good works, might by some occasion change her husband’s holy purpose. Count Rodolphus also, Megenhard’s brother, together with his wife Richardis, expended no small costs for the completion of the work.

Concerning the consecration of the church and of this monastery of Sponheim, by the venerable prelate of Worms, Boggo, vice-archbishop for Adelbert.

Count Rudolphus had begun at the consecration.

When, therefore, the building that had been begun was at last completed, that is, the church formed in the shape of a cross, with the cloister and the necessary houses, the refectory and dormitory adjoining the cloister on the western side, the magnificent Count Megenhard, before he handed over the monastery for monks to inhabit, wished the church, which he had reformed in many respects, to be consecrated anew, as is customary. Therefore, after the clerics had been removed and provided for elsewhere, he approached Adelbert, archbishop of Mainz, concerning the consecration of the church, and also revealed to him the desire of his heart concerning the introduction of monks to Sponheim. That most reverend prelate greatly commended the count’s good purpose; and because he could not come in person to the consecration, as was requested, he designated in his place the venerable prelate of the church of Worms, Boggo, who at that time had for many years been expelled from his see, and whom he kept with himself honorably.

Therefore in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1114, on the Sunday Quasimodogeniti, Buggo, bishop of Worms, consecrated it.

Bishop Buggo in [unclear].

They consecrate this place of Worms.

Eugenius XII. Therefore in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1178, in the second indiction, under Emperor Henry V, Count Megenhard, the renowned founder of this place, handed over this monastery itself, with the church and all their appurtenances, to the order of our most holy father Benedict for perpetual possession, and gave it to monks to inhabit. The first monks, moreover, who from this point first began to inhabit this place, twelve in number, came from the monasteries of Saint Alban and Saint James near Mainz, by order of Archbishop Adelbert, at the urging of Count Megenhard, in the year noted above, on the Wednesday after Passion Sunday. Of these, eight were priests and four were conversi, distinguished and notable men, some of whom, before entering religion, had formerly served as soldiers in the world. These are their names: Bertholdus, priest; Diemus, priest; Adelbero, priest; Anshelmus, priest; Ergenbaldus, priest; Herbordus, priest; Sifridus also, priest; Benno, conversus; Lupoldus, conversus; Hartungus, conversus; and Emicho, conversus. These twelve brothers were taken partly from the monastery of Saint Alban, properly at Mainz, as we have said, and partly from the monastery of Saint James in the same place. When they came to the present place, they were honorably received by Count Megenhard and his wife, and they began to inhabit the monastery solemnly handed over to them. Therefore, after possession had been obtained in the name of God, the aforesaid monks unanimously elected for themselves as abbot and pastor, according to the monastic rule, Bernhelmus, a monk of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Alban, of whom we shall speak later. Bertholdus, a venerable old man, was appointed claustral prior, and for thirteen years he vigorously presided over the office of prior in this place. Furthermore, Adelbero was made cellarer of the monastery and presided for many years; since he was a good and prudent man, he did many good things for this monastery.

The first monks from [unclear].

Names of the twelve monks.

Concerning the first twelve monks who received this place and first began to inhabit it, of whom eight were priests and four conversi.

Of the first abbot.

Of the monk Bernhildus. Sponheim.

On the solemn donation by which Count Megenhard handed over the church and monastery of the order, in the presence of Adelbert, archbishop of Mainz.

After these things the illustrious Count Megenhard, so that what he had done for the place might gain firmness by authority, went to Adelbert, archbishop of Mainz, together with his brother Count Rudolph; and before him, in the church of Mainz, with many persons present, he resigned this church, before the altar of St Martin, with every right and jurisdiction which he had had over it, into the hands of that archbishop, under this condition, namely, that monks should serve almighty God in it for all the days of the world, under an abbot and under the Rule of the holy father Benedict, as is clear in the letters of confirmation of the same archbishop, which he issued concerning this matter, and which read as follows.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Adelbert, by the mercy of God archbishop of this holy church of Mainz and legate of the apostolic see, wish it to be known to all the faithful, both of future and of the present age, how Lord Megenhard of Sponheim and his wife Machthild, Count Rudolph and his wife [Regnat?], moved by the impulse of divine inspiration, came of their own accord to the altar of St Martin, and, for their own safety and that of their people, and in hope of eternal recompense, conferred forever upon the church of Mainz, with pious devotion, the church in Sponheim with all the property and jurisdiction which they had possessed over it by hereditary right up to that day: under this condition, namely, that monks should be established there according to the Rule of St Benedict, by whom continual praises to God and supplications for them should be frequently made in the same church. These, moreover, are the benefices and estates belonging to the aforesaid church: the tithe of the same village, with the household and demesne land, in fields, vineyards, gardens, meadows, pastures, and woods. In Petersheim, two hides; in Rudersheim, three hides; in Auen, four and a fourth part. In [Montzechaarea], with buildings, and twelve iugera of vineyards. In Wergesbach, two hides. In Eselbrunnen, seven malters of wheat and sixteen of rye from the hide which is called Eberhardt. These, moreover, are the things which the aforesaid Megenhard handed over for himself and for the same church as a benefice: nine hides in Hussen and in Stirscheit, with the demesne land and wood which he had possessed there. In Dalen, eleven hides, in fields, plots, vineyards, meadows, and woods. The aforesaid Lady Riggart also added to the aforesaid goods a meadow and a garden suited for planting vegetables, with two fields adjoining the same meadow. And when these things had been done by the above-named men without any contradiction, we confirmed it by the obligation of our ban. Moreover, we endowed the aforesaid church with the same liberty, honor, and [unclear] which the other abbeys and monasteries in our episcopate enjoy: namely, that it should look only to the bishop; and that, when the brothers serving God there are bereft of their spiritual father, they should choose another from among themselves, if only they find one suitable. But if they do not have among themselves a person suitable for that office, they shall have the liberty of choosing another of their own life and institution, from whatever congregation it may happen, yet within our diocese. Furthermore, at the request of the lords already named above, we have forever remitted the payment of the same church which pertained to us; and we have decreed that the parish priest should look to the abbot, in this manner, namely, that he should be invested by him with the benefices of the church, but with the gift of the altar by the lesser provost. This also was decreed or approved on both sides, that the elder of that kin should be advocate of the same church; but if he, forgetful of his name and office, [unclear] the church or those possessions by which [unclear]

[unclear] abbot of St James, Adelhum abbot of St Disibod, Henry provost of St Victor, Cuno dean of the cathedral. Thurimbert the master, Anshelm the provost, Hartmann the provost, Henry, provost of Riganus, Arnold the provost, and very many others from the clergy. Of laymen, moreover: Arnold, prefect of the city; Count Goswin; and his son Gerard; and his brother Emicho; Arnold and his brother Kuperius of Lurenburg; Count Frederick; Bertolf; and his brother Sigefrid; Henry of Katzenelnbogen; Rorich and his brother Gerlach; Ulrich; Fulcold; and very many others of the free men. Of the ministeriales, moreover: Embricho the vicedominus; Ernest the schultheiss; Folbert and Embricho of Bingen; Gerard; Embricho the count; and many others. The donation was received through the hands of the advocate Count Gozwin. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1134, in the second indiction, in the reign of Emperor Henry, the fourth of this name, Arnold being prefect of the city, Ernest schultheiss. Given by the hand of Godescalc the chaplain, on the seventh ides of June.

Therefore, after this solemn donation had been made, as was set forth above, in the church of Mainz by Count Megenhard, and after the monastery had been emancipated with all property, right, and jurisdiction, and endowed with pure liberty, that is, with the liberty which the other abbeys of our order in the diocese of Mainz enjoy, he [unclear] the aforesaid advocacy with all gentleness and goodness Of Sponheim.

of Count Megenhard.
