The aforesaid village of Dalen, moreover, was situated not far from the monastery, between east and north, on a plain at the foot of the mountain which in the vernacular is called [Gauwefberg?]. At that time the parish church was very ancient, and existed long before Sponheim and Bockenau were established. In it there was at that time a parish church, which had collapsed from excessive age; therefore Count Megenhard restored it anew, and had it consecrated by the aforesaid Bishop Bruno, who had then been driven from his church by the emperor’s violence. He wished it to be a chapel, and transferred the parish to that place where it now is, around the monastery, with the consent of the often-mentioned Archbishop Adelbert. Furthermore, he gave the chapel in Dalen, together with the village, plots, vineyards, meadows, fields, and other possessions, to Abbot Bernhelm and his monastery in perpetuity; he assigned the collation of the parish church to the abbot.

In the same year, also, on the same day, Bishop Bruno consecrated the altar before the choir of this monastery church, in honor of the holy and only cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, at the request of Abbot Bernhelm.

In this same year also Abbot Bernhelm transferred his sister Mechtild, enclosed for the love of God at Saint Alban’s, with the consent of Archbishop Adelbert and of Volbert, abbot of the same place, from there and placed her in the new cell which he had founded for her around the monastery, on the slope of the mountain toward the west, a place suitable for enclosure, which place down to the present is called Clusa. She was a most devout virgin nun, who by her example stirred many to fear and love Christ; concerning her more is to be said in its proper place, [unclear].

She also brought with her another woman, named Sophia, a virgin of holy conduct, who herself remained enclosed here with her for many years, serving the Lord, and inhabited the place even after her death.

In these times also the count of Lurenburg founded a monastery of our order within the bounds of the diocese of Trier, which is called Schönau. Over it he first set Hildelin, an abbot of most religious conduct; afterward there succeeded him Egebert, most learned in both divine and secular writings, brother of Saint Elizabeth, nun and mistress of the monastery of Schönau, which the aforesaid Abbot Hildelin built for Christ’s virgins near his aforesaid monastery in the fields toward the south. Adelbert, archbishop of Mainz, confirmed the foundation of this monastery when it was offered to him, as is clear from his letters, which follow and are as follows:

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Adelbert, archbishop of the see of Mainz, legate of the apostolic see, make known to all the faithful in Christ, both future and present, how our kinsman of Lurenburg delivered over to blessed Martin the monastery of Schönau, founded on his own estate and assigned to monastic life under the appointed abbot Hildelein, for the remedy of his soul and of the souls of his parents, with everything belonging to it: households, churches, fields, vineyards, cultivated and uncultivated lands, woods, meadows, pastures, mills, fisheries, waters and watercourses, roads, approaches and exits of the church. He assigned it to the church of Mainz as a perpetual possession, and took care that it should pass to the knowledge of later generations also by this present privilege of ours. He obtained that this abbey should remain free from every service and released from it. When the abbot of the place has died, let the brothers of the same [canon?] freely elect the one whom they find suitable among themselves. But if, which God forbid, no suitable person is found in that college, let them have the power to pass over into another monastery which is known to agree with their religious discipline. The one elected shall be invested by us or by our successors and consecrated by his own archbishop. Each year on the feast of blessed Martin he shall present a clean corporal upon that altar, as a memorial and proof that his [unclear] is from the patrimony of blessed Martin. It also pleased the abbot and brothers that they should celebrate the day of our ordination while we lived, and after our death should perform the anniversary, both ours and that of our successor archbishops, with solemn obsequies. The count himself received the advocacy from our hand on this condition: that whoever, as his successor, shall hold the estate of Mullen with its ministerials and household, and shall be lord in the castle of Lurenburg, shall be the hereditary lawful advocate of the same monastery, yet so that he himself shall not have the power of appointing a second or third advocate after him. And so that this whole act of conveyance may remain firm and unshaken for all, we have written out the page of this present chirograph concerning it, and have secured it with the impression of our seal, by the authority of almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and by our own authority forbidding, under perpetual anathema, that anyone should presume to come against it, seek to undermine it, destroy it, or impair it in any way. But if anyone does this, let him know that he is reserved for the dread judgment of the Holy Spirit, and that at the last examination he will have his portion with the Devil, author of all iniquity. We also record the witnesses of this matter, whose Chronicle of Trithemius

... consented, demanding nothing at all and imposing a burden in no respect, and wished the place and its inhabitants to enjoy perpetual peace and freedom, burdened by no service to anyone. And lest perhaps in future any one of his heirs, who bore the name of advocate, should bring any trouble upon the monastery's possessions or persons, he took care to make provision by letters, which, at the request of Bernhelmus, the first abbot, he issued in the following form of words:

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Megenhardus, by the grace of God count of Sponheim, wish it to be known to all the faithful of Christ, both present and future, that when our father, Count Stephanus of Sponheim, had determined to raise his church, set on Monte Campi beside the village of Sponheim, into a monastery, and, overtaken by death with the work unfinished, had entrusted it to me to complete, I, with the consent to this of Mechildis my wife and of my brother Count Rodolphus, for the remedy of my soul completed the work begun by my father, placed there monks according to the rule of St. Benedict, provided for their sustenance from my patrimony, and freely handed over that place with all its goods forever into the hands of my lord Adelbertus, archbishop of Mainz, legate of the apostolic see, at the altar of St. Martin.

As advocate of the same monastery, however, as long as I live, I have wished no one other than myself to be such. But after my death, the eldest of my sons who shall be lord in Creutzenacht shall hold the advocacy of the aforesaid monastery. If he, forgetting the name of his office, should wish to attack, trouble, or disperse the goods of the monastery or the persons for whom he ought to have been guardian and defender, the abbot with the brothers shall bring complaint against him to the examination of the archbishop of Mainz, who has authority to correct and amend him. But if, after a third warning by the archbishop, he has not amended, making satisfaction for the damage and injuries done to the monastery, the same archbishop shall have power, with the consent and will of the abbot and brothers, to remove him and give them another advocate, whom they themselves shall have chosen. And he shall do this as often as it has seemed necessary to the abbot and brothers, always appointing such a man as is more suitable in power, kindness, and fitness for protecting them.

Let the advocate beware that he ever burden the church in its goods or household; nor shall he demand any ferms, exactions, or precariae, but shall preserve them wholly free. He shall not sit at a public plea within the boundaries of the monastery unless he has been invited by the abbot. But when he comes invited, let him be served in such a way as is fitting for his honor, [unclear], lest by the size of any retinue or retinue of gold and sum the brothers themselves who serve God be saddened. Therefore let him act in all things so piously, kindly, and moderately, showing himself in all things toward the household and the goods of the monastery such that he may be worthy of his name, and, for the office faithfully fulfilled on account of God, may receive from him the reward of eternal life.

That all these things may remain ratified and unshaken for all time, I have caused this charter to be written concerning them, and have strengthened it by the impression of my seal. Witnesses of this my will were present: lord Adelbertus of Mainz, Bruno bishop of Strasbourg, Bernhelmus abbot of the aforesaid monastery, the whole congregation; Adelinus abbot of Disibodenberg, Hermannus provost of Schwabenheim, Goswinus of Lurburck, Count Dudo, Ernestus vice-lord, Adelbertus Warmundus the schultheiss; Henricus, Vdalricus of Stein, peers, and others.

These things were enacted in the year of the Lord's incarnation 1105, in the third indiction, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September.

Finally, for the greater security of the goods of this place, the aforesaid man approached Henry V, king of the Romans, and obtained confirmation of the aforesaid matters as follows:

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Henry, by favor of divine clemency emperor augustus of the Romans: we wish it to be known to all the faithful of Christ who are ours, both future and present, in what manner Megenhardus, count of Sponheim, with the assent and cooperation of Mechildis his wife, moved by heavenly inspiration, for the salvation and welfare of himself and his own, founded a monastery in his county in honor of Saint Mary ever virgin and of Saint Martin the bishop, which he lawfully endowed from his patrimony, establishing in it religious men who, under the rule of St. Benedict and an abbot, would praise almighty God continually in times present and future and pour out devout prayers for him and for his forebears.

He also caused to be written down and strengthened with his seal the right of advocacy, by which he wished them after his death to be free from every service, exaction, precaria, and any other burdens and grievances, and handed it over to the abbot and brothers of the same monastery, which is also called Sponheim. All these things Adelbertus, archbishop of Mainz, in whose parish that monastery was built, confirmed by his ban. Thereupon the aforesaid Count Megenhardus, for an increase of greater stability, requested from us that so holy and pious a work be confirmed by our imperial authority, lest any malice of later men [unclear] by right of imperial [unclear] might be able to alter them, once confirmed by imperial majesty. And because divine compassion has advanced us to the throne of the kingdom so that by royal provision we may care for the churches and monasteries established in our kingdom, and protect their rights and possessions from every injury, and [unclear] the same church or monastery in Sponheim, with all the goods, possessions there, and properties, under the guardianship and protection of the royal defense of our Roman empire forever...

Sponheimense.

In this same year Abbot Bernhelm sent Anshelm, a monk, who after Berthold later became prior, to Rome to the apostolic see, to obtain from Pope Honorius a privilege of apostolic protection for this monastery of Sponheim. On returning, he obtained the privilege from the pope himself, a copy of which has been placed above. Anselm of Bickelheim-[unclear].

1128.

In the year 1128, the fifth year of Abbot Bernhelm's prelacy, after he had most prudently ordered everything that seemed needful for the peace of the brothers, he devoted himself wholly to inward things, and more frequently gave his attention to quiet and to the reading of the Scriptures. Knowing, however, that the requests of many could not easily be disregarded, after taking counsel with his brothers he obtained confraternity with many monasteries round about. And first, indeed, he entered into spiritual association with the brothers of the monastery of St. Disibod, who were nearer neighbors. Its tenor follows, and is as follows. Bernhelm with many monasteries [unclear]. Fraternity with the brothers of St. Disibod.

This is the fraternity of association and fellowship between the brothers of St. Disibod and of Sponheim, a definite declaration and firm confirmation: that, when the brief announcing some deceased brother has arrived on either side, thirty vigils with the same number of Masses are to be performed in the convent; the third, seventh, and [thirtieth?] day is to be solemnly celebrated, namely with three lights kindled before the altar of the Mother, while all the bells ring together. At Masses for the dead, within thirty days, the tract De profundis is to be sung. After Matins the psalm Verba mea is to be recited through the same thirty days, with the other customary things. The commendation after chapter is to be regularly observed for the same time. [Each?] of the priests is to sing ten Masses; the literate are to recite three psalters; those who do not know this are to repeat 450 Our Fathers. The names of deceased brothers are to be written here and there in the Rule; anniversary days with vigil and Mass [unclear]. Brothers arriving on either side go to chapter, and do not leave it except with permission. [Unclear] suffrages [unclear].

This grace of fraternal association is granted in all respects to the brothers of St. James and of St. Alban at Mainz, because these two cloisters are known to have sprung from the root of their religious life. These were the suffrages which were performed here for [them]. The custom shown to the Bearded Brothers is excepted, whose life among them is not [unclear].

[At St. Maximin?] there also; at Seligenstadt; on Mount St. John in the Rheingau; at Hasungen; at Gerode; of the nuns on Mount St. Rupert; of the nuns of St. Peter near Kreuznach; and of many others. As soon as the death of anyone here or in other places in the fraternity had been announced to the confederates, immediately seven offices of the dead were performed for him, with vigils and Masses; besides this, each priest did not delay to say one Mass, those below priestly rank fifty psalms, and the illiterate the Lord's Prayer as many times. There was very great charity among them; this, shame to say, afterwards miserably grew cold and never sought to rise again. Copy of the letter of foundation.

1130.

In the year 1130, which was the sixth of Abbot Bernhelm, Count Megenhard of Sponheim, our founder, offered in perpetuity to the Church of Mainz the canonical monastery founded in Schabenheim, into the hands of Adalbert the elder, archbishop of Mainz. The same pontiff confirmed this donation, as follows. Foundation of the monastery of the Regulars in Schabenheim. The Regulars in Schabenheim. Privilege of the parish church.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Adalbert, by the mercy of God archbishop of Mainz and legate of the apostolic see, make known to all the faithful of Christ, future as well as present, how Count Megenhard of Sponheim, for the remedy of his own soul [and] of his wife Mechthild, [unclear] that which by hereditary right had come to the same Mechthild, his wife, from her ancestors, with the churches in the village called Schabenheim, with all tithes, the ninth part of the demesnes, dependents, villages, fields, vineyards, woods, meadows, cultivated and uncultivated lands, also coloni with certain manses, with every right, [unclear] to the brothers, on this condition: that there, from all the aforesaid goods, we should establish brothers living according to the rule of St. Augustine, lest, cooling from the rigor of the rule, they should ever transgress their institution. If a father of the monastery is to be appointed for the brothers, let him be only the one whom, by common counsel and assent, at the dictation of the Spirit, [unclear]; it shall be permitted to them, in the name of the Lord, to assume a person of the same profession and purpose, whomever they find more suitable. The parish priest also is appointed by the brothers with their father from their college, so that, every disturbance being removed, it may persevere in secure liberty in the praises of God. With the same liberty also which the other congregations of our episcopate enjoy, we have endowed the aforesaid monastery church, so that [unclear]. With which the other congregations of our episcopate enjoy, we have endowed the aforesaid monastery church, so that [unclear]. [The text repeats in corrupt form:] with which the other congregations of our episcopate enjoy, we have endowed the aforesaid monastery church [unclear].

Sponheim.

we receive under perpetual [protection], strictly forbidding, both for those present and those to come, under penalty of the crime of lese-majesty against the emperor, that anyone inflict any molestation, injury, or damage upon the said abbey of Sponheim, which we wish to enjoy every freedom that the other abbeys in our realm are known to enjoy, in goods, persons, household, property, donations already made, or those duly to be made in the future. Moreover, the advocate who shall hold office at the time, if he rashly transgresses the law established for him by the often-named count Megenhard, after being admonished up to a third time by the archbishop of Mainz, when the abbot has made complaint against him, if he does not amend, shall be deprived of such honor; and another, who may be useful to the church, shall be substituted in his place by the counsel and assent of the brethren of the abbey. And so that this charter may remain forever unshaken, and no one’s rashness may presume to weaken it, we have strengthened it by imperial authority with our ban, and, marked by our own hand, have secured it with the impression of our seal. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1125, in the third indiction, in the twenty-sixth year of the ordination of lord Henry V, king of the Romans, the thirtieth of his reign, and the fifteenth of his empire. Done at Mainz. In the name of the Lord. Amen.

Abbot Bernhelm also, in the third year of his institution, obtained from the apostolic see confirmation of all the foregoing, together with certain other privileges. Since the sequence of the order requires it, we shall insert here a copy of their rescript.

Copy of the confirmation of Honorius II, pope.

Honorius, bishop, servant of God, to his beloved son Bernhelm, abbot of the monastery of St. Martin in Sponheim, of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Mainz, and to his successors to be regularly instituted forever. It is fitting to grant ready assent to religious desires. And therefore, beloved son, assenting to the just petitions of you and your brethren, we have taken under the guardianship and protection of the apostolic see the aforesaid monastery of Sponheim, over which, by God’s authority, you preside, and have fortified it by the page of the present writing, decreeing and ordaining that the regular life now newly instituted in that place shall be inviolably preserved in future times according to the rule of Saint Benedict. Nor let anyone have the faculty, after making profession among you, to pass over to another place, under pretext of a greater or lesser religious observance, without the abbot’s permission. But if anyone at any future time departs contrary to this our prohibition, no abbot or anyone else shall dare to retain him. Whenever, with the abbot absent, there must be discussion among the brethren of that place concerning a successor, no one shall be intruded there by any cunning of surreption, or by the violence of any power, whether ecclesiastical or temporal, except the one whom the brethren by common consent, or the part of sounder counsel, shall judge should be elected, according to the fear of God and the rule of blessed Benedict, from the same community or from another, if, which God forbid, no suitable person is found among them. Moreover, the consecration of altars, chrism, holy oil, the blessing of abbots, and the ordination of monks are to be received from the diocesan archbishop of that same parish, if indeed he has the grace and communion of the apostolic see, and if he is willing to provide them graciously and without any depravity. Otherwise it shall be lawful for you and your successors to approach whatever catholic bishop you wish, and from him to receive consecrations and sacraments.

The pope took the monastery under the protection of the apostolic see.

That the monks should not depart.

That no one should intrude an abbot not canonically elected.

We judge also that burial in this place shall be entirely free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and will of those who have desired to be buried there, unless perhaps they have been excommunicated. We also confirm by apostolic authority all the possessions that you hold under the title below, and that you shall acquire in the future by offering or devotion, decreeing that it shall be lawful for no human being at all rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery; and if he does not quickly make suitable satisfaction, let him lack the dignity of his power and honor, and let him know that he stands guilty in the divine judgment for the iniquity he has perpetrated; let him be estranged from the most sacred body and blood of our Lord God and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and at the last examination be subject to strict vengeance. But to all who preserve what is just for the same place, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action, and before the strict Judge find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Given by the hand of the deacon of the holy apostolic see, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1127, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

The pope confirms all the possessions of this church.

The goods of this church [unclear].

When the foundation and institution of the present monastery had been sufficiently confirmed both by the apostolic see and by imperial authority, the monks who had come from Mainz began to inhabit the place and to arrange dwellings necessary for themselves according to the rule. Mechthild, the wife of the founder Megenhard, a woman most devoted to Christ, furnished the monks with everything necessary for life and showed herself a most faithful co-worker in completing the buildings of the monastery. But now, as we are about to proceed to what follows, let us take our beginning from the first abbot.

The place is inhabited by monks.

Countess Mechthild. ... have authority to preach, baptize, and bury; and that it be subject to the archbishop alone, answer to him in all things, and remain free from our service as well as from that of the archdeacon. Among the rest we thought this also should be added: that for as long as the same Count Megenhard lives, he himself shall hold its advocacy over them; and when he has died, if by chance his inheritance has been divided between two heirs, the one who possesses those estates belonging to the castle, namely Dille, not by usurpation but by hereditary right, being instituted by us or by any of our successors, shall be their advocate without any opposition. Therefore, establishing the tenor of this page, we have marked it with the impression of our seal, commanding and forbidding all Christians under perpetual anathema that anyone presume to come against it, assail it, or destroy it; but let its authority remain firm and unshaken for all, by the authority of almighty God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. These things were done in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1130, in the eighth indiction, while Lord Lothar, glorious king of the Romans, the second of that name, was reigning, in the fifth year of his reign.

At the same time also the provostship of Mount St. John the Baptist in the Rheingau, of the order of our holy father Benedict, which Ruthard, archbishop of Mainz, had built a little earlier and decreed to be subject to the abbot of the monastery of St. Alban the Martyr outside Mainz, was raised to an abbey by his successor Adalbert the elder, archbishop of Mainz, as is clear in the letters drawn up concerning it, as follows:

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Adalbert, by the grace of God archbishop of Mainz and legate of the apostolic see, wish it to be known to all the faithful of Christ, both future and present, that Lord Ruthard of blessed memory, our predecessor, handed over to the church of St. Alban a certain mountain in the Rheingau, which is called Bischoffsberg, by his own hand, for this reason: that by the aid of the faithful dwelling round about, the discipline of monastic life might be established there. And when part of a monastery had been constructed in that same place, and our aforesaid predecessor had been summoned to consecrate the altar, wishing to share in the labor of those who had put their hand to cultivating that same place, he assigned as a dowry, upon the holy relics, a certain part of the surrounding wood, as far as the hollow called Hunenklingen, and so from there as far as the place called Kalenberg; on the side of the burial-ground, [unclear], and on the other three sides as far as [unclear] places. In addition he added the rent of half a mansus in Winkel, which belonged to episcopal right; this Ruthard, son of Regefo, and a certain Rabodo of Damburg, enclosed there, conferred on the same monastery for the remedy of their souls. It was also established by the aforesaid archbishop that every year, at the nativity of St. John the Baptist, a fair should be held there by merchants both of Mainz and of the province, and he handed over to the brothers of the same place every profit that could come from it to the bishop.

Furthermore, Count Richolf in the Rheingau, his wife Clanckmodis, and their children, Ludovicus, by common consent solemnly gave to St. John, in whose honor the principal altar of the aforesaid monastery was dedicated, without any opposition, the goods described below: namely, the court which lies nearest opposite the mountain, with the small estate belonging to it, that is, vineyards and trees, a mill, a wine-cellar, meadows, and gardens. Likewise one vineyard near Winkel, which is called Exconis; another in the field; a third near the court; a fourth on Culersberg; a fifth on the eastern side of the same mountain; a sixth at the foot of the mountain, beside the watercourse; four portions of arable land. They also offered their son and daughter in the same place to serve God and St. John; these aforesaid goods would have come to them by hereditary right if they had remained in the world.

In our times, therefore, when the resources of the same church were increasing by the working of divine mercy, and it, being sufficient for itself, sought its own pastor, it seemed right to us that we should change its condition for the better and take action to obtain liberty for it. Therefore, having summoned to us Henry, provost of the greater church, and very many other religious and wise persons, we approached the lord abbot of St. Alban, and by the assent and will of all his brothers obtained that the aforementioned church of St. John, free from its former subjection, should henceforth retain free judgment in electing for itself, and should freely present to us or to our successors the man canonically elected, to receive the staff from the hand of the bishop and to be consecrated. Therefore, after this concession had been obtained from the aforesaid Abbot Wernher and his brotherhood, and after we had released the aforementioned church from their hand and power by the counsel and approval of the abbots, archdeacons, and our other persons, we gave certain goods in Lorch for the use of the aforesaid brothers [unclear]; also a part of the tithe in Burnheim, possessed by the same brothers already for many years, we gave absolutely and without opposition to the abbot and brothers of St. Alban as a just and lawful compensation. In addition, for the daughter of Count Richolf, enclosed beside the monastery of St. Alban, we established that each year during her life a cartload of wine and a mark of silver should be given from Culersberg, and after her death the same benefaction should revert to the church of St. John.

We also granted, at the request of those brothers, that whoever of the faithful should wish to be baptized or buried there may find baptism and burial there in peace, all opposition of his own parish priest ceasing. Furthermore, the tenants of the aforesaid brothers living on the same mountain under its command we endowed with this liberty...

242. CHRONICLE OF TRITHEMIUS. ON BERNHELM, THE FIRST ABBOT OF THIS MONASTERY; WHO PRESIDED 26 years, 9 months, [and] 17 days; AND ON THE DEEDS OF THAT TIME.

In the year, therefore, of the Lord's nativity 1124, in the second Roman indiction, the eighth day of the month of June, Bernhelm, monk of St Alban's near Mainz, sent hither with others, was constituted the first abbot of this monastery, as much by the election of the brothers as by the command of Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz, by whom, ordained, he presided 26 years, 9 months, 17 days. He was ordained at Mainz in the monastery of St Alban, four abbots standing by him—namely [those] of St Alban, St James, St Disibod, and St Ferrutius in Bleidenstadt—with many others, as much of the clergy as of the people, in the aforesaid year, on the nativity of St John the Baptist. This our first abbot Bernhelm was sprung from the county of Sponheim, begotten of honest parents, his father by name Eberhard having strenuously served Stephen, count of Sponheim, for several years. His mother, by name Hiltrudis, was a woman devoted to Christ; whose dwelling was in the village of Sponheim, under the castle. Bernhelm, therefore, a boy prompt and docile in talent, was sent to the schools to be imbued with letters, and, having obtained good teachers, was not only well instructed in the science of the Scriptures, but adorned also with the best morals. In each he greatly advanced, and with time turned out renowned in virtues, and at the same time in erudition: so amiable, and never grievous to anyone even slightly. Whence, his merits advancing, on account of [his] all-round knowledge of the Scriptures, he was made Master of the schools in the same monastery, and at length, made presbyter, was constituted [such]; and he embraced that office of teaching, no less by writings than by daily lessons, magnificently for ten years. He wrote, first of all, On the instruction of boys, 1 book; also Introductions into the seven liberal arts, 2 books; Against a certain Sophist, 1 book; Against the simoniacs, 3 books; on Ecclesiastes of Solomon he published a most beautiful work, [—] book[s]; Against the Jews, 1 book; and some others, which negligence has brought into oblivion.

In this same year Berthold the monk is constituted here the first Prior, a learned and most religious man, who published Commentaries on the Gospel of Mark, 2 books; On the Song of Songs, 2 books; On the humility of monks, 1 book; many sermons and homilies. He presided in the Priorate 13 years, and did many good [things].

In the same year Adelbero was constituted chief Cellarer—a monk, once one of the first sent hither, a good man and of religious conversation, sagacious and much experienced in ordering and disposing temporal matters, who for several years strenuously governed the office committed to him. And straightway the fame of the good and religious conversation of the brothers began to spread round about, and little by little to come to the notice of all the neighbors. Whence, since the new plantation did not yet seem sufficiently abundantly provided for the sustenance of the monks, many, both noble and ignoble, on account of the opinion of [their] good fame and the holy conversation of the brothers serving God, began to donate many alms and benefits.

In this same year a monastery of our order was founded at Ballenstedt, by Otto, count of the same place, in Saxony, and dowered honorably enough by him. [Margin: The monastery of Ballenstedt is founded; today Rudenzhow.]

Bruno, archbishop of Trier, also died, who founded a monastery of our order at Odenheim in the diocese of Speyer, which he dowered with many estates and possessions.

A hail of great mass, too, fell the 9th [day before] the Kalends of August. And the 3rd [day before] the Ides of August there was an eclipse.

[1125.] In the year 1125, the second of abbot Bernhelm, the 13th [day before] the Kalends of September, the church of the village of Dalen was consecrated, in honor of St George the martyr, by Bruno, bishop of Strasbourg, at the request of Adalbert the arch[bishop]… Chronicle of Trithemius

a nun most devoted to Christ. But Saint Jutta, daughter of Count Stephen, was mistress of the virgins of Christ on the aforesaid Mount St. Disibod; under her their number was greatly increased, and many nobles round about offered their daughters, under her governance, to serve our Lord Jesus Christ. All these served under the Rule of our holy father Benedict and under obedience to the abbot, shut away separately in a narrow and well-walled enclosure; no man except the abbot had access to them.

For this custom was then very celebrated in almost all our monasteries and those of regulars: that the nearer the nuns were to men, the more easily, by their vigilance, they might be protected from the snares of the ancient enemy. So it was in the aforesaid monastery of St. Disibod; so in the monastery of St. John in the Rheingau; so in Schönau; so at St. Alban’s; so at St. James’s; so in Hirsau under Abbot St. William; likewise in Frankenthal. Were there not around the monastery of Limburg three convents of our order established for nuns, namely Seebach, Hausen, and Schönfeld, of which the first still flourishes, suitable for holy virgins, while the other two are desolate?

And at the monastery of St. Martin of Trier, beside the walls, above the bank of the Moselle, toward the north, there was the convent of St. Symphorian, in which many most holy nuns of our order were renowned; today no trace of it appears except a single column alone, by which the church was once supported. And Bernhelm, the first abbot of this place mentioned above, built a small convent at the foot of the sloping mountain on the western side of this monastery, as we have also said before; in it he enclosed his sister Mechthild, who had first been enclosed at St. Alban’s for love of the heavenly life, together with another woman named Sophia. And in the same reclusory there were, for many years, several holy and most devout virgins succeeding one another, whose names we do not doubt are written in heaven.

But afterward, when nuns, because of the closeness of the places, began to be a snare and a scandal to men, and when on both sides they walked not according to the spirit, as before, but according to the flesh, we see that almost all the convents, when the nuns failed or were even expelled, were totally destroyed through neglect or some other occasion. For today among us, apart from the name of the place, which is called Clausa from the enclosure of the virgins who once dwelt there, no trace of the convent or structure is seen. But let us return to the history.

Therefore the holy virgin of Christ of whom we have spoken, Jutta, was renowned in this life for many miracles: among other things she changed water into wine, and several times crossed the flowing waves of the river Glan with dry foot. Hence, not without a great reputation for sanctity, she passed from this world to heaven; her life and most holy conduct have been written down with sufficient diligence. After her death the holy virgin Hildegard was appointed mistress of the sisters, under Cuno, abbot of the aforesaid convent. After a few years had passed, with the whole congregation of sisters, by permission of the abbot and forewarned by divine revelation, she passed over to Bingen, and there she remains today; on the mountain of St. Rupert the Confessor she built for herself and her sisters from the alms of the faithful.

1137.

In the year 1137, in the thirteenth year of Abbot Bernhelm, Berthold, prior of this monastery, died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, a man in every respect most religious, and a distinguished cultivator and lover of the divine Scriptures, to whom nothing was ever sweeter than either to write books or to read them. He was so diligent in divine worship that he was always the first in choir and the last to go out after all the others. No one ever saw him idle, no one sad or lax; for in due time he did some good thing: he either read, or wrote, or certainly devoted himself to prayer. He was so frequent in prayer that you would have thought he could think of nothing other than prayer; and again so fervent in the reading of the Scriptures and in manual work that he seemed to love nothing less than prayer.

Anshelm succeeded him in the priorship, formerly a monk of St. James of Mainz, who had been sent here among the first twelve: a good, gentle, sweet, and mild man, born of a military family in Bickelnheim. He presided in the office of prior for forty-three years under three abbots, Bernhelm, Crafto, and Adelger. Under his direction regular discipline advanced greatly, both by the merit of virtues and by the number of persons. Faithfully following also in the footsteps of his predecessor, he enlarged the library of this convent not a little during the time of his office. For around these times the monks of this convent and of St. Disibod had a great zeal for the Scriptures, and with all eagerness wrote books of sacred reading.

In this year Adelbert the elder, archbishop of Mainz, died on the ninth day before the Kalends of July and was buried in the monastery of Eberbach, which he himself had founded. Adelbert the younger, his nephew, provost of Erfurt, succeeded him and presided for four years; few memorable deeds of his are read, because of the brevity of his pontificate. These

Many nuns on Mount St. Disibod.

The ancient [unclear] nuns and pride [unclear] nuns were. Examples.

Why reclusories of nuns were abolished; from this there are [unclear] near the monastery of Sponheim.

The reason why reclusory monasteries are beside monasteries of men.

Whence Clausa Vinea is so called.

Many miracles.

The river Glan.

St. Hildegard is made mistress of the sisters.

Prior Berthold dies.

Anshelm becomes second prior.

Adelbert the elder, archbishop of Mainz, dies.

Adelbert the elder succeeds. 244 Chronicle of Trithemius ... are the names: Henry, provost of the greater church and of St Victor, and many others. Done in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1130, in the eighth indiction, in the reign of the emperor Lothar. Given by the hand of Henry, notary and provost in Mainz.

The Abbey of Schönau was a provostship in Liburna.

And note that the aforesaid monastery had formerly been a provostship, built in that place which is called Lipron, where now there is a parish church with a little village, at a distance of half a mile; and it was subject by right to the monastery and abbot of St Saviour in Schaffhausen, in the diocese of Constance.

1126.

In the year 1126, Abbot Bernhelm began to dig and construct the well of this monastery, which still today remains sound, and completed it in a short time. For previously there was no water here in the monastery, but it was brought, not without labor, from the foot of the mountain, where the larger pond now is. He also completed various other buildings, which Count Megenhard had not yet wholly finished.

In this year Henry, the fourth emperor but the fifth king, died without children at Traiectum and was buried at Speyer; Lothar II, duke of Saxony, succeeded him by election of the princes.

1127.

In the year 1127, a certain nobleman of Sponheim, a kinsman of Abbot Bernhelm, together with his wife, named Judith, for the remedy of his soul, gave to this same [unclear] all his patrimony which he had in Bockenau in Gensingen, namely the church with tithes and all its appurtenances, serfs, fields, vineyard, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, pastures, meadows, mills, fisheries, waters and watercourses, to the altar of St Martin in this monastery at Sponheim, before many witnesses, as is clear in the letter of Lord Adalbert the elder, archbishop of Mainz, who confirmed the same donation, as follows:

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Adalbert, by the grace of God archbishop of Mainz and legate of the apostolic see, make known to the faithful of Christ’s Church, both future and [present?], that a certain nobleman named Udo, [unclear], and his wife Judith, while they still enjoyed the full powers of body and mind, for the remedy of his soul and those of his parents, delegated all their patrimony in Bockenau in Gensingen, the church with tithes and all its appurtenances, serfs, fields, vineyard, woods, cultivated lands, meadows, pastures, mills, fisheries, waters and watercourses, to the altar of blessed Martin of the monastery of Sponheim, to the abbot and brothers living there under the monastic rule, without any opposition, through the hands of the advocate, Count Megenhard of the castle of Sponheim, [unclear]. It also pleased the two aforesaid persons, namely Udo and his wife, since among the serfs they had some of higher and some of lower condition, that, insofar as nature, their own industry, and uprightness had raised them up, they should appoint them ministeriales for the abbot and brothers, and should grant no advocate any right over them; rather, among the better and foremost of the ministers of the other abbots of our episcopate, they should obtain equality in rank with full justice. The rest of the household, however, should remain under fiscal justice, namely so that it should pay each year to the altar of the aforesaid monastery a census of [nine?] coins. In order that this conveyance may remain firm and unshaken, we have caused this charter to be written, marked with the impression of our seal, and strengthened it with the bond of anathema: so that if anyone by perverse contrivance, which God forbid, should presume to [unclear] or annul this same conveyance, he shall lie under our ban, shall be [unclear] by the testimony of the truth itself, and shall know that he has incurred the offense of almighty God and St Martin. The witnesses of this matter are Abbot Folbert of St Alban’s, Werimbold, abbot of St James’s, Adellun, abbot of St [Disibod?], Bernhelm, abbot of the aforementioned monastery, the whole congregation, Richard, archdeacon of the house of blessed Martin, and many others.

This was done on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1127, in the fifth indiction, in the reign of Lothar, august king of the Romans, in the second year of his reign.

After this solemn donation had been made before many witnesses, Abbot Bernhelm peacefully obtained possession of the goods offered in Bockenau and Gensingen; from these, after 138 years, Peter, abbot of this place, conferred the church in Gensingen with the tithes in perpetuity upon the canons of the greater church of Mainz, as an increase of revenues, services, and all dues arising from this donation of Udo. But another estate, which is called the abbot’s, after 205 years William, abbot of Bickelheim, from his own patrimony handed over to blessed Martin and his brothers in the present monastery; concerning this also we shall speak below in its own time.

This Chronicle of Trithemius

of the holy places at Jerusalem; and many other relics were brought to this monastery from the regions overseas at the same time by the aforesaid knight Hildebert.

Henry of Ulmen, a knight born in the diocese of Trier, likewise, when Constantinople had been captured at the same time, carried away, among other relics of the saints, a large piece of the Holy Cross. This he divided into three parts: one he gave to the monastery of Saint Matthias near Trier; another to a certain convent of nuns of the order of Saint Augustine, which is called Stuba, in the same diocese of Trier; and the third to the monastery of Saint Pantaleon in Cologne, together with the head of the same holy martyr. The remaining relics he distributed to Laach and to other churches.

1151.

Udo, a nobleman of Sponheim, who twenty-four years earlier had made to this monastery that solemn donation concerning the estates of Bugenavy and Gentzigen, in the presence of Adelbert the elder, archbishop of Mainz, and many others, after the death of his wife Judith came to conversion in his old age; and in this year, under lord Bernhelm, he was made a monk in this our monastery. After living for three years in great devotion, he at last, under Craffto the First, on the sixth day before the Ides of June, rested in the Lord, a gentle and most devout man.

In this year Abbot Bernhelm, weighed down by old age and labor, began to be more infirm than usual. When he perceived that the day of death was drawing near him, having received the ecclesiastical sacraments with the greatest devotion, and having most prudently ordered the affairs of the monastery, not without the sadness of the brethren, whose number had now risen beyond twenty, he passed to the Lord on the sixth day before the Kalends of April in the aforesaid year, in the twenty-seventh year of his pastoral office, not yet completed, and in the seventy-third year of his age. He was buried with great honor and with many tears of the brethren in the middle of the choir, a man worthy of eternal memory, beloved by God and men; he instructed the flock committed to him most excellently in all religion and holiness by word and example, and converted many from iniquity to the path of justice and uprightness of life.

Concerning Craffto the First, the second abbot of this monastery, who presided happily for 24 years, two months, and five days.

In the year of the Lord noted above, 1151, in the fourteenth indiction, after lord Bernhelm, the first abbot of this monastery, had died, as has been said, and had been buried, on the same day, namely the sixth day before the Kalends of April, the brethren, assembling together, unanimously, with absolutely no one dissenting, elected as abbot Lord Craffto, a monk of this monastery, of whom we spoke above, son of Megenhard, count of Spanheim. He was still new in the order, but mature, religious, and prudent; he did many good things for this monastery, and was venerable no less for humility than for nobility of blood. Though elected, he consented unwillingly, preferring for the love of God to dwell humbly among the monks rather than to be imperiled by the honors of this world. Yet, overcome by the prayers and tears of the brethren, he could not resist longer, but, weeping and declaring himself unworthy, gave his consent. Afterward, on the Nones of June, which was the day of Saint Boniface the martyr, he was consecrated by Henry, archbishop of Mainz, with great solemnity and honor in the greater church of Mainz, with abbots, clergy, and many of the number of the nobles standing by. He was indeed a man of great prudence, competently learned, who understood very well those things that pertained to his station. He was fully grounded in the fear of the Lord; in his conduct with the brethren he was mature, not turbulent, and easily drew to himself the love of all good men. For he was gentle, mild, and humble; he knew how to offend or harm no one, but to benefit all. Having been ordained abbot, he took care with all zeal to show himself a worthy and useful shepherd to the brethren committed to him, and he always went before them in all religion and humility by word and example. He presided over this monastery usefully and energetically for 23 years, two months, and five days, as we shall say in order.

1152.

In this year Adelbero, archbishop of Trier, died; Hillin, dean of the greater church, succeeded him for eighteen years. From this archbishop Hillin, Craffto, the second abbot of this monastery, of whom we have spoken, obtained by many prayers the head of Saint Irmina, virgin, daughter formerly of Dagobert, king of the Franks. She was the first abbess of the monastery in the Horrea at Trier, which she herself, with Saint Willibrord the bishop assisting, had founded anew from the foundations; her feast is observed on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. This most sacred head, from the archbishop himself and the whole congregation of the aforesaid place, both in consideration of his prayers, and Sponheimense.

...let them render service. Likewise we have excluded all advocates from the aforesaid place, and have left it to be protected and defended under the patronage of the archbishop alone. After all these things had been observed in due order, we solemnly consecrated and appointed Lord Eigelward as abbot over the same place, granting and confirming that whenever a father of the monastery is to be ordained for the same brothers, only the man whom they shall have unanimously chosen by common counsel and consent, at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, shall be invested by the archbishop. And so that the sequence of this matter might remain stable and unshaken, we have signed this page with the impression of our image. But if anyone shall attempt to break what has been so lawfully done, we strike him with the sword of anathema until he comes to his senses. The witnesses are Wernbold, abbot of St. James, Henry of the greater [church?], Cuno the custodian and dean, and very many others. These things were done in this year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1130, in the eighth indiction, while Lothar, most glorious king of the Romans, was reigning, in the fourth year of his reign.

On the western side of the aforesaid church of St. John a reclusory was built, in which virgins wishing to serve Christ, almighty God, in purity of mind and body were received under obedience to the abbot and under the rule of our holy father Benedict. Day and night they devoted themselves to prayer and contemplation, and the abbot of the place provided them with the necessities of food and clothing. There also the daughter of the aforesaid Richolf, count of the Rheingau, as is noted in the archbishop’s privilege, was enclosed with the other virgins. But after many years, the holy nuns and virgins succeeding them in order were transferred from the mountain into the valley, for the quiet both of themselves and of the brothers; a monastery with the necessary dwellings had first been built for them, which is called Clusa down to the present day, because virgins were enclosed there.

Around these times also the monastery of our order called Groinavy, within the borders of the diocese of Trier, not far from Schonaw, about which we have already spoken above, was founded by the count of Lurenburg. In it the head of St. Sebastian the martyr is shown, which is said to have been brought there by the count.

1133.

In the year 1132, the ninth of Bernhelm, the monastery of the Cistercian order in the Rheingau, called Eberbach, almost two miles distant from Mainz, was built by Adelbert the elder, archbishop of Mainz.

In these same times Abbot Bernhelm, led by singular foresight, acquired a house and courtyard in Mainz for the use of this monastery, so that, if necessity should perhaps arise, we might use it for the preservation of the goods.

In the year 1135 Abbot Bernhelm obtained by his prayers from Count Megenhard the stream flowing around the castle of Sponheim, and the whole right of fishing, shared with him and his heirs, from that castle downward as far as the middle of the road toward Wimesheim, so that none of the ministerials living around it or of any others whatever, except only the domestic ministerials of the count and of the abbot, ought to fish in it. From the castle upward the fishing right is the count’s, and then to the beginning of the wood, where the boundary of those belonging to the castle extends. In these times the monastery of regular canons at Frankenthal [unclear] as far as Buggenau further on, and thence subsequently as far as the new church, today Naunkirch. The fishing belongs to the abbot by the gift of the aforesaid Udo. The monastery of Frankenthal is founded.

He appointed a mistress, and both were renowned for miracles. In the year 1136 Lutta, a most chaste virgin, daughter of Stephen, count of Sponheim, and sister of Count Megenhard, our founder, rested in the Lord on the second day before the Kalends of January. She was buried in the monastery of St. Disibod, beside the great altar toward the south, where for love of the heavenly kingdom she had been enclosed with certain other virgins for twenty-four years in a strict, although [unclear], service to the Lord. In 1112, in the fifth indiction, with three other virgins, Hildegard of Bickelnheim, who after her death went to Bingen and there founded a monastery on Mount St. Rupert, as will be said in its proper place; another Lutta, a certain noble virgin; and another of the same name, equally [unclear]...

Sponheimense.

Lobenfeld is founded. In these times the monastery of nuns at Lobenfeld, of our order, in the diocese of Worms, in the district called Kraichgau, about two miles from Heidelberg, was founded under Buggo, the venerable bishop of Worms.

At the same time the count of Leiningen founded the monastery of St Peter of Dumeta, commonly Hugen, in the same diocese of Worms. The aforesaid Bishop Buggo consecrated its church and established there the canon brothers under the rule of blessed Augustine, setting over them Hartung, a very venerable man, as their first father and provost. This consecration was performed in the year of the Lord’s incarnation MCLII, on the feast of St Peter which is called “in Chains.”

In this very year Mainz was burned together with the great monastery; Speyer also and Goslar, on one and the same day, for the greater part perished by fire.

The emperor Lothar also died in Bavaria on the day before the Nones of December. This emperor Lothar founded a monastery of our order in Saxony, which is called Lutera Regalis or Königslutter, where, after the nuns had been transferred to another place, he established an abbot and monks; and when he died he was buried there. Conrad III succeeded him and ruled for fourteen years.

In this year, on the night of Good Friday, the body of St Disibod, under Abbot Cuno, was translated with the greatest devotion from the old monastery, where it had once been placed in the altar by Archbishop Willigis, to the new monastery which Archbishop Ruthard and afterwards Adalbert the Elder had built on the mountain where it now stands; and it was honorably laid behind the high altar in a new marble sarcophagus. Abbot Bernhelm was present at this translation with the whole community of this monastery, and obtained the shoulder blade of the same holy pontiff.

MCL.

In the year MCXL Abbot Bernhelm traveled to Rome with Adalbert the Younger, archbishop of Mainz, and Count Gottfried of Sponheim, son of Megenhard, and through the entreaties of the aforesaid archbishop obtained from Pope Innocent many precious relics. Among them was one tooth of the holy apostle Paul; likewise, from the head of St Hippolytus the martyr; also from the hair of the holy apostle Peter; from the wood of the Holy Cross; from the shirt of St Benedict our father and abbot; from the cross of St Andrew the apostle; of Mary Magdalene and Mary of Egypt, together with many others.

In this year Embricho, bishop of Würzburg, founded in the suburb of the same city the monastery of St James the Apostle for the reception of Scots of our order; and he named and appointed as first abbot Macarius, a holy man, a Scot by nation. Among the other miracles of his holiness, as the same bishop declares in the charter of foundation, since out of love for the heavenly kingdom he abstained from wine and had nothing else on the table to drink, he changed the wine set before him into water in the presence of many, and drank it.

In this year St Otto, bishop of Bamberg, formerly a monk of our order, died on the day before the Kalends of October and was buried there in the church of the Mount of Monks, where he had been a monk before his episcopate. He built the monastery of [Aura?], of our order, in the diocese of Würzburg, in which he appointed as first abbot Egard, a religious and most learned man, who composed many little works of fine reading; and he lies buried in the middle of the same church, not without a reputation for holiness. He also founded anew some other monasteries, and magnificently restored several that had collapsed through excessive age, whose names [unclear]. [Unclear] of the martyr was consecrated, and was quite magnificently endowed by him.

The monastery of Schönau is founded. In these times also Buggo, bishop of Worms, founded not far from Heidelberg a monastery of the Cistercian order, which is called Schönau, and obtained a community from Clairvaux from St Bernard.

MCXLI.

In the year MCXLI [unclear], bishop of Mainz, died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August; Marolf, provost of Aschaffenburg, succeeded him and presided for one year and two months.

Marolf, bishop of Mainz.

Two bodies of saints are brought here.

MCXLIII.

In the year MCXLIII Abbot Bernhelm, through the intervention of Count Megenhard, obtained from Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, two bodies from the company of the eleven thousand virgins and martyrs for the monastery. Receiving them with great honor, he brought them here to the monastery and placed them in two gilded wooden reliquaries; their heads, however, had been broken, but the individual parts were arranged with their own body.

Chronicle of Trithemius

In the same year [Marcelsus?], archbishop of Mainz, died on the Ides of July; Henry, provost of the greater church, succeeded him and presided for ten years and eight months.

In the same year Adelbero, archbishop of Trier, expelled Gerard, abbot, and all the monks of St Maximin because of their disorderly life, and introduced other monks, who would live according to the Rule of St Benedict. Over them he appointed as abbot Siger, a religious and learned man. There are those who say that he did this not out of love for regular discipline, but because of his own greed: for it is agreed that he violently plundered much from the monastery of St Matthias for his own use, and obtained the abbey of St Maximin itself from the hand of the emperor; he drove out Abbot Gerard, who for a long time remained in exile on Mount St Disibod and here with Lord Bernhelm and our brethren. After he had thus been driven out, the brethren of St Maximin called the count of Namur, now Luxembourg, to their aid against the bishop, after selling jewels and ornaments, with whose price they hired him. But the archbishop besieged his castle of Rudolsberg while he himself was inside; he fled secretly and left the castle to the bishop. After the fortress had been taken, with many captives, the bishop returned; he [unclear] Manderscheid, Colubria, and thirty fortified castles of the counts, and forced the count himself to come into his favor, whereupon the brethren, deprived of all aid, were expelled by him.

1148.

In the year 1147, the twenty-fourth of Bernhelm our abbot, the holy virgin Hildegard, mistress of the brides of Christ on Mount St Disibod, having been appointed after the death of blessed Jutta, as we have said, was divinely admonished and passed over to Bingen with eighteen holy virgins. She built a monastery on the mountain across the river Nahe, near the tomb of St Rupert, duke and confessor, and brought that place, with all its goods and possessions, partly by purchase from the hand of the count of Hildenheim, dwelling in the parish of Trier, partly by exchange, and partly by donation of the count of Sponheim and other faithful persons, into the right of ownership; and, with the intervention of an apostolic privilege, she commended it for all time to the protection of the church of Mainz. This most holy virgin was born in our county of Sponheim, in the village called Bickelnheim, begotten of her father Hildebert, a most noble knight of Count Stephen, and of her mother Mechthild, likewise a most noble and honorable woman. When she was about eight years old, she was handed over by her parents to be instructed in the fear of the Lord under the teaching of blessed Jutta on Mount St Disibod. After St Jutta died, Hildegard herself, more perfect than all, was appointed mistress of the sisters by unanimous vote; and then, inspired by the divine Spirit, she was compelled to write certain wondrous things. These were brought for examination to the supreme pontiff Eugenius, then at Trier with eighteen cardinals, by Henry, bishop of Mainz, and St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux; they were read publicly before all and confirmed by that supreme pontiff himself. But since many nobles round about were entrusting their daughters to her instruction, the place became too narrow for them to dwell in; with the permission both of the supreme pontiff and of her abbot, she passed over to Mount St Rupert, as we have said, with eighteen sacred nuns. Among them was Hiltrud, daughter of Count Megenhard, a virgin of most holy life, very close to blessed Hildegard; on account of regard for her, her father the count bestowed many benefactions on that place, and we shall speak more fully of his place.

In this same year Adelbero, archbishop of Trier, called Pope Eugenius to Trier; and for many months he kept and maintained him, with eighteen cardinals, archbishops, bishops, and [unclear], together with all their household, most abundantly at his own expense.

In this year a great gathering of Christians from all Europe went overseas to recover the Lord’s sepulcher and the Holy Land. Among them were Conrad, king of the Romans, Louis, king of France, with many dukes, princes, bishops, abbots, monks, clerics, nobles, and commoners; yet they made little progress toward their chief purpose.

In the year 1149, the twenty-fifth of Bernhelm our abbot, Craftho, son of Count Megenhard of Sponheim, our founder, inflamed by the divine Spirit, despising for love of Christ all the pomp of the world and the broad possessions of riches, with his father’s consent became a monk under Abbot Bernhelm in this present monastery of ours at Sponheim. This happened as follows. A few years earlier he had taken Clementia, daughter of Adolf, count of Altena, a most beautiful and most prudent virgin, as his betrothed and future wife, and he loved her with exceeding love. Since she had a vow of virginity, at length by many prayers Sponheim.

[unclear] obtained from him permission to serve Christ in perpetual virginity, the parents of both being unaware. Finally the young man disclosed to his father the maiden’s vow and his own, and humbly begged him not to oppose it; and since he was a good man and most devout in the religion of Christ, he readily gave consent to his son’s prayers. And so he handed over his son’s betrothed, the aforesaid maiden Clementia, to serve Christ most devoutly, in the monastery of blessed Hirmina in the city of Trier, which had once been built by Dagobert, king of the Franks, and was called the Granary of Dagobert, commonly Oeren. In it she served the Lord for many years until the end of her life, in great devotion, holiness, and purity of mind and body. Craffto, moreover, the betrothed of the holy maiden, having been converted by her to the love and vow of perpetual chastity, became a monk in the present monastery, as we have said.

1150.

In these days, when St. Hildegard, the most devout handmaid of Christ, was dwelling on Mount St. Rupert near Bingen with her holy virgins, the necessary dwellings and convent having been built, as we have said, it happened that St. Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, while travelling down the river Rhine from Frankfurt to Cologne, visited in person her whom he knew by reputation and writings. When he had come to her, after the customary prayers and the courtesies of greeting, he himself ordered the volumes that she had written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit to be brought forth. After examining them carefully, and admiring them beyond what can be said, he is reported to have said to those standing around: “These writings were not devised by human means, but divinely inspired through the Holy Spirit; nor can any [mortal?] man understand them unless he has been inwardly reformed in his soul to the likeness of God.”

St. Bernard visits St. Hildegard.

St. Bernard commends the writings of Hildegard.

To this the provost of the virgins, a monk sufficiently learned and of most devout way of life, replied: “Reverend father, what you have said is indeed true; but many people, not only secular laymen, but also religious and learned men, torment the soul of the handmaid of Christ with daily disparagements, asserting that these things are not divinely inspired, but are either women’s dreams and phantasms of a disordered brain, or deceptions sent in by demons.” To him the man of God said: “We do not wonder, dearest brother, if those sleeping in sins think divine revelations to be dreams, knowing that what the Apostle said is true: ‘The animal man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God; for it is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand, because it is examined spiritually.’ For to all who lie as if asleep in sins of pride, greed, and lust, divine admonitions are accustomed to seem dreams, because if they were awake in the fear of the Lord, they would without doubt recognize the signs of divine revelations as true. But those who say that these things are sent in by demons do not know the hidden and mystical signs of divine inspirations. They are to be judged like those who, puffed up, said that our Lord and Savior Christ cast out demons by the power of Beelzebub.” He also said to St. Hildegard: “And you, dearest daughter, do not fear the reproaches of ignorant people, since you have God as protector; for they will perish like stubble, but the truth of the Lord remains forever. We also, for the honor of almighty God, will take care that these writings of yours be read by our lord the pope, just as also those that you sent to Trier to be approved.” Holy Hildegard then gave the man of God, at his request, a small portion of the relics of St. Rupert, duke of the people of Bingen and confessor. Then, bidding one another farewell, St. Bernard continued the journey he had begun, shining everywhere with miracles.

St. [Rupert?] is transferred [unclear] Sponheim.

In this same year Abbot Bernhelm, through the intercession of Count Megenhard the founder, obtained from Henry, archbishop of Mainz, and St. Hildegard the right leg of blessed Rupert, the aforesaid confessor and duke, complete from the knee down to the foot or ankle, with skin, flesh, and bones; and he brought it with great reverence and honor to this monastery of his at Sponheim.

Finally, about these times, after Constantinople had been captured by the Latins, Hildebert, nephew of our lord abbot Bernhelm, a very brave knight who had crossed the sea with other Christians, returning through Greece, brought back many relics of saints, both from Jerusalem and from Byzantium, almost all of which he bestowed on this monastery. For he brought these, received from the church of St. Basil: of St. Lawrence the martyr; of Sts. Mark and Marcellinus, martyrs; three small pieces of the Innocents; of St. Basil; of St. John Chrysostom; and many others. But those that he carried from the Holy Land are these: of the Lord’s sepulcher; of the stone on which the [Lord?] stood when he ascended into heaven; of the stone on which the angel stood when he announced the Incarnation to Mary; of the Lord’s cradle; of the door through which the Lord entered, though it was closed, after the resurrection; of the oil of St. Catherine; of St. Stephen the protomartyr; also of the Mount of Olives; of the sepulcher of holy Mary ever virgin; of the stone of Calvary on which the Lord was crucified; of the Lord’s rock; of the stone of Golgotha that was stained with the Lord’s blood; of the Lord’s table; of the Lord’s bed; of the place of the Lord’s passion; also a mixture of all Sponheimense.

which, obtained for love of the holy virgin Clementia, formerly his betrothed, who was serving the Lord in the same convent, he received with great honor and reverence, and brought here to his monastery, the whole congregation going out beyond the gate to meet it with praises and hymns; which, intact with skin, flesh, and hair, we venerate down to the present day.

In this same year King Conrad died; Frederick, the first of this name, succeeded him and ruled for 38 years.

1153.

An Almeinda is established for the poor.

Abbot Craffto, for the use of all poor persons arriving from anywhere, especially of those who serve the count and the monastery with their conveyances, obtained from his father Count Megenhard the Almeinda which is next to the vegetable garden, which Countess Richart had once bestowed on the monastery at its first foundation, toward the east and on the right side of the road to Mannede, with every right of ownership. He wished it to be confirmed forever with this limitation: namely, that every right and ownership of it should belong forever to the monastery, but that the usufruct should be common both to the monastery and to the household of the villages of Sponheim in Dalen, and to all poor persons arriving with beasts of burden and wishing to remain there as shepherds, unless the count with the abbot should wish to revoke it.

In this year Henry, archbishop of Mainz, by command of Pope Eugenius, was deposed by two cardinals, Gregory and Bernard. Wasted away by disease, he died in the same year on the kalends of September. Arnold, provost of Aachen, chancellor of Emperor Frederick, promoted and assisted by his aid, succeeded him.

1154.

In the third year of Craffto, Machthildis, a consecrated virgin, died; she had once been the sister of Abbot Bernhelm and was enclosed here beside our monastery at the beginning of its foundation, as was said above in its place. She died in her enclosure on the fourth day before the kalends of March. At her passing, angelic harmonies of praise were heard, and certain visions were said to have appeared. She was buried in the choir of the brothers before the steps of the presbytery, not without a reputation for sanctity. She left after her in the same cell five sisters, virgins consecrated and devoted to Christ, whose names are these: Sophia, who had come with her from Saint Alban, and who died in the same year on the day before the kalends of May; Gerlindis, Demodis, Luigardis, and Gertrudis, who served the Lord in the holy purpose of virginity until the end of life. In the course of time some others were joined to them to serve the Lord, but the names of few have remained among us. For after about seventy years the sisters failed in the same place; the enclosure was left desolate in the course of time, the buildings were ruined and utterly destroyed. At length, after many years, Abbot Dieterus had the stones carried away, the place cleared, and a vineyard planted there, which had continued there down to the present.

1155.

In the fourth year of Abbot Craffto, his father Megenhard, count of Spanheim, founder of this monastery, died on the day before the kalends of March: a man magnificent in every respect, father of the poor. For his soul Craffto caused many good works to be done. Finally, with the whole congregation of this monastery consenting and approving, he decreed that his anniversary day should be observed every year with vigils and masses, on which every priest should read one mass; non-priests should read fifty psalms, and those who did not know them, as many Our Fathers and Hail Marys. On that day twelve poor persons were to be fed in memory of the twelve apostles of Christ. Count Gotfridus, son of Megenhard, having obtained the county of Sponheim after his father’s death, governed it quite vigorously. At the urging of Lord Abbot Craffto, his brother, he [unclear] the castle called Coppenstein, with the forest and adjacent hamlets, to this monastery forever as the portion of a lawful inheritance [unclear]. About 170 years later, under Willicho the first abbot, a certain exchange was made by Count Johann [unclear], his brother Simon of Birgberg, Count Heinrich of Katzenelnbogen, Count Conrad of Sponheim, and others, for the little castle of Coppenstein with its appurtenances. This Count Hermann Palatine gave the church in Lainstein, with the third part of the tithes, of no small usefulness, to the archiepiscopal mensa of Trier, and bestowed many benefactions on the same church. For he was a man magnificent and glorious in every respect.

Chronicle of Trithemius. 1156.

In the fifth year of Abbot Craffto, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, the hospital of the poor, with its attached chapel, into which the right of the parish church had long before been transferred from Dalen, was consumed by fire and wholly perished. Therefore the parish church was again transferred to that place adjoining the monastery, where even today it is seen, separated from all human dwellings, so that it cannot easily perish by fire. For the first parish church was in Dalen from the time of St. Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, for almost 278 years. And then, under the elder Archbishop Adelbert, at the instance of Count Megenhard, the right of the parishioners was transferred into the chapel of the hospital, which had been situated toward the south near the monastery. Finally, when in the aforesaid year of Craffto that church with the hospital had been burned, a new church began to be built on the slope of the mountain beside the monastery, into which the entire right of the mother church was transferred. But the hospital was not rebuilt, both because of the monastery and because Count Gottfried seemed at that time to care little about the support of the poor. The graves also of the dead, with their bones for the greater part, were first transferred from Dalen to the hospital, and then to the new cemetery; although in both places many remained which at that time were not found. For often meanwhile, both in Dalen and in the place of the hospital, bones of the dead are found in digging and ploughing.

In this year Hermann, count palatine of the Rhine, etc., died.

1160.

In this year, which was the ninth of Abbot Craffto, on the third day before the Nones of November, in the [unclear] indiction, the parish church at the foot of the mountain around the monastery, newly built, of which we have already spoken, was consecrated by Bishop Henry, vicar of Arnold, archbishop of Mainz, in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity, the Holy Cross, and St. Giles, abbot and confessor. He enclosed in the altar relics of St. Vitus, of St. Maurice, of the holy Moors, of St. Alexandra the martyr, of St. Egricius, archbishop of Trier, of St. Boniface the bishop, of St. Emerentiana the virgin, of St. Irmina the virgin, and of the eleven thousand virgins. But the baptistery had from the beginning been placed in the church of the monastery, and for that reason another was not built in the parish church, because the one that existed before could suffice for so large a parish family.

1163.

At this time, for nine continuous years, the bodies of the holy eleven thousand virgins and of the other saints who suffered with them were found in the suburb of the city of Cologne and raised from the earth; some of these were found even without names. From them St. Elisabeth, a nun and mistress in Schönau, learned, by angelic revelation, the names, merits, and ranks of many, and wrote to Gerlacus, abbot of the monastery of Deutz, of our order.

1168.

In the thirteenth year of Craffto, abbot of this monastery, St. Elisabeth, a virgin nun of our order and mistress in Schönau, passed from this world to the Lord Jesus, whom she had always loved with a pure heart, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the thirty-sixth year of her age, and in the [unclear] of the visitation of the heavenly light, in holy revelations, on Friday at the ninth hour in the morning. This holy virgin, in the twenty-third year of her age, began to be consoled by angelic visitation and address, and thereafter had many revelations from God, which she arranged in part in the German tongue. But her brother, a monk in Schönau and afterward abbot, reduced all the writings and revelations of his holy sister into the more ornate style and into the form in which they are now read. These two precious lights of the world were at one and the same time: Hildegard at Bingen, on the mount of St. Rupert, and Elisabeth in Schönau; both, often visited by divine revelations, brought many secrets, according to the will of God, to the knowledge of men.

1167.

Craffto the abbot, in his sixteenth year, obtained from Pope Alexander III, through the mediation of a certain Cardinal Benedict, a large particle of the wood of the Lord’s Cross, which he adorned for this monastery with gold and gems. Finally, he adorned our church quite well with jewels, crosses, relics, and ornaments, all of which, however, failed with time, except for a precious mitre, which, although under many abbots it was often pawned, nevertheless in time, God willing, was brought back to the monastery. This mitre Craffto himself, in the first year of his promotion, caused to be made of pure silver, gilded on top, throughout with pearls and precious stones, many of which have been removed, with the help and, for a great part, at the expense of his mother.

1168. 260 Chronicle of Trithemius

for years, on account of his most fervent zeal for regular discipline, he was appointed prior under Abbot Baldemar; by word and example he showed himself steadfast to all, and preserved inviolate the integrity of the monastic life. All the time in which he was prior, namely for thirteen years, he spent either in the Scriptures as much as he could, or in prayers and the worship of divine praise. He always fled idleness with the greatest care, knowing what is written: “For in desires is every [unclear],” etc. Therefore he was accustomed to occupy himself usefully at all times, lest through idleness an entrance should lie open to vices. He was, however, as we have said, very learned in the writings of both branches of knowledge; always aided by his natural ability, with continual practice he became more learned every day, and by his own example and instruction he also stirred the brothers who seemed more fit for learning to love and study letters. When he had been ordained abbot, since he was now compelled to have regard for temporal as well as spiritual affairs, he showed himself so diligent and attentive in both that one would have sworn nature had fitted him for either.
