In this same year in which Abbot Rupert was elected, serious disputes arose between the bishop of Worms and his citizens over various matters and ecclesiastical liberties. Emicho, count of Leiningen, Werner of Bolanden, with their followers, involved themselves in these; the count of Sponheim lent them his aid.

A.D. 1200.

Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, entered Hungary to restore peace between the two brothers Emeric and Andrew, who were contending for the kingdom. When agreement had been made between them and he was preparing to return, in the regions of Austria, in the territory of Passau, he paid the debt of the flesh. After his funeral rites had been celebrated, Wolfger, bishop of that place, honorably conveyed his body to Mainz and had it buried there.

Meanwhile a serious dispute arose in Mainz. Some elected Lupold, bishop of Worms, as archbishop; others preferred Siegfried, provost of the greater church. Leaving the city, they came to Bingen, and there confirmed the election which they had begun concerning Provost Siegfried. Hearing this, Lupold came with a strong hand, with the favor of King Philip, and drove Siegfried and his electors out of Bingen. But Siegfried, seeing that his men were making less progress, betook himself with his followers to King Otto. He was kindly received by him, and received the regalia from him. Relying on his authority, he returned to Bingen with the forces of an army; Lupold barely escaped by flight, and he captured many from his side along with the town. And so Siegfried, confirmed in the see of Mainz, presided as archbishop for almost fifteen years. This Archbishop Siegfried, in the first year of his pontificate, ordained our Abbot Rupert, of whom we are speaking, at Mainz in the church of Saint Alban, on the third Ides of November, which was the day of Saint Martin, our patron. Elsewhere I found that he received the gift of benediction from Guido, cardinal of Palestrina, legate of the apostolic see, at Saint Pantaleon in Cologne; I believe this to be truer, especially since Siegfried did not yet have the pallium.

In this same year many princes, bishops, and abbots, with an infinite multitude, signed with the cross, set out for the Holy Land in the service of the Lord’s Sepulchre. Among them was Berthold, count of Neuenburg in Breisgau, who, having received money, handed over his county to the church of Strasbourg as a perpetual possession, with all its appurtenances. He himself, with his son, set out for Jerusalem, and there persevered in the service of the Lord’s Sepulchre until death. Stirred by his example, many noble and powerful men, selling their estates, dedicated themselves with their wives and children to the perpetual service of the Holy Sepulchre. Lutold, bishop of Basel, likewise set out.

A.D. 1202.

Adelbert, count of Sponheim, set out for the Holy Land with many others, and for two years served Christ there as a soldier. In the same year Baldwin, count of Flanders, made his way to Jerusalem with great equipment. Rupert also, abbot of the monastery, since he was a wise and most prudent man, was appointed governor of the county of Sponheim by Count Adelbert, along with certain others, and governed the province quite prudently until his return.

Abbot Rupert made Peter, a monk of Bingen, whom three years before he had ordained prior in his place, after he had been deposed, I do not know for what reason, provost of the nuns on Mount Saint Rupert, at the request of Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, of the mistress, and of the whole convent of that monastery. In his place he appointed as prior the sixth in order from the beginning of the foundation, an old monk named Erenfrid, a venerable man, who Sponheim.

1168.

In the seventeenth year of Abbot Craffto, Arnold, archbishop of Mainz, was cruelly killed by his own citizens in the monastery of St James near Mainz, on the day of St John the Baptist, namely [the eighth day before the Kalends?] of July. The leaders of this conspiracy from the clergy were Gotfridus, abbot of St James and provost of St Peter, with many others. When the slaughter had been carried out, Abbot Gotfridus, with the rest of the accomplices of his impiety, immediately withdrew into the city. They compelled the clergy and elected Rodolph, son of Conrad, duke of Zähringen, as archbishop. When he wished to appease the emperor with gifts, he stripped the church of all its adornment; but the emperor despised both him and his gifts.

But Conrad, count palatine of the Rhine, the emperor’s brother by one parent, drove out Rodolph and raised a certain Christian to the archbishopric; he nevertheless did not on that occasion attain the bishopric. For the emperor, rejecting both of them, raised Conrad, brother of Otto, count palatine of Wittelsbach, to the archbishopric. After two years he also expelled him, as will be said there, and caused Christian to be ordained in his place.

Moreover, after Arnold had been killed, as has been said, in the monastery of St James, that place itself was destroyed, all the dwellings of the monks were overturned, the monks were put to flight, and the abbot was banished from the country. And so for twelve years no divine offices were celebrated there. The monks who had been put to flight betook themselves to various monasteries; of these, four were sustained here for a long time out of fraternal charity, six in the monastery of St Disibod, and others were received in other places. The wall of the city of Mainz also, by command of the emperor, was destroyed all around, so that Mainz stood without a wall for thirty-six years. But all the citizens who had consented to the death of the archbishop, except the poor and beggars, fled before the emperor’s return from Italy.

1170.

In the nineteenth year of Abbot Craffto, Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, bound himself by oath to Pope Alexander. Wherefore the emperor, angered, expelled him from the archbishopric and from the country, and compelled him to flee to the pope; the pope gave him the bishopric of Sabina. Hence, for as long as he afterwards lived, he styled himself archbishop of Mainz and bishop of Sabina. After he had been expelled, the emperor raised Christian, who had been elected before him, as we have said, to the archbishopric. He presided for thirteen years. When he died, Conrad returned to the church of Mainz, as we shall say below in its place.

1183.

In his twenty-second year, Lord Abbot Craffto covered the head of St Irmina the virgin, which at the beginning of his promotion he had obtained from Hillin, archbishop of Trier, with a beautiful silver reliquary, and adorned it all around with precious stones, for the adornment of the church. But after many years, when the condition of temporal affairs had collapsed greatly through the bad governance of the abbots and the wicked life of the monks, under Craffto the second of this name the silver head itself was sold, and a copper one, which is seen today, was substituted.

1175.

Craffto, the second abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, son of Count Megenhard and our founder, died this year on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, and was buried in the same tomb with Bernhelm, his predecessor, in the middle of the choir: a man in every respect religious and most holy, who did many good things for this monastery and acquired many possessions for the support of the brothers. On his tomb verses are seen carved, which, with the names of both men set before them, sound thus in prose:

Illustrious abbots, to whom it has fallen to be entombed here, Both dear to God, I am now in equal peace.

Anselm the prior is believed to have made these little verses, because he was a studious and learned man. Abbot Craffto died, released by the disease of dysentery, in the fifty-eighth year of his age, and in the twenty-fourth year and second month of his abbacy.

Concerning Adelger, the third abbot of this monastery, who presided for six years, one month, and three days; and concerning his deeds and other matters occurring in the present work.

When the most reverend abbot Lord Craffto had died and, not without many tears of the brothers, had been given ecclesiastical burial in the middle of the choir, as we have said, the same brothers assembled in the chapter place on the fourth day before the Kalends of June for the election of a known pastor. Having invoked the gift of the Holy Spirit and held much deliberation among themselves beforehand, at length they unanimously elected Adelger, a venerable monk, custodian of our church, a mature man and so [unclear]

Arnold the archbishop is killed. Rodolph the archbishop is driven out. Christian is [unclear] archbishop [unclear]. Conrad becomes archbishop. The monastery of St James is destroyed. Mainz [unclear] is destroyed. Archbishop Conrad is expelled. Christian becomes archbishop. Irmina’s head is covered in a silver shrine. Abbot Craffto dies. [Blank page in the source scan.]

most skilled in spiritual as well as in temporal matters; he was solemnly ordained by Christian, archbishop of Mainz. He presided over this monastery with sufficient foresight for 6 years, 1 month, and 3 days.

This Adelger was born of his father Theodo and his mother Amalberga, citizens of Mainz, honorable and devoted to Christ. In his boyhood he was entrusted by those parents to letters in the city of Mainz. Through the diligence of his teachers, as he grew older, he made no small progress in writings, especially secular ones, and surpassed many of his contemporaries in conduct and knowledge. Then, when he was twenty years old, out of love of wisdom he betook himself to the University of Paris, then the most famous in the whole world, and, remaining there for seven years, made magnificent progress in every branch of knowledge, both divine and human. When the seven years had passed he returned to Mainz; because of the reputation of his learning he was appointed scholasticus there, where he received many talented young men as pupils. At length, however, after his parents had already died, seeing that many were going to perdition by the broken paths of vices, he abandoned the world with its vanities for the love of God, and coming here under Abbot Craffto he was made a monk. His way of life among the brothers was beyond reproach, humble and quiet, burdensome to no one, never troublesome to anyone. Finally, when he was appointed abbot, he took care with every effort and solicitude to show himself a useful shepherd to the brothers, and to instruct them in living well no less by example than by speech. For under his rule monastic discipline flourished here in praiseworthy fashion.

MCLXXVI.

In the year 1176, Abbot Adelger built the sacristy beside the high altar on the left, for greater convenience. It had previously been beside the northern apse, where the chapter room now is, placed between the refectory and the church.

In this same year died Clementia, a virgin nun in [Horreo Treverensi?], on 21 March, formerly the betrothed of Lord Craffto, count and second abbot of this monastery, daughter of the count of Hochenberg. This most devout virgin was a most fervent lover of Christ; intent day and night on prayer and contemplation, she desired nothing more than to please God in all things. Finally she departed, not without a great reputation for sanctity, in the forty-eighth year of her age, the twenty-seventh of her conversion to our order, in the ninth indiction. Buried in the church of St. Irmina.

MCLXXVII.

In the year 1177, Adelbero, the first cellarer of this community, formerly a monk of St. Alban’s at Mainz, who had been sent here with the first monks, died in this same year on 11 November, in the eighty-sixth year of his age. He held the office of cellarer vigorously for almost fifty-three years, and with great diligence and charity always applied the necessary care to domestic affairs.

Saint Hiltrudis also, a virgin and nun at Bingen, daughter of Count Megenhard of Sponheim, sister of our above-mentioned second abbot Craffto, in this same year on 17 November rested in the Lord; blessed Hildegard, her teacher, bore witness to her sanctity.

MCLXXVIII.

In the third year of his rule, Abbot Adelger sent Erenfrid, his monk, to Rome for the dispatching of certain business of this monastery. Returning from there, among other relics he brought back a notable particle of St. John the Baptist, which was received with great reverence and honor. This same Abbot Adelger, for the adornment of the church and reverence for the relics, had small reliquaries made: some of white ivory, others of wood overlaid with gilded bronze plates, which he filled and adorned with diverse relics of saints. Among the many volumes of sacred reading that he acquired for the use and benefit of the brothers, he also had the New and Old Testament copied in a beautiful script, in three large volumes, by the hand of Godefrid, a monk of this community, who was an excellent scribe and a most vigilant restorer of books of sacred scripture. In this same year the monastery of St. James on the fair mountain near Mainz, which some years before had been destroyed on account of the killing of Archbishop Arnold, began to be rebuilt, with the permission of Emperor Frederick I and the assistance of Archbishop Christian. Archbishop Liutpold of Mainz founded this community in the year of the Lord 1053.

MCLXXIX.

Anselm of Bickelnheim, kinsman of St. Hildegard, the second prior of this monastery, died on 21 December, in the forty-third year of his priorate. He was among the first twelve sent here from the monastery of St. James, as was said above. For he was a good man and a notable lover of regular discipline. At his death he left after him in this community twenty monks well instructed. He increased the library to no small degree and trained very many excellent scribes. After his departure Adelger appointed as third prior one named Eberold, a sufficiently learned monk, who [Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheim.

who held the office of prior for six years, and afterwards, under Abbot Baldemar, was deposed, having no other cause for his deposition except that he seemed too lax in monastic observance and, though more often admonished, scorned to amend; this cause was approved by all as more than sufficient.

In this year St. Hildegard, virgin of Christ, a nun of our order, foundress and mistress of the monastery of St. Rupert near Bingen, died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the eighty-second year of her age, in the thirteenth indiction. She was buried with great honor before the high altar of the aforesaid church, with many honorable persons and the whole congregation standing by. This holy virgin was deemed worthy to be visited by divine revelations from her youth; from these, by divine command, she wrote down many things for the use of posterity. But since she was ignorant of the Latin tongue and had learned nothing from any human being except simple psalmody, taught by the inward instruction of the Holy Spirit she perfectly understood every writing, arrangement, or construction of speech. Her revelations, moreover, and heavenly visions she set forth partly in the German tongue; these Gotfridus, monk of St. Disibod, her chaplain and confessor, made into [unclear] Latin, reducing them into that order and form in which they are read today. Among her other volumes, however, there is a great volume in that same place which contains her letters to various persons, homilies, lives of saints, and other things which, taught by God, she published; the nuns of that place falsely assert that she wrote it with her own hand, since she was ignorant of the Latin tongue and, because of frequent illnesses, wholly indisposed in her damp head for writing. For none of those things which are displayed there today should be believed to have been written by her own hand, since indeed she did not know how to write; but the aforesaid monk either wrote everything or caused it to be written.

MCLXXXI.

In this year Adelgerus, the third abbot of this monastery, died on the sixth day before the Nones of July, about the twelfth hour in the middle of the night. He was buried in the brothers’ choir before the steps of the presbytery. Under this abbot’s rule regular discipline was quite good in the present place, with the greatest charity among the brothers and religious devotion; and when this reputation was laudably spread round about, it earned great reverence from the faithful peoples. Hence very many, conferring generous alms on this place, commended themselves to the prayers of the brothers; and not only those living nearby strove by their benefactions to relieve the brothers’ poverty, but also men from distant places, stirred by devotion to the brothers, sent their alms here. Among many we shall set down at least one, so that the truth of what has been said may be proved. For thus, among other things, the brothers wrote to a certain man who gave his goods generously to this monastery: Wernerus of blessed memory, pastor of St. Columba in Cologne, gave ten marks for the purchase of a vineyard in Monaecha, so that annually the abbot in Sponheim would pay one cartload of wine to his relative Wilhelm. After the departure of his uncle, however, Wilhelm offered the above-mentioned vineyard of the town, after receiving full fraternity, for the use of the brothers, so that in the granary of his Lord, having full charity in bread, wine, and lean fish, they may rejoice in the Lord, giving thanks to him for this benefaction. And so that this may always be held valid, it was confirmed by the attestation of the present page under the abbot’s anathema: that if anyone should wish to annul this, or should annul it, he be blotted out from the book of the living and not be written with the just, unless through repentance and satisfaction he should regain his senses. The other donations of the faithful made to this monastery under Abbot Adelgerus, since they were numerous, we have not wished to recount in this place, in order to remove tedium.

Concerning Baldemar, the fourth abbot of this place, who presided for 17 years, 2 months, and 17 days; concerning his deeds with regard to the present monastery.

After Adelgerus, the third abbot of this monastery, had died and been buried, as we have said, two of the brothers were not present; when their arrival had been awaited, and they had then appeared on the third day, that is, on the third day before the Nones of July, Prior Eberoldus, together with the conventual brothers, began to have discussion concerning the election of a new abbot. After many [unclear], at length they [unclear] gave their consent. He, ordained by Christianus, archbishop of Mainz, presided over this monastery for seventeen years, twelve months, and 17 days, a man sufficiently religious, experienced in both [unclear] of cloistered persons. He was born from the county of Sponheim, in the town of Kreuznach, of parents honored according to the world. Coming to the monastery under Abbot Craffto, he was made a monk when he was eighteen years old, a youth of good character and already, at the beginnings of literary instruction, not moderately learned. He had a sister here in the enclosure, shut up with other sacred virgins for the love of Christ, who of conversion that woman was a very great occasion for his entering religion; her name was Udegeba, a nun very devout and of holy conduct, who converted him by her most sweet admonitions.

After he was made abbot, overcome by the prayers and love of his sister, he enlarged the enclosure, which was too cramped, and gathered in it sisters serving Christ, up to the number of twelve; all of them lived in common from the portion of their paternal inheritances and from the labor of their hands, without burden to this monastery.

1183.

Christian, archbishop of Mainz, died; Conrad was restored, whom the emperor Frederick had expelled because of his adherence to the Apostolic See, and he presided for 17 years. He wrote the title thus: “Conrad, by the grace of God bishop of Sabina, archbishop of the holy see of Mainz: After divine clemency restored us, after our long exile, to the governance of the Church of Mainz, by the office enjoined on us by God, by which we were and are bound universally to provide for our [unclear] church, graciously to reform all things which pertain to the state of rectitude and the vigor of justice ...” He retained this title together with the bishopric of Sabina, which Pope Alexander had conferred on him when he had fled, as was said above, as long as he lived.

In this year, on 20 July, a great fire broke out in the town of Kreuznach, by which many houses were burned and great damage was inflicted.

1184.

In this year Abbot Baldemar built the great house on the eastern side, which is now the lower refectory, with the brothers’ dormitory above, for the reception of guests, away from the abbatial house, in which he constructed various chambers in the manner of the ancients; all of these were afterward changed into another form.

In this same year Lugardis, a virgin nun enclosed here, very devout, daughter of the late Eberhard, knight of Sobernheim, died on 25 October and was buried in the cloister of this monastery. It was said of her that she had often had visions and angelic revelations.

1187.

In this year Eberold, the third prior of this monastery, was deposed by Abbot Baldemar, because he seemed too lax in the observance of regular discipline. Rupert succeeded him in the priorship as the fourth, a very venerable monk, a lover, cultivator, and strenuous preserver of regular observance, who after Baldemar’s death was later elected abbot in his place. He was by nation a Thuringian, sprung from honorable parents, very learned in both divine and human writings; of him we shall speak in his own place. He greatly enlarged the library according to his abilities, and wrote and caused to be written many volumes.

1188.

Abbot Baldemar built and completed the wall around this monastery, which Abbot Craffto had begun long before but, being overtaken by death, had not completed, because not everything necessary could be accomplished at the beginning.

In this same year the virgin Hildegund died on 20 April in the monastery of Schönau, of the Cistercian order, in the diocese [unclear]; she had been received there among the novices, concealing her name and calling herself Joseph. Caesarius, monk of Heisterbach, wrote her history in the first distinction of his Dialogues.

1189.

In this year Ida, countess of Sponheim, became a nun in the monastery of St. Rupert at Bingen, brought to this by a wondrous vision given to her from heaven; there, living in holy conduct and very severe penitence, she was an example to all of chastity and holiness. Her sister was that most holy virgin Margaret of Hohenfels, prioress for many years in the same monastery, who is said to have shone with miracles in her lifetime; the feast of her commemoration is celebrated on 29 October.

1190.

In this year, on the vigil of St. John the Baptist, there was a great general eclipse.

1192.

Abbot Baldemar, in the twelfth year of his rule, had a certain dispute with the villagers of Sponheim over pastures and woods, which nevertheless was settled by Count Gerlach and other good friends with the consent of the parties.

In this same year Albert, afterward called the Great, was born in Lauingen in Swabia. Also in this year Rupert, prior of this place, saw a wondrous vision, both of the punishments of hell and also of the joys of Paradise; when he revealed it rather imprudently, he was gravely [struck] by paralysis Sponheim.

having been gravely struck, he was ill for almost the space of a year.

1195.

In this year Abbot Baldemar purchased the village which is called Argenschwang, with all its jurisdiction, justice, and property, for twenty marks of silver from the count of Sponheim, whose advocacy he gave in fief to Erinfrid of Sponheim, knight.

Also in this same year Conrad, count palatine of the Rhine, duke in Heidelberg, [unclear] of the diocese of Worms, changed [unclear] of the monks of our order in Nuwenburg, appointing as the first abbess Cunegund, a very religious virgin, with Sigenhard, abbot of the monastery of Lorsch, agreeing to everything; to him that provostry of Nuwenburg belonged by full right, without any intermediary. [unclear] Six nuns will die.

1197.

In this year Udegeba, sister of Abbot Baldemar, a nun enclosed here among us, died on the fourth Ides of July, a virgin of holy conduct, who for many years served almighty God in great devotion. Five other sisters died successively not long after her; these are their names: Sister Walpurgis, on the eighth Kalends of August; Gertrude, on the third Ides of August; Adelheid, on the thirteenth Kalends of September; Lucardis, on the seventh Kalends of September; Otilia, on the sixteenth Kalends of December, at night around the eleventh hour, who was the daughter of Henry, knight of Kreuznach, a most beautiful virgin, renowned no less for her conduct than for her blood, who shone with many virtues. There remained, however, six or seven in number, who also died successively within a short time; nor were as many gathered again in their place as before, but far fewer.

1198.

In this year the little village called Bockenau was set on fire on the fifteenth Kalends of January by a certain fugitive peasant, and was entirely consumed by fire. He himself, however, was afterwards apprehended and was judicially burned for so heinous a deed.

In the same year Drutwin, Schultheiss in the village of Sponheim, was captured by Count Gerlach and beheaded on the day before the Kalends of June for the crime of homicide.

1199.

Baldemar, the fourth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, died in this year on the tenth Kalends of July, and was buried in the cloister before the door of the church, in the fifty-fourth year of his age, not yet completed. He was a good and religious man, who profitably governed this monastery both in spiritual and in temporal matters, and did many good things. Rupert, prior of this place, succeeded him in the abbacy.

Concerning Rupert, the fifth abbot of this monastery, who presided for fourteen years and two months; concerning deeds relating to the present monastery.

In the year of the Lord's incarnation 1199, in the second indiction, two days after the death of Lord Abbot Baldemar, that is, on the eighth Kalends of July, the brothers came together to hold the election of a new pastor. Having invoked, according to custom, the grace of the Holy Spirit, they unanimously set over themselves as the fifth abbot of the place Lord Rupert, the fourth prior of this place, a learned man, very religious, no less prudent in counsel than mature in action. After his long and humble excuse of himself, he presided vigorously for thirteen years and three months. He was ordained abbot in the following year by Sifrid, archbishop of Mainz, in the church of Saint Alban, because Archbishop Conrad, returning from Jerusalem, had remained for some time in Italy because of the dissension between Philip and Otto, who were contending over the empire. Afterwards, having returned to Mainz, he died in the following year, as we shall say. This Abbot Rupert was by origin from the province of the Thuringians, of honorable parents of moderate fortune; having been given over to letters from infancy, so to speak, he advanced with age in every branch of knowledge, both secular and divine, and became most learned. And first indeed in his own country he received the rudiments of youthful studies; then he went to Gaul, and returning from there after some years, at the admonition of a fellow-countryman of his, he was detained here and became a monk under the venerable Abbot Adelger, when he was about twenty-four years old. But after he assumed the habit of holy conduct, he was so devoutly, so religiously and blamelessly planted in the midst of the brothers' life that he seemed to be the master of all in regular observance. Hence after some Sponheimense.

... who vigorously held the office of prior for five years and maintained good discipline.

In the same year Conrad, bishop of Würzburg, chancellor of the imperial court, when he was rather steadfastly reproving the vices of the wicked, was cruelly killed by Bodo and Henry, knights of Rabensburg, and by their assailants Herald and Conrad, in the city of Würzburg, in the public street, on the fourth Nones of December. Henry, called Käse, succeeded him, because he held cheese among his delicacies. The murderers, going to Rome, received a very severe penance from Pope Innocent III, which is contained in the bull of the same pope.

1203.

Adelbert, count of Sponheim, returned from the parts beyond the sea and brought to us relics of many saints; and he gave many gifts to Abbot Rupert, whom meanwhile he had appointed as steward. Through his munificence he gave in perpetual right and ownership to this monastery the little village of Auwen, not far from Monzingen, with its household, land, jurisdiction, justice, pastures, woods, waters, fisheries, hunts, and all its revenues or appurtenances, together with the Schultheiss, the scabini, and the leading men.

1206.

In this year, on the day before the Kalends of March, at the tenth hour of the day, there was a quite dreadful eclipse of the sun. For several testified that they had then seen a human head in the sun. Many other signs also appeared at this time in the sun, the stars, and the air. Abbot Rupert, considering that a great danger of souls was arising for the monks, [unclear] that no sister thereafter should be received into the enclosure beside this present monastery of ours, lest by any occasion they become a ruin of souls for posterity; and so none was received thereafter. For at that time there were still six in the enclosure. Two of them died after some years, and the four remaining transferred to Mount Saint Rupert under Abbot Iwan, as we shall say below in its proper place, when we come to the eleventh year of Abbot Iwan.

1208.

Erenfrid, the sixth prior of this monastery, died in this year on the day of Saint Andrew the Apostle, a good man and a special lover of regular discipline, who most zealously bestowed admonitions of salvation on his brothers by word and example. After him Iwan, a monk of this monastery, [unclear].

... bestowed admonitions of salvation on his brothers most zealously. After him Iwan, a monk [unclear] that by no occasion they become a ruin of souls for posterity; and so none was received thereafter. For there were at that time still six in the enclosure; after some years [some] died, and the four remaining transferred to Mount Saint Rupert under Abbot Iwan, as we shall say below in its proper time, when we come to the eleventh year of Abbot Iwan.

In this year Philip, king of the Romans, was killed at Bamberg by Otto, count palatine of Wittelsbach. Otto, duke [unclear] of Brunswick, succeeded him immediately in the empire by election of the princes, and reigned for a few years, namely three. Dispensation of the table allowances of Saint Rupert.

In this year Philip, king of the Romans, was killed at Bamberg. Otto, duke [unclear], succeeded immediately by election of the princes as king in the empire, and reigned for a few years, namely three. At length, after agreement had been made between them by Rupert, our abbot, and also by the abbot of Disibodenberg, at the order of Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, both withdrew, and a third was substituted in their place. Frederick [unclear]. Gertrude, daughter of Emelrich, knight of Mainz, but the other was Beatrix, daughter of the count of Hohenfels. At length, after agreement had been made between them by Rupert our abbot, [unclear].

At the same time Hermann, landgrave of Thuringia, arranged for the son of the former King Frederick to be elected king of the Romans against Otto; and many evils followed: persecutions, burnings, and wars, which lasted until Otto’s death. Emperor Otto is excommunicated.

1211.

In this year Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, by the command and authority of Pope Innocent III, everywhere throughout all Germany denounced Emperor Otto as excommunicated. Hence Henry, count palatine of the Rhine, the emperor’s brother, was moved, and with the duke of Brabant, the count in Sponheim, and the other nobles of Lotharingia and of these regions, he devastated the whole bishopric of Mainz around the feast of Saint Michael with fire and plunder, leaving nothing untouched except cities and castles, but destroying everything. In this year, on the fourth Kalends of March, a great miracle occurred in the village which [is called] Vallis [unclear].

Chronicle of Trithemius

A dead man came back to life and preached many things.

[unclear], commonly called Mannendal, situated not far from here, is so named. In it there was a certain good and respectable man, named Adelbert, who had a wife and children, whom he supported by the labor of his hands. When he was sixty-two years old, he fell into very acute fevers; as they gradually increased slightly, he seemed to be near death. Therefore, after confession and fortified with the ecclesiastical sacraments, he came to his end, and on the aforesaid day, when the sun was already setting, he departed from human affairs. Thus dead, he lay silent the whole night, while his friends around the lifeless body performed the funeral rites with tears, according to custom. But when morning had come, and the sun was now rising, when everything that seemed necessary for burial had been prepared and he was just about to be buried, suddenly, in the presence of all who were there, he sat up alive; and when they all fled from him, he himself also rose from the place where he had been lying and, going at a rapid run to the church, remained fixed in prayer until the ninth hour of the day, nor would he give any answer to those who questioned him.

But when at last he had raised himself from prayer, looking around he saw the crowd standing by, wondering and asking what was happening concerning him. “God has done this well. O folly of men! O impiety! How hidden are the things that await them after this life!” Meanwhile the parish priest of that church, named Udo, who was archpriest, a learned and religious man and one who feared God, came up and said: “What is it, Adelbert? Were you dead at the end?” “I was dead,” he said; “by the mercy of God I am alive, as I was before; but hereafter I must live otherwise than I did before.” The priest said to him: “Did you see anything of the future life?” “I saw,” he said, “many dreadful things.” And when he was asked to tell what he had seen, he answered: “A law has been imposed on me, without which I can neither say nor do anything.”

But when he had been brought back into the priest’s house, he said to him: “Lord pastor, I have been ordered to disclose to you and tell you everything that I saw and heard. I cannot tell all the people, lest the secret mighty works of God come into derision among those who think according to the flesh.” Therefore the pastor sent a messenger here to the monastery and made everything known to Rupert, our abbot, asking him to deign to come without delay to Mandal and hear the mighty works of God. Taking with him John the prior, he hastened there; and a few of the villagers having been summoned, as many as the pastor there judged suitable, they sat in the presence of the man who had been dead, to hear what he would say.

Opening his mouth, he said: “When I was being pressed toward death by a very grave illness, and was lying thus, with all my senses darkened, it seemed to me as if there occurred a very great earthquake, in which heaven and earth clashed violently together. Suddenly my soul, made outside the body as if from darkness into light, in a way I do not know, could see the whole world all together at one time with the greatest clarity. O good God, how far removed is the opinion of mortals from the truth of that life which follows after the present one. My soul, then placed outside the body, was so bright that it beheld so clearly all things that are in the world: all provinces, cities, castles, villages, peoples, men, kingdoms, lands, mountains, hills, waters without matter, indeed the whole sum of the entire universe; and it understood all things properly and distinctly, all together at one time, so that I seemed never to have understood anything in this world so well.

“And what I am about to say is marvelous above all things. For although I knew that I had neither body nor eyes, nevertheless I saw everything that is in the whole world. I cannot now sufficiently wonder at my own ignorance, by which I no longer understand what I then understood. For the soul is a spirit; all things were done with me in the spirit. Now I cannot understand any of those things otherwise than if they had been shown to me through the senses.”

At this point Abbot Rupert, interrupting his words, said: “We understand that what he says is true, and there is no need to linger here longer, since it is established by reason and faith that none of the things which separated substances either [unclear] or suffer can come to our understanding without the service or comparison of the senses. But go on to say what you began to say.”

He therefore continued, saying: “When I stood thus within myself in the greatest wonder, I suddenly saw, as if from the right and the left, innumerable spirits coming toward me with force. Those who came from the right were good spirits, but those from the left were evil and perverse. The good angels, taking me up, suddenly lifted me upward into the air, as if in a moment, in the blink of an eye. It seemed to me that the whole air was filled with demons, who, like sparks flying thickly in the manner of snow, filled everything. Around me, wherever I looked, there was a dreadful fire and flame, which seemed to torture me so much that no suffering of this world ever seemed more grievous to me. Moreover, those malignant spirits, striving to snatch me away while the angels defended me, set before me the very grievous [unclear] of my sins.

“Therefore I was led to the judgment of almighty God, which I cannot remember without horror. What I saw and heard I cannot tell, nor can any mortal who has not seen those things believe it. There all my sins were bare, manifest, and open to all spirits, both evil and good, whatever I had committed in all my life, even in the smallest thought or deed; and for these they accused me most severely. But the very sins that I committed suddenly came back to my memory; I do not know how. Indeed, they themselves accused me so gravely that the accusation of the demons seemed lighter. It is not possible for me to say how heavily there are weighed and punished the things which I did not think were sins. I will say one thing about myself, by which the rest may be estimated. It happened twenty years ago, as I was going to Kreuznach, that I met a poor man asking, a half-beggar, who, when he had asked me the way, I do not know to what place, I said: ‘This is the direct road to the place—’ [Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheimense.

“...with whom you are going. That man, proceeding [unclear], through ignorance turned aside from the right way onto another road, and wandered for several hours in the wood. How gravely I was accused and afflicted because I had not warned him of this, even though he had not asked me at all, I could not express if I had a hundred tongues.

The demons also charged me with another matter, much more serious: once, when in tithing the crops in my field, as is customary, I had not observed the due order, I had kept back for myself one sheaf owed to the church, putting in its place another which seemed to be somewhat more useful to me. I had confessed that guilt of mine to my priest and been absolved by him, and believed that I was now wholly secure. But alas, how wretchedly my confidence deceived me. For because I had not restored the loss inflicted on the church, which was scarcely four denarii, even though absolved, a sentence of eternal damnation was already about to be pronounced against me, had not the most blessed Mother of God and St. Maximinus, together with the holy angels, interceded for the mercy of the Judge.

Nevertheless I was tortured in the unspeakable burning of flames, while demons rushed upon me with what seemed like sheaves of fragments and mocked me with laughter. It seemed to me that I was tortured in that most penal fire for more than four hundred years, and that all the sheaves of the whole world were thrown upon me; although I later learned that I had scarcely been placed in that torture for the space of one hour.

Then, freed by the mercy of God, I was led by an angel to the places of punishments, where I saw torments so horrible, so monstrous and fearful, that no mortal understanding can grasp them and no tongue of anyone in the world can utter them. No comparison can be made between the punishments of this world and those punishments of eternal damnation which I saw in the underworld. So great a multitude of souls also descended into hell during that interval in which I was out of the body, that previously I would not have believed so many people could have died in a hundred years. There were bishops, abbots, priests, monks, nuns, together with innumerable Christians of both sexes, as many as I would have believed were living in the whole world. Moreover the multitude of unbelieving heathens was infinite; like snow from heaven, so they fell into hell.

O how great is the misery of unhappy souls, how pitiable their groaning and outcry, who never cease from wailing, always crying out: ‘Woe, woe is me; why was I born upon the earth, to come into this place of eternal damnation?’ Meanwhile I saw the soul of a certain bishop dragged by demons into hell, with such exultation on their part that it is difficult to say; and she cried out miserably, wailing without end. So great a multitude of demons had poured around that wretched soul that we would never have believed there were so many demons. Fraudulent tithing, the withholding of rents of churches and monasteries, is punished with penalties: they should rather pay a double tithe than subtract from the ministers of the church the value of one denarius.

I saw monks and nuns there enduring horrible punishments, which it is not possible for me to express, because of even slight disobedience, or displeasure or murmuring against their superiors. Of the innumerable multitude of bishops and prelates of the church who were there, some were more tormented because they had no certainty of their liberation. He said that a greater multitude of simple peasants are damned because they commit fraud against one another, especially against the ministers of the church, in tithes, in crops, in pastures, in fields, and in other things; they do not restore what they have inflicted in great measure, and few of them truly and purely confess their sins with true contrition and a firm purpose of amendment. But he asserted that this is a grave sin of subjects: rashly to judge and rebuke the deeds of prelates or ministers of the church, or to speak against those whom God himself will judge.

But it seemed to me, he said, that in the middle of the earth there was a great and very deep well, full of animals foaming with flames and reaching upward as far as the clouds; led to it by the angel, I was ordered to look inside. O good God, how great a horror seized me; if I live a thousand years, I shall never be able to forget it. When I had looked inside, if I had as many tongues as there are drops of water in the great sea, I could not describe the least punishment of those who were being tormented there. For I saw infinite souls of men being horribly tortured there, and innumerable demons mixed among them, tearing them most cruelly. Nothing was heard there but lamentation and ‘Woe’ without interruption, with such blasphemy against God and against every creature that I cannot remember it without horror. So great was the tumult there, so great the crash, so great the tempest, that if a thousand worlds were struck together at once, they could by no means make so horrible a din. I recognized many there whom they had known together long before, who cried out that they were damned forever. For the well was...

Concerning fraudulent tithes. [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Trithemius

That place, as I had learned from the Angel, was a place of hell: whoever once descends into it will by no means come out for ever.

After this the Angel again led me around through all the places of punishments, in which souls were being tormented, as he said, for their purification. Their multitude was countless, and they were being punished in different places by various kinds of torments, according to the nature of their offenses for which they had not made satisfaction in life. O what misery, what calamity of unhappy souls, whom I saw there suffering the bitterest punishments even for faults which in this life they had neglected to confess and wash away with tears as very slight.

Afterward I came to a certain very deep valley, as it seemed to me, in which there was a certain great and very foul-smelling river. There was a slender bridge, slippery and exceedingly narrow, over the river, stretched from one very high mountain to another at such a height that four towers of the castle in Kreuznach could not, if set beneath it, have touched that bridge. It was so narrow that it could scarcely take two feet, and from either side toward the middle it rose gradually, so that one could climb it only with the greatest difficulty. I saw many souls wishing to cross over this bridge; some of them fell into that dreadful river at the very beginning, others about the middle, and others about the end. It was full of dragons and very great serpents, which stretched their heads upward as if to devour those who fell; and it was a pitiable sight.

Those who fell into the river were submerged: some up to the neck, others up to the knees, and others otherwise, either wholly or in part, according to their deserts. By swimming and repeatedly sinking, they labored with the greatest urgency to reach the bank of the river; some reached it sooner, others later. But as soon as they had reached the bank, far more beautiful than they had been before, they were received by the holy Angels with the greatest rejoicing and were led into the palace of the heavenly kingdom. I saw certain people there, laden with gold or silver, or burdened with any other loads of cares for temporal things, wishing to cross; they fell at the very beginning, and after many labors could scarcely at last reach the bank. For the more often anyone fell from the bridge, the longer he remained in the river. There was no possibility of going back, but only of going forward; all were being driven to plunge into the depth. Some, after being tossed about in that river for many years, labored almost to the failure of their strength.

Meanwhile I saw one naked but very beautiful soul come to the bridge and cross with such speed and assurance that it did not tremble even slightly at anything. I asked the Angel what that soul was, and he said to me: “This is the soul of Theodebert the monk, who, because he possessed nothing besides God, therefore walks securely. For when he was a canon of the church of Mainz, wealthy, young, and powerful, he despised everything for the love of God and became a monk in the monastery of St. Ferrutius, which is called Blidenstadt, where until death he served the Lord in all purity and simplicity of mind and tranquillity of heart. And because for God’s sake he despised everything, God granted him this privilege, that in securely crossing the bridge he should not fall. With the same assurance all those crossed who serve God in a monastery in the true observance of the rule, without occupation in worldly affairs.”

Many other things also I saw and heard there, which I cannot tell on this occasion. Then the Angel took my hand and led me to the places of the blessed spirits, who were exulting in such happiness and joy that no mind can grasp these joys and no human tongue express them. What I saw and heard there I cannot tell; nor, if I went on telling it, would you grasp it. There I saw several whom I had formerly known in the flesh. Among them was my lord Hildebert, formerly pastor in Sponheim and afterward a monk there, who had upon his breast a golden star shining like the sun, because of the light of knowledge and doctrine by which he had recalled many in this life, by teaching and admonishing, to the practice of justice.

What very sweet songs I heard there, what beautiful and delightful things I saw, which have been prepared for those who truly love God, which no one understands unless he receives them. Through all the choirs of Angels I was led in some manner I do not know, and I saw secrets which I neither ought nor can tell. And when I had come to those first, most splendid blessed spirits, they invited me to remain with them. The Angel of the Lord answered them: “He must return to the body. If he has washed away past evils through penitence, if he has guarded himself from sinning thereafter, if he has devoted his zeal to works of justice, he will come to us happier.” [unclear] “preach to those who fear God; and what he has forbidden, you shall cover for ever with silent [unclear].”

When these things had been said, I was immediately led back to my body and ordered to enter. O good God! How [unclear] I dare say: all things that are done or suffered there are spiritual, and greater and more sublime than all mortal things by as much as the spirit is more subtle than the body. But to me, as I was taught in writing by the Angel, they were shown in the likeness of sensible and material things known to me, because I was to return to the body.

[Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheim. 265

I had returned; nor could I, now in the flesh, either have retained those things spiritually as they are or revealed them to you, if I had seen them without an aid introducing a likeness of sense. For it is impossible that mortal man should see those things as they are. Yet now I do not understand in the body the things which, placed outside the body, I rightly understood; rather, I am as one cast after a great light into the densest darkness of ignorance. He said many other terrible things about the punishments of hell and purgatory, and likewise about the joys of the kingdom of heaven, all of which it would be too lengthy to write. At the command of the angel he also disclosed to certain men the hidden sins of some, so that they might do penance, and he foretold some future events which afterwards came to pass. These things which we have noted down Udo the archpriest, pastor in Mandal, wrote for the knowledge of posterity. Moreover Adelbert himself, who had been dead and came back to life, undertook so arduous a course of penance that there was no doubt that he had seen greater torments than he described. For he took up a solitary life in a wood not far from Dalen, where he built a small hut of wood and clay, in which until his death he served the Lord in great abstinence for the seven years by which he survived.

1213.

In this year, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September, Rupert, the fifth abbot of the monastery, died; he was buried before the steps of the presbytery in the choir. He was in every respect a magnificent man, who vigorously maintained the observance of regular discipline both in himself and in others, and converted many to righteousness by word and example. For, as we said above, he was most learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, an outstanding preacher of the divine word, and no less suited to the governance of temporal affairs than of spiritual ones, and most prudent in everything that had to be done. His brothers, who were bound to him by the greatest love, did not bury him without many tears. For he did many good things for this monastery: he enlarged its revenues and acquired various possessions, and, what is greater than all, he preserved inviolate to his death the holiness of the spiritual life.

In this same year St. Mary of Oignies, in the parish of Liège, died, a most holy woman in life and conduct, who shone with many miracles in her lifetime. Her deeds were written in a lucid style by James of Vitry, afterwards bishop of Acre, and lastly cardinal-bishop of Tusculum of the holy Roman Church, who had preached the cross against the infidels in the diocese of Liège.

Concerning Ivan, sixth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, who presided for forty years and three months, and concerning the various deeds of that time.

When the venerable abbot Rupert had died, as we have said, and been buried, the brothers of this monastery of Sponheim, coming together in one place in the year of the Lord 1213, in the first indiction, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, unanimously elected as abbot Ivan, the seventh prior of this place, a man sufficiently fit for the governance of souls. He presided in the abbacy for thirty-nine years and three months, and in the same year was ordained by lord Sifrid, archbishop of Mainz, cardinal and legate of the holy Roman Church, at Mainz in the monastery of St. James on the feast of St. Michael the Archangel. This Ivan was the son of Gotfrid, knight of Sponheim, who in his youth, under abbot Adelger, had been handed over by his parents in this monastery to serve almighty God, when he was ten or eleven years old, namely in the last year of abbot Adelger. As his years increased, wisdom and knowledge of the scriptures increased in him, in which he made such progress that he far surpassed almost all his contemporaries. At length under abbot Rupert he was made prior, and he served in that office for almost five years. When Rupert died, as has been said, he succeeded him in the abbacy; and he was a man sufficiently skilled in handling both spiritual and temporal matters, whose reputation for wisdom was widely spread here and there in the province. After himself he appointed as eighth prior a certain monk named John, who presided in the priorate for only three years, and was deposed for some reason I do not know, as we shall say in its place.

1214.

In his first year abbot Ivan obtained a privilege from lord Sifrid, archbishop of Mainz and legate of the apostolic see, that he might bless vestments and ecclesiastical ornaments for the use of the monastery and of the churches subject to it.

In the same year Marquard, brother of John, count of Sponheim, entered the religious life. He brought many gifts to this monastery, and lived peacefully among the brothers, humbly and religiously, without complaint; but he was lame in both feet, so that he could walk only with difficulty, and for that reason he was not of much use to the world, and therefore he became a monk.

Chronicle of Trithemius

In this same year Brother Conrad of Marburg, of the Order of Preachers, began to preach in Germany by apostolic authority; he continued for nineteen years, and caused many, indeed almost countless, persons to be burned as heretics, and he himself was at last killed.

  1. In this year, which was the second year of lord Iuanus the abbot, many princes, meeting at Aachen, anointed Frederick, king of Sicily, grandson of the emperor Frederick I, as king of the Romans, through Sifrid, archbishop of Mainz and legate of the apostolic see, and placed him on the royal seat, Emperor Otto having been abandoned and left almost by everyone. When the consecration had been completed, John Scholasticus of Xanten at once preached the cross there for the relief of the Holy Land. Hence there were soon signed with the cross Frederick the king himself, Sifrid archbishop of Mainz and legate, also the bishops of Liege, Bamberg, Poitiers, and Strasbourg, likewise the duke of Moravia, the duke of Brabant, Henry duke of Limburg, the duke of [Ancei?], the count palatine of Tubingen, the margrave of Baden, the count of Los, the count of Julich, the count of Sayn, the count of [Monte?], also John count of Sponheim, and many other nobles, clerics and laymen; and a great army of horsemen and foot-soldiers was signed. In the same year, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, around the first hour of the day, there was an earthquake.

  2. In this year Iuanus the abbot, with lord John count of Sponheim and many other pilgrims signed with the cross, crossed the sea and went to the Holy Land. At the same time William count of Holland and George count of Wied also went with them, with a great crowd of those signed with the cross. Andrew king of Hungary also, and Leopold duke of Austria, with bishops and counts and a numerous multitude of those signed with the cross, crossed the sea at the same time and set out for the aid of the Holy Land. Moreover Iuanus committed the governance of the monastery to Riginfrid the prior, whom in the preceding year he had substituted after John had been deposed. He was a prudent and noble man, and administered the office of the priorship vigorously for twenty-two years, and maintained good discipline.

  3. In this year Iuanus the abbot and John count of Sponheim returned from the regions overseas and entered the monastery on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. Lord Iuanus the abbot brought back with him many small portions of relics of the saints, and especially from those places which the Lord Jesus sanctified by his bodily presence, stones and pieces of rock cut out; all these holy things he enclosed in a fabricated [unclear].

In these times the monastery of nuns of the Cistercian order in the valley of Saint Catherine, virgin and martyr, near Mandal, was built and endowed through the munificence of Udo, pastor in Mandal and archpriest, and of his associates; he, warned by the vision of the aforesaid deceased [unclear], gave to that place everything he was able to have. A copy of this foundation follows, and is as follows.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. Sifrid, by the grace of God archbishop of the see of Mainz: by the tenor of the present document let it be known to all the faithful of Christ that the beloved sons Gosfrid, provost of Creutzenacht, Udo archpriest of Mannendal, Frederick dean of Hilbersheim, and their fellow brethren, having in their hearts zeal for God, brought their properties together into one, and from them founded the church of Saint Catherine of the Cistercian order. Therefore, arranging that these goods be stripped of every burden of administrators and of service by any [unclear] whatsoever, the advocates, if they held any right in them, renounced their right. Since, however, we are bound to strengthen this donation of property by our authority, so that it may be lawful for those dwelling there justly and lawfully to possess both this property and the things belonging to it, we confirm it by the authority with which we are invested, and we decree that the order of monastic religion, according to the rule of the blessed father Benedict and the institution of the Cistercian brethren, shall always be observed inviolably by those dwelling there. We also firmly decree and establish this for them: that what is known to have been granted by lord Pope Alexander to all of their religious profession, and by several pontiffs of the Roman see, namely that from newly broken lands, enclosed places brought under cultivation by their own labor and at their own expense, and also from gardens and from the nourishment of their animals, they shall pay no tithes to anyone; but they shall enjoy this indulgence granted to them. We have also ordained that the aforesaid overseers of the monastery, in selling or buying the goods of the church, or in admitting sisters or lay converts, shall do nothing without the consent of the abbess and convent; and that whatever is brought or sent to the aforesaid church from remote or neighboring parts shall be kept in a place appointed for this, under the custody of the abbess, the provost, and the servants. The household utensils with their appurtenances, namely wool and dairy produce, shall be kept under the custody of the ladies. The abbess and convent shall arrange nothing in the aforesaid matters without the counsel of the provost; the provost, however, shall dispose of nothing without them. But when the abbess or the provost dies, by no cunning of stealth or by violence shall an abbess [Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheimense.

No abbess or provost shall be appointed except the woman or man whom the convent by common consent, or the sounder part of the council, according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, shall have elected. We also decree that an abbot shall be chosen by the same convent only from their order, for preserving the rigor of the order, or for deciding questions for which the convent shall seem to him insufficient; and he, according to the mandate of our institution, ought not to oppose the election made of him. The lay brothers shall promise obedience to the provost, and the sisters to the abbess, and shall render it according to the Rule of blessed Benedict without murmuring. We likewise command that lay brothers departing from the aforesaid place without due permission shall not be received in any places.

Whoever therefore, with any rash boldness, which God forbid, shall presume to act against this page of our constitution, and shall endeavor to break or disturb the ordinance noted above, secured and confirmed by the impression of our seal, let them recognize that they will incur, unless they make answer, the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, condemned by him with anathema, by the authority of lord Pope Honorius and our own. These things were done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1219, in the eighth indiction, when lord Honorius III presided over the apostolic see, and lord Frederick II, most glorious king of the Romans, ever Augustus, and king of Sicily, was reigning; under these witnesses: Henry, major provost; Poppo, dean; Gotfrid, custodian; Christian, cantor; Henry, provost of Burg; Albert of Cogelenberg; Frederick of Firnenberg, canons of the major church of Mainz; Luano of Sponheim; Hartvernus of Mount St. Disibod, abbots; Henry, provost of Struvabenheim; Philip of Oterburg, abbots; Mechthild, son of the count of Sponheim, with his brothers; Godebold of Wierbach and Micho his brother; Wulfram of Stein; Marquard and Barthold of Strumberg, knights; and very many others, both clerics and laymen, worthy of trust; also Diepold of Eberbach, Eastachius of Hennenrode, Philip of Oterburg, abbots; Mechthild, abbess of the same place, in the 121st year from the beginning of the Cistercian order, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the twentieth year from the beginning of the house in the valley, was absolved from excommunication and interdict.

In the same year also King Frederick, having held an assembly at Frankfurt, set out for Rome, and was invested as emperor by Pope Honorius III.

1231.

In this year Count Silvester Conrad, commonly Wiligraf of Dhaun, was excommunicated by Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, and his land was placed under interdict, on account of the advocacy in Heimbach, which he had violently invaded against the will of Henry, major provost, and the canons of the church of Mainz. At last, agreement having been made between them, and one hundred marks having been received from the canon, the count resigned the advocacy of the church, and was absolved from the sentence of excommunication and interdict.

In the same year Worms was burned on the day of St. Margaret the Virgin, and many houses by a certain knight of Beckelnheim, who was called Henry Spon, which Crafftobas III afterward alienated from the monastery, redeemable by the procurator for Rhenish florins, as will be said in its place.

In the same year Abbot John, in the eighth year of his rule, bought a manor for twenty-five marks of silver from [unclear]; especially around the market and in the adjoining streets they were burned. In those days Bishop Henry, son of the count of Saarbruecken, was there. In the same year also the Friars Minor entered Worms and built a monastery.

1232.

In this year, which was the ninth of Abbot John, Conrad, bishop of Speyer, hearing that the nuns of our order in the monastery called Haulen near the monastery of Limburg in his diocese had slipped too far from the path of regular discipline, and had failed no less in temporal and necessary goods than in spiritual conduct, to such an extent that they were compelled to relieve their poverty by shameful traffic, decreed with the consent of Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, that henceforth no one should be admitted to the order there; and he incorporated that monastery, with all its revenues, into the monastery of Limburg, so that, when all the nuns of that place had died, the abbot of Limburg should have divine services celebrated there by his monks.

1234.

In the eleventh year of John there were still only four nuns, sisters, in our enclosure. Our nuns [unclear] passed over to the monastery of St. Rupert. All the others having died in the course of time, and no one being admitted any longer, according to what Abbot Rupert had decreed almost eighteen years before, as was said above. Hence, with the license and authority of John the abbot, the four who remained were transferred to the monastery of St. Rupert near Bingen, with all their possessions, and there were received into the convent. Their names are these: Agatha, Radegundis, Helwigis, and Margaret. And thus the place of our nuns—

Chronicle of Trithemius

began to lie vacant, and remains vacant down to the present day, containing nothing of its former dwelling or building except only the name by which it is called Clausa, as it was in antiquity. Hence the nuns of the aforesaid monastery of St. Rupert, made bolder by such a contrivance or occasion, obtained from Sifrid, archbishop of Mainz, that their aforesaid monastery should be entrusted for all future times to the abbot of this monastery, as it had been entrusted from the beginning of the foundation of the abbey of St. Disibod. But because religious discipline had grown exceedingly lukewarm in that monastery of Disibod, they could easily obtain from the archbishop what they asked for the salvation of souls. For in this our monastery at that time there was still a praiseworthy observance of discipline. Therefore lord Sifrid, the archbishop, entrusted the aforesaid monastery of the nuns of the monastery of St. Rupert to Iuano, abbot of this monastery of Sponheim; and it remained so entrusted for many years, until at last regular discipline in both places almost wholly perished, and the nuns, seeking liberty, paid no attention thereafter.

1225.

Sifrid the archbishop dies, etc. [unclear] Sifrid [unclear]. Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, is killed by his nephew.

Sifrid the third succeeded and presided for twenty-four years, a man of great deeds and of such authority and constancy that he fearlessly excommunicated and opposed Emperor Frederick, by command of the lord pope.

In the same year, on the eighth ides of November, Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, when on the previous day he had dedicated a church in a certain village, was cruelly killed as the day was already drawing toward evening by Frederick, count of Eisenberg, his brother's son, pierced through with thirty-seven wounds or blows because of [unclear]. Buried in the church of Cologne, he began to shine with countless miracles. But Frederick the count, the impious parricide, with his accomplices numbering twenty-five, soon betook himself to the castle of Eisenberg; but, not trusting the fortification, he fled from there and, lying hidden as an exile for a whole year, excommunicated by Conrad, bishop of Porto and legate of the apostolic see, at last, when the year had passed, was found and captured by a certain knight. He was sold for one hundred and two thousand marks to Henry, the archbishop who had succeeded Engelbert; bound, he was led outside the walls of Cologne on the eighteenth calends of December and broken on the wheel, while his mother stood by beneath the wheel, crying: “Alas for me, these are my entrails to be devoured by crows, just as I saw in a dream when I was still carrying you, my son, in the womb.”

But when Frederick had thus been broken on the wheel, the signs at Engelbert's tomb soon ceased to occur.

1226.

John, a monk of this monastery, who had been prior before Reginfrid, a shrewd, religious, and very devout man, after the death of Peter, provost of St. Rupert's at Bingen, was appointed provost there by Abbot Iuano. He always kept the observance of regular discipline inviolate, both in himself and in others, to the utmost of his ability.

In these times Henry, bishop of Worms, son of the count of Saarbrücken, founded a monastery of nuns at Kirschgarten, outside the walls of the city of Worms, and placed there nuns of the Cistercian order, who inhabited that place for almost [unclear] years under the same religious rule, until the times of Bishop Frederick, who in the year 1443, after the nuns had been expelled, introduced reformed canons regular of good observance. The aforesaid Bishop Henry was in dispute with the citizens of Worms over ecclesiastical liberty. When they would not obey his command, he placed them under interdict. When he made no progress by this, he ordered all the clergy to depart except the parish priests, to whom the care of souls had been entrusted; nevertheless they did not dare to give the body of Christ to the sick unless they promised that they would obey the bishop if they recovered, nor were the bodies of the dead permitted to be buried in holy places. And when these things had lasted for the space of a year, certain of the citizens, affected by weariness of them, turned to the bishop's side and stirred up partisanship in the city. Hence the council, compelled by necessity lest it suffer worse things, entered into peace and concord with the bishop, and they were absolved.

1227.

In this year, which was the fourteenth of Abbot Iuano, Marquard, a monk of this monastery, son of the count of Sponheim, died in the thirteenth year of his conversion, a good man of singular devotion.

In the same year Pope Gregory IX excommunicated Frederick the second, emperor, because, contrary to his promise, he neglected to cross over for the recovery of the Holy Land; and the whole army gathered for this expedition from various parts of Europe was dispersed, whence many evils followed.

Also in the same year, on the third ides of September, Louis the Pious, the fifth landgrave of the Thuringians, the first margrave of Meissen, husband of St. Elizabeth, died in Sicily, in a certain city called Otranto. His bones were brought back to Thuringia and buried in the monastery of Reinhardsbrunn of our order.

1228. [Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheim.

1228.

In this year Ottokar and Wenceslaus, illustrious kings of the Bohemians, gave such a privilege to the church of Mainz: that the archbishop of Mainz, and no one else, must anoint and crown as kings both them and their successors, as is clear in these letters:

In the name of the Lord, Amen. Ottokar and Wenceslaus, illustrious kings, to all the faithful of Christ who shall look upon the present writing, perpetual salvation. We acknowledge and publicly declare that we and all our successors are bound forever to receive royal consecration and the placing of the diadem from the archbishop of the most holy see of Mainz, the metropolitan of our land. But if that archbishop, when requested, should withdraw himself by impulse of his own mind, let him commit his office for carrying this out to another bishop whom we or our successors shall request. And so that this may remain valid and unshaken, we have confirmed this page, with the consent of the venerable bishops of Prague and Olomouc, by the attachment of our seals. Given at Prague in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1228, in the first indiction.

In the same year the emperor Frederick crossed the sea, recovered Jerusalem, together with part of the Holy Land, and made truces there with the Saracens for a fixed time.

1219.

In the sixteenth year of Abbot John, the village called Wimesheim was burned by an accidental fire, almost wholly consumed, and in that fire three infant boys perished by a like misfortune, namely on 21 August; many were impoverished even to beggary.

In the same year the emperor Frederick returned from the lands beyond the sea and, finding his land in Italy harried by troubles through the pope, gravely avenged all the injuries he had suffered.

1230.

In this year a grave controversy and dissension arose among the citizens and the council of the town of Bingen, which went so far that two members of the council were publicly slain in the marketplace through a sedition of the common people; some were wounded; the rest, scarcely escaping by flight, took care to save themselves. But not long afterward a severe vengeance followed against the authors of the sedition. For some were beheaded, others mutilated in their limbs, and the rest, proscribed beyond the borders of the fatherland, endured perpetual exile.

Also in the same year the emperor was absolved by the pope, through the mediation of Leopold, duke of Austria, who, after a treaty of peace had been completed between the pope and the emperor at San Germano in Campania, died; his entrails and flesh were buried in the chapter house of the monastery of our most holy father Benedict on Monte Cassino, while his bones were carried back to Austria.

Also in the same year dissension arose between the archbishop of Cologne and the duke of Limburg over the advocacy of the monastery of Siegburg of our order, in the same said diocese of Cologne.

1231.

In the eighteenth year of our abbot John, Saint Elizabeth died, daughter of the former king of Hungary, widow left by Louis the Pious, fifth landgrave of Thuringia, a woman of many virtues and of most holy conduct, buried at Marburg, which is a town of Hesse; she at once began to shine with countless miracles.

In the same year, in the month of July, in the city of Worms, a fire that arose by chance in the house of Herbord the knight consumed a great part of the city together with the church of Saint Paul.

Also in the same year Louis, duke of Bavaria, when he had gone to the Holy Land with a great army, was killed on his return at Kelheim with a knife by a certain Saracen, a messenger of the Old Man of the Mountains, in the presence of his household, the emperor Frederick having procured this crime, as was afterward confessed. The Saracen himself, however, was immediately cut to pieces by the duke’s attendants. The duke’s body, attended with great honor, was buried in the monastery of Scheyern in Bavaria. His son Otto succeeded him in the duchy; he took as wife Gertrude, the only daughter of Henry, count palatine of the Rhine, who dwelt at Heidelberg, with whom he obtained that whole dominion; thus the duchy of Bavaria and the county palatine were joined into one. That Otto begot from Gertrude, his aforesaid wife, two sons, Henry and Louis, of whom we shall speak in their proper place.

This duke Otto gave the town of Braubach, with the adjacent castle and all its appurtenances, in fief to the count of Katzenelnbogen; the landgrave of Hesse possesses it today, none of those counts now living.

In the same year Ulrich, abbot of Limburg of our order, in the diocese of Speyer, with the consent of his convent, gave to the chapter of the church of Mainz the pastoral church in Heldenberg, with its tithes and revenues, for the increase of the prebends of the church of Mainz, as is clear from their letters, as follows.

The kings of Bohemia must be anointed and crowned by the archbishop of Mainz alone.

Chronicle of Trithemius

Copy of the donation.

In the name of the Lord, Amen. Ulrich the prior, with the whole convent of Limburg, sends greeting in the Savior of all to all who shall see this writing. Lest those things which are done in time should slip away and perish with time, salutary provision has been made for human frailty that all acts be strengthened by the testimony of writing. Therefore we wish it to be made known to all the faithful of the present age and the future that, after mature deliberation had first been held, by unanimous common consent, freely and absolutely, we have handed over to the greater church of Mainz, to be possessed perpetually, the church in Heldenberg, the right of patronage of which is known to belong to us; namely on this condition, that when the pastor who now is there shall resign or die, whomsoever the chapter of Mainz shall choose for the governance of the said church, he shall be presented, with letters of that chapter, to the abbot, or to the prior if there is no abbot; and he, as a sign of recognition of the benefice received from the church of Limburg, shall request from him a [unclear], and shall obtain it without any difficulty; namely so that the same cleric shall be presented with letters of the abbot or prior to the archdeacon, that he may receive from him the care of souls. The same shall be observed in the case of others substituted thereafter. But if either the abbot or the prior, which however be far from the case, should wish on some pretext to refuse, no prejudice shall thereby be generated either to the person substituted or to the chapter of Mainz itself. And so, after a suitable and sufficient stipend has been assigned to that priest, from which he may now be able to answer to the diocesan as well as to the archdeacon of the place concerning their rights, and nevertheless the parish priest himself be suitably maintained, whatever remains from the revenues which the pastors hitherto have been accustomed only to receive, shall go to the improvement of the prebends of the chapter of Mainz, saving in all things the right of the church of Limburg. Furthermore, so that provision might be salutarily made by a firmer bond of charity for the entry of the church of Mainz into the church of Limburg, it has been decreed that, whenever one of our brothers, having entered the way of all flesh, is announced to the church of Mainz, the memory of the deceased shall be performed in vigils and obsequies as for one of themselves. And we likewise, in the customary manner, shall offer prayers and hosts for their deceased brothers. But this must not be passed over: that in all affairs of our church the church of Mainz shall faithfully, as in its own affairs, bring aid and counsel, as often as it can and ought, amicably and kindly. These things were enacted in the year of grace 1231, in the month of October, in the fourth indiction.

Conrad, bishop of the church of Speyer, also together with his chapter gave consent to the aforesaid donation of the abbot of Limburg, at the instance of the provost, the dean, and the whole chapter of Mainz, declaring that it had been made not to the loss of the monastery of Limburg, but rather to its advantage and honor, as appears in the letters made thereupon by him, which we have judged it superfluous to insert into this history of ours. Lord Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, also confirmed by letters that same donation made to his chapter.

1232.
