Abbot John, in the nineteenth year of his rule, had a grave dissension and dispute with the villagers of the village of Sponheim, on account of the woods, pastures, and common land beside the vegetable garden of Lady Richardis, countess of Sponheim, which she had donated to this monastery at its first foundation. Hence, after many contentions, an agreement was at last made between them by Lord John, count of Sponheim, in this manner: first, the woods of the forest were divided and distinguished by signs set between them, so that the abbot separately and also the villagers separately should henceforth possess their woods in peace, and neither party should henceforth presume in any way to inflict damage on the other in the woods or elsewhere, or to hinder the other. The pastures, however, throughout the whole march must be common both to the abbot and to the villagers, except for certain districts of the abbot in which the villagers are to have no power of pasturing. The common land must be common, and remain common in every form for the monastery, the villagers, those of Dal, and the other poor of the [unclear], just as nearly eighty years before it is known to have been established by Count Megenhard and by his son Craftho, the second abbot of this monastery; nor shall anyone be allowed to sell anything from it, neither from its land, since it belongs to the monastery, nor from the usufruct, which the count, the abbot, and the county granted to the poor villagers.

In this year Conrad, landgrave of the Thuringians, waging unjust war on account of a certain [unclear] against Lord Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, caused him much damage. For he took the town of Fritzlar and almost destroyed it utterly, along with certain others. At last agreement was made between them in this manner, as follows:

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Concerning the destruction of Fritzlar, Witzenhausen, the towns, and the other damages which Lord Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, and Lord Conrad the Younger, landgrave, felt on both sides when they had war between them, such a settlement intervened: the old settlement, as it was ordained by Lord Siegfried, formerly archbishop, and Lord Ludwig, of pious memory, formerly landgrave, shall be kept unshaken in every way forever. Likewise the archbishop granted the town in Wolfheim as a fief to the aforementioned Conrad the landgrave, and grants it to his legitimate heirs, even to daughters, if there are no sons to succeed after his death by hereditary right. And if the same Conrad should ask in his lifetime that he grant the same town to his brother or to his brother’s son, this shall in no way be denied him.

[Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheim.

This agreement contains many other articles also concerning the law of the parties alleged, which there is no need to insert now. At this agreement, made between the aforesaid lords Sifrid, archbishop of Mainz, and Conrad the Landgrave, there was present Master Conrad of Marburg, of the Order of Preachers, a man of great learning and authority in the Sacred Scriptures, who had been appointed general inquisitor of heretical depravity by the holy Apostolic See. In this same year, on the third day before the Nones of May, he caused four heretics in the city of Erfurt, condemned to the fire, to be burned. Many, almost innumerable, throughout nearly all Germany, who had long lain hidden as heretics, after being brought to light and examined, he condemned, and handed over to the secular court to be burned.

There are those who say that he was too ready and prompt in condemning simple people, to such an extent that he caused many innocent persons to be killed; for as soon as anyone had been denounced before him, without the cause of the denunciation or the merits of the accuser having been examined, he would pronounce sentence, crying: “Take away, take away the impious heretic, to be burned with fire.” Hence in the following year, which was that of the Lord’s incarnation 1233, it happened that the Count of Sayn was falsely accused before him of heresy. For his excuse or purgation Henry, son of the emperor Frederick II, held an assembly of many princes, bishops, and abbots at Mainz; all of them, with one voice, bore united testimony to the count’s Catholic faith, since, a few years before, not without great loss of his men and goods, he had crossed the sea in aid of the Lord’s sepulchre. He had always honored the Church of God and its ministers. Finally the count himself, standing before all, with tears publicly proclaimed his innocence, gravely injured in so unjust a manner.

For this reason brother Conrad became hateful to all, noble and ignoble alike, since on account of true and fabricated heresies he had caused many nobles and commoners, clerics, monks, nuns, enclosed women, townsmen, and peasants, in various provinces of Germany, to be condemned by an excessively hasty sentence, if it is right to say so, to the punishment of fire, and cruelly killed. For on the same day on which anyone was accused, whether justly or unjustly, with no refuge afforded him by any appeal, any defense or excuse, or even, what was impious, any recantation, he was condemned and thrown into cruel flames, so much so that he seemed to rejoice more in the multitude of the condemned than of the innocent. Therefore, seeing that he could not prevail against the Count of Sayn, confounded and exposed to the hatred of many, he resolved to go from Mainz toward Marburg, and [unclear] safe-conduct both from the king and from the archbishop [unclear].

In the same year the Sultan of Babylon sent to the emperor a tent, constructed with wondrous skill, in which images of the Sun and Moon, moved artificially, [showed] their course with certain proper and due [unclear]. He was killed by certain nobles; and when he had sought pardon and mercy with tears and sighs, he was not heard. He was buried beside St. Elizabeth.

In the same year also the emperor Frederick II took away from the same monastery the principality of a monastery of our order not far from Heidelberg, which is called Lorsch, with all its honor, vassals, ministeriales, [unclear], towns, revenues, rights, and appurtenances, which the abbot of that same monastery had always possessed up to this time, and gave it to Sifrid, archbishop of Mainz, and to his church, as is clear from the letters that follow:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity: Frederick II, by divine favoring clemency Emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus, king of Jerusalem and Sicily. The dignity of the Roman prince is exalted, and the narrow bounds of the empire are adorned, when he restores and preserves by suitable provision the principalities in which the empire, established in its dignity, flourishes, and chooses and appoints over them for their restoration and preservation those persons who, both by the prerogative of the souls committed to them and by the merit of their own dignities, are judged sufficient and acceptable for this. We wish it to be known to all the faithful of the empire, both present and future, that we, considering the weak condition of the church of Lorsch, falling in the course of time from the honor and name of a principality, so that it seems to fail no less the empire than itself; considering moreover that through our beloved prince Sifrid, venerable archbishop of Mainz, whose favor and services daily rendered to the empire present themselves to our sight with much gratitude, not through the same see of Mainz, always effective in obedience to the empire and to our honors, the service owed to the empire by that principality, which because of the weakness of that same church has hitherto been withdrawn from us, can be rendered in full: with our beloved son Henry, illustrious king of the Romans, ever Augustus, standing near us and wishing to provide for these matters, together with the deliberation and counsel of the princes, from our inborn prudence, by the grace of majesty, [we grant] that same principality of the church of Lorsch, with all honor, vassals, ministeriales,” The Chronicle of Trithemius

... those marked [with the cross], who for their transgressions and for withholding tithes had been excommunicated for many years, had shown themselves contemptuous of the ecclesiastical keys; and, often fighting with bishops, counts, and other nobles, they were frequently victors and rarely defeated. But when an army of crusaders came against them, they were defeated, and more than two thousand were killed; the rest fled to the neighboring Frisians.

The Count of Holland is killed. Worms is burned. Henry, bishop of Worms, is dead; Landolf succeeded him. Nonnenmünster is reformed. King Henry opposes his father Frederick and comes to a bad end.

In the same year the Count of Holland was killed in a certain tournament at Corbie in the diocese of Amiens. Also in the same year, on the night of 10 Kalends of July, the city of Worms was set on fire, and a great part of it was burned, not without very great loss to many. In the same year Henry of Saarbrücken, bishop [unclear], died. He expelled the nuns of our order from the monastery in the suburb of the city of Worms, which in the common tongue is called Nonnenmünster, because of their disorderly life, and introduced nuns of the Cistercian order there, who inhabit that place down to the present. Also in the same year King Henry held an assembly of certain princes at Boppard, where he received counsel from certain wicked men that he should oppose his father Frederick, and this he did. For from that time he began to solicit everyone he could, by threats, entreaty, and payment, to stand with him against his father; and he found not a few.

MCCXXXV. In the twenty-second year of Abbot John, Emperor Frederick, returning from Italy into Germany with many treasures, held a council at Worms on 6 Nones of July, where he received his son Henry back into favor. But when Henry did not keep his promises and occupied the castle of Trifels against his will, he was seized by order of his father and first [kept] in a certain very strong house [unclear] because of their disorderly life expelled, and they introduced nuns of the Cistercian order there, which he did. Then at last, after being sent to Alzey and finally to Sicily, he was held prisoner until death, and in the fifth year of his exile and captivity he died there in custody.

In this year, which was the twenty-third of Abbot John, in the village of Gebrad a male child was born with two heads, very monstrous; he lived six months and nine days. His two heads were joined opposite each other at the back, but there was one body, two confused bellies, and lower down they were wonderfully reduced into one; two feet.

In the same year Saint Elizabeth of Marburg was canonized by Pope Gregory. Emperor Frederick was present at Marburg with an innumerable multitude of people when her most holy body was raised from the tomb; he himself was the first to lift the stone from her sarcophagus, and he gave a golden crown to her holy head. Present there were the apostolic commissioners: Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz; Theodoric, archbishop of Trier; and the bishop of Hildesheim, with many other bishops and princes. There are those who write that more than twelve hundred thousand people assembled there at that time. These things were done in the ninth year from the death of Saint Elizabeth, on the day of Philip and James, where among other signs oil flowed from her sacred body.

MCCXXXVII. In the twenty-fourth year of Abbot John, the grange of our monastery situated on the mountain near Dalen, which was called Gauwershausen, with all the surrounding buildings, [unclear] or six, was burned, and afterward was not restored. For on that very mountain, which is called Mount Gauia, commonly Gauwersberg, there was once a small village, which gradually declined and in this year was entirely consumed and so desolated that today no trace of it appears in the place.

In the same year Conrad of Than, bishop of Speyer, died; Conrad of Eberstein succeeded him on the feast of Saint Agnes the Virgin, and he presided for eight years.

MCCXXXIX. In this year, which was the twenty-fifth of Abbot John, Reginfrid, the ninth prior of this monastery, died on the day of Saint Cecilia, virgin and martyr, a good and upright man; after him no one like him in zeal and fervor for regular observance and the keeping of monastic discipline arose in this monastery for many years. When he had died, Abbot John, with the counsel of his brethren, appointed as the tenth prior of this place John, a venerable old man, who held his office for only one year and six days, and died. In the same year the greater church of Mainz was consecrated by Siegfried the archbishop. MCCXL.

272 The Chronicle of Trithemius

with its castles, towns, revenues, rights, and appurtenances, as it is known to belong to us and the Empire, we have, by imperial authority, given and granted in perpetuity to the same church of Mainz, to the said archbishop of Mainz and to his successors; and we have solemnly invested our named prince, the venerable archbishop of Mainz, in the presence of the princes, so that the same church of Mainz, the same archbishop of Mainz, and his successors may henceforth hold and possess that principality, and may foster and preserve it for our honor and that of the Empire, saving the right which shall be owed from it to the Empire. By the authority of the present privilege we command that no prince, duke, margrave, count, sheriff, advocate, ministerial, no person high or low, ecclesiastical or secular, shall presume with rash daring to go against the page of this present gift and grant of ours. Whoever presumes to do this, know that, besides our indignation, to which he shall know himself subject, he will pay, in punishment of his rashness, one hundred pounds of pure gold, of which one half shall be paid to our court and the rest to the party that has suffered injury.

Therefore, for the stable memory and firmness of this gift and grant of ours, we have caused the present privilege to be made, impressed below with the golden seal of our majesty [unclear]. The witnesses of this matter are B., patriarch of Aquileia, and others. The sign of the lord Frederick II, by the grace of God most unconquered emperor of the Romans, ever august, king of Jerusalem and Sicily. I, Sifridus, bishop of Regensburg, chancellor of the imperial court, in place of the aforesaid Sifrid, archbishop of Mainz, archchancellor in Germany, have reviewed it. These things were enacted in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1232, in the month of April, in the fifth indiction, while our lord Frederick II, by the grace of God most unconquered emperor of the Romans, ever august, most glorious king of Jerusalem and Sicily, was ruling, in the twelfth year of his empire, the seventh of his kingdom of Jerusalem, and the thirty-fourth of his kingdom of Sicily, happily. Amen. Given at Aquileia.

This donation or alienation of the principality from the monastery of Lorsch, then still of our order, made by the emperor Frederick, King Henry his son confirmed thus:

Henry, king of the Romans, by the grace of God ever august, to all the faithful of the empire who shall see this page, his grace and every good. It redounds to royal munificence unto glory if [unclear] with worthy honors, if with increased augmentations of property [unclear] the attendants at its side and those privy to its secrets. For from this devotion springs up in subjects, and the number is increased among the devoted, while munificence multiplies by example whatever it could have [unclear] through grace. Hence it is that we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present as well as future, that, when our beloved Sifridus, archbishop of Mainz, appeared in our presence, he earnestly petitioned our highness that the gift and grant of the principality of the church of Lorsch, with every honor, vassals, ministerials, castles, towns, [unclear], made to him and to the church of Mainz by our lord emperor Frederick, ever august, king of Jerusalem and Sicily, with us present and consenting, we ought to hold and preserve as renewed inviolably. We therefore, considering the gracious services which the said church of Mainz is known to have rendered to us and to our forebears, and also considering that the services owed to the Empire, which through the weakness of the aforesaid monastery have hitherto been withheld from it, can suitably be rendered by the said archbishop and his successors, holding the aforesaid grant and gift ratified as made with our assent, have decreed by the edict of the present royal page that no person, high or low, ecclesiastical or secular, shall presume with rash daring to oppose it. But if anyone attempts this, besides the indignation which he thereby incurs, let him know that he will pay fifty pounds of gold, of which we wish one half to be assigned to our court and the other to the party that has suffered injury. The witnesses of this confirmation of ours are B., patriarch of Aquileia. Given at [Chindacum?], in the year of the Lord 1232, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the fifth indiction.

When this imperial gift, together with the royal confirmation, of the principality of the aforesaid monastery of Lorsch had been received, Sifridus, archbishop of Mainz, in order to establish that same principality for himself and his successors with perpetual firmness, induced the monks of that monastery by crafty persuasion, making great promises, to direct letters to the supreme pontiff Gregory IX and to request that their monastery be united with the church of Mainz. Therefore the monks, having no suspicion of their own expulsion, and firmly hoping that they, together with their monastery, would very soon be restored by the archbishop to their former state, wrote thus:

To the most holy father and lord in Christ, lord Gregory, supreme pontiff of the sacrosanct Church, the dean with the devout college of brethren, though small, of the ministerials of the church of Lorsch: continual prayers to Christ, with filial subjection. We have thought it right to report to the grace of your apostolate that, since, at the mandated examination of judges delegated by the Apostolic See, lord Conrad, formerly our abbot, was by sentence deposed on account of the wasting of our property and the other enormities which he had committed, we, perceiving that the reformation of our said church could not consist in anything else, as indeed it cannot, [unclear] our aforesaid judges concerning beneficed counsel and consent Chronicle of Trithemius

... obtained Landshut together with Lower Bavaria. This Louis, Count Palatine, first took as wife Mary, daughter of the Duke of Brabant; having suspected her of adultery, he later had her beheaded at Werde in Swabia, and had no children by her. In satisfaction for this crime he afterwards founded the monastery of Fürstenfeld, in which he too was buried, as we shall say later in its proper place.

In the same year Conrad, bishop of Speyer, died. Henry, count of Leiningen, chancellor of the imperial court, succeeded him on the Friday before the feast of All Saints and presided for twenty-seven years. This Henry, elected and not yet confirmed, together with his brother, the count of Leiningen, invaded and took by armed force a certain castle in [unclear], called Starckenberg, in the diocese of Worms, which belonged to the principality of the monastery of Lorsch. Therefore the archbishop of Mainz, angered, obtained from the pope judges who would compel them to restitution.

1246.

In the thirty-third year of John our abbot, Henry the Landgrave, elected king of the Romans by the princes after Frederick had been deposed, as was said a little above, fought with Conrad, the emperor's son, near Frankfurt, defeated him, and compelled him to flee into Italy.

In the same year Landolf, bishop of Worms, died, and was buried in the monastery of Nonnenmünster, which he had taken away from our order. Cuno, dean of Mainz, succeeded him; when he died within three weeks, Richard of Trier was substituted and presided for about [unclear] years.

In this year, which was the thirty-fourth of John the abbot, Louis, Count Palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, of whom mention was made above, for the defense of Bavaria against the bishop of Augsburg [unclear] a castle which he had taken away from our order [unclear]. Cuno, dean of Mainz, succeeded him; when he died within three weeks, Richard of Trier was substituted and presided for thirty years.

1247.

In the same year the magistracy of Kreuznach was in great dissension with the citizens, because certain liberties and privileges of the city were not being observed for the poor, as it seemed to many at that time; but afterwards concord was made among them.

1248.

This year, which was the thirty-fifth of John the abbot, Conrad, bishop of Cologne, a wealthy and high-spirited man, began to build that great and distinguished church of Cologne, laying the first stone on the vigil of blessed Mary ever virgin. Although that work daily increases through the labor of craftsmen, and has thus now been continued without interruption for 453 years, nevertheless scarcely half of the planned building is now seen to have been completed.

The same Conrad the archbishop built anew from the foundations the church of St. Clement, pope and martyr, which had collapsed and which St. Cunibert, archbishop of Cologne, had once founded. Having lost its former name of Clement, it is today called by the name of St. Cunibert. He built many other things and conferred much upon the Church.

In the same year a very great famine oppressed all Germany and killed many.

1249.

In the thirty-seventh year of John the abbot, Siegfried, archbishop of Mainz, died on the seventh Ides of March; Christian, the second of this name, succeeded him, and presided over the church of Mainz for eleven years, a good man indeed and a lover of the clergy.

In the same year Henry, Landgrave of Thuringia, died; a few years earlier he had been elected king of the Romans, although not all the princes consented to him, nor did he attain the imperial crown. When he died, William, duke or count of Holland, was elected king of the Romans, while Emperor Frederick was still alive with his son Conrad; but he did not attain the crown of the Empire, nor did he live long. Nevertheless he had fairly great obedience, both here and in the lower regions.

1250.

This year, which was the thirty-seventh of John the abbot, Emperor Frederick II died at Tarentum, in the fifty-eighth year of his age.

In the same year Hermann, bishop of Würzburg, died; Iring of Reinstein succeeded him.

In the same year also the winter was extremely harsh and very long-lasting, with snow and ice exceedingly abundant; when these at last melted together into one, a very great flooding of waters followed, so great that it overthrew many buildings round about.

1350 Sponheimense.

... with the consent of the princes who were then governing the Empire, we sought from the church of Mainz that same church of ours as one, especially since our church, without the help of the church of Mainz, which until now has fostered us, could not in any way rise again; since also the said church has reformed our church in many respects, prudently redeeming the castle of that church from the hand of stronger men, in which castle a large part of our church consists; furthermore, by its power it has recovered many other possessions of the same church of ours. Since therefore, pious and merciful father, it is manifest that this was done by the deliberation and providence of prudent men, prostrate at the feet of your holiness we humbly and earnestly beseech you that, regarding our necessity [unclear], and holding our deed and our union with the church of Mainz as valid, you would deign to confirm it by the authority and mercy of the Apostolic See, etc.

When Pope Gregory had received these letters, he wrote back to Sifrid, archbishop of Mainz, for this cause as follows.

Copy of the papal letters to the archbishop of Mainz. The first bull.

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother, the archbishop of Mainz, greeting and apostolic blessing. From the representations made to us by our beloved sons, the dean and convent of the church and monastery of Lorsch, it has become known that, when the abbot of Werden [unclear] and his colleague, performing the office of visitation for the same monastery by apostolic mandate, had removed its abbot from its governance, they committed to you, in whose diocese it lies, the charge, defense, and reform of it, since it had fallen so far in spiritual and temporal matters that it was believed it could scarcely rise again except through your help. You, indeed, have devoted such solicitude to its reform that, besides other gracious advantages which it received through your diligence, you bought back a certain castle for no small sum of money. Therefore, commending your prudence in this matter to the Lord, by apostolic writings we command your steadfastness that, watching over the charge, defense, and reform of it committed to you, as you have laudably begun, you so cherish, maintain, and defend it that its disturbed condition may be brought back to its due established state, so that you may deserve to receive recompense from the Lord and to be commended by us. Given at Perugia, May 4, in the sixth year of our pontificate.

When these apostolic letters had been received, Sifrid, archbishop of Mainz, not only subjected the principality of the monastery of Lorsch, its lordships, castles, towns, vassals, and dependents to his church of Mainz with authority, but also labored to reform the life of the monks of that monastery to the observance of regular discipline. But when the monks perceived that they had lost all liberty for themselves, and that the monastery itself had been left with all honor as lord not to them but to the church, understanding the mystery too late, they grieved not a little, acknowledging that they had been outmaneuvered, and with the help of certain nobles began to oppose the archbishop's commands. Seeing this, the aforesaid archbishop Sifrid obtained from the supreme pontiff that the office of visitation and inquiry be carried out again through the bishop of Hildesheim, who, after the visitation had been made, informed the Roman pontiff that in the monks of that monastery, who [unclear] by thing or by power repeatedly of friends; for this reason he had labored with every effort that, after the monks had been expelled, men of another profession, who would not care for lordships or principality, should be put in their place.

He therefore pursued by such means as he could before the Apostolic See that the monks of Saint Benedict be expelled and that Cistercians, whose order and power do not permit them to have principality or temporal lordships, be introduced in their place, [unclear] of the said monastery as though unjustly taken away or by right assigned to him in future. Whence, after two years, the pope wrote thus to the same archbishop of Mainz.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother, the archbishop of Mainz, greeting and apostolic blessing. The vineyard of the monastery of Lorsch, from which you expected that it would produce grapes, is said to have brought forth wild grapes in the midst, while that monastery itself, in which Mary's office was accustomed to flourish in the beauty of contemplation, and in the abundance of temporal things the solicitude of Martha's office was vigorous, through the malice of its inhabitants, as our venerable brother the bishop of Hildesheim, to whose prudence we committed inquiry concerning this matter, reported, we have learned to have collapsed so far that, Jezebel succeeding in the place of Mary, and prodigality succeeding in the place of Martha, it is even said to have withered in its leaves, so that it seeks and expects nothing else than that the roots of the foolish fig tree, which uselessly occupy the ground, be hidden. Indeed, just as by the skill of an experienced physician wounds which do not feel the medicine of poultices are judged to be cut away, [unclear] they wrapped up the substance of the monastery, dissipating it with the prodigal son, so that, with [unclear] horns put in, it is said, after long expectation, to have withered not only in fruits but also in leaves: because there is no further hope that, with Jezebel and prodigality succeeding in the place of Martha, it may be reformed in its order, it seeks and expects nothing else than that the roots of the foolish fig tree, which uselessly occupy the ground, be hidden. Indeed, just as by the skill of an experienced physician wounds which do not feel the medicine of poultices are judged to be cut away, so that, when the rottenness has been excluded, wine and oil may be poured in and the wounds at last healed, [unclear] lest they be disappointed of their preconceived hope that the field of the inhabitants may be relieved, according to the counsel of the aforesaid bishop, which became known to us by his letters, you, who are the diocesan of the place, [unclear] decree and it is expedient, especially since the time of harvest is approaching...

[Blank page in the source scan.]

[Chronicle of Trithemius]

[unclear], to pull up, with the hoes of correction, the tares of the monks existing in the same place, and to gather the wheat into the barns. Let your fraternity therefore have compassion, since we too have compassion, on the monastery thus collapsed; and, going to it in person, plant in it the Cistercian order, utterly bereft of virtues as it is, so that the order, changed from black into white, may be purged of vices and increased in virtues; and thus, as at the wedding [unclear], water was changed into wine by the working of the supreme craftsman, it may bring forth the flower of honor and propriety, and will not lack the fruit of good work. From this the hope of the faithful may revive; and by watering [the planting] of so great a name and religion, newly planted, [unclear] will foster the little plant more devotedly and willingly with the sweetness of his dew. But if you find any of the monks whom love of the Cistercian order enkindles, you may be able to retain them there, provided that no sinister opinion about them easily arises among good and serious men. The others you shall dispose through the various places of their order in your diocese so cautiously that a diseased sheep may not stain the flock, but rather the lost one may be led back to the sheepfolds; taking more careful provision that the possessions and goods which that same monastery is known once to have had shall not in any way be excluded from the new plantation.

When therefore these letters of the supreme pontiff had been received, Sifrid, archbishop, expelled all the monks of Saint Benedict from the aforesaid monastery of Lorsch against their will, and introduced a convent with an abbot of the Cistercian order, according to the apostolic mandate. This deed greatly displeased the nobles round about, although they entirely [unclear] to withstand so great an authority. The Cistercian monks who had been introduced, as the archbishop handed over the possessions of the monastery that had been left, took possession of them, except for vassals, ministerials, castles, towns, estates, which pertained to the honor of the principality, and turned their fruits to their own use, from which they might live. Meanwhile the former monks, grieving heavily that they had been expelled and that professors of another order had been placed in their monastery, resolved that so great an injury was by no means to be endured without vengeance. Gathering therefore on a certain night, with the aid of certain of their friends, they violently entered their monastery of Lorsch with force; attacking the abbot with the lay brothers and the whole household, they threw them out, captured some and compelled them to swear off the place, wounded others by beating them, and drove them all together from the monastery. The expelled monks of the order brought their complaint to the archbishop of Mainz, declaring that they could not remain amid such dangers. Meanwhile the former monks, possessing the monastery which they had recovered, consulted among their friends about what seemed more useful to them.

But not after much time, when they heard that the archbishop was coming with force, they abandoned the place, not without booty, and withdrew to safer places; [unclear] what he wished to do, [unclear]. Those who had been expelled were, at the persuasion of the bishop, encouraged to return to the monastery of the Lorsch religion, and they continued the manner of living they had begun. And behold, not after much time, when the Cistercians established at Lorsch now believed that they were secure, the old monks, entering the monastery by night with their friends and with force, attacked them, struck them, beat them, and expelled them again, protesting that they would kill them all if they returned again to the monastery of Lorsch. Therefore from that day the Cistercians could no longer be induced to return to Lorsch to remain there.

The monastery therefore remained vacant for some time, since neither these nor those saw that they could safely stay in it. At length Sifrid the archbishop reported the matter for examination to the apostolic see, over which Pope Innocent IV then presided, from whom he received such a reply by letters concerning the ordering of the monastery of Lorsch itself, as follows:

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Sifrid, archbishop of Mainz, greeting and apostolic blessing. Since, as you have taken care to set forth to us, Gregory, pope of most happy memory, our predecessor, having understood that a monastery of the order of Saint Benedict, of the diocese of Mainz, had been diminished not a little in spiritual and temporal matters by the wickedness of those dwelling in it, had given command to you by his letters that, with the monks utterly removed from it, you should reform it from the Cistercian order, you, as a diligent executor of his commands, introduced into it a Cistercian convent. But certain sons of perdition, who, given over to a reprobate mind, persecute the sons of God the more fiercely the more they are held unlike them in their deeds, cast the aforesaid Cistercians out of the said monastery once and a second time by violence; as a result of which, in that very monastery, not without injury to Jesus Christ, given over almost wholly to desolation, the divine voice of praise does not resound in it. But because it is known to pertain to our solicitude that, in churches whose desolation the savagery of the perverse has procured, we come to their aid with swift remedy lest they perish altogether, we grant to you, by the authority of the present letters, free faculty to establish in that same monastery a convent of regulars, or even secular canons, according as your providence shall know to be more expedient for the place and the country, assigning to them the revenues of the former convent. You shall compel gainsayers by ecclesiastical censure, with appeal set aside.

Given at Lyon, [unclear] November May, in the second year of our pontificate.

Fortified by the authority of these letters, the archbishop of Mainz [introduced?] the Premonstratensians [unclear]

The monks of Saint Benedict are expelled from Lorsch. The Cistercians are introduced.

[unclear] [Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheim.

[He] took Premonstratensians from the monastery of All Saints, of the diocese of Strasbourg, and established a convent in the aforesaid monastery, setting over them not an abbot but a provost, and after him he appointed a prior, according to the custom of that order. He confirmed by his letters this establishment of the Premonstratensian order in the often-mentioned monastery of Lorsch; their date is the year of the Lord 1248, the sixth ides of January, in the eighteenth year of his pontificate. Since these are too lengthy and do not serve our purpose, we have reasonably omitted a copy of [unclear]. But the Premonstratensians introduced into Lorsch, at the archbishop’s instance, renounced every right of lordship over the said monastery, as is clear in these letters:

“To all the faithful of Christ, present as well as future: the provost and convent of the monastery of Lorsch, of the Premonstratensian order, in the diocese of Mainz, offer devout prayers in Christ. Since the venerable father lord Siegfried, archbishop of the see of Mainz, by the counsel and consent of the chapter of Mainz, has established us by apostolic authority in the monastery of Lorsch, revenues suitable and honorable having been assigned to us, with which we are also content, namely all the revenues of the former convent and of its offices; by reason of this establishment, and also because our place lies in the diocese of Mainz, we subject ourselves and our place, and acknowledge them subject, to the church of Mainz, to the said lord archbishop and to all his successors, according as is contained in the privilege of our establishment.

“Moreover, since imperial and likewise royal authority, by the counsel and assent of the princes, has seen fit, for certain and legitimate causes, [unclear] the lordship of the church of Lorsch, with every honor, vassals, ministerials, castles, towns, revenues, rights, and its appurtenances, to the church of Mainz, as we have perceived to be contained in the imperial and royal privileges: we acknowledge that the church of Mainz, lord Siegfried the archbishop, and his successors possess a firm and stable right in that lordship itself and in its civil appurtenances; and concerning these matters we shall never raise, nor shall any of our successors raise, any question whatsoever. But if by our establishment, by reason of the monastery of Lorsch, any right had been acquired for us or our successors in that lordship itself, or in the aforesaid goods and rights pertaining to the abbey, we have renounced it, and we give and grant that same thing to the church of Mainz and to the archbishops who shall be in office from time to time, to be possessed by them; since we are wholly unable to restore and maintain the same lordship in its rights and honor, and the statutes of our order forbid us to possess such things. In memory of this act and for its perpetual validity, we have caused the present letters to be written and to be strengthened by the protection of the seals of the churches of St. Peter and St. Stephen of Mainz, and of our own church of All Saints in the diocese of Strasbourg. Done at Mainz in the year of the Lord 1247.”

And so that noble abbey, once famous and most powerful, of the monastery of Lorsch, was taken away from our sacred order, given into the hands of others, and its lordship was, less justly, as it seemed to many, made subject to the church of Mainz; although prudent and religious men of our order, noble and powerful, could certainly have been found who would have reformed that monastery in both estates. Duke Tassilo of Bavaria built this monastery in the time of Emperor Charlemagne, about the year of the Lord [unclear], and endowed it magnificently; in it he later became a monk, and with Theodo his son ended his life in great religion.

Now, after we have described the lamentable ruin of the monastery of Lorsch:

1233.

In the aforesaid year, which was the twentieth of John our abbot, a concord was made at Frankfurt between the bishop of Worms and the citizens on the third kalends of March, through Siegfried archbishop of Mainz, Conrad bishop of Speyer, and the margrave of Baden. In the same year many fires occurred in various places.

In this same year brother Conrad of Marburg, as we have already said above under the preceding year, was slain by the knights of those of Dornbach near Marburg.

1324.

In this year, which was the twenty-first of John the abbot, our village in Dalen, on the fifteenth kalends of March, was burned by an accidental fire at night, and remained utterly desolate down to the present day. For the demesne lands were transferred here to the village next to the monastery, so that today no trace of the former village in Dalen appears. The church also, long ago built in honor of St. Gregory, perished in the same fire, and lay desolate for almost sixty-two years, so that trees grew in it, until the time of Abbot John, when it was restored anew by Hadwig the widow, as we shall say below in its place. And thus the village around the monastery grew and was enlarged by a multitude of people and houses.

In the same year Pope Gregory IX had the cross preached against the Stedinger peoples, situated on the border of Frisia and Saxony, surrounded by inaccessible marshes and rivers—

The provost and convent of Lorsch.

The provostship and convent of Lorsch acknowledges itself to be subject to the church of Mainz, and they renounce the lordship.

[Unclear] foundations of Lorsch.

Concord between the bishop and the citizens of Worms.

Many fires.

Brother Conrad of Marburg is killed.

Dalen is burned and laid waste.

The cross Sponheim.

1240. This year, which was the twenty-seventh of our Abbot Johannes, Johannes X, prior of this monastery, died on the vigil of St Andrew the Apostle, burdened by old age and an abscess. After him Sifridus, a monk born in Trier, was appointed eleventh prior; he presided in his office for four years and was deposed.

Johannes, tenth prior, dies. Sifridus, eleventh prior.

1241. In the twenty-eighth year of Abbot Johannes, David, pastor of the church in Roxheim, was most cruelly killed by peasants in Sommerloch near Waldenhausen, because he defended the rights and liberty of his church. Therefore, excommunicated by Sifridus, archbishop of Mainz, and [unclear] cursed, they paid very heavy penalties for their impiety. For all who polluted their consciences with the contagion of this crime, some in pilgrimage, others escaping by flight, perished from this life in beggary and great want.

The pastor in Roxheim is killed.

[Unclear marginal note concerning Kreuznach and the count of Sayn?]

1242. In the twenty-eighth year. In the twenty-ninth year, Johannes, provost of the nuns [unclear], died. In the same year Conrad, bishop of Speyer, together with his chapter, sold to the count of Sayn all the right of ownership and the possessions that he himself and the canons of the church of Speyer had in Kreuznach, for 1,100 marks of pure silver; with this money they bought properties more suitable for themselves.

Johannes, provost of St Rupert, dies; [Roricus?] succeeds. Worms is burned.

In the same year Johannes, provost of the convent of St Rupert near Bingen, a monk of this monastery and formerly prior in the order, a good and upright man, died. After him Abbot Johannes appointed as provost of the said monastery the monk [Roticus?]; how long he presided I have not found.

In the same year, on [unclear] April at the hour of vespers, the city of Worms was consumed by fire over more than half its extent, and more than 300 people perished in that fire; this loss was wholly irrecoverable.

1243. Frederick II, emperor, long since excommunicated, was deposed from the empire at the council of Lyon by Pope Innocent IV, but he did not care. The pope commanded the princes to elect another emperor against Frederick. And so at length Henry, landgrave of Hesse, son of St Elizabeth, was elected; near Frankfurt he had a battle with King Conrad, son of Emperor Frederick, and defeated him. Holding the name of king for almost five years, he accomplished nothing worthy of memory, and died not long afterward.

This year Pope Innocent granted to the dean of the greater church the use of the mitre or infula on the chief festivals, as appears in the bull that follows:

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the dean of Mainz, our chaplain, greeting and apostolic blessing. You have deserved our [favor] and that of the Apostolic See [unclear] by the purity of fidelity, [unclear], always watching for this, driving all fear from yourself, that under the experience of grievous labors [you might] enlarge the honor of the same see. Therefore, so that from merits of this kind joy may be produced for your heart and an example of devotion for others, by the authority of these presents we grant to you and your successors that in the church of Mainz, on the chief solemnities, in the celebration of divine services, you may forever use the mitre, which the provost and cantor of the same church are said to use. Let no man, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our concession. Given at Lyon, on the fourth day before the Nones of August, in the third year of our pontificate.

And these three, the provost, dean, and cantor of the aforesaid church of Mainz, by force of the granted privilege, use the infula on the highest feasts down to the present.

1245. This year, which was the thirty-second of Abbot Johannes, Sifridus, eleventh prior of this monastery of Sponheim, was deposed. I could not find the cause of his deposition. When he had been deposed, [unclear]. At length, on account of Emperor Frederick and his son Conrad, he was excommunicated by Pope Innocent and began to persecute the clergy. Therefore, when on the vigil of St Andrew he had been joyful with his wife and household, he died suddenly that very night. He left two sons, Ludwig and Henry, who for ten years held their father's principality jointly. But afterward, in the year of the Lord 1256, when they were at odds with one another, they divided the lands and patrimony. Ludwig, who was the elder by birth, received the Palatinate, with certain other things in Upper Bavaria, for his portion; and Henry [unclear].

Otto, count palatine, dies. Sifridus, prior, is deposed. Petrus, prior, is elected.

When he had died, [unclear] succeeded in his place.

In the same year, on the night of St Andrew the Apostle, Otto, count palatine of the Rhine, [of] the dukes of Bavaria, died. At the beginning of his rule he was a pious, just, and vigorous prince.

Sifridus, eleventh prior of this monastery, was deposed. I could not find the cause of his deposition. When he had been deposed, [unclear]. At length, on account of Emperor Frederick and his son Conrad, he was excommunicated by Pope Innocent and began to persecute the clergy. Therefore, when on the vigil of St Andrew he had been joyful with his wife and household, he died suddenly that very night. He left two sons, Ludwig and Henry, who for ten years held their father's principality jointly. But afterward, in the year of the Lord 1256, when they were at odds with one another, they divided the lands and patrimony. Ludwig, who was the elder by birth, received the Palatinate, with certain other things in Upper Bavaria, for his portion; and Henry [unclear].

Otto, count palatine, dies.

When he had died, [unclear] succeeded in his place.

In the same year, on the night of St Andrew the Apostle, Otto, count palatine of the Rhine, [of] the dukes of Bavaria, died. At the beginning of his rule he was a pious, just, and vigorous prince.

Sifridus, eleventh prior of this monastery, was deposed. I could not find the cause of his deposition. When he had been deposed, [unclear]. At length, on account of Emperor Frederick and his son Conrad, he was excommunicated by Pope Innocent and began to persecute the clergy. Therefore, when on the vigil of St Andrew he had been joyful with his wife and household, he died suddenly that very night. He left two sons, Ludwig and Henry, who for ten years jointly [held] their father's principality.

Sponheim.

1251.

In the thirty-eighth year of his rule, Iuanus, abbot of this monastery, began to rebuild the church of St. Gregory the martyr; and, sending his prior with certain brothers to Hugh, Cardinal Priest of St. Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, who was then staying at Bingen, he obtained from him indulgences of this kind.

“To all Christ’s faithful established throughout Germany, to whom these letters shall come, brother Hugh, by divine mercy Cardinal Priest of the title of St. Sabina, legate of the Apostolic See, greeting in the Lord. Since, as the Apostle says, we shall all stand before the judgment-seat of Christ, to receive according as we have done in the body, whether good or evil, it is fitting for us [unclear] eternal life. Therefore, since [unclear] and with a view to eternal things to sow on earth what, when the Lord gives it back, with multiplied fruit we ought to gather in heaven, holding firm hope and confidence, because he who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessings shall also from blessings reap eternal life. Therefore, since, as the beloved sons, the prior and convent of the monastery of St. Martin in Sponheim, of the Order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Mainz, have taken care to inform us, the same chaplains have begun to rebuild their chapel of St. George in Dalheim, consumed by excessive age, at great expense; and since their own resources are not sufficient for this, we admonish and exhort all you Christ’s faithful in the Lord, and enjoin upon you for the remission of your sins, that from the goods conferred upon you by God you bestow upon them pious alms and kindly aids of charity, so that through your assistance the said work may be brought to completion, and you, through this and through other good deeds which, by the Lord’s inspiration, you shall have done, may be able to come to eternal joys. We, trusting in the mercy of almighty God and in the authority of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, mercifully remit forty days of the penance enjoined upon all truly penitent and confessed persons who shall have stretched out to them a helping hand for this purpose; which [unclear] through questors we more strictly forbid, decreeing that, if otherwise done, they shall lack force. Given at Bingen, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the ninth year of the pontificate of the lord pope Innocent IV.”

And so the church of St. George, the rebuilding of which was begun in this year, was not completed. For only the choir, where the altar is, was roofed; the remaining part of the church remained unfinished until the time of Abbot Johannes, as was said above under the twenty-first year of Iuanus.

In the same year also Christian, archbishop of Mainz, died; Gerard succeeded him [unclear] years [unclear]. In the same year Abbot Iuanus began to be sick unto death.

1252.

In this year, which was the thirty-ninth and last of Abbot Iuanus, there died the most devout virgin of Christ, Jutta, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April; she had formerly been the maidservant of blessed Elizabeth, landgravine of the Thuringians, of whom mention was made above. This holy virgin was renowned for many signs and miracles both in life and after death, and while her lady was still living she was always the most faithful witness and helper of all her virtues; and she strove in all things to imitate her most holy manner of life, in which she prevailed so greatly, and was a singular advocate of the poor.

In the same year Iuanus, the sixth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, weighed down by old age and long illness, closed his last day, and died on the fourth day before the Kalends of December. He was buried in the cloister of the monastery with his brothers. Under his rule, in the last years, the observance of regular discipline began to fail.

On Johannes, the seventh abbot of this monastery, who presided for 12 years, 4 months, and 21 days, and on the deeds of that time around this place.

When Iuanus, the fifth abbot of this monastery, had died and been buried, after mature deliberation among themselves the brothers came together as one in spirit and intention to set a new pastor over themselves. Having invoked the aid of the Holy Spirit, in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s incarnation 1253, in the tenth indiction, on the vigil of St. Andrew the Apostle, that is, on the third day before the Kalends of December, they unanimously elected as abbot Johannes, a monk and cantor of this monastery, who presided for 12 years, 4 months, and 21 days. He was a good and simple man, son of the same nobleman of Schönberg, who in his boyhood, under Abbot [Opre Cantoso?], came to religious life through the urging and offering of his parents, and for a long time held the office of cantor. When he was ordained abbot, he found that the observance of regular discipline was gradually failing, but he could not bring it back to its former fervor because of the malice of the time and the conduct of wicked men. And so, in succession from his time down to the most recent reform, which is called Bursfeld from the place where it began, the observance of monastic purity in this monastery, growing lukewarm and failing, was less cared for through [unclear] years, although in the meantime reform was attempted several times, but it did not attain a stable effect. For the monks began to have private property, and little by little always to fall into worse condition, until they wholly failed.

The church of St. George is restored.

Indulgence for the church of St. George.

Christian, archbishop of Mainz, dies; his tutor Gerard succeeds.

Jutta, maidservant and follower of St. Elizabeth, dies.

Abbot Iuanus dies.

The discipline of observance fails.

Johannes von Schönberg, abbot.

Discipline collapses. ...that we may show reverence to [Martin], our patron, the parish church in Gensingen, in the diocese of Mainz, with the right of patronage and all its appurtenances and revenues, which the pastor of that church has hitherto been accustomed to receive, with the consent of the venerable father, our lord Werner, archbishop of Mainz, and of our whole convent, we grant to you, to be held in perpetuity, so that, as soon as it shall happen to become vacant, you may freely and perpetually apply its revenues to your common uses. Yet there is to be left from the revenues of the same church a definite and suitable portion, from which the person who is to serve God perpetually in that church of Gensingen, and who is to be appointed by you, may be able to be honorably supported. In easy remembrance and perpetual confirmation of this, we give you the present letters, strengthened by the protection of our seal and that of our convent. Done in the year of the Lord 1265, on the seventh ides of July.

Confirming this donation, Archbishop Werner delivered the following letters.

Werner, by the grace of God archbishop of the holy see of Mainz, archchancellor through Germany of the Holy Roman Empire, to his beloved in Christ, the provost, dean, and the whole chapter of Mainz, greeting in the Lord. It is fitting that we meet the just desires of petitioners with gracious consent, diligently pursue the same, and, so far as ability suffices, commit them to effect. Therefore, inclined by your prayers, we, holding as very welcome and valid the donation of the church in Gensingen which, for the increase of your prebends, the beloved in Christ, the abbot and convent of the monastery in Sponheim of our diocese, freely and kindly made to you, as is contained in their writing drawn up concerning it, confirm it by the testimony of the present writing. Let no man, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation, or with rash daring to oppose it. But if anyone shall presume to attempt this, let him know that he has incurred the indignation of almighty God and of blessed Martin, and the sentence of our excommunication. Given at Mainz in the year of the Lord 1265, on the tenth kalends of October.

In recompense for the aforesaid donation, the aforementioned Archbishop Werner, with the consent of his chapter, incorporated the parish church in Sponheim, with all its revenues, into the monastery, as is clear from the letters that follow.

Werner, by the grace of God archbishop of the holy see of Mainz, archchancellor through Germany of the Holy Roman Empire, to his beloved in Christ, Peter, elected abbot of the whole monastery in Sponheim of our diocese, greeting in the Lord. We, considering with fatherly affection that your church, on account of the manifold burdens of exactions and through various unfortunate events, has been so diminished in many things that you labor under no small poverty, in order that, so far as we can, we may somewhat relieve your need for our salvation, grant to you the parish church in Sponheim with its attached chapels, to be held by you in full right forever, [unclear] when it shall happen to become vacant, freely and perpetually applying its revenues to your common uses, provided that you present to the archdeacon of the place a faithful and perpetual vicar for that church, to whom you shall assign from the revenues of that church a definite and suitable portion from which he may be able to be honorably supported; and we also freely impart our consent, and that of our archdeacon, to you concerning a donation of this kind. Let no man at all, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our donation, or with rash daring to oppose it. But if anyone shall presume to attempt this, let him know that he has incurred the indignation of almighty God and of Saint Martin.

For the greater confirmation and evidence of this, we have caused this present writing of ours to be strengthened for you by the protection of our own seal, that of the provost, dean, and chapter, and also of you, the elected abbot. Done in the year of the Lord 1265, on the seventh ides of July.

Thus, in order that the church of the village of Sponheim might be incorporated into the monastery, Abbot Peter gave the church in Gensingen with all its appurtenances to the church of Mainz.

In the same year the citizens of Würzburg, because of the many and various injuries which they had inflicted upon Iring, their bishop, and upon the clergy, were condemned to pay him two thousand two hundred marks, and, after the silver had been paid, were compelled to return to his obedience.

1266.

In this year the provost, dean, and chapter of the major [church] bought from Philip the elder of Falkenstein and from his two sons, Philip and Werner, [unclear] which they had held by feudal right from the church of Mainz, with Archbishop Werner consenting, as is clear from the letters of purchase drawn up concerning it, whose date is in the year of the Lord 1261, on the third ides of February.

In the same year Iring, bishop of Würzburg, died; Berthold of Sternberg succeeded him and presided for eighteen years.

1267.

In these times the monastery of the Friars Preachers in the city of Speyer began to be founded under Bishop Henry, with his consent and that of the whole chapter. In the same 280 Chronicle of Trithemius

[1253?].

John the abbot, in the first year of his rule, continued for some time the work begun on the church of St. George the martyr in Dalen, which nevertheless he afterwards left unfinished.

In the same year there was a great and powerful wind in these regions, which overthrew many trees and buildings in various places.

1254.

Conrad the king, son of Emperor Frederick II, died. After his death his son Conrad, whom the Lombards called Conradin, wishing to succeed to the kingdom of Apulia as the legitimate heir, was repelled by the contrivance of the pope, and Charles, count of Anjou, was introduced by deceit. Hence Conradin, having set out for Apulia with a very great army, in the first encounter Charles, with papal aid, was defeated. After the victory, while our men were intent on plunder and spoils, he, having recovered his strength, rushed upon them, conquered the conquerors, killed many, captured others, and put others to flight. There Conradin was captured with many nobles and was beheaded; in him the line of Frederick II and of the duchy of the Swabians failed. Conradin was a youth most beautiful of all, who, by the counsel of the pope, through envy of the German name and especially of his grandfather Frederick, our emperor, was killed with many counts and nobles.

In the same year Godescalcus, abbot of St. James at Mainz, with the consent of his convent and of Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, conferred upon the chapter and canons of the greater church of Mainz, for the augmentation of their prebends, the parish church in Schornsheim with its tithes, revenues, and all its appurtenances, as is clear in these letters:

To the honorable men and beloved in Christ, the provost, dean, and whole chapter of Mainz, Godescalcus, by the grace of God abbot, and the whole convent of the monastery of St. James at Mainz, offer the gift of prayers and a will ready for services. When we bring to mind with due meditation how liberal, how magnificent, in the time of her abundance, the church of Mainz has been toward us and other churches, which, brought forth from her inward parts, through her have been planted and founded in the great abundance of other goods, we can scarcely think of anything by which we may be able to render to her the return that is owed. Yet so that, for the relief of the poverty of our mother, in which the general disturbance of the land has involved us by occasion of the business of the church, our scant means may offer at least some small thing, and so that the filial fervor of devotion and the effect of due compassion in us may shine more clearly: behold, the parish church in Schornsheim of your diocese, whose collation pertains to us, with the right of patronage and all revenues, we give to you and your successors, by concordant will and liberal spirit, to be possessed forever, for the augmentation of your prebends. Thus, as soon as it shall happen to fall vacant, you may apply it to your common uses. In memory of this deed and for everlasting and perpetual firmness, we give you the present letters, strengthened by the protection of our seals. Done in the year of the Lord 1254, on the day of blessed Barnabas the apostle. Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, confirmed this donation by letters in the same year, on the vigil of St. James the Apostle.

In like manner also, in the same year, Otto, abbot, and the convent of St. Disibod, of the order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Mainz, conferred the church in Osternach upon the canons and chapter of the greater church of Mainz; and he gave letters concerning this matter of the following kind:

To the reverend and beloved in Christ, the provost, dean, and whole chapter of Mainz, Otto, abbot, and the convent of St. Disibod, of the order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Mainz, with the affection of filial devotion, offer a will ready for services. Since the distinguished beauty of the honor of your church, our mother, shines forth famously, and the wondrous splendor of the work of excellent dignity [unclear], and we, considering in some measure the poverty of the ministers, as we are bound by the compassion of filial devotion, have resolved to redeem the deformity of this sort of defect, and at least to redeem the ministry of one minister set before your choir: behold, the parish church in Osternach, of your diocese, whose collation pertains to us, with the right of patronage and all its appurtenances which the pastor has hitherto been accustomed to receive, saving the other things which our church has and has had in that same village, with unanimous consent we freely so give and [unclear], so that when it shall first happen to fall vacant, all the revenues of it which, beyond the suitable prebend of the perpetual vicar of that church to be instituted henceforth by you, shall be able to remain, may be wholly converted to the prebend of a perpetual vicar in your church, who is to serve in the name of our church. Thus I, Otto, and my successors, the abbots, may always freely confer that vicarage upon an honorable person and a priest useful to the choir, who, like the other vicars of your church, shall be bound to due service in the choir and obedience to the dean. In memory of this deed and for perpetual firmness, we have caused the present letters to be strengthened by our seals. Done in the year of the Lord 1254. Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, confirmed this donation in the same year, on the Kalends of January, by his letters, in the third year of his pontificate, which he delivered to the chapter of Mainz.

In the same year there occurred at Cologne a certain deed of Albert the Great, of the order of preachers, [unclear], to whom Sifridus of Westerburg, an excessively warlike man, succeeded, and from Pope Gregory X received confirmation with the honor of the archiepiscopal pallium.

1273.

In this year, which was the ninth of Peter our abbot, the princes of the Roman Empire, assembled at Frankfurt, after many deliberations at last unanimously elected as king of the Romans Rudolf, count of Habsburg, then absent and besieging Basel with a great army. When he heard that he had been elected king of the Romans, he at once raised the siege and came to Frankfurt; then, proceeding to Aachen, he received the office of consecration according to custom. There the princes, having sworn obedience, received their feudal holdings from his hand, and they stood firmly by him against all the adversaries of the empire. Therefore in a short time he recovered many things that had been alienated from the empire, and restored peace in the land. He reigned eighteen years and ten months. He had as wife Helizabeth, daughter of Burchard, count of Haerloch, who bore him three sons: Albert, duke of Austria, who afterward was emperor of the Romans, from whom all the dukes of Austria who are today, or have existed in the meantime, were begotten; Hartmann, who was drowned in the Rhine; and Rudolf, duke of Swabia, who took as wife the daughter of Ottocar, king of Bohemia. Of his daughters, the first married Wenceslaus, king of Bohemia; the second, named Machtildis, married Louis, count palatine of the Rhine, as we shall say; the third married Albert, duke of Saxony; the fourth married Charles, prince of Apulia.

In the same year Louis, count of Montfort, the count of Helfenstein, the count of Duckenberg, Count Eberhard of Wurttemberg, with eleven others, conspiring against King Rudolf, sought with all their might either to capture or to kill him. When this became known to him, he brought forth a great army against them, defeated them, and compelled them to obedience to him and to the empire forever. He restored secure peace throughout all the surrounding land, from Italy as far as England.

In the same year Peter, abbot of this monastery, seeing that that division of revenues and proceeds made three years earlier between himself and the convent was the beginning of every future imputation and no small detriment to his authority, grieved vehemently over it. Though all resisted, except Ottuvinus the prior, he publicly revoked it. The monks, angered by this and as if turned to madness, resisted with all their strength; and, after forming a conspiracy among themselves, they resolved rather to kill the abbot than to resign the portion of property once granted to them. When this became known to the abbot, giving place to wrath, he withdrew to Kreuznach and stayed there for more than the space of a year, until at last, when the stronger leader of the faction had died, the matter was composed and settled through the count of Sponheim, the lord.

1275.

In the eleventh year of Peter our abbot, Rudolf, king of the Romans, moved an army into Bohemia against King Ottocar, who, after the death of the legitimate heir, had unjustly occupied Austria, Styria, Carinthia, and Moravia against the jurisdiction of the empire. After an engagement was fought, he defeated and subdued him, and imposed upon him agreements of submission. But when Ottocar afterward scorned to keep what he had promised, Rudolf returned again into Bohemia, overcame the perjured king a second time, killed him, and subjected the kingdom of Bohemia to himself. Furthermore he gave the duchy of Austria to his son Albert, count of Habsburg, from whom Maximilian, today king of the Romans, descends in a direct line of generation continued as follows. Rudolf, king of the Romans from being count of Habsburg, begot Albert, duke of Austria. Albert begot Albert the younger by Helizabeth, daughter of the count or duke of Carinthia, Meynhard. Albert, moreover, begot Lupold, duke of Austria, by Johanna, daughter of the count of Pyrreth. Lupold then begot Ernest the duke, and Ernest begot Frederick the third, emperor, by Simburga, daughter of Duke Alexius of Ancazon in Poland. Frederick the emperor begot King Maximilian. Maximilian begot Philip, duke of Austria, Burgundy, and Brabant, and Maria, queen of Spain, concerning whom it will be said in their place.

1276.

In the twelfth year of Peter our abbot, concord between him and his convent through Simon Sponheim ... of the Preachers, which John de Beka, clerk, recounts in his Chronicles on the deeds of the bishops of Utrecht and of the counts of Holland, speaking thus: As the Epiphany of the Lord approached, King William went to Cologne, so that there he might solemnly offer the sacrifice of praise in honor of the three Magi. In those days the lord Albert, later bishop of Regensburg, of the Order of Preachers, was regent and lecturer there: great in necromancy, greater in philosophy, but greatest in theology. He humbly asked the king to deign to dine with him on the solemn day. The king, hoping to see some prodigious sign, agreed to his request.

When, therefore, the solemn masses were finished, the king hastened to the convent of the Preachers. Albert received him gladly and led him out of the house into a certain garden adjoining the monastery, where he found servants of wondrous beauty, who had prepared everything necessary for a banquet. In those days it was a very harsh winter, and the whole surface of the earth was covered with snow. Therefore all those who were with the king began to murmur against the master, because in such dreadful cold he had ordered his guests to dine outside the house, without a fire, in the garden.

But after Albert had sat down at table together with the king, each person being placed according to his rank, while they were waiting for the meal to be brought in, behold, suddenly all that immense mass of snow and ice vanished in a moment, and summer heat, with the rays of the sun shining forth, grew hot. The earth at once brought forth grass, and flowers of wondrous beauty appeared both on the trees and in the grass itself. A wondrous thing: each and every tree of that same garden put forth leaves and flowers, and at once produced early fruit. The flowering vine gave off the scent of sweetness and in that instant brought forth fresh grapes in great abundance before all. A multitude also of birds of various kinds was seen, which, applauding one another and chattering with varied song close by, made them joyful, so that it seemed one should think not January but rather the season of May or June was present. For the long severity of wintry cold vanished completely, and the fierce heat of summer warmth grew so strong that some of those reclining at table were forced, because of the excessive heat, to take off the clothes in which they were dressed, and many prepared shade for themselves by various devices.

The servants, however, were very beautiful young men, lively and indeed handsome, unknown to all those dining there, who brought in food and drink in very great variety and most abundant supply, whence this was done [unclear], with the greatest decorum and discipline of manners. All marveled with great joy, seeing such great marvels as they had not seen before. At last, when the banquet was completed, the whole crowd of servants suddenly disappeared, the singing of the birds fell wholly silent, the greenness of the trees and grasses suddenly [unclear], and the returning abundance of snow again covered the face of the earth. Immediately such cold grew dreadful that all who had earlier put off their double garments, sweating because of the excessive heat, now, touched by excessive cold, took up their clothes again and hastened as quickly as possible to return to the fire.

When these things had been done, Albert obtained from the king a place for his brothers in the city of Utrecht for building a monastery, with freedom and many gifts of gold and silver. The aforesaid John wrote these things in the aforementioned Chronicles of the Utrechters; whether they are true or false, it is not our purpose to wish to judge in this place.

In the same year, in the month of February, the men of Worms bound themselves for all future time by a very firm perpetual treaty with the men of Mainz, who for many former years had long practiced hostilities and enmities against one another. In these times also Count Emicho of Leiningen was laboring wholly in secret to capture and carry off Richard, bishop of Worms, who nevertheless [unclear] aid [unclear] and the count, with a discord conceived long before, for many days. Great tumult was in the kingdom in these times, and various dissensions, because not all wished to accept William as king of the Romans.

In the same year the castle called Richenstein, beside the Rhine, not far from Bingen, was captured. At the same time also, when King William was staying in the lower regions, Mainz and the other cities of those parts which had adhered to him had no defender against their adversaries. Therefore, when the procurators of the cities of Worms, Boppard, Wesel, Bingen, Oppenheim, Friedberg, Frankfurt, Gelnhausen, Fritzlar, and certain others met at Mainz on the day of Saint Margaret, virgin and martyr, they entered into a treaty, peace, and concord in the year noted above, and they laid aside every toll which they had about the Rhine for the preservation of the good of peace, although most of them were entangled in heavy debts on account of the wars and many hardships which they had suffered in the time of the schism after the deposition of Emperor Frederick II.

  1. In this year, which was the third of Abbot John, when King William was in Worms, his wife the queen on a certain day in the month of December resolved to go with an honorable retinue to the castle which is called Trifels. Perceiving this, a certain knight, Hermann of Rieperg, captured the queen herself on the road, and the count of Waldeck with her, and [unclear] despoiled ...

The magical miracle of Albert the Great.

The queen and the count of Waldeck are captured. with all her jewels, led her captive to Rieperg; after he had held her for some time, he allowed her to depart.

In the same year Hermann, abbot in Bleidenstadt of our order, with the consent of his convent, handed over to the canons of the greater church of Mainz, for the increase of their prebends, the parish church in Kemde, with all its revenues and appurtenances, under the witness of letters secured with his seal and that of the aforesaid convent. I think it superfluous to insert them here, because they were written in the same form as the letter of the abbot of Saint Disibod concerning the donation of the church in Osternach, which we placed above. Henry also, abbot of Fulda, with the consent of his convent, in the same year conferred on the church of Mainz, for the increase of the prebends, the church in Berstatt, with all its rents, revenues, and appurtenances, as is clear in the letters written on the matter, dated at Fulda on the Nones of June, that is, on the vigil of Saint Boniface, in the year 1255.

Starkardus also, abbot of Seligenstadt of our order, together with his convent, handed over to the same canons of Mainz the parish church in Nuhem, with all its revenues and profits, reserving to himself and his successors forever the right of conferring one vicarage, to be established from these revenues in the greater church of Mainz. Done on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1255.

1256.

Gerard, bishop of Mainz, together with the canons of his chapter, greatly troubling our abbot John and the convent of this monastery, pressed them with pleas and threats for the church in Gentzingen, which they desired by every means for the increase of their prebends. But Abbot John would not consent, and with steadfast mind despised both their threats and their pleas. But after his death, at last Abbot Peter gave the church itself to them when they asked for it, as we shall say below in its place.

In the same year William, when he was preparing to go to Rome for the crown of the empire, and had first wished to subdue the rebellious Frisians, led an army against them on the fifth day before the Kalends of January. Going ahead of the army over the ice, to reconnoiter an entrance and passable road against his adversaries, he was sitting on his horse; behold, the ice broke, and in a marshy ford the horse itself was gradually submerged with the king. The king, having none of his servants with him, was almost suffocated. Seeing this, the Frisians who were hiding in the reeds ran together and, not knowing that he was the king, killed him before the army arrived.

1257.

In this year, which was the fifth of our Abbot John, the princes of the empire assembled to establish a new king, lest, if they delayed longer, they should lose the right of election. But being at variance among themselves, Conrad of Cologne, Gerard bishop of Mainz, and Louis count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria elected Richard, count of Cornwall, brother of the king of England, as king of the Romans. But Arnold, archbishop of Trier, with those adhering to him, elected Alfonso king of Castile as king of the Romans and sent solemn envoys to him, promising counsel and aid. But King Alfonso [unclear], promising that he would follow with an army; but, content with his own kingdom, because he was a philosopher and a very great astronomer, he did not come, nor did he involve himself in any respect in the kingdom of the Romans, except for the title alone, which, apart from the honor of those who had elected him, he retained for a time in his letters. Further, Richard, the aforesaid count of Cornwall, summoned from England by Conrad archbishop of Cologne, assumed the title and government of the empire of the Romans, and, with great rejoicing of his men, was consecrated king by the same archbishop in the church of the blessed Mary ever virgin at Aachen. Afterwards, by the favor and votes of his princes, he was received as true king of the Romans by the people of Cologne, Boppard, Wesel, Mainz, Frankfurt, and many other cities. Going on farther, he received all into his dominion and spent much money to obtain obedience. And when he had come as far as Basel, and the money too lavishly spent was now failing, the princes, withdrawing from him, left him alone and abandoned, tacitly making clear that they had followed plunder, not the man. Therefore, seeing himself deprived of the princes’ aid and unable to make any further progress, he entrusted the kingdom of the Wetterau to Philip of Falkenstein, whose sister he had taken as wife because of her great beauty; Alsace to Werner, bishop of Strasbourg; and Boppard and Wesel with their appurtenances to Philip of Hochenfels. Then, taking his wife, he returned to England. For he had bought the kingdom with money; when that failed, he could no longer reign.
