For at the time when the election was pressing, Gerard archiepiSponheimense.

The archbishop of Mainz was being held captive by the duke of Brunswick; Richard himself redeemed him for eight thousand marks, on this condition: that he might deserve to obtain his vote in the election. And this was done. For, released from custody, the same aforesaid archbishop betook himself from Marburg to Frankfurt and elected Richard king of the Romans.

The archbishop of Mainz taken captive.

In the year written above, on the sixth day before the Ides of November, Richard, bishop of Worms, died. Conrad of Durkheim, dean of Mainz, succeeded him and presided only about twenty weeks; and he had discord with the citizens.

Richard, bishop of Worms, dies.

Eberhard, bishop of Worms.

In the same year Louis, count palatine of the Rhine, son of Otto duke of Bavaria, having his wife Maria under suspicion of adultery, as we said above, caused her, while she was staying at Werde in Swabia, to be beheaded on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February. By her he had no heir. This deed seemed excessively cruel to all good men, and was condemned by many, together with the man who commanded and ordered it to be done.

MCCLVIII.

In this year Johannes, abbot of this monastery, removed Petrus the prior and appointed him cellarer of the monastery, because he seemed more fit for governing temporal affairs than spiritual ones. For he was a man, as he himself used to say, born for earthly things; impatient of rest, he was always eager for outward labors. Of him there will be more to say below, where, after the death of Johannes our abbot, he will be recorded as having been substituted in his place. After Petrus, moreover, Nicolaus was appointed prior of this monastery by abbot Johannes, the thirteenth according to the order; he had once been provost of the nuns on Mount Saint Rupert near Bingen. He was a good man, quite zealous for the observance of regular discipline, though he could not restore it to its former fervor. He presided in the office of prior for six years; he died.

In the same year the church of St. Catherine in Oppenheim was erected as a parish church by Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, as appears in the letters that follow.

Gerard, by the grace of God archbishop of the holy see of Mainz, archchancellor of the sacred empire throughout Germany. Since, at the command of our most serene lord, the illustrious king of the Romans, through the older and better inhabitants, the true ancient boundaries having been revealed, which divided the diocese of Mainz from that of Worms, although through negligence they had in part been [unclear], it has been clearly declared that the known city in Oppenheim is established in our diocese; and the people of the same city, numerous and [unclear] in authority, have earnestly represented, with the Lord increasing it, that it ought, indeed that it is expedient for the salvation of souls, to be governed by the rule of a single and proper rector. We, with the counsel and consent of our chapter and of the provost of St. Victor, archdeacon of the place, choose, make, and create the church of St. Catherine, founded in that city, as a parish church, and distinguish it by the use, right, and honor of a parish church; granting to it that it may have the use of its own baptistery for baptizing its little children, and also a special cemetery for the convenience of burial. They shall also have and appoint special [curates?], who shall promote and dispose those things that pertain to spiritual right. In testimony of this deed and for due firmness, we have caused the present writing to be fortified with our seal, that of our chapter, and that of the aforesaid provost of St. Victor. Given at Mainz, on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the year of the Lord MCCLVIII.

In the same year the canons of the greater church of Metz sold all their goods in Odernheim, where St. Rufus, formerly bishop of Metz, remains buried down to the present day, to the canons of the greater church for 1040 pounds of Metz money, as appears from the letters made and sealed concerning this, whose date is in the year of the Lord MCCLVIII, on the Kalends of June.

MCCLIX.

In the sixth year of Johannes our abbot, the monks of our order from the monastery of St. Disibod near Sobernheim, after the death of Otto their abbot, were removed and expelled through Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, and the canons of the greater church of Mainz, as founders of the same place; and that monastery was given to the Cistercian order, as it remains to the present day. Therefore monks and lay brothers coming from Otterberg in the diocese of Worms first began to inhabit that place, appointing for themselves as the first abbot of their order one named Johannes, who bound his monastery to the church of Mainz, as it were in gratitude for the benefit received, in perpetuity, for one hundred malters of rye each year, as appears in the copy that follows:

Copy of the obligation.

To the reverend and beloved in Christ, Wernher the provost, Johannes the dean, and the whole chapter of Mainz, brother Johannes called abbot of the convent of the monastery of St. Disibod, of the Cistercian order, [offers] prayers in the Lord [unclear]. Since you, together with the venerable lord our father Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, 284 Chronicle of Trithemius

[the monastery] of St. Disibod, then of the order of St. Benedict, founded by the church of Mainz, for certain reasons you have said is to be given to us and through us to our order. Lest we should seem ungrateful for so great a grace bestowed upon us through your kindness, [preserving?] the everlasting memory of that immense gift, we freely and steadfastly promise your whole body, and we wish ourselves and our successors to be bound, that for the use of two vicarages newly established in your church we shall give you from the revenues of our monastery, every year in perpetuity, fifty malters each of rye, of the Mainz measure, to be delivered at Mainz in every eventuality at our expense and risk; namely, that for one vicarage in the present month we shall give fifty malters of rye, and thereafter in the next following month, and thenceforth, for each vicarage’s lifetime, every year in perpetuity, we shall give one hundred malters of dry rye without chaff, of the aforesaid measure, to be delivered at Mainz, as has been said, at our risk and expense, between the two feasts, namely the Assumption of Mary and her Nativity. Adding that, as soon as we shall have any plough-teams furnished with beasts of burden, without any deceit or fraud we wish to be bound in perpetuity to bring your wine, which shall have grown for you in Monzingen each year at vintage time, whenever we are requested, to your cellar at Mainz in our wagons and at our expense; provided, however, that if the occurrence of some misfortune should befall, we shall be wholly excused. And for the due firmness of these things we grant the present writing, strengthened by the protection of the seals of the lords abbots in Eberbach and Otterberg, with the consent and knowledge of their convents and of our monastery. Done at Mainz in the year of the Lord 1259, on the day before the Nones of March.

You see how the canons of the greater church of Mainz, in order to make their prebends fatter, sold into annual servitude to the Cistercians, for one hundred malters of rye, a monastery that previously had been free and of our order, to no small loss, injury, and disgrace of our order, unmindful of the benefice received four years earlier from Otto, abbot of the same monastery, the last of our order, who had handed over to them the parish church in Odernheim with notable liberty, to be possessed forever with all its revenues.

In the same year Albertus Magnus, provincial of the Order of Preachers, by the provision of Pope Alexander IV, was made bishop of Regensburg in Bavaria. 1260.

Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, died. Werner of Falkenstein, provost of the greater church, succeeding him, presided for twenty-three years and six months. He governed his church excellently and wonderfully enlarged it in revenues and ornaments.

In the same year Louis, count palatine of the Rhine, of whom we spoke above, who had killed Maria, daughter of the duke of Bavaria, his wife, took another wife, Anna by name, daughter of Conrad, duke of Poland. By her he begot a daughter named Agnes, and a son Louis, an excellent man, concerning whom there will be occasion to speak later in his proper place.

In the same year also Jacob of Lapide and Simon of Guntheim, knights, waging serious hostilities against the Worms people, [took] many of the citizens captive; but afterward peace was made between them, and the captives were released upon payment of money. 1261.

In this year, which was the ninth of John our abbot, there was a very great flood of waters in these regions. The Rhine rose to such a degree that it overturned many houses and buildings; even people living around the Rhine, struck with excessive terror, abandoned their homes, and many fled to the protection of the mountains. In these times there was very great dissension between Engelbert the archbishop and the citizens of Cologne, which endured for many years, not without damage to both parties. 1262.

In the tenth year of John, abbot of this monastery, a certain man came from the lower parts to these lands. He was called Master Theodo, a magician and wondrous conjurer, who performed many incredible marvels. For in the town of Kreuznach, publicly in the marketplace before all the people, he cut off the head of his servant, and after the space of half an hour restored it to the body lying there. He seemed to walk with dogs in the air, as if going hunting, ascending and descending, and shouting in the highest places as if from afar. They thought he had devoured an armed man. He also devoured wagons loaded with wood or hay together with the horses, as those who did not know the method thought. He did other astonishing things too, which I have considered superfluous to write in this place.

In the same year Werner, archbishop of Mainz, excommunicated Philip of Hohenfels and placed his land under interdict because of the excessive and indiscriminate exactions which Of Sponheim.

... he was making in the goods of the clergy of the city of Mainz situated in his domain, and a grave disturbance arose among them.

285.

1263.

In this year, on the day after the Epiphany of the Lord, in the time of Richard, king of the Romans, an agreement was made on Mount St. James between the aforesaid Philip of Hohenfels and the prelates of the church of Mainz, and was confirmed under penalties of proscription and other terrible censures, as is clear in the letters concerning it, which we have omitted because of their excessive length.

In these times also there was a long and very serious dissension between the archbishop and the citizens of Cologne, the former wishing to draw the liberties of the citizens to himself, while the latter fought most vigorously for liberty. At last the citizens, capturing their archbishop Engelbert and Theoderic of Falckenburg, his brother, compelled them to make peace.

1264.

Nicholas, the thirteenth prior of this monastery, died this year on the Kalends of January, a good man and a lover of regular discipline. After him a certain monk, named Otwinus, a wise and very notable man, was appointed the fourteenth prior. He presided in the office of prior for twelve years, and would gladly have reformed the collapsed monastic discipline, but because of the malice of the times he was able to make little progress.

In the same year the Hermit Friars of the order of St. Augustine, entering Worms, began to build a monastery, and, having completed it, they inhabit it down to this day.

The Augustinians of Worms.

John, the seventh abbot, dies.

... concerning the deeds of that time.

... the eighth abbot, buried in the middle of the choir, before the steps of the presbytery.

Concerning Peter, the eighth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, who presided for twenty-five years and three months, and concerning the various deeds of that time.

After Abbot John had died and been buried, when the brethren of this monastery who were then present had assembled to elect a new pastor for the widowed church, a grave disturbance followed. For two men were elected through dissension. Peter, who was cellarer, concerning whom we spoke above, had one part of the convent for himself; and William, a monk who held the office of cantor, obtained the other part of the electors for himself.

And when a serious contention arose between the parties of this one monastery, and each party tried to defend its own elected man, Peter, who was a crafty man, using the former authority of his office, [unclear], surrounded by a band of his household supporters, powerfully invaded the abbacy and [unclear] himself in all things. Yet afterward he resigned the whole case into the hands of Werner, archbishop of Mainz. This contention lasted for the space of a year, not without damage to the temporal goods of the monastery and great danger to souls. Count Simon at first indeed supported the party of William and implored [unclear]. But at last Werner, archbishop of Mainz, summoned both elected men to him, and, carefully examining the manner and form of the election, and likewise the zeal of the electors, repudiated William and confirmed Peter as abbot of this monastery.

After he had devoted himself for some time to letters, he came to the monastery and under Abbot John became a monk; by him afterward he was appointed prior, as we have said, and then cellarer, and finally abbot.

The church in Gentzingen is alienated.

This Peter, in the first year of his confirmation, immediately gave the parish church in Gentzingen in the district of the Nahegau, which from the donation of the late noble man Udo our monastery had possessed peacefully for 138 years, to the chapter of the greater church of Mainz with all its appurtenances, as is clear in these letters:

Copy of the donation.

To the reverend and beloved in Christ, the provost and dean, and the whole chapter of the church of Mainz, Peter, by the grace of God elected and confirmed as abbot of the monastery of Sponheim, sends greeting and, with obedience, devoted prayers in Christ. Since through the aid of our assistance, by which we are bound worthily and reverently to be present to our mother, the slenderness of your prebends may be relieved in some measure, and through you also to blessed MarOf Sponheim.

In the same year a very great sedition arose among the citizens of Cologne. For when the rulers of the city had imposed burdensome extraordinary exactions on the community, the community itself rose up against the consulate, and, attacking one another in arms and war within the city itself, they fought; many on both sides were slain and killed.

The Cologne sedition.

[unclear].

1268.

In this year, which was the fourth of Peter our abbot, William, who, as we said above, had in the dissension been elected against Peter as abbot of this monastery by one part of the convent, but had been rejected by Werner, archbishop of Mainz, as having fewer and weaker votes in the election, after he had long troubled the monastery and the abbot, was seized by that same archbishop of Mainz while running about here and there, and was committed to prison, not to come out until his death. And that very disturbance ceased, which he had carried on against Peter for three years, with certain of the brethren adhering to him, though secretly, because of fear of the bishop.

William the pseudo-abbot is captured.

1269.

In this year a grave discord arose between Bishop Berthold and the counts of Henneberg, Castell, and Hohenlohe; at length, coming together for battle near the town in Franconia which is called Kitzingen, they fought fiercely. Many on both sides were slain, wounded, and captured.

The Bishop of Würzburg is at odds with certain counts.

In the same year the proscribed fugitives from the city of Cologne, having made a hidden passage underground and wishing to occupy and seize Cologne, inflicted many evils on the citizens; and, fighting against one another, they mutually caused themselves irrecoverable losses.

The Cologne sedition.

1270.

In this year, the sixth of Peter our abbot, since regular observance, alas, had too greatly [unclear], the monks now openly [unclear] proprietors [unclear]. Many on both sides were slain, wounded, and captured. The rest, for almost 130 years, had previously flourished in the present monastery in a sufficiently praiseworthy manner. Therefore the convent divided the total of its revenues into prebends, adding to these a certain common distribution, which they call “presences,” in the manner of secular canons, to the grave detriment of the present monastery and danger of souls.

The monks of this monastery withdraw from regular observance.

In the same year John, abbot, and the convent of the monastery of St. [unclear] at Nida, of our order, in the diocese of Cologne, sold to the chapters of Mainz, of the greater church and of Blessed Mary the Virgin at the Steps, the villages Drechtingshausen, upper and lower Heimbach, and Weiler, with their boundaries, and part of the castle of Reichenstein, with the people, land, property, lordship, buildings, vineyards, possessions, cultivated and uncultivated lands, jurisdiction, and actions of every kind, with all rights, appurtenances, and revenues in the aforesaid villages, in the castle of Reichenstein itself, and in all the adjoining bounds, for 1,423 marks of Cologne denarii, as appears in the letters drawn up concerning this sale, whose date is the aforesaid year, the eighth day before the Kalends of October.

Concerning the sale of Drechtingshausen.

Today Drockshaufen.

Also in the same year Gottfried, lord of Eppenstein, and his son Gottfried sold the village called Flersheim, with fields, vineyards, courts, meadows, pastures, waters, mills, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, with the people dwelling there or wishing to return who had transferred themselves to other places and had an inheritance there, with the knights, the boys of the knights from Johann Venator excepted, for 1,500 marks, drawing up letters concerning it, whose date is as follows: Done in the year of the Lord 1370, on the third feria after Dominica Indica.

Flersheim is sold and the church [unclear].

[unclear] our court in Weiller [unclear].

[unclear] they resigned to the monastery, which, having been distributed to the villagers in small portions, were leased for an annual rent.

1271.

In the seventh year of his rule Peter, abbot of this monastery, bought back the goods in Praumweil for 200 marks; from them he made a court and leased it to farmers for an annual rent.

The Bishop of Speyer dies.

In the same year Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, died in the church of Buden [unclear].

In the same year Henry, bishop of Speyer, died; Frederick of Bolanden, his sister’s son, succeeding him on the fourth Nones of March, presided for almost thirty years.

The Bishop of Speyer dies. Sponheim.

... was made with Count Simon, after the death of Siger the monk, who was the chief and head of the whole disturbance; namely, that the division of revenues once made between abbot and convent, as we have said before, should henceforth remain, and that the monks should be bound each year to render an account to the abbot of receipts and expenses. The abbot himself also, lest he be able to alienate anything without consulting his convent, is in every way similarly bound to render an account to the convent each year; and neither the abbot without the consent of the convent, nor the convent without the consent of the abbot, shall presume to sell or alter anything.

In the same year noted above, Ortwin, the fourteenth prior of this monastery, died. Prior Ortwin dies. This division of revenues between abbot and convent was greatly displeasing to him, and with all his strength he labored to prevent it from being made, or to revoke it once made; but he was able to accomplish little, although he brought upon himself the hatred of all the brothers. After him Megenhard, a monk, son of John, knight of Weinsheim, was appointed fifteenth prior; he presided in that office for eighteen years. Megenhard, prior [unclear].

1277.

In the thirteenth year of our abbot Peter, Count Simon of Sponheim, our advocate, died. Count Simon of Sponheim dies. He left two sons, John and Henry, about whom we shall speak more fully in the following year.

In the same year Hermann, son of King Rudolf, was drowned in the Rhine and buried at Basel, not without many tears from his mother.

1278.

In the fourteenth year of our abbot Peter, John and Henry, counts of Sponheim, brothers, sons of Count Simon, of whom we spoke above, had a serious quarrel with each other. Discord among the brothers, counts of Sponheim. John was the elder by birth, to whom his father had left the county of Sponheim to govern, a spirited and steadfast man; since he yielded to his brother Henry in nothing, he made him his enemy and adversary. And so Count Henry, brother of John, betook himself to Werner, archbishop of Mainz, and entrusted himself to his protection; he received a fief of twenty marks of Aachen denarii for annual service, but the castle called Böckelheim, with the adjacent castle-villages there, with revenues of eighty marks, to the grave loss of the county, he sold to the aforesaid archbishop for 1,300 marks of Aachen denarii, as is clear from the letters of sale which he delivered to the archbishop, whose tenor follows.

I, Henry, a noble man, son of the late Count Simon of Sponheim, by the tenor of the present document publicly acknowledge and wish it to come to the knowledge of all, that I have sold my castle of Böckelheim, together with the castle-villages now held there in fief, with the castle-fief there, and revenues of eighty marks, with the consent of Cunegund, my wife, to whom the same castle had been assigned as a marriage-gift, by joint hand, to my lord Werner, archbishop of the church of Mainz, to be possessed in perpetuity as property, for [unclear] marks of Aachen denarii, to be paid at fixed terms, with sureties appointed for me for the same, as is more fully contained in the letters of the same lord archbishop drawn up concerning this matter; promising [unclear] the archbishop of the aforesaid church concerning the castle and its goods for the space of one year and one day, as shall be just and customary, [unclear]. And because the aforesaid lord archbishop has acquired for me, for 400 marks of the aforesaid money, in [unclear] of his castle-fief of the church of Mainz, at Olm or Bingen, the choice having been given to me of selecting a residence in one of these places, I declare and protest that I am bound, after those two hundred marks have been paid to me, to convert them into goods situated at Olm or Bingen, from which they will be able to have revenues of twenty marks annually, or to show to the same lord archbishop, from my goods which I possess by right of ownership, revenues of twenty marks, receiving them from him in the name of the church of Mainz as a castle-fief, to be held. Furthermore, if it happens that the aforesaid lord archbishop has war on my account with Count John of Sponheim, my brother, and [unclear] has stood by him in pursuit of my right, I will accept absolutely no settlement from that count without the knowledge and consent of the same lord archbishop. And he likewise promised me that he would do this. In testimony and firmer assurance of this, I have caused the present letters to be written and fortified by the protection of my seal. I also, Cunegund, wife of the aforesaid nobleman, lacking a seal of my own, in testimony and evidence of my consent, have asked that these letters be sealed with the seal of Lucardis my mother. Given and enacted at Mainz in the year of the Lord 1278, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.

Count John, gravely offended, conceived a hostile mind against his brother and the archbishop; and since he could not obtain from the prelate Werner, either by prayers or threats, the aforesaid castle of Böckelheim, a portion of his paternal inheritance, he resolved to attack the matter by arms. Thus, having become the public foe and enemy of the archbishop, he inflicted much damage on the church of Mainz, by himself and through his men.

1279.

In the fifteenth year of our abbot Peter, a fierce war between Werner, archbishop of Mainz...

Chronicle of Trithemius

to us, over all our goods situated within the bounds of the village of Welgesheim; she freely conferred them upon our chapel of St. George in Dalen, and, in view of pious devotion, assigned them in the name of a dowry. We, in consideration of her kindness, grant to the same Hedwig and to her heirs, by hereditary right forever, the right of patronage, that is, presentation to that same chapel, in this manner: that the aforesaid lady Hedwig, lord Wilderic her son, or the senior heir of the same Wilderic who shall exist at the time, shall confer the said chapel upon, or present to it, one monk-priest chosen in our convent; and he, with the permission of his abbot granted, shall receive the said revenues, [unclear] the chapel and divine services. Given in the year of the Lord 1296. But after 175 years the heir of the aforesaid Hedwig resigned the right of patronage into the hands of Johann of Kulenhausen, abbot, in favor of the new reform, as we shall say in its place.

In the same year Manigold, bishop of Würzburg, died. Andreas, born of Gundelfingen, succeeded him and presided for 22 years; he had many disputes with his citizens, from whom he received and endured many injuries.

1297.

Adolf, king of the Romans, puffed up with excessive pride, stirred up many conflicts and wars throughout every land, disturbing the peace. For at his command Hermann, count of Geroldseck, and a certain other count, appointed provincial prefects in Alsace, were most troublesome to Conrad of Lichtenberg, bishop of Strasbourg, and to all the inhabitants of Alsace, and inflicted many losses. Provoked at last by such injuries, the aforesaid bishop, and also the citizens of Strasbourg, the counts of Lichtenberg, the counts of Zweibrücken, the count of Holloch, together with many other princes, counts, cities, and nobles, unanimously conspired against King Adolf, incited by the excessive insolence of him and his men; nor did they desist from the purpose they had begun until, after many princes had been brought to the same opinion, they finally cast him out of the kingdom, as we shall say in the following year.

1298.

Sifrid, archbishop of Cologne, died and was buried in the church of Bonn. Wichbold, dean of the greater church there, succeeded him. Bohemund, archbishop of Trier, because of his old age, soon took him as coadjutor; this same Bohemund did not live long.

In the same year, when King Adolf was excessively weakening the Empire, nourishing discords and wars, burdening the people with unusual taxes, and despising the princes, Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, together with certain other princes, summoned from Austria to Mainz the duke, son of the late Rudolf, king of the Romans, promising that, once Adolf had been removed, he should be elected king of the Romans. When he had heard this, he came to the Rhine with many princes and a very great army, having on his side Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, Wichbold, archbishop of Cologne, Bohemund, archbishop of Trier, Conrad, bishop of Strasbourg, and also the bishop of Constance, the counts of Lichtenberg, Ochsenstein, Freiburg, Holloch, Zweibrücken, the landgrave of Alsace, and many other princes from Austria, Hungary, Bohemia, Carinthia, and various other provinces. The bishop of Strasbourg brought to Albert's aid against Adolf 80 armed horsemen and footmen. The people of Strasbourg, moreover, sent in his aid four thousand armed men, both horse and foot, who received him at Freiburg with great honor. Hearing this, King Adolf gathered a great army and besieged Rubiacum, but withdrew with the matter unfinished; going to Speyer, he waited to see what the princes gathered at Mainz would decide to do against him.

Meanwhile Albert came to Mainz with very great power, with no one resisting him, and found the leading princes of the Empire assembled. There, therefore, on the vigil of St. John the Baptist, the princes deposed Adolf from the kingdom on account of his grave offenses and unanimously elected Albert king of the Romans, promising obedience, fidelity, and assistance against all adversaries. When this had been done, Albert, the new king, went out from Mainz and with his victorious army came to the town called Alzey, three miles from Worms toward Kreuznach; there, with his princes, having pitched their tents, he settled, and he laid waste the whole town except for the castle attached to it. Adolf, however, having gathered a great army of warriors from the cities sworn to him, Speyer, Worms, Oppenheim, and Frankfurt, together with his princes, Rudolf, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, his son-in-law, and also the count of Eisenberg and many others, withdrew to Oppenheim and for ten days awaited the aid of the friends to whom he had written. But when ten days had passed, before the aid of his friends Chronicle of Trithemius 290

[unclear] of Mainz and John, count of Sponheim, near Gentzingen, not far from Sprenglingen, took place on account of the castle of Beckelnheim, which Henry, brother of John, count of Sponheim, had sold, as we have said, to the same archbishop without his brother’s consent; on both sides many were killed, wounded, and captured. Among others there was a certain butcher of Creutzennacht, called Michael Mort, a very brave and exceedingly bold man, who fought so strongly on the side of the count, his lord, against the adversaries that, like another Maccabee, he deserved for himself an enduring name of praise among posterity. For, standing in the midst of the enemy, brandishing his sword on the right and on the left, he attacked them so strongly that he alone killed more than twenty and made a way for himself through their midst with the sword-point. At length, overcome by the multitude of enemies and wounded in the feet, he fell to the ground; then, immediately recovering his strength and standing on his knees, since he could not rise, defending himself strongly and brandishing his sword fearlessly around him, he struck down five more and wounded several of those standing around. Finally, however, having no helper, since his own men had begun in part to flee, he died gloriously. In memory of such courage, a stone was set up in that same place with his image carved on it, and is seen there down to the present day. Moreover, although the battle was fought for a long time with uncertain fortune, nevertheless the victory at last fell to the archbishop. There, on the side of Count John, the count of the Rhine, the count of Veringen, with many other nobles, were captured by the same archbishop; and John himself, count of Sponheim, fleeing with the help of a horse, barely escaped. He was lame in one foot, and when he was fighting bravely with his own hand, surrounded by the enemy, he was seized. Seeing this, the aforesaid Michael Mort, with the other butchers of Creutzennacht, boldly, as we have said, rushed upon the enemy and freed his lord by his own blood. For so great a benefit the count afterward rewarded the butchers in Creutzennacht with a special privilege of his own. Having won this victory, the archbishop plundered all the count’s villages round about and burned many of them. His knights too, thirsting for plunder, spared neither monasteries nor churches. For, entering the nearby monastery called Schwabenheim, they plundered it, and, robbing the courts and buildings around it, set them on fire and inflicted many losses on the brethren.

In the same year Werner, the aforesaid archbishop, took the castle called Rheinberg and destroyed it utterly, because of the robberies and depredations that were being committed from it.

In the same year also Henry, count of Veldentz, entered into a perpetual alliance with Werner, archbishop of Mainz, as is clear from the letter that follows, whose tenor is as follows:

I, Henry, count of Veldentz, make known to all that, in regard to the fidelity which I owe to the church of Mainz, of which I am steward and vassal, and from which I hold ample fiefs, desiring to remain forever in devotion and service to the same church, I promise in good faith, for myself and my heirs who ought to succeed me in the county of Veldentz, that I and my aforesaid heirs will give aid to lord Werner, archbishop, and to the churches of Mainz, against all who injure them, and will assist them perpetually. The archbishop himself promised to do the same in turn for me and my heirs, as is more fully contained in his open letters. In testimony of this matter and for its perpetual validity, I have caused my seal to be appended to the present letters. Given and enacted in the year of the Lord 1330, on the calends of September.

In the sixteenth year of Peter our abbot, Albertus Magnus, formerly bishop of Regensburg, died, a man most learned in every respect [unclear], both in the church of the saints and in secular [unclear]. William, count of Jülich, having secretly entered the city of Aachen with 468 armed men, with the purpose and intention of taking the city, was killed by the citizens together with his first-born son and all his armed men. In vengeance for this deed afterward, when negotiations for an agreement were held, the people of Aachen were compelled to resign to the count of Jülich for all time the right of appointing the provost in the church of Aachen, together with the receipt of the third part of all offerings accruing in the church of the blessed Mary ever virgin there.

1271.

In the seventeenth year of Peter our abbot, Rudolf, king of the Romans, after matters had gone prosperously in Austria and Bohemia, held a solemn assembly first at Nuremberg and afterward at Frankfurt. All the castles in which robbers and plunderers of the royal road kept themselves were destroyed. Afterward he moved an army against the count of Burgundy, and first surrounded the city of Besançon in order to obtain it. The count, advancing against him with a great army, was defeated and swore submission to the king. Returning from Burgundy, the king [unclear] Columbariam, Thuregium, Beronam, and HaChronicle of Trithemius

and with the intention of setting a new abbot over themselves; and, the grace of the Holy Spirit having been invoked, as is customary, they unanimously elected as shepherd of their souls a venerable old man named Dietlib, a monk of this convent. Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, confirmed him and had him blessed by his vicar-general in pontificals. Dietlib, ordained abbot, governed this monastery for ten years and six months.

He was a native of the city of Trier, born of honorable parents; having been set to letters in childhood, he advanced not a little in learning as he grew older. When he had become more mature, with progress in his studies, at the age of twenty he was received into the chancery of Henry, bishop of Trier, in which he distinguished himself wisely for some years, and gained by experience much wisdom in conducting curial business. After this, John, Count of Sponheim, having tested the man’s prudence, took him as his chancellor and chief secretary of his affairs, and relied greatly on his counsels as those of a prudent and experienced man. Finally, when he was held by a very severe illness of fevers, he vowed a vow of religion to the Lord; he recovered, and so became a monk under John the Second. When John died three years later, he succeeded in his place by the election of the brothers.

He was a good and pious man, very experienced in business; understanding very well that private property was not permitted to monks, he at once, at the beginning of his rule, cut out this vice by the roots, so that, communal fellowship having been restored, the religion of this monastery seemed in no small part to have been brought back to its former state, although not all other things were reformed to regular purity, because at that time things which we weigh were held in less esteem.

  1. Dietlib the abbot, in the first year of his rule, deposed John, the sixteenth prior of this monastery of Sponheim, because he seemed to be somewhat opposed to the holy reform and to the renunciation of private property. John, deposed from the priorship, bore it patiently; not long surviving, he rested in the Lord in the same year. After him Dietlib the abbot appointed as the seventeenth prior Albert, a monk of holy conduct, whose father was John, knight of Bleinich, and whose mother was Elizabeth, daughter of Henry, knight of Sponheim.

This Albert, who [unclear], was a man sufficiently learned, sufficiently inward in morals and conduct, most devout in prayer and compunction, who never consented to the pursuits of the wicked but always strongly opposed them, although he benefited others little. Once appointed prior, he took care with all zeal always to obey the commands of the rule and of the abbot, to cut out the vice of private property by the roots, and, as far as he could, he constrained the monks by word and example to the observance of the rule. Among others he had as a notable imitator his sister’s son Henry, who later succeeded him in the priorship. He himself presided in the priorship for four years.

In the same year Bohemund, archbishop of Trier, died on the fourth ides of November and was buried in the monastery of Henrad, of the Cistercian order. This Bohemund built from the foundations a new castle at Neumagen near Trittenheim. After him Diether of Nassau, brother of King Adolf, neither elected nor postulated, was substituted, ordained, and sent to Trier as archbishop by Pope Boniface VIII, out of hatred for King Albert; he presided for nearly eight years. He was of the order of Friars Preachers. On all the days of his pontificate he opposed Albert, king of the Romans, but, being far inferior in strength, he could do nothing against him. He did not rule usefully; therefore he stirred up the hatred of all against the people of Trier.

In the same year, on the vigil of Saint James the Apostle, Emicho, bishop of Worms, died and was buried in his greater church of Worms, in the monastic habit, as they say. Eberwin of Cronenberg succeeded him in the episcopate and presided for three years and nine months; at the urging of his citizens he consented that [unclear] from the community should be admitted to the council of the senate. In his time the monastery of nuns of the order of the Friars Preachers was founded at Liebenau outside the walls of Worms, not far from Neuhausen toward the south, by a certain citizen of Worms called Jacob Engelman; he himself confirmed the deed.

  1. In this year, which was the second of Abbot Dietlib, Willichco, brother of the wife of Count Henry of Sponheim, came to the religious life, a noble man, wise and very religious. Hearing the good reputation of Abbot Dietlib, namely that he had taken care to reform this monastery so diligently, he became a monk under him and at length succeeded him in the abbacy; concerning him it will be said below in its place.

In the same year, when Pope Boniface VIII had instituted the jubilee at Rome, an infinite multitude Sponheim.

And he took the rebellious cities of Hagenau, the authors of the rebellion being partly killed and partly proscribed; and all the land was quiet before him in good peace.

In the same year King Rudolf, established at Mainz in the month of December with many princes, made peace between Werner, archbishop of Mainz, with Count Heinrich of Sponheim on the one side, and Johann, count of Sponheim, Heinrich’s brother, with Heinrich his son and those adhering to him on the other side, concerning all wars and battles and damages had by reason of the castle of Böckelheim, as is clear from the letters of settlement that follow:

The war between the count of Sponheim and the archbishop of Mainz, which they had waged on account of the castle of Böckelheim, is settled.

Letters of settlement.

Rudolf, by the grace of God king of the Romans, ever Augustus, we make known to all and each who shall read these letters or hear them read, that we have wholly, perfectly, and perpetually concluded, reconciled, and pacified all discord, suit, and contention which existed between our beloved princes, Werner, archbishop of Mainz, his church, Heinrich, brother of the count of Sponheim, with all their friends and helpers, parties on the other side, concerning all deeds committed and perpetrated during that whole time in which discord began and endured between them, in this manner.

First, the aforesaid Count Johann, with his wife and his brother Eberhard, for himself and all his heirs, renounced forever before us the castle of Böckelheim, [unclear] with its men and goods, which the aforesaid archbishop had bought, as is contained in the letters of division made between Count Johann and Heinrich his brother; and under my judgment, under which the said goods are known to stand, he must do each and every thing which the order of law requires with warranty. Count Heinrich ought to be content there with his third part, just as he has held it up to now, and the archbishop, together with the church of Mainz, shall remain in quiet possession of the two parts which Heinrich, brother of Count Johann, sold to him, without molestation from any of them. All captives, after making the oath of peace as is customary, have been set free. Johann and Heinrich, counts of Sponheim, swore upon the holy Gospel of God that they would firmly observe all the aforesaid things. But if the aforesaid counts presume to violate this our concord and peaceful settlement to the injury of the archbishop and the church of Mainz, then we, together with the cities of the realm, Frankfurt, Friedberg, Wetzlar, Gelnhausen, Oppenheim, Wesel, and Boppard, and he with us, will give aid and assistance against them to the often-mentioned archbishop and his church. Frederick, count of Leiningen, nor his son, nor Eberhard, count of Katzenelnbogen, nor Emicho, count of Leiningen, nor any of them, must give aid against these things to the aforesaid counts Johann and Heinrich against the archbishop and the church of Mainz. We have made this settlement of concord and peace with the consent and good will of the aforesaid archbishop of Mainz and of the counts Johann and Heinrich of Sponheim, and at their instance we have caused our royal seal, together with their seals and those of Frederick, count of Leiningen, and Eberhard, count of Katzenelnbogen, to be appended to these letters. Done at Mainz in the year of the Lord 1281, on the feast of St. Lucy.

Captives released.

1282.

In the eighteenth year of our abbot Peter, Johann, count of Sponheim, who in the preceding year, as we have said, had fought against Werner, archbishop of Mainz, at Gensingen, now entered into a perpetual treaty with him and promised assistance against all who should injure him, except Gottfried, count of Sayn, Heinrich, count of Starkenburg, Eberhard, count of Katzenelnbogen, who was the brother of his wife, Emicho and Frederick the younger, counts of Leiningen, as well as the count of Zweibrücken and the landgrave of Hesse, with whom he had previously been allied, as is clear from the letters drawn up concerning this, given at Mainz in the year of the Lord 1281, on the third day before the Nones of May; because they are both too lengthy and contribute nothing to our purpose, we have deliberately passed them over.

A treaty between Count Johann of Sponheim and the archbishop.

In the same year Rudolf took and destroyed the robbers’ castles Reichenstein and Schöneck.

Two castles destroyed.

In the same year, on the Monday after the feast of holy Easter, the citizens of Mainz killed all the Jews who were in the city of Mainz because of a certain enormous crime, and usurped all their goods for themselves. A similar blow followed against almost all the other Jews throughout all Germany.

Slaughter of the Jews.

That year was so temperate that around the feast of the martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, that is, 2 June, the vineyards generally everywhere in these lands had flowering clusters.

The year temperate.

1283.

In the nineteenth year of our abbot Peter, on the day of St. Potentiana the virgin, the counts of Henneberg led an army against Berthold, bishop of Würzburg, burned the town called Schwarzbach, and plundered the monasteries of our order there outside the walls.

War at Schwarzbach.

In the same year Pope Martin IV sent a legate from his side into Germany, the bishop of Tusculum, who, coming to Würzburg in the presence of King Rudolf and many [unclear].

Apostolic legation. Chronicle of Trithemius

[he] held a solemn council of princes, bishops, abbots, prelates, and nobles. There, among other things, the pope began most urgently to demand a tenth penny from the clergy, and the king from the whole people of the kingdom, with many princes giving their consent. But Sifrid, bishop of Cologne, and Henry, bishop of Trier, most steadfastly opposed and contradicted this unusual and excessively burdensome exaction, and made the efforts of both come to nothing.

1284.

In the twentieth year of Peter our abbot, on the second day of the month of April, Wernher, archbishop of Mainz, died, and was buried in the church of Mainz. The see of Mainz was vacant for three years, two men having been elected in dissension, namely Peter, canon of Basel, provost of the greater church, who had once been physician to Rudolf, king of the Romans, and Gerard of Eppstein, archdeacon of Trier. After they had contended for the bishopric at the apostolic see for three years, at last Pope Honorius IV, setting both aside, raised Henry of the Order of Minors, bishop of Basel, to be archbishop of Mainz. But the aforesaid Peter the physician he appointed in place of the said Henry as bishop of the church of Basel.

In the same year Berthold, bishop of Wurzburg, died. Mangold of Neuenburg succeeded him and presided for twelve years; he was the forty-third in the order of the bishops of Wurzburg.

1285.

In the twenty-first year of Peter our abbot, the church of the Blessed Virgin Mary at the Steps in Mainz was burned. In the same year the canons of the church of Wurzburg, together with all the clergy, were violently expelled by the citizens on the sixth ides of January, and were stripped of all their goods.

In these times there came a certain unknown man, very like Emperor Frederick, who said that he was Emperor Frederick; and first indeed in Meissen, then in Wetzlar and in other [unclear], at last, after Pope Honorius IV had set both aside, Henry of the Order of Minors, bishop of Basel, was raised to be archbishop of Mainz. But the aforesaid Peter the physician he appointed in place of the said Henry as bishop of the church of Basel.

In the same year Louis, Count Palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, died, and was buried in the monastery of Furstenfeld, which he had founded [unclear]; he left two sons, Rudolf the count palatine, and Louis, afterwards emperor of the Romans. Rudolf, the firstborn, begot Rudolf, Rupert, and Adolf, of whom mention will be made in their place.

1286.

In the twenty-second year of Peter our abbot, Pope Honorius IV, as we said above, after Peter and Gerard had been contending at the apostolic see over the archbishopric of Mainz, set them aside, and ordained Henry, bishop of Basel, of the Order of Minors, as archbishop of Mainz. He presided for one year, eleven months, and five days. But Peter the provost was made bishop of Basel, and that long-lasting and destructive dissension for the church came to an end.

1287.

In the twenty-third year of Peter our abbot, the Jews secretly seized a certain boy named Wernher, born in a little village called Wamraidt, without his parents’ knowledge, and took him with them to Wesel. On the thirteenth calends of May, piercing him with needles in order to draw blood, they cruelly killed him after many torments. His body, placed in a certain chapel situated on the mountain in the town of Bacharach, is shown to the present day incorrupt and whole in memory of his martyrdom; it is said that immediately at the beginning of his burial it shone with many miracles.

In the same year Frederick, bishop of Worms, died in the sixth year of his pontificate. Simon of Schoneck succeeded him in the bishopric and presided for four years. This Bishop Simon, in the first year of his episcopate, consecrated the church and monastery of nuns of the Order of Preachers near Worms, called Hochheim, then newly built by Rudolf the knight.

1288.

In the twenty-fourth year of Peter our abbot, William the monk died; having been elected in dissension against Peter, and because of the many evils he had done, he had been captured by Wernher, bishop of Mainz, and imprisoned for nearly twenty years, as has been said.

In the same year, on the fifteenth calends of April, brother Henry, archbishop of Mainz, died and was buried in the greater church at Mainz. After his death two men were again elected in dissension, namely Gerard of Eppstein, canon of Mainz and archdeacon of Trier, who had been elected before with Peter, as we said, after the death of Wernher; and Emmerich of Schoneck, scholasticus of Mainz. But while these things were being done at Mainz, Pope Honorius having died, the apostolic see [unclear].

Sponheimense.

The Apostolic See was vacant for ten months, so that the matter of this election could not easily be settled either in those parts or at Rome. Meanwhile Henry, archbishop of Trier, died, and the aforesaid Gerard, against Bohemond, was also postulated as archbishop by one party of the canons of Trier. At length, when he had gone to Rome with a double election, he was ordained archbishop of Mainz by Pope Nicholas IV, and Bohemond, succeeding Henry, presided as archbishop of Trier for sixteen years: a magnanimous and most prudent man, since he vigorously accomplished many things for the advantage and benefit of his church.

In the same year the duke of Limburg died, and [there was a dispute with?] Reinald, count of Guelders, over that same duchy of Limburg, which each of them labored exceedingly to claim for himself by hereditary right, as the nearer legitimate heir. At last it came to war, and the duke of Brabant had with him his brother Godfrey, Adolf count of Berg, Henry count of Windeck, Walram count of Julich, his brother Gerard, Eberhard count of the Mark with his brother, also the bishop of Liege, the count of Looz, the citizens of Cologne, and many other noble and very brave men. With Reinald, count of Guelders, were Siegfried archbishop of Cologne, Henry count of Luxembourg and his brother Walram, John lord in Limburg, Henry count of Westerburg, likewise the count of Falkenburg, and several others. When battle was joined, the duke of Brabant obtained the victory, captured the count of Guelders, and secured many castles and lordships for his release. Siegfried archbishop of Cologne was also captured, in the custody of the count of Berg. Since he did not wish to redeem himself with money, he was detained for seven years, until at last, compelled by necessity, he redeemed himself from captivity at a great price.

1289.

In the twenty-fifth year of our abbot Peter, King Rudolf again moved an army into Burgundy. First he captured the city of Payerne, enclosed by a siege. Then he powerfully subjected to his power the count of Burgundy himself, also the count of Montbeliard and the count of Savoy, and made them obedient to him in all things.

In the same year there died Emicho count of Leiningen, Diether son of Eberhard count of Katzenelnbogen, Walther count of Geroldseck, Gerlach the elder lord of Limburg, the count of Uechingen, and the count of Reineck by the Black Forest; at one and the same time they all perished miserably together.

In the same year also Siegfried archbishop of Cologne, as we have said, was held in the chains of Adolf count of Berg, and for seven years was treated quite miserably.

1290.

In this year Peter, the eighth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, after he had presided for twenty-five years and four months, died on the sixth day before the Nones of May, at an advanced age, being more than sixty-eight years old, and was buried in the cloister of the monastery before the entrance to the church. He was a very active man, but less concerned with inward spiritual matters. He was the first to allow the monks of this monastery portions of revenues, although later he wished to revoke this, but did not succeed. When he was about to die, however, after making a most devout confession, he said that he feared the future judgment of God for nothing more than that, by his agency, the greatest occasion for private property seemed to have been left to the monks of this monastery. Nevertheless, as much as lay in him, even when already placed at the point of death, he revoked with constant perseverance all that had been done concerning the division of revenues, contrary to the Rule of our Holy Father Benedict; but he accomplished nothing. For the monks, having once obtained permission for private possessions, so to speak, paid no heed to the words of a dying man.

In these times a great dissension arose for a slight cause between John count of Sponheim and Henry count of Veldenz.

For the count of Sponheim had caused a certain man from the county of Veldenz to be hanged, who had stolen a considerable sum of money in the town of Kreuznach and, carrying it away secretly, had hidden it in a small village of the aforesaid count of Veldenz. When the money was disclosed by torture, the count of Sponheim wished it to be returned to the man from whom it had been taken; on the contrary, the count of Veldenz asserted that it belonged to his jurisdiction and was in no way to be returned to anyone, because it had been found in his domain. And so, when dissension arose, they were close to attacking each other in war, had not Gerard archbishop of Mainz intervened and restored peace, adjudging that the money ought to be restored to the injured party.

The Roman See is vacant.

The bishop of Trier dies.

Gerard becomes archbishop of Mainz; Bohemond, of Trier.

The duke of Limburg without children.

War over the duchy of Limburg.

The duke of Brabant with his allies.

The count of Guelders and his allies.

The duke of Brabant gains the victory.

The count of Guelders captive.

The king’s second expedition into Burgundy.

Death of the [unclear] counts.

The archbishop of Cologne [unclear].

Peter, abbot of Sponheim, dies.

What sort of man Peter was.

He renewed private property.

Dissension between the count of Sponheim and [the count] of Veldenz. Money that had been taken away ought to be restored to him from whom it was taken, not to the magistrate of the place where it was found or taken. Chronicle of Trithemius concerning John the Second, ninth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, who presided for seven years and eleven months, and concerning various events of this time.

After the death of lord Peter, the eighth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, in the aforesaid year, which was the year 1300 of the Lord’s Nativity, the brothers, left without a shepherd, came together on 3 May with the intention of appointing a shepherd over themselves. After much counsel had first been taken and mature deliberation held, they unanimously elected as abbot John, a monk and cellarer of this monastery. Not long afterward Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, confirmed him when he was presented to him, and in the same year, on the Sunday after the feast of St Urban the Pope, had him ordained at Mainz by Peter, bishop of Suden, his vicar-general in pontificals. John, elected, confirmed, and ordained as abbot, presided over this monastery, as is customary, for seven years and eleven months. He came from Sobernheim, born of honorable parents of middling fortune; when he was still a boy in his twelfth year he was handed over to the monastery by his own parents. He conducted himself fairly well before the brothers according to the customs of that time; he was appointed cellarer by Abbot Peter, and succeeded him, as we have said, in the governance. According to his capacity he ruled temporal affairs fairly well.

1291.

In the first year of his rule Abbot John renewed our inner church with four altars, and had it consecrated anew by Peter of Suden, as we have said, vicar-general in pontificals of Archbishop Gerard, as is clear from his letters.

Copy.

Our church was dedicated anew.

To all who shall see these presents, Peter, by divine mercy bishop of Suden, vicar of the reverend father and lord Gerard, by the grace of God archbishop of Mainz, greeting in the Lord. Since in the year of the Lord 1291, on 8 April, we [unclear] the church of the monastery of Sponheim, of the Order of St Benedict, with four altars for divine worship to be performed perpetually. We granted to all the faithful of Christ one year, [unclear] coming to the altars, forty days, [unclear] in each of the altars, at the time of the dedication, namely on the Sunday nearest after the Nativity of blessed Mary ever Virgin, through all the following octaves, to endure forever; adding also, by special grace, to all benefactors of the aforesaid monastery, after the manner of the venerable father lord Hugh, cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, an indulgence of forty days, likewise to endure. Given, etc.

But here it must be noted that for reasonable causes the day of the aforesaid dedication of this church, with its indulgences, after forty-six years, at the instance of Abbot Wilhelm, was transferred by Albert, bishop of [unclear], vicar of Henry, bishop of Mainz, to the Sunday nearest after the feast of St Martin.

In the same year King Rudolf of the Romans, holding an assembly of princes at Frankfurt, labored with many entreaties and promises to induce the princes to elect his son Albert, duke of Austria, as king of the Romans. The princes entirely refused to do this, saying that they already had a king, and that the kingdom could not support two, since the commonwealth seemed already sufficiently burdened by one.

1292.

In the second year of our Abbot John, on the octave of the Division of the Apostles, Rudolf, count of Habsburg, king of the Romans, died. He was honorably buried in the church of Speyer with his predecessors, kings and emperors. The empire was vacant for one year. In the same year Gerard, bishop of Mainz, held a synod in Aschaffenburg, with his suffragan bishops present: those of Eichstätt, Speyer, Augsburg, Würzburg, Bamberg, and Hildesheim, and many abbots, prelates, and clerics of the province of Mainz. When the council had been dissolved and each man was arranging to return to his own place, Frederick of Bolanden, bishop of Speyer, was captured on the road near the Main, at the village called Kelsterbach, by Gerard, son of Count Eberhard of Katzenelnbogen, provost of the church of Utrecht, and was taken into a fortification; but at last, after an agreement intervened, he was released.

In the same year the princes assembled at Frankfurt around the feast of Philip [and James?] for the election of a new king of the Romans. After many negotiations had first been held, Adolf, count of Nassau, was elected king of the Romans. He ruled for six years, and was deposed by the princes of the empire, as we shall say later. From these things it is concluded that King Rudolf died not in this year but in the preceding year; otherwise the empire would not have been vacant for one year, as the more important chronographers report.

1293. Sponheim.

1293.

In this year the city of Worms, burning by accidental fire, was for the most part consumed. In the same year, on the day of St. Othmar the abbot, Simon, bishop of Worms, died and was buried in the monastery of Schönau. After his death Gerhard, son of the Hirsute Count, was elected; he died before his confirmation. After him Eberhard of Strahlenberg was again elected; he presided over the church of Worms scarcely ten months. When he too had died, Emicho of Badenberg, provost of the major church, succeeded in the episcopate, elected unanimously on the day after St. Thomas the Apostle, and he presided for four years and one month. This Emicho, while he was still provost of the church of Worms, founded a chapel in the suburb of the city in honor of the most blessed virgin Mary, mother of God. In it he established twelve prebendary priests, who were to discharge the hours there in honor of God and the Virgin. Afterwards, when he was made bishop, he confirmed what he had previously done, and joined greater benefices to those already granted. From the first foundation of this same chapel, many miracles and signs are reported to have been performed there by the merits of blessed Mary ever virgin, so that down to the present day there has been a great concourse of faithful peoples to that same church; through their alms and offerings it grew, in the course of time, into the form in which it is now seen.

1294.

In the fourth year of our abbot John, Megenhard, prior of this monastery of Sponheim, the fifteenth in the order of priors from the beginning of its foundation, died in the eighteenth year of his priorate and was buried in the cloister of the monastery with his brothers. In the priorate he was succeeded as sixteenth by John, a monk of this convent, originally from Weinsheim, and he presided in it for nearly five years.

In these times a great quarrel arose between Philip, king of France, and Edward, king of England, which proceeded to a most savage war. The aforesaid king of England hired Adolf, king of the Romans, as an ally for one hundred thousand marks of silver; but Adolf, having received the money which he ought to have divided with the princes of the Empire, kept it alone against their will, and provoked them to the greatest indignation, so that none of them agreed to go with him to the aid promised by him to the king of England. Therefore king Adolf, confounded, was never able to come to the king of the English with the princes, as he had promised, nor alone with his own men at the proper time; and it was a very great disgrace both to that king of the Romans Adolf and to the whole Empire to have received so much money and disgracefully withheld the aid promised for it.

1295.

In the fifth year of our abbot, Albert, duke of Austria, son of the late king Rudolf, rose up strongly against Adolf, king of the Romans, and inflicted many losses on him. When Adolf had tried to depose him from his duchy, he could not, because Albert, favored by many princes and helped, defended himself stoutly.

In the same year Siegfried, archbishop of Cologne, after seven years of his captivity, had at last been released for a high price; [unclear] had detained [unclear], cast into prison and captive, until death, and did not wish to release him for any price, but repeatedly reproaching him said: “Now I shall teach you how you ought to hold an archbishop captive.” And when the count promised that he would return everything that he had extorted from him and would add much greater things if he were released, the archbishop answered: “Saint Peter, even without those things which you promise, can [unclear] his servants; therefore I pay no heed to your promises. You will die a captive.” And this was done. In the same year John, duke of Brabant, died in Hastelitz.

1296.

In the sixth year of our abbot, when the church of the holy martyr George in Dalen, formerly burned down and afterwards begun to be rebuilt, stood unfinished, a certain religious matron Hedwig, wife of the late Hermann, knight of Sponheim, forewarned by divine inspiration, completed it at her own expense and costs, and gave to the same monastery in perpetual possession her court in Winckelsheim with fields, house-sites, meadows, and all its revenues. In gratitude for this benefaction, Abbot John conferred on her and her heirs the right of patronage of the same chapel, yet on the condition that she must confer it on no one other than the senior monk of this monastery, as appears in the letters:

“In the name of the Lord. Amen. We, John by the grace of God abbot, John prior, and the whole convent of the monastery in Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Mainz, send greeting to all forever. Since Lady Hedwig, widow of Lord Hermann, of happy memory, knight of Sponheim, has bought and acquired thirty maldra of rye, by the Bingen measure, in perpetual annual revenues for [unclear]

The fire of Worms.

Three bishops of Worms died in one year.

Emicho, bishop of Worms.

The church of blessed Mary at Worms.

Megenhard the prior dies.

John succeeded.

Adolf the emperor, as a mercenary, promises service but does not perform it for the aforesaid king of England.

Albert the Austrian rises up against Adolf.

The count of Berg is captured by the archbishop of Cologne and dies in prison.

The duke of Brabant dies.

The church of St. George at Dalen.

Winckelsheim, today Welgesheim.

Copy. SPONHEIM. 297.

…[before] the aids of [his] friends had come, too inconsiderately and precipitately, unequal in strength, [Adolf] advanced to battle against Albert, between the village which is called Göllheim and the nuns' monastery named Rosenthal; there it was once sharply fought, and many fell on either side. King Adolf fought most bravely with his own hand, and, when victory now seemed to be approaching him, his [men] began to flee, and he himself was killed in the same place, and his son captured. There fell also in the same battle lord Otto of Oxenstein, the first captain in duke Albert's army; likewise the count of Eisenberg, supreme standard-bearer in king Adolf's army, and a most brave soldier, was killed. Counts, soldiers, and nobles also, more than sixty notable [men], fell in the same place. But the body of the slain king Adolf was buried in the aforesaid monastery of Rosenthal, until the times of Henry, king of Luxembourg, who ordered his bones to be entombed in the tombs of the kings in the church of Speyer. There are [those] who write that all those who conspired against king Adolf perished by an evil death. For they report that Albert himself, the usurper of the kingdom, was slain by his brother's son; the count of Holloch killed; Otto of Oxenstein (as we said) fell in war; the archbishop of Mainz, sitting on his chair, died unexpectedly; the count of Zweibrücken drowned in the water or bank called Blies; Conrad, bishop of Strasbourg, before Freiburg, slain by a sword by a certain peasant; the count of Leiningen made insane and frenzied; and almost all, by a similar kind of death, emigrated from this world. Albert, therefore, escaping victor, with his princes sets out for the city of Aachen, and there is consecrated king of the Romans by Wichbold, archbishop of Cologne. He reigned 10 years. He had as wife Elizabeth, daughter of Meinhard, count of Carinthia, who bore him 5 daughters and 6 sons; of whom these are the names. The first-born was Rudolf, king of Bohemia, who died in the year of the Lord [MCCCCLXX, as printed—recte c. 1307], buried at Prague. The second was Frederick, duke of Austria, who afterward was elected against Louis the Bavarian, the emperor; of whom it will be said in [its] place. The third was Leopold, duke of Austria, Styria, and Carinthia, who died in the year of the Lord [MCCXXXVI, as printed—recte 1326], buried in the monastery of Königsfeld. The fourth was Henry the duke, who died in the year of the Lord [MCCCCLIIII, as printed], leaving [his] wife Elizabeth, daughter of the count of Virneburg. The fifth was Albert the duke, who founded a monastery at Gaming, from whom the line of Maximilian, king of the Romans, descends. The sixth was Otto, duke of Austria, who had as wife a daughter of the duke of Bavaria, by name Elizabeth, and died in the year of the Lord 1344. But of the daughters, the first, by name Agnes, married Andrew, king of Hungary; he being dead without children, she again married the duke of Breslau. The second was Elizabeth, who married Frederick, duke of Lorraine, and bore him Rudolf, who [succeeded his] father. The third was Anna, who married Hermann of Brandenburg. The fourth was Catherine, betrothed to Henry of Luxembourg, the seventh king of the Romans; he being dead before the marriage, she was given to Rupert, king of Apulia, duke of Calabria, and died in the year of the Lord 1434 [as printed]. The fifth daughter, by name Jutta, married Udalric, count of Oettingen, and died in the year of the Lord 1424 [as printed].

In these times the citizens of Cologne, on account of suits and contentions which they had had with Sifrid, archbishop of Cologne, were under excommunication for 7 years, as many months, and nine days, and interdicted, so that through all that time the celebration of the divine [office] among them was suspended. Sifrid the archbishop being dead, Wichbold did not restrain the presumed license of the monks departing far from the integrity of regular observance, but permitted the division of revenues with pernicious private property, as he found [it].

ON DIETLIB, THE 10TH ABBOT OF THIS MONASTERY OF SPONHEIM; who presided 10 years and 6 months; and on the various deeds in these regions.

In the aforesaid year, John, abbot of this monastery, being dead and buried (as we said), the brothers assembled at the chapter-place the 4th [day before] the Kalends of April, in mind… Chronicle of Trithemius

which Johannes Trithemius, his successor, enlarged, and made into a fitting dwelling, raised to the form in which it is now seen.

1312.

In this year Peter, archbishop of Mainz, around the feast of All Saints came to the castle of Beckelnheim and stayed there for six days. Willicho, abbot of this monastery, approached him and, among other things, obtained confirmation of the indulgences granted by thirteen bishops at Rome at the time of the first Jubilee, as is clear in the letters, whose transcript we have placed above in its proper place.

In the same year Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, who at Rome [unclear], with his brother Henry VII, emperor of the Romans, fighting and doing battle in his own person, had accomplished many distinguished deeds, for the expenses incurred [unclear]; Boppard and Wesel were then pledged to the church of Trier.

Copy of the donation.

In the fourth year of Willicho, abbot of this monastery, the altar of Saints Nicholas and Catherine in our monastery of Sponheim was founded and endowed by Stephan, provost of the canons in Ravengiersburg, as appears in the letters given concerning this matter, reading as follows:

In the name of the Lord. Since every professor of the faith bearing the Christian name ought effectively to attend to those things that concern the praise and honor of God and increase the salvation of souls, we, Stephan, by the grace of God provost of the church of Ravengiersburg of the regular canons, in the diocese of Mainz, establish and ordain in the monastery of Sponheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, with the consent and free will of lord Willicho and the whole convent there, one mass to be celebrated every day in perpetuity upon the altar of blessed Nicholas and blessed Catherine by a secular priest, unless he is prevented by lawful causes. In this mass the priest shall hold remembrance and make memorials of our father Emelric, formerly a knight, of our mother Petrissa, and also of our brothers Lambert and Arnold, called Kindelen, formerly knights, and Emelric, formerly an esquire.

To this altar and to the priest serving it we freely give and assign our court at Roxheim, with all the goods and appurtenances of the same, so that the priest may enjoy the court, goods, and all appurtenances quietly and peacefully; we also assign to him in perpetuity one cartload of wine in the village of [Mandel?]. Careful provision has above all been made that through the said priest no prejudice be done to the pleban of the parish church in offerings or in any other dues. The same priest must also be present daily at high mass and vespers. If he transgresses disgracefully, he is to be corrected by the abbot who shall be in office at the time, with [unclear] reserved to the heirs.

We have reserved to ourselves the collation of the altar during our lifetime. After our death, however, Arnold called Kindelin, Emelric his brother, the daughter of our aforesaid brother, Arnold son of Bigela, our kinsman, and their nearer heirs, successively and in alternate turns, shall present. Yet we establish this: that after our death the first collation belongs to the aforesaid brothers Kindelin and Emelric. And so that each and all of the aforesaid things may be preserved with due force, we have had the present letters strengthened by the seal of the lords judges of Mainz, and by the seal of the lord abbot and the aforesaid convent, together with our seal. We also, the judges, at the petition of the aforesaid lord provost, have thought fit to append our seal to the present letters. These things were done in the year of the Lord 1313, on the third day before the Kalends of April.

The heirs gave the right of patronage to the abbot of this place.

The heirs of the aforesaid founders, namely Wilhelm of Lebenstein, Simon Booss of Waldeck, and Hartmann of [Halberg?], knights, together with the consent of their wives, transferred in perpetuity to Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery, for themselves and all their heirs, the collation of this altar of Saint Nicholas, in the year of the Lord 1490, as we shall say below in its proper place.

Death of Emperor Henry in Italy.

Henry VII, emperor of the Romans, in the aforesaid year still being in Italy, at the city of Pisa, having gathered new forces and made agreements with the Genoese and with Frederick, king of Sicily, strove to go against Robert, king of Apulia. He died by poison, through the deceit and treachery, as they say, of Bernard, his confessor, of the Order of Preachers, who had poisoned him on the day of the Assumption of blessed Mary ever virgin in the Host, while he trusted in good faith. And a great persecution against the Preachers followed, although the same Bernard, before the king of Bohemia, son of that emperor, likewise Sponheim.

... a multitude from all Germany made its way to Rome for indulgences; among them was Dietlibus, abbot of this monastery, who, having set out for Rome with the above-mentioned count and many others, brought back to us, among other spiritual benefits, the following letters of indulgences.

“To all sons of holy mother Church to whom the present letters shall come: We, by divine mercy, Basilius of Jerusalem, Ramitus of Cagliari, Adevulphus of Cosenza, archbishops; Thomas of [Etesia?], Bonifacius of Taranto, Adam of Martirano, Nicolaus of [Neccastro?], Bernhardus of [Pace?], Benedictus of [Tracouar?], Nicolaus of Tortiboli, brother Antonius of [Thunad?], Angelicus of Fiesole, brother Jacobus of Chalcedon, bishops: greeting and sincere charity in the Lord. We do not in the least doubt that the joys bestowed through the merits of the saints belong to Christ’s faithful who earn their patronage by worthy services of devotion, and who also venerate in them him whose glory and recompense of rewards he himself is. Therefore, wishing to give the faithful occasion to obtain the aforesaid things, to all who are truly penitent and confessed, who shall come to the monastery of Sponheim, of the Order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Mainz, on whatever days and at whatever hours, for the sake of devotion and prayer, intending to implore from the Lord the pardon of their sins; or who shall extend helping hands for the fabric, lights, vestments, ornaments, or any other necessities of that monastery; or who, laboring at the point of death, shall bequeath, give, or send anything of their means to the aforesaid monastery; or also who shall reverently hear the masses or sermons of the monks of that monastery, as often, wherever, and whenever it shall happen that they hear them or any one of them celebrating divine service or preaching the word of God; or who shall make acceptable offerings to them or to any of them: for each occasion on which they shall do the foregoing, or any of the foregoing, trusting in the mercy of almighty God and in the authority of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, each of us mercifully relaxes in the Lord forty days from the penances enjoined upon them, provided only that the will of the diocesan bishop shall accede to this.”

“In witness whereof seals have been appended to the presents. Given at the Lateran, in the year of the Lord 1300, in the sixth year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Boniface VIII.”

These indulgences, then, Abbot Dietlibus brought with him from Rome, obtained by the labors and expenses of a certain familiar of his, Johannes de Soetern, who was procurator of this monastery, appointed by him, and whom, when he was about to set out for Rome, he had taken with him. But the consent of the diocesan bishop, of which mention is made in the letters, first acceded after twelve years, through Petrus, archbishop of Mainz, as is clear in the charter which he affixed to the letters themselves, secured with his seal; its tenor is as follows:

Another copy of the indulgences.

“We, Petrus, by the grace of God [of the holy and Mainzer see?], archchancellor of the Empire throughout Germany, holding as ratified and pleasing the indulgences of the venerable fathers, archbishops and bishops, contained in the letters to which this our charity is affixed, just as they were given, [unclear], each of them forty days, as is clear in the letters which follow; we confirm them for you after the year, so that they are not drawn by us into public questing. Given in the castle of Böckelheim, in the year of the Lord 1312, on the third day before the Nones of November.”

Of the above-mentioned thirteen bishops, three at the same time gave indulgences to this monastery, to the parish church, and to the chapel of St. Pancras the martyr in the castle of Sponheim. “To all sons of holy mother Church to whom the present letters shall come: We, by divine mercy, Basilius, archbishop of Jerusalem, Ramitus, archbishop of Cagliari, and Nicolaus of Tortiboli, gave them, each of them forty days, as is clear in the letters which follow: We, Petrus, by the grace of God archbishop of the holy and Mainzer see, archchancellor of the Empire throughout Germany, holding as ratified and pleasing the indulgences of the venerable fathers, archbishops, contained in the letters to which this our charity is affixed, just as given in the letters, as is clear in the letters which follow: We, Petrus, by the grace of God archchancellor of the holy and Mainzer see of the Empire throughout Germany, holding as ratified and pleasing the indulgences of the venerable fathers, archbishops, contained in the letters to which this our charity is affixed, just as given in the letters, as is clear in the letters which follow:”
