“To all sons of holy mother Church to whom the present letters shall come: We, by divine mercy, Basilius, archbishop of Jerusalem, Ramitus, archbishop of Cagliari, and Nicolaus, bishop of Tortiboli, eternal greeting in the Lord. The splendor of the Father’s glory, which illumines the world with its ineffable brightness, then especially pursues with gracious favor the pious vows of the faithful, who hope in the most merciful goodness of his majesty, when their devoted humility is aided by the merits and prayers of the saints. Therefore, wishing that the church of the saints Martin, Giles, Pancras, and Benedict of Sponheim, of the Order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Mainz, be frequented with fitting honors and be continually venerated by the people of Christ, to all who are truly penitent and confessed, who [unclear] to the said churches [unclear] by the merits of the aforesaid saints or trusting in their authority, each of us, sealed, mercifully relaxes in the Lord forty days from the penances there enjoined, provided only that the will and consent of the diocesan bishop shall accede to this. In witness whereof we have set our seals to the present writing. Given at Rome, in the year of the Lord 1300.” Its tenor is as follows:

Consent.

To these indulgences the lord Gerardus, archbishop of Mainz, at the request of Heinrich, count of Sponheim, above-mentioned, gave consent and confirmed them by the oracle of his living voice.

Copy of the letters of the twelve bishops.

Abbot Dietlibus brings letters of indulgences from Rome.

Copy of the letters of the thirteen bishops.

Johannes de Soetern.

Consent of the archbishop of Mainz.

Pontificate of the lord Pope Boniface VIII. [Source page illegible in the scan; the page image is the authoritative witness.]

Chronicle of Trithemius. 1400.

Our Clausa is made a vineyard.

Dietlib, abbot, in the third year of his rule, utterly desolated and destroyed the enclosure of the sisters beside the monastery on the western side, built from the beginning of the foundation of this place by the first abbot and at this time collapsed through excessive age; and he had the stones carried away and planted a vineyard in the same place. And thus thereafter nothing remained down to the present day except the name of the place, the Inclusory. For it is still called Clausa from the enclosure of the sisters who once dwelt there, and, apart from the name, it shows no trace of its former condition, as is seen.

1401.

In the fourth year of Dietlib our abbot, on the fifth day before the Kalends [unclear], Frederick, bishop of Speyer, died. Sibodo was bishop of Speyer. Heinrich of Wernberg was archbishop of Cologne. After the death of Wichbold, archbishop of Cologne, Heinrich of Virneburg, the second of this name, succeeded and presided for twenty-six years, a man more inclined to war than to peace, since during all the days of his pontificate he had disputes with the city of Cologne, counts, princes, nobles, and neighbors, and taxed his clergy and religious with very heavy exactions beyond what was customary and due.

In the same year also Gerard, archbishop of Mainz, Diether, archbishop of Trier, Heinrich, archbishop of Cologne, and Rudolf, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, conspiring together, made peace and a perpetual treaty among themselves, which greatly displeased Albert, king of the Romans. Therefore, coming unexpectedly with a great army, he first invaded the land of the aforesaid count palatine; after it had been miserably devastated, he compelled him to surrender. Then, moving his army against the archbishop of Mainz, among other damages and fires inflicted on the region, he besieged the town of Bingen, which belonged to the jurisdiction of the church of Mainz. The nuns of the monastery of St. Rupert, very near the aforesaid town on the other side of the river Nahe, having heard of the king’s arrival, all fled and withdrew to [lbingen], taking with them privileges, relics, and whatever they could carry off in the shortness of the time. Therefore, when King Albert came to the town of Bingen, he stationed war engines and part of the army in the aforesaid monastery of St. Rupert, and made a stable for horses out of the house of those serving God, and began to attack the town vigorously, which also, after a few days had passed, he received into his power. But when the aforesaid archbishop saw that he could in no way resist the king’s power, he sought pardon from him and obtained favor, after resigning into the hand and power of the king himself the towns of Lahnstein and Bingen, with the castles Klopp, Ehrenfels, and Scharfenstein, together with the other conditions.

Meanwhile, while the archbishop, being with the king in that same town of Bingen, was negotiating the conditions of peace, and all who had had residence in the monastery of St. Rupert beyond the Nahe, now that the town had been captured, had betaken themselves into it, leaving the monastery abandoned, empty, and stripped of all things, two wicked men, who out of want were following the king’s army, entered the aforesaid monastery of St. Rupert with the mind and intention of carrying away anything they might find. But after they had examined all the places and corners of the monastery most diligently, they found nothing; for everything had previously been carried off by those who had occupied the place during the days of the siege. Therefore, going out from the cloister, they searched the church, to see if by chance they might find something left in it. Now at that time in that church, before the entrance of the choir, which was in the lower parts above the ground, not raised up as it is now, toward the south, there was in the cloister an altar consecrated in honor of St. Catherine, virgin and martyr; above it, in an arched recess in the wall, an image of the most blessed mother of God and virgin Mary was painted quite fittingly, having a crown on her head, in which there were four crystal stones, artfully fixed into the wall and the crown, and a fifth on the breast of the image itself. When, therefore, those thieves found nothing in the church, one of them, so that he should not go away altogether empty, climbed onto the aforesaid altar and began to dig those crystals out of the Virgin’s crown. The other, rebuking him, said: “What are you doing, wretched man? Stop despoiling the mother of mercy; through her, if salvation ought to come to us, and not through another grace, we shall be able to find it.”

But that sacrilegious and impious man, scorning his rebuke, after he had dug the four crystals out of the crown, also began to dig the fifth out of the breast of the holy Virgin. A wondrous thing happened: as soon as that impious man presumed to violate the sacred breast, the image began to sweat all over. Seeing this, the sacrilegious man shuddered somewhat, but, hardened in wickedness, did not cease from the crime he had begun. Therefore he tore the stone out of the sacred breast of the image; when it had been torn away, immediately blood mixed with milk burst forth from the very wound in great quantity. Seeing this, that unhappy man shuddered all over, and, leaping down from the altar, gathered dust in the church and [unclear] the wound of the image, lest blood should flow— Sponheimense.

[unclear] blood with milk, he began to obstruct it. But the more he tried to obstruct the wounded breast of the holy Virgin, with so much greater abundance did milk with blood flow out. When he had seen this, that impious man hastily went out of the church and, running to the river Nahe as if driven mad, threw himself in and drowned. But his companion immediately fled; later, however, he returned and related the course of the matter to the mistress and the nuns of the said monastery. Then a certain priest arrived, who had celebrated there that same day; seeing a miracle of such novelty, he spread out the corporal before the image and collected the milk flowing with blood. This blood with milk, preserved in a glass vessel, we have seen in the aforesaid monastery down to the present day; at the petition of the abbess we even transferred it with our own hands from an old broken vessel into a new glass. When the miracle was at once made public, King Albert, who was still in the town of Bingen, came with the other princes to the monastery of St Rupert; seeing so dreadful a deed, he was astonished, and for the restoration of the monastery he bestowed many gifts in honor of the Blessed Virgin. In memory of this miracle a chapel was built there in honor of the Mother of God, in which the image, often renewed in the meantime, is seen above the altar.

When matters had been settled with the archbishop of Mainz, the king, advancing further against the archbishop of Trier and the archbishop of Cologne, subjected both to himself and compelled them to seek favor, not without their very serious losses.

1303.

In the fifth year of Dietlib, our abbot, Albert, the seventeenth prior of this monastery, died on the seventh Ides of May, a man of many virtues, who showed the greatest diligence for the restoration of regular observance and restored no small part. After him Abbot Dietlib chose as the eighteenth prior of this monastery Henry, a monk, the son of the sister of the aforesaid Albert, young indeed in years, but in character and wisdom an old man. He presided in the priorship of this monastery for twenty-nine years; of him we shall speak later in his place after Wilhelm. During the whole time in which he was prior there was a sufficiently good reform, although for many years it did not attain the first institution which had existed at the time of the foundation.

1305.

The bishop of Mainz, whom Peter, born of Treviri, succeeded, presided for sixteen years, a shrewd and industrious man, who issued many constitutions and ruled the church of Mainz quite magnificently.

In the same year, on the fourth Kalends of May, Eberwin, bishop of Worms, died. Emerich of Cronenberg succeeded him and presided for ten years, a peaceful and devout man, whom both people and clergy venerated with wonderful affection; when he was sent by the apostolic pope as bishop, they willingly received him.

1405.

In the seventh year of Dietlib, our abbot, on the feast of the commemoration of St Paul the Apostle, King Albert, being at Speyer, celebrated the obsequies of the king of Bohemia with great pomp in the greater church. While the bells were being rung, the great bell fell; and, breaking two vaults, it fell to the ground and was divided into three parts.

At these times the citizens of Koblenz contumaciously rose up against Diether, archbishop of Trier, their lord, forgetful of the fidelity of their oaths. Therefore the archbishop, moved to anger, summoned to his aid many princes and nobles, whom he hired for large sums of money, and encircled Koblenz with a siege. When it was at last taken at the dedication, he constrained the citizens to obedience. For this victory he spent incredible sums of money; hence he pledged almost all the revenues and proceeds of the church, and stirred up hatred against himself among both clergy and laity, especially the nobles of the province of Trier.

1306.

In the ninth year of Dietlib, our abbot, on the day of the Blessed Virgin Mary, otherwise the Purification, when the ice broke up, very great losses were inflicted on the cities and villages around the Rhine and the Main. The bridge at Frankfurt was broken, and many nearby houses were submerged in various places. At Cologne also two towers near the Rhine, shaken by that tempest, fell; many persons of both sexes and of every age were drowned in the Rhine in various places.

At the same time all the Jews were expelled from the kingdom of the Franks, their goods having been confiscated.

In the same year also the Hospitallers of St John of Jerusalem, with the aid of the [Trojans?], [took] the island of Rhodes, with five other adjacent islands, from the hand of the Turks, with they obtained very great power; fighting against those same Turks for four continuous years, until, as has been said, in the year prescribed they were victorious.

1307.

In the ninth year of Abbot Dietlib, the clergy of the Church of Trier, on account of the squandering of the goods and revenues of the church, and various other acts contrary to equity, had Diether, their archbishop, summoned to Rome for examination before the Apostolic Pontiff. But before the appointed date arrived, in the same year, on the twenty-third day of the month of November, he ended his last day; he was buried among his Preachers in the city of Trier. Baldwin, son of the count of Luxembourg, brother of Henry the Seventh, emperor, then in the twenty-third year of his age, succeeded him, Pope Clement V dispensing with him concerning his minority. He presided for forty-six years, one month, and eighteen days: a man in every respect magnificent, who also governed his church with sufficient foresight and usefulness, restoring peace, paying debts, and restoring alienated property.

In the same year Pope Clement V, in the Council of Vienne, annulled and destroyed the order of the Templars, which had lasted almost 184 years from its foundation. It was charged against them that in their profession they denied Christ; whether this was true or false is not for us to judge.

1308.

In the tenth year of Abbot Dietlib, Albert, king of the Romans, because he seemed excessively avaricious, and because he held the duchy of Swabia, belonging to his brother Rudolf, in the name of guardianship, which he ought not undeservedly to have resigned to John, the son of that same brother, now grown up, and although often appealed to by him paid no attention, was slain by the sword near Schaffhausen; after a year he was buried in the church of Speyer.

In the same year the princes, assembling at Rhens on the twenty-seventh day of the month of November, unanimously elected as king of the Romans Henry, count of Luxembourg, brother of Baldwin, archbishop of Trier. Conducting him to Aachen with great solemnity, they had him consecrated king, and he reigned for five years. He had as wife Margaret, daughter of the duke of Brabant.

In these times Peter, archbishop of Mainz, began to build anew and endow a monastery of the Carthusians outside the walls of Mainz.

In the same year, on the sixth ides of November, there died at Cologne John Scotus, doctor of sacred theology, of Paris, of the Order of Minors; he was buried there in his own convent.

1309.

Dietlib, the tenth abbot of this monastery, died on the day of Michael the Archangel, and was buried before the steps of the presbytery, not without many tears of the brethren. For he was a good man, a lover of his brethren, who presided well over the monastery both in spiritual and in temporal matters; because, although he took away the private allowance which his predecessors had granted to the monks, he suitably enlarged the substance of temporal goods. In business he was provident, of perceptive intelligence; his counsel was sometimes used in difficult cases even by the count of Sponheim and neighboring nobles. But although there is no doubt that his deeds, performed praiseworthily, were many, we could not know them all, both because of the negligence of the ancients and because of the distance of time.

Concerning Wilicho the First, eleventh abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, who presided for twenty-seven years, five months, and four days.

Accordingly, when Dietlib, the tenth abbot of this monastery, had died and been buried on the third day before the kalends of October, in the year previously noted, 1309, in the seventh indiction, the abbacy of this community was vacant. After the grace of the Holy Spirit had been invoked according to custom, they unanimously elected as abbot Wilicho, son of the noble man the count of Westerburg, brother of the countess of Sponheim, a very devout religious man, a conventual monk of this monastery, who almost eight years before, under Dietlib, as we said above, had entered the order. Confirmed and ordained by Peter, archbishop of Mainz, he presided over this monastery with sufficient energy for twenty-seven years, five months, and four days, and did much good for this monastery, both in buildings and in increasing revenues. Having been committed to letters in boyhood, as he advanced in age he made sufficient progress in learning and turned out to be a learned and likewise devout man. But when he had reached manhood Sponheim.

...he had arrived, he was girded with the military belt; and after he had for some time led his life in arms and affairs of war, it happened that he fell ill even to the point of death. Given up by the physicians, he turned himself to God, having made a vow of religion on the counsel of his sister, and, to the astonishment of all, miraculously recovered from his illness. Nevertheless, remaining for two years in secular life, he arranged his affairs according to the condition of his purpose, and distributed in alms for the poor a large part of the substance belonging to him. At the urging of the aforesaid sister of his, who venerated Abbot Dietlib and the present monastery with wondrous affection, he came without delay to conversion. Finally, he conferred and gave no small gifts to this monastery.

  1. In this year Henry, king of the Romans, held an assembly of the princes at Speyer, where Elizabeth, daughter of Wenceslaus, the late king of Bohemia, appeared in person, asking King Henry to grant her paternal kingdom to her as a fief. But King Henry, after first taking the mature counsel of his princes, considering that the said daughter of Bohemia was the sole heir of the kingdom, joined her in marriage to his son John, count of Luxembourg, and by imperial authority raised him to be king of Bohemia. Therefore, when the wedding had been celebrated there, he soon sent him into Bohemia, attaching to him Peter, archbishop of Mainz, formerly his physician, with a mighty army. And when John, the new king, came into Bohemia with the queen and the aforesaid archbishop, he soon subjected the whole kingdom of Bohemia to himself and powerfully received it into his dominion. He was crowned by the same Peter, archbishop of Mainz, to whom by ancient right it belonged to anoint and crown the kings of Bohemia, as we have shown far above. And when the coronation had been solemnly performed, at which more than three hundred thousand horsemen and warriors are reported to have been present, the king gave to the aforementioned archbishop of Mainz a golden seat beautifully adorned with gems. The archbishop, taking it with him to Mainz, bestowed it on Saint Martin; it is kept in the greater church down to the present day, and is called by the people the seat of Saint Martin.

In the same year King Henry, with his brother Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, Rudolf, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, Leopold, duke of Austria, and many other princes, dukes, counts, and nobles, set out with a great army into Italy to receive the crown of the empire. On the way he took by force and destroyed many cities resisting him and in rebellion. And when he came to Rome, he was crowned emperor at Saint John Lateran by cardinals ordained and sent for this by the pope, on the holy day of Pentecost. Fighting with the king of Apulia near the bridge of the Tiber, he defeated the Romans, who were denying him entrance into the city, and killed many of them. And after he had been crowned emperor, he created Rudolf, count palatine of the Rhine, and many other princes and nobles knights in the aforesaid church of Saint John. While the emperor was in Italy for two years, his second army, which he had left in Germany specially appointed for this, advanced in battle against the counts of Württemberg, rebels against the empire; from eighty very strongly fortified castles and towns which they held, they vigorously captured seventy-two by arms. For when King Henry was going into Italy, he prepared three armies: the first, gathered from Franks and Bavarians, he sent into Bohemia with his son and with Peter, archbishop of Mainz, as we have already said above; the second against the aforesaid counts of Württemberg; the third he led with him into Italy. The people of Brescia, whom he powerfully defeated by arms, he compelled to obedience to the empire; the Lombards, all the people of Pavia, Turin, Asti, Verona, Piacenza, Genoa, Pisa, Siena, Florence, many inhabitants of other cities, and all who resisted him, he defeated in armed expedition and brought under his power. This emperor Henry was a wise, just, gracious man, vigorous in arms, a most upright worshipper and lover of the Catholic faith, powerful in counsel and spirit, a lover and defender of the clergy; no one like him arose in the meantime.

  1. In this year Willicho, abbot of this monastery, built anew the house of the principal gate of the monastery on the southern side. But after almost 156 years, Johannes of Culenhusen, the first abbot in the reform called Bursfeld, had that gate closed and built a new gate of the monastery on the eastern side. The house of the old gate, constructed by Willicho, he changed for himself into an abbatial dwelling.

Assembly of the princes at Speyer.

John, count of Luxembourg, becomes king of Bohemia.

The war of the empire against the Württembergers.

The house of the abbot’s gate is built.

[unclear]. In this year Henry, king of Germany, who held the aforesaid kingdom, [unclear] with the Danes and the one ruling in Denmark, because [unclear] of the Danes recently from him, ruling [unclear] kingdom of the Danes [unclear] gave, which [unclear] ought [unclear] had given, [unclear].

Sponheim.

...he held that [he?] should be removed from the faithful of the Church. Among the other princes he had with him Reynald, first duke of Guelders, William, count of Holland, his father-in-law, Theodoric, count of Cleves, William, count of Jülich, Theodoric, count of Berg, and many others, all of whom came to his aid at great expense and with a great army.

At the same time, after Matteo Visconti of Milan had died, the emperor Louis, in Italy, as we have said, enfeoffed his son Galeazzo, who was very hostile to Pope John, with the same duchy. This displeased the supreme pontiff more than was fitting, and he said that Louis had not been permitted to do anything in the name of emperor unless he had first been crowned emperor by the Roman pontiff, and that even after coronation he had no right at all in Italy; rather, Italy, indeed the whole world, was subject to the Roman pontiff in spiritual and temporal matters. Since the emperor despised this vanity of the pontiff, at the insistence of Leopold, duke of Austria, the pope, having used counsel not very prudently, excommunicated the emperor himself, and declared that all who called him emperor were excommunicated and that their lands were placed under interdict; and a grave scandal followed in the Church.

In the year noted above Gottfried, bishop of Würzburg, died. Wolfram von Grumbach succeeded him and presided for six years, and compelled the citizens to be subject to his rule.

In the same year also Matthias, archbishop of Mainz, held a synod of abbots and prelates and established many things necessary for ecclesiastical utility.

1328.

In the nineteenth year of Wilicho our abbot, on the fourth day before the Ides of September, Matthias, archbishop of Mainz, of the Order of Saint Benedict, died, and he is buried in the church of Mainz. After his death the archbishop of Trier governed the church of Mainz in the name of administrator for almost three years. In these times there was great dissension between the clergy and the citizens of Mainz: the former were contending for liberty, while the citizens were striving to violate everything. And this was perhaps the first reason why the clergy took Baldwin as administrator, whom everyone knew to be a prudent and magnanimous man, through whose strength the pride of the people of Mainz could easily be subdued. Therefore, after he had been made administrator, to repress their rashness he built from the foundations a castle at Eltville near the Rhine, which Heinrich von Virneburg, who later succeeded Matthias, completed.

Meanwhile, while Baldwin had undertaken this administration, at the request of the canons and clergy of Mainz, Pope John XXII sent the aforesaid Heinrich von Virneburg, consecrated as archbishop of Mainz, with mandates to the clergy and citizens that they should receive him without contradiction as their pontiff. But the canons of the aforesaid church of Mainz, alleging defects and many crimes against the aforesaid Heinrich, appealed against him to the apostolic see, committing for a second time the castles, cities, and fortifications, together with the whole diocese, to the aforesaid Baldwin, archbishop of Trier. But after many disputes and lawsuits had taken place before the supreme pontiff between Heinrich and the aforesaid chapter, at last the pope sent two legates to Mainz, instructing the aforesaid Archbishop Baldwin to hand over the administration, with all the castles and fortifications, into their hands, and commanding the canons, clergy, and people, under sentence of excommunication, to receive Heinrich, destined for them as archbishop. Therefore the legates, together with the often-mentioned Archbishop Baldwin, placed the aforesaid Heinrich in the archiepiscopal see with the favor of the citizens.

Meanwhile, while these disputes were being carried on between the church of Mainz and Heinrich von Virneburg, the citizens of Mainz, fearing a siege by Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, took counsel and on a certain day went out armed and miserably destroyed the monasteries of Saint Alban the martyr, Saint James the apostle on the fair mountain, and Saint Victor, together with the castle at Weisenau, as is clearer than daylight especially in the church of Saint Alban, which shows the traces of the destruction down to the present day. For this rashness, when they were later summoned to the imperial chamber by the prelates of the said monasteries, the citizens of Mainz were condemned in a large sum of money. From that time until the destruction of the city, with God avenging the wrong done to the saints, fortune was always adverse to the people of Mainz.

In the same year, on the fourth weekday before the feast of Saint George the martyr, Emicho von Leiningen, bishop of Speyer, died. He was succeeded by Berthold von Bucheck, of the Order of the Teutonic Brethren, and he presided scarcely one year; afterward he was transferred to the church of Strasbourg by Pope John XXII, as we shall say in the account of the following year.

The Visconti of Milan is appointed by the emperor.

Behold the arrogance of the pope.

Wolfram becomes bishop of Würzburg.

A synod is held at Mainz.

Matthias, archbishop of Mainz, dies.

Baldwin becomes administrator of the church of Mainz.

A castle is built between [Alfiel?].

Dispute between Heinrich and the chapter of Mainz.

The pope destined Heinrich as archbishop.

The monasteries of Saint Alban, James, and Victor are destroyed.

Berthold von Bucheck becomes bishop of Speyer. Sponheimense.

similarly also to the archbishops and bishops of Trier, Milan, Genoa, Lucca, and Strasbourg, he said that he had perished through another’s plots; nevertheless Henry, count of Flanders, and the other steadfast nobles confirmed that he was guilty, and that the emperor had been slain in the Host, as we have said, from his hand; and the Roman Empire was vacant for almost a year.

In these times, after the death of Emperor Henry, a great dearth and plague occurred, and many perished.

1314.

In the fifth year of Willicho our abbot, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, the princes of the Empire assembled at Frankfurt to elect a new emperor; and, when the votes were divided in different directions, Peter, bishop of Mainz, Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, John, king of Bohemia, and [Volmarus?], margrave of Brandenburg, elected Louis, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, as king of the Romans. Against him Rudolf, count palatine of the Rhine, brother of that same Louis, Henry, archbishop of Cologne, and the duke of Saxony elected Frederick, duke of Austria, son of Albert, formerly king of the Romans, as king. But Louis obtained the kingdom and the Empire, and, after defeating Frederick in battle, took him captive. And he compelled his brother Rudolf, count palatine, who sided with Frederick, despoiled of his duchy and every possession, to flee to England, where he remained until death. Yet he restored the principality to his sons.

In the same year, on the fourth day before the Ides of February, Emerich, bishop of Worms, died; Henry, son of count Silvester of Dune, provost of the greater church of Worms, succeeded him, and presided vigorously for almost five years.

Also in the same year, on the day before the Ides of January, Sibodo of Lichtenberg, bishop of Speyer, died; Emich of Leiningen succeeded him, and presided for fourteen years.

1315.

In the sixth year of Willicho our abbot, there was a great famine throughout all Germany and Italy, in which many thousands of people perished from want; and it lasted almost two years, and a great plague followed.

In the same year a battle took place between Louis, king of the Romans, and Frederick, duke of Austria, his adversary, near Speyer; in it Leopold, Frederick’s brother, consumed many villages round about by fire. There was, as we have said, a great famine, and Baldwin, bishop of Trier, a wealthy and most provident man, supplied abundantly to the king and his army whatever had been necessary. Victory fell to Louis, who compelled Frederick with all his men to flee; nevertheless he did not afterward acquiesce.

1316.

In his seventh year, Willicho, abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, around the feast of Pentecost, was appointed by Pope John XXII, together with the other prelates of the church of Mainz, as commissioner concerning the inquiry into the life of Hildegard of holy memory, formerly mistress of the virgins of Christ on the mount of Saint Rupert of blessed memory at Bingen. A commission for this matter had also previously been made by Pope Clement V, who gave his consent to her canonization. But when the inquiry had been made and communicated by letters to the aforesaid supreme pontiff John XXII, she had been canonized; and I do not know by what intervening occasion it was neglected.

In the same year King Louis, Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, and certain others summoned to his aid, besieged the fortifications of Wiesbaden and Scharfenstein against Frederick. When they saw that they could accomplish little, the matter unfinished and the siege lifted, each returned to his own affairs.

Also in the same year King Louis confirmed peace with all the princes and cities of the Empire; Henry, archbishop of Cologne, and the other men who were on the side of Frederick, duke of Austria, paid no heed to it.

1318.

In the ninth year of Willicho our abbot, Andrew, bishop of Würzburg, dies; to him [Source page illegible in the scan; the page image is the authoritative witness.]

Sponheim.

...proscribed, some mutilated in their limbs, so that they might carry about before those who saw them the perpetual disgrace of their impiety.

1322.

In the thirteenth year of Wilicho our abbot, a certain brother named Walter was burned at Cologne, the father and prince of heretics; he had long lain hidden in secret and infected many simple people with his errors. When he was put to torture, he could not be induced to reveal the sharers in his error.

In the same year Isabella, daughter of Philip IV, king of the French, wife of Edward, king of the English, seized that king, her husband, because of the devastation which he had wrought in the kingdom with his servants, and committed him to custody, in which he remained until death; nor by any threats or prayers could he get out.

1323.

In this year, which was the fourteenth of Wilicho our abbot, Frederick, duke of Austria, having gathered a great army of more than six thousand armed men from Hungary and Turkey, came against Louis the Bavarian, king of the Romans. Louis met him with a great military force, and, when battle had been joined between Mühldorf and Oettingen in Bavaria, Louis proved victor. Duke Frederick, captured by John, king of Bohemia, was presented to Louis on condition that he not be killed; Louis committed him to custody in a certain castle not far from Nuremberg. After some time, while Frederick remained thus in custody, a certain magician came to his brother, Duke Leopold, who was staying in Austria, promising that by his art he would snatch Duke Frederick the captive from custody and bring him back safely to Austria in one hour. The duke believed the master of the art, and promised that he would give whatever he asked if he matched his words with deeds. So both enter a circle, on a night appointed in advance. The master summons a spirit accustomed to come at his conjurations. It came in the form of a pilgrim man and received the command to take the duke out of custody and bring him back without delay to Austria. The spirit answered: “Your commands, good master, I will gladly obey, and I will free that captive duke and bring him back to you safe and unharmed, provided only that he does not refuse to come with me.” Immediately the spirit flew away and, in the same form, came by night to the captive duke, who was eating, saying: “Leopold your brother has sent me here to lead you out of the prison-house. Rise, then, quickly; mount this horse. I will lead you safe and unharmed to your brother.” The duke said to him, “Who are you?” The spirit answered: “Do not concern yourself who I am, but mount the horse, if you desire to be freed from this custody.” At once horror seized the duke and all who were with him; and when the sign of the cross had been made, the spirit vanished and returned empty-handed to the master. After this Duke Leopold harassed King Louis with iron and fire for so long that at last, when princes intervened and he was moved to mercy, he released the captive, after receiving from him a pledge that he would no further involve himself with the royal title. Thus Louis reigned, from the beginning of his election until his death, for almost thirty-three years; Frederick thereafter did not involve himself with the title of the kingdom of the Romans. This Louis was the fourth of that name. He had as wife Margaret, daughter of William, count of Hainaut, by whom he had six sons: namely Louis, margrave of Brandenburg; Stephen, duke of Bavaria in Landshut; Albert, duke of Bavaria in Straubing; William, duke of Holland, Zeeland, and Frisia in Breda; Louis, who was called the Roman because he had been born at Rome; and Otto of Brandenburg. And so through this empress Margaret the counties of Holland, Zeeland, Frisia, and Hainaut came to the dukes of Bavaria and counts palatine. For in the year 1345, as we shall say below, after her brother William had been killed by the Frisians, the empress, by decree of the princes, went down to Holland with a most splendid retinue, received homage from the vassals of the land and an oath of fidelity from the inhabitants, enlarged liberties and privileges for all, and made truces with the people of Utrecht. When these things had been done, she handed the county over to her son and returned to Bavaria. William, the father of this empress Margaret, the aforesaid count of Holland, died in the year of the Lord 1436; William his son, brother of the empress, succeeding him, was later killed by the Frisians, as we have said.

1324.

In the fifteenth year of Wilicho our abbot, and the two-hundredth from the first entry of the brothers into this monastery of Sponheim, Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, John, king of Bohemia, who at that time was staying at Luxembourg, and also the duke of Lorraine and the count of Bar, making alliance with one another, besieged the city of Metz with a great army, laying waste and devastating everything around.

A heresiarch is burned at Cologne.

War between King Louis and Frederick, duke of Austria.

Frederick, duke of Austria, is captured.

A magician promises that he will free Frederick.

The spirit that was sent comes to the duke.

Duke Frederick is freed.

Louis reigns as emperor for thirty-three years from his election.

The sons of Emperor Louis.

The county of Holland comes to the duke of Bavaria.

The city of Metz is besieged. [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Trithemius, 1325.

In this year, which was the sixteenth of Abbot Willicho, an exchange of the following kind was made between Johann and Simon his brother, counts of Sponheim, on the one side, and Willicho, abbot of this monastery, with his convent, on the other side. The aforesaid counts gave to this monastery the estate which we still possess peacefully today in Basenheim, with all its appurtenances, free, released, and immune from every service, levy, and exaction whatsoever, to be possessed forever, in return for the castle of Coppenstein with its revenues, together with the little villages of Richweiler and Geilweiler, with tithes, rents, meadows, fields, woods, waters, fisheries, and all other appurtenances, as is clear in the letters drawn up concerning this matter and strengthened with the seals of the two aforesaid counts; their date is the year of the Lord 1325, on the day of St Lawrence, martyr.

This count Johann had as a concubine the daughter of one of his squires, a virgin of considerable beauty, whom he had violated; she at length bore him a son, whom the count his father had legitimized through the emperors Louis IV and likewise Charles IV. When he had been enrolled among the military class, he gave him the title of the aforesaid castle of Coppenstein, whose line of descent, multiplied, flourishes down to the present day. Then, at Count Johann’s request, Abbot Willicho assigned his aforesaid son as his advocate in the monastery’s village which is called Omme, [unclear] chickens to be given to him every year by the inhabitants of the same village as a fief: namely on this condition, that the eldest son of the lineage, by lawful successions, when the advocate has died, receive the fief from the abbot of this monastery, take an oath, and promise fidelity to the abbot in the manner of vassals. He shall have no other right over the men of the aforesaid village except what the abbot has established for him, nor shall he burden them in any respect, because every right in that village, in meadows, fields, pastures, gardens, vineyards, groves, hunts, waters and watercourses, roads and trackless places, cultivated and uncultivated, acquired and to be acquired, with lordly judgment and justice, the appointment and removal of the Schultheiss and the scabini, and universal temporal jurisdiction, belongs to the abbot, to whom alone, and not to the advocate, the aforesaid inhabitants of the aforesaid place owe homage. When it is necessary to make an inquiry in criminal cases for putting malefactors to death or mutilating them, this belongs to the office of the advocate, yet in such a way that from the revenues belonging to the treasury, and from the fine which they call Frevel, the abbot receives two parts and the advocate the third part. But if the abbot, moved by mercy, wishes to remit the fine for poor persons, the advocate shall not have the power to object, but shall also be bound to remit his own part. Finally, both the advocate himself and his heirs after him, after the succession in this year, which was the seventeenth of his rule, Abbot Willicho by writing; nevertheless Abbot Willicho could first come into possession in this year, which was the seventeenth of his rule.

Willicho, abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, in the seventeenth year of his rule, bought an estate in the village of Sponheim for seventy marks of Cologne denarii, three Heller being reckoned for one denarius, from Conrad, Rudolf, and Simon, brothers, and their sons, and with the seals of Johann count of Sponheim; their date is the year of the Lord 1413, on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross. And although the purchase was made in the year described in the letters, nevertheless into possession in this year, which was the sixteenth of his rule, [unclear]. The first duke of Guelders, named Reinald, who had held his father of the same name captive for eight years in the castle called Montfort, after he died in custody on the seventh ides of October, powerfully held the principality for almost twenty years; he had previously governed it for eight years, during which he held his father captive, under the title of administrator.

He was created duke by Emperor Louis IV, with the title of the duchy of Guelders retained together with the county of Zutphen annexed to it down to the present day.

In the eighteenth year of Abbot Willicho, King Louis, having often been admonished by John, the Roman pontiff, to come to Avignon, where the pontiff was then staying, to receive the crown of the empire, because he judged that neither sufficiently just nor safe, set out for Rome with many princes and a great army, writing to the pope that either he himself should come to Rome, or send some cardinals to mark him with the crown of the empire. Since the pope [unclear], he had himself crowned; this so displeased Pontiff John that he [unclear] him from the communion of the faithful.

King Louis sets out for Rome for the crown of the empire. [Blank page in the source scan.]

314 Chronicle of Trithemius

[Your] persons and [the place] in which you are bound to divine service, together with all the goods which at present you reasonably possess, and which in future, by just means, with the Lord’s help, you will be able to acquire, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves.

In particular, your tithes, houses, possessions, woods, meadows, mills, and your other goods, just as you possess them justly and peacefully, we confirm to you and, through you, to the same monastery by apostolic authority, and we strengthen them by the protection of the present writing, saving, in the aforesaid tithes, the moderation of the general council. Therefore let no man be permitted to infringe this page of our protection and confirmation, or with rash daring to oppose it. But if anyone shall presume to attempt this, let him know that he has incurred the indignation of almighty God and of blessed Peter and Paul, his apostles. Given at [Anagni?], on the fourth ides of May, in the second year of our pontificate.

He also did many other things for the utility and liberty of this monastery, some of which we have noted above in the sequence of years; the rest we have resolved to pass over in silence in this place.

Concerning Henry, the twelfth abbot of this monastery, who presided for two years, one month, and six days, and concerning his very few deeds.

Henry becomes the twelfth abbot of this monastery.

Again a division was made between the abbot and the convent.

The books of the library are destroyed.

After the death of Lord Wilicho, the eleventh abbot of this monastery, the brothers, assembling at the appointed place and invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit, elected as abbot Henry, a monk of this convent, born at Kreuznach. Confirmed by Henry, archbishop of Mainz, he received the gift of blessing from his vicar in pontifical matters, Brother Albert, bishop of [Ibingen?], at Mainz in the church of the Friars Preachers, on the first Sunday after the octave of the feast of Easter, and he presided over this monastery for two years, one month, and six days. In his time the discipline of regular observance was very greatly lacking, and the monks again usurped private property for themselves, and a division of revenues was made between the abbot himself and the convent, to the grave loss of this monastery. This lasted until the most recent reform, which was made from the monastery of Saint James near Mainz in the year 1369; and the substance of the monastery, in the course of time greatly diminished, was at last almost entirely dissipated. For when Abbot Wilicho died, who had continued the reform begun by Dietlub, there was no one to care for the integrity of monastic institution; and after the general division the monks began, each one also for himself, to have private property, and to spread out into every license without anyone’s prohibition. They shamefully destroyed the library, from the beginning of the monastery’s foundation filled at different times with many volumes, selling very precious volumes for a low price, so that they could satisfy their [unclear] pleasures. This Henry, moreover, was, as has been said, born at Kreuznach, sprung from humble kin; his father Albert was cupbearer of the counts of Sponheim. Sent to the schools, he devoted himself not to letters but to vanity, and therefore remained an unlearned man. At the petition of the counts, however, he was received into the monastic state of this monastery under Lord Wilicho; and after his death he was ordained abbot, more out of regard for his father than out of fear of God. He did nothing for the utility of this monastery, but on the contrary brought many losses upon it instead.

For first of all, what was the gravest of all losses, he allowed the discipline of regular observance to perish, introduced private property among the monks, and instituted a division of revenues between himself and the convent, contrary to monastic institution. For in the first year of his rule he alienated from the monastery a large part of the groves and woods between Wiler and Argenschwang, and in all his actions he was always incautious and exceedingly negligent.

1338.

In the first year of Abbot Henry, Wernher, the nineteenth prior of this monastery, was made provost of the nuns in Ibingen, at the command of Henry, archbishop of Mainz. After him Philip of Sponheim, called Meyswein, was appointed prior; and he was the twentieth in the order of priors of this monastery, and presided in that office of prior for twelve years. Then, after Wilhelm, he was elected abbot, as we shall say in its proper place.

In the same year the dedication of the church of our monastery was transferred from the Sunday nearest before the Nativity of Saint Mary the Virgin to the Sunday nearest after the feast of Saint Martin, archbishop, by Albert, bishop of [Ibingen?], vicar general in pontifical matters of Henry, archbishop of Mainz, as is clear in the following letters:

We Chronicle of Trithemius

In the same year also sixteen counts, conspiring against John, duke of Brabant, advanced to war against him near Fexhe and Landen. Among them from these upper territories were John, count of Sponheim, also the count of Katzenelnbogen, Henry of Bolanden, and the count of Falkenburg; but the dispute was at last settled by Philip, king of France.

1329.

In this year, which was the twentieth of our abbot Wilicho, Simon, count of Sponheim, after he had divided the castle of Sponheim with his brother John, added, delivered, and resigned his part with all its appurtenances, freely, of his own accord and voluntarily, forever, and [unclear] gave and resigned it to this monastery, freely, of his own accord and voluntarily, forever, and [unclear] by him to all his successors, abbots of this [unclear], of his wife [unclear], to Abbot Wilicho [unclear], those to descend from him, whoever shall be the elder at the time, should receive from the hand of the abbot one half of that castle with all its appurtenances as his fief, according to the tenor of the letters drawn up concerning this, which the same count, strengthened with his own seal and that of his aforesaid wife, delivered to Abbot Wilicho. Their date is the year of the Lord [1329?], on the Sunday next after the feast of St. John the Baptist. This condition having been made, Lord Abbot Wilicho [unclear] the said castle.

Count Simon received the abbot’s fief.

Conrad, bishop of Worms, died.

Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, was administrator of the church of Worms.

Baldwin was rector [unclear] of the priory.

In the same year Cuno of Schoneck, bishop of Worms, died. He had permitted the canonical brothers in Frankenthal to have their own houses and residences, contrary to the regular institution; nevertheless he revoked that permission before his death. When he had died, Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, with John and [unclear] of Sponheim, abbot, and the aforesaid count, granted it anew in fief and received from him the customary oath. This same John was count, brother of Lord Simon, concerning his remaining part of the aforesaid castle, in the sixth year following, as we shall say there.

Sponheim, with all its revenues and appurtenances, was granted anew in fief to the aforesaid Lord Count Simon, and the oath was agreed to by the same. This same John was count, brother of Lord Simon, concerning his remaining part [unclear], in the same also the date is the year of the Lord 1329, on the Sunday next after the feast of St. John the Baptist. This condition having been made, Lord Abbot Wilicho [unclear] the said castle. Conrad, bishop of Worms, died. Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, was administrator of the church of Worms. Baldwin was rector [unclear] of the priory. In the same year Cuno of Schoneck, bishop [unclear] Frankenthal, permitted private houses and residences contrary to the regular institution. When he had died, Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, with John and [unclear] of Sponheim, abbot, and the aforesaid count, granted it anew in fief, and the oath was agreed to by the same. This same John was count, brother of Lord Simon, concerning his remaining part of the aforesaid castle; in the same also the year is given as the year of the Lord [unclear], on the Sunday next after the feast of St. John the Baptist. This condition having been made, Lord Abbot Wilicho [unclear] the said castle. Cuno, bishop of Worms, died. Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, was administrator of the church of Worms. Baldwin was rector [unclear] of the priory.

In the same year Berthold, bishop of Speyer, was, by the authority of Pope John XXII, transferred to the episcopate of the church of Strasbourg, and Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, to the episcopate of Strasbourg [unclear]. In the same year the bishop of the church of Speyer was transferred; Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, in the same year was [unclear] administrator by the chapter of the church of Speyer, and archbishop of Speyer and administrator [unclear], because one man at the same time was archbishop of Trier and administrator [unclear], not elected nor postulated, but violently intruded. In the same year also [unclear] the bishop of Speyer, after the promotion of Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, who after the translation of Bishop Berthold to Strasbourg, as we have said, was administrator of the episcopate of the same church; this same Walram presided over the church of Speyer for six years. In the same year also, when the aforesaid archbishop resigned the administration of the church of Worms, Gerlach Schenk of Erbach, of whom we have already spoken above, assumed the episcopate of the same church and held it for two years.

In the same year also, after a long contest held in the papal curia, the clergy and citizens of Mainz were compelled by Pope John XXII to receive as their archbishop Henry of Virneburg, surnamed Busman, consecrated by the same pope. Through two apostolic legates sent for this purpose, Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, resigning the administration which he had carried on for almost three years, he was introduced into possession of all the goods of the archbishopric and presided for fifteen years. This Archbishop Henry completed the castle called Altavilla, Elfeld, [unclear] by Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, administrator of the church of Mainz, as has been said.

In these times also Emperor Louis, seeing the excellence of the sons of his brother Rudolf, count palatine, whom, because he had sided with Frederick, duke of Austria, he had driven into England, as we have said, said: “Their father sinned against me, not the sons. Shall innocent sons therefore bear the iniquity of their father? Far from it.” He therefore ordered that everything which he had taken from their father be restored to the sons: namely, the principality of the county palatine, with the other possessions in Bavaria, in Amberg, Nabburg, and all the rest which their father had possessed.

The sons of Rudolf, counts palatine, succeed to shares.

Names of the sons of Rudolf, the aforesaid count palatine.

There were three sons of Rudolf, and these are their names: Rudolf, the firstborn, a man not very wise nor shrewd, had as wife the sister of Louis, king of Hungary; by her he begot one daughter, named Margaret.

[Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheimense.

[Mar]garet, who married Charles, king of Bohemia, who after Louis became emperor of the Romans. Rupert, the second-born, died without children and was buried before the choir of the church in Neustadt. Adolf, the youngest, who obtained the principate of the Palatine county and the electoral dignity, married the daughter of the count of Oettingen; by her he begot Rupert, Count Palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, concerning whom the history will later be continued in its proper place.

1331.

In the twenty-second year of Willicho, our abbot, the noble John, count of Sponheim, at the request [unclear], freed the possessions belonging to the monastery in perpetuity from every service, contribution, exaction, and any burden, for himself and all his heirs, with the consent of Lord Simon his brother and of Walram his son, counts of Sponheim. For this liberty the same abbot Willicho and the convent of this monastery handed over to that count and his heirs, in ownership and perpetual possession, the mill in Rüdesheim, formerly in Gensingen, with all their revenues, as appears in the letters drawn up concerning this by the same count, strengthened with his own seal and with those of his brother and of his brother’s son aforesaid, and delivered to the monastery. Their date is the year of the Lord 1331, in the middle of Lent, on Laetare Sunday.

In the same year Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, bought from the abbot and convent of the monastery of St. Matthias the chapel of St. Alban with the adjoining garden outside the walls of Trier, and began to build there a monastery of the order, which he brought to its appointed proper completion within ten years. In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1400 he consecrated the church of the same monastery.

The same archbishop also, around this time, built anew at great expense a stone bridge over the Moselle at Koblenz, decreeing that all people of the diocese of Trier, of whatever status or condition they might be, could pass freely over it. But of the rest, who, being from outside the diocese, wished to cross the bridge, each one, clerics excepted, was to pay one obol for its maintenance, which they call Hallenses from Halls.

1332.

In this year, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, being the twenty-third year of Willicho, abbot of this monastery, Lord John, count of Sponheim, aforesaid, with the consent of his brother Count Simon and of Walram his son, leased to the abbot and convent of this monastery the whole jurisdiction and district, which he calls Bann, of the grist-mill in the villages of Sponheim and Bockenau, at a fixed tenure, that is, in perpetuity, according to the tenor of the letters which the same count had made concerning this and delivered to the abbot. Their date is the year of the Lord [1423?], on holy Easter day.

In the same year, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, Gerlach Schenk, bishop of Worms, died. Salmann, a native of Mainz, succeeded him and presided for almost twenty-three years. Salmann becomes bishop of Worms.

[unclear]

In the same year also, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, Henry, the eighteenth prior of this monastery of Sponheim, died, in the twenty-ninth year of his office and before the sixteenth [unclear] of his age had been completed: a good and devout man, a very notable lover of regular observance. Under his hand and direction a sufficiently fitting integrity of monastic life flourished in this monastery, although it had not been restored quite to the first fervor of its original institution. After him Lord Willicho the abbot appointed Wernher, a monk of this monastery, as the nineteenth prior; he presided in the office of prior for six years. Concerning his life, zeal, and manner of life I find nothing in particular except this alone: that after the death of Prior Henry, when Abbot Willicho had already grown old, the observance of regular discipline began little by little to fail, until at last it lay wholly collapsed for almost 137 years.

In the same year also the consulship of the city, together with the government, was changed in Strasbourg. For when the nobles had governed the commonwealth until then for many years and were excessively burdening the citizens, at last at this time the city rose against its rulers, and the matter was carried so far [unclear]

Lord George, Count of Veldenz, which, with his consent, she sold to the abbot and convent of this monastery for a certain sum of money, to be held in perpetual possession, as appears in the letters which, with the consent of Mechtild his wife, written and sealed, he handed over to his son and to the convent. Their date is in the year of the Lord 1342, on the Sunday in the middle of Lent. The aforesaid goods were in part leased to the villagers in Bockenau for annual rents at farm, and in part distributed by cart-loads for the use of the tenants.

But the aforesaid knight also handed over certain other goods to Abbot Wilicho, his son, and to this monastery, to be possessed forever; we judge it superfluous in this work to make mention of them individually.

In the same year the Count of Eisenburg, at the fair of St. Remigius in the city of Cologne, killed Lord Stephan, knight of Oirsbeck, publicly in a certain social joust, against his will. With his neck broken he suddenly breathed his last, and even when dead he did not fall, but remained upright, sitting in the saddle upon the horse, until he was taken down by the hands of his household; this was a sign of great strength.

In this same year, on the eighth day before the Ides of August, died Wilicho the Second, the thirteenth abbot of this monastery, a man sufficiently provident and experienced in the care of temporal affairs. If he had been able to live longer, he would without doubt have enlarged the revenues and possessions of the monastery. Nevertheless he did not take away private property from the monks, nor did he restore the division of revenues to common use, as he ought to have done.

Concerning Wilhelm, the fourteenth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, who presided for nine years, and concerning his deeds and the various events of that time.

When, therefore, Lord Wilicho the Second, the twelfth abbot of this monastery, was dead, and his body had been committed to burial according to ecclesiastical custom, the brethren assembled in the chapter place to appoint a new shepherd over themselves. Having invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit, in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s nativity 1341, in the ninth indiction, on the day of St. Cyriacus and his companions, martyrs, which is the sixth day before the Ides of August, they unanimously elected Wilhelm of Beckelnheim, a professed monk of this community, a prudent man and, according to the custom of that time, sufficiently religious. Confirmed by Heinrich, archbishop of Mainz, and blessed by his vicar in pontificals, Rudolf, bishop of Salona, and adorned with the mitre according to custom, he presided for quite useful years and enlarged the revenues of the monastery according to his powers.

He came from the village of Beckelnheim, of honorable parents, and was born of a knightly stock, namely from that lineage under which the holy virgin Hildegard, foundress and abbess of the monastery of St. Rupert near Bingen, had once been born. In boyhood he was entrusted by his parents to letters; applying himself diligently to them, he became sufficiently learned according to his measure. Then, when he was twenty-three years old, under the rule of Johann and Simon, counts of Sponheim, he began to serve as a soldier, and for some years continued in that office of the military order. But since he was slender and weak in body, afterward [unclear]

When a storm of clouds arose, thunder was heard, and lightning and flashes appeared, with hail and heavy rain, so that if it had been the middle of summer, there would not have been a greater storm.

In the same year Count Sylvester of Daun, who had already for many years, not without very great loss to himself, carried on enmities against Balduin, archbishop of Trier, at last, wearied and utterly exhausted in strength, came of his own accord and not under compulsion to the palace of that same archbishop of Trier, sought and obtained mercy, and thereafter remained at peace. He publicly acknowledged that the castle of Droneck, with the village of Dalvang and the other revenues there, was held in fief from the church of Trier and the aforesaid archbishop, and as a sign of fidelity he accepted this same fief from his hand.

[unclear] the affair, because the nobles, having left the city, in contempt of the citizens betook themselves outside to various castles, thinking that by this the citizens would be brought to greater obedience and reverence toward them; but the matter turned out otherwise than they had hoped. For when they had gone out, the citizens, after mature deliberation, closed the gates and, then establishing a new council from among the citizens and suitable non-nobles, decreed by public ordinance that none of those who had left the city should thereafter be permitted to return to it. And from that time down to the present day one of the citizens, whom no nobility of birth exalts, has each year customarily been chosen as magistrate of the others and of the whole commonwealth.

MCCCXXXIII.

In the twenty-fourth year of Willicho, abbot of this monastery, Wolfram, bishop of Würzburg, died on the day before the Kalends of July. Otto Wolfskeel succeeded him and presided for fifteen years, having been promoted and ordained at Liège on the twenty-first day of July by Pope John XXII, against Hermann of Leuchtenberg, chancellor of Emperor Louis, out of hatred for that emperor. For, as we said above, after the death of Emperor Henry VII, Louis, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, brother of Count Palatine Rudolf, by the election of the princes, after Frederick duke of Austria had been defeated, was raised to be king in the year of the Lord [unclear], in the twelfth indiction. He soon came into great discord with Pope John [XXII?] on the following occasion. The king’s chancellor, inserting falsehoods as truths into the letters which the emperor had ordered to be written to the pope, called the pope “the beast rising from the sea,” and put in many similar things. By these the pope was provoked to great indignation, and he excommunicated the emperor with all those adhering to him. This same chancellor at last confessed this malice of his at the moment of his death. But afterward, in the year of the Lord MCCCXXVII, Louis set out for Rome, was reconciled to the pope, and, having received the papal blessing and absolution, returned home. To this excommunicated Emperor Louis came William of Ockham, an Englishman by nation, of the order of Friars Minor, a man most learned in philosophy and sacred letters, fleeing after being [unclear] by Pope John [XXII?], I do not know for what reason, and he implored his protection, saying: “Most just emperor, defend me with arms, and I can and will defend you with writings against the pope’s injuries.” And he remained with him until the day of his death, and wrote many dreadful things against the same pope.

In this same year there grew a great abundance of wine, so that at vintage-time, because of the excessive plenty, many lacked vessels, and one vessel after another was filled with the best wine; and two measures of good wine were sold for one Heller penny.

MCCCXXXIV.

In the twenty-fifth year of Willicho, abbot of this monastery, Henry, archbishop of Cologne, died. Walram, son of Gerard count of Jülich, provost of Liège and treasurer of Cologne, a man most learned in both laws, succeeded and presided for sixteen years, six months, and nineteen days. He was a peaceful man, who governed the church entrusted to him in good peace, quite vigorously and usefully. This archbishop Walram, among the many buildings which he constructed in various places during the time of his pontificate, also founded the Carthusian monastery in Cologne, which he honorably endowed for the support of the brothers; although in the course of time it was wonderfully enlarged, both in revenues and in buildings, by the offerings of the faithful.

In these times also Adolf, count palatine of the Rhine, John and Simon, counts of Sponheim, also the count of Nassau and Count Sylvester of Dhaun, were mutually allied with one another against Baldwin, bishop of Trier. The archbishop of Trier [unclear]. The fortress in [Sirendlingen?] is destroyed. The villages of the counts of Sponheim are burned. By setting fire to the town of the same count and by plundering, he reached as far as the gates and caused them much damage in grain and wine. After this, leaving the town of Kreuznach because he could not take it by storm, he came with his army to Sponheim and cruelly laid waste everything he found outside the castle, burning and devastating everything. He burned down with fire the borough that had been before the castle, took the inhabitants, and carried off the spoils and plunder of everything he had found. He consumed by fire all the villages around Sponheim, Beckenau, Beckelnheim, Rudelfheim, Weinesheim, with the others adjoining. But he spared the monastery and the churches, except for the courts situated in the little villages of the county, which the devouring flame, together with the houses,

The villages of the counts of Sponheim are burned.
