...we remember that he wrote. But when everything had been duly completed, entrusting those lands and counties to her William, she returned to Bavaria. Therefore William, Duke of Bavaria and Count Palatine, son of the aforesaid Emperor Louis, having become lord of Holland, ruled those counties for fourteen years, and used this title in his letters: William, by the grace of God Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, Count of Hainaut, Zeeland, Holland, and Lord of Frisia. This William was a proud, restless, warlike man, who inflicted many losses on the church of Utrecht; and after the death of the Emperor he also refused to receive his mother into those lands which she had lent him. Having become [unclear], he received from God, even in this life, the reward of his iniquity. From that time, therefore, down to the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1425, the Dukes of Bavaria possessed the county of Hainaut, Zeeland, Holland, and Frisia for almost ninety years. When these had elapsed, John, Duke of Burgundy, who on his mother’s side was a son of the house of Bavaria, usurped those counties, as we shall say in its place; his heirs hold peaceful possession of them down to the present day.

1356.

In the fifth year of our Abbot William, when Henry of Virneburg, Archbishop of Mainz, was adhering to Louis the Bavarian, the excommunicated Emperor, against the prohibition of the supreme pontiff, and was defending him in his affairs with all his strength, and, though often admonished, would not desist, he was deposed in absentia by sentence of Pope Clement VI in a public consistory at Rome, and was stripped of every pontifical honor. Not accepting the pope’s sentence, and taking as coadjutor of the church of Mainz Cuno of Falkenstein, who afterwards became Archbishop of Trier, he conducted himself in all things as before. But the pope, after Henry had been deposed, promoted Gerlach of Nassau as Archbishop of Mainz; for eight years he did not come into peaceful possession against him and Cuno, his administrator, until Henry himself at last died. While this schism lasted for eight years, the church of Mainz was miserably desolated and suffered infinite evils: monasteries were plundered and destroyed, churches were stripped of their ornaments, and the clergy endured persecutions, fires, and irreparable depredations.

In this same year a dispute over the duchy itself arose between Reynard, Duke of Guelders, and his brother Edward. It lasted sixteen years, with the greatest loss to them and the desolation of the whole land. For as they often fought one another, many thousands of men were killed, villages were left deserted without inhabitants, castles were destroyed, and the land, with the peasants either killed or fled, was left uncultivated. At last, in the year of the Lord 1361, Edward captured Reynard and held the duchy alone, as long as he lived, without anyone’s prohibition, as we shall say below in its proper place.

Also in the same year Pope [Clement] VI, who had long since deposed Louis from the Empire, commanded the princes that, if they did not wish to lose the right of election, they should within a fixed time elect another emperor in place of Louis, the deposed emperor; otherwise he would of necessity make provision for the empire himself. When the princes had heard these things, Baldwin, Archbishop of Trier, Walram, Archbishop of Cologne, Gerlach of Nassau, for whom the pope had provided the archbishopric of Mainz against Henry, John, King of Bohemia, and the Duke of Saxony, meeting at Rhens beside the Rhine, ratified by sentence the deposition of Louis from the Empire. Then, remaining there, in the aforesaid year, the fifth of Abbot William, on the eleventh day of the month of July, which was the day of the translation of Saint Benedict the Abbot, they unanimously elected Charles, who had previously been called Wenceslaus, firstborn son of John, King of Bohemia, as King of the Romans. Leading him with great pomp to Bonn, they caused him to be anointed and crowned by the hands of the Archbishop of Cologne. For they could not come to Aachen, because the people of Aachen [unclear], although the pope immediately confirmed the election. For Adolf, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Margrave of Brandenburg, the Dukes of Bavaria, and almost all the imperial cities followed Louis.

Also in the same year, on the twenty-fifth day of the month of August, war was again waged between the kings of England and France over the duchy of Normandy. In it John, King of Bohemia and Count of Luxembourg, father of Charles, King of the Romans, although struck with blindness, was present in person, and fell after being wounded by an arrow of a certain Englishman. This King John was the son of Emperor Henry VII, of whom we spoke above, and the father of Charles IV. Through him the county of Luxembourg came to the kingdom of Bohemia, namely in the year of the Lord 1310.

The dukes of Bavaria ruled Holland for eighty years.

Henry, Archbishop of Mainz, is deposed.

Cuno of Falkenstein becomes administrator of the church of Mainz.

The pope promoted Gerlach of Nassau to the archbishopric of Mainz.

Conflict over the duchy of Guelders.

Charles, King of Bohemia, is elected emperor.

John, King of Bohemia, count, father of Charles, is killed.

The county of Luxembourg is joined to the kingdom of Bohemia in the year 1310. SPONHEIM. 313.

…consumed [it] in the houses of the peasants. Then he moved [his] army to the castle which was [that] of lord Simon the elder, count—namely brother of the aforesaid John—and walled it with a siege, and inflicted many damages round about, by fire [and] plunder. Seeing which, the wife of lord Simon, born of Falkenburg, niece of that archbishop, countess of that land, went out of the castle with her infants, and, placing herself on [her] knees before the bishop, said: "What do you do, O reverend Father? Do you proceed to bring to want your own flesh and blood, whom you ought to have defended from the injuries of others? Spare, I beseech [you], [your] nephew; spare [your] blood; spare your grand-nephews." These [things] said by the countess, archbishop Baldwin was moved with mercy, and, peace given to the counts, raised the siege. There was made, therefore, between the said archbishop of Trier and the aforesaid counts, peace; and the Sponheim [counts], reconciled to one another, departed in concord. But count Sylvester held himself in a certain fort called Felsberg; which, after archbishop Baldwin perceived [it], encircling [it] with a siege, he took and utterly destroyed, and forced the count himself to surrender. These [things] were done in the year of the Lord 1320, in the 3rd indiction.

After this, in the year of the Lord [MCCXXXVIII, as printed—recte 1338], between the aforesaid bishop Baldwin and the countess of Starkenburg arose a certain contention over certain goods in Birkenfeld, whence the archbishop decreed to gather an army against the countess herself; but by the industry of Henry, count of Sponheim, provost of Aachen, and Emerich von Stein, soldier, laboring for the countess, the archbishop's intention was impeded. [Margin: The archbishop of Trier is captured by the countess of Starkenburg.] It happened meanwhile that archbishop Baldwin, hidden in a small boat, wished to go down the channel of the Moselle to Coblenz; and he, betrayed to the countess, was captured by her, and for some time detained in the aforesaid castle of Starkenburg. At length he redeemed himself from that captivity for thirty thousand gold florins, and renounced all the goods in Birkenfeld over which the contention had arisen. With this money the same countess built a castle called Frauenburg, which is now placed in the dominion of John, duke of Simmern.

[1335.] In this year, which was the 26th of our abbot Willicho, John, count of Sponheim, brother of count Simon, handed over to abbot Willicho and his successor abbots of this monastery, in perpetuity, the part of his castle of Sponheim concerning him, with all its appurtenances—namely so that the abbot, who should be for the succeeding time, should hand it over in fief to the elder of the counts who should be lord in Kreuznach, according to the tenor of the letters which the same count, drawn up thereupon and fortified with his seal, handed to the abbot; of which the date is the year from Christ's nativity [MCCCCXXV, as printed—recte MCCCXXXV], the sixth feria after the day of the beheading of St John the Baptist. And thus the whole castle of Sponheim thenceforth, with all pertaining to it, depends on the fief of the abbot of this monastery. For what John performed of his part in this year, the same Simon his brother, who had received the other part in the division, did six years before (as we said there).

In the same year, on the day of Simon [and] Jude the apostles, the greatest wind was in all these parts about the Rhine, which overturned many buildings [and] trees.

[1336.] In the year 28 of abbot Willicho, on the day of St Augustine the bishop, died Walram, bishop of Speyer, buried at Speyer in the church of the Friars Preachers before the high altar, whom Gerard of Ehrenberg succeeded, elected on the day of St Catherine virgin [and] martyr: he presided 27 years, 1 month, 6 days.

In the same year the city of Mechelen, kindled by celestial fire, was miserably burned up on the day of Corpus Christi.

[1337.] In this year the 11th abbot of this monastery, lord Willicho (who was also called Wilhelm, as appears in the superscription of his seal), the 16th [day before] the Kalends of April, rested in the Lord, buried in the choir before the steps of the presbytery; who did many good [things] for this monastery. First of all, in the 8th year of his rule, he obtained from Pope John [XXII] a confirmation of all the goods of this monastery, as appears in the bull itself, whose tenor is as follows: "John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to [his] beloved sons the abbot and convent of the monastery of St Martin in Sponheim, of the order of St Benedict, of the diocese of Mainz, apostolic greeting and benediction. Since [something] which is just and honest is asked of us, both the vigor of equity and the order of reason demand that, through the solicitude of our office, it be brought to its due effect. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, agreeing with grateful assent to your just petitions, [we take] your persons and the place in which…" Of Sponheim.

We, brother Albert, by the grace of God bishop of the church of [unclear], acting in pontifical matters in the place of the venerable father in Christ and our lord Henry, Archbishop of Mainz; copy of the indulgences, [unclear] of the bishop; to all the faithful in Christ to whom the present letters shall come, greeting and sincere charity in the Lord. Desiring to invite all Christ’s faithful to works of piety by suitable means pleasing to God, to all truly penitent and confessed persons who shall stretch out helping hands to the monastery of St. Martin in Sponheim, or shall come to it for the sake of devotion and prayer on the individual feasts of the glorious ever-virgin Mary, of all the apostles, of the patrons, and of the dedication, or who follow the body of Christ when it has been carried to the sick person or persons, or who shall go around the cemetery or cloister, praying for all the faithful departed there and everywhere, by the mercy of almighty God and the grace of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, relying on the authority which we exercise, we mercifully relax in the Lord forty days of indulgences, together with one quarantine, from the penances enjoined upon them. Moreover, the dedication of the aforesaid monastery, celebrated hitherto on the Sunday next before the day of the Nativity of the blessed Virgin Mary, we have transferred to the Sunday next after the day of St. Martin, to be celebrated perpetually in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Given and enacted under our seal, in testimony of each of these things, in the year of the Lord 1338, on the vigil of St. Bartholomew the Apostle.

In the same year also Edward, king of England, came to the Emperor Louis at Koblenz, asking aid from him against the king of France. Louis, after receiving a great sum of money, promised him support, but did not keep his promises, and the king of England did not get back the money he had given.

In the same year also Reynald, Count of Guelders, who was afterwards first created duke, led a great army against the Liégeois, who in the preceding year, when he was absent and with the Emperor, had miserably devastated his land with fire and plunder; he had with him Adolph, bishop of Liège, whom the citizens had formerly expelled in disgrace.

On the other side the Liégeois led out a much larger army, and they met not far from Upper Maastricht; and when the aforesaid battle had been joined, by a miracle they were defeated by the aforesaid count with fewer men, many of them being captured, from whose spoil he became rich and renowned. In this battle more than nine thousand fighting men from both sides were said to have fallen. Reynald the count, having obtained so notable a victory, became not only rich from the plunder and the ransom of captives, but also named and famous in every land, and pleasing to all the princes; and he built many fortifications and castles, and enlarged his county.

1339.

In the second year of Henry, abbot of this monastery, on the day of St. Kilian the martyr, around noon, there was a great eclipse of the sun, which lasted more than two hours; and later in the same year, in autumn, the [unclear] in Verona killed many persons.

In this same year also Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, lent a very great sum of money to Edward, king of England, receiving from him as pledge the royal crown, a jewel of inestimable value. For in the preceding year the same king had declared war on Philip, king of France, on account of the county of Normandy, which he asserted belonged to him by hereditary right; and, having hired many princes and nobles from Germany for a great stipend, he entered France with a strong hand, and, though it profited him little, he raged with fire and plunder against [unclear].

In the same year the Emperor Louis, having summoned all the princes of the realm, held a court at Frankfurt in mid-Lent. There, among other things, sitting in his imperial majesty, he took Reynald, Count of Guelders, from the number of counts and placed him in the company of dukes, on account of his singular prudence and the magnificent deeds he had performed, creating him duke of Guelders, with the title of the county of Zutphen added. He was the eleventh count in the order of succession who ruled Guelders, and from a count he became the first duke, of whom we spoke above thirteen years earlier. At the same time also William, Count of Jülich, was raised to margrave by the Emperor Louis, with the consent of all the princes, on account of his many virtues and magnificent deeds, by which he seemed worthy.

1340.

In this year there was a very great pestilence throughout all Germany, and it laid low many thousands of people; a great famine also followed, and it was misery to live and danger to die.

A comet in Lent around the [unclear] of the Lord’s Baptist Sponheim.

They received the king of the Romans with reverence. When Charles learned this, he gathered a great army and advanced against Gunther; but, seeing him stronger than himself, through the efforts of Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, he drew the duke of Bavaria over to his side. Although they were joined by blood, nevertheless he married his daughter. Then, after three months, King Gunther returned to Frankfurt and began to fall ill; seeing that he had been deceived, he began to negotiate an agreement with Charles, who was then present, through the mediation of the margrave of Brandenburg. Having received two cities in Thuringia and two thousand two hundred marks of silver, he resigned the royal seal, the royal insignia, and the kingdom into the hands of the aforesaid Charles before the princes.

There was a report at that time that Gunther had been poisoned; for, having received a cup from the physician, he is said to have said to that physician: “Master, if it is good afterward, you drink first, and I shall drink afterward.” When the physician, compelled by necessity, had drunk first, the king drank afterward. On the third day the physician died; the king, made more ill by swelling of the body, followed him after the space of a month, while still alive [unclear].

Therefore Charles IV, elected king of the Romans in the year of the Lord 1346, as we have said, obtained the empire peacefully after Gunther’s death. He ruled for thirty-one years, a good, wise, learned, and magnificent man, perfectly endowed with knowledge and skill in five languages. He had four wives. The first was [the daughter?] of Rudolf, count palatine, brother of Adolf; she died without children. The second was from France; when she also had died without children, he took a third, the daughter of the prince of Sweden, by whom he begot a daughter, whom he gave to the margrave [unclear], afterward king of the Romans. The fourth wife was Elizabeth, daughter of the duke of Stettin in Pomerania, by whom he begot Sigismund, king of Hungary, and John the duke.

In the same year, on the vigil of the Assumption of blessed Mary ever virgin, Walram, archbishop of Cologne, died. William, a canon there, succeeding him by apostolic provision, presided for twelve years and nine months. He ruled well, freed the church from many debts, and redeemed everything that had been pledged.

In the aforesaid year 1349, William, abbot of this monastery, because of the devotion which he had toward the most blessed Mary, mother of God, erected in her honor a new chapel from the foundations in the circuit of the cloister. He completed it in that same year and had it consecrated in the following year, as we shall say there.

In that year also there arose in Hungary a certain new sect of Flagellants, which very quickly stained all Germany with its error. For men went about naked, males and females together, with head covered by hood or cap, and their private parts covered with a linen veil, carrying crosses in their hands and scourges with knots at the tips, to which spikes were fastened. With these, in church and outside it, under the appearance of penance, which they imposed on themselves without the judgment of priests, they scourged themselves, singing certain songs mostly contrary to the Christian faith, very often prostrating themselves on the ground in the form of a cross, praying, crying out, and striking themselves to the shedding of blood. When the ignorant populace began to admire and praise this pernicious novelty as holy and pleasing to God, and many began to imitate it, the bishops of the churches, fearing that the error would grow immeasurably if they dissembled, brought the matter to the examination of the apostolic see. By command of Pope Clement VI, all were either recalled to public penance or handed over to secular judgment and perished by fire. Thus that heresy, refuted in a short time, ceased.

In the same year also the human race was scourged by a threefold plague. For first there was a mournful and pitiable [plague], almost throughout the whole world, beginning from India and everywhere creeping through all the provinces, over the space of three years as far as England; everywhere on earth [unclear] there was no place in all Europe where that contagious calamity did not rage. The second plague was hemorrhoid, that is, a flow of blood, in which also many thousands of people, especially in Germany, perished. The third was that which was called by the name of sacred fire, which consumed the bodies of people, both dead and living, down to the bone. So savage was that calamity that it even consumed the bodies of the buried dead more swiftly in themselves. These times were full of calamity and misery and exposed to such great dangers that from the origin of the world, apart from the universal flood, we do not read [unclear].

Gunther falls ill.

Through the mediation of the margrave of Brandenburg, an agreement is negotiated.

Gunther, poisoned by venom, dies.

Charles, king of the Romans, IV; what wives he had.

William becomes archbishop of Cologne.

A chapel of blessed Mary is erected in our cloister.

A new sect of Flagellants arises.

A threefold plague of the human race.

1. Pestilence.

2. [unclear]; afterward more than sixty thousand people will be absent [unclear].

3. Sacred fire.

In Florence.

All were dying more swiftly. In the city of Florence alone in Italy, more than sixty thousand people of both sexes, miserably infected by this plague, died in the same year. Nor was there a speaker [unclear] in all Europe where this contagious calamity did not rage. The second plague was hemorrhoid, that is, a flow of blood, in which also many thousands of people, especially in Germany, perished. The third was that which applied the name of sacred fire [unclear]: wives carrying a cross [unclear], which consumed the bodies of people, both dead and living, down to the bone. So savage was that calamity that even the bodies of the dead, buried more swiftly [unclear], consumed themselves. These times, moreover, were full of calamity [unclear].

Chronicle of Trithemius ... crossing [unclear], he launched a second expedition into France, and, after many of the French had been killed and many slain, he triumphed gloriously.

Second expedition of the king of England. [unclear]. The castle of [Duna?] is surrounded in a siege. Count Walram of Sponheim. Henry, twelfth abbot of this monastery, dies.

In this same year also Baldwin, archbishop of Trier, surrounded in siege the castle Duna of the count called Sylvester; and to tame his insolence he built a new castle, which he called Mount St. John, and at last compelled the count himself to come to surrender. Walram also, count of Sponheim, perpetrated many things against the aforesaid archbishop; wherefore, stirred to anger, he proceeded against him again, and as far as Kreuznach did much damage in the county by burning and plunder. But Emperor Louis, interposing his authority, made concord and peace.

In the same year, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, Henry, the twelfth abbot of this monastery, died and was buried in the body of the church before the altar of the Holy Cross; and the abbacy was vacant for five days. He left to posterity, however, a testament that was not good: he divided the revenues in the possessions of the monastery with the convent, and again made the monks proprietors, just as Abbot Peter had once done in the year of the Lord 1270, as was said above, not heeding the piety of Abbots Dietlib and Willicho, his predecessors, who, cutting this vice off at the root according to the command of the Rule, magnificently increased the substance and revenues of the monastery with spiritual gain. As soon as the division of revenues was made between abbot and convent, and the monks resumed private property, immediately, along with regular discipline, the temporal substance also began to perish; and within a few years they came to such want and poverty that, although the monks in this place were few in number, they scarcely had enough from all the revenues of the monastery on which to live. But now, directing our pen to continue the history, we shall make the narrative.

Concerning Willicho the Second, thirteenth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, who presided for one year, three months, and four days, and concerning his deeds.

[unclear]

Therefore, after the death of Henry, the eleventh abbot of this monastery, the brethren assembled in the chapter room in the aforementioned year of the Lord's Nativity 1340, in the seventh indiction, on the second day of the month of May; after long deliberation had first been held, they at last unanimously elected as thirteenth abbot of this coenobium the cellarer of the monastery, a monk professed here from his youth, named Willicho, son of John, knight of Sponheim, surnamed Bruder. Confirmed by Henry, archbishop of Mainz, and blessed by his vicar in pontificals, brother Albert, bishop of [Ibina?], he presided for only one year, three months, and four days. He was, as we have said, from Sponheim, of honorable parents of the knightly order. His father John was knight and secretary of Count Simon; his mother was Gertrude, daughter of Wilhelm, knight of Sobernheim. After she died ten years after the birth or nativity of her son, the father took a second wife, Mechthild, daughter of a certain knightly man of Winnesheim. When she had borne several sons and daughters, the preceding sons, by his command, were handed over by their father to various monasteries to serve God. Therefore, when Willicho was in the season of youth, he was made a monk under Abbot Willicho; then, after some years, he was appointed cellarer, and finally, as we have said, was ordained abbot. Immediately at the beginning of his promotion he demanded back from his father the portion of the maternal inheritance concerning him, for which he acquired certain goods for the monastery in Bockenau, as we shall say in the following year. He was a man sufficiently industrious and provident, concerning whom there was sure hope, if he had obtained a longer life, that he would have magnificently increased the substance of the temporal estate for this place.

1341.

Since Abbot Willicho, from the first year of his promotion, had asked from his father the portion of his maternal inheritance, and the latter seemed less willing to give anything to the monastery, at last, induced by the counsel and authority of lord Simon, count of Sponheim, he yielded to his son's requests in this way. First, therefore, he gave to him, and through him to this monastery, as a perpetual possession, the court in Nosbach with fields, meadows, pastures, waters, ways and byways, cultivated and uncultivated lands, with all its revenues and appurtenances, together with houses, a chapel, and all things acquired and to be acquired, by a completely free transfer, without any burden of debts, precaria, or impediment of any exaction whatsoever. In Bockenau also the same knight had certain goods in fields, meadows, and small gardens by feudal right from lord Chronicle of Trithemius

The Rhine, rising, overthrew many houses. In the same year also, on the vigil of St. James the Apostle, the Main River, rising contrary to its nature and custom, suddenly discharged into the Rhine so great a flood of waters that no one living at that time remembered having seen the like. It also inflicted many losses on people, overthrew entire villages, and destroyed fields, vineyards, gardens, and many houses adjoining the Rhine.

At this time died Rupert, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of Rudolf, who formerly, as we have said, had been driven into England by the emperor Louis; and on the twelfth day of February he was buried in the church of the New Town, which he himself had founded. This same Rupert established the general or universal university at Heidelberg, which, raised up by many benefactions, Pope Benedict XII confirmed. He also built from the foundations, with handsome stone vaulting, the collegiate church in the New Town, as we have said, and endowed it quite magnificently.

  1. In the second year of our abbot William, our estate in Bockenau, which is called the Abbot’s Court, with its fields, vineyards, meadows, gardens, and all its appurtenances, came from his patrimony into the possession of the monastery. For when the mother of that abbot died, his father having died long before, a division of the paternal inheritance was made among the brothers; and the aforesaid estate, with certain other goods, fell to his share. With the consent of his brothers he gave it to this monastery as a perpetual possession, and we possess it peacefully.

But the other estate in Bockenau, which is called the Praesentia Court, came into the possession of the monastery by the gift of Lord Udo in the year of the Lord 1127, as was written above under that same year; and with it came the court of the scabini which we have there, with all the rights and liberties contained in its same description. This estate, however, with everything belonging to it, has from the beginning always been, and still is today, wholly free from every exaction, impost, and service. For greater security, Walram, Count of Sponheim, son of Lord Simon, afterward freed it, together with all the other goods which we have in Bockenau, from every burden, as we shall say below under the year of the Lord 1359.

  1. In the same year died Reynard [unclear], duke of Guelders. His son Reynard, a boy of ten years, succeeded him in the duchy; he afterward took as wife Mary, daughter of John, duke of Brabant, and both died without children. But Edward, brother of the aforesaid Reynard, after some years, led by desire of ruling, seized his brother and held him captive for ten years.

In this year Lord William, abbot of this monastery, bought the house and estate which we have in Bingen, with its appurtenances, from a certain Wentzo called [Kipdeck?]; and [unclear], surrounding [Kipdeck?] and Grenzau together in a siege, captured them and powerfully added them, with certain other things, to the possessions of the church of Trier.

In the same year also, the emperor Louis cast John, son of the king of Bohemia, out of the duchy of Carinthia, which he had previously given him; and his wife, taken away without the judgment of the Church, he gave as wife to his own son, to the grave scandal of the Church. Therefore, both for this and for other crimes, he was again excommunicated by Pope Clement VI and finally deposed from the empire, and Charles, king of Bohemia, was elected against him.

  1. In the fourth year of our abbot William, William, count of Hainaut, Zeeland, and Holland, and lord of Frisia, around the feast of the Nativity of St. Mary the Virgin led a great army against the Frisians, having with him the count of Horn and many noble and very brave men. The Frisians came out against him and, using their customary skill, killed some of those shut in the marshes and drowned others; among them Count William himself was also drowned, leaving no children. After his death his sister, the wife of the emperor Louis, coming down with her son William and a most splendid retinue, as the nearer heir, by decree of the emperor and princes, received into her power all the county of Holland, Hainaut, and Zeeland, and the lordship of Frisia, just as above under the year of the Lord 1323 we have already written Chronicle of Trithemius

... was promoted to the dignity, and finally under Abbot Henry, who succeeded Wilicho (as we said above), he was appointed the twentieth prior of this monastery. When he had completed twelve years in that office, after Wilhelm, as it is, he was ordained abbot. For he was a prudent man of many occupations, who would gladly have reformed the monastery in both estates, if he had been able. Once ordained abbot, he appointed after himself as prior, the twenty-first in the order of succession, Gerlacus, a professed monk of this monastery, a man sufficiently mature in life and morals for the quality of that time, elderly in age, weak and infirm. He presided in the office of the priorship for almost eight years; because of his old age he accomplished little.

1351.

In the first year of our Abbot Philip, Emperor Charles IV, to gratify the princes on this side of the Rhine, established many new tolls in various places on the Rhine, by whose help he had been raised to the empire. But when the merchants, being exceedingly burdened by this, avoided the traffic of the Rhine, the people of Strasbourg so closed the Rhine around Strasbourg with chains and timbers that for two years ships could neither go up nor down. Seeing that they were being deprived of the revenues of both the new and the old toll, the princes entered into an agreement with the people of Strasbourg; content with the old tolls, they renounced the new ones.

In the same year Wilhelm, Duke of Bavaria, Count of Hainaut, Zealand, and Holland, lord of Frisia, son of the late Emperor Ludwig, who was the first from Bavaria to rule in Holland, oppressed the people with new and unusual exactions, nor any with the poor [unclear], who was the only daughter of that land (as we said above), they implored; when she admonished him in writing to desist from his presumptuous tyranny, the son despised the command of his mother. Therefore the mother, seeing herself despised by her son, gathered a great army and advanced against her son in a naval battle on the Meuse on the day of the translation of Saint Martin. Defeated by him, she fled with a few to England; the son exercised tyranny against the poor.

1352.

In this year Philip, abbot of this monastery, had renewed before the Schultheiss and the scabini there the complete liberty of the goods of our court in Blenich, exemption from every burden of exaction, precaria, and any servitude, in the presence of Walram, Count of Sponheim, and very many others, as is clear in the instrument drawn up concerning this matter.

In the same year Reynaldus of Sponheim and Ernestus of Molenarck, canons of the greater church of Cologne, were cruelly and less than justly killed for a trifling cause by the leading men of the city of Cologne in the house of the official.

1353.

In the third year of our Abbot Philip, on the eve of Saint Thomas the Apostle, died Heinrich of Virneburg, formerly archbishop of Mainz, long before deposed and excommunicated by Pope Clement VI (as was said above). Gerlach of Nassau remained in peaceful possession.

In the same year, on the day of Saint Oswald, the second division of the duchy of Bavaria among Stephan, Albrecht, and Wilhelm, sons of Emperor Ludwig, was made at Regensburg by Ludwig, margrave of Brandenburg, Adolf, count palatine of the Rhine, and Johann, burgrave of Nuremberg, as is clear in the letters.

1354.

In this year, which was the fourth of our Abbot Philip, the emperor held a solemn court or assembly of princes at Mainz in the month of January, and dealt with many matters for the peace and usefulness of the commonwealth.

In the same year, on the Kalends of February, died Balduin, archbishop of Trier, a man [unclear], and he is honorably buried on the western side of the church. After him Boemund of Edendorff, raised to be archbishop, presided for twelve years and one [unclear]. In the same year died Salamannus, bishop of Worms; Theoderic the Bavarian of Boppard succeeded him and presided for nine years.

1355.

In the fifth year of our Abbot Philip, on the day of December, died Johann III, duke of Brabant, leaving no children; hence, over his duchy, a grave dispute arose between Wenceslaus, count of Luxembourg, and Ludwig, count of Flanders, which finally Chronicle of Trithemius

For after Wenceslaus, king of Bohemia, had died, the aforesaid Count John married Elizabeth his daughter, and with her obtained the kingdom for thirty-six years. When he too died, the aforementioned Charles succeeded, and after him his son Wenceslaus.

1347.

In this year, which was the sixth of our abbot Wilhelm, on the day of Saint Gereon the martyr, Emperor Louis died, and he is buried in the church of blessed Mary ever virgin in the city of Munich. Report says that he perished by the poison of a certain duchess of Austria, whom all were accustomed to call Maultasch because of the foul and hideous shape of her face. This, indeed, we hold as certain: that after returning home from hunting, and after taking food with her at the same table, he at once began to feel ill; and, hoping that by movement of the body he would be better, he mounted his horse and went off again to the hunt. But as his body grew hot, not far from Furstenfeld, he fell from his horse and expired in the hands of his attendants. He was a man for a long time good and peaceable, who always bore injuries with an even mind, and conquered more by piety than by severity.

After Emperor Louis had died, Rupert, count palatine of the Rhine, who was also called Adolphus, son of Adolphus and grandson of Rudolf, brother of the deceased Emperor Louis; Louis, duke of Bavaria, son of the deceased emperor; Otto, margrave of Brandenburg; and Henry, archbishop of Mainz, who, although he had been deposed by the pope, nevertheless conducted himself as archbishop, came together as one. By letters and solemn envoys they invited Edward, king of England, who in that year had most gloriously triumphed against the French, to assume the empire. Giving thanks to them, he sent back word that he was so occupied in governing the kingdoms of England and France that he could by no means attend to the empire of the Romans. When the aforesaid princes had received this from the king of England, they sent letters and envoys to the margrave of Meissen, son-in-law of the deceased Emperor Louis, and elected him king of the Romans against Charles, who, as we have said, had been elected by the other princes while Louis was still alive. He at once consented to the election made of him. Meanwhile the year passed while these things were being done.

1348.

Therefore, after Charles had learned that the margrave of Meissen had been elected king of the Romans against him by the aforesaid princes, without delay he hastened to him,

The king of England is invited to the empire.

Our estate in Blanich is bought.

In the year noted above, Wilhelm, abbot of this monastery, bought the estate that we have in Blenich, with all its appurtenances, fields, vineyards, meadows, gardens, pastures, and houses, for a certain sum of money from Clementia, widow left by Tilmann the knight, with the consent of George of Savvelnheim, her son-in-law, for herself and all her heirs, as is clear in the letters of his consent drawn up concerning this, whose date is in the year of the Lord 1348, on the days of the martyrs Felix and Adauctus.

In the same year Otto, bishop of Wurzburg, died. Albert of Hohenlohe succeeded him and presided for forty-four years. In the sixth year of his pontificate he tightly besieged Wurzburg for three weeks, and powerfully forced the citizens to his obedience, which they were refusing.

Albert becomes bishop of Wurzburg.

Wilhelm, count palatine of the Rhine.

Conrad de Deech is killed.

Günther, count of Schwarzburg, is elected against Charles.

Günther [unclear] to Frankfurt.

In the same year also Wilhelm, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, count of Hainaut, Zeeland, Holland, and lord of Frisia, son of the deceased Emperor Louis, entered the lands of the church of Utrecht with a very great army; miserably devastating everything by fire and sword, he laid waste the whole diocese.

In this very year Conrad de Deet was in the city of Munich, whom a certain nobleman [unclear]. He came with a great army to Frankfurt, and pitched his tents there before the city, as is the custom, for three days and six weeks; him the Frankfurters and the other neighboring cities [unclear] as king

1349.

In the eighth year of our abbot Wilhelm, Günther, elected king of the Romans, with

Conrad [unclear], Louis duke of Bavaria, with certain others, seeing themselves [unclear] by the margrave,

Günther of Schwarzburg they elected as king of the Romans against Charles.

Conrad Swicker of Gondelfingen, holding [him] in hatred, approached in his own house as if to greet [him], cruelly killed [him], and immediately fled.

In the same year also Rupert,

count palatine of the Rhine, Henry, the deposed archbishop of Mainz,

[unclear] of Schwarzburg; Charles is elected.

The Frankfurters and the other neighboring cities [unclear] as king

Günther [unclear] to Frankfurt.

Conrad Conrad [unclear], Louis duke of Bavaria, with certain others, seeing themselves [unclear] by the margrave.

Conrad Conrad [unclear], Louis duke of Bavaria, with certain others, seeing themselves [unclear] by the margrave.

Günther Günther [unclear] of Schwarzburg; Charles is elected.

Günther Günther [unclear] to Frankfurt.
