Conrad Chronicle of Trithemius

In the same year also Hermann Beude, knight, father of our abbot Philip, obtained for the benefit of this monastery letters of indulgences from the twelve bishops who follow.

To all the sons of holy mother Church to whom the present letters shall come: We, by divine mercy Nicholas of Belcastro, Raphael of Archadia, Remigius of Pistoia, Richard of [Bisancientis], Peter of Valona, John of Potenza, Garcias of [Correnchensis], James of Sebaste, Peter of [Otthonensis], Arnold of [Surrensis], Augustine of [Salubriensis], Boniface of [Fodiensis], bishops, eternal greeting in the Lord. The splendor of the heavenly light, which illumines the world with its ineffable brightness, follows with kindly favor the pious vows of the faithful who hope in the clemency of his majesty, especially when the devout humility of [unclear] has deserved and is aided by the prayers of the saints.

Desiring therefore that the monastery at Sponheim, of the order of St. Benedict, in honor of St. Martin, and the chapel of St. Mary the Virgin, founded within the precinct of the said monastery, in the diocese of Mainz, be visited with due honors and be continually venerated by Christ’s faithful: to all who are truly contrite and confessed, who come to the said monastery or chapel on the individual feasts of their patrons, and on all the other feasts written below, namely Christmas, the Circumcision, Epiphany, Good Friday, Easter, Ascension, Trinity, Corpus Christi, the Finding and Exaltation of the Holy Cross, St. Michael the Archangel, on all feasts of the blessed Virgin Mary, the Nativity and Beheading of St. John the Baptist, the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and all the Apostles and Evangelists, on the feast of All Saints, on the commemoration of souls, and on the dedication of the said monastery or chapel, of Saints Stephen or Lawrence, Nicholas, George, of Saints Mary Magdalene, Margaret, Catherine, Elizabeth, Lucy, and Agatha, and throughout the octaves of all the aforesaid feasts that have octaves, on each Sunday and Saturday of the whole year, for the sake of devotion, prayer, or pilgrimage; or who shall be present there at masses, sermons, matins, vespers, and other divine offices and [unclear], and at the burials of the dead; or who shall celebrate there or have or procure celebration there; or who shall go around the cemetery of the said monastery or the precinct, praying for the dead; or who shall follow the Body of Christ or the holy oil when they are carried to the sick; or who at the evening ringing of the bell, on bended knees, shall say the Ave Maria three times; and also who shall extend helping hands to the fabric of the monastery or chapel itself, for lights, books, chalices, vestments, or any other necessary ornaments; or who shall give, bequeath, or procure to be given or bequeathed to the same church or altar gold or silver or any of their property in their wills; and who shall devoutly pray to God for the salutary state of the lord archbishop and for the state of lord Philip Meysz, now abbot of the said monastery at Sponheim, and of Hermann Beude, knight, and Hildegard his wife, and their sons and daughters, the petitioners for the same, while they live, and for the same when they have departed from this light; and who, for the soul of the reverend father and lord Wilhelm, abbot, predecessor of the aforesaid monastery at Sponheim, who is buried in the aforesaid chapel, shall say beside his tomb the Angelic prayer, the seven penitential psalms, or any other devout prayers, and shall piously beseech God: as often as they shall devoutly do the aforesaid things, or any of the aforesaid things, trusting in the mercy of almighty God and in the authority of his blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, each one of us remits forty days of indulgences from the penances enjoined upon them, provided that the will and consent of the diocesan bishop intervene for this. In witness whereof our seals are appended to the present letters. Given at Avignon on the twentieth day of May, in the year of the Lord 1358, in the sixth year of the pontificate of lord Pope Innocent VI.

These indulgences Gerlach, Archbishop of Mainz, diocesan of this monastery, confirmed by his authority, and added forty days to all the aforesaid matters, as likewise appears in his letters:

Gerlach, by the grace of God archbishop of the holy see of Mainz, archchancellor of the Holy Empire throughout Germany, to all Christ’s faithful to whom the present letters shall come, eternal greeting in the Lord. The indulgences of the venerable fathers, the bishops, to which this present charter of ours is attached, given and granted for the monastery at Sponheim of the order of St. Benedict, founded in honor of St. Martin, and for the chapel of St. Mary the Virgin situated within the precinct of the said monastery, of our diocese, we hold to have other equal graces, and we confirm them in the name of the Lord by these presents; and, trusting in the mercy of almighty God and in the merits of his blessed Apostles Peter and Paul and of St. Martin our patron, we add to them forty days of indulgence in like form, in God’s name, in these writings. Yet we do not wish, and under penalty of excommunication strictly forbid, that anyone should in any way carry or export letters of this kind of indulgences outside the monastery and chapel for which the collection is made. In witness whereof our seal is appended to the present letters. Given on the Ides of November, in the year of the Lord 1358.

The total, therefore, of these indulgences of the twelve bishops and of the aforesaid Archbishop of Mainz, for any of the aforesaid works and on any Sunday throughout the circuit of the year, or on any other day expressed in the letters, joined together, makes 520 days of remission from the penance enjoined for those who merit it.

In the same

Sponheim.

In the same year also the residence of a secular priesthood was established in Bockenau by Peter, archpriest of Sponheim, with Lord Philip, abbot, and the convent of this monastery consenting; the collation of this benefice belongs to the abbot, as appears in the letters whose date is the year of the Lord 1358, on the Sunday next before the feast of Philip and James.

The Mass at Bockenau is established.

1359.

In this year Philip, abbot of this monastery, obtained from Lord Walram, count in Sponheim, complete freedom from every service, impost, and exaction for our courts and goods in the marches of the villages of Sponheim, Rudesheim, and Bockenau, for one thousand florins, which he gave to the same count in one sum, as appears in the letters of the same freedom, secured by the seal of the aforesaid count and of Elizabeth his wife; their date is in the year of the Lord 1360, on the day of St Martin. And to this day we possess peaceful possession of this freedom, in all the aforesaid courts, just as it was granted.

Our courts in Sponheim, Rudesheim, and Bockenau are granted freedom.

In the same year Philip, bishop of Châlons, and legate and nuncio of the sacrosanct Apostolic See, being established in the city of Mainz, caused Philip the abbot, Peter the prior, and the senior monks of the convent of this monastery to be summoned to him at Mainz; and, after a diligent inquiry had been made into their state, both spiritual and temporal, when he had learned by the testimony of many that they had failed in both, he appointed for them a manner of living henceforth in holy conduct, first enjoining and commanding that all the monks of this monastery, both those then present and those to come, should especially be instructed in regular disciplines, and should sleep together communally in one dormitory, according to the canonical sanctions and the ancient custom of this monastery hitherto laudably observed, under penalty of deprivation of that day’s prebend and of disobedience. He also commanded them to have integrity of morals, sobriety of diet, propriety of dress, and diligence in divine worship according to the Rule of St Benedict. He instructed the abbot to correct delinquents and to amend the disobedient according to the canonical institutions. Finally, in favor of regular observance, at the petition of the abbot, he confirmed in perpetuity by his authority the incorporation of the parish church formerly made by Archbishop Wernher, Udo’s donation, and all other grants made by anyone to this monastery. These things were done at Mainz in the year of the Lord 1360, on the twentieth day of the month of December, with Hermann, abbot of St Alban’s, and Wiric, abbot of the monastery of St James, present there with many others, in the residence of the aforesaid lord bishop and nuncio of the Apostolic See.

1360.

In the tenth year of Philip our abbot, Emperor Charles IV held a convention of princes at Esslingen. There, when on a certain day he was holding council with his princes among the Friars Minor in the refectory, a tumult arose among the citizens against the emperor; departing from the place, he ordered Count Eberhard of Württemberg, with the aid of the imperial cities, [unclear]. The people of Esslingen, surrounded by a very close siege and seeing that they were placed in danger and could by no means resist such power of the empire, bought peace with money, giving the emperor seventy thousand for the expenses which he had incurred in making war against them by command of the lord emperor.

A convention of princes at Esslingen. A disturbance of [unclear] against the emperor.

At these times also there were grave discords and dissensions between Boemund, archbishop of Trier, and the counts of Sponheim and Starkenburg, on account of certain [things] which the archbishop said belonged to the right of his church, while they protested against it. Walram, count of Sponheim, with his knights, through the mediation of friends, soon returned to concord with the archbishop. But the count of Starkenburg began to devastate the fields, villages, and possessions of the church of Trier with the sword, plundering, and fire, and inflicted many losses upon the church. Against him the archbishop, bringing forth an army, besieged a village near the Moselle which is called Enkirch, and a fortification below the castle of Starkenberg which the same count had built for a toll, and destroyed it utterly. When this had been done, the count, seeking the pontiff’s favor, obtained peace and pardon.

Discord between the archbishop [unclear].

The University at Prague is founded. [unclear] Ingelheim.

At these times also Emperor Charles IV, since he was a learned man, indeed one who with much ornament of his Bohemian kingdom established the University of Prague, which he exalted by enriching it with many privileges, favors, and possessions. He also founded many churches and monasteries of different religions in his time, and provided for them abundantly in imperial magnificence. In the imperial court at the village called Ingelheim, not far from Mainz, he established a monastery of canons of the Order of St Augustine, in which he consented that no one should be received into religion unless he had been born in Bohemia. The first brothers of the same monastery he [took] from the monastery of St Charles in the city of Pra[unclear].

Chronicle of Trithemius

...the times were more dangerous. For, as we have already said, when pestilence was raging throughout the whole world, it consumed more than half of the human race in three years. In that season there died in the town of Kreuznach, which is quite small, more than sixteen hundred people; in Mainz, more than six thousand people, so that both there and in Erfurt and in other principal cities, sometimes in one day [unclear] people were placed in one pit, in such confused order that they could scarcely be kept to a fixed number. Everywhere there was fear, everywhere lamentation and the image of death; and people went about as if dead and out of their minds, struck by excessive fear of sudden death, which each person saw set before his eyes.

The cause of this calamity was laid upon the Jews, namely that they had poisoned the springs and the air; from this there followed a very severe persecution of them by Christians. For in different parts of the world, when such an opinion against them had been made public among Christians, some were miserably suffocated, others cast headlong into the water, others drowned, others beheaded, others burned, others pierced through with swords and lances, and others killed by various kinds of torments. Some of them, seeing themselves set in evil plight, first killed their children together with their wives, lest they fall into the hands of Christians cruelly raging, and then, setting fire beneath, destroyed themselves by burning along with their houses and dwellings. This persecution of the Jews, beginning in the year noted above, lasted two years. Whether it was carried out justly or unjustly is not for us to judge, although it does not seem likely to us that they could have infected all the springs of the whole world with poison, even if they had wished to. But, mindful of the Greek proverb, [unclear], we leave the judgment to be borne by God, who can neither be deceived nor knows how to deceive. In Cologne also, in the same year, for the same cause that we have mentioned, on the vigil of St. Bartholomew the Apostle, the Jews burned themselves up by setting fire to their houses; all the rest were expelled from that city.

1350.

In this year, which was the ninth of our abbot Wilhelm, when the new chapel which he had founded in the ambulatory had already been completed, he had it consecrated in honor of blessed Mary ever virgin, on the 5th day of the month of September, by Rudolph, bishop of Salona, vicar in pontificals of Gerlach, archbishop of Mainz, as appears in his letters, which follow:

To all who shall see these presents, Rudolph, by divine mercy bishop of Salona, vicar of the reverend father and lord Gerlach, by the grace of God archbishop of Mainz, greeting in the Lord. Since in the year of the Lord 1350, on the Nones of September, we dedicated for divine worship to be performed there forever the chapel with the altar of the blessed and glorious Mary ever virgin in the ambulatory of the monastery of St. [Sponheim?], of the Order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Mainz, we have granted to all the faithful of Christ, penitent and confessed, who devoutly visit the aforesaid altar with the chapel, indulgences of fourteen days for criminal sins and of one carena once in the year; and as often as the sacrament is brought to the sick, throughout the whole parish, to endure hereafter. Given and enacted in the year of the Lord as above.

And because, as we have said above, all the monks in this monastery at that time were proprietors and openly possessed money as if lawfully, abbot Wilhelm endowed the aforesaid chapel from the goods of the monastery, and with the consent of his brothers assigned it, with all its revenues, to the office of the priorship: that is to say, that the prior for the time being should celebrate two masses in it each week and should receive all its [pectentes?], as appears in the letters drawn up concerning this, whose date is the year of the Lord 1350, on the day of the Epiphany of the Lord. These things were done before his resignation. The consecration of the chapel, however, was carried out afterwards, after the resignation, under lord abbot Philipp, as can be plainly seen from calculation of the days.

Accordingly, in the aforesaid year Wilhelm, abbot of this monastery, weighed down by age and infirmity, voluntarily and freely resigned his abbacy into the hands of the convent on the second feria before the feast of St. Lawrence the Martyr; and in the same year, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, he died and was buried in the middle of the church which he had founded. He was a pious and good man, who did many good things for this monastery and enlarged its courts, possessions, revenues, and rents. For, as we have said, he purchased with money the court in Blenich and the manor in Bingen as property of the monastery; he also acquired the court in Boekenau, together with certain other goods from his own patrimony, as a perpetual possession for the monastery. In return for these benefactions which he showed to the monastery in his lifetime, the brothers who were then there promised him, while he was still living, a perpetual anniversary to be performed four times a year after his death, on which, after the manner of canons, they were accustomed to divide among themselves portions which they call presences. At his tomb, whoever devoutly says the Lord’s Prayer with the Angelic Salutation, or the seven Psalms, or any other prayers for

The chapel in our ambulatory is consecrated.

Copy of the consecration.

Wilhelm resigns the abbacy and dies in the same year.

Indulgence for being at his tomb. ...he caused to be admitted to [unclear], for whom he appointed a provost according to the custom of the regular canons, subjecting both him and the brothers and the place in full right for all future times. He caused the bishopric of the church of Prague to be raised to an archbishopric, and made it distinguished with many privileges and honors; it had previously been subject to the archbishop of Mainz. He also obtained from the pope the institution of the feast of the Lance and Nails of our Lord Jesus Christ, to be celebrated every year throughout the whole Christian world on the sixth feria after Quasimodo Sunday, with many graces and indulgences for sins.

1361.

In the eleventh year of our abbot Philip, there arose between Edward and Raynald, brothers and dukes of Guelders, a very grave dispute and struggle over that duchy. After they had contended with one another for some time, Edward at last emerged victorious, captured his brother, and ruled the duchy of Guelders alone for ten years. In the same year, in the month of February, the sky on a certain night seemed to be burning. On that same night died William I, duke of Jülich, whom the emperor, at the assembly of Metz, about five years earlier, had made duke, as we said above.

In this same year Gerard, count of Berg, and Arnold, count of Blankenheim, who had long had hostile minds toward one another, attacking each other with sharp lances in a certain joust at Cologne, both died, each cruelly pierced through by the other’s lance.

1362.

In the twelfth year of our abbot Philip, certain petty robbers coming out of England were ranging through France and Spain, devastating everything with sword, fire, and plunder, and everywhere inflicting much damage. When they had increased in number, they set over themselves a captain, whom they called the Archpriest. The very multitude of robbers was called either the Great Company or the English Company, having more than forty thousand fighters. Therefore, after ranging through France and entering Spain and the neighboring regions, they plundered everything. Then they came in a very great multitude to the borders of the Trier lands. When Boemund, archbishop of Trier, heard of their arrival, he sent against them Cuno of Falkenstein, his coadjutor, Wenceslaus, duke of Luxembourg, Walram, count of Sponheim, the count of Veldenz, the count of Starkenburg, with many others both of the counts and of the nobles, with a large army. As soon as they learned that so many princes had come together against them to fight, they fled from the borders of Trier and entered Alsace. They inflicted much damage on the peasants around Strasbourg, carrying off everything they found in the villages.

Coming therefore by night to the city of Strasbourg, they stationed themselves outside the walls, burning Königshofen and certain other villages round about. But before they came, the peasants in the villages everywhere, terrified by the report of them, had brought whatever they could carry to the neighboring cities and safer places to be kept. Then, making quarters in the villages around Strasbourg, they seized whatever remained. The gates of Strasbourg, however, were closed for fear of them, and no one was permitted to enter. Whatever peasants they found in the fields they subjected to unheard-of torments, unless they redeemed themselves with money. Women and virgins, both secular and consecrated to God, whomever they found, they violated with an incredible kind of lust, sparing neither rank nor age. They encircled several towns with siege, but because they did not have the necessary engines, they could not take any at all. It was lawful for no one to pass safely without their safe-conduct; and when they had given it to anyone, they observed it with inviolable firmness. Captives who could not redeem themselves with money they killed without mercy, although many, fleeing under cover of night, escaped safely from their hands. Young males they kept as captives for themselves in servitude.

At last, after they had remained many days in Alsace and had done much damage in the fields and villages by various devastation, they were put to flight by the army of the emperor, the princes, the Strasbourgers, and other cities gathered for this purpose. When our men wished to pursue them, they fled with such speed that the journey which they completed in one day, ours could scarcely have covered in four days. And so this disturbance ceased in Alsace; although the emperor with his men, in departing, inflicted greater damage on the peoples of Alsace than they seemed to have suffered from the English, because the harvest was near, and the grain in the fields was trampled down by the army. From this a great famine followed, which lasted for six years.

In the aforesaid year Boemund of Saarbrücken, archbishop of Trier, weighed down by old age, when he saw that he was insufficient for governing the church entrusted to him, summoned to himself Cuno of Falkenstein, canon of the church of Mainz, formerly administrator before Gerlach under Henry of Virneburg, as we said above, a magnificent man, and caused him to be made canon of the church of Trier; he took him as coadjutor, who Sponheimense.

...shall have said for his soul, he will obtain indulgences of 480 days from the imposed penances, as is clear in the letters obtained by Abbot Philip from twelve bishops in the year 59; a copy of these we shall set down below, in the eighth year of Abbot Philip, the aforesaid year of the Lord.

Concerning Philip Metswin, Fifteenth Abbot of This Monastery of Sponheim, who presided for twenty-four years, one month, and twelve days, and concerning his deeds and those of his time.

After the resignation of the reverend father Wilhelm, which was made on the Monday before the feast of St. Lawrence, lest the monastery long lament the hardships of its widowhood, the brothers appointed the immediately following Thursday as the date for choosing a new pastor over themselves. On that day, gathering in the chapter room, and after the customary prayers had first been said, immediately, with no other discussion intervening, suddenly inspired by the grace of the Holy Spirit, as they maintained, all of them, with no one at all objecting or dissenting, directed their votes, together with the aforesaid Wilhelm, to Philip, called Meysvin, prior of this monastery, and unanimously elected him abbot. They sent him to Gerlach, archbishop of Mainz, to be confirmed, with these letters:

“To the venerable father in Christ and lord Gerlach, archbishop of Mainz, archchancellor throughout Germany, the whole convent of the religious of the monastery of the Order of St. Benedict in Sponheim, in the diocese of Mainz, offers its devout prayers in Christ. Since by divine [unclear], the abbacy of the church in spiritual matters of our monastery through Wilhelm, formerly abbot of our monastery [unclear], lest that monastery long lament the hardships of its widowhood, a day was unanimously assigned by our brothers present, namely the Thursday immediately before Lawrence the Martyr, in the year of the Lord 1350, for holding the election of a future abbot. Meanwhile the absent having been summoned, and all who wished, could, and ought conveniently to be present assembling at our chapter on the aforesaid date, immediately, with no other discussion intervening, suddenly inspired, as we believe, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, all of us, with no one at all objecting or dissenting, unanimously directed our votes, together with Wilhelm, formerly abbot, to brother Philip Mysvin, prior of our monastery, a useful, provident, and discreet man, commendable in knowledge of letters, life, and morals, established in sacred orders and of lawful age, professed of our monastery, born of lawful marriage, and very circumspect in spiritual and temporal matters; and with one spirit we elected him as abbot of us and of our monastery, solemnly sang Te Deum laudamus, and, raising the said elect to the high altar, as is the custom, immediately had his election published to clergy and people. Afterwards, when this election had been presented to the said elect within the due time, and he had been asked to give his assent, he at length, not wishing to resist the divine will, within the time established by law, agreed to our wishes, consenting to the election made concerning him. Therefore we supplicate your Paternity, as devoutly as humbly, with unanimous wish, that you deign to confirm this same election, thus unanimously and concordantly made, and favorably bestow upon the same elect the gift of blessing, so that he may be able to preside over us and our monastery as abbot and usefully benefit us, and that we and the other subjects under his rule may serve God wholesomely. Furthermore, so that your Paternity may know more clearly that the votes of all of us were in agreement in the aforesaid matters, and that in this petition we remain unanimous and concordant...”

[unclear] from the vicar in pontificals of the aforesaid archbishop of Mainz, here in our monastery, with two abbots standing by him, namely of [St. John?] in [the Rheingau?] and of Mount St. Disibod, he received the gift of blessing. At the same time he had the chapel of the Blessed Virgin Mary, founded in the cloister by lord Willicho his predecessor, as was said above, consecrated by the same bishop. This Philip was by origin from Sponheim, from that knightly family which, taking its origin from the late great Philip Meysvin, was called by the same name; born of honorable parents, whose father [unclear]. Set in his childhood to learn letters, he made sufficient progress according to his measure; with nature assisting study, he grew into a sufficiently provident and active man. Then, having been made a monk under the first abbacy of Willicho, and in the course of time advancing to higher things, to the priesthood...

Philip is chosen [unclear] among the abbots.

The decree of election is sent to the bishop.

The Thursday before the day of Lawrence, the day of election.

Commending Philip the elect.

They seek confirmation of the elect.

The family and origin of Philip.

How he was made a monk, and when prior. Of Sponheim.

... was finally quieted through the mediation of William, count of Holland, son of Emperor Louis. The aforesaid duke died in the habit of our order, and was buried as a monk in the monastery of Veleer.

In the same year Philip, abbot of this monastery, had the lease of the goods of our court in Wendelsheim, belonging to the altar of blessed Mary Magdalene, renewed before a notary and witnesses, as is clear in the instrument drawn up concerning it, which is still preserved intact.

In the same year also King Charles entered Italy with a great army of Germans, and, coming to Rome, received the crown of the Empire with great solemnity from the hand of the cardinal of Ostia, whom Pope Innocent VI had sent from Avignon for this purpose. Departing from there, he turned aside to the city of Pisa, where a sedition arising among his [unclear] grew so strong that the emperor himself slipped away in flight and scarcely escaped unharmed with his men. The empress also fled from the city by night with her maidservants; some of them were naked, some in only their shifts, while the rest, half-naked, followed their lady in flight. On the following day the authors of the sedition were beheaded. The like happened to them in the city of Siena.

In this same year, in the month of September, John, king of the French, was captured by the English.

In the same year also, on a certain day around the ninth hour, there was an earthquake at Strasbourg and Basel, so that many buildings and walls collapsed; and a great part of the city of Basel fell in that event and crushed many people. But many very strong castles in the mountains fell as well.

1356.

Emperor Charles, having returned from Italy, held a solemn assembly of princes in the city of Metz with the greatest pomp, where nearly all the princes of the whole kingdom came together and received their regalia according to custom. There was present there a certain archbishop, legate of the Apostolic See, with many princes of the French. There William, margrave of Julich, was then created duke by the emperor; from that time down to the present day the dukes of Julich began to exist. Wenceslaus also, the emperor's brother, from being count of Luxembourg, was raised to be duke by the same emperor, with the consent of all the princes then present. At the same time he raised the county of Bar to a margraviate. He also caused the Golden Bull concerning the election of the emperor, along with many other matters pertaining to the advantage of the commonwealth, to be written with the consent of the princes, and confirmed it. When these things had duly been completed, passing from city to city and from monastery to monastery, he collected many relics of the saints here and there, and carried them with him into Bohemia.

1357.

In the eighth year of Philip our abbot, Pope Innocent VI demanded the tenth penny from the whole clergy of the entire Empire, but did not obtain it from everyone; for many opposed him, especially those of the dioceses of Trier, Mainz, and Cologne.

In the same year also William, count palatine, lord of Hainaut, Holland, Zeeland, and Frisia, was seized by disease and became insane, wholly delirious. Since he had no children, Albert, duke of Bavaria, his brother, son of the late Emperor Louis, undertook the government of his land, which he held for forty-seven years. He had as wife Margaret, daughter of the duke of Brieg; by her he begot a son, William, and a daughter named Catherine, who married Edward, duke of Guelders, brother of Reynald.

1358.

In the eighth year of Philip our abbot, on the seventh day before the Kalends of January, Gerlacus, prior of this monastery, the twenty-first in order, died and was buried in the cloister with the brothers. After him Peter of Schomberg was appointed the twenty-second prior. A professed monk of this monastery, he held the office of prior for fourteen years, a man born more for temporal affairs than for spiritual ones. For in his time the discipline of regular observance had greatly collapsed, and the monks possessed private property; in both spiritual and temporal matters they fell far short.

In the same year Albert, duke of Austria, son of the late Albert, king of the Romans, died; concerning him much has been said above. He left after him Leopold, his son, duke, through whom the genealogy of Maximilian our emperor is continued; Duke Rudolf, who founded the provostship of St. Stephen the Protomartyr in Vienna and subjected the county of Tyrol to the Austrian duchy, whose wife was Catherine, daughter of Emperor Charles IV; Duke Frederick, who died without children; and one daughter named Margaret, marchioness of Brandenburg, and a second named Catherine, who was abbess in the monastery of St. Clare at Vienna, a virgin of most devout conduct.

Ec [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Trithemius. 1373.

In the twenty-third year of our abbot Philip, Albert, bishop of Wurzburg, died. In his place Albert Heßburg was elected by the chapter; against him Emperor Charles obtained from Pope Gregory XI that Gerard of Schwarzburg be promoted as bishop, against the will of all the clergy and people of Wurzburg. Gerard, ordained bishop by the pope, presided for twenty-[eight?] years, and was hated by everyone because of his greed and the unusual exactions that he imposed.

In the same year the dukes of Bavaria sold the Margraviate of Brandenburg to Charles, emperor and king of Bohemia, for two hundred thousand florins, of which one hundred thousand were paid in cash. For the remaining one hundred thousand certain castles, namely Lauf, Hersbruck, Reichenfels, Sulzbach, Rosenberg, and Hirschau, were left in the hands of the dukes of Bavaria under the title of redemption for the aforesaid sum. But the other castles sold to the king of Bohemia in Bavaria were afterwards recovered by Rupert, king of the Romans, and restored by him to the dukes of Bavaria.

1374.

In this year, which was the twenty-fourth and last year of our abbot Philip, Pope Gregory XI, at the request of the same abbot Philip, instructed the scholasticus of St. Peter at Mainz to cause the goods unjustly alienated from the monastery to be restored to the right and ownership of the monastery, as is clear in the bull that follows.

Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved son, the scholasticus of St. Peter outside the walls of Mainz, greeting and apostolic blessing. Inclined by the prayers of our beloved sons, the abbot and convent in Sponheim, of the Order of St. Benedict, in the diocese of Mainz, by the authority of these presents we command you that whatever you find has been unlawfully alienated or disposed of from the goods of that monastery, you take care lawfully to recall to the right and ownership of the same monastery, compelling opponents by ecclesiastical censure, appeal being set aside. And witnesses who have been named, if they withdraw through favor, hatred, or fear, you shall compel by a similar censure, appeal ceasing, to give testimony to the truth. Given at Avignon, the seventh day before the Kalends of March, in the fourth year of our pontificate.

But what the obtaining of this commission accomplished or availed, I do not find, because not long afterwards Abbot Philip died, and Craffto, succeeding him, did not rule very profitably.

In the same year, in the month of February, there was an immense inundation of waters. For the Rhine rose so much that it passed over the walls of the city of Cologne; the town of Bingen too was for the greater part filled with waters, to such an extent that all the gates toward the Rhine and the Nahe were closed, covered by the waters up to the top of the walls. This flooding of the Rhine did many evils and injuries to people dwelling beside the Rhine: for it overturned villages, drowned people, cast down churches and many buildings, and reduced vineyards, gardens, hedges, and roads around the Rhine to nothing.

In the same year also a manic affliction infected many people, which affliction people call the dance of St. John. It attacked many, women and maidens as well as young men, and made them fugitives from their homeland and kin, [unclear]; first, falling to the ground, they foamed, and afterwards, rising, danced until collapse, unless they were restrained by others with a very strong binding. Many deceptions also occurred on this occasion, for many, either so that they might obtain money by begging, or so that they might more freely satisfy their lust, feigned the disease.

In the same year also, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, Philip, the fifteenth abbot of this monastery, died, when the twenty-fourth year of his rule had been completed, with one month and twelve days; he was buried in the middle of the choir before the steps of the presbytery. A stone with an inscription was placed over his tomb, which Johannes Colnhausen, the first abbot in the reformation, removed in order to build the refectory.

Concerning Craffto the Second, the sixteenth abbot of this monastery, who presided for fifteen years, eleven months, and ten days; with various deeds of that time.

After Abbot Philip had died and been buried according to the custom of ecclesiastical tradition, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October, lest the monastery long lament the inconveniences of its widowhood, the brothers soon, on the following day, that is, on the vigil of St. Matthew the Apostle, came together in the chapter place to elect a new shepherd. After many deliberations they elected as abbot Dom Craffto, the second of this name, a monk of the present monastery, whom Adolf, archbishop of Mainz, confirmed through his vicar in pontifical The Chronicle of Trithemius

1378.

In the fourth year of Abbot Crafto, Henry, count of Sponheim, son of Count Walram, set out for the Holy Land for the remission of his sins; Abbot Crafto attached to him as chaplain Wernher of Dille, a monk of this community. But the abbot’s brother, called Eytelwolf of Sponheim, who set out with the count to Jerusalem, received there the dignity of knighthood.

In the same year the tower of St. Martin in Cologne, of our order, was burned up by fire, and a great part of the adjoining [buildings?] perished in the same fire; and the tower itself remained without a roof for nearly 116 years, until at last a certain merchant, Ewald of Bacharach, a citizen of Cologne, when dying bequeathed so much money for its restoration that it was rebuilt in the form in which it is now seen. For his soul a solemn mass in honor of the blessed Mary ever virgin is sung every day in the same church.

Also in the same year, on the vigil of St. Andrew the apostle, Emperor Charles IV died. After him came Wenceslaus, his son, with whom he had reigned for eight years, having been emperor for twenty-two years without the crown of the empire. While still alive, his father had caused him, as we have said, to be elected king of the Romans, namely as a boy of fifteen years, promising each prince-elector one hundred thousand florins. Since he could not pay these, he was forced to assign to the princes, as pledges until the money should be paid, the best cities of the empire. Thus Rupert the Palatine [received] Oppenheim, Odernheim, Ingelheim, and Kaiserslautern, with all their revenues, which his heirs still possess today and will possess until the aforesaid money is paid.

1379.

In the fifth year of Abbot Crafto, Louis, king of Hungary, besieged Venice and inflicted much damage on the Venetians, compelling them to change their seal so that henceforth they would not write themselves “lords of the sea,” a title they had presumptuously usurped for themselves.

In the same year Wenceslaus, king of the Romans, came to Cologne and was received with great honor, having in his retinue a cardinal, legate of the apostolic see.

Also in the same year Otto, margrave of Brandenburg, son of the late Emperor Louis IV, died and was buried in Salzwedel. This Otto, like two of his brothers, William, who held Holland, of whom we have spoken, and Louis called “the Roman,” who was born at Rome, departed without children, leaving to his brothers everything that he possessed.

1380.

In the sixth year of Abbot Crafto, almost all the cities and towns of the empire around the Rhine and in Swabia, together with Pilgrim, archbishop of Salzburg, and the city of Regensburg, having made a league among themselves, attacked with plundering and fire, with an army of nearly eight thousand, the dukes of Bavaria and certain others in their vicinity who were troublesome to them. But after five years, when they had begun to act more insolently, they stirred up against themselves the minds of all the princes around the Rhine and in Swabia, Bavaria, and Franconia. These, after uniting a very great army of their men, advanced against them, inflicted very great losses, and destroyed that league or confederation. Pilgrim, archbishop of Salzburg, was at that time captured in [unclear]; the castle Hoensolms was captured by the citizens of the aforesaid confederation and, fire having been set to it, [unclear].

1381.

In the seventh year of Abbot Crafto, Lampert, from being an abbot of our order, bishop of Speyer, was transferred by apostolic authority to the church of Bamberg. Adolph of Nassau succeeded him in the bishopric of Speyer and presided for fifteen years, a man acute in affairs and of penetrating intelligence, who had certain disputes with his citizens.

In the same year Wenceslaus, king of the Romans, because of the plague, left Bohemia; between [unclear] the count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria serious disagreements arose, which went so far that, becoming public enemies against each other, they inflicted much damage on one another. At length, however, through the mediation of friendly princes, they were brought back to concord.

In this year also a very great pestilence was raging in Hungary and Bohemia, which [unclear] thousands Sponheimense.

who, triumphing most gloriously over the enemies of the aforesaid church, soon at the beginning of his establishment accomplished marvelous things. Therefore Boemundus, rejoicing, obtained from Pope Innocent VI permission to resign the archbishopric of Trier to Cuno, which the pope freely granted. Cuno becomes archbishop of Trier. Boemundus, therefore, after resigning the pontificate to Cuno, received for his support the fortress and castle of Saarburg, with its appurtenances and revenues, for as long as he should live, and, suffering from gout for almost five years, survived there.

In the same year also died Wilhelm, archbishop of Cologne, leaving many possessions in gold, silver, and revenues; the archbishopric was vacant ten months. Meanwhile Johannes of Virenburg, dean of the greater church, was elected by the chapter and went to Rome for his confirmation. Pope Urban V not only refused to confirm his election, but even annulled it entirely, and, after consulting the chapter, raised Adolf, brother of the count of Mark, bishop of Munster, to be archbishop of Cologne; he was young in age and by no means suited to such a dignity. He governed the church of Cologne badly for ten months and eighteen days, and afterward, resigning, took a wife, as we shall say in its proper place.

1363.

In the thirteenth year of our abbot Philip, on the day of the Holy Innocents, Gerlaeus of Ernberg, bishop of Speyer, died and was buried in the greater church. Lampert of Burnen, abbot of the monastery in Gengenbach of our order, in the diocese of Strasbourg, succeeded him and presided for eighteen years; afterward he was transferred by apostolic authority, through Pope Urban V, to the bishopric of Bamberg. To this bishop of Speyer Emperor Charles IV renewed all the privileges of the kings granted to that church, and solemnly confirmed them under the Golden Bull before the princes. In the same year died Theoderic of Boppard, bishop of Worms, whom Johannes Schatlandt of the Order of Preachers succeeded: doctor of sacred letters, apostolic nuncio, inquisitor of heretical depravity, sometime administrator of the churches of Hildesheim in Saxony, Augsburg in Raetia, Kulm in Prussia, and Constance in Swabia. He presided for almost fourteen years, and had many disputes with the people of Worms.

1364.

In the fourteenth year of our abbot Philip, Adolf, archbishop of Cologne, accused before the apostolic see of being a squanderer of ecclesiastical goods, resigned the archbishopric into the hands of the pope, not by force or fear but voluntarily, out of love, as was reported, for a certain girl of the count of Mont, with whom he hoped that he would receive the county of Cleves; and this happened. For after resigning the pontificate, since he did not have holy orders, although he had held the bishopric of Munster for [unclear] years and Cologne for almost one year, he took the aforesaid girl as his wife, and not long afterward obtained the lordship of the land of Cleves, which belonged to her. After Adolf’s resignation Engelbert, count of Mark, bishop of Liege, paternal uncle of the aforesaid Adolf, was postulated as archbishop of Cologne; confirmed by Pope Urban V, he presided for four years. He accomplished little, because he found the church in very great debts and joined new debts to the old.

1365.

In the fifteenth year of our abbot Philip, the winter was exceedingly harsh; the Rhine, frozen for almost three months, offered itself as passable on foot to those crossing it. An exceedingly harsh winter. Many people also in this year [unclear] by a great pestilence. For after resigning the pontificate, since he had not had holy orders, although he had held the bishopric of Munster for [unclear] years and Cologne for almost one year, he took the aforesaid girl as his wife, and not long afterward obtained the lordship of the lands of Cleves, which belonged to her. After Adolf’s resignation Engelbert, count of Mark, bishop of Liege, paternal uncle of the aforesaid Adolf, had been postulated as archbishop of Cologne; confirmed by Pope Urban V, he presided for four years. He accomplished little, because he found the church in very great debts and joined new debts to the old.

1366.

In the sixteenth year of our abbot Philip, there was a great sedition and discord between the bishop and the citizens of Worms over the institution of the consulate of the Schultheiss, and certain other matters pertaining to jurisdiction. Sedition of the citizens. At length, after much contention, it was amicably settled by Rupert, count palatine of the Rhine, who was called Adolf, [unclear] the consulate of Mainz and Speyer, on the day of the Conversion of St. Paul in the aforesaid year. In the same year the king of England brought the king of France, with his son, and likewise the king of the Scots, captured, into England. In these times also a great confederation was made among the cities of the Empire.

1367.

In the seventeenth year of our abbot Philip, Boemundus, archbishop of Trier, died on the day of St. Scholastica the virgin, and was buried in the greater church of Trier; after him Cuno of Chronicle of Trithemius

At the same time also the monastery of Deutz, of our order, which the people of Cologne had destroyed ten years earlier together with the parish church, was rebuilt and consecrated anew.

In this year also there was war between the duchess of Brabant, Joanna, widow of Duke Wenceslaus, and William, duke of Guelders, who emerged victorious against her; and at length an agreement was made between them through Frederick, archbishop of Cologne.

1388.

In the fourteenth year of [Crafto?], our abbot, Adolf of Nassau, archbishop of Mainz, died. Conrad of Weinsberg, canon of the cathedral church, succeeded him by election and presided for seven years, a good and peaceable man.

In the same year a general school, or university, was established in the city of Cologne by the council there, and at its request was confirmed by Pope Urban VI; elsewhere we read that Boniface IX, who succeeded Urban, confirmed it.

In the same year also the citizens of Mainz, Worms, and Speyer, with certain other confederates against the princes, entered the land of lord Rupert, count palatine and duke of Bavaria, with six hundred armed men, and began to lay everything waste with fire and plunder. The duke himself came against them with his army not far from Worms, and, when battle was joined, emerged victorious: two hundred of them were cut down and three hundred captured, so that scarcely one hundred of their whole army remained after escaping by flight. Among the captives were sixty wretched plunderers who, roaming about by night, had oppressed the poor with fire and robbery. The duke ordered them to be thrown into a fiercely burning limekiln, saying: “You burned up my land with hidden fire in the nighttime, and I shall make you burn in broad day, with a very great crowd of people looking on.” The rest were compelled to ransom themselves from captivity with money. These things took place on the Friday before the feast of Saint Martin in the year noted above, not far from Worms. And thereafter the confederate citizens did not dare to attack the princes’ lands in war, except those very nearby, nor did they afterward have peace until they satisfied the princes with money according to their will, and dissolved the league of their confederation among themselves.

In the same year also Cuno of Falkenstein, archbishop of Trier, burdened by old age, with the will and consent of his chapter resigned the archbishopric to Werner of Falkenstein, his kinsman. In May they unanimously received him as bishop, canonically elected and confirmed by Pope Urban VI, assigning to him all the possessions of the church, towns, castles, and villages, with no one opposing. Cuno, however, keeping with him his very great treasures in gold and silver, began to live a private life, taking up residence in the castle called Wellmich. He did not long survive there, but died in the same year, in the month of June, and was buried in the church of Saint Castor at Koblenz. Werner performed solemn obsequies for him, with Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, and Rupert, also called Adolf, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, standing by, together with many other princes. Werner, his successor, found with him an immense treasure, the church free of debts, and most abundantly supplied with every kind of provision.

In the same year the people of Frankfurt led an army against the lords of Kronenberg to fight. The men of Kronenberg, though fewer in number, hastened boldly to meet them; and when battle was joined they were victorious, killed one hundred of the Frankfurt men, and led away six hundred captives; the rest fled in disgrace. For the liberation of the captives, however, the nobles of Kronenberg received seventy thousand florins from the people of Frankfurt, and compelled them to accept conditions of peace.

In the year noted above also the confederate citizens in Swabia took up arms against the count of Württemberg. Against them those counts, supported by the aid of other princes, advanced to battle near the town of Weil in Swabia; after a long contest they became victors, killed many of the confederate citizens, and, utterly dissolving the league of cities, which had lasted almost ten years, reduced it to nothing. All these evils occurred in the land while Wenceslaus was reigning and imprudently looking the other way.

In this year, in the town of Boppard, in the diocese of Trier, an infant was born who was double from the navel upward: he had two heads, four hands, and all the other things required for the perfection of a human being in double form. But from the navel downward all the members were arranged in the form of one human being. This monstrosity did not live long, for within the space of one year both died.

1300 [unclear]. Chronicle of Trithemius

Cuno of Falkenstein, mentioned above, and lord of Münzenberg, born of a mother who was the daughter of the count of Saarwerden, who while he was still living had been ordained archbishop, vigorously ruled the church of Trier for [unclear] years, and did many good things for the church. For the services rendered in many ways to Emperor Charles IV, he obtained Boppard and Wesel, together with half of Sternenberg, which Baldwin, once archbishop, had received in pledge for expenses from Emperor Henry VII, his brother, as a firmer pledge to the church of Trier for a great sum of money, so that this later pledging was greater in amount than the earlier had been.

In the same year there were serious quarrels between Ulrich, count of Württemberg, and the counts of Eberstein. Therefore, when the Württemberger was one day in a natural bath, which we call a woodland bath, the aforesaid counts of Eberstein came secretly with an army and surrounded the place with a siege, hoping that they would certainly capture the count shut up inside. But vain confidence deceived them; for, led at night through the woods by a certain peasant, he escaped from their hands, and a great discord followed in the province of the Swabians. For all the nobles of that land made a conspiracy together against the counts of Württemberg. But the citizens of Esslingen, adhering to the Württembergers, encircled Heisheim with a siege and compelled the nobles to obedience to the aforesaid counts.

Likewise in the same year Engelbert, archbishop of Cologne, weighed down by old age and very great burdens of debts, but weakened by paralysis, feeling that he was less sufficient for the governance of ecclesiastical affairs, by the counsel of his own [unclear] great discord. Therefore, when the Württemberger was one day in a natural bath, which we call a woodland bath, the aforesaid counts of Eberstein came secretly with an army and surrounded the place with a siege, hoping that they would certainly capture the count shut up inside. But [unclear] vain confidence deceived them; for, led at night through the woods by a certain peasant, he escaped from their hands, and a great discord followed in the province of the Swabians. For all the nobles of that land made a conspiracy together against the counts of Württemberg. But the citizens of Esslingen, adhering to the Württembergers, encircled Heisheim with a siege and compelled the nobles to obedience to the aforesaid counts.

Likewise in the same year Engelbert, archbishop of [Cologne?], weighed down by old age and the greatest burdens of debts, [unclear] for the governance of ecclesiastical affairs, by the counsel of his own [unclear] great discord. In the sixteenth year of Philip, our abbot.

338 Chronicle of Trithemius

his intimates, banqueters, and flatterers, who pursued the booty, not the man, and cared very little for the advantage of the monastery. Moreover the brothers, to whom his excessive pomp was burdensome and intolerable, considering the providence of divine counsel, expected better things to come in the future.

Concerning Bernhard, eighteenth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, who presided for 41 years, 3 months, and 9 days; and concerning his various deeds and the events of that time.

When Philip the Second, seventeenth abbot of this monastery, had died and been buried according to the custom of ecclesiastical tradition, the brothers, having the voice of election for choosing a new pastor over themselves, came together to the chapter place; and, after the grace of the Holy Spirit had been invoked, as is customary, they resolved that the greatest care must be taken not to elect an abbot like the deceased, who would consume the remaining goods of the monastery in empty pomp, but rather to promote a useful and provident man, fearing God and having zeal for the common good. Therefore, after mature deliberation had first been held, they at last unanimously elected as abbot and pastor of this monastery Bernhard of Sponheim, a professed monk of this community, then in the thirty-first year of his age. Confirmed by Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, and blessed by his vicar in pontificals, as is customary, he presided over this monastery for 41 years, 3 months, and 9 days: a steadfast and energetic man, and sufficiently keen and fit for the management of affairs.

He was, moreover, from Sponheim, born of knightly stock. In his boyhood he devoted himself for some time to learning letters; and when he had already begun to show understanding in them, by the will and persuasion of his parents he became a monk, and turned out better than those of his own age. Once ordained abbot, he labored with all the zeal he could so that the goods and possessions unjustly alienated by his predecessors might be restored to the ownership of the monastery. Part he restored; part he was forced to leave in another’s possession, because of the poverty of temporal goods and the wickedness of the times. Finally, he often undertook to restore the observance of regular discipline, which had utterly collapsed in this monastery, to the integrity of monastic conduct, but, with the rashness of wicked men standing in the way, he made little progress. Yet he did bring about this: that the monks, so long as he lived, were compelled to eat together in one refectory and to sleep together in one dormitory; nevertheless, immediately after his death this was again laid aside. However, he did not take away the private property of the monks, the root of all irreligion, nor did he restore private possessions to common use. Nonetheless, because of his zeal for rectitude, he often endured many insolences from his monks, not without loss to the monastery and danger to souls.

In the fifth month of his rule, Philippus and Eberhardus Meysvin, squires of Sponheim, resigned forever to the abbot and convent their right, which they had with the abbot, to the altar constructed in our monastery in honor of Saints Mary Magdalene, Lawrence the martyr, and Margaret, virgin and martyr, so that the same altar should henceforth be served by a monk of this community and not by another, as is evident in the letters of this resignation, which the aforesaid squires handed over to the abbot in the year of the Lord 1391, on the vigil of Lawrence.

1392.

In this year, the first of our abbot Bernhard, the University of Erfurt in Thuringia was founded, and was confirmed by Boniface IX, privileges and liberties being granted after the manner of other universities.

In the same year Pope Boniface IX, at the request of Stephen, Frederick, and John, brothers and dukes of Bavaria, granted a jubilee year to the city of Munich, in the diocese of Freising, in Bavaria, from Laetare Sunday until the feast of St. James the Apostle.

Also in the same year, on the Tuesday before the feast of St. Catherine, virgin and martyr, a division was made among the aforesaid three brothers, sons of Duke Stephen, son of Louis IV, emperor, of Bavaria. In this division John received Munich in Upper Bavaria, with its appurtenances, as his lawful portion; Stephen likewise obtained, in Upper [Bavaria?], Baiolzhuett and Rattenberg, with the [50?] things belonging to it; Frederick, however, received Landshut in Lower Bavaria, with its appurtenances, for his portion. Of these, Stephen and Frederick married wives who were daughters of Galeazzo Visconti of Milan, whom Wenceslaus, king of the Romans, after receiving money, created duke. Stephen begot Duke Louis of Ingolstadt, Elizabeth queen of France, and John, bishop of Ratisbon. Frederick begot Henry, duke of Landshut, and two daughters, Magdalena and Elizabeth, of whom the last was taken as wife by Frederick, burgrave of Nuremberg, whom Emperor Sigismund afterwards, at the time of the Council of Constance, made margrave of Brandenburg.

Sponheim.

1370.

In the twentieth year of Philip our abbot, Gerlach of Nassau, archbishop of Mainz, died, and in the election of a successor there was very great difficulty. For first Cuno, archbishop of Trier, was postulated for the church of Mainz; under Henry of Virneburg, Gerlach’s predecessor, he had for some time been its administrator. Content with his own church, he refused the dignity offered to him. Afterwards Adolf of Nassau was elected by the chapter; against him the emperor sought to have his nephew John, son of Wenceslaus duke of Luxembourg, whom the common people called the Gallic, promoted as archbishop of the church of Mainz, a good and vigorous man, who died poisoned by venom.

In the same year lord Cuno, archbishop of Trier and administrator of the church of Cologne, obtained from the aforesaid chapter of Cologne that they unanimously elected Frederick of Saarwerden, his nephew and their canon, as archbishop of the church of Cologne, in a castle not far from Koblenz, called the Chapel: a young man indeed in years, but of good promise and singular prudence. Ordained by Pope Urban V at Rome on the fourteenth day of the month of November, in the presence of the cardinals, he presided for forty-four years, quite usefully and vigorously, and did many good things for his church.

In the same year Emperor Charles IV, now heavy with age and consulting his own repose, obtained from the princes that his son Wenceslaus, king of Bohemia, was made king of the Romans; with him he governed the Roman Empire for eight years.

1371.

In the twenty-first year of Philip our abbot, on the vigil of St Bartholomew the Apostle, a great battle took place between Wenceslaus, duke of Brabant and Luxembourg, brother of Emperor Charles IV, and William, duke of Jülich, near Baesweiler. In it the duke of Jülich emerged victor, and led away Wenceslaus, duke of Brabant, captive with many other nobles and counts, from whom he extorted an incredible sum of money. But after he had held the duke of Luxembourg captive for eleven months, through fear of his brother the emperor he released him free without exaction of money. In this battle more than eight thousand fell on both sides, among whom there were more than forty in number of the knightly class. In the same war Edward, duke of Guelders, who had betrothed the daughter of Albert, count of Holland and duke of Bavaria, was struck in the forehead by an arrow by his own servant called Hermann Leers, whose wife he was abusing, and died. When he was dead, his brother Reynald, released from ten years’ custody, was again accepted by all the people; since he was very fat, surviving scarcely three months, he died, and the stock of the dukes of Guelders failed in him, and William duke of Jülich obtained the duchy.

1372.

In the twenty-second year of Philip our abbot, Peter of Schönberg died in the fourteenth year of his priorate. In his time, and thereafter for many years, there was almost no discipline of regular observance in the present monastery. For they were all proprietors, and cared little for the integrity of monastic conduct. After Peter, Abbot Philip appointed as twenty-third prior of this monastery Frederick, a professed monk, who presided in the priorate for eighteen years, a worldly and secular man, who cared either nothing at all or [unclear] for religion.

In the same year John, archbishop of Mainz, son of Wenceslaus duke of Brabant and Luxembourg, nephew of Emperor Charles IV, died in the castle of Eltville, poisoned by venom, as it seemed. When he was dead the chapter elected as archbishop of Mainz Adolf of Nassau, son of the sister of the late archbishop Gerlach, who before John, as we have said, had been elected. But Pope Gregory XI, wishing to elevate Louis, son of the margrave of Meissen, bishop of Bamberg, as archbishop of Mainz, as he had promised him, denied confirmation and the pallium to justice, as was reported. Adolf, aided by his friends, though not confirmed, obtained the places and fortifications of the archbishopric, and for almost seven years litigated at Rome with Louis. At length Louis himself perished, overtaken by fire, and Adolf, confirmed as archbishop, possessed the church of Mainz in peace. He presided, from the time of his election until his death, for almost sixteen years.

Also in the same year Emperor Charles, with the empress, bishops, ten dukes, nine counts, ten knights, eighty-two nobles, one thousand one hundred horsemen, and another innumerable multitude, came to Aachen; and, after an imperial court had been held there, he freed his brother William, duke of Brabant and Luxembourg, from captivity under the duke of Jülich by threats, not by money, whom he had earlier refused to release for a great sum.

Gerlach, archbishop of Mainz, dies.

John becomes archbishop of Mainz.

Frederick becomes archbishop of Cologne.

Wenceslaus becomes king of the Romans.

War between the duke of Brabant and the duke of Jülich.

The duke of Jülich victorious.

Edward, duke of Guelders, struck by an arrow, dies.

Peter, prior of this monastery, died.

The state of the monastery.

Frederick becomes twenty-third prior of this place.

John, archbishop of Mainz, dies.

Adolf is elected as archbishop.

Pope Gregory wants Louis to be promoted as archbishop of Mainz.

Adolf occupies the places and fortifications of the archbishopric.

Louis perished, overtaken by fire.

An imperial court is held at Aachen. Sponheim.

...had him ordained with pontificals, and he presided over the abbacy of this monastery for fifteen years, eleven months, and ten days. He was by origin from Beckelnheim, born of his father Wolfram, knight of Sponheim, and his mother Margaretha of Sobernheim. In his boyhood he had been handed over to the monastery under Abbot Wilhelm and lived among the brothers according to their custom. But when elected abbot, Regular observance is deficient, he presided, not very usefully, more with regard for his parents than for God, because he instituted no discipline of regular observance and in many respects made the supports of the temporal substance worse. Under his rule all the monks of this monastery, seeking what was their own, not what was the Lord’s, had money; they first began to disperse, violate, and sell the quite precious library, which up to that point had remained intact.

1375.

Crafft, abbot, in the first year of his rule, stripped and laid bare the head of Saint Irmina the virgin in its silver capsule, which Crafft the first, almost two hundred years earlier, had had made for the adornment of the house of God; and, after the silver was sold, he clothed the crown with copper, as it is still seen to be clothed. Other various treasures of this monastery too, which former abbots had bestowed on the church for the honor of God, were afterward alienated and sold by their successors, so that, apart from their old pontifical mitre, nothing remained down to our time.

In these times also there was a grave dissension between Archbishop Friedrich and the citizens of Cologne; many princes formed a [confoederatio?] with the archbishop against them.

1376.

In the second year of our Abbot Crafft, Johannes called Scadlandt, bishop of Worms, of the Order of Preachers, died. He was buried in his convent at Coblenz, where he had entered that order. After him Eckhard of Ders obtained the bishopric of Worms for twenty-nine years, a man very learned both in sacred Scripture and in secular letters, devout in life and conduct, a despiser of the world and lover of God. Contrary to the custom of bishops of that time, in order that simony might be avoided, he was accustomed to confer all orders, both minor and major, in his own person, freely and with complete purity. He was rarely seen in public outside the church, but, fleeing the tumult of men, he rested alone with his own household in his palace at Ladenburg, devoting continual zeal to the reading of the Scriptures and to prayer.

In the same year Abbot Crafft had an action with the villagers there concerning the liberty of our court in Flonheim, and obtained the liberty in every respect, as appears in the letters.

In this same year the townsmen of Deutz, siding with Friedrich, archbishop of Cologne, showed themselves public enemies of the people of Cologne. Hence the people of Cologne, provoked to anger, burned and utterly destroyed the monastery and the parish church. Afterward in the same year, on the eve of Saint Pantaleon the martyr, Archbishop Friedrich besieged Cologne for a few days; when he saw that he could not take it, he raised the siege and returned to Bonn. Then, around the feast of Saint Laurence the martyr, the people of Cologne went out again and utterly destroyed the monastery of Deutz, which they had previously left untouched, together with the parish church, leaving absolutely nothing whole, lest the archbishop perhaps place his garrisons there to attack the city. Moved by this presumption of theirs, many princes publicly became enemies and foes of the people of Cologne; among them these were the more important: Cuno, archbishop of Trier, also the bishop of Paderborn, Wenceslaus, duke of Brabant and Luxembourg, the duke of Austria, also the emperor of the Romans, the count of Ziegenhain, and the city of Aachen. With these they had more than eight hundred hostile men-at-arms declared against them. For eight years also the city of Cologne itself was placed under interdict, and the celebration of divine services in it was discontinued.

1377.

In the third year of our Abbot Crafft, Wilhelm, count of Holland, Zeeland, and Hainaut, and count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, son of the late Emperor Ludwig and brother of Count Albert, died in custody, insane, as we have said; it was reported that he had fallen into that insanity after drinking poison. His brother Albert, as was said above, after his removal into custody, usurped his territory for himself.

In the same year a great battle took place between Eberhard, count of Württemberg, and the imperial cities of Swabia, near Reutlingen; many fell.

In the same year also, through Cuno, archbishop of Trier, a very firm concord was made between Archbishop Friedrich and the citizens of Cologne, but in the usual manner it was not long observed.

Wilhelm, count of Holland, dies.

[Bullum?] of Count Eberhard of Württemberg with the [customarii?] of imperial Swabia.

Concord between the archbishop and the citizens of Cologne.

Deficient in regular observance. The silver head of Saint Irmina is sold.

Dissension between the archbishop and the people of Cologne.

Eckhard becomes bishop of Worms.

The court in Flonheim.

The people of Cologne destroy Deutz.

Cologne is besieged.

The monastery with the parish church is destroyed.

Enemies of the people of Cologne.

Wilhelm, count of Holland, dies.

[Bullum?] of Count Eberhard of Württemberg with the [customarii?] of imperial Swabia.

Concord between the archbishop and the citizens of Cologne.

It was not long observed, not long observed, not long observed.

Sponheim.

... consumed thousands of people; for in the city of Prague 1,116 died in one day.

1382.

In the eighth year of Abbot Craffto, the king of France and the count of Flanders besieged Ghent; and although they had twice emerged victorious, nevertheless the men of Ghent advanced against them to battle and forced them to flee to the city of Bruges. Then, surrounding the city of Ghent with a siege, they took it at the sixth hour after midday, on the Sabbath day, when the blood of the Lord’s circumcision is carried in procession. There more than seventy-seven thousand men were said to have fallen. The count of Flanders, having slipped away in flight, scarcely [escaped?]; the king of France, suddenly gone mad, raged.

In the same year Lupold, duke of Austria, went out to war against the Swiss; defeated by them, he was killed together with many other nobles and commoners, and many were captured.

1383.

In the ninth year of Craffto our abbot, Johannes of Sponheim, brother of Count Heinrich, died without children.

In the same year, on the seventh day before the Kalends of August, Wernher of Dille died, a monk of this monastery, who three years earlier, with Count Heinrich and with the permission of his abbot, as we have said, had set out overseas to the sepulchre of the Lord.

Also in the same year, on the eighth day before the Ides of December, Wenceslaus, duke of Brabant and Luxembourg, brother of Emperor Heinrich IV, died. He had governed Brabant for twenty-seven years, and was buried with great pomp in the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary near Luxembourg, which is an abbey of our order. After his death his wife, who was the daughter of Johann III, duke of Brabant, ruled those lands for almost twenty-two years with the aid of Arnold of Horne, bishop of Liège, whom she had lifted from the sacred font of baptism.

1384.

In this year, which was the [unclear] of Abbot Craffto, Johannes Frie died, a monk of this monastery, who held the office of cellarer for many years.

In the same year, on the seventh day before the Ides of August, Hermann Stumpf died, a monk and custodian here. After the death of Johann, the elder cellarer mentioned above, Abbot Craffto appointed as cellarer Emerich, a monk of this community, son of Philipp Viner, knight of Beckelnheim, who previously had been rent-collector of this monastery for seven years.

1385.

In this year Abbot Craffto sold this court [unclear] for florins to Heinrich Wolff of Sponheim, knight; thus alienated, it remained apart from the monastery until the time of Abbot Johannes Trithemius, for one hundred years. He redeemed half the court, but was compelled to give up the other half, as we shall say in its place.

In the same year, on the eighth day before the Ides of September, Philipp Viner, knight of Beckelnheim, died, father of Emerich the monk and cellarer, a singular benefactor of this monastery.

Also in the same year Wilhelm, count of Holland, son of Albert, duke of Bavaria, and grandson of Emperor Ludwig IV, took as wife the daughter of Philipp, duke of Burgundy, and celebrated the wedding with great pomp and notable solemnity.

1386.

In the twelfth year of Craffto our abbot, a very great abundance of wine grew, so that at vintage-time, because of the plentifulness, vessels were lacking; a cartload was sold for one florin, and a vessel holding a cartload of wine for three florins.

In the same year, on the first day of the month of March, which was the fifth feria of Sexagesima, [unclear] leaving Worms [unclear] of our abbot, whose wife Catharina delivered to us certain goods from his legacy. He was buried in our church before the altar of St. Margaret, virgin and martyr.

In the same year, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March, Johannes, called Reyle, a professed monk of this monastery, died, and is buried in the cloister of the church.

Sponheim.

1389.

In the fifteenth year of Craffto, our abbot, on 11 March, Margaret died, widow of Philipp Viner, knight of Sponheim, mother of Emeric, monk and cellarer of this monastery. She bequeathed thirty florins for making the panel on the high altar, which her aforesaid son Emeric, the cellarer and steward, had made, adding from his own patrimony the remainder of the cost; and he had himself painted below, beside the image of the Holy Trinity, at the foot of that panel, with his arms.

In the same year, on 6 December, Peter of Sponheim, monk of this place, died.

In the same year also Wilhelm, count of Berg, was created duke by Wenceslaus, king of the Romans, with great pomp and solemnity, as is customary.

1390.

In the sixteenth and last year of our abbot Craffto, Diethardus, count of Katzenelnbogen, became a public enemy and foe of the people of Cologne, and inflicted much damage on them, Frederick the archbishop dissembling and furthering the affair.

In the same year also, on the day of St Egidius the Confessor, lord Craffto died, the sixteenth abbot of this monastery, in the fifty-ninth year of his age. He was buried in the choir of the monastery, at the head of Bernhelm, the first abbot, beneath a stone: a laborious man, but not very fortunate, who governed with insufficient foresight in both states, leaving the monastery in many debts and its observance utterly dissipated.

In the same year John, duke of Bavaria, son of Albert, count of Holland, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, was postulated as bishop of Liege; although he had not yet completed the nineteenth year of his age, he was received by the people of Liege with great honor.

Concerning Philipp the Second, seventeenth abbot of this monastery, who presided for six months and eighteen days, and concerning his deeds in that time.

After lord abbot Craffto had died and been buried in the aforesaid year and on the aforesaid day, the brethren assembled at the chapter place on the following day, that is, 2 September, to hold the election of a new abbot. After mature deliberation among themselves they elected [unclear], who soon in the same month was confirmed by Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, and ordained according to custom by his vicar in pontificals. He presided for only six months and eighteen days: an excessively pompous and vainglorious man, who immediately at the beginning of his rule, wishing to appear splendid, hired a large and useless household; he acquired superfluous horses, contrary to the custom of all his predecessors, who used to be content with three horses and a household chaplain. With four or five he began to ride outside the monastery, making great expenses, the magnitude of which the poverty of the monastery could not sustain without utter desolation. The precious golden cross [unclear], which abbot Craffto, the first of that name, had had made 255 years before for the adornment of the house of the Lord, he sold, in order to satisfy the pomp of his rank, and utterly alienated it from the monastery. Furthermore he sold certain possessions which the monastery, from the beginning of its foundation down to these times, had possessed in all peace and usefulness.

Philipp was by origin from Bechtolsheim, son of Heinrich the knight. When he was twelve years old he became a monk under abbot Philipp Meysvvin, and was instructed in the manner of the rest, more toward the luxury and vanity of the world than toward the love of God. When, however, he was in the thirty-first year of his age, after the death of abbot Craffto, he was elected abbot, as we have said. He did evil at the beginning of his rule, and if he had lived longer he would have entirely dissipated the whole substance of the monastery.

In the same year in which abbot Philipp was instituted, on 11 October, Frederick [unclear] regular discipline and observance. For all the monks were proprietors and had separate houses of their own; neither the refectory, according to the Rule, nor the dormitory was common to them. After Frederick had died, the abbot instituted as twenty-fourth prior Rudolf, a professed monk of this monastery, who presided in the office of prior for thirteen years. He seemed little concerned for the discipline of regular life, after the manner of his teacher.

1391.

In this year, on 18 March, Philipp the Second, seventeenth abbot of this monastery, died. He is buried in the choir before the steps of the presbytery; his death saddened no one more than [unclear].

Abbot Philipp dies. Chronicle of Trithemius

... denounced; but because the monks, refusing to undertake the reform proposed at Constance, were working for the transfer of the monastery into a secular status, in which it now is, for that reason the chapter could not be held there, but was celebrated among the Augustinians. At this provincial chapter Bernhard, abbot of this monastery, was present in person. When he had set forth to those presiding the insolence of his monks, who were refusing to undertake reform, it was entrusted to the visitors that they should compel them to reform by ecclesiastical censure. Therefore the visitors came to the monastery, but accomplished little, because they were deceived by the deceitfulness of the monks, who made great promises in their presence but after their departure observed nothing.

In the same year also John, duke of Burgundy, entered France with a strong hand against the king of the French, inflicted very many losses upon him, and took the city of Paris with armed force. There many bishops, priests, doctors, students, and citizens were cruelly slain, and the city was miserably laid waste. But in the following year the aforesaid duke of Burgundy, as we shall say, was beheaded in the presence of the king.
