In these times also there were great discords and dissensions between Theoderic, archbishop of Cologne, and the citizens of Cologne. Proceeding as far as open hostilities, they brought many losses on both sides to the parties, until at last they were reconciled.

1419.

In this year, which was the twenty-eighth of Bernhard our abbot, on the twenty-third day of September, John, archbishop of Mainz, died. Conrad, son of the Count of the Rhine of Stein, succeeded him in the archbishopric, elected at Ruedesheim on the sixth of the Ides of October, a magnificent and powerful man, who presided well for almost sixteen years.

In the same year John, duke of Burgundy, was beheaded in the presence of the king of France, contrary to sworn faith, since they had sworn upon the Lord's body that peace between them was to be kept most firmly; and as evidence of this, they received from the hand of the priest at the altar the host of the Lord's body, divided into two parts. Philip, his son, avenged this murder of the duke with very severe punishment: for, having taken the king of the English as an ally, he devastated all France with fire and plunder, took Paris, killed many thousands of people, almost utterly destroyed the kingdom itself, and forced the king to flee from France for a time.

1420.

In the year of the Lord [1420], the twenty-ninth of Bernhard our abbot, Emericus Ulner of Sponheim died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, a professed monk of this monastery, who for more than thirty years had held the office of cellarer, or provider, quite faithfully and energetically. After his death Bernhard, finding among the monks no one whom he could trust, had the monastery's domestic affairs governed for a time by a secular priest; nevertheless, changing this again not long afterward, he entrusted it to a monk.

In the same year, on the fifth day of the month of May, the third provincial chapter of our order was celebrated in the monastery of Fulda, in the diocese of Wuerzburg. Presiding there were Lambert, abbot of Michelsberg near Bamberg, Frederick of Hirsau, and Henry of St. Godehard's at Hildesheim, abbots of monasteries of our order; many things were decreed there for the reform of the order.

1421.

In the year [1421], the thirtieth of Bernhard our abbot, Conrad, prior of this monastery, died, the twenty-fifth man, as we said above, quite good and honorable according to the customs of that time. Since he had been brought up from boyhood among the unreformed, he neither learned nor cared for the reform of monastic life, believing it sufficient for his salvation if he lived according to the customs he had found. After him Gotfridus of Schmidberg, a professed monk of this place, was appointed prior of this monastery. He was the twenty-sixth in the order of priors from the beginning of the foundation of this monastery, and he presided in the office of prior for almost nine years. He did not care for reform, but rather was always opposed in everything. For the monks of this monastery at that time were excessively lax, rebellious religious against both God and their abbot in everything that pertained to religion.

1422.

In this year, which was the thirty-first of Bernhard our abbot, on the [unclear] day of the month of May, the provincial chapter of our order, with continuation on the following days, was celebrated in the monastery of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, in the town of Seligenstadt; in it there presided Of Sponheim.

he did. But Johannes married the countess of [Gorizia?], by whom he begot Ernest and Wilhelm of Munich, and a daughter named Sophia, wife of Wenceslaus, king of the Romans and of Bohemia.

1393.

In the second year of our abbot Bernhard, after a long dispute, concord was made between Friedrich, archbishop of Cologne, and the citizens, through the mediation of the count of Moers and other friends of both parties.

In the same year, in the archbishopric of Trier, in the village called Brechen, a child of horrible disposition was born. For the lower part of its body displayed the form and arrangement of a human being, but the upper part that of a most foul toad, so that horror even seized those who looked upon it. Many attributed this to the sins of its mother.

1394.

In the third year of our abbot Bernhard, Johannes, duke of Burgundy, who was the son of the sister of Duke Albert in Straubing, came into Bavaria with a great army and proceeded further against the Turks, having with him Rupert called Pipan, count palatine and duke of Bavaria, son of Rupert, later king of the Romans, and very many other counts and nobles with a great army. King Sigismund of Hungary, making known to all Christian princes the great insolence of the Turks, asked for aid. Therefore, when a very great multitude of warriors from the whole Christian world came to the said king’s aid, an expedition was organized against the Turks. And when they had come to a certain city of the Turks called Nicopolis, they surrounded it with a siege. But the king of the Turks came to the city’s aid with two hundred thousand men. King Sigismund of Hungary, going to meet him with his men at a distance of one mile, arranged the battle-line as best he could, appointing the duke of Wallachia captain of the armies. Johannes, the aforesaid duke of Burgundy, taking this badly, usurped the command for himself against the king’s will, and, taking up the army of his own men, who were almost six thousand in number, made the first assault upon the Turks with too little prudence. He was captured by them along with many others, and an innumerable multitude of Christians was slain by the Turks. But Sigismund, king of Hungary, fled and escaped by ship, while Rupert Pipan, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, returned to his homeland in great poverty.

1395.

In the fourth year of our abbot Bernhard, Conrad of Weinsberg, archbishop of Mainz, died in the month of October. After his death, Gottfried, son of the count of Leiningen, was unanimously elected by the chapter, a good and upright man, quite sufficiently learned in secular as well as divine writings. Against him Johannes of Nassau, canon of the church of Mainz, obtained the archbishopric from Pope Boniface IX for seventy thousand ducats, as was said; and, confirmed by the same pope and ordained, with Gottfried thrust aside against the will of the chapter, he presided over Mainz rather providently for nearly twenty-four years, a strict and crafty man, whose counsel was known to few.

In the same year, within the octave of Corpus Christi, there was a great earthquake in the night. Afterward a storm following with a mighty wind overthrew trees and houses.

Also in the same year, on the eighteenth day of the month of August, Albert, duke of Austria, died; he was the first to found the University of Vienna in Austria, as we said above.

1396.

In the fifth year of Abbot Bernhard, Nicolaus of Wiesbaden, bishop of Speyer, who had succeeded Adolf of Nassau, about whom it was said above, died. After him Rabanus of Helmstatt was unanimously elected by the chapter. He presided for thirty-five years; afterward he was raised to be archbishop of Trier, as we shall say in its proper place.

Around these times, Wernher, archbishop of Trier, transferred to Engers, for better profit, the toll which Cuno, first of all, had established from Koblenz to the chapel. He also captured the count of Solms, of the church of Trier, with many nobles in war and led him away captive; he ordered him to be kept in the castle of Montabaur for so long, until he obeyed the will of the one giving the order.

1397.

In his sixth year, Abbot Bernhard leased the monastery’s estate in Flonheim at farm; although he seems to have done this for the monastery’s advantage, nevertheless it is agreed that in the end it did not turn out for the monastery’s useful provision.

In the same year Wilhelm, duke of [Berg?], entered the land of the count of Cleves with a strong army, and indeed in the first encounter he conquered; in the second, by the citizens of Wesel [unclear] their count

Concord between the archbishop and the citizens of Cologne. A horrible monster is born. War of Sigismund, king of Hungary, against the Turks. Nicopolis [unclear]. Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, dies. Johannes becomes archbishop of Mainz. A great earthquake. Albert, duke of Austria, dies. Rabanus becomes bishop of Speyer. Flonheim estate. The duke of [Berg?] was captured by the men of Cleves. Chronicle of Trithemius

...bringing aid, he was defeated and captured with many of his men. Among them were, chiefly, the duke of Jülich, the count of Solms, also the count of Hinsberg, the count of Sayn, the count of Westerburg, and the count of Reifferscheid.

1398. In the seventh year of our abbot Bernard, on the day before the Kalends of September, Henry Viner of Sponheim died, brother of Henry, monk and cellarer of this monastery, a singular supporter and benefactor of the present place; he himself also assisted Abbot Bernard in all the things that he undertook for the honor of the order.

In the same year Wenceslaus, king of the Romans, without the knowledge and will of the princes and electors, created Galeazzo Visconti of Milan as duke; and this was one of the articles on account of which he was afterward deposed from the empire.

1399. In the eighth year of Abbot Bernard, a great fire broke out in the city of Kreuznach, in the new town, and the ravening flame consumed more than half of it. And in the same summer the village of Sponheim was accidentally burned by fire; a large part of it perished in the conflagration, and it caused much damage.

In this year also great wars were waged in the land of Berg, and much damage was inflicted on the poor by burning and plundering; the village of Molenheim too was captured.

1400. In the ninth year of our abbot Bernard, on the twentieth day of the month of September, about the tenth hour or thereabouts, there assembled at Upper Lahnstein Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, Werner, archbishop [unclear], duke of Bavaria, with many other princes, and they deposed Wenceslaus, king of the Romans, from the kingship because of the following articles which they set against him. Item, that he alienated the city of Genoa from the Empire after receiving money, handing it over to the king of the French without the consent of the prince-electors and of the Empire. Item, that without the consent of the princes he created the Visconti of Milan as dukes, as we said above, assigning to them all Lombardy as a title. Item, that territories, dominions, and castles which had devolved to him by imperial right he alienated from the Empire, granting them to others as perpetual property. Item, that he martyred and killed honorable persons, both secular and spiritual, and especially a certain master in theology, and exercised many other cruelties, against learned men and clerics as well as against nobles and the poor. Item, that he fostered robbers, who despoiled merchants and all travelers, and it was safe for no one to go anywhere under his rule, not even by water. Item, that after receiving money he gave parchments under the seal of the royal majesty. Item, that he united and allied himself with the king of Poland, who took his stand with the pagans against the Teutonic lords in Prussia rather than with Christians. Item, that he summoned many men to his court without reasonable cause, solely in order to extort money from them unjustly and without any occasion of justice. Item, that he brought that praiseworthy University of Prague, which his father had established, almost entirely to nothing, expelling the doctors and holding them in hatred; because, always intent on feasting, drunkenness, and luxury, he did not care for the affairs of the kingdom, but, acting negligently in all things, fostered wars and seditions. Item, that, concerning the foregoing and many other crimes and negligences, although often admonished by the princes openly and secretly, he never took care to amend himself even in one matter. These things were done at Upper Lahnstein, in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s incarnation 1400, on the twentieth day of the month of September, about the tenth hour or thereabouts.

Moreover, the duke of Saxony and the margrave of Brandenburg, though summoned for the appointed date, did not come; notwithstanding their absence, the aforesaid princes nevertheless deposed Wenceslaus by themselves as a man wholly useless for the kingship, since he had spent all his time in Bohemia in idleness and lust. After his deposition, the princes who had assembled unanimously elected Rupert, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, as king of the Romans. Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, anointed and crowned him around the feast of the Epiphany of the Lord in the greater church of Cologne. He presided over the Roman Empire for ten years: a man sufficiently Christian, a cultivator of justice, vigorous in military affairs, a lover of the clergy, and a most upright defender of the poor. Pope Boniface IX confirmed his election, holding valid the deposition of the slothful king Wenceslaus. But when afterward he had determined to go to Rome to receive the crown of the empire, Galeazzo, duke of the Milanese, a supporter of Wenceslaus, by whom he had been created duke, as we have said, resisted him with force as he was coming into Italy, and the journey toward [unclear]; therefore into Germany fi- ne be without the imperial benediction, he governed the kingdom energetically; by besieging his castle Mulberg, he compelled the Margrave of Baden, who had rebelled against him, to his obedience. This Rupert, king of the Romans, had as wife Margaret, daughter of the Burgrave of Nuremberg, who bore him six sons and three daughters: Rupert called Pipan, who fought against the Turks, as we said above; Frederick of Amberg; Louis the Bearded, who after his father was Count Palatine and Elector of the Empire; John of Neumarkt; Stephen of Zweibrucken; Otto of Mosbach; Agnes, Margaret, and Elizabeth. The firstborn, Rupert Pipan, died without children and was buried in Amberg; Frederick likewise died before his father, without children. Of the other sons, however, we shall speak in their proper place.

1401.

In the tenth year of Bernard our abbot, Gerard, bishop of Wurzburg, died, leaving the church weak, exhausted, and very much impoverished. For almost everything had been pledged: castles, towns, villages, together with the revenues of the church. He was succeeded by John of Egloffstein, through the promotion of King Rupert, and he presided for eleven years, a good and peaceable man, faithful to his church and in all respects sufficiently useful.

In the same year, on the feast of the Epiphany of the Lord, Rupert, elected king of the Romans, was consecrated in the greater church of Cologne by Frederick, archbishop of that city. But the citizens of Aachen, because they were bound by oath to the deposed King Wenceslaus, refused to admit the coronation of the new king in their city, having hope in the duke of Julich, who had promised them assistance against Rupert. But this did not turn out prosperously for them. For King Rupert, crowned, as we have said, in Cologne, took action against the people of Aachen and subjected them to the imperial ban, until at last, after six years, they were compelled to swear to his authority.

1402.

In the eleventh year of Bernard our abbot, Rupert, king of the Romans, celebrated splendid nuptials for his son Louis in Cologne in the month of May, giving him as wife the daughter of Henry, king of England, named Blanche; she bore him a son named Rupert, who died in the twentieth year of his age without children. But the wife herself also died after a few years, and then he took another, Matilda, daughter of the duke of Savoy, of whom we shall speak below in her proper place at the appropriate time.

In the same year Rupert, king of the Romans, set out for Italy, both to obtain the crown of the Empire and also to bring aid to the Florentines against the Milanese.

1403.

In this year, which was the twelfth of Bernard our abbot, on the feast of St. Hippolytus the martyr, a very great fire arose by chance in the town of Bingen and inflicted many losses on people; for scarcely a fourth part of the town remained unburned. The devouring flame consumed the parish church, towers, houses, and the chapels of Saints Christopher, Nicholas, Giles, and of the Holy Spirit, with everything that it seized; and so powerful was the fire that it could be restrained by no one. It laid everything waste, consumed everything, and in one hour made many of the rich extremely poor.

In the same year, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, Rudolph, prior of this monastery, died, the twenty-fourth in the order of priors; a man according to the manners of that time, when they cared little for the discipline of regular observance. Through him, even after himself, he transmitted the monks of this community to posterity as possessors of private property, incontinent, and secular rather than religious. After Rudolph’s death, Abbot Bernard appointed as the twenty-fifth prior of this place a man named Conrad, a professed monk of this community, who presided in the office of prior for almost eighteen years; he was indeed, according to common human estimation, a man of honorable conduct, who, because he had been brought up from childhood among the deformed, trusted that living by the morals he had found would suffice him for salvation.

In the same year also, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, John, parish priest of our church of Sponheim, died; he had formerly been rector of the scholars here in the monastery, a singular benefactor.

In the same year the duke of Berg placed his captured father in custody in the castle that is called Nuvvenburg, and usurped his father’s dominion for himself, making little of his father’s prayers and despising his mother’s tears, poured out without ceasing. But in the same year, through Henry of Oeyr, who brought help to Archbishop Frederick, he was secretly freed from custody with great cunning and taken away in secret.

1404.

In the thirteenth year of Bernard our abbot, the reform of our order in Bavaria was begun, which is called the Castellan reform, by Otto, abbot of the monastery of Kastl, in the diocese of Ei[unclear]

The Castellan reform of the head.

King Rupert subdues the people of Baden.

The fortunate Rupert [unclear] of the kingdom of the Romans.

John becomes bishop of Wurzburg.

Rupert is crowned king.

The citizens of Aachen are [unclear] by the king.

Louis, son of the king, takes a wife.

King Rupert set out for Italy [unclear].

The town of Bingen perished by fire.

The duke of Berg captured his father. Chronicle of Trithemius

[unclear], who first reformed himself and his monastery to the integrity of monastic observance, and thereafter, in the course of time, drew many other monasteries in Bavaria and Swabia into the same association. But so holy a reform did not last a hundred years in the aforesaid monastery; destroyed by the pomp and pride of the abbots, it has left no trace of itself today. The other monasteries too, which had in a certain way been numbered with the Castellenses through uniformity of life, when the mother failed, almost all fell away from their first institution.

1405.

In the fourteenth year of our abbot Bernhard, his sister Anna, wife of Wilhelm, duke of Mons, came to King Rupert while he was staying at Heidelberg, accusing her son Adolf, who had seized his father and now had expelled both parents from the duchy of Mons, and asking counsel and help against her insolent son. The king, her brother, pitying her calamity, marked the son by an imperial sentence and soon compelled him to reverence and obedience toward his parents.

In the same year, around the Nativity of the Lord, Duke Albert of Bavaria died, son of Emperor Ludwig, Count Palatine of the Rhine, count of Hainaut, Holland, and Zeeland, and lord of Frisia, a pious, good man and a most humane prince; he was buried in Holland. By his wife Margaretha, daughter of the duke of Poland, he left three sons: Albert, who had Straubing with the duchy of Lower Bavaria, who was the first among the brothers to die, without children, and who had no wife; Johann, who was elected bishop of Liege and afterward ruled Holland for several years after the death of the following brother; and Wilhelm, who, after his mother’s death, ruled Holland, Hainaut, Zeeland, and Frisia for a few years, and died in the year of the Lord 1410, leaving one only daughter, named Jacoba, of whom we shall speak in her place.

In the same year, on the day of Saint Scholastica the Virgin, the clergy of Worms left the city for the preservation of their liberties. For one year and eleven months, others say for two years, they remained outside the city, each college in the place anciently reckoned to it. At length an agreement was made, as we shall say below in order in its place, through King Rupert and his son Ludwig.

Also in the same year, on the fourteenth day of the month of May, Eckard, bishop of Worms, was buried in the middle of the choir of the greater church. He was succeeded by Matthaeus of Cracow, who presided for six years, a man learned in sacred letters, a Doctor, who wrote many little works pertaining to the instruction of the faithful and the formation of morals.

In the year noted above, Bernhard, abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, purchased one manor in Winzenheim, with houses, fields, vineyards, meadows, gardens, and all its appurtenances, from Peter, son of Conrad the tailor; and before the Schultheiss and the Schöffen there, as is the custom, he received it as the perpetual property of the monastery. But after some years, as we shall say below, falling into displeasure against his convent, out of anger he alienated both this manor and another without the consent and will of the convent, to no small peril of his soul.

1406.

In the fifteenth year of our abbot Bernhard, on the day of the martyrs Vitus and Modestus, in the morning, about the seventh hour, there was a very great eclipse of the sun. Many wars followed in various lands and provinces of the Roman Empire.

In the same year, after the feast of Easter, certain princes, counts, and other nobles of various rank of this province came together as one and took counsel against the citizens of Mainz. They inflicted great losses on them for the insults and damages which they said they had previously suffered from the people of Mainz. Also, on a certain night, they came in force to the gate of the city, pretending to be associates of that same city, and were let in. Since they were strong and many in number, they beheaded certain of the more powerful citizens, plundered whatever citizens they could, inflicted irreparable losses on them, and withdrew. In this same year, at last, the citizens of Aachen swore allegiance to King Rupert after many losses.

1407.

In the sixteenth year of our abbot Bernhard, around the feast of Saint James the Apostle, an agreement was made between the clergy and the citizens of Worms through Rupert, king of the Romans, and his son Ludwig, count palatine of the Rhine, after many expenses had been incurred by both parties in the Roman curia and elsewhere. And thus the clergy, after they had been in exile for two years and five months, returned to the city.

In the same year the new praetorium in Cologne, which they call the citizens’ house, was begun; it was completed in seven years, and its expenses, as they say, exceed fifty thousand gold florins when each item is counted.

1408. Sponheim.

1408.

In the seventeenth year of Abbot Bernhard, a great dissension arose between John, Duke of Bavaria, elect of the church of Liege (who for almost sixteen years had sat as bishop and had not received sacred orders, contrary to his oath), and the citizens of Liege with those adhering to them. This brought a disastrous defeat upon the people of Liege, whom the aforesaid John overcame in war. For the people of Liege besieged John the elect himself in Maastricht, where they practiced such cruelty that, when women fled from the said city because of want, they cut off the [unclear] garments around their private parts. And although William, Duke of Bavaria and Count of Hainaut, Zeeland, and Holland, brother of John the elect, and also John, Duke of Burgundy, the son of their sister, at first wished to give him no assistance, nevertheless at last, seeing him placed in such great necessity, they came to his aid with one hundred thousand men equipped for war, while he himself, besieged by the people of Liege in the city, did not know it. When the aforesaid dukes came with their armies to the city of Maastricht, they fell unexpectedly upon the people of Liege on the twenty-third day of the month of September, killed more than thirty-five thousand of them, only a few escaping; on their own side scarcely ten died. And thus John the elect obtained the whole diocese.

1409.

In the eighteenth year of our abbot Bernhard, the aforesaid William died, Duke of Bavaria and Count Palatine of the Rhine, Count of Holland and Zeeland, lord of Frisia, son of Duke Albert, nephew of Emperor Louis IV, leaving one daughter, named Jacqueline. She first married the Dauphin of France, afterwards the Duke of Brabant, and finally a certain nobleman of the French, all of whom died without children. This daughter Jacqueline, after her father’s death, was striving to obtain by right the inheritance of that county; against her the aforesaid John, elect of Liege, her father’s brother, obtained it by violence, and as long as he lived he retained Hainaut, Holland, Zeeland, and part of Frisia under his lordship, while the aforesaid daughter of his brother protested. At length, wishing to have an heir after his death, he abandoned the bishopric of Liege and, with the dispensation of the Council of Constance, took a wife, but he did not receive children from her.

In the same year, on the twenty-first day of the month of May, died Blanche, daughter of Henry, king of England, wife of Louis, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of Rupert, king of the Romans, who was called the Duke with the Beard, because he afterwards did not consent to have shaved off the beard that he had grown when he set out for the Holy Land. After her he took as his second wife Matilda, daughter of the Duke of Savoy, a woman of great piety and devotion, by whom he begot three sons: Louis, Frederick, and Rupert. After his death, she married Albert, Duke of Austria, brother of Emperor Frederick.

1410.

In the nineteenth year of our abbot Bernhard, Rupert, king of the Romans, Duke of Bavaria, and Count Palatine of the Rhine, died at Oppenheim on the twelfth day of the month of May, and was buried at Heidelberg in the middle of the choir of the church of the Holy Spirit, with a mausoleum raised high. This Rupert, before he was elected king of the Romans, first founded, built up, and endowed the University of Heidelberg in the year of the Lord 1386, which Pope Urban VI confirmed and honored with various privileges. He also built in the same town a notable church in honor of the Holy Spirit, in which he established many sufficiently rich and good prebends of canons and vicars.

After the death of King Rupert, the prince-electors, coming together, unanimously elected as king of the Romans Sigismund, son of Emperor Charles IV, brother of Wenceslaus, once deposed king, king of Bohemia and Hungary, a strong, vigorous, wise, and most Christian man, who ruled for twenty-seven years and vigorously did and accomplished many things for the benefit of the Catholic Church.

1411.

In this year, which was the twentieth of our abbot Bernhard, there were serious dissensions and discord between Louis the Palatine, son of the late Rupert, king of the Romans, and John, Count of Sponheim, over certain boundaries and liberties in the counties, especially in Kreuznach. In these matters Count John obtained victory by the sentence of the judges against the aforesaid Louis the Palatine. In these times the condition of this monastery in temporal matters was very poor; the monks, casting aside the observance of discipline, lived in great deformity of life.

Dissension between John of Bavaria and the citizens of Liege. The people of Liege besieged John the elect in Maastricht. Savage war against the people of Liege, in which more than thirty-five thousand of the people of Liege died. William, Count of Holland, dies. John, elect bishop of Liege, obtains the county of his brother William. Blanche, wife of Louis, Count Palatine, dies. Sons of Louis, Count Palatine, by Matilda his second wife. Rupert, king of the Romans, died. The University and the church of the Holy Spirit are founded at Heidelberg. Sigismund becomes king of the Romans. Discord between Louis the Palatine and John, Count of Sponheim. What the condition of the monastery was. Chronicle of Trithemius, 1412.

1412.

In the twenty-first year of our abbot Bernhard, John, bishop of Würzburg, died, killed, as was commonly reported, by [poison?] at [Forchheim?] on the eleventh day of January. Another John, of Brunn, succeeded him and presided for twenty-eight years: a man excessively lavish, who on that account pledged to creditors almost everything belonging to the episcopal table.

1413.

In the twenty-second year of our abbot Bernhard, Stephen, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of Rupert, formerly king of the Romans, and brother of Ludwig the Palatine with the Beard, took as wife the only daughter of the last count of Veldenz. She bore him [unclear]: Frederick of Simmern, father of Duke John, now dwelling in Simmern, who obtained the county of Sponheim; Ludwig, surnamed the Black, who was father of Duke Alexander and obtained the counties of Zweibruecken and Veldenz; Rupert, bishop of Strasbourg; Stephen, canon and dean of the church of Cologne; and John, bishop of Muenster, and afterwards archbishop of the churches of Magdeburg and primate of Germany.

1414.

In this year, which was the twenty-third of Abbot Bernhard, the very famous general council was begun in the city of Constance, by the aid and effort of Sigismund, king of the Romans. It lasted for three continuous years. At it John, Pope XXIII, first appeared; afterwards, in the same place, he was judicially deposed by the council, together with the two others contending for the papacy. He entered Constance in the aforesaid year on the fifth day of November, with great solemnity, received honorably as pope, and he began the council and held a session on Friday, which was the sixteenth day of the same month. In this council, over three years, forty-four public and solemn synodal sessions were held, and many things were laudably established for the peace and unity of the Church. A very great multitude of princes, pontiffs, abbots, prelates, nobles, clerics, and laymen came together there from the whole Christian world, all of whom were unanimously obedient to the decrees of the council.

1415.

In the twenty-fourth year of our abbot Bernhard, on the vigil of St. Matthew, Frederick, duke of Austria, was born, afterwards emperor, the fourth of this name. In the same year, while the sacred council of Constance was still continuing, Saint Bridget, formerly queen of Sweden and Norway, was canonized on the vigil of the Purification of St. Mary. In the same year also Sigismund, king of the Romans, with the counsel and assent of the princes, was constituted in the general council at Constance on the twenty-fourth day before the Kalends of May; and from that time the dukes of Cleves began to exist, and they exist down to the present day. In the same year also, when Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, had died, Theoderic, son of the count of Moers, succeeded him and presided for almost forty-eight years, quite energetically.

1416.

In the twenty-fifth year of our abbot Bernhard, the men of Berg burned the village of Deutz, situated opposite the city of Cologne across the Rhine, so that Archbishop Theoderic would not station his garrisons there. For there had been hostilities and dissensions between the aforesaid archbishop of Cologne and the duke of the land of Berg. In the same year a certain cloud, burst open at night, fell upon the town of Muenstereifel; and while all were sleeping it overthrew the walls, gates, and the greater part of it, with many men and livestock unexpectedly submerged. Their corpses were found outside the town at a distance of one mile, and much damage was inflicted on the inhabitants of the place, which down to this day has not been repaired.

1417.

In this year, which was the twenty-sixth of our abbot Bernhard, all the abbots and prelates of our order throughout the whole province were summoned and cited to the Council of Constance, for instituting the celebration of a provincial chapter and beginning the reform of our order in all the monasteries. Therefore the abbots of our order came together at Constance; among them was Bernhard, abbot of this monastery, summoned and cited with the others. By command of the council itself, in the monastery called Petershausen, of our order, in the city of Constance, they first celebrated a provincial chapter. And because there was no one among all the abbots of the province of Mainz who knew how to celebrate a chapter.

chapter; for that reason the council appointed, as presidents for holding the chapter, two men from our province of Mainz, namely Siegfried, abbot in Ellwangen in the diocese of Augsburg, and Johannes, abbot of St. George’s in the diocese of Constance; to these they added Ludovicus, abbot of Tournus in the diocese of Chalon, and Thomas, abbot of Ebrach, who already knew the manner of holding a chapter. In this chapter measures were laudably established for the reform of our order, which are contained in the acts of the provincial chapter. This provincial chapter was held in the aforesaid year of the Lord, begun on the last day of February; from it our reform, called the Bursfeld reform, as we shall say in its place, first took its beginning. From that time provincial chapters began to be held every three years in the province of Mainz, and they are continued down to the present day, as we shall say hereafter in order in its place.

In the same year, in August, Adolphus, Duke of Berg, entered with a strong army of his men the land of Bar, adjoining the duchy of Luxembourg, which he said belonged to him by hereditary right on his wife’s side; but, when provisions had been consumed, he was forced to return with loss and confusion. Then, seven years later, when he had again entered that land with the strong hand of his men and had subjected a great part to his rule, he was captured in a certain convent of nuns and delivered into the hands of the Duke of Lorraine.

In the same year also Johannes, Duke of Bavaria, Count Palatine of the Rhine, son of Albert, brother of Wilhelm, Count of Holland, elect of Liège, a subdeacon, about whom we spoke above, after he had for some time, following his brother’s death, governed that county with Jacoba, his brother’s daughter, resigned the bishopric and, with dispensation from the Council of Constance, took as wife the widow of Anthony, Duke of Brabant. Leaving Liège in the month of September, never to return, he obtained the land against his brother’s daughter with the bloodshed of many, waging many wars with her, and at last came out victorious. 1418.

In the twenty-sixth year of our abbot Bernhard, Wernher of Falkenstein, archbishop of Trier, died on the fourth day of the month of October, and was buried with honor at Koblenz in the church of St. Castor. After his death Otto, son of the Count of Ziegenhain, provost of the major church, a magnificent man, glorious in every respect, was canonically elected archbishop by the chapter; he presided vigorously for twelve years, did much in a short time, powerful in peace and arms, steadfast.

In the same year Bernhard, abbot of this monastery, lost the other eye on the following occasion. While he was at the provincial chapter held at Constance at the time of the council, to which, in going, staying, and returning, he spent more than [unclear] with a servant and two horses, as we find from his manual, he was forced to swear with the others that within the space of one year he would accept without opposition the proposed reform, under penalty of loss of the abbacy and perpetual incapacity. Returning therefore to the monastery, he explained to the brothers the oath which he had made with the other abbots, and urged them most earnestly to accept the proclaimed reform. But when he saw that they were wholly unwilling, he used penalties and threats, and took care first of all to cut away, as far as he could, every occasion of deformity, forbidding by strict prohibition the wandering of the monks and the entry of women into the monastery. But he had within the walls [unclear]. Yet he could not fully draw the monks back from their deformities, whence great discord arose between him and them, which brought no small disaster upon this monastery. Thereafter the abbot himself was rarely in the monastery, but more often stayed in the town of Trarbach, or in Bingen, or in Kreuznach, not without grave loss to the temporal and spiritual affairs of this monastery.

In the aforesaid year, on the first day of the month of September, the second provincial chapter of our order was held at the Augustinians in the city of Mainz. Presiding over it were the abbots of Fulda, Kempten, St. Ulrich at Augsburg, and Reinhardsbrunn, who had been appointed to the office of presidency in the last chapter held at Constance, as we have said. The place for holding the chapter was in the monastery of St. Alban.

The Duke of Berg enters the land of Bar for the third time.

Johannes, elect of Liège, takes a wife.

Otto becomes archbishop of Trier.

Abbot Bernhard lost the other eye.

Abbot Bernhard attempts to reform the monks.

A provincial chapter is held in Mainz. [unclear] Albert of Hirsfeld, George of Castell, and Theoderic of Amorbach, abbots of monasteries of our order.

In the same year Sigismund, Emperor of the Romans, and Cardinal Branda, legate of the Apostolic See, meeting in an assembly with certain other princes, settled for a fixed number of years that long contest and the dissensions among the dukes of Bavaria, which had lasted for a year and six months with great damage and devastation to Bavaria, restoring peace and concord among the dukes.

In the same year also John, Duke of Brabant, founded the University of Louvain, which, at his request, Pope Martin V confirmed, permitting lectures to be instituted in every faculty except theology. But Pope Eugenius, Martin’s successor, afterward granted lectures in theology, as in the other faculties.

In these times also a great expedition of princes, bishops, nobles, and commoners was made against the Bohemians, who had separated themselves from the unity of the Catholic Church by many errors and heresies, Pope Martin V granting plenary indulgences, from penalty and from guilt, to all who should set out to war against them. Therefore, when a very great multitude of Catholics advanced against them, at first our men emerged victorious, many towns, castles, and villages of the heretics being overthrown, and many being killed. But afterward, when our princes began to thirst more for plunder than for the defense of the Catholic faith, they perceived the emperor’s mind stirred against them, whose kingdom they preferred to despoil and divide among themselves rather than to let stand intact. From this point fortune changed, and the Bohemians began to rush more strongly upon our men and to inflict greater losses than they had received from them. O ever-blind ambition of human greed: while it does not know moderation in possessing, it loses even what it has. The matter of the Bohemian heretics would then have been finished, if our princes had not put avarice and ambitious desire before love and defense of the Catholic faith. Thus our men, slain, despoiled, and confounded by the Bohemians, returned in disgrace to their own lands. In this expedition of the faithful John, the last Count of Sponheim, was present in person with his retainers; he fought most bravely against the schismatics, beyond the rest. When one morning at sunrise he had resolved, suddenly and unexpectedly, to attack a certain heretical town with some other Catholics, the gate being open for the sending of livestock into the fields, a little sheep, by chance rolling itself under the feet of the horse on which he was seated, threw him headlong a little before the gate; and before he could mount his warhorse again, the townsmen shut the gates of the town and killed all of our men who had entered at a headlong run. But the count, shut out against his will by the danger, or shall I say the benefit, of the sheep, was saved.

In the same year also Hohenzollern in Swabia was captured by the citizens of the Empire, after which [unclear].

In the thirty-second year of our abbot Bernard, on the vigil of John, Reynald, Duke of Jülich and Guelders, died without children. After his death the people of Guelders accepted as duke Arnold, Count of Egmond, who, after receiving the rule of the duchy of Guelders, [unclear] for his posterity. Further, Adolf, Duke of Berg, obtained the duchy of Jülich for his son Rupert, through the aid of Theoderic, Archbishop of Cologne, down to the present day.

In this same year Abbot Bernard deposed the secular administrator and appointed two monks, Frederick and Wilhelm, who were to collect all the revenues and proceeds of this monastery, expend them for necessary uses, and each year make an accounting for each item.

The condition of the monastery at that time was, however, quite poor, dissolved no less in temporal than in spiritual matters. The monks with the abbot were often under excommunication, sometimes by the order because of disobedience and rebellion, sometimes by a judge because of debts not paid to creditors on time. The divine offices were frequently interrupted; unless a temporary relaxation had been obtained, it was not permitted to celebrate them. The abbot lived in Trarbach and was seldom in the monastery; each man, free from fear, did what seemed right to him. The monks lived without a rule, miserably fallen into every wantonness and pleasure.

In the aforesaid year, after the death of Rudolf and Albert, dukes of Saxony, Sigismund, Emperor of the Romans, conferred the duchy of Saxony, together with the principate of the election, upon Frederick, Margrave of Meissen and Landgrave of Thuringia, and upon his heirs forever, excluding Duke Eric, brother of the aforesaid Rudolf and Albert, who was still living; when the title of Duke of Saxony had been taken away, he wished him to be called Duke of Lüneburg thereafter.

The dissension [unclear] of Bavaria is settled.

The University of Louvain is founded.

A very great expedition against the Bohemians.

[unclear].

Our men are [unclear] by Bohemia.

John, the last Count of Sponheim, fights [unclear].

Hohenzollern is captured by the citizens of the Empire.

Reynald, Duke of Jülich and Guelders, dies.

The Count of Egmond becomes Duke of Guelders.

The duchy of Jülich, Berg, Guelders, [unclear].

Two monk administrators of this monastery are appointed.

What the condition of the monastery was like.

The Margraves of Meissen become dukes of Saxony and electors. [Blank page in the source scan.]

...when Frederick, Margrave of Brandenburg, was steadily opposing this donation and, having received from the Meissners a sum of twenty-eight thousand florins, yielded the right which seemed to belong to him.

1424.

In this year, which was the thirty-third of Abbot Bernard, on Jubilate Sunday, which was the fourteenth day of the month of May, the fifth provincial chapter of our order was celebrated, continuing through the following days, in the monastery of St. Stephen the Martyr in the city of Würzburg. At it presided Baldwin of Lüneburg, Theoderic of Northeim, Appello in Sinsheim, and Helfrid of St. John in [Rinckau?], abbots of monasteries of our order; and many things were ordained and decreed there for the reform of our order.

In the same year died Ernest, Duke of Austria, father of Emperor Frederick III.

In this same year Adolf, Duke of Mont, again entered the land of Bar with a strong army and obtained the greater part of it. While he was spending the nights in a certain monastery, as was his custom, in shameless pleasures with women consecrated to God there, he was betrayed and captured one night and presented into the hands of the Duke of Lorraine. After being held in custody for a whole year, therefore, he could not be freed until he himself, together with his son Rupert, renouncing every right that belonged to him in the aforesaid land, granted it into the hand and power of the Duke of Lorraine and his heirs forever.

1425.

In the thirty-fourth year of our Abbot Bernard died John, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and Count of Holland, Zeeland, and Hainaut, and Lord of Frisia, son of Duke Albert and grandson of Emperor Louis IV. He had once been elected bishop of Liège; by dispensation of the Council of Constance he had given up the bishopric together with the subdiaconate, had taken a wife, and, subjecting Holland to himself together with the other counties, had deprived Jacoba, daughter of his brother William, of her paternal inheritance, leaving no children. When he died, the aforesaid daughter of his brother sought to reclaim the aforesaid counties of her father William as the nearer heir; but the Duke of Burgundy, son of Duke Albert’s sister, resisted and brought all the land of Holland, with the other appurtenances, under his rule. And so the counties of Holland, Zeeland, and Hainaut, with the lordship of Frisia, which the line of the Palatines and Dukes of Bavaria had possessed for eighty years, came into the surrender of the Dukes of Burgundy down to the present day, not without grave injury to the aforesaid Jacoba, daughter of Duke William, and serious loss to the house of Bavaria.

Also in the year noted above Otto, Archbishop of Trier, kindled by the fire of pious devotion, crossed the sea with much patience and humility and visited the holy sepulchre of the Lord at Jerusalem, carrying with him precious ornaments marked with his arms. These, for the honor of divine worship, he bestowed with eager devotion on the Friars Minor living there, as a perpetual memorial of his pilgrimage, and with humble insistence commended himself to their prayers. The sole cause of this pilgrimage was devotion.

1426.

In this year, which was the thirty-fifth of our Abbot Bernard, Louis, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, prince-elector, son of Rupert, once King of the Romans, a pious and renowned man, set out beyond the sea to the Holy Land for love of our Lord Jesus Christ, and visited the sepulchre of our Savior in Jerusalem with great devotion. Returning from the lands beyond the sea, he no longer allowed the beard which he had grown on the holy pilgrimage to be shaved; but as long as he lived he preserved it inviolate in memory of his pilgrimage. And from that time onward he was called by the people the Duke with the Beard.

John also, Count of Sponheim, the last, set out on the same pilgrimage with Duke Louis to the Holy Land, having in his retinue Gobelin, a monk of St. Disibod, his chaplain and secretary, of the Cistercian order. After the death of Bernard, abbot of this monastery, John intruded him, against right, privilege, and the will of the convent, and made him abbot, as we shall say below in its proper place. This Count John of Sponheim, once driven out by his brother Simon, fled to the Margrave of Baden; treated honorably and kindly by him, he promised that in return for so great a benefit he would give to that same Margrave a considerable part of the County of Sponheim. And indeed, after Count Simon died, having returned to his paternal inheritance with the help of the aforesaid Margrave, he gave it as he had promised; and by such means and donation the Margraves of Baden came to the County of Sponheim down to the present day. But when this same Count John attacked Lady Elizabeth, wife of the late Simon, who died in the twenty-second year of our Abbot Bernard, and [unclear] her from the County of Sponheim

The provincial chapter is celebrated.

Ernest, Duke of Austria, dies.

The Duke of Mont enters the land of Bar with an army.

The Duke of Mont is captured.

John, Count of Holland, dies without heirs.

The County of Holland is transferred from Bavaria to the Burgundians.

Otto, Archbishop of Trier, visits the Lord’s sepulchre.

Louis the Palatine, the Beard, crosses the sea.

How the Margrave of Baden’s family came to the County of Sponheim.

How the Palatine came to the County of Sponheim.

John, Count of Sponheim, crosses the sea.

How the Margrave of Baden’s family came to the counties of Sponheim. How the Palatine came to the County of Sponheim. Sponheim.

Having been ordained vicar on the day of St. Lawrence the martyr, he presided here in the monastery for seven years, one month, and fourteen days, and endured many tribulations and adversities, especially after the death of that count. He was by origin from the county of Sponheim, from the town of Kreuznach, born of humble but honorable parentage; his father, Andreas, and his mother, Barbara, citizens there, sustained a modest life by the labor of their hands. While he was still a little boy he was handed over by his parents to teachers to learn letters; after he had devoted several years’ effort to these, he was at last made a monk in the monastery of St. Disibod, of the Cistercian order. There, since he was subtle in intellect, he advanced in many things beyond those of his own age, among other things also laboring over curious arts, and [more frequently devoted?] study to alchemy and medicine. When he had made some progress in these things, he came into the acquaintance and intimacy of the aforesaid last count of Sponheim; by him he was drawn out of the monastery and made first his chaplain, then his secretary, and finally, as we have said, abbot of this monastery. Yet he was rarely here in the monastery, but was accustomed to stay more often at [Trarbach?] with the count. He had his own house there, in which, with the necessary household, receiving support partly from the count’s table and court, partly from the monastery, he lived apart. Mention of his deeds will be made more fully in order.

1433.

In the first year of Gobelin, Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, and Ludwig, landgrave of Hesse, had serious dissensions and enmities between them. After threats, raids, plunderings, and burnings, they at last met for battle in the field; there, after a long and uncertain contest, with not a few killed on both sides, Archbishop Conrad was defeated by Ludwig the landgrave. More than six hundred of his men were captured by that count of the province; these afterward ransomed themselves with money, not without loss to the archbishop.

In the same year Ulrich of Manderscheid, dean of Cologne, who against Jacob of Sierck, as we said above, [unclear] Rabanus, in [unclear] had been elected archbishop, and had been set aside by the pope together with Jacob, bearing a hostile spirit against that same Archbishop Rabanus and despising the apostolic commands, besieged Trier, the most ancient city of Europe, for two years with the help of the count of Virneburg. He placed engines and bombards on the neighboring mountains and sent many stones and arrows into the city. But when he saw that he could make no progress, because of the [unclear] of the citizens, [unclear]. Among the clergy and the citizens of Mainz various discords and dissensions arose, which to such a degree [unclear]. [Unclear], elected and confirmed by Pope Eugene IV, presided for twenty-five years, a good and gentle man, who ruled the church committed to him in peace and quiet, and was the first to confirm, with much goodwill, our reform, the annual chapter, and its constitutions.

In the same year also Abbot Gobelin secretly took away all the privileges, letters, and records of the liberty of this monastery of Sponheim, on what occasion we do not know, without the knowledge or will of his convent, and carried them off to [Trarbach?] beside the Moselle, where he was accustomed to stay; this was not without the gravest and irrecoverable loss to this monastery and to all our posterity. For many of them were lost on that occasion, [unclear] brought back to the monastery. And although he was often admonished by the convent about their restitution, and finally was cited to the Council of Basel before the presidents of the chapter, as we shall say later, by the report of the visitors, and was compelled by the abbot of St. Matthias, a commissary of the council specially deputed for this, to swear that he would restore everything, nevertheless he could never be induced to satisfy his promise and the mandates of his superiors. There were some who said that the privileges themselves [unclear] could not be restored by the abbot. That we may believe this to be true, we are led by a probable argument: for the greater part of the letters and privileges of this monastery Sponheimense.

...when he was striving utterly to expel her, she, using prudent counsel, called upon and appointed the aforesaid Lord Ludwig the Palatine as her guardian; and to him she granted in perpetual possession that part which the Count Palatine today has from of old in the county of Sponheim, apart from what was afterward pledged. And thus the Count Palatine of the Rhine was first admitted into this county. This count was a man much given to curiosities, always desirous of novel things, who often spent much money in useless dealings: now on alchemy, now on mathematics, now on these, now on other curious inquiries. For he always had at his court men devoted to such vanities: alchemists, mathematicians, haruspices, exorcists, magicians, predictors of the future, whom he easily believed, and, though very often grossly deceived, nevertheless paid great honor.

In the year noted above, Johannes de Fleckenstein, bishop of Worms, died. He had succeeded Matthew of Cracow, in the sixteenth year of his pontificate, on the [unclear] day of the month of May, and was buried in the major church. Frederick of Domneck succeeded him in the episcopate for nineteen years.

In the same year also Philip, duke of Burgundy, captured that admirable maiden Joan, about whom Master Johannes Gerson wrote several things. Armed and riding among soldiers, she did wonders in war on behalf of the king of the Franks, and predicted future events. He sent her to the king of the English, and he, after she had long been afflicted with many punishments and torments, finally had her burned with fire; this she had predicted would happen to her. This maiden was from Lorraine. When she was fourteen years old she came to Charles, king of the Franks, in the twenty-ninth year of our Abbot Bernhard, who, as we said above, had been driven from his kingdom by the duke of Burgundy, predicting future events to him and promising him the restoration of the kingdom and certain victory against all his adversaries. Although she was a young and tender girl, nevertheless fully armed she mounted a horse with great agility; by her counsel she arranged battle lines, taught ambushes, predicted dangers, held the banner in her hands, and, riding among armed men, always fought first against the adversaries and everywhere did many marvels.

In the year noted above also, the sixth provincial chapter of our order was held at Erfurt, at St Peter’s, on the twenty-first day of the month of April. From it, arising through the rashness of certain subjects, a destructive disaster came upon this monastery. For when the monks refused to undertake the proposed reform, as we said above, they assailed their abbot with slanders and insults. Moved by these things, since he could not avenge himself in another way, without the consent of his convent he alienated from the monastery two courts in Winsheim with all their appurtenances and their revenues, handing them over for nothing to a certain Jacob of Gmund. Through him they came into the hands of Meinhard of Coppenstein, from whom, though they were often demanded back by several abbots with threats and entreaties, they could never be obtained, down to the present day.

1427.

In this year, which was the thirty-seventh of our Abbot Bernhard, Emperor Sigismund, with the consent of Pope Martin V, levied an immense amount of money from all the clergy and people of all Germany, intending to fight with it against the schismatic Bohemians, although little or no effect followed. He who had a thousand florins gave two; but he who was wealthy in possession to the value of one hundred florins paid a quarter part of one florin. All the rest, men, women, sons, daughters, hired servants, household members, as many as had completed the fifteenth year of their age, with absolutely no one excepted, each paid thirteen Hallenses. It was indeed a great exaction, but little benefit for the Catholic faith followed from it. Yet there were some among the Germans who refused to submit their necks to this exaction. The summer of this year was exceedingly wet; flooding waters brought much damage upon people, and thereafter a great pestilence followed in all Germany.

1429.

In the [forty-seventh?] year of our Abbot Bernhard, the seventh chapter of our order was celebrated in the monastery of Monks’ Hill near Bamberg, on the tenth day of the month of April, which was the Sunday Misericordia Domini, with continuation, as is the custom, on the following days. At it presided George of Castell, of St Peter’s at Erfurt, Henry of [Gul-]...

[unclear] Doctor, of St. Giles of Nuremberg, and Hugo in Albersbach, abbots of monasteries of our order. In this Chapter, however, Bernard, abbot of this monastery, did not appear in person, but in his place sent his monk and chaplain, named Jacob of Cleberg, with the customary mandate and procurations.

At about these times a new reform of the order began in the monastery of Bursfeld, in the diocese of Mainz in Saxony, which Henry, formerly count of Northeim, had founded around the year of the Lord 1098; from it our observance has been called the Bursfeld Union, and it flourishes to the present day. This reform took its beginning from the monastery of St. Matthias near Trier, over which that distinguished abbot, Master Johannes Rode, then presided. Through him, with Archbishop Otto cooperating, all the monasteries of our order which are around Trier were brought back to a better condition.

This Johannes Rode was a learned, upright man of great devotion. Although he was a canon of the church of Metz, provost of St. Simeon, and official of the Trier court, he despised everything for the love of Christ and became a monk in the Charterhouse near Trier. Since he was a man very learned, mature in life and conduct, and very strict and zealous for the observance of the order, Otto, archbishop of Trier, with the pope's consent, drew him out of the Charterhouse and appointed him abbot of the monastery of St. Matthias. There he soon restored monastic life according to the rule of our holy father Benedict, instituted statutes and ceremonies, and instructed the monks in all religion and holiness by word and example.

After the monastery of St. Matthias had been reformed, at the request of the duke of Brunswick he sent brothers to Bursfeld, with the ordinance, statutes, and customs which he had given. Johannes, abbot of Bursfeld, received them with great joy and devotion, and most zealously conformed himself in all things to their holy seniors. This Johannes had once been a monk in Reynhusen; his abbot had sent him by way of procuration to the Council of Constance, at that same time, namely, when all the abbots of the province of Mainz, as we said above, had been summoned to Constance by the council to hold a Chapter. There, when he had seen the zeal and diligence of the fathers for the reform of the order, and had heard how dangerous it is for a monk to live in deformity, he was moved to compunction [unclear] for the reform of the order; and he diligently urged them to amend their life and to undertake the promised and enjoined reform under the penalties prescribed.

At first they began to mock him, and afterwards even to hate him and afflict him with abuse. Seeing that, though he strove, he made no progress, and wishing to provide for his own salvation, he went to Agnes, wife of Otto of Brunswick, sister of the landgrave of Thuringia, who was then staying at Gamundia, not far from Reynhusen, a woman most devout in Christ. He reported the acts and conclusions of the fathers in the council, and asked for help by which he might satisfy his oath. When the holy woman recognized his holy purpose, she promised that she would provide counsel and assistance.

Meanwhile it happened that the abbot of the monastery of Clus died. When the duchess learned this, she prevailed upon the duke her husband that the aforesaid monk of Reynhusen should succeed the dead man as abbot, and this was done. Once that monk Johannes had been appointed abbot in Clus, he applied every effort to reform, and began to go before his subjects in religion according to the rule. When the monks, accustomed to corrupt ways, saw this, they all fled from him. But he, having gathered a few novices, instructed them in the purity of the rule, and living in great poverty began to serve God in all humility.

At that time the above-mentioned monastery of Bursfeld had fallen into such misery that, for its support, there was no income apart from a single cow. The church, that once had been the choir of singing monks, was roofed with straw and had become a stable for arriving cattle. [unclear] Johannes, abbot of Clus, because of the solitude and quiet. Hence, with the will [unclear], Bursfeld being utterly desolate, Johannes, abbot of Clus, transferred to Bursfeld. [unclear] Trier. He continued the reform, as far as he could, in great poverty. But hearing [unclear] that he had reformed his monastery excellently, had made constitutions necessary for preserving the reform, and was a learned, mature man, singularly zealous for the observance of religion, he came to him on foot, saw the praiseworthy institution, and experienced the life of the monks Sponheim.

...he learned by experience that it was holy, and praised the constitutions issued by him as most holy. And so the abbot asked the abbot, the Bursfeld abbot the Trier abbot, the poor man the rich, Johannes Johannes, to attach to him some of his brethren, by whose counsel and help he might complete the reform desired in Saxony. Johannes Rode, the abbot, consenting to his pious desire, assigned certain men of proven conduct from his monks, and sent him back with joy to Bursfeld. From that time the holy reform of the monasteries of our order, originally transmitted through the Trier men into Bursfeld, began to revive, and within a few years was enlarged. For when the princes and bishops of the churches saw the devoted and holy way of life of the monks of Bursfeld, they desired that the individual monasteries subject to them be reformed by them. Therefore, little by little, certain monasteries in Saxony and beyond began to be reformed from the monastery of Bursfeld, and from those others also; and their abbots, making a certain union and confederation among themselves, met once every year, celebrating a synod, which we call, by customary though barbarous and improper name, a Chapter, in which there would be discussion of those matters that pertain to the usefulness of the reform of the order. This union of reformed abbots under the name of Bursfeld, together with the annual Chapter, Pope Pius II confirmed in the first year of his pontificate, and bestowed many privileges upon those united and [unclear], concerning which below, in order, at the proper time, we shall briefly make mention.

And so the aforesaid Johannes, abbot of Bursfeld, the first in this designation of reformer, a good, religious, and devout man, magnificently restored our order in these regions, which had almost collapsed. But after he had died, after some years, he [unclear] successors [unclear] seventeen, an old man, devout and of holy conduct. In the time of his successor, however, the number of monasteries subject to this holy union increased, so that today seventy-five have been reformed, of which these are the names. The first is that distinguished monastery of St. Matthias at Trier, which we have therefore decided to name before Bursfeld, because the source of the whole Bursfeld reform flowed from it into the others that follow. The second in order of reform, but the first by name, was Bursfeld. The rest therefore follow without the order of reform: the monastery of St. James near Mainz, [unclear] monastery, in the year of the Lord 1469. After him Theodericus presided at Bursfeld as abbot, a mild and very prudent man, for sixteen years, and died on the fourth day before the Nones of January, in the year of the Lord 1485. Johannes [succeeded?] him [unclear].

Names of the monasteries of our synod of reformers. In the diocese of Mainz.

After him Theodericus presided at Bursfeld as abbot, a very mild man, for ninety-six years, and died on the fourth day before the Nones of January, in the year of the Lord 1485. Johannes [succeeded?] him [unclear]. The names of the monasteries are indicated here in this time.

The first is that individual monastery in the sign of Saint St. Matthew at Trier, which we have therefore decided to name before Bursfeld, because the source of the whole reform in these regions had almost collapsed: the rest therefore follow without the order of reform: the monastery of St. James near Mainz, a singular monastery, in the year of the Lord 1369. After him Theodoricus presided at Bursfeld as abbot, a very mild man, for forty-six years, and died on the fourth day before the Nones of January, in the year of the Lord 1285. Johannes [succeeded?] him [unclear]. The names of the monasteries are indicated here in this time.

After him Theodericus presided at Bursfeld as abbot, a very mild man, for forty-seven years, and died on the fourth day before the Nones of January, in the year of the Lord 1385. The first is that singular monastery in the sign of Saint Saint St. Matthew at Trier, which we have therefore decided to name before Bursfeld, because the sources of all reforms in these regions had almost collapsed: the rest [unclear] without order...

of nuns of our order were reformed by this holy institution; and although they have for the most part been entrusted to the abbots of our union, nevertheless, apart from those two aforesaid monasteries in Siloe and in Clara Aqua, they are by no means united to our Chapter. There are also certain other monasteries reformed by us which, for certain reasons, are not at this time incorporated into our annual Chapter and union: the monastery in Wissenburg, the monastery in Rasteten by the sea, the monastery in Lutzenburg, the monastery in Steina, the monastery in Hulmershusen, and the monastery in Corbeia. These indeed have been reformed, but not yet united to us.

1430.

In this year, which was the thirty-ninth of our abbot Bernard, Otto de Zegenhan, archbishop of Trier, died at Koblenz from an old disease of the stone; and, carried back to Trier, he was buried before the altar of the Blessed Virgin in the cathedral church: a truly magnificent man, endowed with singular devotion toward God, who governed his church excellently and did many good things. The head of St. Matthias the Apostle, which for many years had been kept in the castle of Ehrenbreitstein near Koblenz among the treasures of the pontiffs, he transferred with great devotion to the cathedral church of Trier, where it is kept in great veneration and honor in that same church down to the present day. In the same church of Trier he instituted the Mass of the blessed Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, so that it should be solemnly sung there every day in perpetuity after matins by the choristers. He was a lover and benefactor of the poor, and a most powerful subduer of the proud. He was the first to reform the monasteries of our order around Trier, with much labor and expense; for this holy work he appointed Johannes Rode, taken out of the Carthusian house, as abbot of St. Matthias, as we said above. But after the death of the most reverend archbishop Otto, many evils followed in the church of God at Trier. For the canons, disagreeing in the election, the greater and sounder part elected Jacobus de Sirck, scholasticus of the cathedral church and provost of Würzburg, a good man and worthy of every honor. The other, weaker part, namely Friedrich de Cracovia, provost of Trier, and another canon called de Pittingen, elected Ulrich von Manderscheid. From this division the church of Trier suffered very great disadvantages. For Ulrich, although weaker in right, was nevertheless more powerful in arms, and with the aid of his people, and of the counts of Virneburg and other nobles, he held the castles and fortifications of the archbishopric against Jacobus, who was unequal to him in strength, and received the customary homages from the subject men of the church. Hence Jacobus, compelled by necessity, invoked the aid of the supreme pontiff. But the pope, after the parties had been summoned and the cases heard, rejected the election that had been made, and, setting both aside, assigned the archbishopric of Trier to Rabanus de Helmstat, bishop of Speyer, through the promotion of Ludwig, count palatine of the Rhine. From this arose infinite evils, and the church of Trier suffered damage amounting to more than 300,000 florins. For the counts, barons, and soldiers of the whole country, adhering to Ulrich, scorned the apostolic mandates; and, raging against Rabanus, they besieged for almost two years the city of Trier, which favored him, hurling stones and balls at it in vain from the neighboring mountains. But at last, with the matter unaccomplished, they withdrew in confusion. Finally the pope, understanding that his commands were being despised, placed the territory of the diocese of Trier under ecclesiastical interdict for almost four years. At length Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, Dietrich, archbishop of Cologne, and Friedrich, bishop of Worms, intervening in their stead, put an end to the disputes by friendly negotiations; and thus lord Rabanus peacefully held the archbishopric for the greater part for almost five years, after, that is, the four years during which those disputes had lasted. The count of Virneburg attacks Rabanus.

In this year, which was the fortieth of our abbot Bernard, Gottfried, prior of this monastery, died, the twenty-sixth in the order of priors, in the ninth year of his priorate. In his time there was either no observance of regular discipline in this monastery, or only a slight one, although abbot Bernard labored not a little for reform. After Gottfried, Friedrich was made prior of this place, the twenty-seventh since its foundation, a man of that time and a zealous defender of the customs which he found; and he presided for seven years.

In the same Sponheim.

In the same year Abbot Bernhard removed Friedrich and Wilhelm, monks and procurators of this monastery, from the office of their provision, which they had held for almost eight years, and he raised thirty-eight articles against the account which they had made. He therefore again appointed a secular provisioner, whom his successor Gobelinus later removed.

Change of the provisioner of this monastery.

In the same year also, in the month of December, a general council was begun in the city of Basel, and it lasted more than thirteen years; in it forty-four public sessions were held. It had a fair and glorious beginning, but a weak and confused end, because Pope Eugenius IV, not agreeing with the council itself, stirred up many contrivances against it. After he was deprived by it of papal honor and dignity, he did not trouble to obey the council, but recalled it, and procured that the Dauphin, first-born son of the king of France, be sent against the people of Basel for its dispersal, as we shall say in its place. From this followed many evils and scandals in the Church, not yet wholly quieted, some preaching that the pope is above the council, others saying the opposite.

The Council of Basel is begun.

In the aforesaid year also a great expedition of bishops, princes, nobles, and citizens was made against the Hussites in Bohemia; but no fruit came of it, while very great loss befell the Catholics. For, because of the ambition and greed of the princes, the heretics again prevailed against our men; many were slain, and the rest fled with loss and disgrace, all their horses, wagons, valuables, money, and the whole equipment being lost.

Expedition against the Hussites in Bohemia.

1432.

In the forty-first year of our abbot Bernhard there was a very harsh winter; and at last, when the ice and snows had melted, so great a flooding of waters followed that many villages, houses, and churches along the Rhine were overthrown in various places by the excessive force of the flood, and great losses to sown fields and meadows followed.

A very harsh winter.

In the same year, on the holy day of Parasceve, during the office, two Jews came to a little village not far from the monastery of St. Catherine, which is called Wiler. With smooth speeches and promises they took a certain little boy, seven years of age, and secretly led him outside the village into the neighboring wood, which is called Dumus lupina, in the vernacular Wolfisheck, and is a possession of this monastery. Cruelly martyring him, they killed him; and, having collected his blood, they went away, leaving the innocent boy’s little body unburied among the bushes themselves. Afterward, when the innocent corpse was found, it was carried with honor to Kreuznach, and for some days it stood unburied in the parish church, many hoping that his martyrdom would be made known by signs and miracles through the mercy of God. But when no miracle appeared, they buried it in the cemetery behind the choir, toward the east, where that stone cross is seen erected today. The Jews too, having been apprehended in Kreuznach, were burned with fire outside the town.

In the same year also, on the eleventh day of the month of May, which was Jubilate Sunday, the eighth provincial chapter of our order was celebrated at St. Ulrich in Augsburg. Presiding over it were Ortwin of St. Peter in Erfurt, of the diocese of Mainz; Johannes in Stein, of Constance; and Heinrich in Amorbach, likewise of the diocese of Mainz, abbots of monasteries of our order; and many things were decreed in it.

In this same year Sigismund, aided by the power of Filippo, duke of Milan, was conveyed to Rome and crowned with the imperial diadem by Pope Eugenius.

In the same year also Bernhard, eighteenth abbot of this monastery, weighed down by old age and the disease of the stone, died on the fifth calends of June, in the seventy-seventh year of his age, and with the forty-first year, together with three months and nine days, of the rule he had undertaken completed. When he perceived that death was near him, having first made confession with tears and received the ecclesiastical sacraments with great devotion, he had the whole community called to him. As they stood by, he said: “Brothers, always indeed beloved to me in Christ, you now see that the end of the present life is upon me, and that I can no longer remain with you. I therefore ask: call to mind the injuries which you have so often inflicted both on me and on God, since, when I wished to bring your conduct back to the integrity of monastic life, you always resisted me with too much contempt. Behold, now I die, and if I have done well, my reward is with me; but you, I greatly fear, after my death will have [unclear], so that, as you were unwilling to hear me as father, you may hear another [not as father?]. Consider therefore, I pray, the brevity of the present life, and amend your ways according to the monastic rule and the decrees of the holy Fathers, lest in the article of death, in which you see me placed, you repent of rashness. Moreover I charge you that, after my death, you seek back as far as [unclear] those farms in Winzheim from unjust possessors, of which I bought one for a price, and acquired the other from my brothers by [unclear] edict for my son. But if that man of Cuppenstein should claim to have any right in them, know that his allegation is most false; for I, as you know, in that discord which was between me and you almost five years before this, may God forgive us for it,” [Blank page in the source scan.]

354 The Chronicle of Trithemius

provoked by excessive indignation, from the violent disturbance and displeasure of my mind I did what [unclear], handing them over without your consent (which cannot be established) to the said Jeckel of Gemunden, which Meynhardus of Coppenstein now possesses by an unjust title; so may God be propitious to me in this my extreme necessity. Behold, I have told you the whole order of the matter. If you neglect to seek back the alienated estates, you shall answer to God; I have discharged my soul. Having said these things, he rested in the Lord. Present, moreover, who heard this protestation, were Frederick the prior, Wilhelm count of the Rhine, monk, Frederick count of the Rhine, monk, Gerard the monk, Frederick of Nackheim, monk, Johannes the monk, all professed members of this monastery; also Jacob of Cleberg, monk and chaplain, Volker the layman, cellarer of this monastery, appointed in the same year on the day of the Innocents, and many others from the household. After Abbot Bernhard had died, the brothers, in accordance with his commission, seeking back those estates, began to mow the hay; but by armed force they were violently driven out by the servants of the men of Coppenstein. And although afterward a complaint was often brought against them by several abbots, as we shall say below, nevertheless they achieved nothing against the violence.

Concerning Gobelinus, nineteenth abbot of this monastery, who presided for seven years, one month, and fourteen days; concerning various deeds both of his and of that time.

After the death of the venerable lord Abbot Bernhard, the tribulation which he had foretold to the monks while he was alive came upon them. For as soon as Johannes, count of Sponheim, the last of the line, heard that the abbot was dead, he came in person to the monastery together with the count of Veldenz, and by a strict prohibition forbade the brothers to elect a new abbot without his presence, consent, and will. Perhaps he would not have done this if the death of the deceased abbot had not by chance been reported to his knowledge so suddenly; and it has been handed down to memory that it happened thus. At the very hour when the bells were being rung here in the monastery for the deceased abbot, it happened by chance that the count himself, with his attendants, had begun to continue his journey from Winterburg toward Kreuznach; and during that ringing he met a peasant not far from the monastery.
