When the count asked him what that ringing of the bells at an unusual hour meant, he replied that the abbot was dead. When the count heard this, immediately turning aside from his journey, he entered the monastery. He made the prohibition which we have mentioned, contrary to justice and the privilege of the monastery, appointing for the brothers the day for the election of a new shepherd at the town of Kreuznach on the third day immediately following, which was the day of the holy martyrs Abdon and Sennen, namely the third day before the Kalends of August.

The count, moreover, had with him a certain monk of the Cistercian order from the monastery of Saint Disibod, named Gobelinus, a shrewd and courtly man, whom he loved greatly; and he was held by him in high esteem, and was first among his secretaries. Therefore, having obtained an opportunity, desiring to honor this monk for his fidelity toward him, he [unclear] to promote him as abbot of this monastery. The brothers, because of necessity and because of their depraved morals and dissoluteness of life, did not dare to oppose him. And so, when the term appointed for the election arrived, the monks of this monastery, compelled by necessity, came to Kreuznach, as had been ordered. When they had been assembled in the count's court, the count of Veldenz himself being present with certain others, the count of Sponheim began in this manner: “Do not suppose, lord brothers, that because I have summoned you to this place for the election of a new abbot, I am either your enemy or an invader of your monastery. For I, as advocate, guardian, and faithful defender of your monastery, especially desire to see your advancement both in spiritual conduct and also in the substantial good of temporal affairs; nor should it be believed that I wish in any way to destroy the monastery which my forefathers built to the honor of God, but rather to advance it in all things toward better things according to my powers. Since, therefore, your monastery of Sponheim has now for many years notably declined in both respects, there is certainly need, if it is to be brought back to its original institution, of a man prudent and experienced in many things, who is willing and able to preside over you usefully. I have such a man with me, known to you as prudent and experienced, lord Gobelinus, whom I advise and ask you to elect as your abbot; for I know that through his wisdom and industry the condition of your monastery will be brought back to a better state.”

When these things had been heard, the brothers were suddenly exceedingly dismayed and were wholly ignorant what they should do. But after much counsel at last, and after many prayers to the contrary had been offered to the count, since they were making no progress at all, they yielded to the advice of the count of Veldenz and of others who knew that the mind of our count was not to be bent from what he had begun. Lest something worse should happen to them, as could be inferred by a likely conjecture from his threats, consenting under injustice, they elected this Gobelinus, in such manner as they could, as their abbot. Therefore Gobelinus, although of another order, was elected nineteenth abbot of the monastery of Sponheim in the aforesaid year of the Lord 1332, in the tenth indiction, on the penultimate day of the month of July; and he was confirmed by Conrad, archbishop of Mainz, through his vicar in pontificals 356. CHRONICLE OF TRITHEMIUS.

…at the time of the last reformation, which was made in the year of the Lord 1469, [the privilege] was found among the letters of the county of Sponheim in the vault of the castle of Trarbach, and by lord Frederick—the illustrious and Christian prince, count Palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, our first reformer—was restored to us and to the monastery. Reckoning, therefore, the years from then to the reformation introduced, no less than 35 years flowed, in which the privileges of the monastery were lost—although not even today are all restored, as we are taught from certain copies and rescripts, whose originals we do not have. But also certain precious volumes of our library, which those former gluttons had left untouched, he carried off with him, which, dispersed in various places about Trarbach, will never be brought back to us. For (as we said before) rarely was there an abbot in the monastery, but he followed the count's court, and was first among his councilors. Whence meanwhile the state of the monastery, both in spiritual and in temporal [things], greatly declined—so much so that, on account of the excessive debts of the convent, [it] was frequently almost in excommunication; and [the brothers], on the principal feasts (as appears from their hand-registers), that they might be permitted to celebrate the divine [office], redeeming [it] with vexatious money, used to obtain for a time a relaxation of the censures from the judges of the see of Mainz. The term of the indulgence elapsed, they fell again into the censures as before, compelled to intermit the divine offices. And this lamentable calamity lasted for several years, up to the last reformation, [that] of Bursfeld, which was made in the year of the Lord 1465 [as printed]. [Margin: Abbot Gobelin carries off the books of the library. The state of this monastery was bad from [that] time.]

In the aforesaid year, the second of our abbot Gobelin, a most grievous, long-lasting contention arose between him and a certain Craffto, altarist of Blessed Mary ever-Virgin in the church of St Martin at Mainz, over twenty maldra of rye of annual rent, [which had been] promised (as is asserted), by a certain instrument, to the aforesaid altar from our goods in Blenich, by lord Bernhard the former abbot, without the knowledge or will of the convent—by what occasion or reason is not known. When, therefore, lord Gobelin the abbot, successor of Bernhard, by the counsel of the brothers altogether refused to give the aforesaid rye unless he were first taught why, he is first impeded before the secular judgment in Blenich by the same Craffto, claiming [arrears] of 40 years, and then is cited to the council of Basel. And this contention lasted 6 years, not without the greatest [and] most grievous expenses; at length a sentence was pronounced—by John, Dean of St Gangolf of Mainz, commissary of the aforesaid council of Basel—for the plaintiff over the possessory [right], against the abbot, to the grave loss and damage of the aforesaid monastery. For the abbot Gobelin himself, in his own person, was twice, on account of this matter, at the council of Basel; he often sent a monk of the brothers to Basel; he made many other expenses through 8 continuous years in the same cause, which he handled less advisedly. [Margin: Contention between the abbot and the chaplain of St Quentin. The abbot was twice at the council of Basel on account of this matter.]

In the same year, too, marvels were seen in heaven: for there appeared 7 circles in the manner of a rainbow, arch against arch, disposed in a marvelous order; and the winter of that year was hard enough, cold and long, which afflicted the poor exceedingly. [Margin: A marvelous sign appeared in heaven.]

Item, in the same year, the dukes of Austria and of Meissen, advancing with a great army of Christians to war against the Bohemian Hussites, slew more than 12 thousand of them. But in the same year, on the 7th day of the month of October, in the night, a horrendous, most violent wind, coming from the north, from the English sea up the ascent of the Rhine, raging through all the adjacent regions as far as Italy, both in the waters and on the land, inflicted infinite damages on men. For, overturning the strongest houses, towers, churches, and innumerable trees, it crushed many men of either sex and every age. [Margin: Expedition against the Hussites in Bohemia. A horrendous wind.]

In this year, which was the 3rd of abbot Gobelin, the provincial chapter of our order was celebrated the 26th day of the month of June—which was the Sunday next after the feast of the nativity of St John—at Basel, at the time of the general council, in the monastery of the Friars Preachers; in which presided Ortwin of St Peter in Erfurt, Frederick of St Mark in Reichenau, John of St George in Stein, and Henry in Faucibus, abbots of monasteries of our order. To this provincial chapter abbot Gobelin, by the authority of the council, was cited, and by the report of the Visitors accused before the presidents on many articles—chiefly that he had alienated privileges, letters of liberties, and muniments from the monastery, made no accounting, and for the most part resided outside the monastery. Who, answering on all these as he could, obtained from the council and chapter, through the mediation of Louis, count Palatine, that the abbot of St Matthias of Trier be deputed to him as commissary, who [should hear] the cause… [Margin: The provincial chapter is celebrated. Abbot Gobelin is cited to the chapter.]

[Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheim.

...in his own person, after the matter had been heard here in the monastery, he would determine it by just counsel; and he promised those presiding over it that he wished to acquiesce in its decree. Therefore in the same year, in the month of December, the abbot of St. Matthias came, supported by the authority of the Council of Basel and of our whole provincial chapter; discharging his commission, as is customary, he found that the report to the chapter had been true, and compelled the abbot to promise amendment in all things. At Kreuznach, before the friends of Gobelin himself, he heard the accounting for the receipts and expenditures of the three-year period, where he composed peace and concord between the abbot and the convent as best he could. The expenses of this visitation, accounting, and settlement at Kreuznach exceeded the sum of 50 florins, as we find from the registers of the procurators, and yet no profit, or only little, came from it.

The abbot of St. Matthias visits here by authority of the council.

In the aforesaid year also, on the day of St. Dionysius the martyr, the abbot Gobelin appointed a certain Johannes, pastor, provider, cellarer, and procurator of the church in Sulm, over this monastery, and entrusted to him the governance of the whole monastery in temporal affairs; and he himself, in his usual fashion, stayed with the count in Trarbach and was very seldom in the monastery.

A secular provider appointed by the abbot.

In the aforesaid year also, on the twelfth day of the month of October, Ernest, duke of Bavaria, caused a most beautiful young woman, the daughter of a certain barber of Augsburg, whom his son Albert loved with excessive love and kept as a concubine, to be thrown from the bridge at Straubing and drowned in the Danube, while his son was far away and knew nothing of the matter. When he returned and heard of his father's cruelty committed against the mistress most beloved to him, from excessive grief of heart he first fell into madness; afterward, having returned to himself, he wept most bitterly, and swore that he would spare neither father nor [unclear] until he had avenged the innocent death of his beloved. Great discord therefore followed between the son, the father, and the nobles who had cooperated in the young woman's death, which at last could scarcely be quieted with the greatest difficulty. Over the woman's tomb, at the son's compulsion, the father founded a new chapel, in which one Mass was to be celebrated every day forever for her soul. There were those who said that Duke Albert had contracted a secret marriage with her, and that his father, moved for this reason because he had disgraced the nobility of his lineage with a person of humble stock, had given the order that she be killed. All cried out that the father had acted wickedly in ordering so beautiful, honorable, and innocent a young woman, most beloved to his son above all others, to be killed because of love, since many formerly most noble kings and princes, overcome by virtue or by love, had taken wives for themselves from the humbler class of citizens or peasants without disgrace.

The miserable deed of Ernest, duke of Bavaria.

In the same year also the winter was extremely harsh for three months, so that trees, sown crops, and vines perished in many places from the excessive cold. Wine too was at an altogether dear price, because, except in Alsace, little grew anywhere, and it was very sour.

An extremely harsh winter.

1436.

In the fourth year of Gobelin our abbot, Johannes, the last count of Sponheim, granted the altar of St. Pancratius the martyr in the castle of Sponheim, with all its revenues, rents, and appurtenances, to be incorporated into this monastery with the right of patronage, which he openly renounced, for the increase of the monks' prebends, as is evident from the letters which he gave to the convent concerning this matter. Their date is on the day of St. Martin the bishop, in the year of the Lord 1436. Theoderic, archbishop of Mainz, afterward confirmed this donation, through Johannes de Lysura, doctor of decrees and his vicar in spiritual matters, at the instance of the abbot and convent of this monastery, as is evident in the letters drawn up concerning it, which were dated in the year of the Lord 1439, on Friday in the month of March.

Count Johannes offers the altar of the castle of Sponheim to this monastery.

In the aforesaid year of Abbot Gobelin, Albert, duke of Bavaria, of whom mention was made in the previous year, took as wife Anna, daughter of the duke of Brunswick, and celebrated the wedding at Munich.

Albert, duke of Bavaria, takes a wife.

In this same year good wine grew in great quantity and was sold for a low price.

1437.

In the fifth year of Gobelin our abbot, Johannes, the last count of Sponheim, died in the castle of Starkenburg near Trarbach, leaving in the hands of Gobelin, his secretary, a written testament; nevertheless, because contradiction by the heirs intervened, it was not put into effect, although Gobelin himself for that reason went in person to the Council of Basel and obtained from it the necessary letters of commission, yet he could not prevail against the powerful [unclear]. For the aforesaid count, almost two years before he died, deposited twelve thousand florins in the keeping of Gobelin our abbot, which the abbot himself, expending them at his command, disbursed in various matters as they arose. But when the count had died, the duke of Bavaria and the margrave of Baden, who had taken the county of Sponheim into possession,

Johannes, the last count of Sponheim, dies.

The deposit of the count entrusted to our abbot Gobelin.

Johannes, the last count of Sponheim, dies. [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Trithemius

They were holding Abbot Gobelinus in Winterburgk, for almost the space of a year, in honorable custody, desiring to have from him, as from the secretary of the deceased count, not only an account of the deposit, but also certain treasures, which, as they asserted, had been entrusted to him by the count. Throughout all that time Abbot Gobelinus stayed in a public inn, a prisoner at Winterburgk by command of the princes, with one very strong servant appointed to guard him; and indeed he could walk about within the walls wherever he pleased, his guard always following his steps, but he did not dare go out of the village. At last, after the months of his captivity had passed, he gave a lawful account of the deposit, a sufficient reckoning, to the princes' counsellors who had been sent to him; concerning the suspicion of the treasures, he confidently asserted that he knew nothing of them. Thus at last he was released and returned to the monastery; no execution of the will followed.

In the same year also, on the last day of December, there died the illustrious and most Christian prince, lord Louis, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, son of the late Rupert, king of the Romans, called the Bearded, or also the blind duke, because after his return from the Holy Land he incurred illnesses, among them blindness: a good, pious, holy man, who had been protector and defender of the Council of Constance, and who kept Pope John XXIII, after his deposition, when handed over to him by the council, for three years in his castle at Mannheim. He left behind him three sons, the first of whom was Louis, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, prince-elector, a pious, just, devout man, who had taken as wife Margaret, daughter of Amadeus, Duke of Savoy, afterward Pope Felix, elected in the Council of Basel against Eugenius; by her he begot Philip, the most unconquered prince, ruling far and wide today, of whom we shall make mention afterward in his proper place. The second son of Louis the Bearded was that most powerful Duke Frederick, who after his brother's death was guardian of the most illustrious Philip; he did not take a wife, and of him also we shall speak afterward. The third was Rupert, Archbishop of Cologne after Theodoric; of him we shall make mention below.

Also in the aforesaid year, in the month of December, Sigismund, emperor of the Romans and king of Hungary and Bohemia, died in Moravia: a most Christian prince, lover of God, defender of the clergy, advocate of the poor, buried at Alba Regalis with great honor, not without a reputation for holiness.

Adolf also, Duke of Berg and Jülich, died in the same year, in the month of December. A great famine [unclear]. Matilda, [wife?] of the Count Palatine and Duke of Bavaria, grandmother of Philip our most illustrious prince, died on the twelfth day of May: a devout woman, holy toward God and most pious toward the poor. In the same year, around the middle of Lent, the prince-electors assembled at Frankfurt and unanimously elected to the rule of the Romans Albert, Duke of Austria, son-in-law of the deceased Emperor Sigismund, a vigorous, pious, good, holy man, who reigned only two years. After the death of his father-in-law he obtained many kingdoms, duchies, and counties by hereditary right, peacefully and without any disturbance, such as the kingdom of Hungary, Bohemia, Dalmatia, Croatia, the duchy of Moravia, and many other lands; and among all the princes of Germany he was the more powerful and the wealthier. He was elected, as we have said, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the middle of Lent: a prince of whom the world was not worthy; therefore, made perfect in a short time, he fulfilled many times.

In the aforesaid year Rabanus of Helmstatt, Archbishop of Trier and Bishop of Speyer, weighed down by old age and seeing that he was less equal to the governance of so great a pontificate, followed the counsel of certain persons and took John, Bishop of Liège, as coadjutor of the church of Trier, against the will of many of the chapter; hence the church of Trier, as many asserted, suffered no small loss, inconvenience, and harm. In the same year also, on the first day of July, Ernest, Duke of Bavaria, died, leaving one son, Albert by name, of whom mention has been made above. In the same year John, Abbot of St. Matthias of Trier, again came by authority of the council

Abbot Gobelinus is held prisoner for almost the space of a year.

Louis, Count Palatine, grandfather of Philip, dies.

The sons of Duke Louis the Bearded.

Emperor Sigismund died.

Adolf, Duke of Berg and Jülich, dies.

Great famine.

Matilda, grandmother of Philip, Count Palatine, dies.

Albert, Duke of Austria and king of the Romans.

The Bishop of Liège was coadjutor of the church of Trier.

Ernest, Duke of Bavaria, dies. 364 Chronicle of Trithemius

of Odernheim, otherwise commonly called [Schiltweck?], who, confirmed by Theoderic, archbishop of Mainz, and blessed by his vicar in pontificals, presided over this monastery for sixteen years and twenty days. He was a native of Odernheim, born of respectable parents, of knightly stock; in his youth he was handed over to the monastery and imitated the habits he found there. He was, however, worldly, frivolous, and inconstant; he was accustomed to take too much delight in games and carousals, and cared little, indeed absolutely nothing, for religion. But when he had been ordained abbot, he did not at once change his former bad habits; for some years, intent day and night on carousals, dice-games, and other things, he seemed to care not at all about the advancement of the monastery. For not rarely, but often, he shamefully squandered much of the monastery’s substance at dice, sometimes staking [unclear] florins, or rings from his fingers, in that very pursuit of vanity, losing them at the same time. At length, after some years, frightened by fear of the Bursfeld reform, whose fame was then exceedingly celebrated, [unclear] of Nicholas of Cusa, legate of the apostolic see, [unclear] compelled him to leave monasteries bound [unclear]. But afterwards, as far as the prudent administration of temporal affairs is concerned, he sufficiently reformed himself; he gave up the games, carousals, and wandering excursions to which he had previously devoted himself, and applied himself more earnestly to the monastery’s advancement. Nevertheless he did not correct either his own morals or those of his subjects to the purity of the Rule, nor did he take care to amend the defect of spiritual instruction. He found the state of the monastery in temporal matters very poor and exhausted, burdened to creditors in more than one thousand sixty florins; over several years he paid off the greater part of the debts and constructed several new buildings. Among other things, he built the house which is now the kitchen, and that which today is the bakehouse; for their expenses he laid out more than 130 florins, according to the tenor of his reckoning. He also repaired the lower mill from the foundations, planted several new vineyards, not without great expense, and completely repaired two fishponds. He also constructed a number of other things, both in the courts outside and within the monastery: buildings, barns, houses, and stables. We judge it superfluous to make individual mention of them all.

1446.

In the first year of Abbot Conrad, Ludovicus, prior of this monastery, died, the twenty-eighth in the order of priors from the beginning of the foundation. After Fridericus, who had died in the sixth year of Abbot Gobelinus, he was [unclear] that he should care for religion. After him, Johannes Mariae was appointed the twenty-ninth prior; for some time he also held the office of cellarer together with the priorate, because of the small number of persons. He remained prior for almost fourteen years, a man born more for temporal affairs than for the cares of monastic discipline. It happened at that time that sometimes the prior himself represented the whole convent, because apart from him there was no monk at all in the monastery. For the abbot had his own dwelling apart; similarly Fridericus of Nackheim, formerly abbot, who had resigned, was accustomed to stay sometimes in the monastery in his own little house, sometimes in Kreuznach. And the monastery, formerly full of monks, was exposed to the mockery of the peasants: abbots, and one monk, of whom the other part was the convent. Nevertheless the number of persons was increased from [unclear] alien monks.

In the aforesaid year of the Lord, on the seventeenth day of the month of April, which was Palm Sunday, during the night the sea in the regions around Dordrecht, with the greatest force, broke through the dike and went beyond its bounds, and suddenly and unexpectedly submerged more than one hundred thousand people, with all their goods and livestock, in a pitiable calamity. On the same Palm Sunday there were also horrible thunders and flashes of lightning in the county of Zutphen, so much so that lightning falling from the clouds into the church of the blessed ever-virgin in the town of Zutphen consumed the tower and bells, seriously injured several people, and killed thirteen in number. On the same day also a great cold wind coming from the north along the ascent of the Rhine brought such a quantity of snow that, all roads being blocked with snow, no one could go anywhere outside the house. And on the penultimate day of the same month of April, in many places the healthy vineyards, injured by excessive cold, perished.

In the aforesaid year Theoderic, archbishop of Cologne, with a great army of his men again entered Westphalia against the people of Soest, but to the great harm and inconvenience of himself and his men. For the citizens, going out and fighting manfully, captured two hundred men from among the better nobles on the archbishop’s side and, bringing them captive into the town, did not set them free until they had redeemed themselves with a great sum of money; from them they extorted more than fifty thousand.

At the same Sponheim.

of the Council of Basel and of our provincial chapter, specially deputed general visitor, and again visited here, leaving a certain instrument of his visitation, in which he especially admonishes the abbot concerning two matters. First, that from then on he should not continue his residence outside the monastery, but rather should remain with his brothers in the monastery, intent on his own salvation and theirs, especially now that the count was dead, by whose service he was no longer being pressed. Second, that he should take care to restore to the monastery as quickly as possible the letters and privileges long before alienated from the monastery by him, as we said above. The first of these two things he did; the other was not within his power to do, although he often attempted it. For, on account of the privileges long shut up in the vault of the castle of Trarbach, to which he himself could not have access, because of the impeded execution of the dead count's testament and his own captivity and detention in Winterburg, he conceived a hostile mind toward Duke Stephen; and, on the advice of legal experts, attacking him judicially, first through the commissioner of the Council of Basel and finally through the most clement prince Louis, Count Palatine, he began to compel him to restitution and satisfaction. But meanwhile, being carried off by death, he left the undertaking begun but unfinished, and nothing further was done.

1439.

In the seventh year of our abbot Gobelin, Pope Eugene, in order to disperse the Council of Basel, stirred Louis, Dauphin of Vienne, the first-born of the king of France, to arms, by entreaties and by money, as was reported, against the Roman Empire and the German nation. Having gathered a great army of twenty-five thousand armed men, he came into Alsace. Around Basel, Strasbourg, and the surrounding cities they committed many burnings, plunderings, and damages in villages and fields. They had a very fierce war with the Swiss not far from Basel, in which they lost no fewer of their own than they had killed of the others. These things were done in the month of March. At length Louis, Count Palatine, with the aid of the neighboring princes, of the cities of the empire, especially the people of Strasbourg, Basel, and Schlettstadt, powerfully drove out of Alsace that troop, which was called the Armagnacs, together with their prince the Dauphin, many of them having been killed, so that out of that whole multitude of twenty-five thousand very few escaped. After this great slaughter of the Armagnacs in Alsace, plague, famine, and dearth followed in all the regions on this side of the Rhine; many thousands died.

In the same year the Council of Basel issued one bull for the reform of our order in Germany, which begins thus: “Among the manifold cares by which, amid the varieties of matters and business that arise, we are distracted for the universal Church,” etc. Given at Basel, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the year from the Nativity of the Lord 1439. In this act of the council, twelve abbots of our order were appointed visitors and reformers of all the monasteries of our order throughout Germany, especially throughout the province of Mainz. Among them was one John, abbot of St. Matthias near Trier, who in this year visited here for the third time, supported by the authority of the aforesaid council. Yet in the end he made little progress, because the monks, accustomed to depraved morals, cared little for the words of the one admonishing them, since, born and brought up in deformity, so to speak, they did not wish to live otherwise than they had learned. For excessive poverty and lack of temporal goods had led them to despair of spiritual life, whereby they believed themselves unable to do what they easily could have done.

In the same year, on the twenty-sixth day of the month of April, which was Jubilate Sunday, the tenth provincial chapter of our order was held at Nuremberg, in the monastery of St. Giles, over which Hartung of St. Peter’s in Erfurt, Nicholas of St. Basil’s in the Black Forest, and Henry Amerbach, abbots of monasteries of our order, presided. In this provincial chapter the bull of the Council of Basel written above, issued for the reform of our order throughout Germany with much maturity, as we have said, was presented to the fathers. Receiving it with reverence, the fathers commanded that it be observed by all.

In the year also noted above, Raban of Helmstatt, archbishop of Trier, considering that his decrepit age, exhausted in strength, was not equal to the burdens of so great a pontificate, after taking counsel with his own men, especially with his coadjutor John, bishop of Liège, resigned that archbishopric of Trier, with the consent of the whole chapter, to Jacob of Sierck, who before him had been elected in the dispute with Ulrich of Manderscheid, as we said in its place. To obtain quiet he returned to his church of Speyer, which in the meantime he had held in commendam. But soon he also resigned the bishopric of Speyer in favor of Reinhard of Helmstatt, provost of the greater church, to whom the pope had made provision for that same bishopric, with the consent of the chapter of Speyer. And thus Reinhard, confirmed as bishop of the church of Speyer, presided for nearly seventeen years in tranquillity. Moreover, Raban himself in the same year, on the fourteenth day of November, at Speyer [unclear].

Raban, archbishop of Trier, resigned to Jacob of Sierck.

The bishopric of Speyer also [to] Reinhard of Helmstatt.

Bishoprics [unclear], of Speyer, Reinhard of Helmstatt.

The provincial chapter is held.

In the year 1438, on Wednesday, in the dispute between the abbots of the Council of Basel and [Ludovicensis?], at the monastery of St. John in Alsace, with their confrères, for the reform of the order, we said: Because no acts of this sort of council are available, nor are we now making an agreement of each side, but let us proceed in this way: to the abbots of the councils Chronicle of Trithemius

he died, and was buried in the body of the church: certainly a magnificent man, and wholly laborious for the Church of God. Jacobus was archbishop of Trier. But Jacobus Sirck, after the resignation of Lord Rabanus, was confirmed by Pope Eugene IV and was consecrated archbishop in the castle of Mayensberg; he presided for seventeen years. He was an excellent man, good and magnificent in spirit, who by his prudence and magnanimity defeated and overcame many rivals and adversaries of the church of Trier. Certain canons of the greater church who were rebellious against him he firmly compelled, with the help of the Supreme Pontiff, to subjection and obedience. At his first entry he found the church of Trier altogether impoverished: all its castles, towns, tolls, and revenues pledged, and all its storehouses empty. Nevertheless he was compelled to give and pay sixty thousand florins to John, bishop of Liege, formerly coadjutor of Rabanus, by reason of his administration.

Also in the aforesaid year, John, bishop of Wurzburg, for what reason I do not sufficiently know, was captured by the Domicelli of Hirtzhorn and detained in their custody for four months. There are those who write that the cause was [unclear], and that he had burdened his church with many debts, had not restored at the appointed time a loan received from the aforesaid Domicelli, and for that reason had been captured and detained by them.

In the same year also, on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, Albert, king of the Romans, died, not yet having completed two years in the kingdom, and was buried in Alba, leaving his wife pregnant. He was a prince renowned for liberality and courage. But it seems to me that there is an error in the histories. For if he was elected on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April in the preceding year, and died on the sixth day before the Kalends of November in this year, he held the kingdom for no more than one year, seven months, and seven days. Therefore four months and twenty-one days were still lacking from the two-year period, as is plainly evident to one who calculates well the intervening months and days.

In his aforesaid year Gobelinus, the nineteenth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, weighed down by illness, departed this present life and rested in the Lord on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, after he had completed in the abbacy seven years, one month, and twenty-four days. He was certainly a man constant in spirit and provident in intelligence, not to say crafty, who during the time of his rule endured many adversities with constant spirit and was readier to conquer than to yield. The greater damage which in the time of his rule he brought upon this monastery was the alienation of the books of privileges, which even to the present day have not yet all been restored to us. The withdrawal of bodily residence also harmed the monastery not a little, since the monks, as though deprived of their head, observed no order at all, either in spiritual or in temporal matters. For from the time of Abbot Philip, the last, down to the most recent reform of this place, for almost seventy-nine years, the providers and procurators appointed successively by the abbot, both monks and laymen, are found, for the most part, as appears from their manual registers, with few exceptions, to have been unfaithful to the monastery. The providers of the monastery were thieves. However few had dealt unfaithfully, each escaped wealthy, and always after the account had been completed they were found to have spent, in a notable sum, more for the monastery than they had received from it in all things by reason of their office. When asked whence they had received the surplus, one lied that he had received a loan from his mother, a friend, or any other person brought in besides. And so, since the monks were laboring, as it were licitly, under the open vice of private property, what else was to be expected from them than to steal, subtract, commit fraud, lie, deceive, and bring the monastery down to extreme poverty or want? Their pitiable way of life brought such ruin and desolation upon this monastery that up to the present day it could scarcely in any degree be restored, even with the greatest labors.

Concerning Fridericus Nackheim, twentieth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, who presided for five years, seven months, and four days, and concerning various deeds of that time

After Gobelinus, the nineteenth abbot of this monastery, had died in the year and on the day noted above, and had been buried according to the custom of ecclesiastical tradition, on the third following day, that is, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, the brethren assembled in the chapter-place with the purpose and intention of establishing a new pastor over themselves. They were few in number. After deliberation among themselves, they at last unanimously elected as abbot Fridericus de Nackheim, a professed monk of this monastery, constituted in the priesthood. Confirmed by Theodoric, archbishop of Mainz, and blessed by his vicar in pontifical matters, he presided over this monastery for five years, six months, and four days. Afterwards he resigned, as in its place Sponheim.

we shall speak in the proper place. This Frederick was born of military stock; having been handed over to the monastery in his youth, he acquired little literary learning, just as nearly all the others of that time, being without education, sang from custom rather than from art. He was a quiet man, unable to endure labors, and for that reason less adequate for the governance of pastoral care. In his time, as far as his own person was concerned, he neither benefited the monastery greatly, nor was he found to have harmed it greatly. He entrusted the care of temporal affairs to stewards, after the manner of those who had preceded him in the abbacy; devoting himself to his own comfort, he involved himself in few matters.

1440.

In the first year of our abbot Frederick, the monastery of St. James on the Fair Mountain beside the walls of the city of Mainz was reformed by monks of Bursfelde in Saxony, at the urging and with the cooperation of Theodoric, archbishop of Mainz, after the old, unreformed monks, who had refused to submit to reform, had been removed far away. As the first abbot for maintaining this most holy reform there was appointed Lubbert, a father of venerable religious life, together with other brothers sent from Bursfelde; he lived devoutly and died in holiness.

In the same year John, bishop of Wuerzburg, died. Sigismund, son of the duke of Saxony, immediately succeeded him and presided for barely three years. For before three years had elapsed, he was expelled from the bishopric by the noble lords of the chapter because of his excessive foolishness and sloth. Fleeing to his brothers in Saxony, he was, as a foolish and ruined man, placed by them in custody in a certain castle, with an annual pension intervening for his support from the church of Wuerzburg, according to the agreements, as we shall say below in its proper place.

In this same year, in the middle of Lent, the prince-electors assembled at Frankfurt for the election of a new king. After mature deliberation had first been held, they unanimously elected as King of the Romans Frederick, the third of that name, son of Ernest, duke of Austria, and nephew through his sister of the late King Albert. He ruled for fifty-three years: a mild and peaceable man, a lover of the clergy, patient under injuries, twenty-six years old when he began to reign.

1441.

In the second year of our abbot Frederick, on the last day of April, the eleventh provincial chapter of our order was held in the monastery of St. Giles at Nuremberg, with continuation over the following days, as is customary. There again presided Hartung of St. Peter’s at Erfurt, together with George of St. Giles’s at Nuremberg, Nicholas of St. Blaise’s in the Black Forest, and Henry of Blessed Mary ever Virgin at Amorbach, abbots of monasteries of our order. They established many things for beginning and continuing reform, but the necessary executors were lacking. In the same year the winter was hard and very severe, and great snows lay on the face of the earth from the feast of St. Martin until the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary the Virgin, to such an extent that many poor and needy people died from cold and want.

In the same year also Louis, duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Hunchback, against his father Louis in Ingolstadt, with the help of Margrave Albert of Brandenburg, encircled the town of Neuburg on the banks of the Danube with a siege. When at last it was taken, after the citizens surrendered, he captured his father and left him as booty to the aforesaid margrave; the latter sold him to Henry, duke of Landshut, his bitterest enemy, for a great weight of gold. But divine power did not long tolerate so wicked a crime of a son against his father to go unpunished; instead, in a short time, when he least feared it, removing him from their midst without children, it presented him to its own judgment.

In this year also Theodoric, archbishop of Cologne, having gathered a great army of his men, besieged the Westphalian city of Soest; but since the citizens defended themselves bravely, he could not obtain it, and at last, after an agreement had been made, he returned to his own with loss.

1442.

In this year, which was the third of our abbot Frederick, in the month of June, Frederick, the elected King of the Romans, with the princes and a great retinue of nobles, descended by ship along the Rhine as far as Bonn, and from there through Aachen; there, by Theodoric, archbishop of Cologne, he was anointed and crowned King of the Romans with the customary solemnity. But he long delayed being crowned by the pope because of the schism that existed between Eugenius and Felix; at last he was crowned by Nicholas V.

In the same year wine grew in great quantity, very good and pleasant to drink, and a cartload was sold and owed for two florins; throughout the whole land there was abundance of wine. For the summer was very temperate and beautifully disposed toward every growth of provisions, with the result that abundance of wine and grain came forth. But at harvest-time the air was very clear, so that the crops, gathered without any hindrance from moisture, could have been kept for many years without corruption.

Chronicle of Trithemius

to remain in force, they annexed in perpetuity to the aforesaid reformed monastery the nunnery at the foot of the mountain, which was called Clausula, with all its revenues and proceeds, after expelling the nuns, who were few and of very dissolute conduct.

In the same year Mehmed, emperor of the Turks, in the third year of his reign, took that most famous city of the Greeks, Constantinople, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, assaulting it by land and sea with the greatest force of arms, on the fiftieth day of the siege; and he killed all persons of both sexes who had passed the sixth year of age. He beheaded the emperor Constantine Palaeologus, and cruelly slew the monks after inflicting many tortures on them. There countless thousands of people were killed, so that the whole city overflowed with blood as if with a kind of river. The Turks also killed virgin nuns and beautiful women with pitiable torment, after perpetrating upon them an unheard-of fury of lust. Nevertheless the patriarch of the Greeks, fleeing with many Christians, was saved. At that time that unspeakable emperor of the Turks, having obtained the royal city, profaned all the churches; he made the church of St Sophia, most famous in all the world, a stable for horses, and ordered all the relics of the saints that he found to be thrown into the mud and trampled by the horses of his soldiers. But when the soldiers refused to inflict such an insult on the bones of the dead, he himself first, with his horse, leapt more savagely upon the relics of the saints, and, turning angrily to the soldiers, said: “Whoever has not followed me, by Muhammad, the great messenger of God, shall die this day.” Terrified by this, the soldiers, by the running and trampling of their horses, sank the relics of the saints, scattered over the mud, into the depth of the mud, an impious deed. The most cruel enemy of God also caused the sacred books of the orthodox fathers of the Christian faith, as many as he found, to be placed on perforated ships and sunk into the depth of the sea, so that no occasion for knowledge of the Christian faith might be left there. And after Constantinople was taken, the cruel enemy consequently obtained rule over the whole empire of the Greeks, while our emperor and princes did nothing against it except words.

In these times also the Prussians, having formed a conspiracy against the Master of the Teutonic Knights, stirred up a revolt of fifty-five cities and towns against him; the greater part of these not long afterward defected from the Teutons themselves and subjected themselves to the king of Poland. A very grave war then arose among them; with the forces of the Teutons [defeated?], the town of Danzig also defected to the Poles. And so the defeated Master, who once could be compared with kings, with his Teutons, having almost lost his dominion, was compelled to yield and be subject to the [unclear]. This is said to have happened to him because his men acted too much according to their own pleasure in tyrannizing over the citizens.

1454.

In the ninth year of Conrad our abbot, the fifteenth provincial chapter of our order was celebrated in the monastery of Saints Marcellinus and Peter at Seligenstadt, on the twelfth day of the month of May, with continuation on the following days; it was the third Sunday after the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection. Wolfram at Hirsau, Christianus of St Peter’s at Erfurt, Ulrich at Wiblingen, and Berthold of St Stephen’s at Würzburg, abbots of very famous monasteries of the order, presided there; many statutes for the reform of the order were made there.

In these times Dracolus Wayda, a most cruel heathen prince or captain, exercised unheard-of and incredible tyranny in Wallachia; he killed many thousands of innocent people of both sexes and every age, especially Christians, by a new kind of torture never before heard of. At last he was captured by Matthias, king of Hungary, and, converted to the faith and baptized, was restored to his dominion after some years; thereafter he conducted himself well and most modestly, and did many good things. His cruel deeds are circulated in part in a single little book printed in the vernacular tongue.

In the year noted above also Mehmed, emperor of the Turks, obtained Lower Moesia and Wallachia, the princes surrendering because they had no help.

In these times also a monastery was founded in the diocese of Trier, not far from Bernkastel-Cues, of regular canons of the Windesheim reform, which is called Eberhardsklaus, from the offering of the faithful. For a certain poor peasant, born from a village situated on the bank of the Moselle, which is called Piesport, made a small hut there, in which he placed an image of the blessed Mary ever virgin holding her Son in her lap at the hour of vespers. Many miracles were reported concerning it, and from that time down to the present day there has been a concourse of peoples to that very image; from their alms the monastery was built there and sufficiently provided with necessities. That peasant, because he was called EberharThe Chronicle of Trithemius. Here the Cardinal Panormitanus grants an indulgence.

In the aforesaid year Frederick, abbot of this monastery, using the counsel of his friends, approached Nicolaus Panormitanus, of our order, formerly an abbot in Sicily, priest-cardinal of the Roman Church, and legate de latere through Germany of the Council of Basel, who was then at Frankfurt on his legation; and he set forth the need and [unclear] of the present monastery, asking that through the granting of indulgences he would deign to stir the minds of the faithful to relieve such great poverty. The magnificent man freely consented to his just request and granted great indulgences of five years in the form that follows.

Nicholas, by divine mercy priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles of the holy Roman Church, commonly called Panormitanus, legate de latere through Germany of the most holy general Synod of Basel, legitimately assembled in the Holy Spirit and representing the universal Church, to all and singular the faithful of Christ who will inspect the present letters, eternal salvation in the Lord. Although he, by whose gift it is that he is worthily and laudably served by the faithful, out of the abundance of his mercy, which exceeds the merits of suppliants, repays those who serve him well with things much greater than they can deserve; nevertheless, desiring to render unto the Lord a people acceptable, a [unclear] of good works, we invite the faithful themselves to please him, as it were by certain allurements, namely remissions, so that thereby they may be rendered more acceptable to divine grace.

Since therefore, as we have learned, the monastery of Sponheim, of the order of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Mainz, because of pressing wars, other extreme conditions of scarcity, and other things which in times past have prevailed sharply, exists greatly diminished and impoverished in its revenues and buildings, and is in very great need of vestments, books, and other jewels necessary for divine worship, for which the resources of the fabric of the same monastery are by no means sufficient, on account of which the suffrages of Christ’s faithful are known to be very opportune: we, desiring that the said monastery be frequented with due honors and that aid be given it in the said necessities, so that the faithful themselves may flow there more willingly, and also may more promptly extend helping hands for repair and preservation of this sort, the more abundantly they shall perceive themselves refreshed there by the gift of ecclesiastical grace, by the mercy of almighty God and by the authority of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul, [unclear], to all truly penitent and confessed persons who shall come to the said monastery on any days whatsoever for the sake of prayer and devotion, to implore pardon for their sins, or who, for the fabric, lights, vestments, or any other ornaments necessary for that monastery, on the feasts of Saint Martin and his octaves, in whose reverence the church in that monastery was founded, of All Saints and of holy women having [unclear], and of the patrons of all the altars belonging to that church, shall devoutly visit the said church and extend or send their helping hands to that monastery, or shall bequeath, give, or send to that monastery something from their means, we mercifully relax five years and as many quarantines from the penances enjoined upon them, by these presents to remain valid perpetually. We will, moreover, that whatever indulgences have been granted to the said church and monastery in any manner, tenor, for a time or in perpetuity, and still endure and have the force of validity, we confirm them anew by the tenor of the present letters. Given in the town of Frankfurt, in the diocese of Mainz, under the attachment of the seal of our cardinalate, on the fourth day before the Nones of August, in the year from the birth of the Lord 1442.

1442. The winter was very severe.

In the fourth year of Abbot Frederick there was a very long and very cold winter, which lasted from the feast of Saint Martin almost until the middle of May; and fodder failed for the draft animals. In many places neither hay nor straw was to be had. Poor peasants were forced, through want, to take down the straw roofs of their houses and to prepare as feed for the beasts straw almost rotted by age. Many also, because of lack of fodder, were compelled to slaughter their livestock; others drove them into fields and woods and voluntarily exposed them to be devoured by wolves.

In the same year also Sigismund, bishop of Würzburg, of whom we spoke above, a foolish man altogether very like one demented, was driven out because of his excessive folly and sent back into Saxony to his brothers. They placed him, as a ruined man, in a certain castle to be guarded perpetually, receiving from the church of Würzburg no small pension for his support, as we said in its place. When he had been deposed, Gottfried of Limpurg succeeded by election of the chapter, and he presided for twelve years.

1444.

In the fifth year of Frederick our abbot, on the tenth day of the month of May, which was Cantate Sunday, the twelfth provincial chapter of our order was celebrated at Erfurt in the monastery of Saint Peter. In it the abbots of the monasteries of our order presided, namely of Saint Peter there, of Saint Gall, of Saint Giles of Nuremberg, and of Saint Stephen of Würzburg; in it many things necessary for the reform of our order were enacted.

In this same year Frederick, king of the Romans, [held] a great and notable assembly of princes at Nuremberg Of Sponheim.

Eberhard gave the place the name Clausa Eberhardi. Jacob, archbishop of Trier, confirmed the foundation of this monastery, and consecrated the new church in his own person. The same archbishop of Trier reformed the convent of the Minors at Koblenz, and established the well-reformed canons regular of Windesheim in the new monastery not far from Koblenz, on a certain island of the Rhine near Vallendar.

1455.

In this year, which was the tenth of Conrad our abbot, Duke Louis, surnamed the Black, count in Veldenz, son of Stephen, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, and count in Zweibruecken, and brother of Duke Frederick in Simmern, rose against Frederick the Palatine, guardian of Philip our prince, and carried out plundering and burnings here and there in his principality.

Duke Frederick warned him by letters once, a second time, and a third time, in charitable fashion, to desist from his evil undertakings and not rashly to violate another's right by injury. But when he saw that he was being despised by him, judging that the matter must no longer be overlooked, he encircled with a siege the town of Bergzabern, which Duke Louis held as a garrison; after three days and five weeks of assault he finally took it on the day of Saint Tiburtius the martyr. But afterwards, in a certain agreement, at the insistence of friends, he restored the aforesaid town of Bergzabern to the aforesaid Duke Louis, under this condition namely: that he should presume and do nothing thereafter against the Palatine. This, however, as will be clear, he did not keep. Thereafter the high-spirited prince Frederick, count palatine aforesaid, provoked by the insolence of Richard of Hohenburg, besieged the castle called Cleeburg, not far from Weissenburg, and took and acquired it with all its appurtenances in two days.

In the year of the Lord noted above, on Tuesday after Palm Sunday, Gottfried, bishop of Wuerzburg, died. John of Grumbach succeeded him and presided for twelve years, a rather warlike man; although unlearned, nevertheless a lover and defender of the clergy, and he ruled his church well.

In these times also, in the aforesaid diocese of Wuerzburg, not far from Iphofen, in a certain place called Bircklingen, in a wilderness, a certain image of the blessed Mary ever virgin, placed in a certain tree, began to shine with many miracles. To it there was a very great concourse of people, and many offerings of the faithful were expended, through which in the course of time a monastery of regulars of the Windesheim reform was built and sufficiently provided for.

1456.

In the eleventh year of Conrad our abbot, the sixteenth provincial chapter of our order was held in the monastery of Saint Peter in Erfurt, on the third Sunday after the feast of the Lord's Resurrection, with continuation, as is customary, on the following days. Presiding in it were Berthold of Saint Stephen's at Wuerzburg, John of Saint Michael's at Hildesheim, Ulrich in Blaubeuren, and Lupert of Saint James's near Mainz, distinguished abbots of monasteries of our order. Many statutes were made in this chapter for the reform and preservation of our order.

In the same year, on the eighth day of the month of May, Jacob of Sierck, archbishop of Trier, died in Palatiolum; his body was brought back to Trier and is buried before the high altar in the church of the blessed Mary ever virgin, in the seventeenth year of his pontificate, a prelate to be celebrated with every praise, who not only kept his own church in peace and tranquility but also often restored peace among princes and the pontiffs of other churches. After his death, the canons of the greater church met on the twenty-first day of the month of June to elect a new pontiff, and, after a long discussion among themselves, were divided into two groups. One part elected Diether of Isenburg, canon of the churches of Mainz and Trier, who afterwards was made archbishop of Mainz, as arch-prelate; the other part, superior in number, elected John, son of Jacob, margrave of Baden, brother of Margrave Charles, then in the twenty-second year of his age. Although Diether tried very hard to obstruct his confirmation at the Apostolic See, nevertheless John prevailed, and was confirmed by Pope Calixtus III, and presides over the church of Trier up to the present day, sound and unharmed, in the forty-sixth year of his pontificate and the sixty-eighth of his age.

In the same year also, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, Reinhard of Helmstatt, bishop of Speyer, died, and is buried in the middle of the church. Sifrid of Venningen succeeded him, elected by the chapter on the twenty-ninth day of the month of March, and he presided for three years, five months, and four days; he did many good things for the church in so short a time.

The monastery of regulars on the lower island is founded.

Agreement between the Palatine and Duke Louis established.

Bergzabern taken by Frederick the Palatine.

Cleeburg is taken by Frederick the Palatine.

John becomes bishop of Wuerzburg.

The fifteenth provincial chapter is held.

The monastery of Bircklingen is founded.

Jacob, archbishop of Trier, dies.

John becomes archbishop of Trier.

Sifrid becomes bishop of Speyer.

Sifrid becomes bishop of Speyer. Sponheim.

At Nuremberg he held [unclear], in which many measures were concluded for the commonwealth, and especially concerning the expedition against the Turks; but either no effect or only a small effect followed from them. For at that time the Turk invaded the borders of the Christians with a great multitude. For on the day of St Martin, in the year noted above, a most savage battle, such as one scarcely reads of any similar one having taken place in Europe, was fought between the Christians and the Turks. In it the struggle was long contested with doubtful issue, but the Turks at last prevailed by their numbers. In this battle more than eighty thousand men were killed. There Ladislaus, king of Poland, an outstanding young man, who was also seeking the kingdom of Hungary by arms, and Julian, cardinal of St Angelo and legate of the apostolic see, perished with many praiseworthy men.

In the same year the citizens of the town of Soest in Westphalia, having rejected their lord, Theodoric, archbishop of Cologne, submitted themselves to the lord of Cleves. From this there followed among them many evils, plunderings, burnings, and wars, to the very great disadvantage of both parties. For the archbishop, having gathered a very great army from Bohemia against the men of Cleves and Soest, and having added his own men, entered Westphalia with great power, laying waste everything by fire and plunder, and utterly destroyed many castles, villages, and fortifications around Soest; and he carried off with him many persons, noble as well as non-noble.

In the same year also Frederick, king of the Romans, brought the Armagnacs from France into Alsace, more than eighty thousand of them, against the Swiss; and they did many evils in the land. In the same year a great dispute arose between the duke of Lorraine and the men of Metz, which grew to such a point that the duke, proceeding against them with a great army of his own men and of Armagnacs from France, in a short time took all the castles and fortifications of the men of Metz, and compelled them to seek peace, with great disadvantage and loss to them.

In the same year also a war was waged between Arnold, duke of Guelders, and Gerard, duke of Jülich, in which the men of Jülich, few in number, put to flight a great multitude of the men of Guelders; some were also killed. At last peace was made. 1445.

In this year, which was the sixth of Frederick our abbot, Frederick, bishop of Worms, died. After expelling the nuns of the Cistercian order from the monastery which is called the Garden of Mary, in the vernacular Kirschgarten, outside the walls of Worms, he introduced the reformed canons of Windesheim under the rule of St Augustine. Louis of Ast, doctor of both laws, provost of the major church, and secretary of Louis, the most serene prince palatine, a good man and one fearing God, succeeded him in the bishopric by election of the chapter; he presided for only forty days. For since he was a prudent man and a lover of God, he considered how dangerous the government of souls is, and therefore, having used the counsel of certain friends, on the fortieth day after his election he resigned the bishopric into the hands of the electors, preferring to remain at rest in holy humility rather than undertake, to his own peril, the care of governing souls. After him Reinhard of Sickingen, a good and peaceable man, was elected bishop of the church of Worms; he presided over his church sufficiently and energetically for almost thirty-six years.

In the same year, while the Council of Basel was still continuing, John, bishop of Lausanne, William, archdeacon of Metz, Rudolph of Rüdesheim, provost of St Paul’s at Worms, and John of Bachenstein, archdeacon of Zagreb, entrusted to Abbot John, for they were auditors of cases of the aforesaid Council of Basel, that he should correct the order of divine services and the manner for our union and annual chapter, reject apocryphal material, and cut away superfluities, as is clear from the letters drawn up concerning this, whose date is the year of the Lord 1445, the seventeenth day of the month of July.

In this year Louis, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria and prince-elector, the son of the late Louis the Bearded, concerning whom we have said more above, took as wife Margaret, daughter of the duke of Savoy, as we have said, by whom he begot Prince Philip. In the same year Frederick, abbot of this monastery, perceiving that because of the poverty of the place and the malice of the times he could make no progress either in spiritual or in temporal matters, and overcome by weariness, resigned the abbacy into the hands of the convent on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, with a yearly pension assigned to him by the convent for suitable support during life; and afterward he survived for eighteen years.

Concerning Conrad Humbrecht, the twenty-first abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, who presided for sixteen years and twenty days, and concerning various deeds both of his time and of that time.

Therefore, when the abbacy of this monastery was vacant after the free resignation of Frederick of Nackheim, the last abbot, in the year and on the day written above, the monks of this monastery, who were then few in number, so that they might not live longer without a shepherd, soon on the same day, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, coming together as one in the chapter place, unanimously elected as abbot Conrad Humbrecht of Gau-[unclear]

A most savage war between the Christians and the Turks. The lord archbishop of Cologne [unclear] of Westphalia.

Frederick, king of the Romans, will fight [unclear]. War of the [unclear].

In the same year a great dispute arose between the duke of Lorraine and the men of Metz, which meanwhile grew to such a point that the duke, proceeding against them with a great force of his own men and of Armagnacs from [unclear]

Frederick, bishop of Worms, was elected.

In the same year a war was waged between Arnold, duke of Guelders, and Gerard, duke of Jülich, in which the man of Jülich, few in number, put to flight a great multitude of the men of Guelders; some were also killed. At last peace was made. 1445. In this year, which Frederick [unclear] from the nuns of the Cistercian order from the monastery which is called the Garden of Mary, in the vernacular Kirschgarten, outside the walls of Worms, he introduced the reformed canons of Windesheim under the rule of St Augustine. In the bishopric there succeeded him by election Sponheim.

In the same year also, the bastard son of Philip, duke of Burgundy, desiring to gain possession of the lordship of Trier, secretly met with two of the citizens, men of no low rank, one of whom, born of a knightly family, was called Wigand Schenck, the other Johann Longus; and, by promising them a great sum of money, he encouraged them to betray the city. But while they were taking counsel about the manner of this betrayal, in a certain inn in the town of Luxembourg, it happened by divine will that a maidservant of the house heard their discussion. Through her the men of Trier were warned, and they put the traitors to torture; after they confessed, they cut off their heads and divided them into four parts. The history of this deed was afterwards sung for a long time by boys in a vernacular song, which has now almost passed from human memory; in it Bulmann, master of the citizens, and another called Master Michael, who was the first to lay hands on the traitors to seize them, are introduced.

1447.

In the second year of Conrad our abbot, the fourteenth provincial chapter of our order was celebrated in the monastery of Petershausen in Constance, on the seventh day of the month of May, which was Cantate Sunday, with continuation on the following days. At it there presided the abbots of our order: of Petershausen there, of St. Giles at Nuremberg, of St. Stephen at Würzburg, and of St. Godehard at Hildesheim. Many things were decreed in that chapter for the reform of the order.

In the same year, after the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, Theoderic, archbishop

The archbishop of Cologne, with the aid of the Bohemians, [unclear]. A monstrous [unclear] follows.

The provincial chapter, the twenty-third, is celebrated.

The attempted betrayal of the city of Trier.

1448.

In this year, which was the second of Conrad our abbot, two monasteries of our order in Cologne were reformed, namely St. Martin’s and St. Pantaleon’s, to the chapter of the union of the observance of Westphalia; against the duke of Cleves he did much damage in the land, yet he did not obtain Soest. When the siege had been lifted, however, the Bohemians roamed through the whole land of the duke of Berg, and laid waste by fire and plunder; they stripped churches and monasteries of all goods and ornaments; they [unclear] the sacred vessels of the Lord’s body, the Sacrament having been poured out on the ground; they burned with fire nuns and virgins consecrated to God whom age had adorned, but young and beautiful women they carried off captive into Bohemia, whom they openly abused with an incredible frenzy of lust.

In this year, which was the second of Conrad our abbot, two monasteries of our order in Cologne were reformed, namely St. Martin’s and St. Pantaleon’s, to the chapter of the union of the observance of Westphalia; against the duke of Cleves he did much damage in the land, yet he did not obtain Soest. When the siege had been lifted, however, the Bohemians roamed through the whole land of the duke of Berg, and laid waste by fire and plunder; they stripped churches and monasteries of all goods and ornaments; they [unclear] the sacred vessels of the Lord’s body, the Sacrament having been poured out on the ground; they burned with fire nuns and virgins consecrated to God whom age had adorned, and carried off young women into Bohemia as captives, whom they openly abused with an incredible frenzy of lust.

In this year Conrad the abbot sought back from Meinhard of Coppenstein those farms at Winsheim which Abbot Bernhard had once, as we said above, in the year ’36, alienated without the consent of his brethren. He summoned him before the advocates of the princes at Kreuznach, Frederick of Lerenstein and Johann of Wachenheim, producing the testimony of certain persons who had heard the revocation made by Abbot Bernhard, now dead, concerning the unjust alienation of those farms. Therefore the advocates, after hearing the parties, entrusted it to the abbot that he should present his petition reduced to writing on another occasion, and that Meinhard likewise should reply in writing; when this had been done, they said that they wished to decree what was just. The abbot did what he was ordered and presented his petition against Meinhard to the advocates in writing. But the advocates, whether entangled in their excessive cares or too much inclined to the opposing party, as was then believed by many, after receiving the request of the abbot and convent, deferred sentence, keeping the abbot’s mind in suspense with fair words from day to day, alleging now this and now that as an impediment. Thus the business remains pending up to the present.

In the same year, after a disagreement had long arisen between Wilhelm, duke of Saxony, and Philip, duke of Burgundy, over the duchy of Luxembourg, the one alleging hereditary right and the other a pledge-right, an end was at last put to the disagreement. Since the noble inhabitants of the land of Luxembourg had begun to hold their lady, the duchess of Bavaria, in contempt, Frederick, king of the Romans, had delivered the duchy itself to the aforesaid duke of Saxony, Wilhelm, for a certain sum of money, and sent there with an army a certain count of Gleichen, who was to undertake to govern the duchy in his name. When the aforesaid count of Gleichen came to Luxembourg, he obtained the greater part of that land; after placing soldiers throughout the region, he himself stayed with some men in the town of Luxembourg. Meanwhile, since the lady of the land had the Saxons as enemies, she had Philip, duke of Burgundy, secretly summoned, promising that she would deliver all her right into his hands. And so, having gained the opportunity, lord Philip sent his captain there with ten thousand horsemen; and while the Saxons acted with too little caution, the Burgundians, in the month of November, on a certain night, by the betrayal of certain ci366 Chronicle of Trithemius

[unclear] having been admitted, they took the town of Luxembourg and the fortress, the Saxons having fled. And this duchy of Luxembourg passed to the dominion of the Duke of Burgundy, and remains under him down to the present day.

In this year the Council of Basel, which had lasted for many years, came to an end.

MCCCCXLIX.

In the fourth year of Abbot Conrad there was a great pestilence throughout all Germany, which in a short time consumed many thousands of people with a miserable plague.

In the same year Albert, Margrave of Brandenburg, with certain princes allied to his aid, namely the Archbishop of Mainz, the Margrave of Baden, the counts of Wittenberg, the Bishop of Bamberg, and the Bishop of Eichstatt, led an army against the cities and towns of the Empire, and especially against the Nurembergers, to whom he was most hostile, raging against them for a year and six months with slaughter, burning, plunder, devastation of fields, and uprooting of vineyards in an exceedingly inhuman manner. The citizens, however, struck with terror at the first assault, kept themselves within the walls. Afterwards, having assembled an army, they powerfully invaded the lands of the princes and began to devastate everything with fire, sword, and plunder, until at length, the stores of both parties being exhausted, they were compelled to enter into concord and keep peace.

MCCCCL.

In the fifth year of Abbot Conrad there was a very great gathering of peoples from the whole Christian world at Rome, for the indulgences and remissions of the Jubilee; and so great was the multitude of people [unclear], in the first year of his age, for whom he appointed his brother Frederick guardian, commending to him that son, his wife, and everything that he had by his own right, namely on this condition: that as soon as the son reached the eighteenth year of his age, he should restore to him without objection the paternal duchy with all its appurtenances. Having arranged these things in this way, he died, and was buried in the church of the Holy Spirit. And so, after his brother’s death, Frederick undertook the government of his whole duchy, and governed, defended, and enlarged it vigorously until his own death, for twenty-six years, down to the twenty-seventh year of Duke Philip; and, waging many wars, driven by necessity, he everywhere with good fortune successfully overcame all his adversaries.

But in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s incarnation MCCCCLVI, on a day of the month of May, after midnight, around the first hour, through the carelessness and negligence of those who had repaired the organ during the day, a great fire was kindled in the greater church of Speyer, which consumed the whole structure of the body of the church, the roof, the organ, the tower, and the bells.

In these times also the art of printing and marking books with characters was newly discovered in the city of Mainz, by a certain citizen who was called Johannes Gutenberg. When, because of the very great difficulty of the new invention, he had spent all his substance in bringing it to completion, he was helped by the counsel and aid of good men, Johann Fust and others, and perfected the unworkable undertaking.

The first spreader of this art after the inventor himself was Peter Schoffer of Gernsheim, who printed many volumes in his time. The aforesaid Johannes Gutenberg, moreover, lived at Mainz in the house called zum Jungen, which house is known down to the present day as marked by the name of that new art.

MCCCCLI.

In the seventh year of Conrad our abbot, the forty-fifth provincial chapter of our order was held on the twenty-fourth day of the month of May, which was the fourth Sunday after the feast of Easter, with continuation on the following days, in the monastery of St. Stephen at Wurzburg, Nicholas of Cusa, cardinal of the title of St. Peter in Chains and legate of the apostolic see, being present and presiding over the chapter, together with the abbots of St. Giles at Nuremberg, St. Burkard at Wurzburg, and St. Gotthard in Hildesheim. In this chapter, indeed, many matters for the reform of the order were discussed by the aforesaid cardinal and the fathers. Finally all the abbots then present, for themselves, and the proctors of the absent for those whose proctors they were, at the Holy of Holies, into the hands of the cardinal ..., after the mass had been sung by him, standing before the altar of St. Stephen, they swore that, under penalty of all their dignities and privileges, within the space of one year they would without delay undertake the reform long since agreed upon, and faithfully preserve it both in themselves and in their subjects according to the Rule and the statutes of the Fathers. O how many thereafter, caring nothing for what had been done, were perjurers. The aforesaid legate Nicholas of Cusa made great effort for the reform of our order, and made no small progress. First, after the chapter, he issued a constitution on the manner and form of reform and visitation, in which he treated rather fully of the integrity of monastic discipline and conduct. He also was the first to confirm the observance and union of the reformed Fathers under the designation of the Bursfelders, which at that time was new; nevertheless it was afterward confirmed anew by Pope Pius II, namely in the thirteenth year of Conrad our abbot.

In the same year King Frederick, accompanied by Ladislaus, king of Hungary and Bohemia, by Albert, brother of the Duke of Austria, and by a great host of nobles, entered Italy with his bride Eleanor, daughter of Edward, king of Portugal; and on the sixteenth day of the month of March he received, from the hand of a cardinal appointed for this by the pope, the iron crown, which he had not been able to receive at Milan because of the duke’s obstinacy. Then on the twentieth day of the same month of March, which was Laetare Sunday, in the middle of Lent, Pope Nicholas V solemnly adorned the king with the golden crown in the church of St. Peter, with great honor. Afterward, departing from the City, he turned his route toward Naples, where, after celebrating his wedding with his betrothed and greeting Alfonso, king of Aragon, he returned to his own lands.

In this same year also, as we have said, Pope Nicholas V sent into Germany as legate, with the indulgences of the Jubilee and with great authority, Nicholas of Cusa, a Mosellan by homeland, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church of the title of St. Peter in Chains, bishop of Brixen, a man most learned in every respect and an outstanding zealot for the Christian faith, to restore peace among the princes of Germany and to stir up the hearts of the faithful for the relief of the Greeks, who were then being attacked by Mehmed, son of Murad, prince of the Turks. The apostolic legate therefore came to Trier, and then to other cities of Germany, and both in his own person and through many other learned men he caused many public sermons to be delivered, exhorting the faithful to the support of Christian fidelity.

In this year, which was the eighth of Conrad our abbot, Frederick, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, brother of Louis [the pious?], of whom we spoke above, on the Ides of January, that is, on the octave of the Epiphany of the Lord, by the consent of all the nobles and counts of the Palatinate, and also by apostolic authority and confirmation, was assumed as guardian and governor, and as father, of the child Philip, his brother’s son, with the title and prerogative of the princely election of the Roman Empire, and at the same time of the Palatinate of the Rhine, so that he was held by all to be, and was, prince-elector of the Empire. The establishment of this prerogative displeased above all Theoderic, archbishop of Mainz, and also Duke Stephen of Zweibrücken, James, margrave of Brandenburg, and his son, and also the counts of Lützelstein, who, conspiring together, devised many things against Duke Frederick. But after many injuries had been done to him by the aforesaid counts of Lützelstein, who were then very powerful, Duke Frederick could no longer dissemble; in the year already noted, with a strong army of his men, he surrounded Lützelstein in a very firm siege for two months and seven days, and at last, on the vigil of St. Martin the bishop, he took the castle together with the town by force. The counts, however, saving themselves by flight, lost everything they had; and so the whole county of Lützelstein has been subject to the Palatinate down to the present day. At that time Schaffhard, count of Lingen, Duke Frederick’s intimate and counselor, was being held captive by the aforesaid counts in the fortress of Lützelstein; when Duke Frederick had obtained the victory, he freed him with great joy. But on the second day after the feast of St. Martin, Sinhartzhusen, whose corrected [unclear], as it now is, he carefully examined and confirmed by apostolic authority.

In the eighth year of Conrad our abbot, the monastery of St. John the Baptist in the Rheingau, of our order, was reformed by monks of the Bursfeld union, taken from the monastery of St. James near Mainz, by the authority and command of Theoderic, archbishop of Mainz. Nicholas of Cusa, the aforementioned cardinal, and Rudolph of Rüdesheim, bishop of Breslau, greatly advanced this reform; and, so that it might be stronger in its [unclear]

1453. [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Trithemius
