In the aforesaid year, on the Ides of October, the high-hearted prince Frederick, Count Palatine of the Rhine, guardian of Philip, with the aid of Theoderic, Archbishop of Mainz, surrounded with a siege Montfort, a castle that was a common haunt of robbers, which is not far from here; and, after vigorously assaulting it for [unclear] days, he took it on the nineteenth day of the month of October and destroyed it utterly. Thus it remains destroyed down to the present day, nor can it be rebuilt without the consent of the Palatine who shall be in office at the time and of the Archbishop of Mainz. For the church of Mainz suffered many losses from this robber-castle through those who were able to have their dwelling there.

Also in the aforesaid year Mahomet, emperor of the Turks, having dispatched a great army of his men, encircled with a very strong siege Nicopolis, a notable city of the Christians, which they call Schiltaw, while the Christians who were within stoutly defended the walls, towers, and fortifications. But when the Turks boldly pressed on toward the walls with engines, our men, animated to fight for the Christian faith by the exhortation of John of Capistrano, of the Observant order of Minors, a learned and most religious man, burst out through the gates of the city, with John, Cardinal of St. Angelo and Apostolic Legate, carrying before them the banner of the holy cross; and they attacked the Turks so vigorously and with such great boldness, cut them down, struck them, killed them, and at once turned them all to flight, that in their excessive haste many of them were drowned in the river, and many too were slain by our men. On account of this victory of the Christians, Pope Callixtus III instituted the feast of the Lord’s Transfiguration, on the eighth day before the Ides of August, to be celebrated every year.

At the same time Mahomet stormed Corinth; many thousands of Christians were killed, and he imposed tribute on the Christians throughout the whole Peloponnese.

In these times also a great gathering of boys from all Germany arose toward St. Michael on the borders of Spain; leaving their parents without counsel, with incredible fervor, led along together in order, they went on, no one being able to prevent them, begging, singing about St. Michael, and proceeding in order under a banner on which the same angel was depicted. Nor could it be written what that spirit was which so strongly urged their youthful age to so hard a journey, so that boys of ten or twelve years would cross so many miles on foot without provisions. Afterwards not only boys, but also men, women, male servants, maidservants, and virgins, suddenly, inspired by I know not what spirit, left everything and girded themselves for the same journey.

1457.

In the thirteenth year of Conrad our abbot, in the month of November, Ladislaus, king of Bohemia and Hungary, a youth of eighteen years, died, killed by poison by the Hussites in the city of Prague; he was buried there in the church of St. Wenceslaus.

In the same year, on the day of St. Matthew the Apostle and Evangelist, Conrad, abbot of this monastery, appointed as provider the cellarer John Mariae, of whom we spoke above; he had for some time been prior-cellarer. Frederick of Nackheim, however, formerly abbot, was living at this time in Kreuznach, living on his pension.

In this very year Abbot Conrad made a reckoning for his convent, in which it was found that they had paid off the greater part of the debts; nevertheless, at the creditors’ request, the brothers were often compelled to undergo ecclesiastical censures and to suspend the celebration of divine services. For, as is gathered from their manuals, four times in this year they purchased relaxation of the censures for a price.

1458.

In this year, which was the twelfth year of Conrad our abbot, on the Friday after the Sunday Invocavit, there was a very great flooding of the waters of the Rhine, the Moselle, the Nahe, and all the rivers in the surrounding region, which inflicted many losses on people. For, when the snows had melted, the flooding of the waters increased so much that they even filled the whole parish church on the island of Kreuznach with water, overturned certain altars, shook the walls, dislodged stones from the tombs of the dead, and, after causing many losses, almost destroyed the church.

In the same year Pope Pius II, in the first year of his pontificate, confirmed the reform and union of Bursfelde and the annual chapter; and, along with the many privileges that he granted, he also extended to our Bursfelde union the privileges of the congregation of St. Justina of Padua, which are many and great.

In the same year also the church of St. James outside the walls of Mainz, of our order, which is now seen, began to be built, and it was completed in the following year. For from the time when the monastery was last laid waste, after the death of Archbishop Matthias, there had been no church on the aforesaid mountain except the chapel of the blessed Mary ever virgin.

In these times also Conrad, abbot of this monastery, great lawsuits and contentions ha[unclear] he had with a certain Nicholas, called Ritter of Mengirfreit, a cleric, concerning the altar of St. Nicholas, which at that time had not yet been incorporated into the monastery, and it lasted a long time. At length judgment was pronounced by the judges of the see of Mainz for that cleric against the abbot; this deed brought great loss upon this monastery.

In the same year also Louis, Duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Rich, son of Henry and father of Duke George, gathered a great army of Bavarians, Bohemians, and Austrians, and besieged the city of Eichstatt; but, when an agreement intervened, he withdrew. From there he led his army against the Margrave of Brandenburg, and took two of his castles, Landeck and Stauff, and utterly destroyed them. Albert the Margrave came out against him with a great army, having with him William, Duke of Saxony; but they did nothing worthy of memory. But an agreement was made in such a way that the Margrave should surrender into Duke Louis’s hands certain letters and privileges given against him by the emperor, and should receive his fiefs from the church of Wurzburg, which before he had refused to do, as Burgrave of Nuremberg; and they departed from one another. Afterwards, on a certain day appointed for this at Nuremberg, the Margrave, as he had promised, delivered the emperor’s letters to Duke Louis in the public town hall, and he at once tore them up in the sight of all. When the emperor heard this he took it very ill, and wished Duke Louis to have incurred the crime of lese-majesty; and for that reason he protested against the agreement made between them, and many evils followed from it.

1459.

In the fourteenth year of our abbot Conrad, on the day before the Nones of May, Theoderic Schenk of Erbach, Archbishop of Mainz, died. Diether of Isenburg, elected by the chapter on the seventeenth day of September, [unclear] on the Kalends of July, was elector for almost five years. Adhering to the Margrave of Baden and Louis the Black, duke, with the other accomplices, against Frederick, Count Palatine, guardian of Philip, he damaged his church in many ways, and exposed the whole diocese to burning, plunder, and devastation by enemies and friends.

In the same year, on the second day of the month of September, Siegfried, Bishop of Speyer, died. John Nix of Hoheneck, called Ensberg, elected by the chapter on the eighteenth day of September, succeeded him and presided for five years. Adhering to the Margrave of Baden and Louis the Black, duke, with the other accomplices, against Frederick, Count Palatine, guardian of Philip, he damaged his church in many ways, and exposed the whole diocese to burning, plunder, and devastation by enemies and friends.

In the year noted above, too, the sixteenth provincial chapter of our order was celebrated after the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, on the second Sunday; at it presided George of St. Giles there, Berthold of St. Giles in Brunswick, Eberhard of Mount St. James near Mainz, and Henry in Ettenheim, most religious abbots of monasteries of our order.

In the same year Emperor Frederick commanded all the cities of the empire to bring aid with all their strength to Albert, Margrave of Brandenburg, against the aforesaid Louis, Duke of Bavaria, guilty, as he himself maintained, of lese-majesty. All in Swabia did this, except the Nurembergers. Therefore Duke Louis, moved by this, gathered a great army of Bavarians, Bohemians, and Austrians, entered the Margrave’s land, took many villages, castles, and towns, practiced burning and plunder, and inflicted boundless losses on him, with no one able to resist. But afterwards the Margrave, having called together the cities of the empire, while Louis was in Bohemia for I know not what reason, entered his lands in like warfare, devastated, plundered, and burned them. Finally agreement was again made through the king of Bohemia, on condition that what had been taken should be restored.

1460.

In the fifteenth year of our abbot Conrad, Albert, Duke of Bavaria, son of the late Duke Ernest, died, leaving five sons: John, who died without children; Sigismund; Christopher; Albert; Wolfgang; and four daughters: Elizabeth, Duchess of Saxony; Margaret, Countess of Mantua; and Anna, a nun, enclosed for the love of Christ in the monastery at Munich. Moreover Albert kept his aforesaid brother Christopher in chains for some time; the history of this is known to all.

In the same year Albert the Margrave, Diether, Archbishop of Mainz, Louis the Black, duke, and Emich, Count of Leiningen, with their adherents, conspiring together against the great Count Frederick, became his public enemies and defiers; with them was Count Ulrich of Wurttemberg, who had previously taken Philip’s mother as his wife. Therefore Duke Frederick, compelled by necessity, gathered an army to avenge the injuries, and first indeed [took] Schavenberg, a castle in Strata Montensis, commonly [unclear] among the abbots of this place [Gelerich?].

Eichstatt is besieged.

War between the Duke of Bavaria and the Margrave of Brandenburg.

Louis, Duke of Bavaria, tore up the emperor’s letters.

Diether becomes Archbishop of Mainz.

John Nix becomes Bishop of Speyer.

The provincial chapter, the fifteenth, is celebrated.

Emperor Frederick summons the cities of the empire against the Duke of Bavaria.

Albert, Duke of Bavaria, dies.

The sons and daughters of Duke Albert.

Three princes, rising together as one, became enemies of Frederick, Count Palatine.

Schavenberg is taken by Frederick the Palatine. Chronicle of Trithemius

(An der Bergstrassen), which belonged to the church of Mainz, was very strong and very well supplied with bombards, provisions, and defenders; he besieged it and took it in eight days, in the year noted above, on the Sunday of the octave of the Lord's Resurrection. In it he found eighteen horsemen and thirty foot-soldiers, with crossbows and bombards casting missiles and stones; all of them were taken without condition of any exception.

In the same year also, since the agreement made between the margrave of Brandenburg and Louis, duke of Bavaria, as we said above, did not please Frederick, count palatine, it was broken off again, and war was renewed between them. For that count palatine himself and Louis, duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Rich, stood stoutly the whole time against thirteen princes, both spiritual and secular. Among them were especially Diether, archbishop of Mainz; Louis also, the Black Duke, count of Veldenz; Ulrich, count of Wurttemberg; Charles, margrave of Baden; Albert, margrave of Brandenburg; William, duke of Saxony; Emich, count of Leiningen; with many other princes their confederates; Louis, duke of Bavaria aforesaid, against the margrave of Brandenburg, the duke of Saxony, and the cities of the Empire.

Frederick leads out the Palatine army against the archbishop of Mainz.

Pedersheim is taken by Frederick the Palatine.

Counts, nobles, and knights [unclear] by Frederick the Palatine [unclear] Mainz [unclear].

Ingelheim is besieged by the archbishop of Mainz.

An agreement is made between the Palatine and the archbishop of Mainz.

An exaction from the clergy near Mainz by Frederick the Palatine.

Frederick the Palatine leads out an army against Louis the Black.

An agreement is made between Frederick the Palatine and Duke Louis.

Frederick the Palatine leads out an army against the counts of Leiningen.

Hasloch is overthrown by Frederick the Palatine; [unclear].

Hentschuchheim, Dobsenheim, with all their appurtenances, he would hold in pledge from the church of Mainz for his expenses, for thirty thousand florins; furthermore, that the people of the Rheingau should give to the same Palatine nine thousand florins for certain revenues near Lorch, which he had obtained by right. But from this agreement Duke Louis of Veldenz, the count of Wurttemberg, and the counts of Leiningen with their adherents were excluded. This victory of the Palatine took place in the year noted above, on the day of St. Ulric the Confessor, which is the fourth day before the Nones of July; in that year it was Friday.

In the year noted above also, but before Frederick the Palatine led out his army to Pedersheim, Diether, archbishop of Mainz, Louis the Black Duke, and Emich, count of Leiningen, with their adherents, having gathered a great army, entered Ingelheim and burned it. But when the peasants fled into the imperial hall and stoutly defended the walls, the adversaries accomplished nothing and withdrew. Meanwhile the Palatine prince was announced as about to come; when they heard this, they abandoned the siege and withdrew. But when the Palatine came with his army, he destroyed near Mainz certain houses of priests at St. Victor, St. Alban, and Holy Cross in the fields; he extorted four thousand florins from those same priests, in order to make them secure from burning, which in the vernacular is called Brandschatz.

But once an agreement had been made with Diether, archbishop of Mainz, as we have set forth, Frederick, the Palatine prince, led out his army against Louis, surnamed the Black, and by besieging him very strongly in Meisenheim, compelled him to petition for peace. And so an agreement was made a second time between them with this settlement: Duke Louis would remit to the Palatine in perpetuity one half of the five hundred florins accruing to him annually in the toll of Bacharach; the remaining part he would receive from him and his successors as a fief, which can never be renounced; he would also resign the castle of Scharpffenburg. But from this agreement the counts of Leiningen and the other adversaries of the Palatine were excluded. After this the magnanimous prince Frederick led an army against the counts of Leiningen. First he encircled with a siege the very strong castle of Hasloch; when it was taken, he burned it, destroyed it, and razed it to the ground. There he freed many of his own men who were captives, and, finding abundant booty of various furnishings, carried it away. Then, moving the army, he besieged another little castle of the counts of Leiningen, Minfelt, stormed it, destroyed it utterly, and carried off the booty.

Sponheim.

In the aforesaid year John, surnamed Mariae, the twenty-ninth prior of this monastery, [died]. After his death the priorship was vacant for almost two years. For the monks were few in number, five in all, namely Peter of Blenich, Andreas of Traiectum, John, Conrad, and Ulrich, afterwards abbot.

1461.

In this year, which was the sixteenth of Conrad our abbot, Pope Pius II wrote and committed and commanded the bishop of Eichstatt that, having taken to himself proven, religious, and learned men, and having summoned those who were to be summoned, he should by apostolic authority reduce into one those three observances of our order newly restored in the German nation, Bursfeld, Melk, and Kastl, and any others there might be, compelling opponents to obedience through ecclesiastical censures. On account of this mandate many labors and expenses were meanwhile undertaken at various times, but up to this day no effect has followed, because of the excessive diversity of those three observances in many matters.

The commission concerning the three observances is entrusted by the pope.

In this same year Diether, archbishop of Mainz, was deposed by Pope Pius II, and provision was made by the same pope for Adolf of Nassau in the archbishopric. They say that the causes of this deposition were very many. The first was that he had not paid the pope the sum imposed on him for confirmation and for the pallium. The second, that within the time fixed for him he had not had himself ordained priest. The third, that he had treated the legates of the Apostolic See with irreverence and temerity, and had been disobedient to and opposed to their mandates. We do not judge it necessary to explain the other causes of the deposition.

Diether, archbishop of Mainz, is removed by the pope. Cause of the removal.

Against this injury and violence done to him, Diether, in no way wishing to be deprived of his archbishopric, invoked the aid of Frederick, the powerful Count Palatine, and deserved to obtain it. Thus with the help of the Palatine, Diether retained nine towns and cities in his obedience, while the rest defected from him. By reason of this assistance the same archbishop Diether gave and assigned to the aforesaid prince Frederick the Palatine the castle of Starkenburg, the towns of Heppenheim, Bensheim, and Morlebach, with all their appurtenances, for one hundred thousand florins, to be held for the use of the Palatinate until he should receive that sum of money from the church of Mainz. Adolf also, calling Louis the Black, duke and count of Veldenz, to his aid, assigned to him for pay the castle and village of Bockelheim, Sobernheim, Montzingen, Nussbaum, and the castle of [Vimam] not far from Mainz, with all their appurtenances, in pledge for a certain sum of money. All these Frederick the Palatine not long afterwards, as we shall say, powerfully tore from him by arms. To the margrave of Baden for assistance he gave Algesheim and Gau-Bickelheim, with all their appurtenances. He hired the count of Wurttemberg to his aid for twenty thousand florins, and likewise, having also purchased Wilhelm of Saxony as a helper, he gave to Henry, count of Schwarzburg, for wages and pay certain towns, castles, and villages in the Eichsfeld with good annual revenues. To the count of Konigstein, who had his sister as wife, he assigned the county of Hohenheim for his pay, lest he serve without reward. From this arose evils, and that once most famous church of Mainz was reduced almost to nothing.

Frederick the Palatine assists Diether against Adolf.

With all these the archbishop of Trier, the bishop of Metz, Johannes Nix, bishop of Speyer, Albert, margrave of Brandenburg, and many other counts, barons, and nobles adhered to Adolf against Diether. Therefore, first of all Diether himself with his men, having with him for help [unclear] Count Palatine and Philip, count of Katzenelnbogen, led an army against the Rheingau. At his arrival the men of the Rheingau abandoned their garrisons; but because of the severity of the weather the siege was soon broken off, since the army could not remain longer. After this there came to Diether an almost certain promise that, if he came again, the men of the Rheingau would pass into surrender to him. He therefore came again with power, and found the promise made to him concerning surrender empty and false.

The Rheingau is besieged by Diether.

But Duke Frederick, taking up a troop of strong men, moved his army against Ulrich, count of Wurttemberg, laying waste everything with intent of plunder as far as Stuttgart, the chief city of the counts of Wurttemberg.

Frederick the Palatine lays waste the lands of Wurttemberg.

Then the great-souled prince Palatine, together with Henry, landgrave of Hesse, moved his army against Louis the Black, duke and count of Veldenz, surrounding the village of Gau-Bickelheim with a siege. He shortly took it, utterly destroyed its walls, towers, and all fortifications, and led away from it as captives sixty horsemen, one hundred foot-soldiers very ready for wars, and all their engines.

Gau-Bickelheim is taken by Frederick the Palatine.

In the aforesaid year, on the Sunday of the Nativity, 1461, Conrad Humbrecht, the twenty-first abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, died on the seventh day before the Ides of March, at the fifth hour after midday, and was buried before the steps of the presbytery. His illness arose from a certain nocturnal apparition [unclear]

Conrad, the twenty-first abbot of this monastery, [unclear].

John, the twenty-ninth prior of this place, dies.

The Rheingau is besieged by Diether.

Frederick the Palatine lays waste the lands of Wurttemberg. Chronicle of Trithemius

In the same year also Ulrich, abbot of this monastery, besides the many debts that he contracted secretly and openly, sold, disposed of, and alienated many things without the knowledge and will of the convent in Gisenheim, Odernheim, Freymersheim, and various other places, to no small loss for this monastery, spending the money not only uselessly but, what is worse, disgracefully, with frivolous persons and those nourishing the tinder of wickedness.

1366.

In the fifth year of Ulrich our abbot, the monastery of St. Godehard in Hildesheim, of our order, newly reformed, was first received and admitted into the chapter and union of the Bursfeld observance, together with Lupold its abbot.

In the same year, on Friday after the feast of the Lord's Resurrection, Johannes de Grumbach, bishop of Wurzburg, died. After him Rudolf von Scherenberg, elected by the chapter on the last day of the month of April, succeeded and presided for twenty-eight years, an energetic and peaceable man, who did much good for his church of Wurzburg, paying off enormous debts and bringing back many things long before alienated from the church by his predecessors.

In the same year also, after Abbot Ulrich had badly governed this monastery for five years and twenty-three days, and had reduced the monastery itself to extreme want and poverty, having no longer anything from which he could live, compelled by necessity, on the third Nones of April he freely resigned the abbacy into the hands of his convent, leaving debts of more than two thousand five hundred florins, besides hidden losses that he had inflicted on the monastery by selling various goods, revenues, and proceeds without the consent of his brothers and utterly alienating them from the monastery.

Concerning Otto Hawysen, twenty-third abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, who presided for three years, four months, and sixteen days, and concerning various events of that time.

After the resignation of Abbot Ulrich, alas, far too late, on the same day the brothers of this monastery, gathering in the morning at the chapter place, at about the tenth hour, began to hold among themselves the necessary discussion about electing a new pastor. They were five in number, and these were their names: Ulrich, formerly abbot; Otto, prior; Peter of Blenich, cellarer; Andreas of Utrecht; Johannes of Kirchberg; and Johannes of Bockenvy, who has now been held in chains for thirty years, as we state the reason in its proper place. Therefore at last, after mature deliberation, they unanimously elected as abbot the aforesaid Otto of Cologne, called Hawysen, thirtieth prior of this monastery, who, confirmed by Adolf, archbishop of Mainz, and ordained by his vicar in pontificals in the year noted above, on the day of St. John the Baptist, in the collegiate church of St. Barbara in the town of Bingen, presided over this [unclear]. Made a monk in the monastery of St. Pantaleon [unclear], he remained there until manhood. Afterwards, when in the year of the Lord 1348 the aforesaid monastery of St. Pantaleon had been reformed, as we have said [unclear], by the fathers of the union and observance of Bursfeld, for some time, at the exhortation of his parents, he persevered in it, to test whether he could endure the rigor of the order, and he learned competently the customs and ceremonies of those of the observance; and yet afterward, wearied and departing from there, he came to this monastery under Abbot Conrad and was incorporated into the convent.

He was, however, mild and peaceable in disposition, and more gentle than the customs of the monks of that time required in the present monastery. In his presidency he made great effort according to his strength, and would gladly have reformed the monastery in both states, but he could not. For in temporal matters it was altogether impoverished, and in spiritual matters destitute of every regular observance. Nevertheless, he made more progress in temporal than in spiritual matters. What he desired and attempted in spiritual matters we shall say in part in the following year. When he was ordained abbot, however, no definite prior was appointed after him during the whole time in which he presided in the abbacy, for three years and four months, until the appointment of Abbot Kolenhausen, as we shall say below.

1367.

In this year Lord Otto, abbot, and the conventual brothers of this monastery, fearing that at the instance of the princes they would be expelled by the fathers of the Bursfeld observance under the severity of reform, which was then often threatened against them, having taken counsel, resolved to reform themselves. They sent messengers and letters of supplication to the abbots of Trier, who then, apart from the monastery of St. Martin, were reformed, and especially to the abbot of St. Maximin, who are not of the Bursfeld union, which was exceedingly hateful to them, earnestly begging for two monks, who might instruct the monks and novices of this monastery in morals and ceremonies, in regular observance it happened: he had had a new fishpond made, which seven years before he had restored and cleaned around the spring on the western side of the monastery, and he placed the fish he had caught in a certain holding-pond constructed there for this purpose. So that they would not be secretly taken away by peasants at night, always ready for such work, he went out alone at night with a staff and kept watch there to guard the fish. And behold, in the dead of night, God permitting it, the Devil terrified him with certain phantasms; soon, as cold blood rose to his heart, he began to fall ill, and after a few days, as we have said before, he died. He was a sufficiently industrious man, who governed the monastery well in temporal matters. But he utterly detested reform, and lived according to the flesh, leaving sons [and] daughters, not without loss to the monastery and grave danger to his own soul.

In the same year also, 1461, after the eleventh hour, at the twenty-eighth minute, in the night after midday, on the Kalends of February, that is, in the very night preceding the feast of the Purification of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin, Johannes Trithemius was born, afterwards the twenty-fifth abbot of this monastery, in the village of Trittenheim, four miles from Trier in the descent of the Moselle, as will be said below.

Concerning Ulrich of Zeiskheim, the twenty-second abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, who presided for five years and twenty-three days; concerning various deeds of that time.

After Conrad, abbot of this monastery, had died and been buried, the brothers who were then conventuals assembled together on the following day, that is, on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the morning at the ninth hour or thereabout, at the chapter-house, to elect a new shepherd. After discussions had been held among them, at length they unanimously elected Ulrich of Zeiskheim, born not far from Germersheim. Confirmed by Adolph, archbishop of Mainz, through his vicar in pontificals, he governed this monastery, once ordained, for five years and twenty-eight days.

In his youth he had been handed over by his parents to the monastery in Fels, in the diocese of Strasbourg, which was afterwards transferred from the order; he gave all his time to ease, games, and feasting, and neither drank in knowledge of letters nor loved the observance of the order. But after many years, when he had lived too extravagantly and prodigally among brothers who were all proprietors and excessively dissolute, weighed down by the burden of his debts, he could no longer remain there, being troubled by the excessive pressure of his creditors. Therefore, with the permission of his abbot intervening, he secretly departed from there, and, coming here, was received as a conventual of this monastery.

But when he was appointed abbot he did not change his former ways. Giving himself to feasting and to wandering and useless excursions, he brought this monastery to extreme poverty and want. For in five years he contracted so many debts, and secretly sold and alienated so many goods, meadows, fields, rents, and revenues, that, all computed together, in the time of his rule he harmed and damaged this monastery by more than three thousand florins. In buying and selling he spent much improvidently and uselessly, since he often sold for six florins a horse which he himself had bought within a few days for twenty gold pieces. In his accounts it is noted that he bought twenty-four horses for his own person in five years, which, as soon as he had bought them, deceived by the words of the sellers, he would habitually sell again at a much lower price.

He sold annual rents and returns without the knowledge or will of his convent in many places, namely: in Odernheim fields for 131 florins; in Meisenheim; in Upper Heimbach he sold three marks of perpetual rent; in Budesheim, near Bingen; in Lorchersheim; in Geisenheim; in Winkel; in Kreuznach; in Heimersheim he sold many precious fields for a great sum of money; in Sobernheim. And in various other places he secretly sold many things, which remain alienated from the monastery down to the present day. In his time he constructed nothing inside or outside the monastery, nor did he restore ruined buildings in any respect. He also paid off, from the substance of this monastery, debts, formerly not small, which he had contracted in Fels. In Mainz also he contracted some debts before he came to this place, which nevertheless were afterwards secretly paid by him from the substance of this monastery.

He also spent much shamefully, after the example of his predecessor; for each publicly kept a concubine, sometimes in the monastery, sometimes in the surrounding villages, on whom they spent much, to the loss of the monastery and the ruin of their own souls. But enough has been said about these things so far; let us pursue the rest of Ulrich’s deeds in order.

1462.

Abbot Ulrich, immediately at the beginning of his ordination, appointed Otto, a monk and conventual of the present place, as provisor and cellarer of this monastery of Sponheim, who [unclear] churches, eight; monasteries having abbots, five; houses of mendicant friars, four; and many other churches and chapels, with convents of nuns and hospitals for the poor. In it also there were more than twenty thousand citizens equipped for war, and an abundance of all things and immense riches. Therefore, when the city had been taken, Duke Charles spared no order, no dignity, no age. He had all the priests taken captive and presented to the bishop, and he even killed some. He consumed all the men, adolescents, and youths by the edge of the sword; the women with their infants, all the widows and virgins, he drowned in the river. O how many thousands of innocents were then killed, who had given cause for this neither by word nor by deed. The walls of the city, all the houses and dwellings, the whole city, the bridges, and all the buildings in it they stripped by fire, carrying away everything they had found: ornaments, books, chalices, monstrances, jewels, and bells. For they left absolutely nothing in the whole city, but, plundering everything, carried off inestimable booty. This miserable destruction of the city of Liege was so cruel that it cannot be sufficiently explained or written by us in any words.

Also in the year noted above, Ruprecht, archbishop of Cologne, oppressed by excessive poverty and want, since he had nothing from which to live, all the things that pertained to the episcopal table having been pawned by his predecessor, asked counsel and help from his canons and feudatories; but there was no one who paid attention, for some had already conceived hatred against him. Hence, compelled by necessity, he called upon his brother [unclear]. Accordingly Friedrich, Count Palatine, his brother, having learned of his necessity, sent him money, grain, and soldiers; with these auxiliaries he was able to recover the things unjustly alienated, and, as we shall say later, he recovered many of them.

1469. In this year, which was the fourth of our Otto, Friedrich, Count Palatine of the Rhine, with an army and engines of war, in aid of Ruprecht his brother, descended into the diocese of Cologne, and with a strong hand obtained very many towns and castles that had been alienated from the church of Cologne under title of pledge. These are the towns that he restored to the hands of the archbishop: Bonn, the toll; Neuss, the town; Lechenich, town and castle; Zuelpich, town; Bruhl, castle and toll; the castle of Deutz; Andernach, town; Rolandseck, castle and toll; Gudenberg, castle; Kempen, castle and town; Erpenrod, castle; Kaiserswerth, castle, town, and toll; Neet, castle; Papenberg, castle; Hersberg, castle; and many others. All the aforesaid towns and castles Friedrich the Count Palatine recovered by arms and threats, without money, from the hands of those to whom they had been pawned, and restored them to Ruprecht, archbishop of Cologne, his brother, and to the church of Agrippina. But for his expenses, which he incurred on behalf of the church of Cologne, he received the town and castle of Kaiserswerth, with its toll and all revenues, in pledge.

In the same year, since the notable monastery of our order in Wissembourg was being badly governed by Jakob de Ponte, abbot, [unclear] from the counts Antonium de Liningen, provost, and had come almost to utter poverty, the illustrious and most renowned prince Friedrich, the aforementioned Count Palatine, resolved to bring it back to a better condition and to reform it completely, at the instance, counsel, and direction of Eberhard, abbot of Michelsberg near Bamberg, and Hermann, abbot of the monastery of St. James near Mainz, of our order, visitors of the provincial chapter concerning the reform of Bursfelde, by expelling the unreformed monks and introducing others of the observance. Therefore, together with the aforesaid abbots, who had apostolic authority, consent, and a bull of the pope for the reform, he sent prudent and learned men from among his military councillors, and, with the consent of the citizens of Wissembourg, who had promised entirely to uphold the matter, he reformed the monastery. But behold what the devil did.

During the divine office, while Jodocus de Kalb, doctor of sacred theology and councillor of the prince, was preaching to the people, a tumult arose among the people against those sent by the prince, and the outcry of the stirred-up crowd was raised on high. At length, when the commotion of the populace had been quieted and satisfaction had been offered to the prince, the work begun was completed. Moreover, the unreformed monks, fleeing secretly, removed the letters, privileges, and jewels of the monastery, placing them in the castles of robber-friends of theirs. But not for long Sponheimense 375

...who had come a little earlier from Cologne, from the monastery of St. Pantaleon, a good and gentle man; yet he did not remain long in this office, but, as we shall say later, was appointed prior by the same abbot.

In the aforementioned year of the Lord’s incarnation, 1462, Charles, margrave of Baden, George, bishop of Metz, his brother, John Nix, bishop of Speyer, and Ulrich, count of Württemberg, gathered together and assembled an army; advancing against Frederick, count palatine, whom they believed to be far absent, they promised themselves all his land as plunder, together with the town of his residence, Heidelberg.

First, therefore, they surrounded the town of Heidelsheim, not far from Bruchsal, with a siege. When this was reported to the Palatine, he personally and secretly entered Heidelsheim with his men; and while the enemies pressed the walls fiercely throughout the day, he himself stoutly defended the town. On the next day, seeing that they could not prevail, they raised the siege and withdrew, moving the army toward the district of the town of Heidelberg, not knowing that the Palatine was in the land. For they thought, having been deceived by certain letters, as is reported, that at that time he was outside his country.

But when the aforesaid princes came by night to the land of the Palatine, not far from Bruchsal, they surrounded [unclear] with a siege. When this was reported to the Palatine, he joined battle with three hundred horsemen. The Palatine men, hiding not far from Seckenheim in a wood, allowed the adversaries, suspecting nothing of their presence, to pass, until, shut in between the Rhine and the Neckar, they could no longer flee. Then the Palatine men burst from the wood and boldly made an attack on the adversaries. The fighting was fierce on both sides, but victory soon fell to the Palatine, and with great honor, by God’s aid, he triumphed over his adversaries.

There were captured by the Palatine Charles, margrave of Baden, together with his brother George, bishop of Metz, John Nix, bishop of Speyer, the count of Württemberg, and five hundred counts, nobles, and knights, all of whom were led bound to Heidelberg. The rest, however, who had not fallen, fled. On the Palatine’s side few fell. These things took place in a very broad field not far from Ladenburg, on the last day of June.

But the aforesaid princes, after they had been held in captivity for some time, since they could do nothing else, redeemed themselves with money. George, bishop of Metz, for his liberation gave the Palatine forty thousand florins, and by letters and oath made himself, with all his soldiery and with three castles, Bergzabern, St. Theobald, and Holy Cross, perpetually bound to the Palatine. Charles, margrave of Baden, for his liberation offered the Palatine [unclear] thousand florins; for these, since the money was not ready to hand, he assigned to that same Palatine in pledge, with usufruct, his share of the county of Sponheim belonging to Kreuznach; likewise he assigned into the hands of the Palatine the towns of [Besigheim?] and Bensheim with the castle, toll, and feudal rights, for the same sum of money. Furthermore, he was compelled wholly to renounce the right of redemption which he claimed to have over Heidelsheim and Eppingen, and also the hunts, waters, and fisheries about which there had previously been a dispute near the Rhine between Germersheim and [unclear]. He also made the town of [Porcesse?] a fief, and made himself and his soldiery bound to the Palatinate by oath and the necessary letters.

Ulrich, count of Württemberg, was assessed at one hundred thousand florins, of which forty thousand were paid, and twenty thousand, on account of the Church of Mainz, were assigned by the superscription of Stratenmont, beyond the one hundred thousand for which, as we said above, it had previously been pledged to the Palatine by Diether, archbishop of Mainz. Then, concerning the remaining forty-one thousand, he promised, with letters and securities furnished, that he would pay a pension of two thousand florins each year. Furthermore he made Marbach a fief of the Palatine, and made himself, with all his soldiery, bound to the Palatine. Once these securities had been provided, the aforesaid princes were released.

After these things, meanwhile, while these things were being done around the Rhine, Albert, margrave of Brandenburg, by command of the emperor, associating the imperial cities with himself, again moved an army against Louis, duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Rich, laying waste his land with fire and plunder...

Four princes proceed against Frederick the Palatine.

He besieged Heidelsheim.

The notable victory of Frederick the Palatine.

Four princes and five hundred counts, nobles, and knights captured by Frederick the Palatine.

The assessment for the liberation of the bishop of Metz. The assessment for the liberation of the margrave of Baden. The town of [Pherencense?] made a fief. The assessment for the liberation of the count of Württemberg. [Barbaricci?] made a fief. Frederick the Palatine [unclear] army [unclear] against the bishop of Speyer. Rothenburg captured by Frederick the Palatine. Concord established between the Palatine and the bishop of Speyer. War between the Brandenburgers and the duke of Austria. [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Trithemius

...devastating everywhere. Against his onslaught Duke Louis, leading out an army with a strong hand, took the very wealthy village of [unclear], together with almost sixty others in number, of which many belonged to the people of Ulm; these he reduced almost to nothing. These things happened around Shrovetide.

Afterward, on the sixteenth day of the month of July, the aforesaid Margrave, with many nobles and a strong army of his own men, of the Counts of Württemberg, and of the imperial cities, beset with a siege Heidenheim, which Duke Louis had previously taken. When Duke Louis heard this, he moved his army against him, and on the nineteenth day of the month of July drove the Margrave from the siege, seized his camp, killed many of the nobles and soldiers, and captured many. The Margrave escaped with difficulty with two men and withdrew into the castle of Albeck. Duke Louis, however, found much wealth in the Margrave’s camp, in gold, silver, horses, wagons, and arms. Then peace was again made between them.

In the same year also, on the vigil of the apostles Simon and Jude, while Diether of Isenburg, archbishop, and Philip, Count of Katzenelnbogen, were awaiting the aforementioned Frederick, Count Palatine, in that very night, through the treachery of certain citizens, Ortwin and Dudo being the leaders of the treachery, Mainz was handed over into the hands of Adolf of Nassau, while Louis the Black, Duke, and the lord of Königstein, with the men of the Rheingau and others, set the city on fire and plundered it wretchedly, many citizens being cruelly killed. Moreover Diether and the Count of Katzenelnbogen, having been lowered over the wall, escaped by fleeing in a small boat along the Rhine.

The enemy found there the plunder not of one city, but almost of the whole country, because many goods from the surrounding villages and monasteries had previously been carried into the city out of fear of the adversaries. The houses of priests and Jews, despoiled by them, were miserably laid waste, and the priests themselves, together with the Jews, were shamefully captured and led away to Eltville and other places. Of those who were in the city, almost five hundred were killed; beautiful women and virgins were raped, and many things were done contrary to the order of Christian charity and honor.

After this, peace was made at Frankfurt between Adolf and Diether of Isenburg under this settlement: that Diether should relinquish the pontificate of Mainz to Adolf with all its debts and burdens; and that he himself, for the support of his life, as long as he lived, should freely possess the town, castle, and toll of Lahnstein, with all their revenues. John the bishop, while the aforesaid wars were going on, had twice besieged it with a great army against Diether, but, because the townsmen stood faithfully with Diether and defended themselves bravely, he could not take it; indeed he was compelled to withdraw, with no small loss to himself and to his church of Trier. Likewise Höchst, town, castle, and toll, and also the town of Dieburg, all with all their revenues. These Diether obtained, and thus peace was agreed between them.

Moreover, to Frederick, Count Palatine, for the expenses and provisions which he had laid out for Diether, a pension of one thousand florins each year was assigned on the toll of Ehrenfels. And for the sum of nine thousand florins, which those men of the Rheingau were obliged to pay him, as we said above in the fifteenth year of Conrad our abbot, he received Petersheim in pledge from the church of Mainz.

In the same year also, near Mainz, Frederick instituted the Court Judgment, to be held four times in the year, which he adorned with learned men in law and with nobles, to declare to each person what is just. This Court Judgment, quite usefully instituted, the most excellent prince Philip, Count Palatine, has laudably continued down to the present day with increased strength and wisdom; in it the lengthiness of many lawsuits is curtailed.

In the same year also, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, Ulrich, abbot of this monastery, appointed as the thirtieth prior of this monastery Otto Hawisen of Cologne, whom almost five months earlier he had made cellarer, after the convent had remained for two years without a prior. He held the office of prior for four years, except for twenty-three days; and when Ulrich resigned the abbacy, as we shall say, he himself was elected abbot.

1463.

In the second year of Ulrich our abbot, the monastery of Michelsberg near Bamberg was reformed and, as is customary, united to the annual chapter of the union and observance of Bursfelde. Pope Pius II conferred the abbacy of the same monastery on Eberhard of Venlo, abbot of St. James near Mainz, and ordered him to transfer himself there for the preservation of the reform that had been introduced. John of Littstein, abbot of the Mount of St. John in the Rheingau, succeeded him in the abbacy of St. James; John of Lutherbach succeeded him there in the abbacy, and both did not preside long in either place.

In the same...

[Blank page in the source scan.]

Of Sponheim.

In the same year, on the Ides of February, Theoderic of Moers, archbishop of Cologne, died in the forty-ninth year of his pontificate and was buried in the greater church of Cologne. After him, in the same year, on the next-to-last day of March, Rupert, son of Louis, Count Palatine and Duke of Bavaria, called “with the Beard,” brother of the magnanimous prince Duke Frederick, guardian of Philip, was unanimously elected archbishop by the chapter; and he presided for sixteen [unclear] years amid many tribulations, as we shall say later.

In the same year also, in the month of November, the above-written agreement between Diether of Isenburg and Adolf of Nassau was made through the mediation of certain princes.

In this same year all victuals increased in abundance and were bought at a low price. Wine was cheap: for in many places one measure of wine was bought for one Hallensian obol, and three malters of rye for one florin.

1465.

In the fourth year of our abbot Ulrich, the eighteenth provincial chapter of our order was celebrated at Würzburg, at St. Stephen’s, on the third Sunday after the feast of the Resurrection, with continuation on the following days. There presided in it Berthold, abbot of St. Stephen there, John of St. Michael’s in Hildesheim, Melchior [unclear] of St. Ulrich in Augsburg, and Everhard of Mount St. Michael, abbots of our order; and little was reduced into statutes.

In the same year, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, Frederick of Nackheim, formerly abbot of this monastery, died; he had resigned the abbacy, with Abbot Conrad succeeding.

In the same year, on the fifth day of the month of May, John of Aldendorf, abbot of St. Burkard’s near Würzburg, of our order, together with his reprobate monks, rashly cast off the holy order and the habit of sacred religion, in which they had been professed and educated, deceiving the pope with false narratives so that they might extort from the Apostolic See permission concerning this; and from reprobate monks they became wicked secular canons, leaving to posterity much example for apostatizing. Our order and the provincial chapter opposed this most impious translation; but, with money and the favor of many who thought against religion being interposed, it accomplished nothing. Those apostates long ago received their reward: they all perished by an evil death, leaving to posterity a manifest judgment of their damnation.

In the same year also, on the eighth day of the month of August, John Nix, bishop of Speyer, who, by waging war imprudently and without cause against Frederick, Count Palatine, brought irrecoverable damage upon his church, resigned the bishopric into the hands of the chapter; and soon, wasting away excessively within himself, he scarcely survived for the space of a year. For besides the evils enumerated above, which Frederick, Count Palatine, inflicted on the church of Speyer because of him, he also, in the first year of our abbot Ulrich, in broad daylight and with no one resisting, burned and utterly destroyed the houses and mills of the priests around the church of St. Germanus outside the walls of the city of Speyer, all of them, both of the vicars and of the canons. On the same day Matthias of Raming, not yet [unclear], chancellor of Frederick, the aforesaid lord Count Palatine, succeeded him in the bishopric by provision of the supreme pontiff Pius II, with the consent of the chapter. He presided for fourteen years, a learned, devout, and magnanimous man, who governed his church very well by virtue and wisdom, and always stoutly defended its rights, privileges, and liberties.

1465.

In this year, which was the fourth of our abbot Ulrich, Adolf, Duke of Guelders, seized his father Arnold by night while he was sleeping naked in bed, shut him up in a certain castle, Bobeck, and held him captive for a long time. Having done this, he compelled all the men of the duchy, after abjuring his father, to render him the oath of homage. But [unclear] punished this impious crime in him with fitting vengeance.

In the same year the people of Liège, after many lawsuits and disputes held in the Roman curia with John of Bourbon, their elected and confirmed bishop, following their inborn savagery without reason, while he had neither resigned nor been deposed, took as administrator of their church of Liège Mark, son of James, Margrave of Baden, brother of John, bishop of Trier, and of Charles. Archbishop Charles, brother of the aforesaid, led him from Cologne to Liège with two hundred horses. But not long afterward, offended by their wickedness and malice and placed near destruction, he departed, leaving everything behind, and could scarcely escape their hands.

In this same year the monastery of Liesborn, of our order, in the diocese of Münster, was reformed with the assent and cooperation of the prelate of the same, with Henry, its abbot, being received into union with the chapter of the Bursfeld observance. The monastery in Isenburg likewise was reformed in the same way and united to the chapter.

Rupert becomes archbishop of Cologne.

Agreement between Diether and Adolf, etc.

Adolf [unclear].

Year of abundance.

The eighteenth provincial chapter [unclear].

Frederick, formerly abbot here, dies.

The monastery of St. Burkard is transferred from the order.

John Nix, bishop of Speyer, resigns the bishopric.

Matthias becomes bishop of Speyer.

The Duke of Guelders holds his future [unclear] father captive.

Nicholas of [Budel?], administrator of the church of Liège.

The monastery of Liesborn is reformed; Isenburg similarly. Sponheim.

...they should instruct [them] in suitable matters; but they could obtain no one from the men of Trier. After this they sent to Cologne, and from there two brothers from St. Pantaleon came. When they first arrived they were received gladly, and were appointed by the abbot as masters to instruct the monks of this convent. But, harassed by the excessive importunity and malice of the monks, especially the young ones, mocked, and sometimes even subjected to blows, when they saw that they could make no progress, they returned to Cologne, whence they had come.

In the same year, on the nineteenth day of the month of April, which was the third Sunday after the feast of the Lord's Resurrection, the nineteenth provincial chapter of our order was held at Monks' Mount near Bamberg. Presiding over it were Johannes of Bursfelde, Melchior of Augsburg, Heinrich of St. Michael's at Hildesheim, and Johannes of Holy Cross in Werdea, abbots of very distinguished and celebrated monasteries of our order.

In this year, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, died Andreas of Lower Utrecht, a monk of this place. He left certain little works of his talent, namely: Soliloquies of Man to God, one book; On the Progress of the Virtues, two books; On Abstinence from Meat, one book; On the Use of Flocci in Our Order, one book; also various sermons, poems, orations, and many letters to different persons, and certain other things, of which some are still extant, and some have been destroyed through negligence.

In these times there came from Basel a certain poor man, having with him his [unclear] son, named Theoderic, six years and two months of age, who in words was so mature and composed, as if he had attained his fortieth year in conduct, that he seemed very like a most eloquent orator; and he could excuse his own childhood and ignorance in both languages so beautifully, and speak about any subjects whatsoever, that he turned everyone to amazement.

In the aforementioned year, in the month of June, died Philip, duke of Burgundy, who accomplished many things vigorously in his life; [he left] a single heir, Charles, duke of Burgundy, who himself also vigorously performed many things. 1468.

In the second year of Otto our abbot, Charles, duke of Burgundy, led a strong army against the people of Liege.

In the aforementioned year Adolf, archbishop of Mainz, by his ordinary authority, brought forth [unclear] and, after [unclear], graciously admitted the privileges also, however granted from the apostolic see, to the aforesaid union and chapter.

In the same year Matthias, bishop of Speyer, on the third day of the month of January, incorporated the church of St. German outside the walls of the city of Speyer, in the diocese of Mainz, into the church of St. Maurice within the walls, because of the previous desolation of the priests' houses of St. German by Frederick, count palatine, against Johann Nix, bishop.

In the same year Charles, duke of Burgundy, with a very great army of armed men, advanced into Gaul against Louis, king of France, and remained there for several days, and throughout the whole kingdom inflicted much damage by fire and plundering. Meanwhile, while these things were being done in France, the factious, inconstant people of Liege, at all times ready for sedition, prepared themselves again for rebellion, and began in their accustomed manner to rage against their bishop. When this became known to the bishop himself, coming from France with seven thousand Burgundians in great array, he resolved to besiege Liege with a strong hand. When he had come to the city called Tongeren, and its provost had made this known to the Liegeois, they entered the city by night with two thousand men, seized the bishop, killed many nobles and counts, while many others slipped away in flight, and led him captive to Liege. Meanwhile, however, agreement was made between the duke and the king of France. Therefore, when report of the deed came to Duke Charles, moved by excessive fury and having a very great fighting army from Picardy and Burgundy, forty thousand armed men, of whom he lost almost two thousand in the siege itself, after many labors he at last took the city and exercised unheard-of cruelty against the citizens. The city was very beautiful in its buildings; in it there were thirty-two parish churches, but collegiate churches [unclear].

Two monks came from Cologne to reform this place.

The nineteenth provincial chapter is held.

Andreas, monk of this place, dies.

Certain little works of the monk Andreas.

The archbishop of Mainz [unclear] confirmed ours.

The church of St. German outside the walls of the city of Speyer is incorporated into the church of St. Maurice within the walls.

The duke of Burgundy devastates France.

... the fidelity promised to the prince for the maintenance of the reformation endured, but it was soon changed, as we shall say in the following year.

In this year, on the third day before the Ides of August, Johannes, abbot of Bursfelde, died, the second in the reformation; Theoderic succeeded him, the third in the reformation, and presided for sixteen years.

In the same year, Frederick, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Adolf, Archbishop of Mainz, and Rudolf, Bishop of Würzburg, joined in alliance, brought out an army against those robbers of Rosenberg, Georg, Arnold, and Michael, together with his adherents. Stirred up by diabolical fury, they despised the prince’s commands, plundered all bishops whom they found anywhere, castrated priests by cutting off their genitals, and, carrying out depredations on the public road throughout all the land between Franconia and the Neckar, perpetrated many evils. They also forced the prince’s messengers who had been sent to them, in contempt of them, to eat the letters they had brought. Wherefore the aforesaid princes, moved by this, in the following year strongly besieged the castle of the aforesaid robbers, Bocksberg, for three weeks, battered it with engines, and took it, the robbers having escaped in flight by night with seventy horsemen. These things were done in the following year, namely 1470, on Thursday of the Lord’s Supper. After this they surrounded with a siege the very strong castle Schupf, and took it in eight days, which they utterly [overthrew?] on the octave Sunday of the Resurrection. And thus the rashness of those robbers, humbled and confounded, was thereafter compelled to obey the princes.

But because our present monastery of Sponheim was reformed in the year noted above, and Abbot Otto was deposed, it is worth the labor briefly to learn the manner, time, persons, and authors of its reformation, according to the sequence and order of time, especially wishing to bring it to the knowledge of [posterity?] by the testimony of writings.

On the Reformation of This Monastery of Sponheim, and the Deposition of the Aforesaid Lord Otto, the Twenty-Third Abbot, and the Other Things Done Here at That Time.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity noted above, 1469, in the second indiction, when the present monastery, because of the bad rule of the abbots and the dissolute life of the monks, had come to extreme poverty, and was wholly deprived of all its beauty both in spiritual and in temporal matters, the illustrious and most devout prince Frederick, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and Count in Sponheim, son of the late Duke Stephen and brother of Duke Louis the Black, who had his residence in Simmern, grieving over the ruin and desolation of this once distinguished monastery, resolved to subject it to reformation to the honor of God, and, according to his powers, to restore it in both estates to the observance of the Rule. Accordingly, with the consent and good will of the most renowned prince Lord Frederick, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and Prince Elector residing at Heidelberg, concerning whom many things have been said above, he obtained from Adolf, Archbishop of the church of Mainz, two commissioners for this work: namely Hermann of St. James near Mainz, and Conrad of Rodenberg of St. John in the Rheingau, abbots of monasteries of our order, with whose counsel and direction he might bring so necessary and holy a work to the desired end. Therefore the aforesaid Adolf, committing to them his authority in ordinary jurisdiction, to visit and reform the present monastery in spiritual and temporal matters, gave them such a mandate, furnished with his seal.

Adolf, by the grace of God Archbishop of the see of Mainz, Archchancellor through Germany of the Holy Roman Empire, and Prince Elector, to the religious and devout Hermann of St. James outside the walls of our city of Mainz, and Conrad of St. John in the Rheingau, abbots of monasteries of the Order of St. Benedict, our beloved in Christ, greeting always in the Lord. Among the other cares of solicitude incumbent upon our shoulders by the duty of the pastoral office entrusted to us, we strive especially to undertake those by which, according to the statutes of the sacred canons and the decrees of the holy Fathers, we are able fittingly to visit those faithfully subject to our care, to inquire more truly into their morals, state, and conditions, to confirm things well done, correct things badly done, restrain insolence, reform things desolate, and lead those who err back to the path of justice and truth, lest it happen that their blood be required from our hands. Indeed recently it has come to our hearing, not without displeasure of our heart, that the monastery in Sponheim, of our diocese and of the aforesaid order, is in many ways deformed in spiritual and temporal matters, and that its rectors have been marked by negligence in the execution of their offices, and deserve correction; matters which, without the application of due remedy, we ought not to pass over under dissimulation. We therefore, grieving fittingly over the aforesaid matters, and [unclear] to the reformation of the monastery and to the correction and reduction of its rectors and members, to

Johannes, Abbot of Bursfelde, Dead.

Those Robbers of Rosenberg [unclear] Their Lord by the Prince.

The Castles of the Robbers, However Bold the Robbers Were, Are Overthrown.

Frederick, Duke of Bavaria, Count in Sponheim, Reformer of This Monastery.

Chronicle of Trithemius

wishing, with paternal and solicitous efforts, to attend to better counsels, but at present hindered by various weighty affairs of ours and of our church, and unable to give special attention to this matter, we commit to you, in whom we have special confidence in the Lord, and to each of you jointly and severally, the completion and execution of this work, with power to visit the said monastery; by our ordinary authority to introduce brothers to be instructed in regular observance and to join them to those who have hitherto been in the same place and have wished to keep the due observance; to remove rebels and opponents; to inquire into the usefulness of the present abbot and of the other officials; and to remove that abbot and the other office-holders who shall seem to you useless, or not altogether, or not so useful as may be expedient for the reformation; and to elect, depute, and appoint another approved abbot from among the reformed, instructed in due observance, and having trustworthy testimonials; and to ordain, establish, and do any things that shall seem useful or expedient for the reformation and its due continuation, which we ourselves would do and could do if we were present; and to compel the abbot and brothers of the said monastery to observe the aforesaid things and to fulfill what, as stated above, you shall judge should be ordained, and also all other persons, spiritual as well as secular, of whatever status, rank, order, or condition they may be, directly or indirectly, under any color sought, under penalty of excommunication, suspension, interdict, and other censures and sentences of the Church, [unclear], with the aid of the secular arm. Witnesses, however, who are to be named and produced, if through favor, hatred, love, or fear they withdraw themselves, are to be compelled by a like censure to bear witness to the truth. In testimony of these our letters, to which our seal has been appended. Given in our city of Mainz on the last day of the month of July, in the year of the Lord 1469.

When this commission had been received, the aforesaid abbots took care to bring it as quickly as possible to the knowledge of the aforementioned prince, Frederick. When he had learned these things, he appointed the nineteenth day of the month of August for coming here to the monastery in the morning, secretly or unexpectedly, so that no one among those dwelling around should perceive anything before they arrived. When the appointed day came, which was the Saturday after the feast of the Assumption of the blessed Mary ever virgin, councillors sent by the aforesaid prince, with an armed band, entered this [unclear] monastery in the morning after Prime, taking the greatest care that none of the monks should escape or that anything could be carried away from the monastery.

Meanwhile, after an hour, there also arrived the [unclear] abbots, Hermann of St. James and Conrad of St. John; and as soon as they had been admitted, they entered the chapter-place and caused the abbot and convent to be present. When these had been gathered, in the presence of the prince’s councillors they had the mandate given them by the archbishop of Mainz read before all by a public notary. But when [unclear] had learned that they could not, nor could they in any way undergo the Bursfeld reformation, which was too austere and unbearable to them, the commissioners, after hearing these and many other things that they brought forward against the reformation, not wishing to condemn anyone hastily, admonished them to deliberate better, and thereafter began the office of visitation, making inquiry into both conditions of the monastery.

On the following day, which was the twentieth of the month of August, namely Sunday and the feast of Saint Bernard, abbot, when the inquiry had been completed and the visitors had discovered that the abbot of this place, lord Otto, both because of the weakness of his body and also because of his lesser experience in regular observance, was not suitable or useful for pastoral care under the reformation to be introduced, after pious admonitions they at last persuaded him to yield the abbatial dignity, lest he should in any way wish to impede the holy business of reformation. Therefore he resigned the abbacy in the aforesaid year and on the aforesaid day, before a notary and witnesses, receiving an annual pension for the sustenance of his body. Not long afterward he was made provost of the nuns on Mount St. Rupert near Bingen; there at last he rested in the Lord.

After the resignation had been made, as we have said, on that day and the next the commissioners, together with the duke’s secretaries sent for this purpose, received from the resigning abbot the computation and accounting of all the revenues and debts of this monastery, drawing up an inventory, as is customary, by the hand of the notary. It was found that the monastery had come almost to the utmost poverty. For everything had been pledged: estates and revenues, so that nothing free remained for the sustenance of the monks. The sum of the debts, for which it had been pledged, exceeded the calculation of two thousand two hundred florins, besides very many other burdens.

[Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheim.

The hardships of poverty. All the buildings of the monastery were ruinous, and the individual things that could be seen were covered with extreme [unclear]. The utensils of the house either did not exist, or had previously been removed through fear of the reform, so that those arriving first found neither table-linens, nor dishes, nor almost anything else necessary for the management of the house. Moreover, as soon as the brothers of the reform began to inhabit this place, they were necessarily compelled not only to take money on loan, but also to ask grain and wine on loan from others for the sustenance of life. The first brothers who came for the reform of this monastery were from the monastery of St. James near Mainz, four in number, namely Johannes of Kolenhausen, who had been cellarer there; he was ordained abbot. Heinrich of Geilenhausen, who remained here until death for eighteen years. Bruno, who did not remain long. Johannes Hocheim, who was appointed cellarer, but did not remain. For indeed, because of the excessive poverty and want of this monastery, having been brought up comfortably at St. James, they despised remaining here. When they returned to St. James, others sent back in their place remained for a time; and when these also departed, still others were sent to this place. Thus for many years none of the monks coming from St. James, except the aforesaid Heinrich, had stable permanence in this place, until at last young men were gathered, coming from the schools, instructed and professed according to the custom of the order, and finally put a necessary end to these excursions. Great at that time was the poverty of this monastery. Fish were very rare in the brothers’ food; but often, instead of fish, pears, cooked by a certain drying in an oven, afterwards softened again in a cauldron and covered with broth, were prepared for the brothers’ meal. In want they had voluntary patience for the love of God, laboring under great extremity both in food and in clothing, desiring nothing more than to relieve as quickly as possible, by their moderate frugality, the monastery from the burdens of its existing debts. The ornaments for the beauty of the Lord were few and exceedingly meager; apart from the pontifical mitre there were no jewels in the church. There was no library, because the unreformed monks pursued not books, but games and pleasures. For only eight volumes, apart from the Bible divided into two parts, of small price or value, were found in this monastery at the time of the reform. For, as we said far above, after regular discipline began gradually to decline in this place, and the substance of temporal goods together with the integrity of monastic life to fail, the monks, who were then all proprietors, dispersed a library once sufficiently precious, secretly selling the books for a low price, so that nothing remained of so many volumes that was of any value. But now, pursuing the institution of the new abbot, let us complete the order of the history; for, just as we cannot explain all the misery of this monastery, so we judge it superfluous to dwell longer on the blameworthy life of the unreformed monks.

Concerning Johannes Kolenhausen, twenty-sixth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, who presided for fourteen years, eleven months, and three days; concerning various deeds both of his and of that time.

Now in the year written above, 1459, in the second indiction, on the third weekday after the feast of St. Bernard, that is, on the twenty-second day of the month of August, about the eighth hour, the aforesaid abbots, commissioners of lord Adolf, archbishop of Mainz, entering the chapter-place of this monastery with the notary and witnesses, caused all the monks found here to be called to them anew. When they came and were sitting in the aforesaid place, in the presence of Johannes of Lansheim, chancellor, and of others who had been sent by the prince, the often-named commissioners and visitors attempted by every means to counsel and persuade them piously and paternally, that, casting aside deformity, they should submit their necks to the reform of the former holy manner of life, and conform themselves, for the salvation of their souls, to the practices of the brothers whom they had brought to reform this place. But since they in no way wished to acquiesce in the instructions and pious admonitions of the fathers, the aforesaid visitors and commissioners, by authority granted them by the ordinary, removed them all from the monastery, depriving them by sentence, for the present, of every right in the election or otherwise concerning the monastery.

Then, directing their intention to the institution of a new abbot, which had devolved upon the archbishop since there were no persons incorporated in the monastery, and using the authority committed to them, with the counsel and consent of the brothers present for introducing the reform, they nominated, deputed, and instituted Johannes Kolenhausen, otherwise of Butzbach, monk and cellarer of St. James near Mainz, then present, in the name and stead of lord Adolf, archbishop of Mainz, as abbot of this monastery. Thus instituted by them, in the year and on the day written above, he took up the burden of rule at the command of his abbot, and, confirmed at Mainz on the third day of the month of October by [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Trithemius

[Sifridus?], bishop of Cyrene, vicar in pontificals of lord Adolf, archbishop of Mainz, by his special commission, and finally ordained by the same man, as is customary, presided over this monastery from the prescribed day of his institution for thirteen years, eleven months, and three days, in great poverty, want, and patience. He came from a certain town of the Wetterau named Butzbach, of knightly stock, which bears the arms of Colnhausen. Placed at letters in his boyhood, he learned most of the first rudiments. Afterwards, when he was about fourteen years old, having left the schools, at the urging of a certain young nobleman, a friend, he began to ride. But since he was slender and delicate in body and did not seem able to endure the labors of horsemen and the burden of arms, after four or five years he gave up the practice of riding along with the office of soldiering, on the advice of his people, and returned again to the schools.

Having therefore recovered the studies which he had for some time interrupted, he went to the general gymnasium at Erfurt, and in a short time, by learning many things thoroughly, made considerable progress. He was inclined to devote himself to mathematics and astronomy, and became sufficiently learned in that science. But because of weakness of the head he could not apply himself to the contemplation of these arts to the degree that the will of his mind required. Therefore, after he had devoted himself to letters for some years in the aforesaid gymnasium, he was made doctor of philosophy by the consent of all, and in that faculty he easily surpassed many masters in learning and knowledge.

After this, having left the public study of letters, he went to his native place, and there began to remain in the house that had once been his father’s, together with a servant. But when household care and domestic anxiety began to vex him too much and make him restless, afflicted with excessive weariness, he did not know what he should do or what state of life he should assume. To take a wife, because of occasions which we deliberately pass over, did not seem safe enough for him; to enter the priesthood and live in secular society he judged dangerous, and so he did not wish it; to remain as he was he could much less endure. Therefore at last, after much deliberation, he resolved to leave the world and enter a monastery.

But since he was very slender and of a delicate constitution, he feared to undertake the arduous path of the rule, lest perhaps afterwards he should be compelled, with great shame, to abandon what he had taken up imprudently and too rashly. And so, for the space of one year, proposing and fearing, he stood in doubt, and could not conclude what was more useful for him. He shrank from the order of the Carthusians as too austere; he did not wish to enter the religion of the Mendicants, because of many things by which he was moved; but to enter our observance, because of the almost continual and perpetual abstinence from meat, he likewise dreaded. But at last, anticipated by the light of divine mercy, he broke off delays and laid aside all fear; having arranged his affairs, he came to the monastery of St. James near Mainz, asked to be received as a monk, and obtained it.

Having become a monk, he lived religiously in all things without offense to anyone, so that he even seemed to be set before the rest as an example. Then ordained priest, and afterwards cellarer of the aforesaid monastery, since he seemed sufficiently suitable, he was finally, as we have said, appointed the first abbot of this monastery in the reform. He was of middling stature, neither too short nor again tall in height, lean in body, slender, and slight in strength; subtle in intellect, mild, very affable, but of swift and vehement anger, whose disturbance of mind came quickly and passed quickly; yet his anger harmed no one more than himself. The reform that had been introduced he continued well, as far as lay in him; he always lived religiously, and at all times conducted himself with the highest maturity and honesty, without complaint.

  1. In the tenth year of John Kolnhausen our abbot, on the tenth day of the month of May, the twentieth provincial chapter of our order was celebrated in the monastery of St. Peter at Erfurt. Presiding in it were Gunther of the same place, Melchior of St. Ulrich at Augsburg, Sebald of St. Giles at Nuremberg, and Paul of St. Mary at Elchingen, abbots of monasteries of our order. In it many statutes were renewed for the [unclear] of the order.

In the same year, on the eleventh day of the month of September, the annual chapter of the union and observance of Bursfelde was celebrated in the monastery of St. Matthias near Trier. In it John, abbot of this monastery, and the present monastery deserved to be incorporated into the union and participation of all the indults, privileges, and graces of the same, in the customary form, with the necessary and customary letters prescribed.

Also in the same year, one of the old unreformed monks who had been removed in the preceding year, John of Bockenau, a young and rash priest, against the reformed brothers [Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheim.

...bearing a bitter mind toward the reformed monks, he secretly labored to harm them, or even to kill them if he could. Coming therefore to the abbot and brothers with a feigned intention, he asked to be admitted to the reform, promising that he wished to obey the commands of the elders in all things, and he hid the lurking poison under the sweet modulation of his words. Why delay? Received for probation, the wolf was joined to the sheep. But when he had learned everything for the sake of which he had come to spy it out, namely the entrance and exit to the dormitory, also the cells of the individual brothers, the arrangement of the beds, and the other things that would serve his purpose, having found an opportunity he secretly fled from the monastery. After two or three months, by night during matins, he entered the brothers’ cells, stole whatever he found pleasing to himself, and threatened that he would kill certain of them. At that time the brothers’ dormitory was on the western side of the cloister, where the dormitory of the donors now is.

Therefore on a certain night he came with a sword into the dormitory of the sleeping monks, and silently approaching the bed of Bruno, whom he pursued with greater hatred, thinking to thrust the sword into his throat, he wounded his foot or shin; for that night Bruno had turned his feet toward the place where he had previously been accustomed to put his head, I do not know whether by design or by chance.
