But as soon as he felt the wound of the one stabbing him, he awoke and cried out; whereupon the terrified thief fled.

Afterwards, when the harvest had already been gathered, returning one night, he set fire to one granary with its crops, burned more than forty malders of grain, and, having taken a horse from the stable, fled through the gate that leads to the vineyards. At length he came to Hornbach, and there, received for a time among the monks in the guise of a guest, he could not long hide his wickedness; but, having stolen money, jewels, and garments in the church from the little chests of the townsmen, placed there because of the immunity of the place, he was detained and put in public custody. Since there he was fed only on bread and water, he wrote to John Kolnhausen, our abbot, whose monk he was not, and begged him more urgently to rescue him from the prison of hard affliction. That good and exceedingly merciful man, although he could have left him, as one subject to him by no profession, utterly expelled by right from the monastery as incorrigible, caught in his iniquity, was moved by mercy; after paying what he had furtively taken in the church, together with the expenses incurred in prison, he freed him from there. He came, therefore, free from prison, but a slave of iniquity; he sought pardon and was received again, but he did not in the least amend his depraved morals. Finally, when with excessive rashness he had troubled everyone, he fled again, perpetrated many wicked and unjust deeds everywhere, until at last, in the third year of the aforesaid Abbot John, captured by the horsemen of Duke Frederick, he was placed here in the monastery in perpetual imprisonment. This is the twenty-ninth year of his imprisonment.

The other old monks, however, attempted nothing of this sort against the reform. The eldest of them, Peter of Blenich, came to the monastery of Sunsheim; there he died in his deformation. Otto, once abbot, having become, as we have said, confessor of the nuns on Mount St. Rupert near Bingen, rested there in the Lord, buried there in the chapel of the blessed Mary ever virgin. The other three young men returned to observance; two of them died shortly afterwards. The third, John Nutigin of Kirchberg, was confessor of the nuns for more than twenty years in Bibelis in the diocese of Strasbourg, until at last, compelled to withdraw because of the impropriety of the nuns, he was again appointed confessor of the nuns at the monastery of Schmerlenbach in the diocese of Mainz by John Trithemius, abbot of this monastery, where he still lives, an old and infirm man.

In the aforesaid year of the Lord 1470, the citizens of the old town of Weissenburg, who in the preceding year had sworn in the words of Count Frederick that they wished with all their strength to maintain the reform introduced by that prince, as we said above, in the monastery of our order there, moved by I know not what reason, changing their decision against the oath they had made, secretly admitted the old deformed monks in women’s clothing; and, after the reformed monks had been driven out with disgrace, they handed the monastery over to the old monks. They also received and fostered with hospitality enemies and foes of the Palatine prince, such as Wirich Hoffart with certain others, and they treated the prince’s prefect in Weissenburg, captured and subjected to exaction, with insults. Whereupon the magnanimous prince, moved to anger, besieged the town of Weissenburg throughout the whole harsh winter with a very strong army of mercenaries, and, after placing a garrison in the deserted provostry of the four towers, began to assault the city vigorously. Meanwhile the people of Strasbourg, together with certain cities in Alsace, were laboring for concord. Peace was concluded on condition that satisfaction be made to the prince for the insult, and the siege was lifted. But the people of Weissenburg did not remain in the agreement they had accepted; for, after sending envoys to the emperor, they accused the Palatine of persecuting imperial subjects, asking that Duke Louis, surnamed the Black, Count of Veldenz, be appointed for them as captain in the emperor’s name against his attack. The emperor did what he had been asked, [unclear] against the Palatine.

He secretly flees from the monastery.

He tries to cut down the monks.

He burns the crops at Hornbach.

He commits a most sacrilegious deed. He is imprisoned at Hornbach.

John our abbot frees him from prison.

He is placed in perpetual imprisonment. What became of the old monks.

The citizens of Weissenburg are besieged by Frederick the Palatine.

Weissenburg is besieged by Frederick the Palatine. [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Trithemius ... otherwise taking offense, and by open imperial letters, in his own name and in that of the whole Roman Empire, appointed the aforesaid duke Louis as captain. Duke Louis, accepting this appointment, though bound by oath to the Palatine, as was said above, began to act against him.

And so Prince Frederick, compelled by necessity, mustered his soldiers and, as if roaring, went out with his army against Louis. Besieging Stralburg castle and the town of Schriesheim, he took them in eight days; after taking the booty, he had sixteen of the foot-soldiers drowned, while the rest were led into captivity. After this he besieged the duke Louis’s town, called Armsheim, which was sufficiently fortified; and, vigorously assaulting it with engines, bombards, and ditches, he received it in surrender on the day of the Commemoration of St Paul. In that victory the Palatine took eighteen soldiers and forty-one horsemen captive. Having assessed the townsmen for money, and sent forty foot-soldiers to Alzey for custody, he destroyed the surrounding wall, overturned the towers and battlements, and carried off the weapons, bombards, and all the military equipment. The captive foot-soldiers, however, who had been led to Alzey, were almost all drowned, because the prince Palatine had this custom: he let no one live who, being his own man and subject to him in servile condition, had presumed to make enmity against him, unless he had an excusable cause.

Then the Palatine besieged Wachenheim castle, and took it after it had been attacked with great assaults; in it he found a large supply of military equipment. He held this little castle as a garrison for some time, but afterwards nevertheless overthrew it utterly, as is seen today. After these things he also besieged the town of Wachenheim; but when he heard that duke Louis, with the counts of Leiningen-Bitsch, was going to come through Alsace with a strong army, he raised the siege, deposited the war-engines at Deidesheim, and advanced to meet them. When they learned of his coming they withdrew, and did not dare come before his face.

Again after this the Palatine besieged the very strong castle of Ruppertseck, which, after being attacked with the greatest assaults, bombards, and ditches, he at last received in surrender. In it he found provisions, horses, engines, and military equipment in great abundance, and twelve nobles and forty-six horsemen, together with several others, all of whom he captured. Among the noble captives were Reinhard, count Hirsutus, commonly called Raugraf, and Johannes of Landeck, captains of all the rest.

In the year noted above, when Frederick, the illustrious count Palatine, was doing those things which we have mentioned against his enemies, the foot-soldiers who, at Wachenheim, held the garrisons on the side of duke Louis against the Palatine, made a sally on the vigil of the Assumption of blessed Mary ever-virgin and entered the monastery of Limburg, of our order. They violently opened the sacristy and the library, and carried off everything they found, both in the church, except the relics, and outside it throughout the whole monastery; and, after taking away the courts [unclear] and the monks’ horses, they brought the plunder to Wachenheim.

In the same year also Mahomet, emperor of the Turks, with a fleet of forty ships and an army of one hundred thousand horsemen, invaded Euboea, the famous island of the Christians, and then took it on the thirtieth day. He miserably killed many thousands of believers in Christ and utterly overthrew the cities and castles.

In the same year, on the Ides of April, Pope Paul II, amid the sacred solemnities of the masses, created Borso d’Este, count of Ferrara, duke; at that time this seemed to many not to belong to the pope, but rather to the emperor. Otherwise, if it is lawful for the pope to create dukes, it is lawful for the emperor, as formerly, to institute pontiffs and abbots. But Emperor Frederick, as scarcely anyone before him would have done, dissembled this deed, like many others, to the desolation of the empire.

In this year, after an almost four-year vacancy in the priorship of this monastery, Johannes Kolnhausen, the abbot named above, appointed as thirty-first prior Donatus, a certain monk, who did not preside long in that office, but was afterwards transferred to Weissenburg, to a certain convent of nuns; he presided for three years.

  1. In the second year of our abbot Johannes Kolnhausen, Frederick, the illustrious count Palatine, leading in person a strong army of fourteen thousand armed men against Louis, duke and count of Veldenz, again surrounded with a siege his town of Wachenheim, which he had besieged before winter. Pressing it hard with engines, arms, bombards, and ditches in a manly assault, he received it in surrender on the day of St Boniface, bishop and martyr. When the town had been taken, together with eight nobles, thirty-five horsemen, and seventy foot-soldiers, he assessed the townsmen for a fixed sum of money, overturned the walls and towers and levelled them with the ground, filled in the ditches, and carried off all the engines. Of the foot-soldiers, however, who had plundered churches and monasteries, killed the poor, or burned houses, fifty-six were drowned. Then they received the reward for the plundering of the monastery of Limburg which they had committed in the preceding year, as the Lord avenged the injury. After [Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheimense.

After this the Palatine moved his army to the greater and the lesser village of Bockenheim, both well fortified with ditches and defenses, which belonged to the counts of Leiningen; he surrounded them both with a siege and took them in eight days, the nobles and knights with certain others having slipped away in flight, except for four men-at-arms, fifteen horsemen, and twenty foot-soldiers, who were found and captured, while some of the foot-soldiers were drowned. All the walls, fences, towers, and every fortification were destroyed, the ditches leveled, the houses burned, and both villages utterly destroyed and laid waste, on the fourteenth day of the month of June.

When these things had been done, the high-spirited Prince Palatine moved his army against Duke Ludwig and besieged the castle and town of Vimen, which that same Duke Ludwig held in pledge from the church of Mainz, and from which he had inflicted many losses on the Palatine. When the canons of Mainz heard this, fearing that if the Palatine took the castle it would be alienated forever from the church of Mainz, they intervened by way of agreement: namely, that the prince should allow the horsemen and foot-soldiers in the castle to depart with their goods; that he should also restore the castle and town to the church of Mainz, no longer to be granted into the hands of Duke Ludwig; and that he himself should receive from the church of Mainz four thousand florins for his expenses.

These things were done and agreed on the day of St. James the Apostle, in the year written above. From there the Palatine, with the very powerful army of his men, besieged Lambsheim, a town very strongly fortified by its site, waters, ditches, walls, and defenses. In it were thirty-four nobles and horsemen, and more than three hundred foot-soldiers hired for wages from the Swiss. When, after two days of siege, they had seen the assaults and strength of the Palatine forces, they obtained security to depart, with an oath that during this dissension they would do nothing against the Palatine, and, leaving the town and the horsemen behind, they departed. Then the prince took the town with a strong hand, captured Philip Luster, the prefect, with fifteen nobles, thirty-one horsemen, and twenty foot-soldiers, but had those foot-soldiers drowned. The citizens were compelled to swear to the arms of the prince on the Sunday after the feast of St. Peter in Chains.

After this the same high-spirited prince besieged Dürkheim, the greatest and most excellent among all the towns of the counts of Leiningen; for its defense and strength those counts themselves, for twenty continuous years, had spared neither labors nor expenses. The prince therefore placed a garrison in the monastery of nuns at Seebach, of our order, and with all effort, by engines, bombards, ditches, and various methods of war, he began to storm the town; and after many labors and dangers he received it in surrender on the Sunday after the feast of the Assumption of blessed Mary ever Virgin, in the year noted above. Its walls, towers, and all its fortifications, as is seen today, he leveled to the ground and utterly overturned. All whom he found there belonging to Duke Ludwig were led away as captives. The townspeople, however, rendered homage and an oath of fidelity and subjection to the same Prince Palatine. Among others three counts were captured: Philip and Diether, counts of Leiningen, and Peter, lord and a certain French count; also twenty-four men-at-arms were captured, one hundred and six horsemen, the best who were in the whole circuit, forty hired foot-soldiers, fifty-one citizens, and seventy men from the county of Leiningen stationed there for defense, who together with the townspeople were assessed by him for money. In this storming of Dürkheim nearly two hundred men, noble and non-noble, fell on the side of the Prince Palatine; on the side of the counts in the town, however, eighty-nine.

After these things the high-spirited prince moved his whole army against Duke Ludwig, and first besieged Sobernheim, a town of the church of Mainz pledged to Ludwig himself with others, as we said above. When the citizens heard this, they at once came into his surrender, knowing that they could neither resist so great an army nor have any help from their duke. Montzingen also, Merxheim, and Nosbaum in like manner, in the same year and on the same day, namely on the vigil of Bartholomew the Apostle, [were taken?] at the siege of the little castle of Landsberg and of the castle and village of Moscheln; and then for the first time Duke Ludwig sought pardon, since by now he had lost many castles and towns and was bereft of all auxiliaries. Agreement was therefore made between him and the Palatine, and on the Monday after the day of St. Aegidius the Confessor it was concluded at Heidelberg with the necessary letters and documents: namely, that all castles and other things which the Palatine had taken should remain in his power. This agreement did not please Emperor Frederick, but he could not break it, because Duke Ludwig thereafter would rather have had the emperor as an enemy than, at his command, offend the Palatine again. The other princes around him also, all fearing the Palatine’s strength, did not presume to mutter against him.

Greater Bockenheim is captured and destroyed by Frederick the Palatine.

Vimen is besieged by Frederick the Palatine.

Lambsheim is captured by Frederick the Palatine.

Dürkheim is captured and overthrown by Frederick the Palatine.

Sobernheim, Merxheim, Montzingen, and Nosbaum are captured.

Beckelnsheim came into [unclear] of Frederick the Palatine.

Agreement is made between the Palatine and Duke Ludwig. [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Trithemius

In the same year also, on Wednesday after the feast of the Eleven Thousand Virgins, the aforesaid prince Frederick, having previously made alliance with Nicholas, duke of Lorraine, and having joined their army, [captured?] the castle of Gerolzeck and the town of Morsmünster, a den of robbers, by Frederick the Palatine. Dorsbach and Waltbach likewise. Certain altars are incorporated to us. A comet appeared. Dissension between the archbishop of Cologne and the chapter. An attempted betrayal [unclear] of Neuss [unclear]. The bishop of Worms is sent to Cologne. [unclear] of the chapters. A robber-castle is taken by the Palatine army. Donatus, our prior, will be sent to the monastery of Weissenburg. Presidents. John [unclear], in place of our prior, is installed. Hermann of Hesse, count, [unclear] governor of Cologne.

Again afterward, in the month of December of the same year, the lion-hearted prince Palatine sent his army to the land called the Odenwald, and besieged Dorsbach and Waltbach, castles of robbers. The first of these he took on the Tuesday after the day of St. Lucy, martyr, and the other on the following day, the inhabitants of each having either escaped by flight, or been captured or killed. Thus the roads through them were made safer for travellers.

In the aforesaid year also, 1471 from the Lord’s nativity, John Kolnhausen, abbot of this monastery, obtained certain altars, namely the chapel of St. George in Dalen, that of St. Anthony here in the monastery, and others; all these, incorporated into this monastery in the reign of Frederick III, emperor, or earlier, were confirmed by Francis, cardinal deacon of the title of St. Eustace of the holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See, as is clear in the letters.

In the same year also, in the month of December and through January of the following year, a dreadful and enormous comet appeared for almost eighty days, fiery in color, glowing red at the beginning of Libra. Stretching out its tail at length, and little by little turning toward the north, it turned everyone to fear and wonder.

1482. In the third year of John Kolnhausen, our abbot, a very grave dissension arose between Rupert, archbishop of Cologne, and the chapter of the greater church. This so stirred the bishop’s mind to fury that in various places outside Cologne he seized by force the revenues of the lords of the chapter and applied them to his own uses. This did not turn out to his good, but rather to his loss and everlasting disgrace, as in the next year and those following we shall say more fully in the proper place.

In the same year also three men were appointed and hired at a great price to deliver the town of Neuss into the hands of the aforesaid archbishop of Cologne. One of them, named Basilius, after also receiving money from the people of Neuss, handed over his accomplices, Frederick Schruff and Eberhard Bock, into their hands. As soon as they came to Neuss and disembarked from the boat, they were captured after a signal had been given by this betrayer; confessing the intent of their crime, they were beheaded and divided into four parts. From this came the pontiff’s fury against the people of Neuss; from this all the evil took its beginning.

In the same year also Frederick the Palatine sent Reynard, bishop of Worms, with certain others of his council to Cologne to attempt a settlement between the archbishop and the chapter. But they returned without effect; on the way up, not far from Rodenkirchen, together with the envoys of the aforesaid archbishop, they were captured, despoiled, and led away.

In the aforesaid year, around the feast of St. Martin, Frederick, count Palatine, sent his army to the Bohemian Forest for the destruction of a certain robber-castle, which was called Diffayve; it was taken by them with violent force, the robbers were killed, and the castle was overturned and razed to the ground. The captain was led away captive to Amberg. And thus the road through Bavaria was made safer for travellers.

1483. In the fourth year of John Kolnhausen, our abbot, after the monastery of Weissenburg had been brought back to observance after many wars and disturbances, Donatus, the thirty-first prior of this monastery, was sent there. After some years he was sent from there to Lobenhelt, became confessor of the nuns, and at last rested in the Lord.

And it should be noted that before and after him there were some sub-priors, whom they call presidents. For immediately from the beginning of the reform the sub-prior was John of Wesel, a monk of St. James near Mainz, indeed a good and gentle man; but, not remaining here long, he returned to his own monastery. After Donatus, John of Leiningen, the thirty-second prior of this monastery, was appointed, a monk sent here from St. James and established here; he presided in the office of prior for almost eight years, except for a short intervening time in which John of Oppenheim, a monk of St. James, was sub-prior, but he did not remain here long.

In the same year the canons of the greater church of Cologne, as their governor and that of the church of Cologne against Rupert the archbishop, chose Hermann, son of the provincial count of Hesse, their canon and provost of the church of Aachen, who after the death [Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheim.

... was made archbishop in place of Rupert. When he had been made governor, the citizens and townsmen of Bonn and Andernach, defecting from their lord the archbishop, did him homage of fealty, and very many evils followed in the church of Cologne. For, having gathered an army of his men, the aforesaid governor Hermann besieged and took certain castles of his lord the archbishop, and brought them under his own power and that of the chapter.

1474.

King Frederick of the Romans came to Trier.

In the fifth year of John Colnhausen, our abbot, Emperor Frederick III came to Trier with many princes and remained there in the Archbishop's Palace for almost two months. Among the other princes at that time at Trier was Charles, the last duke of Burgundy, who had his lodging in the monastery of St. Maximin outside the walls of Trier, and there, before the emperor, the princes, and all the people, displayed the magnificence of his power and riches. There are some who say that he coveted the glory of a kingdom, and for that reason had always invited the emperor to Trier, so that, raised by him to be king, he might carry out the rest with still more conspicuous pomp. As evidence is the fact that a diadem, sceptre, globe, and the other things pertaining to the coronation of a king had been prepared with great splendor. But afterward, when the emperor departed secretly, he was disappointed in his hope.

The magnificence of Charles of Burgundy.

Rupert, archbishop of Cologne, took the aforesaid Charles, duke of Burgundy, as his guardian and defender against Governor Hermann and the chapter of Cologne; and he at once, in the same year, on the fourth day before the Kalends of August, besieged the notable town of Neuss, in the place and name of that archbishop, with a very great multitude of armed men. The aforesaid Governor Hermann was in the town, and throughout the whole time of the siege, for ten months and twenty-seven days, persevered with the townsmen. Charles had many thousands of men in his army, and with engines and bombards often made very great assaults, but nevertheless achieved nothing.

Neuss is besieged by the duke of Burgundy.

In the preceding year the twenty-first provincial chapter of our order was held at Nuremberg.

The twenty-first provincial chapter is held.

Also in the same year, 1474, Philip, the illustrious count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria, on Quinquagesima Sunday, took as wife at Amberg Margaret, daughter of Duke Louis of Bavaria, surnamed the Rich, sister of Duke George. By her he begot Duke Louis, Philip bishop of Freising, Duke Rupert, Duke Frederick, and other sons as well as daughters. Moreover, this wife died in the eighteenth year of John Trithemius, abbot of this place, as we shall say in its proper place.

Philip the Palatine takes a wife.

1475.

In the sixteenth year of John Kolnhausen, our abbot, Adolph of Nassau, archbishop of Mainz, died on the eighth day [unclear] before the Ides of September in his castle of Eltville. After his death the canons of the greater church, using wise counsel, in order that they might bring the revenues of the church back into one, elected again as archbishop Diether of Isenburg, who had once been deposed; he presided a second time for six years and as many months. This Diether built anew a fortress at the end of the city of Mainz, which he wished to be called the castle of St. Martin. This archbishop Diether, as prelate for the second time, first established the university of the studium generale in the city of Mainz; after it had been endowed to some degree, he obtained its confirmation by the supreme pontiff and its enrichment with the customary privileges and graces.

Diether is made archbishop of Mainz a second time.

Foundation of the University of Mainz.

In the year noted above, on the vigil of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, Charles, duke of Burgundy, raised the siege of the town of Neuss and withdrew, by the persuasion and counsel of the emperor, who was then present to aid the people of Neuss with a very great multitude of armed men from all the princes and cities of the empire. After his departure, Hermann, governor of the church of Cologne, gradually obtained the castles, towns, fortifications, and villages of the greater part of the bishopric, so that Rupert's obedience was greatly diminished in a short time, which was pitiable to see. But Duke Charles moved his army against the duke of Lorraine around the feast of St. Martin, and, after the duke had been put to flight, received in surrender all his land and the whole duchy of Lorraine, and compelled all the inhabitants to render him homage.

The siege of the city of Neuss is raised.

The duke of Burgundy obtains the duchy of Lorraine.

In the same year, on the Ides of December, John, archbishop of Magdeburg, primate of Germany, son of Stephen duke of Bavaria and count of Sponheim, and brother of Duke Frederick of Simmern, our reformer, died, a devout and holy man.

John, bishop of Magdeburg, dies.

1476.

In the seventeenth year of John Kolnhausen, our abbot, the twenty-second provincial chapter of our order was held on the Monks' Mountain near Bamberg, on the third Sunday after the feast of Easter; at it presided Martin in Schwarzach, Hermann of St. James near Mainz, Henry in Blaubeuren, and John of St. Giles in Nuremberg, abbots of monasteries of our order.

The twenty-second provincial chapter is held.

In this same year there was in Franconia a certain drummer, a shepherd of brute animals, [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Trithemius

The gathering of the people at Niclashausen. A poor and unlearned man at the little village of Niclashausen said that the blessed Mary, Mother of God, had appeared to him in the fields and had given him commands that, preaching publicly to the people, he should rebuke the vices and greed of the clergy; that tolls and transit-dues were not to be paid to princes; that all waters, fisheries, woods, and hunting-rights were common to all; that the commands of priests and bishops were not to be obeyed, nor their judgments heeded; and that neither tithes nor rents were to be given to anyone. To this fool there was a gathering of peoples from all Germany, as to some most holy prophet; much money was offered, miracles were fabricated, and many things were done contrary to the purity of the Christian faith. That foolish man would stand in some house and, while a certain fugitive monk whispered the word to him, would preach to the people through a window; they listened to him all the more gladly, the more he attempted to injure and diminish ecclesiastical liberty and the lordships of princes. Wondrous madness of fools. When the fame of the new prophet had been stirred up from distant regions, a very great multitude of people flowed together, and they adored that wretched and wholly foolish man on knees bent to the ground, crying, while he heard and tolerated it, “Holy man, have mercy on us.” But they also tore away pieces of his clothing for a shrine and relics, and a man considered himself fortunate if he had deserved to touch, see, or hear him. There was a continual and uninterrupted running thither; people of both sexes and ages lay at night in the fields, meadows, and neighboring woods, and many impurities occurred. At last Rudolph, bishop of Würzburg, in whose parish Niclashausen is, sent his armed men, seized the false prophet himself, caused him, after he had confessed the deceit and presumptuous impiety, to be burned, and so the pilgrimage of fools to that place ceased. 1477.

[Unclear] rashness of foolish men. In the eighth year of John Kolnhausen, our abbot, Pope Sixtus IV, at the instance of lord Frederick, duke of Bavaria and count in Sponheim, and of Margrave Christopher of Baden, appointed him apostolic commissioner over the incorporation of certain prebends of the newly collegiate church in Wolf on the Moselle in the diocese of Trier, which the aforesaid princes had handed over to the Brothers called the Grey Brothers of the Common Life, to be possessed in perpetuity, and he confirmed the whole transaction.

The false prophet [unclear] died by burning. In the same year Eberhard the Elder, count of Württemberg, who afterwards was raised to be duke by Maximilian, king of the Romans, at [unclear], established a gymnasium or general school in his town of Tübingen, in the diocese of Constance. In the province of Mainz he also raised the parish church of St. George into a collegiate church, and caused both it and the university, provided with a sufficient stipend, to be confirmed by Pope Sixtus IV and fortified with the necessary privileges, after the custom of other universities.

The University of Tübingen is established. Also in the same year the duke of Lorraine, together with the confederated Swiss, attacked Charles, duke of Burgundy, by whom he had been driven from his duchy the previous year, and defeated and killed him. After his death the aforesaid duke recovered Lorraine. The king of France brought Burgundy under his scepter, down to the present day; and other princes, seizing some things, diminishing Charles’s dominion, scattered it, and just as it had grown little by little, so it suddenly failed. He left one only daughter, named Mary, betrothed to Maximilian, duke of Austria; with her he obtained Holland, Hainaut, Zeeland, Brabant, together with the duchy of Luxembourg, and granted them to Philip his son, the son of himself and Mary. For the duchy of Guelders he had many labors and wars, but down to the present day he has by no means been able to obtain it.

Charles, duke of Burgundy, is killed. In the year noted above, on the twelfth day of the month of December, died the illustrious and most Christian prince-elector [Frederick?], buried among the Friars Minor at Heidelberg, in their habit, with great pomp: a lover of the clergy, promoter of all observant monks, defender of the poor and of widows, a most upright advocate of churches, who did as much for peace and the defense of all his people asking his aid as no prince in Germany had done in three hundred years past. He, as my opinion holds, if he had been emperor of the Romans, the Turk would not have torn so many kingdoms, so many provinces, so many cities from Christian dominion; or if the emperor had been such as this man was. When he had died, our most excellent prince, happily ruling today, in this very year undertook the governance of the paternal duchy, which he had governed in the name of guardianship after his father’s death for twenty-six years, being in the twenty-eighth year of his age: a renowned prince, gentle, brilliant and subtle in intellect, strong no less in counsel than in arms, a lover of peace, and a very keen defender and guardian of his subjects.

Frederick, count palatine, dies. 1478.

Philip’s principate of the Palatinate. In the ninth year of John Kolnhausen, our abbot, died Matthias of Rammung, bishop of Speyer, chancellor of the illustrious prince, the magnificent count palatine, a distinguished man and of his churches [unclear]

Ludwig becomes bishop of Speyer. [Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheim.

...a most steadfast promoter and defender of his own [church]; he was succeeded in the episcopate by Ludovicus de Helmstat, who today is in the twenty-fourth year of his pontificate over the church of Speyer, a peaceable, gentle man, a lover of the clergy and a supporter of all honorableness and religion, who, as such, deserves from all men the testimony of purity and integrity.

Ludovicus, firstborn of the Palatine, is born.

In the same year, on the second day of the month of July, that is, on the day of the Visitation of blessed Mary ever virgin, at about the third hour after midday, there was born in the castle of Heidelberg the illustrious prince Ludovicus, firstborn of our most distinguished prince Philip, Count Palatine and Duke of Bavaria, who today, being in the twenty-fourth year of his age, does not yet have a wife.

In the same year also, around the feast of Pentecost, Rupert, archbishop of Cologne, according to the report of certain persons, was captured by the soldiers of Henry, provincial count of Hesse, brother of Hermann, governor of Cologne; he was placed in custody in the castle of Blanckenstein, survived there for two years in the greatest distress, and died there.

In this same year Otto, formerly abbot of this monastery, died on Mount St. Rupert near Bingen, where for eight years he had held the office of confessor. He was buried there in the chapel of blessed Mary ever virgin, near the entrance to the cloister.

In the same year also Johannes Schonborn, dean of the church of St. John at Mainz, by commission of Pope Sixtus IV made in the preceding year, incorporated the parish church of this village of Sponheim into this monastery, at the request of Johannes Kolnhausen, abbot.

In the same year also the aforesaid Abbot Johannes closed the principal gate of the monastery, which had been situated on the southern side, where the abbot's residence now is, on account of the excessive movement of those passing through; he made a new one toward the east, where it now is.

1379.

In the tenth year of Johannes Kolnhausen, our abbot, Johannes Ruchard of Upper Wesel, doctor of sacred theology, was condemned at Mainz to recant certain articles which he was said to have preached publicly in the church of Worms, compelled by the doctor inquisitor. All his volumes, while he himself looked on, were handed over to the fire and burned; he himself, to carry out penance, was banished to the convent of the Augustinian friars there, and, consumed by grief, died shortly afterward.

The first article which he was said to have preached was: that the prelates of the church did not have authority to establish or add anything to those things which Christ and the apostles had commanded; indeed, that neither the apostles nor the supreme pontiffs received such power from Christ.

The second article: that it is permitted to no man, however holy, learned, or educated, to expound the words of Christ and the Gospel; that sacred Scripture was not interpreted by the holy fathers in the spirit in which it was first handed down and established.

The third article was against the authority of the pope and the keys of holy mother church: for he said that indulgences were nothing other than pious frauds and deceptions of Christians, and that those were therefore foolish and senseless who went to Rome for indulgences, which they could have found at home, provided they were truly contrite for their sins with the intention of amendment.

The fourth article, following from the first: that the commands of the church, of the pope, and of other prelates do not bind under mortal sin, because they do not have authority to establish law.

The fifth article: that there is not, nor ever has been, original sin; nor are little children conceived in original [sin], nor for that reason damned; and that he himself had never been subject to original sin.

The sixth article was: that all priests are in reality bishops; [unclear] priests confer nothing upon men toward salvation, but that men can be saved by faith, concord, and peace without priests.

The seventh article: that fasting, since it was not instituted by Christ, does not bind us to fast; for the church cannot bind one who is unwilling in that which Christ did not command, since it does not have authority to establish canons and laws, as in the first article.

The eighth article: that extreme unction is not a sacrament, because it was instituted not by Christ but by men; but that oil remains oil just as it was before.

The ninth article was: since it is nowhere read in sacred Scripture that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, but rather the contrary, it is better to believe, with the wise Greeks, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and not from the Son, because the Son said this.

He is also reported to have preached many other erroneous articles, such as that the canonical hours should not be said, that feasts should not be observed, that the continence of clerics should not be observed, that the church also can err and has erred; that blessings of inanimate things in the church, of herbs, lights, water, vessels, vestments, and the like, should not be cared for; and many others. Yet he publicly recanted all of these in the year written above, on the Sunday Esto mihi.

In the same year Ludovicus, king of France, with a strong force obtained the duchy [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Trithemius

The king of France obtains Burgundy.

The war of Maximilian, Duke of Austria, against the people of Guelders.

... of Burgundy, and the County, with many towns and cities of Artois and Picardy, which by right had devolved upon the Duke of Austria together with his wife. In the same year also the aforesaid Maximilian, Duke of Austria, with the help of the Duke of Cleves, entered the Gelders territory with an army, as legitimate heir after the death of Duke Charles his father-in-law. When the inhabitants of the land refused to admit him, hoping that they would receive back their own lord, a captive of the king of France, he besieged Nijmegen; but he made little progress. For, after making a sortie, those who were in the town put his army to flight, carrying off the war engines and no small amount of equipment.

The twenty-third provincial chapter is celebrated.

In the year noted above as well, on the second Sunday after the feast of Easter, the twenty-third provincial chapter of our order was held in the monastery of St. Giles at Nuremberg. Presiding there were Martin in Schwartzach, Leonard in Kastl, Bernhard in Hirsau, and Hermann of St. James near Mainz, abbots of our order; many statutes for the reform of the order were made there.

Louis, Duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Rich, dies.

He left a son and a daughter.

In the same year Louis, Duke of Bavaria, surnamed the Rich, died, a strong and vigorous man, who waged many wars bravely against Albert, Margrave of Brandenburg, indeed, when provoked by Emperor Frederick, against many cities of the Empire, and always came out victorious. He left an only son, Duke George, who had as wife Hedwig, daughter of the king of Poland, and who died in the nineteenth year of John Trithemius as abbot; [and] an only daughter named Margaret, who had married Philip, Count Palatine, a most illustrious prince, of whom we shall speak in her proper place.

1480.

Philip, the second-born Palatine, is born.

In this year, which was the eleventh of our abbot John Kolnhausen, on the seventh day of the month of May, there was born the second-born son of our most illustrious prince Philip, Count Palatine, Duke of Bavaria and prince elector. He received his father’s name in baptism and was called Philip, and later was made bishop of Freising.

Rupert, Archbishop of Cologne, died.

In the same year, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, Rupert, Archbishop of Cologne, died in his wretched captivity in the castle of Blankenstein, as was said, under the pope’s excommunication. His corpse was carried to Bonn and, after some months, was buried in the church of St. Cassius. O fortune, O envy, O the times and morals: what does ambition not presume?

Hermann succeeds.

After his death, Hermann, son of the Landgrave of Hesse, governor of the chapter and church of Cologne, was unanimously elected on the third day before the Ides of August, and now is in the twenty-second year of his pontificate: a good man, excellent, gentle, outstanding in counsel and action, who throughout the whole time of the siege of Neuss fought vigorously for the citizens.

Sigismund, formerly Bishop of Würzburg, dies.

In the same year too died Sigismund, Duke of Saxony, formerly Bishop of Würzburg. After his death Bishop Rudolf von Scherenberg was compelled to pay his brothers more than 33,000 florins on account of a delayed payment.

The mother of Philip the Palatine dies.

In the year noted above also died Margaret, daughter of the famous Amadeus, Duke of Savoy, mother of our most illustrious prince Philip the Palatine mentioned above. After the death of Duke Louis, her first husband, namely Philip’s father, she had married Ulrich, Count of Württemberg, leaving her little son in the guardianship, as has been said, of Frederick.

A singular monastery in Kreuznach.

Around these times the monastery of the Friars Minor of the Observance in Kreuznach was founded by Frederick, Count Palatine, Duke of Bavaria and Count in Sponheim, father of Duke John, who is residing today in Simmern, with the offering of the faithful assisting. For a certain citizen of the aforesaid town of Kreuznach placed a small image of St. Wolfgang, carved from wood, in the chapel or church of that same new foundation. In a short time so great a gathering of peoples began to come to it, and miracles to be proclaimed, that the whole work begun was very quickly completed from the offering of the people. Nor did the repute of miracles cease until the brothers, lovers of peace and poverty, removed the image; then the fame of signs ceased, and the gathering of peoples was gradually reduced.

The island of Rhodes is besieged by the Turk.

1481.

The monastery of Limburg is reformed.

In the twelfth year of our abbot John, the monastery of Limburg of our order, in the diocese of Speyer, was reformed by Hermann, abbot of St. James near Mainz, [and by] our aforesaid abbot Kolnhausen. There Boniface, a monk, was ordained as abbot Sponheim.

1484.

In the first year of Johannes Trithemius, our abbot, Albert, administrator of Mainz, a young man of good promise, died in May and was buried in the church of Mainz itself. After his death the canons of the greater church, on the twentieth day of the month of May, unanimously elected as archbishop Berthold of Henneberg, dean of the aforesaid church, a prudent man, outstanding in counsel and deed, who today governs his church vigorously and is spending the eighteenth year of his pontificate in peace and tranquility.

Berthold becomes archbishop of Mainz. Johannes becomes prior of this place, the 34th.

In the same year Abbot Trithemius appointed as the thirty-fifth prior of this monastery Johannes of Tonna, a Thuringian by birth, first a monk of the monastery of Gerode and later of this place: indeed a good and disciplined man, but without vigor, and for the most part more clouded in brain than was proper. Therefore he could not persevere long in the priorate, because he did not know the measure that should have been distributed to each man according to place and time.

In the year noted above also, on Monday after the octave of Easter, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of this monastery, had the altar in the sacristy consecrated in honor of St. Anne, mother of the most blessed Mother of God, of St. Jerome the priest, of St. Benedict the abbot, of St. Scrutatius, bishop of the Tungri, and of St. Barbara, virgin and martyr, by Berthold, bishop of [Pariadensis?], vicar in pontificals of Albert of Mainz, then administrator and still living; in that altar many relics of the saints were, according to custom, deposited.

In the same year the Friars Minor of the Observance began to inhabit the place and monastery for them in Kreuznach, built by Duke Frederick, count in Sponheim, formerly residing in [Siernem?], as we said above, in the ninth year of Abbot Johannes Kolnhausen.

In this same year there grew a very great abundance of wine throughout the whole land, such as, or as great as, had not existed in human memory. This abundance was first observed at the very time of the vintage, and because of it a great shortage of vessels arose. For one vessel, bought for three florins, which they call a [plausitale?], contained only one florin’s worth of wine, and a wagonload of the best wine was sold for one florin of common money, although the vessel had been bought for three gold coins. For wine had become so cheap in this year that some of the peasants, disregarding water, mixed the mortar of walls with wine; others, so that they might draw new wine, poured the old out upon the ground; and some did not even take care to gather it all, because of the excessive abundance. And for us, as is known, there grew in this year one hundred wagonloads of wine, something which, in human memory, happened neither before nor after; the shortage of the following year offset this abundance. For the ingratitude of the people deserved the vengeance of God, as the matter itself showed.

1485.

In the second year of Johannes our abbot, in mid-Lent, on Laetare Sunday, Berthold, elected and confirmed as archbishop of Mainz, was consecrated by Johannes Camerarius Dalburg, bishop of Worms, at Mainz in the principal church, with Ludovicus of Speyer and Berthold of [Panadensis?], bishops, standing by, and with many abbots also present: Johannes Trithemius of this monastery, of St. James, in Blidenstadt, in Seligenstadt, in Amorbach, in Limburg, in Otterberg, on Mount St. Disibod, and many others, with great pomp and solemnity. When the office had been completed, they were all called to the table [unclear].

In the same year, on the third Sunday after the feast of Easter, the twenty-fifth provincial chapter of our order was celebrated in the monastery of St. Ulrich at Augsburg. Presiding there were Johannes of St. Egidien in Nuremberg, Johannes Trithemius of this our monastery, Heinrich in Weissenburg, and Paul in Elchingen, abbots of monasteries of our order; and in that same chapter many things were established for the preservation of the order.

At about this time the monastery in Salza, in the diocese of Strasbourg, at the urging of apostate monks who sought this by their cooperation, was transferred from the order into a secular college, and from bad monks they were made worse canons. Violating without cause the vow made to God, they will find the wages of their crime.

In this same year God punished the ingratitude shown to him by the peasants in the preceding year with a harsh enough chastisement, since as great as the abundance of wine had been in that year, so great a shortage followed in the next. For very little wine grew that year. And, to measure the others by ourselves: we, who in the preceding year had had one hundred wagonloads, scarcely received one in this year from all the growths, tithes, and revenues together.

L1 Sponheim.

[unclear] of St. James, but he did not preside for long. To this monastery of Limburg, however, in favor of the newly introduced reform, Johannes Colnhausen sent Johannes de Liningen, the thirty-second prior of this monastery, not without harm to this place. After him he appointed as the thirty-third prior Heinrich of Holtzhausen, a Saxon, a professed monk at Northeim, a learned, religious, and devout man, an outstanding zealot for regular observance; he scarcely completed two years in the priorate, and was deposed through the envy of certain men who, walking according to the flesh, hated one who corrected them.

In the same year Muhammad, the great emperor of the Turks, a most bitter persecutor of Christians, died, leaving two sons. One of them, Bayezid, having seized for himself the empire of the Turks, compelled his other brother, named Zyzymus, driven from the kingdom, to live in exile first among the Rhodians, then among the French, and finally among the Romans, 45,000 ducats being assigned each year for expenses to those who held him.

In the same year also died Johannes, duke of Cleves, a great-hearted and warlike man.

1482.

In this year, which was the thirteenth of our abbot Johannes Colnhausen, Diether of Isenburg, archbishop of Mainz, died on the seventh day of the month of May; he was buried in the greater church with this inscription:

Twice made prelate, Count Diether of Isenburg built the citadel of Mainz and also the school.

He was a good man, and greatly loved monastic observance; while living he conferred many benefits and favors devoutly upon God and religious persons. After his death, just as he himself while still living had arranged, Albert, son of Ernest, duke of Saxony and margrave of Meissen, being in the eighteenth year of his age, was received by the chapter as administrator of the church of Mainz, and was confirmed by Sixtus, the Roman pontiff; at his father’s request he also received provision to succeed to the archbishopric. But after completing two years in his administration, the innocent young man died.

In the same year, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, Reinhard of Sickingen, bishop of Worms, died and was buried in the chapel of St. Giles, which he himself had newly built beside the greater church. He was succeeded by Johannes Camerarius of Dalberg, provost of the greater church, a man worthy of greater honor: the glory of pontiffs, the ornament of nobles, the prince and glory of all philosophers and learned men, most learned in every science. Among pontiffs Germany had no equal to him, nor Italy a better. To him Johannes Trithemius, abbot of this monastery, later begins his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, a varied work.

In the same year also Johannes Trithemius, later abbot, became a monk of this monastery quite miraculously, contrary to his intention; it happened thus. When he had set out from Heidelberg with a scholastic companion for his homeland, he entered this monastery, because it lay on the road, for the sake of seeing it, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the morning around the ninth hour, his companion not merely persuading him but rather compelling him. After dinner had been taken, thinking of nothing less than religious life, he departed to continue the journey he had begun. And when, ignorant of the roads, both had come to the mountain adjoining the little village of Bockenau, there suddenly began to arise an immense mass of snow and a dense storm of clouds, which not only covered the path of the road, but, striking their faces from ahead, almost blinded their eyes. Therefore, when his companion on the journey advised a return to the monastery, since it was not possible to go on, Trithemius replied: “It is too shameful to return; rather let us go forward as far as we can.” But when they had waited up to three times under the shelter of trees for the end of the storm, and it was increasing altogether, Trithemius again said to his companion: “We must return to the monastery; behold, you will see me remain there.” I do not know by what divine prompting he said this, for when he said it he was thinking of nothing less than entering religious life. Unwillingly, therefore, but of necessity, he returned to this place; in the aforesaid year and day, in accordance with his own word which he had spoken unknowingly, he changed his mind, induced by the persuasion of Heinrich of Holtzhausen, our prior, and, intending to remain, put off the secular habit on the day of the Purification of the blessed Mary ever virgin. He became a novice on the day of our most holy father Benedict, and in the same year, on the feast of the most pure Conception of Mary, he was professed according to the Rule with three others.

In the year likewise noted above, the twenty-fourth provincial chapter of our order was celebrated at Blaubeuren, after the feast of Easter, on the third Sunday. Presiding at it were Georg of St. Stephen’s in Würzburg, Johannes in Willingen, Ulrich of Mönchberg, and Johannes of St. Giles in Nuremberg, abbots of monasteries of our order.

In the same year Johannes de Bourbon, bishop of Liège, was killed by a certain knight.

In the year also mentioned above, when Heinrich of Holtzhausen, prior of this monastery, Sponheimense.

... judged by most people excessive, for the sake of preserving peace he was deposed and, because of a certain necessity that arose, was appointed cellarer, full of shame.

1487.

In this year, which was the fourth of our abbot Johannes Trithemius, on the fourth day of March died that famous hermit Nicholas in Swida, in the district of the Suitenses or Swiss, not far from the town of Lucerne, in a vast solitude. For many years in that same hermitage, in great poverty, humility, patience, and holiness, he served the Lord strenuously as a solitary; before his death he lived for twenty continuous years without bodily food, as we have learned by the testimony of the bishop of Constance, in whose parish he dwelt, and of several other trustworthy persons. He also had the spirit of prophecy, and foretold to his people certain future things which later came to pass. A great concourse of pilgrims came to him even from distant regions, since his dwelling was not far from the monastery of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of the Hermits. This man of God was a miracle to us in his time: although he was wholly ignorant of all letters, nevertheless he flourished in understanding of the Scriptures with wonderful subtlety, and gave answers to the questions of learned men of every kind, just as that holy hermit Anthony, a most learned philosopher, is said once to have given them without letters. Yet he did not admit everyone indiscriminately to conversation with him, but only those whom he had recognized by the divine spirit to be stirred to speak; finally, he is said to have shone with miracles.

In the same year, since the altar in the castle of Sponheim, long since incorporated into this monastery, had collapsed with its chapel from excessive age and threatened ruin at every hour, so that no one dared to celebrate Mass upon it, Johannes Trithemius, abbot, with the consent of the archbishop prince, transferred it here to the monastery with all its rights and revenues. He, although he was wholly ignorant of all things, nevertheless flourished in understanding of the Scriptures with wonderful subtlety, and answers were given to the questions of learned men of every kind, just as that holy hermit Anthony, a most learned philosopher, is said once to have given them without letters. Yet he did not admit everyone indiscriminately to conversation with him, but only [those?] whom he had recognized by the divine spirit to be stirred to speak; finally, he is said to have shone with miracles.

In the same year, on the third day before the Ides of July, that is, on the day of Saint Margaret, virgin and martyr, our aforesaid abbot Johannes caused the chapel and altar to be consecrated in honor of Saints John, Pancras, Jerome the priest, Bernard the abbot, Catherine virgin and martyr, Catherine of Siena, and the eleven thousand virgins, by Heinrich, bishop of [unclear], vicar in pontifical matters of Berthold, archbishop of Mainz, with the customary indulgences granted. After the meal had been completed, he solemnly blessed here in the monastery two new bells, one of which abbot Trithemius had caused to be cast, and the other he had purchased for a price.

Also in the year noted above, on the third Sunday after the celebration of the feast of Easter, the twenty-sixth provincial chapter of our order was held in the monastery of Saint James near Mainz. Presiding over it were Heinrich of Weissenburg, Conrad at Wiblingen, Bertram of Saint Gotthard in Hildesheim, and Johannes at Seligenstadt, abbots of monasteries of our order.

In the same year, on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, died Conrad of Rodenberg, abbot of our order on the Mount of Saint John in the Rheingau, a very religious, devout, and learned man, a special lover of regular observance. For him our abbot Johannes Trithemius wrote an epitaph, and fixed it to the wall beside his tomb:

Stay your steps a little, and pause a while, traveler, for here you see the tomb of Conrad Rodenberg. The holy Mount, which the famous Rhine river beholds, held him; in character and talent there was no one equal to him. He had been the most renowned abbot of this monastery, a cultivator of virtues, a lover of religion.

Nicholas the admirable hermit died.

He led an exceedingly austere life.

The chapel of Saint Pancras in the valley was built [unclear].

The aforesaid chapel is consecrated.

The twenty-sixth provincial chapter is held. Chronicle of Trithemius

[unclear], since he was striving with the greatest zeal to maintain and enlarge the observance of regular discipline, incurred the hatred of certain men who were carnally minded; and at their insistence, John Kolnhausen, our abbot, moved, alas, deposed him from the priorship, to the perpetual loss of the monastic discipline of this community. Having sent him to Lobenfeld in the diocese of Worms, he appointed him confessor of the nuns; but, not remaining there long, he returned to Northeim, his monastery in Saxony. For the aforesaid lord John Kolnhausen, our abbot, at that time had three convents of nuns of our order entrusted to him, namely Bibelis in the diocese of Strasbourg, Nuvvenburg, and Lobenfeld in that of Worms, for which he was compelled to provide. After him there was no prior for two years, but an interprior or president appointed by the said abbot: Henry Molitoris of Gelnhausen, one of the first reformers sent here from St. James, a good and gentle man, but too lax in correcting offenders; for that reason he was later deposed.

Henry the prior is deposed.

Henry becomes interprior.

1483.

In the fourteenth year of John Kolnhausen our abbot, William, provincial count of Hesse, died. He had as wife the daughter of Philip, the last count of Katzenelnbogen; with her, after the death of his father-in-law, he obtained that county with a very great treasure, and joined it to the county of Hesse down to the present day.

William Ludgerianus of Hesse dies.

The county of Katzenelnbogen is transferred to Hesse.

In the same year, on the seventeenth day of the month of July, after the death of Abbot Reinhard, lord John of Kolnhausen, the twenty-fourth abbot of this monastery, with the consent and will of lord Albert, administrator of the church of Mainz, was transferred to the abbacy of the monastery of Saints Marcellinus and Peter in Seligenstadt, while the convent of this community protested against it and opposed it with all its strength, but accomplished nothing. He afterwards resigned our abbacy into the hands of the convent, on the twenty-seventh day of the same month, which was the Sunday immediately after the feast of St. James. He governed the aforesaid monastery of Seligenstadt for almost nine years; afterwards, weighed down by age and illness, he resigned the abbacy there also. Surviving thirty months, he died: certainly an excellent man, who did many good things for both this monastery and that one.

John Kolnhausen is transferred to Seligenstadt.

Concerning John Trithemius, twenty-fifth abbot of this monastery; concerning certain deeds done by him, and various events of that time. He presided for twenty-three years, two months, and fourteen days, and was transferred to Würzburg.

After the transfer and resignation of John Kolnhausen, abbot of this monastery, to Seligenstadt, Henry the president and the capitular brothers, setting the twenty-ninth day of the month of July for the election of a new pastor, meanwhile summoned by messengers and letters those absent from the monastery. After a three-day fast had first been observed, with the customary prayers, and after the visitors deputed to them by the order had been summoned for the appointed date, namely Hermann, abbot of St. James near Mainz, and Conrad, abbot of the monastery of St. John in the Rheingau, they appeared together with lord John Kolnhausen, formerly abbot here but then abbot in Seligenstadt, and on that very day of Felix, pope and martyr, which is the fourth day before the Kalends of August and was the Tuesday after the feast of St. James, they began in the name of God to hold the business of the election. Therefore, after the Mass of the Holy Spirit had been solemnly celebrated, the brothers assembled in the chapter place adopted the way of compromise, which seemed safer, to be observed in the election. They committed the matter to two abbots, Hermann of St. James and John of Seligenstadt, and three from the convent: Henry of Gelnhausen, president; John of Donna, custodian; and John of Dreysa, master of the donors, so that, after hearing in secret the votes of each before a notary and witnesses, they should elect as abbot of this monastery, in the name of the whole convent, the one to whom the greater and sounder part had directed its votes. When, therefore, the votes of all had been examined, the greater and sounder part elected John Trithemius as abbot, who had been in the order only eight months and seven days after his profession. He was younger in the order than all the professed, seeing that from the time when he assumed the novices’ habit he had lived in the monastery no more than one year, three months, and seven days up to the day of his election. Therefore, when the election was published, all unanimously consented to him, and each signed the decree of election with his own hand. Thus elected in the year and on the day prescribed, in the same year, on the day of the Assumption of blessed Mary ever virgin, he was confirmed by Albert, administrator of the church of Mainz, in the castle of Steinheim, there being present Hermann of St. James, John in Seligenstadt, Melchior in Schöntal, abbots of our order, and very many others. After this, in the same year, on the fifth day before the Ides of November, which was the Sunday before the feast

The form of election was by compromise.

John Trithemius becomes abbot.

He is confirmed on the day of the Assumption of Mary. [Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheim.

On the feast of St. Martin he received the office of blessing in the church of St. James near Mainz from Berthold, bishop of Pariadensis, vicar in pontificals of the aforesaid lord administrator, while standing by him, in the customary manner and vested in pontificals, were Herman, abbot of the same place, and Anselm, abbot of the monastery of Limburg, of our order, whom he had requested.

The native origin of Johannes Trithemius.

This Johannes Trithemius was a Mosellan by country, born in a certain village, Trittenheim, which lies about four miles from Trier, downstream on the left side of the river Moselle. He was born of honorable parents, of moderate fortune, yet free, his father being Johannes of Montegentili and his mother named Elizabeth of Longouicum; the cultivation of vines supplied them with the necessities of life.

When the boy was scarcely one year old, his father died. His mother, out of love for the child, lest the little one be exposed to the injuries of a stepfather, as often happens, remained a widow for seven years. When that time had at last passed, she took a second husband, with whom she also begot several other children; all of them, however, except one son, died in youth. But Johannes, when he was fifteen years old, against the wishes of his parents and all his relatives, touched by love of letters and in a certain way assured by a wonderful vision concerning his future learning, began secretly to learn letters. When this became known to his stepfather, he attacked him with harsh words and harsher blows, and tried with all his strength to draw him away from the literary purpose that he had. Yet the more he afflicted him daily by forbidding him, the more he inflamed him with a more fervent desire for letters. For at night, since by day it was not allowed except on feast-days, and then secretly, when everyone was asleep he would leave the house and go to a certain neighboring friend who had once devoted himself to letters; from him he received the rudiments of elementary instruction in a very short time, so that even the teacher himself, greatly amazed, said that he had never seen so teachable an intellect or a livelier memory in any man. And this prefigured the vision that he had, which, as he revealed it, we have learned to have been as follows.

He had a vision concerning the knowledge of the scriptures.

For the space of one year, with continual fasts and prayers, he asked the Lord God with the greatest intentness for two very great things, one of which was knowledge of the scriptures; the other he said he had never disclosed to anyone. Behold, one night a young man in bright clothing seemed to stand by him as he slept, holding two tablets in his hands, one of which was written with letters, the other painted with certain images. He said to him: “Choose from these two tablets whichever one you wish.” At once, burning with love of letters, which at that time he still knew not at all, even while sleeping, he chose the tablet that seemed to be written. The young man who had appeared said to him: “Behold, God has heard your prayers; he will give you both things that you asked for, and indeed more than you could have asked.”

The next day, although he was thinking nothing of the vision, a more wonderful occasion was given to him as he desired the beginnings of letters. For some time, then, in that same village he devoted himself to letters in secret, because he did not dare do so openly for fear of his parents. He learned the alphabet, the Lord’s Prayer with the Angelic Salutation, also the Apostles’ Creed, the Confession at the altar, and the blessing of food and drink perfectly in seven days, and committed them most tenaciously to memory. After this, he also accustomed himself within one month to read books in the German tongue most perfectly by himself.

With his uncle cooperating, he is permitted to visit the schools.

When his friends, and especially the priests, saw the young man’s great intellect and love for letters, they persuaded his uncle, Peter of Montegentili, a mature and severe man, to test what such vehement desire for letters in him portended. He consented, and, because he was his uncle, presented himself publicly as the young man’s guardian, despite the stepfather’s protest, and from then on began to take account of his patrimony. But how many blows, how many injuries, how many insults the innocent young man endured from his stepfather; how many showers of tears, in distress, he poured forth before he could escape his yoke, more cruel than any servitude.

At last he escaped the stepfather’s house, as the Israelite multitude escaped Egypt, and for love of letters he made a journey of three days through the wilderness; first at Trier, then in the lower regions, and finally in the town of Heidelberg. And thus, when the three-day journey in a foreign land, as we have said, had been completed, at last he offered himself in this present monastery to the Lord God as a perpetual burnt-offering. Once made a monk, he lived among the brothers without complaint, and preferred the study of letters and the solitude of his cell to all the delights of this world; and he seemed to thirst for nothing in this world more than knowledge of the scriptures.

The very great library is assembled by Trithemius.

But the small number of books in this monastery held him back somewhat from his purpose; this, however, as soon as he was ordained abbot, he was eager to remedy. For, as is clear from the inventory of the library, scarcely forty-seven volumes, counting all of them, were found in this monastery at the time of his ordination, of small value and of less use for true learning. But after he obtained the governance of this monastery, he began gradually to acquire many and various books in every facul[Blank page in the source scan.]

... more zealously to acquire, Greek and Latin, so many and so great, that today in all Germany no library is said to be like ours; in it are held so many rare, so many secret, so many varied volumes, known to few. For today in this monastery the number of books is so great that one place does not suffice for storing them; for they are more numerous than can be estimated. Of their number we shall speak in the nineteenth year of John Trithemius, our abbot, because then a registration of the volumes was made by him. For the library of this monastery is today proclaimed in every land to such an extent that many princes, bishops, doctors, masters, nobles, and very distinguished men, not only from nearby but also from distant regions, stirred by the name and fame of John Trithemius the abbot and of his volumes, wished to visit this place and did visit it, men to whom previously not even the name of the monastery was known. Among these it will not be useless to mention even a few, briefly, who, more eminent than the rest, deigned to visit the present monastery because of Trithemius’s fame. John Camerarius Dalberg, bishop of Worms; John Capnion of Pforzheim; Conrad Celtis Protucius, poet laureate; Franciscus Bonomus of Trieste, secretary of the queen of the Romans, a notable orator and poet: these four men are most learned in every science, most erudite orators and poets, truly profound contemplators of theology, most skilled in the Latin, Greek, and Hebrew languages, distinguished no less for piety than for prudence. Some of these, not content to have seen the place and the man once, returned a second and a third time; the longer they remained here, the more they were held by desire for the volumes, the place, and the man.

But that most learned man, Jodocus Beysclidus, a patrician of the city of Aachen; also Henry Bunaugius, knight, well instructed in all scripture, secretary of the princes of Saxony; John Cuspinianus, a Frank, poet laureate, physician of the renowned city of Vienna in Austria; Andreas Stiborius, a Bavarian, theologian and most profound mathematician; Jacob Wimpfeling of Schlettstadt, theologian, notable orator and poet; Rutgerus Sieamber, canon of Deventer, a man of much reading; Aquinus, a Swede by nation, the subtlest of all mathematicians; Wilhelm Monapus, arithmetician, mathematician, and singular theologian; John Palyonidorus, a man of great study; Martheus Herbenus, inhabitant of Maastricht, eloquent orator and most excellent musician; Jacob, prior of the Wilhelmites at Bruges, historiographer; Aegidius Delphius, Parisian theologian and poet, most outstanding of all; John of Westphalia, theologian and most diligent historiographer; John Tholassus, a Bavarian, canon of Regensburg, jurist and truly admirable astronomer; Adam Werner of Themar, jurist and praised poet; Jason the Italian, poet; Jacob Draconcius, celebrated orator and poet; Jodocus Gallus of Rouffach, theologian, preacher of the church of Speyer, most pleasing orator and poet; Franciscus Wiler, poet and theologian; Gabriel Biel, most famous theologian; John Spegeler of the Order of Minors, theologian, most vigorous defender of Mary’s conception against the Maculists; Theoderic Gresmund the Younger, excellent poet and jurist; Mutianus Rufus, rhetorician, historiographer, and most learned poet; John Vigilius of Sondheim, jurist, patron of philosophers; John Lanshemius, provost of Deventer, a studious man composing many things.

All those written above, stirred by Trithemius’s fame, some from nearby places, some from remote ones, but all coming here from their own places, some once, some twice, and several as many as three times and more, came to see Trithemius and the library of this monastery. Among them were many others whose names do not come to memory, stirred by the same spirit; some of them, for a month, others for two or three, and several for the space of one year, with their expenses paid, remained in this monastery out of love for letters, both Latin and Greek, in which Abbot Trithemius was held to be abundantly furnished. But since he was a gentle man and a most upright lover of peace, and had heard that some of the brothers were murmuring because he tolerated either monks or even foreign secular men in the monastery for the sake of learning, although without detriment to the monastery, he dismissed them all. Afterward he could with difficulty be persuaded, although many offered themselves, doctors and other wealthy men, to take anyone on for instruction. For he had simple and untrained monks, among whom, apart from two or three, scarcely anyone who loved letters was to be found; for this reason he preferred to labor in writing with outsiders rather than with his own. But we, since we know that his life has been described more fully by a certain disciple and friend of this place, though an outsider, restrain our pen, especially since he is still among men, knowing that he, placed as it were on a summit, has not lacked the embitterment of those below, which harmed us and the monastery, not him.

1484. Chronicle of Trithemius

In the same year also Johannes Thoringus, the thirty-fourth prior of this monastery, because of his importunity, since he was unable to be at rest in the office of the priorate, was deposed at his own excessive insistence; and Johannes de Dreysa, a Westphalian, formerly and afterward again a monk in Marienmünster, was appointed thirty-fifth prior of this place by Abbot Trithemius. He himself, unable suitably to moderate his behavior, although he was an old man, gray-haired, before he had completed two years in the priorate, was deposed for the sake of peace.

In the same year also Wilhelm of Arburg, who three years before had killed Johann of Bourbon, bishop of Liège, was captured by the brother of Johann of Horn, the succeeding bishop, taken to Maastricht by the Meuse, and beheaded, after peace had first been made between them, since nothing of the sort was suspected. Many evils followed in the whole land of Liège and the county of Horn, and many thousands of men were killed.

In this same year grain was being bought at a low price: for three malters of the best rye [unclear] after the necessary written records had been received. But the [inhabitants?] of the town of Bingen, a few days after the promise, forgetful of it, rashly violated the peace and concord, and again raised themselves up in arrogance against their lords, the canons of the greater church. When this had become known to the aforesaid archbishop, taking up nearly four hundred armed men, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December in the year noted above he came to Bingen; he was secretly admitted by a postern into the castle that lies next to the town, without the citizens knowing. And so, after those to be summoned had been called to him, and counsel had been held, he banished from the town certain of the citizens who had been leaders of the sedition, and forced the rest to obedience to their lords. Then, on the first day of the month of December, deposing the council, the scabini, and the judges, who had done many things wrongly, he appointed new ones. Lest frauds and deceptions continue in judicial business, he gave the city a common seal. For previously each judge or scabin had sealed with his own seal the case handled before him and reduced to writing, and many deceptions of the poor occurred.

In the same year Johannes Trithemius, abbot of this monastery, brought back into the possession of the monastery, as to one half, the estate in Nussbach, which Crafft the second, a knight, about one hundred years before had pledged for a fixed sum of money to his same kinsman, after it had been redeemed with much labor and expense; he could not obtain the other half, because the sale had been beyond the memory of men. That this estate of the monastery had been alienated under a certain title of repurchase, and not the other, could not be shown clearly enough.

In the same year also Johannes Trithemius, abbot, newly built the greater Stube, a guest-house, within the enclosure, and likewise altered the chambers. He also began to have made a new bell, which is rung at the elevation and at the brothers’ collation.

In this year wine, growing in small quantity, rose very greatly in price: for a cartload, which in the first year of Abbot Trithemius was sold for one florin, in this year could scarcely be bought for twenty gold Rhenish florins.

In the same year also, on the sixteenth day of the month of February, in the first week of Lent, Maximilian, duke of Austria, son of Emperor Frederick III, at the very great insistence of his father, was unanimously elected king of the Romans at Frankfurt, being in the eighteenth year of his age. The electors were Berthold, archbishop of Mainz; Johann, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria; Ernst of Saxony; and Albert, margrave of Brandenburg. After the feast of Easter the aforesaid princes, with many others, accompanying their chosen man with the greatest honor, led him to Aachen, and had him anointed and crowned according to custom by the hands of the aforesaid archbishop of Cologne, with the greatest pomp and solemnity, on the fifth day of April.

In the year noted above also Johannes Westphalus, the thirty-fifth prior of this monastery, was deposed because of the disorderliness of his conduct. After some months, during which Heinrich of Gelnhausen was subprior, Nicolaus of Kreuznach was appointed thirty-sixth prior of this monastery; he himself did not preside for long, because his severity [unclear]

Nicolaus, prior Chronicle of Trithemius, 400

For he first laid the foundations of our life, which flourishes illustrious under the name of Bursfeld. Sober and chaste, pious, upright, and quiet, whose food and manner of life were frugal and austere. He also had been seized with great love for the mother of Christ, and he wrote her praises. He himself, pious, was loved with great brotherly affection, and died on the day on which the holy Virgin gives birth. Therefore we all pray to God with just reason that he may grant him to dwell in the starry heaven. Trithemius the abbot set this up for you according to your merit, whom your vows at Sponheim brought as father.

“He laid the foundations of our life”: because he himself, by mandate of the fathers of the Chapter, first arranged the ordinal of the divine offices and the statutes, which we call ceremonies, into the order and form in which they are now held. He was present at the election of our abbot Trithemius; therefore it is said in the epitaph:

Gerard becomes abbot of St. John’s.

“Whom your vows at Sponheim brought as father.”

Gerard of Montabaur, cellarer of the monastery of St. James, succeeded him, and presided for eight years and nine months: a good man and a lover of regular observance, who governed the monastery well in both states.

1488.
