In the year of our abbot John Trithemius, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, Henry of Gelnhausen died, a monk of this community, sent here from the monastery of St. James at Mainz at the beginning of the reform: a man of competent learning, trained in verse and prose, leaving behind certain little works of his talent, not to be despised for reading, namely: On Spiritual Instruction, addressed to certain novices, an exhortation and a long letter; also the Life of Saint Benedict, described in elegiac verse; sermons against plurality of benefices; and various letters.

In the same year Maximilian, king of the Romans, was shut up and captured by the Flemings in the town of Bruges, and was detained for a long time in custody in a certain respectable dwelling, all thirty of his attendants being wholly excluded except for a single cook; others of the nobles were captured, none killed, while the rest took thought for themselves by flight. For the Flemings desired to exclude the king, whom they hated, from the rule of their lands, and to have his son Philip, still a youth and a boy, as lord, whom they themselves would govern according to their own will rather than be governed by him. But the great-souled king refused to give consent to their wicked desire; for that reason he was captured. Meanwhile Frederick, emperor of the Romans, having learned of his son’s captivity, assembled a very great army from the princes and cities of the Empire, all detesting the disgrace done to the king; and with three thousand four hundred twenty-two horsemen, and a company of five thousand nine hundred and [unclear] foot-soldiers, and with two hundred twenty-two wagons, he entered Flanders, devastating the whole land outside the cities with fire and plunder; he besieged Ghent for six weeks and freed his son.

In this year John Trithemius, our abbot, who otherwise was always intent, as far as he was allowed, upon the study of letters, began to commit his thoughts and discoveries to writing, lest his mind should seem to be shut up with harmful thoughts. Secondly, even if the things he wrote should profit no one, nevertheless in the course of time they would perfect his own understanding and, by practice, train his talent to a certain facility. Nor did his opinion deceive him: by the daily and continuous practice of writing he became so ready in dictating whatever came to hand that even the most learned all wondered at the facility of his discourse; and those who saw him writing extempore, on any subjects whatever, without premeditation, affirm that his discourse flowed rather than was written.

Therefore at the beginning he wrote a certain lengthy composition in four parts, On the Origin, Acquisition, Beauty, and Usefulness of the Virtues, in General and in Particular; because he could not polish it, on account of its excessive length and his various occupations, as he would have wished, he gave it to be burned in the fire. He also began a great work On the Praise of Virginity, which he has not yet completed. In the third year of his rule, moreover, he wrote certain treatises, some of which he corrected in this year; and afterward, at the request of friends, he permitted them to go forth in public and to be printed. At the request of a certain Nicholas of Mernich, priest, once his schoolfellow, he wrote On Priestly Justification, one book, which has been printed; also On the Vanity [Blank page in the source scan.]

Sponheim.

also one book on the present life, likewise printed; one book On the Property of Monks, also printed; On Ecclesiastical Writers, a great and laborious work, which he began in the fourth year of his rule and completed in the eleventh, and which likewise was made public in print; two books of Exhortations to Monks. Likewise two books On the Temptations of Monks. Likewise two books on the Rule of Saint Benedict. Five books On the Spiritual Life. An Investigation of the Scriptures. And likewise one book On the True Method of Studying. One book, The Mirror of the Life of a Religious Man. He wrote these in these times; they have not yet, however, been permitted to go out to the public. He delivered many addresses in chapters, both annual and provincial, in due course; some of them have been printed, but the rest have not.

His books not yet printed, which he also published in this year.

In the year noted above, Nicholas, the thirty-sixth prior of this monastery, was deposed for a certain necessity. For some time afterward John of Fulda was interprior, or president, a man excessively licentious; since he seemed less suitable for the preservation of discipline, he was rejected. John of Bingen was appointed the thirty-seventh prior of this place. He presided in the priorate for one year and six months; afterward, because of bodily infirmity, he had to be released from necessity, as we shall say in the following year.

1389.

In this year, which was the sixth of John Trithemius, our abbot, the monastery of our order of Saint Nicholas in Camberg, in the diocese of Wurzburg, with the consent and permission of Pope Innocent VIII, at the instance of apostate monks, was transferred from our order into a college of secular canons. They were made seculars, fit for their prince of perdition; from bad cloisterers they made secular priors, following with their abbot. O patience of God, O times, [unclear], how great is the license of human rashness toward all things.

In the same year Lothar of Bingen, the thirty-seventh prior of this monastery, was deposed because of continual bodily infirmities. John of Cologne was appointed the thirty-eighth prior in his place; after he had presided for two years, he was deposed at his own all too importunate insistence, and afterward was appointed confessor of the nuns in Neuburg near Heidelberg, where he lives today, for how long is uncertain.

The monastery in Ellwangen of our order, in the diocese of Augsburg, exceedingly wealthy, was transferred from our order a few years before these times, at the instance of the perverse abbot and monks, who obtained permission by false accounts, just as all the rest do and had done before.

In the year noted above, John Trithemius the abbot newly composed the following little books: one little book, The Life of Saint Irmina, Virgin, whose holy head we possess; one little book, Praises of Saint Andrew the Apostle; one little book, Praises of Saint Joseph, Foster-father of the Lord; one book, Praises of Saint Benedict the Abbot. He did begin certain other things, but did not complete them in that year. For the study which, before his entry into religion, while he was still placed in the world, he had begun, and which he had now almost neglected for seven years while intent on other things, he took up again in this year with all his strength, lest through him it should be led into oblivion; and in it he thereafter persevered with singular diligence up to the present day. He had two teachers in Greek letters, succeeding one another. The first of them was Conrad Celtis Protucius, a Franconian by nation, orator and poet laureate; from him he received the first rudiments of grammar and of Greek instruction. The second was John Capnion, otherwise Reuchlin, a Swabian by nation, born from the town of Pforzheim, a most learned man of singular grace in teaching; from him he had the fortune to be instructed in the higher precepts of the Greek language and at the same time in Hebrew. In Hebrew he had as teacher at Heidelberg a certain poor baptized Jew, whom afterward, when he had become abbot, he summoned here to himself in the monastery and supported for God's sake as long as he lived. In the aforesaid two languages he gathered together many volumes, written and printed, with great sagacity and also with the help of princes, from Italy and more remote lands, in almost every faculty; of these below, in the nineteenth year of his rule, we shall make some mention in general.

1490.

In the seventh year of our abbot John Trithemius the twenty-seventh provincial chapter of our order was celebrated, on the first Sunday after the octave of Easter, at Saint Giles in Nuremberg. Presiding in it were George, abbot of Saint Stephen's at Wurzburg; John, abbot of Saint Giles's at Nuremberg; Henry, abbot in Blaubeuren; and Blasius, abbot in Hirsau, monasteries of our order. They made many statutes for reform.

In the same year John Trithemius, among other things, composed the Form of Visitation of Mo- [Blank page in the source scan.]

Chronicle of Trithemius

...of the monks of our Order, which afterwards was printed [for?] the provincial chapter. Printed minor works. Also Praises of the Carmelite Life, one book, not yet printed. In this year of Trithemius. The town of Bingen is burned by fire.

In the same year also, on the holy day of Pentecost, a great fire arose by accident in the town of Bingen, which suddenly consumed more than two hundred and forty houses around the market, from the upper part of the town as far as the Rhine. The town hall also, together with letters, registers, and certain privileges, along with the chapels of Saint Lawrence and Saint Nicholas, was wholly consumed by fire; and the whole town would have perished had not the people of the Rheingau come to its aid.

In this year died Matthias, the renowned king of the Hungarians, the hammer of the Turks, who, waging many battles for the Christian faith, often triumphed over the forces of the Turks. After his death, when Maximilian, king of the Romans, was preparing to subject Hungary to his dominion, he was anticipated by Vladislaus, son of the king of Poland and king of Bohemia, who affirmed that he was the nearer heir of the kingdom of Hungary; and he obtained it, an agreement having been made between them.

In the same year René, duke of Lorraine, surrounded the city of Metz with a siege, but, not persevering long, he soon withdrew from there after raising the siege, with loss and damage.

1491.

In this year, which was the eighth of Trithemius our abbot, in the middle of the night on the third Sunday after the feast of Easter, the town of Montabaur in the diocese of Trier, together with its church, towers, and fortifications, having been set alight by accidental fire, miserably perished in the space of three hours, and many irrecoverable losses were inflicted upon people.

In the same year, when a certain wooden granary in this our monastery, consumed by excessive age, had collapsed, and it was necessary that another be built anew, after much deliberation had first been held, Johannes Trithemius the abbot began to construct anew not a wooden one, because it would last only a short time, but a stone one, which could remain longer. Therefore, in the aforesaid year he constructed from the foundations that great stone granary, which is visible up to the present in the upper part of the monastery, roofed with tiles.

At this very time grain was at a high price in these regions, so that one malder of rye was sold everywhere for two florins in gold coin.

Also in the aforesaid year, on the twenty-fourth day of the month of October, Johannes of Cologne the prior was deposed at his own insistence, and Nicolaus Andreae of Reinig, called of Luxembourg, was appointed the thirty-ninth prior of this monastery; today he is in the eleventh year of his priorate. Among all the monks of this monastery who are alive today, after Abbot Trithemius he easily holds first place in the study and knowledge of the Greek language; for he has perfectly learned both to read and to understand whatever is contained among the Greeks in sacred writings. He also knows perfectly how to write, as well as read, both Hebrew and Greek, and he does not interrupt the study of these literatures, as many do, but always continues it.

Clingenmünster is transferred from the order. In the same year the monastery at Clingenmünster, in the diocese of Speyer, was transferred from our order by a dispensation of the Supreme Pontiff obtained through false narratives, although there was no other cause than fear of regular observance. But not long afterward the abbot, leader of the apostates, was removed by a horrible death, just as all who presume such things against God have frequently been accustomed to die.

The betrothed of the king of the Romans is carried off by the king of the French. In the same year also Charles, king of the French, against law and equity, for love of the duchy of Brittany, carried off Anne, the only surviving daughter of the duke of Brittany, who had been solemnly betrothed to Maximilian, king of the Romans, and took her as his wife; Margaret, daughter of the aforesaid king of the Romans, whom he had previously solemnly taken as his betrothed and had long kept with him in France while she was a minor, and whom he had ordered everyone to call queen, was repudiated, not without injury. This deed generated the occasion of a great scandal among the people.

Bingen trades. Around these times the citizens of the town of Bingen had many dangers and losses, not only from the fire written above, but also from other occasions. For, blinded by excessive greed, in the preceding years they burdened with tolls, exactions, and other unaccustomed charges the market which they had been accustomed to hold on each Wednesday; they harassed with exactions beyond measure the clergy and monks, but also the poor coming from the Palatinate with grain; nor would they acquiesce, either to threats or to pleas, so as to lay aside the unusual burdens. Hence, when the rashness of this presumption, and of many abuses which it is pleasing to pass over, had come by the report of many people to the most just prince Philip, count palatine and duke of Bavaria, after taking the counsel of his men, he transferred the market from Bingen to the village of Münster, which at that same time he had purchased from the Rhine counts... The market is transferred from Bingen to Münster. Chronicle of Trithemius

But to me a change of clothing is of no profit, for my baldness betrays me, and my frivolous tongue.

Neuwiller likewise.

The kingdom of Naples [unclear] by the French.

Following in their footsteps, the abbot and monks at Neuwiller, in the diocese of Strasbourg, with the consent of the aforesaid pontiff Alexander VI, laid aside their habit together with the order at about the same time, being made from bad monks into worse canons. Woe to the impious.

In the year also noted above, in the month of November, Charles, king of the French, entered Italy with a very great army of armed men; and, passing through Rome to the kingdom of Naples, after its king had fled, he subjected the whole of it to his rule, placing men of his own as guards in all castles, cities, and fortifications. When these things had been accomplished, he returned to Gaul. After his return, the king of Naples, who had previously fled into Spain, returned to his kingdom; and, after the French garrison had been killed or put to flight, he again recovered the whole dominion for himself.

1496.

In this year, which was the thirteenth of John our abbot, the twenty-ninth provincial chapter of our order was celebrated in the monastery of Seligenstadt, on the fourth Sunday after the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection. Presiding at it were Hermann of St James near Mainz, Bernhard in Northeim, Conrad of St Ulrich in Augsburg, and John of St Giles in Nuremberg, abbots of monasteries of our order. There John Trithemius delivered that very well-known oration, known to all, which is entitled On Pastoral Care.

In the same year, on the fourth day before the Nones of July, there were here in our monastery, to see our library, which fame had everywhere proclaimed precious: John, bishop of Worms, a man most learned in Greek and Latin; John Reuchlin, also called Capnion, doctor of laws, most eloquent in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, secretary of the duke of Württemberg; Franciscus Bononius of Trieste, poet and orator skilled in Greek and Latin, secretary of the queen of the Romans; Heinrich von Bünau, knight, learned in every faculty, secretary of the dukes of Saxony, Frederick and John; and John Vigilius, interpreter of both laws, secretary of Philip the count palatine, patron of all philosophers. All these most learned men, when they had seen so great a multitude of rare volumes in this poor monastery, were exceedingly astonished, praising the order and value of them, and the zeal and industry of Father Trithemius.

In the same year also, on the Kalends of September, died Gerard, abbot of the monastery of St John in the Rheingau, a good man and a lover of monastic discipline, who presided over his monastery well enough and usefully, especially with respect to the substance of temporal goods. He was succeeded by John of Segen, a monk of the same community, an equally good and laborious man, who built the new precinct of his monastery from the foundations in handsome stonework, with windows and vaulting, as it is seen today, aided by alms and by the support of faithful friends.

In the year noted above, the citizens of the town of Kreuznach stirred up a certain sedition among themselves, which turned to the harm of many. For the prefect of the Palatine prince, Albert Goler of Ravensburg, had put a certain citizen in prison because of his offenses; and when certain men had broken it open and led out the captive, and when an assembly had been held in the town, they poured forth words full of insult against the princes. But when the matter had been brought to the knowledge of the princes, the authors of the disturbance were severely punished: some had their fingers cut off, others were branded with iron on the forehead, and others on the cheeks.

In the same year Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, suppressed with force the rebellion of his citizens in Andernach; after certain men who seemed to be the authors of the disobedience had been captured, others punished, and others banished from the country, their contumacy thus ceased.

In the year also noted above, the chapter of the church of Paderborn, because of the old age and continual infirmities of its bishop, took the aforesaid Hermann, bishop of Cologne, as administrator of its church; he administers that same church today.

In these times a certain disease of swelling pustules, passing from the French to the Italians, and from them to the Germans, began to assail and corrupt the human race with a calamity wondrous and hitherto unheard of; most people called this disease [Job?]. It generally begins with a rising ulcer, spreading through the whole body, wretchedly tormenting the sick with continual pain, and contaminating those who come near.

In the same year Philip, duke of Austria and Burgundy, son of Maximilian, emperor of the Romans, took as wife the daughter of Ferdinand, most Christian king of the Spains.

1497. Sponheim.

...had acquired; and there, beside the river Nahe, the market of Bingen was customarily held every Wednesday for more than three years, and throughout all that time no one from all this land, since the Palatine forbade it under penalty, presumed to bring anything to the people of Bingen. They were distressed for a long time by a great shortage of provisions, since, while all those from the Palatinate bought whatever they wished, the people of Bingen alone were excluded from all commerce.

There was also in these times a long dispute, over many articles, between the aforesaid most illustrious Palatine and the church of Mainz; it was the occasion both of the aforesaid removal of the market and of many evils in the land. For indeed, to pass over the other articles, mentioning only one, the people of Bingen, obeying the command of their lords, wished to close the public roads and the bridge over the river Nahe on both sides, near the leper-house and the monastery of St. Rupert, sometimes by day, but always by night, at their pleasure, so that no horseman might pass that way without their consent. Since the most illustrious prince Philip, Palatine, could by no means either tolerate or wish this, since that route necessarily had to be kept open at all times for both his messengers and imperial ones, and since, although he had commanded the people of Bingen once and again that they should not at any time block the bridges and the roads necessary for ascent and descent through that place, but should fortify their own town with an enclosure, they paid no heed, he applied the following remedy. He had as prefect in Kreuznach, whom the common people call an official, Albert Goler of Ravensburg, a Swabian by nation, a man ready in counsel and arms, most daring in all dangers, endowed with singular wisdom and industry; through him he compelled the people of Bingen and their adherents to obedience without any great din of arms. For he, one night, with wonderful ingenuity and skill, burned, broke, and removed the road-closures and barriers, so that no guard of the people of Bingen could in any way frighten him or recall him from what he had begun. And so he opened all the roads that they had closed, both by night and by day, down to the present day, and accomplished many wonderful and illustrious deeds.

1492.

In the ninth year of John Trithemius, our abbot, the emperor of the Romans and king held an assembly of princes in September at Koblenz; in it many matters were handled against the king of the French, who, as we have said, had snatched away the wife betrothed to our king. Against him Frederick Caesar strove most earnestly to rouse the spirits of the princes and an army, in order to avenge the injury done to his son. When he [unclear] them unwilling for the triumph over one woman [unclear], after it had been befouled for more than eight hundred years with Mohammedan filth, he restored it to the purity of the Christian faith.

In the same year also Ferdinand, most Christian king of the Spains, after a long siege, great expenses, and incredible labors, powerfully obtained the kingdom of Granada with all its appurtenances from the hand of Boabdil, the Saracen Moorish king, in a most glorious triumph, after it had been befouled for eight hundred years with Mohammedan filth, and restored it to the purity of the Christian faith.

In this same year John Trithemius, abbot of this monastery, at the request of Gerlach, abbot of Deutz, of our order, wrote one book On the Praise of Scribes, previously noted, and also another On the Manner of Celebrating a Provincial Chapter; both were afterwards printed. He also began in this year a little work On the Illustrious Men of Our Order, divided into four books; because it was laborious, he completed it in the following year.

In these times there were certain utterly lost men, foes and enemies of the archbishop of the church of Mainz, whose names we judge unworthy to come in any way to the knowledge of posterity, although they were born from the military class. They devised unheard-of tortures against the clergy, the priests of the Lord: the testicles of those whom they captured, so that they would follow them to appointed places if they wished to be freed, they enclosed so tightly with certain savage iron fastenings, concealing the form and manner of opening them by a certain marvelous invention, that they could not be opened by anyone other than the one who had locked them, by any ingenuity, any skill, or any filing. No cleric could go out securely, if he belonged to the lordship of the church; but priests were captured hereabouts, tortured, despoiled, and beaten, and some even died from the very torments. But all who were under the protection of the most illustrious prince Palatine were secure, whether they were secular priests or cloistered ones. For the most renowned prince by no means wished to permit anyone who lived in his principality to suffer injury from those robbers. The aforesaid enemies of the clergy had their stronghold in the castle of Kaltenfels, not far from here, from which they inflicted very many losses on the church of Mainz by fire and plunder. In these disturbances...

...the aforesaid young lord Albert Goler of Ravensberg, officer of the Palatine at Kreuznach, stoutly defended all who were under that prince’s protection against all [unclear].

In the same year also, on the last day of the month of December, died Melchior, abbot of Schönau of our order, within the borders of the diocese of Trier, a learned and erudite man, the singular ornament of our observance. Among the other monuments of his talent he left a quite beautifully compiled [unclear], that is, one Gospel out of the four Gospels; also certain prayers delivered in chapters, and sermons and other things.

Also in the aforesaid year, on the eighth day before the Ides of November, there fell from the clouds in Sundgau, near the town of Ensisheim, not far from Basel, a thunderbolt or stone of astonishing size, which, as we have learned by truthful testimony, weighed three hundred pounds. Many people wrote many opinions about its meaning; these we pass over in silence. 1493.

The eleventh provincial chapter is celebrated.

Concerning the unhappy thunderbolt of great size falling.

[unclear] Andreas of Michelsberg near Bamberg, and many decrees were made. In the same chapter, publicly at the table of the prelates and doctors who had come together from the University of Tübingen with others to see the chapter fathers, for three days, morning and evening, there had been read at a suitable time the little Penthic book, that is, the mournful book, concerning the ruin of our order, which our aforesaid abbot Johannes Trithemius had published in the same year at the request of Blasius, abbot of Hirsau, and of the brothers of that monastery. When it had then been read to the end with the greatest attention, all the fathers unanimously decreed, as is contained in the recess of that chapter, that it should for all time be read at the table of the prelates in that chapter whenever it should be celebrated.

In the same year, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, Frederick III, emperor of the Romans, died in Austria. He was buried in Vienna, in a tomb previously prepared for him, leaving one son.

In the same [year], with a very large army of his men gathered together, [unclear] burst into Croatia and Carniola and laid everything waste with plunder, sword, and slaughter. When the Christians, gathering themselves together with such strength as they could, advanced against him to battle, because they were unequal in number, they were cut down, overthrown, and led away like cattle. Nine thousand Christians fell in that engagement. On receiving such sad news, King Maximilian interrupted the funeral pomp which he had prepared to celebrate for his father, and moved a strong army of his men into Croatia against the Turks. When he had learned meanwhile that they had fled, after placing the necessary garrisons everywhere, he returned to Austria to perform his father’s funeral rites. These were solemnly completed in Vienna on the Saturday after the feast of St. Nicholas, in the presence of many princes, dukes, counts, nobles, and envoys of the Roman pontiff, of the kings of France, Spain, Hungary, Bohemia, Naples, Sicily, Dacia, and of almost all the princes of the Christian world, pontiffs, abbots, and prelates, with eight hundred [unclear]. Much was diligently discussed between the king himself, the princes, and the legates about establishing peace among Christians and moving war against the Turks; we saw no result from these discussions.

In the same year also certain islands in the Indian sea were discovered by Christopher Columbus, captain of the fleet of Ferdinand, king of the Spains, entirely unknown before then to all inhabitants of Europe and Asia. On some of them he found naked men living like cattle; since a history of them has been written by him, there is no need for us to dwell at length on them. 1494.

In the eleventh year of our abbot Johannes, Maximilian, king of the Romans, took a second wife, Maria Bianca, formerly the daughter of Galeazzo, duke of Milan, the wedding being celebrated with pomp, as is the custom, at Innsbruck.

In the same year the monastery of nuns of our order on Mount St. Rupert near Bingen was reformed by command of Berthold, archbishop of Mainz, the deformed ones partly departing and partly remaining for a short time. The first reforming sisters, six in number, were taken from the monastery of Schönau. Among them Guda, called Specht, of Bubenheim, was appointed mistress by the consent of all. She presided for almost seven years, a most devout virgin, adorned with holy conduct in old age. But when the devil— Sponheim.

When the devil saw that the brothel of those serving him had been [taken away?], in which all the nuns of that time who were old enough, zealously serving Venus, rejoiced that they were mothers, not virgins, and priests’ concubines, he was grieved, and in various ways and by many contrivances he tried either to obstruct the holy work or at least to disturb it in some lesser degree. For first the deformed women who had previously served the devil, summoned by him, all except two old women unable to go anywhere, fled from the monastery by night, and for a whole three years, with the help of secular persons, by force and power, diverted the greater part of the monastery’s revenues to their own uses outside the convent, in towns and many [unclear]. Finally, amid these things, while a rumor was threatening, [unclear] Prince Philip, count palatine, to attack [unclear].

The devil by rumor [unclear] the people to war.

The people [unclear] the people of the Rheingau, thereafter [unclear] and for some time hostile to the Palatines, I know not by what [unclear].

[unclear]

While a rumor was threatening, [unclear] Prince Philip, count palatine, to attack [unclear].

The devil by rumor [unclear] the people to war.

The people [unclear] the people of the Rheingau, thereafter [unclear] and for some time hostile to the Palatines, I know not by what [unclear]. While a rumor was threatening, [unclear] Prince Philip, count palatine, to attack [unclear], they utterly overturned two small houses placed to the north of the cloister; they also demolished for the greater part the wall of the cloister and the two to the north, lest perhaps the Palatine, when he came, should place there his fortifications against the town of Bingen and from there overwhelm it with engines. But it is most certain to us that the Palatine had wanted nothing less than either to besiege Bingen or to seize the monastery in advance. For if he had resolved openly to attack the hill, the lords of the Rheingau would not have been able to resist. And so they lay for a long time in the church of the aforesaid convent, in the fortifications which they had made, with the nuns shut up in the inner parts, until at last they realized that they had been deceived, and had uselessly spent much without cause. This rashness of the people of the Rheingau, however, harmed the monastery of Saint Rupert not a little in its destroyed buildings, and gave certain persons through them an occasion for no small sum of money [unclear].

In the same year also Johannes Trithemius, abbot, built a new abbot’s residence, partly from the old one and partly from the foundations, sufficiently costly and adorned, as it is seen today, on the eastern side of the monastery, where once the entrance gate had been. In it he made two chambers for the abbot, a third for the master chaplain, one heated room, two lower closets, and a chapel with an altar, of whose consecration we shall speak in the following year. How necessary the construction of this abbatial house was, all know who saw the earlier abbatial dwelling. For the dwelling was too narrow, unsuitable, and to be feared because of the danger of fire, although because of the little house, bare and empty of all things, there was nothing in it. For on the day on which Trithemius entered the abbey, apart from one loaf, a biretta, and a bed with its necessary furnishings, nothing was found in the abbatial house. For Johannes Kolnhauen, abbot, a lover of simplicity, had always been accustomed here at Seligenstadt to build rooms that were excessively narrow and mean.

When he resigned, there were here in the abbey no cupboards, no chests, no tables, no closed or secure receptacles of any kind in which anything could be stored. Trithemius therefore, compelled by necessity, built the abbot’s residence with work costly for his poverty; he made cupboards, arranged chambers, added locks, set up the necessary small chests, and procured many other things, which we see today, at no small expense.

In the year noted above, Johannes Trithemius, abbot, at the request of Rumold of Laupach, prior of the Carmelites of Frankfurt, a very good man and a most upright guardian of regular observance, wrote the book, today very widely circulated, On the Praises of Saint Anne, mother of the most blessed God-bearer, the Virgin Mary, which is held by many in great esteem. In its seventh chapter he makes mention of the most pure conception of the God-bearer. On this occasion a certain man of the Order of Preachers arose, named Wigand Wirt, preacher of the convent of Frankfurt, a man indeed quite learned, but excessively rash and proud. He wished to attack the work as far as it concerns the purity of the conception, and sent letters against Trithemius, the writer’s name concealed under the designation of Brother Pensans’s hand, to him by an unknown messenger, as though Trithemius had written badly about the conception, and reproved him rather timidly. To him Trithemius wrote back in these words: I would bear your insults with difficulty, nameless reader, if I did not understand that you are suffering from a grave disease of the mind [unclear].

Trithemius’s book on Saint Anne.

Pensans [unclear] sets himself against Trithemius. Sponheim.

[unclear] before many princes and very learned men it was published, copied out, read to the greatest admiration of all, and regarded as a new and unheard-of miracle. But since no one, however learned, could understand either the principles or the explanations of the things that were promised there, they expressed an uncertain judgment. Some proclaimed Trithemius a divine man, others a most learned one; some, whose understanding was slower and whose will was readier for rashness, asserted that he was a magician and did these things by the ministry of spirits. But how purely natural are all the things that are reported in that same letter he disclosed at the beginning of the book of the Steganography. Moved by this novelty, many men from the farthest borders of Gaul came here to see and speak with Trithemius; and when they had seen the books and the things themselves, the report of which they had heard from afar, and when Trithemius had given a very clear demonstration, as was fitting, they confessed that the report had fallen far short of the truth of the facts. Some also, though far distant, sent their messengers with letters to Trithemius, desiring to know the truth of the matter which they had known only by report.

To some of these Trithemius wrote back in such a way that they understood that the operation of his marvels was possible naturally and without superstition, though they did not know the principles of the art itself or the method of working such great marvels through it. Among those, however, who approached Trithemius by letter concerning these matters, Vlascus the Portuguese, certainly a very learned man, dealt with Trithemius in his letter with such subtlety, such learning, and such variety of arguments that no one more acute than he in proposing questions of such matters was ever found by Trithemius.

In the same year, on the ninth day of the month of September, the canons both of the major church and of the other churches of the city of Worms, unanimously, after carrying away their goods, went out from Worms, on account of the wrongs done by the citizens, who rashly violated the privileges of the clergy. Today the third year after their departure is in progress, but nothing has yet been found to have been done about their return into the city. Often the most unconquered Prince Palatine of the Rhine interposed his offices for concord, but because of the obstinacy of both parties he accomplished nothing. They keep very careful watch at the gates, lest any of the canons who had gone out of their own accord return to the city of Worms against their will.

In this same year Maximilian, king of the Romans, after suspending for the time being the war of Guelders, moved his whole army against the Swiss, who, beginning rebellion in the preceding year, had inflicted much damage on the king without his knowing it; and coming in the month of March to their borders, they had several battles with one another, so that more than twelve thousand are reported to have been slain on both sides. There Count Pitsch was killed by the Helvetians, another of Westerburg, together with many noble and valiant men. At length, after many dangers and inconveniences, a concord was issued in the month of September.

In the same year died Wilhelm, landgrave of Hesse, son-in-law of the most illustrious Prince Palatine, without children. His wife returned to her father and laments the hardships of her widowhood down to the present day, since she lost so quickly a husband most loving to her, with no offspring [unclear]. Between Wilhelm, son of his paternal uncle and his successor, and the above-named most illustrious prince Philipp, count palatine, father of the widow left by the deceased prince, a dispute arose by reason of the dowry assigned to the daughter of that Palatine by the deceased before the marriage was undertaken. Hence they held several diets at Mainz, Frankfurt, Worms, and most recently now at Würzburg, but they have not yet, down to the present day, been able to come to agreement.

1500.

In the seventeenth year of John Trithemius, our abbot, the following crosses appeared in the linen garments of men, in shirts, in women’s veils, in table linens, not only in those that were in use, but also in those which, shut up in chests, seemed to have no influence of [unclear]. Likewise they often appeared on corporals, altar palls, and albs. They were first seen in Sobernheim and Meisenheim, with the greatest fear and horror of the common people, so suddenly that sometimes, while the Salve was being sung in church, thirty people were found to have crosses who had not had them before. Afterwards they appeared in Kreuznach and the villages lying round about, then in Bingen and in Mainz, and consequently in many places of Germany. The crosses were small, of varied and confused color, as if cloth had been smeared with some grease of mixed color; nor could they be erased by any washing, but after the ninth or tenth day they faded away and vanished of themselves. After two years a great plague of men followed these crosses in many places.

406 Chronicle of Trithemius ... is seen to have prevailed in you to such an extent that the skill of the prince of physicians and of [Aesculapius?] seems necessary for your cure. At the end, moreover, he concluded the letter thus: “If you are a religious man, if you are a lover of brotherly charity, do not neglect now to restrain yourself from insults and curses, nor rashly trust in your own prudence against the immaculate Mother of God. Unless you do this, there will be a time when you will grieve that your writings, most worthy of mockery, have been rejected [unclear] in the Inquisition.”

With these letters and other [unclear] Trithemius sent a certain learned man to Frankfurt (it was in Advent), to investigate subtly among the preachers who that brother Pensans-manus was. When he had come there, using diligence, he discovered that it was the aforesaid lector Wigand Cauponis. When he reported this to Trithemius, a great literary war arose between them, which lasted between them for almost two years. For soon against Wigand several very learned men, defenders of Marian purity, wrote in verse and prose, defending Trithemius’s book and his opinion concerning her most pure conception. At length, after two years had passed, concord was made between Trithemius and Wigand through the rector of the University of Cologne, Ulrich Kreityvys of Esslingen, most famous doctor of sacred theology, canon of the greater church of Cologne and councillor of the archbishop, and through Tomus de Scotia and other doctors of sacred theology, so that Wigand abjured his opinion contrary to the most pure conception of Mary and to Trithemius’s little work, and was compelled by Trithemius himself to seek pardon for his rashness; and, injuries being forgiven on both sides, neither would henceforth write invective against the other. Nevertheless the preachers afterwards in the Roman curia under Pope Alexander VI attempted, or treacherously strove, to obtain something against Trithemius, but they made no progress. For Abbot Trithemius had most firmly adhering to him the University of Paris, that of Cologne, that of Tübingen, the whole order of the Carmelites, the order of Minors, the sacrosanct Roman Church, the greater [unclear] of the cardinals, archbishops, bishops, and many princes, and almost all the clergy in Germany, and innumerable learned and erudite men.

At the same time he also wrote: Soliloquies of a Man to His Soul, one book. On the Origin and Progress of the Order of Carmelites, two books. He also collected, by abbreviating them into one volume, the statutes of the provincial chapter of our order. He also elucidated Greek questions to Rutger Sicambrus on the discordances of the Gospels. Likewise he translated from Greek into Latin a book of Abbot Maximus on the incarnation of the Lord, and certain letters of the Third Synod, likewise of Saint Cyril, archbishop of Alexandria.

Also in the year noted above, in the month of July, Maximilian, king of the Romans, entered Gelderland with a strong army against Duke Charles, who, having heard of the king’s arrival, had fled to Lorraine. Many of the king’s hired foot-soldiers did evil things in the land, with plunder, sword, and fire, sparing no one. For when the men fled together to the city, poor women remained in the little villages; from them those plunderers, not to call them most cruel murderers, wishing to extort money, committed unheard-of crimes with threats, tortures, and killing. From among these, so that the rest may be imagined, let us report one. A certain peasant, hearing of the king’s arrival, betook himself to Nijmegen, the principal town of Gelderland, leaving his wife in the village with the little children. The most wicked bloodsuckers, thirsting more for booty than for the king’s victory, pressed the woman with threats and terrors to disclose her husband’s money. But when they could extort nothing from her by threats, [unclear] that he might by pity compel her to their wish, so that he might be roasted alive in the sight of his mother. But since the mother did not have the money with which to ransom her son, the most cruel robbers, while she looked on and groaned, roasted the boy until he died. They committed many other deeds horrible to tell against the poor. King Maximilian, however, not knowing such unspeakable crimes of his men, left Gelderland without obtaining victory, with loss and grave damage to his affairs.

  1. In the twelfth year of John Trithemius our abbot, a new altar was consecrated in the abbatial house, which he himself had built in the previous year together with the vault and the whole dwelling, by Erhard, bishop of [Venecomponensis?], vicar in pontificals for Berthold, archbishop of Mainz, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, which was the vigil of the feast of the Body of Christ, in honor of Saint Anne, mother of the most blessed ever-virgin Mary, and of Saint Andrew the apostle. These relics of the saints, moreover, Abbot Trithemius had placed in the altar by the aforesaid bishop in a glass vessel: of Saint Andrew the apostle, of Saint Nicholas the bishop, of Saint Boniface, archbishop and martyr, of Saint Lawrence the martyr, of Saint Lucy, virgin and martyr, of Saint Cecilia, virgin, of the garments of the most blessed Sponheim.

...feels the continual pain of the same stigmata, yet on Wednesdays and Fridays she is tormented more severely. Many very learned and distinguished men have seen and touched these stigmata, and they bear witness to the miracle; and we neither wished nor ought to contradict their testimony.

1501.

In the eighteenth year of John Trithemius, our abbot, the thirty-first provincial chapter of our order was held on the third Sunday after the feast of Easter in the monastery of Fulda. Presiding at it were the aforesaid John Trithemius, our abbot, who delivered the address, and John of St Aegidius in Nuremberg, John in Huysburg, and John in Elchingen, [abbots?] of monasteries of the order. Nothing new was decreed, but many matters were nevertheless treated in orderly fashion.

In the same year Christopher, margrave of Baden, was here [unclear], having sent his cavalry ahead to Winterburg so that they might not burden us by their number. He came to see the library and certain secret things, on account of which in the preceding year he had summoned Trithemius to his castle of Lutzenburg, and took them into his notice and knowledge.

In the same year also, on the day of the Conversion of St Paul, there died a most Christian and truly most devout woman, Lady Margaret, wife of the most illustrious prince Philip, count palatine and duke of Bavaria. She was buried at Heidelberg in the choir of the church of the Holy Spirit; her thirtieth-day observance the prince celebrated solemnly in Lent.

In the year also noted above, the theological faculty of the University of Mainz, stirred by the example of those of Paris and Cologne, made a statute on the nineteenth day of the month of October on behalf of the truth of the faith and in defense of the most pure conception of the most blessed Mary ever virgin, determining that she was always preserved, exempt, and immune from every stain of original sin, and judging the contrary assertion impious and erroneous. And it nevertheless decreed that henceforth no one should be promoted in theology unless he swore that he would never in any respect favor the contrary opinion.

In the same year, after the death of a certain tyrant who had wickedly oppressed the poor in Moravia, when his son, succeeding to the paternal inheritance, inhabited a certain castle of his, named Giemps, with his wife and daughter, behold, one day, as he was sitting at table, two evil spirits in human form came to the gate of the castle, asking to be admitted. The porter said to them: “Who are you, or where are you from? For I must report this to my lord.” They answered him and said: “It concerns neither you nor your lord who we are or where we are from; but admit us as quickly as possible, otherwise we shall see to it that an entrance lies open for us.” As the porter ran to announce this to his lord, when he had entered the place where he was sitting, he saw those two men whom he had left outside the gate standing before his lord, and from fear he could say nothing. But they, after many threatening and terrifying words and horrible visions, to be brief in the telling, compelled him with all his household to leave the castle. After their departure, a great multitude of demons gathered and began to inhabit that castle; howling day and night and clapping, they do astonishing things.

In the year noted above, on the day of the Epiphany of the Lord during mass, a certain man of the knightly class, named John of Eltz, came with certain other knights, who complained that their rights and liberties had been violated by the archbishop of Trier. With ships and cavalry, by the Rhine and by land, he seized Boppard in advance, and at once placed his own guards on the walls, held the towers and gates, and took possession of the town without anyone resisting, all those who had been on the archbishop’s side having been cast out. What will follow, we await.

In these times heretics multiplied in Bohemia, who are commonly called Diggers, because they meet at night in hidden ditches and caves, practicing obscenity without distinction of persons, in the manner of beasts. They despise the Church of God and its ministers, mock the sacraments, and teem with endless errors. This most abominable kind of people is growing and increasing astonishingly every day, to such an extent that in the year noted above their number was found to be more than nineteen thousand. But very many nobles and powerful men in the kingdom of Bohemia have turned aside to those most foul heretics; among them one, named Christopher, a noble and wealthy man, distributed forty thousand florins among the same heretics as alms, and became one of them.

In these times in Bohemia there was a certain nobleman, Lawrence Glatz of Rotchausen, a good Christian in faith and conduct, who had bought a certain town called Gurricke. In it he found that almost all the townspeople were heretics of the aforesaid sect. When he had set before them the law that they should either renounce their error or, leaving all their goods in rightful condition, depart from the town, all with one [unclear].

The provincial chapter [unclear] was celebrated [unclear].

Margaret, wife of the count palatine, dies.

Decree of the University of Mainz against the [unclear].

Demons seized a castle in Moravia.

Boppard captured by knights.

Multiplication of heretics in Bohemia.

[unclear]. Sponheim.

of the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, and from the sepulcher of St. Justina, virgin and martyr. The anniversary day of the dedication of the same altar was set for the twenty-ninth day of the month of July, that is, the fourth day before the Kalends of August, on which day Trithemius himself was elected abbot of this monastery, as was said at the beginning of his appointment. At the consecration of this altar there was present Jacob Wimpheling of Schlettstadt, theologian, poet, and most eloquent orator, and he composed this tetrastich ex tempore:

While Trithemius, John, was head of the Sponheim house, a father with cheerful dignity, to you, divine Mary, his mother, and to the venerable Andrew, this present altar was dedicated.

For the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, is the chief patroness of this citadel; after her, her holy mother Anne; and third, the apostle Andrew. Moreover, Mary Magdalene, most fervent lover of Jesus Christ, was two years later assumed as co-patroness, because of her relics, which were brought from Gaul by Trithemius and deposited there. Finally, for the adornment of the same altar, John the abbot in the course of time obtained from various princes, bishops, abbots, and other prelates of churches and monasteries many most precious relics of saints; bringing them with joy into this our monastery, he had them enclosed, as best he could, in panels and beautifully adorned in shrines, and laid up with reverence beside the aforesaid altar. For there are many particles, notable in quantity and in the merit of the saints, to be preserved forever with the greatest honor.

In the same year the aforesaid abbot John described some miracles of the most holy mother Anne, and the Catalogue of German Writers, which he had begun almost four years before, at the urging of Master Jacob Wimpheling of Schlettstadt, named above; correcting it this year from the rough drafts, he completed it as best he could.

In the same year also, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April, Rudolf, bishop of Würzburg, died, a man burdened with old age and with the disease of the stone, and was buried in his greater church. After his death he was cut open, as is customary, by his order, and a stone of incredible size was found, which weighed thirty-three lots; and as a sign of wonder it is preserved and shown in the greater church. He died at the age of one hundred, leaving much money and wealth.

In the year noted above, on the third day before the Nones of January, John of Colnhausen died, once abbot of this monastery and afterward transferred to Seligenstadt, as was said above.

In the same year also, on the second day before the Ides of September, in a certain village not far from Worms, a woman gave birth to a monstrous and unusual offspring, having two bodies, distinct from the head downward, whose heads above were joined into one at the forehead, nor could they by any means be separated from one another. Even today two twin girls are living with heads joined and bodies divided, each carrying out her own function either by sense or by intellect; while one sleeps, the other watches, and while the one weeps, the other can laugh or even do something else. This monstrosity is said to have happened by accident. When the pregnant mother was speaking somewhat merrily with another woman in the cemetery, standing with her face turned close to the other, a certain man came up, for the sake of joking, and modestly knocked the heads of both together at the forehead; terrified by this unexpected event, the woman gave birth to offspring in the likeness of the accident.

In the year likewise noted above, at the summons of King Maximilian, a very great assembly of princes from the whole Roman Empire was held for several months in the city of Worms, amid a great concourse of peoples who could not be counted. There, while the king sat in majesty with the prince-electors, as is the custom, and the other princes, bishops, and abbots stood in their order, on the fourteenth day of the month of July the aforesaid prince-electors, and afterward the rest, having sworn their oaths, received their feudal rights from the king himself according to custom. On the following day Maximilian, king of the Romans, with the consent of the princes, elevated Eberhard, count of Württemberg, into a duke: a vigorous, pious, magnanimous man, and worthy of the honor of the duchy, since he was a singular lover of religious and clergy, a most steadfast defender, and a reformer of many monasteries.

In the same year the monastery in Odenheim, in the diocese of Speyer, was transferred from our order to seculars, with the consent of the supreme pontiff at the urging of the apostate monks, who, having no legitimate cause for their transfer, suggested falsehoods to the pontiff as truths. Concerning the insolent abbot of those apostates, who was the occasion of all the evil, someone composed this tetrastich:

I put off your garment, Benedict, and snatched up Peter’s robe: thus I thought I could deceive [unclear].

Day of the espousal of the aforesaid altars.

Trithemius brings together here many relics of saints.

Works of Trithemius of this year.

The bishop of Würzburg dies.

John Colnhausen, formerly abbot here, dies.

A monstrous birth near Worms.

A very great assembly of princes.

The count of Württemberg is elevated as duke.

Odenheim is transferred from the order. Sponheim. 1497.

In the fourteenth year of Johannes Trithemius, our abbot, the monastery called Sunsheim, not far from Heidelberg, in the diocese of Speyer, following the example of other apostatizing monks, was transferred with its abbot and monks from our order into a secular church, by the permission and dispensation of Alexander VI, Roman Pontiff; and from perverse monks they were made criminal secular canons.

In the same year, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, Johann, archbishop of Trier, led out a great army against his disobedient citizens of the town of Boppard. When they refused to consent to his will, he surrounded them with a very strong siege, having with him certain very powerful princes of the empire hired for pay, with many fighters and engines of war. But when the citizens perceived that they could not resist so great a multitude, on the twelfth day of the siege they submitted themselves to the command of the bishop.

In the aforementioned year also, Laurentius, bishop of Würzburg, after the death of the abbot of the Scots in the suburb of the same city across the bridge, expelled the Scottish monks, of whom there were scarcely two, because of their reprobate life, and introduced observant brothers of our order.

In the same year [unclear] before the Kalends of July, Johann, archbishop of [Würzburg?], [unclear] the abbot of the Scots in the suburb of the same city across the bridge, expelled the Scottish monks, who were two [unclear], because of their reprobate life, and introduced brothers of our order and observance. But when the city could not resist so great a multitude, on the twelfth day of the siege they submitted themselves to the bishop’s commands.

In the aforementioned year also, Laurentius, bishop of Würzburg, after the death of the abbot of the Scots in the suburb of the same city across the bridge, expelled the Scottish monks, who were two [unclear], because of their reprobate life, and introduced brothers of our order and observance. But when the city could not resist so great a multitude, on the twelfth day of the siege they submitted themselves to the bishop’s commands.

In the aforementioned year also, Eberhard, duke of Württemberg, who had succeeded the first duke created at Worms, is said to have committed many things wrongly and shamefully against faith and good morals by his own men; when he proposed to designate for death several of the more important of his councillors, they, having been warned, [unclear] to seize him and [unclear] perpetually from him. When this became known to him, on the fourth day before the Kalends of April he fled secretly with his treasures, first to the king of the Romans, who was then in Ulm, a town of Swabia of no small rank. The king made an agreement in this way between that duke and the regents of the land of Württemberg: with Eberhard renouncing the duchy and yielding to Ulrich, the little son of his brother, the Württembergers were to pay him six thousand florins yearly for life. But the duke, not accepting the agreement, departed, wandering with a few men through the land, first among the people of Strasbourg, afterward in Baden, and then in various other places, always everywhere leaving traces of his instability. Finally he fled to the most unjust prince, lord Philipp, count Palatine; for a time he was in Kreuznach, afterward in Heidelberg; now in the castle of Lindenfels, at the expense of the same prince, he is staying in every abundance and liberty, yet in such a way that he may not flee from there.

In the same year there was a certain doctor at Paris, of the order of the Friars Preachers, named Johannes Veri, a rash and presumptuous man, who on the day of the conception of the most pure ever-virgin Mother of God, as is the custom of those men, publicly preached from the pulpit in a certain town, Dieppe, in the diocese of Rouen, that the most blessed Virgin Mary was cleansed from original stain, not preserved from it. From this preaching a great scandal arose among the people, because almost everyone today, except a few Preachers, believes, holds, and preaches that the Mother of God, most worthy of all praise, was never subject to original sin.

But on the following day, that is, the seventeenth of the month of September, there assembled at Saint-Mathurin in the city of Paris eighty-two professors of sacred theology, very learned men, all promoted with rigor in the same University, in the presence of the whole university, and with one voice and one judgment they enacted and determined that henceforth no one should be enrolled in the aforesaid University unless he confirms by oath that he will be, to the best of his powers, an assertor and vigorous defender of this determination: namely, that the most blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary was immune from and preserved from original stain. They themselves also had all sworn beforehand, as is contained in the statute, that at all times they would adhere firmly to this truth of Mary’s most pure conception. It seems marvelous to us that some dare to oppose such virtues. Stirred by their example, the professors of sacred theology of the nourishing University of Cologne [unclear].

Sponheim.

Another man admirable for his knowledge.

But as we write these things, Ferdinand of Córdoba comes back to mind. In 1445, a young man of twenty years, a knight of the golden spur, Doctor of Arts, Medicine, and sacred Theology, he came from Spain into France with [unclear] horses, and by his marvelous knowledge turned the whole school of Paris to astonishment. For he was most learned in every branch of letters, and most upright in life and conduct; not arrogant and proud like that man of whom we have already spoken, but humble and full of great reverence.

A memorable power of memory.

He held the whole Bible in memory; likewise Nicholas of Lyra, the writings of Saint Thomas Aquinas, Alexander of Hales, John Scotus, Bonaventure, and many others in theology; also the Decretum and all the books of both laws; and in medicine Avicenna, Galen, Hippocrates, Aristotle, and Albert; and all the books and commentaries of philosophy and metaphysics he preserved in memory perfectly, as they say.

A very acute disputation [unclear].

In citing authorities he was extremely ready; in disputation acute, never surpassed by anyone. Finally, he read, wrote, and understood Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Arabic, and Chaldaean perfectly. Sent to Rome as ambassador by the king of Castile, he disputed publicly in all the schools of Italy and France and refuted everyone, while he himself was refuted by no one, even in the least point. Various opinions about him were current among the doctors of Paris, some carping that he was a magician and full of a demon, others holding the contrary. There were some who thought him Antichrist, because of the incredible knowledge of the Scriptures in which he seemed to surpass all mortals. He published certain commentaries on Ptolemy's Almagest and illuminated the Apocalypse of Saint John with a very beautiful exposition. He wrote certain other little works of his own talent, full of learning, whose titles we have not been able to recall to memory on this occasion. This was that Ferdinand who, by an astronomical prediction, long beforehand foretold [his death?] to Charles, Duke of the Burgundians.

The cross-bearers [unclear].

Also in the aforesaid year, the eighteenth of Abbot Trithemius, there came from Italy men clad in gray tunics, with heads uncovered, walking barefoot. They carried in their hands a small cross of wood; they had neither sack nor pouch, nor did they receive money; they also used staffs in their hands. They did not drink wine or beer. Only once a day, except on Sunday, did they refresh themselves, taking vegetables and roots with salt and water, without any fat. In church, prostrate on the ground in the shape of a cross, they prayed, carrying nothing besides the cross and the tunic. They went around through cities and villages and did not remain in one place more than twenty-four hours unless they were ill. Many among them were of the clerical order; they admitted into their company all who wished to do penance, except women. After five years had elapsed, their penance ceased.

The Palatine comes to Sponheim.

Also in the aforesaid year, on the nineteenth day of November, on the feast of Saint Elizabeth, Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, renowned Duke of Bavaria, came here to Sponheim with his sons Ludwig and Rupert, for the sake of speaking with Trithemius and at the same time seeing the monastery and the books. It was Friday, and he sent ahead cooks, bread, wine, fish, and everything necessary for food; for he did not wish to burden us in anything, and therefore provided everything most abundantly from his own resources.

1502.

A great pestilence.

In the nineteenth year of Trithemius our abbot, there was a great pestilence everywhere, in all the places round about, namely in Bingen, in Stauronesus, in Berckelnheim, and in the whole County of Sponheim. It consumed many thousands of people, raging over almost the whole world.

A certain man is burned.

In this same year, on the twelfth day of March, a certain poor man in Waldenhufen, named Leonard, was burned by fire because of coinage of pennies, false money which he had struck in a hidden house.

Henry becomes abbot of Bursfelde.

In the aforesaid year, on the eighth day of May, John, abbot of Bursfelde, the fourth in the order of the reform, died, a man most holy in character and life. Henry, a monk of the same monastery, succeeded him by election of the brothers.

Likewise, a meeting of abbots at Nuremberg.

The presiding officer at the convocation of princes in Nuremberg called to himself Johann Trithemius and certain other abbots. To them he opened his intention, indicating that he had thought of making one out of the three observant branches of our order, Bursfelde, Melk, and Kastl. But since the men of Melk and Kastl were unwilling to subject themselves to our constitutions, they returned to their own places with the business unfinished.

Several desert the Palatine.

Likewise in this year, several, withdrawing themselves from the service and fidelity of the Count Palatine, went over to his rivals, laying the foundations of a future war against him. Among them Emich, Count of Leiningen, was chief; departing from the Palatine, he subjected himself and his possessions to the Count of Hesse.

The Chronicle of Trithemius, 1498

In the fifteenth year of Johannes Trithemius, our abbot, a great war arose between the king of the Romans and the whole Roman Empire, and the confederates who are called the Suitenses or Swiss; many thousands of men fell there on both sides. At length, after many losses had been suffered on both sides, concord was made between the king and the Swiss. This pleased not many people, especially the Swabian nobles of the Swabian League, which the emperor had established ten years before.

In the same year the tomb of Saint Hildegard, virgin, on Mount Saint Rupert was opened with the greatest reverence, in the presence of the whole convent there and of others appointed for this purpose, one of whom was Johannes Trithemius, our abbot. By his prayers he obtained the arm of the same holy virgin from the mistress and convent, for whom he had done many good services in the time of their tribulations. He had these sacred relics, together with others, enclosed in a certain panel.

At nearly the same time the abbot and monks of our order in Blidenstatt, in the diocese of Mainz, by a dispensation of the supreme pontiff obtained through false accounts, apostatized from the order, having no other cause than perverse will and hatred of regular discipline; from dissolute monks they became still more shameful clerics. An evil matter, without doubt contrary to God. Therefore let both those who consent to, and those who assume, such an unjust transfer consider what they will one day answer to God.

In the year noted above a great assembly of princes with Maximilian, king of the Romans, was held in the town of Freiburg for many days. There many matters were discussed for the peace and advantage of the commonwealth, but no result, or only a small one, followed. Many counsels were held about moving war against the Turks, about continuing the judgment of the imperial Chamber, instituted at Worms three years earlier, and about correcting rebels; but because, the sinews of money being lacking, the body of the Empire was not sufficient for especially difficult wars. Many agreed in words to contribute, but in deeds many did not fear to do the contrary.

In the same year also Wilhelm, provincial count of Hesse, took as wife the daughter of the most illustrious prince Philip, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria. The wedding was celebrated in Frankfurt with a very great gathering of princes and nobles.

In this same year there was a great tumult of wars in the duchy of Guelders. The king of the Romans in his own person, with other princes, received many fortifications in surrender; but when the war of the Swiss unexpectedly supervened, as we shall say in the following year, he was compelled to leave the people of Guelders and move his army against the Helvetians. Then the people of Guelders again defected from the king to their duke.

1499

In the sixteenth year of Johannes Trithemius, our abbot, the thirtieth provincial chapter of our order was celebrated in the monastery of Saint Stephen at Wurzburg, on the fourth Sunday after the feast of Easter. Presiding over it were the same Johannes Trithemius, who delivered an extemporaneous oration and was leader of the word; Andreas of Monchsberg, Johannes of Saint Michael in Hildesheim, and Thomas in Seligenstadt, abbots of monasteries of our order of the observance.

In the same year the theological faculty of the nourishing University of Cologne established and decreed, by a most firm constitution, that it was to be held, thought, believed, preached, and most constantly defended by all its subjects: that the blessed Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, by the singular prerogative of divine power, has always been preserved, exempted, and privileged from every stain of original sin. Whoever should do the contrary was to be cut off from the University itself and entirely deprived for all time of the honors and emoluments of the theological faculty; and no one was to be promoted in that faculty unless he swore that he would always observe this statute.

In the year noted above, on the Monday after Palm Sunday, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of this monastery, having been asked by letter by Arnold Bostius, a Carmelite staying at Ghent, a most learned and most religious man, what he was writing, and intending to reply to him as to a true friend, wrote back that he had in hand a great work of Steganography, at the request of a certain prince, which had not previously been known to any men, as the work itself proves. But before the letter came to Ghent, Bostius himself, to whom it had been written, on the day before the Nones of April, that is, on the fifth day after the feast of Easter, Trithemius not knowing it, migrated to the Lord. Therefore the prior of the convent at Ghent opened the letter sent to Bostius, read it, and everywhere proclaimed it as a miracle; within a short space of time it spread through all Gaul and Germany [unclear]

War between the Swiss and the king of the Romans.

Relics of Saint Hildegard obtained by Trithemius.

Blidenstatt is transferred from the order.

Assembly of princes in Freiburg.

The landgrave of Hesse takes the daughter of the Palatine as wife.

War of Guelders.

The thirtieth provincial chapter is celebrated.

The word led.

Statute of the University of Cologne against the Maculists.

Arnold Bostius dies. Chronicle of Trithemius

In the same year a certain stonemason, who had for some time worked on the construction of the tower of St. Stephen at Mainz, stole the head of most holy Anne, the mother of Mary ever virgin, which was kept in that church enclosed in a little silver vessel, together with the silver itself; and, departing secretly to the town of Düren, in the duchy of Jülich and the diocese of Cologne, he carried off the sacred head, which was received with honor by the citizens. Thus the holy head was held in great honor by the people of Düren; and what at Mainz lay almost wholly unknown is today visited at Düren with the greatest concourse of people from our own and from other more distant provinces, with immense honor, heaped almost beyond measure with prayers and offerings. They say, moreover, that at the invocation of holy mother Anne signs and miracles have occurred there; but since nothing is established for us concerning these, we do not wish to report what is uncertain. The canons of the aforesaid church, making efforts and expenses for the restoration of the most holy head that had been taken away, summoned the townsmen of Düren before the royal hearing, but they accomplished nothing, being deprived of the holy pledge down to the present day. For they cannot by any argument be induced to restore the holy head. What the people of Düren will do hereafter, however, we cannot know at this time.

In the year noted above, Johannes, archbishop of Trier, burdened by old age, took as coadjutor Jacob, son of Christoph, margrave of Baden, his nephew through his brother Karl, a man excellent in talent and character; Pope Alexander VI confirmed him in his assumption, with provision for succession. This act has not pleased four of the canons of the major church, namely the dean and three others, down to the present day. Hence great dissension is feared in the church of Trier after the archbishop’s death, unless God should be willing to forestall it.

In this year the greatest concourse of peoples from all Europe was made to the Roman curia for the indulgences of the jubilee year, and much money was brought to Rome. Men and women, widows and virgins, young and old, monks and nuns, ran together, mingled and confused, and the matter was [unclear]. Many, consumed by hunger and plague, perished on the journey; some also were killed, and some, sold, were brought to the utmost dangers. There is a certain convent of nuns of our order, built in the diocese of Speyer near Limburg, committed by papal authority to Johannes Trithemius, abbot, whose abbess, without permission either of the bishop or of the abbot, set out for Rome for the indulgences of the jubilee and died on the return, and left her place after her [unclear] desolate. To her in the abbacy, by canonical election, succeeded Richmodis de Horst, a noble and devout virgin, sufficiently learned in the Latin language, a nun of the convent of the Maccabees in Cologne, a lover of regular discipline and its most upright guardian, who, among other monuments of her talent, composed an entire history of St. Anne with melody.

Also in the same year, on the [unclear] day of the month of July, Bayezid, emperor of the Turks, in his own person and with an army of thousands of armed men, besieged Modon, a great and most beautiful city of the Venetians; and after many labors and assaults, on the ninth day of the month of August, he violently captured it, cruelly killed many thousands of Christians, and led the rest away into most shameful servitude.

Also in the year noted above, the inhabitants of our village of Auen, when required by Johannes Trithemius our abbot to render him the homage of fidelity, quite insolently refused to obey, alleging prescription, because within memory they had rendered homage to none of the abbots. But when the abbot referred the matter to the most unconquered Prince Palatine, the peasants, fearing dangers and losses, rendered and displayed homage, and not undeservedly. For since they have always recognized the abbot of this monastery, whoever he may have been at the time, as their lord, and no other, they ought deservedly to swear to no one else.

In these times there flourished in Italy, in the city of Ferrara, a certain most devout virgin, a most fervent meditator on the Lord’s passion, named Lucia, a professed sister under the third rule of St. Dominic of the Order of Preachers, visibly and perceptibly marked with stigmata, which every Friday openly emit flowing blood from her. And although the aforesaid virgin conSponheim.

[unclear] he set forth. Therefore in the aforementioned year, the twenty-first of Johannes Trithemius as abbot, in the month of May, at the command of the most sacred Emperor Maximilian, Ulrich, duke of Wurttemberg, Wilhelm, landgrave of Hesse, Alexander, duke of Bavaria and count of Veldenz, who was staying in the little town of Zweibrucken, together with many counts and men of the military order, took up arms in these lower lands against Philip, count palatine of the Rhine, prince-elector. With one mind they invaded the Palatine lands and wrought great destruction.

For Ulrich, the magnanimous duke of Wurttemberg, powerfully took certain Palatine fortifications, towns, and castles alike, and subjected Besigheim, Meckmuhl, Lowenstein, the monastery of Maulbronn, together with certain others, to his dominion. For he was indeed a young prince, but prudent and devoted to God in religion, and he did not exceed the Christian manner of waging war: indeed he neither set Christ's churches on fire nor plundered monasteries, but, vigorous in spirit and virtuous in power, so far as could be done, he spared the innocent and the ministers of the Church. He powerfully besieged Bretten, a town of the Palatine; when he saw that he could not take it, he raised the siege and turned his army elsewhere. He subjected Weinsberg, with all its appurtenances, to imperial authority; and unless at last the king's edict had intervened, wishing to spare the man who had been cast down, he would have inflicted heavier losses on the Palatines.

Meanwhile, while these things were being done in the borders of the Swabians, Wilhelm, landgrave of the Hessians, having led his army through Frankfurt, surrounded Bensheim, a town of the Palatine, with a siege. But when those who held the garrison in the town defended themselves bravely, and the Palatine's army was approaching, he withdrew with the matter unfinished. Nevertheless he plundered the villages round about, and whatever belonged by right to the Palatine, and gave them to the flames. He plundered Lorsch, a monastery of the Premonstratensian order, and assessed it a sum of money so that it should not be set on fire. He set fire to the Palatine's most beautiful new castle, which from its founder was called Friedrichsburg, and utterly destroyed it. He also received into surrender the castle of Stein, not far from Worms, through the betrayal of the castellan. Descending from there to Mainz, with the people of Mainz favoring him, he brought his army across and seized, caused to be burned, and utterly destroyed everything round about that belonged to the Palatine's jurisdiction.

Then, moving his army, he pitched camp near the town called Alzey, and everything round about, both in the fields, because it was harvest time, and in the villages, he seized and granted as plunder to his soldiers. Nothing was safe except what had been fortified by the protection of walls; for he did not have at hand the machines necessary for attacking towns and stronger fortifications, and therefore he never conquered anyone resisting him, but took only the dwellings of fleeing peasants and poor people. All the Palatine hamlets round about that he could reach he burned with fire. Whatever was found anywhere, both in churches and in villages, without delay, without distinction of persons, without reverence for places, fell as common plunder.

He took Gauodorum by the surrender of the inhabitants, and, taking plunder from there, let it go, whether by fire [unclear]. In wine, grain, and other necessary human utensils, he had great plunder from the land of the people of Gaw, which, reserved for his own uses, he sent at that time into Hesse. When these things had been done with excessive cruelty around the town of Alzey and in its Gau, the aforementioned Wilhelm, count of the Hessians, led his army to Kreuznach; and, having pitched camp around Bosenheim in the Nahegau, he laid waste everything round about.
