There, while he was staying in the tents together with the duke of Brunswick, Duke Alexander came to him from Meisenheim, having long since been allied with him, because both seemed to have not only the common causes of the Empire, but also private ones against the count palatine.

But before these things happened, Alexander's men, on the vigil of Peter and Paul, burned certain little villages of the Palatine around Sobernheim, and in the morning entered the monastery of the Wilhelmites called Marienpforte with carts and [unclear]. Carrying off to Meisenheim whatever they could find, after receiving two hundred gold pieces from the prior for security, they promised to preserve his monastery from fire. It was Friday and, as has been said, the vigil of the Apostles.

When Johannes Trithemius, our abbot, heard this, terrified by fear of the enemies, on the same day he withdrew to the nearest town of the Palatine, which the ancients called Stauronesus and which our people call Kreuznach. Having gradually brought in the books, privileges, and all the utensils of the house, lest they lie open as plunder for the adversaries, he remained there for five months and fourteen days, until the end of the war, and on the vigil of St. Andrew returned to the monastery.

Meanwhile, while the count of Hesse was residing in tents in the province around Kreuznach with a very large army, his soldiers plundered everything round about that belonged to the right of the Palatine, sparing absolutely no person or place. Count Emicho of Leiningen was set over the burning, a savage man, regarding neither God nor men, who burned with fire all the Palatine villages round about, except a few which the payment of money had freed. That he did not fear God, by works contrary to God [unclear].

The duke of Wurttemberg takes certain fortifications, towns, and castles of the Palatine.

Bretten is besieged.

The Hessians [unclear].

Bensheim is besieged.

Friedrichsburg, the new castle of the Palatine, is destroyed.

[unclear] they went out with their staffs, leaving behind everything they had, and departed to other companions of their error, by whom they were received with joy and honor as martyrs of Christ, and were most abundantly provided with all necessities. They profess themselves imitators of the apostles: men without God, without heart, full of the Devil. They are, however, very cunning men, and in their sect wonderfully skilled in teaching, disputing, and defending, so much so that they cannot easily be overcome by anyone in disputation by arguments. No one is found of such dull understanding, provided he has the free use of reason, who, once he has professed this sect, does not immediately become, in defending it by arguments, most learned, as it seems to him. But lest anyone think the matter some kind of miracle, we shall state the cause of so great a change, so that all may understand that it is not God but a malignant spirit working in them. Whoever desires to be admitted by prudence into that secret society first enters a church while some Catholic priest is celebrating, and, standing in a corner or in some secret place, throughout the whole Mass speaks certain insulting words, which it is not fitting for us to express on account of the weak, against the sacraments under his breath, with the intention proposed to him by his teacher. When these have been completed after the end of Mass, a fly of large body flies to him, and, by the noise of its wings indicating that it is present, seeks entry into his mouth. But as soon as he opens his mouth, it enters him, and the man is filled with a diabolical spirit, and becomes learned and wonderfully cunning in that sect. Yet they themselves affirm that the evil fly is not a demon but the Holy Spirit, who, descending upon them, as upon true imitators of the apostles, just as once on the day of Pentecost upon those men, makes them learned and steadfast. And in truth they become not steadfast but obstinate, nor could they ever be brought back from their errors to the right way by any kinds of torments. We knew one convert who, deceived by the counsel of the heretics, did and said under Mass the things we have mentioned; but when he heard the noise of the fly circling his head, he became terrified and fell to the ground, and was scarcely able to drive away the fly so that it would not enter his mouth. Yet not all who profess that sect of error [unclear]

Armsheim, Bafenheim, Lansheim, Wendelheim, Heydelheim, Budesheim, Laubersheim perish by fire.

showed: for he did not even fear to burn churches consecrated to God, and he did not spare the sacred vessels of the mysteries. The village of Armsheim, together with its new and very beautiful church, was burned to the ground by his command and miserably destroyed; the village of Bafenheim, together with the church and our court lying next to it, was reduced to ashes by his order; likewise the village of Lansheim with its church and bells utterly perished by fire; likewise Windesheim, Heidesheim, Budeseheim, Laubersheim, and very many other villages, the names of all of which it would be too tedious to recount, were burned in like madness and wholly perished.

There was a village near the river Nahe, close to the town of Bingen, which by its old name they called Monsterium, having a very beautiful church. A few years earlier the Count Palatine had bought it from the hands of a certain Count of the Rhine, against the protest of Berthold, archbishop of Mainz, placing in it a garrison against the attacks of the men of the Rhine. Hence very grave dissensions had arisen between the church of Mainz and the Palatines; and on their account the men of Mainz, having at this time gained the opportunity of evil wars, supplied the cause, not to say the pleas, for its burning. For for a long time, in the name of the Palatine, a certain Albert Goler of Ravensburg, prefect of the Stauronenses, had harassed them and had made them subject to various inconveniences. Therefore, when the occasion they had long desired had now been given, the men of Bingen obtained from the Count of Hesse, by their entreaties, the burning of the aforesaid village.

But when the village was already burning, Master Henry, pastor of the church of Bingen, was summoned to rescue the most holy body of Christ from the fire; for when he came to the church, already burning in its upper part, he drew the sacrament from the hagiotheca and, suffused with tears, said before everyone: “O most wicked of men, who do not even spare the Lord God your creator, but strive to drive him who contains all things from his dwelling: believe, dukes, believe, prince, that Almighty God will not long let so rash an injury go unavenged.” How truly he spoke, the vengeance that followed proved by divine judgment.

Moreover Wilhelm, Count of Hesse, after spending [unclear] days in the aforesaid place near Stauronesum, and after all things round about, far and wide, had been consumed by dreadful devastation, led his army through the town of Bingen. On the following day, advancing against Ingelheim, he set his battle line in order and thought to attack the castle, which they call the palace of Charlemagne; but his attempts were checked in the following manner by the diligence of the Palatines. As the Hessians approached the castle, when they saw the gates open, they thought the garrisons had turned to flight. And so, bursting forward in a mass to the gate, each, gaping for plunder, hurried to get ahead of the other. Behold, suddenly the Palatines who had lain hidden inside, setting fire to engines prepared beforehand in a concealed arrangement, which from their sound we call bombards, directed them against the enemy, killing many by the blows of the instruments and turning the rest to flight. And soon, when the castle was shut, they rushed to the walls and towers and by the violence of the engines stoutly kept all away from access to the castle.

Meanwhile, while these things were being done around the castle, the adjoining village, having been set on fire, was burning, while all the villagers within that castle protected themselves by the defense of the walls. Indeed many of the Hessians, entering the houses of the burning village for the sake of plunder, were led astray by their own negligence and perished in the fire. The Hessians, thrown into confusion and having suffered a great slaughter of their men, raised the siege and crossed over to Mainz; having crossed the river, they took by surrender a certain castle of the Count in Hanau, which is called Homberg or Alteburg.

While these things were being done by the Hessians, Alexander, Duke of Zweibruecken, assisted by the forces of his allies, surrounded Pilickheim with a siege. Pilickheim is besieged. Since he could not overcome the strength of his adversaries, he withdrew ingloriously from the siege of the town. Therefore, when the army had been removed from the siege, it attacked and plundered the villages and monasteries round about, situated under the lordship of the Count Palatine, and whatever was not redeemed with money it laid waste by fire and burning. The Alexandrians attacked and plundered the church at Clingenmonster, which a few years earlier was remembered as belonging to our Order, and also the monasteries of the Cistercian order, Vtersdal in Otterburg, together with Hartvigshausen of the Holy Spirit, and also that of the nuns of St. Lambert; they extorted money for remitting the burning. Our courts [unclear]. And evils were multiplied in all the land of the Palatine.

But while the enemies were raging everywhere around us against the Palatine, almost all the courts of our monastery of Sponheim were either destroyed by fire by the Hessians or utterly desolated by the incursion of plunderers. For with the fruits of the earth consumed by the army of the enemies, we suffered an intolerable loss of temporal goods, scarcely recoverable in thirty years. Since Trithemius our abbot remained in Stauronesum for several months, with the enemies around the monastery day and night, we fear that our losses cannot be recovered in our age.

While Chronicle of Trithemius

In this same year Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, sent several messengers and letters here to Abbot Trithemius, whom he wished to have with him.

Reymundus, cardinal of Santa Maria Nuova, legate of the Apostolic See, entered Mainz on the Saturday before Palms. The grace of the Jubilee was proclaimed, although, because of the scarcity of people, the gathering was slow and tardy. Nevertheless afterward devotion increased with time, and a great sum of money was offered in various places to the Jubilee chests; this, not yet converted to the promised use, is kept shut up.

In the same year Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot, reviewed the books of the library. There were found in it 1,646 volumes, all of which, apart from forty in number, he himself had brought together in one place during the time of his rule. Finally, in the Greek language, knowledge of which he had acquired, he purchased many volumes. In Hebrew also he reviewed some volumes brought together in this very year; all of these are kept separately in one register, carefully written out by their names.

In this same year, on the eighth day of the month of April, Gerlach of Breitbach, abbot of Deutz, while on his way to the general chapter at Trier, was captured near the little palace by the officials of Jacob, from the Margraves of Baden, administrator of the church of Trier, and was held in custody for four months, on account of his brother, a canon of the greater church, who, with his adherents, was opposed to the same margrave, as we have said.

In the same year also, on the octave of St. Lawrence the martyr, Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot, had the larger bell, broken ten years before, made anew and larger than it had been before, weighing fifteen hundredweight of the best bronze. Later, on the day of Cosmas and Damian, he solemnly blessed it himself, in the presence of Conrad Celtis Protucius, poet laureate, and Ladislaus of Sontheim, historiographer, envoys of Maximilian, King of the Romans, sent to Trithemius himself on a certain business.

In the year noted above, when the dreadful plague of epidemic disease was raging all around, it also invaded the present place; within the space of almost one month it removed and consumed five brothers from our midst. At last half the people of the little village of Sponheim were carried off by the same disease.

Likewise in the same year Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot, had the summer refectory painted with images and names of the abbots of this monastery of ours, Sponheim, in order from the beginning of the foundation down to this year, his nineteenth, together with their coats of arms. In this same year the annual chapter was celebrated at St. Peter’s in Erfurt, on the Sunday after the feast of St. Bartholomew the Apostle. There our abbot Trithemius, before an assembly of fathers, abbots, doctors, and students, delivered a distinguished oration in praise of the monastic life; received with great favor by all, he returned not without [unclear].

1503.

In this year, which was the twentieth of our abbot Johannes Trithemius, the winter was exceedingly harsh and long, and here around us there was great mortality of livestock and human beings. Afterward the greatest drought of summer followed in almost all Germany, so that in very many places it did not rain for four months. Hence the hay and oats dried up completely and were high in price, to such a degree that the poor sold their livestock.

In the same year, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, Jacob, from the Margraves of Baden, archbishop of Trier, died. He was buried with honor in the greater church of the people of Trier. His obsequies were performed among the people of Koblenz in Lent after Reminiscere Sunday, with great pomp. Our abbot Johannes Trithemius was present at them, sent and appointed, as is customary, as envoy in the name of the most illustrious prince, lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, and prince-elector. Afterward Jacob, from the Margraves of Baden, son of Margrave Christopher, formerly coadjutor of the deceased archbishop, as we said above, was confirmed as archbishop of Trier by Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, and was accepted by the greater part of the chapter, people, and land: an elegant and learned man, a most worthy lover of all learned men, than whom hardly any better man could at this time have been found for the pontificate, about thirty years old.

In the same year also, in the month of June, the aforesaid Christopher, Margrave of Baden, again came here, without burden to us, as he is accustomed, to see and speak with Abbot Trithemius; with him he discussed certain secrets in the hidden mysteries of nature, and shared some matters with him.

In the year noted above also, the lord Johannes, abbot of this place aforementioned, [a new stu-] Sponheim.

He built from the foundations a conventual heated room for the brothers’ winter refectory, adorning it inside all around with fine wooden paneling, out of love for the brothers, because it was very necessary for them, since from the time of the reform they had had no conventual heated room, but both in winter and in summer had been content in the summer refectory with its underground fireplace. He also rebuilt anew from the foundations, with stone walls, the mill that was lower down, which in the vernacular is called ter Leymule, since it had completely collapsed from excessive age. Through neglect of the cattle, too, in this same year one house utterly collapsed; because of necessity he immediately built it anew from the foundations with a wooden wall and four chambers.

In the same year, just as the plague had taken hold in the preceding year, indeed in the preceding three years, fevers, heats, and pains of the head, together with dysentery, attacked many thousands of people throughout this whole region; consumed by these, many died everywhere. For this illness was so great and widespread in Kreuznach, Bingen, Mainz, Frankfurt, Worms, Speyer, and the neighboring villages, and here in Sponheim, that there was scarcely a house in which someone was not lying sick with fevers or dysentery.

In the same year also the lord Johannes, abbot, obtained for himself and his successors a privilege concerning the use of a portable altar from the lord Raymond, cardinal, legate de latere of the Apostolic See to all Germany, whose tenor follows and is as follows.

Raymond, by divine mercy priest cardinal of the holy Roman Church of the title of Santa Maria Nuova [unclear].

Chronicle of Trithemius

After [his?] death Pius III was appointed pope; when he died within the space of one month, Julius II was ordained by the consent of all.

In the year also noted above, namely on the third day of the month of September, the annual chapter of our order was held at Mainz in the monastery of St. James; and Johannes Trithemius was present and delivered an oration to the fathers.

In these same days, little by little, the preliminaries of wars began to boil up against Philip, count palatine of the Rhine and duke of Bavaria; from these afterwards countless evils followed, both hereabouts and in Bavaria.

In the prescribed year of the Christians, in the month of October, the prince-electors assembled at Frankfurt, an imperial town: Berthold, archbishop of Mainz; Hermann, archbishop of Cologne; Jacob, archbishop of Trier; Philip, count palatine of the Rhine; and Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg; and, in the name of Frederick, duke of Saxony, the orator Heinrich von Bunau, knight. They treated certain affairs of the empire in common. The most reverend legate of the Apostolic See was present, Reymund, cardinal priest of Santa Maria Nova, bishop of Gurk, together with the orators of Maximilian, king of the Romans, ever august. Johannes Trithemius, our abbot, was present, summoned by letters and messengers by the most serene prince Joachim, the aforesaid margrave, who had already for a long time burned with desire to see and hear Trithemius. He remained with him for ten continuous days, while, to the best of his ability, he gave an account to the prince of the things that the prince desired to hear from him. While our abbot was staying at Frankfurt, the apostolic legate was invited to the margrave's table; Trithemius himself was invited, and when at last he was about to depart, our magnificent abbot was presented with gifts by both. In taking leave of the abbot, the legate used the words of the most blessed Antony, saying: “O how late you are known, how soon you depart.” The abbot was called four times to the cardinal's table; the cardinal promised him great things if he was willing to go with him to Rome. The same legate, by apostolic authority, confirmed the Office, the Rosary, and the treatise of prayers in praise of St. Anne published by Abbot Trithemius, granting eighty days of indulgences to each and all, as often as they should pray that Office, or the prayer, or his Rosary. Likewise, to those visiting with devotion the altar of most holy Anne, mother of Mary, which the same abbot Trithemius founded in the abbatial house, on the feast day of St. Anne, that same patroness, and also on all feasts of the blessed Mary ever virgin, of Andrew the Apostle, of Mary Magdalene, on the day of the dedication of that altar, which is the fourth day before the kalends of August, on the day of Easter, Ascension, Pentecost, Corpus Christi, Martin, Benedict, the Ten Thousand Martyrs, All Saints, the Epiphany of the Lord, all the Apostles, and St. Joseph, foster-father of our savior the Lord Jesus Christ, as often as they should do so, he granted eighty days of indulgences, to last in perpetuity.

1504.

In the twenty-first year of our abbot Trithemius, and the forty-third of his age, a most dreadful war arose between Emperor Maximilian and Philip, count palatine of the Rhine; its cause and beginning were as follows. When George, duke of Bavaria, had died, who had received from his father the name “the Rich” together with abundance of goods, Rupert, his son-in-law, duke, son of the aforementioned count Philip, palatine of the Rhine, said that the duchy of Bavaria and all the riches of his father-in-law belonged to him by right. He had George’s only daughter as wife, by whom he had already received legitimate children as successors. But Albert, duke of Munich Bavaria, was forearmed by certain agreements and letters formerly made between him and Duke George himself, sealed by both parties, by which it was provided that daughters should not succeed in the duchy, but that if one of them died earlier without male seed, the other should obtain his principality. Though warned in every way, Rupert refused to accept this, but persisted in his own opinion against the imperial decree. Therefore the most gentle emperor Maximilian, moved by zeal for justice, after he saw that he accomplished nothing by exhortation, subjected Duke Rupert, as a rebel, contumacious and disobedient to the constitutions, to the imperial ban by sentence, and punished all who adhered to him with the same penalty.

What meanwhile was Rupert’s father Philip to do, pressed too hard from both sides? “For if I abandon my son,” he said, “I shall violate the right of fatherhood; but if I show myself a father to my son, I know that Caesar and the whole empire will wage war against me.” At last the love of fatherhood overcame the advantage of his own utility; an army was sent to aid his son, and he made himself subject to the incursion of all the princes—

The annual chapter is held.

Preliminaries of wars against the Palatine.

Assembly of princes at Frankfurt.

Trithemius called to Frankfurt.

Confirmation of the works of Trithemius.

Indulgence.

Impious war against the Palatine.

Rupert, however, otherwise [unclear]

What meanwhile was Rupert’s father Philip to do, too sorely pressed from both sides? “For if I abandon my son,” he said, “I shall violate the right of fatherhood; but if I show myself a father to my son, I know that Caesar and the whole empire will wage war against me.” At last the love of fatherhood overcame his own advantage of utility; an army was sent to aid his son, and he made himself incur the hostility of all the princes.

Sponheim.

...he granted with certain liberties, and, honoring him with splendid gifts, dismissed him from his presence with goodwill.

In the same year also, after Trithemius, our abbot, had returned from Cologne to Speyer, there came to him a certain doctor of medicine named Narcissus, from the kingdom of the French, with letters from a certain bishop of [Cahors?], who summoned Trithemius to him in France, proposing great gifts and having much and sufficient money ready at hand for travel expenses. For the aforesaid prelate, moved by Trithemius’s reputation, desired to have him with him in France, either permanently or for a time, and for that reason promised many things. But Abbot Trithemius, who had promised the Margrave Joachim that he would follow his steps to Ursulum, and had already received from him fifty florins for travel expenses, desiring above all to keep the faith he had promised, could by no means enter France with the doctor who had been sent. Therefore, answering the prelate by letters concerning certain questions, he sent the doctor back to the French, declaring to him that on that occasion he could not come at all.

In the year noted above also, on the seventh day of September, Reymundus, cardinal priest of Santa Maria Nuova, bishop of Gurk, died and was buried at Viterbo. For three continuous years he had been legate a latere of the Apostolic See throughout the whole German nation: a man most holy in morals and life, conspicuous for all integrity, a great friend and singular patron of our Abbot Trithemius, a great cultivator of justice, and at the same time the most constant despiser of all the honors and riches of the world. Our age had no one like him.

In the same year, on the twentieth day of October, John our abbot, in the March, with the aforesaid prince Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, [unclear] new...

...cardinal of Santa Maria Nuova, bishop of Gurk, buried at Viterbo, who for three continuous years was legate a latere of the Apostolic See for the whole German nation: a man most holy in morals and life, and conspicuous for all integrity, a great friend and singular patron of our Abbot Trithemius, a great cultivator of justice, and at the same time the most constant despiser of all the honor and riches of the world. Our age had no one like him.

In the year noted above also, Maximilian, king, ever august, launched an expedition into Hungary; after peace had been arranged, he immediately returned to his own lands.

1506.

In the twenty-second year of Trithemius our abbot, the winter was quite harsh and very prolonged.

In the same year the aforesaid prince Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, established a new universal school in his town of Frankfurt an der Oder. On the twenty-sixth day of April, which was the second Sunday after the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, he inaugurated it with great solemnity, Abbot John being present. Its first rector of the university was appointed from the faculty of theology: a lecturer from Buchen, an East Franconian, a Leipzig doctor called [Wimpina?].

At these times, while John Trithemius our abbot was staying in the March, our monastery, both because of his long absence and because of the recent losses which it had lately suffered in the war, was sufficiently afflicted in both conditions; there was no one to furnish help. But certain of the brothers, by their incautious speeches and foolish complaints, all of which were reported to Trithemius himself by a messenger going between, wounded his mind very deeply and finally alienated him completely from us.

In the year noted above, on the fourteenth day of May, John Trithemius our abbot, honored with gifts and presents by the most wise Margrave Joachim, and having obtained permission to depart, left Ursulum with an honorable company, set out on the journey toward the regions of the Rhine, and on the second day of June reached the city of Speyer. From Frankfurt he had sent ahead Brother Theoderic, his chaplain, to Sponheim, so that he might diligently inquire into the condition of the monastery, investigate whether there was any disturbance by rivals, and summon his prior to Heidelberg; for the abbot was unwilling to return to the monastery unless he had first understood the brothers’ feelings toward him. He therefore remained with the abbot of Limburg until the end of September at [Budoras?], silently awaiting the outcome of the matter. But after he understood that the feelings of certain brothers toward him were less sincere in the ardor of charity, and that the mind of Duke John of [Simmern?], a prince otherwise very pious, had been somewhat moved, as he was told, by the careless denunciation of certain rivals, he judged it altogether safer to leave this abbacy of his own will than to place himself in the midst of disturbance.

Of Sponheim.

...would be willing to accept what was offered. Philip, Count Palatine and Duke of Bavaria, the illustrious prince and elector of the empire, promised most generously to provide Abbot Trithemius with all necessities, so long as both should live, or either of them.

Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, elector of the empire, of whom we spoke above, embraces Trithemius with such longing down to the present day that he seems to desire nothing more than to have him with him. This is now witnessed by many frequent letters written in his own hand, both to the Bishop of Würzburg, asking for his benevolent consent, and to Trithemius himself, asking him, of his good will, to agree to come. The substance of that prince’s request is this: since Trithemius will not consent to remain with him outside the monastery permanently, he should not refuse to be with him for a short time. These things are true, proved not only by the very frequent letters of the aforementioned man, but often also shown by splendid gifts and presents. For the Margrave himself honored Trithemius with many splendid gifts, and to this very day has not ceased to heap frequent benefactions upon him. For from the time when he departed from us, it is agreed that he has been honored by him to the value of at least five hundred gold florins; nor meanwhile has there been a year, six of which have now passed, in which the often-mentioned prince did not honor Trithemius either with a gold or silver cup, or with some other gift. Moreover, at his own expense he sent him salted fish, pike, and others, with many vessels, to Würzburg.

Finally Hermann, Archbishop of Cologne, promised that his assistance would be available to Trithemius in every need, and several times loaded him with money and silver cups. The Abbot of Fulda also, hearing that Trithemius had departed from us and did not wish to return, had him solicited through Hartmann, Count of Kirchberg, to turn aside to Fulda, promising him a provostship for the support of the rest of his life. With similar generosity many other powerful and wealthy men in the world followed after Trithemius, who promised that they would have him with them and provide for him most abundantly; nor even today are there lacking those who would receive him with honor and provide for him on honorable terms, if he agreed to turn aside to them.

But Johannes Trithemius himself, having from the beginning been laudably received and instructed in the observance of monastic discipline in the present monastery of Sponheim, when he was about twenty-three years old, did not consider it sound or safe for himself to associate in the courts of princes, nor honorable to withdraw from the holy union of observance. Therefore almighty God, having pity on his desolation and unwilling to abandon the afflicted man at the end, looked upon him mercifully and provided, in observance, a place suited to his studies and way of life.

For Conrad, the aforementioned Abbot of St. Stephen at Würzburg, whom we said had been sent from the chapter at Heidelberg to Trithemius with another, after he heard the many reasonable causes by which he was moved and compelled to yield, since he was his friend, had no small compassion for him. Hence he promised that he would give his effort so that Trithemius, elected canonically, might obtain the abbey of St. James at Würzburg with good peace and a pure entrance. At that time the abbot of the said monastery was a certain Cilianus of Ochsenfurt, who had resolved to resign that abbey for certain causes. When he had heard that it was possible for Trithemius to succeed in his place, he rejoiced greatly, saying that he would yield to no one in the world more gladly than to so great a man, and asked that the desired matter take effect as quickly as possible and that no obstacle intervene.

And so Conrad, Abbot of St. Stephen, brought the business to the most reverend Bishop of Würzburg and magnificent Duke of Eastern Franconia, Lorenz, asserting that Trithemius could be induced to give up the abbey of Sponheim and take up that of St. James, if this indeed were pleasing to his paternity. The most reverend prelate, who had previously heard many proclamations of praise concerning Abbot Trithemius, and had seen him before at Heidelberg at the table of the Prince Palatine, had addressed him graciously, and long before would freely have advanced him to the abbey in Schwartach, if, when twice summoned, he had appeared after the death of the abbots Michael and likewise Paul, answered that it not only pleased him but that he especially desired to be able to have Trithemius as abbot in his diocese.

Therefore, once the bishop’s will was heard, a messenger was sent as quickly as possible to Heidelberg, to Trithemius at Würzburg. Trithemius secretly set the matter before the prince, lord Philip, Count Palatine, and with his consent went up to the place to which he was called. And so on the third day of the month of October he came to Würzburg. After the voluntary resignation of Abbot Cilianus, on the twenty-second day of the aforesaid month, which was Monday after the feast of St. Dionysius the martyr, after a commitment made by the brothers into the hands of the lord bishop and two abbots, he was elected and appointed abbot of the often-mentioned monastery; on the fourth day of the same month after the tenth he was confirmed by the same most reverend prelate, and immediately on the next day, which was solemn on the feast of St. Burkhard, he was introduced into real possession of the abbey of St. James.

The Count Palatine likewise.

The Margrave of Brandenburg [unclear] most gladly.

Trithemius is magnificently endowed with gifts by the Margrave of Brandenburg.

The Archbishop of Cologne promised Trithemius every assistance.

The Abbot of Fulda Sponheim.

While these things were happening in our lands, very grave wars were being waged throughout all Bavaria against Philip, Count Palatine, and his son Duke Rupert. For Maximilian, most powerful King of the Romans, wishing to humble the proud and recall the rebellious to obedience, took with him certain princes, namely Duke Albert of Munich, Frederick also, Margrave of Brandenburg, who was staying in Ansbach, and also the bishop of Augsburg and the citizens of the towns of Nuremberg, Ulm, Augsburg, and other imperial cities, and devastated almost all Bavaria, and took many fortifications of his adversaries. Amid these events the monastery of Waldsassen, of the Cistercian order, not far from Eger near the entrance to Bohemia, was cruelly plundered and burned by the army of Margrave Frederick, and was utterly destroyed. But King Maximilian, having arranged matters in Bavaria for victory, led part of the army into Alsace, and whatever right the Palatine had around Strasbourg he received in surrender without bloodshed: namely Geroldseck, Offenburg, Schottern, Ortenburg, and Gengenbach, with all things which up to that point seemed to belong there to the Palatine. Finally, on this side of the Rhine likewise he received into his power the whole advocacy of the province, Lutzelstein, Haguenau, and Wissembourg, with all castles, villages, and towns belonging to it, down to the present day.

In the year noted above, when the Hessians seemed to be occupied around Alteburg and the Alexandrians around Biliekheim, Philip, Count Palatine, sent an army of his men from Alzey and Heidelberg into Stauronesum on the nineteenth day of the month of July, and they remained there eight days, awaiting their increase in numbers and the engines necessary for war. But on the twenty-first day of the same month, which was the feast of the most holy mother Anne, leaving Stauronesum in the morning, they directed their battle-line toward the lands of Duke Alexander, adjoining the county of Sponheim, and surrounded with a siege a small town of that duke, Cotirodorum, commonly called Dreckodernheim, which was taken on the following Sunday, that is, on the twenty-eighth day of July. Its walls and towers were thrown down to the ground; except for the people, everything was given to the soldiers as plunder. The Palatines also entered the monastery of the holy bishop Disibod, and, after driving off the garrison which Duke Alexander had placed there, devastated everything and left nothing untouched except the library. For even the country multitude carried off the lead from the roofs and windows, and what it could not carry away, it labored with all its strength to destroy; they also carried off as plunder all the wine and grain, and likewise the livestock. But while these things were being done around the monastery of Saint Disibod, which is only one mile distant from Sponheim, Matthias, abbot of the same, was being held captive by a certain tyrant; at last, through the justice of the Count Palatine, he was released and sent away free. After Cotirodorum had been taken, the Palatine army was led through the Alexandrian lands toward Lutern, and on the way they attacked and plundered certain little villages; they also gave some over to fire. On the eighteenth day of the month of August after this, Wilhelm, Count of Hesse, gathered a great army and set up camp in the mountains of the Rhine opposite the city of Bacharach on that side of the river, and surrounded with a very strong siege a small town of the Palatine called Kaub. He used great force in order to take the little town, but, when the Palatine sent aid to those shut inside, all the efforts of those pressing the siege were broken. For in that village there were men appointed for its defense, many and very strong, whose number was increased daily. The army of the Count Palatine set up camp on the mountain near Bacharach, opposite the Hessians; and so the Rhine, flowing between, separated those men from these. Various devices were devised by the Hessians, but all failed because of the height of the mountains. They tested one another with cannon-shots, and, after some had been killed on both sides, at last on the twenty-fifth day of September the siege was lifted and the prince of Hesse returned to his own lands, not without loss among his men.

In the year written above, on the twentieth day of the month of August, that is, on the feast of Saint Bernard, Duke Rupert died, the son of Philip, Count Palatine and Duke of Bavaria, prince-elector; and after a few days his wife also died, daughter of the late Duke George the Rich.

At the same time afterward Louis, bishop of Speyer, also died, a most excellent man; Philip of Rosenberg, cantor of the church, succeeded him, a man constantly afflicted by illnesses, prudent, and a very vigorous defender of the affairs of the church.

Also in the year noted above, on the penultimate day of the month of August, which was Friday and the second day after the feast of the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist, the garrison of five hundred men, which Philip, Count Palatine, had placed on the mountain for the protection of the monastery of Limburg against the Count of Leiningen, was recalled by him and sent to certain other places of his principality. After their departure the monastery, left empty of men, [unclear]

King Maximilian devastates Bavaria.

The monastery of Waldsassen is taken.

Army of the Palatine.

It is called Dreckoderheim.

The monastery of Saint Disibod is plundered.

Kaub is besieged.

The Palatine army.

Duke Rupert dies.

Philip becomes bishop of Speyer.

The garrison is recalled from Limburg. Chronicle of Trithemius

remained, the monks having previously taken counsel for themselves in flight because of the threats of their adversaries. On the same day, after the departure of the Palatine garrison, certain petty robbers of the adversaries’ party assembled, entered armed into the monastery of Limburg, now empty of people, stripped everything, plundering it, and carried off to their own places whatever they could find. Finally, when all its goods had been carried away, they set fire to the monastery, burned it, and utterly destroyed it. In that fire all the monks’ dwellings, and also the houses, barns, stables, and all the buildings, together with the notable church, were entirely consumed and reduced to ash, so that apart from stones absolutely nothing remained. This fire lasted for twelve continuous days, the ministers of impiety returning daily and kindling the fire anew, lest anything remain intact.

The church of the aforesaid monastery was great and very beautiful, built sumptuously in honor of the Mother of God, the inviolate Virgin Mary, and of the Holy Cross, by Conrad II, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1030. Its two inner parts were supported by twenty columns of solid stone, each of which was twenty feet in length and two geometrical cubits, that is, at least twelve feet, in thickness. The length of the church itself, from the outer western door to the high altar, contained 450 feet; its breadth, 140. In it there were twenty altars, six bells, and very many altar ornaments, panel-works, and images on the altar, all of which, as we have said, were either first carried off by the enemies of the cross of Christ or consumed by fire.

The count palatine, protector of the monastery, had in time made the abbot more cautious, so that whatever he wished to be safe he should have carried to the cities. Being so advised, he ordered the ornaments of the church, the sacred vessels, the books, and whatever could be transported to be brought to the city of Speyer, where at that time he lay ill. The monks and all the donati, through fear of the enemies, had previously betaken themselves to safer places. For because of the cruel threat of the enemies, who were staying nearby in the castle of Duroburg, no one remained in the monastery except one old man, wholly unfit for flight. When he saw the monastery on fire, rising from the place in which he was hiding, he entered the church crawling as best he could; hiding himself in the [unclear], he was burned. So violent was that burning of the church that it consumed not only all the timber, but by the violence of its heat broke almost all the stone columns, solid, large, and very strong, of which we have spoken. Nothing in that whole monastery remained sound and intact except the single tower of the church. Indeed, as we afterwards saw the place restored, it would more easily have seemed possible to build a new monastery from the foundations in a known place than to restore that one again after the fire.

This savage and bloody war of almost the whole empire against the aforesaid Philip, count palatine, lasted about five months. On its account many, almost infinite evils were committed against God and men: many mortals were killed, others were driven into the utmost poverty; monasteries were either burned or plundered, churches burned or overturned, villages utterly laid waste by fire. The monastery called Waldsassen in Bavaria, not far from the town of Eger, situated at the entrance to Bohemia, of the Cistercian order, was burned in the same year and war by certain satellites of Frederick, margrave of Brandenburg, in a similar fury of the impious; but not long afterward two principal authors of the burning paid the penalty, dying shamefully.

In the year noted above, around the feast of St. Michael the Archangel, the renowned King Maximilian, after he saw that the palatine had been afflicted harshly enough by his rivals, was moved by mercy and applied the hand of piety. Forbidding to all the power of making war, he established peace for the humbled prince and those set in motion [unclear]; by edict he appointed a day for pleading at Cologne, on the first day of July in the following year, to which he summoned all.

In the year prescribed above, on the vigil of St. Andrew the Apostle, Johannes Trithemius of Sponheim returned to the monastery, after he had necessarily absented himself from the monastery for five months and twenty days, withdrawing because of fear of the enemies, nor did he judge it safe to return sooner, since the peace was not yet sufficiently established. On account of this war our monastery [suffered] very heavy [unclear]. For our estate in Bosenheim perished utterly by fire; our rents and revenues, especially of provisions, were for the greater part either consumed by the enemies or, because of the malice of the times and of men, did not come at all to our use. For all the goods of the household property by which we should have lived perished badly.

  1. In the twelfth year of Johannes Trithemius our abbot, in the eighth indiction of the Romans, around the middle of Lent, Philip, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, and [unclear] of the empire Sponheim.

The Archsteward and most worthy prince-elector summoned to Heidelberg all the prelates, bishops, abbots, counts, nobles, and communities of the cities and towns of his principality, and with them held counsel and negotiation concerning certain conditions pertaining to the reform of peace between himself and the princes of the empire.

In the same year noted above died Berthold, of the counts of Henneberg, a prince worthy of eternal memory and the most prudent of all men in his time, of great wisdom, and also of much experience in conducting the affairs of the Church and the empire. He presided well over his church, recovered many things that had been alienated, paid its debts, and loved peace.

He was succeeded in the pontificate by the dean of the greater church, Jacob of Liebenstein, a Swabian by birth, a good and very modest man, who did not complete a fourth year in the archbishopric, being afflicted with stones throughout the whole period of his rule and held back by various bodily illnesses.

In the year noted above, on the first day of the month of April, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of this monastery, setting out from the monastery in the morning at about the seventh hour with the messenger of the prince palatine and one servant and [unclear], took the road toward Heidelberg, having been summoned by the command of that prince and likewise by letters, in the matter of the burned monastery of Limburg, to give counsel that it be built at Wachenheim. At that time, however, he was rather weak in body, suffering from tertian fevers. When he had come to Heidelberg, disordered by the intemperate air, his illness was increased, to such an extent that he could not return as quickly as he had arranged. While he was thus ill at Heidelberg, on the fifth day after his departure from here, at the instigation of the Devil, there occurred here a grave disturbance, which, judging it very injurious to himself, he bore heavily. May almighty and merciful God pardon all who either gave counsel for this evil or aid. This deed, undertaken very rashly and without counsel, provided the abbot with cause for many tribulations and persecutions, and stirred up more rivals against him.

But he, since he was cautious through prudence and endowed with singular patience, committed the whole matter to be settled by divine mercy. Thereafter he has not returned here to the monastery up to the present day, not because he was prohibited by anyone, but because he feared that afterward he could never have peace with his rivals. Therefore, giving place to wrath, he left the place out of love of quiet, as we shall say later.

Also in the year noted above a great assembly of princes was held at Cologne at the beginning of the month of July, summoned by royal mandate, as we said above, for the confirmation of peace and concord, and it lasted until the end of the same month. In this assembly the following princes appeared: Maximilian, king of the Romans; Hermann, archbishop of Cologne; Jacob, archbishop of Trier; Lorenz, bishop of Würzburg; likewise the bishop of Bamberg, the bishop of Utrecht, the bishop of Liège, the bishop of Gurk, Petrus Bonomus, bishop of Trieste, and certain others whose names do not occur to us at this time.

Furthermore, the names of the secular princes then present are these: Philipp, count palatine and duke of Bavaria, elector of the empire, and his two sons, Ludwig and Friedrich; Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg, elector of the empire; Friedrich, duke of Saxony, elector of the empire, and his brother Johann; Friedrich, margrave of Brandenburg, who lived in Ansbach, paternal uncle of the aforesaid elector Joachim; Heinrich, duke of Brunswick; Erich, duke of Lüneburg; Wilhelm, duke of Jülich; Heinrich, duke of Mecklenburg; and certain others with many counts and nobles.

When he was about to go from the March of Brandenburg to the aforesaid assembly, Joachim, the prince-elector named above, sent ahead a mounted messenger with letters to our abbot Johannes Trithemius, who was then staying ill at Speyer in the house of the abbot of Limburg. By these letters he asked that he come down to him at Cologne, sending him travel money. Trithemius gladly agreed to the request of so great a prince, in whose eyes he had already before found great favor. Therefore, although he was still weak in part, and on account of a fall with his horse was suffering from a flux in his left leg, and for that reason limped a little, nevertheless, to please the prince, he hired a carriage and together with the messenger went down to Mainz, and from there by boat as far as Cologne, where he remained for a whole month with that margrave.

But in truth, since he could not yet fully know the authors of the injuries done to him, he resolved to delay his return to the monastery for some time, until he should see what the intention of his rivals was aiming at. When this became known to the often-mentioned prince, he urged him more insistently to go with him to the lands of the Margraviate of Brandenburg, to stay with him for some months. Trithemius did not wish to do this without the counsel of the illustrious prince Philipp, count palatine, whose great kindness he had experienced both then and before. Therefore, after obtaining that prince’s consent, the abbot promised the margrave that he would do what he had requested. Thus, when the assembly...

Concerning Nicolaus, twenty-sixth abbot of this monastery of Sponheim, who presided for twenty years, six months, and twenty-one days, and concerning certain deeds of that time.

After the voluntary resignation of our abbot, lord Johannes Trithemius, and his transfer to Wurzburg, as was said above, this monastery of ours at Sponheim was vacant for nearly two months. When these had at last passed, two abbots came together with us for the election of a new pastor: namely Thomas at Seligenstadt and Johannes of the Mount of St. John the Baptist in the Rheingau. Since they had been deputed to us as visitors according to the custom of the annual chapter, we gladly and honorably admitted them as directors of the business at hand.

Therefore in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s Nativity 1506, Roman indiction 9, on the fifth day before the Ides of December, that is, on the day after the feast of the Immaculate Conception of blessed Mary ever virgin, in the morning at about the ninth hour, or thereabouts, the prior and brethren of the convent assembled at the chapter-place together with the aforesaid visitors. After the customary prayers and declarations had first been made, they began the business of the election in God’s name by way of a compromise mixed with scrutiny, in the presence of the notary and witnesses. Accordingly, when the votes of each had been examined, as is customary, and set down in writing by the notary, the greater part of the voting brethren directed their votes to Nicolaus of Remich, prior of the convent, and elected him abbot, although the visitors themselves would gladly have set someone from outside over the monastery. But the prior and convent, not thinking it honorable or useful for themselves if they appointed over themselves as abbot some monk from another monastery, because several among them judged that there were suitable men among themselves who certainly both could shrewdly undertake so great a burden and would by no means refuse it, steadfastly agreed that no one other than some excellent man from their own congregation, why should I not say ours, was to be elected. Having so agreed, they prevailed, receiving the aforesaid Nicolaus as abbot. They say the agreement did not sufficiently please the abbots, who would have preferred some one or other of their own. Therefore Nicolaus, elected abbot by his own brethren and confirmed according to custom by Jacob, archbishop of Mainz, after Johannes Trithemius holds the abbacy today, for as long as he shall wish who alone knows and can do all things, God blessed forever. Amen.

His native place was a certain village in the duchy of Luxembourg, which the inhabitants call Remich, not far from the town of [Namercum?]. His father, named Andreas, sought his food by hand and craft, a man of simple and innocent life. He had a wife, Catharina, who was mother to this Nicolaus; but all his brothers died in boyhood. Nicolaus himself, while still a boy, at his parents’ command devoted himself to letters, first in his homeland, then at Trier, and afterward among those Wetterau people who border on the Hessians, whom we commonly call Butzbachers. At that time he made moderate progress, but afterward in the monastery much greater progress.

In the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1481, when he was about eighteen years old, he came to this monastery of Sponheim with two other schoolboys, and was received into the novitiate in regular observance by Johannes of Cologne, prior under the abbot, and after a year had passed was admitted to monastic profession according to the custom of the order. In the year of his probation he had acute fevers, on account of which there had almost been among certain men in the convent a refusal concerning his becoming a monk; and not long after his profession he was ordained subdeacon and deacon at the promotion of Johannes of Cologne, abbot. He lived a quiet life among the brethren without disturbance, and by his conduct never harmed or offended anyone.

When Johannes of Cologne, the abbot, was not long afterward transferred to the monastery of Seligenstadt, Johannes Trithemius succeeded in the abbacy. Because of the gentleness of Nicolaus’s life, he pursued him with the singular goodwill of affection: first he had him ordained priest, then attached him to himself as chaplain and familiar servant, and more frequently stirred him to the study of letters both by counsel and example. At his command Nicolaus became at once a scribe and a reader of Greek, a better Latinist, and in time and with practice an excellent Hebraist. After about four years, Abbot Trithemius, wishing to promote him gradually to higher things, appointed him cellarer, so that he might learn not only internal matters but also, in external matters without which the internal do not subsist, might gain experience with time. But when not yet fully three months had been completed in that office, since he was a lover of quiet and desired more to cultivate inner things than earthly ones, he urgently begged Abbot Trithemius to deign to have him released from so great a labor and burden of office, because he saw that he was by no means adequate for managing affairs and cares. Trithemius granted his petition and recalled him to inner matters. But lest he be thought to have suffered disgrace, he soon appointed him prior, and in that office he indeed remained continuously for fifteen years. In these fifteen years he devoted labor to both Hebrew and Greek letters, with Trithemius as teacher, and became an especially good Hebrew scribe. But how much he advanced in the rest, that is, either in the learning of the Scriptures, or in those things which [unclear].

The election takes place on the ninth day of December.

The greater part direct their votes to Nicolaus.

The lineage and origin of Abbot Nicolaus.

He is ordained subdeacon and deacon.

He is appointed prior. Chronicle of Trithemius

...that of the princes having at last been dissolved, Joachim the margrave, travelling through Saxony, returned to his own lands, after first assigning to the abbot abundant provisions for the journey and a quite honorable retinue. And so, in the year noted above, on the sixth day of the month of August, Johannes Trithemius the abbot left Cologne with his companions and went by boat up to Mainz. For he did not wish to enter the March unless he had first made to the prior the necessary report concerning the monastery. From Mainz, therefore, he again went up to Speyer and, summoning to himself Nicolaus de Reinig, his prior, entrusted to him all care and administration of this monastery; and, having arranged matters as he could, he entered the March through Thuringia. Coming to the town of Berlin, where the margrave has his residence, he was received by him with great joy and honor, and was abundantly provided for in all things according to princely munificence. He remained with that prince in the March for nine months, composing various little works for his praiseworthy instruction. For that same prince was most learned in every variety of writings, then in his twenty-fourth year, but in prudence and wisdom famous far beyond his age and very distinguished; burning exceedingly with love of saving knowledge, he had for many years desired to have Trithemius as teacher.

In the year noted above, while the assembly of princes was continuing in Cologne, Macharius, abbot of the burned monastery of Limburg, was present, wishing the cause of his men against Emicho, count of Leiningen, to be examined and judged by justice before the royal majesty. Therefore, at the king’s command, he offered his petition in writing, in which he most plainly accused the aforesaid count concerning the burning of the monastery, because it had been done by his command. The count, on the other hand, denied that he had ordered the burning, and said that he did not know who had set it on fire, because at that time he had been lying sick with fever in Grevenstein. But the abbot was able to prove by the testimony of many that the plundering incendiaries of the aforesaid monastery had gone out from Durenburg, commonly Hartenburg, the count’s nearby castle, and had returned there with the monastery’s spoils; and, what was of greater proof, he said that they were still living in that same castle. But Maximilian, greatly occupied by the war against the Venetians and by other affairs of the realm, entrusted the case to the archbishop of Mainz, who was then absent, to be amicably settled. In his hearing many matters were conducted over two years, but no agreement between the parties followed. Meanwhile the count nonetheless occupied Mount Limburg, where the monastery had stood, and the fields, meadows, woods, pastures, and fisheries around the abbey, and retained their revenues, with their useful profits, for almost six years, until the death of that abbot. When he finally died, his successor entered into an agreement with the count concerning the plunder; under its conditions no mention was made of the burning, but it was left to the abbot’s discretion whether he wished to proceed against him at law.

In the same year the aforesaid Abbot Macharius, wishing to find a secure place in which he might serve the Lord God with his monks in peace, received the parish church in the town of Wachenheim, after a lawful exchange had first been arranged, from the hand of the provost and convent of the Premonstratensians in Lautern, with the bishop of Speyer and also the prince palatine, whose town it is, consenting. The exchange having been made, and the necessary written instruments having been given and received on both sides, the aforesaid abbot established the place of his residence there and decided to make the aforesaid parish church into a monastery, in which he intended to remain with his monks. For it is agreed that he was moved by many reasons and considerations not to restore the monastery burned on the mountain; of these we know two to have been principal. One was that the place, lying open, was not fortified, and he feared that in the future the same thing might happen which he now grieved had been attempted. The other was that on the mountain he suffered great scarcity of water. Therefore he chose a place in the aforesaid town for building a monastery, where there would be both abundance of water and walls would easily prevent the incursion of impious men. And so he built certain necessary dwellings in the parish courtyard, in which he used to remain with a few monks; the rest, because of great poverty, he sent away to various monasteries of our order. But on all the days afterward during which that same Abbot Macharius lived, there were disputes and lawsuits between him and the aforesaid count because of the causes written above.

Likewise, in the aforesaid assembly of princes, in the year written above of Trithemius our abbot, King Maximilian, on the thirtieth day of the month of July, restored peace and concord among the mistrustful princes, and commanded it to be observed by all under imperial penalties. In the same assembly of princes, King Maximilian, on the twenty-ninth day of the month of July, summoned to himself Johannes Trithemius the abbot, who was with the lord margrave, as we have said. The king asserted that he had often heard his reputation from the report of many, and he had a long disputation with him concerning various questions of the Scriptures; whereupon the king, not a little delighted by his eloquence, [unclear] to him the privilege of an imperial chapel with Chronicle of Trithemius

Meanwhile it happened that the annual chapter of our order was held at Mainz at the end of the month of August, according to custom. Its presiding officers sent two prelates to Heidelberg, to our abbot Johannes Trithemius: namely Conrad, abbot of St. Stephen at Würzburg, and Johannes, abbot of Schuttern, who, in the name of the whole chapter, that is, of all the abbots then present in great number at Mainz, were to ask him to return here to the monastery of Sponheim, promising that they would take pains to remove all impediments from the midst.

By authority of the chapter they had appointed two others, Thomas in Seligenstadt and Johannes in the Rheingau, abbots of monasteries, to approach Duke Johann, who was staying in Simmern, and, if his mind were offended against him in any matter, to recall him to favor on behalf and in the name of all the fathers of the order. When he had heard these things, Johannes Trithemius is said to have given this reply:

“From the time when I began to be a monk, I was always willing, ready in mind to obey in all things the commands of my fathers; rashly I never departed from their statutes. Only on this occasion I can by no reasoning give consent to their commands, so as to return to Sponheim to remain there again, because I have no confidence that I shall henceforth have peace with them. For it is manifest how badly certain of them have plotted against me; whether through malice or through the simplicity of ignorance, I do not judge, but commit it to the judgment of almighty God. They have raised up many rivals against me; wherefore, if I returned to the monastery, neither would I be able to have trust in them, nor do I know that their minds would trust me perfectly. It is better, therefore, that we be separated from one another than that we live in perpetual dissension; for the salvation of souls must always be set before the advantage of bodies. And a shepherd who considers that he cannot make the sheep entrusted to him better provides salutarily for himself and for them if he resigns his office.

“Today the twenty-third full year has passed since I, unworthy, was ordained abbot of Sponheim, always overcooked in the furnace of extreme poverty, continuous in misery and labor, and, what more than all things has been accustomed to burden me, never relieved by the help of my brothers in so many necessary cares. Nor among the reasons for my departure was this the least: that one of my monks, by no means the least, whom I always sincerely loved as an intimate son, whom I defended as the pupil of my own eye against whatever molesters, unmindful of all benefits, lately, while stationed at Mainz, by the counsel and aid of a certain other good brother, issued against me letters full of insults, in the name of the whole convent, although it is clearly established to me that he had no commission or consent at all from the convent concerning this matter. If this was done, or could be done, by the man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who walked with me before the poor little flock in the pastures of the Lord, what will the weaker ones do, whom I have by no means heaped with such benefits? If my right hand, bound to me, could so rashly deny me, what will alien hands do?”

[unclear]

Since, therefore, God by manifest kindness had decreed to free me from such calamities, to the honor of his name, I shall yield gladly and commit myself to divine providence; lest, if I consent to remain longer in office among the ungrateful, I incur danger to the body and detriment to the soul. Nevertheless, before I do this, it will be necessary for me to provide a place for my future dwelling. The Lord God, who does not spurn the prayers of the poor, but sends help to those who ask at the proper time, will himself provide for me, I do not doubt, a place in which I may be able to serve him more freely and more quietly, and work out my own salvation in silence.”

Having said these things, he fell silent; and, both because of the causes noted above and because of certain others set forth by him to the abbots, persisting in the opinion he had begun, he did not consent to return here to the monastery. Whether this action of his pleased or displeased the divine majesty, we cannot know. This one thing we do not think should be passed over in silence, because we know that [unclear] among whom, if he had wished, he would at all times have found an excellent condition of living. For Maximilian, king of the Romans, both in person and through Matthaeus, bishop of Gurk, urged him many times, wishing to have him with him, or in one of his cities, for writing histories and other things of that kind; by him he would still be magnificently provided with an annual stipend, if the office [unclear].

Chronicle of Trithemius 428

Now the aforementioned monastery of St. James the Greater, of our order, was once built and endowed in the suburb of the city of Würzburg by the most holy prelate Embricho, around the year of the Lord’s nativity [MCXXX?], as was said far above, in the sixteenth year of Bernhem, our first abbot. In it monks of the Scottish nation were accustomed to dwell from the beginning, who lived commendably for many years according to the Rule of our most holy father Benedict; but little by little, with time, at last falling away from the first fervor of their institution, they finally brought the monastery itself down into utter poverty, and they themselves failed entirely. For in the year of the Lord 1397 Philip, the last abbot from the Scots, died, and left no monk in the community.

After his death the most reverend lord prelate of Würzburg, Laurentius, by apostolic commission and at the same time by ordinary authority, commendably undertook to reform the vacant place in both estates. For the sake of this good reform, [unclear] he introduced from the monastery of St. Stephen in the same place; he supplied them with the necessities of life, and paid in full almost all the debts contracted by the Scots. He made the church, darkened by age, as it were new and very beautiful; he gave ornaments, chalices, and several books for the library; and, restoring the community magnificently almost more than the first founder had done, he generously gave vineyards, annual rents, ready money in no small amount, and many other things.

Finally, even down to the present day, not ceasing from the good work which he began, he has bestowed more upon Trithemius himself and upon the monastery, and promises without doubt that he will do greater things, conferring notable annual rents and money in no small quantity and number for buying new [unclear].

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1506, in the ninth indiction of the Romans, on the fifteenth day of the month of October, Johannes Trithemius, elected and confirmed abbot of St. James at Würzburg, accepted real possession in the presence of Conrad the abbot, Master Peter the seal-bearer, Caspar the fiscal officer of lord Laurentius the bishop, and also the notary Master Martin Mosius, and very many witnesses and other notable men. These things were done when he had not yet completed the forty-fifth year of his age, but when twenty-two years, two months, and eighteen days had been completed and passed in many tribulations and labors from his assumption of the abbacy of this monastery in Sponheim.

While these things were being done concerning Abbot Johannes Trithemius at Würzburg, we were here in the monastery daily expecting that he would return to us, having hope and consolation that the abbots sent to him from the annual chapter at Mainz would by their exhortations induce him to return. But our confidence deceived us, because, without our knowing it, he assumed the aforesaid abbacy of St. James, and afterwards resigned this one.

Accordingly, in the aforesaid year, on the fourteenth day of the month of November, letters sent by that lord Abbot Johannes Trithemius came to us at Sponheim; by them he informed us that he had accepted the often-mentioned abbacy at Würzburg and had resigned ours, advising and exhorting us that in his place we should elect as abbot whomsoever we wished, according to the Rule. Therefore our abbacy of Sponheim was vacant after his resignation for almost two months, both because knowledge of Trithemius’s resignation came to us late, and because, being less experienced in the installation of a new abbot and necessarily seeking the counsels of many, we also awaited for a rather long time the arrival of our visitors, who had to be present.

But after the transfer of Abbot Trithemius to Würzburg had been reported to us by his brothers, Master Jacobus Trithemius and Johannes Damius, a monk of our monastery, now confessor and provost in the nuns’ community of Neuburg near Heidelberg, who had been summoned and had gone up with him, we all marveled beyond measure, since we had not thought that the matter would have such an outcome, and that he would abandon us so suddenly, who for so long a time had been our prelate and abbot. Many would have believed that, at least for love of the library, which he had assembled precious and rich in every variety of writings, he ought to have remained with us, held back no less by the beauty and convenience of the new abbatial house, which he had built at great expense, than by regard for his friends and the fame of his great name.

But all these things, being both vain and nonetheless someday to be left behind through death, he abandoned of his own free will, and humbly committed himself to the mercy of almighty God, knowing that divine Scripture has promised: Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you, who is Jesus Christ, God blessed forever. Amen. Here is the end of the abbacy of Johannes Trithemius, abbot in Sponheim, whom Prior Nicolaus of the land of Luxembourg succeeded, DE Sponheimense.

In the same year also, on 25 February, Louis, Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria, Arch-Steward of the Holy Empire and prince-elector, celebrated solemn nuptials at Heidelberg, taking as wife the daughter of the late Albert, Duke of Bavaria, namely the niece, through his sister, of Emperor Maximilian.

Thus far Trithemius.

1526.

On Johannes of Siemern, twenty-seventh abbot of this monastery of Sponheim.

Nicholas, abbot of Sponheim, died [on the Kalends of July?] in the present age, a pious and merciful man, devoted to all religion and honor. He never saddened anyone by his own presumption, nor did he burden the monastery with the expenses of his person; rather, he maintained regular discipline excellently, both in himself and in his subjects, until the end of his life. He was buried in the middle of the choir, amid the outpouring of many tears by his brothers.

After the death of the reverend lord Nicholas, abbot, the abbey of Sponheim was without a shepherd for nine days. When these had been completed, two abbots arrived: Johannes, abbot of St. James at Mainz, and Frederick, abbot of St. John in the Rheingau, called by us for this purpose according to the ordinances of our chapter.

Therefore, in the aforesaid year 1526, on 4 July, around the eighth hour, the prior with the brothers of our convent betook himself to the chapter place, with the aforesaid prelates presiding and witnesses and notaries also present. After the invocation of the gift of the Holy Spirit had first been offered, and after a canonical summons had first been held, as is customary, he began the election by way of scrutiny in the name of God.

Thus, when the votes of the individual brothers had been heard, the greater part of the brothers directed their votes, recorded by the notary, to brother Johannes of Siemern, at that time prior. For when the election was proclaimed, all consented to him, and they subscribed with their own hand to the decree of election. The man elected was, in the same year, on the [unclear] day next after the feast of St. James the Apostle, confirmed by Albert, cardinal of the Apostolic See and archbishop of Mainz; and on the same day he received the office of blessing from Bishop Johannes, vicar in pontificals of the aforesaid lord Albert, in the church of the Mount of St. James, with the aforesaid abbots assisting in pontificals.

The family and origin of Johannes, our abbot.

This Johannes Siemern was, by native country, of the [Cynonoti?],* born of honorable parents in a certain town, [Argenthal?], not far distant from the city of Siemern. His father, named Peter, was from the said town; his mother, named [Helena?], came from the village of Mirsbach. They sought their livelihood by rustic labor. Johannes himself, in his boyhood years, was entrusted by his parents to scholastic letters, to which he devoted himself until his twenty-third year. In that year he entered the monastery, with no mortal person urging him on. He lived under regular discipline for nineteen years, and, promoted to the priestly [office], as a preacher of the divine word for sixteen years [unclear] with vigilant zeal. And now, made abbot, he presides for as long as He shall will who alone governs all things; to whom be praise and glory forever and ever.

  • Hunsrucker.

Louis the Palatine took a wife. Chronicle of Trithemius ... exactly compose and adorn a prelate, there is no need to write, since none of us who daily associate and live with him can fail to know it.

But when Abbot Johannes Trithemius, as we have said, had been transferred to Wuerzburg, Nicholas the prior succeeded in his place; he presides as long as God shall have wished. As far as bodily disposition is concerned, he is a man of middling stature, his body midway between fatness and leanness, dark of face, bald-headed, unsteady in his walk, leaping with a headlong gait.

He is pressed by daily poverty, because of the scantiness of the rents and revenues of the monastery; he can by no means attain the fortune of his predecessor, and therefore in many things he is compelled to have patience. For Johannes Trithemius, known and familiar to many princes, prelates, and doctors because of his learning of every kind, had from various persons many supports, all of which are now denied to his successor.

For, as we heard from Trithemius' own mouth and know by manifest proof to be true, in twelve years he acquired as a gift, from various princes, prelates, and other friends, more than a thousand florins for his labor, study, counsel, or editions of various writings; all of these he turned to the common use of this monastery and of the brethren. Nevertheless, as far as the increase of property is concerned, [unclear]. For [unclear] began to be present; he was not able to advance the governance to such a degree, because he obtained very few suitable and useful helpers. Hence, unless he had had frequent assistance from outsiders, he too would have borne the same poverty that we suffer today. Therefore it is no wonder if Sponheim is today pressed by great poverty, since the Trithemian subsidies have failed. I believe without doubt, indeed I dare to say that I truly know, that if Trithemius had remained with us in the abbacy down to the present day, we would now have been freed from all debts. For moments began to be present in which the familiarity of the greatest princes would by no means have abandoned him in his former poverty; how true this is we know from the report of those who associated with him at Wuerzburg after he had resigned our abbacy. But what? He understands too late who says after the deed, 'Alas, why did I do this?'

The chief reason why Trithemius left us is believed to have been this: that he was not unaware that our affections were less in agreement with him; then, that some seemed by clear signs to be panting after his prelacy; that there was no one among us who wished to come forward as a faithful, suitable, and zealous helper and co-worker for him, as much in spiritual matters as in temporal; and no less that those who presumed with the greatest certainty that they would be abbots in the future said nothing good of him anywhere, but rather whatever evil came into their mouths, both at Mainz, among the abbot and brethren of St. James, and in whatever other places, to whatever persons; through this much lay hidden from Trithemius, who clearly recognized the devices and hatreds of his rivals.

What was the good and learned man to do in the midst of rivals, when, because of the aversion and folly of certain men, he could neither profit himself usefully nor, with suitable co-workers lacking, provide useful things for his subjects? Therefore, since he was astute, he turned aside from evil and, by the Lord's mercy, found a place better than this one and suited to his holy studies. We, however, have fallen into the pit which some of us prepared for the undeserving Trithemius. Man sees in the face and is very often deceived in his judgment; but God, who searches hearts and reins, knows all things. 1507.

In the first year of Nicholas our abbot of Sponheim, Maximilian, the renowned king of the Romans, assembled a great and long-lasting gathering of princes at Constance, in which many things were seriously discussed concerning the continuation of peace throughout the kingdom, and concerning the undertaking of war against the proud, rebellious, disobedient Venetians, whose inborn rashness had inflicted many losses on the Church and had perpetrated very many deeds against the Roman Empire; it would be tedious to make mention of them here.

In the same year Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg, arch-chamberlain of the Roman Empire and prince-elector, sent letters with a messenger and gifts to Abbot Trithemius at Wuerzburg, asking him that he would deign once more to enter the March and to remain with him for the space of even two months, for fuller instruction both in the Greek and in the Latin language and for the completion of the other good arts. But Trithemius, a lover of monastic quiet, did not consent this time to go so far away, although the margrave promised him many things, and had earlier given him many.

Maximilian also, king of the Romans, in the same year, from the gathering of princes held at Constance, summoned Trithemius to himself by messenger and by letters, who, however [unclear] he deferred his arrival until the following year, because of the wondrous work of the Polygraphia, to be dedicated to the king, which was not yet completed.

1508.

In the second year of our abbot Nicholas, on the twenty-sixth day of February, the illustrious prince Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, Arch-Steward of the Holy Empire and Prince Elector, died and was buried in the church of the Holy Spirit at Heidelberg.
