He left seven sons: namely Louis, who after his father obtained the principality; Philip, bishop of Freising; Frederick, guardian of the sons of Rupert, his deceased brother, Duke of Bavaria; John, bishop of Regensburg; George, provost of Mainz, later bishop of Speyer; Henry, provost of Aachen; and Wolfgang. He also left surviving him four daughters: namely Elizabeth, who had first married William, landgrave and count of Hesse; when he died shortly afterward without children, she was given in marriage to Philip, Margrave of Baden. The second surviving daughter of the Palatine was Amalia; the third, Magdalena, not yet married; and the fourth, Catherine, a nun of our order in the monastery of Neuburg near Heidelberg, in the diocese of Worms, by the Neckar.

In the same year, a few days after the death of the Palatine, that is, on the sixth feria after the first Sunday of Lent, Albert, Duke of Bavaria, called “of Munich,” also died. His elder son, named William, later, in the fourth year of our abbot Nicholas, received the governance of his father’s duchy by the common consent of the procurators.

In the aforementioned year our abbot Nicholas took down the old wine-press house, which Abbot Conrad had formerly built of fragile wood and which was ruinous from excessive age, and built the new one which is now seen.

In the same year Lord Johannes Trithemius, formerly abbot among us but now abbot at St. James in the suburb of Würzburg, after he had already been summoned for the third time by messengers and letters, and after sufficient travel money had been sent, came to Emperor Maximilian at Mainz and farther on to Cologne. There, having found the emperor, he remained with him for almost three months, and afterward, rewarded by him, returned to his own place. What he did with the emperor, or why he was summoned by him, is not known to me.

In the aforementioned year Jacob, archbishop of Mainz, died; Uriel von Gemmingen, the dean, succeeded him, and in the following year, on Mid-Lent Sunday, when Laetare is sung, he was consecrated in the church of Mainz.

In the same year also, in the month of August, Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, died, a prince more munificent to the poor, and especially to cloistered persons, than all men of our age; on them he bestowed many benefactions. He reformed many monasteries in his diocese, both of virgins and of men, and bestowed many great benefactions on all cloistered persons who lived according to the purity of the monastic rule. In the town of his residence, Brühl, which is not many miles from Cologne, he built from the foundations, at his own expense, a new monastery of the Order of Friars Minor of the Observance, which he handsomely supplied with relics of saints, books, and necessary ornaments. He was succeeded in the archiepiscopate of the church of Cologne by the major dean Philip von Oberstein, son of the elder Wirich, who for a long time held the first place in the court of John, archbishop of Trier.

1509.

In the third year of our abbot, Emperor Maximilian, summoned into Italy by Pope Julius II, gathered forces and attacked the Venetians, who were not only rebels against the Empire but also disobedient and rebellious toward the Roman Church and Pope Julius himself just mentioned, and for that reason bound by the bond of excommunication and anathema; and he afflicted them with a great calamity. Yet before this fierce and long-lasting war began, [unclear] with the king of the French, Charles [unclear], whom he later called upon for aid against the Venetians, and he did many things with him powerfully and bravely. And so, around the beginning of the month of June in the aforementioned year, with Pope Julius and Louis, king of the French, bringing aid, Emperor Maximilian powerfully attacked the dominion of the Venetians, struck down many thousands of them, and forcefully subjected several of their very strong fortifications to his empire.

In the same year, in the month of May, an assembly of the princes and communities of the cities of the Empire was held at Worms, where Emperor Maximilian, through his orators, sought aid against the Venetians, enemies of the Empire; on that occasion he did not obtain it, although a long consultation was held. Thereafter, in the same year, on the twenty-sixth day of June, Emperor Maximilian again commanded the princes more earnestly by imperial letters to bring aid as quickly as possible against the Venetians, and refuted the reasons alleged against him at Worms.

In the same year also, on the last day of the month of May, by a public sentence to the fire 432 The Chronicle of Trithemius

Four of the Order of Preachers burned at Bern.

[unclear] and burned to ashes among the Bernese in Switzerland were four brothers of the Order of Preachers, namely the prior, the lector, the subprior, and the custodian, on account of certain deceitful and impious contrivances which, chiefly against the immaculate conception of the blessed ever-virgin Mary, to the scandal of many, they had devised with most wicked and damnable presumption. Since the history of this deed, together with the proceedings held against them, has been published everywhere by the art of printing, there is no need for it to be rewritten here in every detail.

In the aforesaid year, in the month of August, William, provincial count of Hesse, whom our people call landgrave, died after a wretched and prolonged illness, leaving an infant son and the government of the county in the hands of guardians.

In the same year died John, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, count in Sponheim, whose father, Duke Frederick, once reformed the present monastery, with the consent and cooperation of the other Frederick, then indeed the guardian of his uncle Philip, count palatine, of whose death I spoke a little before. This John was a most excellent prince, devout, a lover of peace, just, upright, and most humane; he restored peace and concord wherever he could among those at variance, and for that purpose spared neither expense nor labor. Finally, he governed his subjects, poor and rich alike, with such prudence, and protected them with such security, that he had no equal in the whole Empire. He heard the subjects who came to him with the greatest kindness, and always bestowed counsel and aid on each with great liberality. He never burdened his poor in anything, but did not allow those whom he could at times, even justly, have drained of goods or services to be burdened by anyone.

He was always a pious defender and protector of monasteries and religious persons, whom he never burdened with requests, services, or exactions. By nature he was most gentle, and therefore was loved by all. Accordingly, we and our successors rightly ought continually to pour out most devout prayers to almighty God for his soul.

He left behind him one son, called by his father’s name, John, happily succeeding his father in the principality; we trust that he will be not only equal to his father in every adornment of virtue, but we also experience, perceive, and plainly see that he is daily becoming better than the best man. May the compassion of piety long preserve him unharmed.

Also in the aforesaid year, on the sixteenth day of the month of September, Macharius, abbot of the burned monastery of Limburg, died. He is buried in the parish church of the village of Wachenheim, which he had incorporated into his abbey for the construction of the monastery; he was a good man of most honorable conduct, who spent his life amid many tribulations. Werner succeeded him in the abbacy, formerly a monk of this monastery of ours at Sponheim, very unlike his predecessor.

In the same year also, John Damius Cortensius of Cologne, a monk of this monastery, whom John Trithemius, once our abbot, almost twelve years earlier had advanced, to please John Dalberg, the most learned bishop of Worms, as confessor of the nuns in the monastery of Neuburg near Heidelberg, was driven out through the envy of certain rivals, not without the greatest injury, embittered contrary to the faith promised him, and returned to us. How true that distich of Gerard Groote is, he now experiences too late:

No favor is lost which is only the favor of sisters. Thus it was, is, and will be: ingratitude at the end of labors.

Also in the aforesaid year, Jacob, abbot of the monastery of Gottesaue, of the diocese of Speyer, while residing in the Roman curia, rather imprudently began a lawsuit against Christopher, margrave of Baden, concerning certain escheated property; through it a grave danger was feared to be threatening his monastery. Hence John Trithemius, abbot of Saint James the Apostle, and Conrad of Saint Stephen’s at Würzburg, by commission of the provincial chapter of the order, summoned him from the Roman curia by letters to Würzburg, promising that they would devote their diligence to his peace and advantage. Acquiescing in their counsel and writings, he came to Würzburg, where, in the presence of the procurators of his convent, sent for this purpose with full mandate, on the fourteenth day of November of the year written above, the aforesaid abbot resigned his prelacy of his own free will, and received for his support an annual pension of thirty florins for the days of his life.

1510. Sponheim.

1510.

In the fourth year of Nicholas our abbot, a great assembly of princes was held in the city of Augsburg, and lasted almost three months. At it Caesar Maximilian appeared in his own person, and discussed with those same princes many matters concerning renewing and continuing the war against the Venetians. At the same assembly of princes Ludovicus Helianus of Vercelli, ambassador and envoy of the king of the French, appeared; on the tenth day of the month of April he delivered an elegant oration to the senate of the princes and cities of the Empire, in which he enumerated the perfidy, frauds, deceits, and many poisonings impiously and cruelly perpetrated by the Venetians, and declared in lofty style how great disasters they had publicly brought upon the Roman Church, and likewise upon the Empire, and no less upon the whole commonwealth of Christians, by their treacherous plotting. In the name of his king he urged the Emperor and the princes not to put faith in their deceitful promises, nor grant peace to them when they were falsely humbled, but by war, as they had begun, to humble their insolent pride utterly and wholly extirpate their unjust dominion; for the completion of this affair he promised every effort of his king. From Augsburg the same ambassador went down into Hungary, bearing letters and petitions in the name of his king of the French, by which he strove to forestall the Venetians, so that they might not be able to hope for any assistance of support from the king of Hungary.

In the same year a great dissension arose between the citizens and consuls of the town of Erfurt among the Thuringians. Growing within a short time to immeasurable proportions, it was a seedbed of many evils; wherefore many of the citizens of the council either fled from the town of their own accord, fearing the fury of the lower citizens, or, captured by the inhabitants, were consigned to very harsh prisons. Of these, a leading and more powerful citizen, named Hans Keller, was hanged on the gallows; the others laid this crime against him, that since he was the highest of the senators and the most powerful chief guardian of the treasuries, he had secretly stolen many things and spent them for his own uses.

Finally, from the aforesaid sedition a serious discord arose between Uriel, archbishop of Mainz, and Frederick, duke of Saxony; each of them contended that he was lord of Erfurt. The dissension gradually grew so great that, after troops had been gathered on both sides, they mutually prepared themselves for war. When this became known to Caesar Maximilian, he ordered them by imperial authority, through envoys and letters, not to proceed to war.

He entrusted the matter between them, to be attempted amicably, to the most wise prince and reverend father, lord Lorenz, bishop of Wurzburg, duke of Eastern Franconia, so that, taking to himself advisers of the archbishops of Trier and Cologne, and also of Margrave Joachim of Brandenburg, and of the towns of Frankfurt and Nuremberg, he might restore peace between them as soon as possible. If he could bring them back to peace, the matter would have been well handled; but if he could not, he was to refer the business back to Caesar.

Therefore about the middle of the month of August the aforesaid prelate, by imperial authority, summoned the dissenting parties to him at Wurzburg, that is, Uriel archbishop of Mainz, Frederick duke of Saxony, and the consulship of Erfurt. They sent their spokesmen and advisers, while the princes themselves, by way of caution, were not far absent. There were also present advisers sent by the archbishop of Trier, and also by Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg, and the consuls of Frankfurt and Nuremberg. But before the case had fully begun to be heard, Caesar’s letters arrived, by which it was ordered that that assembly ought to be transferred and held in the town of Schmalkalden, nearer to the Erfurters, for the proving of the witnesses in the matters that were being discussed. The appointed day was observed; the parties were heard; but no agreement could intervene, and therefore the matter remained suspended.

Likewise in the year noted above, throughout all Lent, crusade indulgences for the Master and the order of the Teutonic Knights in Prussia, against the Tartars and Ruthenians, adversaries of the Christian faith, were preached throughout the diocese and duchy of Wurzburg, and they lasted from the first Sunday of Lent until the feast of the Holy Trinity, to the salvation of many.

Also in the year noted above, Wilhelm of Bavaria, the elder son of Duke Albert, with the counsel and assent of his men, received into his hands the rule of his father’s principality, and rules until [unclear] Christian, who was burned with them, they had bought for nine groschen, and had cruelly martyred, with punctures dripping blood; yet he allowed the rest, innocent of such a crime, to depart.

Also in the year noted above, Wilhelm of Bavaria, the elder son of Duke Albert, with the counsel and assent of his men, received into his hands the rule of his father’s principality, and rules until [unclear] Christian, who was [unclear] with them, they had bought for nine groschen, and had cruelly martyred, with punctures dripping blood; yet he allowed the rest, innocent of such a crime, to depart. Also in the year noted [unclear] that Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg, Wilhelm, duke of Bavaria at Munich, of Caesar, a woman most devoted to Christ, Duke Albert her husband, in the eleventh year of Nicholas the abbot, as [unclear].

Of Johannes Trithemius.

no adversity will be able to prevent them from everywhere accompanying our journey. Let that tyrant Comastes rage against us as much as he wishes; let his fury attempt [unclear]: he will take away nothing that true philosophy has conferred on us, which the love of God through faith in Jesus Christ has confirmed in us. What concern have I for woodland gnats, which cannot move a mind steadfast in its purpose? Every land is my homeland, and from every side there is one agreement toward those above. It matters little where I live, so long as I live as a mortal. I prefer to live in exile, sound in mind and very poor in possessions, than to flatter Comastes, whom scarcely anyone could praise without fault. What sort our adversaries are, and to what games they are devoted, you will note in the verse appended below:

[unclear]

By the rule of this sentiment lives the crowd, together with their prince, of those who have persecuted me; against whom, in due time, we have taken care to write [unclear], to their perpetual confusion. Farewell, mindful of us before God. From Speyer, on the sixth day of the month of May, in the year of the Christians 1505.

VII.

Joachim, by the grace of God prince-elector of Brandenburg, to Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, his preceptor: greeting.

Reverend father, most celebrated of preceptors, we are shortly to set out on a journey to the sacred majesty of the King of the Romans, desiring on that same journey both to meet and converse in person with Your Paternity, as you know we have already long wished to do, and to confer with you about many things that are in our mind. Therefore we entreat and ask Your Paternity that, setting aside any other occupations of yours, you come in your own person to the town of [unclear] on the Rhine, on the first day of the coming month of July, where we too shall be present at that same time, with divine mercy favoring us. In this matter Your Paternity will do us a singular pleasure, to be repaid toward the same with favor and every grace. May Your Paternity fare well forever. Given from our Cologne by the Spree, on the eleventh day of the month of June, in the year of the Lord 1505.

VIII.

To the most serene prince Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg, elector of the Roman Empire: the letter of reply of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim.

I shall come to Your Highness, most serene prince, on the day and at the place appointed for me by you, most gladly, although because of various ailments of my body I seem scarcely able to move my foot anywhere. For nothing more pleasing to me, nothing sweeter, could have happened at this time than to approach you, a most wise and most learned prince, to spend time with you, to speak and discuss; not indeed about small, very slight, or common matters, but about difficult and very great ones, worthy of your most fertile intelligence, which do not shrink from our threefold philosophy. For whenever the memory comes to my mind of those discussions of ours which two years ago at Frankfurt we were accustomed to carry on far into the night, so often my mind is much more greatly kindled with love for our heavenly philosophy. Therefore, as soon as, after receiving the letter of your serenity, I understood that you would come to the regions of the Rhine, all bodily distress withdrew from me, and because of the exultation of my mind the feeble limbs of my poor body, which had long lost their strength, recover it, and all my bones hasten as quickly as possible to come to Your Majesty. Meanwhile, most serene prince, continue to attend your Trithemius, as you are accustomed, with kindly favor, since he who of his own free will delivered himself to you as a servant has withheld from your command nothing of those things which he can do, knows, possesses, and understands. Therefore by right you ought henceforth to show yourself a favorable patron to your Trithemius, from whom you have received all that was his own, indeed what he was to himself. I know that you deem me worthy beyond my merit, on account of which, almost forgetful of the excellence of your serenity, I could scarcely restrain my loving frenzy. But spare me, most illustrious prince, since I have been bolder than befitted my littleness. I wish Your Highness good health. From Neumagen, on the twentieth day of the month of June. In the year of the Christians 1505.

(as has been said before) having died, she entered the religious community of the sisters of the Third Rule of St. Francis in the town of Munich, sought and received the grey habit, in which she remains, and will henceforth remain.

Also in the year noted above, after the assembly of the princes at Augsburg had been dissolved, the Venetians, considering that on account of their deserts they were despised both by the king of the French and by Caesar and the princes, and that they could not obtain what they had wished, took counsel among themselves and sent an embassy to Pope Julius. Up to that point he had agreed with the kings, was an adversary of the Venetians, and, as was said above, had excommunicated them as rebels. They asked mercy from him; finally, by letters and by the persuasions of their ambassadors, they at length brought it about that the pontiff, moved by mercy and judging that the bosom of mother Church should not be closed to the penitent, received them back into grace and absolved them from the bond of excommunication by which they had been bound. How much this deed displeased Caesar Maximilian and Louis, king of the French, will become manifest to posterity not by my words, but by their deeds. For the pontiff seems to be especially blameworthy in this, not only to those kings themselves but also to many others: that he summoned Caesar and the French king of the French by his commands against the Venetians, and now, when the affair had come to its final crisis, he himself grants pardon to the enemies without their consent, and, after the treaty and compact which he had made with the princes had been concluded, he breaks and violates the conditions of the war which he himself, first establishing them, had commanded. From this point the pope stands for the Venetians against Emperor Maximilian and at the same time King Louis of the French; he wages wars, leads an army, and for several months now the pontiff himself has learned to live in tents. We await the end of this matter.

Likewise, in the year so often noted above, the abbot and monks of the monastery of St. Januarius the martyr in Murrhardt, in the parts of Swabia, of the diocese of Wuerzburg, consenting to the malignant machinations of Satan and wishing, after the example of Camberg, to apostatize from the Order of St. Benedict, which they had professed, sent their prior to the Roman curia with letters, money, and false narratives, so that by whatever rashness they could they might obtain permission to withdraw from the order. When he came to Rome, he obtained letters of consent and an indult for transferring the monastery into a secular church. Yet they have by no means been able to bring this into effect, nor can they up to the present. For Ulrich, duke of Wuerttemberg, in whose dominion Murrhardt is situated, hearing that the bull of transfer had been obtained by the prior not as he wished but as he could, and that it had been deposited with merchants in a bank at Augsburg, sent a messenger and intercepted it, and did not allow it to come into the hands of those who desired to apostatize. And so the thoughts of the impious were mocked, and they did not come to their end. They spent much money for the same useless bull, and on that account fell into great want. But the prior, having returned to the monastery, because he had exceeded the limits of the mandate entrusted to him and had spent a huge sum of money for a bull, not of the kind he ought to have had but such as he could obtain, was seized by order of the duke and with the consent of the abbot, and was consigned to prison in a certain very harsh castle; in it he is now paying the deserved penalties of his rashness for a second year. For the mandate ran thus: that if the pope consented that all presentations to the benefices of the aforesaid monastery should pass to the one who desired it, I do not say who he was, there is a reason, he should receive the bull, the money being paid through bankers; if he did not consent, he should by no means presume to do so. But in that transfer the pope did not wish to remit anything either of his own right or of that of the bishop of Wuerzburg, nor did he wish entirely to grant to those who desired to have it the presentation to the benefices. The prior, however, caring little who should have the presentations to the benefices, provided that he himself might be allowed to put off the monastic habit and become a secular canon, and desiring all too much to apostatize from the order, spent two thousand florins and more for the aforesaid bull of transfer, and transgressed the law of the mandate imposed on him by those who had sent him.

Therefore in the same year, in Advent, Lawrence, bishop of Wuerzburg, ordinary of the place, greatly indignant at the rashness of the abbot and monks of Murrhardt, took counsel and sent his councillors there, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James, and Conrad, abbot of St. Stephen, with certain others, to visit the place and the monks; the abbot of Lorch, with certain others, agreed with the bishop in the same matter. When the visitation had been carried out, and a summary reckoning of the debts received, they placed certain brethren there for the reform, and also established for them an order of life. Further, for the fuller execution, they appointed another day to meet there again, at Lent after the second Sunday of the following year.

1511.

In the fifth year of Nicholas our abbot, the winter was very hard and quite long, and abounding in snows for a long time, not leaving the face of the earth until the end of the month of February.

In the same Two Books of the Familiar Letters of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Various Princes, Bishops, and Men Eminent in Learning in Germany.

To the most distinguished man, Lord Matthias Held, imperial councillor and pro-chancellor of Germany, Jacob Spiegel of Sélestat sends greetings.

[unclear]

Since, in view of your uncommon prudence, you are by no means unaware, most distinguished sir, that the writings of very learned men have always been dedicated to the highest men, you will judge it less intrusive, or even unfitting, for me to publish under the auspices of your name these books of the familiar letters of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim. For when I consider in my mind how splendidly you have deserved of good letters and of all students, to say nothing now of the benefits you have privately conferred on me, I thought I would not be acting quite candidly if I offered these to another rather than to you. And since you are engaged at the imperial Majesty’s court in this kind of sacred chancery business, so that in writing letters to the highest and most excellent princes and men you are always exceedingly occupied, you will, I think, be declared [unclear] also to read these at your leisure, which Trithemius wrote to the most eminent princes of Germany and also to all the most learned men of his age, and which they in turn wrote to him. Nor do I think it will be unpleasant to you if you grant a little time to reading them, so that you may form in your mind, as it were, a certain image of the former age, in which it first befell me to be received into court under the incomparable hero and most praised emperor Maximilian. I for my part confess that I am affected with no slight pleasure whenever in these letters I enjoy the recollection of excellent men, some of whom we know to have departed this life, while others are still surviving. And although the remoteness of time can do very much in human affairs, so that many things are obliterated by it, or even changed, yet by the benefit of this reading I no longer think of as dead those who among them have fallen asleep, nor any longer as absent those who remain alive. Nor can it be hidden from you in how great esteem Trithemius was everywhere held, on account of his incredible keenness of intellect and his most vigorous zeal in every kind of literature; and in prudence indeed he was so great that he was held in the highest honor by kings, princes, and by Maximilian himself, in every way the greatest emperor of his age, and was very often asked to enroll himself in the order of councillors. And it is fitting that the princes of our age imitate this singular humanity and benevolence of the most illustrious men of the former century toward men outstanding in learning, and foster with the greatest zeal those through whose service they attain so greatly to immortality.

But if Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, Frederick, Margrave of Brandenburg, and Hermann, Archbishop of Cologne, electoral princes, pursued the learned men of their age with such favor, it is right that in our own time, too, all the most learned should be liberally fostered. Moreover, in these letters one may see how religiously Trithemius thought about the Christian religion, with how great zeal he defended it against the preachers of that age, who more often cited Aristotle or Porphyry than Christ or the apostles from the pulpit, judging it most unworthy that the doctrines of the Christian faith should not suffice for the instruction of the Church of God, and indeed that the utterly empty inventions of the Aristotelians should be preferred to them. It is very pleasant, and full of consolation, that besides Christ, the apostles, and indeed all the saints, he so often by his own example also exhorts to patience, and says that the mind must be drawn back from the desire for vengeance, which is the greatest virtue of all, not so much in great and most powerful men as in the ministers of the Word of God, whom it is fitting to endure all things with a patient spirit for the glory of Christ to be made illustrious. But how rare this virtue is at this time in very many people, daily experience Dedicatory Epistle.

[unclear] teaches. As often as he makes mention of the Apostle Paul, he calls him, with a most apt epithet, “lover of Christ.” For what blessings did God not bestow upon this apostle? Or from what dangers did he not deliver him, so that the truth of his promises might be established? All these things have this end: that all of us everywhere should display this most beautiful virtue, especially those upon whom hands have duly been laid in the churches for the office of teaching.

Moreover, although he was of a most blameless life, for he was familiarly known to me for many years, and always with the greatest zeal intent upon the divine Scriptures, so that no one could doubt that he proved himself a very pious and faithful abbot of his order, it is remarkable that he attributed so little, or almost nothing, to his own holiness before God, whereas in this age of ours even those are accustomed to boast under this name who are utterly alien from every pious and honorable manner of life, which proceeds only from living faith.

But lest I be burdensome to you by the length of my letter, I now present to you Trithemius himself, abbot of Sponheim. I trust that he will be all the more welcome to all learned and excellent men, not only because he comes forth into the light under your patronage, which is of very great weight with everyone, but also because, through your intercession, he has been granted an imperial privilege and will thus come more freely and with greater commendation into men’s hands. Nor, I think, will it deter anyone from reading so great a man that he seems to have spoken in the familiar language of his own age, and to have said some things in a manner which the more learned men of this century do not accept, since one must look not so much at the words as at the matter itself.

Therefore, since you have bound me by many kindnesses of your humanity, and, after recently having been appointed Count Palatine, have now so obliged me by sending this privilege that I can scarcely ever repay the debt, I judged it most equitable that the fruits of your labors should return first of all to you also. Farewell, most distinguished man, and I pray you to take in good part this devotion of mine toward you. I shall render greater offices of gratitude whenever God offers the occasion; to him I pray and desire that you be most highly commended. From Sélestat, on the third day of March, [1536].

The Familiar Letters of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim. Book One of the Familiar Letters, to Jacob Trithemius, his most beloved brother.

I.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James the Apostle at Würzburg, sends greetings to Jacob Trithemius, his most beloved brother.

You have reminded me quite opportunely, dearest brother, that we should gather into one volume the letters, witnesses of our calamities, which it is known that we sent familiarly from the day of our departure from Spanheim down to that day on which we undertook the governance of this abbey of St. James, and that we should send them to you, so that you may always have at hand a remembrance of us. You have reasonably added what moved you to ask these things of us: that no one will say it impossible that a man growing old hastens toward his setting, and that he who entered the world earlier will depart it earlier. Since, therefore, you are joined to us by the bond of brotherhood, we can deny you nothing, especially when you ask for that which in no way lacks the rationale of honor. Receive, then, now, as a witness of our love toward you, this last Spanheim book of letters, so that you may have with you a reason for remembering us diligently, and, if our writings have any power, for your consolation. We rejoice that you survive us and are the heir of our studies, so that, although it is necessary for us to be dissolved in body, it may at least befall us to live with you after death in memory. Yet to us it is a thing of very little estimation to commend one’s memory to posterity, since no account either of praise or of blame can reach the dead. Having entered upon this one fate, we ask this of you: that as often as you serve God at the altar, you humbly interpose remembrance of us. It will aid the soul, enlarged after the completion of its purgation, we do not doubt, if you, purified, offer for it the saving host. Farewell, remembering us before God. From our monastery of St. James the Greater in the suburb of Würzburg, on the fourth day of the month of November, in the year of the Christians 1506.

II.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, to his dearest sons in Christ, the Prior and Convent in Spanheim: greetings and sincere charity in the Lord.

On the ninth day of the month of April, Brother Theoderic, a monk, came to us at Budorim [Heidelberg?], bearing news not very pleasant; by this occurrence we were disturbed in no small measure, especially because none of you set himself against the rashness of those malignant attendants, none contradicted it. Who will be angry with me, my brothers, if I suspect some of you of being both aware of and consenting to so great a rashness perpetrated against us? An argument conspires toward suspicion: that not only did none of you intervene on our behalf, but not even did any of you think of reporting to us a deed too rash indeed. We know also that some of you were present at the prelude, when the agents of rashness first broke down the doors and rushed upon the servants, and laughed at the insult to our men when they were ordered to leave. O always pernicious sloth of the unskilled: what great calamity and desolation you are accustomed, through neglect, to bring upon the commonwealth from a slight beginning. And indeed, brothers, gravely harmed in this matter, we very much fear that this presumption will soon do harm no less to you and to the poor monastery than to us. For I certainly am not ignorant of the hidden causes of the Cynonoti’s hatred toward me; nor shall I be able to love the rule of him who, without cause and contrary to justice, opposes me. Yet it cannot yet be sufficiently clear to me by whose urgent command such things were attempted against our men. For I cannot easily be brought to believe that the Prince [unclear] thundered such decrees against us. Even if perhaps he has given credence to the unjust denunciations of the Battologi against us, shall we therefore abandon our holy purpose of philosophizing? Or because of one man’s hatred shall we interrupt our studies of literature? Let him who is born to avarice think anxiously on riches; we were born to letters, Johannes Trithemius.

...we shall pursue the sacred delights of books. For us, placed in this mortality, to live is nothing other than to toil in the pursuit of true wisdom. Therefore, if one of the two must be done, we shall bid farewell rather to the abbacy than to the study of letters. Meanwhile, dearest brothers, lest the state of our community be more gravely disturbed on account of our absence, let each one of you diligently attend to his own order and the office entrusted to him, until we deliberate better what it is useful for us to do in this disturbance. To the abbot of Speciosus Mons, who does not follow Saturn’s motion very gracefully enough, we give thanks; we do not have them. For he is the chief cause of all evils against us, inciting ministers of crime against our people, by whom he was never harmed, nor indeed could have been harmed. What have our innocent familiars to do with the threats he feared from outsiders? As if we lacked the aid of princes, whom the wanton tongue and intemperate insolence of the old man offends no less. We are staying at the town of Büdor belonging to the prince palatine, and we are indeed awaiting the most serene prince Philip, now absent by necessity; to his judgment we shall refer everything that occurs to trouble us. For we shall do nothing in this disturbance of ours without the counsel of the most mild prince, whose favor and clemency [unclear] has provoked hatred against us. Farewell from Büdor, a town of the prince palatine, on the tenth day of the month of April, in the year of the Christians 1505.

III.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Jacob Trithemius, Doctor of Arts and Philosophy, his most sweet brother, greeting.

What the rashness of our rivals has presumed against us, we have learned from the report of Brother Theoderic. See to it and take care that you guard our books and the things entrusted to you, especially [unclear], [unclear]. For we do not intend to return to Sponheim unless we have brought to the knowledge of very many people this insult inflicted undeservedly upon us and ours. The keys of our possessions, especially [unclear], which on our departure, suspecting nothing adverse, we entrusted to your good faith, you are to hand over to no one without our commission. For we are held by a vehement suspicion of a conspiracy of certain brothers against us, especially of the prior of the other, to whom he was always hostile. But you, sweetest brother, are not to be moved by these evils, if indeed those things should be called evils through which a road to God is being prepared for us. By experience they will learn that they have begun no childish game, when at last they themselves have fallen into the snare which they prepared for us. Brother Theoderic, who carries our letter to you, has received certain instructions from us; give him the trust of belief, and render him aid. For among our people we have found him, a foreigner, faithful to us, one who grieves at our lot and gladly carries out whatever we have ordered. Farewell. From Buri, on the tenth day of the month of April, in the year of the Christians 1505.

IV.

To his prior in Sponheim, Brother Nicolaus Remitius.

The old proverb has been fulfilled in me, by the permission of divine providence: no [unclear] without leaves. Power has been given to the adversary to rage against us, and he has not spared us, first stripping us, by the example of the innocent man, of our goods, friends, and sons whom we brought forth in the Lord, and then now tearing the body with various wounds; the mind alone, with God’s compassion assisting us, he will by no means penetrate. We lie here grievously afflicted by fevers, full of swollen ulcers, deserted by our own people, and, what is more serious, exposed without cause as a reproach and a tale to the adversaries of letters. No one from all our dear ones consoles us; no one of our old friends, being far away, visits us; no one appears beside us in our grief. But you, Lord God, compassionate and merciful, raise me up again; I shall repay them, not evil for evil, for this has been forbidden to us through your word, but by reviving in good I shall overcome evil, so that I may do what your word most rightly commanded to be done by his disciples toward enemies who persecute them. For, with you taking pity on me, this casting-up of temporal inconveniences will be for my salvation, if, while the little body outwardly suffers insults and weaknesses, the mind perseveres immovable amid the internal [unclear]. I know that I was born for labors, and that through many tribulations I am to return to him from whom I withdrew through disobedience. I, perhaps, before God, suffer what I deserved; but let those who persecute me though I am innocent see by what zeal they are moved. One thing is what they utter with their mouth about their estimation of us, and another what they have known in their mind. But concerning these things, at another...

440 Familiar Letters ... regard must be had for the time, since we shall disclose not one unjust cause of hatred against us, but several. Meanwhile we must patiently bear what necessity enjoins, until the Sun, whom a mist has somewhat intercepted, [sends] his rays upon us, driving away all the darkness of sorrow. Send to us, with the bearer of the present letters, the following volumes from our Greek library, so that we may have them at hand in the bed of our sickness, and may be fruitfully occupied with them in the intervals by studies of writings. First, I should like you to send the Greek dictionary printed by Aldus Romanus. And then the Psalter, issued in type by the same man at Venice. Likewise the Greek letters copied out by our own hand. Also Zenobius, and those Latin poems which we have made from Homer. We likewise instruct you to send our smaller bronze astrolabe, with the remaining items recorded in the little list. Farewell, mindful of us before God. From Speyer, on the last day of the month of April, in the year of the Christians 1505.

V.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, to Master Jacob Trithemius, his brother, greetings.

I betook myself some time ago to the city of Speyer, not for pleasure but from necessity, lest I burden anyone by my illness; preferring to be with acquaintances and friends, and especially with those on whom I formerly conferred benefits, rather than with strangers in Neuenburg, where I remained ill for fourteen days. I have been received in hospitality at the house of the Abbot of Limburg, and I have not yet sufficiently recovered from all my illnesses. We do not wish you to remain longer in Spanheim, lest our rivals, who we understand bear our absence heavily, perhaps devise some evil against you. For he fears, as we gather by conjecture, that perhaps their wicked counsels may be brought by us to the notice of very many princes; and this indeed they fear not without cause, since, with their own conscience bearing witness against them, they understand how presumptuously they have inflicted insult on us because of the prince’s clemency toward us. But what will they say to this: that, though never harmed by us in anything, they persecute us with hatred because we are well disposed toward the most serene prince of [unclear], who has always been most gracious to us? O envy, always blind, harmful to no one more than to yourself, whom you think you are persecuting. The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness; for love of him the whole world is my fatherland, and the loss of one monastery is easy. But these things, brother, must be covered in silence between you and me, because the time has not yet come for the hidden counsel of my mind to be set forth in public. I follow a hidden divine will. After you have taken your books and clothing with you, hasten to come to us at Neamatricum, that is, Speyer, with brother Theoderic as soon as possible. We have prepared for you a place, not the last, among the household of the Abbot of Limburg, by whom you will be taken on as secretary, until the light shut off from us shines again. Once our books and goods, [unclear Greek], have been duly arranged according to the order and manner of our will, which that brother will tell you, hand over all the keys of our abbatial house into the hands of the prior. Bring with you our Greek little books of devotion, which we cannot be without for longer. But put away in the appointed place all the other things necessary for the more sacred philosophy, until our [unclear] reach their end. Farewell, my only and sweetest brother. From Speyer, on the last day of the month of April, in the year of the Christians 1505.

VI.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, to Roger Sicamber, most constant of friends, greetings.

We have read the list of your lucubrations, which you sent to us through Laurentius, our courier, the day before we wrote to you, and we cannot sufficiently admire their multitude. It is plainly worthy of admiration that you, a single man, always most occupied day and night in the observance of regular discipline, have completed, in a decade, one hundred and thirty-six works, both in verse and in prose, and not commonplace ones; even their titles alone delighted us in a wonderful way. I beg you, sweetest Roger, take care that as soon as possible we may be refreshed by the reading of so many works of yours. For I know that it does not escape your prudence by how many injuries our rivals have shaken us, and by what adversities we are oppressed. Against all their assaults one consolation has been left to us; one impenetrable shield remains: the confidence of our mind in God, and zeal for sacred reading. For no impiety will ever be able to remove from us these faithful companions of our pilgrimage; no...

Familiar Letters IX

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to his beloved brother Nicholas, his claustral prior: greetings and sincere charity in the Lord.

Our affairs having been disturbed by the malice of wicked men, the mind is drawn away to other matters, and rightly considers where at last it may find rest. The authors of rashness do not spare innocence, and those who cannot harm us extend, as we have heard, a lying and slanderous tongue against our people. But we, setting little store by their curses and praising God’s mercy, bless him; of his protection at the fitting time we are certain. For why should we care for the follies of men raging in continual fury like the sea, men in whom everything is settled by foolishness, and nothing by wisdom? For we know that through many tribulations the kingdom of heaven lies open; nor do we refuse to suffer what chance offers, keeping Christ’s passion continually before our eyes. Sorrows have never been absent from us from the day on which we were elected to the abbacy; but we have placed our mind, furnished with the supports of the divine scriptures, in that place from which, by God’s mercy preserving it, it will be able to be overturned from the state of its tranquility neither by prosperity nor by adversity. For we are not ignorant how destructive a thing unrestrained sadness is for men, if once it has clung to their minds, although it is not easy to pass life without sadness. Innocence alone consoles me as I suffer injuries, and the Cynonoti will see what sort of Christian philosopher I am. Nor does their quibbling satisfy me, by which they say that what they rashly presumed was not done out of hatred of me, since it concerns the account of our name in no small degree.

But these times demand something else. At the beginning of the month of July there will be an assembly of princes in Cologne, to which we also have been summoned by the most serene prince elector Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg. Therefore, lest because of our long absence the established order of the monastery’s affairs should collapse, we entrust our office meanwhile to your charity, yet without prejudice to our dignity, until either we shall decide to return to the monastery, or [unclear] this same most serene prince elector [unclear].

My cellarer and universal procurator for [unclear] years, a man indeed shrewd and cunning, but stirred up too much by hatred against us, together with a few from the number of the donated brothers, favoring the Transylvanian parties, is laboring in unjust machinations against us and our prince. We do not need another’s testimony, since we intend to keep the prior’s words in lively memory. When he was lately here with us, among other things he confessed that the duke’s officials had said such words about us: “If the abbot had adhered to your parties, just as he is commonly said to have favored the Palatine ones, he would not have fallen into all these evils.” I know that their testimony in this matter is true. But who stirred up the duke’s mind against us, unless, as the prior himself reported, the aforesaid brother Heilmann and that donated brother Claudius, who, always slandering the Palatine parties, made the Transylvanians hostile to us without cause? Almighty God, who knows all things before they happen, knows that I am not lying. Whenever any one of the ducal officials entered the monastery, known to the aforesaid informers, mention of us was brought into the midst, as though we favored the Palatine affairs too much. This was the one and first cause of the Cynonoti’s rivalry against us; although the charity of the brothers made it known to us almost ten years ago, nevertheless we were unable to remove it safely enough. Let us add also another, concerning the fief of the castle of Sponheim, which you too are not unaware of. The third cause of the man’s hatred against us is the unwearied continuation of our studies in good letters; to him, to speak in his own words, the sight of books is the greatest horror. These two oxen Johannes Trithemius. 443

[unclear], men ignorant of all good writings, enemies, adversaries, and despisers, have increased it not a little, since they have always, to the extent of their powers, disparaged our excellent studies, for which we were born. A fourth cause for our rivals against us was supplied by the most atrocious war which the conspiracy of many waged in the previous year against our most mild prince, Philip, Count Palatine. What things were attempted against us by our rivals while that war lasted you know well, since during its whole duration you were always with me in the town of the monastery of Kreuznach for twenty-two weeks.

What if we add also a fifth cause of hatred against us to those already stated, one which the words of our Prior confirm, although we know for certain that it is more certainly fabricated? For he reported to us some time ago, after returning to us at Neumagen from the Cynonoti, that a certain chief secretary, provoked by us in words I know not what, was ill-disposed toward our affairs, and that for this reason he had devised everything against us in the name and by the command of the prince, who had been misled, and had entrusted to the servants of the prefect the office of robbery. We do not remember ever having spoken wrongly against him, not even this very thing of which he seems to accuse us: that he is an unlearned and shifty man, gaping too eagerly after his own advantages, as one who came to the prince as a needy scholar and very poor, and in a few years became very rich by serving.

If I had ever spoken these words, I would indeed have spoken words suited to his conduct, and therefore true, and uttered not against his prince but against the man who had done such things. The character of the Duke seems to me sufficiently clear: he is mild, quickly humane, excessively credulous. Nor do we think it difficult to recover his favor, lost through false accusations, unless a hidden cause should prevent us from being obliged to do so. Too credulous toward his own people, he has unjustly persecuted us. Therefore we shall not seek pardon from him whom we have never injured. We shall try fortune, even when it threatens heavier things, appointing as our protector him by whose nod all things stand.

We would deservedly be ashamed if we seemed to have spent freely so many sweats and labors on the study of letters through thirty continuous years, both before and after our entrance into the monastic religion, only not to be able to command our own mind, surrounded by the strongest defenses of threefold philosophy: both to despise the hatred of the unskilled and to endure with meekness and patience whatever things are adverse to us, for the desire of the heavenly kingdom. For however grave the things which the wicked envy of fortune has prepared for us, they are for that very reason especially to be despised, since, being subject to an end, they cannot continue very long.

The victory of Christ’s holy martyrs teaches us by a most illustrious example how laughable the adversities of this world are to a wise man. For the love of their redeemer they patiently endured torments lasting for a very short time; for these they now enjoy without end the eternal joy of the angels. Christ has wiped away every tear from their eyes, for whose testimony they received adversities in this life; and now there will be among them no more crying, nor fear, nor mourning, nor pain, since all these things have passed away like smoke in this age. But they are in peace, and their names live for everlasting ages.

Let us too endure, most loving brother, for the love of Christ, with patience and for the remission of our sins, those adversities which befall us, knowing that Theophilus spoke faithfully: that through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of heaven. Let us attend to our head, our creator, JESUS CHRIST, God and man, with what meekness, long-suffering, and patience he endured for us the adversities of this life, the loss of innocent reputation, mockeries, contempt, hunger, thirst, cold and heat, and immeasurable labors for our salvation; and finally a passion full of infinite bitterness, horrible torments, and death on the gibbet of the cross, his side pierced by a spear, exceedingly bitter.

And so if our prince, Lord, and master first had to suffer such things and thus enter into his glory, how shall we Christians, we monks, finally we unjust men, and by the very necessity of nature mortal and corruptible, promise ourselves, so to speak, another’s glory, without labor, without adversities and the manifold endurance of sufferings? No one will reach the glory of our prince who has not persevered in his charity by FAITH AND WORK, living Christianly unto death. But what it is to persevere in Christ by living piously, holy Christophilus did not pass over in silence, saying: All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution. A Christian cannot live without adversity, since the master himself says to us: If they have persecuted me, they will persecute you also. The servant is not greater than his lord, nor the disciple above the master, nor the Christian better than Christ. If we are members of Christ, let us follow our head in adversity, so that we may deserve to be numbered as reigning in his fellowship, in whose imitation we are now grieved as sufferers. Suffi[Blank page in the source scan.]

Familiar Letters

For it is fitting for a disciple of Christ that, in sufferings and adversities, after the example of his teacher, he should daily, and [unclear], with anxious mind imitate his Lord. Those who suffer for Christ. In this life struggles of sufferings are never lacking for a Christian, although not all who are called Christians use them, through patience, unto merit. For not everyone who suffers in this world truly shares in the sufferings of Christ; but only he is made glorious by the testimony of Christ who either suffers for love of Christ and of justice, or, for his own sins, judges himself deserving of every adversity, that he may gain Christ. For the great martyr of Christ, Cyprian, said among holy men: “Punishment does not make the martyr, but the cause.” If, when we suffer, Christ is the cause, let us not be sad, but let us keep our grief within ourselves and bear it bravely, since Christ himself, for whose love we patiently endure, will send us swift help from heaven. For you know what holy Christophilus said: “Tribulation works patience, and patience proof, and proof hope.” And lest we should think hope vain, he added: “But hope does not confound, because the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.” Did not also a certain wise man, considering tribulation necessary for just men, say: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests just men.” Whatever adversities befall us must be borne patiently, since, although the tribulations of the just are many, nevertheless they are delivered by the Lord from all of them after a very brief and momentary hour. It is foolish to fear what you cannot avoid, and on account of bodily adversity to fall into sickness of mind. Let the authority of Menander’s verses put us to shame, if, when struck by adversities, we have been womanish. For he says: [unclear].

Therefore, my brother, since we are both monks and Christians, our spirit must always be strengthened against all adversities that can threaten, and made firm in the love of Christ, so that no circumstance of the present life may ever be able to meet us against whose assault the mind has not already been sufficiently fortified. And this we shall indeed be able to do very easily if, through the fervor of inward love, we continually refer all our thoughts and works, and even the desires of our heart, to the memory of Christ. Great are the things promised us in heaven by our prince; if the constant memory of them faithfully clings to our minds, we shall certainly fear no adversities of this world. O most beloved brother, if with discerning mind you turned over the gifts of future happiness, which are here reserved in heaven for those troubled for Christ, the adversity of the present life would bring you joy, and worldly prosperity immense sadness. The joys of eternal delight are very great and wholly incomprehensible to mortals, because, as divine Scripture promises: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, the estimation of the good which almighty God has prepared for those who love him.” Thinking on these things more often, dearest son, you will both bear your illness more lightly and not weep over our misfortune. Although we do not at all doubt that you bear our injury more heavily than every weakness of your body which you suffer. For measuring your spirit by our own, believe us, we have more compassion for you than we ourselves suffer. We have known you to be subdued by many tribulations from tender age, and for that reason we now grieve the more for you, burdened as you are by age and ill health. But suffer patiently whatever adversity comes to you: the time of the evils of our pilgrimage is very brief, but the reward of those who labor in tribulation for Christ is eternal. We hope shortly to temper your sadness by our presence; but if the envy of Satan has shut off bodily presence, then, present here in the spirit of love, in the future life of the heavenly fatherland, by the gift of the Savior of all, we shall rejoice forever in one another’s sight. The day after tomorrow we are to go down to Cologne, called by letters of my most merciful prince Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, whom you know, and whose benefits conferred on us you have seen, one among those princes who have the right to elect the Roman King. Therefore, not knowing the day of our return, we have appointed our prior Nicholas, under a certain limitation, as vicar general, so that meanwhile he may carry on anxious care concerning the state of our affairs and the care of both [unclear], lest anything be done amiss in the business of the monastery while we are absent. For this reason we have thought it right paternally to admonish also your charity, in which we have very great confidence, that you keep sharp eyes upon him and assist him in all matters that come up for handling, as much as your weakness permits, lest the condition of the poor monastery suffer any harm because of his inexperienced levity, by which he trusts that he can do everything. Farewell, most beloved bro— ...by which you may both teach the people well and, by living rightly, not condemn them. Take care to resist, with continual battle declared, the three especially deadly adversaries of priests, by whom many perish today, as manfully as you can; when these have been overcome, you will easily vanquish the whole crowd of evils attacking you. The three vices of priests, by which very many are swept away and slide down to hell, are avarice, pride, and lust, [unclear Greek]. Happy is that priest who in this time has kept himself unconquered by these demons, and has not walked in the public road of priests. We have written to our common friend Beiselius about the things that are happening around us; so that you may not be ignorant of them, we send you enclosed a copy of the letter which we gave to him. We ask, moreover, that you send back to us our translation of the Mystical Theology of Dionysius, together with the Greek copy, which we lent you two years ago when you were with us at Spanheim. Farewell. From Cologne, on the eighth day of July, 1505.

XV.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, sends greetings to Johann Capellerius, mathematician.

On the sixth day of this month I came to Cologne with the most serene prince Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, which I did not wish to remain hidden from you any longer, because you have always kept inviolate the rights of our old friendship. We ask, therefore, that you come to us as soon as possible, accompanied by the Muses and the lyre, since the place is suitable for us, and there is time very abundantly sufficient for philosophizing and pursuing our plan. Do not wait for the sextile of melancholizing Saturn, which on the day when we entered Agrippina did not pass by very auspiciously, a swelling of the left foot having been inflicted upon me. How long we are to remain here is uncertain to us. Therefore cut short delays, and come as quickly as possible, because much discourse that must be brought forward presents itself to us for you. Farewell. At Cologne, from our lodging, which is in the street that they call potoplaetae, because it truly abounds in drinkers. Looking for the Margrave’s insignia at the doors, you will by no means go astray. On the eighth day of the month of July, in the year of the Christians 1505.

XVI.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, sends greetings to Jakob Kymolanus, of the Carmelite order, his friend.

When a few days ago I had come by boat to Cologne, I heard that you were there in the convent of your order; and today our Jakob of Maaseik, doctor of medicine, invited by us to luncheon, made me certain of this, though I had been somewhat doubtful. Soon, when the dishes had been removed from the table, I asked for pen and paper, and wrote you the letter which I am sending, unable any longer to defer my longing for you. And so we wish, and earnestly beg, that tomorrow morning you come to us, to dine with us and to grant the whole day to our disputations. There will be no one present to hinder us; for I am alone with my attendants and with one necessary mathematician of the Margrave of Brandenburg, a man indeed exceedingly courteous. Let nothing delay you from coming. You will recognize the lodging by the report of this servant of mine. Farewell. From the very house of our residence in Cologne, today, the ninth day of the month of July, in the year of the Christians 1505.

XVII.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, sends greeting to the excellent father and friend Ger[ardus?] Laco of Breitbach, Abbot of the monastery of Deutz.

What adverse things fortune, not to say the perverse rashness of men, has fashioned for me cannot be wholly hidden from you. For the report has been spread through all the land that Abbot Trithemius is living outside his monastery, although the cause is not equally known to all; hence many circulate various rumors among the common people that are by no means true. Since, therefore, we are situated not far from one another, you indeed in Deutz in that most holy monastery of yours, but I at Cologne in a lodging arranged for me by the prince on whose account I came, in order that I may make you more certain concerning our affairs, come to me tomorrow, to dine and feast on noble fare from the table of the most serene prince Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, by whose munificence we are copiously provided. I, for my part, am prevented from coming to you for two reasons: one on account of the aforesaid prince, whom I cannot leave; the other because of the swelling of my left leg and foot, which forbids me every ability to go about. On my descent by boat to [unclear], five...

Of Johannes Trithemius.

... me, brother, and pray to God that his most holy will may be fulfilled in us. From Neumagen, on the twenty-fourth day of the month of June, in the year of the Christians one thousand five hundred and five.

XI.

To Lady Richmodis de Horst, abbess of the monastery of [Sebacensis?], a virgin dedicated to God, etc.

It had been our intention, beloved daughter in Christ, together with Jacob, abbot of [Carsae Dei?], now nearer to us, to come to your convent and to fulfill the office of visitation entrusted to us. But while we were considering these things in our mind, behold, there came a messenger of the most excellent prince Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg, who by his letters summoned me to Bonn for the first day of the month of July. Therefore, since the shortness of time does not allow me to turn aside elsewhere, and since to comply with so great a prince is not only honorable but also necessary, we are compelled to change the plan that we had formed for the act of visitation.

Accordingly, since we are to go down by boat on the following day, although we think that it is not fitting to instruct by our letters your charity in the Lord, very venerable to us, how you ought usefully and fruitfully to preside over the virgins entrusted to you, since from childhood at Cologne, at St. Maccabees, in a monastery most excellently reformed to the purity of the rule of our divine father Benedict, you have fully learned both sacred letters and, in holy conduct, have perfectly attained regular observance; nevertheless paternal solicitude prompts us to admonish and exhort your gentleness, so that with good will you may more fully accomplish in deed and speech the right thing that you have learned.

For no one is found among cloistered persons so learned, so holy, so devoted to God, that, by the very fact that he desires to be good, he is not made better whenever another's exhortation of holy charity is applied to his own will. But of your love we cannot doubt that you will both gladly receive the words of our exhortation and keep them at all times to the best of your power. Therefore we exhort your devotion in the Lord Jesus Christ: so live always that it may have no cause to fear death. For perfect love of God alone has no cause for fearing death, inasmuch as it does not doubt that, after the dissolution of the prison of this present life, it will remain forever in him whom, while placed in the flesh, it loves with all its strength.

But the sluggish and lazy servant, knowing the will of his lord and not doing it, fears to come into his sight, whose commandments he recognizes that he has despised. He, however, who has always loved his lord with his whole heart and has been eager to carry out his will in all things, not only does not fear to appear before him, but rather longs to come into his sight, by whom he knows he is to be rewarded. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself set forth clearly for us a likeness of this matter in the holy Gospel, when he commended the faithful usurers for the profit they had brought.

You too, most beloved daughter in Christ, having received the money of our Lord and Savior, have received from him the gift of understanding, by which you ought to bring back a great profit of holy love. We beg you to take the most diligent care not to hide this precious gift of God in the earth of carnal passions, nor to indulge the flesh more than is fitting, nor, having been set over sacred virgins, to grow numb in idleness. Remember how the precious benefits of a very short time have been granted to us, and how many good things it is permitted us, by living well and rightly in the very few days of this life, to send on ahead.

Be an example of purity to the sisters entrusted to you, a standard of a more sacred life, mindful of the saying of our lawgiver Benedict: Whatever the abbess has told her nuns to be contrary, let her show in her own deeds that it must not be done. Then indeed, O daughter, you will rightly carry out the office of Christ in the monastery, when you precede the virgins subject to you in all purity of mind and body, in word and conduct. First of all, therefore, consider yourself diligently, so that, cleansed of all faults and adorned with good and holy virtues, you may please God through the continual fervent longing of love; and then, with whatever earnestness you can, diligently exhort those entrusted to your rule to think and will the same thing in the Lord Jesus.

With all care and solicitude keep watch over the souls entrusted to you, lest any perish through the snares of the malignant tempter, who always prowls about roaring like a lion, and gnashing his teeth from malice, seeking some virgin dedicated to God whom he may devour. Remember, daughter, how you carry the precious treasure of virginity in earthen vessels; and always keep watch lest the malignant enemy be able to penetrate the house of your heart, lest he steal away this treasure of yours, venerable to the holy angels of God.

Close your hearts, virgins dedicated to God, since they are the earthen vessels in which you carry the incomparable treasure; they are the caskets in which you contain the ointment of angelic composition, and you must keep the highest watch lest it flow out. For holy virginity surpasses the condition of human nature, through which human beings [unclear] Ange are said to be like the angels, equal in the reward of inestimable happiness, unequal in action. But the victory of virgins is greater than that of angels, and the contest differs in manner, time, and condition. For the angels, living without flesh, by the confirming grace of God became victors once for all by willing rightly; but virgins, living in the flesh beyond the flesh, aided by divine mercy and fighting in a long contest, never triumph securely. And therefore it is more blessed in the flesh to imitate the life of angels than from the flesh to increase the mortal number of pleasure. For an unmarried woman and a virgin, as that holy Christophilus declared, thinks on the things of the Lord, how she may be holy both in body and in spirit, nor has she any place into which she may flow away through vanities, but is always borne toward God with a most pure love, to whom she has wholly vowed herself, cleaving to him by desire the more happily, the more she has made herself a stranger to every consolation of this life. But married women have many and various and useless cares, by which they are oppressed the more unhappily, the less they are accustomed to think on the things that are the Lord’s. We ask you, virgin, most vigilant guardian of the brides of Christ, to apply your mind attentively to the few things we are about to say. Show yourself, as is fitting, the faithful executrix of our commands, which in our last visitation we handed over to you after mature deliberation, especially concerning the enclosure of the monastery, which is to be opened to no one except for a cause of necessity. Likewise let none of the sisters be permitted to approach the speaking-window alone, nor to speak with any person without prudent and suitable witness, whether he be father or brother, mother or sister, or sent by anyone on any occasion whatsoever. Let the dangers of others make us cautious, we who are not ignorant of the cunning of the evil spirit, and have known certain most abominable imitators of him; when these were permitted to speak alone with virgins at the window, they said that they were the brothers and kinsmen of those very women whose sacrilegious corrupters they were found to be a little afterward. We hand over to you both our decree and that of the ordinary, the bishop of Neumagen, by which before all else we forbid you to allow any of the men from Duroburgium either to be seen within the precincts of the monastery or to speak alone at the window with any woman. For you know with what zeal they strive to carry out the works of demons, and how pernicious the speech of such men is to chaste virgins dedicated to God. These are the things which I thought should usefully be made known to you at this time. If you have anything to be conveyed to your people in Cologne, we shall gladly perform the office of carrier. Farewell from Neumagen, 24 June, in the year of Christ 1505.

XII.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot, to Roger Sycamber of Duemeten, a studious and excellent man. Greeting.

We have written, Roger, to our beloved daughter in Christ, Lady Richmodis, that on the day after tomorrow we shall go down to Cologne, which we also want you to know, excellent Roger, so that if you wish to write anything to our Beifelius, or to Herbenus, or to the rest of our friends, you may conveniently do so through us. Whatever you are going to do, let it be done as quickly as possible, since we shall not remain here longer than two days. Send us something new from your nightly studies, so that we may relieve the tedium of travel by boat with useful occupation. For how troublesome sailing is to us without reading, you, who lived with us in our Spanheim monastery and know our custom from association with us, are not ignorant. For leisure, as Seneca bears witness, without letters is death, and the burial of a living man. Fortune, not industry, gave me the ability to philosophize according to his counsel. “If you wish,” he says, “to be free for the mind, be either poor or like a poor man.” For riches have obstructed many men from philosophizing. Poverty, however, is unencumbered and secure. And so no one can at the same time be free for the studies of letters and for riches; nor does wisdom deign to inhabit a soul which it has seen either infected by desires or entangled in cares for temporal things. Indeed it has happened to me rather often up to now to be entangled in cares, but poverty has never departed from me from the time when I became a monk. For by long familiarity it has become so familiar to me that henceforth it is in a certain way necessary.

By long study I have learned many things, but have I finally been able to grasp this itself, so that I may know the thoughts of a wealthy man? I indeed do not think that I shall ever understand whither the thoughts of the rich direct themselves, but I have made a virtue for myself out of necessity, and with a tranquil mind I thus sing:

[unclear Greek verses]

I praise the excellent opinion of Euripides, who says:

[unclear Greek verse]

that a noble man is by no means poor.

Menander confirms this, saying:

[unclear Greek verse]

Not Johannes Trithemius

447

“It is not,” he says, “the part of every man, but only of the wise man, to endure poverty. Let greedy, luxurious, ambitious men, who do not consider that they are mortal, have riches and be possessed by them. Let us follow the ways and life of the lovers of Christ, who admonishes us that, having food and clothing, we should be content. We would deservedly be burdened by want if the rich were either immortal, or if, when dying, they carried away with them the riches they had loved. But now, since they themselves die and, naked, receive burial along with the poor, my poverty does not greatly burden me, since, being about to depart from here, I trust that I can be all the less saddened in proportion as I have possessed in this world nothing transitory that I might love.

But the exercise of the mind toward the understanding of truth, which through the study of the Scriptures is pursued in this life, with ordered delight, toward the final end by studious men and contemners of vanities, brings no bitterness to those about to die, since they understand very well that the perfection of their understanding, which they desire to attain by study, cannot be completed before they are released from the corruption of the flesh. For the human intellect is like an unpolished precious stone: if it is polished it will become capable of light, and will be beautiful, bright, and transparent, in which the beauty of God may shine forth. Yet in this mortal life there cannot be a perfect polishing of the human intellect. Nevertheless it has certain degrees and fixed modes assigned to it by nature, by which, after death in the purgatory of souls, whatever has here through negligence been less applied to its polishing is necessarily added. Therefore our stone is polished here imperfectly, more perfectly in purgatory, but most perfectly in heaven. And so the common study of all ought to be to exercise and polish the intellect, so that a pure and upright understanding of the universal principle, which is God our creator, the never-failing light of the intellect, may arise.

The continual reading of the Scriptures shows us the way of this exercise, if in reading we do not interrupt the practice of prayer, and if in praying the mind is raised to God through the longing of love. Nor should we be frightened by labor, which, if it is strenuous, conquers all things. Long-continued study of letters gradually increases the intellect, as Hesiod beautifully sings in verse:

[unclear Greek verses]

For if you add a little upon a little, and do this very thing often, certainly this will become great. For there is no virtue without labor, nor victory over enemies without struggle. Therefore, Roger, we who desire to come to the sweetness of wisdom must always labor and never cease from the study of the Scriptures, because one does not otherwise come to the taste of inward sweetness than through a vehement application of the mind to that most beautiful light of the intellect which we seek.

Let us look at the ancient wise men of the gentiles, to pass over our own in the meantime, and, comparing their studies with ours, measure both in an equal balance: it will appear clearer than daylight that, in comparison with them, we should be laughed at rather than called studious. Demosthenes, when he had completed seven years of age above a hundred and was now dying, groaned that he would die at the age at which he had first begun to be wise. Socrates, the teacher of Plato, in his ninety-eighth year of age received [unclear] while studying. Cato the Roman, studious at all times, began Greek as an octogenarian. The tongue of Nestor, as Homer bears witness, when he was already aged and decrepit, poured forth speech sweeter than honey in a public assembly.

But let us come to our own men, who at the beginning of Christian philosophy handed down to us the norm of the studies of the saints, so that we may see how little our own estimation of ourselves amounts to. Adamantius Origen, son of Leonides, martyr of Christ, a man most studious of all in the divine Scriptures, is said to have worked out six thousand books in the Greek language, and to have persevered in the study of the Scriptures always, up to extreme old age, poor and humble for the love of Christ. Augustine the African, bishop of Hippo, the most holy founder of your order, a man truly the most learned of all the learned, is found to have written more than one thousand thirty books or treatises.
