Ambrose, bishop of Milan, is said to have published three hundred treatises. Jerome, the most holy priest of Bethlehem, besides the edition of the New and Old Testament, is read to have published more than six hundred books and treatises.

We pass over the rest, almost innumerable: Dionysius the Areopagite, disciple of the apostle Paul and bishop of Athens; Tertullian, presbyter of Carthage; Cyprian, bishop and martyr; Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria; Lactantius Firmianus; Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine; James, bishop of the city of Nisibis among the Persians; Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria; Hilary, prelate of Poitiers; Gregory Nazianzen, bishop; Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; Aurelius Clement Prudentius; Clement of Alexandria, presFamiliar Letters.

[the pres]byter, John Chrysostom, patriarch of Constantinople; Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe; Boethius Severinus, martyr; Cassiodorus, abbot of Ravenna; Gregory, pope, formerly abbot of St Andrew’s, the first in the city of Rome; Fortunatus of Poitiers; Isidore of Seville; Bede, the English monk; Albinus, abbot of Tours; Haymo, abbot of Hersfeld; Rabanus, abbot of Fulda; Strabo, monk of Fulda; Notker, abbot of St Gall; Peter Damian, cardinal-bishop; Anselm of Canterbury; Honorius of Autun; Sigebert of Gembloux; Bernard of Clairvaux; Hugh and Richard of St Victor; Rupert of Deutz; Hugh of Barcelona, cardinal; Bonaventure, cardinal; Albert the Great; Thomas Aquinas; Vincent the Great of Beauvais: all of whom, before the other writers of ecclesiastical matters, produced many distinguished volumes.

What are our studies, Roger, compared with the lucubrations of those men? They handed over the whole time of their life to letters, always reading or writing something, so that they might raise their understanding to the knowledge of the highest truth and provide useful things for posterity. Finally, what are our lucubrations, by which we are thought to be something above the rest, if they are compared with the little works of the aforesaid fathers, except chaff set beside wheat, certain unripe fruits, for which neither time nor place was present, indeed nor was the seasonable tempering of the air granted, so that they might grow together into the desired food. We write, as Flaccus says, “learned and unlearned, we everywhere write poems”; too desirous of empty esteem, we do not keep back our little works, altogether childish, not for the ninth year, to say nothing of that, but not even for a second year.

Although all these things are so, nevertheless we rightly praise the talents of our own men, since each one does this very thing that he can, out of love of wisdom. For the more assiduous anyone has been in the sacred scriptures, the richer an understanding he receives from them. For beautiful and fruitful is the occupation of the mind of a studious man in the divine scriptures, which illuminates the understanding of the soul reading or writing, and sweetly kindles a man withdrawn from the vanities of the world to the love of God. Hence the divine Ambrose admonishes us, saying: We ought long to wear down and polish the utterances of the heavenly scriptures, turning them over with our whole mind and heart, so that that juice of spiritual food may diffuse itself into all the veins of the soul. And that most holy priest Jerome says: Read the divine scriptures more often; indeed, let sacred reading never be put down from your hands. For if you love knowledge of the scriptures, you will not love vices. For ignorance of the scriptures is ignorance of Christ. For if, according to the Christ-loving Paul, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, he who does not know the scriptures does not know the power and wisdom of God, which is rightly understood by us only through them.

We are ignorant of many things which would by no means be hidden from us if, after the example of the ancient Fathers, continual reading were familiar to us. Therefore let us do what Democritus advises, Roger, and in time we shall be more learned: [unclear]. If you are, he says, desirous of learning, you will certainly be learning many things. And, wishing to strengthen the memory of the pupil, he finely added: [unclear]. Preserve by meditations those things, he says, which you have learned; but grasp from those who know the things which you have not yet learned. For it is equally shameful for one hearing useful discourse not to learn, and not to accept some good thing given by friends. Farewell. From Neumagen, 24 June, in the year of Christians 1505.

XIII.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to his Jodocus Beissel, doctor of both laws, greeting.

On the first day of this month of July I came to the town of the archbishop of Cologne which they call Bonn, where on the next day, according to the agreement, that most wise and most learned prince Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg, chamberlain and elector of the Roman Empire, met me; summoned by him, I had come down there from the city of Neumagen. Then, at dawn on the sixth of the same month, we came to Cologne, where an assembly of many great princes of Germany is being held, with our most serene king of the Romans, Maximilian, present and hastening an expedition against the Sicambri. When we had come there, on the very next day I thought it appropriate to write to you, so that you would not be ignorant of the movements and terrors of my fortunes, because I count you among all men as a proven friend. For if the possession of no thing is pleasant without a friend, how will communication of sad things not bring relief to one who is saddened? Although adversity, which only the envy of rivals has stirred up against an innocent man, grieves me little, since I gave them no occasion at all. If fortune has played with me, she will take away nothing which she did not give, she who rather Of Johannes Trithemius.

perhaps adversity will profit me more than flattering and prosperous fortune, since her gifts are snares, not gifts, and should be called injuries rather than benefits. But if we believe Cicero, not only is Fortune herself blind, but she also commonly makes blind those whom she has embraced. Therefore, when Chilo the philosopher was asked what fortune was, he answered: Fortune is an ignorant physician, for she blinds many. But hear with what weapons blind fortune, stirred up by the envy and ill-will of our rivals, is trying to rage against me, so that you may understand that you are not the only one among mortals for whom his own household has raised up grievous wrongs. For Truth, which knows all things, cannot lie, when in the holy Gospel it foretells that its faithful would suffer tribulations and enmities for justice and most sacred religion, not only from outsiders, but also from their own household and intimates. By what means these things have happened to us, both from our own people and from strangers, we shall inform you in a brief account.

Since in the year just past, as can hardly be unknown to you, a conspiracy of many princes was waging a most savage war, utterly contrary to the customs of the Christian religion, against the most clement prince Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, under whose protection my monastery is known to stand secured by right of the county of Sponheim, I was compelled by fear of the enemy to withdraw to Stauropolis, the town nearest the monastery. Kreuznach.

Meanwhile Pyrophorus, that count of the Hessians, carrying out plundering, burnings, and devastations of sacred buildings, villages, and the most beautiful villas around Stauropolis without mercy, among other things devastated the better courts of my monastery and burned them with fire. But we remained with our notable library, which you once examined among us, in the aforesaid town for five months, until at last it was permitted to see an end of the evils. When peace had at length been restored to the province and we returned to the monastery, we gradually learned of various schemes against us by certain rivals, with some of our own people consenting, which had arisen meanwhile. Since, trusting in the innocence and uprightness of our mind, we had disregarded them, not considering or weighing the hatred of the Cynonoti that lay hidden against us, the fury of the malignant grew with time.

It happened, however, that on the first day of the month of April of the present year, having been summoned to Budoris, a town of our most serene prince Philip, Count Palatine, in the matter of the burned monastery of Limburg, I went out from my monastery, fearing nothing less than the evil that afterward happened in my absence. For on the fifth day thereafter, while I was at Budoris on the common business of my order, certain attendants of the Cynosnoti, sent to my monastery, broke the locks, took away clothing and such goods as they found, seized certain members of the household, and, laying upon them I know not what false crimes, delivered them over for not a few days to the public custody of the aforesaid town, to our manifest insult and reproach. When these things were reported to us at Budoris, they moved our mind not moderately, and not undeservedly did it distress us that we had received so signal an insult from those whom we had never offended even by a word.

Yet, deliberating with friends as to what would be useful for us to do, we concluded at last that we should not return to Sponheim before we knew that so great a wrong had been corrected by lawful satisfaction. And so we remained among the Budorites and Neometes for almost three months, not doubting that our people grieved more over the prolongation of our absence than we ourselves were saddened. The Cynonoti have some causes of hatred against us, and invent others. The love and loyalty with which we have always favored the affairs of the most clement prince Philip was not the least cause of the persecutions against us. I shall therefore give rashness room for a time; I shall go with the most serene prince into the March of Brandenburg, something which, though asked of me for many years, I had never before been able to accomplish. Nor shall I return soon, unless that commotion against us grows quiet.

You have, excellent Beifeli, the whole story of my misfortune, if indeed it is to be called misfortune, through which the malice of fortune is made manifest. For if we are rightly wise, fortune will not be able to harm us, as Menander says:

[unclear] [unclear]

For whatever fortune brings upon men who are truly wise will turn out for good, and often it happens that from adverse events a better fortune follows. Therefore in every event we need courage and temperance, so that we neither at any time cast down our mind in a time of things opposing us, nor in prosperity are vainly lifted up beyond what is fitting. Though fortune take away everything she has given, diminish riches and honors, annihilate dignities, if the mind, sustaining the divine ray, perseveres on its summit, she has harmed nothing. The mastery of affairs, as Valerius says, is accustomed to collapse; a good mind is preferred to riches, for the possession of a good mind undergoes no assault of a harsher fortune. Let us recognize that we are morJohannes Trithemius.

[it] moves toward salvation. With what zeal? So that that which moves more powerfully toward love may be pursued more ardently. With what end? So that it may be directed not to empty glory and display, but to one’s own salvation and that of others. But just as there is not one single intention among all who hasten toward knowledge, so also there is not one single end. For some desire to know many things only for this end, that they may know, and they receive the vain fruit of their curiosity, consisting in nothing. Others wish to know for temporal advantage, namely so that they may obtain riches, honors, and dignities; what else are they doing but practicing a base trade, and they must be judged wholly unworthy of the sacred name of knowledge itself? And how many today will be found to apply themselves to knowledge for this end. And there are some who wish to know so that they themselves may be known by men; the fruit of their knowledge is vanity. The intentions of all the aforesaid in seeking knowledge are blameworthy, and their end is subject to the reckoning of guilt and judgment.

But there are others who desire to know so that they may instruct and more ardently build up their neighbors in the love of Christ; their end is charity, and the fruit of [unclear] doctrine, eternal happiness. Others, again, wish to know so that they themselves may be built up in the law of the Lord; their end is prudence, and their reward is the due recompense of the life of good everlasting blessedness. You see now, friend, what the end of our knowledge ought to be, and in what manner we ought to know. Since, therefore, the end of speculative knowledge is truth, and of practical knowledge is work: we apprehend only so much from the knowledge of almighty God, who alone is truth, and we know only so much as we love. For true and saving knowledge begets knowledge of God; love begets frequency, frequency familiarity, familiarity trust, and trust the easy obtaining from the Lord Jesus of all things that you shall have requested.

Indeed, knowledge precedes the cultivation of virtue, because no one can faithfully seek what he does not know. Knowledge of the true and love of the right prepare a most certain entrance to happiness. But [unclear] truly precedes what it inwardly does not know. Therefore the Lord Jesus Christ said to the Father in the Gospel: This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. What else is that enjoyment of the supercelestial delight of the blessed spirits, if not knowledge and love of the divine majesty? For the knowledge of saving learning has love joined to itself; nor can the intellectual mind have fellowship in everlasting enjoyment if either knowledge is without love, or love without knowledge. Evil demons do know, but because they do not have love, they by no means attain the enjoyment which is born from both and not from one alone.

Certain gentile philosophers, and perhaps today many placed outside Christianity, are held to have love of the one highest truth; but because they do not know the Father of the universe, the only true God, and him whom he sent, our Lord Jesus Christ, they have become vain in their thoughts, and by no means arrive at the enjoyment of the highest goodness. And our savior himself, the Lord Jesus Christ, says in the holy Gospel about those who do not know by faith that he came into the world: He who does not believe has already been judged. And Saint [Christophilus?] says: Without faith it is impossible to please God. For true knowledge is from faith, and love from knowledge. Therefore the man who does not have faith does not have knowledge; he does not have love. And he who does not have love cannot have enjoyment. For this is what the Lord Jesus himself, when about to ascend into [heaven?], revealed to his disciples, saying: Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature. He who has believed and has been baptized will be saved; but he who has not believed will be condemned.

Thus the first road to God is knowledge or cognition through faith, without which no one will be saved. Let all other knowledge and your studies be referred to this true knowledge, O mathematician; but if you do not do this, you will be consumed in empty and foolish labor. This is true knowledge, which moves the one who knows to compunction and love, not exalting him; nor does it make those whom it has filled proud, but groaning, according to that saying of the wise man: He who adds knowledge also adds sorrow, because in much knowledge there is much indignation. Now therefore, friend, let us provide for ourselves at the opportune time, so that we may make our studies good while we have time, as the holy Apostle says: [unclear].

Familiar Letters

...such, and always liable to the common and necessary dissolution, that, laughing at all the assaults of fortune with one judgment, we neither praise prosperity nor accuse adversity. Indeed, as Cicero holds, to praise fortune is folly, but to blame it is arrogance. Farewell, constant and sound. From Cologne, while the council of the princes was continuing, on the [unclear] day of the month of July, in the year of the Christians 1505.

XIII.

John Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, sends greetings to Matthew Herbenus.

I congratulate you, my friend; I have rejoiced many times because at last, after the various wavering opinions of your mind, you have dedicated yourself at the sacred altars of the Lord, our Savior Jesus Christ, as a minister, priest, and sacrificer. This is the safer way to happiness, if in mind, works, and office you agree with what you have undertaken. For divine Scripture says in Leviticus: He who has a blemish shall not offer the loaves to his God, nor approach his ministry. If he is blind, if lame, if with foot or hand broken, he shall not approach to offer victims to the Lord, nor loaves to his God.

A priest has a blemish who, gaping after earthly affections, has stained the purity of his conscience with the foulness of vices. He is blind who, because of ignorance of the divine Scriptures, does not behold the light of heavenly doctrine with the understanding, and for that reason is rendered unworthy of the priestly office, because he is wholly useless for instructing the household of God in salutary doctrines. For since the office of a priest, according to the prophet's saying, is to answer when questioned concerning the law and to announce the will to the Lord's people, because he is called His angel, how will he teach the peoples entrusted to him, when he himself is wholly turned about in the darkness of ignorance?

But we readily believe that you can become learned in the law of the Lord, if you turn the zeal for secular letters, in which you have been fully instructed, with the desire of love to meditation on the holy Scriptures. For you flourish with a most noble talent; lifted up by its keenness, you may very easily grasp with love whatever you wish of divine instruction. And when you have escaped the vice of spiritual blindness, which indeed you easily can with the aid of the grace of the Holy Spirit, you must take the greatest care that you not be marked with the most shameful reproach of the limping man.

For a priest is lame, and broken in foot and hand, who in life and conduct does not walk toward the purity of evangelical truth, nor takes care to show himself, before the sheep entrusted to him, a follower of good works. Against him it is read in Exodus: Let the priests who approach the Lord be sanctified, lest perhaps I strike them. And again Scripture commands the priests, saying: Be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord.

For the priests of the Lord ought to be adorned with a twofold doctrine: namely, with uprightness of work and with the word of sacred preaching, so that they may not corrupt by wicked deeds the good which they preach to their subjects as something to be chosen. Certainly the doctrine of truth is always useful to the people of God, whether the one who teaches lives well or badly; nevertheless, in a priest it does not suffice without the example of good conduct, since by living badly he has made fruitless the good which by preaching he usefully set before the peoples entrusted to him.

Therefore no one, as Augustine holds, harms the Church of God more than he who, acting perversely, has obtained the name or order of priest. For none of his subjects presumes to rebuke this man when he sins; he is drawn more forcefully into an example of fault, when, vicious as he is, he is honored out of reverence for his order. Since, therefore, bad priests are the ruin of the people, we must provide with great caution that no one, scandalized by our example, should fall into the pit by reason of our occasion for sinning.

The multitude of those like you does not excuse you when you sin; rather flee the examples of the many who do not turn purely to priestly instruction. For it is a most foolish consolation to wish to be lost with many, rather than to be saved with few. For there are many priests, as Chrysostom says, and few priests: many indeed in name, very few in deed. See therefore how you sit upon the chair, because the chair does not make the priest, but the priest makes the chair. The place does not sanctify the man, but the man the place. He who sits well upon the chair receives honor from it; he who sits badly does injury to the chair.

You sit in judgment: if indeed you have lived well and taught well, you will be judge of all. But if you have taught well and lived badly, as judge of yourself alone you will condemn only yourself. For by living well and teaching well, you instruct the people how it ought to live rightly, and you show that you are a faithful minister of the Lord, to be rewarded by Him. But if you live well and do not teach well the people entrusted to you, you have sinned, because by not instructing the people you destroy them; and when they perish through your fault, how will you, a priest without a people, be saved? But when, living badly, you teach well, you prescribe to God the form in which He ought to condemn you.

For this reason I exhort you, Herbenus, dearest brother: take care as diligently as [unclear], so that you may be able to be adorned with both kinds of beauty [unclear].

452 Familiar Letters

At the house of the most reverend archbishop of Cologne, Hermann, we rested for some days in Bonn; he relieved us of the cost of lodging at his own expense and gave us a most welcome gift. We also mentioned you more than once in conversation, as you will hear when you come, [with the highest regard for you?]. The bearer of this letter will make clear at what lodging I am staying. Farewell, best father. From Cologne, on the 10th day of the month of July, in the year of the Christians 1505.

XVIII.

John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, sends greetings to Jacob de Maseck, physician, wise man, and friend.

Yesterday evening you sent us a gift most welcome indeed, namely the books of Kyranus, written on parchment in an ancient and very beautiful script; although we had searched for them through almost all Germany, we had nowhere been able to find them complete. We give you immense thanks, and, if ever it is permitted us, we shall give you the greatest possible thanks for this kindness of yours toward us. For you have honored us more with such a gift than if you had offered us much money, because the reading of so great an author can contribute somewhat to the perfection of our understanding, whereas money contributes nothing. Money is easily consumed, but wisdom, illuminating our understanding, suffers no loss.

For what use to a philosopher professing the religion of Christ Jesus, and striving through poverty toward the riches of paradise, is the money of this world, which is the cause to human beings of all evils and crimes? For money is acquired with labor and with no small danger to the soul; once acquired, it is kept with fear; and often it is lost with the gravest pain of mind. Add that the satirist sang, not unwisely, about avaricious men, saying:

Meanwhile, while the money-bag swells with full mouth, Love of coin grows as the money itself grows, And he who lacks this resource desires it less.

And perhaps we despise it the more easily the less we have; we would have it even if we did not despise it. But why [unclear] part, but requires the whole man. Avarice, however, and the boundless love of possessing, are so contrary to wisdom that, once they have begun to possess someone in part, they do not allow him any longer to be free, but subject him wholly to their most restless tyranny. The mind in each person is one, and cannot be open to two contrary loves, as our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ testifies in the holy Gospel: [unclear]. And in another place he says: “See and beware of all avarice, because a person’s life does not consist in the abundance of the things he possesses.” And in the Gospel of Mark: “Little children, how difficult it is for those who trust in riches to enter into the kingdom of God. It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of heaven.”

Our most learned teacher Christophilus, too, wishing us to be fortified against avarice, says: “The root of all evils is desire; some, seeking it, have strayed from the faith and have pierced themselves with many sorrows. But you, O man of God, flee these things. We brought nothing into this world; there is no doubt that we cannot carry anything away from here. Therefore, having food, and garments with which we may be covered, let us be content with these. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil, and into many useless and harmful desires, which plunge human beings into ruin and destruction.”

For he who serves money is both bound by the fetters of present evils and made ready for future and everlasting evils. For it is difficult for one who has riches not to set his heart on them, not to desire more, not to be anxious, not [unclear] from the belief in acquiring wealth. The precepts of Phocylides are to be kept by philosophers, by which both tranquillity of mind and the community of [unclear] is preserved:

[unclear]

[unclear]

[unclear]

Likewise, strongly enough detesting avarice and gold as the cause of all evils, after a few words he adds the following maxim: Of Johannes Trithemius.

[unclear]

Accordingly, after some passages, he warns that, if riches are ours, they must by no means be spared, since we may neither carry them away with us nor bring them into Pluto’s darkness, saying beautifully as follows:

[unclear]

Among the ancients who took up the precepts of philosophy, it was above all necessary to despise riches as certain impediments to wisdom, for they understood with sufficient foresight that a mind occupied with earthly things could in no way be free for divine teachings. And why do I speak of men of the world, who did not find the path of true philosophy by which one comes to eternal happiness, when the chief apostles of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and their disciples and followers, in order to attend more freely to heavenly things, despised all the perishable riches of the world through love of things above? For rightly a certain imitator of the saints, calling us to true wisdom, sang thus:

Wisdom fills a tranquil mind, empty of cares; she will be the guest of a peaceful breast.

And the Holy of Holies himself says through a certain prophet of his oracle: Upon whom shall the Spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words? How many today do we see among Christians, arrogating to themselves the name of the more sacred philosophy, who are covetous, greedy, luxurious, unclean, and given over to every animal passion; who think themselves to be what they are not, because they have made themselves such as they ought not to have been. Of them the holy apostle of Christ says: Know this, that in the last days perilous times will come. For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, without natural affection, implacable, slanderers, incontinent, fierce, without love of good, traitors, rash, puffed up, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having a form of godliness but denying its power; and from such turn away.

How the greater part of Christians today has everywhere given free rein to the passions just listed, none of us who has lived even moderately among men is ignorant. Most of all we see that avarice, which is slavery to idols, has infected almost the whole human race, and, if it is right to say so, even those who, by the preeminence of their dignity, ought above others to be despisers of riches. Hence very few today betake themselves either to the priesthood for love of God or to the study of letters from desire for wisdom; rather, what is greatly to be lamented, in both cases temporal advantage is sought by many, and worldly honors and riches are thought of more than reverence for God, so that the prophecy seems to be fulfilled to the letter in which it was said: And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest. From this arises contempt for the priesthood; the word of the Lord is blasphemed all day long. If even the life of a priest is despised, what wonder if his teaching is despised by the ignorant people? To such a man the holy apostle of Christ, rightly reproaching his evil life, is shown to have said: You who teach others, do you not teach yourself?

But our Lord Jesus Christ prescribed for us a model of teaching, concerning whom the holy evangelist Luke reports at the beginning [of the Acts?] that, after giving commandments through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen, he was taken up. Hence Saint Ambrose says: Life must be sought before teaching. A good life without teaching has grace; teaching without life does not have integrity. For to teach and not act, as Chrysostom bears witness, not only contributes nothing, but brings very much harm. For great condemnation belongs to one who indeed composes his discourse, but shamefully neglects his life in deed. Therefore, before all else, let a holy life confirm teaching, lest that saying written in the sacred Gospel be said to anyone: Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your eye; then you will be able to see the speck sticking in your brother’s eye.

But we, O Jacob, leaving aside the multitude of those who do not philosophize rightly, should direct our studies to true philosophy, which consists in the knowledge and love of the highest truth. For the most holy attainment of this we need neither gold nor money, but only the tranquility of a purer mind, together with desire for divine love, observance of the commandments of God, in all gentleness, patience, and long-suffering. Farewell, and do not neglect to visit us more often, lest we be consumed by idleness. At Cologne, from our lodging, on the twelfth day of July, in the Christian year 1505.

XIX.

John Trithemius, abbot, to John [Capellius?], [unclear]. Familiar Letters

[unclear]

20.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Roger Sycamber, his very dear brother, greetings.

Most loving Sycamber, in order to satisfy your desire, which, at your request, I promised before I left Neumagen, I wished briefly to disclose to you in my letter what fortune I have had in sailing, and what is being done publicly here. On the twenty-fifth day of the month of June I left Neumagen with Master Narcissus, lately sent to me from Paris, and with certain other members of our household, and that same evening, carried by carriages, we entered Mainz. The next day, having boarded a ship, and sailing with a favorable wind, we went down, furrowing the Rhine, and on the first day of the month of July we put in at Bonn. It was the solemn vigil of the Visitation of the most blessed Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary. There we waited for two days for the arrival of the most serene prince Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, meanwhile being most abundantly provided in all things by the munificence of the most reverend Hermann, Archbishop of Cologne. But on the third day of the month of July, around sunset, the prince himself whom we were awaiting also came, with sixty horsemen; the archbishop received him honorably and detained him for three days. On the morning of the sixth day of that same month, leaving Bonn, we came to Cologne around the tenth hour. And now we are here, having no certainty at all about our departure. There is a report, not a common one, that our king is planning an expedition, and that aid will not fail in the future for your Sycambrians. Continuous negotiations are being held among the princes before the king for the restoration of peace and concord between our prince Philip, Count Palatine, and the others who are at odds with him. Macharius, abbot of the desolated monastery of Limburg, Johannes Trithemius

... our guests, most devoted to you, might happen to enjoy [unclear]. We have sent this servant of ours on certain business to Neomete and Sebach; through him, if you wish to write anything to us, you will be able to do so with the greatest certainty. For he will soon return to us at Cologne. Farewell, my brother, and pray to God for us. From Cologne, on the 12th day of the month of July, in the year of the Christians 1505.

XXI.

John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to his most beloved daughter in Christ, Richmod, abbess of the monastery in Sebach, sincere charity in the Lord.

As soon as an opportunity of speaking with the archbishop of the people of Cologne was given me, which occurred at Bonn on the second day of July, I set forth the matter of your patrimony, which you have with William, knight of Horst, your brother, and at the same time I asked for counsel and assistance. After he heard from me that you were in good health, he rejoiced with you and promised that he would apply all his effort so that you might obtain some part of your paternal estate, as far as possible. But since nothing can be done unless your brother is present in person, we postponed the whole matter at Cologne, where we hoped he would come. And because he did not appear, the prince’s counsel is that you appoint someone at Cologne by letters as procurator, who may suitably pursue the case before him whenever your brother is personally present here in Cologne, as often happens. I have no doubt that the archbishop, out of love for you, will exercise in the case all the diligence that he promises. Therefore appoint before a sworn scribe [unclear], so that [unclear] in Cologne as procurator. Yesterday, invited by the master, I had dinner in your monastery of the Maccabees, and I set forth your case to Master Elias, who also willingly promised that he would cooperate to the best of his ability. He, together with Master Gisbert, would seem to me not unprofitable to be chosen as advocate of the case. The mistress of the convent greets you, and Sister Margaret of Dauerckhusen, formerly prioress in Sebach, and all the other sisters most devoted to you. They are putting off writing letters to you until my departure from Cologne. This servant will make you more certain about my condition and health. Farewell, most devoted virgin of Christ, mindful of us in your holy prayers. From Cologne, on the 16th day of July, in the year 1505.

XXII.

John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to Johann Gryposius, baker, citizen of Stavelot, a most distinguished friend, greeting.

Since, sweetest Johann, you have always shown yourself a true friend to us, according to that saying of the wise man: “He who is a friend loves at all times; and a brother is proved in distress,” you strive to persevere to the end. For with letters no less elegant than sweet you console us most affectionately, as though we were cast down in spirit because of that insult raised against us by a rival; you also promise that, to the best of your ability, you will never fail us in body or substance. And although no dejection has penetrated our mind, since we have placed our hopes in safer things, and have been instructed to bear patiently all the assaults of raging fortune in view of the reward to come, nevertheless we give you immense thanks, for you keep inviolate the rights of true friendship. For this is the integrity of perfect friendship: it is not separated from those whom it has held for the sake of advantage. For the brothers of a poor man hate him; moreover, even his friends have withdrawn far from him. But he who takes mercy away from his friend abandons the fear of God. That is not true friendship which deserts a friend when he is placed in necessity. But true intimacy, according to Saint Jerome, is that which is joined by the glue of Christ, which is brought about not by the usefulness of private property, not merely by the presence of bodies, not by deceitful and flattering adulation, but by the fear of God and the study of the divine Scriptures. For in friends one seeks not property but good will, because substance is often supplied even by those who are not friends; but only the charity of friendship grants good will. For to will the same things and not to will the same things among equals and good men is firm friendship; where it remains, nothing is easily believed, nothing is easily received, as Chrysostom says, that could produce distrust. But if enmities once occupy minds, all things all things that are, that are said, that are heard, are so received that they tend toward greater enmities. True friendship is rare today among mortals, because private good is preferred to common advantage, and those whom a gift, not grace, has joined cannot be faithful in friendship, since, as soon as they receive no more, [unclear] men abandon all charity. For love that is glued together by a gift is dissolved when the same is suspended. Therefore true friendship is that which seeks nothing from the possessions of the beloved except goodwill alone, namely that he should freely love the one who loves him. Equality of minds, indeed, brings friendship together, not ambition for things, so that a friend is in a friend through goodwill, as if another self or one soul, as Aristotle used to say, dwelling in two bodies. Since, therefore, there can be no true friendship among mortals unless true charity binds it together among those who love, which, shame to say, is exceedingly rare in our times, great diligence is needed in acquiring friends, lest we love without counsel one whom it later happens that we hate. Therefore a certain wise man, making much of the value of true friendship among mortals, used to say: There is no comparison for a faithful friend, since a faithful friend is a strong protection; he who finds such a one has certainly found a precious treasure. And Menander, confirming this very thing, says: [unclear] [unclear] In adversities a friend is preferable to money. Having friends, consider yourself to have treasures.

How rare faithful friends are, we all experience every day: in prosperity we find many, but when fortune has changed we find no one, as Menander himself also said: [unclear] If you are rich, perhaps you will have friends in abundance.

That wanton poet also bears witness to this in the Tristia, saying: So long as you are fortunate, you will count many friends; if times become cloudy, you will be alone.

But farewell, my faithful friend: time heals all things. From Cologne, on the 16th day of the month of July, in the year 1505.

XXIII.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Johannes Capellerius, mathematician, greetings.

Steganography.

That part of our lesser Steganography to which we gave the Greek title [unclear], that is, “fertility of language,” and which you long ago requested from us, I have had copied out for you: a secret work, as you know, seen by no one up to now, which we send on this condition, that it be kept hidden. I do not reproach your love and your unfailing zeal for Greek letters and the other sciences of worldly philosophy; rather, I would praise them and extol them with great commendations, if you ordered all these things rightly toward divine love. For all studies of mortals, when they have not been ordered toward the charity of God, are empty, vain excesses to be despised by every Christian. We must therefore take care that our mind, mindful of salvation, never cling to worldly studies, but rather use them for the ministry and service, not continuously, but only when necessary, by turns, of spiritual philosophy and wisdom; through this, by loving, it is led into the knowledge of God, and, by knowing, is strengthened in the sweetness of love. We are mortal under the pressing statutes of nature; we all necessarily die, carrying with us only this: what progress we have made, by learning and studying, in the knowledge and love of the highest good, our creator. But all the fruits of other studies vanish like a mist, once the labor has been undertaken. Every art acquired by human means, which does not adhere to divine knowledge, although in this life it usurps for itself the name of knowledge, however celebrated, and attains a demonstrative habit, can remain in a person only as long as life with reason remains in the body. But it ceases completely when the person dies; it expires with the other actions of life. Concerning this vain knowledge of the world, Saint Christophilus says in a certain letter: If anyone thinks that he knows anything, he has not yet learned how he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by him. Saint Bernard, most beautifully explaining his meaning in the Meditations, said: You see that he does not approve those who know much if they do not know the manner of knowing. You see how he establishes the fruit and usefulness of knowledge in the manner of knowing. What then does he say, except that you should know in what order, with what zeal, and to what end each thing ought to be known? In what order: that first, which more maturely moves [Familiar Letters]

[unclear]

... there is need, if we desire to obtain the fruit of true wisdom with the most blessed apostles of Christ in eternal blessedness. For Saint Christophilus says again in a certain letter: “Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no one will see God.” In Leviticus too the Lord said to Moses: “Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel, and say to them: Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy.”

But what holiness is to be thought to be, Dionysius the Areopagite did not pass over in silence in chapter twelve of On the Divine Names, saying: “Holiness, to speak according to our manner, is purity free from every crime, perfect, and utterly unstained.” Our God is holy; we, however, are sinners and unclean. Since, therefore, there is no union between unlike things, how will there be concord between God and us? Let us hear the divine teacher, Saint Augustine: “No holy and just man is without sin; yet on that account he does not cease to be just and holy, so long as he holds holiness in affection.” For Scripture says: “Seven times in a day the just man falls, and will rise again; but the wicked will fall into evil.”

“If he falls,” says Jerome, “how is he just? If he is just, how does he fall? But he does not lose the name of just who always rises again through repentance.” And not only to one sinning seven times, but even seventy times, if he is turned to repentance, sins are forgiven. And although no one becomes holy by his own powers, since it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy, nevertheless our good will is necessarily required for our sanctification, so that the grace of God may work holiness in us. For indeed, just as neither a man without a woman, nor a woman without a man, begets a human being from himself or herself, so neither does the good will of a human being without the grace of God sanctify anyone, nor does divine mercy sanctify anyone unto good without that person’s own will.

God gave free choice to man, whereby he might have his will in his own power: not so that by himself he could do the good which he wills, but so that he might will what God himself has granted him to be able to do. Hence also the holy Christophilus said: “To will is present with me; but to accomplish it I do not find.” Why is this, O holy observer of divine things, when nothing is so sufficient for a good will as it is for itself? But, he says, “it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy.” This saying of Paul many who are carnally wise do not understand soundly, especially because of this...

Of Johannes Trithemius.

... and impure things to the most holy, heavenly things to earthly ones, so that the mind may equally savor the things that are above and the things that are upon the earth. Farewell, Capellerius, and toil in salutary studies, whose fruit is promised in heaven, and whose end is held subject to no end whatsoever. And again, farewell. From Cologne, on the 18th day of the month of July, in the year 1505.

XXIII.

Johannes Trithemius to Johannes Steinemoel, priest of Mechelen.

An opportunity of writing to you has been offered me through this man, both known to you and, as he asserts, joined to you by the singularity of a certain close relationship, who was going to pass from there to Mechelen. We write, therefore, so that you may know what seems to us should be arranged concerning your return to us, lest you run in vain. First, then, we make known to you that, by reason of the war raging around us in the previous year, our affairs have collapsed, and, fortune being blind, a grave envy of rivals has arisen against us. Reason has persuaded us to yield place to it for a time, so that either the enemies themselves may deliberate better, or we, by the counsel of friends, may provide for our affairs elsewhere. We are therefore going to the March of Brandenburg with its most serene prince, now present here in the royal convocation, who long ago desired this of us many times by letters and messengers, but now in person by words. But we shall go wholly uncertain about our return, because, after the grave insult received from our own people, we think of nothing less than returning to Spanheim, unless the divine will shall have ordained otherwise; to it our weakness must always be subject and consenting. You must therefore defer your return to Spanheim until you hear that we have at last returned there, unless perhaps you wish to make a journey of sixty miles in vain. We have been unable to attend to the affairs of your Vincentius because of the unrest of the times; nor indeed can they any longer be of concern to us, since you, vainly and all too boastfully, carry about for sale, for shameful profit, those secrets of the more hidden philosophy which you received from us, as we have been made certain, thinking yourself to be someone great because you can boast that you were a disciple of Trithemius. This is not the path of true wisdom, my Johannes, nor does it befit your age to place hope in vanity and to cast pearls before swine for the price of a cheap reputation. You proclaim certain great things about us, so that you yourself may be regarded as great in the estimation of the people; and while you overstep the rule of true praise, you do us a grave injury, forgetful of the very ancient proverb: praise sparingly, blame more sparingly. Your praises displease us most vehemently, because they are rather reproaches of us than commendations. For it does not belong to all men to understand the secrets of nature and to discover, in known things, something hidden beyond common use. But when you promise certain things about us which others do not understand, what else do you believe remains, old man, except that they will say that we are either given to superstitions or sunk in vanities? We know that you were not introduced by us on that condition; but because you have transgressed the law of fairness set between us, what you would do in greater matters had reasonably to be foreseen by us. Cease, therefore, from these vanities, we exhort you, and consider that you are a minister of Jesus Christ and mature in old age, whom it does not befit to hunt after mortal glory by vanities. Farewell, mindful of us before God. From Cologne, on the 20th day of the month of July, in the year of Christians 1505.

XXV.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, to Johannes Bracht, of the monastery of St. Matthias, greetings.

I believe that you are by no means unaware, ornament of friends, of that tribulation which that malignant enemy has stirred up against me, who, armed with the dart of envy, drove the first men from the paradise of innocence. He has driven me too from my monastery, not indeed unwilling, but willing through the recollection of injuries, and he has brought upon my mind nausea and a certain horror of the former place, which I had loved most tenderly. I am now living here by a certain necessity as a courtier, soon to go with the most serene prince Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, Elector of the Roman Empire, to the borders of the Saxons, and perhaps to return late; meanwhile, may the persecution stirred up against me either cease, or, if it has gained strength from my absence, may mature providence furnish us a remedy. For the earth is the Lord’s and the fullness thereof; his power is immeasurable, and the compassion of his utterly inexhaustible piety is such that we trust help from him will be present for us everywhere at the opportune time, and we in no way doubt his protection. But you, brother beloved in Christ, we ask that you deign to pray to God for us incessantly in this commotion of the restless sea, so that [unclear]

To you in some manner, although to have you even from me, not content, but rejoicing as I consider that you will come to me, and that nevertheless now I seem to see you, provided namely that I came before you, and afterwards I seem to see you. Since if I see you, and see you who sees me, and with us conversing, and us conversing, and all looking on, and all hearing, and all will see, as they could have seen, when they could have seen, and hoped, and hoped. And if I hear you, and seeing, and you see, and you will see, and you hear, and of one seeing, and you see, and you will see, and of one seeing, as he comes, and he comes, and he has been heard, and they have been heard, and he will be seen, and he has come, and they have come, and he would be seen, and they would come, and they would be seen, and they would come, and they would be seen, as he has come, and let him come, and he has come, and he comFamiliar Letters

[so that] the good which our merits cannot attain may, through your prayers, be granted to us by the mercy of God. For I know that the prayer of one who humbles himself penetrates the clouds and will not return empty, as our Savior promises in the holy Gospel: “Ask,” he says, “and it shall be given you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks it shall be opened.” For as James, the apostle of Christ, says: the constant prayer of the righteous man avails much. Nor, when you pour out prayer for us, will you lack benefit, as Pope Gregory says: whoever strives to intercede for others, rather aids himself out of charity, and deserves to be heard more quickly for himself, the more devoutly he intercedes for others. For to pray for oneself, as Chrysostom bears witness, is necessity; but to pray for others belongs to brotherly charity. Sweeter before God is the prayer which not necessity sends forth, but which the charity of brotherhood commends. And the holy bishop Ambrose says: if you ask only for yourself, you alone will pray for yourself; but if you ask for all, all will also ask for you. Prayer, moreover, is then perfect and easily obtains what is desired when cause, tongue, heart, deed, speech, life, and the whole thought cry out, as Menander too expresses in a few words, saying: [unclear]. That is: God is the hearer of righteous prayer. But he cries to the Lord with a great voice who, even if he is silent with his tongue, nevertheless cries out perseveringly by good works. Since we know you to be such an intercessor, distinguished by purity of mind and holy in life, again and again we ask you: pray for us, and farewell.

From Cologne, on the 22nd day of the month of July, in the year of Christians 1505.

XXVI.

John Trithemius, abbot of Saint James, sends greetings to Jacobus Kymolanus, theologian. Of Johannes Trithemius

I agreed to go into the March, especially because my aforesaid most serene prince, the Palatine, not only gave me his consent for that very thing, but also advised it. Meanwhile perhaps my brothers will experience what benefit our absence brings them; their charity toward their father has grown too cold, since, when it could have resisted the rashness of rivals in our absence, it disdained to do so.

On the fourth day of August we left Cologne; on the vigil of Saint Lawrence the martyr, after vespers, we entered Neometum. The prince Margrave, however, after assigning us expenses for the journey with three servants, left Cologne with his men on the penultimate day of July itself, making his way through Westphalia and Saxony to his own region. We left the Abbot of Limburg in Cologne, and with him our brother Master Jacob, whom we would rather have taken with us into the March, had the abbot's requests not stood in the way. In his cases against his adversary the Count of Leiningen, whose officials burned the monastery of Limburg [unclear], he obtained from the royal majesty as commissioner Jacob, Archbishop of Mainz, who, after hearing the parties' allegations and examining witnesses if any are produced, will try to bring about harmony between them not by law but amicably. And if the matter can be reconciled, it has gone well; but if it cannot, which I rather believe, the whole business, with the acts, will be referred back to the king.

That impious tyrant, hateful to God and men, a count whose name is unworthy of memory, denies the most audacious [unclear] knowingly before the majesty, but he plainly lies, since he is convicted by open testimonies. The man full of the devil seeks evasions; he seems to sigh for the Greek Kalends. O evil head among the sons of the devil, more like your father, [unclear], do you think that you can escape the vengeance of God? By your own authority you caused the monastery, with its distinguished church, to be burned, out of hatred and vengeance; therefore you have incurred the penalty of the canon which is set forth in 23, question 8, chapter Pessimam. You are a member of your father the devil, rightly to be punished, as in 41, question 2, Cum devotissimam, and in the following chapter. Almighty God is not ignorant of your horrible crime because he dissembles for a short time; nor will you therefore escape the wrath of the just judge because you have not at once paid the penalties you have deserved. Divine power indeed takes vengeance slowly, but it will compensate the delay by the severity of the punishment. But let the man go to ruin, unworthy of any man's memory.

But you, Roger, we ask that you come to us at Neometum as soon as possible; we have many necessary matters to discuss with you before we proceed into the March. We shall remain here some days for certain affairs of ours; when these are settled, we shall soon be on our way. We have written to your prior, asking that he permit you to come to us, which, as we trust, he will not refuse. Farewell, from Neometum, on the twelfth day of August, in the year 1505.

XXXII. Johannes Trithemius to his most beloved brother Johannes Nuntius, greeting.

We grieve for your illnesses, most loving brother, from our whole heart, and we suffer with you more than we can either say or commit to letters, humbly beseeching the mercy of the Almighty that he may deign mercifully to pour out over you the bowels of his compassion, and may grant you in all your adversities, for love of him, patience and the everlasting consolation of his inward sweetness. You exhort us, and with suppliant devotion ask that we return to our monastery, not doubting that very shortly all our adversaries will return into favor with us, since they are not a little sorry that they began this game of rashness, and all desire our return with great longing.

The same things that you write we have heard from others, and we do not doubt that they are true; but at this time we cannot return to the monastery. We are going into the March of Brandenburg, and will remain there for some time; for this journey the most serene prince, the Count Palatine, at the request of Margrave Joachim, not only gave us his consent but also advised that we go. Meanwhile it will become possible to see what [unclear] are plotting against us, and how much they favor holy religion, who, armed with envy and malice, have persecuted me without cause because of hatred for the Prince Palatine. My prior was aware of every conspiracy of the rivals against me; we are not ignorant of what moved him. For he believes that, if we, provoked by insult, should withdraw from the monastery, he would succeed us in the abbacy. And in truth both things can happen: that we may withdraw shortly, and that he may succeed us. For we were long ago forewarned by a most certain revelation that we shall not remain in the abbacy of Sponheim until death, although we are still ignorant of the time of withdrawal. We do not yet have a successor designated for us, although we can plausibly suspect that the prior will thrust himself in. But let the will of the Lord Jesus be done, which can never be unjust, even if to our thoughts JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS

...they brought forward the most holy doctrine of Christ, the promises also of the prophets, and the ordinances of the apostles. But our preachers, in greater number, mingle the purest words of God with Aristotelian and Julian opinions, citing more often the philosophers of the Gentiles than Christ’s apostles. Shame! So celebrated has the authority of the Peripatetics become among the heralds of the word of God that in the chair of Christ Aristotle is more often cited in public than Paul or Peter, the most holy chiefs of the apostles.

What do sermons of such men profit the simple, unlearned people of God, in which everything is introduced for display, but nothing for compunction? Those little harlots and traditions of the Gentiles must be sent back to the schools of the Gymnosophists, so that in the school of Christ nothing be preached except the pure and unstained doctrine of Christ. For whoever first devised this manner of preaching mixed bran with the purest flour.

Turn over, I pray, the sermons of all the holy fathers of old, together with their most celebrated homilies; see whether you find the bran of Gentile philosophers mixed with the flour of Christian purity. Examine, I beseech you, as diligently as possible, the homilies and sermons of Origen, Hippolytus, Cyprian, Hilary, Gregory Nazianzen, Ambrose, Basil, Chrysostom, Jerome, Maximus, Severian, Augustine, Fulgentius, Pope Gregory, Isidore, Bede, Rabanus, Haymo, Peter Damian, Anselm, Bernard, and other most holy ancient fathers: you will find in them nothing other than the true, solid, pure doctrine of Christ, free from all leaven of Gentile traditions. There is not cited there that Peripatetic Aristotle, not the apostate Porphyry, not Plato, not Averroes, not Cicero, nor finally anyone from the remaining troop of the Gentiles, but only Christ Jesus himself, the wisdom of God the Father, and the apostles of that highest truth, the holy patriarchs and prophets.

It is plainly an unworthy kind of teaching, in my judgment, that in the school of Christ, as though for confirmation of the sayings of the Holy Spirit, the names should be heard recited of those whose spirits are without doubt wholly alien from Christ. For the wise men of this world did not know the wisdom of God; therefore in their vanities they shamefully came to nothing. There are otherwise among Christians petty scholars who, presumptuous with excessive rashness, dare to assert that the philosopher Socrates, in life as in death and doctrine, prefigured our Savior, making a comparison of him to Christ that is excessively absurd, insolent, and by no means tolerable to Christian ears, as though he had been alien to the worship of idols, when, as he was already about to die, as Plato records in the Phaedo, he spoke this as the last of his words: “O Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius; pay it, and do not neglect it.”

But grant that no mortal knows the counsel of the Lord, and that for this reason no certain condemnation of such great men can be brought forward by us, especially of those who preceded the birth in the flesh of Christ our Savior: what necessity drives the preacher of the words of God to mingle, in the holy Church, which is the school of Christians, the words of Gentile philosophers ignorant of Christ with the doctrine of the highest truth, when sacred Scripture is abundantly sufficient for us for the instruction of the Christian life, and there is no need to borrow anything from elsewhere? Every preacher is foolish if he thinks the doctrine of Christ must be adorned with the sayings of Gentile philosophers; concerning it the holy prophet sang, saying: “The law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to little ones.” And again: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold.” Our Lord Jesus Christ himself also says in the Gospel according to John: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” What agreement, then, has death with life, or what comparison has light with darkness? If the words of Christ are spirit and life, surely the words of those dead outside the Lord must not be mixed with them.

But hear what Firmianus Lactantius says: “Divine instruction,” he says, “does not require dialectic, in which the whole method of speaking is contained, because wisdom is not in the tongue but in the heart; nor does it matter what manner of speech you use, where things are sought, not words. And we are disputing not about the grammarian or the orator, whose knowledge is how it is fitting to speak, but about the wise man, whose teaching is how one ought to live. But if neither that physical reasoning is necessary, nor, besides this, logical reasoning, because they cannot make one blessed, it remains that the whole force of philosophy is contained in ethics alone, to which Socrates is said to have turned after casting all other things aside; yet in this part too the philosophers erred, because they did not comprehend the highest good, for the sake of desiring which they were born.”

It is therefore evident that all the philosophy of the Gentiles is false and empty, and for that reason must by no means be mixed with the sacred teachings of Christ, because it neither instructs in the duties of righteousness nor confirms the office and principles of man. But the office of a preacher established in the Church of God is faithfully to set before the people the law and doctrine of Jesus Christ the Savior, to impress compunction and devotion upon the minds of the hearers, and them to righteousness

Aristotelian preachers.

1 Corinthians 1.

Socrates is impiously compared with Christ.

Psalm [unclear].

Psalm [unclear].

John 6.

The law and the Gospel ought to be set before the people. Of Johannes Trithemius.

XXXIII.

Germanus de Ganay, to the most illustrious man Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, splendor of our age, greetings.

[unclear]

Most worthy sir, the radiance of the sun cannot be hidden when it strikes our hemisphere, nor withdrawn from human sight; rather, it spreads the most brilliant rays of its light into the eyes of all, and draws them into admiration of its brightness. So too the most luminous splendor of your learning can by no means lie concealed, but sends forth the ray of its light to all, however far removed by distance of place. Hence among foreigners your name is held most celebrated and is exalted with wondrous praises; stirred by the fame of your singular learning, they desire nothing more ardently than to be illuminated by the ray of your distinguished knowledge.

And I too, relying on confidence in your kindness, have not feared to send you this letter, both to congratulate your dignity and to explain my desire to you. A letter from you came into my hands, sent to a certain Johannes Steinenmoelen, whom, in the very opening of the salutation, after the expression of your name, you call a man of desires in sacred matters. It certainly contains a rare and admirable philosophy, both concerning numbers and concerning elements, yet so veiled in enigmas and hidden in secret words that understanding of it is only partly open to me, and far exceeds the grasp of my mind.

Therefore, if there were with you some interpretation of it which you would not refuse to share with me, I myself should wish to read nothing more gladly. For my mind conjectures that a very worthy and lofty meaning lies beneath those words, and that from your same workshop other works have come forth, which go beyond the accustomed mode of philosophizing and contain a secret and sacred knowledge. If, by your assistance, I should attain these, things more desirable than Attalic wealth and the riches of Croesus would fall to me. I beseech you not to refuse to impart them to me, a most observant devotee of your name.

Our Carolus Bovillus, who in former years, when he was traveling through Germany, came to visit your excellence, has often mentioned you to me, and, to tell the truth, has wholly led me to become an observer and admirer of your virtues. Finally, the bearer of this letter, known and friendly to your excellence, Master Narcissus, will explain more fully the greater wishes of my mind, which I could not easily include in a brief letter. Farewell, glory of our age and unique exemplar of learning. From Paris, the third day before the Kalends of August, in the year 1505.

XXXIV.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, to Germanus de Ganay, a most learned man, greetings.

[unclear]

Your envoy Master Narcissus came to us at Neumetum on the fifteenth day of the month of August, bringing your letter, and at the same time welcome little gifts. We detained him with us for almost twelve days, so that he should not seem to have undertaken so great a journey in vain. For the matters which you indicated to us through him are great, and it was not within our power to give him an answer without mature deliberation. We have fully understood your mind from his report, and, as far as it has now been permitted to us, we have taken care that you should understand that you have not been disappointed in your desire.

Yet we have by no means been able to satisfy you in all things on this occasion, because from the first day of April of this year we have not been in our monastery; the reasons for this matter we have entrusted fully to Narcissus himself to report to you. For the understanding of our letter which we wrote in the previous year to Johannes Steinenmoelen, we have given Narcissus some entrance, from whom you will understand the foundation of the hidden matters for knowledge of which you are striving. The ternary must altogether be reduced to unity if the mind wishes to attain a perfect understanding of these matters. For the unit is not a number, and from it every number arises. Let the binary be rejected, and the ternary will be convertible to unity.

But, O Germanus, as Hermes says, without falsehood, certain, and most true by kinship with unity. Narcissus is not capable of all things. That which is above is like that which is below, and that which is below is like that which is above, because every number consists of units alone, to perpetuate the many wonders of one thing. Do not all things flow from one thing by the goodness of the one? And whatever is joined to unity cannot be diverse, but bears fruit by the simplicity and fittingness of the one. What is born from unity? Is it not the ternary? Understand: the unit is simple, the binary composite, but the ternary is reduced to the simplicity of unity. I am not Trithemius of a triple mind, but rejoicing in one mind in the ternary number, which truly brings forth a wonderful deed. Its father is the sun, its mother the moon. The wind carried the seed in its womb; the earth nourished it. This is the father of all perfection of the whole world. Its power is complete and immense. If it has been turned into earth, you will separate earth from fire, the dense from the subtle, and the ternary, now restored to itself, with skill and great sweetness will ascend from earth into heaven, and again by power and Familiar Letters

...to kindle with all one’s powers the observance of righteousness and the inward love of God. But this cannot be done otherwise than by the doctrine of Christ, because the holy Spirit of God does not pour in the gifts of his grace where he finds not the words of Christ but the folly of the Gentiles. We do not read that any of our people, from a discourse supported by testimonies of Gentile philosophers, received the grace of the Holy Spirit or ever felt the sighs of inward compunction. For the Spirit of God is accustomed to make fruitful his own seeds, not those of another; the Son of God confirms by the infusion of virtue his own words, not the empty babblings of Gentile philosophers.

O golden ages of the fathers of old, when the Spirit of the saints spoke through them his own words to the people, not words proper to them or alien ones; for then he bestowed his grace upon the minds of the hearers when he recognized in them his own things sown and cast forth, not those of the Gentiles. For the holy preachers, burning with the inspiration of the divine Spirit, spoke fiery words of God to the people with humble sincerity; and they, kindled by their ardor, were rendered willing and most steadfast for every observance of Christ’s commandments. At that time the words of the preachers, kindled by the grace of the Spirit, prepared the minds and hearts of the peoples aflame; and then the mercy of God worked many wonders among Christians, granting to both alike, that is, to preachers and hearers together, increases of all virtues. Sinners were suddenly converted to repentance; an incredible grace of compunction imbued the minds of the hearers; and the fervent and glowing love of God sweetly set all hearts on fire, and, inducing contempt for earthly things, armed them bravely for the endurance of every tribulation for the love of Christ.

For the discourse of all teachers then was Christian, simple, pure, and whole: not defiled by the opinion of the Gentiles, not [unclear] by a confused citation of [unclear], nor interrupted by fables and words provoking laughter, nor swollen with curious and useless quibbles, nor devised for the vain esteem of the preachers. It is fitting for you, Kymolanus, to be an imitator of these fathers, who, as lovers of true wisdom, sought in all things not their own glory but Christ’s, and the advantage of their hearers. Beware of becoming an imitator of those who do not preach Christ in a Christian manner, who seek either glory from men or the advantage of temporal property.

You have girded yourself for the true philosophy, which professes, preaches, loves, praises, and imitates Christ, the power and wisdom of God; in love of it you ought to remain faithfully, so that you may deserve to receive the fruit of everlasting blessedness. But those who imitate false wisdom cannot come to true wisdom. And what is false wisdom, except that which seems great to the lovers of this world? This is the wisdom of the world, with Gregory as divine witness: to cover the heart with machinations, to veil meaning with words, to show as true the things that are false, to demonstrate as false the things that are true. Those who know this wisdom despise the rest in pride; those who do not know it, being subject and fearful, admire it in others. It commands those who obey it to seek the heights of temporal goods, to rejoice once the vanity of temporal glory has been obtained, to repay evil for injuries, and to love the advantages of this life more vehemently.

But our wisdom, O Kymolanus, is to feign nothing for ostentation, to disclose meaning by words, to love true things as they are, to avoid false things, to offer good things freely, to endure evils more willingly than to do them, to seek no vengeance for injury, and to reckon insult for the truth as gain. The fear of the Lord, as Scripture says, is the beginning of wisdom. Blessed is the man who finds true wisdom, and to whom Christian prudence has flowed abundantly. Its acquisition is better than the trade in gold and silver. Its first and purest fruits [unclear], because it is more precious than all riches, and all things that are desired cannot be compared with it.

For true wisdom is that by whose splendors the mind, once illumined, both understands the truth which it loves and loves the good which it knows. Let us take an example of wisdom from the sun, so that we may be able to distinguish between knowledge and love. The sun does not warm all those to whom it gives light; and wisdom indeed teaches many what is to be done, yet it does not at once set all on fire so that they wish to fulfill in deed the good that they know. For just as it is one thing to know many riches, another to possess them, and knowledge does not make a man rich, but the possession of riches does, so to know many things and to understand wisely does not make a truly wise man if the display of works does not follow. For all our wisdom consists in this one thing: that we know God, and, worshiping him devoutly above all things, because he is the highest good, love him with all our powers. This is the philosophy of Christians, this the certain wisdom of the faithful, to which all other sciences are chiefly to be referred. This is consummate wisdom, which all the philosophers of the Gentiles sought throughout their whole life and were never able to find, comprehend, or hold, because they either retained a depraved religion or utterly abolished every religion. But whoever has deserved to obtain familiarity with this perfect wisdom is truly wise, and to him thereafter whatever of talent and labor Of Johannes Trithemius.

[unclear] he will gladly devote his labor; and, having scorned all public and private affairs, he turned himself to the study of this contemplation. For he thinks, and certainly is not mistaken, that it is far more excellent to investigate and know the reason of divine and human things than to cling to the piling up of perishable wealth or the accumulation of empty honors. Since these things are fragile and earthly, and pertain only to the cultivation of the body, no one can be made better by them. For wisdom is nothing other than truth, in which the highest, immutable good is held and discerned; it is in no place and is lacking to no one, because it is wholly everywhere. This alone is our reason for philosophizing: the desire for blessedness. But the true blessedness of our mind arises from knowledge of the Highest and love of truth.

Now therefore, O Kymolanus, let us seek true wisdom, which consists in the sole faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, once formed; without knowledge and love of him no one has ever become blessed, as the holy bishop Augustine says in a certain place. For whoever wishes to have salvation without the Savior, and thinks that he can become prudent without the true wisdom, which is Christ, will labor not as sound but as sick, not as wise but as foolish, in continual sickness; as a fool he will remain in the darkness of ignorance. For true wisdom Christ is the way, faith the guide of the journey, unstained humility the guardian, contempt for all earthly things the adornment and garment. Exhorting us to this, holy Christophilus says: “Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, that he may be wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly before God.” The wisdom of God is despised by those who glory in the wisdom of vanity.

A good Christian, a lover of God, a despiser of the world, an enemy of vices and cultivator of virtues, is truly wise, even if he knows none of the wisdom of the world; nothing is alien to him except what is inconsistent with virtue. Wherever he goes, he carries all his own things with him; the whole world is his possession, because he uses all of it as his own. He is not broken by fear, nor changed by power; he is not lifted up by prosperous things, nor cast down by sad ones. For where true wisdom is, there is strength of soul, there is constancy, there is fortitude. The wise man, founded in the love of Christ, is always the same: he is not diminished, as Ambrose says, nor increased by changes of circumstances; nor does he waver like a child, so as to be carried about by every wind of doctrine, but remains perfect in Christ, founded in charity, rooted in faith. Therefore the wise man knows no want of things, knows no changing passions of the soul, but shines like the sun of justice, without stain, before God and men.

But that we may become such men, O Kymolanus, we must labor with the greatest care, since there is no greater or more miserable care than to apply oneself to vain, earthly, and perishable things, which not only confer no good at all upon the soul, but rather afflict it with the greatest evil. Let us learn useful and necessary things, the knowledge of which promises blessedness; and let us not imitate those who do not know necessary things because they have learned superfluous ones. Farewell. From Cologne, on the 22nd day of July, in the year 1505.

XXVII. Johannes Trithemius to Johannes Cantherius Frisius, doctor of medicine, greeting.

Because all things are succeeding prosperously for you, as we truly rejoice with a friend, we admonish you above all in this: pass through temporal goods in such a way that you do not lose eternal ones. You have taken a wife; you have not sinned, but nevertheless you have sold your freedom. For married life and the freedom to philosophize cannot coexist in one man. For you write: “I have married a young wife, beautiful, noble, and of the very best conduct.” A rare bird is a woman beautiful, noble, and well conducted. And according to Euripides in the Medea: [unclear]. “Safety,” he says, “has been achieved through very great deeds, when a woman does not disagree with her husband.”

For beauty in women has often been accustomed to [unclear] pride, from which disagreement and rashness take their origin against the commands of men, as Menander says: [unclear]. “A beautiful woman is a proud thing.” And another certain man finely noted the troublesome rashness of women, saying: [unclear].

“Every woman is anger, yet she has good hours: one in the bedchamber, the other in death.”

That is, one when she sleeps, the other when she lies dead, because she harms no one, offends no one, and does not use abuse. Whence comes that saying of Menander: Familiar Letters

“[unclear Greek].”

“He says, ‘It is better to bury a woman than to take her as a wife.’ Since, then, it is very difficult to find a good wife, we greatly rejoice with you that you have found such a one, concerning whom you may persuade yourself of all the best things. It remains that, as Saint Christophilus says, those who have wives should be as though they had none, because the fashion of this world passes away, and nothing among mortals is lasting.

The evil things that happened around us in the commonwealth in the preceding year, no doubt as our sins required, we have thought it worthwhile to report to you briefly, as far as we can, insofar as they concern those known to you or your friends.
