In the year of the Christians just past, namely 1504, in the month of May, many princes of Germany, at the command of Maximilian our king, conspired against Philip, count palatine and duke of Bavaria, and elector of the Roman Empire, and waged very grievous wars against his commonwealth, both here in our region and in Bavaria. Between Worms and Kreuznach, and likewise on the other side of the Rhine, whatever was under the dominion of the Palatine outside cities and castles fell as plunder to the Hessians; respecting no one, they consumed with fire almost all the villages round about, together with their churches, many and very beautiful. The better courts or granges of our monastery also, and almost all of them, from which we had been accustomed to have all our substance, either perished or were utterly laid waste by the incursion of the Hessians. Because of this war we have suffered the greatest hardships, by which we have been driven almost to the final point of poverty.

That distinguished monastery of Limburg, in which you once fulfilled the office of teaching, was burned and utterly laid waste on the thirtieth day of August of the aforesaid year, by the setting of fire by the attendants of the count of Duroburg. For the fire lasted for twelve continuous days, the servants of Duroburg going out daily and always setting a new fire, so that nothing might remain. The church, with all its altars, bells, panels, and paintings, was completely burned. And, to embrace everything briefly, all the buildings, with all their structures, were reduced to ashes in that fire, and nothing at all remained except the stones. The abbot is here in Cologne; he is imploring the king’s aid against the count, but as yet he has obtained nothing. His monks, because of want, have been scattered from here and there to various monasteries.

Our Rogerius is still alive and well, and philosophizes in his own manner; his monastery remains intact, although it too has undergone many hardships. Many of the brothers of my monastery also, from the time when you were with us, have departed this life; some, too, driven by the want which the affliction mentioned above brought upon us, we have sent to other monasteries, so that few now remain in the place. Nor has the envy of impious men spared me; they persecute me for this reason, that I have necessarily adhered to the side of the Palatine prince and my defender. But the Lord Jesus, who knows all things before they come to pass, will himself be my helper, and I will not fear what man may do to me. Farewell, in good health. From Cologne, on the twenty-fourth day of the month of July, in the year 1505.

XXVIII.

To the reverend father in Christ, her lord and superior, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, Richmodis de Hoerst, humble handmaid of Christ, unworthy minister of the poor sisters serving God in Sebach, with continual prayers, prays eternal salvation.

[unclear] I hear that you, father always reverend to me in Christ, have the favor of many princes, and especially of the lord archbishop of Cologne, a thing I also knew long before; therefore, compelled by necessity, humbled [unclear] may you deign [to aid] your poor daughters, whom you were accustomed to feed with the milk of heavenly doctrine. For we are oppressed by the hard and unbearable yoke of the count, and by continual servitude, against justice, we are being reduced to the utmost poverty. Until now, twelve times a year only, and only at vintage time, we had been accustomed to send his father a cart with three horses for service; but now, at his command, he demands from us a cart with four horses for service twice or three times in almost any week, and this at our expense; indeed he violently compels our household, threatening prison and death. He does not distinguish day from day, nor does he observe reverence for any feast, but in the building of his castle of Duroburg near us, on feast days as well as on other days without distinction, both men and beasts of burden are worn out. For on the feast of the Lord’s Ascension, and also of Pentecost, of Trinity, of Corpus Christi, on Sundays, and on all other days whatsoever, he always has workers on the walls.

Of Johannes Trithemius.

walls. Your fatherhood knows our poverty, and that the temporal substance by which we might for any longer nourish so great a multitude of persons serving God, burdened with services to others, is very slender, and that provision has been made for us in no way sufficiently. Therefore, bending our knees to the ground, we all ask that, if it seems advisable to your fatherhood, you speak some good word on our behalf to the Archbishop of Cologne, and one conducive to our advantage, so that he may intervene for us with the Count and, by his intercession, see to it that so heavy a yoke of Pharaoh be removed from our necks, or at least mitigated somewhat. I send with the bearer of these letters the procuratorial document in my case, together with the brother, just as you instructed me. I beg you to be willing to arrange the rest in such a way that I am not entirely deprived of my paternal inheritance. Farewell happily. Given from Seebach, in the year 1505, on the 24th day of the month of July.

XXIX.

John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to Roger Sicamber, his sweetest brother.

On the 18th day of this month of July, in the morning at about the tenth hour, our most serene monarch Maximilian, King of the Romans, left Cologne with many princes, about to undertake an expedition against your Sicambrians. They all went down armed by ship along the Rhine, directing their line first toward Arnhem, the town of your Guelders, which the royal army had already for some time surrounded with a hard siege. The princes who had gone down in the ships with the King, together with their retainers, were these: Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, my prince-elector; Frederick the Margrave, his paternal uncle, who resides at Ansbach; Louis, firstborn son of Philip, Count Palatine and Duke of Bavaria, our prince-elector; Frederick, Duke of the Saxons, prince-elector; John his brother, Duke of Saxony; George, Duke of Saxony; likewise the Duke of Mecklenburg; the Duke of Brunswick; the Duke of Luneburg; the Duke of Julich; the Landgrave of Hesse; and many other princes, dukes, and counts, whose names I did not observe. When they came to Arnhem, the townspeople at once surrendered themselves to the King, and all the Sicambrians, struck by fear, swore submission to King Maximilian. But the Duke of Guelders himself also accepted the royal conditions, and peace was restored in the land to men after a long interruption. On the 28th day of July, however, the King, returning to Cologne together with the princes, entered in the same order and array in which he had gone out. On the following day all the bells throughout all Cologne were rung for many hours, for congratulation on peace and concord. These are the things that were done with your Sicambrians; I did not wish the sequence of them to be unknown to you. There are, however, very many who do not believe that the Sicambrians will keep their promises to the King, because the people readily despises oaths and is always too prompt for novelties. But between the Archbishop and the citizens of Cologne it is not yet certain that any agreement has been made, although it has been attempted several times. These are the things, Roger, which seemed to us to be written this time. We ourselves also shall very soon follow the letters themselves to Neometum. Farewell, and pray for us. From Cologne, on the 29th day of the month of July, in the year of Christians 1505.

XXX.

John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to Johannes Capellarius, mathematician, greetings.

My departures from Cologne are now already near at hand; therefore, if it is irksome to come to us, farewell. This morning my most serene prince Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, left Cologne, to return to his own territories through Westphalia and Saxony. I shall follow him after three days, when first certain letters and affairs concerning my person have been dispatched in the royal chancery. We ask, therefore, if it can be done, that before we leave here you visit us once more, so that we may bid one another farewell in brotherly charity, especially since we know not at all whether henceforth we shall ever see one another mutually in bodily sight. For I have been sworn into the March of Brandenburg, wholly uncertain about my return, chiefly for this reason: that, having been too gravely offended by the insults of serious rivals, I know that I could not easily be persuaded to return to Sponheim, although, if I wished, there would be very many at hand who would avenge these insults with signal vengeance. But I long ago persuaded myself that the Lord’s precepts must be obeyed and that injuries are not to be avenged; rather I shall imitate that saying spoken by the Lord Jesus to the apostles: “If they have persecuted you in one city, flee into another.” For we must have greater care for the soul than for the body, according to which we were made in the image of God. For Saint John the Bishop says: “If we neglect the soul, we shall not be able to save even the body.” For the soul is not [unclear]

Matt. 10.

More account must be taken of the soul than of the body.

of the body.

Familiar Letters

... for the body, but the body was made for the soul. Therefore he who neglects what is first, and takes up what is lower, corrupts both. But he who preserves the order, and cares for what is first, even if he neglects what is second, nevertheless through the salvation of the first the second also will be preserved. We must therefore take care that we have a soul sound, beautiful, and unharmed, rather than the body. Now in the face shines forth the appearance of beauty, from which we are accustomed to judge the whole person. But the face of the soul is conscience. Therefore, just as a beautiful face is pleasing in human sight, so a clean conscience is beautiful in the eyes of God. Sometimes a change of place benefits a person for the salvation of the soul, so that a face which did not please those who knew it through familiarity may in another place, by novelty, appear more beautiful. For often, when the place is changed, the disposition of the mind is also changed. And although no fault of my own moves me to change place, but rather another’s envy, still I yield somewhat to it; I am less attached to any particular place. For I know that one Lord reigns everywhere on earth, under whose command I shall serve wherever I shall be.

You praise our letter in friendly terms, which we sent to you almost twelve days ago; and wishing to adorn it with wondrous commendations, you asserted that it had come down from the oracle of Apollo. We understand that by a pagan word you wished to designate our Jesus, who alone with the Father and the Holy Spirit presides in the high heaven; his dignity is so immense, and his majesty incomprehensible, that nothing among all things can be compared with him. Beware henceforth, our friend Capellerius, we pray, lest you attribute to this highest and inaccessible majesty any other name than Christian religion is accustomed to give. For we think it very unworthy to attribute the polluted names of idols, which were not gods, to the highest God, and to address the divine substance with the most filthy terms of the gentiles. Nowhere will you find in the whole sequence of the Scriptures that the true God, whom we worship and adore, has taken for himself the names of false gods, or called himself Jove or Apollo, or anything else belonging to those vanities. We do not lack most honorable and most holy words in the sacred Scriptures, by which with sobriety we can designate in speech that unnameable and superdivine majesty. There is no need, nor is it permitted, nor is it fitting, to express among ourselves the true divinity of the creator of all things by the names of demons and the words for false gods. If we wrote correctly, if we sent a letter worthy of praise, the true God bestowed it, not Apollo; Jesus Christ gave it, and it came from nowhere else. Illumined by truth, we wrote true things, by which we desire to call your mind away from earthly, perishable, and transitory things, so that you may turn yourself to true philosophy, which most befits us Christians, through which alone we shall be able to arrive at the felicity of eternal blessedness, which is the highest good and the final end of the rational creature. For whatever we perceive in the world is corruptible; whatever we possess is transitory; the very body also by which we live is mortal; only our mind, by which we live, is immortal. For the bishop of Le Mans once said:

All mortal things hang beneath uncertain chance, And by their own instability promise flight. Whatever you have today may perhaps leave you tomorrow, Or even now, while you speak, ceases to be yours.

Matthew 24. Death is not evil.

Finally, we all die, as sacred Scripture bears witness, and we flow down like water into the earth, which does not return again. For there is one entrance for all into life, and a like departure. Therefore it is fitting that we always be mindful that it has been appointed for human beings to die once; and that death does not delay, but when it is least expected, then it stands at the doors. For this reason our Lord Jesus Christ, wishing us always to be prepared for death, commands in the holy Gospel, saying: Watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come. We must always live in that state in which we desire to die, because that death is not to be thought evil which a good life has preceded. For what follows death does not make death evil; rather, the evil life which preceded death itself makes it evil. And so we, who otherwise must die by necessity, should not be greatly concerned with what happens to bring about our death, but before all else this should rather be our concern: that life be so ordered, adorned in good works with the adornment of virtues, that it does not allow death to be evil. Yet death cannot be evil, since it is nothing other than the abandonment of the body, the laying down of a heavy burden, and the road from toil to rest. But he who has lived well, rooted in the love of the Lord, will never be able to die badly, even if people have judged otherwise of him.

Now death is threefold: namely, that of nature, about which Saint [Christophilus?] said: It is appointed for human beings to die once. And this death is not to be feared by the brave, but rather to be desired by those wise in the philosophy of Christ, and to be awaited by the wretched. About it this was excellently said: Johannes Trithemius.

[unclear] excellent [things]. But for others there is sadness, whose whole concern is now in pleasure. For we shall escape immortal. For death, as all philosophers affirm, is nothing other than the end of all these evils.

The second is the death of guilt, of which it is written: “The soul that has sinned, it shall die.” And again: “The death of sinners is very evil,” whose birth also is evil, and a worse life has followed. This death, O [unclear], let us fear, which not only kills the body but sends the soul into eternal pains.

The third, however, is the death of saving grace, which brings about the death of worldly pleasures, in which not nature but sins die. This is the saving death by which, baptized in Christ, we are reborn, and with him himself are graciously buried in the Lord. Therefore the first death is to be despised by all the wise; the second is to be detested by everyone; the third is most greatly to be desired by all Christians.

Those, then, are wretched and rightly to be lamented, who die by the second death, whom hell receives from this life to be tortured forever, not those whom the heavenly court receives to be made glad forever. For precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints. And truly precious: through it the desired end of labors will be present, the preservation of victory is granted, the gate of life is opened, and entrance into perfect security is conceded.

The quality of death depends on the merit of life, just as life itself is good if it is lived virtuously, evil if with crime; so death must be weighed from the acts of the preceding life. Thus it happens that if life has been spent in the love of God and the knowledge of truth, death cannot be evil, because it is a transfer to immortality. If the other life has existed, death must necessarily be evil, since it sends one to eternal punishments. Death is to be feared by all who, not walking wisely in the law of the Lord, have preferred earthly things to heavenly, perishable things to eternal.

O wretched we, O unhappy, what must we necessarily do, being about to die, we who especially dread common death because, conscious of our evils, we dread the sentence of the judge whom we have offended? For it is necessary for all who lead life on earth to die. But now, O you [unclear], at last thinking that we are already about to die, let us amend our life, fearing death in such a way that before it comes we may die to sins. For we shall not fear the death of the flesh if, our vices having been mortified, we have lived in the love of God through works of holy piety. Who indeed should fear temporal death, to whom eternal life is promised for the merit of justice?

Yet we must never forget that our death is pressing life toward its end, since he who daily remembers himself [unclear] from his labors. Let us beware, friend, lest we die worse than we were born, and lest, with [unclear] sins, [unclear], we depart from the world, we who entered it without actual sin.

Familiar Letters

as though not perceiving it, they are carried with the ship to the destination to which it had to sail; so also we, O Philobius, whether waking or sleeping, whether lying down or, indeed, willing it, are carried each day, through every single moment of time, toward our end, without thinking of it. We promise ourselves empty hopes, full of deception, when we think that we shall live for very many years, though we must nevertheless necessarily die at some time. For what if we have lived for a long time? Shall we therefore not die? Between him who has lived thirty years and him who has lived a hundred, after the same unavoidable end of living, death, has arrived, tell me, O Philobius, whose condition do you think is the better? Both were born, both lived, though not for equal years, both died. Have you not read the senarius of Menander, who says: [unclear] For he whom God loves dies young.

“Happy is the death of men,” says Boethius, “which neither inserts itself in sweet years, and, often called, comes in sorrowful ones.”

There are two things that frequently make death in old men unhappier than the passing of the young. One is that the dying old man sets out with a heavier burden of sins; the young man, however, could sin so much less, in proportion as he lived for a shorter time. For, as Seneca says, we make life restless for ourselves through fear of death; so great is human madness that by a certain fear of death men are driven to death. Therefore it makes no difference at what time we die, but we must take the greatest care that it befall us to die well. And we shall die well if we have lived well, walking not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. For the holy Apostle says: [unclear] Let us walk in the spirit; let us not fulfill the desires of the flesh.

Wherefore let us abandon all things that are in the world, seeking nothing more than what is necessary for the sustaining of the body, and even that itself scarcely, as the last thing, so that, free and unencumbered, we may be able to await our end, which threatens daily. For we grow old in silent years; even as we grow, life little by little decreases. We have lost infancy, then [unclear], then adolescence also passed away. Youth too has swiftly gone by; whatever time of our life passes has wholly perished and cannot be recalled. Of the time that remains there is no certainty, nor any moment of standing still; indeed, we divide with death this very day which we are spending. Why, then, do men, since they do not fail to know that they are mortal, devote themselves so greatly to gathering perishable riches, which they know they cannot carry away with them when they die? Nature can be content with few things, because, loving the middle, it shudders at extremes, as Palladas said very beautifully and prudently in a Greek poem: [unclear] For moderation is the best thing, since heights are apt to bring on dangers, while extremes contain insult.

Let us therefore tear our minds away from all desires of the world; let us abandon the way of perdition and fraud, so that, the more we now see, as the years incline toward old age, that day drawing near on which one must necessarily depart from this life, the more we may consider how pure we may depart, how innocent we may come to judgment. Nor should we imitate those who, accustomed to crimes, when the powers of the body are now failing and they ought to have remembered that they are about to pass from here, plunge themselves into heavier sins, so that those who in youth had been wanton may now in old age not undeservedly be called mad. Let each person shake off from himself every bond of the world, the flesh, and the devil, while it is permitted him, while there is opportunity, and turn himself to God with his whole mind, so that he may be able to await securely that day on which he will put off the present life and assume another. Before old age let him take care to live well; in old age, to die well. Farewell, always anxious about the end. From Cologne, on the thirty-first day of the month of July, in the year 1505.

XXXI.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Roger Sycambrius: greetings.

I wish you to know, dearest Roger, that the most serene prince Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, has obtained by his prayers from our most illustrious prince Philip, Count Palatine, with my consent, that I should follow him into the March and remain there for some time. For during four years, having a desire for us, he has very frequently solicited me by letters and messengers, wishing to have me with him in his realm for a while. For the prince is a young man, in the twenty-second year of his age, competently instructed in letters, very strong in intellect, and has the greatest affection for the study of letters. Until now, however, it could not conveniently happen that I should absent myself for so long a time from my monastery; but now the envy of rivals has given a cause by which I can absent myself no less cheerfully than willingly for any length of time...

Familiar Letters

...which, since we often live according to the flesh, may seem contrary. But woe to our prior, swollen with such a vice of ambition; his progress will never be good in the abbacy into which his entrance was perverse. Let him think what he will with his Cynonoti; I cannot but favor the party of the most merciful prince Philip, Count Palatine. For he is a lover of all learned men, gracious, gentle, and always generous to all. By his virtue I could easily ward off the injuries of the Cynonoti, if I did not fear him who said: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.” Rather, I shall give place to wrath for a time, until either the rash men repent of their injuries, or we deliberate in due time what it is useful for us to do. For for every business there is a time and an opportunity. And many things that cannot be overcome by strength are conquered by time. As Plato also says:

[Greek verse unclear.]

Time bears all things; long time knows how to change name, and form, and nature, and fortune.

But Sophocles the comic poet also said most truly in the Ajax:

[Greek verse unclear.]

All things grow slack in a long time and are consumed; it brings hidden things into the light and hides manifest things. The day casts down and again raises up all human things.

If the almighty has willed that I be struck by adversity, who am I to contradict him? Or how great am I, that with his help I should not bear it patiently? I myself am prepared, the Lord Jesus knows, and I am not troubled: for the glory of his name, also for my sins, and for love of the heavenly kingdom, not only willingly to give up the abbacy and all favor of this world, but even to subject myself to utter poverty and devote myself to beggary. I have endured undeserved injuries and insults from the prince of the Cynonoti; although I could turn them back upon his own head, I preferred to embrace patience rather than stir up vengeance against the will of God. There is a God in heaven who sees the injuries that I suffer without cause; I do not doubt that he himself will avenge them. For time will bring all things to light, as Menander says:

[Greek verse unclear.]

Time is the judge of merit among men. In time also all things are done and judged. Therefore no counsellor is more useful than time.

For nothing that has an end is long; and compared with eternity, all time is short. I know that I am mortal, and that I must necessarily die soon; and therefore, since one of the two must be, I prefer to suffer injuries rather than inflict them. For St. John Chrysostom says: Whatever we shall have suffered from any human being, either we shall receive remission of all sins, or, if there have not been such great offenses in us, we shall be honored with more splendid crowns.

For thirty years, in peace and tranquillity, I may say usefully, I have devoted myself to Christian philosophy. Day and night I have spent almost continuous study in reading writers, as is known to all who have known me; but how much I have profited, experience will now for the first time show. All the time that I studied has prepared for me the hour of temptation, which imposes the necessary voyage. I must test what sort of skilled sailor I have become, who for so many years have not spared the labors of learning. More than two thousand volumes, not common ones, nor only printed ones, but, as you know and as is evident, very ancient ones, and written by the pen, I have gathered with the greatest diligence and at very heavy expense into the library of Sponheim. In reading and most studiously turning them over for nearly twenty-three years, what I have profited, this time demands that I declare. For, as the wise man has long since usefully said, the learning of a man is discerned through patience. If therefore I come through such great adversities patient, I shall judge that I have learned enough. And indeed the spirit is ready, but the flesh is weak.

Therefore, dearest brother, with what charity I can toward you, I ask that you assist me with your prayers and diligently intercede for me with the mercy of the Almighty, so that through your prayers he may grant me constancy in adversities, may also grant pardon for my sins, and may make me willing to follow his will in all things. I have sent letters to the prior, by which I have summoned him to me at Neumagen; if you wish to write back anything, you can. Farewell, from Neumagen, on the thirteenth day of the month of August, in the year of Christians 1505.

XXXIII. Ger-

Familiar Letters

adorned with beauty it will return to the earth, and it receives the superior and inferior force, and will now be powerful and glorious in the brightness of unity, fit to produce every number, and all darkness will flee. The one is the pure beginning; the binary is composed by departing from unity, because it is impossible that there be two beginnings. Therefore only the ternary, [unclear], virtuous, and powerful, having overcome the binary, returns into its own beginning, not by nature, but by participation in likeness; in it, without contradiction, the mind understands all the mysteries of the beautifully ordered secret.

This is the most beautiful virtue of all strength, which conquers all worldly things and penetrates every solid body, dyeing each thing with desirable beauty, just as the alchemists indeed promise in composite bodies; but they err and deceive all by whom they have willingly been heard. They wish to imitate nature, and to make by art what belongs to the universal alone, since they do not understand the root of the virtue of nature. Do not assent to the most foolish alchemists, for they are fools and pupils of apes, enemies of nature and despisers of heavenly things, without whose intelligible kinship alchemy is nothing.

But he who does not understand earthly things, as our Lord Jesus Christ had said, how will he find heavenly things? Our philosophy is heavenly, not earthly: that by the gaze of the mind, through faith and knowledge, we may faithfully behold that highest principle which we call God, truly believing, purely knowing, and always adoring with the service and worship of most fervent love the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, one principle, one God, and one supreme good, existing eternally in a Trinity of persons, from whom are all things that can exist by any power. Unless the animated mind rises up to him, it will understand none of the things that are beautiful, but will waste away in its own ignorance.

This ascent, O Germanus, is not for common people, nor is it sufficient by imitating those who are borne upward on only one wing, but it is familiar to very few indeed, namely to those who have not rashly reduced themselves into unity. Many indeed try, but the ternary is not in the mind of all. Do we not, when about to look up at the sky, necessarily first lift the head, and lower it afterward when we have looked upward? It is permitted to the eyes alone to behold the sun. Ears do not see. Therefore, for the soul to climb up, let it become not an ear, but an eye and a heart; and from the ternary let it become unity by participation in goodness toward the beginning, because there is one omnipotent good, not two nor more. For unless unity comes to be, there will not be a conjunction of likeness in the mind, nor participation in the good, and without these there is no transcendence; and unless these precede, it will be able to attain neither the understanding of superior things nor the proper operation of inferior things.

Things, however, both universal and singular, necessarily, and the conditions of things, are in some cases manifest, in some most manifest. And some are hidden, others more hidden, others most hidden, both to sense and to reason. The nature of the things themselves produces this diversity. Hence it happens that certain men become wiser than the rest. He is called the wiser, however, who perceives things less perceptible. Number consists in order and measure. Order also cannot exist without number and measure. Measure, moreover, consists in number and order. Here unity and the ternary do not admit the binary, but, stripped of all multitude, they stand in the first principle by the simplest purity innate in them.

This is the way to the higher things, O Germanus, by which the ancient sages [unclear] intelligible [unclear] are now considered wise by our own wise men. Do you wish to hear more fully? Study begets knowledge; knowledge gives birth to love; love to likeness; likeness to communion; communion to virtue; virtue to dignity; dignity to power; and power makes a miracle. This is the one path to the end of magical perfections, both divine and natural, from which everything superstitious, deceptive, and diabolical is kept far away and confounded.

Indeed, by magic we wish nothing else to be understood than wisdom, that is, the understanding of physical and metaphysical things, which consists in the science of divine and natural virtues. You must know that a heavenly harmony, not material, but spiritual consonance, is to be perceived by us, where number, order, and measure come together through the ternary into unity; and to this consonance all our inferior things must be conformed. It is foolish to think that heavenly harmony forms a sound perceptible to the ears, caused by the motion of consonant stars. Heavenly harmony, however, is the inviolable consonance, in number, order, and measure, of the distributions of bodies. But it is necessary to go beyond this, so that through the ternary an ascent may be prepared to that harmony which is supercelestial, where there is nothing material, but all things are spiritual. From there the likeness must be assumed by the mind, whence it came. For stellar harmony neither gave the mind nor flows into it.

A certain Philocryphus used to speak thus: Whoever [unclear] the condition of heavenly harmony ...if he had it known, he would know both past and future. But who will be given me, one out of thousands, who understands this heavenly harmony? The mind was born for the supercelestial realm, in whose likeness it lives. The stars understand nothing, nor indeed do they feel; whence they neither confer wisdom upon our mind nor have any dominion over us, who walk in the spirit, confessing the Lord Jesus Christ, who has all things in his power, to whose likeness we must faithfully conform ourselves as far as we can. For he is the wisdom of God the Father; he is the fountain and origin of knowledge; he is the center of the soul, through whom all things were made. Let rash men go away, vain men and lying astrologers, deceivers of minds and babblers of trifles. For the disposition of the stars contributes nothing to the immortal mind, nothing to natural knowledge, nothing to supercelestial wisdom; but body has dominion only over its own body. The mind is free, and is not subjected to the stars, nor does it receive their influences, nor follow their motion, but communicates only with the supercelestial principle by which it was both made and made fruitful. The rest that had to be answered to your inquiries, O Germanus, we have enclosed in a more sacred chest, to be presented through Narcissus to you alone; and to him we have entrusted also the key to be brought to you, who do not know enough, lest you possess a chest full of secrets without profit. But we have not been able to come to you in person this time, since we have been called elsewhere. Nevertheless you will learn more fully from Narcissus our intention, how and when an opportunity may come to us of coming to you. In other letters we have written everything that seemed to us ought to be written to you. Farewell, mindful of us and not forgetful of yourself. From Neumagen in the city of Speyer, on the 24th day of August, in the year of Christ 1505.

XXXV. Wolfgang Hopilius to Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim: greeting.

Recently, my Trithemius, I received from you a most elegant letter, which was pleasant to us and brought admiration to my mind: that you yourself, a most learned man and altogether more excellent than I, did not disdain to write to me, a country ant living a rustic life, and by that token wished to declare the affection of your mind toward our uncultivated talent. But whence this has happened I think I know by conjecture. Our Narcissus, a most diligent investigator of all good sciences, perhaps reported to you about us things like dreams and phantasms, indeed greater than our smallness can furnish; and you give credence to his words, for those who have an honest mind and kindly disposition easily believe whatever good they hear about others, but believe evil slowly. You were moved, as far as I can conjecture, to share with me your most ornate letter. I give immortal thanks, as one who greatly values the letters of so great a man. For whatever in human affairs can be known, I know is not hidden from you, since today you easily surpass and excel all mortals in talent, knowledge, and literary experience, as your writings and the testimonies of the most approved men make clearer than light. Hence you embrace all singularly learned men; indeed, even those whom report has brought to your notice as skilled in anything, and if they are men inferior in praises, by your inborn goodness toward you [unclear] you magnify and esteem very highly. The remaining secrets of our breast you will understand from our Narcissus, our common friend, who has inscribed your immortal name upon marble breasts. Him I commend to you very greatly, although there is no need; and I should like you to persuade him to beware of the dangers of Arisleus and Alehindi, of whom the one ended his life most wretchedly, while the other fell into madness, as you easily know from their little works. Farewell, and love us. From our Parisian workshop, on the 3rd day before the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord 1505.

XXXVI. Johannes Trithemius of Spanheim to Wolfgang Hopilius, citizen of Paris: greeting.

Our Narcissus, coming to me at Neumagen on the 15th day of the month of August, delivered your letter to me [unclear], and explained the rest entrusted to him by you. You wonder that I judged you worthy of my letter, thinking that I had been too credulous toward Narcissus, as though I had not known you before he came to me. For how great you are I had already learned from the report of many. But you do well by imitating the counsel of the wise man who says: The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and before God you will find grace, since the great power is of God alone, and he is honored by men. Likewise the very power and wisdom of God, the man Christ Jesus, said in the holy Gospel: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. Our heavenly fatherland is lofty, Familiar Letters

...to which we all hasten; but Christ Jesus is the humble way by which one goes into heaven. Therefore whoever desires to ascend the lofty mountain of eternal happiness must not neglect the way of humility. And so, however much in this world we have advanced either by learning or by living well, we ought to think more about what is lacking in us than about what is present in us. For we know more things not than we have learned, and we have neglected more than we have done good things.

Considering this faithfully, blessed Augustine said in a certain passage: “More praiseworthy is the mind to which its own weakness is known than one which, without regard to that, would examine the walls of the world, the paths of the stars, the foundations of the earth, and the heights of the heavens.” And holy Jerome, in a certain letter: “This,” he says, “is the sole perfection in all things: the true knowledge of one’s own imperfection, because a great ascent to God is the judgment of one’s own weakness.” The sacred virtue humility is the foundation and guardian of all virtues.

Let all the proud therefore blush, who grant a place to pride in their hearts, since they know that only through humility is there a path of the mind into heaven. Let those who reckon themselves great among the wise men of this world hear that Socrates first obtained the palm of wisdom from Apollo when, after the studies of many years, he at last professed that he knew this: that he did not know. For we are called Christians in vain if we have not followed Christ, who for this reason called himself the way in the Gospel, so that the conduct of the master might become the disciple’s rule of living, and the Christian might imitate that humility which Christ always displayed.

Humility is the stable foundation of the virtues; if it is omitted, what will the gathering of the other virtues be called except a kind of ruin? For the first thing for a man pursuing wisdom is to consider what he himself is, what is within him, what is outside; likewise what is above him, what is against him, what is before him, what is after him. This contemplation bears a fourfold fruit: low esteem of oneself, charity toward one’s neighbor, contempt of the world, love of God. And this is the way to true wisdom, since without humility all human learning is useless, and with pride it is altogether contemptible.

Therefore pride must above all be guarded against by all who strive toward wisdom through the study of the Scriptures, since just as no wise man is proud, so one who is proud will never arrive at wisdom. For pride is the beginning of every sin among angels and among men. Envy does not produce pride, but rather pride makes envy. For only love of excellence envies. But love of excellence is called pride; since it is an evil in men, it does not please God, as sacred Scripture says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” Therefore we must fear lest, growing proud, we fall, with God permitting it, even on a slight occasion, as Sophocles says:

“[unclear] “[unclear] “Rather, a man ought, even if his body has a great nature, “To think that he can fall, and that from a small evil.”

And Phocylides gave a fine warning against pride, saying:

“[unclear] “[unclear] “Do not be lifted up by wisdom, nor by strength, nor by riches; “One God is wise, powerful likewise, and [unclear].”

The other vices have force only in evil works, but pride must especially be guarded against in good works. Since pride is hateful before God and men, you do rightly, my friend, by humbling yourself before both, so that you may obtain grace.

Narcissus, too curious in investigating rather hidden matters, I have urged, both now and often before, to abandon vain studies; dreaming of some great thing or other, he promises himself that mountains of gold will shortly arise for him. Let us allow him to go on, blind, along the road he has begun, until he understands that he has been cheated of his desire, just as all the others before him who labored under the same foolishness. He has begun to waver somewhat on hearing from us of the danger and difficulty of those matters which he pursues without a teacher. But from him you will receive the answer to your petitions. Farewell in health. From Neumagen, 24 August, in the year 1505.

XXXVII.

Libanius Gallus to Johannes Trithemius, most worthy abbot of the monastery of Sponheim, greetings.

I have no rest of mind, O Father Trithemius, until we overcome this hour, I would not say of evils, but of trial. We were born for labor, by doing labor and at the same time by suffering it, since this is altogether necessary and advantageous for us. Do not fear this envy of men against you, for in a short time he will give your affairs a better lot. For love of him, endure patiently, who for...

Johannes Trithemius 475 who died for you on the cross, do not be saddened, but silently, with tranquil mind, follow the counsel of God, since you are called [unclear] of others. Keep your purpose, and care neither for riches nor for the most empty honors of the world. Think of the end toward which we are tending; love the beginning from which we are. I beg you, recognize Trithemius as thrice great in the sharpness of his mind: a Christian by imitating Christ, a monk by despising the world, and a philosopher by not admitting disturbance; when you have become great, in the love of Christ you will at last come forth blessed. Know that Saturn, since he is not moving quite prosperously enough for you, as I had also foretold when I was present with you in your monastery, is to be avoided a little. By Mars indeed and Mercury, in a short time, believe me, you will be relieved with a good though humble condition. For neither God will abandon you, O Trithemius, nor Libanius. Hear the counsel of him whom it is not permitted to despise. Give place to envy; better things are being prepared for you. After fifteen moons, follow when called, and not before. Go now when called by the great [philoctyphus?], with heaven opened, to return; then you will see either me or my messenger at Neometum. But take care lest Saturn behold the books that are witnesses of secrets. Be ready for the journey; forget nothing of those things which are useful for our affairs. Keep the [anacrisis?] in silence, and do not release the dove before the time. Lift up your head and do not turn aside. Leave the lying Phoenicians, so that he may understand too late what is good. Beware, O Trithemius, lest you bring the rays of the sun into caves, since the dragons are destructive. Do not hide the higher air in the earth except once. Do not offer your bread to oxen and goats, nor send out the spirit through the lesser doors. Be one with yourself, and beware lest [you be] alone. Flee every multitude, because one is all things, and without one there is nothing. Do not lead a blind man by the hand, but only with a staff. Do not mix water with wine, nor let there be double bread on your table. Do not feed birds in the sun but in the shade, and do not show glass or a mirror at all to dogs, because it is dangerous. Do not strike the shadow, since it is an injury to the sun. Use ants, if perhaps you take pleasure in catching birds. Divide light in water, lest, when frozen, it creak. Be more even in soul, and do not fail, O Trithemius, because if no one else is willing to have care for you, certainly Libanius will. We have kings and powerful men as friends, who will most gladly favor you even by name alone. The Almighty permits nothing without cause, and one must not despair of the mercy of the highest goodness. I know that you fear God, and, raised up by sharpness of mind, neither care for the prosperous things of the world nor fear adverse ones. Therefore, having found such a disciple in you, I have gladly communicated to you all that is mine. Only remain faithful; in the one thing alone, which you lawfully can, be a Pythagorean. Farewell, more than my other self, in him who alone always is. From Saint-Quentin, the sixth day of the month of June, in the year 1505.

XXXVIII.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to his Libanius, his only teacher, greetings.

I received, read, and understood your most sweet letter, best of teachers, on the fourteenth day of the month of July at Cologne Agrippina, where an assembly of the princes of Germany was being held, with our king present. I shall follow the counsel that you gave, although there will be a very serious muttering among our men, whose tongue will rage against me. Melantius, with his people, stirred up the whole evil against us; we do not doubt that he will fall into the pit which he prepared. Our Astrophilus advised us the same things in your words, nor did he indeed depart in one point from your opinion. The prince, the Margrave, summoned me to Cologne, and prevailed upon me to go with him, to remain for a time in the March. I shall keep not only your precepts, but also your counsels themselves, to the best of my strength. I have withdrawn hay from the oxen and goats, and I have a great war with the apes, but thus far I have come out the victor. Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, a prince worthy of eternal memory, a young man of twenty-one years, skilled in the Latin language, and a most zealous lover of true wisdom, burns with a great desire for you. O, if it could ever come about that he might deserve to see and address you in person. He is a most humane prince, and one who not only does not blush to learn, but also very greatly desires it. I would like you to write to him as soon as possible, taking the subject from us, and send something from the workshop of Pelagius. Thus I would wish you to act: insofar as whichever of us two departs first, let the one who remains be heir of his other self. By your consolations my mind has been made stronger, and it gladly inclines to you in the return that it owes. Pray with me, I beg, to God, that he may grant us what we wish, and what we ought especially to wish.

I write to a wise priest beloved of God, who can help us with prayers and vows, having obtained the grace of the one highest good, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit, of the beginning from which [one] slips into multitude and is re-formed to him by unity. Would that, O most faithful after God of all teachers, even now at last it could come about that Familiar Letters

...we have often desired, that it might be permitted us to imitate true and holy wise men, who, through abstraction, truly united [unclear] to themselves, with the most ardent desire of love, held the path of salvation toward God. What have we to do with the world, since we are soon to depart from here? Behold what reward the lovers of the world have given me, because, as a prelate of monks, I could not serve God without the world. Never, as you know, have I sought anything worldly; I have loved nothing earthly; I have fled and despised all the pleasures of the world; I have suffered persecution from men undeservedly, without demerit, without cause, without fault. But almighty God, whom alone I desire to please, has permitted this tribulation upon me neither unjustly nor without cause; and I give thanks to his goodness, because in truth I have recognized that this injury of my rivals against me is of no little profit to me. I accept what is mine with patience, insofar as the Lord Jesus grants it. Those who inflicted insult before men upon one who did not deserve it may see with what zeal they were led to inflict it. I am not moved by the injury done to me, while I seem [unclear], but with tranquillity of mind I can say: A mind conscious of right despises the falsehoods of fame, knowing as true what they, credulous, have disturbed into blame. Have no doubt about me, most loving teacher: I shall do, according to my strength, what befits a lover and disciple of Christ, and with a tranquil mind I shall bear the things he has set before us to be borne. Why should I not bear patiently, who am a Christian monk, not ignorant of the great reward? Pray for me, and farewell. I wrote this from the city of Neumagen on the twentieth day of the month of August; I arranged for it to be presented to you, by Narcissus the physician, at Paris in the house of Carolus Bovillus, theologian, born at Saint-Quentin, whom you know, our friend; nor do I doubt that it will be faithfully delivered to you. Farewell again. In the year of Christ 1505.

XXXIX.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Carolus Bovillus of Saint-Quentin, theologian at Paris, greetings.

I was surprised, Carolus Bovillus, at Narcissus, the bearer of this letter, because he departed from us for Paris without your knowledge, since I wished to have letters from you. Yet he reported that you are well; from him you will hear the state of our affairs, and what we have in mind concerning these things. We remind you of your promise made last year, when you were with us in our monastery of Sponheim for fourteen days: that you should complete as soon as possible those very profound questions of sacred Scripture, the headings of which we long ago set down at Sponheim, and transmit them to us, as you promised. For they will be for us an everlasting memorial of your name, a mutual testimony of affection. Everything you set forth in letters delights us greatly, because, after the manner of the ancient doctors, you are a solid, lucid expounder of truth, neither excessive through multiplication of words nor cut short by deficiency in matters that are necessary. The things you wrote about the intellect greatly pleased me. For they contain the true theology of Christians, pure and complete, which confers knowledge on the mind and desire for the highest good on the affection, existing in itself pure, whole, bright, without the scars of external traditions. Never has the curiosity of certain men pleased me, who mingle human things with divine, and defile sacred Scripture, which is pure and sufficient for us in itself, with the loquacity of the Gentiles. Against these blessed Jerome speaks in a letter to Pope Damasus: One disputing from the Scriptures ought not to seek out the arguments of Aristotle; nor should a little stream be drawn from the river of Tullian eloquence; nor should ears be soothed by the little flowers of Quintilian in a scholastic declamation. Rather, a discourse of plain, everyday likeness is necessary, redolent of no lucubration, which explains the matter, sets forth the sense, and makes obscure things manifest. For the Scripture of God is manifest; the testimony of God is lucid, granting wisdom to little ones. The divine letters do not need folds, nor enfoldings, nor refoldings, because these do not grant wisdom to little ones, but leave their minds in confusion and compel them, striving through their whole life, to wander from men. Not those who fold, not those who refold, but those who explain and elucidate me, says sacred Scripture, will have eternal life. Farewell. From Neumagen, on the twenty-second day of the month of August, in the year of Christians 1505.

XL.

Johannes Trithemius, to the sisters beloved in Christ, Richmodis the abbess, and the whole convent of the monastery of St. Lawrence in Seebach, greetings.

On the day after tomorrow, as by divine mercy we are to take our way toward the Mark, we judged it necessary and opportune, before we departed from Neumagen, to write to you, O dearest daughters in Christ, Johannes Trithemius.

[it was] fitting, so that you might have consolation from us, and we from you the support of prayers to God. Therefore we exhort you in the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom you have been betrothed, that according to the rule of the cenobitic institution you should always walk worthily, having your conduct in the monastery pure, holy, and immaculate, as befits virgins consecrated to the heavenly king. Keep your minds always occupied, as far as possible, in the law of the Lord, applying yourselves with the sweetness of divine love to the readings of the divine Scriptures, so that while you are working with your hands you may never lack material for holy meditations.

All the delights of this world are forbidden to us; and it is clear that you too renounced them of your own free will, when at the beginning of your profession each one of you sang out in a clear voice: “The kingdom of the world and all the adornment of the age I have despised for the love of my Lord Jesus Christ, whom I have seen through the most certain hope of faith, whom I have loved, in whom I have believed, whom I have cherished.” It is not permitted to you to seek again what once, for love of Christ, you despised; rather you must persevere in contempt of worldly things until death, as our Savior himself says in the holy Gospel: “He who has persevered to the end, he shall be saved.” Therefore, having once despised the world and whatever is beautiful and lovable in it for the love of God, it is not fitting for you to love it any more, unless you wish, with the foolish virgins, to receive rejection from the bridal chamber of the bridegroom and, with the apostate spirits, eternal damnation.

Remember, dearest daughters in the Lord, to whom you have promised faith, and live in such purity of mind and body that, through the good display of works, continually fervent in desire for divine love, after the end of this life you may be able to come to him. Do not wish to love the world, as Saint John says, nor the things that are in the world. For if anyone loves the world, the charity of God the Father is not in him. But the world passes away, and all its concupiscence; he who does the will of God remains forever. Know this, however, [unclear], that the love of God and of the world cannot dwell together in one heart, just as the eye by no means looks at heaven and earth equally at the same time.

This world is rightly compared to the sea, because it is exceedingly bitter with falsehoods, restless with various temptations and adversities, everywhere full of the creeping things of vices. This great sea, dangerous to mortals, you, O daughters, have escaped by fleeing to the monastery through the mercy of God; and by loving God in purity of heart [unclear], you renounced that very sea of the age at the beginning of your profession. Each one of you must take the greatest care not to entangle her mind in the vanities of the age, because it is of no profit to have fled the world in body if the heart is still occupied in love of it. You escaped the world in body for this reason: lest any occasion should bind the mind into love of it. For a person’s own desire is like a tempest of the sea; if by sinning he consents to it, whether he is in a monastery or outside, he is worldly and is overwhelmed by the waves of the sea. If by loving God you resist the desires of the world, you walk above the sea and come to salvation. But if you have walked after your desires, the tempest of the sea will without doubt swallow you up. For the world is accustomed to sink its lovers into the depth of hell, not to carry them; no one ever trusted the world and was not deceived.

Therefore the world must be despised by us, O virgins of Christ; nothing at all must be loved: not riches, not honors, not joys, not pleasures, not conversations with people, not greetings, not little gifts, not praises, not the comforts of the flesh, not any ornament in clothing. Your riches are the love of God and the testimony of a pure conscience; to acquire and preserve these you must always keep watch with every zeal. Nor is it fitting for you, betrothed to the Son of God and attendants of the Virgin Mary, his undefiled mother, to have any care at all for the world and perishable things, but at all times you ought to provide for this alone: that you may be able to please him to whom you have offered yourselves as a holocaust.

Your honors, however, are fasting, abstinence, tears of compunction, and avoiding the sight of all secular outsiders, detesting conversations, spurning greetings, despising little gifts and familiar letters, loving nothing worldly at all. The joys and pleasures of nuns are to apply themselves to the readings of the divine Scriptures, to occupy themselves with holy meditations, to be always intent on prayer, to mortify the flesh, to adorn the mind with virtues, and to spend no time unfruitfully. The adornment of cloistered virgins is humility and purity of heart; without these no one has ever pleased God. For Christ Jesus, the Son of almighty God, justifier of faithful souls, is your bridegroom; to him you have bound yourselves, mind and body, to serve faithfully in perpetual purity. He requires in you your adornment: not of the flesh but of the heart, not of the body but of the mind, not of garments but of virtues, not of outward beauty but of inward purity. Adorn yourselves for him, O virgins, not for the world; strive to please him, not human beings. Whenever a virgin nun adorns herself with more elaborate garments in order to please human beings in their eyes, to Christ Jesus, to whom she is betrothed, 478 Familiar Letters

...does an insult. For your adornment, bride of Christ, is to flee men and, as we have said, to turn away from conversations at the window. For St. Ambrose says: In a virgin, let modesty everywhere be the companion of each virtue; it ought to be inseparable from virginity, so that [unclear] may be kept away and virginal honor preserved. Let a virgin's speech be prudent, modest, rare, not so much prized for eloquence as for shamefastness. Let all admire, when the virgin is silent, her bashfulness; when she speaks, her prudence; and in her conduct let them proclaim the discipline of a most religious life. Let your heart, O bride of Christ, monastic virgin, be pure from every stain of worldly desire; let it be clean from every spot of disordered affection, so that it think of nothing in this life except Jesus and love nothing except his sweetness. Let the sweet name of Jesus resound in your mouth whenever it must be spoken; let your whole mind sigh continually in his love; let no consolation be sought in this world except Jesus; let constant remembrance of Jesus be kept in the virgin's heart. For this above all befits Christ's bride: in love of him to keep her heart constantly occupied nowhere else, so that, truly burning in remembrance of him, she may be able to say: I languish with love, not worldly but heavenly, not carnal but spiritual, not for any mortal man but for Jesus Christ, the eternal King, who is judge of all the living and the dead, of whom the holy martyr Ignatius said in a certain letter: My love has been crucified. And let the monastic virgin, knowing that her love is the Lord Jesus Christ, and that he was piteously crucified for all of us, be always engaged in the exercise of his most bitter passion by reading, meditating, and suffering with him; and let her pass no day on which she does not at least once recall the labors endured for her by so great a loving bridegroom. For she is not a true lover of Christ who does not occupy her mind, even to tears, in meditating on his most bitter passion, but rather, given over to the laughter and frivolities of the world, forgets her most sacred lord and bridegroom. How, indeed, you ought to exercise yourselves usefully in remembrance of the Lord's passion, you have long since heard from us in many sermons. For the continual remembrance of Christ's benefits toward us is the greatest exercise of devotion and the most fruitful exercise of spiritual progress. Therefore, in order that you may be able to please him alone to whom you have devoted yourselves, all things that are transitory must be despised by you for love of him, because you cannot serve God and attend to the vanities of the world. Pray for me, sweetest daughters in Christ, that the Almighty may bring me back unharmed and keep me everywhere in his most holy will. About to give place to those who wrong me, I go into a far country, uncertain of the day of my return. Farewell in Christ.

From Speyer, on the 26th day of the month of August, in the Christian year 1505.

XLI.

John Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. Martin in Spanheim, to the prior of the community and to his sons in Christ, his most beloved brothers, with most loving [charity?].

When on the twenty-seventh day of the month of August we were leaving [Neometum?], about to enter this March of Brandenburg, it had been our intention to hasten our return before the feast of St. Martin, and to betake ourselves to [unclear], to the most serene prince, until the rashness of our rivals against us should be brought to its proper end. But when we came to Berlin, the town of the most illustrious margrave's continual residence, on the eleventh day of the month of September, we were received kindly by him and are also being treated generously. Since we ought not resist his will, we have agreed to remain with him until the feast of Easter, and indeed not without advantage to ourselves, as we trust.

But lest the necessary change of plan be hidden from you, or some unfavorable suspicion about us arise among you, we have decided to send to you Brother Theodoric, our chaplain, this bearer of the letters, so that, when he reports our situation, you may know everything. Concerning our return to my monastery of Spanheim, brothers, this [unclear]: I could ever, if I wished, pursue the advantages of my own interest. There are not a few kings and princes known to me who are sympathetic; by their favor I could, if I wished, not only avenge the wrongs done to me, but also find sufficient provision for my state. But for love of him who endured death on the cross for us, I wish neither to avenge the insults done to me nor to abandon you, unless perhaps [I am] first abandoned by you. But if this happens, you will find that I have wandered so long through uncertainties not for my own sake, but rather for yours. Bring also your duke, hostile to me without fault on my part, back to acknowledgment of the truth, which rashly against us...

Johannes Trithemius

... if lying men have proceeded against us, instruct them; but if not, behold, I again declare to you that I shall not have him as lord who does not have me as prelate, nor shall I submit myself to the command of one who, armed with injustice and tyranny, does not wish to be subject to the justice of God. I have favored Palatine affairs. For this reason they have persecuted me without cause. What will my rivals do if I say, indeed, that I shall favor them as long as the breath of life remains in me? The lord defender of my monastery, as you know always a most gracious prince to us, Philip the Palatine, in those things that are not against the Lord of all, I shall never be able to disown. Permit to each man his right inviolate. Farewell, brothers; pray for me, placed in a foreign land. From Berlin, on the twentieth day of the month of October, in the year 1505.

XLII

To the most serene and unconquered prince, Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Bavaria, prince elector. Johannes Trithemius sends greeting.

Most serene prince, I am compelled to remain in the March longer than I had intended, detained by the command of the most excellent prince Joachim, Margrave, whose most holy will I ought not to oppose. For he pursues my smallness with much kindness; he has often pressed me with a great request, desiring that I not depart from here before the feast of Easter. At last, with this condition interposed, I consented to remain until Easter: that, when a messenger with letters has been sent to your Serenity, permission to remain may also be obtained from you by your excellence, as he requests. I thought your clemency should most humbly be asked that meanwhile you deign to have regard, in your piety, for the brothers and my monastery, lest the rashness of my rivals also burst forth against the sheep, which did not spare the shepherd. They have indeed persecuted me, innocent and without cause; they have hated me without reason. Therefore, with the consent of your serenity, I willingly withdrew for a time, so that a more useful plan may be prepared for me with delay. But, most serene prince, the rashness of my rivals is not hidden from you; you consider exactly whence they are moved against an innocent man. Nor is there need to describe to you the characters of men very well known to you, since they sufficiently showed their minds hostile to your affairs at that time when the enemies raged against your people; nor now, as they persecute me secretly under the appearance of good because of your blameless favor toward me, do they conceal them. But I shall overcome their insolence by patience; they themselves will at last waste away in their own envy. Farewell, magnificent prince. From Berlin, on the twentieth day of October, in the year 1505.

XLIII

Johannes Trithemius to Jakob Trithemius, his sweetest brother, sends greeting.

If you are well, it is indeed well. For we, by the mercy of God, are well. Intending to enter Neometum, on the twenty-seventh day of the month of August we departed from here with our household by carriage, while you were still staying in Cologne; on the eleventh day of the month of September we entered the town of the Margrave’s residence called Berlin. But the prince was then occupied in hunting, according to his old custom. On the next day a messenger was sent to him, to report that we had come. When he learned that I was present, he rejoiced, and asked the messenger why I had not brought you with me. We are now living in a foreign land indeed, but an excellent one, abundantly supplied with all things necessary for the body. The prince is munificent and most gracious to us; by his providence we have been most richly provided for in all things. We had resolved to return to the regions of the Rhine around the feast of Saint Martin, but the prince’s insistence changed our plan and brought us to the point that we consented to remain until Easter. Therefore we exhort you to betake yourself to the New Castle, to stay there with our faithful Johann Damius until we come. We do not wish you to wash a brick, to serve those lacking a brain, but rather we desire you to be occupied with the study of letters, especially divine letters, through the knowledge of which the mind rises up to the knowledge and love of the highest truth. Do not be ashamed to flee curiosity, and detest those [unclear] which are opposed to divine love. For there is a great difference between a curious man and a studious man. The curious man is eager for knowledge of those things which contribute nothing of honorable usefulness. But the studious man is eager for knowledge of those things whose cognition pertains, by honorable ordering, to nourishing and adorning the soul in a liberal way. We desire you to be studious, not curious, since, as Saint Bernard says, curiosity is the first step of pride, contrary to the grace of the Holy Spirit, whose teaching does not sharpen curiosity but kindles charity. Therefore Scripture says: Do not seek things higher than yourself; do not search into things stronger than yourself. Ecclesiasticus 2.

More curiously.

More studiously.

Ecclesiasticus 2. Familiar Letters

For if you have searched very much into them, you will often wonder. Necessary and useful things must be learned by us, the knowledge of which may illuminate the mind, separated from earthly things, into the knowledge of the highest truth, and may inflame it with love of everlasting goodness. It is foolish, while useful and necessary things have been omitted, to learn vain and useless things, and, with the Creator neglected, to occupy the mind with created things. Pernicious and plainly damnable is the curiosity of many men of this age, who, having despised the most salutary humility of Christ, in order that they may seem learned and great, most diligently investigate what Plato, what Aristotle, what Anaxagoras, what Democritus, what Pythagoras, and the rest of that kind thought, men who, it is agreed, were far removed from the knowledge and teaching of the highest truth, as though from among our own there were lacking philosophers and most learned men, by imitation of whom [unclear]. We have many better than the philosophy of the gentiles, whose teaching, as seems clear to us, we ought to imitate: namely the holy apostles of Christ, Peter, Paul, and John, and their followers, Origen, Athanasius, Hilary, Irenaeus, Chrysostom, Basil, Eusebius, Firmianus, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, Bede, Rabanus, Bernard, and the remaining teachers of the catholic faith, whose certain wisdom concerning truth instructs Christian minds unto justice, truly illumines the understanding, forms charity, and gives life to souls. Imitate these wise men according to your powers, and by reading and learning their books frequently turn over useful things; do not allow the times of youth given to you to pass uselessly. Flee idleness as a pernicious plague of the soul, since it is especially contrary to industry and study, and consumes the mind as rust consumes iron. One must occupy the talents with good study, and the desire for true wisdom must be implanted more deeply, so that when old age arrives, the mind, formed by heavenly teachings, may stand firm before any faces of fortune whatever. And we pray that you not be ashamed to imitate us, your brother, who, as you know, after the years of life have passed, have spent all our time on the study of the Scriptures, even to the envy of frogs. For if we had not done this, where now, brother, do you think we would be, with fortune stinking against us, except lying everywhere? For although we have come out only a little learned, nevertheless with God's help we have learned to stand firm in ourselves, to despise the various deceitful faces of fortune, and to understand what the end of ignorance is. No one will take from us what is ours, since we have learned to carry our own things with us, making little of every loss of earthly things. Nor do we fear that the necessities of this life will be lacking to us, having the most certain promise of God in the holy Gospel, since he himself has care for us, and for those who seek first heavenly things neither want of food nor want of clothing will occur. Therefore, brother, we exhort you: imitate the studies of good men, not for vanity and profit, but for the cultivation of the mind, so that you may recognize the light of truth, love it when recognized, and possess it without end when loved. Again we warn you to flee idleness, since every idle man is in desires, and idleness, a spring of many vices, is hostile to the soul. Idleness softens the powers, destroys the light of minds, and makes a living man like a trunk and altogether useless. No one was ever made great by idleness, no one learned, no one excellent or of immortal memory. How does he live who lives for no one? But he lives for no one who is always idle. We were born for action, since nature, which has given us nothing more precious than time, abhors idleness and emptiness. After labor let there be rest for you, and not sloth, as much as is enough, so that you may rise stronger for action, not so that, with labor relaxed, you may grow completely numb in idleness. Love the study of the holy Scriptures, and you will never be idle. For what that carnal lover used to say about his own love, we have found true in the study of the Scriptures: let him who does not wish to become slothful love. True love is never idle. But farewell, and love good, honorable, and useful things. Again farewell. From Ursulus in the March of Brandenburg, on the twentieth day of the month of October, in the year of Christians 1503.

XLIIII.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, sends greetings to Roger Sycambrius.

Intending to send my chaplain to the regions of the Rhine, excellent Roger, I could not prevent myself from making you, by letter, more certain concerning the condition of our affairs. We live here by the mercy of God healthy in body, regarded as being in no low place with the prince, yet almost destitute of the consolation of learned men. The men are indeed good, but too barbarous and unlearned, more given to feasting and drinking than to the study of good letters. Rare here is the man devoted to the study of the Scriptures; but by a certain inborn [unclear] the customs of the inhabitants are pleasing, since they burn with great observance and devotion toward the religion of Christ. They visit the temples of God most diligently, the feasts of the saints [unclear].

Of Johannes Trithemius.

...they reverently celebrate the feasts of the saints, and most tenaciously observe the fasts imposed upon them; and they are the more fervent in the worship of God inasmuch as they are known to have been converted to the faith of Christ among the newest peoples of Germany. Only excess in drinking does not have the name of a vice, although many abstainers are also found among them; the immigrant Franconians and Swabians, as we have often experienced, exceed more in drinking than the natives of the land. But you, Roger, pray to God for us, that at last, departing from here in safety, we may return to our homeland: not because we are weary of the March, for it pleases us greatly, but so that, having returned to the Rhine, we may bring our affairs to their due conclusion. For [unclear] is easy for us for Christ’s sake, since wherever we shall have been in the Lord’s will, we think ourselves to be in our homeland. Before the feast of Easter we shall not see the Rhine, because we must please the most serene prince, who insisted that we remain longer than had been our purpose. We wished you to know these things. If you have anything, write back. Farewell, mindful of us. From Berlin, on the 20th day of the month of October, in the year of Christians 1505.

XLV. Johannes Trithemius to Johannes Vigilius Sunszhemius, doctor of both laws, greetings.

We have sent both my letter and that of the prince Margrave, excusing my rather prolonged stay in the March, to the most serene prince Philip, Count Palatine, by the hands of our chaplain Theodoric, very well known to you; we ask that it become your duty to present them to the prince. You will learn from the bearer what is being done concerning me; receive in these few words how it pleases us here. The land is indeed good and very fruitful, but it needs hard-working cultivators, since it is itself vast, broad in extent, and the peasants are few and very lazy, given more to drinking and leisure than to labors. Of them we may say: among the March-men, feast days hasten leisure and poverty, fasts hasten illnesses, and drinking hastens death, because in these three things they seem to exceed the other nations of the Germans. For they are men born, as it were, by nature for leisure; they are forbidden to work on many feasts of the saints, and are oppressed by constant want, especially those who live in the countryside. Yet of all whom we have seen they are most observant of fasts, and in this one thing they are rightly to be judged praiseworthy before many. But the greater multitude of them, too much given to drinking, shamefully stains the merit of fasting, to such a degree that here living is almost nothing other than eating and drinking. These things concerning the customs of the people.

There is nothing new here, nothing unusual is being done, except that very serious quarrels are arising between the Duke of Mecklenburg and the Lübeckers; unless they are extinguished by the counsel of friends, they will certainly run together into war. But my prince, the most serene Margrave, whose sister the duke is to have as wife, has interposed his offices and has labored much for concord. Through his mediation truces have been made until Easter. Meanwhile there is peace; yet sometimes confidence in peace is never [secure]. We desire to know from you the good health of our most serene prince Palatine, before whose majesty our necessary delay has been suitably excused. Farewell. From Berlin, on the 20th day of the month of October, in the year of Christians [1505?].

XLVI. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, to Johannes Damius, monk, greetings.

[unclear]

We wish you to know, most loving brother, that, by God’s mercy, first of all we are well, and are being kept in good condition with the most serene prince Margrave, and most abundantly provided with all necessities. Assenting to his will, we have promised to remain here until Easter. Moreover we have written to our brother M. Jacobus Trithemius, instructing that he betake himself to Neuenburg, to remain there with you until we come. Meanwhile let him remain with you, by the kindness of the mistress, lest he be compelled any longer, with salutary studies interrupted, to live fruitlessly, as up to now, with unsettled brains lacking memory. For it is most troublesome to serve the ungrateful; it is too grievous that an obedient man should be deprived of his fruit, and that one to whom a reward ought to have been repaid should be forced to carry off disadvantage. The men dwelling in the land of Nayth are exceedingly ungrateful, as we have experienced because, for many benefits often shown to them not without our loss, [unclear]; therefore not without cause do we forbid the brother to serve the ungrateful. You will make us more certain what our brothers are doing, if you have ascertained the [unclear] of the Cynonoti. Deceit will assuredly be checked by deceit, if they have not changed their plan of impiety. We have no concern about their machinations, because we desire neither favor nor hatred...

Familiar Letters

[unclear]. Nor, however, do we strive to avenge the injury, but rather to despise it, knowing that the reprobate will fall into the pit which they have made. We have not bound our mind to a place, as though we could not live outside Spanheim. For, if it should be necessary, the whole world is our fatherland.
