One heaven covers one earth; wherever I shall be, I am on earth, continuous with this one, a pilgrim yearning not for Spanheim but for the heavenly fatherland. The one almighty God is everywhere, and is nowhere absent; in him we are, live, and move, wherever we may be. Therefore the loss of one monastery will be easy for us, if it shall please God, in which we have experienced much poverty and labor, never any delight or rest. But farewell; pray for us, that the will of God alone may be fulfilled. From Berlin, 20 October, in the year of Christ 1505.

XLVII.

Johannes Trithemius to Johann Bracht, prior of St Matthias at Trier, greetings.

We have already written to your charity from Cologne Agrippina about the cause of our absence from the monastery; but now we have thought it right to inform you by letter of our stay in the March, likewise from Cologne, but the other one, on the Spree near Berlin in the March itself, so that, knowing our condition, you may by no means be distressed on our account. By the protection of divine mercy we are healthy and unharmed, and we have provided for our affairs in such a way that, if need be, we can live freely outside Spanheim. We have a prince favorable to us in all things; provided for by his munificence, we have want of nothing. We shall not return to the Rhine before Easter, having meanwhile been persuaded by the will of that prince to remain, so that we may bring to its proper end what we have begun for his honor. And in truth, if we did not know that it is contrary to our profession, and by no means fitting for our state, to dwell in the courts of princes, we would never depart from here. For the very best terms are proposed to us, if we should wish to remain wholly with the prince; but lest we do injury to the monastic purpose, it is necessary not to love the courts of princes. Yet we pass through this journey, reasonably marked out, in such a way that we refuse nothing offered to us according to our judgment, until we see what necessity at last indicates should be undertaken. Therefore, God granting, we shall return after Easter to the Rhine; but we shall never enter the monastery unless the rashness of our rivals has first happened to be humbled. But if, with [unclear], they decide that they must persist in their obstinacy, then, with the abbacy of Spanheim voluntarily laid aside, we shall follow God’s ordinance. For we trust in the goodness of almighty God, since to the end he will not despise one whom he himself knows to have been harmed, without fault, by the envy of rivals. Yet it is something we must consider not a little, lest perhaps by the ordinance of the supreme will of God we are called elsewhere, like a useless tree to be transplanted into better soil for the bearing of more abundant fruit. For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor? Therefore we must always fear, and follow the divine counsel in silence. For he who made and created us has care for us; his mercy is more useful to us than all our own counsel. I shall go on, then, gladly and voluntarily following God’s counsel, wherever I must go; and, if it please him, as a useless tree uprooted, I shall be transferred, that I may bear richer fruits of patience. Farewell happily. From Berlin, 20 October, in the year 1505.

XLVIII.

Theodoric, bishop of Lübeck, to Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, greetings.

That you very greatly desired us to lend you Iamblichus, best father, we learned from the account of our magnificent [unclear] de Lapide, a knight both of the golden order and a candidate of letters. Although we keep him in our house in the place of a most dear and most honorable philosopher, nevertheless we have sent him to you, together with Proclus, Porphyry, Synesius, and the rest of his fellow philosophers gathered together with him, no less willingly than cheerfully, instructing him to go and greet you, our noble guest, in our name. For we believe that such great men of wisdom will be all the more welcome to you, the more you have long enjoyed familiarity with them. Receive, then, best father, these noble messengers of ours, addressing you most pleasantly from the hidden recesses of philosophy, bringing, by heaven, nothing harsh or rough, but savory seasonings from the philosophical academies of the Greeks, skillfully and festively prepared by their hands. When you have enjoyed their familiarity to satiety, see that they return to our house. Farewell, bright cabinet of the scriptures, and love us, who love you dearly. From Lübeck, on Friday, 24 October, in the year of Christians 1505.

XLIX. Of Johannes Trithemius.

XLIX.

To the most reverend father in Christ, Theodoric, bishop of Lubeck, Johannes Trithemius sends greeting.

Iamblichus, priest of the Academics, brought into my house by the hand of our most serene prince, greeted me in your name. Gladly I admitted the philosopher, who at times intrudes himself upon our studies; when I read him together with Proclus, his fellow philosopher, and look more deeply into him, I often find that I am reading not them but Dionysius the Areopagite. And this practice, after the manner of the ancients, pleases me, since for the present I am content to drink from the little stream until I may be allowed to reach the spring of the purest fountain. I thank your kindness, most learned prelate, for honoring me, though I did not dare ask, with such guests. I shall make use of reading them for a short time, and shall soon arrange that they return to your bookcases. I recently brought with me from Cologne a Life of Apollonius of Tyana printed in a certain handbook; the occupations of my prince do not permit me, on this occasion, to enter into judgment on it. For I fear to give a hasty opinion, especially because Saint Jerome, in the preface to the Sacred Library, seems to have introduced Apollonius not without praise. Each point must first be examined by me as soon as leisure permits; afterward I shall state my own view without prejudice to anyone.

For I fear to give a hasty opinion, especially because Saint Jerome, in the preface to the Sacred Library, seems to have introduced Apollonius not without praise. Each point must first be examined by me as soon as leisure permits; afterward I have to state my own view without prejudice to anyone. I shall make use of reading them for a short time, and shall arrange that they soon return to your writings. since he himself, simple in his honesty, does not sufficiently understand the tricks of the crafty. Consider, finally, most revered father, your only brother, Master Jacob Trithemius, a very dear friend to me, lest, laboring in vain among the Limburgers, he suffer the loss of a noble talent. For he will be able to obtain no profit from those men who, turning over stones and logs, have no commerce at all with the study of the Scriptures. He is a man slight by nature, born for philosophy, not for the labors of peasants; if he hopes that he will attain anything great, among those men he will feel himself most certainly led astray. Be dutiful toward your own, you who have always been most merciful toward strangers. For since you are known and familiar to so many and such great princes, it will not be difficult for you to obtain some ecclesiastical office for your brother, from which he may lead an honorable life with letters. You who have so often interceded for strangers and been heard will suffer no refusal when intervening for your own. May your dignity prosper through many ages. From Speyer, on the Ides of November, in the year of salvation 1505.

52. John Trithemius to Eucharius Heimerius of Neometa, greetings.

You advise well, Eucharius, that we should return more quickly to our own affairs, as though there were not a fatherland everywhere for us, whom the Christian religion commands to leave father and mother for the love of God, and the monastic institution enjoins the renunciation of all earthly things. For we follow the prince, compelled by a certain necessity, not as courtiers, but rather as men needing counsel and assistance, since, being abandoned by those necessary to us, we fear graver dangers. It is hardly unknown to you what an outrageous insult we have endured from the Cynonoti, under whose rule we shall not easily consent to serve for long. With them certain of our own, filled with a spirit of faithlessness and conspiring against us, added the poison of malice; going about, they increased the envy of many rivals against us. It therefore pleased us to yield to evil for a time, until our own men at last learn by experience what good our presence hitherto brought them. And what was not sufficiently discussed when we left our fatherland? Those who were the authors of such great evils against us, those who from among our own were said to have conspired with our rivals, all cried out that they were innocent. Overcome by the counsel and assent of my most illustrious prince Philip, Count Palatine and of Brandenburg, we consented to leave our fatherland, by God's bounty to return to the Rhine at the feast of Easter. Meanwhile, if our rivals repent of the rashness committed against us, it will be well done and we shall return to the monastery; but if they persist in their stubbornness, if they do not acknowledge themselves for their injuries, if our brothers have dealt with their leader no differently than hitherto, we shall adhere to our own counsel, nor shall we humble ourselves before our enemies, nor shall we return to the monastery, but we shall provide for ourselves another dwelling where, with peace and tranquility, we may serve almighty God in the order. For, having a just cause of indignation at the injuries, we cannot easily forget them, nor henceforth do we ever trust those men who, though harmed by us in nothing, presumed to carry out so great an insult against us. Let it suffice our rivals that, having patience for the love of Christ, we do not seek vengeance, although we could avenge ourselves; we pass over insults in silence. They thought us so bound in mind to one place that we would necessarily not care about what they did to our contempt, as though outside Sponheim there were no place for us to remain. We trust in the Lord Jesus, who has never abandoned anyone crying out to him in tribulation, that he will have mercy on us and will prepare a place for us where, with greater peace and tranquility, we may devote ourselves to him than we ever could at Sponheim. The courts of princes do not delight us, as you suppose, nor have we resolved to adhere to an earthly prince unless it is necessary, although there are not lacking several who would admit us with great desire to be supported permanently. The continual study of the Scriptures has given us this: that we fix our mind not on place, but on truth. What you advised about your brother we received gladly; perhaps for him a richer lot will arise in time. Farewell; pray for us to God, who alone can do all things. From Berlin, on the eighth day of the month of January, in the year of the Lord 1506.

53. To the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord John Trithemius, [unclear], Nicholas the prior, faithful in all things, greetings.

Reverend and most loving father, I received the letters of your reverend paternity with immense joy, and beyond what can be said I rejoiced at your good health and excellent condition with the prince, as Theodoricus reported to us; all the brothers rejoiced with me. But with immense Johannes Trithemius.

The very long delay of your return to us has affected me with sorrow, since on account of your absence we are in great tribulation, and are harassed, mocked, and reviled by everyone, as if we were the cause of your most just indignation; and a great outcry of all has arisen against us, saying that we are worthy of burning or of perpetual exile, because we drove away our abbot, a good and holy man, wise and most learned, without cause. So great are the reproaches of men against us that we do not know what we must do, and we greatly fear that we shall soon be expelled from the monastery. But your paternity knows that, apart from the son of perdition, none of us was at fault; rather, we all grieve deeply, and the rash deed of the rivals never pleased us. Now all who were present say that they did not act with the intention of doing injury to your paternity, but because of threats made by the abbots of Mount St. James, by Magnus and Frederick, our familiars. And in truth I believe that it is so, because there was no other cause for their being seized than the threats. The duke’s official, who sent the satellites of his wicked soldiery against our household, has now been removed from his office, and in his place Meginhard of Coppenstein, your sworn vassal, has been substituted. In the name of the prince palatine, however, the prefecture is held by Francis of Sickingen, most devoted to you, who both, together with the neighbors and all the friends, [unclear] especially your arrival. The abbot also of Mount St. James grieves over your absence more than all. Therefore we ask most humbly, most reverend and most beloved father, and by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ we entreat and beseech you, that you would deign to return to us as soon as you can, and not desert the whole flock of your sheep because of the crime of a few. Why do you remain outside so long, sweetest father, when there is no one who either can or wishes to harm you? For even that Duke John loves you greatly and desires that you return, saying that he never thought any evil against your person. All our brothers also, the dearest sons of your paternity, most ardently desire your return to us, except Judas, the most impious traitor. Yet even he pretends that he greatly desires your coming, but wickedness lies to itself; the outcome of the matter will prove this. For I know that he will flee from the monastery as soon as he hears that your paternity is approaching us. Brother Johann Nutius, our senior, and all the brothers desire your well-being and humbly commend themselves. Farewell from Sponheim, on the twenty-second day of the month of November, in the year of the Lord 1505.

LIIII.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to his beloved son in Christ, Nicolaus Remittus, his prior, greeting.

Your letters, dearest son, would have moved our mind from its purpose, so that in the middle of winter we would have hastened our return to our homeland, had not the condition of our promise bound us to the prince to remain longer. For the promise commands us to remain until Easter, lest we offend so great a prince, who is very favorably disposed to our affairs, contrary to his wish. You write that our return is desired by many; we believe it, and in due time, as we promised, with the Lord granting it, [unclear] about to receive the reverence of the promises. But we greatly wonder that the abbot of Mainz grieves so much over our absence, since he himself is the chief author of all the evils against us; at his clandestine and false instigation our familiars [unclear] into scandal for us, and the tongue of the unblemished old man did not spare our most serene prince and legate, the archbishop of Cologne, the count palatine, and the margraves; if we had shown it to even one of them to be read, he would long since have paid the penalty for his rashness. That good abbot acted most unjustly against us, and, out of hatred of others, persecuted us unjustly, whether knowingly or unknowingly. May God forgive him and not impute to him the sin that he committed against us. A strange reflection for an old man: he grieves over our absence, he who first gave the counsel that we should withdraw for a time, avoiding envy. But the fact that an outcry of men has arisen against you does not relieve us at all, nor does it delight us in any way, but rather saddens us, especially for those among you who are innocent of the evils against us. For we know that you did not all conspire against us, nor for that reason do we believe you all innocent. In all these things nothing saddens us so much as that the innocent are reviled together with the guilty. Our innocence consoles us, to which even you, our enemies, will bear witness: how justly among you and without offense we lived, always putting your advantage before our own convenience. Lastly we exhort you to look diligently to the worship, now diminished; do not sadden the brothers without reasonable cause, and yourself and 486 Familiar Letters

that you keep them religiously within the monastery, and preserve monastic observance inviolate. Remind the brothers to pray to God for us; we greet them all in the charity of Jesus Christ. Farewell, from Berlin, on the eighth day of the month of January, in the year of the Christians 1506.

LV.

To the Reverend Father in Christ, Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, Brother Jacobus Trithemius Sends Greeting.

[unclear]

The letters of your paternity brought me great joy, by which I learned that you are safe and well. Moreover, you wish to know my condition. Know briefly: it is middling. By God’s goodness I am healthy, and rich without money. After your departure from Neometum I came to Wachenheim, and after staying there a few days, I soon perceived that men, forgetful both of my services and of your benefactions, were casting grim little glances at me, and, envying my studies, were recalling me, unwilling, to stones and mud. Therefore I did not wish to remain longer with ungrateful and cold-hearted men, who neither remember benefits nor fulfill promises. As you know, I served the abbot for many days at Cologne as a scribe, and on account of him I offended those whom I could have had as friends; I spent time with him without profit, wore out my clothes, and obtained absolutely nothing from him as wages. The church which he wished to assign to me is very poor, in the valley of the willows; the priestly dwelling-house, together with the village, has been consumed by fire. Let him have it for himself and be well, because I have no mind to remain with him. Would that I had yielded to you rather than to his requests, and had gone on with you into the March; it would be better for me than to have served him for nothing. Therefore, despising that most empty hope, I went down to Trier and stayed for some time with my parents, until I advanced through the several grades to the priestly order. Now hereafter I shall do what you urge, and I shall remain with our Damius until you come. Farewell, in health. From Speyer, on the second day of the month of November, in the year 1505.

LVI.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, to Jacobus Trithemius, His Most Loving Brother, Greeting.

[unclear]

By God’s grant we are still well; if you too are well, it is good. It was not unknown to us whom you served, whose ungrateful [unclear] divinity we knew very well, having long since experienced it. But since it pleased you so, if you have lost your labor, you will know that it must be imputed to yourself. As soon as you can, write to our parents that we are safe and sound, and that they should have care for their old age, not being anxious about us. Almighty God, by his mercy, will, as we trust, provide what is necessary for us without the anxiety of our parents, even if we never return to Spanheim. The prior Remittit wrote humble and very sweet letters, desiring that we return to the monastery as soon as possible; answering him, we gave words in return for words, until we may examine the minds of the men more fully. For henceforth we shall not easily believe, having once been so enormously deceived. Therefore, when we have returned to Neometum or Budoris, we shall act so that the dispositions of the brothers do not escape us, and then at last we shall do what seems to us more useful. But if it should happen that we remain outside, it is nothing to us, since we choose rather to lack an ungrateful monastery than [unclear] wicked men. Farewell, from Berlin, on the eighth day of the month of January, in the year of the Christians 1506.

LVII.

Theodoricus, Bishop of Lübeck, to Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, Greeting.

[unclear]

The worthy and renowned philosophers Iamblichus and Proclus, with the others, whom we formerly sent to you to greet you, best of fathers: in what manner they have conducted themselves with your paternity, whether they have now nearly performed their duty, or whatever you required of them, [unclear]; and we judge that, living, you can most abundantly [unclear] them excellently, according to your generosity, and with the bowl of Tantalus for the sake of strengthening friendship. Therefore, lest they grow sluggish either through idleness, or, with new and more pleasing things [unclear], be held, as usually happens, in a lower place and in contempt, and become dirty with dust, we have thought they should be recalled. We also believe that they have been wearied by you to such a degree that now that monastic discipline, rather strict, which you, very religious father, employ, has become very tiresome to them. But if you have judged it so, permit them, with your honorable peace, to return. But if to you Of Johannes Trithemius.

It remains to compare what you have, to complete it, and to enjoy the most honorable men to satiety; and finally see to it that they visit our house. Farewell happily and prosperously, and love us, who love you dearly. From Lubus, on the 27th day of the month of January, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1506.

LVIII.

To the most reverend father in Christ, Theodoric, bishop of Lubeck, Johannes Trithemius sends greeting.

Iambicus, who had been entertained very honorably among us for almost three months, as the beauty of his face will show, we have permitted to return to you, his lord, now that the duty of his embassy has already been well discharged, most holy prelate. He agreed willingly, although he by no means disliked our lodging, since, having long enjoyed our familiarity, he is now touched by no fear. He does not fear monastic censure, inasmuch as, accustomed to our ways by long habit, he now understands very well that we imitate the counsel of the wise man, whereby we know how to have conversation with each person according to his capacity. For we know, on the testimony of Iamblichus, that neither must one treat with a monk about philosophy, nor among philosophers must one dispute about the religion of cloistered men. We keep each thing in its own place, exercising the monk with the former, the philosopher with the latter. This one thing perhaps could have been troublesome in our hospitality, that in Ursul he remained alone with us, he who had been accustomed to live in our monastery with almost three thousand. For here we are sojourning away from our own people among a few, philosophizing not as we wish, but as we can. Receive your Iambicus, most learned prelate, whom we send to your house, giving thanks for your kindness toward us; and use our service as you please. Farewell, and regard us as commended to you. From Ursul, on the 4th of the month of February, in the year 1506.

LIX.

Johannes Trithemius to Hermann Bu[unclear]schius, poet of Munster, greeting.

When we were making a journey from the regions beyond the Rhine through the town of Leipzig to the March of Brandenburg, it was by no means clear to us that you were there. For we had heard at Cologne that you were professing your letters at Louvain, and therefore at Leipzig we made no inquiry for you. But now, through the report of Georgius Sibutus the poet, we have learned that you have been provided on the best terms for the youth of Leipzig in more elegant letters. We congratulate you that your affairs have been well established, admonishing you of this one thing: that you must live in such a way that you do not destroy learning by your morals. It does not befit an educated man, even if he is a poet, to be wanton, a follower of drunkenness, womanish, and given to luxury; all of which things quickly destroy a man, as someone sang, saying:

[unclear]

Wine and baths, and love concerned with Venus, prepare a swifter road to hell.

This also that Maro of yours is said to have warned most beautifully in his little treatise on wine and Venus, where he completes many matters in a few words, saying:

Do not be seized by love of Venus or of wine, for in one way wine and Venus do harm. As Venus by force enervates the powers, so an abundance of wine weakens the steps and enfeebles the feet. Love compels many men, when overcome, to confess secrets; mindless drunkenness discloses what is hidden, etc.

When Anacharsis was asked by what means someone might become abstinent, he answered that, if he were sober, he should set before his eyes the shameful movements of drunkards. For he says that the vine bears three grapes: the first of pleasure, the second of [unclear], the third [unclear] a famous saying. The first bowl, he says, pertains to thirst, the second to cheerfulness, the third to pleasure, the fourth to madness. Nothing is more shameful than a drunken man, who has a stench in his mouth, trembling in his body, frenzy and forgetfulness in his mind, who promises stupid things and brings foolish hidden matters out into public; his heart throbs, his face reddens with blood. Flaccus, embracing all these things with beautiful brevity, used to say:

What does drunkenness not devise? It unlocks hidden things, bids hopes be held as certain, drives the unarmed man into battles, 488 Familiar Letters

It removes the burden from anxious minds, and teaches arts; Whom have fruitful cups not made eloquent?

There is nothing among demons, as Chrysostom says, so pleasing and friendly as drunkenness and lust, which is the mother of all vices, and nothing so contrary to them as sobriety, which is the mother of all virtues. What else shall we think drunkenness to be than a man’s voluntary madness, which overturns the mind, removes memory, brings on forgetfulness, weakens the body, and kills the soul? No one given over to wine and drunkenness will ever be able to be a good man, nor wise, nor learned, nor faithful, nor useful to anyone, nor worthy of any honor or remembrance. Therefore you, Buschius, flee all plagues of the soul, especially wine and sexual pleasure; by their excessive use all virtue is enfeebled, the mind is blinded, and one’s reputation is exposed to reproach before all. Spare your eyes, which, struck by both evils through your own excessive willing, are now almost destroyed by discharge and redness. Spare your property and substance, which you acquire laboriously by teaching, lest, when you have become older, you be forced to beg. Remember that, as the poet says: “By wine beauty perishes; by wine age is corrupted. Through wine often the mistress does not know her own man.” And what Aristotle said: that one who is sober and watchful cannot easily be attacked; but one who is drunk and sleeping, like a dead man, is easily captured. We beg that you both be sparing with our admonitions and acquiesce in them; for you are not unaware that we love you, and we know that you need a bridle. Around the feast of the Lord’s Ascension, when we are about to return to the Rhine, by the Lord’s bounty we shall meet with you, to confer with you more fully on those matters that are in our mind. Meanwhile, farewell in health.

From Berlin, the first day of March, in the year 1506.

LX.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Conrad, venerable Abbot of the monastery of Saints Ulrich and Afra in Augsburg, greeting.

After the most turbulent Palatine war had arisen, the envy of certain men against me on account of my prince himself, when I was with him at Heidelberg on the sixth day of the month of April, made it seem good to me to withdraw for a time from my monastery, lest something worse should follow. Meanwhile our king Maximilian summoned a meeting of the princes at Cologne Agrippina for the beginning of the month of July; and I too, called by certain princes, went down by boat. At last, after thirty days, when the council had been dissolved and the princes were returning to their own places, I, having often and much been asked by the most serene prince-elector Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, with the consent of my prince, the elder Palatine, entered the March, having meanwhile entrusted the government of the monastery of Sponheim to my Prior. And now indeed I am here, having the intention, after the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection, of returning to my own affairs and, according to the ordering of matters arranged, as I shall find them, either to change or to continue my plan. How gladly I would have come to Augsburg for the provincial meeting of our order, if the Prince had agreed that I should leave here before Easter, and if I hoped to find good counsel for my affairs among the fathers. But because it is necessary to comply with so great a prince, I have thought that my place should be entrusted to your paternity, so that, according to the tenor of the procuration which in the preceding year, when the provincial meeting of the fathers was being begun because of the war, I had sent to you with the money, you may act, and appear before the presidents on my behalf, and in my name carry out each matter according to the custom of the order, and render my necessary absence excused. That you would be willing to do this, and would do it, in view of the mutual friendship between us, I ask you again and again. If you wish me to know anything of your thoughts, write back, and hand your letter itself to this messenger of my prince, since, setting out for Salzburg, after completing his embassy he is to return to us through Augsburg. Remember that the chirograph of our account for the past presidency is to be delivered to the abbot of Nuremberg. Farewell. From Berlin, 24 March, in the year 1506.

LXI.

Johannes Trithemius to Georg Sibutus, poet laureate, greeting.

We have heard that you have entered into a contest with Hermann Trebelius; we would judge that you had done better not to do this. It is not fitting for your age to provoke old men with writings, and, as someone says, to wage war over goat’s wool. It is more becoming for you, a young man, to listen to your elders and learn from them, not to despise or envy your betters, even if you are wiser. In you is verified the saying of the poet Hesiod, who says: xxi Of Johannes Trithemius.

[unclear Greek verse]

And the potter hates the potter, and the craftsman the craftsman, and the poor man envies the poor man, and the poet the poet.

Envy, moreover, is the worst evil, harming no one more than its own author: the daughter of pride, a death-bearing poison of the mind, by which the devil, most guilty, overthrew the first man. But consider what Scripture says: “The little one,” it says, “envy kills.” Saint Pope Gregory, in explaining this, says: “We cannot envy any except those whom we think better than ourselves in some respect. Therefore he is little who is killed by envy, because unless he himself were inferior, he would not grieve over another’s good.”

No loss is more monstrous than envy, which rightly must be called the abyss of erroneous agitation, the hell of the human mind, the spur of contention, the sting of corruption, the entrance of diabolical obstinacy. Envy bears more heavily upon its own author, the mind from which it takes its origin; like a viper it kills its parent, and through it, by the devil’s deceit, death first entered the world.

Hence Solomon, instructing a well-disposed hearer, says in Proverbs: “Do not eat with an envious man, nor desire his foods.” For envy devours all things with a pestilential heat: it troubles the soul, consumes the understanding, burns the breast, fastens upon the mind, and feeds upon the human heart like a kind of plague. Envy is an inextinguishable fire. For as a moth eats a garment, so envy consumes the one who is jealous. Seneca advises that one should beware a friend’s envy more than enemies’ treacheries. If you have not envied, you will be greater; for he who envies is lesser. The envious man makes another’s good his own evil; that evil is far from the learned, wise, and good man.

Misery alone lacks envy. Therefore it is better to suffer envy than to practice it. If you wish to be free from envy, do not hunt after vain glory by your night studies, but imitate your Tibullus, saying in the fourth book:

“There is no need of envy; let the glory of the crowd be far away. Let him who is wise rejoice in silence by himself.”

Show yourself modest in all things; you will be more gloriously without envy. Modesty, moreover, is the virtue that moderates the passions of the soul, rendering a man pleasing and estimable to all who behold him, so that he utters words examined by the balance of justice, and there is seriousness in his meaning, weight and measure in his words.

It does not befit men devoted to the study of letters to be inflamed with contentions, to neglect more useful matters and wage war over useless speech; by this the minds of teachers are torn away from the state of rectitude, and the hearts of hearers, clouded over by the mist of vanity, are prevented from reaching the hidden things of wisdom. Everyone willingly admires, praises, and widely receives the teaching of that man in whose speech modesty shines together with gravity, where no contention of perverse rivalry is seen, no arrogance of pride, but calmness of voice, mind, and mouth is displayed with sweetness, and humility, the friend of wisdom, shines forth.

For no wise man can be proud and arrogant; but he who is exalted and proud is not wise. The condition of our mortality is the greatest cause for humility for us; for pride we have absolutely no cause. For what are we, O poet, except human beings, necessarily destined to die shortly? We are like a shadow in the wind, as Sophocles says in the Ajax:

[unclear Greek verse]

For I see that we are nothing other than images, all of us who live, or a light shadow.

“It is a point,” says Seneca, “that we live; indeed less than a point.” But nature has divided this smallest thing by a certain appearance of a longer span: it has made one part of it infancy, another childhood, another adolescence, another a certain inclination from adolescence into old age, and from old age it has established a certain return to childhood, through which all things are enclosed by death.

What else is man than foul seed, the juice of dung, food? After being a man we shall be a rotten corpse; from the corpse, worms; after the worm, the worst stench, the greatest horror. And thus every man is turned into this form. For as Solomon said in Ecclesiastes: “Just as man came forth naked from his mother’s womb, so naked he will return to the earth; he will take nothing with him from all his labor.” Truly pitiable is the weakness of man: as he came, so he will return. What therefore will it profit him that he labored for the wind? All the days of his life he eats in darkness, amid many cares, hardship, and sadness.

“O deceptive hope of man,” Cicero cries, “and fragile fortune, and our empty conceptions, which are often broken and collapse within a moderate space, and are overwhelmed in the very course of their progress before they have been able to sight the harbor.” Therefore always think upon your end, [Sibute?], and know yourself to be mortal; never in your mind touch pride, the mother of all evils. For the fates are inexorable, as Martial says, 490 Familiar Letters

No one has had it fall to him to entreat the three wool-working maidens; they observe the day which they have appointed.

We all die, and, as it were, we are poured out like water upon the earth, as that man said: We are owed to death, and we and our mortal deeds will perish, and death is the final boundary of things.

Sweat over useful studies, by which you may provide not only what is necessary for the body, but also that the mind may be kept immune from dreadful death. When, about to return to our own affairs, we shall shortly be with you in your Albiburg, we shall disclose in conversation what moved us to write these things rather boldly. But you, knowing our love toward you, will not curse the exhortation which we have made. Farewell, mindful of yours. From Berlin, on the 20th day of the month of April, in the year of the Christians 1506.

LXII.

To the Most Serene Prince Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, Duke of Stettin and Pomerania, Count of Ruegen and Cassubia, Prince Elector, etc., Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, wishes happiness.

On the fourteenth day of the month of May I left Berlin, the town of residence of your Serenity, as you know, most illustrious prince, at about the eleventh hour. According to the predictions of our Astrophilus many adversities befell us, but by God's mercy we overcame them all. For, suffering for six days from the disease of stone in the bladder and gravely afflicted, I was compelled to remain in Leipzig and to entrust myself to the hands of physicians, something I had never done before. And when we had come to the Rhine, through the retainers of a certain most wicked count, the incendiary of the monastery of Limburg, I, together with the messenger of your Serenity and my servants and one monk of the aforesaid burned monastery, were captured on the feast of the Most Holy Trinity at about the eleventh hour, and led to a nearby castle. Yet that same evening, recognizing that I was kept under royal protection, they released us all, giving no other reason why they had seized us except that they thought I favored the affairs of the burned monastery of Limburg. By this insult it happened, as you will understand from your messenger, that I could not carry your commissions either to the Archbishop of Cologne, or to the Archbishop of Trier, nor even to the Archbishop of Mainz. Yet I shall act as soon as possible so that they may have your letters and understand your will.

Concerning my own affairs, however, I can write nothing certain until I have spoken with my most excellent prince, who is now absent, and until I have understood more clearly the state of my brothers and likewise the minds of my rivals. For I shall in no way be seen at Sponheim unless all obstacles have first been removed. But if the rashness of my rivals has not been turned aside, I shall do one of two things: either I shall return to you, as you requested, or I shall choose for myself a place in the order suited to my studies, where I may be able to make your Serenity a participant in my studies. You have often heard me saying what I think: that following courts is [unclear], and neither suits my purpose nor plainly agrees with my institution. Therefore I shall seek a place suitable for me in the breadth of my order, if it can be done; if I cannot find one, I shall necessarily do what I can. To your Serenity, however, I give immortal thanks for your very great benefactions toward me, not only those already shown, but also the greater ones promised, if there should be need. I desire that your Excellence, with all his people, may remain unharmed for Nestor's years. From Heidelberg, on the 18th day of the month of June, in the year of the Lord 1506.

LXIII.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to the brothers beloved in Christ, his sons, the prior and convent in Sponheim: sincere charity in the Lord.

Having at last returned safely from the March of Brandenburg to our homeland, we sent ahead to you from Frankfurt our chaplain Theodoric, so that, with him reporting the things which we entrusted to him, you might understand our state and mind. Returning to us at Budoris, he reported to us your desire, by which you pray that we return to you as quickly as possible, and that there is and will be no one who can or wishes to trouble us. We indeed believe that what you say is true in your hearts; nevertheless we have not thought that trust should be placed in rivals, whose presumption against us is judged by no one. Therefore we shall do nothing without counsel, especially since certain men among you, full of ambition and faithlessness, are manifestly proved to consent to Cynonotus rather than to us, their pastor. We call almighty God to witness, from whom nothing can be hidden, be unknown, that we would indeed gladly return to you, if we could have your integrity toward us ascertained; but we are compelled to doubt it, because, though so often warned by us, you have done nothing with the Duke against our rivals. But send to us the prior, or someone else from among you, to whom we may be able to explain our mind more fully. For although we fear no one who could harm us, since we remain outside not through fear of anyone, but only through indignation at the memory of the deed, nevertheless we by no means intend to return to Sponheim without the counsel of the prince palatine. Farewell, praying God that his most holy will may be fulfilled, which can never be other than right. From Heidelberg, on the twentieth day of the month of June, in the year of Christians 1506.

Of Johannes Trithemius.

63.

To the most holy father in Christ, Pope Julius II, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, offers the most humble kisses of the blessed feet.

[unclear]

The fire which our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the eternal Father, sent upon the earth, and wished to be kindled vehemently in the hearts of men, compels me, most merciful father, the least of your subjects, of no weight before the divine seat of your pontificate except in faith and devotion, merit or consequence, to plead before your most merciful paternity, at the instance of the most Christian Duke George of the Saxons, the cause of blessed Benno, formerly bishop of Meissen, most worthy in merit and holiness, a cause higher than my powers; since I cannot do so with words, I do it at least with mute letters.

He, as we are taught by ancient monuments, was from infancy anticipated by the divine Spirit and devoted himself wholly to the service of God: distinguished in faith, untiring in virtue and constancy, strong in hope, and at all times most fervent in love and charity toward God and neighbor. From being a monk of the rule of Saint Benedict, he was appointed first abbot of the monastery called Goseck, situated in the diocese of Naumburg not far from that city itself, and presided for almost three years in all religion and holiness. When this time had passed, stirred by the envy of his monks and by the assaults of the advocate, a count, he left the monastery together with the abbacy and entered the wilderness to serve Christ in tranquillity. From there, summoned by Pope Victor II, he was made rector of the church of Goslar, while the merits of holiness were always increasing in him; finally he obtained the episcopate of the church of Meissen by the canonical election of the brethren.

And so that he might not seem to have taken on the name of so great a dignity without fruit, he turned himself wholly to the usefulness of all the flock of Christ the highest shepherd, constant in prayer, wondrously devoted in preaching the word of the Lord, both to the Slavs, whom he converted to the orthodox faith, and to his own faithful and those round about, with an [unclear] and fervor. In that persecution also in which Emperor Henry III, disobedient enemy and rebel against the supreme pontiffs of the Roman Church, troubled the whole Church, especially in Germany, Benno, man of God and also a magnificent prelate, formed in faith and love of his Lord, always most faithful to the Apostolic See, resisted the tyrant to his face, rebuked him in his sin, and confidently thundered against him the sentence of anathema which the pope had decreed, publicly proclaiming and denouncing him to all the faithful as schismatic, accursed, rejected by God unless he did penance, to the judgment of the vicar of Christ.

For all these things he was cast into chains and prisons, suffered injuries, insults, reproaches, and blows as well, and always with a cheerful mind sang: “It is good for me to cling to God, since the vicar of Christ must be obeyed rather than a man of evil speech.” O man full of virtues and lofty merits, thrice holy and four times most holy, who, strengthened on the rock of apostolic constancy, confidently set himself as a wall for the house of God at a necessary and dangerous time, and, fighting most bravely for the honor of the most holy Apostolic See, feared no chains of tyrants. O pontiff to be extolled with everlasting praises, whose life, shining with all virtues and every holiness, is rightly set before us as an example; and that it pleased God most high is clearly declared by almost infinite miracles down to the present day, to such an extent that, if the integrity of saints is judged to be proved by the testimony of miracles, no one in these times seems to be judged holier than blessed Benno.

Every day astonishing miracles are done at his tomb, and things still more wondrous always succeed the wondrous. And although, most blessed father Julius, Benno has already received from God, the best and greatest, the eternal reward and glory in the heavenly palace for his merits, and, joined to his ineffable principle of spirit by grace, not by nature, blessed without end, he by no means requires our honors, since he has all things in that highest good, nevertheless provision must be made for us and for the faithful posterity, who need the patronage of the saints, by the authority of your most holy see. Miracles bear witness that Benno is holy; virtues cry out that he is to be honored; the experience of healings promises him as a faithful patron. This one thing stands in the way of the prayers of all and impedes the benefits of individuals: that, although by the authority of the Apostolic See Familiar Letters

Benno does not yet seem among us to have been enrolled in the catalogue of the saints, though we do not doubt that he reigns with the saints in heaven; [lest] we be compelled to desist from venerating him, and it not be permitted us to invoke the intercessions of so great a man. But since his most holy life, full of virtues, is clearly described by older men and by his own contemporaries, and since many miracles are done daily in the church of Meissen at his tomb, the aforementioned George, most upright and most Christian prince of the Saxons and duke of Meissen, lover, cultivator, and defender of Christianity, moved by pious devotion, judged that efforts should be made for his canonization, and obtained from your Holiness's predecessor, Pope Alexander VI, commissioners to examine each point. But Alexander, carried off by death, could not carry through the matter of the holy Benno, and perhaps ought not to have done so, because divine providence assigned the honor of so great a man to your times, and reserved for you the prelate most dear to itself for the catalogue of the saints. Therefore, most blessed father, we beg your Holiness with what humility we can: grant that Benno, an apostolic man, be venerated by us, and enroll his name to be celebrated with the holy confessors of God, and do not allow what has been reserved for your gift to pass into the glory of another. Believe me, greatest of pontiffs: by conferring Benno upon the holy fathers you will have enlarged the worship of God in no small measure; you will also obtain everlasting remembrance on earth for your most celebrated name, and, with the holy Benno interceding, for the enlarged divine worship you will receive a good reward in heaven. This we all, as many as have experienced the merits of the holy Benno either in ourselves or in others, unanimously ask of your most holy majesty. May we be heard by you, most merciful father; again and again we beg it, and you will do a thing pleasing to God, useful and honorable to the Christian people, and to be remembered by us, your suppliants, with perpetual gratitude. May almighty God, whose vicar you are on earth, long preserve your Beatitude unharmed for our salvation.

From Büdingen, 21 June, in the year of the Christians 1506.

LXV.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to his beloved [sons].

To his most beloved sons in Christ, sincere charity in the Lord.

How quickly the minds of men change we experience daily enough, not only among strangers, but also, what we greatly wonder at, among you, if indeed the things reported to us in your name by your prior are true. You beg that we return to the monastery; yet the obstacles which not undeservedly offend our mind, about which we have often given orders, you have not yet removed. Consider, brothers, whom this negligence of yours can rather harm. Do not think that I am panting after Sponheim, for elsewhere, with God's help, I can easily provide better for myself. I only have pity on you; unwillingly do I abandon you, whom, gathering together in Christ, I nourished. But if through you occasion should be given me whereby I may justly abandon you, know for certain that I shall never for all eternity agree to return to you, but shall follow the fortune offered me. You are not ignorant what rash injury our rivals have done us, although they themselves now say that they planned nothing out of hatred of us, but rather took up the injury against those who brought threats against the abbot of Mainz. But why you advise letters of request to the duke is a cause forbidding us, especially since it is manifest that we have never sinned in anything against him, whereas he is [unclear] in mind against us, and for what reason is not hidden from us. But you, as seems good to you, deal with him; we indeed shall not write to him on our behalf. It has pleased us, not without reason, to defer the whole matter until the annual chapter, which will shortly be held at Mainz, so that we may both ascertain the opinion of the fathers and be shown not to have passed them by in so arduous a matter. Meanwhile bear with it a little, since, when the chapter has been held, we shall make our mind manifest to you in deed. Farewell, and keep the memory of your pastor before God.

From Büdingen, the 6th day of July, in the year of the Christians 1506.

LXVI.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, sends greetings to Jacob Wimpheling of Sélestat, his friend.

In the whole two-year period no occasion was ever given me by which I could write to you with certainty, since a very grave war was raging against us and, God so permitting, our affairs were undergoing a great change. For in the year of our salvation the fourth above the five-hundredth and thousandth Johannes Trithemius.

... around the feast of Pentecost, the Bavarians, Swabians, and Hessians, conspiring together as one, with certain other princes and cities, ranged everywhere with hostile incursion through all the land of our most serene prince Philip, Count Palatine, both here around the Rhine and in Bavaria, and carried off whatever they found not sufficiently fortified, sparing no place, showing respect to no religion, and reverencing neither sex nor age. They plundered churches, robbed monasteries, carrying away whatever they found: chalices, coverings of altars too, bells, all utensils, both those belonging to divine worship and those belonging to human use. Many villages around us, quite fine and large, with most richly adorned churches, were burned by the enemies and lie utterly consumed by fire. That notable monastery of our order also, Limburg near Durkheim, was reduced to ashes with its church and all its dwellings by the retainers of the Count of Leiningen, and completely destroyed. Those two monasteries around us, one the Porta Mariae of the Wilhelmites, by the [Alexandrines?], the other of St. Disibod, of the Cistercians, by the Palatines, were then stripped of all movable goods found there; they were redeemed with money so that they might not be burned. The farms of our monastery too, almost all of them, lie either burned or otherwise utterly destroyed.

Meanwhile, while these things were being done here around us, I was forced to remain for twenty-two weeks in the nearby Palatine town of Kreuznach, to which I had withdrawn on the vigil of Peter and Paul from fear of the enemies, not without very great loss to the household property. For whatever was in the monastery, lest it fall to the enemies as plunder, had to be carried there. And indeed many things, in the carrying and carrying back, were scattered or even damaged, since none of us could be present who might have applied the necessary care to the goods.

When at last the tumult of the raging people had somehow been calmed, I returned to my monastery, almost empty of grain and necessities, all of which had been consumed by reason of the war. And behold, after a few months had passed, while I was at Budor, certain men from our hooded monks, whom we call donati, led by I know not what spirit, were noted as having conspired against us with the Cynonotes, who were secretly hostile to us on account of the Palatine; they made the Duke of Transylvania hostile to us. He, giving credit to false accusations, had certain persons of our household detained under ecclesiastical immunity, alleging fabricated causes, although everything proceeded from another source.

When I at Budor heard what had been done, moved by the indignity of the matter, from the first day of the month of April in the one thousand five hundred and fifth year of our salvation down to this day I remained outside the monastery, not from fear of the duke or of anyone else whatsoever, but indignant at the memory of the injuries. I was in the March of Brandenburg for nine months with the most serene prince Joachim, elector of the Holy Empire, having for many years been desired and requested by him; and, having now been rewarded by him not inconsiderably, I departed and returned to Budor, and am remaining here until I see what may usefully be done by me.

There are many reasons and causes with me on account of which I shall not readily consent to return to Sponheim. Yet lest I seem to have done anything without consulting the fathers of the order, I shall await their assembly, which will be held, according to custom, at Mainz at the beginning of September. If they are able to provide for my affairs by some useful plan, it will be well done; but if they cannot, or certainly if they neglect to do so, necessity itself will give me counsel, so that I may follow the fortune that presses me. Nor am I the first who, after suffering injury, abandoned the place committed to him, lest he serve the ungrateful, since many before me, not only abbots but also pontiffs, by resigning their dignities and prelacies because of the wickedness of their subjects, have provided for their own safety.

Almighty and most loving God, who feeds the birds of heaven and gives food to beasts of burden in due time, will, I do not doubt, provide for me too the means by which I may live, since I neither desire many things nor covet great things. For having food and clothing, according to the word of St. Christophilus, I have already learned to be content with these, as a certain one of the Greeks said:

[unclear]

I do not seek or wish to be made rich; but let it be mine to live among modest things, with no evil possessing me.

We desire to know what new thing you have forged; nor do we believe that you grow feeble in idleness, nor that you can spend even one day without continual lucubration. Farewell, mindful of us before God. From Budor, on the last day of the month of July, in the year of the Christians 1506.

494. Familiar Letters, LXVII.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, sends greeting to his very good brother Johannes Nuntius.

[unclear]

The prior came to me without letters from anyone, indicating orally that the heads of the factions had met at Bingen on our account on the fourth day of the month of August. He himself also took part in their council, together with his colleague from Bingen, and he reported to us certain things said and at the same time concluded by our rivals in that impious council; the substance of their opinion is comprised in these words. They say that they very greatly desire that we return to the monastery, and that on the part of the Duke and his people there is nothing for us to fear, since he too greatly desires our return, and has often said openly that he has never felt or thought anything against us. But if it does not please us to return to the monastery, the Duke, together with those lying old priests, desires that we resign the abbacy; yet they would rather that we return than that we withdraw. This is the sum of the counsel of the wicked, concerning which Melantius the prior desired our answer, which he might report.

We said that the chapter to be held at Mainz at the beginning of the month of September was drawing near, in which we intend to set forth the case for examination by the fathers, and to hear what they advise. Having learned these things, the prior departed, to report them to the Duke. After his departure, on the very next day Johannes Damius disclosed to us that he had seen, in the prior’s possession, letters addressed to us in the name of our convent; when the prior was asked what they contained, he answered: an invective against the abbot. And Damius said, “Does the convent write against the abbot? O most foolish and senseless men, what are you doing?” And snatching the letters from the prior’s hand, he opened them, read them, and marveled at the prior’s rashness. For they contained certain brothers, fabricated by our prior alone at Mainz with the help of that ruined man Peter Slarion, and falsely written in the name of our convent, while they themselves knew nothing of it. But after Damius had read the note, he tore it up, lest it should fall into our hands.

Moved again by this injury done by our prior, we have resolved with ourselves, brother, and we do not wish you to be at all unaware of it, never to return to Sponheim, but to provide for ourselves elsewhere as best we can. For now the prior’s faithlessness is clearly evident to you, he who up to this point pretended to be faithful to us. We know that he aspires to our abbacy; for that reason he contrives plots against us, with sweet words in his mouth, but he devises deceit in his heart. Therefore we shall yield, not unwillingly but voluntarily; and although we could hold our abbacy even while absent from the monastery, against the will of both the Duke and all of you, nevertheless after a few days we shall freely relinquish it and without any bargain, just as twenty-three years ago we were canonically elected to it without any bargain and without our knowledge. The earthly loss of dignity is easy for us, who know that we are mortal; nor do we weigh what we are called, but rather have judged that attention must be given to what we are.

But we marvel at the ingratitude of the prior, whom we have always exalted with singular goodwill and pursued with many benefits. O prior, most faithless of all monks, not undeservedly to be compared with Judas the betrayer, how impiously you have acted against us, unmindful of all the benefits we have bestowed upon you. Did we not, out of love for you, receive your parents, fugitives from the land of Luxembourg because of war and fire, poor and needy; did we not cherish them, and for twenty-three years now support them from the substance of the monastery, contrary to the opinion of many brothers; and did we not freely give them a dwelling with every kind of liberty in the village of Sponheim? We also arranged that a full prebend, sufficient for both of them, should be served to them daily from the monastery by our servants.

You too we caused to be ordained priest; then we took you on as our chaplain and table-companion; afterward we first appointed you cellarer of the monastery, and when it had become necessary to remove you from that office because of your fickleness, so that no disgrace might arise for you, we raised you to be our prior, though many protested. We never denied you anything you reasonably requested. You also, as you will not be able to deny, we always guarded like the pupil of our eye; and against all the murmurings of the brothers, which your negligence had stirred up, I, too trusting toward you, upheld and defended you for almost fourteen years now. But what kind of return you have made to us in this very tribulation of ours, we do not doubt that almighty God, who knows, will cause you to understand in his own time. We too, not in vengeance, but so that you may recognize that we have understood your ingratitude, shall write you a repayment in due time.

What now, most beloved elder Nutius, does it seem to you? Are we moved justly or unjustly to yield, we who have found such ingratitude and malice in our own man, in whom we used to trust above the rest? He writes eulogies against us under the name of the convent, while all are ignorant of it, he who could never with truth write anything evil about us. Perhaps the stupid man, full of ambition, thought that if letters of this kind should come into the hands of [Blank page in the source scan.]

[unclear] had come to ours, that, moved by insult, we should turn our arms against the convent, and by writing rather harshly make the brothers themselves averse to us, and by this means an entrance to the abbey would be afforded him. But we have resolved to dissemble everything, because we have no thought at all of returning to Sponheim. We shall not easily change our plan in this matter, unless perhaps, God forbid, we are compelled by the authority of our superiors. What hope of safety, what confidence of peace could there be for us with such men, who, forgetful of benefits, neither fear God nor reverence men, nor even consider the account of their own salvation? These things for now, most beloved brother, until the day comes for carrying out the plan. Farewell, mindful of us before God in your prayers. From Budori, on the fourteenth day of the month of August, in the year of Christians 1506.

LXVIII.

To the reverend fathers in Christ, the presidents, definitors, and the other abbots celebrating the annual council of the Order of St. Benedict at Mainz, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, reverence and honor.

I had determined, most beloved fathers, to come in person to the sacred convent of the order which you are now celebrating, on account of causes and business of no small importance that concern me, as you will understand partly from this letter of mine, partly from its bearer, Johannes Damius, my professed monk. But fortune, raging too fiercely against me, prevents it. For that most wicked tyrant, the count of Leiningen, who last year utterly destroyed the monastery of Limburg by fire, has occupied with robbers all the roads leading to Mainz, so that he may capture either me or the abbot of the said monastery, as we have been informed by many, both secretly and openly. For he lays snares for the aforesaid abbot because he accused him before the royal majesty and the princes concerning the plundering and burning of the monastery. He persecutes me for the same reason, because not only at Cologne but also in other places I always favored and advised the abbot's just cause, and was often present at many discussions against the tyrant. Offended by this, he pursues us both with grave hatred, and if we fall into his hands, we could not escape without danger.

Recently too, when I had returned from the March of Brandenburg with my whole household, which was then with me, the retainers of the same tyrant took me while I was staying in the monastery of Seebach, which has been committed to me, seized lodgings in the house, and led me to his neighboring castle, the tyrant himself being then absent. When he returned the next day and learned what had been done, he severely rebuked his men because they had let me go, and now he plots against me with even greater madness.

As for my affairs, I believe none of you is unaware how severely all of us who are placed under the protection of the most serene prince palatine were afflicted last year by the war and cruelty of the [Pinaleones?] Hessians, who, running through everything around us, plundered it, consuming churches along with villages by burning. From fear of them, since they did not even spare religion, I withdrew into the nearest town, and remained there until that whole disturbance had subsided. At length, returning to the monastery, I discovered that many things had been wrongly done in my absence, and that the morals of certain brothers had terribly degenerated from regular observance, and that they had committed such things as did not seem to be passed over entirely in silence, but rather deserved to be corrected according to the form of regular discipline.

But the authors of these crimes, fearing the punishment which they knew they had deserved, began by hidden machinations to defame and carry about on their tongues certain members of our household, about whom they suspected that I knew all the things that had been done from their report, first to the officials of Duke Johann, and then to certain others, laying upon them I know not what insult. Meanwhile it happened that I was summoned to Heidelberg in the case of the despoiled monastery of Limburg. When I had been there for several days, the officials of the aforementioned duke, by whose command I do not know, seized certain members of our household and put them in chains, at the insistence, as report has it, of the abbot of Mainz, who preferred to give credence to one fugitive monk rather than to me and my whole convent of Sponheim.

When news of this deed was brought to me, I seemed to myself not a little offended, and indeed not undeservedly, especially because, while I was absent and without first being warned, they presumed such things contrary to the order of law. For I feared what did happen: that the common crowd, otherwise too ready to believe evil, might suspect something unfavorable about me, as though those arrested were being detained on my account. Soon many things were being said by the people in varying opinions, and so great a rumor arose round about that I resolved not to return to the monastery before the rashness of those doing the injury should be punished with fitting satisfaction. I referred the whole affair to the prince palatine, with whose counsel and assent.

Familiar Letters

I could have, but I never wished to bring evil upon those who were causing harm, hoping that the Lord Jesus will reward the patience which he gave. Above all, it would have been grievous for me to leave my monastery with my friends forever; to have built the very beautiful structures which I built for another, perhaps an enemy and an ungrateful man; and, what surpasses everything, to leave behind me the library of two thousand very precious and very rare volumes, which, as is manifest, I alone brought together, without which I seemed to myself unable to live. This indeed held me back for several years by too great a love of it, so that I would not consent to richer abbacies, which were offered to me, as you know; it always drew me back too much. But now, after the persecution of rivals began to rage against me, I have bravely broken the bonds of love; for the love of Christ I have resolved to leave not only the library most dear to me up to this point, but also the monastery with everything belonging to it, my country, and my friends, lest perhaps, placed in the midst of rivals, the memory of injuries corrupt my mind. Nor, daughter, should you therefore think yourself deserted, since, God calling us, we depart to the Franks. For the Lord Jesus is able to give you a better provider, one who can look after the affairs of your monastery, both spiritual and temporal, much more usefully than I. Your bishop of Metz, in whose diocese your monastery is known to be situated, will not abandon you, but without doubt will provide you with a better abbot. Farewell, with all the sisters committed to you, praying to God for us. From Metz, on the twentieth day of the month of September, in the year of the Christians 1506.

LXXVI.

To the reverend father in Christ, Dom Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, Richmodis, abbess, Anna von Helmstatt, prioress, humble daughters of the whole convent of the monastery of St. Lawrence in Seebach, with prayers, would that they were devout, desire eternal happiness.

We wish your fatherhood to know that we have been saddened almost to death after reading the letters you sent us, in which you signify that you will leave your abbacy of Sponheim and proceed so far away from us. O why do you leave us, most reverend father, or to whom do you entrust us, most poor little sheep, whom you have been accustomed to feed so sweetly with the milk of heavenly doctrine? Who will there now be, most [unclear] father, who, in your manner, will distribute to us the sweetest sermons on the passion of Christ, on divine love, and on the delightfulness of the heavenly kingdom? Or who hereafter will console us in tribulations? To whose counsel shall we flee, or whom shall we call upon, bereft of your presence? Would that you could see the tears of your daughters; would that, having pity on the sheep committed to you, you would return to your monastery, since there is no one, as we have truly been informed, who does not most greatly desire your return to Sponheim. For the prior of Sponheim was here with us recently, and he said that that Duke Johann, together with all the rest, greatly desires that you return to Sponheim, and that he wishes always to be kind and gracious to you, and not to permit you to suffer any trouble. This same thing your brothers all desire, pray for, and beg; likewise the abbots of the order, who are said to have been at Mainz in chapter, all desire the same thing. Woe to us poor little women, captives enclosed, who are bereft of every human consolation, placed in the midst of enemies: the one refuge which we had, a father and faithful and most loving shepherd, we are compelled to lose while he is still living; we shall never be able to find one like him, who may have such power in learning, [unclear]. If it were lawful for us poor little women to leave the place in which we have been enclosed together, we would follow you wherever you would move, if only we could obtain the permission of the pontiff. But since it is necessary for us to remain fixed in the place, we humbly ask, petition, and beseech your fatherhood by this one thing always to be observed by us, for the shedding of the most precious blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom you have always been accustomed to honor in your preaching, that if you have altogether resolved to leave the abbacy of Sponheim, you should by no means on that account renounce the charge of this our monastery, which the lord bishop once gave to you, but should remain our visitor hereafter, just as you have already been until now for many years. For although Würzburg is farther from Seebach than Sponheim, your fatherhood will nevertheless be well able to visit us in its own time, if not every year.

496. FAMILIAR LETTERS.

…I remained outside [the monastery] up to the present day. My rivals, seeing that I was unwilling to return to the monastery, began to rage the more; whose threats I cared for little. I remained at Heidelberg and Speyer for two months, sick and infirm with fevers and the indignity of the deed, without the aid or consolation of my [friends], until at length, called by the most serene prince Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg, I went down to Cologne; and thence, my own Palatine prince consenting, I entered the March of Brandenburg itself with the margrave. Thence, after nine months, returning to [my] homeland, when I believed the tumults of [my] rivals settled, I found [them] stirred up by the ambition of certain agitators, as is said. Having considered each [thing], therefore, with myself, I resolved by no means henceforth to serve the ungrateful, nor to be under the dominion of one with whom lies prevail more than truth, and with whom the integrity of anyone's life took no confidence, [but] only the flattery of the impious took firmness. For I am of a will to leave the monastery, with the abbey of Sponheim, unless you reasonably decree otherwise—whom I desire to obey to the [best of my] powers. What [have] I [to do] with the Cynonoti [men of the Hunsrück]? Or what rest of mind can there be for me, set in the midst of the perverse? I trust in the LORD JESUS CHRIST, faithful Savior of souls, that he will not despise me, a poor servant, in the end, even if I be desolated by you all. For twenty years now and more (as you yourselves know) I have continuously labored for the community of the order and the chapter—by writing, speaking, [and] visiting, [and] by expediting innumerable causes and commissions of ours before bishops and princes and various others; nor does anyone live today in the order who has tolerated such great labors for the common good as you know me to have borne. Through Swabia, all Franconia, and Alsace, [and] through the dioceses of Trier, Cologne, Mainz, Speyer, Bamberg, Würzburg, and Strasbourg, not once or twice, but many times, at your command I visited; and for a long time, absent from my monastery at your command, I neglected my own [affairs], caring for others'. What reward have I obtained for all these? Unless the omnipotent God, in that future retribution of the just, confer on me, through his mercy, the reward of [my] labors, I should say all [is] lost before men. See what I have done, and you will understand how unjustly I suffer. For many years these evils have sprouted upon me, especially on this occasion: that, I being long occupied in visitations, my brothers did not live religiously enough, and secretly provoked the Cynonoti—of whom I now have experience—to hatred of me. I do not write from opinion: for manifest are the [things] which I say. But the faults of my brothers I neither will nor ought to bring into the light; rather, embracing patience, after the example of the holy fathers, I shall dismiss the incorrigible sheep. The rest I have committed to the aforesaid bearer, to be set forth to your paternities. I wish you well in Christ, mindful of me. From Boppard, the 20th day of the month of August, in the year of Christ [1506; the source misprints 1566], indiction 9.

JOHANNES TRITHEMIUS, to the abbot of the monastery of Saint Stephen in the city of Würzburg, greeting and charity. Reverend father, friend, and dearest brother: since, according to the common proverb, in necessity a true friend is proved [to be] whether he is true or false, I ask nothing of you in this my desolation more than that (if in any way it can be done) you come to me at Boppard, the chapter being celebrated. For there are many [things] conceived in my heart to be told you, which I can by no means commit to dead letters. Nor do I think it hidden from your charity by what storms of persecutions of certain Cynonoti I am driven—who think [it] a service to God if they have persecuted me gratis, laboring no less from envy than from hatred of me. But I, who know full well that through many tribulations the entrance to the kingdom of heaven lies open, have armed myself, as far as I could hitherto, with patience—the LORD JESUS bestowing [it]—not willing to render evil for evil, but rather to give place to wrath; and, absent from my monastery, I have remained to this day for the seventeenth month. The cause, indeed—not one only, but several—persuaded me never to return to the monastery. The duke of the Cynonoti, too credulous to my rivals, favors [their] evil parties, although he seems to wish that we return. But I will not follow the command of him who is reported to have said: "Let your abbot return to the monastery, fearing nothing; for I will do him neither evil nor good." You have sufficiently declared your mind toward us, O prince, nor is any interpreter needed, for we understand how well you favor our affairs—you who manifestly promise us nothing good to be done, just as you have not before done anything. Therefore, farewell; since henceforth I will not consent to be subjected to your dominion in eternity… forever. I shall follow the counsel of the Almighty, who permits nothing without cause; trusting in his mercy, I shall not fear what wicked men may do to me: ambitious, ungrateful men, who persecute me for this reason, that their ambition might be satisfied, as the outcome of the matter will prove. As report has it, my prior wrote against me, in the name of the community, [unclear] full of lies, fabricated without reason. Wondrous is the man’s deceitfulness. With almost continual letters he importunes me; with words too, and tears, whenever he comes to me, he prays, begs, asks, both in his own name and in that of the community, that we return to our monastery, promising all subjection and obedience, while in secret he contrives adversities against us. Moved by the scandal of this injury from the right hand, although with the favor and assistance of the most serene prince Palatine and of others I could repel these wrongs, and retain my abbacy even while absent from the monastery at all times, with the Duke and all my rivals not considered, nevertheless I have brought my mind to resigning, preferring to keep my conscience innocent of those evils that might follow, rather than avenge the insults inflicted. Therefore I resolved within myself to yield to such burdens of pastoral care, and henceforth in no way to serve the ungrateful, after the example of our most holy father Benedict and of very many fathers following him, who, provoked by the ingratitude of their own monks, left the pastoral care of sickly sheep and betook themselves to other places to provide for their own salvation. But we shall discuss these matters fully when your charity comes to us at Heidelberg, where I, the abbot of Limburg, await you together with the [Schottern?] abbot, and we altogether hope that you will come. I pray that your paternity may long fare well and safely.

From Budori, on the 20th day of the month of August, in the year of the Lord 1506.

LXX.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, sends greetings to Henry, Abbot of Bursfelde.

God alone, best and greatest of all, who is ignorant of nothing, knowing the hidden things of hearts, he himself knows how unwillingly I absented myself from the chapter, having no small cause, under whose pressure I would more than gladly have been present at its celebration, had not the savagery of the tyrant count prevented me, just as it prevented the abbot of Limburg. For by the counsels of many we were advised not to expose ourselves to so great a danger of the roads. For we are not ignorant of his malice, which is so great that he neither fears God nor reveres man. He is full of a demon, almost mad, as one who in the preceding year, when war was raging against the poor, not only the monastery of Limburg but also several other most beautiful churches, doing the devil’s work, utterly destroyed by setting them on fire. Hence he always presumes with a savage and disturbed conscience. If he should capture me again, which God avert, who would free me from the hands of a madman? The issue is for body and life, which I have held should be preferred to the whole world. I have determined with myself what I shall do, having deliberated maturely by the counsel not of one night but of several months. I intend shortly to resign my abbacy and, with God’s help and the prince’s favor, to provide for myself elsewhere, where I can do so more quietly.
