I do not desire to return to Sponheim, nor do I wish for reconciliation with the Duke, since he who showed himself hostile to me without cause will not hereafter have me under his dominion. There are two men in Sponheim who were the instigators of the whole evil, of whom one is the prior, the other was the cellarer; each aspires to the abbacy. Let the fathers allow them to prevail if they wish; I shall turn myself to the path of peace and avoid the company of the impious. The abbot of St. James at Mainz would have forestalled all these evils, if he had not believed falsehood more than truth. For the cellarer, publicly detected in crime, while I indeed was absent, fearing punishment, fled to that abbot himself; in order to defend his own vices, he falsely invented another’s. The latter believed the liar rather than the truth, and thought the whole thing a Gospel which the brother had devised in his own defense. When I returned to the monastery and had learned the history of the deed, I was indeed deeply grieved not only at the brother’s crime but also at the rashness of the abbot, who was defending such a criminal fugitive against the testimony of all the brothers. Meanwhile, since I had been unwilling to follow the precipitate opinion of many, it happened that I was called again to Heidelberg, where, while I was occupied for a rather long time in the business of the burned monastery of Limburg, that same brother, out of hatred for those who had disclosed his deed, with certain of the lay-brothers consenting to him, brought about so much that some of them were captured, with the aforementioned abbot no less procuring it. What followed afterward your paternity will understand more clearly from the brother whom I sent you. Farewell, best father; pray to God for us.

From Budori, on the 30th day of the month of August, in the year of the Christians 1506. And in his own hand, very hastily.

Familiar Letters. LXXI.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, sends greetings to his excellent brother Roger Sycambro.

There came to me at Budori, on the fourth day of this month, John in Schorteren, Conrad of St. Stephen’s at Würzburg, and George in Schwarzach, abbots of monasteries of our order, sent by the annual chapter lately held at Mainz. In brief, they had these instructions: that by their words they should persuade me to return to the monastery. They said also that two other fathers had been appointed by the chapter, who were to approach the Duke in the name of the whole Bursfeld union and make him reconciled to me.

When I heard this, I answered that there was no need for men appointed on my account to approach the Duke, since I neither seek nor desire his reconciliation or favor. Far be it from me hereafter to be subject to the lordship of a man with whom falsehood has very great power and truth can do nothing. Having suffered an exceedingly rash injury, both from the Duke and from three men of my community, I shall not return to them any more, but shall resign the abbacy as soon as I have made some provision for my affairs.

After receiving this answer, when they saw that my opinion was fixed, the envoys troubled me no further, but wrote back to the abbots appointed by the chapter that there was no need of any effort with the Duke, because I had altogether resolved not to return any more to Spanheim. God will provide for me where I may remain, with greater peace than I have ever lived in at Spanheim. But if you wish to know whither I intend to betake myself, I do not know what I should answer. Three great princes await me, but it does not please me to follow the courts of princes. Three abbots also, more powerful men of the order which I have professed, ask me to come to them.

But lest you think it a fable, I shall give the names of each. Maximilian, most serene King of the Romans, has several times, as our men know, caused me to be solicited to enter his service. There is no need for me to bring the Margrave of Brandenburg forward, since you know how highly he esteems me. Philip also, Duke of Bavaria, Count Palatine of the Rhine, a most gracious prince, has promised to provide for me abundantly as long as I live, either with the Abbot of Limburg, or in his own principality, wherever I may wish. Lastly, the above-mentioned Abbot of St. Stephen’s has now told me that the abbey of St. James the Greater, apostle, in the suburb of Würzburg, will shortly become vacant through the resignation of the present abbot; if I am willing to take it up, he said that he would make effort that the matter should take effect as soon as possible.

I have agreed to the plan, preferring to live in poverty under monastic discipline than to live richly in the courts of princes. These matters being thus concluded, the fathers sent to me by the chapter departed on the eighth day of September, to return to their own places. But I await the answer of the often-mentioned abbot, namely whether the matter so pleases the most reverend father, the Bishop of Würzburg; when that has at last been received, I shall make you more certain about everything.

Farewell, from Budori, on the twelfth day of September, in the year of the Lord 1506.

LXXII.

Conrad, Abbot of St. Stephen’s at Würzburg, sends greetings to Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim.

Reverend father, in accordance with the departure from our mutual conclusion most recently made in the monastery of the nuns of Neuburg near Heidelberg, as soon as I arrived home I approached the lord most reverend Bishop of Würzburg. Among other conversations concerning the monastery of St. James, I made mention of your paternity, asserting that it would be possible, if it pleased his most reverend paternity, for your paternity to be placed over the same monastery. Hearing this, he said that it was greatly pleasing to him, and he promised that he wished graciously to favor your paternity and faithfully to lend helping hands; he also enjoined me to signify these things to your paternity as soon as possible.

Therefore let your paternity now make no delay, which our most reverend lord himself is accustomed to take very ill in all matters. The rest I reserve for mutual conversation, which may the Most High deign to make prosperous and pleasant. Given at Würzburg on the day of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, in the year of Christians 1506.

LXXIII.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, sends greetings to Conrad, Abbot of St. Stephen’s.

Your letter, venerable father, dated the sixteenth day of this month of September, I received at Budorras, in the new castle monastery; when it had been reread, the mind of the most reverend Of Johannes Trithemius.

at the same time I have understood your paternity's [unclear]. I give you very great thanks for your charity toward me, and I shall gladly give greater thanks, if ever I am able. For although, by the favor and piety of princes, sufficient provision could have been made for me, yet because I am a cloistered man and devoted to the study of the Scriptures, I prefer to lie hidden in a poor monastery rather than be held most illustrious among courtiers. I shall imitate that man of innocence who said: I have chosen to be lowly in the house of the Lord, rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners. I shall come, therefore, around the end of September, meanwhile dispatching certain affairs of mine here and at Neometum; when these have been completed, I shall take care to be with you without delay. And I beg that it not be irksome to make this intention of mine known to the most reverend bishop of Würzburg. But if some circumstance intervenes by which I shall be unable to be present at the end of September, do not think at once that my coming is to be despaired of, because I shall certainly come, if God prolongs my life with health, and I shall not disappoint you in your expectation. Meanwhile farewell happily, mindful of me in your prayers to God. Again farewell. From Budori, on the 17th day of September, in the year of the Christians 1506.

LXXIII. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, to Roger Sycambro, greetings.

What I had promised you, most beloved Roger, in my last letter to you, I now do, though in this very brief one, with great willingness. I received the letter of Conrad, abbot of St. Stephen, on the 16th day of this month at Budora, in which he indicated that the most reverend prelate of Würzburg, Laurence, was well disposed toward my affairs; and also that he was offering me the abbey of St. James, formerly of the Scots, not only willingly but indeed most cheerfully, and had commanded me to hasten as quickly as possible to accept it. I shall therefore remain here at Neometum for only a few days, for the dispatch of certain affairs of mine; when these have been arranged, we shall direct our journey toward Würzburg. But before we depart from these regions, we wish to see and speak with you. Yet since, as you know, we are quite unable to come to you because of the savagery of the incarnate demon, who is to be called a devil rather than a man, not by nature but rather by imitation, we urge, ask, and beseech you again and again to come to us. For we are turning over in our mind many things to discuss with you which we cannot commit to letters. We have also written to your prior, asking that by his authority he grant you permission to come. Bring with you your little book on the varied use of letters; for there are certain things written in it, if I remember rightly, for which a more delicate file will be necessary, especially in those matters that concern the Greek language, in the understanding of which you have not yet made sufficient progress. I shall assist as much as I can, lest this little work of yours go out from your workshop into public uncorrected. Break off delays, since we shall not remain here beyond four days. Farewell. From the city of Neometum, on the 20th day of September, in the year of the Christians 1506.

LXXV. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Spanheim, to Richmodis von Horst, abbess in Sebach, greetings.

Today, dearest daughter in Christ, the eighteenth month is passing since we have been living away from our monastery, moved by the rashness of rivals. Whence, after many counsels and mature deliberation, having resolved that we must by no means return to Spanheim any more, it has at last been worthwhile to make provision where we should stay. A certain abbey is offered to us, situated in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, which we know well: poor and modest indeed, but very quiet and tranquil, and, as we hope, sufficiently suitable for our purpose; persuaded by the counsel of friends, we have judged that it should not be spurned. Your charity knows very well with how many labors we have been afflicted for twenty-three continuous years now in Spanheim, not only in the government of our own monastery, but much more for the common utility of the whole order. But now, after we have plainly experienced the brothers' ingratitude toward us, we do not believe it safe to remain with them any longer, since neither will they ever hereafter be faithful to us, nor shall we truly be able any longer to trust those by whom we have been so enormously deceived. And while we, for our part, are living so fearfully, who does not understand how great a danger to souls would follow, when neither can the shepherd entrust himself to the sheep Familiar Letters.

to believe, nor could the sheep henceforth have secure access to their shepherd. And although perhaps I could put away every grudge from my heart, nevertheless the brothers who are the authors of these evils would neither believe this very thing, nor would they easily change their depraved habits. For we know well how difficult it is to recall monks depraved by evil habit to the rectitude of newness. For the wise man says: “A young man according to his way, even when he has grown old, will not depart from it.” For habit is likened to nature, which no one resists without difficulty, as blessed Gregory says: “Depraved habits hold him whom they have once seized, and, growing harder every day, are ended only when the sinner’s life is ended.”

There are, besides, many reasons by consideration of which I am moved to yield, but very few by which I could be induced to remain. Most of all, however, I have been moved, as I might say, into hatred of the place by the duke’s inconstancy and the rashness of his people, to such a degree that I can no longer put faith in his promises, nor believe him when he asks pardon, nor accept the favor he offers. Let the men of Sponheim henceforth live in the countryside with peasants, since it had seemed excessively grievous to them to have someone of whom even princes might boast. For the sake of seeing me, learned men, and men most highly educated in every faculty, were accustomed to come to Sponheim from almost all Germany, from Italy, Gaul, and the other adjacent kingdoms. Princes and powerful men of this age sent to me their messengers and envoys in literary matters, as the whole neighborhood knows; and I certainly neither ought nor wished to send them away unheard, or without the honor of hospitality, although several of them lawfully made satisfaction for their expenses. All those around saw these things and praised what was done. Only two monks from among my subjects, and all the lay brothers, whom in the usual word we call donati, could not look on it with an even mind; but they murmured in secret, as is the custom of such men, and by their unjust denunciations gradually stirred up against me the duke himself, who did not sufficiently value students and learned men. I shall therefore give place to wrath, that they may prosper with the peasants, they who have always despised saving doctrine. The Most High, I trust, will provide for me a place more suited to my studies; for the many labors in which I have sweated at Sponheim, he will deign to grant me rest elsewhere.

But you, dearest daughter in Christ, together with the holy virgins committed to you, stand firmly in the purpose of holiness until the end, so that, when the journey of this present life has been completed, you may deserve to be admitted with the holy virgins to the marriage-feast of the bridegroom, the eternal king. Always love with your whole heart your Lord Jesus Christ, to whom you have devoted yourself entirely, and love him above all things, who for love of you became man. The more you have loved him, the more fit you will become for entry into the kingdom of heaven, since he himself is the way by which one goes to the fatherland; he himself is the truth through which the highest good is known; he himself also is the love of God, by which all the plagues of the soul are swiftly healed, the understanding also is wondrously illuminated for knowledge of all things, and the affection is cleansed from every dustiness of worldly attachment. For whoever loves the Lord Jesus with his whole heart leaves in himself no place at all for vices and sins; nor is the devil allowed to enter the soul which is wholly occupied by divine love, because the devil thoroughly considers a soul empty of virtues more suitable for himself. Happy is that conscience in whose secret chamber, besides the love of Christ, which is wisdom, chastity, patience, purity, and justice, no other love has its place; where the heart of one who loves God never sighs even at the recollection of a human being, nor desires to see anything transitory in the world.

Let your love for God be constant and perfect, O virgin betrothed to the company of Christ, so that, if it should be necessary, you may die for love of him who for love of you deigned to die peacefully and kindly. O how sweet, pleasant, strong, and powerful is your love, Lord Jesus, which makes the mind despise eternal [unclear], keeps the conscience pure from every uncleanness, perfectly illuminates the soul of the one who loves, and most robustly strengthens the heart of the weakest human being against all adversities of this world. Therefore love God, O virgin of Christ; love wholly with your whole self, so that you may be able without labor to conquer all things and destroy sins, because charity covers a multitude of sins, makes a human being near to God, and glorious in all the adversities of the world. For it belongs to tender service and delicate combat to carry off victory over all enemies by love alone. Therefore, that you may bravely conquer all the evils of this age, stand bravely constant in the love of God. For you will conquer the more powerfully the more strongly you have loved, as Saint Bernard says: “O yoke of holy love, how sweetly you take captive, how gloriously you ensnare, how pleasantly you press, how delightfully you burden, how strongly you bind, how prudently you instruct.” O happy love, from which arises accessible. Music teaches song; astronomy teaches the ecclesiastical computus, without knowledge of which no one is found sufficiently fit for the priesthood. But if we wish to describe a master of the seven liberal arts, those things which we said pertain to a priest will not suffice. For the method of a master teaching in the schools is one thing, and that of a priest preaching in the Church is another. For the latter, indeed, a use of the sciences drawn from an art in a certain general way is sufficient; but upon the former the necessary office of teaching enjoins that even the particulars of the individual arts be examined particularly in their special character, so that he may know not only how to use the sciences he has acquired, but also how to give rules and precepts to his pupils for acquiring them. But you, who, after receiving the mastership and leaving the schools of the artists, have betaken yourself to Christ’s school, having been made a priest and minister in the Church of God, retaining only the necessary use of secular letters, turn yourself henceforth wholly to the study of the divine Scriptures, in which true saving knowledge is contained, and heavenly wisdom sweetly illumines the mind. For all the knowledge of this world is vain if it has not been turned to the worship of God. But sacred Scripture, which we rightly call divine, far exceeds all the knowledge and teaching of this world, since it proclaims true things without ambiguity, calls the mind of the gentle reader from earthly things to heavenly ones, and, for the love of God, renders it humble in prosperity and strong and constant in adversities. This is the force of the sacred river which makes glad the city of God, at once shallow and deep, in which both the simple and little lamb may walk and the greatest elephant may swim. Wondrous is that river, in which the simple Christian, even without literature, may, so to speak, pass securely to salvation with dry feet; and the great and subtly learned man can swim by being soberly wise, and, if he searches too deeply, be submerged. For it has, in public, that from which it nourishes little ones, and it keeps hidden that by which it leads the minds of the lofty into wonder. For in one and the same utterance, while it narrates history, it unfolds manifold mystery; on the surface it sweetly refreshes the simple, and in the secrets of mystery it sublimely exercises the wise. In what is open it is drink, because it needs no breaking; in the more obscure parts it is food, because it cannot be swallowed without the breaking of exposition. Therefore Saint Ambrose instructs us, saying: We ought long to rub and polish the utterances of the heavenly Scriptures, turning them over with our whole mind and heart, so that that spiritual juice may spread into all the veins of the soul. Rich and most fertile is the field of the divine Scriptures; it has within itself all delights and brings forth every sweetness. And just as manna tasted in the mouth according to the will of each person, so the divine word will furnish in your heart every flavor you wish. Nothing can be better, sweeter, or more pleasant for a Christian priest than if at all times he occupies himself with the sacred Scriptures with the desire of his heart, and keeps himself clean from this wicked age. For blessed Jerome says: Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. Therefore let the divine Scriptures always be in your hands, and let them be turned over in your heart by continual meditation; and do not think it sufficient to keep the commandments of God in memory and to forget them in works, but read them often for this reason, that you may do what you have learned. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of God’s commandments who receive from him the crown of righteousness. Live in such a way that you may deserve to attain the wisdom, the knowledge of divine and human things, necessary for you, because there is no more pitiable poverty, or more shameful want, than for one established in the priestly order to lack wisdom, and for him who is commanded by office to teach others to be a foolish man and without learning. Farewell, and pray to God for us. From Würzburg, on the 24th day of the month of June, in the year of Christ 1506.

II.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James in the suburb of Würzburg, to the prior and convent at Sponheim: to have continual fear of the divine name.

Almighty God, whose power is eternal and whose will is never unjust, holy and just in all his works, who permits nothing without cause. He himself, just, holy, and merciful, has made all things in true judgment, since he is good and almighty; he does absolutely no injury to anyone, he who keeps truth forever and ever, who executes judgment for those suffering injury, who gives food to the hungry. The Lord raises up those who have been cast down; the Lord loves the righteous. The Lord kills and makes alive; he brings down to the lower world and brings back. The Lord makes poor and enriches; he humbles and exalts. He raises the needy from the dust, and from the dung lifts up the poor. He will preserve the feet of his saints, and the impious shall be silent in darkness. If it had not been that the Lord was among us, let Abbot Trithemius now say, if it had not been that the Lord was among us, when wicked men rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive. When madness was enraged Of Johannes Trithemius.

...the vigor of morals, the purity of affections, the subtlety of understandings, the holiness of desires, the brightness of works, the eloquence of virtues, the dignity of merits, and the sublimity of rewards. Divine love is an unfailing treasure: whoever has it is rich; whoever does not have it, even if he possessed the riches of Croesus, is the poorest of all. God first loved us, not with a common love, but sweetly, wisely, and strongly.

Sweetly indeed, because he assumed human flesh for us; wisely, because he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth; strongly, because for us he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Behold, virgin, Christ in his very self showed you beforehand the form of divine love which you must follow, if you wish to enter his bridal chamber. Love Christ Jesus himself sweetly, so that you desire nothing besides him; prudently, so that you are not deceived by the vanity of the flesh; love strongly, so that in the adversities of this world you are never cast down from your holy purpose. For there is need of these three columns of divine love, since whoever loves Christ sweetly loves him alone and desires nothing contrary to him, as Augustine says: “He loves you less, Lord, who loves anything together with you which he does not love for your sake.” Therefore you love sweetly if you love Jesus for no other thing than for himself, and indeed for him alone. For you know what he himself says in sacred Scripture: “I am the Lord your God, strong and jealous.” He alone wishes to be loved by you; he admits no partner, nor can love be sweet if it is shared among a diversity of objects. You should also love the Lord Jesus wisely, since he is the wisdom of God the Father, who wishes to be loved not only sweetly but also wisely; otherwise the spirit of error will very easily mock your zeal, when you have neglected the knowledge of a wise lover. For the cunning enemy has no more effective medicine for removing the love of Christ from a person’s heart than if he can bring it about that one walks in it without reason and incautiously. Therefore Scripture commands salt to be offered in every sacrifice, just as God made and ordered all things wisely. The manner of loving God is that you love him as much as you can, since the more you have loved him, the better it will be for the beloved.

Love your Lord Jesus strongly too, O virgin, that is, perseveringly, so that neither prosperity nor adversity may soften or turn your mind away from love of him. Jesus must be loved with the greatest fervor unto death, no less in adversity than in favorable circumstances, and not on account of any accessory thing, but for himself alone, because Jesus is the most worthy cause of love for him. Let the Lord Jesus be your portion, O cloistered virgin: nothing is to be cared for by you, nothing thought of, nothing loved except Jesus himself, to whom you have devoted yourself in mind and body, whose love is sweeter than all honey; whoever truly loves him desires nothing in this world except him. The love of Jesus is sufficient in all things for the one who loves; it suffers no want, neither yields to adversity nor is softened by prosperity; it is constant in itself, abundantly sufficient for itself, since inwardly in the Lord Jesus it possesses all things, requiring none of those things that seem to be outside. For whoever wishes to have Jesus as a friend necessarily despises all things. Therefore, as the cloistered virgin approaches the love of Christ, let her stand in fear and prepare her soul for temptation, since whoever seeks the friendship of Jesus should know that he must endure the enmities of many; and for this reason let him prepare himself for humble patience, lest he lose holy friendship before he perfectly attains it.

Indeed, when the soul has joined itself to the Word of God, let it know without doubt that it will at once have enemies, and that those whom it formerly had as friends will very often be turned into adversaries. Therefore one must persevere strongly in the love of God, and the spirit must be strengthened against whatever adversities occur, lest, placed in the middle of the road, it fail on the journey or, terrified by the magnitude of its labors, turn back. For if Christ Jesus, who had no sin, had to suffer and so enter into his glory, how much more must we wretched human beings, conceived, born, and brought up in sins, who by sinning daily make ourselves worse, necessarily endure many adversities; we who suffer by our own demerit whatever evil befalls us. If Scripture does not hesitate to recall the many tribulations of the just, let it seem wonderful to no one if we sinners, stripped of works of righteousness, though converted and penitent, endure many adversities.

Hence [unclear] says: “For patience is necessary for you, so that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promise.” It belongs to Christians, and especially to the cloistered, to overcome injuries by keeping silent and fleeing, rather than by answering or resisting; and the more the profession of monastic life binds us to perfection, so much less is it permitted for us to repel force by force, but rather we must endure whatever adversities with greater patience. We are Christians and cloistered persons, very greatly bound to humility; for this reason all grievous and bitter things must be borne patiently by us for the love of Christ. In order that I might prove myself a servant of Christ, though a useless one, behold how many things I have endured without deserving them, which I could have turned back upon my rivals,

Hebrews 10.

Monks most of all lack the showing of patience. in years, at least once every two or three years, and meanwhile more often to be comforted by the sweetest letters, as was formerly customary. For you know that I can find no other abbot nearer to us who is fit to preserve in us the holy institution of regular discipline, which your reverend paternity planted with great labor and has laudably continued up to the present. Therefore we beg again and again, by the most innocent death of our Lord Jesus Christ: hear us in this petition of ours, if it cannot be done for another, since we seek things just and holy, salutary for us, and not impossible for you. We send with these letters our procurator, through whom we unanimously request and await the response of your reverend paternity. May almighty God long preserve you, sweetest father, for our advantage and that of many. From Seebach, on the twenty-first day of September, in the year 1506.

LXXVII.

John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, to his sweetest daughters in Christ, the abbess and convent in Seebach: sincere greeting and charity in the Lord.

The letters of your charities we received at Neumarkt, in which you signify your tears and sighs for us. We do indeed grieve with you from the heart, but it cannot be otherwise. Sponheim, as we have resolved, we shall abandon because of the ingratitude of the monks, not caring for the words of the prior, whom we know to be deceitful. For he says one thing and ponders another in his heart. We do not heed the mind of the duke, nor do we care for the wishes of those who are with him, since, if either must be, we have resolved at all times rather to beg than henceforth to be subject to his rule. We know and have learned by the report of many that he is greatly pained at what has been done, that he desires us to return to the monastery, and that he promises faithfully to maintain us; but we do not seek the favor of one whom we have experienced as provoking us so ill-advisedly, unjustly, and rashly.

As for the commission long ago made to us concerning you through Ludovicus the bishop, we shall gladly do what you unanimously request: namely, that we retain the name of visitor together with the office, until better provision can be made for you. For although I shall by no means be able to come to you personally as often as hitherto, nevertheless I shall come in writing, until at last it may someday happen that I come in person. But while the affairs of the Limpurgers are set in turmoil, no abbot or monk of our order will dare to approach your Seebach because of the savagery of your count, much less I, who am charged with having always adhered to the just causes of the Limpurgers against the count. Hence you will necessarily remain without visitation for some time, until concord has been restored between the abbot and the count himself.

Therefore we ask you in the Lord, dearest daughters, to attend diligently to your calling in all charity and patience, living humbly according to the Rule of our most holy father Benedict, so that, advancing daily in the peace and love of God, you may have the Holy Spirit as visitor, who is accustomed to rest upon the humble, quiet person who keeps the admonitions of God. Do not sadden the mother who presides over you in solicitude, but imitate her fervor in the service of God, obeying humbly in all things. For she herself, as you perceive by word and example, always precedes you first in the choir in all holiness, so diligent and careful in divine service that she seems to have no occupation in temporal matters; yet so occupied in external matters that no time for prayer can seem to remain.

Before all things preserve mutual charity among yourselves, since where charity is not, there can be no justice. For love of neighbor works no evil. Charity, indeed, the bond of perfection and the fount and origin of all virtues, covers a multitude of sins; without it no one will be able to have true contrition of heart, no one will obtain pardon for crimes. Love of neighbor, conformed to divine love, is a wave of peace, a shower of charity, the seed of concord, the merit of eternal happiness. Therefore almighty God commands each one of us, saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. This neighbor is to be considered not by nearness of blood but by fellowship of reason, in which all human beings are companions. For this reason you have been gathered in a monastery, that by the mutual aids of charity you may protect your weakness; therefore always keep the mutual observance of love, so that you may satisfy the monastic institution, just as the holy Apostle commanded: bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. For charity alone is what conquers all things; without it all things are of no avail, which if Familiar Letters.

... if it has truly existed in you, will make you true brides of Christ. May almighty God cause you to burn in his love; and that you may render him favorable to us by your prayers, we most earnestly ask, mindful of our labors, which for your common benefit we have now borne for many [unclear]. Farewell, living without stain in the Lord Jesus. From Neumagen, on the 22nd day of the month of September, in the Christian year 1506.

LXXVIII.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, to Brother Johannes of Frankfurt, greetings.

Beloved brother, for certain reasonable causes we intend to leave our monastery of Sponheim and to resign its abbacy, which we have possessed for twenty-four years. But lest on that account the convent of Christ's brides at Seebach should incur some danger, we shall continue for a longer time the commission over it made to us by the bishops of Speyer, at the humble entreaty of the abbess and convent, until they can find for themselves a more suitable visitor. Therefore we entrust and command to your charity that you execute and guard with all diligence and solicitude those things that concern the office entrusted to you, just as you heard from us when we were lately present in that monastery. Refrain from wandering excursions outside the convent, and do not ever enter the enclosure alone. Obey the commands of the abbess, knowing yourself to be the servant, not the lord, of Christ's virgins. In the remaining matters, strive to conform yourself to the little rule prescribed to you. Farewell. From Neumagen, on the 22nd day of the month of September, in the year 1506.

LXXIX.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of the Monastery of St. James the Apostle, [unclear] in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, to James Trithemius, his very dear brother, greetings.

To your desire, sweetest brother, as far as I could, I have yielded a little; and copies of certain letters of mine, which I wrote from the day of my departure from Sponheim down to the present day, as many as remained, I have brought together in the present volume. For we did not keep copies of all of them with us, because we were rather often compelled to make haste in writing. But in this volume itself we have gathered sixty-six letters of ours, and have joined to them twelve letters from others sent to us, all of which, together with this one to you, make seventy-nine in all. In them, in our customary manner, we seem to ourselves to have used a familiar style of writing, not pursuing eloquence out of admiration for ourselves, for there has never been any eloquence in us, but using scholastic speech, by which we may easily be understood. You know, moreover, that on the first day of the month of April I left my monastery, and have never returned there afterwards down to this day. We departed, then, in the year of the Christians 1505, on the first of April, as we have said; and we received this abbacy of St. James on the fifteenth day of the month of October of the following year. Thus all the time between our departure from Sponheim and our entry here amounted to eighteen months and thirteen days. The present letters belonged to this period, which we have handed over to you, most pleasant brother, not for your instruction, but rather as a memorial of ourselves. Those, however, which we wrote earlier we left at Sponheim, not yet gathered into order; if at some time we put them into order and you should wish to have them, you will easily obtain them. But those which we have given afterwards, or shall write in the future, comprised in another volume, we shall likewise not withhold from you in their own time. Farewell from our monastery of St. James the Apostle Major in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, on the 28th day of the month of December, in the year of Christ 1506.

End of the Sponheim Letters of Trithemius, Abbot.

Joan- The second book of the familiar letters of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James of Würzburg, to Jacob Trithemius, his most dear brother.

I.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of the holy Apostle James in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, to Master Jacob Trithemius, his only and most dear brother, greetings.

[unclear] In order that we may be approved by a full brotherly affection toward you, we have thought it proper, for a fine reason, to connect this first book of our Würzburg letters with the last of the Sponheim letters, which we dedicated to you. For in that one you read the miseries of our calamities; in this one, the compositions of a mind rightly and gladly at leisure after quiet had followed. For we wrote the letters of the previous volume as abbot of the monastery of Sponheim; those sent in this book, however, we issued nevertheless as abbot of St. James of Würzburg.

What we did in the first, we promise also in this one: that we have not copied out the forms of all the letters, but only of those which we thought would please you. Also letters of friends sent to us, not all indeed, but a few out of many, which we judged worthy of your reading.

We exhort you, brother: imitate the studies of the wise, and flee the sloth of fools, knowing Solomon’s saying that a wise son makes his father glad, but a foolish son is the sorrow of his mother. While age permits and memory is strong, one must learn, since, as Seneca truly said, studies will make you renowned and noble; thus without studies the mind is sick, with no distinction among its marks. Human understanding is compared to gold, which lies fouled with the dust and mire of ignorance unless it is continually cleansed by the file of exercise; and neither gold attains its beauty, nor understanding its natural knowledge.

There are three things which are often accustomed to obstruct those intent on the study of the Scriptures: namely negligence, imprudence, and fortune. Negligence hinders us whenever we either extravagantly abandon or pursue with too little zeal those things which are profitably to be learned by us. Against this corrupter of salutary study, the venerable company of studious men and of those who continually exercise themselves in the arena of the Scriptures offers the best remedy; it is found in public schools in many places, but in the cloisters of monasteries in few. For today the study of the Scriptures is despised by many cloisters of almost all orders, and seems to flourish in few monasteries.

Imprudence, however, overturns us while we are studying when we do not preserve the proper order in the things we learn. For either we desire to learn things that are not suitable for us, or, sometimes neglecting the more useful, we rashly take up the less useful, or we do not distribute even good and useful things to the proper time. It is highly improper for nobler minds to be dishonored by lesser studies, and for those whom arduous and weightier studies await to be occupied with vain and useless exercises. Lest we fall into this evil while learning, the best teachers must be chosen by us, by whose instruction and likewise example we may attain a suitable order of studies.

Fortune also lies in wait for the studious in many ways, as each one of us experiences daily who strives for the ascent of true philosophy. For by various events, poverty, riches, illness, honors, prosperity and adversity alike, by which at times individually the mind of a studious man is intercepted, he is prevented from apprehending the knowledge he desires. The natural slowness of the intellect, lack of books, and scarcity of suitable teachers have drawn many back from progress in salutary study. Riches have often harmed philosophers; they have recalled more people from study than poverty has. Honor, beauty of body, and prosperity teem with the same poison, and have provided more people with an occasion for ignorance than for wisdom.

But love conquers natural slowness of intellect, if diligent continuation of studies is applied. The ancients could allege lack of books; but abundance has rather made us poor, since the art of printing, invented in our days at Mainz and now spread throughout the whole world, brings to light so many renewals of ancient and new doctors that now, for a small amount of money, anyone can be learned. Nor are teachers of good studies lacking today, but everywhere on earth they abound in every variety of discipline, not only in the Latin language, but also in Greek and Hebrew. These are truly golden times, in which the studies of good letters, neglected for many years, have flourished again.

Nor do I wish you to drink more deeply of secular literature than is necessary for attaining the divine Scriptures, lest there be verified in you what a certain wise man said concerning lovers of vanity, such as many are today, saying: [unclear]

Where and when the art of printing was invented. Familiar Letters

They do not know necessary things, because they have learned superfluous ones. True knowledge is that which leads to the knowledge of God; it corrects morals, restrains pleasures, purifies affection; it enlightens the intellect in those things that pertain to the salvation of the soul, and inflames the heart with love of the Creator. This is salutary knowledge, which affects the mind in the love of God and does not puff it up, which does not make men proud but makes them lamenting, which does not follow vanity, but, drawing all things to one, is most sweetly made firm in divine love. Brother, we desire you to be devoted to this knowledge, by which alone there is the completion of all the sciences.

Let not the degree of mastership exalt you so as to make you less intent upon the study of the Scriptures; but know that you must [unclear] so much the more, because you have received a manifest sign of knowledge, and especially the name of doctor. I do not esteem highly a bright degree without knowledge, or a great title with little learning; rather, we seek learned men, since we have many doctors. Knowledge commends the degree, not the degree knowledge. It is shameful for a master not to know, and for one who publicly bears the sign of knowledge not to have necessary learning. What is a hoop displayed before a house where no wine is sold? Or what is a royal sceptre in the hands of a fool? A sign is bestowed without the thing signified whenever an unlearned man, and one without knowledge, is raised to be a doctor. And, shame to say, how frequent today in the schools among certain people is that abuse, by which the degree of mastership is given as a sign where a sufficient thing signified is not found.

Does it not seem to you that I have spoken the truth, since the world swarms alike with masters and doctors, among whom fewer learned men and many unlearned are encountered? You must take care, my dear, to adorn mastership with knowledge and priesthood with holy morals, lest you be confounded by a double reproach, if you are regarded both as a doctor without knowledge and as a priest without the merit of holiness.

The noble office of priest: a degree without knowledge.

The knowledge necessary to you is, first of all, to know God, to understand the divine Scriptures, to know the canons of the fathers, not to be ignorant of both human and divine law insofar as it concerns your office, to cultivate virtues, and to love God above all things with a pure heart. It pertains to a master to know the principles of the arts he professes, so that he may know how to unravel knots, clarify tropes, and explain all the figures of the Scriptures.

The seven liberal arts.

You are called master of the seven liberal arts; let us see how much knowledge you have attained of each one, so that you may understand how their use becomes necessary to you. First, through the art of grammar, which is the foundation of the seven liberal arts, you ought to know how to write in Latin, speak fittingly, and utter correct speech without fault. Rhetoric, surpassing the common manner of speaking, seeks a certain beautiful adornment in speaking, uses tropes and various colors, and strives to set forth the cause proposed to it in beautiful and most pleasing speech; when it has persuaded, it has arrived at the end of oratory with the reward proposed to it. Logic, the rational science, teaches you to discern the true from the false, lest you be deceived by subtlety of speech or fall into the syllogisms of deceitful arguments. For knowledge precedes the cultivation of virtue, because no one can faithfully desire what he does not know; and evil, unless known, can by no means be avoided.

Arithmetic teaches how to multiply given numbers, also to divide them, and in every variety to find the certain root. All things consist in number, and he who is ignorant of arithmetic has the perfection of no science. By knowledge of the art of geometry you will understand the measurement of the earth, arising from numbers and measure: a beautiful science indeed, and adorned with the figures of arithmetic, through which human reasoning rises in no small measure to the knowledge of the highest principle. This measures the broad circuit of the world, describes all the spaces of sea and land, and, when completed, ascends into cosmography. Nothing is more beautiful than this contemplation, in which the mind, transcending the whole structure of the world, marvels at the incomprehensible wisdom of the Creator of all things.

Music, prefiguring heavenly harmony and consonance, is necessary for you both in art and in morals, so that, ordained a priest in the Church of God, you may know how to sing rightly and sweetly with modulated voices, and, adorned with holy virtues, may not depart from the proportion of priestly morals. How necessary astronomy is for you as a master, if you do not know, you are not [unclear]. This teaches the courses of the stars, distinguishes time, divides the year, distinguishes hours and days; from its science arises the ecclesiastical computus, giving the reckoning of movable feasts, which Christian priests ought to know.

Behold, priest, how necessary to you is knowledge of the seven liberal arts, so that you may not be compared to an ape in [unclear], nor to a fool sitting on a royal [unclear]. For grammar contributes this, that you may fittingly understand and utter Latin speech. Logic teaches you to discern the true from the false. Rhetoric furnishes you with the virtue of speaking, so that you may be able usefully to persuade your hearers of the good and true thing that you understand. Arithmetic, moreover, together with geometry, besides the fact that they benefit you in household matters, also furnish a good support for divine contemplation, so that you may be regarded as a master fitted not only for things already discovered but also for those still to be discovered. For the greatest secrets are contained in numbers and measures, which, if mathematics is unknown, are by no means accessible, [Blank page in the source scan.]

[Blank page in the source scan.]

Familiar Letters and their fury against us, perhaps the waters of the malignant would have covered us. Our soul passed through a torrent of injuries and insults, unless the Lord Jesus had been present; perhaps our soul would have passed through the [water?] of intolerable despair, or at least would have avenged the injury in a manner not sufficiently religious. But blessed be the Lord Jesus, who did not give us as prey to the teeth of our rivals, so that we should be forced to remain longer under the rule of depraved men. Our soul, like an innocent sparrow, has been freed from the snare of the malignant hunters, whose envy knows how to spare no good man. The snare has been broken, and the vain confidence of the Cynonotes has been shattered, by which they tried in vain to recall us from holy studies into hatred of the just prince. But we, by the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, have at last been freed from the many miseries that we endured in the governance of the monastery of Sponheim. The snare of worldly entanglement, wholly contrary to our studies, has by God’s providence been broken, and we have been freed from the servitude of most ungrateful men. The Lord Jesus has freed my soul from wicked lips and from the too-deceitful tongue of rivals.

You know, brothers, if only you were willing to bear witness to the truth, what unjust injury I received from the Cynonotes, who, having no case against me, moved by envy and spite, did not fear to violate ecclesiastical immunity. They now bring excuses for their rashness toward us, saying that they did what they did not from hatred of us but rather from love. But theirs was an evil love, and intolerable to us, by which our name, always innocent of every crime, is turned through the mouths of many into suspicion, as though on account of some wantonness of ours it had been necessary to rage so against the household.

Today the twenty-fourth year is passing since, canonically elected abbot of Sponheim, all the time that could fall to me for leisure, you yourselves being witnesses and judges, I always turned not to any pleasure of the flesh whatever, but entirely to the study of the Scriptures, intent day and night on reading, always writing or learning something. None of you ever found me idle; none saw or heard that I was given to the consolations of the flesh, or uselessly occupied in wandering excursions or walks inside or outside the monastery, nor devoted to feasting or drinking or conviviality beyond what was necessary, or sweating over any other frivolities or vanities. Nothing was ever sweeter to me than to search out the sacred Scriptures, and to be occupied in them at suitable times by day and by night, and always to read or write something good.

As testimony to our studies I summon and cite that distinguished library which I brought together by my labors, zeal, and expenses, not without vigilance and continual weariness, gathering no small multitude of volumes in every variety of studies, not only newly printed books but also books written by hand and pen, the total number of which exceeds two thousand. It would be superfluous to list our lucubrations, which we wrote at intervals in the midst of pastoral care and anxiety over temporal affairs; by them the name of the monastery of Sponheim, previously unknown and obscure, has been made quite famous. Nor, because we were intent on our studies, did we therefore neglect temporal property, as many monuments of our labors will testify; nor will you yourselves be able to deny it, seeing plainly what necessary and very beautiful buildings you have been raised in, and what ornaments we acquired in the church, and little bells, and various sacred vessels of the mystery, and also the most splendidly renewed registers of revenues. All these things, with how great labors and expenses we accomplished them, even if you do not understand, will nevertheless bring admiration to posterity.

Finally, for almost twelve years now, since we came into the acquaintance and friendship of certain princes and nobles, we brought you no small advantage from those things which had been bestowed on us by their munificence. Nothing was ever special to us, nothing our own, just as indeed it ought not to have been; but all things were always common to us with you, and there was never any singularity in us at all, neither in clothing nor in drink, and none of you is ignorant that this is true. We also always had the greatest care lest any of the things that seemed necessary to you should be lacking, and we saw to it that you suffered want in nothing, so far as was entirely possible for us. In spiritual matters, however, we never failed you, although few of you, after the departure of our brothers to whom holy studies were pleasing, loved spiritual exercises, but always occupied themselves with vain things. We wrote, we spoke, we continually preached the word of God to you, and we exhorted you, in season and out of season, publicly and privately, to the worship of true wisdom; but how much we accomplished, we blush to confess openly.

And because you made yourselves unworthy of our exhortation, perhaps by divine prudence we have been transplanted, lest the tree among thorns be pricked too long without fruit. The day has come which we desired for many years, on which the opportunity was given us to pour the blood of ungrateful sheep upon their own heads, and, shaking the dust of our feet against them, to pass by deaf [asses?], according to the Gospel precept. Hear, if you please, the chief points of what you committed against us, so that you may know that you have been abandoned by us for a most just reason. Our sacred studies always displeased you, and for all our writings you returned laughter instead of reverence, and our lucubrations never pleased anyone less.

Johannes Trithemius.

...than to our sons. Nor was it enough to have mocked even the little works that we composed at the fathers’ command, unless you also attacked them before the unlearned common people in your discussions. You have always lived in opposition to fatherly exhortations. Often you contrived many conspiracies against us, and, after an oath had been imposed in chapter, under penalty of losing the voice, that no one should reveal to us the secrets of your conspiracy, you fabricated against us falsehoods about debts; these, through the goldsmith of Worms, who was said to be a hidden creditor, we showed before you all in the chapter room to be fabricated and false. Both witnesses are alive today: Gerlacus, abbot of Deutz, and Johannes, abbot of Schönau, then appointed visitors, who by their entreaties prevented us from taking due vengeance upon you.

Likewise, heavily oppressed throughout the whole time of our rule by care and anxiety over temporal and spiritual affairs, we could never find anyone among you who either felt compassion for our labors or truly grieved over the condition of the poor monastery. How many cloister priors did we appoint for you? Apart from one, Nicolaus of Kreuznach, and another, Johannes Damius of [Curtius?], we could never find any zealot for regular discipline. We are ashamed to say with how much hatred you always persecuted those who tried to persuade you to accept the discipline of monastic observance. But how much diligence in household affairs was shown by those whom we took as coadjutors to ourselves, we have learned by painful experience; it cannot be hidden from any of you. O with what groans and sighs we have until now borne among you the burden, full as it is, of pastoral care, having no faithful helper from among you either in spiritual or in temporal matters. You have proved useless to us in everything, having no zeal for uprightness or for the common good; you sought nothing but the comforts of the flesh. Among you there was no one who stretched out helping hands to us; whenever we took some outsider as helper in temporal care, you at once tore him apart with the bites of slander. For four years we were compelled in our own person to collect and renew all the rents of the monastery, bereft of every comfort from you; as often as we appointed one of you cellarer, so often we suffered serious loss in the monastery’s affairs. But we, who often had to obey the command of the fathers of the order, and for twenty years have for the most part spent ourselves by visiting through all the neighboring provinces, carried [unclear]; with us absent and you neglecting everything, indeed seeking your own comforts, at last a by no means fair appearance of affairs in each estate emerged.

Yet, through the intervention of our greatest solicitude, you never felt any lack of the things necessary for sustaining life, until at last, in the year of the Christians one thousand five hundred and four, when war was raging against the most illustrious prince Palatine, most dear to us, the monastery’s farms, from which on every side we used to live, were either burned or laid waste by the Hessians and the Alexandrines. Nevertheless we had a sure hope of recovering everything, but your folly, not to say treachery, put itself in the way; with presumptuous rashness you spoiled every plan of ours, which, mindful of no wrong, we had prepared for your good. We know that for twelve years the seeds of discords had preceded, from which it is clear that every evil arose. Certain men among you, by their hidden machinations, rendered the duke of the [Cynonoti?], otherwise a most pious prince, hostile amid common chatterers, bringing forward as a cause, so that the reason might seem sufficient, fabricated charges, as though we had judged the side of the prince Palatine, with some great attachment, to be preferred to the rights of that duke. For what if this fabrication of yours had even been true? Were we on that account to be torn apart by your slanders, or justly liable to the duke’s indignation? What did our attachment contribute to the Palatine? What did it profit him, or what advantage did he gain from the matter? Or what harm did it do the Duke that we favored the Palatine’s affairs? We frankly confess that we have always truly favored the most serene prince Palatine, most gracious and munificent to us, and today we favor his honor, good fortune, and prosperous affairs, although this favor of ours has contributed nothing to his majesty. Nor should we therefore be thought to have hated the Duke, or to have ill-favored his affairs; even if we had wished to do so, what loss would we have brought upon his affairs? If he believed your false denunciations, I am inclined to cry out against the duke and his men, with Aristophanes, who says quite finely in a certain passage: at the beginning of Plutus.

Concerning all these things we would indeed gladly persuade ourselves that the prince was innocent, were not manifest indications of a seduced mind seen to stand in the way. We speak truths; we write what is known about a powerful man, fearing no proscription of his, since he will not be able to proscribe us, for we are in no way subject to his command. Yet we refrain, lest it seem a kind of revenge to have written the truth. We report to you things known and manifest; contradict them if you dare, indeed if you can. Who found that monk, whom you know, on the threshold of the church with the wife of [unclear]...

[Blank page in the source scan.]

[with the wife?] of a peasant, mingling? Were you not, prior, with many others? Could such a man rightly have been defended by you, and, to the destruction of others, while we were then absent, summon to himself the aid of secular men? He publicly denied the deed which had been proved by the testimony of many; and, lest he should pay the punishment due for his misdeeds, he, against all justice, charged with guilt our innocent familiars, by whose diligence he had been caught in the crime, though we had consented and given aid. Why did you not await our arrival? For all these things were done while we were then at Heidelberg and ignorant of them. With your favor and counsel, by his lies he deceived the abbot of Mount Speciosus, who was too credulous, and certain officers of the duke of the [unclear], and stirred them up so that, to no small contempt, insult, and reproach of us, they seized some and put others to flight: namely, our innocent familiars who, from the eleventh hour until the second, had watched him alone in a dark place of the church, remote from human access, with the manifest signs of his crime, which the greater part of you also saw and knew to be true, had found him, and had reproached him as he came out of the church. We have learned with certainty that all these things were done by your counsel and urgency, and were presumed by ducal ministers in our absence, together with the rest which shame does not allow us to write. When the indignity of this deed was at last reported to us, we resolved to remain outside the monastery for a time, until we should understand more fully your dispositions toward us and have explored the mind of the duke, why and whether he had committed such things. Meanwhile eighteen months passed, in which, apart from the prior, we saw none of you, received no letters from you except one in the March, and lived at others’ expense, sustained by the munificence of princes: understanding the dispositions of your men well enough from the display of their conduct, unless perhaps the prior disdained to be a faithful go-between, which time without doubt will bring to light. What is it, brothers, that you have so often wished to press us with prayers to return to the monastery, as though you did not know our mind, which we long ago made known to you by letters through the prior? If you wished us to return to you, why did you not obey our commands? Why did you not approach your duke, so that he might have restored a gracious disposition toward us? But we have heard that he said to several of his men: Why does the abbot not return to his monastery, when no one has been troublesome to him, no one has disturbed him, no one ordered him to leave, no one forbids him to return? For we do not doubt that the duke would rather that the deed had not been done, which he ordered to be done at the urging of that fugitive monk, and that, led by repentance, he desired that we return; but, after the manner of the princes of this world, he fears that if he wrote his desire to us, he would seem to have acknowledged the injury which he did. Rather, however, he expects humility from us, so that we who have suffered the insult should beg pardon. We cannot deny that this would befit our monastic institution, and we would have done it most gladly for the love of Christ, had not your too long-standing ingratitude toward us stood in the way of our returning. For the duke’s innate clemency is sufficiently known to us, and we do not at all doubt that it could have been obtained even by a single letter. We consider the faults of ingratitude committed by you against us and often repeated; and, unwilling to tolerate their insolence any longer, we accepted, albeit with bitterness, the occasion given to us by which we might be freed from you, knowing that up to this point we had cultivated a barren field. You are exceedingly slothful and simple if you think that I did not foresee your tricks and deceits, when you caused me to be asked repeatedly in words to return, and yet feared nothing more than my return. Do you believe that the plans discussed in the assembly of the malicious at Bingen are hidden from us? Or will you think that the eulogies which the prior, in the name of all of you, contrived at Mount Speciosus against us, causing them to be written by the hand of Peter Schlarp, are not at all known to us, although, intercepted by the diligence of a certain brother at Budoras, they have not yet come into our hands? These manifest signs of your ingratitude and ill will at last reasonably moved us, so that, departing from you, we would no longer endure such great insolence. Would that we had done this earlier, when we were called by many to several abbeys, all of which, with one decision, we despised for love of you. For there were then among you several most religious brothers, distinguished in character and prudence, out of regard for whom we despised the fortune offered to us. But when these were at last either dead or called to other monasteries, you harassed [him?] with so many injuries, insults, and mockeries, until you drove him not only from the priorship but also from the monastery. Likewise the venerable brother and most upright man Johannes Damius Curtesius of Cologne, sufficiently instructed by us in every sort of literature, not only Latin but also Greek and Hebrew, you refused, with equal madness, to endure in the priorship, because, walking according to the purity of the rule, he would not consent to your sins. How great this man turned out [Blank page in the source scan.]

Johannes Trithemius.

Today you see among strangers him who displeased his own, whom henceforth you will by no means be able to recall to yourselves. Your wickedness could never endure the best men, because they would by no means consent to your frivolities. O Sponheim, Sponheim, always abhorring good and useful men from the beginning of your reform, with how many efforts I wished to reveal your miseries, and you refused to agree. Behold, then at last, full of weariness, I am compelled to follow better brothers whom you repelled by injury. Did not the envy of petty men compel Henry of Northeim, an excellent man and a most zealous guardian of regular discipline, to return to the Saxons? After him, by the equal madness of rivals, John Thoringus, now prior in Pegau, was driven out from you; likewise John of Dreifa, now prior in the monastery of Mary; Nicholas of Stauro[polis?], cellarer of Limburg; John Damius, provost of the nuns in Newcastle near Budorim; and John Venatoris, instructor of the novices in the aforesaid monastery of Pegau. Each of these, succeeding one another in turn, performed the office of prior in you; and because they had zeal for monastic discipline, you refused to bear them. I pass over the rest, not priors, monks as well as novices, to whom the envy of your men granted a place of better fortune. This, Sponheim, was always your weakness and nausea: to vomit up what was sound and whole, but to retain in the stomach of the belly what was sick and useless, not without danger. Good, mature, and useful men, in whom I might have rested secure, you cast out through envy, so that, deprived of their aid, you might at last more easily rage against the shepherd. When the harmless members of the household have been expelled, what remains except that the father of the household be expelled? Fabricated words do not bring a lawful excuse, since the one who gives occasion for damage is considered to have caused the damage. For besides those things wrongly committed by you against us, which we have listed above, your lying detraction stirred us no less to indignation, since, God being witness, we have committed none of the things which you fabricated against us with an impious mind. We blush to speak of the crimes of certain of you, which are manifest to you all; but since these things which we write this time will remain secret among us, and since integrity compels us, let us bring back to your memory things of which you were never [unclear]. Good brothers, we exhort you by the strict judgment of God, in which the secrets of hearts will be manifest: cease to persecute an innocent father, concerning whom you know that whatever crime has been spoken was fabricated and lied. Rather examine yourselves and do penance, since it is small consolation if your crimes lie hidden from men, when they cannot by any means lie hidden from God. Read the schedule enclosed with these writings, and you will understand how much penance you need. We cannot sufficiently marvel at your rashness, by which you seek to involve innocents in your dangers, not fearing your own, to such a degree that you have not even known how to spare us. If shame had not prevented us, we would have caused your reprobate way of life, by which in our absence you always advanced toward worse things, to be brought to the knowledge of the fathers, so that all might recognize how great an injury we have suffered from you. But we trust in the Lord Jesus, who alone knows our innocence, that all the things which you have committed against us will come to light even though we reveal nothing, and that by the just judgment of God you will pay deserved penalties in this time, lest you perish in the future examination. You indeed gave us occasion to believe this by your wickedness, committing against us such things as good cloistered men never committed against their shepherd.

Therefore the abbacy of the monastery of the divine bishop Martin at Sponheim, which, having been canonically elected and confirmed long ago, we undertook, and for twenty-three years, two months, and twenty days, with God’s aid and according to our strength, took care to rule, maintain, and govern according to the purity of the rule of our most holy father Benedict, today by the handwriting of our own hand, on account of your incorrigible rashness and the manifold injuries received both from you and from others, before the crucified Jesus Christ, into the decision of the convent, not induced nor persuaded or compelled by anyone, but of our own free will, in the name of God, we resign, content with those things which on the day before the feast of Saint James the Greater, Apostle, in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, we received to govern, offered by the most reverend bishop Laurentius. Moreover we confess and publicly protest in these writings that we believe, hold, and pronounce John Nutius the elder, John Pingionita the elder, and Nicholas, son of Scultetus, innocent, guiltless, and free from all injuries and insults inflicted upon us by you. For their innocence and integrity are sufficiently clear to us: they always obeyed our commands with pure devotion, and everywhere withdrew themselves from the pursuits of your depravity. Therefore we declare them exempt and guiltless of all your injuries, insults, and detractions, by which you brought it about that we departed from you. Likewise, among those dead in life, except for Haymo, we believe and pronounce all innocent of your conspiracies. May almighty God forgive you the things that you have committed against us, and not impute them to you as a sin unto death, but remit in this life both the fault and the penalty due for it. I, even though you do not ask, willingly forgive you for the love of my Lord Jesus Christ, from whom also Familiar Letters

...has conferred, or what harm has it done to your duke? It certainly benefited the former not at all, and harmed the latter not at all. What will a poor and humble monk be able either to confer on, or to take from, the great princes of this world? Yet we favor, and always shall favor, the most sacred prince Palatine as well as we can; but your duke we favor in proportion as he is proved to have favored us. For thus he caused word to be sent to us through his own men: “Let the abbot return to his monastery, fearing nothing, because we are going to do him neither any good nor any harm.” What a fine promise of a Christian duke, in which the disposition of his mind toward us is made manifest. But let the fickle crowd at last fare well with its prince. Trithemius will not be fed on these beans. I have set God as my helper, to whom I have entrusted the whole cause of my injuries, certain that he does injury to no one, but will repay each one according to his works. For I know that through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God, just as our Lord Jesus Christ himself deigned to go before us in many sufferings of tribulations, wishing by his example that we be steadfast in adversities. For love of the heavenly fatherland we must patiently endure all adversities, so that before the angels of God we may deserve to find the company of the saints, we who do not avenge the insults of rivals. For, as Hugh of Fouilloy, our monk, writes in the first book On the Cloister of the Soul, four things are necessary for a good man.

First, that he make all men his friends. Second, that if he cannot make all men friends, at least he not make enemies. Third, that if he cannot avoid even this, so that enemies are made, he withdraw from them. Fourth, that if anyone pursues him as he withdraws, he not avenge injuries. But I, who have always striven to show myself a good man, desired, so far as lay in me, to have all men as friends, especially those who seemed adorned with virtues and with learning in letters, from whose intimacy, namely, there would arise for me not reproach but a proclamation of praise. And indeed I made many friends by the fellowship of studies, whose faith and constancy I afterward experienced in adversities. One class of men only I could never admit into friendship, because it always showed itself hostile to good studies and never ceased persecuting learned men. These are the swollen and most idle haters of letters, who, proudly despising learned men, hunt after nothing more than money and the vain honors of the world. I never desired their friendship, nor, if I had sought it, could I easily have obtained it, because all their friendship consists in the largess of money and gifts, not in love of Christ or of truth. But they hated me because I devoted myself wholly to virtues and to the sacred study of the Scriptures, of which they always showed themselves despisers, and also because, as a boy, I had been chastised and beaten by the excessive and indiscriminate flogging of teachers. I have said these things not as an insult to the duke, but so that you may recall to memory what you do not fail to know: what sort they are who wished to show themselves enemies to me without cause. But I, following the counsel of a good man, withdrew from them, preferring to have peace in a foreign land rather than continual disturbance in my own.

Perhaps our rivals thought the spacious orb of the earth was confined within the narrowness of one little boot, so that Trithemius could not find anywhere outside Sponheim to remain, and for that reason would be forced to submit himself to their wishes and live as a slave at the command of [unclear], he who has always been accustomed to live in inborn freedom under the service of Christ alone. Yet I seem to myself certain that, if they had foreknown the outcome of the matter, which now, after my withdrawal, they recognize, this [unclear], since not only is there no one to forbid it, but rather all around, together with us, friends and at the same time those who previously seemed enemies, vehemently desire your return? I admit that no one ordered me to leave, no one compelled me, no one forbade my return. Of my own will, not bearing the insult of rivals, I resolved to remain outside, where I was, until the outcome of the affair should be seen. But to return to the monastery of the most ungrateful men would seem to me folly rather than piety, where an insulter stands daily at the doors, but no helper is present. Hence, fearing to be crushed between two millstones, it seemed better to abandon both the abbey and the people in peace than, in the midst of a corrupt nation, continual [unclear] of mind and body...

... I myself await pardon for my offenses. Believe me, brothers, as I speak the truth before Christ Jesus, the savior of all: I have always spared you, and I have never brought to light your misdeeds, which you committed against God and me, deeming it unworthy that a pastor should say anything bad, even truthfully, about his own sheep. From this, I know, your boldness increased, and the drunken poor man took up horns against us, so that you invented false things about me, while I always kept silent about true things concerning you. I therefore thought it better to leave the monastery than to accuse your wicked conduct in the chapter of the fathers, by word or in writing. For I am certain and have no doubt whatever that, if I had brought the case as it is to the knowledge of the fathers who held the annual chapter at Mainz at the beginning of September of the present year, my innocence would have been proved, and none of you would thereafter have remained in Spanheim. I willingly bore your disgrace before men, so that I might prove myself a true disciple of Jesus Christ. For I judged it better that one should yield to many than that, on account of one, many should be scattered. I do not doubt that the Lord Jesus, who is to come as judge of the living and the dead, will repay me for these insults and injuries, which I endured innocently, with a reward beyond what I would dare either ask or hope. For the rest, brothers, provide for your consciences according to the fear of God, and choose over yourselves such a pastor, not one who suits wicked morals, but one who by word and example [unclear] you. You have two leaders of factions, each of whom aspires to the abbacy: the one long since encouraged by the prophecy of a certain little fool, whom you all know, the other trusting in his own prudence. They do not seek God, but the comfort of their own flesh, which you can easily prove from the past life of each, and hereafter you will learn it not without danger. Let this warning alone suffice, although I fear I am telling a tale to the deaf. Fear the Lord God, and observe his commandments, lest, piling sin upon sin, you store up for yourselves double wrath on the day of the revelation of the just judge. For the Lord is an avenger, and he compensates for his long-suffering toward those who sin and do not practice repentance by the severity of punishments. Farewell, and at some time be rightly wise.

From Würzburg, on the last day of the month of October, in the year 1506.

III.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James in the suburb of Würzburg, to Johannes Brachius, prior of the monastery of St. Matthias the Apostle outside the walls of Trier, his friend: greetings and charity.

How all mortal things hang under uncertain chance, if you did not know it before, my friend, the Trithemian history now makes plain to you. I am that Trithemius, formerly abbot of Spanheim, whom learned and unlearned alike used to regard as an oracle of Apollo; who, praised in the mouth of all, seemed to be the head and pillar of the Bursfeld congregation. Kings and princes thought me something great; and prelates of churches, drawn together by the fame of our name, wished to see me, to speak with me, and to enjoy my presence. Great and learned men were happy if I had admitted them to my intimacy [unclear]; princes too and pontiffs of churches visited [me] with their letters and gifts. You wonder who could have moved me, such as I was, held in esteem among men far and wide, so that I should leave the place which I had made distinguished by writings and vigils, and also my brothers, whom I had nourished in Christ, together with that most precious store of books, which I had gathered from every variety of writings, and transfer myself to this obscure place, known to very few. We wrote to you in the month of July of the previous year that, because of certain injuries done to us through the envy of the ancient enemy, we had fallen into disgust with our monastery of Spanheim; moved by the recollection of these things, after leaving the monastery for a time we withdrew into the March of Brandenburg. Returning from there to Neumagen, we found such dispositions among our rivals that it seemed better to us to abandon the monastery entirely than, with continual weariness pressing upon us, to live any longer with the ungrateful and treacherous.
