To the poor, humble abbey of St. James in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, offered to me by the most reverend bishop Laurentius, I knowingly and willingly betook myself, and I resigned Spanheim, full of useless and vain occupations. For, born for studies of the Scriptures, I found a place suited to my training, in which the peace of poverty is joined with tranquility, and peace accompanies want. You know very well my custom of living: that I scarcely ever sought many or great things, but always lived on few and small things Familiar Letters, V.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St James at Würzburg, to Johann Damius Curiescius, provost of the nuns in New Castle. Greetings. [unclear]

Since the reasons, most beloved brother, which move our mind to the resignation of the abbey of Sponheim are not unknown to you, we have thought that few words should be used, signifying this alone first of all: that on the fifteenth day of this month of October we obtained real possession of the abbey of St James by canonical election, in which we hope that we shall live with greater peace than we ever lived at Sponheim. Hence we have sent letters to the convent in Sponheim, in which we both reprove their ingratitude and announce that for that reason we have resigned the abbey of Sponheim. It will be your part to deliver them, and to take care that they find a useful abbot, not one consenting to their vices. Wherefore it would seem advisable to us that your charity, about to announce these matters to the foul abbot of Speciosus Mons, from whom all their counsels depend, and as if from Apollo all responses, should first go down to Mainz, if perhaps it will be necessary to send for visitors, lest the wickedness of the impious prevail.

Wherefore in the bowels of Jesus Christ we exhort you: so far as lies in you, do not omit to provide that a suitable and useful person be set over the poor monastery, just as necessity itself seems to demand. For you know how those two, Prior Melantius and the lying Pingionita, both very foolish and stupid, especially pant after the abbacy; and you know their life and manners. In our judgment each of them will be not only useless to the monastery, but also harmful in no small degree. But although we have suffered an exceedingly grave injury from our own, nevertheless we wish every good for the monastery, for love of him who said in the holy Gospel: Pray for those who persecute and slander you; do good to those who hate you. May almighty God forgive them, who have persecuted us unjustly and without cause, perhaps not knowing what they have done, having a zeal neither good nor according to knowledge, but of bitterness and indiscretion. Farewell, praying continually to God for us. At Würzburg, on the last day of the month of October, in the year of the Christians 1506.

VI.

To the most serene and most unconquered prince, Frederick, duke of Saxony, etc., Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St James in the city of Würzburg, sends greetings.

To Fulda, concerning the deeds of the Saxons.

When I was lately returning from the March of Brandenburg, Conrad Mutianus, doctor, set forth the desire of your serenity, which Henry of Bünau, knight and once your envoy, also explained with no less diligence. Both reported one and the same opinion: that your serenity desires me to complete the history concerning the deeds of the Saxons, which Adam of Fulda once began, but, prevented by death, did not finish. My mind indeed has always been prompt and willing to obey your commands; but with various occupations presenting themselves in the meantime, up to now I have by no means been able to satisfy either your desires or my vows.

Now, however, at last having obtained quiet by a change, I have resigned the abbey of Sponheim and have taken up that of St James at Würzburg, in which I now live poor, in the manner of a philosopher, one suited to my studies and more tranquil by the opportunity for quiet. If therefore there is any strength in me by which I can render pleasing service to your highness, you will always find me prepared, because before many others I have known you, by the mouth of all men, as a prince worthy of praise, since in wisdom, in knowledge of the greatest matters, and in favor toward learned men you have no equal.

I once lent to the aforementioned Henry of Bünau, when he was among the Wangiones suffering from a broken leg, certain volumes, of which I have enclosed the list with these letters, on his pledge that they were to be restored as soon as possible. But he, restoring nothing in his usual manner, entered the way of human dissolution, leaving his brother as heir of all his affairs, with whom those very volumes of mine are said to have remained. Wherefore I beseech your serenity with the humblest submission, that by your command you cause these same volumes of mine to be restored to me. If I shall obtain this by your authority, you will have bound me wholly to your affairs. May almighty God long preserve your excellency unharmed; to him I commend myself with humble diligence. From my aforesaid monastery of St James at Würzburg, on the sixth day of the month of November, in the year of the Christians 1506.

VII. Joa- Johannes Trithemius.

[unclear] I lived content. I despised several rich and wealthy abbeys that were offered to me, knowing that in great abundance of things there are many disturbances, and that nothing is so contrary to my purpose as to be immersed in temporal affairs and to have no quiet left for the pursuits of salvation. For I know who said: “Wisdom fills a tranquil mind, free from cares, and will be the guest of a peaceful breast.” I was therefore content with familiar poverty, and, having despised the pomps and riches of the world, I did not refuse to lie hidden in the little hut at Sponheim. [unclear] saw this and envied it; and, thinking that I must either be enslaved to the cares of princes or necessarily entangled in earthly affairs, he prepared all the poison of his treachery against a poor and humble man. Twelve years ago he had infected the hearts of certain brothers, who favored the party of the most serene prince, the Count Palatine, badly; by their hidden plotting the envy of wicked men at last rose up against us. The favor of the Palatine prince toward me increased the envy of the Cynonoti; the consideration of unequal power furnished the cause of their hidden hatred. They saw me very often admitted among his intimates and honored by the munificence of divine Jove, and they wasted away, dreaming of gains greater than there were. As long as the strong lion stood in his flower, the little dogs dared nothing, but they waited for a time when they could exercise their malice upon the innocent man. That day desired by wicked blasphemers came, on which impious robbers, disturbing the whole principality of the Palatine, laid it waste with plunder and fire, sparing neither monasteries nor the churches of God, and showed themselves not Christians but rather faithless Turks. Meanwhile the most valiant lion, with the eagle pursuing him, gravely worn down by the forces of the whole empire, began to suffer no small loss, so that the faith of many might be tested. Many thought the lion prostrate, [unclear], and suddenly extinguished; and those who earlier had seemed friends through fear, not love, abandoned the prince when he was set in adversity and sided with his adversaries, according to that common proverb among the Greeks: [unclear]. Thus we all fell with him. From this envy took the boldness of rashness, and attacked me, poor and harmless Trithemius, having found the long-desired opportunity by which it might boast itself powerful among gnats. For while I was staying at [Budoras?] with the most sacred prince, the chief followers of the Cynonoti, at the urging of certain of my brothers who had been caught in crime, entered the monastery, seized certain members of the household who had observed what was done, stripped them of all their possessions under ecclesiastical immunity, broke down the doors, and threw them into chains. When this was reported to me at [Budorim?], it displeased me not a little, because I considered that it had been done out of hatred for me, fearing what happened: that it could in some respect injure the purity of my name among those ignorant of the truth. I therefore determined within myself not to return to the monastery before I had avenged by justice the cause of the injury committed. I remained away eighteen months, moved, as it seemed to me, by reason in recollection of the deed; and the longer it went on, the greater a nausea at returning began to come over me. Indeed the ingratitude of my brothers moved me not a little to yield; I had often experienced it gravely, but, with shame forbidding, I did not wish to bring it to light, judging it better that I should suffer injury than that, even with the truth, I should defame a multitude. Let the occasions of my departure remain entrusted to God and, so far as concerns me, covered in silence; knowledge of them could have brought scandal to hearers rather than edification. Believe me, my friend, I should wish you to know that, unless the injuries had been grave and the cause of my departure exceedingly reasonable, I would not have resigned my monastery, over which I presided for twenty-three years with the greatest solicitude, nor the most precious library. God permits nothing without cause. Who knows whether he wished me to be transferred to another place? I know indeed that not a few wonder that I gave up the abbey of Sponheim, which I made most beautiful with books and buildings, to such an extent that in all Germany there is nowhere found a library in which there are so many precious and very rare volumes, both new and old, in every science of the scriptures, written not only in Latin but also in Hebrew and Greek, in a very ancient hand. For, as you saw, I brought together more than two thousand volumes, rare and very ancient, from diverse kingdoms of the world; all these, together with the buildings and various possessions, I gave up for the love of peace. If any grief over their loss had begun to strike my soul, I formed for myself the likeness of death, by which I persuaded myself not only to forget the books, without which at one time I could not live, but even, so to speak, to hold myself in contempt. I confess that once I was held by a great love of the library, and I preferred my books to all the riches of the world; but after I perceived that the change of my affairs was at hand, I despised as dung all the things I had previously loved, and I commanded my soul henceforth to believe nothing its own except itself, and to learn, while living in the flesh, much more not to love those things which in death it would necessarily have to leave behind. Once the vain confidence of the world deceived me, by which I thought that the practice of monks was favor, blandishments to possession of which I entered on the fifteenth day of the month of October of the present year. The place is indeed small, poor, and modest, but very well suited to my purpose and studies, where I may always be intent, at my pleasure, both upon myself and upon letters. And so, for love of peace and quiet, I gave up the abbey of Sponheim, full of useless occupations, together with its most ungrateful monks, after I had presided over it into the twenty-fourth year.

This deed not only has not caused me regret, but delights me to such a degree that I would not wish to have remained there even with peace of every kind. I should bear the death of Libanius, my sweetest teacher, heavily, if I knew for certain that he had died. For I hope, through the mercy of God, that he is still living and, as he promised me in the previous year, will come to me shortly. In the month of August I sent him letters, both those of Your Serenity and my own, but I am still uncertain whether he has received them. I shall do what I can to know the truth; and if indeed he is dead, which may almighty God avert, [I shall take care that he not] seem to have been utterly taken away from us. For he has left very precious little works, composed by his brilliant talent; the more of these we shall be able to gather to ourselves, the less he will seem to have departed from us. But from the day on which I left your March and Your Highness down to the present I have been able to write nothing, because I could have neither a quiet place nor a suitable time. As for the praises of Saint Joseph, foster-father of the Savior, I shall begin the treatise as soon as possible, and the remaining items, marked in order on the schedule by Your Highness’s hand, I shall see to publishing as quickly as I can, according to the powers of my talent. Meanwhile I ask that Your Serenity patiently endure this delay, since, if the Lord Jesus has mercy and prolongs my life, in due time you will receive from me completed all the things you request.

But as to this, that Your Highness again asks for my return to you in the March at the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection or of Pentecost, I can write back nothing certain, because, having resigned the former abbey and undertaken this one, I have now subjected myself to the lordship of another prince. As far as lies in me, I could easily be persuaded, and I am both ready and willing to obey the just desires of Your Majesty in all things to the best of my ability; but on this occasion there are two things that seem to hinder the readiness of my mind. First, because in this new abbey I can in no way depart so soon and so far away, and remain abroad for a long time, without the consent of my most reverend prince; and the consent which the former Palatine gave is of no force today, since, the prince having changed, the privilege too must necessarily be changed. The other thing which seems to stand in the way, although it is not great, has nevertheless saddened me somewhat: that certain fathers of my order are scandalized at me because I frequent the courts of princes, chattering I know not what frivolous and fabricated things, as though I had previously gone to Your Highness to teach certain profane matters, and not for the honor of the Christian religion and to transmit understanding of the divine Scriptures. The credulous crowd rages against innocence in its customary way into vice; and since it does not possess the principles for knowledge of natural things, whatever it does not understand it ascribes to evil operations. No ignorant person grasps that what he marvels at can be possible, and each measures the force of nature according to the capacity of his own intellect, and is thereby deceived altogether like a blind man. But a mind conscious of right pays no attention to their cavils, rather laughing at the sloth of the unskilled, who despise the good which through sloth they have never learned. Yet let Your Serenity write to my most reverend lord bishop, and if he consents that I come, sufficient provision will have been made for each of us. Although, saving the will of Your Highness, it seems to me more advisable in many respects that my entry into the March be deferred until the year one thousand five hundred eight, lest, if I depart so soon, the tongue of rivals again spit out against me something of ill-speaking levity.

I have learned that the promise of the king of the Danes has been delayed, and I grieve. But I fear that he will have little success with the Swedes; and the more he tries to crush them, the more he will tear himself apart. For God Most High rules the kingdom of men, as Scripture says, and gives it to whomever he wishes. May almighty God deign to confirm your principate in every goodness and make it glorious, granting you every desire of your heart; this without doubt he will do, if with a perfect heart you walk innocently in his commandments with holy David, as you have begun. The reason why the messenger of Your Serenity returns later is that, deceived in his expectation, he sought me at Sponheim. May the Most High preserve Your Majesty unharmed; to whom I most humbly commend myself. From my aforesaid monastery at Würzburg, on the 25th day of the month of November. In the year of Christ 1506.

IX. DO- Familiar Letters

I deemed the honor of nobles; and whatever pleasing thing fortune offered, I thought eternal. It will not go on to sadden me a second time, since, taught now by experience, he has learned not to trust vain things, and that the false hope of men always fails in tribulation. Do you not see, man, that a small viper kills a broad bull with its bite, and that monks hidden in secret undermine the rule of a shepherd? A drop hollows stone not by force but by falling often; and often a humble crowd has cast down a proud ruler. For many years now, through the envy of certain brothers, whose infamy for public crime had long held them, a seedbed of wickedness began to sprout. So dangerous is it for a ruler to punish contumacious sources, who ascribe deserved penalties to injury, always covering with silence the time in which they may destroy the censor who corrects them. But the Lord Jesus, who will not forget his poor unto the end, will be my consolation; in him I have placed all my hope. He will give peace to my heart in a fitting time, and, when he judges the hidden things of mortals, will bring them into the light. I beg you again and again to pray to his mercy for me. Farewell. From my aforesaid monastery at Wurzburg, on the last day of the month of October, in the year of Christians 1506.

IV.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James at Wurzburg, to Johann Gotfrid, pastor of the church of the Valley of Men [Manthal], greetings.

That you attend upon me with brotherly love I have plainly enough; and therefore I could not conceal, nor perhaps ought I to have concealed, from you the whole sequence of my affairs. For true friendship, confirmed by the love of Christ, is not accustomed to hide from a friend anything that befalls by fortune, so that if favorable things come to pass he may rejoice with him, but if adverse things, he may suffer with his suffering friend. I do not write to you the causes of my long wandering from the monastery of Sponheim, since they are known to you, but rather that, moved by the injury of rivals, I have at last made provision for my affairs. Why should I not do so, after receiving so notable an insult beyond my deserts? It was necessary for me not to spurn the peace offered, and to embrace among strangers what was denied by my own. Indeed, what the face of regular observance among the monks is today at Sponheim, and what it was once when I was present, you, as a neighbor, cannot be ignorant; and how much I long ago [unclear] for ungrateful men, who care for nothing less than spiritual things and pursue nothing more zealously than carnal things. With the greatest cares and labors for their advantage I afflicted myself for twenty-three continuous years; you see what reward I bring back. Those among them who had more influence, siding with our rivals against us, stirred up against us the most pious duke, using lie, fraud, and deceit, until, persuading him of false things as true, they brought about what they had long been planning. We resolved to yield the monastery for a time, so that the opportunity might not be lacking for sounder counsel, by which envy might pay its deserved penalties. After dwelling nine months in the March of Brandenburg, we thought it certain that rashness would change its counsel, and that the brothers, at least the innocent ones among the wicked, would approach the mind of the prince. Meanwhile they often asked us by letters to return to the monastery; but the duke, whom, without our being consulted, they had rendered hostile to us by false teaching, they disdained, moved by shame and fear, to persuade to the contrary opinion. Returning at last to Budoras, we called the prior to us; from his accustomed report we learned that all things were at peace and that absolutely nothing was to be feared, and that not only all the neighbors and brothers, but also the duke with his men, were asking [unclear] that we should return to the monastery as quickly as possible. At last he persuaded our mind to return, once the annual chapter had soon been celebrated, which was due to be observed at Mainz at the beginning of September. On hearing this he pretended to be glad and departed, though in truth he was sad at heart, because we are certain that he had always dreaded rather than desired our return to Sponheim. For unless our opinion deceives us, the picture 26 painted in the refectory gave him hope of the abbacy. But when the prior had gone away, soon through Johann Damius it became known to us what eulogies, written at Mainz on the mountain of St. James by the hand of a certain monk of the monastery of St. Johann at [Rinckaug?], Peter Slarpion, he had caused to be written in the name of the whole convent of Sponheim; yet these, intercepted by the caution of the very man who reported it, did not come into our hands. When this treachery of our men became known, we stood firm in our decision that henceforth we would by no means return to Sponheim, nor yield in this matter to any persuasions of any men whatsoever. Truly that saying of Christ in the Gospel has been fulfilled in me: that a man’s enemies will be those of his own household. O brief memory of benefits among cloistered men, since there is little faith in monks who seek not God but themselves. Who would have believed that Trithemius, an abbot always kind to his subjects and burdensome to no one, Familiar Letters, X.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James at Wurzburg, to Roger Sycamber, Dumetensian canon: greeting and sincere charity in the Lord.

That you rejoice with us over our peace and tranquillity, you do well, and what befits a true friend; nor are we ungrateful, as in duty we must not be, for your wishes and efforts toward us. For the friendship long since formed between us is great, and great it can be, because it did not take its beginning from the vanity of temporal things and the fleeting consolations of the world, but consists wholly in the strong love of Christ and in zeal for the sacred Scriptures.

And this is the height of our philosophy, we who are Christians and cloistered men bound to God: always to love with pure affection the Lord Jesus, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is one God in a trinity of persons, and, despising all the vanities of the world, to keep the mind continually occupied in the divine Scriptures with sobriety. For this is the true friendship of cloistered men, which divine love binds together among brothers; having God as its beginning and end, and, rejecting the fellowship of vanity, it walks the solitary way of God’s commandments without stumbling, with the companion of its vow.

For the prophet Jeremiah says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; he will sit alone, because he has lifted himself above himself.” For the sinew of cloistered friendship is to love solitude for the love of Christ, and at all times to avoid the conversations of men who are carnally wise. The only firm friendship of cloistered men is that which the fellowship of equal vows has joined in the love of heavenly wisdom, without regard for earthly advantage. Here there is no need of perishable gifts, no gold, no silver, because for true friendship this alone is required: that God be loved purely by both.

Love, however, arises from knowledge; knowledge is generated from continual study of the Scriptures; and study is nourished by desired solitude, as Saint Prosper the bishop said:

The quiet may search out the law in whatever way they can, if hearts, free from the world’s noise, are at leisure.

And again he says:

Wisdom fills a tranquil mind, empty of cares, and will be the guest of a peaceful breast.

In body, indeed, you are solitary; you dwell in a grove with a few brothers of the same profession under the yoke of silence; you are fervent in sacred study of the Scriptures. If the invisible noises of the world have not penetrated the inmost parts of your heart, you have now prepared an easy way toward knowledge of the highest good, which is God. The mind, too, must be restrained, lest it be shaken from without by disturbances of excited frenzy, or touched by animal passions, but rather be peaceful and tranquil, always fearful before the divine word, because it is written: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful; but he who is hard of mind will fall into evil.” And the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “To whom shall I look, except to the poor little one, contrite of heart, and trembling at my words?”

For because you burn with zeal for saving knowledge, so that you may understand the true wisdom which is from above, first purify your mind from every pleasure of earthly things, and then further [unclear] in the study of the Scriptures; and the more you advance in knowledge, the more [unclear] you will love. And the more ardently you love the Lord your God, the more you will approach true wisdom. For what else is that enjoyment of eternal happiness by the mind after the dissolution of our body, than a certain unfailing exultation of the spirit, which, consisting at once in knowledge and love of the unchangeable good, with the grace of God cooperating, has taken its beginning in this mortal life through holy studies from our free will?

Roger, I do not esteem you highly as a poet, nor do I admire you as a rhetorician, nor do I praise you as a lover of worldly wisdom; but because you are a lover of sacred theosophy, and worship God with a pure mind, and are held to be a despiser of the age, this is what I venerate and praise in you, and at the same time love most strongly. For this alone I have admitted you into friendship, and inscribed you in my heart as a true friend; without it there is no firm friendship among cloistered men.

Thus, Roger, I would wish us to proceed as constant friends by the love of Christ Jesus alone, so that, with our hearts continually purified by readings of the divine Scriptures, and devoted with sobriety to them, we may through the continuation of actual study attain to knowledge of the unchangeable good, and may always love that incomprehensible God, known by faith, with the whole intention of the mind, despising for love of him all the prosperous things of this world, and fearing no adversities. For the Lord Jesus, the wisdom of God the Father, is our philosophy, and the true bond of cloistered friendship; without him you ought to have no friend. The more fully you come to know him through study of sacred Scripture and the exercise of spiritual compunction, with the greater affection, the more fervently you will love [him], Of Johannes Trithemius.

... I am burdensome to none, troublesome to none, but cherish all with fatherly affection, treat all charitably, and love them in true affection, so suddenly and without cause to be abandoned by his own sons, whom he gathered, cherished, and nourished in the Lord? O prior, not undeservedly to be compared with Judas the betrayer, how treacherous a vicar you have shown yourself to us, you who, in order to obtain our abbey, have plotted against us with manifest treachery. Remember, even now at last, most ungrateful of all men, how greatly we always took care, with the zeal of humanity, to do good not only to you, unworthy indeed and never deserving it, but also bestowed our benefits on your parents with the greatest piety. For you know, faithless man, and cannot be ignorant, that when war was laying waste the duchy of Luxembourg, they were compelled by want to leave their homeland naked and beggars; finding no one to receive them, they came to you, who were then living with us as a novice at Spanheim, and at the gate of the valley of men they lived for the space of [unclear] year in great poverty. At last, when we were called to the abbacy, moved with compassion, and with you also urging it, we summoned them to the village of Spanheim; we granted them an excellent dwelling free of charge, and from the monastery we assigned them each day a sufficient prebend in food and drink, for God’s sake and out of love for you, which today, into the fourteenth year, just as we established it for them from the beginning out of love, [unclear] cannot be ignorant.

Finally we made their children free from every servitude, exaction, and burden of villages and princes; we gave them clothing; in every necessity we always provided for them abundantly down to the present year. You too, first from our domestic chaplain, we appointed to the ecclesiastical office of our monastery, having singular confidence in you. But when after a few months, because of your inexperience and much negligence, we were compelled to remove you from that very office of cellarer, lest you incur any stain of unfavorable opinion, we appointed you cloister prior, against the will of many. We have also upheld you in that same office now for sixteen years against the murmurings of all the brothers; we have always defended and excused you. We are ashamed to recall our kindness toward you, which we confess was liable rather to negligence and remissness than to virtue. You never conducted yourself in the monastery as a worthy prior, because you neither greatly cared for regular observance nor loved zeal for the inner life. When we were often occupied in visitation of the order, you, without cause, without necessity, and without our permission, which was by no means lawful for you, used to run off to the convents of the nuns of Saint Catherine, Saint Rupert, and Ibingen, seeking [unclear] comforts, and were accustomed to wander to villages and towns within a circuit of three miles, contrary to the rule of monastic institution, while you begged those whom you restrained not to report your wandering to us. But when we did at times learn what had been done, burning with excessive charity toward you, we either entirely dissembled for the sake of peace, or corrected it less adequately than we should have. We always bore toward you a most pious mind; but you, imitating Judas the betrayer, have repaid us evil for our goodness toward you. But because, though we easily could have done so through you and through others, we did not desire to avenge the insult done to us, we passed over the rest of the crimes of your malice, not doubting that you would fall into the pit which you made, by the just judgment of God raging against you, you who have faithlessly, without cause, and unjustly persecuted us.

Yet we fear, not without a foreboding of future things, which the good brothers will learn by experience too late, how useful and pious a pastor they lost in us, by their own will rather than ours; whether they who thought to come to our aid in time of necessity, out of love or out of hatred of rivals or of us, themselves despised it. They very often asked that we return to the monastery; but that they never did this with a whole heart toward us has been made persuasive to us by two considerations. The first of these is that they could never be induced even lightly to attempt to soften the mind of the prince of the [Cynonoti?], whom certain men by their lie had rendered hostile to us, fearing to be accused of duplicity if they later praised again one whom they had previously blamed. The other testimony of their faithlessness is sufficiently manifest, since those who previously were always insisting that we return, changed, or rather abominable, among the [Pingiones?] in the council of the malicious, asked that I yield the office of pastoral care. But we judged that we should provide for our affairs according to our own decision, not theirs; and we yielded when it pleased us, not when they themselves wished. We grieve that the prince, otherwise humane, gentle, and to that point a lover of uprightness, on this occasion proved too credulous toward the accusations of the depraved, although we never contradicted his command even by a word, to the detriment [unclear]. We confess that we have always favored the just party of the Palatine, because we recognized that prince as most Christian, devoted to God, always kind to good and learned men, gentle and most pious; his many benefits toward us would deservedly charge me with ingratitude if we felt otherwise. What good that supporter of ours [unclear] to our most illustrious prince the Palatine...

Johannes Trithemius

[unclear] to fear danger. No rashness of my own impelled me to withdraw, nor, without the example of the fathers who preceded me, did I dismiss wicked monks, whose ingratitude deserves such a shepherd as I never wished to show myself to be. That Rabanus Maurus, sixth abbot of Fulda, certainly a most learned man, because of the wickedness of his monks abandoned that abbey itself after he had governed it for twenty-four years; fleeing to Louis the Pious, the emperor, he withdrew, and by him, after two years had passed, after the death of Otgar, archbishop of Mainz, he was appointed in his place. Regino also, the very illustrious and likewise most learned abbot of the monastery of Prum, who wrote many useful things, was driven out by the injury of his monks, abandoned the abbey, and fled to the archbishop of Trier. Benno, the first abbot of the monastery of Goseck, harassed with injuries by his brothers through the count, the founder, left the abbey together with the monastery and, for the love of Christ, fled to the wilderness. At length, by the consent of all, he was ordained bishop by the priests of the church of Meissen, and in testimony of his holiness he shines with frequent miracles down to the present day. The writer of the Chronicle of Pegau did not pass over in silence how badly and wickedly his monks thought of him.

Why should I speak of abbots of almost the most recent times, when the prince of monks, our holy father Benedict, left the first abbey to which he had been ordained because of the faithlessness of those subject to him? I am not better than my most holy and most learned fathers, whom almighty God willed to suffer injuries from the father of monks, so that in them he might increase the merit of holiness, or, after the manner of a wise farmer, so that he might produce richer fruit if he transplanted them to a more suitable place. For from reading the ancients we have learned that many most excellent fathers left their abbeys because of the ingratitude of monks; some indeed compelled by fear of tyrants, others by their own free will. After the example of these fathers I dismissed the obstinate monks together with the abbey; the crimes they committed against us I did not think fit, out of shame, to commit to the pen. But just as in these evils I cannot judge all my monks innocent, so neither would I say that all are culpable, although, if they had wished to have me as shepherd for longer, they would have informed otherwise the duke who had been offended by false accusations. For it is quite clear to me that Johannes Nutius, Johannes Cusensis, Johannes Damius, Johannes de Sobernheim, and Nicolaus Sculleteti were always innocent in all the conspiracies of the brothers against me, nor do I affirm that I was harmed by them in any respect. But to name those who armed their teeth against us is of little use, for you know very well who and what sort they are. Among them two heads of factions, Remigius Melantius, the prior, the most ungrateful of all men, and that younger Pingionita, whose malice is surpassed by his folly, having obtained certain supporters of their rashness, both strive with all their efforts for the abbey.

Therefore, so that their faithlessness may at last become better known, we give place and time, taught by long experience how greatly the destructive rashness of monks obstructs the progress of the mind. The abbey offered to us, that of the monastery of Saint James the Greater, Apostle, in the suburb of the city of Wurzburg, through the most reverend bishop Laurentius, by the counsel of friends, we accepted on the fifteenth day of the month of October in the present year; the former one, Spanheim, over which we presided for twenty-three years, two months, and twenty days, we left of our own free will because of the ingratitude of the monks and the persecution of your duke. Farewell now to my rivals, who persecuted a humble and innocent man; farewell to the duke with his envious [Cynonoti?]; farewell to the prior Melantius, lover of iniquity, with all his conspirators. So much, God permitting it, could the envy of rivals do against me, that forgetfulness of my benefactions suddenly arose among my beneficiaries; they returned evil to me, though I did not cease to do them good. But whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s. I have set God as my helper, in whom I have placed all my hope; he has transferred me from the midst of a depraved nation and established me in a place of peace and quiet. To him be praise forever. Amen.

Would that those who so greatly desired my contrition might now be armed with zeal for God and with purity, to provide for the desolate monastery such a shepherd as may be willing and able usefully to take thought for its poverty. For I feel compassion for the poor monastery; for the innocent brothers I bear the bowels of compassion, although they seem to have had little regard for me. You have the whole history of my transfer; [unclear], knowing the judge of all to have said: vengeance is mine, I will repay. For I endured all things patiently and withdrew, fleeing from the face of the persecutor; although, had I wished otherwise, neither support nor strength to repel the injuries would have been lacking. Farewell; do not cease to pray to God for me, and stand by the poor monastery of Spanheim devotedly in its need as patron, as you have been accustomed to do up to this point. Farewell again. From Wurzburg, the last day of the month of October, in the year of Christ 1506.

Of Johannes Trithemius.

VII.

Joachim, by the grace of God Margrave of Brandenburg, prince elector, to the reverend father Johann Trithemius, abbot of Saint [unclear].

Our great love and goodwill toward you, most learned father, together with the recent memory of those evidences of pious learning which you lately presented to us, strongly impel, urge, and move us to write to you often, making known first of all by this present writing of ours the happy and unharmed condition of ourselves, and also of our wife, son, brother, and sister. We greatly grieve with your paternity on account of the envy of rivals who are stirring up adversities against you, as we understood from your last letter and received from the report of our messenger. Yet we trust that by the counsel of your wisdom, and likewise by divine aid, you will easily overcome all the contrivances of human depravity.

We have learned by an exceedingly bitter report that your once most learned teacher Libanius has laid down the burden of the flesh and rendered his spirit to the Most High who created him; concerning his death, if indeed he is dead, for we still hope that he is alive, [unclear] than if any one of our dearest friends had departed. We always loved and admired in him his distinguished learning, his inestimable knowledge of almost all writings, and the singular subtlety of his intellect. We ask your paternity, therefore, that if you find him dead, you apply every diligence regarding the books left by him, so that they not come into the hands of strangers, especially those which you understand to be useful to us. For we shall gladly pay whatever you decide must be paid.

Moreover, most loving teacher, we beseech you again and again, most urgently, that you not be reluctant to return to us around the feast of Easter or Pentecost. For, as you know, your service is necessary to us in many matters; without it we cannot long be lacking without detriment to our affairs. Write back to us your counsel on these matters through this messenger of ours, whom for that reason we have sent to you. But if you consent to our requests, as we have full confidence in you, indicate the time; we shall send the same courier back to you on the appointed day with the expenses necessary for the journey, nor will you depart from us unrewarded.

Nor should it escape you, uniquely beloved one, that the new teacher whom, on your persuasion, I admitted is doing well in all things, and I have some slight hope of greater progress from him in time. We have also marked on the schedule enclosed with this letter certain volumes of which we do not have a copy, asking that, as soon as you can, you refresh us with the reading of them. We also wish you to know that our sister will consummate the marriage contracted with the Duke of Mecklenburg here in Werder, with solemn celebration of the wedding, in this Shrovetide. Again we ask you that in all the foregoing matters you show yourself toward us such as the confidence we have in you expects; you will always have us grateful to you in all things. Farewell, loving and mindful of us; may the friendship long since contracted between us remain inviolate. Again farewell, and ever fare well. From our town of Tangermünde on the Elbe, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1506, on the day of Saint Burchard. And by our own hand.

VIII.

To the most illustrious prince and lord, Lord Joachim, Margrave of the Brandenburgers, etc., Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, but formerly of Sponheim, wishes happiness.

I rightly rejoice greatly, most serene and most pious prince, in the well-being of you and yours; I have rejoiced at the prosperous successes of your affairs more than I could either say in person or write while absent. For the compassion of your excellence over my troubles I give and hold immortal thanks, and I shall repay them if ever I can by some opportunity.

I hope, moreover, that by prudent counsel I have at last escaped the envy of my rivals, with God’s help. And so we make known to your serenity, unconquered prince, that when I departed from your highness I did not return to Sponheim, because, although [unclear] seemed desired for my monastery, nevertheless certain contrivances on the part of my unfaithful monks intervened, by which I was provoked to such great weariness that, by a firm conclusion in my own mind, I resolved that henceforth I must by no means return to Sponheim. Therefore I remained outside, not without counsel, with my most serene prince Philip, Count Palatine, Duke of Bavaria, and prince elector, at [unclear] for four months, until at last the most reverend prelate of Würzburg had me called, elected, and confirmed to the abbey of Saint James, formerly of the Scots, in the suburb.

[Jacobus?] Trithemius, brother of your most reverend Paternity, brought us your letters, from which we understood that you not only live, but live happily. As humbly as I can I give thanks to almighty God, whose mercy has made you stronger than all your rivals, so that those who thought you should be harmed have gravely harmed and confounded themselves, and have made themselves worthy of everlasting reproach. Those most treacherous scoundrels thought that they could extinguish your famous name and the renown of your most holy reputation throughout the whole Christian world; but I trust in him who knows all things, that not only will the unjust persecution of the envious do you no harm, but because of it, after being transferred to Francia, you will shortly shine forth much more brightly than you did before.

No one gave greater occasion for all the evils you endured than your monks, together with those two most treacherous abbots, the one of Mainz and the one of Rheingau, who, as I have heard by truthful report, stirred up the chancellor and the officers of Duke John into hatred of you. For while you were in the March, your monks were running ceaselessly here and there to Mainz, and to the duke himself, who was continually residing at Fortiburgium beside the Moselle, and they tried to provoke against you whomever they could. The unlearned [unclear] of the duke, formerly well disposed toward you, readily believed the reports of the envious, as one who had long regarded your learning and wisdom with suspicion, always fearing, as is now publicly reported, that this duke might take you as his councillor. Wishing therefore to forestall the duke’s plan, he persuaded that overcredulous man of everything that was being fabricated about such matters. But the justice of almighty God will bring all things successively into the light; and certainly it has already begun actually to become plain how very unjustly you have been treated.

Your rivals launched many rash accusations against you when you were stationed in the March, wishing to blacken the most splendid reputation of your holiness, and they spread abroad among the people certain dreadful lies, for which they are now being confounded in the sight of all men. For although we all knew that you were with the most serene prince Joachim in the March, nevertheless certain pestilent and very envious men of your most sacred name were saying: “Where do you think Abbot Trithemius is? With the Margrave of Brandenburg? He is not, they say, with him, but in despair has gone away to Rome, never to return thereafter.” Others dared to say that, touched by excessive desolation of spirit, he had hanged himself with his own noose. Others again falsely declared that he had been consigned to perpetual chains. Many also, giving credit to the words of your enemies, believed that you had perished, saying: “Alas, that splendid light, which was wont to illumine the whole world with its learning, how has it been obscured by the darkness of shadows? Who would have believed that Abbot Trithemius, glorious in nearly the whole Christian world for the fame of his learning and holiness, would come to such dejection of spirit that he would so rashly desert his fatherland and his friends?”

But I, who knew your learning, your prudence, and also the holiness of your life very well, always resisted these blasphemies and curses of the impious with all my strength, and I showed openly by many arguments what a rash injury they had done to your most holy name. For having spent two years in your monastery under your teaching, to learn Greek and Hebrew letters and to draw in the saving knowledge of the Scriptures, I could never see anything in you, never hear anything of you, except what was holy, upright, and religious; indeed, we saw you conducting yourself at all times in such purity that we greatly marveled. While the others slept, you kept watch in the holy study of the Scriptures, always either reading or writing something for the common benefit of many. No one ever found you idle; no one heard that you were given to feasting or drinking; no one saw you dissolved in laughter or any levity; no one ever found you speaking or associating with women in a way from which an evil suspicion could arise.

O my sweetest teacher Trithemius, gracious father, whenever I recall to memory that most holy manner of teaching by which you were accustomed to teach and exhort me, and at the same time your brother Master Jacobus Trithemius, to the knowledge of the divine Scriptures, I cannot keep back my tears for sorrow. For you used to pour forth to us such profound, such mystical, and such ardent words concerning the holy Scriptures that they could have moved hearts of iron to the love of God. Hence I cannot sufficiently wonder by what judgment of God, permitting it at last, your rivals could have invented such unworthy things about you, when you were never harmful to anyone, when you wronged no one by injury, but rather showed yourself pious and generous to all, always seeking all your consolation, without injury to anyone, in the study of the Scriptures alone.

But with firm confidence I believe that almighty God has provided by his disposition that you be placed elsewhere, so that, finally rescued from the midst of a wicked nation, you may persevere in the holy study for the rest of your life with peace and tranquillity, to the common benefit of many. The monks of Sponheim were never worthy of your prelacy; nor did Duke John himself deserve to have in his dominion such a man as you are, excellent Trithemius. It was therefore necessary for you to go out through tribulation from the midst of the wicked, just as once the sons of the saints, when they were to leave the land of Mizraim, first [unclear] in mud Of Johannes Trithemius.

IX.

To Lady Elisabeth de Longovico, his most honorable and sweetest mother, Johannes Trithemius, her son, abbot of St. James at Würzburg, formerly indeed of Sponheim, with all honor and reverence, offers in all things a son’s affection, ready with due service.

[unclear]

I know, mother (for I cannot doubt it), that since our affairs have now been disturbed for more than a year, you are on that account not a little troubled. For although we have passed beyond childhood, yet so long as your sons survive you do not cease to show yourself a faithful mother. I have sent to you with this letter master Jacob, my only brother, so that through one son you may learn everything that has happened to the other son, and, through the presence of the one, grow accustomed to bear more lightly the absence of the other.

I do not wish you to have any anxiety for me, nor to think me wretched because rumor has perhaps spread that I was expelled from Sponheim. Rather believe me, who write the truth: that I departed not by force, not from fear, not under compulsion, but of my own free will; after mature deliberation beforehand, I resolved to remain outside, and I resigned the abbey. I accepted this one in which I now live in peace, for many reasonable causes inducing me to this; if you wish to know some of them, you will learn them from my brother’s report.

I trust in the Lord Jesus, who permits nothing without cause, that this change will have given me material for progress toward the salvation of both man’s parts, since I have been freed from many useless occupations and have obtained good peace with tranquility. For no one knows better than I how ungrateful the men are whom I have served until now at Sponheim. On that account I am not saddened, but rather rejoice that an occasion has been given me to withdraw from those whom I had often before considered leaving.

But there is one thing which, as I think, may seem able to torment your mind somewhat: that henceforth you will see me living in this flesh either more rarely or never, because of the greater distance between the places in which we dwell apart from one another. Remember that you are the mother of a necessarily mortal man, from whom, whether you wish it or not, you must at some time be separated, even if he should live with you for many years, whichever of you dies first. For what consolation can the very brief human sight of the flesh contain in itself, when at last it is necessarily extinguished by death with greater bitterness than it ever seemed before to be possessed with sweetness?

Let us therefore refer these desires of our vanity to that vision of eternal blessedness, in which sweetness will endure without end, and when once it has shone upon us, it will never be extinguished for ever. Let us hasten to that, O mother, for participation in which we were created, and which then without doubt we shall be able to attain, when, meditating day and night on the Lord’s commandments, we shall always have loved the Lord God himself, our Christ, with a pure mind, a whole heart, and the desire of eternity burning within us.

What need have we of fleshly sight, who ought to seek the spiritual? I have vowed that I shall serve God; it is not permitted me henceforth to take delight in the comfort of parents. I have despised everything for the love of Christ; I have already begun to be like Melchizedek, without father, without mother, without genealogy. I acknowledge God alone as father; I have no mother except the Church. Nor am I now any longer my own, nor am I your son, since I have been solemnly offered to God and enrolled forever in his service; therefore I have no need of your anxiety.

Take care of what is yours; almighty God will without doubt take care of what is his, and will not despise what has been offered to him by free will. I thank you, because when I was yours, you nourished me with pious solicitude; but now, after I have offered myself to God’s service, he who created me will nourish me, and he does not need your care, nor will he any longer entrust to you what is his. Be therefore tranquil in mind; bear no anxiety for me, since the Most High has so provided for my affairs that here in Würzburg I am much better and more gladly situated than I ever was at Sponheim.

For God, who has ordered all things well, has mercifully bestowed upon me such grace that, through the favor of many princes, if I had wished, sufficient provision would have existed for me, so that there is no need to implore the assistance of parents. I have made God my helper; therefore the whole world is my fatherland, in which I shall pass through all adversities. Thus must we live, mother, so that after death we may enjoy the eternal vision of God in heaven.

Farewell. Pray to God for me; nor do I wish you to be mindful of me otherwise, since I am accustomed to have no remembrance of you except in my prayers. Farewell again. From my monastery at Würzburg, on the eighth day of the month of November, in the year of the Christians 1506.

you will love, since, just as no one loves an unknown good, so whoever has recognized that supreme, unchangeable good through faith, by the zeal of formed belief and holy fervor, will love nothing except it alone. I thank you, Sycamber, because, mindful of me, you pray for us while offering sacrifice to God the Father. May the love of Christ, which made you our friend, always burn in your heart with spiritual sweetness. Farewell, healthy and unharmed, for Nestor’s years. From Würzburg, on the eighteenth day of the month of November, in the year of the Christians 1506.

XI. Of Johannes Trithemius. 523

To the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James at Würzburg, most revered teacher and friend, Rogerius Sycamber, claustral canon in Hegen, sends greetings.

I received your letter, most learned Trithemius, exhorting me to the love of Christ, with great reverence and joy. Would that you might often send me such exhortations, by which I may always be able to advance in the love of God and become better than myself. For your letters are sweet to me and [unclear] than honey, nor can I read them so often that they do not please me more when reread.

But I rejoice greatly with you that you have found a place quiet from the cares of secular affairs and suited to your studies, hoping that from now on you will compose many things for the common benefit in leisure and monastic quiet, which previously at Spanheim, because of the manifold cares both private to the monastery and public to your order, you were compelled to interrupt. But I was greatly afraid, after you did not wish to return to your monastery of Spanheim, that you would betake yourself to the courts of princes, since there are many, as I have heard, who greatly desire to have you with them.

But what good man would not rightly be angry with your monks at Spanheim, reproach and curse them, who, out of their envy and malice, did not fear so injuriously to confound you, a man most gentle, excellent, and learned beyond all, dear to kings and princes, and to be revered by all good and learned men, such as the order of Saint Benedict has had no one for three hundred years, and to provoke you to indignation? I, no blind examiner of cloistered men, when ten years ago, with the consent and will of my superiors, at the request of your paternity, I stayed with you for the space of six months, as you know, in Spanheim, your monastery, and copied out for you, at your request, two volumes of my compositions with my own hand, carefully noted the manners and inclinations of your monks, and found almost all of them, except Henry of Cologne and Johannes Damius, of whom one is now dead and the other provost of the nuns in Neuenburg, to be haters and contemners of all good arts, and detractors of your useful studies.

I wondered at your moderation in food and clothing, and I took up your continual observance of regular discipline, together with your constant study of the scriptures, as an example for my spiritual edification; nor shall I forget it as long as I live, but I shall take care, according to my powers, to be your imitator. I have also heard from many that that envious Duke Johannes does not love learned men, nor has anyone in his court who is well disposed toward studious and learned men. I believe this to be true from the fact that, when I was with you in Spanheim at that same time, since for some cause unknown to me he necessarily had to write to the Roman supreme pontiff and to the college of cardinals, he could find no one in his whole duchy of such learning who could write in Latin. Afterwards, if I remember rightly, he was compelled to send his chancellor to you and to ask that you write in Latin to the pope and the cardinals.

Therefore I rejoice and am very glad that you have found a place suited to your studies, where there are many who take delight in your compositions and in your most lucid learning. Certainly I have no doubt concerning your monks in Spanheim, who were never worthy of you, that, with God, the just judge, taking vengeance, they will receive punishment for their rashness after a short delay of time. There is one thing that afflicts me with sadness in this change of yours: because, on account of the greater distance between the places, I cannot henceforth receive your letters so often.

Our Veldicus in Dirmstein, who is most devoted to you, greatly rejoiced when he heard that you had established yourself in monastic peace; for he feared, as I did, that, attaching yourself to the courts of princes, you would evade the quiet of cloistered life. He especially asks, moreover, that you cause some part of his works, after it has first been corrected by you, to come forth into the light through the printers for the common benefit of readers. I also hope that someday you will cause at least one of my little works Familiar Letters

... you will have [them] printed by the printers, of whom there are many in Nuremberg near you. If with kindly favor you are willing to meet my wishes, I shall see to it shortly that I send you two or three of my works. I recently wrote a certain prognostication, full of jokes and witticisms, which pleases many; but since your censorious severity disdains all jokes, I did not judge it proper to send these things to you, who, by the maturity of your life and words, are wont to be exceedingly formidable to trifles. I have also written to Jodocus Rubecacensis, a theologian most devoted to you in the church of Neometa, a single little work of familiar poems, which we both ask to have printed. I have written four volumes of my lucubrations, as you know, in each of which are contained thirty-four little works; if you order these to be given to the printers for printing, I shall send them all to you, when you have appointed for me a definite messenger to carry them. Our Johannes Canter, the Frisian physician, our common friend, has paid the debt of the flesh; remember him before God. Farewell, and pray for me. From Hegen, on the first day of the month of December, in the year of the Christians 1506.

XII.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James at Würzburg, but formerly of Sponheim, sends greetings to Roger Sycamber, his most steadfast friend.

I do not doubt that you rejoice together with me, if I myself rejoice. But if I myself do not rejoice, then you too will not rightly rejoice with me when I am not rejoicing. I do rejoice, however, that I have overcome the envy of my rivals, and at last, with the help of the Lord Jesus Christ, have escaped the company of my most ungrateful monks, whose ways, opposed to my purpose, I was forced to bear for twenty-three years not without bitterness. I have escaped wretched, ungrateful, and most foolish men, and have come to a place, as I hope, sufficiently quiet, in which I can both attend to my own salvation and continue the holy studies of the Scriptures. Yet I grieve that good and innocent men have had to depart because of the wickedness of the faithless, although they too at that time can provide for themselves safely enough elsewhere, if they are burdened by the company of the depraved. You feared that I would thrust myself into the courts of princes, because there were many who delighted in my service. You were not alone in fearing this. But in all my adversities I resolved this in my heart, with God showing mercy: by no means to abandon the way of the Lord, but to keep inviolate until death the profession of holy religion. Hence, let this be said in your ear without boasting: the more my rivals raged against me, the more I felt the grace of God present to aid me; by it it came about that, although with the help of many nobles and princes I could quite worthily have avenged the injuries done to me, I wholly neglected every vengeance. For unjust tongues, depraved by their habit of lying, moved against me, inventing such things as had never been thought by us. But in truth the principal cause of the whole persecution against us was that, being well disposed toward the most serene Prince Palatine, I was cherished by him with singular clemency. For this is plainly enough known to very many. It was notorious that Duke [Cyno-?] did not favor Palatine affairs; this was clearer than light at the time when, in the past war, the provincial Count of the Hessians devastated Naganium with plunder and fire. Therefore, out of hatred for the Palatine, not only the [Cynonori?] persecuted me, but also certain men from among our own, such as the abbots of the Mount of St. James at Mainz and of the Mount of St. John at Rheingau, who, together with their monks, for many years back have never ceased to assail with curses a most gentle prince, although he has done them no harm. They also always envied me both my name among students and my good reputation, bearing it with a most unjust spirit whenever I had been honored by any of the princes. When, in the year 1503, the princes, electors of the Empire, had assembled at Frankfurt in the month of October for certain affairs of the realm, it happened that I too, having been summoned, was present at the court of the most serene prince Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg. There were present Raymond, cardinal priest of Santa Maria Nuova, at that time legate de latere of the apostolic see, and the archbishops Hermann of Cologne, Berthold of Mainz, and Jacob of Trier. I was a continual table-companion of that same Margrave Joachim; I was called to table four times by the cardinal and twice by the archbishop of Cologne, and on my departure was presented by them with very beautiful silver vessels and held in great familiarity. Hearing these things, the aforesaid abbots and monks were torn in their hearts by envy, and since they could do nothing else, they began to persecute me with slanders...

Of Johannes Trithemius.

they began, thundering out things which the cloistered men were by no means saying. May the Almighty pardon them, since their envy provided the occasion for all the evil that I suffered. For if they had not favored those reckless attempts, my brothers would never have raised their horns openly against me. But let these things pass into everlasting oblivion, and in the future recompense of the righteous may he who gave the virtue of endurance render to us the fruit of patience.

If our Veldicus has any of his works that he wishes to be printed, let him send it to us polished, and we shall take care that it is printed as soon as possible. Concerning your little works also, send whatever you wish to have printed, and you will find our diligence. Roger, you have written many little works in a few years, by day and by night, while nevertheless carrying the burdens of canonical religious life; at this quite a number, indeed, are amazed. I praise and commend the diligence of your studies; I would praise it more if, leaving secular matters aside, you turned yourself to spiritual ones. You have already composed almost one hundred and forty little works, among which there are very few (yet I do not know whether there are any) whose reading either builds up faith or advances the mind into devotion to spiritual exercise. I beg you, my Roger, change your purpose in writing, and you who until now have written many things for the sons of the world, from now on bring forth something for the worshippers of God. [Boys'?] songs do not always befit [a man?]; studies must be matched to one's age, and, according to the [unclear] of Saint [unclear], when one is a man one must put away those things which seem to belong to children. You are strong in talent and at the same time in facility of writing; it is not enough unless you write such things as may benefit readers either in knowledge or in love of the highest good, which is God, and may prepare a reward for you in the future. Farewell, praying to God for us. From Würzburg, on the eighteenth day of the month of December, in the year of the Christians 1506.

XIII. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James at Würzburg, sends greeting to Johannes Damio Curiesto, confessor of the nuns at Neuburg near Heidelberg.

From your letter, dearest brother, I have now been made more certain both what the form of the election was, and who has been elected abbot of the monastery of Sponheim in my place. Did I not long ago predict that Melantius the prior was panting after the abbacy, and that for this reason he had earnestly devised all methods and ways by which he might induce, or at least provoke, me to resign? What he ambitiously coveted he has obtained; let him himself see by what means, since the Lord God is just, who gives grace to the humble and is wont to resist the proud and swollen. This must be imputed to the foolish and inexperienced visitors, who badly arranged the difficult business of the election. And so that you may recognize what seems to me to have been wrongly done in an election of this kind, we shall recount in order what we noted from your letter. First, indeed, the visitors left a bad precedent to posterity, in that they summoned laymen to the monastery for counsel at the time of an election, with such great display, as a bad example; this had not been done before, nor was it then necessary that it be done, unless perhaps in the [council of the brothers?] they feared an outbreak of schism. Then, since they could clearly have known that on that occasion none among the brothers then present at the election was fit for the charge of pastoral solicitude, why did they not postpone the day of election until [the absent ones?] were compelled to be present? Why did they not elect some fit man from wherever? Only five conventual monks were present at the election; the rest, and likewise you too, were absent out of indignation at what had been done; and, after a conspiracy had been made among them, they swore that they would receive no one as abbot unless he was contained in their number of five. Once this conspiracy had been allowed by the visitors, there could be no doubt that no one except Melantius would be abbot. What sort of election of monks is this, in which the way is barred to the Holy Spirit, and the votes of all the electors are maliciously restricted contrary to the norm of equity? In such a manner the prior was elected abbot, who [unclear] of our father Benedict [unclear]. For they elected as abbot one consenting to their own vices: sluggish, afflicted with acedia, and having no zeal for regular discipline, unless perhaps from now on, by God's mercy, he rises to better things; that this may happen, we do not cease to pray to God with continual prayers. For, to confess the truth, we do not hate the man, many evils though we have received from him, but we rightly detest his vices enough; unless he corrects them, he will be a useless shepherd. The man Familiar Letters

You know, and therefore there is no need for us to write much about him. For this reason they did not notify us in time of the day of the election, so that we too might have been present for guidance and counsel. If any man can know the characters of men, none of the monks of Spanheim was unknown to us. But Prior Melantius, knowing how great the evils were that he had committed against us, dreaded our presence, fearing that he could not obtain the abbacy if the election had been held with our counsel. Therefore, if any evil has followed upon this election, let it be assigned to the visitors, who neglected to summon us when they ought to have done so. You write that, after the election had already been completed, they departed from the monastery in indignation, because, forestalled by the brothers’ conspiracy, they were unable to appoint an abbot suitable for the place. We do not wonder that they were forestalled by the brothers’ fraud and scheming, since both of them are altogether inexperienced in the actions they had presumed to undertake. For the one, the abbot of Seligenstadt, accustomed to stay at home, has never been engaged in public affairs of the order. The other, however, the abbot of Bischofsberg, what is he but a skin without understanding, puffed up with banquets and cups? By foolish and ignorant prattling he is accustomed to throw into confusion and overturn whatever he undertakes. But since we cannot take back what has been done, let us pass over it in silence. For the Lord God is able, through mercy, to raise up the fallen, so that the elected man himself, with whom now no one seems to be content, as divine grace advances in him, may become much better than anyone could have judged. Nor will our exhortation be lacking; but as soon as we have the opportunity of a reliable messenger, we shall take care, for the love of Christ, to urge him by our letters toward better things. Farewell. From Würzburg, on the fourteenth day of the month of January, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XIIII.

Joachim, by the grace of God Margrave of Brandenburg, prince elector, to John Trithemius, abbot of St. James at Würzburg, greeting.

[unclear]

Reverend father and most beloved teacher, with gracious affection we congratulate you on the new abbey which you have lately received, in which, as we hope, you will have greater peace than it is agreed you had in Spanheim. We devoutly and humbly beseech almighty God that, according to his most holy will, he may long preserve your paternity in it healthy, fortunate, and unharmed, just as from our heart we favor you. We very much desire to know what has happened concerning your teacher Libanius, whether he is still alive or has departed from human affairs. But if he is dead, we earnestly ask your paternity not to sleep over the acquisition of his books. For you know how useful and necessary they are to us. In your last letter to us you promised that, as quickly as you could, you would complete those things which we requested to be published by you. We ask that, in your accustomed manner, you apply diligence, and that as soon as you have completed the things agreed upon, you not be slow to send them as quickly as possible, after hiring a faithful messenger at our expense. We send you, O our glory, one cask of salted pike and two of herrings; we ask that you receive them with a grateful mind, not as a gift but as a remembrance of us. This time, however, we were unable to have a supply of sturgeon and [unclear]; otherwise we would have sent those to you too very gladly. For whatever good we shall be able to bestow upon your paternity, we are prepared to do with singular favor; your fidelity, diligence, and munificence, abundantly shown to us, deserve that we do this. For we would rightly be charged with the fault of ingratitude if we seemed to forget your kindnesses toward us. With the most fervent desire, moreover, we long for your return to us around the feast of Pentecost, or sooner if it could be done; and we shall take diligent care that this happen without inconvenience to you. For we have many things to discuss with your paternity which we cannot entrust to letters. But so that, for this very matter, you may have suitable access to your lord the bishop, and our friend, since you cannot come without his consent, we send you our letters to him, in which we earnestly ask that he consent to us concerning your return to us, not at all doubting that your paternity will most diligently cooperate with us before this same friend of ours for the obtaining of this matter. Whatever you finally obtain, please write back to us through a messenger to be hired at our expense, and you will have us ready to gratify you in all things according to your wish. We desire that your paternity fare most happily. From our Ursulum, on the day of Saint Anthony the abbot, with our own hand, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation one thousand five hundred seven.

[unclear]

To these Of Johannes Trithemius.

I first replied to these letters in the Easter season, since they were presented to me not by a regular messenger, but by a chance carrier, who brought us fish given by the prince himself on the sixth day of the month of March, which was the Saturday after Reminiscere in Lent.

XV.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James at Würzburg, to the excellent brother Nicolaus Basellius, monk of Hirsau, once his hearer and disciple: greetings.

I feel compassion for your sickness, and I pray the mercy of almighty God that he restore you as quickly as possible to your former health. And indeed, as you write, devastation and solitude befell me, according to the prophecy of Isaiah, not without great contrition, since, while the war of many men was raging against my most serene prince, the Palatine, almost all the estates of my then monastery of Sponheim perished either by fire or by hostile devastation. When at last the war had been quieted by the authority of the King of the Romans, certain men from [Cynonotis?], not very favorably disposed toward the Palatine prince, rose up against me in hatred of him and, secretly raising up rivals against me, made Duke Johann hostile. What evils afterward followed upon me, when you were with me at the end of the month of June at Neumagen in the year one thousand five hundred and five, you heard more fully. But afterward, in time, I learned what I had not known before: that all the things which my rivals attempted against me they undertook at the urging of certain of my brothers, together with the abbot of Mainz, an enemy of all studious men. For indeed, unless he had supported the wicked men while I was absent and suspecting nothing of the sort, they would never have committed [unclear].

Do not wonder, Basellius, nor suppose that it was rashly done, that, provoked by the injury of my rivals, I resigned the abbey of Sponheim. In it, through twenty-three years, how many useless occupations opposed to my purpose I endured, neither can I say nor would you easily believe. Yet you are not wholly uninformed, since you lived with me for a whole year, carefully weighed the character and pursuits of each man, and found among us many haters of good letters. What were we to do any longer with ungrateful monks, whom we could never persuade to correct their manners according to the purity of the Rule and to devote themselves to the sacred study of the Scriptures, which would especially become monks? We dismissed them when the opportunity was received; nor does it repent us, having obtained a place which, though poor, is nevertheless quiet and by no means unsuitable for our studies, in which we shall be able usefully to devote ourselves both to ourselves and to the reading of the Scriptures. Since you wish to know who are the heads of the faction against us, recall to mind what you once heard at Sponheim, and you will easily separate the good from association with the bad.

Blessed be the Lord God almighty, who delivered me from the midst of Babylon and rescued my soul from the depth of useless occupations, so that henceforth I may walk before him in peace and tranquillity of mind, which indeed I had always desired with my whole heart. Concerning the chronicle of your monastery of Hirsau, I want you to know, dearest [Irbusius?], that I left it unfinished, together with the books and all the collected materials, in the monastery of Sponheim. There seek whatever is of your right, and think about its completion as you will; for the former agreement no longer pertains to me, because I have renounced the abbey together with all things belonging to it. I shall nevertheless be ready to do what I can for the honor of your monastery, if your abbot wishes. Farewell, mindful of us in your prayers to God. From Würzburg, on the fourteenth day of the month of March, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XVI.

To the most reverend father in Christ, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Würzburg, his most learned teacher: Johannes Cemurianus of Clusardia, pastor of the churches in Trittenheim, sends greetings.

It can hardly be said, nor indeed would anyone easily believe, most learned of all teachers, with how great joy and exultation I was suffused when Master Jacobus TriJohannes Trithemius.

to writings, although fabricated, because the matter escaped men’s notice, hearers would give credence no less readily, especially since noble philosophers seemed to proclaim these things, than to those things which unlearned fishermen had announced concerning the Savior. Taking boldness, therefore, from the true miracles of Christ, they devised similar things about their own teacher, promising themselves no less belief among the people than they saw believers had given to the holy preachers, whom they despised as simple and unlearned. Hearing that Christ, led from the midst of the Jews to the precipice, passed through untouched, they fable that their Apollonius vanished suddenly from Caesar’s sight and was made far outside the city. Likewise, the Lord Jesus recalled three dead persons to life in the mystery of baptism; they lie that Apollonius raised a dead girl at Rome. Over the baptized Lord the Father’s voice was heard; Apollonius is said to have been addressed by Hercules and the other gods of the Gentiles. If this is true, they were necessarily phantoms of demons; if it is not true, Damis, certainly, or Apollonius himself, invented this as he did many other things. Likewise, after his resurrection the Lord Jesus entered to his disciples though the doors were closed; Damis lies that Apollonius, bound in fetters at Rome, made himself free as often as he wished.

It would be far too long and tedious to hear if I wished to bring back to the pen all the miracles which Philostratus narrates concerning Apollonius; no reasoning supports how he could have performed them, because it is manifest that he was a mortal man and a worshipper of idols, and that he often held the pernicious error of many things concerning the transmigration of souls into bodies.
