He introduces a noble young man among Hiarchas and the wise men of India, slandering letters and all philosophy out of hatred of Homer, because, although he had once been a high-souled commander in the Trojan war, through Homer’s envy he had received no remembrance among the illustrious. Then, therefore, the man, clothed again [in a body?] and mindful of the former injury, assails all writers with one obstinate judgment. What is more insane than this folly: that a man should remember what he had been twelve hundred years before, for they report that so much time elapsed between the destruction of Troy and the age of this Apollonius of Tyana, when he cannot know where, or what, or how he was before he came forth from his mother’s womb? Or how will this fable be able to have even according to the Pythagoreans and Platonists any likeness of truth, who place very many years for transmigration’s return to the first point? But, since shame forbids me to speak longer about these most vain ravings, which are vainer than dreams, I ought not do so; rather, the remaining matters must be pursued in brief narration.

Such is that manifest fiction of Damis, contrary to every reason of nature, in which, in the meeting of Apollonius with the Indian philosophers, with Hiarchas presiding, he introduces miracles unheard of and nowhere seen: that the seats of the philosophers burst forth from the earth; that the sun supplied perpetual fire for the sacrifices; that a bowl, often drained by the philosophers with a little cup, again suddenly sweated forth abundant full liquid, so that as often as it had been drunk up, so often it would again overflow full. I pass over the other things devised with similar presumption: singers raised on high, demons expelled from men by letter, predictions of the future, declarations of hidden names and things, the interpreted twittering of swallows and birds, the exposed crimes of disguised specters. Whatever miraculous thing his followers wrote concerning Apollonius, in a few words I shall disclose to you, most reverend father, as you command, my opinion concerning the miracles of the Tyanean.

The miracles, signs, and prodigies which in the eight volumes of Philostratus are read as ascribed to Apollonius, in my opinion, firmly and without doubt to be held, are either fabricated and false, or, if they did occur, were perpetrated without any hesitation by the cooperation of demons. That they are fabricated, lying, and false is strongly persuasive to me from Damis himself, the disciple of Apollonius, who, as often as he writes something great, difficult, and miraculous about him, always introduces his fellow disciples as absent, and himself either alone or present with very few; and more often he records that no one was with Apollonius when he did great things or spoke with specters. But if the persuasion mentioned should not sufficiently win trust for my words, and someone should wish to defend the miracles of the Tyanean, whoever he may be, let him tell me first: if Apollonius performed the miracles ascribed to him, by whose power could he have done them? By his own, namely, or another’s? Certainly not by his own; nor had he obtained any natural science for performing them, since the power of natural magic by no means extends itself to most such things as are narrated about him. For Apollonius was a corruptible and mortal man, who must be believed to have been able to do nothing by his own power beyond the common order of nature that deserves the name of miracle. It follows, therefore, that if he did anything of this kind, it was performed not by his own power, but by another’s. But true miracles are performed by divine power alone, and the Tyanean could in no way have done these, since, being a worshipper of idols and full of much superstition, he was far removed from knowledge of the true God. Also by the proper power of the intelligence of his spirit, or of natural magic, most of the greater things which concerning Johannes Trithemius.

...they had been afflicted in many ways by the Egyptians with mud and brick. The apostles of the Lord also, beaten with rods by the Jews, cast into prison for the name of Jesus, and having suffered many insults, afterwards passed over to salvation. By their example you too, indeed, suffered injury and insult from your monks, lest, when you were to be transferred elsewhere by the will of God, you should seem to have abandoned the wicked without cause. The monks of Sponheim, strengthened by the counsel and assistance of depraved men, full of the poison of malice, were trying to bring your holy name into contempt and reproach, but they had no power at all, since, by the justice of God taking vengeance upon them, they are now all terrified and confounded, falling into the pit which they made. But you, most learned teacher, remain glorious in the esteem of all good men, and your name is celebrated more and more from day to day. Farewell, most reverend father, and hold me, your disciple, commended. Given from Trittenheim on the eighteenth day of the month of April, which was the second Sunday after the feast of Easter, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1507.

XVII.

To the Reverend Father Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of the monastery of St. James at Wurzburg, his most sweet teacher. Johannes Gotfridi, useless pastor of the church in Mandal near Kreuznach, sends greeting.

Most loving teacher, by your letters, at once most sweet and exceedingly bitter, I was so overcome, with little eyes weeping unceasingly from bitterness, and so disturbed over your resignation, that the bitterness of the death of all my parents and friends could never have saddened me so much. For I alone am not now saddened by your perpetual absence, but all the priests, masters, and learned men round about lament your departure most bitterly. For to whomever I showed your letters, and I showed them to many, as soon as they had begun to read them they were compelled by tears to interrupt their reading. Now it is said with one voice by all: Alas, that so great a man, so learned, so experienced, and celebrated in every land, one whose like Germany does not have, excelling in wisdom and religion, compelled by the envy of monks to abandon his monastery and his country alike, has transferred himself to foreign nations.

That most unjust chancellor of Duke Johannes, made your slanderer and enemy unjustly through I know not what mules, unless through your monks and subjects, at the instigation of the abbot of St. James at Mainz and of your brothers, made the most pious prince offended with you. For love of you I did not blush recently to reproach him for this to his face before many people, at the time when your successor was being elected in Sponheim. Answering in fury, he said: Who drove out your abbot Trithemius, whom you commend so highly? Or who harmed him, saddened him, or offended him? Why did he not remain in his monastery? Or why did he not return, since there is no one who would have prevented him? Why did he not acknowledge Duke Johannes as equally his lord and the protector of the monastery, just like his Palatine, whom he always preferred to all? That useless beast was saying many other things too, by which he publicly declared his envy against you, the best of men.

It was the day of the month of December when the election was being celebrated, and the monastery was filled with knights, so that the fathers of the order, together with the monks, could scarcely have a suitable place for electing. O most sweet teacher, how bitter a spectacle it was to my heart to see, in the place of you, my most loving father and the best and most upright of men, another man raised up, and one unworthy, unlearned, inexperienced, [unclear], who in fact betrayed you like Judas and, under the appearance of humility, was always secretly opposed to you. I was present at the election, as you know; I heard and saw everything that was said and done, and, when I called you back to memory, all my inward parts trembled, and amid the song of gladness my little eyes poured out tears without interruption.

Do not suppose, most learned teacher, nor take it that I write these things from zeal for vanity or with the intention of flattering, since not I alone, but the whole neighborhood, of laymen as much as of priests, is affected by your most grievous departure with sorrow of mind and body. And not undeservedly. For you were the glory of the whole country, the light of Christians, the teacher and mirror of cloistered and religious men, the defender, instructor, and advocate of rural priests, also the father of the poor and the physician of the sick. We all used your prudence and learning according to necessity at will, and there was no hesitation that was not removed by your counsel. For you were a most ready comforter to all who fled to you, and whatever could be requested from you lay open without envy to the poor as to the rich. O how often, when I was troubled now by patrons, now indeed by peasants, did I flee to your wisdom as to an oracle, seek counsel, implore aid, and, always protected by your defense, come out victorious in all things. Never from you without...

Trithemius’ kindness. XXIII.

Joachim, by the grace of God Margrave of Brandenburg, Prince Elector, to Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St James at Würzburg, greetings.

[unclear]

Reverend father in Christ, most distinguished man: let your Paternity know that by divine mercy I am sound and unharmed, together with my wife and son. This same thing I wish for your Paternity above all; I pray and beseech, because it greatly delights me to hear often of that same happy condition.

My lord brother, the Archbishop of Cologne, Prince Elector, sent letters to me, and with them he sent your Paternity’s letters, which you gave to him in the month of March, containing an excuse and impediments why you would not come down to him in person after returning from me to your homeland, and why you cannot send without a sure messenger the things entrusted to you by me; all these things pleased me. His Paternity, moreover, gives infinite thanks for the books and other medicines which I entrusted to you to carry to him, if you could, in person together with my letters.

But since at this time you do not intend to go down to him, and since he could ill do without the gifts sent by me for longer, I have sent this messenger of his to you, by whom I again and again ask that you send to him the things that are to be sent. But the other, more secret matters, which I entrusted to be carried by word of mouth, should remain with you until you are able to approach him in person. Farewell, sound and happy, praying to God for us.

From my Cologne on the Spree, on the 28th day of the month of May, in the year of Christ 1507.

XXIIII. Re- Familiar Letters

I departed from you without consolation, and whatever counsel you gave me, I always received its useful and honorable effect. Whatever had been spoken as your opinion was always and everywhere held firm and stable by the learned and likewise by the unlearned. O, who will now console me, wretched and unhappy, in my tribulations? Who will teach me in my ignorance, or who will instruct me, doubting, toward the truth? To me, and to all who fled to you for refuge, you were accustomed to be the fountain of true wisdom and the inexhaustible ark of the covenant, since you used to disclose to us, in whatever matters we could be in doubt, the clear truth confirmed by the sacred Scriptures. Finally, taught by your instruction, I confess that whatever I know in the sacred Scriptures I have acquired; and if I write in Roman style, it is not my own doing, but the service of your training. Hence I shall always take care, to the best of my ability, to imitate not only your manner of speaking, but also the character of your writing, moved no less by love of you than by the example of my fellow pupils whom you instructed: namely Jacob Trithemius your brother, Johannes Centurianus, Nicolaus Basellius the monk, Adam Pantomoranus, and others doing this same thing.

Would that I could truly imitate you not only in learning, but also in character and in the merit of life; nothing more desirable could ever happen on earth. For I have done what befitted a faithful pupil: I have fixed you as master in my heart, so that from it the memory of you may never depart, and my mouth at all times may utter Trithemian praises with favor. For the Trithemian name is imposed upon me to such a degree that it is sweeter to me than every sweetness, and more honorable than every honor. For I do not blush at the name of my most learned and most innocent teacher, but I shall magnify it and celebrate it with praises as long as breath shall govern these limbs. Let him perish who does not favor, speak well of, and wish well to Trithemius.

Sometimes, most loving teacher, your rivals say to me, whenever I bear your name to the stars: Where now is that most famous Trithemius of yours, the abbot whom the princes of the world and the pontiffs of the churches, and also all men, learned and unlearned, used to admire, to honor with letters and gifts, and greatly to venerate? What prince or pontiff now sends either messengers to him? Where now are the most learned men, who used to flow together to him at Sponheim from every region that is in Europe? Is he himself as honored and glorious before bishops and princes as he was before? To them I am accustomed to answer what is true: You are wrong, fools, you are wrong. For it was not the place that made Trithemius, but rather Trithemius himself who by his learning made the place of Sponheim distinguished. What was Sponheim before Trithemius was in it? Or who heard its name far away? Certainly it was nothing, and its name was obscure, cast down in darkness, [unclear], and unknown. My Trithemius by his learning and lucubrations made the name of Sponheim illustrious, and made it renowned throughout the whole world with immense glory, though before it had been utterly unknown. Princes, bishops, nobles, and learned men venerated him, not the place; they cared to see and address him, not the monastery.

And behold, my Trithemius has left the place which he had made distinguished; he still lives, and has been transferred elsewhere with glory. Where do princes now run? Where do they now send their messengers? To Sponheim, or to Trithemius? Certainly no learned man henceforth now comes to Sponheim; none of the princes or bishops any longer sends his men, knowing that Abbot Trithemius is not at Sponheim. Therefore it is manifest, and needs no proof, that princes venerate not the place but the man; and now, hearing that he has been transferred to Würzburg, they send their messengers to him, as they used to do before. They have no concern for the monastery of Sponheim, since, as I have said, they seek not the place but Trithemius. But I know, informed by a truthful report, that the fame of Trithemius is greater and more glorious today among princes than it ever was before. For as Truth says: A prophet is not accepted in his own country; so Trithemius attains greater glory in a foreign land than he had in his own.

O what a foul face of a monster the monastery of Sponheim is now seen to have, where, because Trithemius is absent, almost everything is perceived to have collapsed. Regular observance has fallen, integrity of morals has been corrupted, and the name of cloistered discipline remains only in the habit of the monks. I know, my teacher, that Duke Johannes already greatly grieves over your resignation, and many with him; and all would wish, except the chancellor, that you would [unclear] at Sponheim, because only now do they recognize how useful a prelate they have lost, and how faithlessly your monks dealt with you. Hence no one favors them, no one feels compassion for them, no one comes to their aid when they are in necessity, but they are despised by almost everyone, and people publicly say of them that the monks of Sponheim are worthy of burning, who did not fear to circumvent and supplant so excellent and distinguished a man with such great faithlessness. The abbot himself, your successor, companion of Judas the betrayer, an inexperienced, lazy, and foolish man, pleases none of the neighbors, is despised by the officials of princes, and is held in contempt by all.

Of Johannes Trithemius.

...is held. To him I am accustomed often to say: “Look, the blood of my Trithemius is being sought; and as you have done to him, though he did not deserve it, so it will be done to you according to your deserts.” Duke Johannes himself would not have thought, nor, as I have heard, would he have believed, that you ought to have reckoned that deed, in the capture of your servants, as an injury to yourself, or taken it so much to heart that on that account you would leave your abbey. For if he had known this, he would never have allowed it to be done. But I, knowing what you have written to me, am accustomed to answer those who say such things with that Virgilian line:

“The herdsmen came late.”

The snare of the impious has been broken, and innocent Trithemius, my own, has been delivered, God preserving him. These things, most reverend teacher, I wished to write back to you from the sincerity of my heart, and I ask you again and again graciously to understand them in that spirit. For I am yours, whatever I am; therefore I write confidently whatever comes into my mouth. Master Conradus Antonianus of Cologne read your letter not without tears; as you know, he loves you greatly, honors you in every way, and greets you. Farewell, excellent teacher, and remember to write to me more often, because your letters are more precious and dear to me than gold. Farewell again. From my house in the village of Mandal, on the fourth day of May, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1507.

XVIII.

To the Most Serene Prince, Lord Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, Duke of Stettin and of the Pomeranians, Prince of Rügen and Cassubia, etc., Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James at Würzburg, wishes eternal happiness.

What shall I repay to your majesty, most wise Prince, or in what way shall I ever be able to make return for your benefits? Behold, with how many gifts you have already honored me, a humble and lowly man. First, at Frankfurt, with a golden cup, sufficiently precious and very beautiful. Secondly, when I was staying with you in your March of Brandenburg, you adorned me with very many gifts in gold, silver, and precious stones, whose price was of quite great value. But now, wishing still more abundantly to provide for my poverty, you have sent me three vessels filled with salted fish, the use of which during this Lent has been no little useful and timely for me and my brothers. For what shall I repay to your most sacred majesty for all these things, O most noble Prince, except that I most gladly devote all that I am, can, and am worth to your service? For I am in no way able to return thanks to your Highness; I have and offer as many immortal thanks as I can, offering myself at all times for the services of your Serenity, according to my strength, from the heart of the fathers. Let your Serenity know, excellent Prince, that our Libanius, my dearest teacher, is still living, and healthy and safe; and he promises that he will come to me in the present year, if this can be done in any way. He writes, however, that he was ill almost to death for nearly two months.

Concerning my return to you in the March, most gracious Prince, I presented your letter to my lord, the most reverend bishop of Würzburg; when he had read it, he also handed it to me to read. He would indeed gladly grant assent to your desires, unless he feared that my absence for so long a time would be harmful to me and to my monastery, especially because I am still new in the abbacy, and the rashness of the Scots threatens us with snares. But in order that your Serenity may know his friendly disposition toward you, at length he concluded, as you will clearly understand from the letter of his most reverend Paternity which I am sending, that I should complete for your Highness whatever things have to be written; and when these have finally been finished, I can betake myself to your Serenity, to remain in your March for one or two months. I desire above all to obey your commands in everything, so far as I can with God, and to serve your majesty before all princes. But because I am a man placed under authority, it is necessary for me to submit to the command of a superior. This, however, I ask and advise: that your Serenity deign to have patience until the next coming year; meanwhile I will write here what you have ordered, and when I come I will bring it with me completed. For I trust without any hesitation that, at the appointed time, at the feast of Easter of the following year, my aforesaid most reverend lord bishop, in accordance with his promise, will not deny me leave to come to your Magnificence. I have been able to send nothing remarkable this time, since I have not yet sufficiently corrected the things I have written; nevertheless I shall take care to bring all these with me, and to the best of my ability I shall strive so that I may not seem to have been honored by your Highness in vain, nor your confidence in me be deprived of the fruit hoped for. I have again sent the Greek manner of writing which I had given when present, since the earlier one in the last letter...

532 Familiar Letters

[unclear] your Highness marked as lost. May almighty God preserve your Serenity unharmed. From Wurzburg, on the 9th day of the month of April, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XIX. Joachim, by the grace of God Margrave of Brandenburg, Prince Elector, etc., sends very many greetings to Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James in the suburb of Wurzburg, with prayer for all good fortune and prosperity.

Reverend father in Christ, my most beloved abbot, I received the most welcome letters of Your Paternity, and at the same time the messenger whom you sent; by his report I learned that you were sound and unharmed, and that your condition was quiet and fortunate [unclear], for which I congratulate you from affection and give due thanks to the immortal God. Your Paternity gives me very great thanks for the munificence and benefits bestowed on you, which are in no way owed to me, since all the gifts that I have conferred on you are small and cheap; indeed, they do not even deserve to be called gifts, and for that reason they require no acts of thanksgiving. Even if they had been of some value or price, they are nevertheless not such and so great as you deserved to receive from me and as were especially fitting for you. For through them I wished only to show the affection and goodwill of my mind toward you; I ask you again and again to be willing to weigh that rather than the utterly cheap gifts themselves.

I rejoice that Libanius, your teacher, is sound and unharmed; if it could by any means be done, I would desire to see and speak with him. I have also received the letters of our friend the lord of Wurzburg concerning your return to me in the March, promised for next year, which saddens me not a little because of the ordering of my affairs and the nature of the causes to which your long absence can bring harm, since your return to me is not only useful to me, but very necessary. But since it cannot be otherwise, I am compelled to be content and breathlessly await the promised time. Yet I ask that Your Paternity not defer your return to me beyond the promised time, since your coming again is necessary to me. I have also written back to my friend, the lord Bishop of Wurzburg, asking [unclear]; do not be reluctant to present my letters.

I have also given letters to your prince, the Palatine, in which I asked that he assist you in obtaining the books necessary for you. And so that it may not at all be hidden from you by what writings of yours I desire to be delighted, I refer you to the note sent from Tangermunde the previous year, in which I had marked for you the names of certain subjects on which I wish to have splendid treatises from your workshop. Whatever Your Paternity judges conducive to true wisdom and to living blessedly, I shall count as my delights.

I give Your Paternity infinite thanks for that very beautiful and most exquisite method of writing [unclear], which you have again sent me; in my secret affairs I would not wish to lack it for a great deal of money. Let Your Paternity not distrust my person, because I shall never be able to forget the faith and charity conceived between us. For my mind toward you is sufficiently open, sincere, upright, and most loving.

[I send?] one silver cup, gilded inside and out, not as a gift, but as a sign of my love toward you and of the stable friendship long since contracted between us and destined to endure until death; I pray that you receive it with a glad heart and use it rather often in remembrance of me.

I wish to know concerning my letters whether they have reached the hands of Libanius or not. Palestinus, about whom you asked, is still with our King Maximilian, and we do not know when he will come. Let Your Paternity apply diligence in those matters which you know to be useful to me, and you will have me grateful to you in all things as long as I live. Farewell, ornament of Germany and chest of all wisdom, mindful of me before God and loving, we who love you exceedingly. From Berlin, in my own hand, on the twenty-ninth day of the month of May, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XX. [unclear] Of Johannes Trithemius.

XX.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James at Wurzburg, to George [unclear], prior of the Friars Preachers in Berlin and vicar general throughout the March, his dearest friend, greetings.

[unclear] [Mindful of your merits?], venerable father, I cannot but favor you as well as I can, and be concerned for your welfare as a supporter. And therefore I wish to know from you what you are doing and how you are faring, although I know very well that you have felt the envy of your brothers, who, as my judgment stands, are in no way worthy of you. But these, if I may so speak, are vices inborn in many cloistered men: to resist holy and excellent prelates, and to expose them to various murmurings and detractions. Slanderous monks. When troubled, all come to the prelate for consolation; but if it should happen that the ruler himself is troubled by some occasion, which of the brothers will console him?

Having experienced these disturbances in the abbey of Sponheim for twenty-three years, I long ago wrote a book On the Misery of Cloistered Prelates. Although not all suffer these things equally, nevertheless few are found altogether immune from them. For many are the miseries and tribulations of cloistered rulers, which I could enumerate the more certainly, the more numerous and bitter I have always experienced them to be. This one thing alone consoled me: that I knew from the rule of my institution that I had undertaken the care of weak souls. For that reason, for the honor and reverence of the supreme shepherd, I endured all things patiently as far as I could, hoping that I would receive my reward from him who did not refuse to die for our infirmities.

In all these things one thing was still lacking in my tribulations, which, apart from death, was the last of miseries. And when, with the envy of rivals raging against me, I at last began to experience that, and had seen the hardened hearts of the wicked, I resolved to give place to wrath; I refused any longer to serve ungrateful cloistered men. For you know the causes of my disturbances; therefore I shall be briefer. Returning from the March to my homeland, I found certain of my monks not thinking rightly toward me. Provoked by their ingratitude and perfidy, I went to Wurzburg when summoned, and accepted the monastery of St. James in the suburb to govern. But I resigned the abbey of Sponheim because of the wickedness of the monks and the envy of rivals, preferring to live with few monks in peace rather than with many in continual disturbance.

I wished briefly to recount to you the history of my tribulations, so that in your adversities you may know that I am a sharer, sympathizing with you from my heart. I have written a word in your defense to the most serene prince; what sort of word it is, the little sheet enclosed with these letters will report. I should like you to write back to me what is being done with you, and not allow this messenger of mine to depart without your letters. Please greet in my name all our friends, whoever they may be, those who remember me for good. And you, excellent father, take care to be well, praying to God for us. From our monastery, on the tenth day of the month of April, in the Christian year 1507.

XXI.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James in the suburb of Wurzburg, to Johannes de Segen, abbot of the Mount of St. Peter at Erfurt, greetings.

[unclear] Reverend father and friend, since I was about to send this servant of mine on certain business to the most serene prince Joachim in the March of Brandenburg, I could not, and certainly ought not, let him go without my letter to you, since he must necessarily pass through Erfurt. First of all, I give immortal thanks to your paternity for your kindness toward me, and I shall repay it if ever I can. I have not found such charity in the whole Bursfelde Union, except in Antonius, abbot of St. Matthias of Trier, who seemed to vie with you in benefactions toward me. Hence I would deservedly place you two foremost among my friends, thinking without forgetfulness of your benefits toward me.

I resigned my abbey of Sponheim of my own free will, because of the ingratitude of the brothers and the envy of rivals, at last seeing and openly recognizing the hardened heart of Pharaoh, who gave credence to falsehood rather than to truth. But I came to Wurzburg, called through the abbot of St. Stephen by command of the most reverend prelate, and, canonically installed on the fifteenth day of the month of October, poor myself, I took up the poor abbey of St. James the Apostle, formerly of the Scots; in it I trust that henceforth I shall live with greater peace and tranquility than I have been able to dwell in at Sponheim up to this time.

Familiar Letters

it incomparably far excels, since it teaches true and solid things and invites the reader to the enjoyment of eternal happiness; it also recalls the mind of its lover from earthly things, and instructs it the more in knowledge, the more diligently it has been ruminated in meditation. There is no weariness in it; by use it pleases, by neglect it displeases, and the more it is read, the more it is loved. It bestows two most precious gifts on its lovers, since it both sweetly enlightens the understanding by instructing it, and gently inflames above all things, with the ardor of divine love, the mind withdrawn from the vanities of the world.

Commending this, Saint Jerome says: “The divine speech is most rich; it has in itself all delights. For whatever good you wish is born from it, just as manna, when it was eaten, tasted in the mouth according to each one’s will.” Hence Saint Paul, beautifully wishing to express the breadth of the divine Scriptures, says, writing to his disciple Timothy: “All Scripture, divinely inspired, is useful for teaching, for arguing, for correcting, for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be made perfect, instructed for every good work.” Therefore the effect of sacred Scripture is to teach truth, to refute falsehood, to rescue from evil, to lead toward good, and to raise the mind of the diligent reader to perfection.

Hence divine Scripture is deservedly to be preferred to all sciences, since whatever good is contained in each of them is commended wholly and universally in it. For in it is contained the instruction of all philosophy, since all causes of all natures, as holy Augustine says, are in God the creator, whose holy knowledge Scripture promises and establishes for us. In it also ethics is seen to be surpassed, since a good and honorable life is formed from nowhere else than when those things that are to be loved are loved by us, namely God and our neighbor, which truly divine Scripture alone teaches. Here is logic, since the truth and light of the rational soul is nothing but God; and sacred Scripture itself proclaims this to us. Here is the praiseworthy welfare of the commonwealth, here the laws of princes and the rights of nations. For a citizenry is not best guarded except by the foundation and bond of faith and firm concord, when the common good is loved, the highest and truest good, God, which sacred Scripture alone pours into us.

Therefore men intent with piety upon the sacred writings are to be preferred to all teachers and placed before the students of any sciences whatever, since, as someone says: “Nothing is better for a man than, by reading divine things, to fix his mind there whence life comes to him.” For the study of the divine Scriptures is a ready, beautiful, and pleasant way, which with sweetness leads us into the knowledge of the highest and unchangeable good. When the mind of the studious man has come to this, exulting broadly in the Lord it will cry out: “The king has brought me into the wine-cellar; he has ordered charity in me.” Happy is that conscience in which, besides the love of Christ, who is the wisdom of God the Father, chastity, patience, and justice, no other love has dealings; nor has it sunk back to the lowest things, but with a spirit always desiring heavenly things, it sighs for them.

O mind thrice happy and four times most happy, which, inflamed by zeal for divine love, can say with the most blessed martyr of Christ, Ignatius: “My love has been crucified.” O yoke of holy love, how sweetly you bind the humble mind to the plough of Christ, how gloriously you draw it when ensnared, how gently you press it, delightfully burden it, strongly bind it, prudently instruct it. Your sweetness is known to no one untried, since no one understands what love is who, always slothful, has never truly loved.

The love of God is a most powerful fire, which the Lord Jesus came to cast upon the earth, and he wished it to burn, illuminate, and consume in the hearts of his faithful with continual charity. That fire of divine love makes the mind which it inhabits burn with desire for heavenly goods; and, sweetly illuminating it, leads it into all truth; and, powerfully consuming in it all things of vanity, makes it rich by participation in divine goods. The rational love of the mind is Christ; therefore whoever wishes to taste true affection beforehand should learn to love Christ sweetly. For divine love is an unfailing treasure: whoever has it is rich; whoever lacks it, even if he abounds in all the riches of the world, is truly and rightly to be called most poor.

For whoever loves God with his whole heart, and with his whole soul, and with his whole strength, leaves no place for fault, since the devil does not enter when the soul is full of God. For, as the Lord signifies in the holy Gospel, the devil desires an empty mind, and seeks one stripped bare, swept, and cleaned. But where he finds God present through love, he immediately departs in great confusion. For just as visible vessels of material things, when they are full of some liquid, do not receive the increases of things poured in besides, so, if divine charity has wholly filled us, there will be no place by which crime can enter. But the love of God is never idle, as has been said; rather, always watchful for the worship and increase of the mother [unclear], it works great things, and with every care is circumspect, lest even in a small matter it offend its beloved, but [unclear] in all his [unclear].

Familiar Letters

[unclear] reward; so far as men are concerned, I have labored in vain. Finally, in the common causes and affairs of the chapter, the order, and the union, by making visitations, by speaking, and by carrying out embassies before princes, bishops, and very many others on many occasions, I have labored not a little, although I have received no reward from men. Yet I hope that the almighty and merciful Lord will bestow eternal good for these things. I have had few faithful helpers for the common good, and, as we plainly see, I have left behind still fewer followers of my works on behalf of our observance. Few there are, I say, not to say very few, who have the necessary zeal for holy religion: all seek what is their own, not what belongs to the commonwealth. Hence visitations are neglected, regular observance perishes, and no one is found who grieves over it. I know certain monasteries of our union and observance, and indeed not few in number, in Swabia and in our eastern Franconia, some of which have not been visited by the fathers in eight years, others in ten, and others in fourteen. Indeed, there are found today in certain monasteries of our union monks and abbots alike who publicly and privately eat meat, in contempt and insult of regular observance, and no one comes forward to correct those who offend so outrageously. The holy endeavors of the former fathers have been brought at once into oblivion and contempt; they, with great labors, vigils, and expenses, splendidly restored in our own times, under the title of the Bursfelde Union, in Saxony, in the regions of the Rhineland, and in the other adjoining parts, the observance of regular discipline, which had long since utterly collapsed. I grieve deeply, and not without cause, that through the negligence of these times the holy labors of the fathers of the past are perishing. It would be worth the trouble to admonish the fathers, when they are at some time assembled in chapter, so that they may forestall the evils that follow and compel those who walk carnally to return to the path of regular observance. Farewell, remembering me before God in your prayers. From the monastery of Saint James in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, on the tenth day of the month of April, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XXII. To the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Dietrich, Bishop of the Church of Lübeck, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James at Würzburg, prays everlasting felicity.

Most reverend prelate, most learned father, and ever-honored teacher, you will not wonder that I have changed the title of my abbacy, if you weigh with an even balance the reasons that stirred my mind to yield to my rivals. You are not unaware of the injuries I received without deserving them; lest the abbey suffer more grievous ones, I exchanged it on reasonable grounds. For I am a lover of peace, and therefore I refused to dwell any longer amid disturbances. Why your most reverend paternity wishes to learn from me what I think about the life of Apollonius of Tyana the philosopher, which Philostratus described in eight books from materials gathered by Damis and his other disciples, I cannot sufficiently wonder. For since you yourself are most learned in every variety of both divine and human writings, nothing can be hidden from you that I could either understand or write. Therefore it is rather shamefacedly that I answer your command in this matter, since you surpass me beyond comparison in talent and learning, and whatever I can bring forward is certainly already stored up in many ways in the cabinet of your breast. But to strive against it and to be unwilling to obey your commands would seem to me a manifest sign not only of a rash mind, but also of a mad one, the stain of which I have always been accustomed to keep far from myself. For if I must incur one of the two, I prefer to be accused of foolishness before your paternity rather than of disobedience or rashness. Briefly, therefore, and without the order of disputation, in a confused manner as best I can, I shall set forth in simple narration what I think about Apollonius, without injury to anyone who judges better.

Apollonius lived at the time when the apostles and disciples of Christ, throughout all Greece and Asia, preached the Catholic faith with signs and miracles shining forth, and announced to the Gentiles the life, doctrine, powers, passion, and miracles of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ himself, converting those who had been predestined to the knowledge of the highest truth, and arousing among the people great admiration and reverence for themselves. Hearing these things, which the holy preachers had spread throughout the whole world concerning the life and miracles of Christ, Damis and the other followers of Apollonius, although they did not believe the deeds that were said of the Savior, nevertheless invented similar things about their own teacher after his death, so that they might persuade foolish men that the one whom they had known as a philosopher was something above man, and for that reason not inferior to Christ. For they thought that by miracles written about Apollonius, then a very famous philosopher,

When Apollonius of Tyana flourished. Of Johannes Trithemius.

... conforming himself in all things to the will, with sagacious mind he ponders the commandments. For thus says the Lord Jesus in the Gospel: If anyone loves me, he will keep my words, and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him, and make our dwelling with him. O holy dwelling, O sweetest visitation of the mind, in which God almighty, the creator of all things, incomprehensible, deigns to hold a joyful banquet, where the creature is joined to its maker through the grace of inward love, and all worldly affections are powerfully extinguished. There are peace, piety, goodness, light, virtue, honor, joys, gladness, sweetness, everlasting life, glory, praise, rest, love, and sweet concord. This, reverend father, is the fruit of our friendship; sighing after its sweetest acquisition in continual meditation, let us walk with gladness in the way of God’s commandments, lest harmful weariness of the journey overtake us; may the consolation of the divine Scriptures always be with us. For as the holy [unclear] writes to the Romans: Whatever things have been written were written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.

Since, therefore, the study of the holy Scriptures prepares for us an open, safe, and most beautiful road to the knowledge of God, and knowledge leads the soul by the most pleasant and sweetest way of the Holy Spirit to love, from these two things, in this mortal life in which we live, the observance of God’s commandments happily occupies the mind; and after the death of the flesh, in that heavenly fatherland, there succeeds the enjoyment of the highest good, destined to endure without end. Those, then, must be judged happy who, despising the vanities of the world and rejecting useless and curious doctrines, have wholly devoted themselves, with pure sobriety, to this most holy philosophy of divine traditions. Among their number, Frederick, most learned preceptor, I have considered that you should be placed among the first; for just as a rose among thorns sweetly attracts the reader by its beauty and fragrant scent, so you, among many nobles by blood of our own age, canons and prelates of the Church of God, shine and gleam with learning in the divine Scriptures and constant study of them, and also with holy morals and innocence of life, and you have so bound me wholly to yourself that in loving and honoring you I shall yield to no one.

Therefore I wish you to be persuaded that I am such a man as has known and wishes to observe most holily, and to preserve with inviolable constancy and unharmed, the rights of the friendship contracted between us. For if rarity increases the price of things, you are to me the more precious a friend to be embraced, inasmuch as among the noble ministers of Christ known and dear to me, applying themselves today to the divine Scriptures, you are held almost uniquely alone. How many today, I say it with shame and reverence, are found among the nobles, canons and prelates not only of cathedral churches but also of other churches, despisers of sacred reading, who therefore think the knowledge of the Scriptures disgraceful to themselves, because, not born of rustic blood, they boast that as nobles they are ignorant. How great a madness turns the breasts of mortals! If contempt and ignorance of the Scriptures made men noble, such men would rightly be called most noble, because they understand less than nothing, since they do not know themselves and are ignorant of God. But it is not our office to censure the haters of saving wisdom; therefore let the blind fare well, groping in darkness, who detest the light of knowledge.

Let us continue on the journey we have begun, the study of the Scriptures, so that by continual meditation on them our understanding may delightfully rise up to the knowledge of the highest truth, and our affection may constantly burn in the love of God. For this is the true friendship of Christians: by common study to believe in God through faith, one in substance, three in persons, according to the tradition of the holy Scriptures, and to love him truly above all things with equal desire, equal virtue, and equal consent. And therefore, Frederick, most loving father, you are to me a more precious and dearer friend, since in loving me you seek nothing earthly, you hunt after nothing perishable, you burn sweetly with zeal for the divine Scriptures, you pant toward God at once with knowledge and with longing for inward love; for that reason you desire to have me as a friend, whom you believe to be inflamed with like fervor. But although I am in no respect to be compared with you, yet I frankly confess myself a lover of the holy Scriptures, and I promise myself as a companion on the journey to the delightful knowledge of the highest good, in love of which may our inviolable friendship remain founded: now committing the seed of good works to the soil of one’s own pure heart, from which we may obtain the fruit of eternal enjoyment among the sons of God’s election.

I have completed, with God’s help, the little book of Saint Joseph, containing the praises of the foster-father of our Lord and Savior and inscribed to your most renowned name. Since I have determined that some things in it must be made clearer, it will necessarily have to be written out again, so that it may come into your hands, worthy of more polished things, as corrected as possible. Meanwhile I ask you to bear this delay patiently until it is brought into the light, because it will admit no other patron than you, reverend father and lord. You urge that I enter your house by right of friendship whenever it happens that I go up to Bamberg; this offering of yours I gladly accept, and I give thanks as much as I can.

Chapter 35.

Noble [unclear], despisers of sacred Scripture.

The true friendship of Christians. Familiar Letters

As for the things that are narrated of him, I am persuaded by certain reasoning that he could by no means have been able [to do them]. Nor is it to be believed that an idolater had anything in common with the holy spirits of God. It remains, therefore, to be held as an undoubted conclusion that, if he performed those miracles which his followers wrote about him, they were accomplished by no other cooperation and power than that of demons; for it is not difficult for them, by false miracles, to deceive even in greater matters the senses of men devoted to them, since by nature and by skill, through long practice, they are more subtle than we are in producing illusions.

But his followers do not allow Apollonius to be accused of magic. I therefore adhere to the former opinion which I stated: that the miracles ascribed to Apollonius were devised, fabricated, and falsely invented either by him or by his disciples. Nor do I think I can easily be led to think otherwise, unless perhaps they concede that they are to be attributed to the deeds of demons. What wonder is it if men devoted to worldly wisdom and philosophy, and wholly ignorant also of divine knowledge, most eager for praise and esteem among men, fabricated about their teacher greater false miracles than the apostles preached throughout the whole world about our Savior and truly performed in his name? Therefore, to sum up all the miracles of the Tyanean: if he did the things which his followers wrote in his praise as wonders, he was certainly a magician and an enchanter of demons and infernal specters. If he did not do them, as is my opinion, no one can doubt that all were devised, fabricated, and falsely invented by Damis and his other disciples, so that they might adorn their master with false praises and thereby themselves obtain eternal glory among mortals.

If you marvel at the rashness of the deed, consider what the audacity of Greek writers has not presumed from the beginning. It is the opinion of many that the histories of the Greeks teem with fabricated tales; that great Trojan destruction is a fiction of the poets. We readily believe that demons devoted their efforts to the fictitious Apollonian tales, so that through these imaginings of Damis and his companions the Christian religion might become cheap among the gentiles, since the Tyanean seemed to have done among the Greeks no less than they had heard Christ had worked among the Jews.

Perhaps they also thought that men would easily be persuaded that Christ was not God on account of the display of miracles, since Apollonius himself, a worshiper of idols, who for that reason wished no divinity to be proclaimed about himself, had been no less distinguished in performing them. How desirous this Tyanean was of the glory of human esteem is testified in many places by the things written by Damis, especially where Apollonius himself recounts to his disciples that gods, the souls of the dead, appeared to him in the temples of idols and spoke great things. Whoever, therefore, believes that the Tyanean performed the miracles written about him either by his own natural power, or by philosophical wisdom, by purity of sanctity, or by natural science, which they call physical magic, should beware lest he do injury to Christ, the Savior of all; for if he did them, he was an enchanter of demons rather than a philosopher.

This, most candid prelate, is my opinion concerning the miracles of Apollonius, which you wished to know. If anyone wishes to oppose it, he seems to me not sufficiently to understand how far the powers of human nature extend. Farewell, most illustrious pontiff; keep your Trithemius commended.

From Würzburg, on the 16th day of the month of April, in the year 1507.

Of Johannes Trithemius. 24.

To the most reverend father and most serene prince and lord, Lord Hermann, archbishop of the church of Cologne, duke of Angaria and Westphalia, administrator of the church of Paderborn, archchancellor of the Holy Empire throughout Italy, prince-elector, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James at Wurzburg, wishes happiness.

Most reverend prince, I send to your highness, with the bearer of these presents, your messenger, whom for this reason the most illustrious Prince Joachim sent to me from the March, the book and those things which in the previous year were entrusted to me by the same prince, to be delivered by me in person, as I recently wrote to your most reverend paternity. I had indeed resolved to come down to you and to hand over the remaining matters which had been entrusted to me to be conveyed orally; but, my affairs being in a state of disturbance, as your serenity very well knows, I have necessarily been compelled to defer this intention to another time. I did not receive in writing from the prince mentioned the manner of using the things which I send; yet I shall take care, as soon as I can bring it about, that it too be sent to your highness by a trustworthy messenger. For at present I do not have at hand the written replies which would seem necessary for the things sent. I trust, however, that at some time time and leisure will be granted me to come into your sacred presence, so that I may dispatch the remaining matters which did not seem fit to be entrusted to dead little letters. May almighty God long preserve your most reverend paternity unharmed. From Wurzburg, on the fifth day of the month of June, in the year of the Christians 1507.

25.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James in the suburb of the city of Wurzburg, to Roger Sycamber, canon of Dumetum, greeting.

The great and continual tribulations of Macharius, abbot of Limburg, I share all the more deeply the longer I have lived with him. Who would not have compassion for one who has suffered so dreadful an injury, unless he were altogether estranged from the faith of Christ, as are those who burned to ashes by fire such a distinguished monastery as Limburg? For unless they had been utterly estranged from the faith, that savage, impious, and wicked Count of Leiningen, and the satellites of impiety who serve him, would not have destroyed the temples of God, would not have violated altars, nor converted to their own uses things consecrated to almighty God. But what are the princes of the earth doing, who, appointed for the punishment of evils, punish their own injuries, even small and sometimes childish ones, so severely, yet do not notice insults to God? It is no wonder, in my judgment, Sycamber, that the Christian faith is today everywhere in danger, devotion perishes among men, charity is extinguished together with religion, and impiety with cruelty rules everywhere. By our deserts, Roger, we suffer evils, because we do not truly love that supreme good. Since today there are no princes to correct the vices and crimes of tyrants, many are found who alone are to be corrected. Therefore the Church is shipwrecked, the empire is diminished, the number of the unbelievers is increased. What once most Christian princes, with devout intention, bestowed on the churches of God, tyrants today seize, and this very often with impunity, sparing neither God himself nor men. Whence the Church of Christ now justly laments, saying: In peace my bitterness is most bitter. But since our discussion of these matters is fruitless, we are compelled to be silent, lest we seem to have set our mouth against heaven. Your letter announces to me that Johannes Cantherius the Frisian physician from Groningen, a learned man, has departed this life. There is nothing new, nothing strange, if one dies who was mortal by nature, since he entered under this law, that at some time he should go out again. Behold, he has now gone out; he has paid the debt owed to nature; he has conquered what is most terrible of all, and has made past for himself what we all fear will be future for us. If he lived well in Christ, he has gone out happily, since, as Saint Augustine says: He cannot die badly who has lived well, and he can scarcely die well who has lived badly. O that we might live with such constant prudence as we desire to have lived when it is necessary to die. Cantherius has gone before us, has overcome death, and has now shaken off human fear. Let us therefore consider, dearest Roger, that we shall soon arrive where we grieve that he has arrived, and let us so live the very small moment that remains that we may suspect any hour at all to be our last. For, as Saint Christophilus says, we have here no abiding city, nor are we more enduring than our fathers, who have all preceded us to death. We also, as the bishop of Le Mans says:

We are all taken from the midst, with the fates pressing on, And we are drawn where life, once completed, calls us.

No [unclear] of religion. Isaiah 39.

For whom death becomes good. Hebrews 124.

Familiar Letters

Happy are those mortals in whom holy devotion ever burns in the love of God, who, recognizing themselves as pilgrims of this world, sigh in spirit for the heavenly homeland, and, loving nothing of corruptible things, long with constant desire to be brought into the eternal mansions. Death will be pleasant to them, not dreadful; through it they go with joyful prayers from prison, receiving the end of all evils and the beginning, without end, of good things. Death is terrible to those who live in such a manner that after death there is no hope of any good for them, who die in mind and body together, receiving eternal oblivion as the reward of their despair. Farewell from Würzburg, on the fourteenth day of the month of June, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XXVI.

Hermann, by the grace of God Archbishop of Cologne, Prince Elector, etc., to the venerable, sincerely beloved by us in Christ, Johann Trithemius, Abbot of St. James at Würzburg: greeting.

The matters which you sent to us, entrusted to you on behalf of and by commission of the most excellent prince lord Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, arch-chamberlain of the Holy Roman Empire and Prince Elector, our kinsman and brother, we have received with a grateful mind. And since we do not have, according to our will and judgment, the necessary manner of using those same matters, we desire of you with special longing, wishing that by our present courier you send us in writing full information about each of them; or certainly, if it will be possible for you in any way, that within the space of fifteen days you come down to us in person, to some place of our principality near the Rhine, since we do not intend to remain in these regions beyond fourteen days. For we desire to obtain from you complete knowledge of those matters. Show yourself diligent and willing toward us in these things, as our confidence in you holds. For in these matters you will do us a special kindness and a pleasing service, to be acknowledged with favor and grace, without forgetfulness. Given at Aldenahr, on the Saturday after the feast of Barnabas the Apostle, in the year 1507.

XXVII.

To the most reverend father and most serene prince, Lord Hermann, Archbishop of Cologne, etc., Johann Trithemius, abbot of St. James at Würzburg, wishes happiness.

Most reverend prince, there would indeed be in me a very ready will to come to you in person, were I not this time prevented by two impediments. The first is that the excellence of your most reverend paternity set for me a period of fourteen days for coming; interpreting these from the sending of your letters, I found them exceedingly short. Hence, fearing that perhaps, when I came down, your serenity would either, as usual, be in Westphalia, or elsewhere far away from the Rhine, and that I would have labored without fruit, I did not dare to undertake so long a journey unless I was certain. The second, which also drew my mind not a little back from the plan, was the absence of my most reverend prelate, stationed outside the homeland; without his will and consent it did not seem to me sufficiently fitting to enter upon so great a length of journey, especially because, by his munificence and kindness, having been placed in charge of this poor monastery, I have placed my whole hope after God in his humanity. I add a third impediment to a voluntary journey, since hitherto, being ignorant of your highness’s counsel in the matters proposed, I have not prepared those things which seemed to me necessary for their completion. But to please, according to my strength, your most reverend paternity I am wholly ready, willing, and prompt. Lest I delay longer, I have decided, around the feast of St. Michael, when your most gracious highness is accustomed to return from Westphalia to the Rhine, God having mercy and my most reverend bishop consenting, to come down to Bonn to your sacred presence, bringing with me those things which in so short a time I have been able, which seemed to me to have to be sent, because the most serene prince of Brandenburg handed over to me nothing except the bare forms themselves of the matters, which I sent some time ago; the rest he sent to be carried by word of mouth. Now, however, I send to your most reverend paternity, by the messenger sent to me, those things which he commanded, namely the manner of using the matters sent long ago, together with the rest tied up in a little bundle; with these would that I may have presented to your most serene highness a pleasing gift of service. May almighty God [unclear] your highness, illustrious prince, long Johannes Trithemius.

may preserve long unharmed; to him I commend myself, his humble servant. From Würzburg, on the twenty-third day of the month of June, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XXVIII.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James at Würzburg, to Friedrich von Redwitz, canon and cantor of the church of Bamberg and provost in [Oringau?], his friend, greeting.

[unclear]

Most distinguished sir, as to the fact that I return a reply rather late to your most elegant letter, do not think it was done through forgetfulness of you, but because of my usual literary occupations. That you have admitted me among your friends I both greatly congratulate myself upon and render you immortal thanks. For what sweeter thing could have happened to me, a man who is a stranger and established in a foreign land, than to obtain the friendship of a most excellent and most learned man? Not only nobility of birth and integrity of morals have made him worthy of regard, but also an education in every kind of letters, adorning him with all virtues, has deservedly rendered him glorious.

It delights me all the more to have entered into friendship with you, O most reverend father, because, according to the opinion of divine Jerome, I understand this bond of ours to be true: one joined by the glue of Christ, brought about not by advantage in household affairs, not merely by the presence of bodies, not by crafty and fawning flattery, but by the fear of God and the study of the divine Scriptures. This is perfect friendship, by which a friend is loved in God, and, through the love of Christ, there is one mind in two bodies, for no other reason than the likeness of studies by which both friends strive together toward the summit of the highest and unchangeable good.

Therefore true friendship cannot exist among evil and reprobate men, since, as Aristotle says, perfect friendship exists only with respect to one thing, because what is perfect cannot be directed toward many things but toward one. But the evil and reprobate always live in disturbance, never peaceable, never quiet, never ceasing to foam forth wickedness; they are carried away to many things, unity being neglected, and for this reason their associations should be called not friendships but rather conspiracies. For friendship is an equality of minds, standing firm in understanding and reason; wherefore it has never happened that there is any friendship among the wicked, who live by appetite and not by reason. The aforesaid philosopher expressed this very thing sufficiently in the Ethics, saying that only the friendship of good and honorable men is unchangeable.

No equality of minds, however, can be more constant than that which is born from divine love, by which the one, true, and only unchangeable good is known through faith with pure devotion, and is loved with fervent desire by friends in equal consent. Concerning this very bond the wise man says: “There is no comparison with a faithful friend,” because “a faithful friend is a strong protection; he who has found him has found a precious treasure.” Hence I rightly consider myself blessed, since I have found you a true friend, namely one who loves nothing else in me than the glue of Christian charity, which is the love of heavenly wisdom and the study of the divine Scriptures.

Who does not know that the enjoyment of eternal happiness, to which all our studies must be ordered, consists in the knowledge and love of the highest and constant principle of all things, which in our custom we call God; and that in the kingdom of blessedness that very enjoyment is common to all the good, and that by adherence to that good the perfect friendship of all the elect of God is confirmed, never to be dissolved by any intervening division? For the friendship of all who are united to their principle through the grace of enjoyment is therefore indissoluble and firm by an everlasting covenant, because they will one thing, love one thing, and consist in the enjoyment of one thing.

Therefore we, who have established the foundation of our friendship in Christian love to be made firm, approach that heavenly bond all the more nearly, the more we shall be in agreement in study and will upon the way that leads to it. There is, moreover, a threefold road to that friendship of eternal enjoyment, which directs those walking upon it into one way. Knowledge of divine goodness is acquired by the study of the sacred Scriptures; the love of heavenly desire is nourished by the exercise of virtues; and the worship of God is declared by the observance of the commandments.

Knowledge, therefore, causes love, because no one rightly loves what he does not know; love, moreover, demands worship, as Gregory says: “The love of God is never idle. For it works great things if it exists; but if it refuses to work, it is not love,” since the showing of work is a true sign of love. This is the threefold cord of true Christian friendship, which is not easily broken, because whoever walks in agreement with a faithful friend upon this road will easily overcome his adversaries: the flesh, the world, and the devil. Therefore Saint Jerome exhorts Paulinus, walking upon this road, saying: “Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh.” For sacred Scripture shows the way to the knowledge of God to those who love it, and every doctrine [unclear]

[unclear] Commendation of sacred reading, 546 Familiar Letters ... haters of [unclear], and utterly ignorant of the sacred Scriptures. Understanding, therefore, that it would not be sufficiently safe for me henceforth to associate with rivals and dog-eared scoundrels, I decided to move myself to other, safer places. Accordingly, poor as I was, on the fifteenth day of the last month of October, I accepted this poor abbey of St James at Wuerzburg, offered to me by lord Lawrence, the most reverend prelate, and afterwards of my own free will resigned Sponheim with its most ungrateful monks. Let the men of darkness and the rivals now fare as they may, those to whom our holy studies were not pleasing; and we, with the Psalmist, shall sing gladly: The snare of useless occupations has been broken, and we have been freed. For I do not regret what has been done, since, having obtained a quiet place, I now seem to myself for the first time to have found a beginning for philosophizing. I left my whole library at Sponheim, the loss of which I do not greatly esteem, since by now I have learned in large part to philosophize without it. The most illustrious Prince Palatine had been ready to provide me with the necessities of life as long as I should live, and no less the aforesaid Margrave of Brandenburg, if I had wished it; but it did not please me to live among courtly flatterers. I therefore chose, poor, to dwell in a monastery rather than, rich, to live in the world contrary to the monastic rule. You now have, most loving brother, the history of my calamity written in summary form; from reading it you may recognize that men are not to be trusted rashly. These things were done to me by those who seemed friends; these things sons perpetrated against a father. But I fear that the evil which they prepared for me may meet them in their own draughts, and that they may fall into the pit which they made. My abbey of Sponheim Prior Melantius has obtained; in it, without doubt, he will receive a share of the injuries done to me, which he has prepared by his own desert. Our Vigilius, Maecenas of philosophers, has obtained a canonry at Worms, but since the clergy has not yet returned to the city, he is staying at [unclear]. Farewell, and write to me more often. Again farewell. From Wuerzburg, on the first day of the month of July, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XXXIIII. To the reverend father in Christ, lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St James at Wuerzburg, his superior and special friend, Bilibald Pirckheimer sends very many greetings.

Reverend and most esteemed father, I have received two letters from you, to which I have until now made no reply, both because of my business and because of my absence [unclear]. For we know that almost all great and good men in every age have been persecuted by the wicked. Therefore you too should trust in the Lord, who gives and takes away, exalts and casts down, and again consoles. For he is not worthy of favorable circumstances who cannot bear adverse ones. Thus the wise man is distinguished from the fool, when he knows how to endure adversities with a great spirit. You therefore [unclear].

For we know that almost all great and good men in every age have been persecuted by the wicked. Therefore you too should trust in the Lord, who gives and takes away, exalts and casts down, and again consoles. For he is not worthy of favorable circumstances who cannot bear adverse ones. Thus wise men are distinguished from the fool, when adversities are borne with a great spirit. He knows. You therefore [unclear Greek quotation].

And [unclear Greek quotation].

Therefore one must not despair, but rather trust and hope, and, as Corydon says in Theocritus: [unclear Greek quotation].

But enough about these matters. For what swine will teach Minerva? Let us therefore come to the matter. Celtis, and especially Peutinger, have asked me to write to you and ascertain whether you were minded, once a stipend had been obtained from our most serene King, to betake yourself to Augsburg; for they would exert themselves so that an honorable condition might be offered to you. They offer both a house and very many other things, by the possession of which you may be able to philosophize at leisure, far from all noise. It will therefore be for you to consider what you must do, and then to inform me, so that I may be able to write to our friends about this matter. Be assured that I shall strive earnestly to attend to everything that is to your advantage. Farewell, and love me as one most devoted to you. From Nuremberg, on the Kalends of July, in the year of the Lord 1507.

XXXV. Jo- 548 Familiar Letters

...did not despise a friend. To you also, magnificent sir, I give undying thanks for your kindness, goodwill, and charity toward me, though I have no merit in your eyes and am not fit to repay thanks. Yet whatever I am, whatever I can and am worth, all that must always be subject to your command. When you write back to my friends and most generous men, Peutinger and Celtis, convey thanks in my name. Farewell from Würzburg, on the eighteenth day of the month of July, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XXXVI.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James in the suburb of Würzburg, to Georg von Rotenburg, most distinguished doctor of medicine, greetings.

When, in the year just past, on my return from the March of Brandenburg to the Rhine, I directed my journey through Erfurt, I made a most diligent inquiry for you, most distinguished sir, desiring to see and speak with you because of our old acquaintance and affection, mindful of the goodwill and kindness once honorably shown to me on the Mount of Saint Peter by you and your sons, young men of great talent, in the presence of the whole congregation of fathers; for this I shall be grateful to you as long as the power of remembering remains with me. But I sought and did not find you, because you were not in the city. Therefore, after waiting three days with longing for your arrival, since you did not come at all, I departed sadly. For I was held by a great longing for you. And quite often indeed I wished to send letters to you, but I always lacked a sure and faithful messenger who would carry them through.

Today at last, by the Lord’s will, the bearer of this letter, a priest and gymnosophist of Erfurt, met me quite opportunely, through whom I might satisfy my desire. And so I write you innumerable greetings; I signify, as best I can, my love toward you; and I desire that our old friendship remain firm and endure forever. As for the rest, the misfortune of our affairs and the change in our weak condition, whatever adversities have met us, we believe you have learned from the abbot of Saint Peter’s.

I suffered a grave insult and injury from my monks at Sponheim, with certain scoundrels attaching themselves to them; by them my spirit was so provoked into displeasure with the place and the people that my indignation advanced to nausea. From that there then arose in me a horror of my monastery, which over time grew so strong that it finally persuaded me altogether to abandon the ungrateful monks and to provide for myself honorably wherever I could. Meanwhile there was offered to me by the most reverend father, lord Lawrence, bishop of Würzburg, the abbey of St. James, very poor but quiet, and sufficiently suitable and appropriate for my studies. Accepting it for love of peace and tranquillity, I resigned Sponheim, together with its Spatic persecutors, of my own free will.

For twenty-three years I endured the greatest labors in the abbey of Sponheim; for these I received the envy of rivals, to whose rashness I thought it better to yield than, by continual cohabitation, to endure destructive madness. I left behind two thousand volumes, old, precious, and very rare, which with incredible zeal and love I had brought together at Sponheim during the time of my presidency, not without many expenses and labors, in every variety of writings: very many manuscripts, many printed books as well, Greek, Latin, and also Hebrew, of which before me there had been none there.

I confess that my spirit was broken, that so great a store of books had fallen entirely to unlearned and ungrateful monks; and, to restore it wholly to itself, I had to recall the image of my death. I began the experience of death in life; by a certain cosmetic art I tempered what was necessary with what was voluntary, so that one might pass into the nature of the other. And so little by little the pain began, as though afterward, to cool down; and, carried away toward future things, to say with holy Job: Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return into the earth whence I was begotten. And that saying of the holy Christ-bearer Paul: We brought nothing into this world; without doubt, neither can we carry anything away.

Therefore, among all the things of this world, the chief thing in which I was wont to take delight for the sake of the final end was that very library; for love of peace it was indeed necessary to despise it, though the separation was beloved to a spirit that had been accustomed to use the familiar consolation of writings in adversity. Yet with God’s help I overcame this intolerance of mind, making a virtue of necessity, so that I might turn more freely toward the highest good, which no one has ever rightly loved with a companion. I rejoice indeed that at last in life I have been released from useless cares of earthly occupations, so that henceforth I may philosophize more quietly in tranquillity. I gladly followed the counsel of Saint Ambrose, who says: It is better to depart with favor than to remain amid quarrelling. The place, however, in which I dwell is small and very poor, and in its buildings and structures largely ruinous. But the word of a wise man consoles me

Of Johannes Trithemius.

... of the Wise Man, who says: “For a little with justice is better than many revenues with iniquity.” For wealth, just as I did not possess it, so I never loved it. I have been content with moderation; every extreme is excessive and full of hardship. But enough about these things. I am most eager to know how you are, what your talented sons are doing, whom I heard delivering speeches many years ago when they were still quite young, how far they have advanced in learning, and what they profess in the Athenaeum. For I think that with age they have become most learned, since already in childhood they flourished with such wonderful talent. The education of your sons undoubtedly redounds to your praise, since you trained them in ancestral virtues, performing the duty of the best of fathers in morals and of a most learned teacher in philosophical studies. May almighty God, through his most merciful kindness, deign to make you joyful and happy in the wisdom, prosperity, and safety of your sons, and to preserve you forever, mindful of us. From Würzburg, 20 July, in the year of Christ 1507.

XXXVII.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James the Greater the Apostle in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, to Johannes Gotfridi of Mandel, most vigilant pastor of the church: greetings and love.

Whenever an opportunity is given me, I neither ought nor can restrain myself from writing to you, a friend truly most dear to me, to inform you of my circumstances. It is plainly most sweet to me to see letters from you often, and more frequently to send mine to you. My brother, Master Jacobus Trithemius, recently delivered to me your letter, when he was directing his journey from Trier through Sponheim to us. In it you lament that I am absent far away, and you declare that you are vehemently afflicted in your mind because I have utterly resigned the abbey of Sponheim. You assert that not only are you troubled and cast down in mind because of my resignation, but also that all the priests round about are lamentably saddened because I have deserted my place and departed into foreign lands. This was done after mature consultation with friends; nor does it repent me, nor, if it did repent me, could it be recalled. I thank you, and all my friends too, who grieve over the injuries done me. Repentance will not move me. Nor will it repent me to have resigned the monastery of Sponheim, if perhaps he should wish that he had not inflicted insult. For it is better for me to pass my life in peace of mind than, under a captive prince, to be driven by continual waves of disturbances. Nor do I greatly weigh the poverty of this monastery which I have taken up, since I know that at Sponheim I always lived in the utmost poverty. Nevertheless, as far as moderation requires, I have been sufficiently provided with all things necessary for the body, both for myself and for those who dwell with me; I seek no more. For no one can despise riches so easily as one who has always lived in moderation. For me, as a Christian philosopher and at the same time a monk, the richest thing is the mind, since I have always been content with my lot, and never either loved riches that I did not possess or desired to possess them.

That my rivals think that after my departure from Sponheim I am unknown to bishops and princes, I count as nothing; nor is there any need for them to know our fortunes, if any have been favorable, lest they waste away from greater envy on that account. But you, who are accustomed to rejoice in the peace and tranquillity of a friend, will understand most fully from the account of this brother, who has delivered these little letters of mine to you, how differently our affairs stand from the judgment of our rivals. For rivals are not to be cared for, nor will their envy disturb the uprightness of my mind.
