As for the fact that the officials of the neighboring princes round about detest the monks of Sponheim on my account, just as it does not benefit me, so it does not please me. For I understand well enough that this aversion of men will harm in no small degree that poor monastery, whose poverty I especially pity. I continually pray God that he may deign mercifully to provide for it in its necessities. You also, since you are neighbor to the place, I admonish, ask, and exhort with what love I can, that you not set great store by the injuries of the sons, which they inflicted on a father who did not deserve them, but rather attend to the place dedicated to God and to Saint Martin; whenever you see them oppressed by want, do not neglect, as far as you can, to bring help for the love of God. For they have been afflicted enough; they have paid heavy penalties for their rashness. The abbot who desired the abbey is infirm; he was not the last cause of my resignation, and I have heard that his appointment has not pleased everyone. I fear very much, though may the Almighty grant that it be in vain, that just as he secretly persecuted me, his pastor and abbot, so, God permitting, who is just, he himself will one day suffer open persecution from his own subjects. All things that are being carried on around me, from Proverbs 10, Familiar Letters

... great, knowing you to be a true friend and faithful from the heart. For unless your friendly presence delighted me beyond all things, I certainly would not be a true friend. For who would not take delight in being wholly with himself? Or who would endure being divided? But he cannot be wholly with himself who does not wish to be with his friend. For when Aristotle was asked what friendship was, he answered: “It is one soul dwelling together in two bodies.” And another indeed spoke beautifully of his friend: “half of my soul.” Therefore he who is with a friend is with himself. And I feel that half of my soul is in you, most steadfast of friends, by reason, of course, of the force of love; therefore, although you are absent in body, yet present in spirit, I suffer I know not what. From this it happens that I think I am speaking with you, and, carried away by the greatness of love, I cannot find an end to my words. Therefore I am compelled to restrain myself, lest the letter exceed measure. I beg you, be indulgent to these unpolished writings; if I have written with too little prudence, know that it must be imputed to friendship, by whose driving power love for you has seized me, divided as I am. For as often as I think of you as my friend, I know that half of me, not the whole, is in my possession. Farewell, my other self, loving and mindful of you, since I am a lover mindful of myself through the mirror of friendship in you. Again farewell. From Würzburg, on the 12th day of the month of July, in the year 1507.

XXIX. To the reverend father in Christ, Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James at Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, his most honored teacher: Johannes de Woesbruck, moneyer of the most serene king of Castile and master of the great toll at Bruges in Flanders, sends greeting.

Reverend Father, almost five years have now passed since I was last in Sponheim with your paternity. Afterward I could nowhere hear or learn anything certain about the same: what you were doing, or how you were faring. For I would hear nothing more gladly than of your good health, your happy condition, and your prosperous fortune in all things. The fame of your name is great among us; you are praised in the mouth of all learned men, and also of noble magnates. There are many in all our land who desire to see you and wish to be taught by your learning.

Among them is one venerable doctor of decrees, named Nicolaus de Pulchro Monte, a man universally most learned in philosophy, in mathematics, in astronomy, in medicine, in theology also, and excellently skilled in many other disciplines of the scriptures. He has been so inflamed by the fame of your name that he has judged neither expenses to be spared nor the dangers and labors of a very long journey to be feared, so that he might come as soon as possible to your paternity. Having asked and received from me letters of recommendation to so great a reverence, last year he undertook a sufficiently dangerous journey to you, because of the unrest of the Sicambri, and came to your monastery of Sponheim on the twenty-fourth day of the month of February. But when your most reverend paternity was not found, he returned with great sadness to our town of Bruges, from which he had set out, leaving his letters and mine at Sponheim with your prior, to be presented to you at hand as soon as possible.

From this it came about that, both of us ignorant of the state of your affairs, we began to pass our life with much weariness, and of necessity ceased from inquiring about you. For it was being reported there that your most reverend paternity was with the margrave of Brandenburg in the March, but about your return to the monastery we heard nothing certain. At last, God so ordering it, from Master Nicolaus Beifelius, whom your paternity knows very well, canon of St. Germanus at Utrecht and doctor of medicine, who, coming from Italy, was with you at [Neometum?], we learned that you were healthy and safe, that your affairs had been well provided for, and that, after resigning the abbey of Sponheim, you had betaken yourself to [unclear], there in peace and tranquility to philosophize. On this we greatly congratulate you, knowing that you are by no means going to lead your life in idleness, but rather, in your usual manner, will always write something that may profit many unto salvation.

But the aforesaid Doctor Nicolaus de Pulchro Monte, who, because of his exceeding desire for you, always thinks of you when awake and dreams of you at night when asleep, can give himself no rest until at last he satisfies his purpose, by which he desires to see you and to mingle sweet conversations with you about true knowledge. For he is a man not unworthy of conversation with you, as one learned and skilled in many languages, and also experienced in many matters and in the customs of diverse peoples. Twice he has been in Jerusalem; he spent a considerable time in Turkey; at Venice also, Naples, Bologna, Paris, Oxford, Salamanca in Spain, and many other places he lived as a pilgrim for love of wisdom and of the scriptures. Therefore, so that at last satisfaction may be given to his holy desire, we both [unclear].

both together most earnestly ask that you write back to us by the bearer of the present letter, where and when he can most conveniently come into your presence, because he has many things to speak and discuss with you which he cannot entrust to letters. I certainly hope that his conversation will not be unpleasant to you. Farewell, most loving teacher. From the town of Bruges in Flanders, on the 4th day of the month of March, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1507.

XXX.

John Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, but formerly of Sponheim, to John de Woesbruck, master of the Great Customs of Bruges, greeting.

On the twenty-seventh day of the month of May, dearest friend, we received your letter, together with that of a certain Nicholas of Fair Mountain, doctor of [unclear], through a certain young man; and since he said that he necessarily had to depart at once on the next day, we wrote back more briefly than had been our intention. What you mentioned, that we had been with the most serene prince, the lord Margrave of Brandenburg, and that I had given up the abbey of Sponheim and taken up another, is true; the man who reported it was not mistaken. It was done not without very great cause; so that you may know it, I shall set it down in this letter as briefly as I can. In the year of the Christians one thousand five hundred and five, on the first day of the month of April, I left my monastery of Sponheim, having been summoned to Heidelberg by the most serene Prince Palatine. While I was staying there for some time, certain of my monks, having allied to themselves certain [unclear], arranged a certain hidden conspiracy against me, and made that Duke John, whom you have known very well from long ago, hostile to me, to such a degree that he ordered certain members of our household, who seemed to favor my side, to be put in public chains as if they were wicked criminals. When these things were reported to me in my absence, moved by the rashness of the deed, I had resolved not to return to the monastery unless the authors of so great an evil had first expiated the insult by suitable satisfaction. Therefore I remained outside [unclear], in no way doubting the justice of God, since the wicked will fall into the pit which they have made. Accordingly, on the fifteenth day of the month of October just past, I took up this abbey in which I now remain; because of the unfaithfulness of the monks and the hostility of the duke, I resigned Sponheim of my own free will. Here, then, I now live as long as the Most High shall will; I devote myself to my writings, and always await, timid, the final calling which no one can escape. But if that good doctor of yours should wish to approach me, I hope he will find me here, unless perhaps meanwhile I must turn aside somewhere for a time, summoned as before. For you know how necessary it is for us sometimes to obey the commands of princes. Farewell, remembering and loving me. From Würzburg, on the twenty-eighth day of the month of May, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XXXI.

To the most reverend father and lord John Trithemius, abbot of the house of St. James at Würzburg, a man of the first rank among the Germans, Nicholas Gerbellius of Pforzheim wishes greeting and eternal happiness.

Since indeed, most reverend father, [unclear] in this most happy age, in which so many illustrious men, and men of no obscure fame, have appeared everywhere in Germany, among whom you are one: you who have made Latin, Hebrew, and Greek letters richer among the Germans; among whom you have such power and shine so brightly that I am in doubt, and waver like Terence’s Chremes, whether I should compare you with anyone or prefer you to all. But I do not doubt thoughtlessly, since we behold in you not one virtue or three, but all of them firmly gathered and massed together, as though we were watching a most seemly spectacle. Magnificently adorned with these, you [unclear] the minds of many, and the literary exercise of very many, of all you too have plausibly turned your eyes, who eagerly love you, greet you in turn, and look upon you in crowds. Stirred by them, I too have hastened quickly, and this love, which with long inward longing has laid waste to and burned up our heart, I display significantly, as we think, in these letters of mine, such as they are. By them I believe that I shall be most closely joined to you, since you do not disdain to enroll familiarly in your list even writers of the lowest bench. But if I am enrolled in the company of you and yours, I confidently affirm that it has gone very well with Gerbel, since you will judge, not without care, that I am not mortal but endowed with immortality. As for what remains, most reverend father: whatever it is that is now being most elegantly fashioned and overlaid beneath your hammer, do, I pray, let me know, who am yours and consecrate my whole self to your school; or write out what you greatly desire this new follower and soldier of yours to know. For I eagerly await your letters, which, assuredly with that veneration with which I am accustomed to receive the writings of the most learned, I shall kissingly adorn with everlasting cedar, perpetual ivy, and eternal honor. Farewell, most reverend father, and deign to number me among your own. From Cologne, the fourth day before the Ides of June, in the year of the Lord 1507.

XXXII. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James at Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, sends greeting to Nicholas Gerbel of Pforzheim.

Long ago, when I received your letter, excellent Gerbel, I resolved in my mind to reply at the same time to your wishes, as was proper, so that you might not be disappointed in the outcome of your confidence in me, and so that our friendship might become the more pleasing the sooner it had grown together. But because I delayed for a while, you should not therefore think that you have been either neglected or despised by me; and you will of your own accord pardon the delay, if you weigh exactly the inextricable occupations of servants of the sanctuary. It was also necessary that a volunteer letter-carrier be at hand to carry our little letter to you, lest, if entrusted to rascals, it perish midway on the journey. You ask first of all that we enroll you among our friends, requesting a thing that is certainly not difficult, since it has always been most pleasant for us to have all students of good letters among our brothers and dearest friends. But men of darkness and the greediest brooding spirits of riches we are never accustomed to admit into our friendship, because they oppose good studies, and because it is always their habit to snarl against learned and educated men. You, however, studious Gerbel, whom your most elegant letter declares learned and thoroughly virtuous, we willingly receive with open hands into our friendship, though we are quite middling, and we promise faith and charity in unshaken constancy. Although, in your estimation of us, deceived by report, you have erred greatly, if I may say so with your leave, since your praises far exceed our merits, nevertheless we accept the integrity of your mind toward us with the benevolence that is fitting. For I know that you do not imitate those utterly vain flatterers, who, when they seem to praise someone, deceive him, lying with fabricated proclamations, because they pursue not the man himself but gifts and rewards. You, however, have praised from love; trusting in deceptive report, whose judgments are blind, yet any intention of lying or will to deceive was far from your mind. But consider whether I am a truthful paraphrast of your letter, so that you may understand that I have grasped the meaning of your right opinion. Let the testimonies of truth be unstained, because you have conceived in your mind a matter sufficiently plain and manifest: that the man who denies that the friendship of the most illustrious men in the literary arena is immortal should be considered out of his mind rather than of sound head. For all the glorious deeds of former men would long since have perished with their authors, if they had not been endowed with immortality by the monuments of writing friends. Therefore antiquity judged those men fortunate who, doing things worthy of remembrance by talent, wisdom, or courage, had fallen into those times in which there was an abundance of the most learned and most illustrious men, by whose urgent friendship whatever seemed worthy of praise received immortality through the support of letters. Rightly, therefore, you promise yourself immortality from the friendship of illustrious men, men most renowned in the matter of letters; for just as the stars of heaven, joined by friendship with glittering rays, so too those illumined by the light of immortality often remain glorious among posterity. All learned men write good and honorable things to their friends, and they are accustomed to make their name and fame immortal no less than themselves among all posterity. But no one has ever endowed with immortality in writings an enemy or a man lurking in obscurity. I, however, my Gerbel, although I know that I am neither learned nor a giver of immortality, but only moderately studious, nevertheless shall take care, as far as my powers allow, that you have not entered into friendship with us—

It is agreed that the friendship of learned and distinguished men gives immortality.

An elegant comparison. Thus far I have served ungrateful monks more than enough. But this monastery, over which I now preside unworthily, although it is burdened by poverty, has neither such great anxieties nor so many ruinous, contentious occupations with peasants. By God’s grace I live content with my lot; and the poorer the place is in transitory goods, the richer I reckon myself in abundance of peace and tranquility. Indeed, according to the counsel of the holy Christ-loving Paul, having the necessary food by which the little mortal body may for a time be sustained in life, and clothing to keep off Boreas, I seek nothing more. The globe of the earth, sea, and islands, which you write is for sale at Worms, beautifully drawn, I would indeed wish to be able to obtain; but to spend forty florins on it, no one would easily [unclear] me. A few days ago [unclear] for a modest sum a beautiful sphere of the world in small size, recently printed at Strasbourg, and likewise, in a large arrangement, the globe of the earth spread out on a plane, with the islands and regions newly discovered by Amerigo Vespucci the Spaniard in the western sea and toward the south almost to the tenth parallel, together with certain other things pertaining to that inquiry. As for your advising me to put the cause of this matter before my most reverend lord the bishop, you are certainly doing your duty; but you seem to me to weigh too little the occupations of princes, and their perpetual and very great affairs, since you think the studies of men at leisure should be recommended to minds most occupied. Do not doubt that I am most tenacious of our old friendship; and no distances of lands will ever weaken the affection which I once poured out toward you. Therefore, what you bid me do, I exhort and ask that you too not be reluctant to do. I pray that we may live as friends in such a way that the memory of each in the other may avail before God. For this is the true cause of friendship: that we seek nothing other than equality of hearts in the manifestation of God, and the advancement of souls from mutual exhortation. But if one of the friends should fall into some calamity of the raging world, he must be consoled by the other with all his strength. If he has erred, he must at once be recalled by his friend to the way of truth. If he has grown lukewarm in saving study, he must be stirred up; for friendship will be true and rightly commendable if it accomplishes that for which it was instituted. And therefore the holy fathers judged the law of friendship to be most just, by which it is commanded that each man love his friend no less than himself. I heard that Heinrich von Buna died long ago; but I have not heard that his books and the globe of cosmography which he once bought from your workshop remained with the princes of Saxony, as you suppose. For he has a surviving brother, to whom, when dying, he consigned everything. I congratulate you warmly on your prosperity, and rejoice with you as a true friend, yet wishing that you remember the little verses of Hildebert, archbishop of Tours, who says: All mortal things hang on uncertain chance, and by their own changeableness promise flight. Whatever you have today will perhaps leave you tomorrow; or even now, while you speak, it ceases to be yours. You indicate that you have composed marvelous little works by lamplight since the time when I was with you in Dirmstein, which you promise to show me when I come to you. But since there is no reason for me to come to you, indeed not even the will to interrupt my quiet, you will do well, and do what most befits a friend, if you send me as soon as possible the titles of all your works, or certainly, what I would more desire, the little works themselves; once read by me, or even copied, I promise they shall be faithfully returned to you as quickly as possible. Perhaps you wonder that I said I had no reason to come to you; but hear the reason. The monastery over which I preside, though unworthy, is not yet known to be subject to the annual chapter of the Bursfeld fathers, since it has been newly reformed; for this reason they cannot at all burden me with the office of visitation, as they did before for twenty continuous years, not without great expense to me. Hence, by Jesus’ providence, the opportunity of resting is granted me, and no occasion for wandering, as before, is offered. And that is why I said I had no reason to come to you. Yet I would very much wish that you were with me even for one day; I too would show you little works at which you would marvel. But we shall see one another sometime, if the Lord Jesus, who can do all things, wills it. Meanwhile, whenever opportunity offers itself to us, let us mutually exhort one another by letters in his love. Pray for me, brother, to God, that he may keep me in his way and mercifully forgive me all my transgressions, of which there is no number, on account of the grief of his most bitter passion. Farewell. From Würzburg, on the 12th day of the month of August, in the year of Christians 1507.

...that he may regret the friendship. You urgently ask that we disclose to you what is now being fashioned under our anvil. We are treating a rustic Camena, and we sing, as far as cast-off scraps permit, a Muse suited to our purpose. We have completed a moderate-sized book on Saint Joseph the Christ-bearer. We have also brought the [Nepiachum?] of our Annals from the hour of the nativity down to this day. At the prayers of friends we have begun a great work of twelve books on demons, in which we have resolved to destroy all the profane arts of magicians, both in general and in particular, and to censure by name and properly their causes, inventors, books, methods, and deceptions. Amid these things we are also applying ourselves to the newly invented Steganography, which we do not yet promise to publish, being deterred by the malice of scoundrels. Someone used to say: “He who does what no one does, all admire.” But now one must say: “He who does something new, all disparage.”

From Würzburg, on the sixteenth day of the month of July, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XXXIII.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James at Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, to Conrad Celtis Protucius, poet laureate, brother and dearest friend, greetings.

Augsburg. I had hoped, brother, that you would come to us from Augsburg, so that I might have explained to you the whole history of my affairs, lest you either accept false things as true about me, or appear ignorant of a friend’s fortunes. But since you have turned your journey back toward Austria, I have been compelled to do by letter what I had prepared to do in speech. Therefore this nephew of yours by your sister, Nicolaus Wilandt, has met me quite opportunely; through him you may obtain knowledge of the things that have happened around me. In the year of the Christians 1504, our most serene king of the Romans, Maximilian, with the help of many princes, declared a most savage war against the Palatine forces; and, after crossing the Rhine at Mainz and entering the Nagau, the Hessians with the [Wedreffs?] carried off everything found around Alzey, a town of the Gau, and Kreuznach, under the rule of the Palatine and of the duke of the [Cynonoti?], while churches, castles, and little villages, unless they were ransomed with much gold, were burned and destroyed. There was one frenzy and incredible [unclear] among all against the most merciful Palatine prince; they thought they would cover his name and memory with the shadows of hell. Terrified by fear of the Hessians and by dread and threats of the neighboring [Melantagori?], I was compelled to leave my monastery, which is subject by command of that Palatine to the equal authority of the duke of the [Cynonoti?], because Alexander, son of [Melantagus?], who has now long since performed the duties of life, had already then given his right hand to the Hessians and was bringing them aid, devastating all the Palatine countryside and sparing neither age nor religion; and against me in particular, through hatred of the most illustrious prince, the count of [Budorianus?], he had prepared [unclear]. I therefore betook myself to Kreuznach, where I remained for twenty-two weeks, for so long did the fury and madness of the [Spatic?] Hessians last.

Meanwhile, while these things were being done, two of my monks, [Melantius?] Remigius the prior, and Johannes [Pingionita?], together with some [petronibus?] who had been given, long accustomed to favor the party of the [Cynonoti?], began to assail me first with hidden hatred and then with open hatred. Above all they made hostile to me the duke of Transylvania, who rules the country people of the [Cynonoti?], inventing many things, the principal charge of which in sum was that they always grieved that I had very strongly favored the Palatine interest. All the rest, however, was contrived and falsely invented. Then in the following year, which was the year of the Christians 1505, on the first day of the month of April, summoned to [Budoricm?] by command of the prince, I betook myself there on account of the monastery of Limburg, which had been utterly burned by the wicked enemies of the Palatine. While I was necessarily staying there for some time, the [Cynonoti?], by order of the duke, invaded the monastery, and, seizing certain members of the household in hatred of me, violated ecclesiastical liberty with reckless daring. When these things had been reported to me at [Budorim?], they indeed displeased me greatly; and, after taking counsel with friends, I resolved to defer my return to my monastery until a fitting expiation should follow so great a wrongdoing. I therefore remained at [Budoris?] and [Neometis?] for three months, until the assembly of princes with the royal majesty at Cologne, whither I went down at the beginning of July, summoned by Joachim, margrave of Brandenburg and prince elector, and I stayed there also for five weeks. From there, at the insistence of that most illustrious prince himself, I entered the March after him. Finally, after nine months, having returned to my homeland, I clearly learned that the aforesaid monks, together with the abbot of Mainz, had been the authors of all the evils, men who did not favor my affairs sufficiently well, because they are Of Johannes Trithemius. XXXV.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, sends greetings to Willibald Pirckheimer, senator and patrician of Nuremberg.

My magnificent Willibald, it has been most sweet to me, not without great pleasure of mind, to reread often your letter, full of consolation and learning; in it I clearly understood both your [unclear] and the common and sincere compassion of my friends toward me.

To you, therefore, most distinguished man, and no less to all my friends, I have and give undying thanks. If any opportunity is given me to repay it, I shall see to it that I show myself willing and most ready. I embrace your admonition, by which you finely and most modestly exhort me to endurance. Everything done against me without my deserving it I have already before now committed to God, and I have resolved not to seek vengeance, knowing [unclear]. [unclear]. How I served ungrateful monks, now [cast out?], I seem already to have learned sufficiently. [unclear]. For although I knew very well the saying of the wise, that [unclear], I always hoped for better things, until suddenly, with experience as my teacher, I was compelled to know that [unclear]. Hence Hildebert, archbishop of the Gauls, spoke finely:

All mortal things hang beneath uncertain chance, and in their own mobility answer to flight. Whatever you have today will perhaps leave you tomorrow, or even while you are speaking, it ceases to be yours.

But there is an eternal providence in heaven, to which all lower things are subject, which governs all things with just and right judgment. We, created by it, saved by it, and to be made blessed by it, ought always and everywhere to praise, bless, and glorify it, giving thanks from the purest minds no less in adverse circumstances than in prosperous and favorable ones. For it is to me a sign of salvation, and a hope by no means small of the compassion of God that will come upon me, that the persecution of the wicked has gone before, as the holy [unclear] says: “For all who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution.” 1 Tim. 3.

I have withdrawn from the territories of evil men, lest an occasion for taking vengeance be left to me, and lest it fall to me any longer to hear the snarling of creatures of darkness, to whom nothing has usually been more burdensome than learning, nothing sweeter than idleness, nothing more familiar than envy. May they prosper, to be changed for the better when he wills it who is judge of all, in whose decision I have placed the insults inflicted upon me.

The position proposed to me through Celtis and Peutinger, as your letter indicated, is not fitting for me to accept, since I am a monk and a professor of regular discipline, and especially for this reason: lest I seem to have disappointed my most reverend lord, my bishop of Würzburg, and his expectation, trust, and confidence concerning me. For he has set me over this poor monastery, holding a singular hope about me; he pursues me graciously and supports me most mercifully. I must not be ungrateful for the benefits of so great a prince; nor is it fitting for my religion to have a dwelling outside the monastery in cities. For if I had wished to live on the stipends of princes, it certainly would not have been necessary to dwell here in poverty. For there are many who would receive me with a large provision and maintain me with honor.

But I could never be induced to allow myself to be joined to courtly flatterers, since philosophy forbids it no less than religion; and I do not know how religion can be preserved unharmed in the tumult of a court, if anyone has ever been able to do so. I was born for letters, whose constant study dreads the tumults of courts, loves solitude, and detests a public gathering in the city. Poor in possessions, I live here in poverty, I who have never loved riches, knowing that Seneca prudently warned his disciple that one cannot have leisure for studies and for acquiring riches. And it is written in the Gospel: [unclear]; “You cannot serve God and riches.” Beautiful is that distich which the poet Theognis sang:

[unclear] [unclear]

Content, therefore, with my condition, whatever it is, I shall not seek riches. To serve princes, just as it is contrary to my purpose, has likewise never pleased my will. According to the saying of the holy Christopher Paul, “having food and clothing,” I wish to be content with these. Yet I give those men, my friends Celtis and Peutinger, the greatest thanks I can, who, having concern for me, do not disdain to take thought for my poverty and desolation. May almighty God render them grace and mercy at the opportune time, because me, a poor man,

not Familiar Letters

...you have begun; if you have not yet completed it, the work is indeed either very great, or you are the slowest compiler of all. I greatly fear, however, that what we know happens today to many cloistered men placed under obedience to prelates may happen to you: men endowed with very noble talents are compelled to take up the base burdens of worldly business, and those whose mind is most fit for the study of letters are forbidden to handle a book with their hands.

I sent you recently, as you requested, the names of the twelve months by which they are called among the Greeks and likewise among the Hebrews, written in their own letters; nor do I sufficiently understand how they are useful to you in the publication of chronicles. But the Greek epigrams which you say are preserved among you, inscribed on a golden cross, have caused me no small wonder: how they came from Constantinople to Ghent. For the inscription states that the cross itself was made by order and at the expense of the emperor of Constantinople. My wonder ceased at once when it came to mind that Constantinople was once captured and despoiled in the time of Emperor Henry IV by Godfrey, count of Bouillon, who, because of the magnificent deeds he performed in the land of Lorraine, deserved to be distinguished with the title of duke and to be raised up as king of Jerusalem. For he, intending to lead an army through Hungary and Bulgaria into Palestine, provoked by the injuries of Emperor Alexius, captured Byzantium; and he gave the spoils to the soldiers, many of whom afterward returned to Germany and brought to Latin churches relics, crosses, and golden and silver tablets taken from the Greeks.

Remember, Christianus, in the publication of your chronicles, that almost all chronographers have gravely erred in the reckoning of the years of the Lord, omitting twenty-four years which passed under the consuls without being correctly reckoned; you will find this subtly calculated from Marianus Scotus the monk and Augustine Wesgallus, theologian of Louvain. I wrote to you more fully about this very matter three years ago from Spanheim through John Steinen Moelen, priest of Mechelen. Meanwhile we too have written a chronicle, of no small size, of the monastery of Spanheim, over which we then presided, beginning from its first foundation, which took place in the Christian year 1040, down to the year 1502; in it we led the sequence of the narrative through the succession of all the abbots down to the nineteenth year of our prelacy, inserting many matters done in Germany which seemed to us worthy of memory.

Please hasten at last to put the final hand to the work, so that at some time we may deserve to see it. As soon as possible make us more certain about the things that are going on around you. Concerning ourselves, we inform you that for love of peace we have resigned our abbey of Spanheim, and have taken up the one in which we now live, St. James at Würzburg, certain rivals giving us the occasion, men to whom our sacred studies were by no means pleasing. Farewell, and pray to God for us. From Würzburg, on the sixteenth day of August, in the Christian year 1507.

XLVII.

John Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, to Johannes Damius Curtensis: greetings and sincere charity in the Lord.

Brother Wilhelm Orphanus, the bearer of the present letter, nephew of Abbot Macharius of Limburg, has reported to us a tale of great rashness, which, if it is true, makes us wonder greatly. For he says that the abbot of Bursfelde, together with I know not what other man, recently performed the office of visitation at Spanheim, and, among the other commands of his authority, ordered Abbot Nicholas, our successor, under certain penalties, to take care to alienate, dispose of, and sell from the monastery all volumes written in the Greek language, both manuscript and printed, which we, as you know, gathered from Greece and Italy with great labor and heavy expenses.

If these things are true, for they cannot be hidden from you, we most earnestly ask that you go as quickly as possible to the monastery of Spanheim, and [unclear] those Greek volumes together with the Hebrew ones, which were bestowed on us by the generosity of princes, [unclear] to gather enough money for us, by which we may redeem the books put up for sale. Yet we cannot rashly give credence to what has been said. What reason could have moved that good abbot to order Greek books to be sold, in which nothing evil is contained? Or perhaps does he labor under hatred of us, or, led by a zeal of bitterness, does he think that by this the memory of Trithemius must be wiped from the earth, as the Romans are read once to have done to the blessed Pope Gregory I, who after his death consigned to the flames all the books composed by him that they could find? But we cannot believe this abbot...

Familiar Letters

from the bearer’s report, if you wish, you will understand it more fully. Farewell, mindful of me in your prayers to God. From Würzburg, on the twenty-seventh day of the month of July, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XXXVIII.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St James at Würzburg, to Jakob Wimpfeling of Sélestat, his singular and dearest friend, greeting.

[unclear] letters from Strasbourg, which you sent to me on the twelfth day of the month of July, I received on the twenty-second of the same month. But those which you write that you had given before have not yet come to my knowledge. Lord Gaspar, bishop of Bethlehem, vicar in pontifical matters of our most reverend general prelate, brought me the little book destined for me by you, ascribed to the holy abbot Bernard, on the seven penitential Psalms. The man who delivered to me your aforesaid letter at the same time handed over in your name two little books lately printed at Strasbourg, one by William, bishop of Paris, on the holding and plurality of benefices; the other by Albert the Great, bishop of Regensburg, on the fervor of charity. Do not doubt that I received them with a most grateful mind.

With the afflictions that you suffer I sympathize from a most faithful heart; and if you think that I can do anything for your peace, let me know, and at once you will find me ready for everything. Trust in the Lord Jesus, and walk firmly in the way of truth, and truth itself will set you free. This one thing only I warn you: do not hereafter be over-ready to occupy yourself with the business and affairs of cloistered men, because what is outside you and the condition of your state is no concern of yours. For what is it to you whether Augustine was cowled or toga-clad?

You wrote in that battle of yours concerning integrity that Bede was not a monk, and likewise very many others whom I counted among monks in the book on ecclesiastical writers; and, unless you were yielding to me as a friend, you promise that you would easily prove it. Let us engage with one another, if you please: those whom I wrote were monks, and especially Bede, you will by no means show not to have been monks. You seem to me not to have surveyed sufficiently the histories of past time, since you do not know that Bede was a monk. But I have thought that you should be spared, since I understand that you are afflicted more than enough by the vexations of the hermit brothers of St Augustine.

You wish to know from me whether there could be a place for you with my successor in Sponheim, and who he is, since you wish utterly to flee the company of worldly men. Indeed in the abbacy of Sponheim the prior whom you know succeeded me, no small part, although hidden, of my persecution. But I fear that you will not have a place to stay there, because the prince of the [Cynonoti?] is little inclined toward men devoted to letters; you will experience this if you go there. I do not utterly reject your desire to live with me, but I advise this first: that after having examined the people and the place you yourself should come, and if the matter is to your mind, we shall discuss by counsel on what condition you may attain the result. For whatever I can do, I shall do most willingly out of love for you. I have a poor and small little monastery, but quiet and sufficiently suited for one philosophizing; only the lack of books troubles me, in which, as you know, at Sponheim I was very rich.

Farewell, my Jakob, and persuade yourself that I am with you, I who shall never desert you. From my monastery near Würzburg, on the twenty-seventh day of the month of July, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XXXIX.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St James in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, to his most loving confrater Simon, abbot of the monastery of Laach, greeting.

[unclear] What is this, dearest confrater and friend, that you marvel that I resigned the abbacy of Sponheim, in which you say I was famous and distinguished, and blessed with many friends? Marvel rather that for so long a time I was able to endure the deceits and insolences of the monks, and to overlook, as if I did not know them, the plots of the [Cynonoti?]. For the twenty-fourth year I presided over the monastery of Sponheim amid many labors and no small poverty; and when, with buildings, books, ornaments, and many necessary things, as you yourself saw, I had at last adorned it beautifully, and had brought it back to a good condition of temporal affairs, when the war of the empire came upon us against the most illustrious prince Philip, count palatine of the Rhine, duke of Bavaria, and prince-elector, under whose protection the monastery is known to be established, it sustained a grave loss of its possessions and goods from the enemies. There were were among the [Cynonoti?], who, because I favored the affairs of the Palatine for the most just reason, were unjustly persecuting me: at first secretly, fearing the power of that most benign prince; but at last, when the war at the king’s command was cooling, thinking him humbled and exhausted of strength, they began to rage against me with open hatred, the more powerful of my monks consenting. What and how great lies they then devised against me, time has already partly brought to light, and has left no doubt that it will very soon bring the rest to light. But this one thing was the chief cause of all evils against me: that my rivals held in hidden hatred the most clement prince, whom, as I ought, I always loved. Nor only certain of the [Cynonoti?], but also almost all my brothers, together with the abbot and all the monks of the monastery of Belli Montis. But I, seeing that the wicked had prevailed against me, changed my place; and, having accepted the abbey in which I now dwell in peace, I resigned Spanheim together with its most ungrateful monks. And perhaps thus it pleased almighty God, by whose providence, as Saint Jerome says on Ezekiel, all things are governed: adversity dispensed to us by him, which is thought to be punishment, is medicine. To what great miseries the pastors of cloistered men are subjected, and by what great inconveniences they are battered, you yourself experience by daily [unclear]. Up to that point I judged that all things were to be endured patiently for the love of God. But when the betrayal of my own men had entered in against me, patience thereafter would have been wholly without fruit. Therefore, following Saint Benedict, leader of monks, I, a lover of peace, left the monks whom, hardened as they were, I could not advance to sounder things. Farewell, sound in mind and happy in body, praying for me. From Würzburg, on the twenty-eighth day of the month of July, in the year of Christians 1507.

XL.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James in the Würzburg suburb, to Roger Venray the Sicambrian: sincere greeting and charity in the Lord.

On the first day of the month of August I received, by an uncertain messenger, your letter sent to me, as appeared in the subscription, on the Kalends of May; in it [unclear] certain poems into my book [unclear] by no means reached my hands. After two days another man appeared, who presented me with your letter written on the seventeenth day of the month of July; he said that it had been entrusted to him by some other man, I know not who, together with two little works of yours, written in your hand. One of them contains certain familiar odes in various verse; the other, composed in prose, comprises a certain [unclear] disputation. The subject does not displease me, nor am I averse to the argument of your inventions, but I would wish you to devote your effort to more important studies, which your time of life, your age, seems to require of you. You have passed the fiftieth year of your life; what studies should henceforth become you is especially for you to consider. Youth advised us to one thing; old age bids us search out another. The sun of our vital strength is declining toward its setting; the evening hour gradually consumes the bodily powers that midday supplied. Henceforth care must now be taken of the soul, which remains immortal. We have yielded enough to the flesh. Let the little ass be nourished only with necessary fodder; all wantonness will fall far away. Let childish lucubrations give way; since in age you present a man, embrace compositions becoming to gray hairs, not fables. You have composed one hundred and thirty-six little works. It is a great thing, and in my judgment praiseworthy, that you have turned the leisure that regular discipline permitted to the study of letters, and have directed your mind rather to composing books than to the pleasures of the flesh. Yet little works are not to be weighed at all by number, but by usefulness: if they instruct the mind and understanding of the reader toward true wisdom; if, lifted from earthly things, they raise it to heavenly things; if they truly pierce it with compunction in divine love. The world now everywhere bubbles forth innumerable writers, as Flaccus says:

Learned and unlearned alike, we write poems everywhere; everyone likes to rave as poets.

But the lesser part of those who write thinks of the edification of souls. From the abundance of the heart we all write, and in writing commit to letters those thoughts with which we are occupied. Hence we cannot write spiritual things that induce the fervor of divine love, because, shameful to say, we seethe, full of worldly and carnal thoughts. For no one without faith and the charity of Jesus Christ, who is the wisdom of God the Father, will be able to attain true and salutary wisdom, so that, namely, one who savors carnal and transitory things should write spiritual things. Therefore I urge you, my Sicambrian, since you know that you are sworn to the monastic religion, that just as in outward conduct you walk without offense in the midst of your confreres, so, with [unclear] despised Familiar Letters

from childish studies, which contribute little to the soul’s salvation, and turn your mind and pen with all your strength to spiritual things. I ask that hereafter you [produce?] such little works, the working-out of which may sweetly increase the love of God in you, and lead the reader’s mind to contempt for worldly things. Let childish games now give way: poems of poets do not befit an old man; you must proceed in prose, in keeping with the honor of old age. Let immature youth play with tortuous little verses; we love the plain road. But if you like to write verse, I say again that an old man ought to compose no poems except penitential ones, perhaps epitaphs for the dead, unless he is such a paraphrast as has always had practice in verse and never in prose, so that, with Prudentius, Sedulius, Juvencus, and their like, having turned to penitence, he may apply the weapons of worldly wisdom to the praises of divine Scripture. We read no poems of the old holy doctors, Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, Origen, John Chrysostom, Basil, Cyril, and very many others, except hymns composed to the praise of God and a few epitaphs for the dead, although we do not doubt that they possessed the art. For, wishing by their lucubrations to benefit the salvation of souls, they preferred to write in prose rather than in verse, because it is difficult, in all the things that usefully present themselves to be written, to observe the law of meters; and this kind of teaching would seem more fitting for young men than for old men, and rarely does it happen that anyone is found perfect in both. You ask that I write out for you an account of all my lucubrations, their titles and subjects, especially of those which I composed after the publication of the book on ecclesiastical writers. For you say that you have a most honorable reason for seeking an account of them. I shall satisfy your desire as soon as I have leisure, which could not now be done, since the messenger was hurrying and I was occupied with other matters. I do not doubt that Herbenus is most loving toward me; I love him no less than I am loved by him. Greet in my name, whenever opportunity is given, our Herbenus, our common friend and most upright fellow-philosopher, who is worthy of the friendship of all good men, being distinguished no less for holiness of life than for learning in letters. Farewell, sound in mind and body, mindful of me before God. From my monastery of St. James at Würzburg, on the 12th day of the month of August, in the year of Christians 1507.

XLI.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of St. James at Würzburg, to Wilhelm Veldicus Monapius, parish priest in Dirmstein, theologian and mathematician, our very dear friend: greetings.

My friend, I received on the first day of the month of August the letter that you sent to me on the fifth day of the month of July, together with Roger’s, and I have resolved to answer them in order if I can. And first indeed I give you great thanks for your goodwill toward me, by which you rejoice in my tranquillity, and are glad that I have found a place suitable for philosophizing with freedom. I myself indeed rejoice not a little. Greet in my name, whenever opportunity is given, our Herbenus, our common friend and most upright fellow-philosopher, who is worthy of the friendship of all good men, being distinguished [unclear] for life than for learning in letters. Farewell, sound in mind and body, mindful of me before God. From my monastery of St. James at Würzburg, on the 12th day of the month of August, in the year of Christians 1509.
