Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St James in the suburb of the city of Wurzburg, sends abundant greetings to Master Matthaeus Herbenus, most upright of friends.

[unclear]

The excessive distance of places causes me to be able to send letters to you rather rarely; yet I am not therefore separated from you in spirit, although in body I am far absent from you, whom I have always loved in the true charity of Christ and set among my foremost friends. Two years have passed since I sent my last letter to you from Cologne Agrippina; with it I had also sent a copy of my letter to Briselius, our common friend, so that you might be made more certain about the things that were then being done with me. Meanwhile, for lack of messengers, I have written nothing to you, nor have I seen any letters of yours, which I think has happened for the same reason. When the assembly of princes at Cologne had been dissolved, I entered the March of Brandenburg with the most serene prince Elector Joachim, and I stayed with him for nine months.

But afterwards, having returned to Budoris with the intention in mind of returning to Spanheim, when I had plainly learned that my brothers, Melantius the prior, whom you know especially well, together with my Cynonotian rivals, had conspired against me [unclear], I changed my plan; and, having accepted the abbacy offered to me, in which I now live, that of St James near Wurzburg, I resigned Spanheim with its wicked monks. For what was I to do in the midst of rivals, who were always carrying on either hidden or open enmities against me, so that there could never be any security for me, but continual suspicion of plots would immediately arise on both sides, according to the saying of Achilles to Hector in Iliad X, speaking thus:

[unclear]

[Greek unclear]

Paraphrase.

There is no firm concord between lions and men, Nor do wolves and sheep have one mind, But they devise evils against one another on both sides; So it will not be that I and you love each other mutually.

The fathers of our order interposed their efforts and tried to call us back to mutual concord, and with all their strength attempted to persuade me to return to the monastery; but it did not seem safe to me to trust enemies reconciled by their necessity, not by their will, remembering the wisdom of Pittacus, who finely warns: [Greek unclear]. That is:

[unclear]

Nor should you regard an enemy as your friend.

And Menander:

[unclear]

[Greek unclear]

that is:

You will think speech from an enemy friendly.

I therefore yielded to envy and rivalry quite seasonably, and I do not regret it, having by God's favor obtained good quiet and peace, where henceforth it may be freer for me to be attentive to myself. For I have always hated the tumultuous occupations of the world, and have loved rather solitude of place and tranquillity of mind, even to the envy of certain men, as you yourself are not unaware, who for not a few days once stayed with me in the monastery of Spanheim for love of Greek letters, and saw quite thoroughly both my own habits and those of my brothers. But I shall dismiss these matters. Rather I shall set forth for you the circumstances of our friends, since I do not doubt that you very gladly wish to know them. Johannes Damius, who once learned Greek letters from me along with you in the monastery of Spanheim, is provost of the nuns in No Of Johannes Trithemius.

...in Neuburg near Heidelberg, and, immersed in perishable affairs, he has almost put aside every study of letters. Our [Rogerius?] Sicamber, in his fashion, makes books and produces innumerable offspring, so that it would be tedious for me even to list merely the titles of each of the little works he has composed by lamplight. For he has completed, to use his own word, 136 little works of his lucubrations in four codices, and to this day he does not cease writing.

Jacob Wimpfeling is at Strasbourg, enduring a grave persecution from the hermit friars of Saint Augustine because, in a certain work of his entitled On Integrity, he wrote that Augustine himself was not a monk or hooded religious. Wimpfeling’s persecution by the Augustinian hermits. I feel compassion for the man, who bears trouble almost beyond his strength, whose noble talent, now in old age, is being compelled to the quarrels of lawyers. For they arranged for him to be summoned in person to the Apostolic See; I sent you, with my letters, his apology, composed in one hundred short verses [unclear], so that you may understand the man’s defense.

Sebastian Brant is still living at Strasbourg, employed on a public stipend of the senate. Johannes Nutius, that monk of Spanheim who never consented to the conspiracy of the wicked against me, is dead. I ask you again and again to intercede with God for his soul. In the abbey of Spanheim, Prior Melanius, whom you know, has succeeded me, because he did not prove sufficiently faithful to his pastor. May God not impute it to him, since perhaps he was deceived unknowingly. Farewell, sound and safe for Nestor’s years, remembering us before God. From Würzburg, on the sixteenth day of the month of August, in the year of the Christians 1507.

43. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Saint James at Würzburg, sends greetings to Johannes Capellerius, mathematician at Paris.

Most learned Johannes, I would send letters to you more often if I did not lack a supply of messengers. I believe it is not unknown to you that I left the abbey of Spanheim because of the envy of rivals, and therefore I did not judge it necessary to write to you about this change of mine. I made known to you two years ago the causes of everyone’s rivalries against me, when you were with me at Cologne in that great assembly of princes.

You ask what success I had in the March of Brandenburg, what I did there, with what gifts I was presented by the prince, and what I am now doing. This is the substance of your letter, and what your desire presses you further to know from me. By the mercy of God, who disposes and orders all things, I entered the March after a prosperous journey; and though I was lame from a flux in one leg, as you saw me at Cologne, I recovered completely in the March under the care of the prince’s surgeon.

I remained in Berlin with the margrave himself for nine months, performing the office of teacher. For I handed down precepts and rules to the prince, by which he became more learned in the Latin language without great labor. At his urging I also wrote certain synthemata, in the reading of which he will rejoice. For now he writes Latin elegantly enough, speaks fluently, and perfectly understands whatever he reads. At last, graciously rewarding me as I returned, he gave me three hundred ducats, and promised that he would give greater things in time. Later, when he heard that I had been established in this abbey, he also sent other splendid gifts. You have, briefly, the answer to what you asked.

And behold, here I now live for myself and for the study of writings so much more freely as I am less occupied with the cares of temporal affairs. The monastery over which I preside is rather poor and small, and for that reason involved in few affairs. Trithemius’s writings. If you ask for the list of my lucubrations produced meanwhile, I shall also set this out for you in a brief account. Two books of familiar letters. My familiar letters, which I sent to friends from the day on which I left Spanheim, namely the first day of April in the year of the Christians 1505, up to my entrance into this abbey, which was the fifteenth of October of the following year, I gathered into one book. To this I added a second also, which contains only the letters of the first year of my prelacy in this monastery; into it I inserted this one too.

Then I wrote an itinerary of my whole life from the time of my birth up to this year. After this I composed one book On the Praises of Saint Joseph, Foster-father of the Savior. The work Polygraphia. Likewise this summer I wrote a large work, which I entitled Polygraphia, in six books, for the aforesaid prince, Lord Joachim of Brandenburg. I also wrote certain other smaller works, the titles of which I think it superfluous to set down. Besides, when I have completed the things now in hand, perhaps you will learn of them.

Why he is unwilling to publish the Steganographia. But my Steganographia, the first two books of which you saw at Cologne, I do not know whether I shall ever publish, for three reasons. The first reason that holds me back from publishing it is consideration of the future and fear of Familiar Letters

of a likely evil, which could occur through the misuse of depraved men, since evil men will use our inventions for evil no less than good men for good. The second is the undertaking of very great labor and the repayment of a small reward. For, as you have seen, the work is an arduous one of the keenest speculation, which cannot be completed without the greatest labor. And what recompense is there for so much labor, except perhaps a small weight of gold, which is transitory, and for that reason should rather be despised by a Christian monk? I have never had the mind to labor for temporal reward, since I see myself called into the vineyard of the eternal King. The third cause is the judgment of the unlearned common people, by which they ascribe everything they do not understand to evil arts. I have written nothing so far at which anyone could justly marvel; I have done nothing astonishing. Yet I suffer the opinion of the crowd, since many think me a magician, asserting that I have raised the dead, summoned demons from below, foretold future things, and brought back thieves by incantations and bound robbers. All these things are invented and false; I have never done them, nor indeed even thought them. I admit that I have read very many books of magicians, not so that I might imitate them, but so that by refuting them I might one day confound their most wicked superstitions, which, with the Lord Jesus Christ granting it, I trust I shall do shortly. What do you think the foolish rashness of unlearned men in the future will think of me, when I bring the Steganography into the light, which has invented such lies about me when it has as yet seen nothing of the secret? Although I do not greatly value these chatterings of the inexperienced, being content with the testimony of conscience, nevertheless I do not intend, so far as it is possible, to give occasion for evil suspicion. Farewell, healthy and happy, firm and constant in the strength of our old friendship. From Würzburg, on the 16th day of the month of August, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XLIIII.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of St James at Würzburg, sends greetings to Jacob Kymolanus, theologian and mathematician of the Carmelite order.

Kymolanus, I received on the last day of the month of July, through a certain merchant, your letter which you wrote to me from Ghent on the first day of May; in it you show yourself, as is your custom, very eager for my affairs, for which I give you immortal thanks. I therefore wish you to know that, by the mercy of Christ Jesus, I am safe and well; that, as you write you have heard by the report of many, I have resigned the abbey of Sponheim; and that by my own willing choice I have accepted the one in which I now dwell, poor as it is. You heard from me the reasons for this exchange when two years ago we were together in Cologne. The precious library of two thousand volumes, which you once saw, I left entire in Sponheim, because it had been acquired from the substance of the monastery. For nothing is my own, since I profess myself a monk according to the rule of our most holy father Benedict. I did, however, bring with me to Würzburg certain little books on the mystical secrets of nature, whose reading is not suitable for everyone, which never belonged to Sponheim. The Greek volumes, too, and the hundred Hebrew ones, apart from that small printed Bible, I left in the monastery together with the rest. Afterwards, however, I acquired for myself volumes in both languages with money given to me by the Margrave of Brandenburg; if I need any more, I shall provide for myself in time. The prior succeeded me in the Abbey of Sponheim, certainly a man whom I knew inwardly in [unclear], who does not greatly value the study of the Scriptures; from him, if I wished, I could easily buy back the Greek books at a low price. But it does not please me to take away from the monastery of Sponheim its adornment, which I acquired at a sufficiently great price. My poverty is sufficient for me, since I have learned to be content with few things, for the time now seems to me to be at hand when multitude ought to be reduced to unity. I have read many things almost unbelievable; it is enough: let works sometime follow, as time demands. What need is there to run through many things by reading, when a few things can suffice for necessary learning? Today the world abounds in volumes, and so many books come daily into the light that there is no one who can read them all. For the art which they call printing, invented in my infancy at Mainz, the metropolis of the Franks, brings forth into the light every day almost infinite volumes of old and new writers. Johannes Amerbach, a citizen of Basel, a learned and wholly upright man, last year printed all the books of lord Augustine, as many as he could find, in fifteen volumes, with sufficient correction. With similar diligence he struck off in type all the works of Saints Jerome and Ambrose, and he is also going to print anew the little works of the divine Pope Gregory, some of which indeed have never been printed. But thus far about these matters. I wish to know from you what was done with the letters which I had handed over to you at Cologne for Libanius Of Johannes Trithemius.

...to be sent to Libanius Gallus in France; for [he has written?] to me in the meantime, and makes no mention of them, with the result that I doubt whether they have come into his hands. Johannes Palconydorus, your fellow Carmelite, when he last left me at Sponheim, promised that he would return in a short time; behold, four years have now passed, during which I have been able to hear or learn nothing of him anywhere. If you know where he is, or whether he is alive or dead, I ask you to inform me as soon as possible.

I, sitting here in a place of solitude and quiet, victory over my enemies having been granted to me, devote myself to sacred letters, and I find true what divine Scripture promises: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke of the Lord from his youth,” [unclear]. Pray humbly to God for me, who raises the poor man from want, that he may deign to keep me in his will. For I know that the time of my pilgrimage on earth is short. As Seneca says, what we live is a point, or rather less than a point. And this very least thing nature has divided by a certain appearance of a longer span. For she wished one part of this to be infancy, another childhood, another youth, another a kind of decline from that into old age; and this, heavy with its own inconveniences, she does not allow to be quiet, so that a certain wise man in Ecclesiasticus said with just consideration: “Great occupation has been created for all men, a heavy yoke upon the sons of Adam, from the day of their coming forth from their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the earth, the mother of all.”

For all things that are from the earth shall be turned back into the earth. And therefore man has been made like vanity, since his days pass like a shadow. Behold, the brief years pass away; we are tossed by storms of vicissitudes. For what are we wretched mortals, if not wind, a shadow, we who live in turmoil and, falling in a moment, appear no more? As Sophocles in the Ajax introduces the raging Odysseus speaking:

[Greek unclear]; that is:

For I see that we, being nothing, are nothing other than images, all of us who live, or a light shadow.

Hence Homer, prince of poets, contemplating the misery of man, groans and says in the Iliad, [unclear], as you yourself know:

[Greek unclear]

For certainly there is nothing more wretched than man, of all things that breathe and creep upon the earth.

We are to be compared with the leaves of trees, as the same Homer says in the sixth book, since just as leaves fall from the trees when winter hastens on, and others grow up in the season of spring, so of the race of men one generation is born, and another dies. A leaf which has once fallen does not rise again to the tree; after a man has once died, he will by no means return thereafter to this life. Ah, gods above, how much blind night mortal hearts have! We mortals live and do not consider that we are going to die. [unclear], let us rejoice, we embrace perishable things as though we were going to live forever; when we least expect it we are snatched away from here as if we had never been born. O Kymolanus, let us think on our last things while it helps to have thought of them, lest too late we lament the sloth of life.

The Greek grammar of Lascaris, which I lent you at Cologne, is yours, since it is not necessary to me. For I have another like it, recently printed at Venice. I know no one here devoted to Greek letters except the one Engelhard Funck, dean of our monastery, a learned man, practiced in verse as well as in prose. Farewell, mindful of us before God. From Würzburg, on the sixteenth day of the month of August, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XLV.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Saint James in the suburb of Würzburg, to Christian Masseus, priest of Ghent, residing in the monastery of Saint Jerome, his very dear friend, greeting.

How great is the desire with which I long to know what you are doing, how you are, what new thing you are writing, or whether you have completed your chronicle, I cannot express in letters, nor, since we are separated far from one another, make known to you in words. Most of all, however, I would wish sometime to see your lucubrations on the reckoning of times, which you long ago promised to transcribe for me. Five years have now flowed by from that time when you began to write the Chronicle...

Of Johannes Trithemius.

... that the abbot of Bursfeld, bound by devotion to Christ, should think this, he who knows that we have deserved better in the reform of the order, although our concern for having remembrance among posterity is either none or small. Rather, we believe that he was moved by pious consideration: since he found no one at Spanheim skilled in Greek letters, he therefore judged the books almost useless to the place and ordered them to be sold, and the price turned to the necessary uses of the brethren.

Although that sale does not please me, because I would very much wish all the books, acquired by me at great cost, to remain in their own place for the perpetual adornment and honor of the monastery of Spanheim. For you know that we have spent more than fifteen hundred gold ducats on books in the twenty-four years of our prelacy, and have gathered a great quantity and multitude of them together. Indeed, three years ago we counted two thousand volumes in the library of the monastery of Spanheim, when Henricus de Bunau, golden knight and most learned orator of the dukes of Saxony, was with us; none of these was in the place at the time of our entry into the abbacy. This, brother, you can by no means be ignorant of, since you entered the monasteries with me and for a long time were my servant as chamberlain.

In every faculty of learning we gathered many volumes, not only printed ones, but also several written on parchment, precious and rare, so that I would dare confidently to say that in all Germany there is no similar library in which so many rare and very ancient volumes are found, in every variety of writings, both divine and secular, and also in diverse languages: Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Chaldaean, Arabic, Indian, Ruthenian, Tartar. I deliberately pass over the rest, which use our characters, such as Italian, French, Bohemian, and the like. For I know that the number of Greek volumes, manuscript and printed together, exceeds a hundred; concerning these we most earnestly ask you to take care. And if they are for sale, let them be acquired for us. For we shall give the price of a fair valuation, which no one else will give, since today we know no one in the whole province of the Rhineland learned and devoted to Greek letters. But if the books are not for sale, we are very well content that they remain in their own place. Come, we pray that we may find your diligence in harmony with our desire. Farewell, remembering us before God. From Würzburg, on the twentieth day of August, in the year of the Christians 1507.

XLVIII.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, to Johannes Virdung of Hassfurt, most learned mathematician, greetings.

Henricus Gronigerus, secretary of our most reverend prelate, delivered to me your letter, from which I plainly learned that my petitionary cause before the most illustrious prince Philipp, Count Palatine, had been advanced by you. For this reason I give you the greatest thanks, and I shall repay them according to my powers whenever the opportunity is given me. Concerning the prince’s books, however, I shall act according to your advice, although I fear lest delay bring danger, since men are for the most part lacking in vigilance and apply little care even to arduous matters.

The book of yours which you lent me I entrusted to the hands of a scribe; as soon as it has been copied, it will be returned to you without delay. But my books of Berengarius, which I had left with you at [Büdoris?] to be copied, when you have finished them, order them to return to me.

That man about whom you wrote to me, Georgius Sabellicus, who dared to call himself prince of necromancers, is a vagrant, a chatterer, and a [unclear], worthy to be chastised with lashes, lest he henceforth rashly dare publicly to profess such unspeakable things contrary to holy Church. For what else are the titles he assumes for himself but the most foolish and insane signs of a mind by which he shows himself a fool, not a philosopher? For thus he fashioned for himself a title suited to him: Master Georgius Sabellicus, Faustus the younger, fountain of necromancers, astrologer, second magus, chiromancer, pyromancer, second in the hydra art. See the foolish rashness of the man, with what madness he is carried away, so that he presumes to profess himself the fountain of necromancy, when truly, ignorant of all good letters, he ought rather to have called himself a fool than master.

But his wickedness is not hidden from me. When in the previous year I was returning from the March of Brandenburg, I found this very man at the town of Gelnhausen; about him many frivolous things were said to me at the inn, promised by him with no small rashness. As soon as he heard that I was present, he fled from the inn, and could be persuaded by no one to present himself before my sight. The title of his folly, such as he gave to you...

whom we have mentioned, he also sent to me through a certain citizen. Certain priests in the town reported to me that, in the presence of many people, he said that he had such knowledge and memory of all wisdom that, if all the volumes of Plato and Aristotle, together with their whole philosophy, had utterly perished from human memory, he himself, by his own genius, like another Hebrew, would be able to restore everything with greater elegance. Later, while I was at [Neometum?], he came to Wurzburg, and, driven by the same vanity, is said to have declared in the presence of very many people that the miracles of Christ the Savior are not to be wondered at, and that he too could do everything that Christ did, as often and whenever he wished. In the last Lent of this year he also came to Stauronesus, and, boastful of himself with similar folly, promised great things, saying that in alchemy he was the most perfect of all who had ever existed, and that he knew and could do whatever people might wish. Meanwhile the scholastic office of teaching in the aforesaid town was vacant; to this he was appointed through the promotion of Franz von Sickingen, bailiff of your prince, a man very eager for mystical matters. He soon began, namely with boys, in a most unspeakable kind of [fornication?]; when this was immediately brought to light, he escaped the prepared punishment by flight. These are the things that are established for me by most certain testimony concerning that man, whose coming you await with such great desire. When he comes to you, you will find not a philosopher, but a foolish man driven by excessive rashness. Farewell, mindful of me when there is a princely opportunity. From Wurzburg, on the twentieth day of the month of August, in the year of Christians 1507.

XLIX.

To the most reverend father in Christ, and most illustrious prince and lord, Lord Hermann, Archbishop of the Church of Cologne, Duke of Angaria and Westphalia, administrator of the Church of Paderborn, archchancellor of the Holy Empire throughout Italy, prince elector, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James of Wurzburg, wishes happiness.

Most reverend Prince, in the last letter that I sent to Your Reverend Paternity at the end of the month of June, I had promised that I would come around the feast of Saint Michael the Archangel; and this I would most gladly have done, had not the plague of epidemic disease meanwhile begun to rage too greatly in almost all the places on this side of the Rhine through which I was to descend, and had it not continued up to this very day. For this reason it was necessary for me to remain at home, knowing that the presence of any man who has passed through places where pestilence is strong is usually distasteful to princes. Therefore, fearing lest this very thing should happen with Your Reverend Paternity, since today this evil is raging in almost all places around the regions of the Rhine, I have decided, on necessary consideration, to defer my coming to another time, unless Your Serenity shall judge that this plan of mine should be changed. Meanwhile I shall see to it, as far as I can, that what remains to be added to the things prepared for that same Serenity of yours may be completed as abundantly as possible. May almighty God long preserve your most reverend Paternity unharmed; to whom I commend myself as humbly as possible. From Wurzburg, on the twenty-fourth day of the month of August, in the year of Christians 1507.

L.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Saint James the Apostle in the suburb of Wurzburg, to Jodocus Beifelius, most perceptive jurisconsult, greetings.

I believe, Jodocus, that you have been informed by our common friends Rogerius, Herbenus, and Kymolanus, and by others, of the change in my affairs according to the genesis of circumstances, so that the prediction of the stars might be fulfilled, if it is to be believed to have any force, which the astronomer of King Philip prophesied twenty years ago. Often, I confess, I myself in the meantime, after making the calculation, found the figures threatening; but, persuaded by the counsel of Saint Augustine, I treated the prophecies of the stars as laughable. At last there happened to me what they seemed to promise, and an occasion has been given to me by which experience may necessarily make me more cautious hereafter. The envy of rivals furnished a place for the prophecy; and, so that the prediction of the astrologer should not falter, some malignant demon, no one doubts, stirred it up. For if God permits, demons gladly cooperate with human prophecies, by which they may catch, on the path of error, minds too credulous of vanities. The rashness of rivals, driven without doubt by the instigation of a demon, prevailed against me; and although the stars may have foretold that it would happen, nevertheless it came about by the freedom of human will. For no one for it provoked rivals, unwilling though they were, to rage against me; nor did anyone compel me to give up the abbacy of Sponheim. Rather, I yielded of my own free will; but the reason why I wished to do so was furnished by the ingratitude of the monks, about which I remember writing to you long ago from Cologne at very great length. But now I live here much more quietly than at Sponheim, free for myself and for the reading of the Scriptures; poor indeed in possessions, but, as it seems to me, rich in spirit, since I have never loved the vain occupations of the world. Your urging me to come to you, promising me all the necessities of this life as long as I live, is the greatest token of love toward me; for this I give you, as far as I can, immortal thanks, and I shall repay them if ever the opportunity is given me. But to come down to you and remain there thereafter, which you seem especially to desire, you know does not accord with my profession, since I am bound to the monastic religion and sworn to the words of my most holy father Benedict. For it in no way accords with my purpose to leave monastic solitude and to dwell continually in the world with secular men, however good and just they may be. For although perhaps there would be no danger for me to live together with you there, yet it would be scandalous to many in my religion, since just as not all things please all men, so neither are all things expedient for all men. I have therefore resolved to abide in some monastery of regular order and observance, lest I give anyone occasion to think ill of me. Otherwise I would have had not the least among the great princes of the world to provide for me most abundantly in the necessities of the present life, if I had wished to enroll myself among their cares and service. Hence, even to this day, I have known very many who, with a fixed annual stipend proposed, invite me quite richly to their courts. But life is not for fish on dry land, nor is conversation without a cloister safe for a monk. Therefore, lest I make myself a liar, I chose, poor and cast down, to dwell in a monastery, rather than to appear rich and glorious with princes in the world. For what is more fitting for a dead man than to lie hidden in a tomb? And a monk who has once renounced the world: what do you think befits him more than that, despising all the business of the world, quiet in body and tranquil in mind, free for himself and for the divine Scriptures, he should remain in a monastery? For the greatest and principal cause why I resigned the abbacy of Sponheim, full of useless worldly cares, and took up this one of Saint James, than which there is none poorer in the order, was love of solitude, peace, and tranquillity; not so that I might be carried off into idle leisure, but so that I might be able to apply myself more freely to the study of the Scriptures. Nor indeed did my spirit find the envy of rivals so far insuperable that I could not easily have mastered it by the favor and aid of the most serene prince Philip, Count Palatine, if I had wished, especially since all the fathers of the order of the observance desired nothing more than that I should not abandon the abbacy of Sponheim. Hence they sent to me at Budenheim two abbots from the synod which they were holding at Mainz, to persuade me to return to the monastery. But I, moved no less by love of peace and tranquillity than by consideration of the injuries, kept fixed within myself what I had resolved, patiently enduring the occasion given me, by which it might at last, even if late, remove me from the vain and restless occupations of the world. And so, by the bounty of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the savior of faithful souls, I have attained the peace which I always desired; I now enjoy the peace I longed for; and I shall follow peace as long as the spirit of life remains in me in the flesh. Nor have I thought the poverty of the present place which I have taken up hard to bear, knowing that when the brief span of this life is finished, in the end nothing from all the things possessed in the world will pass with me from here. Therefore, having food and clothing, the Christian is commanded to be content, because those who desire to become rich fall into various temptations of demons. But a monk who loves riches is neither a monk nor a Christian, but rather an apostate and unbeliever, because he both transgresses the Gospel and, as a despiser of his vow and of the monastery, lies to his Lord. But farewell, and also make me more certain of your affairs. From Würzburg, on the twenty-sixth day of the month of August, in the year of the Christians 1507.

LI.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James at Würzburg, to Rogerius Sycamber, greetings and charity.

I received your letter, dearest Rogerius, sent to me on the first day of the month of August, on the sixth day of the same month. In it you ask again and again that I send you the titles and account of all my lucubrations; and I am not unaware that you had asked this of me before, and that I had pledged it by promise. I shall therefore now do what you urge, and I shall set out for you a list of my editions in the order of the time in which they were made, Familiar Letters

First of all, when I was twenty-three years old, I compiled from the writings of learned men a little summary of the virtues in two books, which I have not yet been able to bring to light. This work begins thus: “Great is the virtue of the soul: to love virtue.”

At the urging also of Johannes Curtenefius, now provost of the nuns at Neuburg near [Budorim], then a monk and my chaplain, I wrote two books on the temptations of monks, which have not yet been published. This work begins thus: “The human race.”

Finally, at the urging of Nicolaus Stauronefius, then my claustral prior at Sponheim, I wrote two books on the Rule of our holy father Benedict, which begins thus: “Come, children, listen to me; I shall teach you the fear of the Lord.”

At the request also of the aforesaid Johannes Damius, I wrote two exhortatory books for monks, which lie hidden with him. This work begins thus: “It befits Christian warfare.”

At the urging of a certain friend, I wrote one book on the misery of the present life, in which I tried to lead the reader’s mind to contempt of the world. This work was printed some time ago; it begins: “Since life is nothing,” etc.

Against the vice of private ownership among monks and cloistered persons, I wrote one book, at the urging of a certain monk in Blidenstadt, which was printed at Mainz many years ago. This work begins thus: “All and life,” etc. [unclear]

I also composed, with great labor, the chronicle of my then monastery of Sponheim, from the time of its foundation down to the year of the Christians 1502; in it I arranged most diligently, as far as I could discover them, the successions, times, and deeds of all its abbots from the first down to myself, making a large volume of histories, in which under individual years I inserted, by way of digression, many matters worthy of remembrance in Germany. This work begins thus: “In the year of the Lord.”

On the manner and form of visiting cloistered persons I wrote a book, which some time ago was printed at Nuremberg by command of the fathers. It begins thus: “You will visit your brothers, if rightly.”

On the manner and form also of celebrating a provincial synod I wrote one book by command and order of the fathers, which was printed together with the preceding one. It begins: “Since in celebrating.”

The statutes also of the provincial chapters, from the time of the Council of Constance down to the chapter celebrated at Hirsau, I compiled by command of the fathers, abbreviating them into one book; this was printed at Nuremberg together with the two preceding works. It begins thus: “Since for one wishing each [unclear] of the order statutes.”

The statutes also of the annual chapter of the fathers of the Observance I reduced, at their order, into one book by abbreviating them in a more polished style; it is kept at Cologne in the monastery of Martin, and it is kept at Sponheim. It begins thus: “To the reverend in Christ.”

At the urging of Johannes, abbot of Bursfelde, I described the manner and form of celebrating the annual chapter. Before I completed this work he died, and the little book remained at Sponheim with the others. It begins thus: “To the reverend father lord Johannes.”

At the prayers of Blasius, abbot of Hirsau, I began to write the chronicle of that same monastery and completed the greater part; but when he died I discontinued the edition, uncertain with what reward his successor would be going to compensate me.

At the prayers of the same abbot Blasius I wrote a book on the ruin of our order, which I entitled “Mournful.” This work was printed at Mainz; by command of the fathers it has been customary for it always to be read at table in the provincial chapter. It begins: “Since the most ancient beauty of our order.”

At the urging of Gerlach von Breitbach, abbot of Deutz near Cologne, I wrote one book On the Praise of Scribes, which was printed at Mainz. It begins: “To the venerable father lord,” etc.

At the prayers of certain fathers of the Carmelite order, I wrote two books: in the first of these I set forth the beginning, growth, and praises of that same order; in the second I recorded the illustrious men who shone in it. This work was printed at Mainz. It begins: “By the prayers and urgency of the venerable,” etc.

On the praises also of Saint Anne, mother of the untouched and most chaste Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, I wrote one book at the prayers of Rumold, prior of Frankfurt, of the aforesaid order. It has been printed and begins: “The necessity of a vow compels.”

At the prayers of a certain newly ordained priest, my fellow student, I wrote one book on the instruction of the priestly life, which has been printed; it begins thus: “You ask of me, Nicolaus, dearest brother.” To JoJohannes Trithemius.

To Johann Camerarius Dalberg, the most learned bishop of the Vangiones, I wrote a book entitled On Ecclesiastical Writers, which was printed at Basel; after the letter it begins thus: “Having often been asked at the urging of many.”

At the request of Jakob Wimpfeling of Schlettstadt, a most distinguished poet, orator, and theologian, I wrote a little work on the illustrious writers of Germany, which I entitled Catalogue of the Lights of Germany. This work, printed at Mainz, begins thus: “Since there are some, Jacob.”

I also wrote four books On the Illustrious Men of Our Order, which have not yet come to light. The first speaks of the beginning and growth of that order itself in general. The second is a catalogue of the saints canonized from that same order. The third contains the Roman pontiffs chosen from it. And the fourth describes the distinguished men of the order, who magnificently adorned the Catholic Church no less than the order itself by their writings and their own lucubrations. This work begins thus: “As I was thinking, and more often [unclear].”

To brother Albert Latro of the Order of Minors I wrote one book on ecclesiastical computation, which has not yet been brought before the public. It begins: “Johannes Trithemius, abbot,” etc.

At the command of the fathers of my order, concerning our observance, which is called Bursfeld from the place of its origin, I wrote an arduous work On the Threefold Region of Cloistered Men, taking the occasion from certain [unclear] in the prologue; the first of these describes the region of cloistered beginners, the second that of those making progress, the third that of the perfect. This work was printed at Mainz; after my letter to the presidents it begins thus: “Since the state and condition of the monastic life.”

At the request also of a certain friend, after the end of the aforesaid work on the three regions of cloistered men, I appended a single epitome on spiritual exercise, which I extracted at the petition of the same friend; it was printed together with the preceding works, and begins thus: “Even if the form of spiritual [unclear].”

After this I undertook to write the great and exceedingly arduous work of the Steganography of wondrous [unclear], to be divided into eight books. I brought the first book and indeed the second through to the end, but left the third unfinished and all the rest abandoned down to this day, buried in spirit, persuaded by many considerations, since the labor would be great and perhaps the reward small. It therefore remains unfinished, imperfect as it lies, until usefulness persuades otherwise. This work begins thus: “The most ancient sages, whom the Greeks call philosophers.”

At the request of Ulrich of Esslingen, theologian and canon of the greater church of Cologne, I wrote a little book, according to the Greek text, on certain doubtful questions in the Gospel and John, which has not been printed. It begins: “By the frequent [unclear] of friends.”

To the same man I wrote another little book on certain doubtful passages in the Psalter according to the copies of the Greeks, of which I made a brief resolution. It begins: “When recently at Cologne.”

Concerning the most holy mother Anne I also arranged a rosary divided into fifty articles, out of my devotion toward her, together with the hourly prayers which we are accustomed to call the course, the office of the mass with the sequence “Let them rejoice on this day,” and another which begins: “Let us praise the holy [unclear] of the king of the heavens.”

At the request of Macharius, abbot of Limburg, I wrote two books on the misery of cloistered prelates; they have not yet been brought to light, but remained at Sponheim. This work begins thus: “As to the misery of cloistered prelates,” etc.

I wrote many orations delivered in chapters of the order outside, more than twenty in number. Some of these were printed at Mainz, while others were dispersed among friends.

I also wrote many rosaries concerning various saints, Peter, Paul, Mary Magdalene, and others; collected proses or sequences; and very many supplicatory prayers, without a fixed number, at the urging of devout men. I did not retain copies of all of these. I also wrote several small works besides, whose titles I cannot now all recall to memory. Some of these, brought into the light, have already appeared long since; others, not yet sufficiently worked out, I left at Sponheim, perhaps to be completed in the future.

On the origin and progress of the dukes of Bavaria I also wrote a history, at the command of the most serene prince, Lord Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine; the opening of this work has slipped from my memory.

I wrote many letters to friends, but gathered only a few of them into one book, namely those which I had sent out at the beginning of my abbacy at Sponheim. The rest, however Familiar letters, without order, still lie scattered in loose papers; if I can, I shall take care at some time to gather them into one volume.

These are my writings, dearest Roger Sycamber, which I remember having written up to the present in the abbey of Sponheim, amid continual occupations with household affairs and very frequent visitations in the order, as you know, from the year of the Christians 1483, on the twenty-ninth day of the month of July, when I was elected abbot of Sponheim, down to the year 1505, namely the first day of the month of April, when I left Sponheim for the last time, never again to return. From the time of my departure from Sponheim to my entrance into this abbey of St. James, there passed eighteen months and fifteen days, during which I was able to write little, except certain familiar letters, which I afterwards here reduced into one book. But during the nine months in which meanwhile I had remained with the most serene prince Joachim, Elector in the March of Brandenburg, a fact not unknown to you, I was by no means idle, but at his command I composed certain little works, some of which I completed, while I left the rest unfinished. For at that prince’s urging I abridged the histories of several saints, with devotion to whom he burned most fervently, and I gathered many various supplicatory prayers concerning the same into one volume, which begins thus: Great and arduous work, for love of you, Prince, etc.

At the same time also, while I was staying in the March, at the command of the aforesaid prince I wrote, on various and different matters concerning antiquities arising from daily discussion, fourteen books in one volume, a work which I entitled Panalethia; its prologue begins thus: There are many things, great teacher, etc.

I also wrote another hieratic work for the same prince, necessary for driving away various diseases, divided into thirty-four sections; its first prologue begins thus: The things which I undertake to write for your majesty, etc.

The three volumes written above I completed to the end; but no one compels me here to state the titles of the remaining works which I have not yet finished.

These, dearest Roger, are the little works which I composed in twenty-three years as abbot of Sponheim; those which follow I wrote afterwards as abbot of the monastery of St. James the Apostle in the suburb of Würzburg, over which I now preside, unworthy as I am, being free for this application to letters so much the more freely as, because of the poverty of temporal affairs, I am less occupied in external matters. For knowing the place to be poor and quiet, I took it up the more willingly, because I hoped that there I could be more freely at leisure for the study of the Scriptures. For you know that several great, rich abbeys had been offered to me; trusting that this poor little one suited my purpose, I took it up, in which I have not yet completed a whole year, whence I have composed few works.

First I wrote one book in praise of the most holy Joseph, the foster-father of our Lord and Savior JESUS CHRIST, to which I added a rosary of fifty articles from the proclamations of his merits. Also an office with prayers, and a prose, which they call a sequence. This work begins thus: Often with great desire I resolved to satisfy my own devotion.

After this I wrote to my brother Jacob Trithemius two books of my familiar letters, the first of which contains certain letters, sixty-six in number, which I wrote to various persons throughout all that time from when I left the monastery of Sponheim until my entrance into this place. The second likewise contains sixty letters, which in this first year of this abbey I wrote to various persons. This work begins thus: You have reminded me quite opportunely, sweetest one, etc.

Besides this, in this very year I wrote a great and laborious work divided into six partial books, which I entitled, with a Greek word, Polygraphia, which in Latin means “much writing.” For it teaches, with wondrous natural subtlety, many, indeed infinite, modes of writing, of communicating most secretly and most safely and without any suspicion, universally in every language of the whole world, whatever shall have to be communicated or written. This work begins thus: We read that very many of the wise men of old, etc. But it should be noted, Roger, that it is fitting for no one to possess this work so much as great and powerful princes, by means of which they can communicate their most secret affairs to those absent without fear, so that the whole world could not discover their secret without knowledge of this book; and that knowledge is easily learned once the volume has been obtained and is retained in memory without labor. Therefore I resolved to offer this work to a certain prince, whose wisdom and virtue deserve every good thing.

Against also the pernicious disease and vice of simony and of claustral proprietorship Of Johannes Trithemius.

[unclear], especially of nuns, in responding to the question put to me, I wrote one book, which begins thus: “There is a certain convent of nuns,” etc.

These also, Roger, are the works which, being established in this present year in this abbey of Saint James, I composed by lamplight, the sequence of whose titles you have so often desired to know. Some things are still in hand unfinished; I shall let you know their prefatory titles when they have been brought to completion.

I have resolved, however, hereafter, if the Most High wills it, who alone can do all things, to compose a work, indeed the greatest of all my works, which is to be divided into twelve books. Its subject will be: concerning demons and the profane arts and malefices of the same, by which they wretchedly deceive the human race. And it is my intention, to the extent of my powers, to drive out and refute all the little superstitions of demons’ arts among men, and to demonstrate in many ways from the very books of the fools who handed them down how utterly vain, pernicious, and detestable they are. For the work seems to me necessary, especially in these times, in which men are excessively curious, some learned, and likewise some unlearned, seeking out things which they would better not know.

Nevertheless, being not a little deterred by the magnitude of the arduous labor, I have thought it useful to put off this intention of mine for a time, so that meanwhile the material necessary for so great a work may gradually be gathered into one. These are the things which, in my judgment, had to be written back to you in reply to your letters. But if hereafter I add anything to the light, you shall not be among the last to know. Farewell, mindful of us before God. From Würzburg, on the last day of August, in the year of Christians 1507.

LII.

To the Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Saint James in the suburb of Würzburg, his distinguished and most learned preceptor, Bartholomew Lescanius, unworthy priest, chaplain of Margrave Albert, wishes eternal salvation.

Although I spent only a short time with you, reverend father, in Ursulo, yet I gained no small benefit from that very association, since by your medicine, through the mercy of the Lord God, I was cured and fully recovered from the very grave pain in my head, which for eighteen years continuously and without any interruption I endured and from which I could not be relieved by any of the physicians. For this I give your paternity infinite thanks, and I offer, give, and devote myself wholly as your possession. May almighty God deign to preserve your reverence safe and sound forever in body and soul, just as your kindness mercifully looked upon me, a wretched man deserving pity, and cured me of so grave and long-lasting a pain of the head, concerning which all our physicians, as many as I consulted, always despaired. O my only hope after God, excellent promoter of health, I cannot set down with my slender pen how greatly I am bound to you in love and inclined toward you, so much so that, if it pleased your paternity, I would wish and desire to bind myself as your servant for all the days of my life, together with those things which I possess. For the remembrance of your gracious paternity is always with me, nor can it ever be erased from the memory of my heart for a single moment, since there is no hour in which I do not think of your presence. And I am very sad; many of the citizens of Berlin grieve deeply with me over the continual absence of your paternity, all of us desiring nothing more than, if it were possible, that you should sometime return to us. For many of us know that our most illustrious prince greatly desires your return; he is said daily to await your arrival. O, if your paternity should quickly return to us, with how great a joy you will be received by us! Let your paternity know that, through the promotion of Lord Georg, prior and your very dear friend, I have been made chaplain of the illustrious and magnificent prince Albert, Margrave, with whom I seem to myself to be in a place of paradise, because, although he is young, yet he lives very religiously and conducts himself most honorably in all things. Praise to almighty God, who does not abandon those who hope in him; may his kindness deign to preserve your paternity, deservedly to be honored by me, happy forever. Amen. From Berlin, on the thirteenth day of the month of May, in the year of the Lord 1507.

Familiar Letters, LIII.

John Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Saint James at Wuerzburg, sends greetings to Bartholomew Lescanius, priest.

Most loving man, to your letter, in which you give me great thanks for your health, what else can I, or ought I, reply except what John Mesue the physician says in the preface at the beginning of one of his compilations: God alone heals illnesses, and from the soil of frailty, in his abundance, he has brought forth medicine, blessed, glorious, and exalted. Therefore thanks must be given not to me but to God, since in his goodness he not only heals the sick, but, being almighty, even gives life to the dead. I, however, profess myself not a physician but a Christian monk; if his counsels have benefited you in any way, he deservedly must be blessed and praised, from whom we have received all the good that we understand.

Know that the remembrance of me which you testify that you continually keep, when by interceding for my sins you turn to God, is most pleasing to me: namely, that whenever at the altar, about to offer to almighty God the sacrifice of our redemption, you celebrate the remembrance of your friends, you should also say mentally in prayer: I beseech you, holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, through the pain of the wounds of Jesus Christ our Lord, remember also your servant, though wicked, John Trithemius the abbot, and whatever he has sinned against you, through the blood of the same your Son mercifully forgive, your Church petitioning through me.

If you keep this remembrance of me diligently, dearest Lescanius, you have given me the greatest possible benefit. I rejoice with you no little that you have found the favor and grace of a good prince; in his service it is fitting for you to live in such a way that you never put off the progress and salvation of your soul for the enticements of the flesh, nor love the advantage and peace of the world so much that you forget the consolation of the heavenly kingdom. As for my return to the March, just as I do not dare to promise it to you friends who ask for it together with the prince, so I do not rashly deny it. For God, whose will and volition it is the salvation of every creature to follow, can do all things. But no determinate knowledge of future things is given to mortals. Farewell, mindful of me. Wuerzburg, the penultimate day of August, in the year of the Christians 1507.

LIV.

To the most reverend father in Christ, lord John Trithemius, abbot of Saint James at Wuerzburg, his most dear teacher, brother Theodoric, monk of Fulda, offers reverence and honor, with his most humble commendation of himself.

Reverend father and most loving teacher, on hearing that your paternity had received another abbacy and resigned Spanheim, I was beyond measure troubled in spirit, wavering within myself and in a certain way divided; I became saddened and glad. Saddened indeed for this reason: that the envy of your rivals was permitted to prevail so far that it gave you occasion to leave your monastery, which by your talent, writings, and books you rendered notable, known, famous, and distinguished throughout almost the whole world. For what was the monastery of Spanheim before your reverend paternity was placed over it? It lay hidden in obscurity and darkness, so that for more than ten miles around there was no regard or knowledge of its name. By your studies you made it glorious and known far and wide, as I saw for myself, who served as a disciple under your instruction for more than three years: from the school of Paris in Gaul, from Louvain in Brabant, from Tuebingen in Swabia, and also from Italy, Germany, and other more remote places of the earth, very many most learned men, and princes and bishops too, stirred by the fame of your name, flocked eagerly to Spanheim, not without the advantage and profit of that monastery. All these certainly did not come for this reason, to see the monastery; indeed, what must be held without doubt, they came there because of you and your learning. You also adorned the monastery with new and very beautiful buildings, and with many most precious books; concerning these I am deeply pained, that they must remain in the possession of those unlearned and most ungrateful monks of Spanheim.

But I rejoice and congratulate your paternity no little that you have found a quiet place suited to your studies, although I would rather have advised that you remain with the most illustrious prince in the March, who, as it then seemed to me, was offering you terms not to be despised. Blessed be God, who has granted peace to your paternity and has now left your adversaries in their confusion. They thought that they could bend the mind of your paternity to their side, but they were in no way able to do so. It has happened to you as to our holy father Benedict, and to Rabanus, once of Fulda Of Johannes Trithemius.

... befell the abbot of Fulda, who, although they were suitable and excellent shepherds of souls, incurred the hatred of their own monks because of justice; and those whom they ought to have revered with the highest honor they persecuted with envious plots. But those men, soon leaving behind the sheep, not to say the most ungrateful and perverse goats, transferred themselves to other places. At last, led by late repentance, they lamented that they had lost the best shepherds, whom, blinded beforehand by their depraved ways, they had not recognized.

I do not doubt that a similar thing will shortly happen to the monks left at Spanheim: despising and contemning the pillar of the whole order, now living under the barren, foolish fig tree, that is, under the stupid prior whom they set over themselves as abbot. One day they will confess, with sorrowful heart and deep sighs, that they have gravely done wrong and sinned against their father and most gentle shepherd, who was troublesome to no one contrary to equity, burdensome to no one. Then without doubt they will say, perhaps indeed they already say it, making an incomparable comparison between the condition of this monastery in which they now live and that in which they shone under your rule: “We, senseless and the most wretched of all men, why did we provoke to indignation, by our injuries and insults, so useful, distinguished, and most humane a shepherd? Why did we believe the detractors and rivals of so great a man? Behold how we now sit cast down, despised, and contemned under a foolish and inexperienced shepherd, while he is considered great before kings and princes among learned men of both ways, and is honored with various gifts.”

Let your reverend paternity believe me, since soon they will undoubtedly grieve that they sinned against your person, when there shall come upon them, by the just judgment of God, the vengeance which they have deserved, and they will bring back the fitting reward of their ingratitude.

As far as my own condition is concerned, let your paternity know that, last year, after I departed from you from Speyer with the letter of permission of my abbot of Wissenburg, I came to Fulda, and there, in the greater monastery, having now been professed and established, I promised to remain henceforth. The fathers of the place at once entrusted to me the business of the station of St. Boniface in the lands of the Thuringians and Buchonians to manage; by reason of this I trust that I shall shortly come to Hamelburg, and from there, if it can in any way be done, I shall approach your paternity. Concerning the rest, [unclear] more fully.

I have always found you most humane in all tribulations, both mine and those of my former monastery of Wissenburg, in which we were for fourteen years, when that most impious tyrant John of Drade, brother of the bishop of Merseburg, marshal of the count palatine, unworthy of the name of knighthood, raged against us, together with the satellites of Acheron who adhered to his rash undertakings. Our abbot, avoiding the cruelty of the tyrants, was contending for the affairs of the monastery at the Apostolic See in Rome; our rivals, meanwhile, exercised so many and such great cruelties against us miserable monks in our homeland that we were nowhere safe.

Meanwhile almost all the fathers of the order, especially those of the Bursfeld observance, withdrew their hands through fear of the tyrants. Since through the extreme poverty of the monastery it was necessary for us to be dispersed, scarcely anyone dared receive any of us in lodging, especially the nearer neighbors, who feared the burning of their farms more than the violation of brotherly charity. But your paternity feared God more than mortal men; although our enemies were very near to you, nevertheless, like another Tobias, you treated us most humanely, not only receiving us in hospitality, but also admitting several of us into your convent for a long time. Among them, finally admitting me kindly, you kept me for a fourth year, supplying me freely with all necessities, and, what is greatest of all, you took care to imbue me in the studies of good letters. For this I give undying thanks to your paternity, nor shall I cease to give them as long as I am in the flesh.

For you have always been an advocate and patron not only to me but also to all desolate and wretched monks; you have led many back to the way of truth, nor has anyone ever gone away without consolation who implored your counsel. Because of this, as I do not doubt at all, the merciful God, who permitted you to be troubled for a little time, afterward appointed for you, by provident dispensation, a more quiet place, suitable for the study of the Scriptures.

May your paternity pardon me for my lengthy and foolish writing. May you live long in the health of both men; to you I most humbly commend myself. Given from Fulda on the twenty-eighth day of the month of August, in the year of the Lord one thousand five hundred seven.

Familiar Letters, 55

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, sends greetings to Brother Theodoric de Eltz, monk of Fulda.

I congratulate you on your health, dearest Brother Theodoric, and I greatly rejoice in your peace. Your merits have required me, by the most just reason, to do this; and I should deserve to be accused forever of the fault of ingratitude if I so quickly handed over to oblivion the many services you have rendered me. For, to pass over the rest, no forgetfulness will ever erase this one thing from my memory: that when I was at [unclear] with the most serene prince Palatine two years ago, for several days, in the matter of the burned monastery of Limburg, and meanwhile certain retainers of the prince [unclear], while my monks dissembled, not to say consented, had conspired against me in contempt, because they were aggrieved that I was a supporter of the party of the aforesaid Prince Philip, you were the first and only person to report to me their rash presumption, with charity making the journey safe for you through their threats and swords. But what the monks, professed to me in regular fidelity, faithlessly conspiring with my rivals, committed against me, there is no need for me to recount to one who knows.

Nor did you only disclose to me the conspiracy of my rivals, which otherwise, unknown to me, would have been exceedingly harmful; but by your diligence and fidelity you also brought over to me, from the hands of my rivals, our books and instruments of knowledge and of secret matters at Stauronesus and the monastery, and you did not abandon me when I was sick at Neometum and Neuburg. You always stood by me as an unwearied companion and servant when I went to Cologne Agrippina and from there to the March of Brandenburg, while in all these matters not even one of my brothers cared to come. Therefore it is worthy and seems just that, for your services toward me, I should acknowledge your fidelity with fitting benefits, as far as I can with God.

From your letters, then, which you recently sent me, I have noted two things that concern the peril of your soul, unless you provide for your salvation as quickly as possible by fleeing from them. One of them is that, contrary to equity, you have declined from the regular observance of the order to deformed monks. The other is that, by reason of the ministry entrusted to you, pursuing public gain, not without injury to the purpose of the monastic life, you run about here and there as a beggar and wanderer. I beg you, brother, listen to my counsel, whom you affirm always to have been a faithful patron to you.

You have done a thing exceedingly harmful to your soul and, beyond any doubt, dangerous: departing from the lawful ways of our fathers and abandoning the observance of the regular life, which in the monastery of Wissembourg you publicly professed, swore, and solemnly promised before God and his saints; and now you live among deformed monks a life in no way fitting your profession. How will you stand in the judgment of God? Or what will you answer, if you die in such a state, which is altogether contrary to your profession? See, you are now doing those things which the holy father Benedict forbade to you and to all: you devote yourself to meats, games, and drinking; you possess private property; contrary to the monastic institution, you wander about in the world with dissolution of mind; and the pen blushes to express one by one the things that follow from these.

You were not instructed so at [unclear] of the Helvetians, nor did you learn this manner of living with me at Sponheim; nor did you ever see from me examples of such conduct at any time, nor note even the least trace of it. Rather, the contrary was manifest to you in me, you who both at Sponheim and elsewhere were always a witness of my life and conduct for more than four years. For you know, and it cannot be hidden from you, that many kings and princes have often had me solicited, with the promise of a quite ample stipend, to turn aside to their courts; nor even today do they entirely cease from the insistence of their petition once begun. Yet thus far I have always resisted, and I have not wished to comply with their gifts or promises, so that I might in any way withdraw from the regular observance which I once professed, although a greater occasion than yours was given to me for turning aside to others.

Remember, brother, I beseech you, your first instruction; remember your vow; remember your promise, and return to your heart, because what you do is not lawful, but altogether prohibited, damnable, and apostatic: to depart from the holy reformation of the regular life and to migrate to a deformed monastery. It has always been lawful for each person to advance to what is better, and it has always been praiseworthy to increase a vow in good things; but to fall away from good into evil has never been lawful, nor has it been permitted to anyone to violate and diminish a vow solemnly made to God. No necessity compelled you to transfer your purpose of regular observance to those not living regularly; therefore you will by no means be able to be excused. You are a monk professed under regular observance, and for that reason you can in no way be saved outside observance. Therefore either, if you wish to be saved, return to observance; or, if you have persisted in the deformation of life which you have assumed, know that you are to be damned by him whom you have despised as a transgressor of your vow. Return, therefore, yourOf Johannes Trithemius.

I urge you, since repentance is profitable, and consider that your letter of license does not extend to the deformed. I promise that I will take care that you have an honorable place in observance, either with me or elsewhere as you please. Farewell, sound in mind and body, receiving charitably the admonitions of a friend. I shall write to you more fully about these matters at another time. Farewell again, remembering us before God. From Würzburg, on the first day of the month of September, in the year of the Christians 1507.

LVI.

To the Most Reverend Father and Lord in Christ, Matthaeus Lang, Bishop of the Church of Gurk and Provost of Augsburg, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Saint James in the suburb of Würzburg, sends greetings.

Joh. Rummel.

Most reverend prelate, the man who presented these little letters of mine to your most reverend paternity, Johannes called Rummel of Nuremberg, asserting that he had been sent by the royal majesty, came to me some time ago and tried in many ways to persuade me that, in order to approach that same majesty, I should undertake the journey with him toward the city of Augsburg. For he said that he had received thirty-two ducats for travel expenses from the hands of your highness in the king’s name, and that he had been ordered to see that I was presented as soon as possible before his sacred gaze. But because he produced no letters, neither royal ones nor yours, by which he might show that truth supported his assertions, I began to have some doubt, lest perhaps he himself had been the solicitor before the royal majesty concerning me, promising certain great things, useful to his majesty, which I had never professed. I am a man established in the monastic religion under authority, to whom it is not permitted to wander lightly outside the monastery without evident reason. Therefore I have thought it right humbly to ask your most reverend paternity that, if he announced true things to me, and things entrusted by you in the king’s name, you would deign to hold my absence reasonably excused; but if it was otherwise, do not reckon it to me as presumption that I wrote, having been deceived by the man. Indeed, if he had shown me the necessary letters, who am I, who would not most greatly desire to please the imperial majesty, although I know nothing in myself worthy of so great a highness? For our studies promise nothing great: they are humble, such as are accustomed not to delight great princes, but to suit men of middling station. Nevertheless, if there is any strength in me that could delight the royal magnificence, the bearer will open ways by which I may be permitted to speak with the prince in person. Farewell, glory of bishops. Würzburg, the first of September, in the year 1507.

LVII.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James in the suburb of Würzburg, to Eberhard Senst, dean of the same Church of St. James of Bamberg, royal chaplain, sends greetings.

That I send my letters to you, though I am unknown to you, most humane sir, the bearer of the same, known to you, has brought about. For he reported to me that you pursue me with great favor, and often mention my name with praise before the Majesty, and that you especially desire both to have acquaintance with me and familiar friendship, and that for this reason you have solicited the imperial majesty to have me stand in his presence, to confer especially about those matters that pertain to the publication of histories. I give you undying thanks for your goodwill toward me, which I shall also, if ever it is permitted, take care to repay according to my strength. But I have deferred coming in person to the imperial majesty on this occasion because I feared being marked down for levity if I had believed myself summoned by the royal majesty at the urging of one unknown man, when there were no testimonies of letters present by which the majesty’s good faith could have been established. I would be judged by all to be frivolous and full of ambition if I were so easily moved by persuasions confirmed by no proof. Therefore, if the royal Majesty wants me to be present before him, let him make me more certain by letters. For I have no intention of wandering anywhere at the urging of an unknown man; to his wishes in this matter I have yielded only so far as to give my letters to you, by which occasion might be offered to you of writing to me and of revealing your mind not by another’s words, but by your own hands. Farewell, remembering us. From Würzburg, on the first day of the month of September, in the year of the Lord one thousand five hundred seven.

576 Familiar Letters

LVIII.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of Saint James in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, sends greetings to Conrad Peutinger, doctor of both laws.

[unclear]

Willibald Pirckheimer, our common friend, wrote to me a few months ago that, at your urging and that of my friends, Royal Majesty had arranged this condition for me: namely, that, under a fixed and sufficient provision for as long as I live, I might henceforth freely philosophize in the city of Augsburg; that a suitable house, too, together with the other necessities of life, would be abundantly provided; and that nothing further remained except that I should merely give my consent in these matters. I give thanks to Caesarean Majesty, and I also have no ordinary thanks for you and the rest of my friends in the community, for such great goodwill of yours toward me. But I can in no way accept the condition that you propose to me, because to desert my place, which the most reverend lord prelate and prince of Würzburg entrusted to me with singular trust and confidence, would be not only most shameful, but also full of the vice of ingratitude. For I would rather lie hidden here in the little monastery, in my accustomed poverty, all the days of my life, than by my departure offend so great a prince or disturb in any small way my patron. Indeed, as far as lies in me, I shall never weaken the confidence that he once seems to have had in my person. Nor does it accord with my purpose, since I am a monk and long ago swore of my own free will to the Rule of the holy father Benedict, to leave the monastery and live in cities, and, after having tasted in some measure the sweetness of the heavenly secret, to be occupied again with the tumults of the world. For it is not fitting, indeed it is not lawful, for men who have once bound themselves to divine services to return to secular actions, nor for those devoted to monasteries to dwell in cities. A fish in the kitchen and a monk in a prince's court seem to be in no way far from the utmost danger, since each is nearest to death: the one, that is, to death of life and flesh; the other, to death of spirit and mind. For just as it seems impossible for a fish brought into the kitchen to be long deferred from death, since it is brought there for this very reason, to be eaten by men, so it is not possible for a monk in a prince's court, or in the turmoil of worldly action, to keep his monastic purpose inviolate, especially if the desire of ambition or avarice draws him outside the monastery. A different judgment is to be made if the consideration of piety compels someone to this very thing. But I, a lover of quiet and peace, who for this reason left the tumultuous abbacy of Sponheim, after the envy of rivals had offered me the occasion, and took up this one, truly rather poor, so that, somewhat free and released from the cares of the world, I might have leisure for myself and for the study of the Scriptures, have already long since determined in the counsel of my mind to hold and continue the pursuit of solitude, and, so far as it can be done without injury to pastoral care, to have no concern with the business of the world. But if Royal Majesty is pleased with my service for the publication of chronicles, I am willing and ready here in my little monastery to do whatever he shall enjoin to be worked out by night, provided only that this labor of mine be in some measure recompensed for the necessity of the place, and that my person, intent on the affairs of others, not be judged burdensome. Yet I thank you again and again for your most friendly affection toward me, and I beg you not to take this opinion of mine amiss. Farewell, healthy and happy, and safe for a long time. From Würzburg, on the sixth day of the month of September, in the year of the Christians 1507.

LIX.

Johannes Trithemius of Saint James at Würzburg sends greetings to Master Libanius Gallus, his most learned teacher, and perpetual charity in the Lord.

[unclear]

I do not know, Libanius, what evil fortune has brought upon us, or what good it has envied us, so that, although nature and grace together have made us of one mind in mind and spirit, fortune has willed that in body we be distant from one another by so great an interval of places. From this it comes about that we are unable to console one another with mutual words except, for the most part, after several months and years, and sometimes not even that, because of the rare occurrence of those who might carry our letters and bring them back. Recently, at the end of the month of September, I received the letter that, as appeared, you had given in Spain on the twenty-fourth day of the month of June to a certain merchant intending to go to Frankfurt, adorned and at the same time full of many mysteries of our philosophy; and at the fourth reading, often repeated again and again, I was so greatly amazed and rejoiced that I almost seemed to have been made outside myself, and not to be in Francia with myself, but in Spain, or in Majorca, with you. These letters of yours will be for me, as long as I live, an everlasting memorial, and a refuge laid up after our Lord Jesus Christ alone; through them, in adversities, I shall experience constancy, and in doubtful matters, truth— Index.
