truth. They teem with great and marvelous secrets in philosophy, which in my judgment the understanding of no mortal will grasp who has not first been imbued with your teaching. You propose soon to enter the cell of the master, whom, after imitating him in holy conduct for a short time on earth, you will never be ashamed of forever in heaven. But meanwhile, teacher, to whom do you entrust the pupil to be instructed, if for the love of Christ you inhabit the wilderness, and he inhabits the world? O Libanus, half of my soul, if it is possible, hear me as I entreat you, so that before you carry out your too harsh purpose in this matter, you may approach Melanius, faithful to you, indeed most faithful, with whom the most wise arch-count Theophilus is constantly present; perhaps by his prudence he will raise up for you a new Pelagius from the disciple. Will you thus depart to Majorca, Libanus, exposing Triandricus to confusion, and Megalopius also to grief, of whom the one promised, the other has long, breathless, been awaiting your arrival? You understand what I mean; see to it that even now we experience your very strong love toward us as still stronger. The books of the divine Pelagius on heavenly doctrine, which we requested from you through Melanius as intermediary, we now acknowledge that we have obtained; for them we both thank you and, according to agreement, will faithfully send them back. Libanus, eager for my affairs, I live here so much the freer for myself, the poorer I am in the things of the world, reducing the ternary according to my powers to unity, and restoring the mind to itself, so that a purer understanding may escape to the goals of the principle rightly set before it. I have had a contention for a long time with the Melantians, who are trying to overthrow part of the binary, and for some time they have possessed, not by right but by a certain violence, the seventh portion of the little field under the equinoctial. That dealer in pigments of ours revolves in his usual fashion in a circle, little fixed in place; as often as he returns to us, he always thrusts new winds upon our ears. Know that the sea, by the bounty of God most good and greatest, is calm, so long as it shall please him who has given everything whereby we may sail happily, we who have this sad leaf: that, when the storm has passed, it makes us ashamed to remember inconveniences. If at any time you learn that the arch-count, the most vigilant teacher of Melanius, is nearer to you, I would wish you not to pass him by, inasmuch as he is most loving toward you, and is in Christ the common friend of many, and has often done good to us. I have given this letter of mine to a certain man unknown to me to be carried to you; he testified that he was going to use [his journey] into Gaul, with instructions that he should deliver it at Paris to Carolus Bovillus, prince of theologians among the philosophers, through whom it may come safely to your hands. When you decide to write back to me, arrange for your letter to be carried to me through the same Bovillus, if you cannot otherwise, a man both known to me and a friend. Farewell, mindful of us before God. From Würzburg, 6 October, in the year of the Christians 1507.

LX.

To the most serene and unconquered prince and lord, Lord Joachim, Margrave of Brandenburg, Duke of Stettin and Pomerania, Archchamberlain of the Holy Empire, prince-elector, Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James at Würzburg, sends greetings.

Most serene prince, first of all I make known to your Excellency that I, the most humble petitioner of your Serenity, by the mercy of God most good and greatest, am sound and unharmed, well in my usual manner, and desiring nothing more than that all things concerning the state of Your Serenity, and also of your wife, son, and brothers, may be carried on with prosperous success. The book for which your Serenity kindly wrote to me in the month of May I gave, according to your wish, to my scribe to be copied; when it was finished in the month of September, I had it bound in covers with as much grace and beauty as was possible for me, and, according to your custom, gilded throughout on the outside surface. I wished, moreover, to send that book to your Majesty as soon as possible, and I would not delay even a few days, except that quartan fevers are keeping back the messenger whom I was going to send; as soon as he has recovered, he will carry the book to your Highness. The other things, however, which your Serenity entrusted to me to work out by night, I have already partly published and partly they remain in my hands to be completed up to this very day. For I shall take care, to the best of my powers, that I be found mindful and grateful for your benefits toward me; although I cannot repay thanks for them, nevertheless I shall by no means cease to have and to give thanks.

As for the fact that I have not sent the truly desired volume to your Serenity with the bearer of the present letter, you must judge that it was done with reason. For he is a young and poor scholar, who for some time was my servant; by my encouragement he is about to return to the study which he had interrupted, and will go to that Frankfurt gymnasium of your Serenity. To him I indeed entrusted this letter, but I did not dare entrust the book because of fear of dangers. Yet I hope that, when my messenger has shortly recovered, he will go more joyfully to your Grace. The silver cup, gilded inside and out, which your Clemency sent me by the same messenger, I confess that I received with the greatest gratitude of mind. For it I give as many thanks as I can, and hold them immortal. For it will be for me a great memorial of your Serenity and a sign of your benevolence Familiar Letters

manifest toward me. With the Lord’s help I have completed the work of my Polygraphy, divided into six parts, or books, which is known to be dedicated to your majesty. I shall take care that it is presented to your sacred sight as soon as possible. May Almighty God long preserve your Highness, illustrious prince, unharmed and perpetually happy; to him I commend myself with humble supplication. From Würzburg, on the tenth day of the month of October, in the Christian year 1507.

LXI. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of the monastery of St. James in the suburb of the city of Würzburg, sends greetings to Jacob Trithemius, his dearest brother. Of Johannes Trithemius.

to suspend, to freeze springs, to dissolve mountains, to raise up the shades, to weaken gods, to extinguish the stars, to illuminate Tartarus itself; or, as Virgil sings:

“This woman promises that with spells she can release what minds she wishes, but impose harsh cares on others; stop water in rivers and turn the stars backward; she calls up the spirits of the night; you will see the earth groan beneath your feet, and ash trees descend from the mountains.”

Then there are the things Lucan reports about that Thessalian witch, and Homer about Circe’s omnipotence. Of these, I admit, very many are of such false opinion, such superstitious diligence, and such harmful labor that, although they cannot fall under a non-wicked art, they nevertheless presume that they can be clothed with the venerable title of magic. Since these things, then, stood so, I greatly wondered, and was no less indignant, that no one had so far appeared who had vindicated so sublime and sacred a discipline from the charge of impiety, or had handed it down to us purely and sincerely.

For those among the more recent writers whom I have seen, Roger Bacon, Robert the Englishman, Peter of Abano, Albert the German, Arnold of Villanova, Anselm of Parma, Picatrix the Spaniard, Cecco d’Ascoli the Florentine, and very many others, but writers of obscure name, when they promise to hand down magic, have offered nothing except certain ravings supported by no reason, or superstitions unworthy of all honorable men. Hence my spirit was stirred within me, and, because of both wonder and indignation, I wished to philosophize, thinking that I, who from earliest age have always been a curious and fearless investigator of operations full of mysteries and marvelous effects, would be undertaking a work not unworthy of praise if I restored magic itself, the ancient discipline of all the wise, redeemed and purified from the errors of impiety and adorned with its own principles, and vindicated it from the injury of calumniators.

Although I had long deliberated on this with myself, nevertheless I had not until now dared to descend into this arena. But after the discussion held between us at Würzburg about these matters, your surpassing skill and learning, and your ardent exhortation, gave me boldness and courage. And so, having selected opinions from philosophers of proven trustworthiness, having purged away the introduction of the malicious, who, lying with feigned knowledge, taught that the traditions of the magi and marvelous operations were to be sought from the very condemned books of darkness, as though from the very [adepts?], and having dispelled the shadows, I have composed in these recent days three books on magic, embraced in a compendium of brevity, and have entitled them, under a less offensive title, On Occult Philosophy. These I now submit to your examination, since you possess the fullest expertise in these matters, to be corrected, assessed, and judged, so that if anything has been written by me in them that could tend either to contempt of nature, or offense against the heavenly beings, or injury to religion, you may condemn the error; but if the scandals of impiety have been dissolved and purged away, you may defend the handing down of the truth; and so that you may deal with these books of ours and with magic itself in such a way that nothing which could be useful is hidden, nor anything approved which can do nothing but harm, so that at last these books, approved by your examination, may be worthy sometime to go forth into public under favorable auspices, and may not fear to undergo the judgment of posterity. Farewell; spare these bold undertakings.

Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James at Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, sends greeting and affection to his Henry Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim.

Your work, most distinguished Agrippa, marked with the title On the More Occult Philosophy, which you offered to us for examination through the bearer of the present letters: with how much pleasure we received it, no mortal tongue can ever express, nor can the pen of a writer relate. We are moved with the greatest admiration at your uncommon learning, you who, though young, penetrate such secrets, hidden from many even very learned men, and have been able to bring them to light not only beautifully and truly, but also properly and ornately. Therefore, first of all, we give thanks for your goodwill toward us; if ever we can, we shall undoubtedly repay thanks according to our powers.

We approve your work, which no one, even of the most learned men, will be able to praise sufficiently. Next, with whatever urgency we can, we admonish you, ask you, and beg you to proceed with zeal to the higher things with which you have begun, and not allow such excellent powers of your intellect to grow lukewarm in idleness, but to exercise yourself by your labor always toward better things, and to show, even to the ignorant, the light of true wisdom with which you are especially illumined by God. Nor should the consideration of any good-for-nothings draw you back from your purpose; of them it has truly been said: 574 Familiar Letters.

The weary ox plants his foot firmly. Since, in the judgment of the wise, no one can be truly learned who has sworn allegiance only to the rudiments of a single faculty. But God has endowed you with a broad and lofty talent. Therefore do not imitate oxen, but birds; and do not think that you must linger over particular things, but confidently direct your mind to universals. For each person is considered the more learned, the fewer things he is ignorant of. Your talent, truly suited fully for all things, should reasonably be occupied not with few or lowly things, but with many and loftier ones. Yet we admonish you to keep this one precept: that you communicate common things to common people, but higher and hidden things only to higher and secret friends. Give hay to the ox, [sugar?] only to the parrot: understand the meaning, lest you be subjected to the hooves of oxen, as has happened to very many. Farewell, happy friend; and if there is anything in our possession that can be of use to you, command it, and you will understand that it has been done without delay; and, so that our friendship may daily gain strength, write to us rather often, and send something of your lucubrations, we urgently ask. Farewell again.

In our monastery at [Peapolitanus?], on the eighth day of April, in the year 1510.

The End.
